**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIMES OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH SOME MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST COPIOUS EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH NEVERTHELESS POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY WITH RESPECT TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH COUNTLESS INDEXES, BUT ABOVE ALL WITH TWO IMMENSE GENERAL INDEXES—ONE OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER not merely this or that Father, but every one of the Fathers without exception, has written upon any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented upon each individual verse of the biblical books, from the first of Genesis to the last of Revelation. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one weighs the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, uniformly maintained throughout the course of the entire work, the low price, and, above all, this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology, in the likeness of the Church itself, consists of and is divided into two parts: Latin and Greek. The Latin, fully published, is substantial and immense in two hundred and eighteen volumes, and is sold for ninety thousand francs. The Greek is subdivided and has been issued in two typographical editions. The first contains the Greek text together with a facing Latin translation, and will perhaps exceed one hundred volumes. The latter presents this translation alone and will therefore be contained in approximately fifty volumes. Each Greco-Latin volume costs eight francs, and each solely Latin volume five francs.

### I. ON PETER OF RIGA

[Col. 0009A] Peter of Riga, first a canon and cantor of Blessed Mary at Rheims, then a regular canon of the Order of Saint Augustine in the abbey of Saint-Denis at Rheims, a Frenchman by nationality and a native of Vendôme, flourished, according to Charles du Fresne du Cange in the *Index of Authors* prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 138, from the year 1160; or in 1170, according to William Cave in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1170, p. 682. John Trithemius calls him the most learned among the learned men of his age. Since he flourished at the same time as Peter, canon and cantor of Blessed Mary at Paris, they have often been confused, both in the titles of manuscript codices and in the attribution of works.

He wrote, in varied verse, a work entitled *Aurora* [Col. 0009B] or *Library*, in which he expounds a great many books of Holy Scripture in poetry altogether remarkable for its age. The work is found in manuscripts in many libraries of France, England, and Germany. Fifteen manuscript codices of it are in the royal library of France, namely 4139, 4140, 4141, 4142, 4143, 4144, 4145, 4146, 4392, 4393, 4394, 4395, 4396, 4397, and 4398; two manuscript codices are in the Paris library of Saint-Germain, of the Benedictine Order; several are in the Colbert and Victorine libraries. The same manuscript is found twice in the libraries of Prémontré, of Bonfontaine, Cistercian, and of Belleval, Premonstratensian, in the diocese of Rheims; and in the library of the Dominican friars at Lyons. No author has been copied so extensively and so frequently, although this truly excellent work has not been printed.

Thomas James’s *Eclogue*, which he calls Oxonio-Cantabrigian, lists four manuscript copies of this *Aurora*, book II, p. 53: at Oxford, in the library of Magdalen, codex 3; at Cambridge, in the library of Saint Benedict’s College, codices 43, 371, and 395. I formerly had Peter’s *Aurora*, collated against various manuscript codices, ready for publication. [Note: [Col. 0009B] While Caspar Barth, Christian Daumius, Andreas Rivinus, and Casimir [Col. 0010B] Oudin were undertaking an edition of the *Aurora*, fate intervened. FABRICIUS, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin*, vol. V, p. 277.] Certainly no one rendered Scripture in verse with such success.

His *Tropes and Phrases of Scripture* is in manuscript in the aforementioned Saint Benedict’s College at Cambridge, codex 395. Under the title *On Theological Tropes*, the same work is in manuscript in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, shelfmarks GG. 13 and E. 17. Likewise, under the title *Summary on Tropes of Speech*, it is in manuscript there, shelfmarks PP. 10 and B. 6. It begins: “We now see [Col. 0010B] through a glass and in an enigma,” etc.; but this work belongs to Peter the Chanter of Paris, whom scribes and copyists often wrongly confuse with Peter of Riga, cantor of the Church of Rheims.

In his *Dominican Library*, under the year 1263, p. 19, Ambrose of Altamura assigned this Peter of Rheims to his own Dominican friars without authority or reason, perhaps because a manuscript *Aurora* by this Peter is found in certain conventual libraries of the Dominican friars. But Peter of Riga had died before the Dominican Order was born. Almost all others place his floruit about the year 1160; others, about 1170, as Cave maintains, though he spoke very sparingly and in a scattered manner of Peter of Riga. I stated only these matters in the first undertaking of this work; but we judged it worthwhile to speak more fully of Peter of Riga’s *Aurora* in this second edition, which is not compelled to be concise.

The prose prologue to the whole *Aurora*, which is composed in varied verse, begins: “The frequent request of my companions, with whom in their company I spent the flower of my childhood, that I should make the book …” The order of the *Aurora* is such as Antonio Possevino describes in his *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. II, fol. 265, under “Peter of Riga.”

**The poems on Genesis begin.**

> On the first day, two things are said to have been made: heaven and earth;  
> And on the following day, the sphere of the firmament, etc.

**Exodus begins.**

> These are the twelve names of the fathers, who, as seeds  
> Of the Jewish people, gave rise to so many tribes, etc.

**Leviticus begins.**

> But the voice of the Lord calls Moses and commands him  
> To bear his words and sow them in the people’s ear, etc.

**Numbers, or the Book of Numbers, begins.**

> God addresses Moses and commands that the host  
> Strong for war be numbered from every tribe, etc.

**Deuteronomy begins.**

> These are the words by which Moses instructed the Hebrews,  
> And that work is called, as it were, a second law, etc.

**The book of Joshua begins.**

> After Moses, Joshua rules the Hebrew people;  
> The land which Moses did not give, he gave, etc.

[Col. 0011C]

**The book of Judges begins.**

> After Joshua, let the account be made of the Judges,  
> From whom the Hebrew tribe received help, etc.

**The book of Ruth begins.**

> Peter’s pen hastens to Ruth, that a brief discourse  
> May depict her deeds in slender verse, etc.

**On the books of Kings begins.**

> After the book on Judges, sacred reading, treating  
> Of the titles of Kings, sets forth a noble work, etc.

**On the Song of Songs begins.**

> Though Origen surpassed all learned men  
> In other books, nevertheless in Solomon’s book, etc.

**On the book of Tobit begins.**

> You who read Tobit’s history, investigate the meaning  
> That lies hidden: from the rock you will drink streams from afar, etc.

[Col. 0011D]

**On the book of Daniel begins.**

> After the king of Babylon had conquered and afflicted  
> The Hebrews subject to him by sword, suffering, and hunger, etc.

**The book of Judith begins.**

> Jerome, favouring Eustochium and Paula, translated  
> Judith’s outstanding deeds and history, etc.

**The book of Esther begins.**

> Until one comes from India to the lands of the Ethiopians,  
> The land lay subject to King Ahasuerus, etc.

**The prologue to Maccabees begins.**

> Great Alexander, by whose rule Greece first  
> Flourished, carried away great trophies from the earth, etc.

**Recapitulations of the Old Testament begin. First it is treated in verses without the letter A.**

> At the beginning of things, after five days, the first human being  
> Is believed to have been made on the sixth day, etc.

[Col. 0012A] Then follow others without the letter B, others without C, others without D, and so successively, with every letter of the alphabet excluded. The work is indeed ingenious and most laborious, but its verse could not be entirely pure and polished.

**The prologue to the New Testament begins.**

> After the old law, breathe again, Peter: the new law shines forth;  
> Make new verses concerning this newness, etc.

**The prologue on the Acts of the Apostles begins.**

> I said that I had finished the book; but again I am asked  
> To continue my pen upon the Acts of the Apostles, etc.

**The Acts of the Apostles begin in Leonine hexameters.**

> In the nineteenth year of Tiberius’s reign,  
> While Judaea still served the cruel tyrant, etc.

[Col. 0012B] These latter two poems on the Acts of the Apostles are falsely attributed by Luke Wadding to Alexander of Villedieu, a Franciscan, although they are part of this *Aurora* of Peter of Riga, who preceded Alexander of Villedieu by many years.

The author of the *Great Belgian Chronicle* says that he died at Rheims in 1209, that he had been a regular canon of the Order of Saint Augustine in the abbey of Saint-Denis at Rheims, and that he was surnamed “Library.” Yet in manuscript codices he is commonly called clerk, cantor, or priest of Rheims, and he was a native of Vendôme. Thus that author. But decisive evidence that he was a regular canon is [Col. 0012C] the authority of the poet Giles of Paris, who, somewhat after Peter of Riga’s death, corrected his *Aurora*. It is quite probable that he was Peter’s contemporary and had formerly been his familiar friend.

This Giles, therefore, who was writing about 1210 or 1220—indeed in 1200, as we shall say below—expressly states in the prologue which he prefixed to the *Aurora* corrected by him, beginning, “Brotherly charity seems to taste somewhat of sweetness,” etc., that Peter of Riga was a regular canon of Saint-Denis at Rheims. He says:

> We state first that a certain regular canon of Saint-Denis at Rheims,  
> Peter by name, Riga by surname, according to the verse:  
> “I am called Peter Riga, whose heart Christ the Rock waters,” etc.

We have this from the manuscript codex of Saint-Victor at Paris, [Col. 0012D] shelfmark KKK. 27, fol. 62, where the said *Aurora* of Peter of Riga appears with the commentaries and corrections of Giles of Paris. At the beginning of this work the following little verse is prefixed as a heading:

> Here begins the *Library* of Peter of Riga.

Since this work is sacred, he proposes that schoolboys read it in place of profane authors:

> Therefore, rather than the melodious sayings of poets,  
> Schoolboy throng, love to have this set before you.

At the end of the work, the corrector asks the masters of Paris and Orléans to lecture upon it to their pupils:

> Paris, teach beforehand the verses which your land gives you,  
> Nursling of Vendôme; let Orléans possess them.

And a little earlier he says thus to the book and to his own verses:

> Far be it from you to employ Walter’s hexameters;  
> Vendôme’s nursling loves elegiac pentameters.  
> I have chosen you rather, O elegies, because you are friends of reading;  
> I judge you worthy to be read by the metrical rule of metre.

[Col. 0013A] Caesar Egassius Bulæus, as he reports in the fourth century of his *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 768, had seen in a catalogue of distinguished academics two manuscript codices of this author in the possession of Master Jacques Mentel, doctor of medicine, illuminated by the hand of some master with glosses and scholia. We too saw one, mentioned above, in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris; another in the library of Prémontré; and two others at Belleval, in the archdiocese of Rheims.

But I think that these verses commending the *Aurora* in schools do not concern Peter of Riga, but the commentators, because they do not appear in several, and especially in the older, manuscript codices of the *Aurora*, as we ourselves have seen. In the Belleval manuscript, the following are appended after the *Aurora*, though absent from the older Bonfontaine manuscript of the Cistercian Order in Thiérache:

**Prayer of Peter of Riga, who composed the book.**

> By these things, Peter, your own …

See below, at the end of the fragments.

**Likewise, the prayer of someone who restored what had been ruined.**

> When I, in the sequence …

See the same place.

[Col. 0013]

### ANOTHER NOTICE ON PETER OF RIGA

(Polycarp LEYSER, *History of Medieval Poets*, Halle-Magdeburg, 1721, octavo, p. 692.)

[Col. 0013B] Peter of Riga, an Englishman [Note: [Col. 0013C] See the title of the manuscript codex in the *Catalogues of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, vol. I, part II, p. 120, no. 1068, 4, I.], a master [Note: [Col. 0013C] See the cited place and Thomas Smith’s *Catalogue of the Cottonian Library*, p. 113, Vespasian D. V. I.], a cleric of the Church of Rheims [Note: [Col. 0013C] See Henry of Ghent, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 22.], or a canon of the church commonly called Saint-Denis of Besturne [Note: [Col. 0013C] See the catalogues, cited place.]. Hence in one manuscript codex I found his name written: **PETER OF RHEIMS**. If he was the Peter whom Giles of Paris records as living in the time of Pope Celestine III, who presided over the Roman see from 1191 to 1198, he must be assigned either to the end of the twelfth century or to the very beginning of the thirteenth. The said Giles says: [Note: [Col. 0013C] In the *Carolinus*. See François Duchesne, *Writers of French History*, vol. V, p. 323.]

> We lament that Peter, pursuing divine heights only in words, grew lukewarm.

Unless I am mistaken, Giles refers to Peter’s old age and to the *Aurora*. I therefore think that the author of the catalogue of manuscripts of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, is not far from the truth in maintaining that Peter flourished in 1170. [Note: [Col. 0013C] See the catalogues, cited place, p. 53, no. 1655, 188.] William Cave also observes [Note: [Col. 0013C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 592.] that he flourished in 1170 or a little later. Others believe that he died about 1263. [Note: [Col. 0013C] See Ambrose of Altamura, *Dominican Library*, [Col. 0014C] p. 19, in Johann Albert Fabricius’s notes to Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 388.]

[Col. 0013C] He wrote: I. the Heptateuch, the two books of Kings, and also the Gospels in metre, briefly expressing, as far as he could, not only the historical but also the allegorical meaning, according to Henry of Ghent [Note: [Col. 0014C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 22.], followed by William Cave. [Note: [Col. 0014C] *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ed. 1688, p. 682.] John Trithemius gives a fuller account of the work [Note: [Col. 0014C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 388.], as follows:

> “Peter wrote a distinguished metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled *Aurora*, as follows: On Genesis, book I, opening: ‘The beginning of the world, what changes.’ On Exodus, book I, opening: ‘These are the twelve [names] of the fathers.’ On Leviticus, book I, opening: ‘But the voice of the Lord [calls] Moses.’ On Numbers, book I: ‘God addresses Moses.’ On Deuteronomy, book I: ‘These are the words of God.’ On Joshua, book I: ‘After Moses, Joshua.’ On Judges, book I: ‘The Hebrew sins, he says.’ On Ruth, book I: ‘Peter’s pen hastens to Ruth.’ On Kings, book III: ‘Estra, dwelling upon a mountain.’ On the Song [Col. 0014B] of Songs, book I: ‘Though Origen surpasses all.’ On Fourth Kings, book I: ‘Solomon reigned.’ On Daniel, book I: ‘After he had subjected to himself.’ On Tobit, book I: ‘You who read the history.’ On Job, book II: ‘Some say that Moses [wrote] the Book of Job.’ On Judith, book I: ‘Jerome, favouring Eustochium and Paula.’ On Esther, book I: ‘As far as the Ethiopians, which.’ On the books of Maccabees, book I: ‘Great Alexander.’ On Gospel history, book I: ‘Herod’s rule was distinguished.’ On the Acts of the Apostles, book I: ‘In the nineteenth [year] of Tiberius.’ On the Recapitulations, book I: ‘These things on the new and old law.’”

In the manuscript codices which I have used, the book mentioned is entitled *Aurora*, and also *Library*. Perhaps this is why a certain author was thought to be Peter of Aurora, who wrote on the Bible in metre. [Note: [Col. 0014C] See the *Catalogues of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, vol. I, part II, p. 12, no. 476, 8, and the index.]

The catalogue of the Bodleian Library from the gift of Thomas Bodley wrongly reports that the *Aurora* contains a paraphrase of the Old and New Testaments as far as, and including, the Epistle to the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0014C] See the cited catalogues, part I, p. 145, no. 2702, 103.] No less falsely, the catalogue of manuscripts of University College, Oxford, declares that the entire biblical history [Col. 0014C] from Genesis to Revelation is narrated in the *Aurora*. [Note: [Col. 0014C] See the cited catalogues, part II, p. 5, no. 143, 4.]

The verses in the *Aurora* are counted at 15,056. [Note: [Col. 0014C] See the cited place.]

The following material in the Wolfenbüttel manuscript codex makes clear that not only Peter is acknowledged as author of the *Aurora*, but also a certain Giles as its interpolator:

> You wish to know, reader, who is the author of this codex.  
> I am called Peter Riga, whose heart Christ the Rock waters.  
> The prologue of the man who corrected this book and added supplements of his own; and wherever, throughout the book, an obelus between two points is found, there are his sayings and verses.

A little later the following is added in the same manuscript:

> You wish to know, reader, who is the author of this codex.  
> Hear what the book briefly says on this matter.  
> Peter and Giles wrote me; but the former  
> Was the author, and the latter the final corrector.  
> The former was a native of Rheims, the latter of Paris;  
> This man was a levite in rank, that one a priest.  
> This one a simple clerk; that one a professor of sacred order.  
> Both weighed down by years: this one a man, that one an old man.  
> One invented the work, but erring in its arrangement,  
> He let everything proceed in wandering meanings.  
> The other, distinguishing the verses with a pointed needle,  
> Sewed the work into one body and bound it together again.  
> One possessed abundant learning; but the other knew better  
> What order ought to be followed in setting things forth,  
> So that what had been composed in the modulation of verse  
> Might taste more sweetly.  
> Here begins the *Library* of Peter of Riga.

[Col. 0015A] Hence Peter of Riga’s *Aurora*, enlarged and corrected by Giles of Paris, is cited by Henry Langton in his catalogue of manuscripts of Trinity College, Cambridge. [Col. 0015B] [Note: [Col. 0015C] No. 35; see the *Catalogues of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, vol. I, part III, p. 96, no. 290.] It ought to have been called: “Peter and Giles,” not “Peter Giles’s book, called *Aurora*,” in the catalogue of codices donated by G. Laud to the Bodleian Library. [Note: [Col. 0015C] D. no. 94. See the cited catalogues, part I, p. 60, no. 761.]

A certain manuscript chronicle among Thomas Bodley’s manuscripts makes not Peter of Riga but Peter Comestor the author of the *Aurora*, [Note: [Col. 0015C] No. 14, tract 10; see the catalogues, cited place, p. 100, no. 1979.] perhaps deceived by the similarity of their first names.

The books of Scripture rendered by the author are in elegiac verse, except the Song of Songs, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, the book of Job, and the Acts of the Apostles, which were written in rhythmic hexameter verse. Thus it is not sufficiently accurate to say that the *Aurora* uses hexameters and pentameters in the catalogue of Bodleian manuscripts from the gift of Thomas Bodley [Note: [Col. 0015C] No. 103. See the catalogues, cited place, p. 145, no. 2702.]; or elegiac verse [Note: [Col. 0015C] See the cited catalogues, part III, p. 96, no. 287, 32.]; or heroic verse. [Note: [Col. 0015C] See the cited place, no. 290, 35.]

There exists an *Abridgment of the Aurora* by Peter himself as author, [Note: [Col. 0015C] See the cited place, p. 133, no. 1319, 43.] and an *Epitome of Peter of Riga’s book entitled Aurora*. [Note: [Col. 0015C] See Thomas Smith, *Catalogue of the Cottonian Library*, p. 130, Titus D. XX, 10.] I think that the Recapitulation to be mentioned below is indicated here.

[Col. 0015C] The complete *Aurora* has not yet been printed; Casimir Oudin testified that he had it, collated against various manuscript codices, ready for publication. [Note: [Col. 0016C] *Supplement*, p. 475, in William Cave, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 592.]

The book of Esther was published by Caspar Barth. [Note: [Col. 0016C] *Adversaria*, book XXXI, ch. 15.—The variant readings which Leyser here gives from the Helmstedt codices have been used in correcting Barth’s text. EDITOR.]

Thomas Rudborne inserted two distichs about Reuben, taken from the *Aurora*, in his *Greater History of Winchester*. [Note: [Col. 0016C] Book III, ch. 3, in *Sacred England*, London ed., 1691, p. 204.]

[Col. 0016A] The same Rudborne has a distich about Ehud taken from the *Aurora*. [Note: [Col. 0016C] Cited place.]

The same author presents two distichs on Judas Maccabaeus drawn from the same *Aurora*. [Note: [Col. 0016C] Cited place, ch. 7, p. 209.]

We do not now wish to publish the entire *Aurora*, but only certain specimens from it. We have especially consulted three manuscripts: two from Helmstedt and one from Wolfenbüttel.

I shall first set out the order of Old and New Testament books preserved by the Helmstedt codices. In the first the sequence is: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the book of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, First, Second, and Third Kings, the Song of Songs, Fourth Kings, the Lamentation of Jeremiah, Daniel, Job, the book of Tobit, Esther, Judith, Maccabees, the Gospel of Luke, Mark, and the Acts of the Apostles. The second Helmstedt codex proceeds in this order: the Pentateuch, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Kings, Tobit, [Col. 0016B] Daniel, Judith, Esther, Maccabees, Job, Luke, Mark, the Acts of the Apostles, the Song of Songs, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

It is noteworthy that, at the conclusion of Acts, the later codex reads: “The Old and New Testament ends. The prologue on the Song of Songs begins.” The author seems not to have claimed that book for the common canon.

In place of specimens I shall give:

1. The prologue from the earlier Helmstedt and the Wolfenbüttel manuscript codices.

2. In the earlier Helmstedt manuscript codex of the *Aurora* is appended a Recapitulation of both Testaments, which in the other is placed between the books of Maccabees and Job. It resembles Fulgentius’s book without letters. We shall give the text itself from the two Helmstedt codices.

3. Certain individual excerpts from Peter of Riga’s *Aurora* [Col. 0016C] which seem to depart especially from the text of Holy Scripture, and are historical, will be noted.

II. Peter of Riga’s *Mirror of the Church*, in verse, exists in manuscript in the library of Charles Theyer, no. 288. [Note: [Col. 0016C] See the *Catalogues of the Manuscripts of England and Ireland*, vol. II, vol. I, p. 202, no. 6658.]

III. Manuscript poems of Peter of Riga likewise exist in the Bodleian Library, from the gift of Kenelm Digby, no. 104. [Note: [Col. 0016C] See the cited catalogues, vol. I, part I, p. 82, no. 1705.]

[Col. 0015]

### II. NOTICE ON GILES OF PARIS

(OUDIN, cited above, p. 1723.)

[Col. 0015D] Giles of Paris, a deacon by rank or status, taught the liberal arts and especially grammar [Col. 0016D] at Paris for a long time, and particularly excelled in the art of poetry. He is counted among the leading poets of his time [Col. 0017A] by William the Breton, at the end of his *Philippid*:

> O, if Walter or Giles had been present in that  
> Age, how brightly would your wars shine in the tragic buskin!  
> Alexander entire, and Antiochus, descended from him,  
> And the twice-six commanders would grieve to be mere common people  
> In comparison with the splendour of your regard; and even  
> The biting, sluggish Gyra, composed concerning you in a little book, would yield,  
> If it deserved to possess a poet like these.

About the year 1200 this Giles wrote a *Child’s Instruction*, arranged in five books, which he dedicated to Louis, the still young son of Philip Augustus. In it he exhorts him to the love of virtue by the example of Charlemagne; hence he entitled the work *Carolinus*. It survives in manuscript in the distinguished Colbert Library, [Col. 0017B] codex 4507, whose title is written in red letters: “The *Carolinus* begins, [Note: [Col. 0017C] Book five of the *Carolinus* appeared, but mutilated, among the writers edited by Duchesne, vol. V; later, more completely, in *Collection of the Historians of France*, vol. XVII. EDITOR.] written by Giles for the instruction of the illustrious boy Louis, son of the king of France.” Jacques Mentel had another manuscript codex of this work in Paris; Marquard Gude copied it in his own hand while he remained in Paris, as is clear from the catalogue of Gude’s library, printed at Kiel in 1706, quarto, by Barthold Reuther. There, among manuscript codices, no. 334, quarto, p. 572 of the said catalogue. The prologue consists of several verses:

> If this work seems to contain any inner marrow,  
> Let it now be added to what has been prefaced.

The beginning of the first book:

> The first [book], pursuing apostolic honour, declares  
> That seven-year-old Charles bore the insignia of a king.  
> It adds how the father, formerly a consul, became king;  
> Idle Hilduin sat down, shut up within cloisters, etc.

[Col. 0017C] At the end of the fifth book he deals with teachers originating from the city of Paris, in order to blunt the injury of those who said that no learned men were natives of the city itself in which the Academy had been established. The fourth century of the *History of the University of Paris*, under the year 1198, fols. 526–527, reports these men as supporters and guardians [Col. 0018A] of Parisian honour.

The same Gilo, or Giles of Paris, considered an outstanding poet of his age, completed in four books a history of the First Crusade after Fulcher. [Note: [Col. 0017C] Oudin is mistaken. This history was written by another Gilo of Paris, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Tusculum, who died in 1142; see *Patrology*, vol. CLXXIII, and *Literary History of France*, vol. XVII (quarto, Firmin Didot, 1832), pp. 26 and 36.] You have these books in André Duchesne’s *Collection of French Historians*, vol. IV, p. 898, under this title: “Here begins the fourth book by Lord Gilo of Paris, elegantly written together with the remaining books.” He used Leonine verse, to imitate Fulcher, whose work he continued.

He also interpolated and corrected the *Aurora*—the work so called of Peter of Riga—which had already occupied school lecterns, and arranged it in a better order. This *Aurora* of Peter of Riga, with the commentaries of Master Giles of Paris, is in manuscript in the library of Saint-Victor [Col. 0018B] outside the walls of Paris, shelfmark KKK. 27, fol. 62. The prologue of Giles, who corrected the *Aurora*, begins: “Brotherly charity seems to taste somewhat of sweetness, and whoever casts his care upon the Lord,” etc. The following is read in the preface of the manuscript codex of the Pauline Library at Leipzig:

> You wish to know, reader, etc., the remaining verses of which have already been given above from Leyser.

[Among other things, Giles added to the *Aurora*: 1. a metrical preface addressed to Odo, bishop of Paris, which Leyser prints from the Helmstedt codex, p. 737; 2. an epilogue. A certain narrative follows the epilogue; it does not bear Giles’s name, but is not implausibly assigned to him. The aforementioned [Col. 0018C] Leyser printed it, p. 740.

Also appended to the same *Aurora* is Giles’s metrical treatise *On the Punishment of Hell*, in the same place, p. 742.

*A Mystery of the Paschal Lamb by Master Giles* is listed as a separate writing among the manuscripts donated by G. Laud to the Bodleian Library, though it seems to be only an excerpt from the *Aurora*.]

[Col. 0017]

## FRAGMENTS FROM THE BOOK OF PETER OF RIGA ENTITLED *AURORA*, INCIDENTALLY INSERTED IN VARIOUS PLACES, WITH ADDITIONS BY GILES OF PARIS

### I.—PROSE PROLOGUE

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin*, V, 277.)

[Col. 0017D]

The frequent request of my companions, with whom [Col. 0018D] in their company I spent the flower of childhood, urgently persuaded me to depict the book of Genesis in metrical style and then to draw some allegories from it. I confess that, in response to this [Col. 0019A] persuasion, my mind remained in doubt, uncertain whether it should write or fall silent. For I saw that the powers of my talent were by no means sufficient for so great a work. But on the other hand I feared to oppose the request of my companions. For it was not right to offend those with whom I had associated in the schools from childhood, with whom I had run through the books of grammar, read and selected Cicero’s golden flowers, and entered somewhat into Aristotle’s Labyrinth—not with Daedalus’s thread but with the Son of God as guide. I examined it, but did not enter it wholly.

Thus conquered by the continual prayer of my companions—or rather by brotherly charity—I undertook the task imposed upon me. I intended to weave the history of Genesis in verse and strove to draw some allegories from it: as a kernel from a shell, grain from chaff, honey from wax, fire from [Col. 0019B] smoke, marrow from barley, wine from unleavened bread. In this work I laboured so strenuously that you may see certain things agreeing with one another in harmony: namely, Christ’s pearl with Moses’ diamond, the flowers of the Church with the herbs of the Synagogue, the gold of Christians with the iron of Jews, the new law with the old law, millstone with millstone, wheel with wheel.

Moreover, it seemed suitable to give this little book, in accordance with the character of its work, the name *Aurora*. Nor is this undeserved. For just as dawn puts an end to night and shows that the beginning of day is at hand, so this little book, dispersing the darkness of shadows and the obscurities of the old law, shines throughout with the splendour of truth and with glittering sparks of allegory. Or indeed I marked this page with the majesty of so bright [Col. 0019C] a name because, just as the angel—according to the history which I am recounting—said to Jacob after the nighttime struggle, “Let me go, for dawn has come,” so after the struggle and labour which I expended upon this work I in some fashion addressed my little book with the same words: “Let me go, for it is dawn”; that is to say: I bring this work to an end, because I have explained the figures and shadows, and truth’s splendour has openly shone forth.

### II.—METRICAL PROLOGUE

(LEYSER, p. 701.)

> The beginning of the world: what changes it underwent  
> In its first origin from the Creator’s making;  
> What the completed fabric gave; what were the seeds of things;  
> Every gift and work of God the Creator—  
> These, under Moses’ guidance and by a certain written warrant of this poem,  
> My mind has been moved to commemorate.  
> Still, as one digging deeply into this well,  
> I wish to penetrate to the force of its figurative meaning.  
> Thus I shall draw forth mysteries enclosed beneath a figurative seal  
> By means of historical meanings.  
> And lest I accomplish nothing, I must all the more pursue what is best;  
> Our serious matters ought not therefore to be read with ridicule.  
> I believe that I do not indulge in useless labour;  
> I believe in the reader; I believe that I am able.  
> For, since these things accord with the faith and with our salvation,  
> No other love leads me to speak them.  
>
> [Col. 0020A] By these merits I seek for myself brotherly love;  
> By these I seek to have God generous toward me.  
> Grant, O God, that I may pursue your deeds with a faithful voice—
May your utterance be in the mouth of your prophet.

Direct my steps. Enlarge my heart.  
Open my understanding. Rain words upon me.

Moreover, let him be with me who professes himself  
a receiver of the faith and your worshipper, O Christ.

Let the mythologists yield [Note: [Col. 0019D] Perhaps *Mythologi*.]—and in the schools of the poets  
let this work hold the first and foremost place.

Here one who fixes his eye upon realities will at the same time see  
the refinements of grammar and sacred eloquence.

Here, applying study beside every kind of Latin  
expression, he will find and draw forth a manner of speaking.

Therefore, rather than the tuneful utterances of poets,

[Col. 0020B]

love to have this learned throng set before you.

Here is a great harvest: whoever has looked upon it once, even if  
at first he disbelieves, afterward let no one deny it.

Endure, therefore, and allow me to proceed,  
if it can be done, with your permission despite your envy.

For you would accomplish nothing, where I hope  
to employ so many guides; rather, you would need to close your lips.

Reader, observe now what, as I have already prefaced, must be said,  
and first mark this with a wakeful ear.

### III.—A SECOND METRICAL PROLOGUE, WHICH IS BY GILES OF PARIS AND IS PREFIXED TO THE NEW TESTAMENT

(LEYSER, p. 737.) The prologue to Odo, bishop of Paris, begins.

[Col. 0020C]

Since I have endeavoured to mingle profit with delight in my study,  
when I enclosed these mysteries within the law of metre,

the matter possesses in itself that it may be loved; modulation contributes  
so that it may be more easily drunk in by the ear.

Nothing do I desire so much as that the fruit of these things  
may be the edification of my reader’s mind.

Therefore I am brought back to treating sacred matters after those  
which perhaps once proceeded from a frivolous mind.

And so it was fitting—had I not already played amid so many affairs—  
that I should wish even now to be drawn to better things.

Receive, I pray, the gift sent to you by Giles,  
great father, Odo, bishop of Paris.

I often wished to seem to have rendered you some service,

[Col. 0020D]

yet I had not sufficiently perceived how this might be done.

Until, in that book which is called the *Bibliotheca*,  
a cause suited to the matter and sufficiently fitting was given.

For a great deficiency wounded the little book,  
which did not even have the appropriate opening doorway.

Then, making a leap, it says nothing that I recognize concerning Easter.  
It spoke, failing and languishing, at this point.

Perhaps the subject seemed too difficult for one singing;  
perhaps also the author, wearied, laid aside the burden.

Accordingly, often and earnestly requested by my companions,  
I undertook to wish to remove this defect.

Moreover, in the books of Tobit, Judith, Esther,  
and the Maccabees, I supplied many mystical matters.

Afterward I filled out the whole body of the Old Law,

[Col. 0021A]

so that I might more readily observe whatever was lacking there.

Whatever did not appear to the oars to deserve being of gold,  
most people inserted into their own books. [Reading uncertain.]

Then, whatever he omitted in the Gospel, as though wearied,  
there was the greatest care and labour to supply.

And there were so many things that I scarcely conceived the hope,  
if I attempted them, that I could avoid harm to myself.

Afterward I gathered, chapter by chapter, the things for which  
the text itself and the ready expositor were everywhere the same.

Behold, I copied them out and sent them to you in a very small work,  
as to a beloved and most eminent father.

Not because a measure was not to be made worthy of the ears  
of so great a pontiff, from the lofty mouth of the lyre.

But let things be given such as are fitting and sufficiently suitable  
for the majesty of the subject.

[Col. 0021B]

There are some things for which I ask pardon, not well dispatched;  
but it was necessary that this be done by the law of metre.

May the reader likewise be kindly in every respect,  
for the form of these elegiac verses is not very beautiful.

Nor let them quickly spring forth to be known publicly; rather,  
let them first begin to be read privately and without witness.

Indeed, let them first come under examination. Then, under your title,  
if they have deserved it, let them receive favour.

Then at last let them call these works of ours supplements.  
And you, reader, understand that this is fitting.

For, since I have everywhere become the patcher-up of the book,  
the name of my verselets is prefixed throughout.

### IV.—FRAGMENTS FROM GENESIS

(LEYSER, p. 727.)

[Col. 0021C]

**Genesis II.** He reports that the first language was Hebrew; that Adam, when sleep was laid upon him, became a prophet and committed his visions to writing.

Then God brought forward each living creature of the earth,  
that Adam might give names to all things.

Speaking Hebrew, he gave names  
to all things. That was the first language.

Afterward divine power sent sleep into Adam;  
that sleep was not sleep, but ecstasy.

In it he is said to have seen the causes of clear heavenly things,  
and, awakening, he became a prophet from it.

He saw judgment by water, judgment by fire, and the birth

[Col. 0021D]

of Christ; and he learned beforehand the faith of the Church.

There likewise he knew the mysteries of prophecy,  
and Adam disclosed these things in his books.

**Genesis III.** He reports that Adam was created from Damascene earth:

Afterward God cast Adam out of paradise  
into the land from whose dust he had been made.

And in the field of Damascus, from which He had previously  
taken him away, He placed him, that he might cultivate it there.

**Ibid.** He states that Elijah and Enoch came into the earthly paradise:

Paradise is shut off, and a fiery sword,  
guarding the tree of life, is set before its gates.

And therefore the sword is said to turn about,  
because God would at last wish to remove it.

[Col. 0022A]

When Elijah and Enoch were to enter paradise,  
He provided a passage for a time, the sword having been removed.

**Genesis IV.** He says that trembling of the head was the sign given by God to Cain:

God therefore gives Cain a sign, lest he quickly be killed;  
and it was movement and trembling of the head.

**Ibid.** He discloses the name of Cain’s wife:

He dwelt as a wanderer in the land of Noth with his wife;  
the name of that wife was Calmana.

**Ibid.** He reports that Adam set up columns recording future events:

And Adam, as it were, knew and was first to say: “A double judgment  
will come—namely, of fire and water.”

He wrote the art upon two columns and set them up:  
one was of brick; the other was of marble.

[Col. 0022B]

So that this one should not perish through water, nor that one through fire;  
if one should fail, the other might remain.

As the writings of Josephus declare to us,  
Syrian land still preserves the marble column.

**Ibid.** He explains how music was invented:

With his ear Jubal observed the various strokes of ironwork;  
he weighed their weights and made every sound harmonious.

By this method the art of music was first invented, although  
they say that Pythagoras taught it earlier.

**Ibid.** He expands the history of Lamech with various circumstances:

Lamech was a hunter, powerful with javelin and bow,  
who through long seeing was poor in sight.

For the pleasure of livestock or hides,  
he carried a bow; the eating of flesh did not yet exist.

[Col. 0022C]

He had a young man as his guide; by whose direction  
he wounded Cain, thinking him a wild animal.

Lamech learned the matter, grieved, and then pierced  
the young man with his bow, making his limbs livid.

Afterward Lamech, fearing his deserts and seeing what punishment  
and penalty Cain had justly received,

began to fear that perhaps his wives might kill him  
or treat him badly.

And he feared this because he was hateful to them,  
now a feeble and decrepit old man.

Therefore, wishing by cunning to fortify himself against this,  
he strove to put such words to his wives:

[Col. 0022D]

“For Cain who sinned, punishment shall be sevenfold;  
but for me the punishment is seven times seventyfold.”

**Genesis IV.** He reports that Adam mourned Abel’s death for one hundred years:

Now, after Abel, whom he had mourned for a hundred years,  
Adam again made his wife pregnant.

The Lord had commanded this, intending to assume flesh  
and unwilling to take it from Cain’s reprobate flesh.

**Chapter XIX.** He relates that four cities perished with Sodom:

After these things, fire pierced Sodom, and equal ruin carried off  
four cities equally.

Five cities fall, and the Lord rained upon them  
fire that vomits flame and balls of sulphur.

**Chapter XXVIII.** He assigns twelve rungs to Jacob’s ladder:

It had, as it were, twelve steps, because twice six

[Col. 0023A]

are the disciples who taught the faith.

**Chapter XXXVII.** He declares this concerning Joseph’s beauty:

Nature, having used less wakeful labour upon other faces,  
gave here whatever wealth she possessed.

She was so lavish of beauty upon the boy’s face  
that after this gift she was left nearly poor.

The boy’s beauty is commended by a rosy mouth, blooming cheek,  
sparkling eye, pious mind, and pure flesh.

Mouth, light, teeth respectively imitate, render, and equal  
the lily, the star, and ivory: pure, shining, snowy.

**Genesis XXXIX.** He mentions Potiphar’s illicit love for Joseph:

This Potiphar is said to have been marked by the sulphurous vice,

[Col. 0023B]

being captivated by love for Joseph.

For who knows whom Love will not catch in its snare—  
a mouth in which lilies contend when mingled with roses?

He was accounted the king’s high priest; and thus  
Potiphar was not free from vice.

Even now such men are swallowed up and suffer from this—  
men who hold the government of the world and the highest offices.

### V.—FROM THE BOOK OF EXODUS

**Exodus XXVI.** From the fifty golden rings he derives the number of canonical books:

Ten times five rings of gold were prepared,  
by which the joining of the curtains was made.

By the fifty golden rings are denoted

[Col. 0023C]

the books which the golden words of God fill.

As many rings, so many books. The New Law has eight books;  
the Old Law contains forty-two.

These are the thirty-two books and twelve books  
of the Old Law, if you count them:

Five of Moses; Joshua; Judges; Chronicles; Job;  
twice two books of Kings; Ruth; David; and Solomon;

Ezekiel; Daniel; Isaiah; Jeremiah;  
Ezra; Philo; Sirach; Judith, full of vigour;

Esther, lovely of cheek; Tobit; and the Maccabees;  
and twelve writings of the prophets altogether.

For the book of Ezra gave hospitality to Nehemiah;  
and Ruth became a guest subordinate to Judges.  
[Note: [Col. 0023] The book of Ruth was already counted above; if it is removed, the total rises to forty-one, not forty-two.]

Jeremiah receives the book of Baruch, its author,

[Col. 0023D]

after the later parts of his own book.

From this point the four writers of the Gospel increase  
the number of books and continue their own books.

Afterward the Apocalypse, Paul’s volume, and Acts  
come into the number—the canonical book.

Then, more clearly concerning the books of the New Covenant:

The Hebrews are enriched by forty-two books;  
your people, Christ Jesus, flourish in eight books.

Of the Gospels there are twice two books; the fifth  
is the Apocalypse, bearing mystical words.

The sixth book brings forth the apostolic Acts into the light;  
the seventh is Paul’s writings, exceedingly profound.

The last book is drawn and put together from the writings  
of James, Peter, John, and Jude.

[Col. 0024A]

**Exodus XXXIII.** On the guardian angel of the Israelites, he writes this:

Moses had heard: “My angel shall go with you.”  
He asks Him to explain this more fully to him.

To every nation its own guardian angel is given. Hence  
the nation of Judaea lies under Michael.

No one except Michael was a helper in all these matters.  
You have this in the books of Daniel.

### VI.—FROM THE BOOKS OF KINGS

**III Kings IV.** On Solomon’s wisdom:

He discovered utterances by which he was accustomed to aid  
the diseases of the sick and provide relief.

He discovered words effective against evil spirits;  
thereby he drove them away, not allowing them to return.

And he was the author of characters which he engraved upon precious

[Col. 0024B]

gems, working marvels powerfully.

Placing them, with a root known to him, at the nostrils of the sick,  
he drove away every kind of demon.

**Chapter X.** The author reports that the Queen of the South foretold certain things concerning the wood of the Cross:

After her return, what the queen did not wish to say in person,  
she taught while absent through her writings.

By sure tokens she informed the king that a noble wood had been placed  
in the forest near his house,

upon which a man would hang and be deprived of life, and because of whose  
death the Hebrew tribe would lose its royal right.

Fearing this, King Solomon hid the wood  
in the depths of the earth, and it remained hidden for a long time.

Until, near the Pool of Bethesda, it deserved, O Christ,  
to serve your time.

[Col. 0024C]

They say that this moving wood was the cross, whose  
power extinguished your light, O Hebrew.

### VII.—FROM THE BOOK OF RUTH

Peter’s pen hastens toward Ruth, that brief discourse  
may depict these events in slender verse.

In the land of Judah, under a certain judge, grievous famine,  
confounding the people, began to prevail.

Pressed by this famine, Elimelech feared; he fled and departed  
from Bethlehem, remaining in the region of Moab.

Naomi his wife clung to him, with twin sons:  
one was called Mahlon, the other Chilion.

But by dying Naomi’s husband left her there a widow  
with her sons. Each son took a bride.

[Col. 0024D]

One is called Orpah, the other Ruth; and after ten years  
death made both brides widows.

Bereft of her children and widowed of her husband,  
the woman pours out tears and gives forth sighs.

The welcome report which tells that the land of Judah has food  
redeems these tears.

Therefore she prepares to return. Ruth follows her as she returns,  
having left her people; Orpah likewise follows as companion.

Naomi urges them to remain: “My people,” she says,  
“and sharers in God, are not yours.

Nor can I hope for descendants from you;  
death has taken both sons whom I bore.”

Orpah hears, departs, and then returns; but Ruth follows Naomi,  
although Naomi resists her.

[Col. 0025A]

Though Naomi hinders her and orders her to return  
to her people, Ruth persists and says to her:

“Wherever you decide to go, I shall go.  
Your God and your people are mine.

The land that receives you when you die  
will grant me a grave after life’s end.”

Ruth signifies the holy Church arisen from the Gentiles,  
which at first worshipped idols full of deceits.

Now it worships and reveres true sacred things, and confesses  
as God Him alone whom the holy fathers worshipped.

It hopes that it will reach that place to which Christ’s flesh  
ascended after He had endured the cross.

Ruth follows Naomi when the converted nation has imitated  
the former fathers in conduct and merits.

Ruth enters with Naomi the land of the Hebrew people

[Col. 0025B]

when they began to reap the new barley with the sickle.

She seeks the fields of Boaz, where she gathers ears as she goes,  
making herself pleasing by her services.

There it was ordained by her destiny that a man descended  
from Abraham’s seed should marry her;

and one said to be nearer to her in kinship,  
but such a man denies that he can marry her.

At once he yields to another, removes his shoe,  
and deprives himself of his right and place.

This Boaz was the first to say to those harvesting crops  
with the cutting sickle: “The Lord be with you.”

Ruth is given to him by the favourable praise of ten elders,  
for he was her second nearest kinsman.

Attend to this passage, you who read these things. It contains

[Col. 0025C]

the figure of John the Baptist.

For as the nearer kinsman refuses to marry her,  
but afterward she is united with Boaz,

so likewise the Forerunner—whom the Hebrew people believed  
to be Christ—said to them: “I am not called Christ.

The bridegroom is one whom you do not know; and his friend  
stands outside, believes, rejoices, and hears him.”

By this saying the Forerunner removes his shoe:  
“I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen his sandal-strap.”

And in this manner Christ puts on a shoe when He is clothed  
in the garment of this flesh, so that we may be joined to Him.

Therefore Ruth signifies the Church, and Boaz the Crucified One.  
She is joined to Boaz; this one is joined to God.

And the word of ten elders blesses the two,

[Col. 0025D]

that He who can give all things may give them fruit.

That blessing of ten signifies that the nation to be saved  
is always blessed in the name of Jesus.

Consider the name of Jesus: the first letter is called iota;  
it points to Jesus and signifies ten.

Through this name life is given to all, and no one can be blessed  
except through the name of Jesus alone.

That Boaz begot Obed by Ruth; this father  
became Jesse; this one became the father of David.

### VIII.—FROM THE BOOK OF JUDITH

In the prologue to the book of Judith he teaches in these words that Nebuchadnezzar and Cambyses were the same person:

Jerome, favouring Eustochium and Paula,  
translated the illustrious deeds and history of Judith.

Following meaning more than words from words,

[Col. 0026A]

he produced his writings through his labour.

King Nebuchadnezzar, called Cambyses, accomplished a great work  
in the twelfth year of his reign.

### IX.—THE BOOK OF ESTHER

(BARTHIUS, *Adversaria*, book XXXI, chapter 15, p. 1456, folio. We have emended Barthius’s text with the aid of the Helmstedt manuscripts, whose variant readings Leyser gives in *Historia poetarum medii aevi*, p. 697.)

Until one comes from India to the lands of the Ethiopians,  
the land was subject to King Ahasuerus.

A region of a hundred provinces, serving this king alone,  
lay prostrate and humble beneath the king’s foot.

He set his throne in the city of Susa, which did not permit  
any cities to be counted its equals.

[Col. 0026B]

It was the third year of his reign when the king prepared  
lavish banquets for his leaders and princes.

Here he provided a feast for a hundred and seven days  
in the king’s famous and starry palace.

How festive that house was, if you consult the deeds  
of King Alexander, you may know by reading.

A mass of silver gave strength to columns  
which the hand of an artisan had carved with new skill.

The vaulted roof shone like heaven,  
almost rivaling heaven in equal beauty.

There gems, surpassing the stars, laughed;  
starry light and brilliance filled the chambers.

In seven gems you could see the seven wandering stars  
moving in their wandering courses.

[Col. 0026C]

Chrysoprase held the sun; emerald the moon;  
jasper Mercury; and chrysolite Jupiter.

Onyx is joined to Mars, Venus to beryl,  
while magnet laments the presence of aged Saturn.

Moreover, the carving of twelve gems in their figures  
was equal and like to the twelve signs.

Ram, Bull, Twins, Crab, Lion, Virgin, Balance—  
all these signs shine in seven gems.

Scorpion, Archer, Capricorn, Water-Pourer,  
and Fishes flourish in five gems.

Thus the twelvefold company of gems plays with equal honour  
alongside the twelvefold order of the signs.

After the royal dishes had come to an end,  
the royal table invited other guests.

[Col. 0026D]

The king orders the people dwelling in the city of Susa  
to assemble and celebrate the feast for six days.

Outside the walls of the house stood a colonnade,  
near a flower-bearing garden given over to delights.

Here the king orders splendid dishes to be prepared for all the people,  
cupbearers to stand ready, and cups to be replenished.

From the garden abundant charm flowed upon the guests  
and seasoned the served foods with sight and fragrance:

feeding the eyes by appearance, the nostrils by scent;  
the noble garden served the palate by taste.

Every tree there confers three things: it becomes medicine  
for diseases, shade for the weary, and food for hunger.

Wise nature left none sterile;  
no tree can live there as a virgin.

In the midst stands a noble vineyard, shining with gold,

[Col. 0027A]

silver, gems, fiery, bright, and glittering.

Its vines were of silver, its branches of gold;  
the workmanship surpassed the material.

Clusters distinguished by the varied starlight of gems  
seemed almost about to produce wine.

There shone painted tents; the columns were  
silver, the cords purple, and the cloth linen.

The gleam of silver and redness of gold adorn couches,  
and emerald colour mingles with both.

The sweet, fragrant, exceedingly savoury drop of pure wine  
which laughs in gold makes the guests laugh.

Where their material was not golden, servants made  
every vessel endure exile. [Meaning uncertain.]

[There taste makes the guests dine, impoverishing  
earth, air, and waters.]

[Col. 0027B]

The earth with beasts, the air with birds, and the sea with fish  
refresh the guests, not without attention to the palate.  
[Note: [Col. 0027D] The verses enclosed in brackets are absent from the printed text.]

That Bacchic liquor delights the guests in fragrance, taste, and colour,  
disdaining outward appearance.

No tavern-keeper adulterates that drink with spices;  
there no one marries Bacchus to Thetis.

No guest is compelled to drink;  
each takes his own cups as he pleases.

Moreover, the decorous Queen Vashti prepared in the royal palace  
banquets worthy of companions equal to the king.

Here she gathers the ladies of the country, whom purple clothes,  
whom lineage ennobles, and whom beauty of face blesses.

After this, the king, cheerful after Bacchus’s cups, sent  
eunuchs and ordered Vashti to appear before him.

[Col. 0027C]

He wished to show the leaders with what starry splendour  
her face, eyes, neck, and cheeks shone.

She refuses to come. The king conceives anger and, by counsel  
of his nobles, deprives her of her honour.

At once the king orders girls to be sought throughout every region,  
distinguished and worthy of the king’s bed and love,

to replace Vashti in face—girls whom graceful form,  
honour, intellect, and noble birth ennoble.

The king’s servants hasten to fulfil the commands;  
excellent maidens, bright of cheek, are present.

Among them Esther is more pleasing to the king than all,  
whom the Hebrew tribe brought forth as a rose among thorns.

The others aided their natural beauty by art and cosmetics;  
she seeks no assistance from any art.

[Col. 0027D]

Each maiden increases nature’s beauty with pigments,  
myrtle oil, and snowy adornment.

Hegai the eunuch, their guardian, gave them varied adornment  
and denied them nothing.

For this woman alone the grace of nature suffices,  
which poured many riches into her appearance.

Lilies mingled with roses are joined in her face;  
no adulteration of art separates those two.

Nature showered her with such beauty that one judges  
her cheeks more than mortal.

The king orders the summoned maidens to enter before him after a year;  
entering in the evening, each returns in the morning.

No one among them dared come into the king’s embrace unless the prince called her by name.

[Col. 0028A]

The welcome time was therefore at hand when Esther ought,  
at the king’s command, to approach his bed.

She was one whom death had deprived of both parents,  
whom Mordecai cherished with a father’s love.

He was a Jew; she was his daughter only in affection,  
but his niece by paternal blood.

She zealously strove to follow firmly in every action  
his counsel, instruction, and commands.

From the land of Babylon, whence he had migrated,  
he brought her to Susa and remained there.

But now let the pen return to the sequence of events. Esther  
prepares, as a suppliant, to go to the prince’s couch.

The king’s eye clings to her, and no less does love;  
lovely beauty plunders the whole man.

[Col. 0028B]

The king knew her and loved her kindly;  
in place of Vashti he made her possess the dignity of the kingdom.

He therefore joins her to himself, gives her the diadem, and orders  
the wedding festivities to last for one month.

Peace given in the kingdom flourished during that month,  
and sword, thirsty and needy of blood, was idle.

So that the sword might not break the peace, the king’s marriage  
became a trumpet-call for the whole kingdom.

For through couriers the royal majesty had ordered  
peace to be firmly maintained throughout the kingdom.

Two eunuchs guarding the king’s doors  
during this time planned harm and death for the king.

This sorrowful plot of murder did not escape Mordecai;  
he reported the treachery to his niece.

[Col. 0028C]

Horrified at such a crime, Esther made the king know everything  
in Mordecai’s name.

The matter was investigated, the matter discovered, and the prince’s anger  
ordered the guilty men to be hanged on a cross.

This deed is committed to the books in which the writer’s pen  
is accustomed to record the acts of kings.

After this the king exalts Haman, descended  
from the unhappy stock of King Agag—

the king whose life Saul’s sword spared,  
whom Samuel, brandishing a sword, consecrated to God.

Haman, rich in wealth and exalted in honour,  
flourished in the city of Susa with many goods.

The people, nobles, and great throng of powerful men  
often bend their knees to him as he walks the streets.

[Col. 0028D]

Mordecai alone, following the commands  
of the Hebrew Law, scorns to bend his knee.

Haman, having experienced this often, began with evil heart  
to ponder by what device he might avenge this insult.

Nor does it please him to punish this man alone; rather, he intends  
to punish the whole Hebrew race dwelling in the kingdom.

Therefore, colouring his words with rhetorical ornaments,  
he draws the king’s inclination toward his wishes.

He obtains that the prince seal his documents and that all  
the Jews dwelling in his realms should perish.

Through various messengers he sends instructions to the various cities  
which you, Hebrew people, inhabit:

that they should perish by fire, endure hanging from wood, be beaten,

[Col. 0029A]

by scourging, and be pierced by wounds—the written orders so decree.

A day was appointed and a time fixed  
when the mournful work of slaughter must be done.

This grievous report strikes Mordecai’s ears; grief fixes  
dreadful wounds in his heart.

He covers his limbs with sackcloth, shakes the palace with shouting,  
tears his garments with his nails, and wets his face with tears.

He instructs the queen to be a remedy for grief,  
that, speaking with the king, she may then bring forth prayers.

Esther orders Mordecai to fast, and that all  
her people dwelling in the city of Susa should fast.

Esther approaches the king. In mercy he stretches toward her  
the golden sceptre which he holds in his hand.

The queen kisses the sceptre; the prince kisses  
the standing queen, each astonished at the other’s star-like beauty.

[Col. 0029B]

And, while he fed his eyes on her beauty, he said:

“If, Queen, you ask for gifts, you shall receive what you ask.  
Your beauty deserves half the kingdom;

therefore ask what you desire; it shall happen without delay.”

Esther says to the king: “I pray that on this day  
the king and Haman may deign to come to my banquet.”

They are present; they enjoy the feast and applaud Bacchus,  
whom golden vessels shower upon the guests.

The king, made cheerful after the stream of abundant nectar,  
spoke these words: “Esther, ask for what you desire.”

She says: “I pray that the king and Haman alone may come  
to my banquet tomorrow; then I shall tell the king my requests.”

Haman goes out joyful. The crowd rises as he passes;  
one bows his head, another bends his knee.

Mordecai pays him no honours

[Col. 0029C]

and does not honour him even by moving from his seat.

Concealing his anger, Haman goes away and tells his friends  
how great his glory and how great his honour are,

adding that Esther had invited him together with the king  
to eat with her on the following day.

Yet he thinks all his splendid honour is nothing  
so long as Mordecai is permitted to live.

His wife and kinsfolk gave him this answer:  
let him quickly prepare a great beam,

on which the Jew may perish when hanged, and let him first  
suggest this and move it in the king’s ear,

so that, with the cloud of grief wiped away by a festive foot,  
he may go joyfully to the queen’s banquet.

He trusts their counsel; therefore he prepares a beam like a cross,

[Col. 0029D]

whose summit rises from sight toward the stars.

The king takes no sleep that night and orders  
the books to be brought and the royal writings read.

And while Mordecai’s fidelity was being recorded—the deed  
by whose aid the royal life had been preserved—

the king says: “What reward has been rendered  
for such fidelity?” He is answered: “He received no rewards.”

At this time Haman enters the royal court, intending

[Note: [Col. 0029D] These are omitted in the printed text.]

[to disclose his premeditated wishes and proposed counsel,

[when he has obtained the opportunity, to tell the king]

every evil thing about Mordecai.

He is recognized; the doors are opened, and he is summoned by the king,  
to whom the king directs these words:

[Col. 0030A]

“What ought to be done for the man whom the king’s favour  
wishes to exalt, so that his honour may increase?”

Thinking that this had been said concerning himself by the king’s mouth,  
he burst forth and opened his throat to say these things:

“Let him whom the king wishes to make distinguished be clothed  
and adorned in shining purple and a glittering diadem.

Let him sit upon the king’s horse, whose bridle gleams with gold,  
which trappings ornament and a painted saddle covers.

Let the foremost of the princes lead the horse; swiftly let him enter  
the city and summon the citizens by a new command,

proclaiming with such a cry: ‘He whom the king’s favour honours  
ought to enjoy honour thus splendid.’”

“Bestow this honour upon Mordecai,” says the king;  
“take care that you omit nothing from it.”

Fearing the royal command, Haman, though unwillingly honouring

[Col. 0030B]

the Jew, hastens and performs everything.

Then, clouded, he returns home and explains this to his friends,  
groaning in heart, troubled in face, and snarling in speech.

The king sends servants to Haman, that he may hasten to Esther’s

[Note: [Col. 0030D] Barthius omitted these verses.]

[banquet. The prepared table received the two.

The king, made cheerful after a draught of pleasant nectar,]

says to the queen: “Ask for what you desire.”

The queen replies: “I ask for the life of my people,  
whose ruin and death an enemy people thirsts for.”

The king says: “Who has dared devise this crime?”  
She replies: “This bloody Haman does it.”

These words produce anger in the king and astonishment  
in Haman; the latter grieves, the former is stunned.

The king, angry, enters the garden, that the serene beauty of the place  
may wipe away the cloud of his sadness.

[Col. 0030C]

The author of the crime falls before the queen’s throne,  
begging her to soften the king’s threats.

When the king returns and finds him leaning close to his wife’s couch,  
he utters words exceedingly harsh:

“Shame! This enemy, to the king’s disgrace, not fearing me,  
wishes to violate Esther’s honour itself.”

Harbona replies: “There stands the timber whose arms  
Haman prepared for Mordecai’s death.”

The king says: “Let Haman expire, hanged upon it;  
let the punishment prepared punish its own author.”

The king’s command promptly takes effect:  
life leaves Haman, suspended on the cross.

The queen again obtains from the king through prayer  
that he condemn the former written decrees with new writings;

[Col. 0030D]

that complete salvation be given to the Jews and their enemies  
perish and be subjected to death;

that the ten sons of cruel Haman, slain,  
provide food for ravens upon the wood;

that Mordecai may deserve the king’s favour  
and possess all that Haman had possessed.

The king quickly orders all things to be done; all are done;  
the royal commands experience no delay.

Codex Helmstad. 1 adds:

The king who holds feasts while He is in the Virgin’s womb  
prepares festive joys for the world.

The Synagogue is invited to enter the king’s feast,  
but she disdains it and refuses to come.

Christ rejects her and adopts for Himself the captive

[Col. 0031A]

Church. Thus it comes about that He marries her as Esther.

Every worldly tyrant, Haman, persecutes her;  
but his scheme perishes and her honour remains.

The following verses are added in both Helmstedt manuscripts:

Then, rejoicing that it had escaped the danger of death,  
the Hebrew people held a feast for the most high God,

which the ancients established as an observance due from posterity  
and gave the festival the name Purim.

The Jew still solemnizes it, and Esther still honours  
that ancient dignity by perpetuating it.

### X.—ON SAINT SUSANNA

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 1287, among the miscellaneous poems of Hildebert of Le Mans.)

### XI.—ON REUBEN

(WARTON, *Anglia sacra*, I, 204.)

[Col. 0031B]

You are my firstborn, my strength, and the beginning  
of my sorrow, first in gifts and authority.

You are like water poured out: you could never  
increase, for you violated your father’s bed.

### XII.—ON EHUD

(Ibid.)

That he may save the people and crush the enemy’s right hand,  
the mercy of God sends Ehud for the people.

### XIII.—ON JUDAS MACCABAEUS

After his father’s death Judas Maccabaeus prepares arms, that he may

[Col. 0031C]

destroy enemies and crush the nations.

Supported and assisted by brothers, companions,  
kinsmen, and friends, he wounds the enemy.

### XIV–XVI.—FROM THE GOSPEL: “TOUCH, CAMENA”—“HE RECEIVED THREE”—“THE THREEFOLD HOUSE”

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, cols. 1388–1389, among Hildebert’s miscellaneous poems.)

### XVII.—FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

(*Hist. litt. de la France*, XVII, 35.)

Seeing Mary pregnant, Joseph wonders  
and seeks to depart and leave her secretly.

But an angel warns him in a dream that she should become his wife,

[Col. 0031D]

and that he should think no evil to be in his spouse.

Let him believe that the conceived child is from the Holy Spirit,  
and honour him by giving him the name Jesus—

he who saves the people, cleanses the world from every  
sin, and becomes hope for the wretched, medicine for the guilty.

The man obeyed the sacred warnings, rejoicing to be the Virgin’s husband,  
remaining a virgin with the holy Virgin.

### XVIII.—A RECAPITULATION OF BOTH TESTAMENTS

(LEYSER, p. 703.)

The prologue begins to the brief recapitulation which follows, of all the matters treated more fully above.

[Col. 0032A]

Having completed these volumes concerning the New and Old Law,  
I was about to make an end, if it had been permitted.

Here I ought to have stopped, had not, behold, a different desire  
and a new plan arisen in me.

For, reader, whatever matters I previously treated more fully,  
I now recapitulate for you, so as to make all things easy to learn.

Above I described persons, things, and many names,  
if you retain them well in remembering mind.

Lest these should be lacking to you, I recapitulate them for the most part,  
in brief words and a briefer style.

You will ask: why, having now conducted myself by hexameter law,  
do I again travel here in closed wheels?

Why do I again use pentameter verses,

[Col. 0032B]

for I cannot endure the tedium of a long delay.

It delights me to hasten to the goal, which seems near  
and will halt for me the journey poured out thus far.

Moreover, what I add is new; I pursue a certain novelty  
in words and an artful method.

And do not, in a spirit of blame, call what I have seriously said  
leisurely amusements; do not consider our works trifles.

Whatever it may be, attend gladly.  
Our care and labour serve your instruction.

The prologue ends.

## THE RECAPITULATIONS OF BOTH TESTAMENTS BEGIN

### First division, without A

At the beginning of things, after five days, the first man  
is believed to have been created on the sixth day.

[Col. 0032C]

Here he signifies Christ, who, entering the world at the sixth age,  
became man in redeeming us by the cross.

A wife is made from the man’s bone when sleep is sent upon him,  
and that sleep was Christ’s death.

She was the sign of the Church; from Christ’s body  
the origin of the earthly race received faith.

By the taste of the forbidden tree that man killed us;  
by His blood upon the cross He redeems us.

### Without B

Cain’s sword pierced his brother’s inward parts; blood,  
poured out from the earth, cries in God’s hearing.

The Jew pierced Christ with a spear; His  
blood thus cries out because it washes us from evil.

Enos signifies the wicked established upon the earth,  
from whose name you read that cities were made.

[Col. 0032D]

Seth, whose name is said to mean “rising,”  
shows Him who, rising from the cross, holds the highest things.

Enos, who first invokes the Lord’s name,  
suggests those who seek true joys in hope.

Lamech is an image of Christ, whom He redeems after  
seventy-seven generations.

Enoch was translated, the seventh from the first father;  
he signifies those whom the seventh rest receives.

### Without C

Lest the world perish, Noah guided the wood upon the waves;  
through wood, through waters, O merciful Christ, you wash us.  
[Note: [Col. 0031D] In *Christus*, C in *Ch.*—or at least the letter C in the word *Christus*—is present contrary to the ordinary rule; in ancient manuscripts *Ch.* is generally written in *Christus* by means of the Greek Χ. Although this word may be excused, in other verses the author or scribe violated the principle according to which the letter C ought to have been absent.]

[Col. 0033A]

Shem signifies certain righteous persons, and other profane persons,  
from whom that offspring of the fathers sprang.

Japheth can be a figure of the Gentile people,  
which thereafter knew how to live among the Hebrews.

The brother who mocked his father signifies the Hebrews,  
who laugh at Christ’s reproaches and deny the cross.  
[Note: [Col. 0033D] “And the faith” (*fidemque*) would be more correct, so that the word may lack C.]

He whom the righteous man cursed on account of his father  
signifies the Jews whom the world now has.

Those whom the fathers made guilty of Christ’s blood,  
their offspring, after our evils, washes with these words.

Nemroth, who built the tower threatening the stars, signifies Satan, seeking the heights yet holding the depths. [Note: To eliminate C, it might have been written: “He who built Nimrod’s tower,” or: “Nimrod who built a tower.”]

Heber signifies the dwelling-place where the original language remained: your house, O Christ, in which the one faith abides.

The king and lord of Salem offered bread and wine, in whom Christ is signified as mighty in both.

Without D.

Father Abraham is a type of the eternal Father: he consecrates his own son upon the altar; the latter, his own. Isaac suffers nothing; a ram becomes the victim. Christ’s divinity suffers nothing when the man dies.

Ishmael and Isaac figure the holy testaments: the former represents the Old, the latter the New.

Hairy, red Esau denotes—represents—those who stained their hands with your blood, O Christ.

Jacob, preferred before his brother, denotes that race which preferred to the Hebrews the one who marks heart and deed.

Laban is Satan, whose name sounds like “white”: for Satan is often covered with a false colour.

Rachel remains sparing in childbirth, yet the generous brightness of her countenance makes recompense for a greedy womb’s loss.

Offspring ennobles Leah’s womb; yet she had cheeks poor, barren, and without bloom.

Fair, barren Rachel is the mind intent upon things above, sparing of being useful for a brother’s gain.

Leah thrives in childbirth, because holy action produces in the churches the seed of the word for the useful profit. [Note: I read “because” (*quo*), since the letter D must be absent.]

Without E.

While the man sent from on high wrestles with Jacob, the patriarch is made lame in an instant.

When the Synagogue thus wrestles, wearying Christ, it limps and staggers, thereby preparing many evils. [Note: More correctly: “and.”]

Lot denotes the holy, whom the end of the world separates from those consumed by the evil flame and saves.

Lot’s wife denotes those whom Christ’s grace first drew, but who afterwards make a path back to their former evils.

That country in which Samaria now exercises authority is denoted by one of Lot’s daughters, the last-born Zion: the population inhabiting either place is stained by teachings wickedly opposed to the Lord.

Without F.

Reuben is the firstborn: he denotes that people whom the supreme grace of God first chose.

He violates his father’s bed when he compels the flesh, which Christ joins to himself, to undergo the cross.

Simeon denotes those who killed the prophets and, after the prophets’ bodies had been slain, Jesus—whom their hand pierced with sharp nails, he who remains our wall and our rock.

Levi denotes and points out the Levites and priests as authors of the crime in Christ’s death.

Judah signifies Christ, whom the angel praises on high and humankind, bowed down, worships upon earth.

The lion’s cub is accustomed to sleep through two days of light, and after two days rises and wakes. Thus the third day of light awakens him from sleep, who is called the lion of Judah’s stock.

Issachar is a strong ass lying down near the boundaries, seeing what a good resting-place, an excellent land, there is. He denotes the teacher who performs strong deeds, having the eyes of the mind directed toward true rest; who recalls what the boundary of life and what the world’s end may be, and strives to lie down among these things in mind.

Zebulun denotes the Church, which is battered by the waves of this life and exposed to punishment.

Dan is a judge, a serpent upon the broad path, a horned serpent coming upon the narrow one: the wicked man will stand upon the horse. From him Antichrist will derive his origin, as Scripture declares in speaking thus.

He will be like a serpent that bites, and like a horned serpent to those who wish to walk with straight steps. The horse is this world; everyone proud is its rider. The end of the world is the horse’s hoof.

When he comes amid the world’s storm, he will destroy, biting and casting backward, all whom he can.

Gad, girded for wars, will set these in motion by going before him; girded as he comes, he too will stand behind. He denotes disciples equipped for Christ’s battles, whom the abundant grace of God both precedes and follows.

Asher’s bread is rich, abounding in the richness of bread: he will give its delicacies to kings. The holy food of the altar is denoted by that bread which feeds kings, peoples, and the Church.

Naphtali is called a released hind, ready for every course and possessing words of beauty: he denotes swift men sent by the Lord to carry the splendid words of God throughout the world.

Without G.

Joseph was sold, and Christ was sold: the former is placed over peoples; the latter rules over all.

Benjamin, formerly a wolf seizing prey for himself in the morning, later seizes and divides food. I turn to the typological sense: he denotes Saul, who is said to have been born from that tribe.

At first he seized prey for himself in wolfish fashion, while raging against the saints and persecuting the devout. But, now made Paul, he ceases to be proud as he sows devout words among the Lord’s people.

Manasseh is first among the peoples and Ephraim second, whom, behold, God preferred to the former.

Tamar is the Church, which conceives holy actions while leaning, as upon a staff, upon the cross.

She whose hand clung with a scarlet thread denotes the Hebrews polluted, O Christ, by your blood. But the other brother seems to denote us: the bosom of Mother Church nourishes both.

The holy woman, forced to lie with the prince of the land, signifies the foolish soul drawn along by empty evils.

Patient Job denotes Christ suffering; his friends, schismatics, whose proud hearts swell.

This son of Sarah, *de bassa* [of lowly status?], shone as the fourth successor in the kingship of Idumea after Esau. [Note: *Bassus* otherwise denotes “lower.” Perhaps Hagar is denoted by that name as Sarah’s handmaid and inferior.]

But this man is believed to have been born from the line of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, as the Hebrew says. This is found at the beginning of the book which he wrote, where that passage of the codex places it first.

For Nahor’s wife Milcah bore eight sons, and Uz was the first among them. Accordingly, because he descended from Uz, he is said to have been a man named Job in the land of Uz.

Without H.

The prince of Egypt commands that the female sex be allowed to live and compels the males to be drowned in the river.

The demon loves feminine and soft deeds, and hates and persecutes holy men.

At this time Moses comes forth alive into birth, through whom the law of God arose for the Jews.

A little basket of rushes, set upon the river-bank, steals from death the weeping child, who increases the waters. The king’s daughter hears the little one’s cry; she orders him taken up, has him nourished, and loves him.
