She denotes the holy Church, which in faith sees Christ present at the font of holy washing.

Moses weeping upon the bank denotes Christ weeping: each wept as a child in a cradle.

Aaron, who cleanses peoples by blood, signifies Christ, who washed all things with his own blood.

Moses’ sister, whom leprosy touched, is the Synagogue, which suffers leprosy because it stubbornly refuses belief in God.

Without I.

Amalek, making war, languishes before the weapons as though made into a cross, when the Hebrews’ hands are raised.

It prevails and overcomes the Hebrews when he relaxes his palms and the fruit of prayer from his mouth ceases.

But when they hang down, Hur and Aaron, with the immediate help of a stone, support the upright hands.

Thus their weapons grow weak while the mind is raised to heaven in crying aloud, praying in heart or speech.

Thus also, as he handles the mysteries, the priest performs the rite, standing as a suppliant with both hands raised.

The Amorite ruler, called in our language “the one who spreads before the eyes,” is said to harm Zion. Know Satan through him, when he transforms himself, as it is written, into an angel and deceives the good by every art he can.

Og, ruler of Bashan, whom the author calls “shut in,” or “one who shuts in,” denotes Satan. For he is shut in, seeking to shut out heaven; he is present in the world, tearing us in this manner.

Moreover, the sacred ardour completes six days out of seven; and there are as many utterances that teach sacred words. Through them believers burn with the Holy Spirit; such are the sayings which the world now has.

Without K.

A cluster hangs upon wood; Christ hangs upon the cross: from this flows wine, from that salvation.

The Hebrew and the Gentile are the two bearers of the cluster: the former goes first, the latter follows; the former is blind, the latter sees.

The Hebrew, who goes first, is blinded as he bends his back, lest, hardened, he see and believe in Christ. But the Gentile people that follows, with clear sight, clings to this Christ, seeing in mind and faith.

The man who despises the sabbath and gathers wood denotes those who multiply evils and remain without peace.

Dathan, Abiram, and Korah attempt, as with censers, to oppose God’s commands and denote schismatics. But as the earth swallowed such lumps, so God’s wrath will punish schismatics—those who make a new altar, seek schisms, renew baptism, and oppress the Church.

Balaam was hired to curse the Hebrews, but the magician’s curses became greater blessings.

He sits upon an ass; the dumb beast speaks; the rider does not see the angelic sword, but the she-ass sees it.

The Gentile people, formerly dumb, now speaks your praises, O Christ: the speaking she-ass denotes this. Anyone who taught false rites to be worshipped was her rider, until she rejected the gods; until Christ came, who was the angel of great counsel and subjects the nations to himself.

When Phinehas strikes Zimri’s prostitute, he denotes the person who cuts away every evil thing with the sword of the word.

Without L.

Joshua is a type of Christ: he divided his father’s earthly kingdoms among the Hebrews; Christ gives kingdoms to his own.

If he sends men of ours to the city of Jericho, they may learn the condition of the people and city through them.

Jericho is the world; the Redeemer sent the two Testaments into it, testing human deeds through them.

The scarlet cord hanging and clinging to the window preserves Rahab, her property, and her family from the enemy. The rosy blood shed upon Christ’s cross saves us; his opened side, pierced by the spear, was that window.

The Hebrew people circles the city of Jericho seven times with sound; then its wall falls, and so it triumphs over it. Not by weapons but by the power of sacred words did faith conquer in the world those who love the world.

When its sound resounded, all the superstition of the world and the condition of unbelief immediately fell.

Achan sins by taking gold; the stone avenges the sin of gold; God condemns golden thefts.

He denotes schismatics who mix golden words with sacred writings: God’s wrath will punish them.

The fierce tribe of nobles, enriched by descent of blood, stood upon Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessing there. The six lower tribes, not flourishing so in blood, stand upon the opposite mountain, uttering stern words.

Those upon whom blessing rests figure hearts which do good from love of supreme peace. Those upon whom curse rests figure hearts which avoid vice from fear of punishment.

The altar denotes the mind, which crushes the heat of the flesh and restrains the motions of the soul under reason.

Two gifts of the altar are given us by the Father; both gifts are granted by the Father who reigns. When the flesh fasts, dry land is given to the petitioner; when the cheek is wet with dew, moist land is given.

Without M.

After Joshua, there will be an account of the leaders from whom the Hebrew tribe shone forth as far as Joktan.

Thus after you, devout king, devout leader, devout Christ, skilled rulers come and wage our wars.

If the Hebrew people sinned by worshipping vain sacred things, God’s wrath gave them over to enemies. If, abandoning vain sacred things, they struck heaven with prayer, their enemies turned their backs, God bringing this about.

Thus, when you despise God’s commands, your enemy prevails; if you strike the sky with prayers, you shall be victor.

The Hebrew still sins: King Eglon prevails against him; oppressed and afflicted, he prays to God.

He laments and sighs; in him Gideon breathes again, who hopes that God, pleased with weeping, prepares to be present.

Ehud fights with his right hand and a sword is placed upon his right thigh: King Eglon falls, and he returns.

Ehud denotes the righteous, who, so that they may have no part of the left, make everything right-handed on the right.

Shamgar strikes six hundred enemies with a ploughshare and denotes teachers who sow sacred words.

The fleece flows with dew while first the threshing-floor was dry: the fleece denotes the Jews; the dry ground, the Gentiles.

God first watered the Hebrews with the cloud of the law, but the people was a stranger to so great a good.

After the fleece was dried, the threshing-floor then flowed: the Jews having been rejected, abundant grace was given to the Gentile people.

The basin is filled with water from the squeezed fleece: the holy womb of the Virgin is filled with sacred liquid.

Deborah or Jael, the worthy woman who pierces the enemy’s head with wood, was each a figure of the Church. For by sacred wood, as by a sign, Sisera—Satan—is conquered, stripped of the honour of his authority.

Next follows Jephthah, for whose praise in triumph a daughter was made an offering to God. Christ shines forth in this: his flesh hanging on the tree was made an offering for our salvation.

Samson exults in the jawbone of an ass; Christ upon the cross: there the enemy is struck down, here Satan is conquered.

A new spring gushes forth and benefits the thirsty: the sacred cross washes and renews us with a holy fountain.

Without N.

The mighty leader goes to Gaza to join a friend; Christ descends to hell in order to lead out the Church.

The hostile crowd buries the leader by deception: a Hebrew company places guards at Christ’s tomb. [Note: So that the letter N may be absent, substitute “adds,” or a similar word.]

The former, burdensome to his enemies, rises at the time of the stars; the latter, beneath joyful dawn, bears trophies.

The former carries off the city’s gates; the latter, blessed spoil. The former prevails over his own; the latter prevails over his own.

The victorious leader, having subdued the enemy, climbs the steep rock. Christ, conqueror of the Hebrews, returns to the stars.

That his beloved stripped his head of its sacred hair; that he was delivered to cruel enemies; that he loses his sight; that he plays; that he turns the mill—investigate this, reader who reads sacred words.

Reason is like a frail man; flesh devoted to sweet luxury may rightly be called Delilah.

She cuts off the hair when slippery flesh deceives you: the hair cut off is God’s grace taken from you.

For this reason your enemy mocks you: he who fell from heaven and does every evil.

Thus you lose your eyes, because he blinds you with the dust of vices, so that you may cease to see God with the heart.

And he makes you turn the mill while he circles the world and whirls your wretched heart through many evils.

Without O.

Ruth denotes the Church from the Gentiles, whom Christ, her husband, chastely joins to himself.

Hannah, first found barren, then became Samuel’s mother by a heavenly gift. Having become fruitful from being barren, she figures the same Church as full of devout fruits.

The rejection of Eli and the birth of Samuel denote the withering of the old law, after the succeeding law has been given.

The young men of Eli, the armed father, and the capture of the ark signify the honour of the law’s passing to the Gentiles.

King Saul strives by craft that the royal weapon may drink bloody drops from the little harpist. Thus the faithless Jew, too, hungers and thirsts for Christ’s wounds, bonds, and cross.

We find that the least of Jesse’s little ones was anointed: thus abundant grace acts among the least. He looks upon the humble; he rejects and resists those who pride themselves upon what belongs to others.

David rightly represented the true David, because the blessed mother brought forth Christ from David’s stock.

Naked Bathsheba pleased the king because Christ loves the law, whose bright words shine.

The king deprives Uriah of her: thus Christ deprives the Hebrew of his law; neither knows his own loss.

The letter which Uriah bears destroys Uriah; the Hebrew perishes through his own writings.

David destroys the Gittite, and Christ the proud one who said: “My foot shall be above the stars.”

Without P.

Solomon shone, abundant in wisdom and possessions beyond any human being, possessing this and that in abundance.

He dedicates to God a house worthy of praise, with whose splendour no others dare contend.

Christ builds the Church, which he has blessed with much honour, out of righteous and heavenly men.

No axe was heard in the king’s sacred house; no tumult will be in the heavenly dwelling.

To know human natures, birds’ songs, the medicines of herbs, the stars of heaven, the depths of the sea, the force of wind, the powers of gems, the fury of rivers, and the secrets of things—this has been granted you.

A throne is made of ivory; Solomon clothes ivory with gold. The world did not deserve to possess a like throne.

King Solomon is Jesus; the gold is the majesty of divinity, the ivory virginity, and the Virgin Mary the throne.

Under Rehoboam and Jeroboam the kingdom was divided in two, God bringing this about.

Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, denotes those who gave faith to the Lord at his birth; Jeroboam shows those Hebrew servants whom that son of death kills at the end.

Without Q.

A fiery chariot carries Elijah to the heights; God is not borne to the stars by help or by a chariot.

A needy woman, a guest, feeds Elijah, and he feeds her: she is fed more, he less. Her oil and the substance of her meal do not fail; neither food can diminish.

The woman denotes the Church and the prophet Christ: she feeds and refreshes him by good conduct.

The food is Christ’s body and the anointing of chrism: from it the abundant grace of God feeds the Church.

This food is always consumed; it always overflows and can neither diminish nor perish.

The bread spent upon the altar remains whole: you always receive it and always have it to receive.

“Go up, bald one!” the boys cry to Elisha; but a bear kills and devours them together.

The bald one rightly denotes Christ: for Calvary is said to be the part of the place where Christ dies.

Those two bears are Titus and Vespasian: the former cuts down, the latter kills Jerusalem’s citizens.

Those crying, “Crucify Jesus! Crucify him!” are killed, and the whole offspring pays for their fathers’ sins.

You give the staff to the servant; you entrust it to Elisha’s minister. Nothing is done: the child rises when you come. The letter of the law sent beforehand does not save a human being; we began to live at your coming, O Christ.

Without R.

Naaman is completely cleansed when he enters the water: holy water wholly cleanses us whom it washes.

Uzziah sinning denotes Judaea: its polluted head stinks with flowing corruption.

Thus impiety defiles the Jews who deny the Lord and faith, and evil report destroys them.

Hezekiah, to whom the judge added years, denotes those to whom blessed rest must be given.

Josiah performs the holy Passover and removes idols; Jesus, making the Passover, puts every idol to flight.

Zedekiah is blinded and delivered to enemies; subjected to Satan, he lacks the light of the mind.

Holy Isaiah opens mystical places, as one whose own tongue speaks evangelical things.

The chaste man born at Anathoth, through suffering and speech, gracious Jesus, signified you in this praise.

Your tongue taught these things, O Jesus; your passion washed us: one teaching and the other were useful to the churches.

Without S.

Ezekiel, who rebuked evils, denotes him, ruler of the world, who teaches all things rightly.

While he speaks to the people, labour and pain overwhelm him; when he teaches the people, he bears and suffers the cross.

Bright electrum and two rods seen by him—what a wondrous figure lies hidden here!

In electrum shines the brightness of silver and the redness of gold; in the Lord, flesh shines together with divinity.

Silver denotes flesh; gold, divinity; the Word of God in flesh joins these two.

The first rod is called the Virgin; the other rod, the cross. The former pleases in beauty; the latter is strong in power.

Life is given to the world by the maiden bearing Christ; the blessed cross breaks the serpent’s head.

Modesty flowered and flourished in Daniel; through him both strength and modesty are represented and indicated.

Daniel is made one who flourishes in chaste flesh, whom blind desire does not draw to vice.

Whoever mortifies the flesh and shuns the summit of worldly things flourishes with Daniel when he despises slippery things.

Without T.

When you take an adulteress, Hosea, you signify the Crucified One: the adulteress, as a go-between, signifies the adulterous Church joined to her husband.

O Church, formerly you had indeed been an adulteress in heart, worshipping vain idols, deceitful toward God. But now, converted, you are the beloved of the heavenly king, avoiding false divinities and singing true songs.

Now you celebrate praises to the Lord, sing hymns to the bridegroom, and glorify him in conduct, speech, and faith.

For your bridegroom you now give praise in psalms, words, and hymns; with him you shall rejoice and sing without end.

Without V.

Moreover, Joel at the beginning means “seeking a human being”: it may denote the first sacred gifts to the mind.

In Amos the shepherd you will note the shepherd of the people: the former benefited a flock, the latter God’s people.

Obadiah, feeding one hundred prophets with bread, denotes lofty teachers and bishops.

Such men ought, with the heavenly nectar of bread, to feed believers and the faith of the Church.

Such persons the grace of speech commends: they feed the slow with milk and strong hearts with solid food.

Without X.

Jonah, both by his word and by his shipwreck, denotes him who is the Father’s Word, teaching shipwrecked hearts.

He is sent; having been sent, he fears; fearing, he flees; fleeing, he enters a vessel; received in the vessel, he begins sleep.

The wave swells; the lot cast causes him to be plunged into the sea; the man is swallowed by a fish; he entreats God.

The fish is commanded to vomit up the morsel it holds; it obeys its maker’s word.

When the third day first brought light to the world, the monster, commanded, vomits Jonah onto land.

A servant is said to be sent by his lord and a son by his father: the former obeyed his lord, the latter his Father.

Jonah sleeps in the stern; Jesus dies upon the cross. The former’s sleep was that of a servant; the latter’s death was precious, that of the Lord.

The vessel’s timbers denote the cross; the whale’s throat, the Lord’s tomb. In it he slept three days.

The third day having come, it vomited the prophet from its belly; that day raises the Lord from the tomb.

Without Y.

Micah sees the place in his mind and proclaims it, where the royal mother will bear God.

By the witness of his name Nahum denotes him who consoles us and speaks good words.

Habakkuk, the mighty wrestler who saw horns in the hands of the Lord, denotes every faithful person: whoever believes in the Lord, preaches that the world has been saved by the cross, and spreads faith throughout the whole world.

Zephaniah denotes those watchers who despise Martha and wish to be Mary.

Haggai commands that the Lord’s house be renewed, that the work which he sees has grown old may grow young again.

There is one stone adorned with seven eyes, which Zechariah sees with wondering mind.

This is the sun of righteousness, whom sevenfold grace fills, and to whom all things lie wholly naked.

The angelic Malachi announces the gifts of the devout, the punishments of the wicked, and the day of judgment.

He figures him who is called the angel of great counsel, who is the fountain and origin of good.

Mathan, Achiam, Sadoch, Abian, Aian, and Tobi magnify Jesus, together with the three youths; Ezra, Zerubbabel, Esther, Judith, and the Maccabees—not without Susanna, who was just toward her husband.

The Old Law contains these men, together with those mentioned above, in the pure order of the poem.

Here ends the section on the ancient fathers. The section on the new begins.

Without Z.

These are under the New Law: John the Baptist with his father and mother; the Virgin Mary, mother; Peter and Andrew, Paul, James and John, the virgin guardian who was without stain; Thomas, Matthew, Philip, Bartholomew, James and Judas—not evil but indeed good; Matthias, Mark, Luke, Simeon, Timothy, Barnabas, and Titus. These taught the faith.

Here ends the section on the fathers of the New Testament.

## XVII. Epilogue

Prayer of Peter Riga, who composed the book.

May Christ, Peter, through the merit of your labour, join you to and number you among the good, so that, when he frees you from the muddy prison, he may make you a sharer and participant in his kingdom.

So that you may not be deprived of this reward, may he grant you holy life and an unstained death.

Amen.

Likewise, a prayer by someone who restored what had been ruined.

I, who brought the broken sequence of the book back into order, was here your servant, Peter, not your companion.

But I do not say who I am, for I wish to remain hidden and to be known less by the eyes of the world and more by the eyes of God.

For the Lord knows, for the public benefit of the brothers, who moved me to this and what vows I made.

And since that work is one which your mind drew from heaven alone, the blessed multitude will sing it as divine.

This was done for the brothers’ benefit in reading. If any reward of yours exists in the region of heaven, may some portion, however small, of everlasting good also enrich me because I completed the little book.

And you, reader, grant a share of this prayer to both of us. If you desire this for us and pray that it be done, say, “Let it be”; I answer: “May you too, who so desire, be granted by this prayer the power to enjoy it.”

Amen.

[Col. 0041]

# Verses of Aegidius of Paris on the Number of the Books of Each Testament and the Method of Reading

(LEYSER, *Historia poetarum medii aevi*, p. 741.)

On the number of the books of each Testament, and the method of reading.

This book is enclosed in forty little books. The Old Law gives thirty-two; the New, eight.

The little books are thus arranged with remarkable brevity, so that the order of the prescribed number may show them to you.

The canon of Sacred Scripture, arranged by God’s mouth and pen and published to the world, is believed to be so constituted.

Yet it excludes these: Tobit, Judith, Maccabees, Baruch, Jesus [son of Sirach], and the pseudonymous book.

But though excluded, the practice of the Church, the rule of faith, and the writings of the Fathers authenticate them.

Know that these things were ordered by God’s finger. Here is a deep well; a great abyss lies within.

You would not grasp everything even if you lived through many ages, vigilant in study and strong in reason.

The Spirit, who is also the Creator, teaches these things; he who gave what must be known also enables one to know.

He enables one to know if you study with your mind and diligently persist, giving study with prayer and prayer with study.

Thus the Fathers studied, so that the sacred page might lie open. Thus the saints unseal the closed seals of the book.

The simple bark here contains manifold food: the letter is like bark; the threefold sense like food.

Examine the historical, typological, and moral sense, if you wish to be satisfied with this typological food.

When you read the text of history, a sweetness is drunk, as it were, like milk—or rather, a draught of plain water.

It does not help much here. Yet, when one desires it, the Spirit acts so that one may be refreshed by its examples.

In the typological sense the pungency of wine is felt. This drink intoxicates and gladdens more fully.

Whoever drinks this wine of Scripture hunts on high mountains, finds, and pursues Jesus.

But when reading gives you the moral sense, then you suck in your mouth a honeyed comb.

These are the delights by which the human mind is inwardly fed and thereby becomes rich in good morals.

By whichever of these you learn what rewards are borne by the righteous, or what scourges must be borne by the wicked, you will be nearer to God because of honour’s seasoning, and thence reverent and well guarded.

[Col. 0043]

# Verses of the Same Author on the Punishments of Hell

(Ibid., p. 743.)

Treatise on the proposition that punishment in hell is not eternal, and again, conversely, that it is eternal. Either position can indeed be maintained. This is taught in these verses of Master Aegidius.

Punishment, which punishes reprobates or guilty persons in Tartarus, is often mentioned in sacred writings. Therefore, after the end of this book, some mention of punishment ought properly to follow.

Here teachers seem to disagree among themselves, and perhaps set forth some minor doctrines. Whether that punishment is or is not everlasting is their mutual dispute; they have arguments by which they maintain themselves in this matter.

Accordingly, the distinguished Matthew, a native of the city of Laon, said that he would set forth something brief in these verses.

### Verses of Master Matthew of Laon

Punishment is not everlasting for the spirits in hell, for a twofold punishment is given to the guilty among them.

I believe that unceasing glory is granted in heaven, since in eternal things there is no movement that is unceasing.

Punishment is thus everlasting for the spirits in hell, because no escape is granted to the guilty who have fallen among them.

### Verses of Master Aegidius

He has, as it were, touched upon what might support either position; I was pleased to examine both statements.

And since his view, in some respect, is more concise, it seemed right to pursue it in a fuller style.

Most maintain that punishment is everlasting for the spirits in hell; many opponents deny the same.

One must consider what both these and those maintain. So that you may consider this, I have set forth this brief doctrine.

By making distinctions, they customarily understand punishment differently; thus each school arises in diverse ways from different senses.

### That the Punishment of Hell Is Eternal

The instrument which punishes is called punishment: thus the thief’s gallows bears the name “punishment.”

Punishment may also be called pain in the sufferer, or distress arising from evils inflicted.

In each of these senses punishment in hell is eternal: the fire is perpetual and the snows perpetual.

Likewise, the suffering of those undergoing punishment never ceases. Whoever suffers, here or elsewhere, always feels pain.

### That the Punishment of Hell Is Not Eternal

It remains to consider the proofs of the other school.

Augustine says: punishment is, as it were, twofold; there is a transition from snows to the heavy heat of fire, and again from fire to icy clouds.

Here the distress itself is no longer present, nor does he call the burning, cold, or snow itself “punishment.”

These two constitute a twofold punishment. One punishment is snowy cold; the other is fiery heat.

But these are contrary to one another, and, retaining what belongs to them, cannot exist together.

They cannot exist at the same time: just as in a single subject, two discordant punishments cannot coexist.

For while the sufferer endures one, the other ceases in the meantime. Therefore neither will be eternal.

One is felt by the sufferer, but never both at once; and so neither is perpetuated in his experience.

The judgment is similar. Therefore none among all these can be called eternal when it has alternation.

For punishment could truly be called eternal if heat or cold were always present in them.

But now heat is felt, and now cold; and in one instant neither can be present at the same time.

Indeed, if one inquires more physically, where one persists the other punishment must be absent.

For there is no heat of fire in snow, but the cold of snow; nor is the cold of snow felt in fire.

Indeed, when the person punished passes into fire, the heat of fire then punishes him in the fire itself.

### Consolation: Where It Is Shown What Ought Better to Be Maintained

He does not depart from the truth who understands it thus and proceeds in the same subtle and artful way.

I have explained what this means, but I reject this evil assertion: that no punishment in hell is eternal.

For it is said, as it were, in the same way as if one were to say that no one ought to be punished there, or that those who fall there have redemption from it—contrary to Scripture’s intention and the holy sayings of the Fathers.

### “No Punishment in Hell Is Eternal”

A simple person might easily be deceived by this expression, although in its own sense the statement is true.

### Qualification

For if “eternal” is understood from the standpoint of the subject, the false expression then produces a false meaning.

But after “hell,” the sense of the word “eternal” is more concealed, though sound and true.

### The Earlier, Better, and Easier Opinion: That the Punishment of Hell, or That Inflicted in Hell, Is Eternal

The former opinion is held to be truer, since it is true, whereas the other seems intended to nourish heresy.

Therefore I reject the latter; I would not have it commonly professed, lest it perhaps become a ruinous evil for the weak.

It is safer to say what everyone confesses, plainly apparent without any coverings or cloud: glory in heaven is everlasting for the righteous; correspondingly, punishment is to come for the wicked.

For the greater the one offended, the greater must be the punishment undertaken in satisfaction to him.

But God is infinitely great. Therefore his guilty offenders must bear an infinitely great punishment.

God is eternal, and eternal punishment must be borne by those against whom God has been offended through evil deeds.

What I have now said is sufficient: I think I have explained all things well to you.

The muse of Aegidius of Thérouanne does not know how to be brief in matters in which it has entangled itself for teaching.

For whenever it leads everything forth into an open course, as the mind dictates, it thinks itself foolish.

And whenever I read something, proper order is at once sought there, so that everything may be clear and in good sequence.

If I find it otherwise, I often cannot restrain my hand from desiring to supply the rest.

This was the reason why Peter Riga’s work grew into a library through added verses: for it could not be taught with full completeness unless everything lacking there were known.

But now that this has been added, no mutilation disfigures the book, and its full total appears.

This also caused me to add, after your words, these verses of mine written on a similar theme.

Yet, learned Matthew, I would not have these verses prejudice your verses.

You are concise; I am prolix. You proceed subtly; a broad path is sought for me.

I have spoken in my own manner. If I have done so more fully or aptly, let your muse not therefore be vexed with mine.

Let envy cease in this matter. Let there be mutual goodwill between us, and let each in turn say farewell to the other.

Here ends the section on infernal punishments.

[Note: On Aegidius of Paris’s book entitled *Carolinus*, “written for the instruction of the illustrious boy Louis, son of the king of the Franks,” and not yet published in print, see *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XVII (4to, Paris, 1832, Firmin Didot), p. 36.]

ANNO DOMINI MCCVIII. ODO DE SOLIACO, BISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0047]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VII, col. 78)

[Col. 0047A] After the death of Bishop Maurice, if credit is to be given to Ralph, abbot of the monastery of Coggeshall, in his English Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0047C] *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. V, p. 846.], Peter, cantor of the Church of Paris, was elected bishop by the whole clergy and people, with the king’s assent. He refused the honour of the pontificate, lest the fall should be more grievous from a higher rank. This man, commended in the writings of nearly all authors of that age, was born, according to Ralph, at Paris or Reims. As a youth he applied himself to letters; having become learned beyond his years, he publicly taught them in the Parisian Academy with great distinction. But what was the outstanding ornament of his mind was that he was a champion of ancient morals and a most diligent enforcer of stricter discipline. Shining with these virtues, he readily obtained the highly honourable office of precentor of the Church of Paris [Col. 0047B] in that church. Once summoned to the see of Tournai, he humbly declined the call [Note: [Col. 0047C] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 214.].

Finally, after likewise refusing the bishopric of Paris, as Ralph relates, when William, archbishop of Reims, together with the clergy and citizens, asked him to undertake the deanery of that church, he set out for Paris to obtain permission for this from the chapter. He came to Longpont, a Cistercian monastery, where, laid low by a grave illness, he received the habit of the holy religious life and ended his life in a blessed death. When his body, because of building works, was moved from the place where it had been buried, it gave forth a most sweet fragrance. His epitaph is read in the cloister of the monastery of Longpont, where his death is recorded as occurring on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1180; but the epitaph is more recent. William of Nangis, Vincent of Beauvais, Alberic, and the monk of St Marian, authors contemporary with these events, therefore speak more accurately of Peter’s death under the year 1197; or Ralph himself assigns his death to 1198, since he is still mentioned in a charter of Odo dated 1197.

In the Parisian Necrology [Note: [Col. 0048C] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 214.] one reads of him:

[Col. 0048A] “On the seventh day before the Kalends of October died Peter, precentor and deacon, who gave us forty pounds for purchasing revenues.”

He composed various works, which are still preserved in manuscript in different libraries. Only his *Summa*, called *The Abbreviated Word* (*Verbum abbreviatum*), was printed at Mons in 1639. Some maintain that his teaching was blemished by certain faults. Caesarius relates that Peter and his disciples fell into the error of believing that bread consecrated in the Eucharist is not consecrated unless the consecration of wine is also added, and conversely.

Leaving Peter aside, Peter of Blois states (*Epistle* 126) that many aspired to the Parisian see when it fell vacant through Maurice’s death. Among them, certain old men, having for a long time amassed money to purchase the bishopric [Col. 0048B], were not ashamed to bargain for this sacred dignity. But the chapter thwarted their schemes: for they elected a man who was not in the least thinking of it, much less desiring it, Odo of Sully, adorned both by distinction of birth and nobility of character. For by blood he touched three of the most celebrated and noble families of the whole Christian world: namely, those of the kings of France and England and the counts of Champagne. He was the son of Erchembald of Sully, and descended in the direct line from Henry Stephen, count of Champagne, and Adela, daughter of William, king of England. Their other son, Theobald the Great of Champagne, had begotten Adela, wife of Louis VII, king of the Franks. He also had a brother, Henry, archbishop of Bourges.

Peter of Blois, in the cited letter, vividly portrayed Odo’s life and character [Col. 0048C] before his episcopate, relating what he himself had seen; from it we have excerpted these few particulars. Odo undertook the first exercises of the scholarly profession at Paris, but amid the pursuits of the liberal arts heavenly doctrine infused into him better gifts. As his tutor Peter of Verne—who had been a disciple of Peter of Blois—testifies, he seasoned his almsgiving with tears. Having scarcely reached the years of puberty [Col. 0049A], he went to Rome, at the time when Gregory VIII succeeded Urban. There Peter of Blois saw honour shown him by the pope scarcely inferior to that given bishops. Although from childhood he had possessed his body in sanctification and honour, he nevertheless subdued the unruliness of the flesh by vigils, fasts, and disciplines. He distributed to the poor the abundant income that he possessed in England, and from it endowed three worthy scholars.

While occupied in such good works, he was elected by the unanimous agreement of the Parisian chapter, so that he who had already begun to bear fruit as cantor in the Church of Bourges might bring forth still more fruit as bishop at Paris. Peter of Blois expounds these matters more fully, and at the end of his letter adds some points concerning Odo’s royal lineage, by which he was related to the kings of France and England; Peter Gussanville explains these at length in his notes. Yet neither of them calls Odo a regular canon, as the Victorines maintain.

Moreover, Odo is called “elect” in letters of Ameline, abbess of Calais, dated 1196, in which she appointed him—dean, cantor of Paris, and prior of St Martin—as arbitrators in the dispute that had arisen in Maurice’s time between the Church of Paris and the monastery of Calais concerning the liberty and exemption of the monastery of Calais from the Church of Paris and from the jurisdiction of bishop and archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0049D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 214.]. Odo himself still calls himself elect in the judgment delivered by him and the arbitrators between that monastery and the archdeacon in 1197 [Note: [Col. 0049D] Ibid.]. In this same year, the first of his episcopate, he subscribed a charter recording the cession made by Peter of Donjon, knight, to the Church of Paris [Col. 0049C] at Jard, in the court of Adela, queen of the Franks. In the same year he granted the Victorines the annual income of the half-prebends of the Church of Paris [Note: [Col. 0049D] Ibid., p. 292.]. He dedicated the basilica of St Peter at Latigny, renewed after a fire.

In 1198 the Order of the Most Holy Trinity was founded. Its founders, Felix and John, were sent by Innocent III to Odo, bishop of Paris; assisted by Odo’s counsels, John wrote the Rule, which the supreme pontiff approved with certain additions toward the end of that year. In the same year Fulk, a priest of Paris, preached publicly throughout all France by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0049D] *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 520.]. Countless people flocked to his sermons, and the whole country was changed for the better.

At that time there flourished in the Church of Paris [Col. 0049D] a certain wicked custom, or profane festival [Note: [Col. 0050D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 216.], which its foolish inventors called the Feast of Fools. It was celebrated on the Kalends of January. During it innumerable abominations and unspeakable enormities, as Odo himself says, were shamefully and scandalously committed by laypeople—and, horrible to say, by the clerics themselves—in church on the altar steps amid the solemnities of Mass and the divine praises. This inveterate custom had long taken root in many churches; the Fathers and councils had risen sharply against it [Col. 0050A], yet had not been able to abolish it.

Odo therefore undertook to uproot this wicked festival from his church. Relying on the authority of Peter, apostolic legate of the Holy See, he issued a decree in 1198 by which he not only utterly prohibited that abominable festival, but also ordered the feast of the Circumcision of the Lord to be celebrated solemnly in its place. Yet those profane festivities were not removed and antiquated by these decrees; see Du Cange’s *Glossary* under *Kalendae*, for traces of them remained in certain churches almost into the preceding century.

In the same year Odo rendered judgment for the canons of St Victor, who were litigating with Guy, lord of Villiers-le-Bel, concerning the rights to their houses and lands. He also reconciled [Col. 0050B] the disputing monks of Compiègne and the canons of St Clement in that city, together with Hugh, abbot of St Denis, and Peter of Corbeil. In 1199, the second year of his episcopate, he granted land at Marne for holdings and rent, on the condition that the men should come to the bishop’s court at Saint-Cloud.

He also added to the great solemnities of the Church the feast of St Stephen, patron of the Church of Bourges, in whose bosom he had been nourished from earliest youth. On that feast no less was done than on the day of the Circumcision. In the third year of his episcopate, he assigned from the episcopal table stipends to clerics and canons both for the feast of St Stephen and for the Circumcision.

He received a bull from Innocent III on the third day before the Ides of November [Col. 0050C], in the second indiction and the second year of that pontificate, reciting and confirming all the bishop’s privileges in accordance with the practice of his predecessors. The supreme pontiff wrote him Letter 4 of Book I, urging him to use the authority and favour he possessed with Philip Augustus, by prudent counsels, to induce him to receive Ingeborg after rejecting Agnes.

Odo was most observant of the interdict imposed for this reason upon King Philip and his kingdom. He was expelled from his see by the king’s soldiers [Note: [Col. 0050D] *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 529.], compelled to go on foot, and stripped of his horses, baggage, and all his possessions. But after the interdict was lifted, in recompense for the injury inflicted on Odo, the king exempted him in 1200, for his lifetime, from every military expedition and mounted service which bishops were bound to furnish to the king when he went to war.

[Col. 0050D] About that time, when Octavian, apostolic legate, came to the house of St Geneviève for a visit [Note: [Col. 0050D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 280.] and wished to sit at table with them, a disturbance arose which was not quieted until Octavian issued letters declaring that no prejudice to the liberty of the church of St Geneviève would result from this. At the same time Odo transferred the nuns of Champelle, being incorrigible, to the monastery of St Fara, then reformed as it remains today, and substituted in their place twelve secular canons [Col. 0051A].

Summoned by the clergy of the Church of Bourges, from which he had been raised to the episcopal height, to the election of its archbishop, he was present in the same year. Being chosen to name whom he wished as archbishop, he elected William, abbot of Charroux, on 23 November. The fourth year of his pontificate is equated with the year of the Incarnation 1200 in the cartulary of St Evurtius of Orléans.

In 1201, the fourth year of his episcopate, he confirmed the gift made by Guy de Lévis to the brothers of the Wood of Guy, and declared them free of tithes. Together with Peter, archbishop of Sens, in the same year he made two houses out of several diverse houses for lepers: one at Melun for men and the other at Corbeil for women, so that all might live honourably [Note: [Col. 0051D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 220.]. He settled [Col. 0051B] with the abbot of St Magloire concerning tolls; in place of them the abbot assigned him thirty shillings. Thomas of Bruyères ceded to him after his death every right which he possessed in the chapel of Plessis.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of his pontificate, Innocent appointed him, together with the abbot of Latigny, to secure from the clerics of Rebais the obedience and honour due to Anselm, bishop of Meaux. By letters issued in January, he recognized as legitimate the offspring Philip had begotten by Agnes, which had already been approved by the same pope.

The case between Odo and John, abbot of St Geneviève, concerning possession of the parochial right of St Stephen of the Mount—contested with strong party feeling from the beginning of Odo’s episcopate [Note: [Col. 0051D] Peter of Blois, pp. 794 and 795.]—was decided according to the bishop’s wish at the end of that year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January [Col. 0051C] [Note: [Col. 0051D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. V, p. 597.], in the fourth year of Pope Innocent. In March 1201 the delegates informed the Genevièvans of his judgment: it prohibited an interdict on the borough of St Geneviève and prohibited the bishop from instituting or removing the chaplain of the Mount, while confirming all other matters belonging to parochial right.

In the following year, lest lawsuits should revive, the bishop and abbot made a settlement in June [Note: [Col. 0051D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 153.]. Every parochial right remained with the bishop; the abbot ceded to him the chapel of St Geneviève des Ardents, together with a prebend and vicarage in the Church of Paris. Elias, abbot of St Columba of Sens, approved this settlement in the name of the supreme pontiff in January 1202 [Note: [Col. 0051D] Ibid., p. 281.], and the pope himself approved it on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth year of his pontificate. After this settlement was made, Theobald, canon of St Geneviève, received from Odo in June 1202, the fifth year of the episcopate, the care of souls for the parish of the Mount.

In that same year Odo gave the abbot of St Victor authority to remove at pleasure priests from the parishes which they held in the diocese of Paris. He consented to the construction of a chapel in the parish [Col. 0052A] of St Saturninus of Champigny [Note: [Col. 0051D] *Historia Sancti Martini a Campis*, p. 489.]. In 1202, the sixth year of his episcopate, he wrote letters for the foundation of the chapel of Renemoulin, whose chaplain was to be a brother of the Holy Trinity, subject to the bishop’s institution and removal. He established statutes for the chapel in the almshouse of the Queen’s Cross [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. III, p. 73.].

In the same year, the sixth of his episcopate, he granted the countess of Troyes 120 pounds in Provins currency. These had been given as a fief by Theobald, former count of Blois, to Erchembald, former lord of Sully, father of Odo and grandson of Theobald; Erchembald had pledged them to Count Henry, his kinsman, for 550 pounds in Provins and Meaux currency.

In this year Odo had a dispute with the chapter of Saint-Cloud concerning a church which he had built [Col. 0052B] in the place called the Wood of Marne, which he had caused to be cleared. To settle it, the canons submitted themselves to the bishop’s arbitration. A dispute arising between the bishops of Paris and Beauvais over the boundaries of their respective bishoprics at Moinel was settled in November 1202, on the morrow of St Martin’s day, by defining boundaries and setting up markers [Note: [Col. 0052D] Ibid., vol. II, p. 221.]. In the same year he issued a charter concerning the ovens of Adam of Montreuil, canon of Paris, at Champelles [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Historia Sancti Martini a Campis*, p. 198.].

In the following year, by the command of the supreme pontiff, he blessed a cemetery for the lepers of Villepétrouse, in the sixth year of his episcopate. He assigned to the church of Vanves the parishioners of Issy living on the land of St Peter at Latigny, in compensation for the exchange made with the Genevièvans. He exchanged thirteen rent-pennies at Saint-Cloud for the holding of William of Meudon [Col. 0052C]. At the command of Innocent III, he visited the monastery of St Medard in May, where he issued certain statutes in the presence of Robert, abbot of St-Germain-des-Prés, John, abbot of St Geneviève, and many others. He also visited the monastery of St Magloire on the Nativity of St John the Baptist and established several provisions for its good government.

In the same year he regulated the collegiate bodies of canons in his diocese [Note: [Col. 0052D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 221.], and in October enacted decrees concerning the election and residence of the dean and cantor of St Germanus of Auxerre. He made the same provision in the churches of St Marcellus and Saint-Cloud in January, the seventh year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0052D] Ibid., p. 222.]. He approved the foundation of the chapel of Cramoël in 1203, the seventh year of his episcopate. In the same year Adam of Montreuil, canon of Paris, gave him the tithe of Épiry and four Parisian pounds for four permanent matricular priests. Odo established these priests, together with three laymen, out of both his own and the chapter’s resources in 1204, the seventh year of his episcopate, so that the church might be guarded day and night by churchmen against robbers and irreligious persons [Col. 0052D] [Note: [Col. 0052D] Peter of Blois, p. 788.]. In the same year, to increase the matriculars’ income, he ceded to [Col. 0053A] the Parisian chapter the prebend and vicarage which the Genevièvans had granted them after the settlement [Note: [Col. 0053D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, II, p. 223.].

He also conferred many other benefits on the Church of Paris, in consideration of which the chapter assigned him an anniversary observance [Note: [Col. 0053D] Peter of Blois, p. 792.]. For it he himself bestowed sixty Parisian shillings at Brunel, and in 1204, the eighth year of his episcopate, forty Parisian pounds upon the choir clerics for purchasing income-producing property. In the same year he granted the abbey of St Anthony at Paris the same immunities enjoyed by the other Cistercian abbeys [Note: [Col. 0053D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 209.]. In June 1204 he bought the tithe of Soisy from Guipon of Caproisie for thirty Parisian pounds. In the same month he gave the chapel of St Nicholas to the nuns of Foutel for the use [Col. 0053B] of the infirmary.

In the eighth year of his episcopate, he established in his chapel at Saint-Cloud a chaplaincy founded by Guibert and endowed by himself for the anniversary of his brother H., archbishop of Bourges. In the same year he approved the grant of several arpents of land for constructing the presbytery of Gapelle near Paris. He confirmed the founded church of St Honoratus [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., vol. III, p. 76.]. He gave Guy of Caproisie authority to build and endow a church in the village of Loisy and a chapel in the village of Méencourt [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., vol. II, p. 226.]. He received from William of La Ferté the fief at Port-Royal, for establishing nuns there [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., vol. II, p. 225.].

In 1205, the eighth year of his episcopate, he set the residence requirements of the canons of St Marcellus in proper order [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., p. 226.]. He also reformed the college of canons at Champelles, increasing its prebends from eleven to twenty-two to enlarge [Col. 0053C] the service of God [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., p. 228.]. This had already been decreed by the supreme pontiff on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh year of his pontificate. He bought the tithe of Orsay and Maudétour from Burchard of Orsay [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., p. 230.]. He acknowledged to Guy, abbot of Fossés, that no prejudice would arise to the monastery from the bridge which the abbot was permitting to be made in the port called Olins.

In 1203 he secured for the monks of Dilo the parochial right of the valley of Derland. In return they ceded to the bishop what he assigned in 1205, the ninth year of his episcopate, to the church of St Geneviève: one measure of grain, to be received before the feast of All Saints in their grange at Gonesse. In the same year he confirmed legacies made to Parisian churches by Malcion, the king’s chamberlain [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., p. 295.].

[Col. 0053D] Odo should deservedly be regarded as the first founder of the monastery of Port-Royal [Note: [Col. 0054D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, p. 225.]. With Matilda of Garlande, wife of Matthew of Marly, he founded this convent for virgins in 1206 from various donations, especially those made by the Montmorency family. Like the abbey of St Anthony, he entrusted it in the same year to A., abbot of Cîteaux, to be organized [Col. 0054A] [Note: [Col. 0054D] Ibid., vol. II, p. 209.]. The cartulary of Calais records that he granted the right of mortmain for the tithes of Pomponne in April. By his care and effort Geoffrey of Landa, archdeacon of Paris, was summoned in this year to the metropolitan see of Tours.

In December there was such a flood of waters as had nowhere been seen or heard of at Paris. Odo therefore proclaimed a solemn supplication to Blessed Geneviève. When her relics had been carried to the greater basilica, the waters subsided. In the same month Matthew, count of Beaumont, granted Odo the place in which St Denis was said to have been confined in prison. It was called the chapel of St Catherine and was situated not far from the church of St Denis in the Prison, on condition that the count should establish one priest and Odo two there. Odo agreed, erected there a more solemn chapel, and in August 1207, the tenth year of his episcopate, established four chaplains to serve in it [Col. 0054B] [Note: [Col. 0054D] Peter of Blois, p. 792.]. These were the beginnings of the church of St Symphorian.

William of Garlande entrusted Odo in April with the institution of the chaplain of Groussy. In July he attended the elevation of the body of St Benedict at the monastery of Fleury. In August he ratified the chapel built by the monks of St-Germain at Choisy. In the same month he settled a dispute between the chapter of St Germanus of Auxerre and the house of the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0054D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. III, p. 74.].

He was the first to order the feast of St Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, to be celebrated in the Church of Paris, assigning stipends for that purpose, on the morrow of St Bartholomew the Apostle [Col. 0054C] [Note: [Col. 0054D] Peter of Blois, p. 789.]. He granted the chapter the tithes of all newly cleared land, whether to be cleared or already cleared, not assigned to others in the diocese of Paris [Note: [Col. 0054D] Ibid., p. 791.].

Together with Hugh the dean and other judges appointed by the Apostolic See, he ratified on the seventh day before the Kalends of September the settlement made between the monks of St Denis and the nuns of Foutel concerning the priory of Argenteuil. On that same day was at last terminated the lawsuit [Note: [Col. 0054D] *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 72.] between the bishop of Paris and the monks of St Denis concerning the monastery of Argenteuil. By judgment of the judges it remained a priory dependent on St Denis, but subject to the jurisdiction of the bishops and archdeacons. In return, the abbot and monks assigned the bishop six measures of grain at Herblay [Col. 0054D]. Odo assigned one of these to the chapter for the annual *mandatum*, the ceremonial feeding of fifty poor persons [Note: [Col. 0054D] Peter of Blois, p. 790; *Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis*, vol. II, p. 302.].

Recognizing that residence of the chancellor of the Church of Paris and of the university was especially necessary, he drew up in the same year a statute concerning it with the dean and chapter of Paris. In that year also, after the death of the archbishop of Reims [Col. 0055A], Alberic, the other archdeacon of the Church of Paris, was appointed in his place, chiefly through Odo’s efforts. In 1207 King Philip granted Odo that only sixty pounds should be paid as a tallage by the men of the Church of Paris when the regalian rights came into royal hands. He further declared that no bishop thereafter, nor the Church of Paris, should suffer loss from the sum of 240 pounds which, beyond the amount mentioned, had been levied after Maurice’s death.

In the same year Odo made certain further regulations for the church of St Germanus of Drancy [Note: [Col. 0055D] *Historia Sancti Martini a Campis*, p. 297.], and approved a donation made to the monks of St-Germain at Boulogne by Milo, son of Theobald Cocherel. Finally, the pastoral vigilance which he exercised over his entire flock shines most clearly in those excellent statutes [Col. 0055B] which he framed in two synods not only for the instruction of his own diocese but also for the benefit of the whole Church. Purged of many blemishes according to the manuscript codex of St Victor of Paris, they were printed by authority of François de Harlay, archbishop of Paris, in 1674.

How highly Pope Innocent III valued Odo for his outstanding wisdom is sufficiently clear from the many matters of great importance which he referred to his judgment. For example, he made him, together with Michael of Corbeil, canon of Paris, judge of a controversy between Stephen, bishop of Tournai, and Bernard of Lille concerning a prebend of the church of Tournai granted to Bernard by Celestine III. [Col. 0055C] In Book I of the Decretal Letters, chapter *Cum olim*, Innocent likewise appointed him arbitrator between the bishop of Langres and his chapter. To him he directs chapter 5, *Ex parte de corpore vitiatis*, where he says that Michael, a priest who had amputated his genitals to avoid leprosy, may minister at the altar. In the same first book of the Decretals, he also entrusts Odo with investigation and examination concerning the life and character of the bishop-elect of Cambrai.

The letter begins thus:

> “We have such confidence in your discernment that whenever we entrust to you matters known to concern divine honour and ecclesiastical benefit, you will strive to advance them, setting aside favour and fear. In this matter act as our helper, for by the duty of the service laid upon us we ought, according to the prophet, to uproot and to plant whatever in God’s Church must be uprooted and planted.”

There survives in vol. I of the *Anecdota*, col. 669, a letter written to Odo, bishop of Paris, by Adam, abbot of Persigny; it is wholly about love and humility. Toward its end he thanks Odo for charity shown to two poor women during a famine. Also found in vol. I of the *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 1014, is a letter from A., a monk—perhaps the same Adam—to Odo. He reproaches him for imposing tallages on the priests of his diocese and suggests and casts up several other matters against him.

At last, after Odo had fulfilled the duties of an excellent and holy shepherd for about eleven years, while still of mature age [Col. 0056A]—for he was forty or forty-two years old—but worn out by labours, he entered upon the way of all flesh on the third day before the Ides of July, in 1208. Since he had put, as it were, the finishing crown upon the church largely built by his predecessor Maurice and had conferred many benefits upon it, he was buried, as its founder and benefactor, in the middle of the choir, the first among the bishops of Paris, beneath a bronze tomb bearing the image of a bishop, with these verses inscribed around it:

> Whom the honour of the chair adorned, whom ancestral blood,  
> Whom gravity of character: here lies Odo.  
> Rare in the bishop of these times were  
> A sincere mind, clean hand, and chaste flesh.  
> Gentle toward the gentle, clothing for the naked, food for the needy;  
> Bright was his life as a young man, approved as an old.  
> In the twelve-hundred-and-eighth year of Christ,  
> Odo passed away on the thirteenth day of July.

[Col. 0056B] The Necrology of the Church of Paris says of him:

> “On the third day before the Ides of July, Lord Odo of Sully, bishop of Paris, died from the house of St Mary. He gave us a distribution of bread, wine, and meat to be rendered on the feast of Pentecost. He instituted that henceforth the feast of St Stephen should be solemnly celebrated in the Church of Paris alone; and that each cleric who sang the responsory or Alleluia at Mass in triple or quadruple organum should receive six denarii yearly from the prévôté of Paris.  
>   
> He gave also three denarii to the choir clerics, though not to the canons, who attend the nocturns on the Circumcision of the Lord; [Col. 0056C] and two denarii to every boy, to be received from the revenues of the chapter. Moreover, he gave to the clerics of Matins half the offerings of the cross arising on Friday in the Passion of the Lord.  
>   
> He likewise instituted that the feast of Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux should henceforth be celebrated as a half-double in the Church of Paris on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, and for this he assigned the tithe which he had bought at Buch. Furthermore, he gave one measure of grain, to be received yearly from the tithe which he held from the peace of St Denis, for performing the *mandatum* through the hand of the subcantor, who shall provide what is necessary for the *mandatum*; and whatever remains shall belong to the subcantor.  
>   
> He also gave one pallium, two copes, one chasuble with a dalmatic and tunicle of samite, and a prepared alb with prepared stole and maniple and amice [Col. 0056D], and a missal for the service of the high altar, and a psalter for the service of the choir, and a basin with crystal, an ornamented pallium with gold fringe, an ordinal book, sandals and stockings, and an episcopal carpet; moreover, an image of the Blessed Virgin of eight marks of silver, for enclosing the sacred girdle.  
>   
> It was decreed by the chapter that his anniversary should be solemnly celebrated at the high altar when the canons hold the choir. The chapter also granted that whatever priest serves the altar of St Stephen should be equal to the canons in the distribution.”

A splendid commemoration of Odo on this day is also found [Col. 0057A] among contemporary writers. In an old Martyrology he is called a singular benefactor of the church; his diligent vigilance in guarding the flock is readily discerned from his most holy constitutions and other synodal commands on the seven sacraments.

The chronicle of Auxerre says:

> “Odo, bishop of Paris, died, a man zealous for virtue and an outstanding persecutor of vices. Among the other good qualities in which he excelled, this was especially notable: in conferring ecclesiastical benefices he looked not to birth, gift, or entreaties, but to character and learning, and promoted none but worthy men to ecclesiastical dignities. Hence through his efforts William was promoted to the archbishopric of Bourges, Geoffrey to that of Tours, and Alberic to that of Reims [Col. 0057B]. The first had been abbot of Charroux; the other two, archdeacons of Paris, succeeded one another. They were distinguished men, fearing God, [Col. 0058A] and eminent followers of honour and justice. Moreover, through his earnest action and counsel it came about that the lord pope stirred princes and peoples throughout Gaul to war against the treachery of the Albigensian heretics.”

Stephen should be read in Letter 218, where Odo is celebrated for nobility of birth, integrity, the authority of his dignity, and prudence. Peter of Blois’s Letters 160 and 227 to him survive, besides the one mentioned above. From all this it is plainly evident how rashly Rigord, in his book *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus*, and St Anthony, vol. XVII, chapter 9, wrote that Odo differed greatly from his predecessor Maurice in character and life, when all writers of his age rank him among the most celebrated, wisest, and most devout bishops of his time [Col. 0058B]. How aptly Antony Pagi observed in this connection [Note: [Col. 0057B] Vol. IV, p. 715.] that writers sometimes misuse the pen and relate falsehoods!

[Col. 0057]

# SYNODAL CONSTITUTIONS OF ODO OF SULLY, BISHOP OF PARIS

(Mansi, *Councils*, XXII, 675.) In the name of the Holy Trinity begin the prohibitions and commands to be observed by all priests, issued by the venerable Odo, bishop of Paris.

## CHAPTER I. On the manner and time of celebrating the synod

1. The synod is held on the Thursday nearest to St Luke. It is repeated on the third Thursday after the ensuing Easter.

[Col. 0057C]

At the beginning of the synod, before *Come, Creator Spirit* is sung, inquiry shall be made whether the abbots and priests who are bound to attend the synod are present. When this has been done, the bishop shall begin in a loud voice, *Come, Creator Spirit*. When it has ended, the prayers shall be said, preceded by these petitions: *Our Father*; *And lead us not*, etc.; *Let us bless the Father*, etc.; *After childbirth*, etc.; *Rejoice in the Lord*, etc.; *Let there be peace*, etc.; *The Lord be with you*, etc.

Prayer: “Almighty everlasting God, who hast given to thy servants,” etc. “We beseech thee, O Lord, direct our actions,” etc. “O God, who art the author of everlasting salvation,” etc. “Be gracious, we beseech thee, O Lord, to us thy servants [Col. 0057D], through the glorious merits of thy saints whose bodies or relics rest in this present church, so that by their loving intercession we may ever be protected from all adversities.” “Look upon our infirmity, we beseech thee, O Lord,” etc. “O God, from whom are holy desires,” etc. “Through the Lord,” etc.

When the prayers have ended, they shall sit down and a lesson shall be read; after it has been read, a sermon shall be delivered.

## CHAPTER II. On the same matter

[Col. 0058C]

1. When the sermon has ended, the bishop shall dismiss the laypeople, scholars, and other clerics who ought not to attend the synod. This having been done, the synodal commands shall be read.

2. When these have been completed, the additional chapters shall be stated, and at the end it shall be strictly commanded that they be observed by the priests. Then follow prayers for the needs of places and persons.

3. Priests are strictly commanded to enter the synod fasting; for it must be conducted in fasting and prayer.

4. It is strictly commanded that priests enter the synod held in Eastertide clothed in albs and stoles; but that held in September, [Col. 0058D] in surplices only and stoles.

5. Priests are forbidden to bring lawsuits to the synod, or any business which does not concern certain persons; and they are forbidden to have themselves bled when they ought to attend the synod. [Note: [Col. 0057D] That is, someone must not have a vein opened in order to draw blood on a pretext of illness, so that, perhaps conscious of some offence, he may be absent from the synod and not be condemned for contumacy [Col. 0058D].]

6. It is more strictly commanded that all priests, especially those having the care of souls, come to the synod; [Col. 0059A] and if prevented by grave illness or another unavoidable necessity, they shall send their chaplain or a cleric in their place.

7. It is commanded that priests conduct themselves honourably in going to and returning from the synod, and seek respectable lodgings, so that they may behave circumspectly there, lest the estate of clerics be turned into contempt and reproach among the people. We command, by the power of our Lord and God and by obedience, that the highest honour and due reverence be shown to each sacrament of holy Church, especially by priests and clerics; and likewise that laypeople show them, insofar as priests admonish and exhort them to do so.

## CHAPTER III. Chapters concerning baptism
1. Let baptism be celebrated with reverence and honour, [Col. 0059B] and with great care, in this form: “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Let him take the greatest care in distinguishing and pronouncing the words, in which consist the whole efficacy of the sacrament and the salvation of children. And, using the Roman form, priests shall frequently teach that laypeople ought to baptize children in cases of necessity; and after immersion the priests shall perform for the children those rites which are customarily performed after immersion.

2. Let nothing whatever be demanded beforehand for baptism; but afterwards a customary offering may lawfully be requested.

3. Let the fonts be kept locked, on account of sorceries. Likewise let chrism and holy oil be kept under lock and key.

4. Let the priest always carefully question the layperson [Col. 0059C] when he has baptized a child in necessity, as to what he said and what he did. If he finds that the layperson baptized discreetly and in the proper manner, and pronounced the form of words in the Roman rite in full, let him approve what was done; otherwise let him baptize the child in the proper manner. And this is the manner: “Peter, if you have been baptized, I do not baptize you; if you have not been baptized, I baptize you,” etc.

5. No more than three persons shall be admitted to lift the child from the font; for whatever is beyond this is from evil.

## CHAPTER IV. Articles concerning the sacrament of confirmation

1. Let priests frequently exhort the people to have children confirmed.

[Col. 0059D] 2. After baptism, the sacrament of confirmation must be received.

3. If the person to be confirmed is an adult, let him first confess and then be confirmed.

4. Let laypeople often be told not to wait long for the bishop’s arrival in order to confirm children, but to bring them to him, unless they hear that he is nearby; and that children’s names may be changed at confirmation, if they wish or if this seems expedient.

5. Let no priest presume to confirm or consecrate virgins. It belongs to the bishop alone to confirm, consecrate virgins, dedicate churches, and confer orders.

## CHAPTER V. Articles concerning the sacrament of the altar

[Col. 0060A]

1. Let the greatest reverence and honour be shown to holy altars, especially where the most holy body of the Lord is reserved and Mass is celebrated.

2. Let altar-cloths and vestments be frequently washed, in reverence for the presence of our Saviour and of the whole heavenly court, which is present with him whenever Mass is celebrated.

3. Let the chalices from which the sick communicate be ornamented and kept clean, so that the sick may communicate more devoutly.

4. Let the small vessels of wine and water used in the ministry of the altar be kept clean and unbroken; likewise the vessels of chrism and holy oil.

[Col. 0060B] 5. Let priests not permit deacons—upon those who do not observe this the bishop threatens penalties—to carry the most holy body of the Lord to the sick, except in necessity when the priest is absent. Rather, let the priest always carry it with great reverence and composure in a well-closed ivory pyx, lest it fall, with a lamp going before, while they sing the seven penitential psalms with the litany for the sick, both on the way there and on the return.

[Note: [Col. 0059] He means the priest together with an accompanying cleric and all others who attend.]

If the journey is long, let them add the fifteen psalms and other prayers. Thus they discharge their duty to the sick and invite those who hear them to show God reverence, honour, and prayer.

6. Let laypeople frequently be admonished that, wherever [Col. 0060C] they see the body of the Lord being carried, they are immediately to bend the knee as before their Lord and Creator and, with hands joined, pray until it has passed.

7. Let the most holy body of the Lord be kept in the more beautiful part of the altar, with the greatest diligence, decorum, and under lock and key.

8. Let no cleric be permitted to serve at an improperly adorned altar [perhaps: unless the prescribed custom is observed] in the principal church, except in a surplice or closed cope.

9. Let no one dare celebrate Mass twice in one day, or with a double introit, except in great necessity.

10. Let no one presume, without some necessity, [Col. 0060D] to celebrate Mass before saying canonical Matins and Prime.

11. At the Hours of the Blessed Virgin the third verse shall always be said at the chapter, as H. observes: “Holy Mary, Mother of grace”; and they shall be sung in church with musical notation and devotion, or in governing or guarding [reading uncertain].

## CHAPTER VI. Articles concerning confession

1. Let priests use the greatest care and caution concerning confession: namely, let them inquire diligently into sins—ordinary sins individually, unusual sins only indirectly through some circumstance—yet in such a way that the sins provide matter for confession.

2. For hearing confessions priests shall choose for themselves a more public [variant: prominent] place in the church, [Col. 0061A] so that they may ordinarily be seen by everyone; and let no one receive confessions in concealed places or outside the church, except in great necessity or illness.

3. In confession the priest shall keep a humble countenance and his eyes lowered to the ground. He shall not look at the face of the penitent, especially of a woman, for the sake of due propriety. Let him patiently hear what is said in a spirit of gentleness, and by every means in his power persuade the penitent to confess completely; otherwise, let him tell the penitent that the confession is of no avail.

4. One who commits incest, deflowers a virgin, or is a murderer—

Seek the pontiff; seek the pope, if you have set a fire.

A sacrilegious person, one who strikes his father, or a Sodomite—

If you have struck a cleric or have been a Simonist.

[Col. 0061B] 5. Let priests reserve greater cases in confession for greater authorities: homicide, sacrilege, sins against nature, incest and the seduction of virgins, laying hands upon parents, broken vows, and the like.

6. There are three matters in which no one has power to absolve, except the lord pope or his vicar, unless in necessity: namely, laying hands upon clerics or any religious persons, and arson, through which sentence they are called Simonists. Nevertheless, those guilty of such matters are to be referred to the bishop.

7. In doubtful cases the confessor shall always consult the bishop or wise men, unless necessity prevents this. [Col. 0061C] Having been made certain by their counsel, he may more safely loose or bind, especially his own prelates.

8. Having heard the confession, the confessor shall always ask the penitent whether he wishes to abstain from every mortal sin. Otherwise he shall not absolve him or impose penance upon him, lest he thereby become presumptuous; rather, let him exhort him again to do whatever good he can, that God may enlighten his heart unto repentance.

9. In imposing light penances, priests shall take care. The character of the penance must correspond to the gravity of the fault and the capacity of the penitent; otherwise what is lacking will be required from them.

10. From theft, robbery, and Simon’s usury—

Alms are made by them from possessions thus acquired.

[Col. 0061D] 11. In matters of theft, robbery, usury, and fraud, priests shall take great care: they shall not impose other penances, namely masses, almsgiving, and the like, before restitution has been made; for such a sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored.

12. Let no one celebrate the masses which he has imposed, whether a thirty-day series or an annual observance; and much less a three-year or five-year series.

13. Let priests frequently exhort people to confession, and especially from the beginning of Lent earnestly command them generally to come to confession.

14. In confession confessors shall take care not to inquire [Col. 0062A] into the names of persons with whom penitents have sinned, but only into the circumstances and kinds of sin. If the penitent identifies someone, the confessor shall rebuke him and keep the matter secret, as he does the penitent’s sin.

15. Let no one dare, through anger, hatred, or even fear of death, to disclose a confession to anyone by sign or word, whether generally or specifically, as by saying: “I know what sort of people you are.” If he discloses it, he must be degraded without mercy.

16. Let all command the appointed fasts to be observed: the fast of Lent, Ember Days, vigils—unless a grave and reasonable cause requires otherwise—and Fridays; for they are bound by obligation to observe such fasts.

## CHAPTER VII. Articles concerning marriage

[Col. 0062B]

1. Let marriage be celebrated with honour and reverence, not with laughter and jesting; nor shall it be treated with contempt, even if it is a second or third marriage. Before it is celebrated, on three Sundays or three feast days equally spaced apart, as though by three proclamations, the priest shall inquire of the people, under pain of excommunication, concerning the lawful eligibility of the bridegroom and bride who are to be joined; and this shall be done before the pledge is given for contracting marriage. Before these three proclamations no one shall dare in any way to celebrate marriages.

2. Under excommunication, let them strictly forbid laypeople to practise sorcery. Let sorcerers also, and those concealing consanguinity and other impediments to marriage—[Col. 0062C] a vow, orders, consanguinity, affinity, disparity of worship, spiritual kinship, which excludes only four persons from marriage: the godfather, godmother, godchild, and the godchild’s spiritual brother and sister, namely the godparent’s son or daughter—be publicly excommunicated.

[Supplement: let them be publicly excommunicated.]

3. Let no priest dare to complete a marriage in a doubtful case without consulting the bishop; rather, whenever necessary, he shall always refer every doubt concerning marriage to him.

4. Under pain of suspension, it is strictly forbidden that any priest or chaplain demand anything before the nuptial blessing, whether for giving testimony or celebrating the marriage, on the pretext of the dishes owed for weddings. After [Col. 0062D] the marriage has been celebrated, however, let him receive and, if necessary, demand his dishes, as is customary.

5. Let the priest publicly forbid in church, under excommunication, either spouse to enter religion or be received into it except through the bishop.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the sacrament of extreme unction

[Note: [Col. 0061D] See the Council of Nantes, chapter 4.]

1. Let holy oil be carried to the sick with reverence; and let priests anoint them with great honour and with the solemn prayers appointed for this purpose. Let nothing whatsoever be demanded for it, whether from poor or rich; but if anything is freely given, let it be freely received.

2. Let priests exhort [Col. 0063A] the people to the sacrament of extreme unction—not only the rich and elderly, but all poor and young people who have reached the age of discretion, especially those fourteen years old and above—and generally all, that they may present themselves prepared when necessary.

3. Let them frequently teach the people that this sacrament may lawfully be repeated and received often, namely in every grave illness in which there is fear of death; and that one who has recovered from illness may lawfully return to marital relations after receiving it.

4. Let every parish priest possess the book called the *Manual*, containing the order of service for extreme unction, catechism, baptism, and the like.

5. Let each possess the Penitential Canons and [Col. 0063B] the ordinary office of the Church, according to the use and manner observed in the principal church.

6. Let priests be warned not to make their wills through a layperson; and let them frequently forbid laypeople to make their own wills without the presence of a priest. Let the bishop say that they are not to make them “in one” [passage corrupt and something is missing].

[Note: [Col. 0063D] This passage is corrupt, and something is missing.]

Here begin the common synodal injunctions.

1. Priests are commanded to write all the revenues and possessions of the church in their missals; and priests and parishioners are altogether forbidden to alienate from the church anything belonging to churches or priests, except by counsel of the bishop.

2. It is strictly forbidden that the burial of a body be delayed because of the *interragium* [a burial due]; [Col. 0063C] let customary payments be demanded after burial. We say the same concerning similar matters.

3. Whoever rebuilds in a cemetery shall be excommunicated, if the principal part of the house has collapsed by itself.

4. A person who is to be excommunicated shall be summoned on three successive days; unless he submits himself to justice and gives assurance that he will appear on the day assigned him, and informs his opponent of that day, let him be excommunicated. One excommunicated shall in no way be absolved except by a superior authority, save at the point of death; and even then only upon giving security that he will submit to the judgment of the Church.

5. In making citations, priests may trust those who have given assurance; but in pronouncing excommunications, they shall not trust without letters. Let them pronounce [Col. 0063D] sentences boldly and enforce sentences once pronounced strictly, [the Latin then reads, with defective syntax: “sooner than the sentences fail”], sparing no one through fear or favour, and not regard them as absolved unless this has been clearly established for them.

6. Women who die in childbirth shall be cut open if the child is believed to be alive, provided that their death is clearly established.

7. When priests hear of the death of their parishioners, let them immediately absolve them with the psalms for the dead and the collect.

8. It is likewise forbidden to place the presentation of churches in the hands of abbots or any patrons, but rather in the hand of the bishop or their own prelate.
