[Col. 0064A] 9. Let preachers not be permitted to celebrate upon chests, ring bells through the streets, speak in churches, or display relics; but let them merely carry what is to be carried, and let priests speak on their behalf.

10. Let priests always exhort the people to recite the Lord’s Prayer, the “I believe in God,” and the salutation of the Blessed Virgin.

11. Let them always warn the people, especially women, not to make vows except with great deliberation, their husbands’ assent, and priests’ counsel.

12. Let no priest or chaplain keep a woman in his house for any reason unless she is his mother or sister, or one concerning whom the bishop judges [Col. 0064B] that all suspicion of impropriety is absent.

13. All priests are entirely forbidden to play dice, attend entertainments, participate in dances, enter taverns for drinking, enter other people’s houses without a garment—namely a cope, cloak, or surplice—and without a clerical or lay companion, or wander through streets and squares. They are also entirely forbidden to have winged copes or disorderly garments.

14. Let no cleric or religious receive a tithe from the hand of a layperson except through the hand of the bishop.

15. Let no cleric act as surety for a Jew or moneylender, nor in any way pledge church ornaments or books to a Jew.

16. Let no one be received to preach unless he is [Col. 0064C] an authorized person or has been sent by the bishop or archdeacon.

17. Let no cleric take an oath before he has been presented to the bishop.

18. Let laypeople frequently be warned not to withhold tithes, which they retain at the peril of their souls.

19. No cleric may retain for himself tithes possessed by hereditary right; but by authority of the bishop clerics may receive the fruits, provided that they always cultivate them and that they revert to the church.

20. On the Sunday preceding the synod, priests who have no chaplains in their parishes shall always inquire publicly in church whether anyone in the parish is sick; and on the following third day they shall visit those who are sick, even if not requested, and do whatever concerns the salvation of souls, lest the delay they will make at the synod become an occasion of danger. Nevertheless, they shall also provide for their welfare through the provision customarily made by neighbouring chaplains who remain behind and by their own deacons.

21. On the eighth day priests shall always renew the sacraments at the font with blessed oil and chrism, and the holy Eucharist, lest through age any should be led into irreverence or error.

22. If through negligence, after the Canon has been recited [Col. 0065A] and the consecration completed, neither wine nor water is found in the chalice, both must immediately be poured in, and the priest shall repeat the consecration from that point in the Canon: “Likewise, after he had supped” (Luke 22), to the end; provided, however, that he omits the two crosses which he made separately over the bread. But if consecration is performed with plain wine or with water without wine, the wine is regarded as sacramental, but the water is not; therefore negligence in placing water without wine is the graver matter and must be corrected by a greater penance.

23. If any of the Lord’s blood falls upon the corporal, that corporal must be cut up and kept in the place for relics; if the altar-pall is stained by it, that part must be cut off and preserved [Col. 0065B] as a relic. If it runs upon a mitre, chasuble, or alb, the same is to be done. If it falls upon any other garment, that part must be burned and the ashes placed in the sacrarium. If it falls upon the ground, the ground must be licked; the place itself—whether stone, wood, or earth—must be wiped and scraped, and the dust placed in the sacrarium.

24. Moreover, if a fly, spider, or similar thing falls into the blood itself, because it cannot sometimes be consumed without vomiting and danger to the body, it must be burned in fire, and then the Lord’s blood is to be consumed. Yet that which fell into it must first be steeped in wine in the chalice and, as cautiously as possible, washed; then it must be burned over the piscina, and the priest shall consume that washing. But if anything from the body [Col. 0065C] of the Lord falls upon any other garment, it shall not be cut off, but washed with wine, and the minister shall consume that wine. If what was first given [perhaps: if it] is rejected, let it be recovered as carefully as possible and consumed mixed with wine in the chalice; but it cannot be consumed whole, because it was expelled from another’s mouth.

25. The person guilty of this negligence, and anyone sharing in his fault, shall undergo suitable discipline. But if it falls upon wood or stone, the above-mentioned procedure for the Lord’s blood is to be observed.

26. Priests are forbidden to hurry too early to Paris on the occasion of the synod, and to linger long in visiting and feasting, whether on the journey or in the city. For some set out on the preceding Sunday, or early Monday morning, and delay until the following Sunday; and great danger threatens the salvation of souls.

27. It is strictly commanded that every priest have one hand-towel at the celebration of Mass, for cleanliness of the vestments around the altar.

28. Priests are commanded that, when in the Canon of the Mass they begin, “Who, on the day before,” while holding the host, they shall not at once raise it too high so that it can be seen by all the people; rather, they shall hold it, as it were, before the breast until they have said, “This is my body” (Matthew 26). Then they shall elevate it so that all may see it. After such reception of both the body [Col. 0066A] and the blood, and of unmixed wine, they shall refrain for some time from spitting; if they cannot refrain, they shall do so gently and properly into the piscina. Red wine should preferably be served in the chalice, because white wine resembles water.

29. Priests are strictly forbidden to keep with them children whom they have begotten after receiving holy orders, because of scandal; and they are altogether forbidden to keep chessboards, dice, or gaming pieces in their houses.

30. Priests are strictly forbidden to accept leaseholds or farming contracts except concerning tithes, since that would be a form of trade; and they shall have no pieces in their cloaks except of blue or black colour.

31. Likewise priests are commanded to leave to their churches alone immovable property acquired from church goods [Col. 0066B] (for by law they cannot do otherwise); but from their movable goods let them make a reasonable bequest.

32. Priests are also commanded frequently, on Sundays and other feast days, to set forth faithfully to the people in some part of the sermon the Creed of faith; carefully distinguish for them the articles of faith; and, as far as they are able, confirm the people in each of them by authorities and arguments from Holy Scripture, because of heretics.

33. Know that all those who have given or received a pledge to conceal marriages have been excommunicated in synod; and let this excommunication be recited in the parishes by every priest.

34. Priests are forbidden to have chaplains [Col. 0066C] wearing sleeved copes, just as those incumbents themselves ought not to have them. For all holders of churches are commanded to present themselves for ordination at each season of orders; and this is understood in the oath which they have taken.

35. Priests are likewise commanded most strictly, under pain of a heavy penalty, to observe the synodal injunctions written in their booklets. For some, although three years have already elapsed since they received the said booklets, are so negligent that they still have neither an ivory pyx nor a tabernacle in which the body of the Lord may be reserved with honour, nor fonts under lock and key, nor chrism or oil in any container.

[Col. 0066D] 36. Let priests forbid dancing, especially in three places: churches, cemeteries, and processions.

37. On every Sunday, especially during the vintage season, let priests frequently forbid, under excommunication, any Christian to keep in his possession a measure of vintage-wine which Jews have in any way trodden, because of the horrible defilement which they commit in contempt of the sacrament of the altar. If any remains, let it be given to pigs or spread out for use as manure.

38. Let them frequently forbid under excommunication butchers to permit Jews to cut up their meat, unless the Jews retain the whole of it.

39. Priests are likewise strictly commanded never to give hosts, [Col. 0067A] even unconsecrated ones, to children; and they are forbidden to celebrate without stockings.

40. Priests are likewise strictly forbidden to carry a pointed knife, nor may their clerics do so.

41. Priests are likewise strictly forbidden to permit unknown or unlearned persons to preach, even outside church, whether in roads, squares, or other places in their parish. On Sundays priests shall frequently admonish, and even forbid under excommunication, their parishioners to hear such persons, because of the dangers of heresies and errors which they sow.

42. Priests are likewise strictly commanded to exhort their male and female parishioners to provide for the Church of Paris, which greatly needs [Col. 0067B] albs, stoles, towels, and similar things.

43. Let them likewise diligently and continually exhort their parishioners to arm themselves against the Albigensian heretics; and they shall again have the same indulgence which they had previously.

44. Under pain of excommunication, priests shall likewise warn all who have taken the cross but have not pursued their vow that they are to propose resuming their cross and bear it.

45. All priests are likewise commanded to excommunicate generally all those who have entered into conspiracies against their priests or their churches.

46. Priests are likewise commanded that whenever anyone [Col. 0067C] confesses to them that he has pledged himself to a woman to contract marriage with her, and after the pledge has carnally known her, they shall not give him permission to contract with another woman, because the subsequent carnal union with the woman to whom he gave his pledge confirmed the marriage.

47. Priests are likewise strictly commanded, under excommunication, not to join or bless anyone in clandestine marriage.

48. Let all those who cause themselves to be clandestinely joined or blessed be excommunicated, along with all priests who presume to participate.

49. Priests are likewise commanded that whenever there is doubt about when certain appointed fasts or processions ought to be held, as on the feast of Saint Mark, they shall ask the local dean and not presume to perform them without his counsel.

[Col. 0067D]

50. Priests are likewise commanded that when women [Col. 0068A] come for purification after childbirth, they give them only blessed bread and in no way administer the body of the Lord, unless they expressly request it and have first confessed.

51. In confessions and preaching, priests shall likewise exhort their parishioners to visit the Church of Paris on pilgrimage at least once a year.

52. All priests are strictly commanded to make a special commemoration for the lord king whenever they are able.

53. Priests are likewise commanded each to write down the names of their parishioners who are confreres of the Church of Paris, and also to record the amount for which each is a confrere.

[Col. 0068B] 54. Priests are likewise commanded not to receive chaplains without the knowledge of the bishop or archdeacon.

55. Priests are likewise commanded to demand nothing from their parishioners because they give testimony for them when they are to contract marriage.

56. It is likewise strictly forbidden for deacons in any way to hear confessions, except in the most urgent necessity; for they do not possess the keys and cannot absolve.

57. We command all deans henceforth to inquire into and put in writing the names of all priests who die in their deaneries, and bring them to be read at the synod, that we may pray [Col. 0068C] for them. Let every priest be admonished to perform a special service; for they ought most willingly to do this, since, when they die, the same will be done for them.

58. All priests are likewise strictly commanded to excommunicate three times yearly—at Easter, at the Nativity of the Lord, and on the feast of the Church—all those who knowingly conceal the fiefs of Paris, and all those who know anything concerning this unless they disclose it to the bishop of Paris or his representative.

59. We likewise command every priest that annually, namely on the day after Holy Trinity, the anniversary of all confreres of Blessed Mary be celebrated throughout the whole diocese of Paris.

60. We command that people be warned not to lend wheels to Jews, [Col. 0068D] according to what has been prescribed; otherwise let them be compelled by excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] Binius wrongly assigned these constitutions to the pontificate of Gregory VIII, who died in 1187, since Odo was not bishop of Paris until at least nine years later. He succeeded Maurice, who did not die until 1196. Gabriel Cossart.]

[Col. 0069]

# STATUTES AND PIOUS DONATIONS OF ODO, BISHOP OF PARIS

(From the Appendix to the Works of Peter of Blois, edited by Pierre de Goussainville, p. 778 ff., passim; and *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, Documents, p. 79 ff., 1227.)

## I. Charter of Odo by which he granted to the Church of Saint Victor of Paris the annual revenues of the half-prebends of the Church of Paris

(From the manuscript annals of Saint Victor, under the year 1197.)

[Col. 0069A]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all whom this present writing shall reach, eternal salvation in the Lord.

The more the venerable Church of Saint Victor sweetly diffuses abroad in every direction the purity of its reputation and the fragrance of its good repute—within which the fervour of regular observance does not grow lukewarm, but by God’s grace receives day by day ever more pleasing increase—the more ought we to embrace with abundant charity the brethren there devoted to divine service and to attend with special concern to their [Col. 0069B] tranquillity and welfare.

Although the annual revenues of vacant prebends in the Church of Paris had formerly been granted to that church by the pious generosity of our predecessors, the bishops of Paris, and confirmed by authentic instruments, it nevertheless often happened that, when a half-prebend was vacant and the person who had been a half-canon became a full canon, the Church of Saint Victor was deprived. Therefore, considering that the same church was being deprived without reasonable cause of the benefit granted to it, and understanding that a half-prebend becomes vacant whenever a half-canon is invested with a full prebend—especially since, according to the custom of the Church of Paris, he ought not to hold both a half and a full prebend together, and a full prebend cannot be divided in half—we, after fuller deliberation on this matter and consultation with prudent men, have granted, with the concurrence and assent of the chapter of Paris, to the aforesaid Church of Saint Victor that whenever a full prebend is conferred by us or our successors upon a half-canon, the Church of Saint Victor shall in the first year receive without diminution the annual benefit of the half-prebend, just as it is accustomed to receive the annual revenues of full prebends.

That the aforesaid grant may therefore obtain perpetual force and firmness, we have caused it to be recorded in this present writing, fortified by the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1197, in the first year of our pontificate.

## II. Letter of Odo, bishop of Paris, for abolishing the Feast of Fools and restoring the solemnity of the Circumcision of the Lord

(Year 1198.)

[From the cartulary of the most illustrious lord Jean-Baptiste de Contes, dean of the Church of Paris, charter 156.]

[Col. 0070A]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop; H., dean; R., cantor; MAURICE, HEIMERIC, and ODO, archdeacons; GALO, subcantor; Master PETER, chancellor; and Master PETER OF CORBEIL, canon of Paris, to all whom this present writing shall reach: eternal salvation in the Lord.

When Lord Peter, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church with the title of Saint [Col. 0070B] Mary in Via Lata, was exercising the office of legate in the regions of Gaul, he delivered to us his mandate concerning the correction of certain matters which he had heard required correction in the Church of Paris, in the following form:

“To the venerable father in Christ and most dear friend Odo, by the grace of God bishop, and to his beloved H., dean; R., cantor; Maurice, Hameric, and Odo, archdeacons; G., subcantor; Master P., chancellor; and Master P. of Corbeil, canon of Paris: P., by divine mercy cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

“The more the noble Church of Paris, established in the head city of the kingdom and in so celebrated a city, from whose fullness all receive, [Col. 0070C] spreads purer rays in every direction and is more famously praised throughout the world, the more abundant prudence and diligence must be applied to ordering the state of that Church and utterly uprooting what has there grown up under the pretext of corrupt custom. Thus, from the fountain from which streams of learning flow to nearly every region of the world, the cup of life and moral propriety may be tasted; and where the mastery of letters flourishes, there the elegance of conduct may shine forth as an example to others.

“Indeed, while carrying out the office of legate in the regions of Gaul, at the very beginning of our visitation we came to that Church and learned from the trustworthy report of very many persons that on the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision so many enormities and shameful acts were customarily [Col. 0071A] committed in that church that the holy place, in which the glorious Virgin chose a dwelling pleasing to herself, was often polluted not only by the foulness of words but even by the shedding of blood. This invention of so ruinous a recklessness had gained such strength that the most sacred day upon which the Redeemer of the world willed to be circumcised was customarily, and not without reason, generally called the Feast of Fools.

“Therefore, considering that in these days of calamity and mourning, which the disturbance of times and lands—and especially the desolation of the Eastern land—has imbued with a more grievous bitterness, we ought rather to devote ourselves to prayers and tears than to serve such vanities and indecencies; and desiring also to exclude from the sanctuary of the Lord every filth and occasion of defilement, by the authority of the legation which we exercise [Col. 0071B] we most strictly forbid that henceforth, in your church, anything be attempted by anyone on the aforesaid solemnity that does not befit the clerical profession or appears to diminish reverence for God. Under threat of anathema, we forbid that the same solemnity henceforth be observed with its customary enormities.

“By that same authority we command you strictly, in this matter having before your eyes the fear of God and moral propriety alone, to arrange the aforesaid solemnity—without delay or pretext—and carefully cut away whatever you see must be cut away, so that nothing contrary to propriety may be found concerning the worship of the Church or the condition of clerics. But if anyone [Col. 0071C] should presume, through any rashness, to act contrary to the form established for this matter by you, relying on our authority suspend him from office and benefice and, moreover, from entry into choir and chapter; and regard him as suspended until he gives fitting satisfaction for his presumption, having announced the suspension to the chapter.

“Furthermore, we command that all those be bound by the same sentence who, on the pretext of this prohibition or of your constitution, maliciously withdraw themselves from the service of the Church on the vigil or day of the same solemnity. If all of you cannot be present to carry these things out, or if, God forbid, any one or more of you present should show yourselves discordant concerning them, you, brother bishop, together with the dean [Col. 0071D] and the rest of those named above, shall take care promptly to fulfil and execute what we enjoin upon you.”

Accordingly, having learned and recognized that the aforesaid solemnity of the Lord’s Circumcision was being celebrated with insufficient regularity, and wishing to restore to canonical order what is known rashly to have arisen to the scandal of the Church, we, by authority of the aforesaid legate and after mature deliberation, have arranged the said solemnity as follows. On the vigil of the feast, at Vespers, the bells shall be rung in proper order, as for a simple double feast. The cantor shall properly prepare the roster in every respect; we forbid the performance of rhymes, dramatic characters, and torchlights except only upon iron wheels, and upon a feather, if the person who is to render up the cope wishes it. We also decree that the lord of the feast shall not be brought to the church in procession [Col. 0072A] or with singing, nor be led back from the church to his house. In choir, however, he shall put on his cope, with two subdeacon canons attending him; and, holding the cantor’s staff, before Vespers begins he shall commence the prose, “Let us rejoice in gladness” (*Laetemur gaudiis*). When this has ended, the bishop, if present, or the dean in the bishop’s absence, or the bishop’s chaplain if both are absent, shall begin Vespers, to be celebrated duly and solemnly. This proviso is added: the Responsory and *Benedicamus* may be sung in triple or quadruple form, or with organ; otherwise the Responsory shall be sung by four subdeacons wearing silk copes. Compline shall be sung duly and solemnly.

After a single peal has been rung before Matins, as at the highest solemnities, Matins [Col. 0072B] shall be begun by the bishop, dean, or chaplain, and completed in due order. This is added: the third and sixth Responsories shall be sung with organ, or in triple or quadruple form. The cantor shall arrange the Responsories of Matins. Mass likewise, together with the other Hours, shall be celebrated in proper order by one of the aforesaid persons. The Epistle with its farce shall be said first by two persons in silk copes and afterwards by the subdeacon; moreover, the Responsory shall be read through, while the Alleluia shall be sung in triple or quadruple form, or with organ, by persons in silk copes; and four shall proceed in the Mass. The following Vespers shall begin, like the former, with “Let us rejoice in gladness”; and *Laetabundus* shall be sung in place of the hymn. *Deposuit* shall be said in its place five times [Col. 0072C] at most; and, if the staff has been taken, after the *Te Deum laudamus* has ended, Vespers shall be completed by the person by whom they were begun. The final Compline likewise shall be said duly.

Throughout the whole feast, at all the Hours, canons and clerics shall conduct themselves in their stalls duly and according to rule. We therefore forbid anyone to presume to disturb this arrangement; and whoever refuses to observe it shall incur the sentence expressed in the foregoing authenticated instrument of the lord cardinal. In order that this ordinance may endure more firmly in future, we have caused it to be commended to writing in the present instrument, secured by the impression of our seals.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1199.

### III. Other letters of the same Odo, bishop of Paris, concerning the solemnity of the Lord’s Circumcision and Saint Stephen. (1199.)

[From the Great Pastoral of Paris.]

[Col. 0072D]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all whom the present document shall reach: greeting in the Lord.

Although unworthy, we have been established by divine dispensation in the office of this prelacy so that we may apply ourselves more zealously to the enlargement of divine worship and root out whatever we know to have arisen irregularly in the house of the Lord contrary to ecclesiastical propriety. Therefore, since the venerable solemnity of the Lord’s Circumcision was formerly celebrated with insufficient regularity in the Church of Paris [Col. 0073A], and under the pretext of an evil custom had been reduced to the ruinous condition of such disorder that abominable excesses and shameful deeds commonly occurred on that very day, at last, when Lord Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, was then exercising the office of legate in our regions and had learned of the aforesaid transgressions and enormities, he wished that this solemnity should be ordered by us and certain of the senior members of our Church.

Accordingly, responding with devotion to the command of the aforesaid cardinal together with those persons, and desiring to remove from the sanctuary of the Lord every occasion of disorder, we took care to regulate the said feast of the Circumcision—in which both our actions and our lips ought to be circumcised—and to cut away what we believed [Col. 0073B] required cutting away, as is more fully contained in the authenticated instrument composed on this matter and secured by our seals and those of the aforesaid persons. Since, moreover, the feast of the blessed protomartyr Stephen was subject to almost the same evil of disorder and recklessness, and was not customarily celebrated in the Church of Paris with the solemnity that was fitting and that the martyr’s merits required, we—who are especially indebted to that martyr, because we had him as patron in the Church of Bourges, in whose bosom we were nurtured from earliest youth—have decreed, with the will and assent of our beloved Hugh, dean, and the chapter of Paris, to restore that feast to regular observance and to number it among the great solemnities of the Church. We decree that on that feast [Col. 0073C] as much solemn celebration shall take place as is customarily held on the other annual feasts.

Further, wishing that these ordinances should bring not only spiritual benefit but also temporal advantage to the servants of the same Church, as a token of devotion and in reverence for the protomartyr himself, we graciously grant that, in perpetuity, there shall be received from our provostship of Paris [Col. 0073D]: six Parisian denarii by each canon of Paris or cleric serving at the high altar who attends Matins on the Nativity of Saint Stephen; four denarii by each non-canonical choir cleric; two denarii by each choirboy; and six Parisian denarii by each cleric who sings the Responsory or Alleluia at Mass with organ, in triple, or in quadruple form.

On the feast of the Circumcision, we give and grant in perpetuity that each non-canonical choir cleric attending Matins shall receive three Parisian denarii, and each choirboy two denarii, annually from the revenues of the chapter of Paris; and we bind our successors in perpetuity to pay the aforesaid revenues. Nevertheless, should these solemnities by chance be restored to their former enormity or disorder—which God forbid—both we and our successors would be wholly released from payment of those revenues.

Therefore, in order that what has been established for the increase of divine worship may remain valid with perpetual force, we have ordered the present instrument [Col. 0074A] to be made for greater security and fortified with the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1199, the third year of our pontificate.

### IV. King Philip exempts Bishop Odo from the burdens of war. (1200.)

[From the Great Pastoral.]

PHILIP, by the grace of God king of the Franks. Let all present and future persons know that, because of the special affection which we bear toward our dearest kinsman and faithful servant Odo, bishop of Paris, and also on account of a certain insult inflicted upon him by our serjeants [Col. 0074B]—of which, when we heard it, we were greatly grieved—we wholly absolve and quit him personally, for as long as he lives, from every military expedition and mounted service, both in our own time and in that of our successors, the kings of France. Our due claim to the soldiers whom the said bishop is bound to send into our service is reserved. In order that this may be ratified and firm, we have caused the present charter to be confirmed by the protection of our seal and by the character of the royal name written below. Done at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1200, the twenty-first year of our reign, in the presence in our palace of those whose names and signs are appended: there being no seneschal; the sign of Guy the butler; the sign of Matthew the chamberlain; the sign of Drogo the constable. Given while the chancellery was vacant. [Col. 0074C]

### V. King Philip confirms the liberty of the Paris cloister. (1200.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, amen. Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks. Let the whole body of present and future persons know that we hold valid, approve, and confirm to the Church and cloister of Paris the liberty and immunity which that church and cloister possessed in the times of our predecessors and in our own time. Thus, whoever infringes the liberty or immunity of the aforesaid church and cloister shall make amends to the Church of Paris in one hundred pounds [Col. 0074D] of Parisian money; or, if he cannot pay one hundred pounds, we shall deliver to that church the person who committed the offence, provided he can be found. Otherwise, we shall hand over and expose for seizure, without contradiction, to the same church, all the possessions of him who committed the offence, with the services and customs preserved which lands owe to the lords in whose fiefs they are and from whom they are held, until satisfaction has been made to the church. Done at Paris, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1200, the twenty-first year of our reign; there being no seneschal; the sign of Guy the butler; the sign of Matthew the chamberlain; the sign of Drogo the constable. Given while the chancellery was vacant.

### VI. Odo, bishop of Paris, confirms Guy of Levis’s gift to the abbey of La Roche. (1201.)

[Col. 0075A]

Odo, bishop of Paris, to all whom these present letters shall reach: greeting in the Lord.

Let all know that Guy of Levis, appearing before us, with the praise and consent of his wife Guiburge, for the salvation of his soul, gave and granted in perpetual alms to God and the brethren of Nemus Guidonis [Guy’s Wood] two modii of grain, to be received annually from his tithe at Loges, and three modii of wine from his vineyards at Marly. He also gave the same brethren one ploughland of land adjoining that land which he had formerly granted them in the same place, [Col. 0075B] and, in addition, the grange which he had there.

Moreover, with the assent of A., priest of Saint Non, it was ordained and established through our hand that the brethren of that place shall pay no tithe to the priest of Saint Non from the increase of their animals, but shall be altogether free and exempt from its payment. In order that this may remain firm and stable, at the request of the aforesaid Guy and A., priest of Saint Non, we have caused the present charter to be made and fortified with the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1201, the fourth year of our pontificate.

### VII. Letters of Odo concerning the legitimization of the children of the lord king, begotten of the daughter of the duke of Merania, in the time of Pope Innocent. (1201.)

[From the royal archive of the Sainte-Chapelle at Paris.]

[Col. 0075C]

ODO, etc.

Let all of you know that we have seen the authenticated instrument of our most holy father Pope Innocent, in which it is contained that he endowed with the title of legitimacy the son and daughter of our most excellent lord Philip, king of the Franks, whom he had begotten of Agnes, daughter of the noble duke of Merania, so that no defect arising from their birth should exist in them.

[Note: For Innocent III’s letter concerning the legitimization of the children of King Philip, see among the *Registers of Innocent*, *Patrologia*, vol. CCXIV, col. 1193.]

We, therefore, as sons of the most holy Church, humbly receiving the apostolic mandate and considering them legitimate, by apostolic authority, the mandate of which we have received in this matter, have excommunicated and anathematize [Col. 0075D] and exclude from the thresholds of Holy Mother Church all those who in any manner attempt to oppose or derogate from this apostolic decree.

Done publicly at Sens, in the year of grace 1201, in January.

### VIII. Odo, bishop of Paris, grants the abbot of Saint Victor authority to remove at will priests from his parishes. (1202.)

To all the faithful in Christ to whom the present instrument shall reach, Absalon, abbot, and the whole convent [Col. 0076A] of Blessed Victor of Paris: greeting.

We make known that, whereas in those parish churches which we possess in the diocese of Paris—namely, formerly in the churches of Atheis, Villaribel, Vallis Jocosa, and Saint Paul—both I and my successors are bound to present a regular canon to the bishop of Paris for the care of souls, our venerable father Lord Odo, bishop of Paris, with the assent of his entire chapter, out of the affection with which he embraces us and our church, has granted and conceded to us from his own liberality in perpetuity that it shall be lawful for me, the abbot, and all my successors, whenever we wish, to remove without objection a canon who has been presented, without consulting the bishop of Paris or seeking his assent. [Col. 0076B] Nevertheless, within fifteen days after his removal, we must present to the aforesaid bishop, or to his successors, another person of our choice for the pastoral care.

If any of the aforesaid canons presently serving in the said churches and instituted for pastoral care appears insufficiently suitable to the bishop or his successors, and this is communicated to me, the abbot, by the bishop, or to the abbot then in office, we shall remove that canon without any objection and shall be bound, within fifteen days after his removal, to present to the bishop or his successors another person of our choice, as stated above. In perpetual confirmation of this matter, etc. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1202.

### IX. Letters of Odo, bishop of Paris, concerning Theobald, canon of Saint Geneviève, presented to him for the pastoral care of the parish of Saint Stephen of the Mount by the abbot of Saint Geneviève. (1202.)

[Col. 0076C]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who examine these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that Theobald, canon of Saint Geneviève, was presented to us for the care of souls at the Mount by Amaury, canon of Saint Geneviève of the Mount, who delivered to us the open letters of John, abbot of Saint Geneviève, on behalf of that abbot. The same Theobald received from us the care of souls of that parish, and, with [Col. 0076D] the most holy Gospels present and kissed by him, promised us, as bishop of Paris, upon his priestly word and upon his order, justice, obedience, and fidelity for as long as he should govern the said parish.

All this was done at Paris in our upper chapel, in the presence of Archambaud, dean of Bourges, and Master Jordan, his companion; Geoffrey of Lenda; Master Lothair; Master Bernard; Master Geoffrey of Pissy; Master Nicholas; Gregory; Rodulf of Lineriis; Guy, archpriest, and his clerk Leodegarius; Odo, priest of Viceour; Peter, nephew of the bishop of Angoulême; Robert of Bourges; [Col. 0077A] Peter of Lineriis, clerk; Nivelon; John, clerk of Master Lothair; Odo of Saint Médéric; William Escuacol; John Maurin, then also presented by that same William; Brother Otran; and Brother Peter of Saint Lazarus. In memory of this matter, we have caused the present charter to be fortified with the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of grace 1202, in June, the fifth year of our pontificate.

### X. Letters concerning the settlement of the boundaries between the dioceses of Beauvais and Paris. (1202.)

[From the cartulary of Paris.]

PHILIP, by the grace of God bishop of Beauvais, and ODO, bishop of Paris, to all who examine these present letters [Col. 0077B]: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, whereas a dispute had arisen between us over the boundaries of the dioceses of Beauvais and Paris at the place called Moynel, on the eastern side near the head of the church, we finally came in person to the site. After careful inquiry had been made in our presence, and in the presence of the abbots of the Valley of Blessed Mary, Saint-Just, and Hermeries, and of many other worthy men, among the neighbours of both dioceses, we determined the boundaries by mutual will and consent and set the boundary marks as follows: the first stone marker at the source of the spring of Moynel, which lies in the brothers’ pond; the second directly in the roadway; the third in the narrower field; the fourth and final marker directly beneath the oak tree beside the wall [Col. 0077C] enclosing the brothers’ gardens and beside a certain stream which issues from the aforesaid spring. Thus, what lies on the side of the church is in the diocese of Beauvais, and what lies on the other side is in the diocese of Paris; all the other bounds and boundaries of the aforesaid dioceses remaining in the condition in which they were.

In order that this may remain ratified and unshaken, we have fortified the present charter with the protection of our seals.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1202, in November, on the day after Saint Martin.

### XI. Letter of the same Odo concerning the tithe of Espiers, given by Adam of Montreuil to four matricular priests. (1203.)

[From the Cartulary of Paris.]

[Col. 0077D]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who examine these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, when we had instituted four permanent matricular clerics in our Church of Paris, and had given from our own revenue in perpetuity for this institution, while the dean and chapter of Paris likewise gave from theirs, our beloved Adam of Montreuil, canon of Paris, from charitable concern, gave in perpetual alms to that institution his tithe at Espiers, which he held, and four Parisian pounds, to be received annually in perpetuity from the oven of Loures. He divested himself thereof into our hand for the use of the said matricular clerics. [Col. 0078A] His mother Alix, his sister Helvis, and the knight Robert Ferratus, husband of the same Helvis, approved this donation made by him, held it ratified, and promised on pledged faith that they would observe it.

For the perpetual confirmation of this matter, with their consent, we have caused the present charter to be fortified with the protection of our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1203.

### XII. Letters of the same concerning the institution of four matricular priests in the Church of Paris. (1204.)

[From the cartulary of the lord dean of Paris, charter 161.]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all Christ’s faithful to whom the present instrument shall reach [Col. 0078B]: eternal greeting in the Lord.

What is established for the increase of divine worship deserves to be recorded in writing, lest it should easily be erased from human memory by forgetfulness in the passage of time. Therefore, we wish it to come to the knowledge of both present and future persons that, when, with the consent and will of our chapter, we had decreed the institution in the Church of Paris of four matricular priests, whose appointment shall belong perpetually to us and our successors, our beloved Adam of Montreuil, canon of that Church, concerned for the salvation of himself and his relatives and mindful of the benefit of so pious an institution, gave and granted in perpetual alms for the support of those matricular clerics—with the approval and ratification upon pledged faith of Alix, mother of the same Adam, Helvis, Adam’s sister, and Robert Fortis, Helvis’s husband—the tithe of Espiers, together with every right which he possessed in collecting that tithe, and four pounds of Parisian money to be received annually from the oven of Loures. He possessed that tithe and oven by hereditary right.

Whoever holds that oven shall be bound to render to the matricular clerics sixty sous at Christmas and twenty sous at Easter, without any outlay or expense on the part of the matricular clerics. If, however, the matricular clerics must spend anything on improvement or repair of the oven, they may receive and retain the income, with the appurtenances of the oven, until they have fully recovered both the expenses [Col. 0078D] incurred upon that oven and the revenue of the aforesaid four pounds. Furthermore, it should be known that we have given and assigned to the aforesaid matricular clerics in perpetuity seven pounds of Parisian money which the chapter of Paris was bound to pay annually to us and our successors as the income of a prebend. The abbot and chapter of Saint Geneviève are known to have given and granted this prebend to us in perpetuity under the settlement made between us and them. In addition, after the death of Master Albert, we have given them sixty sous, likewise to be paid annually by the chapter, or by those whom the chapter shall appoint, from the vicarage of that prebend granted to us by the chapter of Saint Geneviève, together with all that pertains to the vicarage.

The dean and chapter [Col. 0079A] have given the same matricular clerics ten pounds of Parisian money. They shall therefore be bound to pay the aforesaid matricular clerics annually, in two instalments—at Easter and on the feast of All Saints—the ten pounds, the aforementioned seven pounds, and the sixty sous which we have specified.

Taking account of Adam’s devotion, we have established and ordained that two of the four aforesaid priests shall serve in one week and the other two in the next. Each, on every day of his week, shall in good faith celebrate in the same Church, at the altar or altars appointed for this purpose by the chapter [Col. 0079B], a Mass of the Dead for the soul of the said Adam; for the souls of his parents, brothers, and sisters; and for all those who have increased or shall hereafter increase this benefaction. They shall say both the commendation and the three-lesson vigils, except on Sundays and on the feasts of the Nativity, Circumcision, Epiphany, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension of the Lord, and Pentecost; of the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross; on the solemnities of Blessed Mary; on the feasts of the apostles’ births; on the feast of the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist; of Blessed Mary Magdalene; of Blessed Michael; on the Nativity of Blessed Denis; on the deposition of Blessed Marcellus; on the feast of All Saints; and on the Nativity of Blessed Stephen.

The two who are not serving in a given week shall be bound to say the three-lesson vigils with Vespers three times in their non-serving week. Moreover, at the beginning and end of their Masses, whatever Masses they may be, the aforesaid four priests shall be bound to say a special prayer with the secret for Adam [Col. 0079C] while he lives and for the other living persons to whom the granted inheritance belonged. Any priest unable through illness or other necessity to perform the aforesaid offices shall in good faith provide someone to make up his deficiency. If he neglects this, the chapter shall provide a substitute at his expense. If any of these benefices happens to be given to a person who is not a priest, the portion of the benefice which would belong to him were he a priest shall be given, in proportion to the time, to the priest who serves in his place. It is also established that, unless he is ordained priest within a year, the bishop shall then have authority to confer the benefice upon a priest.

The aforesaid [Col. 0079D] four priests, when instituted by us or by our successors, shall be bound to swear in our presence, or in that of our successors, that they will faithfully observe the aforesaid provisions. If they refuse to swear within ten days after their institution, they shall know that from then on they are subject to anathema if they receive anything from the aforesaid benefice before taking the stated oath. The oath of the four priests shall also include that they shall attend so diligently to the custody of the church that at every time, by day as well as by night, at least one of the four may be found in the church in good faith, and that two of them shall sleep in the church at night; the church shall never be closed during the day.

When the aforesaid matricular clerics have been instituted by us [Col. 0080A], sworn fealty to us, and performed homage, they shall be bound to come to the chapter and swear fealty there to the chapter, as a lay matricular has customarily done from ancient times. There the dean and chapter shall assign them the altar at which, as ordained, they must celebrate, and shall invest them with that altar.

Furthermore, whereas there was formerly only one lay matricular in our Church, and he was unequal to the weight of so great an office, we have decided, with the chapter’s consent and will, to associate with him three other lay matriculars, who shall serve the Church in their own persons. Each shall receive annually one hundred Parisian sous from the revenues of the matricular office, while Andrew the matricular lives, payable by Andrew in equal halves at Christmas and the Nativity of Saint John. [Col. 0080B] Upon Andrew’s resignation or death, however, all revenues and proceeds of that matricular office shall be divided equally among the four lay matriculars, except that the senior matricular—namely Andrew’s successor, who shall enjoy the ancient liberty and immunity—shall receive alone, beyond the fourth share accruing to him, three and a half modii of wine annually from the eleven and a half modii which the matricular received from the bishop; and, in addition, six sextarii of grain out of the eighteen sextarii of winter grain which he received from the bishop’s granary, as well as the dishes which the matricular was accustomed to receive in the bishop’s household. [Col. 0080C] The remainder of the wine, grain, and all revenues and proceeds, both those already conferred and those which, God willing, shall hereafter be conferred, shall be divided into four equal parts among the four matriculars.

All the aforesaid lay matriculars, like the clerical ones, shall be instituted by us. Once instituted by us and after having sworn fealty and performed homage to us, they shall be bound to come to the chapter and swear to it the fealty which the matricular customarily rendered from ancient times. If, however, the senior lay matricular fails to perform his service of the church diligently, he shall provide in his place a suitable servant, who, together with the remaining three matriculars, shall discharge the office of matricular both in ringing the bells and in the other duties incumbent upon them.

In [Col. 0080D] the oath which these matriculars shall make both to us and to the chapter, it shall be expressly stated that they shall attend so diligently to the custody of the church that at every time, by day and by night, at least one of the four—as was said above concerning the priests—may be found in the church, and that two of them shall sleep in the church at night. If there are any other obligations which we wish to attach to the office of matriculars, clerical as well as lay, once they have been ordained by us and the chapter, they shall be reduced to writing; and the matriculars shall be bound to observe and perform them.

In order that this may have perpetual force, we have caused the present charter to be drawn up and confirmed by the protection of both our seal and the chapter’s seal.

[Col. 0081A] Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1204, the seventh year of our pontificate.

### XIII. Institution by the chapter of Paris of Odo’s anniversary. (1204.)

[From the Great Pastoral.]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all faithful persons who examine these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, when our dearest H., dean, and the chapter of Blessed Mary of Paris, had instituted our anniversary to be solemnly and perpetually celebrated in the Church of Paris, and had graciously and liberally assigned for this purpose forty sous of Parisian money to be received annually from the chapter’s common fund [Col. 0081B], we, taking account of their devotion, have given and granted in perpetuity to the said chapter, as an increase of the aforesaid benefaction, sixty Parisian sous to be received yearly from our rent at Brunel.

It should be known that these sixty sous, together with the forty sous to be paid by the chapter as stated above, shall be distributed on the vigil and the day of our anniversary to the canons of Blessed Mary and to the clerics assigned to the service of the high altar who attend our anniversary. To the other choir clerics of Blessed Mary, we have given forty pounds of Parisian money for the purchase of rents, likewise to be distributed among the choir clerics both on the vigil and on the day of our anniversary.

For the perpetual confirmation [Col. 0081C] of this matter, we have caused the present document to be fortified with the impression of our seal.

Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1204, the eighth year of our pontificate.

### XIV. Odo, bishop of Paris, grants a prebend and vicarage to the chapter of Paris. (1204.)

[From the Great Pastoral.]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all Christ’s faithful to whom the present instrument shall reach: eternal greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to come to the knowledge of all that, when the venerable men, the abbot and chapter of Saint Geneviève, had wholly granted and quitclaimed to us and our successors the prebend and vicarage which they possessed in the Church of Blessed Mary of Paris [Col. 0081D], under the agreement which had been made between us and them, we afterwards granted and quitclaimed the said prebend and vicarage to our beloved brethren Hugh, dean, and the chapter of Paris, to be possessed in perpetuity. They may dispose of both the prebend and the vicarage as they wish, provided that the aforesaid chapter, beyond the ten pounds of Parisian money which it has granted in perpetuity to the matricular priests newly instituted by us in our church, shall be bound to pay those matriculars seven Parisian pounds annually and, after the resignation or death of Master Albert, sixty [Col. 0082A] sous of the same currency annually.

In order that this donation and grant may remain valid with perpetual force, we have caused the present charter to be fortified with the impression of our seal. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1204, the seventh year of our pontificate.

### XV. Donations made to Port-Royal. (1206.)

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who examine these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, when Lord Matthew of Marly had formerly set out for Jerusalem, he assigned fifteen pounds of annual rent at Mantes for the salvation of his soul and that of his wife Matilda, and placed them at the disposal of us and of Matilda herself [Col. 0082B], so that we might assign and grant them as seemed expedient to us. Accordingly, on the counsel of worthy men, we assigned and granted them in perpetuity to the church of Porrois.

Moreover, since the said Matilda had acquired certain rents at Gallardon—namely, a third part in the mill of Herchenout, a half part in the mill of Bourg-le-Riche, and a fourth part in the mill of Freteval—she granted in perpetual alms to the same church ten modii of annual grain-rent from the revenues of the aforesaid mills, free from every exaction and from repairs to the mills, to be received by the measure of Gallardon, namely sound grain of the kind which the mills [Col. 0082C] earned. Thus, if one or two of the aforesaid mills should, by some mischance—which may God avert—be reduced to ruin, the aforesaid church shall be paid its ten modii from the revenue of the surviving mill, insofar as it can suffice.

Bouchard and Matthew, brothers—namely the sons of the aforesaid Matthew and Matilda—approved and, on pledged faith, granted this assignment and donation to the aforesaid church concerning the said money and grain. Matthew, lord of Montmorency, from whose fief the said fifteen pounds were held, likewise approved and granted the same assignment. In testimony of this matter, with the consent of the same Matilda and her sons, we have caused the present charter to be fortified with the impression of our seal. [Col. 0082D]

Done in the year of the Lord 1206.

### XVI. Letters of Odo, bishop of Paris, establishing the feast of Saint Bernard in the Church of Paris. (1207.)

[From the Great Pastoral.]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who examine these present letters: greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, since the dean and chapter of Paris have generously and graciously granted us, at our request, that every year on the day after the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle they shall celebrate in the Church of Paris the feast of Blessed Bernard, first abbot of Clairvaux, as a half-double feast, we have assigned and granted [Col. 0083A] to them in perpetual alms the tithe which we purchased at Buc, toward Châteaufort. From it, every year at Matins on the aforesaid feast, six denarii shall be distributed to every canon present and to each of the four matricular priests. Whatever remains from the proceeds of the fruits of the aforesaid tithe shall be distributed among the choir clerics of Paris, insofar as it can extend to each of those attending the aforesaid Matins.

For the perpetual confirmation of this matter, we have caused our seal to be attached to the present charter.

Done from the Incarnation of the Lord 1207, in August.

### XVII. Letters of the same Odo, by which he grants newly cleared lands to the chapter of Paris. (1207.)

[From the Great Pastoral.]

[Col. 0083B]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to his beloved sons in Christ, Hugh, dean, and the whole chapter of Blessed Mary of Paris, in perpetuity.

And the uprightness of your conduct, as well as the benefit of the Church, moves us all the more willingly to provide for your advantage and peace, since we are especially bound to you and to your Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, considering your devout zeal, in all places of our diocese in which you possess, or shall possess, the right to tithes, we grant, give, and by the protection of this present writing confirm to you and to your Church, to possess peacefully and freely in perpetuity, [Col. 0083C] the tithes of all lands newly brought under cultivation, whether to be made or already made, which have not been assigned to others—saving the right of another Church which may have a share of the tithing in the same territory.

Done in the year of grace 1207, in the month of August.

XVIII. Instrument concerning the sale of certain estates made by Guy, lord of Caprosia. (Year 1207.)

Odo, by the grace of God bishop of Paris.

Let all know that Guy, lord of Caprosia, acknowledged in our presence that he sold, for eight times twenty Paris pounds, to the new house of Porrois the mill which he possessed at Germeville, together with the land and meadow which he possessed beside the aforesaid [Col. 0083D] mill; the meadow called Great Roschia, which he possessed below the mill; and his wood situated near Porrois, on the other side of the stream, as the markers and bounds determine. He also granted that his fief might be acquired by the same house, as its boundaries and markers show, if it can acquire it from those who hold the lordship.

He likewise granted to the animals of the aforesaid house, except goats, pasture in the common woods. Nor may the house’s livestock enter Guy’s other woods after the manner of a herd within five years, except as the community of the land enters them, unless Guy himself specially grants this; and if he or his heir wishes to clear his woods, the aforesaid house may not object. [Col. 0084A] Avelina, the wife of the same Guy, granted and approved this; and both he and she gave their pledge to provide warranty. In testimony of this matter, at the will of the said Guy, we caused this charter to be drawn up and fortified with our seal.

Done in the year of the Lord 1207, in August.

XIX. Foundation of the Church of Saint Symphorian. (Year 1207.)

Odo, by God’s mercy bishop of Paris, to all to whom these present letters shall come, greeting in the Lord.

What is established for the increase of divine worship ought fittingly to be commended to the witness of letters, lest it be brought into oblivion with the passage of time. We therefore wish it to come to the knowledge of all [Col. 0084B] that there was in the city of Paris a certain place of ancient reverence and religion, in which the glorious martyr Dionysius is said to have been held in prison, and which the Lord Jesus Christ is likewise reported to have honored by his presence, when he gave there to that martyr the sacrament of his body. In that place the devotion of the faithful had also erected a chapel, which afterwards, through neglect, had been reduced to desolation and abandoned.

At last, through the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, the noble man Matthew, count of Bellimont, who possessed the right of patronage and ownership both in the chapel and in the adjoining little house, transferred to us and to our successors, by pious generosity, whatever right he had there. We therefore, wishing to restore that place to a more worthy condition, [Col. 0084C] erected there a more solemn chapel in memory and veneration of Saint Dionysius, and appointed chaplains to serve in that church and in good faith personally maintain residence there.

For their support Eleanor, illustrious countess of Vermandois, for the salvation of Lady A., formerly most serene queen of France, gave in pious intention one hundred marks of silver. With these we purchased from the abbot and convent of Montis-Etivi the oven which they possessed in Paris, called the “Hell Oven,” with all its appurtenances, for one hundred and thirty Paris pounds. From the remaining seventy Paris pounds, revenues shall be purchased for the use of the chaplains [Col. 0084D] whom we have mentioned, once the tithe of William Buignel, knight, has been redeemed; it is now pledged as security for those seventy Paris pounds.

For the use of this same chapel Garner of Saint Lazarus, citizen of Paris, and Agnes his wife, mercifully granted the following to the same place: their entire house situated before the gate of Saint Julian the Poor, as it extends to the great street, free of one penny of quit-rent and every customary due; the right which Simon of Pissy, knight, had in that house, and which he quitclaimed into our hand; three arpents of vineyard in the valley of Saint Martin; and one and a half arpents at Lervel. It is to be understood that all the aforesaid proceeds and revenues shall be distributed in equal [Col. 0085A] shares among the four persons, as stated, who serve in the same chapel. One of them shall celebrate perpetually for the soul of the said queen, and three for Garner and Agnes. Their appointment shall belong solely to the bishop of Paris.

But whoever receives any of these chaplaincies, or of others to exist in the same church, shall at the time of appointment be bound to swear that he will personally reside in the chapel in good faith, and that, if he is not a priest, he will receive priestly orders within a year; thus he may receive nothing from the revenues of the church until he has been promoted to priestly orders. In the meantime, the revenues shall go toward the needs of the church.

It is also to be understood that the divine offices shall be solemnly celebrated in the aforesaid chapel at Matins, Mass, Vespers, and the other [Col. 0085B] canonical hours; and bells shall be rung as is customary in a church endowed with prebends. All Masses other than the conventual Mass, however, shall be celebrated without chant or ringing of bells.

We further grant that the said count of Bellimont may establish one chaplaincy in the same chapel, and that he and his successors, the counts of Bellimont, may confer it upon a suitable person to be presented to us and our successors, to whom that person shall be subject in all things. Whenever any of the said chaplaincies becomes vacant through the death of a chaplain—we do not wish an annual payment to arise from any other manner of vacancy—we decree that half of the annual income be assigned to the fabric and other needs of the chapel, while the appointed person shall receive the other half according to the aforesaid arrangement. [Col. 0085C]

That this may remain ratified, we have caused the present charter to be fortified by the impression of our seal.

Done at Paris, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1207, the tenth year of our pontificate, in August.

XX. Appointment by the same Odo of two priests in the Church of Saint Symphorian at Paris. (Year 1207.)

[From the royal charter treasury preserved in the Sainte-Chapelle at Paris.]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord.

We make known that the noble man Matthew, count of Bellimont, for the salvation of his own soul and those of his ancestors, [Col. 0085D] and in recompense for the journey to Jerusalem, gave and granted in perpetual alms to God and to us, in honor of Saint Dionysius, that place in which Saint Dionysius is said to have been imprisoned, called the Chapel of Saint Catherine, together with the building situated in the same place—namely, from the outer little meadow to the street in front which runs between that place and the Church of Saint Dionysius of the Prison—for the building of a church in which priests shall serve God and Saint Dionysius forever; provided that the little meadow and all the rest of his buildings shall remain entirely and freely to the count himself and to his heirs.

We granted that we should appoint two priests there; and the count himself, for the salvation of his soul, [Col. 0086A] should appoint from his own resources one priest in the church which we shall build there. Whenever, or in whatever manner, that benefice becomes vacant, the same count and his heirs may freely confer it upon another suitable person; but they shall be bound to present that person to us, the bishop of Paris, and to our successors. That person shall swear to the bishop that he will reside and serve in that Church, and that, if he is not a priest, he will receive priestly orders within a year. The two priests appointed by us and by our successors shall likewise make the same oath concerning service and residence.

That this may remain ratified, we have caused the present charter to be fortified by the impression of our seal.

Given in the year of the Lord 1206, in December.

XXI. Odo, bishop of Paris, confirms the agreement concluded between the abbot of Saint Dionysius and the abbess of Footel. (Year 1207.)

[Col. 0086B]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop; HUGH, dean; and the chapter of Paris, to all who shall inspect this present charter, greeting in the Lord.

We make known that, whereas an agreement has been made concerning the church of the priory of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil and its dependencies between the venerable abbot and convent of Saint Dionysius on the one hand, and the abbess and convent of Footel on the other, before me the bishop, myself the dean, and many others of the chapter of Paris, and before judges delegated by the Apostolic See—namely Giles, prior of Saint Victor at Paris; Simon, precentor of Senlis; and Master Robert of [Col. 0086C] Corchon, canon of Noyon—we approve and confirm that agreement as ratified and acceptable.

The form of this agreement is as follows: the abbess and nuns of Footel renounced every right, if they had any, in the said church of Argenteuil and its dependencies, according to the form written below: namely, any right they had in the town of Argenteuil and its dependencies, and in Sartouville, Cavenolium, Trapis, Eranceri, Bardini, Ademville, Chrisi, Mellay, Saint-Leon, Mostrol, Momeliam, and the dependencies of those same towns; and in one mill at Melun and its dependencies; and in the tithe of Asnières.

They also ceded to the Church of Saint Dionysius every right and every action, if they had any, by which they might claim the said Church of Blessed Mary and all the aforesaid things. It was, however, particularly agreed and understood by consent of the parties that this aforesaid renunciation and cession should not be understood to include anything which we, the bishop, or the Church of Paris, or the monastery of Footel, or any outsider deriving a claim from us the bishop, the Church of Paris, or the monastery of Footel, held and possessed at the time when this agreement was made. If there are things not expressly named which had belonged to the said church of Argenteuil, each party retains intact the right which it possessed before the agreement.

[Col. 0087A] The abbess and nuns of Footel also delivered to the aforesaid judges, with the consent of the Church of Saint Dionysius, the documents belonging to this case, and renounced the future use, against Saint Dionysius or any person deriving a claim from it, of either those documents or any others, in respect of these matters; that is, so far as these matters are concerned, they shall be regarded as cancelled. For if there were any documents that concerned the aforesaid case and other matters, they shall be considered cancelled as to these matters, but shall remain fully valid as to the others.

It was further agreed between the parties that we the bishop and the Church of Paris should have and retain in the said church of Argenteuil and in all the aforesaid matters, both expressed and unexpressed, every right which we possessed before [Col. 0087B] this agreement, saving the agreement made in the presence of the aforesaid judges between me the bishop and the Church of Saint Dionysius concerning the right in the church of the priory of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil.

The aforesaid abbess and convent of Footel also swore bodily that they would in good faith observe the said renunciation and cession and the other matters stated above, and would not contravene them. If they did contravene them, and, having been admonished by the abbot and another monk of Saint Dionysius who presides over the order in the first place after the abbot, refused to desist within thirty days after the warning, they should make good every loss thereby incurred by the Church of Saint Dionysius; nevertheless, this agreement shall remain in force.

[Col. 0087C] For the sake of peace, moreover, the abbot and convent of Saint Dionysius quitclaimed to the said abbess and nuns every right, if they had any, in the Church of Saint Nicholas situated near Mont-Mélian, together with its house and enclosure; the three sextarii of grain which the said Church of Saint Nicholas is due to receive annually from the grange of Monmeliant; and the four arpents of land which the same Church of Saint Nicholas holds there toward the field. They also ceded to the same abbess and nuns every right and every action, if they had any, by which they might claim the aforesaid matters, saving nevertheless the field-side and the right of the field-side, except that the nuns shall not be compelled by the Church of Saint Dionysius to sell.

They likewise gave the monastery of Footel four arpents of land around the said Church of Saint Nicholas. [Col. 0087D] Nor shall they compel the nuns to sell houses, vineyards, or any other things which they possess under the Church of Saint Dionysius or its dependencies; rather, they shall permit them peacefully to possess them wherever they hold them, as they now hold or possess them, and shall not henceforth raise any dispute concerning them.

They also assigned to the same abbess and nuns, in specified lands in the territory of Tremblay, a tithe worth ten Paris pounds annually, and shall cause the said nuns to hold that tithe perpetually in peace. Furthermore, the said abbot and convent of Saint Dionysius promised to pay four hundred Paris pounds to the aforesaid abbess and nuns on the coming feast of Saint Andrew, and another four hundred [Col. 0088A] Paris pounds on the same feast in the following year.

The aforesaid abbot and convent of Saint Dionysius likewise swore bodily that they would in good faith fulfill all the aforesaid provisions and would not contravene them. If they did contravene them, they should make good every loss thereby incurred by the monastery of Footel; nevertheless, this agreement shall remain in force.

For the perpetual validity of this matter, we have caused the present charter to be fortified by the impressions of our seals.

Done at Paris in the year of the Lord 1207, in August, seven days before the Kalends of September [26 August].

XXII. Odo, bishop of Paris, and Henry, abbot of Saint Dionysius, disputing concerning the Church of Argenteuil, are reconciled. (Year 1207.)

[Col. 0088B]

I, HENRY, abbot of Saint Dionysius, and the whole convent of that same place, make known to those present and future that, whereas there was a dispute between us on the one hand and Odo, bishop of Paris, on the other concerning the right in the church of the priory of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil, we have amicably settled it through mediators in the following manner.

Namely, the same bishop, his successors, and the chapter of Paris shall not henceforth do, nor shall they be able to do, anything whereby there might be an abbot or abbess in the aforesaid Church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil. Rather, [Col. 0088C] it shall remain a priory of Saint Dionysius; nor may they bring it about that the monks of Saint Dionysius be removed from that church.

In the same Church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil, the aforesaid bishop and his successors shall have in perpetuity two procurations each year: one without assessment, as is customary, and another not exceeding sixty shillings. The archdeacon of Paris and his successors shall likewise have there in perpetuity two procurations each year: one without assessment, as is customary, and another not exceeding twenty shillings. Nor may the bishop have more than two procurations there in a year, nor likewise may the archdeacon have more than two.

[Col. 0088D] All other episcopal rights shall remain forever to the bishop of Paris and his successors in the aforesaid Church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil, on account of [Note: [Col. 0087D] “Besides those.”] those other rights which the presently existing privileges of Saint Dionysius take away from [Note: [Col. 0088D] “They offer.”] that bishop. Nor may we henceforth obtain any other privileges against the bishop or chapter of Paris concerning the said Church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil.

Nevertheless, should it ever happen that the bishop of Paris or his successors place Argenteuil under interdict—which it is lawful for the bishop of Paris to do notwithstanding any privilege—they may likewise place the said Church of Blessed [Col. 0089A] Mary of Argenteuil under interdict, provided that the monks of that church may not receive persons under interdict or excommunicated persons, nor ring bells, but shall perform the divine service in a low voice and behind closed doors. We may not invoke against this any privilege now held or hereafter to be held.

We also assigned to the same bishop and his successors six muids of grain, namely half winter grain and half spring grain, measured by the Paris measure, to be received annually before the feast of Saint Remigius from our tithes at Herblay and Montigny: three muids from one grange and three from the other. If one has less, it shall be made up from the other; and if both are insufficient, it shall be supplied from another tithe [Col. 0089B] in the diocese, namely at La Pierre-Laye.

We wish this assignment to remain for a long time [Note: [Col. 0089D] “So long.”], until we have acquired six muids of grain—half winter grain and half spring grain, by the Paris measure—from tithes situated in the diocese of Paris, in at most three suitable places, or in two suitable places, or in one suitable place if we wish; and have assigned those acquired six muids in perpetuity to the bishop of Paris and his successors. Then the other assignment shall cease.

For the perpetual validity of this matter, we have caused our seals to be affixed to the present charter.

Done in the year of grace 1207, seven days before the Kalends of September [26 August].

XXIII. Of Odo the bishop, Hugh the dean, and the entire chapter of Paris, declaring that Provost the chancellor swore to observe the statute made by the bishop of Paris concerning the chancellor’s residence. (Year 1207.)

[DUBOULAY, *History of the University of Paris*, III, 36.]

[Col. 0089C]

ODO, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, HUGH dean, and the entire chapter of Paris, to all who shall inspect these present letters, greeting in the Lord.

We make known to all that, considering the residence of the chancellor of Paris necessary to our Church of Paris and to the community of scholars, by the counsel of good men and common consent we have enacted in the chapter of Paris that whoever shall henceforth be chancellor of Paris shall be bound to reside personally and in good faith in the Church of Paris as long as he holds the chancellorship; and that neither by himself nor through another shall he in any way procure release from the aforesaid oath.

We further enact that he may receive none of the revenues of the chancellorship until he has taken in the chapter of Paris the aforesaid oath. After Master Provost had been made chancellor, we asked him to take the said oath before the chapter and bind himself to the necessity of maintaining residence. He willingly and graciously gave his consent to this. He was the first to swear in the aforesaid form, in which [Col. 0090A] his successors as chancellor shall likewise henceforth be bound to swear.

That this might remain ratified and firm, we have caused the present charter to be fortified by the impressions of our seals.

Done in the year 1207.

XXIV. Foundation by the same bishop for the performance of the Mandatum on Maundy Thursday. (Year 1208.)

[From the Little Pastoral.]

HUGH, dean, and the whole chapter of Blessed Mary of Paris, to all Christ’s faithful who shall inspect this present page, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to come to the knowledge of all that the lord Odo, of pious memory, formerly [Col. 0090B] bishop of Paris, compassionately assigned one muid of grain from his acquisition—which the monks of Saint Dionysius had assigned to him at Herblay—for performing the Mandatum for fifty poor persons on Maundy Thursday.

Since we observed that on the other days of Lent the Mandatum of the poor was conducted less solemnly because there were only two poor persons, we took care, with common consent, to order that from the Monday after the Sunday on which is sung “He has called upon me” (*Invocavit me*) until the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, thirteen poor persons shall be received each day of Lent, Sundays excepted, by the hand of the priest serving the week, or by the hand of the precentor whenever the weekly celebrant is a monk or regular canon and is absent. [Col. 0090C] Their feet shall be washed in the refectory by the ministers of the high altar—that is, the priest, deacon, and subdeacon—assisted by three boys.

The precentor of our Church then in office shall be bound to attend the washing and the Mandatum. If, owing to evident necessity, the precentor cannot attend and devote himself to this duty, the master of the choirboys shall perform the duty in his place, taking care that it be performed devoutly, in order, and in the manner established. If both are absent for a just and necessary reason, the precentor shall be bound to have this performed by one of the ministers of the high altar.

After the washing of feet, the precentor, or the person who carries out his office as stated above, [Col. 0090D] shall give pennies to the priest, deacon, and subdeacon. With these, he shall offer each poor person four pennies for refreshment, with a kiss of the hand. He shall additionally give four pennies to the priest, four to the deacon, four to the subdeacon, and one penny to each of the boys.

When the Mandatum has ended, before the poor persons or the ministers themselves leave the refectory, there shall be said for the souls of the aforesaid Odo the bishop, Hugh the dean, Peter the precentor, who were priests, and for the souls of those who increase that benefaction: *Out of the depths* (*De profundis*), with the Lord’s Prayer, the prayers which follow, and the collect [Col. 0091A] in this form: “Absolve, we beseech you, O Lord, the soul of your servant, the bishop, and the souls of your servants, the priests, and the souls of all the brethren of our congregation, and of all the faithful departed,” etc. When these things have been done, they shall return to the church, as is customary.

We do not alter in any respect the ancient custom concerning the two poor clerics whose feet were customarily washed. Rather, they shall come to the refectory with the thirteen poor persons, do what they have been accustomed to do, and receive the ancient benefaction of the hospital of Blessed Mary.

But on Maundy Thursday fifty poor persons shall be received by the precentor. Their feet shall be washed by all priests and deacons, canons, and other priests and deacons serving the high altar, assisted by the canonical subdeacons. The precentor shall distribute to each of the aforesaid poor persons four pennies, as stated above. [Col. 0091B] For making the aforesaid payment and distribution of the benefaction, we have assigned the muid of grain given by the aforesaid Bishop Odo, as stated above, and twenty Paris shillings piously contributed by Peter the precentor.

XXV. Letter of Odo to Pope Innocent III.—He reports what was done in the matter of the divorce between the king and queen.

(See among the *Registers of Innocent III*, *Patrologia*, vol. CCXIV, col. 884.)

XXVI. Peter of Nemours, bishop of Paris, confirms Odo’s donations. (Year 1208.)

[From the Great Pastoral of Paris.]

[Col. 0091C]

PETER, by the grace of God bishop of Paris, to his beloved sons HUGH the dean and the chapter of Paris, in perpetuity.

What is established for the increase of ecclesiastical benefit and divine worship is worthy of being strengthened with perpetual force, lest in the course of time it be weakened by anyone’s malice.
