We therefore wish it to come to the knowledge of all that the lord Odo, of happy memory, formerly bishop of Paris and our predecessor, wishing to eliminate certain abuses that had arisen in the Church of Paris under the pretext of a corrupt custom, decreed that the feast of the Lord’s Circumcision and the Nativity of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, should be restored to a regular condition and solemnly celebrated.

To every canon and cleric serving at the high altar who attends Matins on the Nativity of Blessed Stephen, he generously gave and granted six Paris pennies; to every non-canonical cleric of the choir, four pennies; to each choirboy, two pennies; and to every cleric who sings a responsory or Alleluia at Mass in triple or quadruple organum, six pennies, to be received annually, peacefully and freely, in [Col. 0092A] our provostship of Paris.

For the feast of the Circumcision, he liberally assigned in perpetuity, from the revenues of the chapter, three Paris pennies to every non-canonical cleric of the choir and two pennies to every boy.

He also gave in perpetual alms to the chapter of the Church of Paris a provision of bread, wine, and pork, to be paid annually at Pentecost by the bishop of Paris then in office; and he established that every canon of Saint Dionysius of the Passage should receive a half-provision on the same day. He further gave and granted the chapter of Paris sixty Paris shillings in rent from Brunello, to be received annually on the day of his anniversary and distributed as he ordained.

Moreover, he granted and quitclaimed to the chapter of Paris the prebend and vicarage which the Church of Saint Geneviève had customarily held in the Church of Paris and which that bishop had acquired for the chapter of Paris, so that they might dispose of both the prebend [Col. 0092B] and the vicarage according to their will.

Furthermore, with the chapter’s consent he established eight matricularii in the Church of Paris and assigned fixed and perpetual support for them, both he himself and the chapter. He likewise granted and liberally bestowed upon the chapter and Church, to possess peacefully and freely in perpetuity, the tithes of all newly cultivated lands to be made or already made which had not yet been assigned to others, in all places of the diocese of Paris where the Church of Paris possessed or would possess the right of tithes—saving the right of another Church which might have a share of the tithing in the same territory.

He also transferred by pious donation to the right and ownership of the chapter what he had bought at Buc, to be distributed as Matins payments on the feast of Saint Bernard. Further, he assigned and granted to the Church and precentor of Paris, for performing the Mandatum on Maundy Thursday, one muid of grain by Paris measure, half winter grain and half spring grain, at Herblay, from the grain which he had acquired and held from the monks of Saint Dionysius. If the abbot and monks of Saint Dionysius assigned that grain elsewhere to the bishop of Paris, the precentor should receive the aforesaid muid where the bishop’s grain was assigned.

He further gave to the clerics of Matins that portion which [Col. 0092D] he received from the offerings of the Cross made on Friday in the Passion of the Lord—namely, half of all the offerings.

We therefore approve and ratify the aforesaid donations, grants, and institutions; by this page of the present writing we confirm them and strengthen them by the protection of our seal; and we decree and command that they remain perpetually unshaken.

Given at Paris, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1208, the first year of our pontificate.

[Col. 0093]

ACCOUNT of a notable miracle, performed in the time of Odo, bishop of Paris, through the merits of blessed Geneviève, concerning the flooding of the Seine, which threatened the city of Paris with destruction. (Year 1206.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VII, Instrument 228, from Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, I, 662.]

[Col. 0093A] Glorious is God in his saints: in the abundance of sins he shows the superabundance of his grace, and in the afflictions of his people he reveals not only his own glory but also that of his saints. This glory and mercy of God has been manifested again and again before their eyes in the afflictions of the kingdom of France and in the miracles of the blessed virgin Geneviève, beloved of God. Therefore it is our purpose to bear witness to the truth concerning those things which we have seen with our own eyes, so that we may be among the disciples of him who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14): the way in example, the truth in promise, and life in reward.

Thus, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1206, in the ninth indiction, in the month of December, God chastised the kingdom of France by a violent inundation of rains and by the force of rivers overflowing [Col. 0093B] their proper bounds and banks. In this flood of many waters, tall trees were uprooted, the earth’s produce was torn out by the roots, and the buildings of cities, towns, and villages were utterly overthrown.

Among the disasters of the whole kingdom, the city of Paris—head and mistress of all the cities of the realm—was shaken from its very foundations by the violence of the River Seine overflowing its usual limits. The inundation was such that those passing through the city’s lanes and streets required boats; its buildings were partly overthrown, while those still standing, for the most part, threatened collapse under repeated flooding and the washing force of the waves. The stone bridge also, called the Little Bridge in comparison with the larger bridge of the same city, [Col. 0093C] struck and battered by the waters’ violence, promised ruin. On the bridge itself one could see very open and extensive breaches: masonry demolished, stones separated from one another, and the bridge itself ruinous and about to fall, like the water’s surface, tossed by the wind through the continual collision of the river’s waves flowing hither and thither.

The city, full of riches, was desolate; the mistress of provinces sat in sorrow: “her priests groaning, her virgins dishevelled, and she herself oppressed with bitterness; nor was there anyone of all her loved ones to comfort her” (Lam. 1). The sole hope, after God and his blessed Mother Mary, for the people in danger lay in the Blessed Virgin Genevieve, through whose benefits enduring memory had rendered the people—and Paris in particular—subject and devoted to that virgin. The people had one voice, all raised one cry, every person one petition: that the Blessed Virgin Genevieve should come forth from her holy place; that by her presence she should protect the supplicating and groaning people and help the perishing city, lest the righteous be swept away with the unrighteous and the devout with the ungodly. Let her stand as a wall for her people; let her break God’s wrath by humble supplication; let her obtain God’s mercy by her prayers, so that the merciful God might forgive the offence, command the winds and the waters, and bring about a great calm.

Accordingly, at the supplication of Bishop Odo, clergy, and people, a solemn procession having been prepared and the relics of the saints brought to our church, the Blessed Virgin Genevieve came forth from her holy place. With the saints’ relics going before, Saint Genevieve led her people as a pillar [Col. 0094B] of fire in the night of adversity. We came, therefore, to the city’s stone Little Bridge, where there was no turning to right or left, but the way lay through the middle of the bridge. Once, with the Ark of the Covenant going before, the people of Israel crossed through the midst of the Jordan dry-shod. Likewise, with Blessed Genevieve and the saints’ relics going before across the broken bridge, close to collapse, the entire people followed her, safe under her protection despite the imminent danger of the flooding waters and of the bridge rocking under the collision of the waves.

Moses divided the waters of the sea for the people of Israel to cross; but the Blessed Virgin Genevieve crossed with the people of Paris over the swollen waters of the river, sustained not so much by the broken bridge as herself sustaining that bridge by divine protection. At last, when Blessed Genevieve entered the church of Saint Mary situated in the city of Paris, immediately—as we heard and also saw in the city of God—the powers coming from his holy mountain, everything that had previously been disturbed at her arrival became peaceful and calm. The city itself, earlier shaken and disturbed from its foundations, was tranquil and still. The people, who had been grievously afflicted before, breathed freely in praise of Blessed Genevieve; and, as it is written, something like the appearance of electrum appeared among the people through the presence of the Blessed Virgin and the most certain hope of divine consolation. They saw, as Moses did in the bush, the flame of fire without burning, because the chastised people of the Lord were being enlightened unto knowledge; and when the sun had set upon them, they sought [Col. 0094D] him, and came to him at daybreak.

The people of Paris bear witness to this: from that day—which [Col. 0095A] was a Saturday—on which Saint Genevieve crossed the swollen waves of the river, the receding waters diminished until the River Seine had gathered itself again within its bed. From that day the Lord did not send rain upon the earth until the earth’s surface was completely dry. Then, when all had been pacified and had conceived hope of salvation in the virgin’s presence, the Blessed Virgin returned, the whole people following her over the broken and swaying bridge. Its collapse was deferred until it might render the Blessed Virgin, returning to her own place, a marvellous and memorable service.

More wondrous events followed upon the wondrous. For after Blessed Genevieve had returned to her own place and had been solemnly installed, as was fitting, in her shrine, and after the people accompanying her had returned home, scarcely half an hour having passed, [Col. 0095B] at nightfall the Little Bridge collapsed. The bridge which a little before had sustained the people as they crossed despite its ruinous condition, fell after the people had passed, injuring and drowning no one. Its collapse was a sign and testimony of the preceding miracle.

Therefore it must be ascribed to the praises of the Blessed Virgin that the broken and ruinous bridge was able to sustain that Lady Virgin and all the passing people, and that it fell after the crossing of that virgin and the entire people, with no one hurt. Moreover, it was by her power that the swollen Seine drew back and confined itself; and the ensuing serenity of the weather was likewise so great. By the merits of Saint Genevieve, God’s grace bestowed these things for the salvation of the people of Paris, the deliverance of that city and the whole country, divine glory, and the honour of Blessed Genevieve, by whose intercessions those who worthily venerate her memory are freed from every danger. Let us therefore marvel at the miracle, [Col. 0096B] venerate the mystery, adore God, and long for the reward of eternal life. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1212. Gunther, Cistercian Monk

[Col. 0095]

## Notice

(Oudin, *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings*, II, 1651.)

[Col. 0095C] Gunther, first a schoolmaster and afterwards a monk of the Paris monastery in the diocese of Basel, of the Cistercian order—not of the famous French city of Paris—flourished in the years 1190 and 1200. He committed his name to posterity when, from the mouth of his abbot Martin, who had been present at the events and had returned from the East to the abbey, he wrote a history of Constantinople’s capture by the Latins in 1204. Henry Canisius published it in volume V, page 358, of the *Antiquae Lectiones* (new edition, vol. IV, pt. I). Since he himself reports that he received what he writes from the lips of that Abbot Martin, who had been present at the siege of Constantinople, we may thereby understand both the author’s date and the degree to which he is trustworthy. See Gerard Johannes Vossius, book II, *On Latin Historians*, chapter 55, p. 445 of the last edition.

The same Gunther wrote thirteen books *On Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving*, published at Basel in 1504 and 1507 by Michael Furter, quarto. The same Gunther is also credited with a heroic poem, certainly not inelegant, in ten books, concerning the deeds of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in Italy and especially Liguria, called the *Ligurinus*. It received this title because the Red-Beard’s chief conflict was with the Ligurian city—that is, Milan—whose inhabitants he calls his Ligurians. For this reason Gunther himself is also, though wrongly, called “the Ligurian” by Baronius in his *Annals* under the year 1160.

Gerard Johannes Vossius, however, absurdly errs in book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 53, p. 431 of the last edition, when he writes that Gunther composed ten books on the deeds of the Red-Beard while the latter was still alive. For in this poem Gunther mentions another work written by himself, *On the Holy War*, which he calls the *Solymarium* and which he scarcely composed before 1210. [Col. 0096D] Therefore, since the work *On the Deeds of Frederick Barbarossa* was composed after his *History of the Holy War*, or of Constantinople’s capture by the Latins in 1204, it was necessarily written after Frederick’s death.

That work first appeared separately at Strasbourg in 1500, folio; then there again in 1531, folio, with the very extensive notes of Jacob Spiegel; and finally at Basel in 1569, with Otto of Freising. Justus Reuber also published it among the *Writers of German Affairs*, at Frankfurt, folio, 1584, volume III, p. 275, with Jacob Spiegel’s notes; and it was published elsewhere with the notes of Conrad Rittershusius. Certainly Justus Lipsius, *Polyorceticon*, book II, dialogue 4; Isaac Casaubon, in his *Polybius*, p. 171; and Gerard Vossius, book II, *On Latin Historians*, chapter 53, p. 432, commend this Gunther, whoever he may ultimately have been, to us as a poet of no ordinary spirit and talent, indeed as remarkable for the age in which he lived. William Cave mocks them in [Col. 0098A] his *History of Literature*, under the year 1210, p. 706. Valerius Andreas, in the *Belgian Library*, p. 336, attributes all these little works to a certain Gunther, a monk of Elnone at Saint-Amand, mentioned by Sigebert in chapter 166 of *On Illustrious Men*. But Andreas is absurdly mistaken: that Gunther was a hundred years earlier, flourishing, according to Trithemius, around 1090 in the time of Henry IV. To him Sigebert, chapter 166, attributes only the martyrdom of Saints Cyriacus and Julitta in verse, preserved in manuscript at Saint-Amand; Gerard Johannes Vossius mentions this work in book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 46, p. 381 of the last edition.

> [Note: [Col. 0097] For Gunther’s life and writings, see the dissertation prefixed below to the *Ligurinus*, which came into our hands too late. —Patristic Editor.]

[Col. 0097]

# Gunther the Cistercian: Thirteen Books on Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving

According to the Basel quarto edition of 1507, entitled: “A most beautiful work on the three customary acts of Christians—namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—containing thirteen books by the venerable Father Gunther, of the order of Saint Benedict; a work most elegant and most Latin, as well as most useful, for the public delivery of sermons and conferences; long hidden, but recently found and printed.” At the end one reads: “The little work on the three acts of Christians—namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—is finished. Printed at Basel by Michael Furter in the year 1507, on the fifteenth day of March.” The same volume contains Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, three books; and at its end: “Thomas Anshelmi of Baden printed [this] at Pforzheim, in copper type and with most careful workmanship, in August, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, 1505, under the illustrious prince Christopher the Elder, Margrave of Baden.” Mr Jung, librarian of Strasbourg, most courteously shared this book with us.

## Brother Conrad Leontorius of Maulbronn Wishes the Benevolent Reader Happiness

[Col. 0097]

The thoughts which I suppose, benevolent reader, you have sometimes entertained and will still entertain have often troubled me as well: why such an abundance of books is appearing everywhere in our age. But when I consider more closely the purpose of this immeasurable abundance of books, I readily perceive that the singular and inexplicable benevolence of almighty God, joined with mercy, has graciously and sweetly resolved in this last age of mortals to come to the aid of us negligent people, us slothful people, us human beings enervated by unclean pleasures.

For now, in this corrupt age, perhaps scarcely one or two persons could be found to copy all those most excellent things which our ancestors and elders composed and wrote with great care. Therefore, lest their memorials and labours perish and the most excellent arts of every discipline be wholly forgotten, the best and greatest God has granted to the German nation this most beautiful distinction and ornament: the invention and art of printing books. Thus, in a single operation and labour—great though it is—more is now printed in one day, by means of those most skilfully devised forms, with the utmost cleanness and accuracy, than many men could write in a thousand days. Accordingly, in this happy age of ours, even the largest, best, and most carefully selected volumes in every kind of letters and disciplines can be purchased for a small and trifling sum.

Let it therefore be most welcome to you, candid reader, that you can now most easily acquire and obtain letters, sciences, the arts of all disciplines, [Col. 0099] and finally every cultivation of the mind, even from the humblest books, by a modest outlay of money—as we are told that Pliny the Elder used to say: “No book is so bad that it does not prove useful in some respect.”

On this occasion, one distinguished citizen of the great city of Basel, Master Michael, surnamed Furter, a native of Augsburg, devoted to book-printing and eager for more correct learning, brought forth for publication this new little book which you see, diligent reader. As it had never previously been printed, certain learned men, and especially the most reverend Lord Telamonius, bishop of Tripoli, suffragan of the bishopric of Basel, outstanding professor of sacred letters and their public and highly eloquent lecturer, urged him not to permit this treasure—not large indeed, but exceptional and precious, containing three virtues—to remain hidden longer, exposed to dust and moths, and finally perish.

A single copy at Basel, written in an older script, was recently discovered. It was immediately inspected, read, examined, divided into chapters and books, and, wherever the old writing was uncertain, corrected and emended as fully as possible. It has been multiplied in the edition which you see, benevolent reader, and publicly offered for sale to you and to all who desire it: the work of the excellent, distinguished, learned, and eloquent Gunther, a most devout monk of Saint Benedict. Joining philosophy and humane letters to sacred theology, he composed and published, with great diligence, this work on the three most excellent virtues—prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—which no one before him, so far as was known, had undertaken.

But if you ask, reader, who or from where this Gunther was, I find that he was a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, whom the reverend, learned, and eloquent Johannes of Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, mentions in his catalogue *On Ecclesiastical Writers* as a man learned in both secular and ecclesiastical knowledge, from the monastery of Elnone. Among other works, he wrote in elegant verse the life and passion of Saint Cyriacus, and Trithemius states that he flourished in the time of Emperor Henry IV, under the year of the Lord 1100.

Do not neglect, therefore, friendly reader, to acquire and keep familiar this most elegant little book of Gunther—whoever he ultimately was—most suitable whether you wish to speak rhetorically to the people concerning these customary virtues of which it treats, to debate in an assembly, or to stir yourself to devotion. Together with me, offer and give immortal thanks to the distinguished printer, Master Michael, citizen of Basel, often recalling that Virgilian line:

> Your honour, name, and praises shall endure for ever.

Fare well, excellent reader.

From the narrow valley beyond the Basel hide-market, 18 February 1507.

## Preface

[Col. 0099]

Among the many volumes of the holy Fathers by which God’s Church has been illuminated and adorned, to produce something new for reading is almost nothing other than to help the sun’s rays with a lighted torch, add a handful of dust to the sands of the shore, or pour a few drops of water into the fullness of the sea. Yet, since it is the nature of mortals to delight especially in new things, we resolved to try whether we might compose something worthy of the pen on these three subjects—prayer, fasting, and almsgiving.

We took all the more care to put this purpose into effect because the Scriptures so often admonished us concerning the virtue and praise of these matters; yet a special treatise on them either exists nowhere or has never come our way to read. We did, therefore, as we had conceived in mind, and treated these subjects with the greater care because we know them to be pleasing to God, useful to humanity, and especially suited to our profession. We have chosen, however, to labour more fully and diffusely upon prayer, because in this matter we act jointly with God; whereas in the remaining two, one is to be performed in relation to ourselves and the other in relation to our neighbours.

Having completed this little work and carried it, so far as we could, through to its conclusion, we divided it into thirteen books, so that the narrower their contents, the easier they may be to understand. We have also thought fit to set down in advance the chapters of each book, so that, upon examining them, the reader may readily observe what is chiefly treated in them. First, then, comes the prologue to the entire work. In it, according to Cicero’s precept, the reader’s goodwill is won, teachability prepared, and attention aroused, by introducing the subject, demonstrating its usefulness, and commending its authority.

## Chapters of Book I

The first book begins to treat prayer, which it divides into four kinds: grammatical, dialectical, rhetorical, and catholic prayer. Having briefly touched on these and left the others aside, it takes up catholic prayer, teaching what must be investigated concerning it: namely, what it is; what it contains in itself; in what cases it obtains its effect; what pertains to it; what is fitting for one praying; and what results from prayer. It then defines prayer and carefully explains its definition. Next it shows the various modes of praying or worshipping. It also shows various divisions of certain matters relating to definitions, and some other points.

## Chapters of Book II

The second book teaches what prayer contains, namely these six things: who asks; what he asks; from whom he asks; for whom he asks; why he asks; and how he asks. It then treats the first component of prayer, namely who asks, and on this occasion sets forth the various classes of faithful and unbelieving persons, and among unbelievers shows various sects. It also teaches what living or dead works are, how they are subdivided, and many other things useful to the reader.

## Chapters of Book III

[Col. 0101]

The third book treats the second component, namely what one asks: good, evil, or something intermediate. It sets forth the various kinds of good: preparatory good, inspiring good, meritorious good, merit, and remunerative good, which is eternal life, together with certain other matters.

## Chapters of Book IV

The fourth book treats meritorious good, that is, virtue; and merit, that is, the interior or exterior movement or act of virtue.

## Chapters of Book V

The fifth treats remunerative good, that is, eternal life, which is nothing other than God: why it is called eternal life; why God cannot properly be called by any name, since he is neither substance nor accident; why privative names are more truly said of God than positive ones; and why God is more truly called eternal than everlasting, perpetual, perennial, and the like.

## Chapters of Book VI

The sixth treats the various kinds of evil: prejudicial, hardening, privative, and meritorious evil; merit deserving death, punitive evil, namely eternal death; and the opposition of evils to goods. It treats intermediate things in the soul, body, and external circumstances, and divides them into joyful and sorrowful. It then treats the third component, namely from whom one asks; the fourth, namely for whom one asks; the fifth, why one asks; and the sixth, how one asks.

## Chapters of Book VII

The seventh treats the topic, namely, in what cases prayer obtains its effect, that is, is heard. Here there is a comparison of all six components: who asks, what he asks, from whom he asks, for whom he asks, why he asks, and how he asks. From these the effect of prayer is drawn out; and it is shown that spiritual goods—such as the forgiveness of sins, virtues, and their works—are granted both to the elect and to the reprobate, though with dissimilar fruit. It also treats intermediate things of body, soul, or those external to the nature of either: why their joyful or sorrowful aspects commonly happen to both groups. It also treats there one who prays for another: namely, who can obtain eternal life for whom, and under what additional conditions. It likewise treats the four remaining spiritual goods and intermediate things which one person can obtain for another by prayer.

## Chapters of Book VIII

The eighth enumerates the matters pertaining to prayer: time, place, manner, and form. It also treats the first three—time, place, and manner—with several rather necessary discussions interposed on the differences among days, nights, and hours.

## Chapters of Book IX

The ninth treats the form of prayer and enumerates four forms: the Lord’s, domestic, monastic, and ecclesiastical. On this occasion it also treats the Lord’s Prayer: its first four petitions are considered there in the order in which the Lord set them forth; and the four gifts of the Holy Spirit, four virtues, and an equal number of beatitudes are assigned to those same petitions.

## Chapters of Book X

The tenth treats the remaining three petitions, to which are fitted three corresponding gifts of the Holy Spirit, three virtues, and three beatitudes pertaining to them.

## Chapters of Book XI

The eleventh treats the aforesaid petitions in reverse order, beginning with the last and proceeding to the first. In the same order, the aforesaid gifts of the Holy Spirit, virtues, and beatitudes are likewise assigned to them.

## Chapters of Book XII

The twelfth treats fasting: what it is, how many kinds it has, what is fitting for one fasting, and the usefulness or effect of fasts.

## Chapters of Book XIII

The thirteenth treats almsgiving: what it is, how many kinds it has, what is fitting for one who gives alms, and what results from it.

The list of books ends.

## Here Begins the Prologue to the Little Work of the Religious Prior, Lord Gunther, on Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving

[Col. 0101]

The Saviour himself disclosed how great is the power of prayer and fasting, and what effect almsgiving has, when he said: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by fasting [Col. 0102] and prayer” (Matt. 17). And elsewhere: “Give alms,” he says, “and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). You see that in the first two he established the prerogative of power, and in the third the purity of cleanness. From this it is indicated that there is no affliction caused by demonic power which is not driven away by the former, and no stain of sin which cannot be cleansed by the latter.

Knowing this, our same Saviour, desiring us also to experience it fruitfully, took care to show it not only by teaching in words but also by the example of his own actions. For we read that he prayed frequently and fasted continuously for forty days. And, leaving aside those benefits which he bestowed daily upon the needy—feeding the hungry, healing the sick, giving sight to the blind, raising the dead—his entire life in the flesh must be regarded for us as almsgiving, because *eleemosyna* means mercy, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Show us your mercy, O Lord, and grant us your salvation” (Ps. 84). By the Lord’s mercy and salvation he means his presence in the flesh, through which he deigned mercifully to save those who had justly perished through the sin of the first-created man.

This is that mercy by which the Samaritan was moved toward the man who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, who stripped him, inflicted wounds, and departed, leaving him half dead. “The Samaritan,” he says, “when he saw him, was moved with mercy. And coming near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine; and setting him upon his beast, he brought him to an inn, entrusting him to the innkeeper to care for him until, health recovered, he could safely return to his own city, from which he had incautiously departed.”

Jerusalem [Col. 0103C] is the vision of eternal peace; Jericho, interpreted as “moon,” is the failing of our mortality. The descending man is the first-created man with all his posterity; the robbers are demons; the plundered spoils are the loss of gratuitous goods; the wounds inflicted are the corruption of natural gifts. The Samaritan, also meaning “guardian,” is our Redeemer; his drawing near is his assumption of our infirmity. The binding of the wounds is the sacraments of our salvation; oil is spiritual grace, the hope of life, remedies of consolation, and the soothing comfort of promises. Wine, however, is the austerity of commandments, the piercing pain arising from the recollection of sin, the bitterness of threats, and the biting, continual remembrance of unending punishment.

The beast is the Redeemer’s body; the inn, the bosom of the Church; the innkeeper, the order of prelates, to whom the man redeemed through mercy is meanwhile left to be cared for, until he can safely be restored to the visions of eternal peace. From what has been said it is plain how greatly these three matters introduced above please our Redeemer within us, since he taught and fulfilled them with such zeal, as it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

Indeed, for the perfection of a higher life, all virtues must be joined together and one’s manner of life must be formed by them, after the example of the man who, wishing to sculpt a most beautiful statue, ordered many of the maidens of Croton, all of them beautiful, to be presented to him, so that, considering each face and limb, he might bring together into one the most elegant feature of each in order to express the grace of the beauty he intended to portray. But for us, who are devoid of and ignorant of all such matters, since they are known only through experience, it may suffice to say something about those matters set forth above, perhaps bringing in some others incidentally—like a blind man who marvels at and praises the brilliance of gems.

And this we do in a humble style and plain speech: both because the coarseness of our intellect permits us no other course, and because we do not wish to seem to imitate certain especially superstitious persons [Note: [Col. 0103C] Or *suscipiosos*?] who suppose they have said nothing unless they have spoken so excellently that [Col. 0104C] they do not understand themselves. Let such people keep their hateful and obscure subtlety; although perhaps they alone do not know everything, they glory that they alone know everything. Our purpose in this work, however, is not so much to tickle ears with elegant words or shadow meanings with obscure subtlety, as to investigate clearly the truth of the matters under discussion, and to communicate in plain and tangible speech to simple persons like ourselves what he has inspired—he without whom nothing can rightly be done or said.

The prologue ends.

# Book I: On Prayer

## On the Division of Prayer into Four Kinds: Grammatical, Dialectical, Rhetorical, and Catholic Prayer

[Col. 0103]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0103C]

First, therefore, we must treat prayer and implore him who both commanded and taught his own to pray, that he may deign to show us not only that prayer is necessary, but also what may suitably be said concerning prayer itself. Since the term *oratio* is equivocal, applying to several things, we must first set forth a division of prayer, so that, leaving the others aside, we may choose the kind which we intend to discuss.

Prayer or discourse is therefore of one kind grammatical, of another dialectical, of another rhetorical, and of another catholic. Grammatical discourse is the fitting arrangement of words, made in conformity with their accidents. Dialectical discourse is the statement or proposition which a disputant employs [Col. 0105A] in syllogizing. Rhetorical discourse is the whole speech employed by an orator in persuasion. Catholic prayer is the devout invocation of God by which a person supplicates in order to obtain something.

The first concerns the agreement of words; the second investigates the consequence of things; the third debates a contested action; the fourth implores the clemency of divine mercy. In the first, syntax—that is, construction—is formed according to the agreement of accidents. In the second, a *thesis*, interpreted as “position,” is demonstrated: that is, a doubtful matter or one doubtfully set forth, by the necessity or probability of arguments. In the third, a *hypothesis* is treated: that is, a rhetorical question together with its circumstances, marked by this verse:

> Who, what, where, by what means, why, how, when—

according to the authority of the topics. In the fourth, God is appeased by humble and pure simplicity of voice and heart.

The verse given above is not to be understood merely as a list of circumstances—as many think, who examine the matter less carefully—but rather indicates all those things that are customarily handled in rhetorical discourse. The first two, namely “who” and “what,” constitute the hypothesis itself and are, as it were, the foundation and substance of the rhetorical question: when inquiry is made who did something and what he did, the hypothesis—that is, the rhetorical question—is principally constituted and founded in these. The remaining five indicate certain adjuncts of other matters, which are called circumstances, without which the action either could not occur or would be incredible. Of these, “where” determines the place of the act; “by what means,” its aid or resources; “why,” its cause; “how,” its quality or manner; and “when,” its time.

We thought these matters should be briefly mentioned because this distinction may soon assist us when the question is raised which things belong to the substance of catholic prayer and which are attached to it, as it were, from outside.

The first kind of discourse has as many parts as it has words, since a part of speech and a word are the same thing. Thus when you say, “Priscian reads,” this discourse has two parts. But if you say, “Priscian reads a book,” this discourse has three parts; and so with the rest [Col. 0105D] in the same way.

The second has as many parts as it has extremes or terms, which can be neither more nor fewer than two: subject and predicate. Either both are expressed, as when I say, “Socrates reads,” or one is understood in the other, as when I say, “It rains” or “It thunders.” For these words, and similar ones, have an implicit meaning belonging only to God, and in each of them the subject term must also be understood: thus when it is said, “It rains” or “It thunders,” it is as if one said, “God rains” or “God thunders.” Other expressions are normally understood by resolution: “It is being read,” that is, “the act of reading is being performed”; “one is standing” or “one is sitting,” that is, “such a bodily posture is maintained”; and the rest in this manner.

Rhetorical discourse has as many parts as it has distinct divisions, namely six: introduction, narration, division, confirmation, refutation, and conclusion.

Catholic prayer has as many parts as it has petitions, which vary in subject matter and number according to the choice of the person praying. They vary in subject matter because one person asks differently from another; in number because one asks for more or fewer things than another. Yet all things rightly asked—that is, for the salvation of the soul—however numerous they may be, may suitably be called one, because of the one end to which they ought to tend. The Lord marked this in the Gospel when he said, “But one thing is necessary” (Luke 10). And David in the Psalm: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26).

Yet in the form of prayer which the Lord gave, because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, with which he came full from the heavenly school and which he wished to pour into us also, he set forth seven petitions. With his help, something will be said concerning them when we begin to treat the form of prayer. The other kinds of discourse are expressed in the indicative mood; catholic prayer, however, is ordinarily made in the imperative. Yet when this mood is directed toward God, it should be called not so much imperative as supplicatory, because of the excellence of the Creator, whom no one is worthy to command. For a person praying need not be concerned with what Priscian commands, but with what a Christian owes to his God.

Having thus set forth the four-membered division of prayer, leaving the others to their own practitioners, [Col. 0106C] let us carefully consider this kind of ours, which belongs only to the faithful and seems especially to concern us: what it is; what it contains in itself; in what cases it obtains its effect; what pertains to it; what is fitting for one who prays; and what results from prayer. Accordingly, so far as the requirements of the work undertaken are concerned, it seems sufficiently fittingly defined if it is stated as follows:

### Chapter II
Catholic prayer is a regular and earnest imploring of the divine mercy for the salvation of the soul, or for those things which may benefit it. Let us now explain the definition itself more carefully, so that the thing defined may become clearer. “Imploring” is placed here as the genus and principle of prayer; because, as the philosophers say, [Col. 0106D] the definition of every thing must be drawn from its genus. Thus, if you wish to define man, you must begin from the genus and say: “Man is an animal.” But since this does not yet show what sort of animal man is, substantial differences must be added, so that by their addition you complete the definition thus: “Man is a rational, mortal animal.” “Animal” is indeed the genus; “rational” and “mortal” are substantial differences, also called specific differences, because, when added to the genus, they constitute the species. Porphyry teaches these matters very learnedly in his *Isagoges* to those entering upon the first lessons of logic. We needed only briefly to recall them, in order to show that this definition of Catholic prayer, which has been given by God, is perfect and convertible with the thing defined, so that nothing [Col. 0107A] should be removed or need be added. Therefore, “imploring” is the genus of prayer, just as “animal” is the genus of man; while the remaining additions serve as substantial differences, just as “rational” and “mortal” do in the definition of man.

## CHAPTER III

### The first difference

The first of these is expressed thus: “of divine mercy.” Of these words, namely “mercy,” the meaning is that the whole purpose of the person praying ought to tend toward gaining God’s graciousness and favour. For this is always the end of true prayer: whether God grants what is desired, as with Peter praying for the raising of Dorcas (Acts 9); or whether he refuses what is requested but bestows greater things, as with Paul asking that [Col. 0107B] Satan’s angel depart from him (2 Cor. 12); or even when he seems to act cruelly, as in the drowning of the Egyptians while the children of Israel cried out (Exod. 14); in the overthrow of Amalek through Moses’ hidden prayer (Exod. 17); in the burning of the king’s messengers, when the prophet was praying rather than calling down a curse (4 Kings 1); and in the crushing of the nations while the Maccabees cried to heaven (4 Maccabees).

For it is beyond doubt that all these works of divine power, and similar things scattered throughout the Holy Scriptures, flowed from the fountain of mercy: either that God might powerfully rescue his faithful, oppressed by the wicked; or that he might cut off from the wicked themselves, whom he foresaw could become still worse through prolonged life, the opportunity for subsequent evils by hastening their death; or that, if any among them were less [Col. 0107C] harmful, by punishing them temporally he might either wholly remit or mitigate eternal punishments; or that, by dealing gently with the wicked, he might establish for others examples of innocence to be followed, or, by scourging evildoers, frighten others away from imitating them; or for some other rational cause, plain to him but hidden from us.

For we are not so unwise—or rather, so shameless—as to dare to investigate all the causes of divine works or examine their ends. Since the things mentioned above and others of this kind are customarily both sought and obtained through prayer, it is unquestionably clear that in every true prayer the intention is to obtain mercy, and its end is mercy obtained. For what rhetorical speech does before an earthly judge, Catholic prayer does more truly and more effectively before the heavenly Judge. As the forensic speaker strives to win the judge’s favour for himself, so that he may persuade him more easily of his purpose, so the faithful petitioner seeks the grace of the supreme Judge, that he may obtain what he desires—or something else, according to the good pleasure of the giver.

But this prayer differs greatly from that speech; nor is the difference in effect less than that in disposition. By the former, what is unjust is often persuaded; by the latter, nothing but what is right and devout. The former consists in a noise of words, the latter in purity of mind. Hence that kind of speech is called *oratio*, as though it were *oris ratio*, “the discourse of the mouth,” as the philosopher says: “By *logos* I mean reason uttered by the mouth.” But this may more truly be called the discourse of the heart—that is, its rectitude and purity. By the former, falsehood frequently wins belief from the judge; through this alone [Col. 0108A] truth does not merely become known, but pleases.

Of the former the satirist says:

> Then the hollow bellows breathe out immense lies.  
> (Juvenal 7)

Of the latter the Lord says: “Those who worship [God] must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). The former is set in shouting and litigation; the latter in silence and love. By the former injustice is often defended and innocence condemned; by this guilt is forgiven and purity commended. The former is stronger the more cunning its practitioner; the latter, the simpler it is. The former requires the support not only of the judge, but also of assessors and witnesses; the latter is content with the favour of the Judge alone. The former is strengthened by a multitude of words; for this, the intention of the spirit alone suffices. “God is spirit,” says the Saviour, “and those who worship him must worship [Col. 0108B] in spirit” (ibid.).

And it was said to Moses (Exod. 4), “Why do you cry out to me?”, although one does not read that he uttered even a single word there. Therefore God, who is spirit, must be addressed spiritually, so that he may understand what we ask, and, understanding, assent; assenting, hear us. Yet words of the body are often added to the intention of the spirit, so that the devotion of both our inner and outer person may be approved. Whether, then, you pray in both ways or only in one—that is, by the spirit alone—it is certainly plain that prayer is nothing other than an imploring of mercy, as the preceding definition states.

“Divine” is expressly added for this reason: if you implore God in prayer, with the other requirements for this being present, that is finally prayer; and it belongs to what [Col. 0108C] the Greeks call *latreia*, that is, divine service; or *theosebeia*, that is, the worship of God; or *eusebeia*, which we may call good worship. But when you implore something other than God, though still on account of God—for example, heavenly spirits, called by the Greeks *kalodaimones* (“good spirits”); or those human beings whom no Christian doubts have been received into eternal glory—it cannot properly be prayer, especially since it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4).

Certainly, since to worship is nothing other than to direct prayer to someone or something, just as it is permitted to worship God alone, so neither is it allowed to pray to anyone else. The Psalmist understood this well when he said: “Let all the earth worship you, O God” (Ps. 65), [Col. 0108D] and elsewhere: “Worship him, all his angels” (Ps. 96). For we do not intend to pray to them, but to entreat them that they themselves may pray for us when we say, “All saints, pray for us,” and similar words. These are therefore not prayers, strictly speaking, but certain devout supplications; and they belong to *dulia*, the honour due to a creature out of reverence for the Creator.

But if you implore any creature whatsoever—not for God’s sake but as though it were God—for example, the sun, moon, stars, evil spirits, whom the Greeks likewise call *kakodaimones* (“evil spirits”); or dead human beings, such as Jupiter or Saturn; or some manufactured thing, such as an idol; if, I say, you implore anything of that kind, this is neither of the foregoing but is rather called an execration or sacrilege. [Col. 0109A] It belongs neither to *latreia* nor to *dulia*, but rather to an affront to the Creator. This is what the Lord complains of concerning the children of Israel in the words of the prophet: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know” (Deut. 32). And shortly afterward: “They provoked me by that which was not god, and angered me with their vanities” (ibid.).

### The second difference

The second difference is that prayer must be regular; that is, it must be regular prayer performed within the bosom of the Church. For just as, in Augustine’s witness, there is no place for true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, so neither is there for true prayer—especially since the Psalmist offers prayer itself as a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord: “Let my [Col. 0109B] prayer,” he says, “be directed as incense before you” (Ps. 140); and elsewhere: “The lifting up of my hands [is] the evening sacrifice” (ibid.).

For if one must worship in spirit and truth (John 4), and the Holy Spirit is not possessed by grace outside the nest of the Church; and again, if there is no truth apart from integrity of faith, since Christ himself is Truth, then it is evident that those outside—namely Jews and Gentiles who have never accepted faith in Christ, or heretics who have torn themselves away from faith once received through schisms or heresies—are permitted neither to pray nor to worship. But because the meaning of these terms is customarily extended also to things which can be done outside the Church, or which are customarily offered within the Church not to God alone but also to other things, it is worthwhile to provide a useful [Col. 0109C] division concerning these matters.

### Division of worship

Worship is therefore of one kind divine veneration; of another, devout supplication; another, devout remembrance; another, mystical signification; another, vain display; another, feigned pretence; another, just satisfaction; another, perfect humility; another, due submission; another, mutual affection; another, wicked mockery; another, compelled necessity; another, deceived vanity; another, detestable impiety.

Divine veneration is that which is offered to God alone, of which the Psalmist says: “Worship him, all his angels” (Ps. 96), and elsewhere: “All kings shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71). Devout supplication is that by which those worthy of seeing holy angels or holy persons already blessed—such as Daniel, John, and many others—venerate them with due honour; and by which we too, though sinners, humbly entreat them to help us before God, as is customary in a litany. Devout remembrance is that by which we venerate, with whatever reverence we can, holy places, relics of the saints, or anything that recalls to our minds the mysteries of our salvation, such as the Lord’s cross or his tomb, for the honour of him who sanctifies these things. This may be the sense of: “We shall worship at the place where his feet stood” (Ps. 131): [Col. 0110A] that it should be referred to those places which the Lord, in the flesh, pressed with his sacred footprints; just as the prophet’s words also say: “His tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. 2).

Due submission is that by which we humble ourselves, even in bodily posture, before our prelates and rulers, or before those persons to whom we are lawfully subject; as Esther is read to have worshipped King Ahasuerus (Esther 5, 10), and, by the very right of subjection, as a captive woman [worships] a king or a wife her husband—apart from the mystery in which he signified Christ and she the Church. Mutual affection is that by which we incline toward one another, not through any legal obligation but through affection of charity alone. This seems especially fitting for persons of our profession, because they ought above all to pursue humility; as we read that certain holy men, not unequal in merits and life, prostrated themselves to one another in mutual humility, asking each other for blessing and prayers.

Just satisfaction may be called that by which a guilty person entreats one whom he remembers having offended to forgive him, whether kneeling or prostrate with his whole body; as Jacob worshipped his brother Esau when Esau came to meet him, whom Jacob had defrauded of the birthright (Gen. 33). Feigned pretence is that by which heretics, or thoroughly wicked Christians living among us in the Church, outwardly venerate with counterfeit piety those sacraments which they despise in their hearts. I do not know whether there has ever been a more fruitful pestilence of such persons than there is now, except that they are restrained by fear of the Church’s vigorous discipline.

Mystical signification was that by which Rebecca, as a type of the Church coming from the Gentiles, worshipped Isaac under the image of Christ; [Col. 0110C] when he, as it is written in Genesis, had gone out into the field to meditate (ch. 24): certainly upon nothing other than the salvation of the human race. Of this meditation the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jer. 29); and in another prophet: “I have turned and thought in these days to do good to the house of Judah and Jerusalem” (Zech. 8).

Vain display is when someone prays publicly for empty glory. This is characteristic of hypocrites, of whom the Lord says: “They love to pray standing in the streets, that they may be seen by men” (Matt. 6); and elsewhere: “They devour widows’ houses under the pretext of lengthy prayer” (Mark 12). Among their number was that proud Pharisee who, despising the publican’s humility, [Col. 0110D] prayed thus within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, unjust men, adulterers, or even like this publican” (Luke 18).

Wicked mockery was that by which the Jews, kneeling, mocked the Lord, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews,” and so forth (Matt. 27; Mark 15; John 16). Like them are those who pray for their sins but nevertheless do not fear to repeat them. Unless perhaps those who despised the true man will seem less harmful than those who, in contempt, spit upon and strike by provoking the face of divine brightness, present everywhere, which they seek to appease by prayers. For when someone says to God, “Show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 7), and then despises and more gravely provokes him as he looks upon him and wishes to spare him, what else does he do but importunately strike and spit upon the face [Col. 0111A] of the God whom he falsely implores?

Perfect humility is that by which someone voluntarily subjects himself in humility to one inferior, as Solomon did. Although, as a most powerful king, he was bound to rise for no human being and worship no one except God, yet when his mother came to him he rose and humbly worshipped her, as is set forth in the book of Kings (3 Kings 2). We call compelled necessity that which occurs through fear or some pressing necessity, as Joseph’s brothers are related to have worshipped him in Egypt (Gen. 42–45).

Deceived vanity is that by which foolish people, deceived by empty error, reverence in foolish fear creatures even inferior to themselves or works of their own hands. Of such persons the Psalmist says: “Let all who worship carved images and glory in their likenesses be put to shame” (Ps. 96). The final kind, called detestable impiety, is that by which certain people, not so much foolish as impious, both worship and invoke demons themselves as gods, to the Creator’s insult. Of them the Psalm says: “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95). Therefore, though there are so many forms of worship, the first, which is due to God alone, belongs to *latreia*; all the others that savour of piety belong to *dulia*; and the rest certainly belong to injury and contempt toward God.

### The third difference

Thirdly, prayer is said to be earnest—[Col. 0111C] that is, diligent, solicitous, and attentive—lest, if you pray negligently, you fall into the fault rebuked by the Lord through the prophet: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 49; Matt. 15).

The earnestness of prayer consists in two things: devotion and compunction. In devotion, because, if you do not pray devoutly, you either disregard or do not understand what prayer is. For it is highly improper to say to God, “Attend to the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 60), when you yourself do not take care to attend through devotion. In compunction, because whoever is not pricked by contrition of spirit is not anointed with the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Where nothing hurts, medicine is not usually applied. For the Lord heals only the [Col. 0111D] contrite in heart, who say to him with the Psalmist: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40).

Again, devotion is considered in two respects: love of God and desire for the kingdom. In love of God, because you cry out in vain if you do not love, since God is the examiner of hearts. As he graciously hears those who love him, so in anger he turns his ear away from those who do not love him (1 Kings 16). For both are written: “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8), and “I shall repay those who hate me” (Deut. 32). And to Mary: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7).

In desire for the kingdom, because you ask in vain if you do not desire; for the kingdom of heaven is not given to the fastidious and ungrateful—as temporal goods are here, which often come more abundantly to the contemptuous and proud—[Col. 0112A] but rather to those poor persons whose desire the Lord hears. Of them it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Compunction likewise consists in two things: hatred of sin and fear of punishment. In hatred of sin, because he who does not hate wickedness does not deserve grace. Hence, after the three verses in which he humbly sought pardon, the Psalmist added, as though giving a reasonable ground for obtaining it: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50). In fear of punishment, because he who does not fear being punished deserves not to escape punishment; as it is written to the Thessalonians: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them” (1 Thess. 5). And in Job (ch. 21): “They spend their days in prosperity and in a moment descend to hell.”

Three things invite us to the love of God: forgiveness of sins, the bestowal of merits, and certainty of promises. Of the first the Apostle says: “God has bestowed grace upon us in his beloved Son, in whom we have forgiveness of sins” (Eph. 1); of the second, the same Apostle: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4); of the third he says elsewhere: “I am certain that the just Judge is able to keep my deposit until that day” (2 Tim. 1).

Likewise, three things urge us to desire the kingdom: fellowship with angels, the immensity of rewards, and the eternity of joys. Of the first the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will confess him in the kingdom of his Father and [Col. 0112C] of the holy angels” (Luke 12); of the second, the Psalmist: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30); of the third, Isaiah says: “Everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isa. 61).

Three things also ought to intensify our hatred of sin: the foulness of guilt, the soul’s wound, and the loss of innocence. Thus Paul said to those whom he wished, through the foulness of guilt, to lead into hatred of sin: “What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). Of sin’s wound in the soul the prophet Isaiah says: “A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore” (Isa. 1). Of the loss of innocence John says in the Apocalypse (ch. 2): “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent.”

Three things can instill fear of punishment in us: fellowship with demons, the severity of punishments, and the perpetuity of evils. All these are indicated in what the reprobate will hear: “Depart, cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). By “fire” is signified the severity of punishment; by “eternal,” its perpetuity; by “the devil and his angels,” fellowship with demons.

### The fourth difference

Let us now come to the fourth difference, which, owing to the lack of a word, we have chosen to explain by this circumlocution: “for the salvation of the soul, or for those things which can benefit it.” For this is how it was placed in the preceding definition. It should be observed that a circumlocution of two or more words—which the Greeks call *amphilogy* (*amphilogia*)—is sometimes used in place of a single name already found. Thus, instead of the already established name “rational,” following “animal,” the genus in the definition of man, one might use the construction “capable of reason,” or “fit to use reason,” or “that which is fit to use reason.” [Col. 0113A]

But sometimes an *amphilogy* supplies the place of a single word not yet invented. If, for example, the aforesaid name “rational” had not yet been invented, one of those circumlocutions would necessarily be used in its place. Thus this whole circumlocution, “for the salvation of the soul, or for those things which may benefit it,” ought to be understood as a single word not yet invented—either because usage has not yet so approved it,

> In whose power are the choice, right, and rule of speech;  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 72)

or because it could not easily be done that one name should express the meanings of so many words. The same is true of the two expressions “divine mercy”: they must be understood as jointly and necessarily placed in the definition of prayer in place of one word expressing a difference, which has not yet been invented.

These points, we believe, have been explained sufficiently carefully: first, so that, if anything of this sort should occur in the Scriptures, it may be more easily recognized; and second, so that nothing might remain obscure in the definition of the matter we wish to treat—especially since a definition is so called because it defines and limits a thing as though enclosing it within certain boundaries; whence it is also called a *term* by the philosopher. [Col. 0113C]

Let us now consider the meaning of this differential amphilogy. “For the salvation,” he says, “of the soul, or for those things which can benefit it,” because whether you implore the salvation of the soul or body, or things necessary to both, such as virtues and material resources, in a fitting manner, it is manifest that all are referred to one end. For as the body is the instrument of the soul for living rightly, and external goods are aids to the body, so we are commanded first and principally to pray for the soul’s salvation; secondarily, we are neither commanded nor forbidden to ask for bodily safety and other temporal things. The Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added [Col. 0113D] to you” (Matt. 6).

Whatever else you attempt to ask beyond these things is either superfluous, harmful, destructive, or even execrable. It is superfluous if you seek many resources when you can be content with few; harmful if you seek an occasion for sin, such as a beautiful wife; destructive if you seek an enemy’s death; execrable if you seek the eternal perdition of his soul. Therefore, instructed by the Lord’s command, let us seek the kingdom of God—that is, eternal blessedness—with every urgency of prayer. If other things are lacking, let us either leave them to his providence, which knows best what is expedient for us, or, if we wish to ask for them, let us ask only so as to refer their use to obtaining that which is to be enjoyed—namely eternal life, which is God.

For we are commanded to enjoy eternal goods—or rather, the one eternal good: for there is only one, and it is God. We are commanded, I say, to enjoy that eternal good; we are permitted to use temporal things.

To enjoy is to cling in love to a thing solely [Col. 0114B] for its own sake. This ought to be done only in relation to God, who alone is to be loved for his own sake and not for another; all else, however, for God’s sake. To use, on the other hand, is to refer whatever has come into one’s possession to obtaining that which is to be enjoyed; otherwise it is more rightly called abuse than use.

If, therefore, all things rightly loved among temporal things are to be loved for God alone, and God for his own sake, it is surely plain that in everything we love in due order, causally speaking—if one may speak thus—we love nothing other than God. For just as a man who fights in hope of praise and the crown which he confidently expects from his emperor is said to love not so much the art of fighting or the weapons he uses as the commander for whose sake he does this and from whom he awaits the reward, so in all things which we love for God’s sake, we must be understood to love God.

## CHAPTER IV

### Recapitulation of the definitions

[Note: [Col. 0113] Ed.: “He summarizes the definition. Final chapter of the first book.”]

Now, if it please you, let us collect in a concise and brief epilogue, for the clearer understanding of the matter, the points scattered throughout the definition. Prayer, then, was called, by its general name, “imploring,” because in every prayer we regularly intend to implore something. “Of divine mercy” was added, lest you suppose that anything is to be sought from anyone other than God; and such a thing as you can request devoutly and he can grant mercifully. Prayer must be regular, so that it is performed within the bosom of Catholic [Col. 0114D] truth; and earnest—that is, diligent and attentive—for the salvation of the soul or the things pertaining to it, so that nothing which hinders or turns one away from it, indeed nothing that does not assist and advance toward it, may be sought in prayer.

# BOOK II

On the contents of prayer: namely, who asks, what is asked, from whom it is asked, to whom it is asked, why it is asked, and how it is asked.—On the first content of prayer

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115A] Although a lengthy investigation of words has sought, as far as possible, what prayer may fittingly be called, let us now proceed to matters which seem no less suitably capable of being said concerning it. First among these, we must see what prayer contains. It contains who asks, what he asks, from whom he asks, to whom he asks, why he asks, and how he asks. Prayer thus contains and embraces these things, not as parts of itself—for none of them is customarily placed in a prayer—but as parts of its matter. For all these things taken together are the matter of prayer; prayer moves in and around them and treats of them, to such an extent that if one should be missing, it could not even be called prayer.

There are other parts of prayer, both simple and composite. We have already assigned some of them when we said that Catholic prayer has as many parts as it has petitions. This, however, must be understood only of composite prayer. For prayer is found to be either simple or composite. Simple prayer is that which is expressed by one deprecatory verb only, whether it seeks only one thing, as in: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18); or several things, as if you say: “God, give me forgiveness of sins and eternal life.”

This corresponds to a categorical proposition, which is expressed by only one indicative verb and which logicians also call simple: whether that one verb joins only one predicate, as “Socrates is musical,” or several, as “Socrates is musical and grammatical.” Likewise, each of these is simple: whether you say, “Tully sees Socrates,” or, “Tully sees Socrates and Plato.” [Col. 0115C]

We call composite prayer that which is expressed through several deprecatory verbs, as if you say: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner; grant forgiveness of sins; bestow eternal life,” and whatever similar matters you may wish to continue. This again corresponds to a hypothetical proposition, which consists of several verbs and which the same logicians call composite: whether it consists of two categorical propositions, as this: “If Socrates were a man, Socrates would be an animal”; or of four, as this: “If everything laughable is a man, and every man is an animal, then if Socrates is laughable, Socrates is an animal.”

And as in a hypothetical proposition every categorical proposition is both a proposition and a part of the statement, so in composite prayer every simple petition is both a prayer and a part of the prayer. Simple prayer, following the model of grammatical discourse, has as many parts as it has words; but these are understood differently. For in Catholic prayer both the utterances and their meanings are considered, whereas in grammatical discourse attention is given only to utterances, with no concern at all for meaning. The grammarian begins with sound, proceeds from sound to letter, from letter to syllable, from syllable to word, and from word to speech; and he considers all these according to the mere propriety of sound. Afterwards he hands over the grammatically constructed speech to the dialectician and rhetorician as an instrument suitable for treating thesis and hypothesis.

## CHAPTER ONE

We believe it has been shown quite clearly that, although prayer has other parts, these six matters now to be discussed are by no means parts of prayer. Nor, again, can we call them *per jocos*, that is, circumstances, for there are other circumstances more properly assigned to it, of which we shall not be reluctant to speak in their proper place. [Col. 0116B] For the present we must treat these matters, and first consider who asks in prayer: namely, whether a believer or an unbeliever.

For the term “prayer,” taken more broadly, extends also to those acts which may be performed by unbelievers, as was shown above. Thus we read in the Gospel of certain Gentiles who had come to Jerusalem to worship (John 1). The publican and the Pharisee are also said to have gone up to the Temple to pray (Luke 18).

Every unbeliever is either a Gentile, a Jew, or a heretic. The first not only does not accept the salvation offered by faith, but through folly despises even hearing and recognizing it. The second does recognize it and understands it from his own Scriptures, but rejects it through envy and contempt for Christ. The third both recognizes and accepts it, but afterwards tears himself away from what he has accepted through pride. The first, therefore, is wicked and ungrateful; the second envious and obstinate; the third faithless and arrogant.

Since the Saviour came into the world for the salvation of all, bringing both words of teaching and precepts of righteousness, let us now see how great an insult is inflicted upon both by this threefold class of unbelieving persons. For an example of contempt for the precepts, we may take three wicked and destructive citizens who must, willingly or unwillingly, live under one and the same great ruler. The first neither reads nor accepts that ruler’s most just laws, already written and publicly promulgated; the second indeed reads them but does not accept them; the third reads and accepts them, but later perverts what he has accepted and stubbornly urges all whom he can persuade to overthrow them.

For contempt of the Saviour’s teaching, let three shameless disciples serve as an example. One neither hears nor approves the word of a teacher who teaches excellently; the second indeed hears it but disapproves; the third hears and approves [Col. 0117A] it, but later, through pride, obstinately attacks it and joins to himself all whom he can for attacking it. These three classes of reprobate persons differ from one another not only in their whole manner of life—if it can indeed be called a manner governed by reason—but even within each class some oppose others by differing opinions. Nor is it surprising that those alienated from Truth, which is Christ, should be entangled in various deceits of error.

For when many run outside the path, there is no reason why one should be said to run more rightly than another. Although one is nearer to the way and another farther away, all nevertheless run uselessly so long as they remain outside it; nor will they ever reach the place to which it leads unless they enter the way.

Among the Jewish people there were perhaps formerly several sects, but two were especially notable. One was that of the Pharisees, who both confessed the resurrection of the dead and received all the Scriptures of the Old Testament. The other was that of the Sadducees, who neither expected resurrection nor cared to receive any Scriptures of the old page beyond the five books of Moses.

Among the Gentiles too, they say, there are many varieties of error; yet all divide principally into two groups: those who trace their origin from Ishmael, Abraham’s son, accept circumcision, and are called Ishmaelites; and the others, born uncircumcised, who are especially called Gentiles and remain in the condition in which they were born. [Col. 0117B]

The plagues of heretics are innumerable. Isidore, in his book of *Etymologies*, describes about seventy sects differing from one another both in name and in their particular articles of error. Since listing them now involves more labour than benefit, it is better to consider that heretics are customarily named for four causes. Some are named after provinces, such as the Cataphrygians; some after the founders of their heresies, such as the Marcionites; some after the distinction of sanctity which they arrogate to themselves above others, such as the Cathars, “the pure”; some after an error which they invent or follow, such as the Anthropomorphites, who falsely suppose that God the Father is transformed into the shape of a human being. For *anthrōpos* in Greek means “human being” in Latin, while *morphē* means “form.”

It should also be observed that the term “heretic” is sometimes taken more broadly and sometimes more strictly. In the broader sense, “heretic” denotes both one who stubbornly tears himself away from the unity [Col. 0117D] of the Church and one who perverts that Church’s sacraments; likewise one who knowingly misunderstands the Holy Scriptures, or who, for temporal advantage and especially for the sake of his own honour or leadership, either devises or follows false and novel opinions. This final sense, although Augustine treats it separately, nevertheless seems capable of being fittingly joined to the three preceding senses.

In the narrower sense of the aforesaid name, the following division may be made. Of those who, after receiving the sacraments of faith, decline and fall away from the rule of truth by living wickedly: one remains hidden within the Church and disturbs it by depraved conduct, as a false Catholic; another utterly renounces the Christian faith, though he cannot cease to be a Christian, as an apostate or apostatical person; [Col. 0118A] another, while retaining the form of faith, violently severs himself from the unity of the Church, as an antipope or schismatic; another knowingly corrupts the sense of Holy Scripture, and may be called errant; another perverts the sacraments of the Church or the articles of faith, and this one is properly called a heretic. Now “heretic” is derived from the Greek *hairesis*, meaning “choice,” because each person chooses, according to his own judgment, what he will follow.

Therefore, although all unbelievers disagree in their impiety, they nevertheless have one lot and an equal condition: namely, in that all are outside, and through the demerit of their unbelief are cut off from those things which can either be done or be of benefit only in the Church. Some of them stand far away, namely the Gentiles, who, apart from the nature by which they are human beings, are joined to us by no fellowship either of morals or of faith. [Col. 0118B] Others come nearer, namely the Jews; although they reject the grace of Gospel truth and the sacraments of faith, they nevertheless share with us in participation in the Old Scripture. Others are near, namely heretics, who, using the same writings, morals, and sacraments as we do, differ from us in a few matters.

Yet they are not for that reason to be loved more, since they approach us not with the affection of peace but with deceit; nor are they to be feared less, because, as the philosopher says, no pestilence is more effective in doing harm than a familiar enemy. Yet among these classes of people there are degrees and boundaries—not only between their different sects, but also among different persons within the same sects—not indeed of virtues, for among them there are none, but rather, to put it more truly, of greater or lesser wickedness.

For I judge the Gentile less depraved who, fulfilling by upright works the natural law written in his heart, lacks only the faith requisite for perfection of life—such as Cornelius was (Acts 10), even before he began to consider Christ’s faith in his mind—than one who both despises the salvation of faith and profanes the law of nature by many and grievous crimes: such as Herod, both he who without cause slaughtered so many thousands of infants (Matt. 2), and he who, defiled by adultery with his brother’s wife, made his banquets dreadful by the murder of a most holy man as the price of an obscene dancer (Matt. 14).

Again, we consider less impious the Jew who, not yet acknowledging the light of Gospel truth, [Col. 0118D] faithfully observes the commands of the old law according to the tenor of the letter—such as Nathanael, of whom the Saviour said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John 1)—than one who both rejects grace and transgresses the law by wicked living. Such were those whom the same Saviour, when they refused to hear the words of his most holy preaching, rebuked even for transgression of the Mosaic Law, in which they gloried while professing to keep it, saying: “Did not Moses give you the Law? Yet none of you keeps the Law” (John 7).

And among heretics, less pestilent is he who, differing in a few and minor matters, shares communion with us in many and greater sacraments: such are the Pelagians, who, agreeing with us in other things, say that free choice is sufficient without grace for attaining life. He is less pestilent than one who agrees with us in a few and lesser matters, but perverts and defiles more numerous and greater things by profane impiety: such as the Donatists, who falsely assert that the Son is less than the Father, and the Holy Spirit less than both; and that, just as there are three persons, so there are three substances in the Trinity.

Indeed, to add something boldly: the best Jew, Gentile, or heretic ought to be considered less hateful to God than the most disgraceful Christian. It has now sufficiently appeared that no unbeliever, however upright, has fellowship in true prayer, although many even among them—whether contemplating the Creator from created things, or taught by the testimonies of Scripture—by supplicating with all the humility they can, do not indeed pray, but imitate one who prays. This, however, is not blameworthy; for if they return to faith, this very thing may, once their works are made alive, turn to their salvation; but if they remain in their error, perhaps it may mitigate their punishment.

But whether the works of a preceding life, however good, can please God and can avail even for obtaining faith itself, is something which makes us doubt because Augustine says that Cornelius was heard before he believed in Christ, while elsewhere we read: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11); and Gregory says that he came to works through faith. Yet some resolve the difficulty of this question by saying that Cornelius, at the time when he prayed and bestowed alms, had faith in the future Incarnation, but not at all in the Incarnation already accomplished; [Col. 0119C] and thus was in part a believer and in part an unbeliever. They therefore say that Peter was sent to him in order, by instructing him more fully, to supply what was lacking. But since this is quite disputable, let us leave it to those able to investigate the matter more certainly.

## CHAPTER II

What was said a little earlier—that certain works can be made alive—seems necessarily to require the following distinction: all the works we do are either living or dead. We call living those that are useful for eternal life; dead, those that are liable to eternal death or useless for life.

Of living works, some are vital and others made alive.
