Vital works are those which, as soon as they are done, are good and therefore pleasing, because they are done in charity and have in them the spirit of life, such as the prayers and alms of the saints. But those are called made alive which, though they have the form of goodness, are not nevertheless good because they are not done in charity. If they were done in charity, they would certainly be good and vital; but when charity comes to them, they are animated and receive, as it were, a certain vital spirit, so that they too may be useful for life. Such are the prayers and alms of sinners who are converted, whether believers or unbelievers.

For we cannot judge equal in reward those of whom one, before conversion, amid many evils did nothing praiseworthy, while the other often prayed humbly, fasted greatly, and bestowed many alms upon the poor, if after conversion they either lived equally or departed this life immediately and at the same time. [Col. 0120A] For this seems greatly at variance with the judgment of the most just Judge, who rewards every good and permits no evils to pass unpunished.

Of dead works, however, some may be called mortal or death-dealing; others mortified or lifeless; others inanimate or unformed; others diseased or disease-producing. Mortal or death-dealing works are those which, as soon as they have been done, make their author guilty of Gehenna, such as murders, adulteries, fornications, and everything whose commission even once is sufficient to merit death. Hence it is called mortal sin.

Mortified or lifeless works are those which had formerly lived through charity but, when charity withdraws, expire and die—not so as to become mortal, but as becoming useless for life. [Col. 0120B] Otherwise those would seem equal of whom one, after many good works, fell into some grave sin, like David or Peter, while the other, destitute of all good works, defiled himself with many great crimes, like Herod or Pilate.

Those are appropriately called inanimate or unformed which, although they belong to the class of good works, are done apart from charity; and therefore, as lacking soul and form, they cannot move toward or attain the merit of life unless, as has already been said, they deserve to be made alive by the coming of charity.

Diseased or disease-producing works are what we call venial sins. They proceed not so much from the malice of the mind as from the sickness of human nature; nevertheless, they defile the soul and make it diseased, though not to the point of meriting eternal death, unless, having been multiplied, they become pleasing. For there is no sin so venial that it does not become mortal when it pleases. [Col. 0120C] From this distinction of works we must also derive the following distinction.

### Division of Works

Of good, evil, or any kind of works: some live from the beginning and never die, such as those of persons who, having once possessed charity, never abandon it, as Paul. Others live at first and die afterward: namely, those of persons who take no care to retain the same charity which they had begun to practise, as Solomon. Others are dead from the beginning and are afterward made alive: such as the good works done by Paul or Cornelius while they were still held by the sin of unbelief. Others are dead and are never made alive, nor can be made alive, such as all mortal or venial sins, which can never recover strength sufficient for the merit of life, even though they are corrected through repentance—not in order that they may contribute to salvation, but that they may not lead to death.

There are likewise other works which at first live, afterward die, and again return to life: namely, those of persons who, after some works of charity, fall into a mortal sin and are restored again through repentance, as David. There are likewise others which at first are dead, then, after being made alive, die again: namely, those of persons who have done certain works belonging to the class of good works because of charity, then are converted, and afterward relapse into wickedness. [Col. 0121A] I believe such persons are far easier to find in large numbers than to demonstrate by a single example, because it is very doubtful whether one whose first and last states we see to be wicked had true charity in the intervening period.

From this it is easy to observe that some works cannot in any way be had without charity: namely, all good works which we have called living, in either category. Some, however, are never had when charity is present: namely, all those which it pleased us to call dead, except venial sins alone. For if these could not be committed together with charity, Scripture would not say: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (John 1 [probably 1 John 1]).

Since, then, there are two kinds of living works, the first are said not only to be living but also to be vital—which is more—because they have always lived in charity. Thus we call someone “seeing” who has always seen, that is, who has never lacked the power of sight. The second, however, are called living works made alive, because, having first been dead, they deserved to be made alive by the coming of charity. Similarly, one is said to be seeing who has not always seen but received sight after long blindness, such as he who said: “One thing I know: whereas I was blind, now I see” (John 9).

But dead works, as we have said, are of four kinds. The first are called not merely dead but, more seriously, mortal or death-dealing, because they have never lived, are full of death, and bring death; and they cannot be made alive for the merit of life, even though they may be wholly erased through repentance. It is as when ice is called cold because it can never be warmed but is always cold and always makes things cold, although it can be dissolved so as to cease altogether to exist. [Col. 0121C]

The second are called not merely dead but mortified or lifeless, because after first living they ceased to live, just as we call a human corpse dead because it lived and ceased to live, and, when life departed, was mortified.

The third are called dead not because they first lived and were deprived of life, but because they are inanimate and do not yet live; just as we are accustomed to call a fetus dead before the infusion of the soul, not because it lived and ceased, but because it has not yet begun to live. These same works are also called unformed because they have not yet been formed by charity; they are like [Col. 0121D] an unformed fetus before the arrangement of its limbs, or like certain outlines made by a painter before color has been applied.

The works of the fourth kind are called dead because they are not merely useless but also harmful, though short of deserving eternal death. They are sins, but venial sins, unless they begin to please through contempt; for then, as has been said, they take on the effect of mortal sins. They are called dead according to the manner of speaking by which we call a dead person “dead,” who is not only useless to himself and others but also harmful. [Col. 0122A] They are also called diseased or disease-producing because they show the sickness of the human condition from which they arise and bring sickness upon the soul. Thus physicians speak of diseased signs and symptoms, because they both reveal and aggravate the disease from which they arise.

## CHAPTER III

But having lingered over these matters long enough, and not, we believe, without purpose—unless perhaps the reader thinks otherwise—let us proceed to what follows. Concerning unbelievers, enough has now been said, as far as the truth of the matter seemed to require.

But if a believer asks anything in prayer, he must be either just or unjust. If just, he will either persevere finally in his justice or relapse into wickedness. Likewise, an unjust person will either depart in his iniquity or return to justice. [Col. 0122B]

Thus the just person who will persevere in justice prays, as Elijah did when he shut heaven by prayers and opened it again (3 Kings 17). The just person who will relapse into wickedness prays, as Solomon did after happily completing the building of the Temple (3 Kings 8). The unjust person who will return to justice prays, as David did when stained alike by adultery and murder (2 Kings 11). The unjust person who will depart this life in his iniquity prays, as Judas did; the Saviour taught him to pray with the other apostles, though he was a thief and robber (John 12). Of him it is written in the Psalm: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108).

Everyone who will depart in justice undoubtedly belongs to the lot of the elect; but everyone who will depart in iniquity belongs to the number of the reprobate, whatever he may have been, whether a good or evil believer, a Gentile, a Jew, or even a heretic. Here, however, we mean by elect and reprobate those who have been either reprobated or elected from eternity. For both terms are used sometimes according to God’s eternal foreknowledge, and sometimes according to present justice or wickedness, which may perhaps not endure.

The Apostle speaks of the first election: “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1). Of the second, it is said in Job (ch. 40) that “the food of Behemoth is chosen,” because the malignant enemy sometimes devours and incorporates into himself those who seemed chosen because of their present justice. Again, of the first reprobation we read in Malachi [Col. 0122D] (ch. 1): “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? Yet I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated.” God’s hatred is reprobation. But concerning the second, the same Apostle says: “For this reason God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting” (Rom. 1). This must not be understood of eternal reprobation, for which there is no cause; rather, it must be understood of those reprobate persons who, because of a lesser wickedness which they refuse to abandon, fall, God abandoning them, into a greater one: “Let him who is filthy become filthier still” (Rev. 22).

# BOOK THREE

Concerning the second element of prayer: namely, what a person asks for—whether good, evil, or an intermediate thing. Concerning inspirative good.

[Col. 0123]

[Col. 0123A] We have treated the first element of prayer—namely, who asks—with care, because from this distinction and those which follow we shall have to draw out, insofar as God deigns to disclose it, a matter difficult to seek out and most difficult to know: namely, the obtaining or effect of prayer. Now, therefore, we must inquire with no less care concerning the second: what he asks for.

## CHAPTER I

For it matters what the person praying asks: whether he asks for good, or asks for or entreats against evil; or whether he asks for something which in its own nature is neither good nor evil, and which may suitably be called intermediate or indifferent.

By “good” we mean both eternal life and everything which cooperates with and assists in meriting and attaining it. By “evil,” conversely, we mean either eternal death or whatever impels toward it and aggravates it. By “intermediate” we mean that which in its own nature is neither good nor evil, according to the aforesaid sense of good and evil, but becomes good or evil through the use made of it by those who use it well or badly.

Each of these three is divided into different species. Good, then, is either remunerative—that is, eternal life—or the merit of eternal life; or meritorious, inspirative, or preparatory. The good which is eternal life is nothing other than God, who is supremely good and the highest good, and the cause and end of all goods. The merit of eternal life is a good work—that is, a good act, whether inward, as of the mind, or outward, as of the body. [Col. 0123C] Meritorious good is virtue—that is, a good quality of the mind, which is like an instrument of good work. Inspirative good is especially the infusion of grace, from which that good quality of the mind is produced. Preparatory good, however, is the remission of sins through contrition of heart; while sins remain, a human being could never be fit for the other goods.

Yet this contrition of heart, remission of sins, and indeed all that follows from the same grace of the Holy Spirit, have their cause, attain their effect, and receive their reward. For the Holy Spirit first cleanses, second breathes, third forms, fourth creates, fifth rewards. He cleanses guilt, breathes grace, forms the mind, creates good action, and rewards unto the crown. Hence Solomon says: “The Spirit goes round, surveying all things, and returns to its circuits” (Eccl. 1): not by local movement, but by a power absent nowhere. Likewise, since the Holy Spirit is frequently signified by the name of water, as in: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7), [Col. 0124A] according to what has been said, this too may fittingly be said here: “To the place from which the rivers come forth, they return, that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1).

## CHAPTER II

Concerning these five goods which those praying ought to ask for, and which are likewise gifts of the Holy Spirit, we must show, as he himself grants, how they arise. We listed them a little earlier, however, in reverse order, because there the first place had to be given to that which is the cause and end of all the others, and then we had to descend in reverse order to the lower things. Here we judge it more proper to treat them in the order in which they arise.

The first good, therefore, and the first necessary one, without which the others will not follow if it has not gone before, is contrition of heart. This occurs when the guilty person, visited by divine grace, begins to grieve over sin and is pierced through with his whole mind: “My tears became my bread day and night” (Ps. 42), in imitation of him who said: “Every night I shall wash my bed with my tears; I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6).

When this begins to occur, remission of sins is at once present; there is no interval of time between this and that, Scripture testifying: “In whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18), that is, worthy of salvation or fit to merit salvation. In the Gospel the sins of Magdalene were forgiven, as it were, in a moment, because she was deeply contrite and loved the Saviour greatly (Luke 7).

For the operation of the Holy Spirit, by whose agency this is done, is swift and is never delayed by any difficulty in the matter. Just as water simultaneously flows in and washes away filth; or as the breath of a blowing breeze simultaneously blows and drives away dust; or as the heat of fire or sun simultaneously strikes wax or ice and melts it: so the Holy Spirit, being cleansing water, enters and washes the human heart at once; being a purifying breeze, he breathes upon it and at once scatters every defilement of vices; being softening heat, at the first touch he dissolves all hardness of compacted or hardened malice. [Col. 0124C] For, as Scripture testifies, he disdains fellowship with vices and “will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1).

Concerning the first, God says through the prophet: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). For the second—that the Holy Spirit is a blowing breeze—you have in the Psalm: “His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147). That sins are dust, Isaiah says: “Arise, arise; shake yourself from the dust” (Isa. 52). Therefore, as the breeze of the Holy Spirit blows and the waters of tears flow through contrition of heart, all the dust of sins is altogether blown away.

Concerning the third, in reference to wax, we read in the Psalm: [Col. 0125A] “As wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 68). Concerning the same thing in reference to ice, we read in the book of the son of Sirach: “As ice in fair weather, so shall your sins be dissolved” (Ecclus. 3).

This good is called preparatory because through it we are prepared for the things that follow, for which we could never be fit unless this came first. Although this designation more especially befits this first good, it can nevertheless suitably apply to every one except the last. For this is the order of spiritual graces: the prior always prepares for that which follows, while first we receive grace freely, and then “grace for grace” (John 1), advancing “from strength to strength,” until “the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Ps. 84). For remission of sins prepares for [Col. 0125B] justice; justice, from the root of charity, produces virtue; virtue moves one to good action; good action receives the recompense of eternal life. Thus the order and progress of these goods are such that what precedes is naturally the cause of what follows, while what follows is the effect of what precedes.

## CHAPTER III

There is also another sort of preparatory good, which may also be called preordinative. It is as much more ancient than these in order and dignity as a fountain is worthier and more excellent than its streams: namely, eternal predestination, which prepares and preordains us for eternal goods, and eternal goods for us—namely eternal life—and, in addition, those temporal things through which we may attain it, namely those designated by the names of the remaining four species.

We excluded this from the foregoing division because the effect of prayer, which we intend to discuss, always depends upon the future; whereas the order of divine predestination was most certainly fixed from eternity and cannot be shaken by any reasoning. No one, therefore, asks that God may predestine him or may have predestined him, although all desire and request that which can happen only to the predestined, namely eternal life.

For imperative words, which we use as supplicatory words when praying, necessarily concern the future: either when the matter has already begun and the command is that it continue longer, as when you say to a boy who is already reading, “Read”—that is, persist in reading; or when it has not yet happened but is commanded to happen at once, as when you command a servant whom you are sending, “Return immediately”; or after some interval of time, as when you say, “Return tomorrow.”

Yet among the Greeks—bold and prolific inventors of words—there are imperative verbs of past time, when something which is not yet so is commanded to come about in such a way that it can be past in a subsequent time. Thus, if on leaving home you should command your servant: “When I return tomorrow, let the door be open for me.” In this expression, those same Greeks, who suffer nothing to be lacking to them in grammar, possess one imperative word in place of these two words, “open” and “let it be.” Because it commands that a thing shall in the future be past, they either boldly affirm or subtly falsely maintain it to be of past time. Yet that such words refer to future time and for that reason are more truly to be judged future in tense will not be doubtful to one who considers more carefully.

Since, therefore, nothing can either be commanded or prayed for except what is future or as though future, it is evident that the good of eternal predestination, which is more ancient than all things, cannot be subject to our temporal prayer, which concerns only the future. For this reason too, as has been said, we excluded it from the preceding division.

It is called the preparatory good of all the others because it prepares us first for grace, second for justice, third for merit, fourth for reward: for grace, by predestining according to the election of grace, because predestination is nothing other than the preparation of grace; for justice, by remitting sins through contrition of heart, [Col. 0126B] for once these are remitted, justification is immediately present; for merit, by producing virtues through a good quality of mind, without which we could never be fit to merit; and for reward, by bringing us to completion through good action, without which we should be judged unworthy of the reward of eternity.

Of the first preparation, which is for grace, Isaiah says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man, what you have prepared, O God, for those who love you” (Isa. 64). Of the second, which is for justice, we read somewhere: “The heart of man is prepared by the Lord.” And in the Psalm: “Your truth shall be prepared in them” (Ps. 89), that is, justice through faith in the apostles. Of the third, which is for merit, the Psalmist rejoiced when he said: “I am prepared and am not troubled, to keep your commandments” (Ps. 119). Of the last, which is for reward, that saying occurs in the Gospel: “The bridegroom came, and those who were prepared entered with him into the wedding” (Matt. 25; the printed citation reads Matt. 28).

And the first of these preparations, which is according to election, was completed and consummated from eternity, before there was anyone for whom anything could be prepared or predestined, as the Apostle says: “He chose us before the foundation of the world,” etc. (Eph. 1). The remaining three indeed happen temporally in us, who are subject to time; yet they descend from that eternal predestination by a most certain order. For before there was a human being to whom either sin might be remitted, virtue infused, or a good work bestowed, it was ordered by God’s preordination that the human being who would later exist should, by using the benefits of divine grace in this order, arrive at the blessedness prepared for him.

Therefore the first and highest of all goods is the election of divine goodness through eternal predestination; the second is remission of sins through contrition of heart; the third, justification through purity of soul; the fourth, the attainment of virtue through a good disposition of mind; the fifth, the consummation of justice through the performance of a good work; the last, the attainment of eternal blessedness through just recompense.

## CHAPTER IV

From this distinction, then, it has now, unless I am mistaken, become clear that every good is either preparatory and not prepared, prepared [Col. 0127A] and not preparatory, or both preparatory and prepared.

Preparatory and not prepared is eternal predestination, by which it prepares all other things and is prepared by none, because nothing precedes it. Prepared and not preparatory is eternal blessedness, for which all other things are prepared, and which itself prepares nothing, because nothing follows it. Both prepared and preparatory is any of the other things placed in the middle, because each of them both precedes another and follows another. They are rightly called prepared in respect to what precedes and preparatory in respect to what follows.

## CHAPTER V

### Concerning Inspirative Good

Enough has, we believe, been said at length concerning the first good which one praying ought to ask for—namely remission of sins, which we have also called specially preparatory. Let us now consider what may be understood by the second, which we have chosen to call inspirative.

Inspirative good, then, occurs when the Holy Spirit, having found for himself an entrance which was previously blocked by the filth of vices, flows more freely into the now-purified soul and gradually breathes into it the gifts of his grace. Yet he does this so subtly and secretly that neither the person in whom it occurs nor another can perceive it, as it is written: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his sound, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3).

First, indeed, he either creates or re-creates justice in the soul itself. He creates it through faith, which justifies the ungodly, if it was not there before; [Col. 0127C] but he re-creates it through the purity of innocence, if faith had previously been present but lay bloodless and dead, choked by vices. Then he continually breathes in other charisms of spiritual graces as well, namely virtues and good works, as it were by an unceasing breath.

For the breath of the Holy Spirit, unlike this airy wind, does not now begin to blow and now cease of its own accord. Once it has begun to breathe, unless it is again shut out by the filth of vices, it never interrupts or ends the course of its breath. Hence this designation too—inspirative—applies generally and equally with the preceding designation to any of these five goods except the last, because there is no gratuitous human good which the same Holy Spirit does not pour in by breathing it forth.

But the last good, eternal life, does not admit this designation. When that point has been reached, the soul, now placed in safety, is to be said not so much to be breathed upon in order to advance, as to enjoy and rest—just as a ship, once it has reached harbor, no longer needs the blowing of the wind, although by that wind’s service it was brought to the harbor itself.

For the whole life of a human being, from the first conversion until the attainment of the blessed life, is, to use a common illustration, a kind of spiritual voyage. To one about to sail, the first breath of a healthful breeze promises a prosperous sea journey and the desired end of the undertaking. Delighted by the mildness of the caressing breeze, he thrusts into the waves, with great exertion and labor, the ship clinging to the mud of a long-standing mooring; [Col. 0128A] he renews the rudder, arranges the rowers, and, with the mast raised, spreads the folds of the sails. Then, as the same breeze presses on more frequently and more beneficially, it does not cease to drive forward and attend the ship until it brings it, with all who are in it, to the harbor of the desired resting-place.

Mystically interpreted: the mildness of the breeze is the Holy Spirit; the sailor, the sinner wishing to correct his ways; the ship stuck in mud, the mind impressed with the filth of vices; the rudder, reason; the rowers, the faculties of the mind; the sail, the expansiveness of hope; the sea-voyage, the difficulty of a more austere life; the harbour, the attainment of eternal life. By experience of the things themselves I have learned how troublesome the beginnings of this voyage are. But what its end or [Col. 0128B] fruit will be, He knows whose office it is to measure the outcome of things by their certain end.

During these five years, whenever, having left the world behind, I both wished and feared to undertake better paths, for almost the whole of another ten years I heard, with the ear of my heart, the alluring breeze of the Holy Spirit calling me, as it were, out into the deep. And thus it was scarcely at last achieved that I moved the ship of my mind from the mud of its earthly station, to which it had always clung firmly—after much and prolonged struggling, and with very great help from Him who cooperated. Although I rejoice that this beginning of sailing has turned out happily for me, I nevertheless cannot help fearing errors and dangers amid the great and so uncertain sea of this present life, knowing that beginning belongs to many, but arriving belongs to those to whom God grants it.

I fear this great and spacious sea, [Col. 0128C] “wherein are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103). I fear waves and storms; I fear pirates and robbers; I fear the Syrtes and the Ceraunian rocks, the uncertain Cyclades, and the wave-tossed clashes of the Symplegades; and, to conclude briefly, a thousand causes of shipwreck. And, if those things which that greatest of Greek poets devised concerning the labours and dangers of the most experienced Ulysses—not so much poetically as philosophically—are to be referred to a mystery: I fear the Lotus-eaters and the Sirens; I fear the Laestrygonians and Cyclopes, Scylla’s barking and Charybdis’ devouring maw; Circe’s spells, the charms of Leucothea and Calypso, Neptune’s wrath, and the delights of the Phaeacians; and, after all these, when the smoke of his homeland was already in sight, the winds bursting out when the bags had been cut open, [Col. 0128D] and the repeated, lengthy wanderings of the fleet that had fallen back.

What mystical meaning all these may have among us—although it is tedious and difficult to determine what the secular philosophers who invented them themselves understood by them—we shall explain as briefly as possible, for the sake of the simpler readers for whom we write these things.

The waves of the sea, then, are the scandals and disturbances of the world; storms coming from the air are manifestations of wrath from above, that is, the indignation of divine vengeance. Both are to be feared by one sailing spiritually, lest either the flood of temporal concerns swallow him up while he is overly occupied, or the visitation of divine vengeance envelop him because he has deserved it through returning to iniquity. Hence David: “Let not the tempest of waters overwhelm me” (Ps. 68).

Storms [Col. 0129A] coming from the air may also be understood as the raging of the aerial powers, that is, demons, who never cease to shake and terrify with great and frequent storms of temptations those persons converted to God who desire to cross the sea of the present age without offence. As the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6).

Pirates—so called in Greek from fire, because they burn ships by throwing fire upon them—and robbers, who despoil, are malignant spirits. They consume human souls with the evil flame of desires and strip them of virtues. In this way was despoiled the man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, “who also stripped him” (Luke 10).

[Col. 0129B] The Syrtes, so named from *syrin*, “to draw,” because sands dragged along by waves are heaped up in the midst of the sea and hem ships in so that they cannot struggle free by any means, are the entanglements of earthly business. Surrounded by these, the soul is intercepted and hindered from reaching the harbour of its desired salvation. The Apostle warned Timothy to beware of these Syrtes when he said: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2); and elsewhere, addressing certain persons, he says: “I desire you to be without anxiety” (1 Cor. 7).

The long and renowned voyage of Ulysses, that most shrewd man, through so many labours, winding errors, and dangers, signifies the life of those who strive to return to their heavenly homeland through the sea of this age, full of hardships, treacherous through errors, and menacing with shipwreck [Col. 0129C]. They may say with the Apostle: “We have no abiding city here, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13); and elsewhere: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

The interpretation of his name itself also seems to allude to this. For Ulysses is said to be, as it were, *holoxenos*, that is, “a stranger to all.” For *holos* means “whole” or “all,” while *xenos* means “stranger”; and this suits those to whom the Apostle says: “I beseech you as sojourners and strangers” (1 Pet. 2). They may also say: “As long as we are in the body, we are away from Christ” (2 Cor. 5). Concerning this sojourn the Psalmist says: “Your statutes were my songs [Col. 0129D] in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118).

The Ceraunian rocks, which are interpreted as “horns of the sea,” are very high crags projecting from the middle of the sea; and the uncertain Cyclades are rocks which now appear and now are covered by water. They are the innumerable stumbling-blocks of the present life, whether manifest or hidden, against which the same soul is frequently dashed in the sea of this world: hidden ones, such as the slanders of those with whom one must live; manifest ones, such as outward persecutions. All these repeatedly strike, tear, and batter the mind of one sailing incautiously.

The Symplegades, that is, the floating rocks which, as the poets imagine, the earth hurled after the first ship because it resented being abandoned, are anxieties that pursue those leaving the world over things done before, or [Col. 0130A] left behind them. These often crush and overwhelm the wretched and heedless soul, while the person who has not renounced the world with sufficient purity both wishes to have greater power himself and to benefit his own people more than he previously could in the secular condition; and thus he suffers the pitiable shipwreck of the voyage he began.

Scylla, who has a maiden’s head but below, with her body divided, is girded with dogs, can signify those who present a good appearance and a simple countenance, but in their slanders assault us with the barking of dogs.

Charybdis, the sea’s whirlpool, which with insatiable greed swallows and spews back the waves, represents those who cruelly seize what belongs to others and squander with prodigal frivolity what has been wickedly acquired. Of them the poet says:

[Col. 0130B]

> They strive to seek in order to consume,  
> And, what consumed, seek yet again.

> And their very vices feed one another in turn.

Charybdis may also signify the instability of an unquiet mind, which is ceaselessly agitated, now drawing in and now casting out the waves of temptations.

The Lotus-eaters, called a sea-monster, and the Laestrygonians and Cyclopes, most cruel men who feed on human flesh, are monstrous demons. They incorporate into themselves, as if by devouring them, carnal sins—or rather, human beings themselves who live carnally. Of their master the Apostle Peter says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). They may also signify most wicked people who, by perverse and deceitful schemes, [Col. 0130C] openly or secretly plot the ruin of the possessions, bodies, or even souls of the innocent and unsuspecting. Of such the Psalmist says: “Those who devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. 52).

Neptune, the god and ruler of the sea, as the poets imagine, who pursued the aforesaid man with such rage that he would often have overwhelmed him with his waves unless the fates had prevented it, is he whom the Saviour calls “the ruler of this world,” but the Apostle “the god of this age.” Unless restrained by the power of divine predestination, he would suffocate beneath the entire weight of his malice those who strive toward the heavenly homeland.

Circe, daughter of the sun, who is said to have inhabited [Col. 0130D] an airy island, and to have been so powerful in spells that she changed unsuspecting guests into beasts by monstrous potions, is earthly abundance. It springs from the earth through the warmth and benefit of the sun, and is received and fostered by the pleasant mildness of the air. Those who misuse it she changes—not so much in body as in character—some through pride into birds; others through cruelty into beasts; one through laziness and stupidity into an ass; another through gluttony and foul pleasures into a pig; and others into other kinds of beasts.

She had changed into a bird the man who said: “Is not this Babylon which I myself have built in the glory of my power?” (Dan. 4). She had changed both Herods, and also the utterly impious Nero, into beasts; their cruelty is known to all.

Leucothea and [Col. 0131A] Calypso, most beautiful nymphs of the sea, are said to have detained him for a long time, enticed by sexual pleasures, so that he could scarcely be torn away even when his companions reproached him. They signify lust, which frequently ensnares even the wise person while reason protests and the faculties of the mind dissuade him. Solomon may serve as an example of this (3 Kings 11): at last his wisdom was overthrown by love of women. As Jesus son of Sirach says, such women “make even wise men apostatize” (Ecclus. 19).

The Sirens, whose name means “those who draw,” are, in poetic account, sea-monsters who sing so sweetly that any sailors hearing them are carried, even against their will, by the sweetness of the song to shipwrecking crags and rocks, and perish. But according to the truth of the matter, it is said that in certain places [Col. 0131B] the sea has a perpetual current like a very swift river, continually dashing against thick-set rocks, and thereby producing a piercing and very sweet sound. When sailors approach those places closely enough to hear that sound, they are drawn headlong onto the rocks and perish by shipwreck—not so much through the power of song, as the story claims, as through the force of the sea itself. Yet this is difficult to verify, or rather impossible, since no one caught in those places can escape the peril of certain death.

The Sirens’ songs signify everything that either idly occupies our hearing, curiously draws it, artfully entices it, luxuriantly affects it, or maliciously corrupts it. Those things occupy it idly which, though they do little harm, nevertheless build up nothing: such as the deeds [Col. 0131C] of Hercules, Achilles, Hector, or Alexander. Those things draw it curiously which, although they have no cause of evil in themselves, nevertheless appropriate to themselves the attention due to God: such as astronomy, which is forbidden because of mere curiosity. Those things entice it artfully which are fictitious, yet please all the more because of the very art of falsehood: such as the tales of Naso [Ovid] and similar works. Those things affect it sensually which excite lust by their very hearing: such as Sappho’s lyric poetry, Naso’s elegies, and the comedies of Menander, Plautus, or Terence. Those things corrupt it maliciously [Col. 0132A] which either overthrow faith, such as necromancy, or publicize others’ evils or fabricate falsehoods, such as satirical invectives, even the recitation of defamatory pamphlets.

The winds bursting from the cut-open bags, which his companions, thinking them money, had pierced with a knife, and by which the fleet was driven back from the harbour of its homeland which it had reached, signify the danger of fraternal discord: when a man already regarded as perfectly mature, pierced as it were by a knife through his brother’s insult and abuse, pours out from the bag of his heart—where he was thought to be full of the treasure of wisdom—the winds of anger and the whirlwind of rage. By this he is driven from the harbour of secure repose into peril of character and life, scarcely at last to return, after much time and labour, [Col. 0132B] to that state of virtue which he abandoned.

The Apostle understood this very well. After listing in sequence many kinds of dangers, he added after all the rest: “Dangers among false brethren” (2 Cor. 11). These are the things which Gentile philosophers wisely devised concerning the labours and endurance of a most prudent man beneath a certain covering of fables—not so much from a desire to lie as from regard for public benefit—so that they might become instruction in life and morals for many.

And, to give one example among many: just as that man escaped the enticing songs of the Sirens by making the ears both of himself and of his companions deaf with poured-in pitch, as it were by a deaf rowing; so we must stop our ears and become, as it were, deaf to everything that can draw us, through corrupted hearing, toward shipwreck of character, saying with [Col. 0132C] the Psalmist: “But I was like a deaf man and did not hear” (Ps. 37).

But since, in following the voyage of this man, of whom we have now spoken often, we too, driven by I know not what spirit, have run farther under extended sail, it is time to bring the pen back to the subject. And since we have treated, as far as possible, the two kinds of good already mentioned—namely, preparatory and inspirative—we must now come to the third, that is, meritorious good.

## BOOK FOUR: On Meritorious Good

[Col. 0131]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0131D]

By meritorious good we mean a good quality of the mind, which the Holy Spirit, the inspirer of all good things, breathes into it. For when the breeze of the Holy Spirit begins to breathe, like a gentle west wind, upon a soul already cleansed from vices and thereby justified, it immediately creates in it, as it were, spring flowers: certain good qualities of mind. By these the mind itself is moved, first indeed to inward acts, and then the hands to the performance of outward work; both of these [Col. 0132D] will shortly be discussed more clearly.

These four things—namely, the purification of the soul through forgiveness of sin, its justification, the inspiration of good will, and inward action—are so contiguous and interconnected that they can be distinguished by order rather than by time. For since the Holy Spirit is active, as Scripture says (Wis. 7), he does not permit the mind upon which he has breathed to remain idle and sluggish. At nearly the same moment he cleanses and justifies, endows it with a good quality, and stirs it to its actions; [Col. 0133A] just as a ray of sunlight enters, illuminates, warms, and rouses those looking on as soon as a window has been opened.

Outward action, however, being bodily, is slower; nor can it be performed except when a suitable opportunity has been found and external circumstances provide assistance. This good quality of mind is not called meritorious good merely because it prepares and makes us fit to merit—for the two preceding goods do this also—but much more because it moves and excites us and is, as it were, an instrument of good work, which those other goods are not.

This same quality is also called virtue: either from greenness (*viror*), because it makes a mind formerly dry grow green so as to bring forth the fruit of good work; or from strength (*vires*), which it supplies for action; or from manliness (*virilitas*), because it permits nothing womanish or languid to remain in it, but by its goads sharpens it into a kind of manly intensity.

[Col. 0133B] We have thought it necessary to pass over the virtues—what and how many they are; what the effect of each is; how some arise from others, though all spring from the root of charity; which vices they oppose or between which vices they lie; and very many other matters that might suitably be inserted here. Otherwise, we might either take away the material of a most beautiful work from those who could treat it better; or, by diminishing great matters about which it is safer to be wholly silent than to speak little, commit an insult against them; or we ourselves might be unable, should we later happen to experience or understand something better, [Col. 0133C] to take up these same matters anew as material for a separate and proper treatise.

But this must not be unknown: no quality of the soul is truly and properly called a virtue unless charity, the mother of all good things, produces and forms it. In many pagans—for example, Diogenes, Plato, and very many others—there was a praiseworthy disposition of mind, partly given by nature and partly acquired through the study of philosophy: harming no one, wishing to benefit all, extinguishing evil desires in themselves, condemning them in others, and whatever else of that kind could belong to the purpose of an innocent life.

Cicero, being an unbeliever ignorant of true virtue, calls this disposition of mind virtue, defining it thus: “Virtue is a habit of a well-ordered mind.” And indeed such a disposition of mind, formed by charity, is virtue; but when that charity is absent—[Col. 0133D] which could not be present in them because of faith—it is judged unworthy of the name of virtue. For, as Augustine says: “Where recognition of the true and unchangeable truth is lacking, virtue is false even in the best moral conduct.” Hence Augustine himself seems aptly to have defined virtue when he says: “Virtue is a good quality of mind, by which one lives rightly, which no one uses badly, and which God alone works in a human being.”

Now it is pleasing to proceed to the fourth kind of good, which we have chosen especially to call the merit of eternal life. Why this is so will be stated shortly; meanwhile, let us see what it is.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0134A] Merit, then, is an act or affection of virtue: virtue is as the instrument, and the act is the work of the instrument. When virtue begins to move the mind, an act must arise from that movement, because virtue cannot be ineffective. For, as blessed Gregory says: “If it is present, it performs great things; but if it refuses to act, it is not virtue.”

An act of virtue is either inward and hidden, or outward and manifest. The inward act is that which operates inwardly in the mind itself, invisibly and secretly, with every bodily service removed. The outward act is that which is carried out visibly and openly through the service of the body, with the assistance of external things.

To give an example: the inward act of justice is to weigh in one’s heart the causes and merits of matters on the scales of fairness; the outward act is to render to each person his due in external affairs. The [Col. 0134B] inward act of fortitude is to prepare a courageous mind for everything that may happen; its outward act is bravely to overcome adversities when they arise. It is easy to reason similarly about the other virtues for anyone able to recognize the effects of each.

The same virtue produces both acts, but one through itself and the other through the service of the cooperating body. To show this by whatever example we can: in children who rejoice greatly at some occurrence, or in people who dance, the mind is first stirred by joy, and then the body exults through the motion of the feet or the tossing of the hands. So virtue first rouses the mind, and then the body too, to its actions.

You will find something similar in vices, but in contrary matters. [Col. 0134C] For just as someone struck by a great and sudden misfortune is first troubled in mind, then claps his hands, tosses his head, and adapts his whole bodily bearing to grief, so the mind is first infected by vices and afterward transfers them into bodily action.

When outward action does not immediately follow inward action, this results either in virtues from the counsel of maturity, or in vices from the uncertainty of a confused mind, or in both from lack of opportunity or external means.

This point is also noteworthy: all virtues have definite and distinctive inward acts; their outward acts are likewise usually definite, but in some cases you will not easily find acts that are fixed or exclusive. For if you are asked what inward actions [Col. 0134D] faith, hope, and charity have, you will answer without hesitation: faith’s act is to believe in God; hope’s, to hope for eternal goods; charity’s, to love God and neighbour. So it is possible to proceed through all the rest: the inward act of humility is to think humbly of oneself; of mercy, to feel pity in one’s mind; of obedience, to prepare one’s mind to obey; and similarly with all the rest.

All the other virtues besides faith, hope, and charity also have proper and distinctive outward acts. Thus prudence’s outward act is to act prudently in external matters; temperance’s, to restrain oneself from evil deeds; and so with the remainder. [Col. 0135A] But it is not easy to demonstrate what private and distinct outward acts faith, hope, and charity have in external matters.

For if you say that faith’s act is to profess faith itself with the mouth and affirm it in words, the same reasoning will have to be applied to hope and charity as well: hope’s act will be to say that one hopes and to extol one’s hope in words; charity’s, to commend love of God and neighbour both in oneself and in others. And thus one may reason in the same way about them all.

If this is accepted, it will surely follow that all virtues have one outward act; and consequently none of those three will possess an act proper and distinctive to itself. Indeed, this further absurdity will follow: that we must admit some virtue to have an effect contrary to itself. Thus humility’s act would be to profess oneself humble and to extol humility itself in words, whereas it seems rather to belong to pride to declare that [Col. 0135B] exceedingly many virtues are present in oneself.

Therefore, since those three virtues have neither these private acts, nor can you discover any others, nor yet can they be wholly without action as though weak and languid—for then they would not be virtues—it remains that we must admit that they manifest their inward actions through the outward works of the other virtues.

When I see you faithfully fulfil the divine commandments by action itself, which belongs to obedience; when you afflict your body for sins, which belongs to fear; when you show yourself humble toward all and despise temporal things, which belongs to humility; when you feed the poor, clothe the naked, and assist those in need, which belongs to mercy: from these and similar things I understand that you believe in God, whose commands you diligently obey; that you [Col. 0135C] hope for eternal goods, for the desire of which you esteem transitory things lightly and even afflict your body for the forgiveness of sins; and that you love God, for whose love you strive before all else with every effort.

Proceeding similarly through individual cases, you will find that all virtues, both themselves and their works, serve those three as primordial and chief virtues by bearing witness to them. Nor should the reader be troubled [Col. 0136A] that what we have preferred to call inward acts of the virtues are also commonly called movements. For, since to move is nothing other than to act, movement too must be an act. If, however, you prefer to call it a passion or affection, it must be referred to the soul that is affected. But in respect of the virtue which moves and acts, it can be called nothing but an act.

It is clear that all acts of the virtues, both hidden and evident, belong to the merit of eternal life. Yet this designation, as has also been said of the other goods, suits each of the preceding kinds quite well, because there is no special grace in a human being through which that person does not merit—especially since the Holy Spirit, as was said a little earlier, can never be idle. [Col. 0136B] Nevertheless, we judged this designation more fittingly assigned to the good that consists in action, because all merits are completed in good work, and nothing further remains except to await the reward, of which we must speak next.

Yet first, at a kind of boundary between the two goods—merit and reward—we wish to insert a division composed of both: every human good is either merit alone, reward alone, or both merit and reward.

Merit alone is the first grace, given undeservedly in order that one may merit; it also begins to merit through contrition of heart and forgiveness of sins. Reward alone is eternal recompense, bestowed after all preceding merits; [Col. 0136C] beyond it we shall merit nothing further, because, once it has been reached, there will no longer be any further meriting, but only enjoyment of the reward.

Both merit and reward is any one of the intermediate goods: merit, indeed, of the subsequent good, but reward of the preceding good, while we receive grace from God as a reward for the grace that had previously been given in order that we might merit.

## BOOK FIVE: On Rewarding Good

[Col. 0135]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0135D]

Accordingly, we have come to that highest and most excellent kind of good which we have thought should be called eternal life, because this designation seemed to correspond more fittingly to the preceding matters. But what sort of good this is, how it should be defined, or by what name it should most rightly be designated—I not only am unable to know, but I believe that no human being clothed in mortal flesh can either conceive or express it. I think nothing truer can be said of it than that it is altogether ineffable.

For this good is the root, fountain, and principle of all other goods—yet not in such a way that any among them, as in things having generative or seed-bearing propagation, shares the nature of that same principle. This good, I say, is perfect through the totality of all goods—yet it does not consist in any diversity of parts or accidents. This good is indeed prior to all others in antiquity and subsequent to them in duration—yet every temporal quantity must be excluded from it. It is best of all, without a form of quality; greatest of all, without addition of quantity; the principle of all, without temporal relation. It always is, without the passage of time; it is everywhere, without local extension. It possesses all things and knows no possession; it fills all things by its presence, [Col. 0137A] and knows no position. It created all things, knowing no motion of acting; it sustains all things, unaware of every passion.

From all this it is evident that the good of which we speak is nothing other than God; and that it cannot truly be nor properly be called a substance, since no accidental predicate can be affirmed of it. For what is such that nothing can belong to it accidentally is not aptly called a substance either. For “substance” is so called because it stands beneath and is subject to accident. Still less should this good itself be called an accident, since an accident is inferior to substance precisely because it cannot exist except in it: as soon as it departs from substance, it is extinguished and perishes; whereas this good remains whole and subsists whether the accident be present or absent. The whiteness of a human being, for example, can exist only in a white human being, and it wholly fails when that same person ceases to be white; but a white person, even when whiteness departs, nevertheless continues and remains a person.

I pass over for the moment what might most truly be said: that all substances and accidents begin in time, and that all accidents and very many substances end in time. For when that state of eternity is reached in which nothing can either be present or absent temporally—the characteristic of an accident—accidents will be wholly removed, and so will very many substances. More worthy substances, however, such as angels, souls, and our glorified bodies, [Col. 0137C] will remain forever. From these foregoing points it may be inferred that the good in question is neither substance nor accident, and therefore belongs to none of those predicaments treated by the Peripatetics.

Their chief teacher, Aristotle—the same man most keenly searching after truth—divided all things which he thought could be comprehended by human sense into two, so to speak, kinds of reality: substance and accident. This was a most correct judgment by a man of great intellect and a diligent investigator of natural things: that everything subject to human knowledge must unquestionably either be substance or be in substance. He retained all substances, as fewer in number, under one and the most general predicament; but accidents, which were more numerous—for one substance can receive very many accidents—he distributed, according to their different modes, into nine predicaments, which the Greeks call *categories*, under an equal number of most general classes. Their names are these: quality, relation, quantity, where, when, having, position, acting, and being acted upon.

Therefore the wise man neither wished—indeed, he could not—confine Him from whom he understood all things to derive their being within unworthy names of created things, associating the eternal with temporal things, the uncreated with created things, the immeasurable with small things, or the immutable with mutable things. For terms properly found and established for temporal things can never suit eternal things in the same proper sense. [Col. 0138A] All this confirms the assertion already made: that supreme good of which we speak is neither substance nor accident. No one, we think, will call it an accident, except perhaps a madman, because the falsity of that is evident. If it is at times called substance out of necessity of speech, that is a divine and heavenly predication, not belonging to the philosophers’ predicaments.

The same judgment should be made of all those terms which we are accustomed to use of God by transfer and, as it were, by sufferance: nature, thing, essence, majesty, power, strength, and whatever else may be found. Whatever we attempt to say in mortal words about that ineffable nature of the supreme good, we are like stammerers. Yet they cannot fully form even elementary sounds, and consequently cannot convey a perfect knowledge of things; while we utter words with an unimpaired sound, but cannot grasp by understanding the things that ought to be unfolded through them. Thus the defect they suffer in syllables, we suffer in the things themselves.

Even what we are about to say, though true, may perhaps seem strange to less diligent readers: namely, that God neither is nor can be, neither lives nor reigns—if the meaning of these words remains that in which they are predicated of human beings. Yet these and similar things are not said of him falsely or vainly, but faithfully and piously; still, they are insufficient and unworthy in relation to their subject matter, because their signification cannot rise to [Col. 0138C] the purity of that divine nature.

The Lord himself seems to have given us an indication of this when he spoke to Moses from the bush, saying: “I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3). By these words he seems to have indicated a certain singular and proper mode of his essence, as though he said: “I am in a different manner from you or those to whom you are sent; I am far more purely and worthily than any creature; no other essence can be compared with mine.” For this is how we commonly speak when we wish to show that someone surpasses others in certain matters: “This is the man who sings, runs, fights”—that is, he sings most elegantly, runs most swiftly, fights most bravely.

Since, then, no terms which either exist or can be devised by human beings are sufficient significantly to express so great and simple a reality, those names seem more fittingly, or less improperly, applied to God which take away and remove: such as *uncreated*, *immutable*, *invisible*, and similar names, which common usage also calls privative. For among terms whose significations are found in created things—the very things for which the terms were devised—such as king, father, lord, and very many like them, there is none whose function can fully and properly signify the divine essence. But privative terms perfectly take away and remove those things which are not in God.

Therefore, according to the functions of the words themselves—though perhaps present usage recoils from it—I judge it more fitting to call God uncreated and immutable, and whatever else is of that kind, than king, father, or lord; although both these and those, whenever speech requires, are predicated of him piously and faithfully. Conversely, the affirmative terms are more splendid than the privative ones. For the latter remove either fault, as *innocent*, *undefiled*, and similar terms do; or defect, as *immutable* and *impassible* do; or capacity, as *invisible* does; or the condition of an inferior nature, as *uncreated* does; and so forth. The former always ascribe praise—of power, as king, prince, or lord; of piety, as father; of work, as creator; or of other things which seem to pertain to his honor. Thus it comes about, rather strikingly, that terms said of God which have less propriety have greater elegance; [Col. 0139B] and conversely, those more familiar in proper predication are less glorious.

You may take an example of this from some great prince. If you call him great, strong, noble, and wise, you praise him greatly, because these names convey praise. But if you call him unconquered and fearless, you do not praise him so much, because those words remove certain less honorable things. Therefore, if you attend to the propriety of words, in which they were devised by human beings for temporal things, privative terms outweigh affirmative ones in propriety of predication, while affirmative terms surpass privative ones in dignity of praise.

But with reference to the purity of that utterly simple reality, in which there is nothing various or unlike, all things are rightly said of it and are equivalent. To be king or lord is no different for God from being immutable and uncreated; and these and other names may be combined with one another in whatever manner—except relative terms, which, although they determine persons and what is proper to them, nevertheless signify nothing other or different. But it is not our purpose at present to discuss these matters further. Rather, we must pursue the point with which we began: namely, that the divine essence cannot be shown by any word.

For I would grant that a thing capable of being conceived or even imagined by the mind can be defined through the service of speech. But as for that which is altogether unthinkable, let whoever can say how it may be named; I confess that I do not know. This seems to be alluded to by the Athenians, among whom philosophical studies once flourished. Having discovered by the guidance of reason, from visible things, the invisible author of all things—the very God of whom we speak—but being unable to understand what he was, they are said to have set up an altar in the place called the Areopagus. Yet, keeping silence concerning him as unnameable, they inscribed upon the said altar the title “To an Unknown God” (Acts 17). When the Apostle read this title, he expounded to them, as far as could be known by a human being, the true and supreme God. But neither he nor any other person clothed in mortal flesh could ever express him by his true name, except the one of whom John says in his Gospel: “No one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1).

For if someone were to say that there is a certain reality from whose authorship [Col. 0140A] all things exist, but did not know what it is because it is neither substance nor accident, then, since nothing else can be thought and he attempts to apply a name to a thing which he cannot comprehend, I cannot see how this could be done. For *name* (*nomen*) is said to derive from *notamen*, or from *notion*, because it marks and makes known a thing; or rather from the equivalent Greek *onoma*, itself likewise derived from Greek *nemein* (“to distribute”), because it assigns its proper quality to each thing. It follows that what can neither be known nor made known, and shares in no quality, cannot be defined through the office of any name.

For in every imposition of a name there must precede some conception of the thing to be named. Thus the person who first called the common species of human beings “men” must certainly first have conceived in the mind that universal form which no one can lack and which could be denoted by such a word. Similarly, those who designated the individual members of the same species—Plato, Socrates, or any others—by their respective names must necessarily have done so according to forms perceived in the mind. So too in things which neither are nor can be, but which are nevertheless imagined—such as the logical “conceivables”—some form of the fiction had to precede: thus the chimera, an animal with a lion’s head, a fiery breast, and a serpent’s tail; and another creature, partly of goat and partly of stag nature, the goat-stag (*hircocervus*). Both received their names as fictitiously as they were monstrously.

Moreover, even in those terms which signify no real or imagined thing at all, but are expressed by negation—whether of two, as *neither*, or of all, as *none* and *nothing*—the same fact is found: in these and all similar cases, the form is a removal. From this follows something quite remarkable: what is false or nothing is more easily conceived by a human being than that which is believed to be the truest and purest reality of all. For such a reality becomes better known to a human being by participation than by thought, by the gift of fruition than by the sound of speech.

We read in ancient tales of genealogies that the ancients, among other errors of their vanity, worshipped a certain god, as fictitious as he was detestable. They imagined him immersed in Stygian darkness, as far beneath all the infernal beings as those were beneath the heavenly ones—foolishly, indeed, but with a certain appropriateness. With no less folly they made him the father of all the rest. And because, without penalty, he was permitted to behold the petrifying face of the Gorgon—which no one had ever seen without turning to stone—they used to call him Demogorgon. For *daemon*, they say, in a certain Greek language, means “seeing,” “considering,” or even “knowing.” They wished him to have another, most secret name, known only to sorcerers, and to very few even of them; at its invocation the earth could never fail to be shaken from its foundations.

If, then, deceived human beings did not think that that monster could be invoked by its fictitious name without a most violent earthquake, do you suppose that the supreme Father of all and the true God—who transcends even the angels themselves, so far superior to us, by incomparable loftiness, and who immutably beholds all things subject to change—can so easily be addressed by a true and proper name? Since, therefore, the beauty of so great a reality cannot, as we have said, be worthily and properly expressed by any word, we nevertheless call it by very many names, so that multitude may make up for the lack of propriety. In this also we seem to imitate stammerers, who, wishing to correct by the following word the defect of the preceding one, persist in their fault and do not cease to stammer. So we too harass a reality wholly ineffable and never to be named as it is with countless terms; and what cannot be achieved in one, we hope to achieve in many.

Yet the divine goodness does not reject this endeavor of pious boldness; rather, it approves it and willingly inclines its ear, after the example of a good mother who hears more affectionately and kisses more sweetly her little child calling upon her in half-formed sounds.

Thus we weary him with so many names, though all of them derive their ground, likeness, or some sort of occasion from created things. When he is called either God—from the Greek *theos*, interpreted “seeing,” or “fear,” as others think—or essence, from “to be,” which human beings can discern only in creatures; or king or lord, from power; or anything else that we believe pleasing to him: [Col. 0141C] it is evident that all these derive their rationale from created things. The very name God, which almost everyone considers especially proper to his being, may be seen not to be proper from this: it is extended not only to certain human beings who are called gods either through error or through grace, but also to wood and stones; indeed, what is more debasing, even to the foulest demons. Far be it from that most excellent creator of all things to possess elegantly as his own what he shares with unclean spirits.

If anyone, however learned, should try to attach to him some newly devised vocal form in place of a name, with no reference to substance or accident, he will be seen to have tried in vain. Beyond those two, he can find no form of a thing to be named which must be preconceived in the mind in every imposition of a name. Yet our God has, in the kingdom of eternity, a name most renowned and glorious, “the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2): a name not composed of letters but adorned with glory; a name of another idiom than our names, which the children in the furnace praised, saying: “Blessed is the holy name of thy glory” (Dan. 3). In this life that name can indeed be praised and blessed, but it cannot be known or uttered. This is truly the ineffable name of God, concerning which more will be said later when we treat of the sanctification of the divine name.

But when the kingdom for which we pray daily comes—saying, “Thy kingdom come” (Matt. 6)—that is, when our Lord Jesus Christ hands over the kingdom to God the Father, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 15), then the name which is now ineffable will be understood, and it will resound everywhere, as is written at the end of Tobit concerning the heavenly Jerusalem: “They shall possess thy land in sanctification; they shall call upon the holy name within thee” (Tob. 13). In that name we too shall be sanctified, and it in us, as the faithful people daily pray in the same Lord’s Prayer: “Hallowed be thy name” (Matt. 6). Although this petition comes first in the order in which it is spoken, in usefulness it is last, as the end and completion of the others.

Meanwhile, while we live here, where it is not permitted to praise our king by his true and proper name, we nevertheless do not cease faithfully to extol him with countless terms taken from our own idiom, drawing them from those ten genera of all things which can either be comprehended by bodily sense or thought by the mind. When all these are transferred to the essence of divine simplicity, they must wholly fail of their prior sense, so that they may serve so great a reality, though by an office less worthy. Therefore they attribute to him none of the things they formerly signified, but reject and banish them as wholly unworthy.

Thus God is called essence, or even substance, without the meaning of substance; good and just, without quality; great, without quantity; creator and lord, without a temporal relation existing in him, but rather in the creatures of which he is called creator and lord. For nothing must be believed to have happened to God when he began to have a servant [Col. 0142C] or a creature; rather, it happened happily to them when they began to have such a Creator and Lord. For what if herbs and flowers newly sprung up should be warmed by the gentle breath of the sun? Would you say that this happened to the sun, which had no need whatever of them, or to those plants, which could neither be born nor, once born, grow without its benefit? Yet no such or any other analogy can be found among created things that supplies a fitting example for that uncreated and all-creating reality.

Created things have some relation both to one another and to their creator. But what relation the uncreated has to created things, or the eternal to temporal things, I cannot conceive, since it has often already been said that he is incapable of any accident. You see, therefore, that nothing subject to the first four predicaments can fittingly be attributed to God. It would not be difficult to show the same concerning the remaining six, if one who understands what has been said of these could not easily think similar things concerning the others.

Our God is also customarily called eternal life; yet this too is not sufficiently excellent and proper, because, as has often been shown, nothing truer can be said of him than that no property of temporal things or words can suit him. He is called life because he is not merely life, but more than life; he gives all things their cause of living, and he himself lives in himself and from himself in a certain excellent and ineffable manner, because he is wholly vital and, as blessed Hilary says, “Life living throughout the whole.” [Col. 0143A] From this vital fountain comes the cause of living to all things that live. In it even those things which do not seem to live were living before they came into being, since all things that were afterwards made “were life in him” (John 1), as that searcher of heavenly mysteries says.

Therefore, since all things, whether living or not living, lived in him from eternity; since those which live temporally receive from him their cause of living; and since those which either now enjoy blessed life or will later enjoy it possess it only by participation in him: common usage not inappropriately calls this vital fountain of all things “life,” using that figure of speech by which the name of the effect is customarily attributed to the cause.

This life is also called eternal, though this too, like nothing else, is not fully expressive; but the name seems to come nearer than others to that unbounded state of the divine essence. The word *eternal* (*aeternus*) is derived either from *age* (*aetas*), as some wish, or rather from *aeon* (*aevum*), as though *aeviternus*, according to Varro, who says: “The earth, the everlasting home of humankind.” Both terms just mentioned, *aetas* and *aevum*, are names of time; thus we call those equal in age *coevals* or *contemporaries*. But *aetas* can denote even a very brief time, as in infants whom we call of tender age. *Aevum*, however, more commonly denotes either some great span of time, as “the age of Nestor” or “the age of Methuselah,” or the whole extent of temporal duration, as when it is said that Wisdom always existed with God [Col. 0143C] and existed before the age.

In view of this rationale, the name was transferred, by philosophers as well as Catholics, to designate the uninterrupted continuance of existence, also called eternity. The philosophers do so, as Boethius says (*Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, metre 9):

> Creator of earth and heaven, who commandest time  
> To proceed from the age, and, remaining steadfast thyself,  
> Grantest all things to be moved.

The Catholics do so as the son of Sirach says when speaking of heavenly things: “Each shall not press upon his neighbor unto the age” (Ezek. 16). Therefore this name *eternal*, taken from them, and its derivative *eternity*, seem more suitably applied to designate the stable and enduring essence of divine purity than *everlasting*, *perennial*, or *perpetual*, or their derivatives—perennity, perpetuity, sempiternity—or any other terms of this signification that may be found.

For *aevum*, in its original institution, signifies either some great quantity of time or the whole of time in such a manner that it produces no conception at all of parts. When I say “the age of Methuselah” or “the age of the world,” I understand the whole together and no part; and similarly in words derived from it, such as *eternal* and *eternity*. But when it is said, “The world is always,” “always” means the whole of time in such a way that I also remember its parts. For I understand the world to exist in this moment and in every other; and there is marked there a certain continuous progression of existence through individual moments. The same applies to terms arising from this, such as *everlasting* and *everlastingness*. *Perennial*, however, seems compounded from *year*, and thus marks a certain temporal distinction which cannot suit divine simplicity. *Perpetual* properly describes what can endure and subsist until the end of time; this is wholly unworthy of him who either suffers nothing or perceives no duration at all.

It is therefore clear that, among all temporal names, none is so fittingly applied to God as *eternal*, although neither this nor any other designation can wholly attain the dignity of the divine essence. Combining, then, these reasons concerning eternity with those concerning life, we are accustomed to call God eternal life, because he lives eternally in himself and from himself in an ineffable manner, while we receive temporal life from him and hope for eternal life in him.

This, therefore, is that supreme good which alone—or for whose sake—whatever is sought in prayer ought to be sought. From it all other things proceed and to it they are referred. Unless it comes first, the others do not follow; unless it follows, what precedes is useless. It is evident, therefore, that every human good receives the cause of its origin from eternal predestination, which is God, and is consummated in the blessedness of eternal life, which we have likewise taught to be God. You see, then, the whole course of our salvation proceeding causally from God and returning finally to him in the manner of a line, so that he is both fountain and conclusion of all goods, just as in a circle the circumference receives the principle of its beginning, end, and entire circuit from the unmoving center. Therefore what that Greek philosopher Parmenides—who, beneath an Egyptian rock, investigated the secrets of heavenly things—is reported to have said of the divine essence is true: “It turns the moving sphere of things, while itself preserving itself unmoved.”

# BOOK SIXTH. On the Different Kinds of Evil, and on the Third Element of Prayer, That Is, from Whom One Should Ask; on the Fourth, to Whom One Should Ask; on the Fifth, Why One Should Ask; and on the Sixth, How One Should Ask.

[Col. 0143]

# CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0143D]

But since enough has been said, as necessity required, concerning the different kinds of good, I think it follows that some observations should be added for purposes of explanation concerning evil, its contrary, because it must be fled in every way and prayed against. For good ought to be known in order that you may desire it; evil, in order that you may flee it. Balsam is known in order that it may benefit; poison, lest it harm.

Evil was already defined above when we said that evil is eternal death, or whatever drives toward it and makes it worse. This is so true that nothing else can properly be called evil, although ordinary usage also applies this name to certain other things, such as bodily punishments or labors and adverse fortunes. Even if these seem evil to those who suffer them, they are not evil, but are often good and salutary for the soul.

The first evil of a human being—and that without which the others either do not follow or do very little harm—is the misery that hangs over the soul even before it exists, because by the eternal divine judgment it has been rejected and is to be one of the reprobate. No calamity can be greater than this. But this evil does not concern the prayer of which we speak; and therefore it is neither to be prayed for nor prayed against, because the intention of prayer extends to the future, whereas the effect of this evil has been foreseen and fixed with absolute certainty from eternity.

Thus this first evil is contrary to that first good which we above called preparatory or preordinative. Accordingly, by a corresponding contrary designation, nothing prevents us from calling it prejudicatory or precondemnatory. Both are excluded from the goods and evils subject to prayer, because, as we have just said, prayer tends toward what is future, while these have been certain and completed from eternity: the one in the preparation of grace, the other in the foreknowledge of misery. Therefore, before speaking separately about them, let us, if it please you, begin from a somewhat higher starting point.

# CHAPTER TWO.

As I consider the many things that the practice of human devotion commonly predicates of God, I do not know whether anything occurs more general or more inclusive than when he is called knowing, wise, understanding, cognizant, or anything else having the same function of signification. For all these terms show of God not only the one essence of a simple and unchangeable nature—for they are understood of him according to substance—but also mark a certain relation between him and temporal things. Yet this relation is not in God, to whom nothing can happen; for every temporal relation is an accident.
