Rather, it is in the things themselves, because they are subject to divine knowledge or cognition.

Thus when God is said to know, or to be knowing—to take one example for all—this term principally signifies the divine essence, but secondarily marks a certain temporal relation to him. Its sense is as if one said: God is, and all temporal things are subject to his knowledge. For since for God to know is nothing other than to be, and to be is nothing other than for God to be, temporal things are subject to God in the same way that they must be subject to his knowledge.

Because of the unchangeable simplicity of his nature, this knowledge could be contained in one name alone and simply called knowledge. But because the different states of things subject to it vary with time, it is customarily called by different names. Since there are three times through which temporal things run—the present, the past, and the future—God, who created time and possesses knowledge of all things, can neither forget the past, nor be ignorant of the present, nor fail to foresee the future. He retains the past in memory, sees the present, and foreknows the future. Yet he judges all these things not as a human being does, according to the nature of things themselves or the variation of times, but as God, beholding them in the one simple manner of eternal knowledge.

Before things were created, when all were still future, his eternal knowledge could be called foreknowledge, on account of future things, because he foreknew them all. But once things had been created, it could no longer be called foreknowledge in relation to them; nor could knowledge, so as to be different from what it was before, come to it in any way. The same holds for things that newly begin to exist or happen each day: before they exist or happen, they are held under God’s foreknowledge; once they have begun to exist or have happened, they cease indeed to be under foreknowledge, but remain immovably subject to knowledge.

This eternal knowledge, which is nothing other than God, has, so to speak, two effects concerning human beings: predestination and reprobation. One is seen in the blessedness of the elect, the other in the condemnation of the reprobate. Predestination is the preparation of eternal blessedness; reprobation is the certain foreknowledge of just condemnation. Since both have been certain and fixed from eternity, neither can concern prayer, which extends toward the future. For no one, as we have also said above, prays that God may predestine him or may have predestined him; just as no one prays that God may reprobate him or may have reprobated him.

From the fountain of divine predestination, which is the principle and cause of all goods, arise those goods of which we treated a little earlier, by whose help we are assisted in obtaining the blessedness that predestination prepares. This is like a most indulgent father who, for his beloved son, prepares an inheritance of a kingdom and also provides other aids by which he may worthily obtain it. Evils, however, do not proceed causally from divine reprobation, lest God be found the author of evils as well. Rather, they are from or done by the human being, according to that knowledge which cannot be deceived, lest the person whom God foresees as justly to be condemned be punished without his own desert.

From this it is most certainly clear that God makes, approves, and crowns good things; but evil things he neither makes nor approves. He tolerates, disapproves, and punishes them. That God loves good things the Psalmist testifies, saying: “The Lord is just and has loved righteousness; his countenance has beheld equity” (Ps. 10). That he hates evil things, the same Psalmist says: “Thou hast hated all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5). That he rewards the former and punishes the latter, the Apostle teaches thus: “To those indeed who by patience in good work glory and honor and incorruption; but tribulation and distress upon every soul that does evil.” And concerning goods, indeed, something was said a little earlier. Let us now speak briefly concerning evils, so that it may appear what ought to be prayed against.

# CHAPTER THREE. On Evil.

We have already defined evil as eternal death, or whatever impels toward it and makes it worse. Therefore every human evil that should be prayed against is either eternal death, or the desert of eternal death, or that which makes one deserving of it; or it is privative evil or hardening evil.

The evil which is eternal death is nothing other than the deprivation of eternal life, which is God—just as bodily death is nothing other than the loss of bodily life. The evil which is the desert of eternal death is an evil act: either inward, an act of the mind, such as hatred or envy; or bodily, such as theft or murder. The evil which makes one deserving of eternal death is a vice of the mind: that is, an evil quality of the soul by which a person is impelled toward evil acts, and which is, as it were, an instrument of evil action.

Privative evil is nothing other than the deprivation of righteousness, when one does not deserve to be cleansed and justified through the infusion of spiritual grace. The evil called hardening is hardness of heart: when a sinner, abandoned by divine grace, is so hardened in evil that, pierced by no contrition of heart, he does not receive remission of sins.

These evils, then, must briefly be discussed, not in the order in which they have been listed, but in the order in which they usually happen to human beings, as we treated the goods a little earlier. But in order to approach this more fittingly, something must first be said about another evil, prior to all these in order and more miserable than them all.

# CHAPTER FOUR.

[Col. 0147D] First, then, among the evils of humankind—and the one upon which all the others follow—is that misery impending over a person because, by the eternal judgment of God, he has been condemned and reprobated. Yet this divine reprobation neither supplies the cause of his future evils nor imposes necessity upon them. Considered in God, this reprobation is holy and simple, and is nothing other than the eternal foreknowledge of the Judge, who most certainly foresees future events. But if that reprobation is considered in the human being, it is supreme misery, admitting of no remedy: namely, to displease the judgment of so great a ruler even before one begins to exist. For what can be more miserable than not yet to have been born and already to have been condemned?

By “condemned,” however, we do not mean that divine knowledge is already punishing one who has committed no sin; rather, we mean that God’s foreknowledge sees that he will sin mortally and will be punished according to his own merit. Therefore, because this misery of the condemned person, though it supplies no cause for all evils, nonetheless establishes their fixed order, it has seemed fitting to call it the prejudging, or pre-condemnatory, evil.

[Col. 0148A] It stands in opposite relation to that first and highest good, predestination, except that predestination supplies both the cause and the prescribed order of every good, whereas this evil prescribes an order for subsequent evils but does not produce their cause. By “cause” I mean that from which something comes to be, not merely that without which it cannot exist. For there are two kinds of causes: one from which something exists and without which it cannot exist; another from which it does not exist, but without which it nevertheless cannot exist. Thus God is the cause of this bodily life in both senses, since we live from him and cannot live without him. Mortality, however, is a cause of our death not because death comes from mortality, but because it cannot exist without mortality. Accordingly, predestination is the cause of all goods in both senses; reprobation, on the other hand, can be called the cause of all evils only in the latter sense. [Col. 0148B]

But this evil, although, as we have said, certain and fixed from eternity, cannot be an object of prayer whose effect depends upon the future. We shall briefly proceed, then, to those evils which ought to be deprecated in prayer. The first of these is what we have called the hardening evil; and we should examine its nature.

Since a human being cannot be saved when God’s grace has been withdrawn, God, who foreknows all things, judges the person whom he has most justly reprobated from eternity worthy to receive saving grace. If this grace were received, he could indeed be converted and contrite, and thereby receive forgiveness of sins. Deprived of this grace of God and left to himself, the sinner is hardened into a certain insensible wickedness—like ice which, touched by a ray of the sun, could soften and melt, but when that ray is removed congeals, as it were, into the nature of stone.

[Col. 0148C] This evil is thus contrary to the good which we called preparatory, because that good prepares the way to salvation, whereas this obstructs and closes it. The former had prepared the ways of salvation for Jacob, whom the Lord loved from eternity; the latter had closed them against Esau, whom the same Lord declares that he hates.

From this evil called hardening there follows, not so much in time as in order, the privative evil—that is, the deprivation of righteousness, which may be called unrighteousness—because righteousness can arise only from the forgiveness of sins. For just as a house is clean when its filth has been removed and unclean when it remains, though the removal or presence of the filth is not itself the cleanliness or uncleanness of the house but supplies its cause, so, when sins are forgiven, righteousness is immediately present; when they are retained, unrighteousness is at hand. Yet the forgiveness or retention of sins is not itself this righteousness or unrighteousness, but merely provides the occasion for it.

[Col. 0148D] This evil, therefore, is contrary to the inspirative good, because through that good purity of soul is acquired by the departure of vices, whereas through this evil impurity follows from their presence.

Again, from this privative evil arises the evil which merits eternal death: that is, the perverse quality of a vicious mind by which a person is incited to earn eternal death through greater crimes. Let dry, uncultivated ground serve as your example. If it were watered and cultivated, it could certainly produce wholesome and useful fruits; but now it brings forth thorns and thistles, or even deadly plants—hemlock, hellebores, and poisons—in its pestilential fertility.

[Col. 0149A] This evil is therefore contrary to the meritorious good, because that is an instrument for earning life, whereas this is an instrument of perpetual death.

Moreover, from this evil—that is, from this perverse quality of the soul—proceeds another evil which is no longer meritorious, but rather the actual merit of death: namely, an evil act, whether inward, belonging only to the mind and also called a movement, or outward, belonging also to the body and specially called an act. For just as bodily illness sometimes afflicts a person inwardly only and does not appear externally, as in excessive heat or cold and other hidden ailments, but at other times both presses within and afflicts outwardly, for example through tremblings, spasms, and tossings of the limbs, so this perverse quality which we call vice, being indeed a languor and disease of the soul, sometimes moves the mind alone toward evil acts, such as anger, hatred, envy, and other perverse affections; at other times it moves the mind and incites the body as well to most wicked deeds, such as thefts, robberies, fornications, homicides, or whatever similar acts you may find.

[Col. 0149B] From this it is clear that this evil is opposed to the good which we called the merit of eternal life: because that proceeds from a good quality of mind, whereas this comes from a most evil one; eternal life is reserved as the reward for the former, but perpetual death for the latter.

[Col. 0149C] It should also be observed, as we said above concerning goods, that the succession of these four evils, proceeding one from another, occurs almost simultaneously and without distinction, so that it can be discerned not so much by time as by order—except for bodily action, which is often delayed either by the hesitation of a mind still uncertain, by lack of means or assistance, or by some other cause.

## CHAPTER V. On eternal death

After all these things follows that evil which is worst of all, and for which the other evils themselves are causes: namely, eternal death, the end and culmination of all evils, and as it were a sea into which all the rest flow by a fixed course. You may infer how terrible and dreadful this evil is from the fact that it surpasses all other punishments, just as we understand bodily death to be the ultimate penalty because a judge can inflict nothing more severe, however great human crimes may be.

[Col. 0149D] Eternal death, then, is to lack him whom we showed above to be eternal life—namely God, who alone is the life of the soul, without whom it cannot live blessedly—just as temporal death is the deprivation of the soul, without whose presence the body itself cannot live even for a moment.

This evil is opposed to the good which we called eternal life, not only because that is to enjoy God while this is to lack him, but also because the former is the reward of righteousness and the latter of iniquity; the former belongs to the predestined, while the latter awaits the reprobate; the former is supreme happiness, the latter extreme misery.

[Col. 0150A] In these five kinds of evil you may observe that what precedes is always the cause of what follows, and what follows is the punishment of what precedes. Thus the first evil, called hardening, is cause only and not punishment as well. The three middle evils are both causes and punishments. The final evil, which may also be called punitive—eternal death—is punishment only for all that precedes it and not a cause as well. It is a punishment to which none can be compared, in comparison with which any other punishment, however severe, may be regarded as a remedy. And while this punishment has not yet been experienced, it may be imagined and feared, but can in no way be known—except at last, when it can no longer be avoided.

## CHAPTER VI. On intermediate things

[Col. 0150B]

Let what has been said concerning goods and evils suffice for the capacity of our limited understanding; let us now examine intermediate things. By intermediate things we mean those which in themselves are neither good nor evil, but become good or evil for those who use them according as they are used well or badly. Some of these are in the soul, some in the body, and some outside the nature of both; these last are also called external things.

In the soul are certain endowments not given by grace—for then they would be virtues, and thus belong to the class of goods discussed above—but either naturally inborn or acquired by effort: such as knowledge of the arts, practical foresight, acquaintance with many things, and memory of events; and their opposites, such as indolence, imprudence, forgetfulness, dullness, and the like.

[Col. 0150C] In the body are health or sickness, agility or sluggishness, strength or weakness, beauty or ugliness, and similar things and their opposites. External things are those attributed to fortune: wealth or poverty, nobility or low birth, freedom or servitude, renown or obscurity, and whatever is similar, together with their opposites. These are divided into pleasant and grievous things and are mutually opposed. No one can lack or possess all of them at once; when some are present, others must be absent.

[Col. 0150D] With respect to all these things, I think that one should pray only that God may grant us to turn either their use or their absence to our salvation: that, if pleasant things are present, we may give him thanks for them yet hold them of little account in our minds; and, if they are absent, that we may not desire them at all, or only slightly. If grievous things are present, we should endure them courageously and attribute them to our own offenses; if absent, we should not fear them at all. For I believe it matters little, as regards the matter’s usefulness, whether you reach eternal life learned or unlearned, healthy or sick, rich or poor, free or enslaved—except that those who here have used pleasant things humbly rejoice there in increased happiness, while those who have patiently endured adversity glory that they have happily exchanged a wretched lot.

## CHAPTER VII. On the third constituent of prayer, namely, from whom one asks

[Col. 0151A]

Since, I think, we have inquired with sufficient care into what should be sought in prayer, the matter placed second, let us briefly add something about the third constituent: from whom one should ask. This chapter has already been considered in part in the definition of prayer itself, when we said that prayer is an imploring of divine mercy; there we explained that prayer must be directed only to God.

This question—namely, from whom one asks—must, like the two preceding matters, be considered in every prayer, so that if it is removed, the act cannot properly be called prayer at all. Whoever the petitioner may be, and whatever may be sought, if there is no one from whom it may be hoped for or obtained, the prayer is not merely ineffective but is not appropriately called prayer. Therefore prayer must always be directed to a definite person, one capable of bestowing what is sought. To ask from one who cannot give is either hidden error or manifest folly. If you do it unknowingly, you are secretly deceived; if deliberately, you are plainly mad.

[Col. 0151B] Since nothing is to be requested in prayer except eternal life, which is God, or what pertains to it, every prayer must certainly be directed to God, because no one can give him to a human being except he himself. For he willingly gives himself to those who seek him and freely offers himself, as the Apostle said to those to whom he spoke: “God offers himself to us as to most beloved children” (Heb. XII).

Nor can anyone besides him bestow those goods which cooperate in and assist toward life, because they are gifts of spiritual graces, which can be conferred upon another by no human being or even angel. They are charisms of the Holy Spirit, which he alone imparts to whomever he wills and in whatever measure he wills, “apportioning to each individually as he wills,” as the Apostle says (I Cor. XII). Yet he does not do this apart from the Father and the Son, who not only bestow those gifts with him, but also bestow him himself with them upon human beings. Hence the same Holy Spirit is most rightly called the gift both of the Father and of the Son.

[Col. 0151C] Do you wish to know whether the Father gives the Holy Spirit? The Savior says in the Gospel: “If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI). And elsewhere: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all truth” (John XIV).

Do you wish to know whether the same Father bestows the gifts of the Holy Spirit? See what Scripture says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I). That the Son too can give the Holy Spirit is made explicit in the Gospel: breathing upon the disciples, he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX). He also afterward sent the same Holy Spirit to them from heaven, as he had previously promised, saying: “When I have been taken up from you, I will send you the Spirit of truth, and he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV).

[Col. 0152A] That the Holy Spirit gives gifts, and likewise the Son, the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. LXVII); and John says in the Gospel: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I). The Holy Spirit also gives himself when he mercifully pours himself into our minds. He also gives his gifts, apportioning to each individually as he wills (I Cor. XII). Therefore the same Holy Spirit is most rightly called both giver and gift: giver, because with the Father and the Son he gives himself and his gifts; gift, because he is given by the Father and the Son, and also by himself.

You see, therefore, that God alone can bestow that supreme and unique good of eternal life, or what pertains to it; and therefore these things must be sought from him alone.

[Col. 0152B] Some intermediate things, however, one person can confer upon another, and they can benefit those using them well in relation to life—for example, worldly material resources, which, if applied to good uses, may greatly assist toward the merit of life. But the best and more praiseworthy element in this, namely the good manner of using them, no one except God can bestow, because it is a spiritual gift and is numbered among the charisms of grace.

From what has been said, therefore, it is clearly inferred that all petitions in our prayers must be directed to God alone, as the Apostle says: “In every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God” (Phil. IV). Eternal life can be hoped for and obtained from him alone, who is eternal by nature—not from those who either do not possess it or have received grace but cannot give it, such as the holy angels or the blessed souls already received into glory.

[Col. 0152C] But it is most foolish to ask it from things unworthy even of temporal life, such as idols; and most impious to ask it from unclean demons, who have not only been deprived by their own merit of the blessedness of that life, but have been assigned to perpetual death.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fourth constituent of prayer, namely, for whom one asks

The fourth matter among the constituents of prayer follows: namely, for whom one asks—that is, who and what sort of person is the one on whose behalf prayer is offered, whether that person is the one praying or another. A person sometimes prays only for himself, sometimes for another, and not so much for himself as for the other. In either case, one must consider the condition of the person for whom the effect of prayer is desired.

[Col. 0152D] For it matters greatly, as regards the usefulness of the matter, whether he has *commercium* in the thing requested—that is, whether he is capable or incapable of obtaining it. In the language of jurists, a person is said to have *commercium* in a thing when he is qualified to acquire and obtain it by civil law, just as a freeborn person has *commercium* in any dignity or magistracy because he is qualified to obtain any magistracy or dignity.

If eternal life—the only thing, together with what pertains to it, for which prayer is to be made—is requested for someone whom God has reprobated from eternity, nothing is accomplished with respect to that person, because he is not qualified for it and cannot have *commercium* in it. But if it is requested for someone predestined to it, the prayer is not deprived of its effect, because he is qualified for it and has obtained *commercium* in it through God’s eternal predestination.

[Col. 0153A] Hence there is a noteworthy consequence: often a person worthy of life—being, for example, full of virtues and merits, and one who, if he died in such a state, would without doubt be transferred to glory—is nevertheless not qualified for it, because he is reprobate and will relapse into wickedness; and therefore he cannot have *commercium* in the thing itself. Conversely, someone wholly unworthy of that life—for example, defiled by every crime, and one who, if he died in such a state, would certainly be carried off to eternal punishment—is nevertheless qualified for life, because he is one of the elect and will return to righteousness; and for that reason he cannot be deprived of *commercium* in the thing itself.

Saul, before his conversion, while still a blasphemer and persecutor of the Church of God, was not worthy, but he was qualified, because God had predestined him from eternity to life. Judas, however, whenever he was righteous, was certainly worthy, but not qualified, because God had reprobated him from eternity.

[Col. 0153B] From these four distinctions, paired with one another, a fourfold division may be made as follows. One person is worthy of eternal life and qualified for it, as a righteous elect person; another is worthy but not qualified, as a righteous reprobate person. Another is unworthy yet qualified, as an unrighteous elect person; another is neither worthy nor qualified, as an unrighteous reprobate person. We have the first example in John the Baptist, the second in Judas, the third in Matthew, and the fourth in Herod or Pilate.

No one should wonder that we have assigned this distinction between “worthy” and “qualified,” because a person is called qualified according to God’s eternal foreknowledge, but worthy according to the present requirement of merits. That one who is presently full of all goods, though he will afterward be wicked, is judged worthy of life belongs to fairness and justice. That another, full of all evils yet destined afterward to be good, is deemed qualified for life belongs to predestination and grace.

[Col. 0153C] [Col. 0153D] It is thus clear that these two are neither equal, so that they must always be present or absent together, nor altogether contrary, so that the presence of one necessarily removes the other. Rather, in relation to a person they stand as exceeding and exceeded: sometimes they are present together, sometimes absent together, and sometimes, when either is present, the other is absent.

I think it sufficiently evident that the supreme good which is called, and is, eternal life cannot be obtained by prayer for anyone except one qualified for it. But spiritual goods—such as virtues and their works, and the good use of intermediate things, itself also a spiritual gift—can be acquired by both elect and reprobate persons; by the elect finally and fruitfully, but by the reprobate superficially and therefore without fruit.

## CHAPTER IX. On the fifth constituent of prayer

[Col. 0154A]

The fifth constituent of prayer is why one asks: namely, whether with a good or evil intention. Whatever is requested, unless it is requested with a good intention, not only does not benefit the petitioner but also harms him. For if someone asks for life in order to be able to mock the torments of the wicked; for the grace of the Holy Spirit solely in order to perform miracles; for knowledge in order to gain temporal praise; for bodily health in order to satisfy pleasures; or for riches because of luxury—such a petition should no longer be called prayer, but a certain foolish and wicked superstition.

Moreover, if an evident evil is requested for an evil purpose, such as the accomplishment of theft, homicide, or fornication, this is so far from prayer that it should more truly be considered its opposite, namely an imprecation. For if the prayer by which evil is requested with a good intention is not good, and worse still is that by which good is requested with an evil intention, it necessarily follows that the petition by which evil is requested for an evil purpose is not only evil but should not even be called prayer.

[Col. 0154B] In every petition, then, the reason must be considered to such an extent that we should believe God less displeased if you ask for an evil with a good mind than if good is requested with an evil intention. Thus Elijah was heard when he sought the burning of fifty soldiers—a great evil indeed, had it not been requested with good intent (IV Kings I); and Simon Magus was denied the reception of spiritual grace (Acts XIII), a great good indeed if he had requested it with a good intention.

Likewise Paul and the sons of Zebedee, because the former wrongly requested release from the angel of Satan and the latter a seat in a temporal kingdom, were respectively denied and corrected. To the former the Lord said, “My grace is sufficient for you” (II Cor. XII); to the latter he said, “You do not know what you are asking” (Matt. XX). You see, then, that in every right and properly ordered prayer one must consider not only whatever one asks, but also why—that is, with what intention—one asks it.

## CHAPTER X. On the sixth constituent of prayer

The sixth and final constituent of prayer is how one asks: namely, worthily or unworthily. We are not now speaking of that worthiness or unworthiness of merits by which a person is in himself worthy or unworthy to be heard, which is called righteousness or unrighteousness. We mean a certain suitability or unsuitability of accompanying circumstances which must be present or absent both in the righteous person and in the sinner: for example, piety, humility, devotion, and the disposition of the person praying, together with similar qualities or their opposites.

[Col. 0154D] For it matters greatly before him to whom prayer must be presented whether you imitate the tax collector humbly and devoutly, with tears, lamentation, and great contrition of heart, or whether, proud and arrogant, you display the frivolity of the Pharisee with, as I may speak poetically, inflated phrases, haughty eyes, and vain bodily display. Thus, conscious of them both, the Savior said of the one, “This man went down justified to his house” (Luke XVIII); but of the other and those like him: “They love to pray standing in the streets so as to be seen by men; they have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

[Col. 0155A] But these matters, because they are customarily considered in connection with the person praying, must be discussed more carefully later, when we treat the question of what is fitting for one who prays. [Col. 0156A] Yet they ought not to have been entirely omitted here, because in them the worthiness or unworthiness of praying is assessed.

# BOOK VII. On the attainment and effect of prayer.—Recapitulation of the six constituents of prayer

[Col. 0155]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0155B]

Having now investigated, with all the diligence we could, what prayer contains, let us consider in what cases it attains its end—that is, obtains an effect. The explanation of this question, however, is not merely difficult but, more truly speaking, impossible, since it exceeds human capacity to comprehend in thought or define in speech which prayers God accepts or rejects. For, as the Apostle says, “His judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. XI).

Nevertheless, having invoked him to whom every prayer must be directed, let us attempt, from what has already been set forth and what still occurs to the mind, to gather some account, however limited, of the effect of prayer. If we say anything rightly, let it be attributed to divine grace; if anything absurd or improper, let it be imputed either to our weakness or to the difficulty of the matters themselves.

## CHAPTER II. On the effect of prayer

[Col. 0155C] First, one must recall what we taught above: outside the bosom of the Church there is no place for prayer, because one must pray only for eternal life or what pertains to it, and eternal life cannot be hoped for outside the unity of the Church. For, says the Savior, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

We read that certain unbelievers supplicated God for their necessities—for example, Ahab, who fasted and covered his flesh with sackcloth because of Naboth’s death. But because such supplication lacked the final cause it ought to have had, it could not be regarded as prayer.

[Col. 0155D] As was also said above, prayer must be regular, offered in spirit and truth; and this cannot occur outside the Church. Therefore, when all unbelievers have been excluded—that is, Gentiles and Jews, indeed also heretics who have torn themselves away from the unity of faith through the various plagues of heresies—only believers, both good and evil, are permitted to pray. For the wicked person ought to pray in order to become good, and the good person in order to become better.

Just as, in the household of some great master, a servant who knows that he has displeased his master because of his fault seeks pardon by prayers, while one who presumes that he pleases him strives to obtain still greater favor, so in the Church of God the sinner ought by prayer to strive for pardon, and the righteous for fuller grace, so that both may be regarded as sharers in the kingdom, though unequal in merit.

[Col. 0156B] But now it is time to address the question proposed. To determine anything more certain concerning it is almost no different from treading with bare feet upon embers hidden beneath ashes.

## CHAPTER III

Since, then, there are six constituents of prayer, which we have treated in order, one must infer from the concurrence of them all which prayer should be believed to be heard by God or rejected. One must consider who asks, from whom he asks, what he asks, for whom he asks, why, and how; and from these draw, so far as possible, a conjecture about the matter.

First, who asks: if the petitioner is not a believer, whatever the condition of the matters that follow, he is said neither to pray nor to be heard, because apart from faith God can neither be prayed to nor hear one who prays. Thus the four hundred and fifty priests of Baal were not heard when they sought heavenly fire to consume the sacrifice, whereas Elijah alone deserved to be heard because of his faith (III Kings XVIII).

[Col. 0156C] Second, what he asks: if he asks for something other than a good, he deserves neither to pray nor to be heard, because prayer concerns goods alone. Even if he obtains the evil he requested, he is not believed to have been heard but rather condemned, because to his harm he obtained what he requested—like the children of Israel, who desired flesh wrongly (Num. XI) and were severely punished at the graves of craving.

Third, from whom he asks: if he asks from anyone other than God, he neither prays nor is heard, because he does not direct his petition to him who alone is to be prayed to and who alone can hear one praying. Thus the aforementioned priests of Baal were rightly rejected because they asked for divine fire not from God but from Baal himself; Elijah, however, was heard because he asked from the one able to give it (III Kings XVIII).

[Col. 0156D] Fourth, for whom the request is made: if the person for whom it is made is neither worthy nor qualified, prayer has no effect upon him, as Samuel, though holy, did not deserve to be heard when praying for Saul, whom the Lord had reprobated (I Kings XV–XVI).

Fifth, why he asks: if he asks without a good intention, he likewise neither prays nor is heard, because God cannot be prayed to with an evil mind and does not approve evil human wills. Hence it is written in the Epistle of James: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, in order to spend it upon your desires” (James IV). Likewise the disciples were forbidden to ask for fire from heaven to burn the city of Samaria (Luke IX).

[Col. 0157A] Sixth, how he asks: if he does not ask worthily—that is, piously, humbly, and devoutly—he likewise neither prays nor is heard, because God is not prayed to by the negligent and does not assent to their petitions. Thus, when the two men went up into the Temple to pray, the Pharisee, less a praying person than one proudly recounting his good deeds, went out more blameworthy than when he entered; but the tax collector departed justified in his humility (Luke XVIII).

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0157B] You see, therefore, that for someone to be heard in prayer all these things are required: that a believer ask; that he ask God; that he ask for a good; that it be asked for one who has *commercium* in the thing requested; that he ask with a good intention; and that he ask in the proper manner.

The petitioner, as we have said, must be a believer. Yet this is not sufficient, whatever the state of all the other matters may be; rather, receive the following distinction. Every believer, as was also said above, is either righteous or unrighteous; again, both the righteous and the unrighteous must be either elect or reprobate. By righteous or unrighteous we mean according to the present quality of life, which can change; by elect or reprobate, according to God’s eternal foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived.

Thus there is a believer who is righteous and elect, persevering in grace; there is one who is unrighteous and reprobate, persistent in wickedness; there is one righteous and reprobate, who falls from righteousness; and there is one unrighteous and elect, who will rise from sin. Therefore all believers are either righteous and elect, righteous and reprobate, unrighteous and elect, or unrighteous and reprobate.

[Col. 0157C] You have an example of the first in Peter, of the second in the disciples who went back, of the third in Levi the tax collector, and of the fourth in Simon Magus. All unbelievers, however, are generally unrighteous, because apart from the faith which justifies the ungodly there can be no righteousness. [Col. 0157D] Yet among them also some are elect, who are converted through grace, such as Cornelius; while others are reprobate, who die in their unbelief, such as Pilate. Thus they are contained in a twofold division: some are called unrighteous and elect, others unrighteous and reprobate, because, as we have said, none among them are righteous.

## CHAPTER V

A believer who is righteous and elect, then, if in prayer he asks God—who alone can give it—for himself the supreme good, eternal life, with a good intention and in the proper manner, is certainly heard and obtains it: both because of his present righteousness, by which he is worthy, and because of God’s foreknowledge, by which, destined to become better, he has been predestined to life. A good intention is required because, as we said, even this good can be desired with an evil intention, as when someone desires eternal life in order to mock there the torments of the wicked.

[Col. 0158A] A proper manner is required so that, by conforming the disposition of mind and body to prayer, we may obtain the things requested more readily.

But if the believer who prays is righteous yet reprobate, he certainly does not obtain but is rejected—not because of his present righteousness, by which he is good, but because of divine foreknowledge, by which, destined to become wicked, he is foreknown for eternal death. If he is unrighteous yet elect, he is certainly heard and obtains—not because of present righteousness, which he does not possess, but because of divine foreknowledge, by which, destined to become good, he has been ordained for eternal life. But if he is both unrighteous and reprobate, he is wholly rejected for two reasons: both because of his present wickedness, by which he is evil, and because of divine foreknowledge, by which, destined to become worse, he has been assigned to eternal death.

[Col. 0158B] It is therefore clear how precious this good of eternal life is, since it is granted only to the elect; and how ample it is, since it abounds for and suffices for all of them. Accordingly, it alone should be sought in prayer; or, if anything else is sought, it should be sought only insofar as it can assist in attaining that end.

## CHAPTER VI
The remaining four kinds of the preceding goods, because they can be possessed in this life, commonly befall both the elect and the reprobate while they live in this world. For remission of sins through contrition of heart, justification through the infusion of spiritual grace, the good qualities of the soul called virtues, and good acts, whether interior or exterior—all these happen to both groups, [Col. 0158C] but in different ways. For they come to the elect finally and fruitfully; to the reprobate cursorily and therefore without fruit. The elect, retaining them perpetually, are happily brought to that highest good which they serve—I mean eternal life. The reprobate, however, abandoning them before the end, never attain that state of blessedness which cannot be reached without them: like sailors who, before gaining the harbour, throw away their oars and thus cannot reach their desired station.

Therefore, either all these things are beneficially granted to the elect, or some are denied without danger; for example, the virtue of continence and the practice of fasting, without which a person may be saved and with which one may perish. For not [Col. 0158D] all the elect are continent, nor again are all who are continent elect. Likewise, not all the reprobate are incontinent, nor are all who lack continence reprobate. There are continent elect, such as John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast (John III); and there are continent reprobates, such as the foolish virgins who are excluded from the marriage-feast (Matt. XXV). Conversely, there are elect who are married, such as Abraham and Sarah, who nevertheless used marriage for the grace of offspring; and there are reprobate married persons who, under the title of marriage, serve the lust that must be fed. Likewise, not all the elect fast, nor are all who fast elect. There are elect who fast, such as Elijah (III Kings X) and John in the desert (Matt. III); and there are reprobates who fast, such as the Pharisees who fast twice in the Sabbath-week (Luke XVIII). [Col. 0159A] Conversely too, not all who eat are reprobate, nor do all reprobates eat. There are elect who eat, such as the disciples who did not fast while the Lord was present (Matt. IX); and there are reprobates who eat, such as those whose god is their belly, as the Apostle testifies (Phil. IX).

## CHAPTER VII. On spiritual goods

It is therefore evident that these spiritual goods are either all granted to certain elect for the perfection of virtue, or some are withdrawn from certain others without danger to salvation. To the reprobate, however, either some of them are granted permanently, or all are granted for a time, without profit, or all are unhappily denied. I say “without profit” with regard to obtaining the life which cannot belong to them, not with regard to the mitigation of punishment, which may be lessened by them. When all are entirely withdrawn from certain persons, this is surely because God foresaw them to be such that no gift of special grace ought to be imparted to them.

They are bestowed upon the elect, therefore, so that by them they may earn the rewards of eternal happiness. They are granted to reprobates who are moderately evil, so that, although they have nothing by which to excuse themselves from punishment, they may nevertheless have something by which their misery is alleviated. They are wholly withdrawn from the worst, lest their wickedness share in any good. To the first they are usefully conferred for attaining eternal joy; to the second they are mercifully allowed as a remedy for punishment; to the third they are justly denied for the increase of their deserved condemnation.

## CHAPTER VIII. On intermediate things

[Col. 0159C]

The pleasant intermediate things commonly befall both kinds of human beings, but for different reasons. To the elect they are granted either as consolation amid the labours without which this life cannot be lived, or that they may be an aid to good work, an instrument for earning blessedness, a foretaste of future delight, and a sign of paternal love. To reprobates who are moderately evil they are granted either lest their removal make them worse and deserving of greater punishment; or as recompense for the few good things in them that are insufficient for life; or so that by this they may be warned how much those who live well might hope for from him who does not withhold the gifts of his generosity even from those living badly. [Col. 0159D]

But to reprobates who are likewise very evil, the prosperity of the present life is allowed to occur either as evidence of their ingratitude, since not even temporal benefits can induce them to live rightly; or lest they have anything by which they may excuse their own wickedness or accuse divine goodness; or for the instruction of the elect, so that from this very fact they may understand how contemptible such things are, since they see even the most shameful people abound in them more plentifully.

## CHAPTER IX. On sorrowful things

The sorrowful intermediate things commonly befall the elect either to purge the stains of their former life, or for the exercise of virtue, the testing [Col. 0160A] of patience, and the earning of a more abundant reward; or to restrain wrongful desires for pleasures; or so that later they may be more grateful and enjoy fuller delight when they remember that they have been transferred from present miseries to eternal joys.

To reprobates who are moderately evil, these same sorrowful things are mercifully inflicted: first, so that, with some part of their vices purged here, they may be reserved for a lighter punishment hereafter; and second, so that, when the fulfilment of their wrongful will is denied them, they may be liable to a lighter penalty. But upon reprobates who are very evil they are most justly imposed: first, so that by this they may recognize what recompense they deserve; second, so that present calamity may be for them a certain beginning of future condemnation, and that they may taste in some measure even here what they will afterwards suffer; and also lest the elect suffer scandal [Col. 0160B] if they see themselves continually pressed by miseries while the worst people always flourish.

For these and any other reasons that are hidden from us but manifest to God, who foresees all things, we judge that pleasant or sorrowful intermediate things befall both elect and reprobate. Since we believe that some of these are obtained by prayer, we thought they should be included in the present chapter, namely, on the efficacy of prayer. For many desire and request pleasant things of mind, body, or fortune: for example, mental ability, bodily health, and resources of greater wealth. Some, however—indeed very few—prefer to seek troublesome things, such as pious simplicity, bodily illness, and no property or only scant property. [Col. 0160C] For that most wise Solomon asked neither riches nor poverty, but only what was necessary for sustenance (Prov. XXX); and the Apostle declares that he knows nothing except Christ (I Cor. II); and he glories in his weaknesses, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, and in the other hardships of intermediate things (II Cor. XI). Thus, in seeking these things, both elect and reprobate are heard and obtain what they ask for the reasons stated above, while others are rejected for other reasons.

## CHAPTER X. On one who prays for another

Let this be enough, so far as we judge, concerning those who pray for themselves. Now let us consider, as far as we can, what one who asks God on another’s behalf may rightly think. Thus, either a worthy person prays for a worthy person, [Col. 0160D] a worthy person for an unworthy person, an unworthy person for a worthy person, or an unworthy person for an unworthy person. By “worthy” we mean one presently just, and by “unworthy” one presently unjust, whatever this or that person may later become.

Likewise, either one fit person prays for one fit person, one fit person for one unfit person, or one unfit person for one unfit person. By “fit” we mean an elect person, whether already worthy of eternal life according to the present quality of merits, or not yet possessing that worthiness but destined to obtain it later. By “unfit,” however, we mean a reprobate person, according either to the present or to the future quality of merits. You see, then, that from these two distinctions, worthy and unworthy, each applying to both persons—the petitioner and the person prayed for—there arises a simple [Col. 0161A] fourfold division; and again, from fit and unfit there likewise arises another simple fourfold division. Two of these distinctions posit, namely worthy and fit; two negate, namely unworthy and unfit.

Again, from these four distinctions, two applying to each person, there results a composite division of sixteen members. The first is when a worthy and fit person prays for a worthy and fit person; the last, when an unworthy and unfit person prays for an unworthy and unfit person. For brevity’s sake, we leave the intermediate fourteen to be constructed by the reader’s discernment. Since to discuss every case in order would involve more labour than benefit, let us give examples of only four simple cases.

If, then, an elect person asks eternal life for an elect person, the one who asks is heard and the one for whom the request is made receives, whether because of the present worthiness of both or because of the worthiness that will exist later—which is already present and visible to God, who sees all things and for whom nothing is past or future, but all things stand in the present. The case is like this: a ruler of some great city is said, in promoting one whom he loves, to hear another whom he likewise loves. [Col. 0161B]

But if one who is fit asks for one who is unfit, such a petitioner is rejected with regard to the person who is unfit for the thing requested, namely eternal life; not with regard to the petitioner, who by the very fact that he devoutly entreats for another earns greater favour with God. Something similar happens when a faithful servant, beloved by his master, intercedes with the master for a wicked and shameful fellow-servant, and is rejected, yet is judged worthy of greater love precisely because he laboured to intercede devoutly for another. [Col. 0161C]

If, however, one who is unfit prays for one who is fit, we say that this petition too is heard not through the petitioner’s favour but through that of the one for whom it is made: just as someone hated and despised by a ruler thinks himself heard by that ruler in the case of a person whom the ruler has raised up because of that person’s own merits, since he himself had asked on that person’s behalf. For someone is said to be heard in two ways: properly, when something is done at that person’s request and because of that person; and more improperly, when it is done while that person asks, though not because of that person’s merits but for another reason.

Such is the saying in the book of the son of Sirach (Ecclus. IV): “Do not turn your eyes away from the poor man; for he will curse you and will be heard, and he who made him will hear him”—as if God were to punish the despiser because of the poor person’s curse, although he would have punished him even had that person remained silent. [Col. 0161D]

But if one who is unfit prays for one who is unfit—that is, a reprobate for a reprobate—this petition is wholly rejected for two reasons: the fault of the petitioner and the fault of the person for whom the request is made, who has no eligibility for the thing requested. By “eligibility” we mean fitness for obtaining a thing, just as, under the laws, a servile person has no eligibility for the consulship or praetorship, and, under the canons, a lay person has no eligibility for an ecclesiastical office. An example of this final rejection occurs when a harmful citizen, and therefore deeply hated by the ruler, intercedes for one whom the ruler has resolved justly to condemn for crimes: he is repelled with inexorable severity, both because of himself and because of the one for whom he pleads. [Col. 0162A]

And so, as we have said, this may perhaps not unfittingly be understood concerning that prayer in which eternal life—promised from eternity to the elect alone—is requested by one person for another. For an elect person is the same as a fit person, whom divine election has predestined to eternal life. Therefore, as has often already been said, the blessedness of that life can be obtained by prayers for no one except one who is fit. If, then, the person for whom the prayer is made is fit, the prayer has effect, whatever the other conditions may be; and the more positive distinctions concur in either person, the more reasons there are why what is requested is obtained. But if that person is not fit, the intention of the one praying is ineffective; and the more negative distinctions concur, [Col. 0162B] the more reasons there are why what is requested is denied.

With the other four kinds of spiritual goods the reasoning is different, because they can happen to both elect and reprobate, though with unequal fruit. The elect retain them until the end and are saved; the reprobate lose them before the end and perish. Both kinds of people, therefore, can obtain these gifts by prayer both for themselves and for others, for the reasons stated above.

For unless remission of sins, called a preparatory good, could be obtained for one person through another’s prayer, the Lord would not say in the Gospel: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V); nor would Stephen say of those stoning him in the Acts of the Apostles: “Lord Jesus Christ, do not lay this sin to their charge” (Acts VII). They had already committed the sin; but that it might not be laid to their charge—indeed, that it might be removed through remission—the outstanding martyr prayed. Likewise, unless righteousness through faith, which we have preferred to call an inspirative good, could be bestowed beforehand upon one person through another’s prayer, the Apostle would not say to the Ephesians: “For this reason I bend my knees to God the Father, that he may give you strength, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. III). [Col. 0162C]

Nor would he add in the same place, concerning meritorious good, namely the good quality of mind called virtue, if it could not arise in one person through another’s prayer: “Rooted and grounded in charity”—one must supply, “that you may be.” See how he prays for them for virtue, faith, and charity. Moreover, unless good action, [Col. 0162D] called merit, were stirred up in one person by another’s intervention, it would be superfluous for the same Apostle to say: “We pray the Lord that you may do no evil, but that you may do what is good” (II Cor. XIII). He prayed for the good works of others when he said: “May God give you all a heart to worship him and to do his will” (II Macc. I), that is, to perform good works. From all this it is evident that these spiritual goods may both be requested and obtained for one person by another’s prayer.

## CHAPTER XI. On intermediate things that come to one person through another’s prayer

You will likewise find that intermediate things, whose use alone involves merit or guilt—namely their pleasant or sorrowful forms—have often [Col. 0163A] happened to some people through the prayers of others. Elijah, by prayer, withheld rain when heaven was shut, and again by prayer opened the clouds and gave rain (III Kings XVII, XVIII). The same Elijah, by prayer, consumed the soldiers of King Ahaziah by fire coming down from heaven (IV Kings I). Peter, by prayer, raised the lame Aeneas (Acts IX); Paul condemned the magician Elymas to blindness (Acts XIII). The same Peter, by prayer, raised Tabitha (Acts IX) and cast the flying Simon Magus down to the earth. Elisha restored the widow of Sarepta’s son to life (IV Kings IV); he inflicted the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian upon his servant Gehazi (IV Kings IV). Isaac obtained for his son Jacob abundance of grain, wine, and oil (Gen. XXVII); Moses, by prayer, suffocated the firstborn (Exod. XII). The same Moses overwhelmed Pharaoh and his army in the waves of the sea (Exod. IV). [Col. 0164A] He defeated the Amalekites less by war than by prayer (Exod. XVII).

We read in the Scriptures of very many deeds of this kind frequently accomplished by prayer, some of which concern the soul, some the body, and others fortune. Let this suffice concerning the obtaining or effect of prayer, not as it perhaps ought to have been said, but as we were able to say it; for it is not easy for human judgment to determine which prayers God receives or rejects.

Having thus completed three chapters concerning prayer, let us now try to consider the fourth matter, namely what pertains to it. Four things pertain to prayer: time, place, manner, and form.

# BOOK EIGHT. On the matters pertaining to prayer, namely time, place, manner, and form

[Col. 0163]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0163B]

The time of prayer is of one kind continuous, of another discrete. Continuous time is the entire span of human life, because prayer, as has often been said, is nothing other than the imploring of divine mercy. A human being’s whole life ought to tend toward this end: to win divine mercy. Whatever you do with this purpose, that you may deserve to have God favourable to you, is prayer. Holding this purpose, you pray when speaking; you pray when silent; you pray when eating; you pray when drinking; you pray when keeping watch; you pray when sleeping; you pray when doing something; you pray when doing nothing. For, as was said before our time as well: “One does not cease praying who does not cease doing good.” In this sense may be understood what was said in the Gospel: “One ought always to pray and never grow weary” (Luke XVIII). And the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V). [Col. 0163C]

Discrete time of prayer is that part of continuous time which is specially and properly assigned to the office of prayer. Such time is either daytime or nighttime.

## CHAPTER II

*Dies* (“day”) is derived from the Greek *dian*, which is interpreted as “brightness” or “serenity.” One day is greater, another lesser. The greater day is always equal: namely, the span of twenty-four hours, that is, the time in which the sun returns from east, through west, to east. Night does not divide this day but is a part of it, as an integral part within an integral whole. The lesser day is always unequal [Col. 0163D] in duration, being longer or shorter than the preceding one; and, together with night, it divides the greater day into portions of hours proportionately distributed between them. For only twice a year, at the vernal and autumnal equinoxes, are day and night equal in number of hours; each comes to twelve hours of the greater day. [Col. 0164B] The lesser day is the sun shining above the line of the horizon; night is the absence of that same sun.

From the vernal equinox to the autumnal, more hours fall to the day and fewer are left to the night. Again, from the autumnal to the vernal, more serve the night while day is content with fewer. Philosophers say that this results because in summer the arc of day is greater and that of night smaller, while in winter the arc of night is greater and that of day smaller. By the arc of day we mean that portion of the daily circle traversed by the sun in the day, that is, for as long as it is above the horizon; and by the arc of night, that portion which it completes by night, that is, [Col. 0164C] while it is hidden from us. For this reason poets, or great philosophers, attribute a bow to the same sun, whence it is called the bow-bearer. The arrows which it shoots from that heavenly bow to the earth are the darts of its rays.

Since, therefore, from the vernal equinox to the autumnal the arc of day is greater and that of night smaller, as was said, while from the latter to the vernal the arc of night is greater and that of day smaller; and since the twenty-four hours are equally distinguished and measured according to the extent of the aforesaid circle: it necessarily follows that in summer more hours fall to the day and fewer to the night, whereas in winter the contrary happens. These are the hours of which twenty-four constitute the greater day; they are called natural hours.

There are other hours, however, which philosophers [Col. 0164D] call artificial hours. They assign twelve to the day at all times and as many to the night. In these, day-hours cannot equal night-hours except at the two equinoxes; but as day increases, its hours increase, while night [Col. 0165A] and its hours diminish; and again, as night increases, its hours increase, while day and its hours become shorter. For since, as stated above, now the arc of day is greater than that of night and now conversely, while each is divided into twelve equal hours, it necessarily follows by the clearest reasoning that the hours themselves are now longer and now shorter.

In this sense, so far as the literal meaning is concerned, may be understood the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John XI). In its mystical sense, however, he intended by the designation of twelve hours to signify the twelve disciples. Whatever is rendered from these hours of day or night in the service of prayer is aptly called the daytime or nighttime time of prayer. This time is either ordinary, voluntary, or necessary.

Ordinary time is that appointed by the holy Fathers for celebrating divine praises or offering devout prayers. Such time at night is only one: it is called the nocturnal office or vigils, because night has been granted to rest, and human weakness could not, by rising more frequently to pray at night, combine nocturnal labours with daytime labours. [Col. 0165B] *Nox* (“night”) is said to derive from *nyx, nyctos*—Greek *νύξ, νυκτός* (“night,” “of night”)—by transposition of the two vowels, namely *i* and *o*.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0165C]

Night, according to the institution of the ancients, is divided into four watches. The ancients, and especially soldiers, used to divide the night into four equal parts. They called them watches because, after setting guards, they were accustomed to keep watch by turns in camp. The first watch began at the first hour of night and continued to the fourth; when it ended, the second guards were awakened. Hence the poet:

> “The third hour had now roused the second watch.”

The second begins at the fourth and continues to the seventh; when it ended, the third guards took their place. The third, beginning at the seventh, reaches the tenth; when it ended, the guards of the fourth watch were summoned. The fourth began at the tenth and, continuing to the end of the twelfth, as it were brought the night itself to an end.

The first watch was called *serotinum*, “the late-evening watch,” from the *sero* (“late”) of the preceding day; for what happens after the day is already ended [Col. 0165D] plainly happens late. Thus, if someone who ought to have come during the day—that is, while it was still day—arrives after its end, we complain that he has come late. The second is called *conticinium*, “the time of silence,” because at that time every kind of living creature on earth, pressed by deeper sleep, becomes silent. The third is called *gallicinium*, “cockcrow,” because at that time of night the domestic bird which we call a cock begins by its song to awaken those keeping watch. The fourth is called *matutinum*, “morning-time,” as if *manuninum*, from *mane* (“morning”), because of alternation, as Priscian says, since it reaches the morning of the following day; or rather from *Matuta*, the name by which the ancients called the dawn.

Those engaged in military camps used to observe this order in distinguishing the hours of the night. But we, who serve in the camp of the Church [Col. 0166A] under Christ our leader, secure under his protection against spiritual wickedness, rise once in the night when half the night has passed, or a little more, our bodies restored by sleep and our food digested. Dedicating to God, as is fitting, the firstfruits of our works, we call the office of that time nocturnal vigils. The Psalmist says of this night office: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII). When these have been completed, we add the morning praise—which nevertheless belongs to the following day—with no interval or only a small one, because it commonly continues until the morning of the next day. When it is finished, many return to their beds; but we, judging this unlawful, gladly spend whatever time remains until daylight in prayer or holy meditation, keeping continual watch. [Col. 0166B]

## CHAPTER IV

The daytime time of prayer is divided into seven parts, concerning which holy David said to the Lord: “Seven times a day I have uttered praise to you, for the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII). Their names are morning praise, of which we have already spoken, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and that which, because it completes the rest, we call Compline. No person of sound judgment doubts that these seven divine offices were instituted in order that the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit might be sought at all times. The office of the Mass, however, celebrated in honour of that holy and saving sacrifice, is not assigned to a fixed time as the others are; therefore it is customarily varied among different times. [Col. 0166C]

Voluntary time of prayer is that which someone, compelled by no rule of institution and by no necessity, but led by personal will, wishes to assign to prayer. We believe this is most rightly done when we happen to have respite from the cares of temporal matters, so that the mind may be directed to God more freely insofar as it has been released from earthly business. For it is fitting and wholly consistent with reason that, when you wish by prayer to approach him who is above all things, you should bring the whole affection of your heart to him and put every temporal care away from your mind.

For if, while petitioning an earthly ruler, through carelessness or contempt you should occupy your mind with something else amid your very petitions, would you not, by your own testimony, be unworthy to be heard if he knew what you were thinking? How much more, if you address in prayer him whom nothing can deceive, while in the very words of prayer you turn over in your mind vain, disgraceful, or even shameful matters: you not only fail to appease him but rather provoke him. [Col. 0166D]

Of such prayer may be understood the saying: “May his prayer become sin” (Ps. CXVIII). For that prayer is rightly judged to become sin which, lacking all devotion and consisting only in the clatter of words, provokes God against the one praying rather than appeases him. Therefore prayer must either be begun with a pure and tranquil heart, or, if it finds the heart disturbed, it must be purified by the power and devotion of prayer, so that the purer the affection of the one praying, the more excellent the effect of the prayer. Hence, after humbly and purely saying certain things, the Psalmist, trusting in God’s mercy, says: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer” (Ps. VI). [Col. 0167A]

## CHAPTER V

Necessary time of prayer is that chosen neither by the will nor prescribed by an institution, but brought about by necessity. This necessity is divided into two kinds. One binds a person to perform the due measure of service because, through a legitimate occupation, forgetfulness, contempt, or negligence, that person omitted to discharge it at the time when it should have been discharged.

By a legitimate occupation we mean an excusable reason for a matter: for instance, a journey or voyage; [Col. 0167B] pleadings in conducting legal cases; deliberations in taking counsel; or very many such matters. Being often hindered by these, we are unable to render the service of divine praise with its due honour. But if someone says that he was occupied with wine, dice, theatrical entertainments, hunting or bird-catching, or even robbery and other harmful things, such occupation is not legitimate; it is rather reckoned contempt and insult. Therefore, if we expect a legitimate occupation to arise that will prevent us from fulfilling the vows of our prayers, I think it safer to anticipate rather than postpone the customary time of prayer, according to the Psalmist’s admonition: “Let us come before his face with confession” (Ps. XCIV). And elsewhere, turning to God, he says: [Col. 0167C] “My eyes anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your words” (Ps. CXVIII). In the preceding verse he had already said: “I rose early and cried out” (ibid.).

But if an unforeseen occupation happens to come upon us, it is not blameworthy to compensate late for the service of divine praise that was prevented by lack of time. Thus one of the courtiers, who, occupied with business of the court, had omitted the Compline of the preceding day, softly whispered it at the hour of Prime on the following day. When the ruler, putting his ear close, perceived this, the man was not only praised but even raised to episcopal rank, the emperor saying to him: “Have this bishopric, because you gladly sing your Compline.”

But if the time for prayer [Col. 0167D] has passed through forgetfulness, it is necessary not only to make up what was omitted but also to make satisfaction by some compunction of heart. For ignorance of a matter that could have been known and ought to have been known involves fault; otherwise the Psalmist would not say: “Lord, do not remember my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV). We are said to be ignorant of, or not to know, those things which we ought to know; and each expression implies a fault, according to the saying: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (I Cor. XIV). Things which it is not expedient to know, however, are not said to be matters of ignorance or of lacking knowledge (*ignorare* or *nescire*), but simply matters of not knowing (*non scire*).

But if the time of divine prayer has been omitted through negligence and contempt—through wine or dice, theatrical spectacles, foolish and indecent actors’ tales, wantonness and impurity, such as the seductive allurements of female pleasure; [Col. 0168A] or through the malice of an unjust mind, such as frauds, traps, and deceits against the innocent, or even quarrels, robberies, and the desire to shed blood, and very many other things customarily done vainly, impurely, or impiously—if, I say, anything has been omitted for such reasons, it must not only be humbly repaired but also punished by the retribution of most severe penitence. One must mourn penitently that what ought to have been done was not done, and that what was least permitted was done; that time belonging to piety and devotion was given to vanity and malice; that when one ought to have been sober in church, one was drunk in a tavern; when one ought to have devoted oneself to contemplation of angels, one attended the spectacle of games; when one ought to have been in the service of the holy Mother of God, one was in the hut of an incestuous prostitute; when one ought to have prayed for one’s persecutors, one hastened to oppress an innocent person; when one ought to have handled or received Christ’s body, one ran to shed one’s brother’s blood. [Col. 0168B]

You see, then, that whatever divine service has been omitted for one of the three aforesaid reasons must be humbly repaired; but in the first failure the fault is slight, in the second it is considerable, and in the third it is most grave.

## CHAPTER VI

There is also another necessity concerning the time of prayer, whenever some unexpected event arises so that we must resort to prayer beyond the customary practice. This commonly happens in two ways: either to avoid danger or to obtain a benefit. [Col. 0168C]

## CHAPTER VII

Danger concerns either the soul alone, the body alone, both together, or outward things such as reputation or fortune. Danger to the soul alone occurs when, though the body is safe, the salvation of the soul is endangered—for example, by the prompting of mortal sin. Against this danger Solomon prayed when he said: “Lord God and ruler of my life, do not abandon me to my own thought. Turn my desire away from me; take away my lusts, and do not hand me over to an irreverent and unrestrained soul” (Ecclus. XXV).

Danger to the body alone occurs when the soul, conscious of no grave sin, is safe, but bodily death is feared—as in one who expects death to be near, [Col. 0168D] for example amid wars, shipwrecks, fires, or an extreme illness. Against this danger the Saviour prayed as a true human being, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XX). So also did the three youths in the furnace (Dan. III), Paul in shipwreck (Acts XXVII), and Hezekiah at the extremity of illness (IV Kings XX).

Danger to both together occurs when bodily death is believed to be immediately at hand and the soul’s eternal death is feared—as in one guilty of many crimes, uncorrected by any satisfaction, who believes death to be near. Against this danger the Ninevites prayed (Jonah III), as did the thief hanging on the cross, so that he might at least avoid one of the two deaths, namely the death of the soul, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke II). [Col. 0169A]

Danger to reputation occurs when we fear for our standing, lest, having lost it, we become infamous, as commonly happens to those accused of grave and monstrous wrongdoing. Against this danger to reputation, and also against danger to the body, Joseph prayed in prison (Gen. XL), and Susanna when she was being led to death (Dan. XV).

Danger to fortune concerns the loss of liberty, friends, or things sufficiently necessary for our use. Danger in the loss of liberty occurs when we fear losing liberty itself, as with one captured by enemies in war and preserved alive in order to serve. For slaves are said to be named both from being preserved (*servando*) and from serving (*serviendo*). Against this danger [Col. 0169B] the Jews, that is, the children of Israel, prayed when Pharaoh pursued them with thousands of horses and chariots, fearing that he would bring them back to the slavery of mud and brick which they had fled (Exod. XIV).

Danger in the loss of friends occurs when we believe that those whom we love, or by whom we are loved, will be taken from us by death or by some event such as captivity, travel, or exile. Against this danger the Jews besieged by Holofernes prayed, when they implored the Lord that their children might not be given as plunder and their wives be divided up, as is read in the book of Judith (ch. IV). Danger in the loss of possessions occurs when we believe beyond doubt that we shall lose things necessary to us, as in shipwrecks, fires, robberies, and other such events. Against this danger [Col. 0169C] the children of Israel prayed that their city might not be given over to destruction and their holy things to defilement, as is read in the same book of Judith. When any of these kinds of danger come upon us at whatever time of day or night, we must pray humbly: reason teaches this, and many examples admonish us.

## CHAPTER VIII.

The benefit which we ask from God in prayer may likewise be distinguished in just as many ways, by considering the corresponding contrary things. There is a benefit of the soul, such as virtue; of the body, such as soundness; of both together, such as the preservation of each; of reputation, such as the standing of good repute; of fortune, such as freedom, an abundance of friends, and sufficient means for the things one must use. Whenever there is need, all these things [Col. 0169D] must necessarily be asked of God with the utmost urgency of prayer.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Place of Prayer

The place of prayer is either universal or particular. The universal place is the whole world, since everywhere throughout the whole world God must be prayed to, praised, and blessed, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. X). And elsewhere: “Let all the earth worship you, O God, and sing psalms to you” (Ps. LXV). Likewise the Lord says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII).

A particular place is this place, that place, or another; and in each of them God is wholly present, no less wholly in one than in another, as the Psalmist says: “If I ascend [Col. 0170A] into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII). If he does not refuse to be in hell, where, I ask, can he be absent, or from what place can he be missing?

A particular place is either sacred or profane. We call sacred that which is dedicated to divine worship, such as a church; profane, that which is not sacred, such as a house or country estate. Both sacred and profane places are either public or private. A sacred public place is, for example, a church or cemetery; a sacred private place, an oratory. A profane public place is a marketplace, theatre, or harbour; a profane private place, a house, field, or garden.

Again, a sacred place is either assigned, chosen, or encountered. An assigned sacred place is, for example, the episcopal church, assigned to the whole people of the city, who are bound to resort to it [Col. 0170B] at least once a week, if they cannot do so more often. It is likewise generally assigned to all its diocesan members, who are bound to resort to it at least once a year, except those excused by a reasonable cause, such as sex, age, or bodily illness. Likewise, the baptismal church is assigned to all its parishioners, who are bound to resort to it once a week if they cannot do so more often. Every collegiate church is assigned to its clerics, who live from a common fund but not in community, and who are bound to be present at every canonical hour of prayer. An oratory, however, is assigned to its monks or regular clerics, who live communally from a common fund; they may never be absent except by command of the provost or abbot.

A chosen place is one which anyone selects of his own will for the sake [Col. 0170C] of devotion: such as the Lord’s tomb, the thresholds of the Apostles, and the many other places throughout the world possessing monuments of divine mercy. An encountered place is one which is neither assigned nor chosen voluntarily, but unexpectedly presents itself by chance, as often happens to those travelling abroad by road or ship, when they come to unknown places.

In all these places, each person’s assigned place must be honoured with the greatest reverence, unless, prompted by great devotion and penitence, he has selected for his prayer another place farther away and more renowned for religious observance: as do those who honour the Lord’s tomb, the thresholds of the Apostles, or other holy places, by voluntary labour and humble devotion [Col. 0170D]. Permission to visit such sacred places is granted to secular clerics by the blessing of their bishop, and to laypeople by the blessing of their parish priest; but it is altogether forbidden to monks and regular clerics without the permission of the supreme pontiff.

## CHAPTER X. On the Manner of Prayer

The manner of prayer consists in two things: namely, the duration of time and the quantity of words. Duration is considered in the fact that some pronounce more words more quickly in psalmody, while others pronounce fewer more slowly. The quantity of words is discerned in the fact that some lengthen or shorten the psalmody of day or night by omitting or adding certain psalms [Col. 0171A].
