In this matter, nothing seems more consonant with reason than that each person should endeavour to conform himself, both in duration and in number, to those persons with whom he must live. For since singing psalms to God and praying are a most holy work, there should be no discrepancy there, but uniformity and harmony, so that we may say with the Psalmist: “In the house of God we walked in harmony” (Ps. LIV).

# BOOK NINE

On the fourfold form of prayer: namely, the Lord’s Prayer, domestic, monastic, and ecclesiastical prayer. On the first four petitions of the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 0171]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0171B]

There is one form of prayer that is the Lord’s, another domestic, another canonical or ecclesiastical, and another monastic. The form of prayer called the Lord’s is that which the Lord God delivered when those asking him to teach them to pray; he spoke as follows: “Thus, then, shall you pray.”

## CHAPTER II. The Lord’s Prayer

“Our Father who art in heaven,” etc. (Matt. VI). The disciples had heard the Lord preaching about the power of prayer; they had also often seen him praying. Yet, desiring to worship at his exhortation and example, they did not know what above all they should pray for, or how they should pray. Therefore, lest they should be ignorant and negligent in a matter so great and necessary, they humbly [Col. 0171C] asked him to deign to give them a certain and fitting manner of prayer.

The heavenly teacher granted their holy request. Knowing for what purpose he had come, and what he had brought from that heavenly school to teach and preach, he prescribed for them a form of prayer complete and perfect, containing every necessity. It was enclosed in words so plain and few that even little children and womenfolk may easily understand its literal meaning; yet so profound in mystery that it can scarcely be grasped in thought or expounded in speech by any mortal. “Thus,” he says, “you shall pray the Father: ‘Our Father,’ etc.”

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0171D]

This Lord’s Prayer contains seven petitions; yet each one is itself a prayer, since asking is almost nothing other than praying. Nothing prevents a catholic—that is, universal—prayer from being part of a catholic prayer, just as was shown above, by way of example, concerning rhetorical speech and dialectical speech called a proposition.

Some, perhaps simpler people or those fleeing the labour of deeper inquiry, think that these seven petitions should be followed in the order in which the Lord set them down: the first being the hallowing of the divine name, the second the coming of the heavenly kingdom, and so on to the end. Others, whether more acute or more carefully considering the order of the things themselves, adorn the matter by a certain artifice and, beginning [Col. 0172B] with the petition in which we ask to be delivered from evil, proceed in reverse order until the hallowing of the Name.

Wishing to follow the practice of both, we shall try to treat them in both their order and the others’ order, leaving it to the reader’s judgment whether this order or that is better or truer. We shall likewise attempt to correlate, according to each order, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated by prophecy, the seven virtues mentioned in the Gospel, and the seven beatitudes applied to those virtues. Therefore, having invoked him who willed us to pray and gave us the form of prayer, let us discuss, insofar as he grants it, the prayer which he himself taught.

First, then, we should consider how worthy of thanksgiving it is that the true and natural Son of God, our blood-relative through the human nature assumed by him, deigned on earth to make his Father—whose only Son he was in heaven—our common Father. He did not begrudge any one of us the inheritance of the paternal kingdom, not to divide it into shares, but to grant the whole of it to be possessed fully with him. He therefore wished us to address God in prayer by the name through which he knew God could most readily be moved to mercy: “Our Father,” he says.

## CHAPTER IV

The title “Father” is customarily attributed to God in Scripture in different ways: by nature, creation, governance, bestowal of benefits, protection, and adoption.

By nature, God is Father of one alone: namely, [Col. 0172D] his only-begotten Son, begotten of him before the ages. Just as the Son has always had a Father, so he must be believed always to have been Son. Therefore, as the former is truly proclaimed eternal Father, so the latter is truly proclaimed eternal Son. Of this fatherhood the same Son says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father” (John V). Elsewhere: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (ibid.). And again: “He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (ibid.).

By creation, he is Father of all things that exist apart from the Creator himself, visible and invisible alike; for he brought all things out of nothing into the being which they possess. Thus all things originally received from him the cause of their existence, as is read in Malachi: “Do we not all have one Father? Has not one God created us all?” (Mal. II). Hence, because of this authority to create, he is not inappropriately called Father of all creatures, in the manner of speech by which someone is called the father of a thing of which he is the first inventor, such as a poem or an art. Isaiah speaks to him of this fatherhood: “And now, Lord, you are our Father, and we are clay; you are our maker, and we are all the work of your hands” (Isa. LXIV).

By governance he is also Father of all, because he governs and rules all things created by him according to the nature implanted in them. Hence he may be called their Father, just as the one who presides over a household and rules its family is, by ancient custom, called *paterfamilias*, “father of the household,” that is, father of the family. This is after the example of the Greeks, who form the genitive in *-as* from nominatives having a pure *a* before it: thus from *sophia* they customarily say, in the genitive, *sophias*. Of this governing fatherhood Augustine says: “Nothing happens on earth which is not either commanded or permitted from that most orderly household of the great father of the family.” Hence elsewhere: “Father, you govern all things by your wisdom.”

By the bestowal of benefits he is Father only of sentient beings: namely, those able to use the benefit of intellect, reason, or sense. To these, according to the capacity of their nature, he lavishly grants the benefits of his goodness with a fatherly affection, like a most indulgent father. To angels and the other orders of heavenly powers, and to holy souls now freed from the body, [Col. 0173C] he shows the presence of his divine majesty. To the righteous still placed in the flesh he grants the necessities of this present life and inspires them with his grace. But to wicked human beings and brute animals he administers only bodily necessities.

For this benevolent providence he is called Father of all living things, because he does not cease to bestow his benefits upon them insofar as either nature or merit permits. This is the meaning of: “That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and unjust” (Matt. V). And elsewhere: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father [Col. 0173D] feeds them” (Matt. VI). And again: “Are not five sparrows sold for two small coins, and not one of them is forgotten before your Father?” (Luke XII).

By protection he is Father of all who are unjustly oppressed, inasmuch as he both has compassion on them in affection, like a father for his children, and aids them by fatherly goodness. Such is what is said in the Psalm: “They shall be troubled at the presence of him who is father of orphans and judge of widows” (Ps. LXVII). Among those whose Father he is by protecting them, he is especially called Father of orphans, so that he may be understood particularly to rule and protect those deprived of the comfort of natural parents.

By adoption he is Father only of believers. Having rescued them from the power of the devil through knowledge of the truth, he joins them, as an adoptive father, to his only-begotten and natural Son in the share of the divine inheritance. Hence: “God sent [Col. 0174A] his Son, made under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. IV). Again: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry: ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII).

Adoption is a civil-law institution by which someone takes another’s son as his own son and into the share of his inheritance, whether he himself has children or none. Adoption imitates nature to this extent: no one may adopt another unless he is older than the adoptee by full puberty, that is, eighteen years—an interval sufficient, by reason of age, for him to be the other’s father.

There are two kinds of adoption: one called *adrogatio* [adrogation], and the other called, more specifically by its generic name, *adoptio* [adoption]. *Adrogatio* is that by which someone who has been emancipated from his natural father and made legally independent is adopted as a son in such a way that he passes wholly into the authority of the adopter. *Adoptio*, however, is that by which someone is adopted by another while nevertheless not ceasing to remain under the authority of his former father. This distinction is briefly expressed in these two little verses:

> I adrogate one who is his own master: he must become mine.  
> I adopt the son belonging to a father, yet he does not cease to belong to his father.

A certain parallel to this twofold distinction is found in spiritual adoption. Some are adopted by God the Father through faith in catholic truth in such a manner that, rescued from the power of the devil—whom they had previously had as father, not by nature but through fault—they are wholly transferred into God’s authority and receive with Christ the right of the paternal inheritance. Such are those who, having received faith and been aided by divine grace, persevere [Col. 0174C] to the end in good works. Of them it is written: “If you are Abraham’s seed, then you are children of God” (John VIII). “And if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

Others, adopted by faith alone, pass into adopted sons in such a way that their former father, the devil, retains paternal authority over them. These are those marked only with the sacrament of faith, but who take no care to practise works of faith, piety, and righteousness. Of them one may understand what was said of the Jews: “Alien sons have lied to me,” etc. (Ps. LXXVII)—that is, those whom I had adopted through faith have, while remaining in wickedness, limped or wavered (ibid.). Nor is it surprising that those retained under the devil’s power can, by faith alone, be transferred into adopted sons, since their father the devil himself both confesses and believes, as it is written in the Gospel: “Demons came out from many, crying: ‘You are the Son of God’; and he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was Christ” (Luke IV). Observe that to cry out is more than simply to confess, and to know more than to believe.

By that kind of adoption in which the adoptee passes wholly into the authority of the adopter, those who have both faith and works of faith become children of God. Therefore he is most rightly called their Father through the same adoption—not so much by civil as by heavenly law. Such persons may fittingly and truly turn to him and say:

## CHAPTER

“Our Father”: as though they said, “Father of your only-begotten Son [Col. 0175A] by nature; ours by grace. Father of all by the authority of creating; ours by the mercy of re-creating. Father of the universe by the power of governing; ours by the clemency of saving. Father of all living things by the bestowal of benefits; ours by the promise of eternal life. Father of the oppressed by the protection of divine power; ours by the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit. Father of all believers by reception of the sacrament; ours by faith and good works.”

## CHAPTER VI

“Who art in heaven.” Although God is wholly present everywhere, he is nevertheless more often said to be in heaven, since heaven appears to be the more excellent part of the whole creation, on account of the reverence due to divine majesty. But we must consider in [Col. 0175B] which heavens, and in what manner, he is to be believed present.

For “heaven” or “heavens” has many meanings in Scripture. Heaven or heavens can mean the splendour and sublimity of eternal divinity. “Heaven,” as in: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven” (John V). “Heavens,” as in: “Rejoice, because your names are written in the heavens” (Luke X).

Again, heaven or heavens can mean the empyrean heaven, which the Greeks call *empyreon*, which was filled with holy angels immediately upon its creation; and in it the orders of heavenly powers were distinguished according to the grace granted them by the Creator. “Heaven,” as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Their angels in heaven always see the face [Col. 0175C] of the Father” (Matt. XVIII). “Heavens,” as elsewhere: “For the powers of the heavens shall be moved” (Matt. XXIV).

Likewise, heaven or heavens can mean the firmament, called *ouranos* in Greek, which God made to divide the waters from the waters, as is written in Genesis (ch. I): “God made the firmament and divided the waters which were below the firmament from those which were above the firmament.” According to the philosophers, all stars except the seven planets are fixed in this firmament. They think they prove this from the fact that they are always carried along with the firmament itself at equal intervals from one another. Moses too seems to support this philosophical opinion when he says in Genesis (ibid.): “God made the stars and placed them in the firmament.” This firmament is now called “heaven,” as in: “God called the firmament heaven” (ibid.); but at other times “heavens,” as in: “Bless the Lord, all you waters that are above the heavens” (Dan. V).

Again, heaven or heavens can mean the region of the world extending from the firmament down to the sphere of the moon, called *aether* by the Greeks. In it the seven wandering stars, which the Greeks call planets, are arranged in this order: Saturn is first and nearest to the firmament; Jupiter second; Mars third; the sun fourth; Venus fifth; Mercury sixth; and the moon seventh. The nearer they are to the firmament, the larger the circle in which they travel; but the nearer they are to the earth, the smaller a circle they describe in each of their two motions—the motion of the world, [Col. 0176A] that is, and their planetary motion. Accordingly, although all are believed to have the same speed, some complete their revolutions more quickly and others more slowly: Saturn only once in thirty years, but the moon every month.

Scripture now calls this region of the world of which we speak “heaven,” as in: “The moon is perfect for ever, and a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII); but now “heavens,” as when someone says: “Sun and moon, praise the Lord from the heavens,” that is, from that region of the ether. Moreover, Scripture calls without distinction either “heaven” or “heavens” the space extending from the lunar sphere down to earth—the windy and stormy air. “Heaven,” as in: “The kite in heaven knew its time” (Jer. VIII). “Heavens,” as in the Psalm: “They ascend unto the heavens and descend unto the abyss” (Ps. CVI), that is, to the height of the air and the depth of the sea.

The holy Church is also sometimes called “heaven” in the singular, as in Revelation: “The stars of heaven fell, and heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up” (Apoc. VI). In the plural, “heavens” means the holy Apostles, as in the Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII); and again: “Mercy shall be built in the heavens” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Moreover, any holy soul is called “heaven,” and several together are sometimes called “heavens.” For since the Lord says through the prophet, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI), and elsewhere it is written, “The soul of the righteous is God’s throne,” it is clear [Col. 0176C] that every holy soul can be called heaven, and several or all together heavens in the plural, as in the Psalm: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens,” that is, in the souls of the righteous (Ps. CXXII).

Since the page of sacred Scripture has attributed the name “heaven” or “heavens” to so many things, whether literally, typologically, or morally, it has dared spiritually to designate itself by the same terms, lest it remain deprived of so beautiful a name. Scripture is called “heaven,” as in the Psalm: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” (Ps. CIII); and now “heavens” in the plural, as in: “Your magnificence is raised above the heavens” (Ps. VIII), that is, above all Scriptures, because the glory of Christ, to whom [Col. 0176D] the prophet speaks, cannot be expounded by any Scriptures.

The sequence of sacred Scripture is rightly called heaven or heavens, since it is not only studded, after the fashion of heaven, as with a variety of stars, with divine commandments, holy exhortations, and examples; but also conceals from us the hidden mysteries of heaven. Therefore, in these heavens—and in any others besides these which may be found—we truly profess that God, who is absent nowhere, is present. But how he is to be believed present in them must be investigated with the utmost care. For we do not judge it fitting to suppose that the Creator is in creatures in the same manner in which one creature is thought or seen to be in another.

## CHAPTER VII

There are, then, diverse and distinct ways in which philosophers, especially the Peripatetics, have discerned something to be in something else [Col. 0177A]. Something is in something locally, that is, as a thing contained in its container—for example, wine in a flask. Something is in something as an accident in a subject—for example, whiteness in a human being—because neither can a subject exist without an accident nor an accident except in a subject.

Something is in something materially, that is, as matter in a material thing: whether the matter remains in it, as iron in a sword, or loses its own character, as flour and water in bread. Something is in something originally, as that which derives its origin from another: whether it remains under the same species, as a son from a father—according to which authority testifies that we all were present in the loins—or is transformed into another species, as a chick from [Col. 0177B] an egg, grass from a seed.

Something is in something naturally, as an element in a composite thing—for example, fire or water in beard or hair. Further, something is in something finally, as happiness in a good life and victory in war, because the former is the end of a good life and the latter the end of war. Something is in something causally, as virtue in praise, because praise follows from virtue.

Furthermore, something is in something as a genus in a species, as animal in human being, because the designation “animal” is most properly applied to a human being: every human being is an animal. Something is in something as a species in a genus, as human being and horse in animal, because both are included under the designation “animal.” Something is also in something as a species in individuals, as human being in Socrates and Plato, because the designation “human being” belongs to both: each is a human being. Something is in something as individuals in a species, as Socrates and Plato in human being, because each is included under this species.

Again, something is in something as a whole in its parts, as a human being in soul and body, because a human being subsists wholly in these two. Something is in something as parts in the whole, as soul and body in a human being, because a human being is constituted only from these two.

Although philosophers say that something is in something else in all these ways, and perhaps in more, God must not be believed to be in heaven or in any thing in any of these ways. He is not anywhere as a thing contained in a container, because he contains all things [Col. 0177D] and is contained by none. Nor is he in something as an accident in a subject, because he is not an accident but a pure and simple essence of ineffable nature. Nor is he as matter in a material thing, because he is the maker of all things and the matter of none.

Similar things could be said of the remaining categories, if we were not avoiding prolixity; from them it could most easily be proved that God is neither in heaven nor in any creature in any of the aforesaid ways. Nevertheless, if something may be ventured on so great a subject, it may fittingly, I think, be said that God exists and subsists in himself, upheld by his own power; in the heavenly angels and holy souls now stripped of the body, through the present glory of the divine majesty; in holy persons still placed in the flesh, through indwelling [Col. 0178A] grace; and in all remaining things through essence, power, and presence.

## CHAPTER VIII. The First Petition: On the Hallowing of the Name

“Hallowed be thy name.” After the invocation of the Father, which the Son himself showed, knowing the Father’s disposition and by what words he might most readily be moved to hear us, let us first endeavour to treat the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer in the order in which he himself placed them. “Hallowed,” he says, “be thy name.” The first petition concerns the hallowing of the Name; and therefore let us take care to examine what this Name is and how it may be hallowed.

## CHAPTER IX

The name of the Father—whether one says “God” or “Father”—can be distinguished in two ways [Col. 0178B]. It consists either in sound alone or in the thing itself alone. A vocal name is one existing only in the sound of speech; it can be uttered from elementary sounds and represented by visible signs. Such is the word *Deus*, “God,” understood as residing so completely in the utterance of the voice that it may be heard at one and the same time in the mouths of different persons and in different places.

A real name, however, is nothing other than the thing itself: that is, the glory of the divine majesty. Someone is said to be “of great name,” not because his name contains more letters, but because he himself possesses great authority and reputation. A vocal name, since it is devised by human beings, can likewise be defined by human beings, so that it may be said to be “a meaningful sound by convention, whose parts have no meaning independently.” But a real name was neither invented by human beings nor can be defined by them—unless perhaps someone defines it as a thing that, because of its greatness, is indefinable: so pure and simple that no parts or accidents can be found in it.

Moreover, since a vocal name rests upon human choice, it varies according to the different idioms of languages. Thus, for what is called *Deus* in Latin, the Hebrews customarily say *hel*, and the Greeks *theos*. Likewise, for our *pater*, “father,” the Hebrews use *ab*, while the Greeks use *pater*. But the real name, because it does not rest upon human choice but upon the nature of divinity—or rather is divinity itself—varies in no respect, but by its own nature and proper stability [Col. 0178D] remains firm and incorruptible, as it is written: “And his name remains for ever.”

This indeed is the Name of which the Saviour says: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world” (John XVII). For if he were speaking of the spoken name, what great thing would it have been for so great a teacher to reveal to the people whom he had chosen from the whole world the name of God, which in that language has scarcely three letters—or rather two—namely *hel*? But there was another Name, exceedingly great and immeasurable, which no one could teach except himself, and which no one then was capable of understanding except those persons: that Name, indeed, of which the Psalmist says: “Blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and for evermore” (Ps. CXII).

This is the Name which the three youths praised in the furnace, saying: “Blessed is the name of your glory, which is holy” (Dan. III). “His name is great in Israel,” he says (Ps. LXXV). Certainly not that monosyllable, or the two-letter word *hel*, than which scarcely anything can be smaller or shorter; but that Name which is above every name named in heaven and on earth, by which the whole world is governed, which angels and human beings must fear, and at which even Tartarus trembles.

For that Name is great in Israel, that is, among those who see and understand through contemplation the glory of the divine loftiness. For, however Israel may be interpreted, it is the name of eternal Divinity: great, immense, and altogether ineffable. This is the Name operative in the sacraments of the Church, in which the Lord commanded the Apostles [Col. 0179B] to baptize, saying: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). He said “in the name,” not “in the names,” because although there are three names of persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—there is only one Name in the reality itself: one majesty, one power, one sublimity.

Let us therefore endeavour to inquire, insofar as he himself grants it, in what manner this Name may be hallowed—the Name concerning which the Lord instructed us to pray.

Before the Savior’s advent, when God was known only in Judaea (Ps. 75), and there only by very few, while all the surrounding nations, having no knowledge of the true God, worshipped wood and stones, the spoken name “God” was, as it were, cheap and profane. For it applied not only to impure [Col. 0179C] human beings, such as Jupiter, Mars, and Mercury, but also to stones and wood, and indeed even to demons themselves. But after the Savior first, and after him the apostles, began to preach that there was only one being to whom this name ought uniquely to be ascribed, that name began to be sanctified in the hearts of those who heard it, and to be judged holy and worthy of God alone. Then the commandment of the Law which had been almost effaced among the Jews—“Hear, O Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. 6)—became known even to the nations; and consequently the multitude of gods was rejected. And because this was to occur in the time and through the office of the apostles, the Lord first instructed them to ask for the sanctification of the name.

[Col. 0179D] Likewise, that real name—which is nothing other than the very nature of the Godhead—was holy to very few before people acknowledged it by faith: not because it could fail to be holy, but because it was not even thought to exist. But when Christ preached, and after him the apostles, and people began eagerly both to believe in and confess the one true God, this name was sanctified: not because it began to be holy, but because it became known to be holy. For the Psalmist had already said of the same name: “Holy and fearful is his name” (Ps. 110); and elsewhere: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and let all that is within me bless his holy name” (Ps. 110). Of this sanctification of the name the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying: “When I shall have been sanctified among you” (Ezek. 36).

[Col. 0180A] This was fulfilled when, through the apostles’ preaching, the spoken name that had formerly been blasphemed among the nations was received, out of reverence for the one God, into honour and glory; and when the real name—that is, the very essence of the Godhead, which had formerly not even been thought to exist—was, as the nations turned to faith, discovered both to exist and to be most holy.

Moreover, by the designation “the Father’s name,” the only-begotten Son of God may suitably be indicated. Through his presence and preaching the heavenly Father became known to the world, just as someone previously unknown ordinarily becomes known through the manifestation of his name. This was taking place when the Lord said in the Gospel: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” (John 17). For when the Son was glorified through the glory of the resurrection, [Col. 0180B] the Father himself too became known to the world in glory.

Of this name the prophet says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, and his brightness fills the whole earth” (Isa. 30). The Son of God came from afar because he came from heaven to earth, not through a change of place, but through the incarnation of the Word. He came from afar because he came from the divine nature into the human: not by abandoning the former, but by assuming the latter; not by laying aside power, but by taking on our weakness. Of this name the Lord said through Ezekiel the prophet: “I shall sanctify my great name, that all may know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 36).

This name, therefore, was sanctified when, as the Lord died and rose again and ascended into heaven, the divine power which had formerly lain hidden in him as though in a mortal human being—[Col. 0180C] the power by which all these things could be accomplished—began to be regarded as great, ineffable, and worthy of every holiness. The Savior was speaking of this sanctification of the Father’s name, that is, of himself, when he spoke to the Father concerning his disciples and others who were to believe in him through them: “For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17).

This sanctification of the name takes place through the spirit of fear. When Isaiah spoke of him who was to descend from heaven to earth, he placed this last among the spiritual gifts, beginning with the spirit of wisdom and descending through the intervening five to this one:

> “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, [Col. 0180D] the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11).

But for a person wishing to return from earth to heaven, this same spirit of fear is necessary before all else, so that, humbled by it, he may ascend step by step to the higher gifts of grace—going, that is, “from strength to strength,” so that “the God of gods may be seen in Zion” (Ps. 85). Thus, humbled to his benefit through this spirit of fear, having acquired the virtue of humility and subjected himself to the Lord, a person begins to wonder at and worship that holy and glorious name, saying with the Psalmist: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. 8).

To this first virtue, humility—which is nothing other than [Col. 0181A] spiritual poverty alone—the kingdom of heaven is promised, lest it seem to run in vain. For the Savior says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). And this is fitting: those who in this life subject themselves through voluntary humility to divine service shall glory with him in the kingdom of eternity.

## CHAPTER X. The second petition: concerning the coming of the kingdom

“May your kingdom come.” The second petition concerns the coming of that kingdom, the sanctification of whose name has been preceded by so glorious and clear a report. This order is admirably arranged. Just as people who have no king desire to have as their king some great man whose authority is renowned and distinguished, and say: “May he come, whom report has proclaimed to us as such a man; may he come and reign over us”; so it is worthwhile to consider what this kingdom is whose coming must be so earnestly sought.

For God, our king before the ages, is not content with only one kingdom: he rules over several kingdoms. He reigns in heavenly glory; he reigns in every creature; he reigns in the Church; he reigns in every holy soul. In the first kingdom he reigns through the present and visible glory of his majesty, by which he delights, feeds, and satisfies the heavenly angels and blessed spirits. In the second he reigns through the unbounded power of divine might, by which he governs, sustains, and preserves all things created by him. In the third he reigns through the ineffable mercy [Col. 0181C] of his loving-kindness, by which he calls, gathers, and cleanses those who had withdrawn from him through unbelief. In the fourth he reigns through the indwelling grace of his goodness, by which he cherishes, instructs, and saves the holy soul.

The first kingdom is that of majesty and glory; the second, of might and power; the third, of piety and mercy; the fourth, of kindness and grace. None of these can come to God, to whom all things are present and for whom nothing is either newly acquired or recent. For just as he has nothing that can be lost, so he receives nothing that can be added. Although nothing is coeternal with God, nevertheless, because he could never be ignorant of anything and all things have always been present to him, even those things which began to exist in time [Col. 0181D] in some manner always stood present before him.

Therefore God reigned from eternity in heavenly glory, that is, in himself, even before there was a creature able to share in his kingdom. He also reigned in all creatures, because, though they did not yet exist in the order of things, they were already subject to him in his foreknowledge. He reigned in the Church because, although he had not yet gathered it through mercy, he nevertheless foresaw in his eternity that it would be gathered. He reigned also in holy souls, because, although he had not yet saved them through grace, he nevertheless had them most certainly inscribed for life.

You see, then, that none of these kingdoms either could or can come to God. Therefore this coming of the kingdom is to be desired and requested, not for him, but for us. The kingdom of eternity comes to us [Col. 0182A] when it happens that we attain it. The Creator’s kingdom comes to a creature when, as it begins to exist, it happily receives such a Creator and Lord. God’s kingdom comes to the Church when it beneficially passes, through the Catholic faith, from the devil’s kingdom into his kingdom. His kingdom comes to the holy soul when he begins, through indwelling grace, to console and cherish it.

The first kingdom, indeed, is above all others to be desired and sought, as the fruit, reward, and end of the rest. But according to the foregoing order of exposition, these words should be understood of the kingdom of the Church, whose coming, at the time when the Lord spoke these words, was to be desired and urgently implored with every persistence in prayer. Thus the apostles in the time of the primitive Church continually devoted themselves to prayer, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They,” it says, “were unanimously persevering in the prayer of God” (Acts 1), namely, for the advancement of the Church itself.

For his kingdom in all creatures ought indeed to be welcome and pleasing; yet it is superfluous to desire or request it, because, whether we will or not, the Maker of all things rules and reigns over the things he has made, as it is written: “In your will, O Lord, all things are established, and there is none who can resist your will; for you made all things: you are Lord of all” (Esther 13). But concerning the kingdom of the Church—which at that time was recent and had begun to take shape in only a few—the disciples then ought to pray that it might grow and prosper, like the yield of a good crop; and every day the faithful, until the end of the age, ought to desire that it may endure and flourish.

For all who through faith, in the succession of times, are incorporated into the kingdom of the Church—we believe that this kingdom comes to them, as we have already said. And nearly the same may be said concerning his kingdom in holy souls. For the Church is nothing other than the gathering of holy souls; thus what is said collectively of the Church is to be understood individually of them.

This coming of the kingdom occurs through the spirit of piety, when the soul, inspired by the Holy Spirit and thereby made devout and gentle, voluntarily subjects itself to God who reigns; and this is the highest piety. Conversely, to repel him from oneself is cruel and impious, as did those of whom the same Lord says: “They have rejected me, that I should not reign over them” (1 Sam. 6). To this virtue of piety the possession of the land is promised, when the Lord says: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5). Certainly not this present land, in which the cruel and impious chiefly rule, but that of which the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). Note that this is stated in a strongly moral sense: just as kings are accustomed to give land to possess to those who voluntarily submit to their authority, while wresting it from the proud and rebellious.

## CHAPTER XI. The third petition: “May God’s will be done”

“May your will be done,” etc. The execution of the royal will follows the coming of the kingdom, because it is most necessary that, having chosen someone as your king, you should strive to fulfil his will. For whoever resists the will of the one reigning over him not only gains no grace from humility, but also earns punishment for obstinacy. For it is written: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12).

It is useful, then, to examine what this will of the Father is which we ask may be done. God’s will is understood in various ways. Sometimes his will and good pleasure mean his eternal disposition, by which he ordains and orders only good things. Of this the Apostle says: “The will of God is good, well-pleasing, and perfect” (Rom. 12): good, because God wills—that is, ordains—nothing except what is good and well done; well-pleasing, to those who understand it, or because he never repents of it; perfect, because it is brought to completion by the sum of all good things.

God’s will is also called his permission, by which he permits and tolerates only evil things to occur. This is not because it is his will that evils should happen, but because, though he can prevent them, he does not prevent them; therefore some think that he seems voluntarily to consent to evils. His will is also called counsel or command, because it is a sign of his will: through it he indicates that he wishes something to be done or not done. God’s activity too is commonly called his will, because God, who cannot be compelled, does nothing except willingly; and for him willing and acting are not different, as it is written: “The Lord has done all that he willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 14).

[Col. 0183C] The first will is the effective cause of all good things, which either God himself does or another does through him as author. The second is the voluntary and just permission of all evils, which either the devil himself does or another does through him as author. Therefore, whatever God does by his own goodness, or permits others to do through his grace, or justly decrees in accordance with his righteousness, all proceeds from the first will of God: for example, the creation of things, the redemption of humankind, the bestowal of temporal or spiritual goods, and the just recompense of rewards and punishments.

But whatever the devil himself does, or drives others to do, all belongs to the second [Col. 0183D] will: for example, the first transgression of angel or human being; the devil’s perverse and unwearied suggestion; and in the human being, wrongful delight in consenting and the carrying out of an evil deed. These are said to belong to God’s will not because God wills them, but because he permits them. In ordinary human usage, one seems to will something when, though able to forbid it, one does not forbid it.

God’s effective will, therefore, as has been said, concerns only good things; his permissive will concerns only evil things. Yet this permission itself is sometimes of guilt alone, sometimes of punishment alone, and sometimes of guilt and punishment together. For when God, as Scripture says (Job 34), permits a hypocrite to reign, that permission is of guilt alone: for reigning is guilt to the hypocrite, not punishment. But when he permitted Paul (2 Cor. 12) to be buffeted by a thorn in his flesh, he permitted punishment alone and not guilt, because in that temptation there was punishment and no guilt. But when he permitted Judas to strangle himself with a noose (Matt. 27), he permitted both, because Judas’s hanging was at once guilt and punishment.

Yet guilt, which is never without fault, proceeds by permission; whereas punishment, which either produces merit or punishes guilt, descends rather from God’s eternal disposition. Therefore, as has often been said, God’s will is either effective, giving origin only to good things, or permissive, not preventing evils from being committed. Counsel or command, however, of themselves are the cause of neither good nor evil; they are called God’s will only because we assume that God wills what he commands or counsels.

Nevertheless, we find that God both commanded what he did not will to be done, as in the command to Abraham concerning the sacrifice of his son (Gen. 22); and commanded not to be done what he nevertheless willed to be done, as in the case of those whom he forbade to publish his miracle, but who went away and spread his fame throughout the whole region (Matt. 9).

Concerning God’s will which is called his activity, Augustine says: “Nothing happens which God does not will, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.” You see that Augustine says God wills both by permitting and by doing; therefore his will is both his permission and his activity. This was the will which the leper implored when he said: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8): he knew that action lay in the Lord’s will.

Therefore, since God’s will is spoken of in so many ways—namely, as his good pleasure, permission, counsel, command, or even activity—there is no need at all to pray that his good pleasure may come to pass, since it is always inevitably fulfilled either by us or concerning us. It would be futile, then, to ask that something be done which cannot possibly be prevented from being done. Nor ought we pray that his permission may be fulfilled in us, since that would be nothing other than asking him to let us do some evil thing. Nor ought we ask that the will of God called his activity may be done, since even among human beings something already in process cannot be altered so as not to happen. For God’s will is not called activity before it begins to be fulfilled by the effect of the work.

[Col. 0184D] But concerning counsel and command—of which the latter is a matter of necessity, while the former rests in freedom—the heavenly Father must be earnestly prayed to, so that, with the help of his grace, the former may be fulfilled in us necessarily and the latter voluntarily, and both happily. This, indeed, is the will which we ask may be done when we say: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” This does not mean that there is counsel or command in the kingdom of eternity, where nothing is lacking that needs either to be commanded or advised; rather, just as all things there accord with the divine will, so here may his counsels be fulfilled in us through perfect virtue, or at least his commands through ordinary righteousness.

This will of God is fulfilled through the spirit [Col. 0185A] of knowledge, which concerns earthly things. When a person receives it, he considers that there is no blessedness in temporal and passing things. Grieved that he was deceived because he had once placed his hope in them, he turns to doing God’s commands or counsels; and when a person has done these things, he shall live by them (Ezek. 20) and receive from God the rewards of eternity. Hence, moved by a double sorrow, he wholly gives himself to mourning and tears: both because he pursued these temporal things to no purpose, and because he delayed so long to serve the one from whom true rewards are to be hoped for.

To this mourning eternal consolation is promised, as the Savior says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). This will undoubtedly be when God wipes every tear from the eyes of his saints, and there shall no longer be either mourning or pain, because the former times have passed away (Rev. 2).

[Col. 0185B] It may also be said in another way: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”—that is, as angels are heavenly by origin, so may human beings, formed from earth, obey your most holy will. In a third sense: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”—that is, in both the soul, which is heavenly by nature, and the body, formed of earth, may nothing be found contrary to your will.

For this to come about, it is necessary that meanwhile, in this valley of tears, we should be sustained by his continual benefits as servants hungry for food. For *famulus* (“servant”) is named from *fames* (“hunger”): that is, one who in time of need is fed in order to serve, serves in order to be fed, [Col. 0185C] and, when service is ended, receives a fitting reward. So too, while serving the Lord in this life, we need both temporal and spiritual aids; and after our labour ends, we await the reward of eternal blessedness. Therefore, as we ask, at the prompting of the Son, for the benefits of God the Father necessary for gaining life, we customarily add:

## CHAPTER XII. The fourth petition: concerning the nourishment of bread

“Give us this day our daily bread.” The term *bread* (*panis*) is derived, by affinity of sound, from the Greek *pan* (πᾶν), meaning “everything” or “the whole.” Among the ancients it signified everything taken as refreshment in food. Thus in Genesis (ch. 28) Jacob is read to have said: “If the Lord my God is with me on this way which I am travelling, and gives me bread to eat,” and what follows.

It is neither improper nor wrong to ask God for bodily food when necessary, provided that it is asked without excessive anxiety. For in asking for necessities, humility in petition is allowed, but anxiety is forbidden. The Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat, or what shall we drink?’ For your heavenly Father knows what you need” (Matt. 6). Yet if this petition were understood only of bodily food, it would seem unworthy of so great a teacher’s authority. Therefore it appears to concern not so much bodily food as spiritual bread, [Col. 0186A] whose nature we shall examine as far as we can.

Spiritual or mystical bread, then, just as it differs in kind, has different flavours, effects, and modes of reception. Bread is the word of divine teaching; bread is Christ’s flesh; bread is the grace of the Holy Spirit; bread is compunction of soul; bread is love of God and neighbour; bread is contemplation of heavenly mystery; bread is hope of the reward to come; bread is the joy of the kingdom; bread is everything by which we are spiritually nourished during the pilgrimage of this world.

Of the first bread the Prophet says: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4). Of the second, the Savior says in the Gospel: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” [Col. 0186B] (John 6). Of the third, in the book of the son of Sirach: “Better is one who labours and abounds in all things than one who boasts and lacks bread” (Ecclus. 10). Of the fourth the Psalmist says: “You will feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79); and elsewhere: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41). Of the fifth the Savior again says in the Gospel: “If he asks for bread, will he give him a stone instead of bread?” (Luke 11). It is as though he said: If someone asks you for the affection of love, you ought not to harden yourself against him into the severity of a stone.

Of the sixth, Solomon’s Proverbs has: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant” (Prov. 9). These are the words of the foolish woman—that is, of heresy—which sets its secret doctrine and contemplation of heavenly things above Catholic teaching and fellowship. Here water refers to doctrine and bread to contemplation. Of the seventh the Church is praised thus: “She has become like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar” (Prov. 31). Of the eighth, again in the Gospel: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 14), that is, who in the kingdom of eternity shall be satisfied by God’s presence. Of everything by which we are spiritually nourished in this life, the words of the prodigal son may be understood: “How many hired servants in my Father’s house abound in bread!” (Luke 15), because all in the Church who serve God for an eternal reward are refreshed by the manifold nourishment of divine grace.

The first bread tastes of discipline; the second, of healing; the third, of holiness; the fourth, of sharpness; [Col. 0186D] the fifth, of goodwill; the sixth, of sweetness; the seventh, of strength; the eighth, of delight. The first digests and regulates the diet; the second refreshes and invigorates; the third guards and strengthens; the fourth pricks and spurs; the fifth moves and softens; the sixth attracts and invites; the seventh cherishes and encourages; the eighth feeds and satisfies.

The first is received by ear and heart: sometimes by ear alone, sometimes by heart alone, and sometimes by ear and heart together. It is received by ear alone when the word of God is heard with the ear but not grasped in the heart. It is received by heart alone when it is not received by the ear but is thought upon in the mind. It is received by ear and heart together when it is both heard by the ear and retained in the mind.

The second is received by mouth and mind: sometimes by mouth alone, sometimes by mind alone, and sometimes by mouth and mind together. It is received [Col. 0187A] by mouth alone when the sacrament of Christ’s body is received with the mouth, but its reality and benefit are not grasped in the mind; this commonly happens to those who receive unworthily. It is received by mind alone when the sacrament is not received, but the reality itself operates in the soul; this belongs only to the righteous, whether they are bodily within or outside the bounds of the Church.

From this it is clear that sometimes a little woman hiding in a corner of the church, or even a labourer working in a field, receives this bread more truly and better than a priest or bishop standing at the sacred altars. Augustine seems to have held this view when he said: “One who eats does not eat, and one who does not eat eats.” For often one who eats sacramentally does not eat in reality, whereas one who does not eat sacramentally eats in reality and benefit.

All the rest except the eighth are received by the heart alone, because by the heart alone we receive the grace of the Holy Spirit; by the heart alone we are pierced with compunction; and by the heart alone we love, contemplate, and hope. The eighth, however, shall be received with all the full faculties of soul and body in eternal blessedness, when all the elect, having received their bodies again, are satisfied with the glory of the divine vision. Thus the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16); and likewise: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in joy” (Ps. 17).

These seven breads, therefore, are necessary in the sevenfold course of this present life and are to be sought, so that, travelling toward our homeland, we may be sustained on the way as by provision for a journey. But the eighth is reserved to be set before us in our homeland in that eighth day of the universal and great resurrection. All the saints shall enjoy it in eternal blessedness—a miracle greater indeed than that by which the five Gospel loaves sufficed for the refreshment of so many thousands of people for a single hour (John 6).

It is clear, then, that the bread of eternal joy, reserved for children in their homeland, may indeed be desired and asked for in this life, but cannot be obtained or possessed here. But we ask from the heavenly Father—who “gives good gifts to those who ask him” (Matt. 7)—for the other seven breads necessary to us on the journey, when we say: “Give us this day our daily bread.” “This day” is today; “this day” was yesterday; “this day” will be tomorrow; “this day” is the entire span [Col. 0187D] of this present life. Therefore, when you say “this day,” it is as though you said: “As long as we are in this temporal life.”

“Our daily bread,” he says: that is, bread necessary every day, to be enjoyed every day, nourishment of such a kind that we ought never, while we are on the way, beneficially to lack it at any time. For the bread of divine discourse through continual meditation, the bread of Christ’s body through the sincerity of faith, the bread of spiritual grace through inward refreshment, the bread of compunction through contrition of heart, the bread of love through the affection of charity, the bread of contemplation through hidden delight, and the bread of hope through secure expectation—all these [Col. 0188A] must always be present to us in reality, according to the capacity of our weakness.

We do not mean that we can exercise the actions of all these things without ceasing, but that the things themselves can and must always be present in us. No one can always hear, read, or meditate upon the words of sacred Scripture; but one who always has the will to do these things is judged to do them, following the example of him who said: “I shall always meditate upon your statutes” (Ps. 118), and elsewhere: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (ibid.). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “If you love me and my words remain in you, whatever you ask shall be done for you” (John 15).

Likewise, no one can actually receive the sacrament of the altar every hour; but one who through purity of faith and union of charity incorporates Christ into himself and is incorporated into Christ eats this bread of the Lord’s body without ceasing. Those who said, “Lord, always give us this bread” (John 16), thought this bread should be chewed without ceasing, since, once received, it never ceases to be eaten except because of mortal sin.

We likewise say that one continually eats the bread of spiritual grace when he is constantly cherished by the grace of the Holy Spirit and makes progress: as John the Baptist, filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb (Luke 1), as the angel had promised his father concerning him, continually remained and progressed in that same grace of the Holy Spirit.

Similarly, a person receives the bread of compunction continually not when he is always pierced by compunction—for this is impossible or rare—but when he always has the purpose of holy compunction, following the example of him who said: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me” (Ps. 50). James also says: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. 8 [sic]).

A person also always eats the bread of love not when he always exercises the act of loving, which, we believe, no one does, but when he never changes his loving disposition. The Apostle shows how this bread can and ought continually to be eaten: “Before all things,” he says, “keep unceasing brotherly charity among yourselves” (1 Pet. 4).

The same is to be understood of the bread of contemplation: a person is always refreshed by this bread not when he always contemplates, which human weakness does not permit, but when he never loses the desire to contemplate, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Set your minds on the things above, not on things on earth; seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3).

Likewise, a person is always cherished and fed by the bread of hope not when he is always engaged in the act of hoping, but when that security of mind never departs from him, following the Psalmist’s example: “But I shall always hope” (Ps. 70). Therefore, when we ask for daily bread, it signifies not an unbroken act but the continual intention of a holy purpose.

The spirit of strength is especially appropriate to this fourth petition, because, as we said a little earlier, that Spirit is bread; and as bodily food strengthens and fortifies [Col. 0189A] the body, so it strengthens and fortifies the soul. To one hungering for this bread—which is nothing other than righteousness, since righteousness cannot be possessed except through the power of the Holy Spirit—satisfaction is promised when the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, [Col. 0190A] for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5). This will surely be when what the Savior says is fulfilled: “That you may eat and drink at my table” (Luke 22), so that eating refers to hunger and drinking to thirst for righteousness.

# BOOK TEN. Concerning the remaining three petitions of the Lord’s Prayer

[Col. 0189]

## CHAPTER ONE. The fifth petition: concerning the remission of debts

[Col. 0189B]

Therefore, after the Father’s name has been sanctified in us, after we have at last chosen him as our king, desired that his will be done, and received the daily bread by which we may be nourished in his service, there seemed to remain no reason why we should thereafter be troubled by our offences. For it is certainly most wicked to provoke anew by repeated injury the one whose excellent renown you have received, to whose rule you have voluntarily submitted yourself, whose will you have asked to be done and have promised yourself to do, and from whom you have obtained the sustenance of daily food.

But because not even an infant of one day can live without sin upon the earth (Job 25), and “the righteous person falls seven times a day and rises again” [Col. 0189C] (Prov. 24), while he cannot rise except through the remission of sin, the following is necessarily added in this prayer:

## CHAPTER II.

And forgive us our debts. In the Scriptures we find different kinds of debts; and therefore we must ask which kind is meant here. There is debt arising from contract, debt arising from office, debt of nature, debt of justice, debt of piety, debt of propriety, debt of necessity, debt of gratitude, and debt of fault.

Debt arising from contract is that by which one person is bound to another to give or do something, by the consent of both. By this kind of debt we are customarily bound both to God and to human beings. We are bound to God when, under his power—which is [Col. 0189D] absent nowhere and therefore can be ignorant of nothing—we promise, for love of him, that we shall give or do something. We promise to give, as Zacchaeus did, who promised that he would give half his goods to the poor (Luke 19); or to do, as those do who privately or publicly promise either to preserve continence, to fast on certain feast-days, to visit the shrines of the saints, or even altogether to renounce the world. We are bound to another person, as commonly happens in formal stipulations, when, one party making the stipulation, another promises that he will give or do something, in this manner: “Maevius, do you promise to give one hundred gold coins on the Kalends of January?” “I promise.” “Will you give them?” “I will give them.” “Do you promise?” “I promise.”

What has been contracted between human beings by the consent of both may be dissolved by their contrary consent. But what has been promised to God [Col. 0190B], if it can reasonably be fulfilled, God does not release unless something equally good or better is done instead, since it is written in the Psalm: “Make vows and fulfil them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75). Nor should one ask him to release it, since that would be to wish him to favor our own frivolity and instability.

Debt arising from office is that which a person is bound to do by the requirements of the role he bears—that is, what he ought to do in accordance with the dignity of his own person. For an office is an action fitting to a person according to the customs and institutions of the community. The Apostle sufficiently copiously defined the variety of such debts when, marking out the duties of different persons, he said: “Husbands, love your wives; wives, be subject to your husbands” (Eph. 5); “children, obey your parents; fathers, do not provoke [Col. 0190C] your children to anger; slaves, obey your masters, and you who are their masters, refrain from threatening them, knowing that one is both your Master and theirs” (Eph. 6). And elsewhere the same Apostle says: “The one who presides, with diligence; the one who exhorts, in exhortation” (Rom. 12). And again: “Owe no one anything, except that you love one another” (Rom. 13).

By this kind of debt likewise we are frequently bound both to God and to human beings: to God, that each person render him the service due according to the rank of his station; to human beings, that among people themselves the duties appropriate to the respective conditions of persons be fulfilled. God neither remits this kind of debt nor should be asked to remit it, lest he seem to authorize some great [Col. 0190D] disorder by allowing what is due to himself to be denied him; for the Savior says in the Gospel: “Render to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). Nor should we ask God that we may be permitted to deny our neighbor the service owed to him; for that would be to ask him to consent to our overthrow of what is fair and good. For from fairness and goodness comes the principle that every person should render to his neighbor the service due by the proper order of things.

Debt of nature is that which nature demands by unavoidable necessity: for example, that everything born must necessarily die. Hence someone who has already died is said to have paid nature’s debt. In this debt we are bound neither to God nor to human beings, but to nature alone—unless perhaps you say that we are bound to God because we are subject to the nature that he himself created. Therefore a human being cannot remit it, nor need he be asked to remit [Col. 0191A] it. God, to whom nothing is impossible, could indeed remit it; but he should not be asked to do so, since that would be to ask him to violate nature and to act contrary to his own ordering. Therefore no one should ask God to be released from the natural debt—that is, not to hunger, thirst, grow weary, or finally die. Rather, each person should earnestly ask that he may meet the former things patiently and prudently, and await the latter happily.

There is another debt of nature, consisting not so much in necessity as in regular order. Neither God remits it nor can a human being remit it; nor should either be asked to remit it. This is divided into two parts. One is that what nature commands to be done should be done, such as the rearing of one’s own [Col. 0191B] offspring, and things of that sort; it is so natural that every kind of living creature is bound to it. The other is that what natural use requires should be done also in the natural order: such as the carnal and ordered union of different sexes within the same nature—not that of the same sex within the same nature, nor of different sexes across different natures. Both of these are so detestable that in the Old Testament they are punished even by bodily death, as Scripture says: “Whoever lies with a male or even with a beast shall surely die; they shall stone him” (Lev. 20).

Debt of justice is that which justice requires—that is, what ought to be done according to justice: for example, that you give to each his own right, namely, to God, to yourself, and to your neighbor. To God, that you worship him [Col. 0191C]; to yourself, that you live rightly; to your neighbor, that you love him as yourself. Justice is simply the constant and perpetual will that gives to each his own right. God does not remit this debt of justice, nor wishes to be asked to remit it, because this would be wholly contrary to divine equity. For if you entreat God to grant that you may either despise him, live wickedly, or fail to love your neighbor, you act foolishly in asking him for what, if he granted it, would mean that he was not God. Nor can any human being relax this debt, since it derives both from the moral precepts of the Law and from the Gospel, in which no dispensation can be admitted.

Likewise, temporal things justly due to God, such as tithes and offerings: if they can be paid, God neither [Col. 0191D] remits them nor is rightly asked to remit them, since their payment pertains to the payer’s salvation. But temporal things which one person owes another may be remitted by the consent of both, because everyone may renounce his own right, provided that the one who remits it is neither deceived nor compelled.

Likewise, the debt of piety—which is to sympathize with the wretched and assist those who labor; the debt of propriety—which is to yield to one’s superior and honor one’s elder; the debt of necessity—which lies in providing those things required for use; and the debt of gratitude—which lies in remembering and repaying, so far as it can be repaid, a benefit received—God does not remit, nor can a human being remit them, nor should either be asked to remit them [Col. 0192A]. For this would be nothing other than consenting to our vice or fault.

There are also other debts of various kinds found in matters that ought to be done, such as the works of the virtues. Of all these one may reason according to the principle already stated: none of them belongs to this petition. We must therefore diligently inquire what debt it is that we seek in this petition. It seems to us, then, that only the debt of fault is intended here; let us consider what it is.

The debt of fault appears to be nothing other than contempt and transgression of the other debts—that is, the omission of those things which ought rightly to have been done. When the debt of a good work is not paid, when what ought to be done is neglected, when what has been promised by contract [Col. 0192B] to God or a human being is not rendered, when the dignity of one’s office is not fulfilled, the requirements of nature are not observed, the rule of justice is not maintained, the works of piety, propriety, and the other virtues are not performed, and gratitude for a benefit received is not shown: by contempt for all these we become bound by a certain more grievous and ruinous debt. This is nothing other than fault—or, if you prefer, sin or transgression. For sin or transgression is believed to be nothing other than the absence of the good which ought to be present or done.

This is the debt that the Gospel lender forgave the two debtors who had nothing with which to repay him, in the parable which the Lord proposed to the Pharisee (Luke 7). Therefore it is this debt of fault, incurred by neglect and transgression of the others, that [Col. 0192C] we ask God to forgive when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Observe the condition; understand the form of the undertaking. For if we desire our heavenly Father to release us from the debts of our faults, we too must forgive from the heart those things in which others have sinned against us. Thus the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “For if you do not forgive your brothers, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6). We must take great care lest that also be found spoken against us: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you asked me. Ought you not therefore to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. 18).

The Spirit of counsel is most fittingly joined to this fifth petition [Col. 0192D], because the best counsel is to forgive others, so that God also may forgive you. Thus the Savior instructs us in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6). Hence the same Savior pronounces blessed those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 6). For they have abundant matter for forgiving; and thus, their sins having been forgiven, they can readily attain the kingdom of heaven, which is promised to those who forgive.

But because temptation does not cease even after sins have been forgiven, but sometimes grows stronger and prevails, after sins have been forgiven one must pray—not indeed that we should never again be tempted, for this cannot happen to a human being placed in the flesh [Col. 0193A]—but that we should not succumb to temptation and enter into it by consenting to fault. Hence the following petition follows:

## CHAPTER III. The Sixth Petition

**And lead us not into temptation.**

God leads into temptation not by forcing someone unwilling and resisting into fault, but by withdrawing the grace of resistance from one who is slothful and negligent.

Every testing of a human being is either for proving, for teaching, or for harming. Testing for proving is done either by God or by one’s neighbor. By God, as when God tested Abraham—not that by testing he might learn what Abraham was like, but that he might show him to be approved to others [Col. 0193B]. Such also is what Moses says to the children of Israel: “Your God tests you, that he may know”—that is, that he may remind you yourselves and make others know—“whether his fear is in you and whether you walk in his ways.”

A person is also tested by a neighbor for proving in three ways: either that the person’s character may become known to the tester, or that the person himself may be reminded, or that he may be shown to others. In the first way Nebuchadnezzar tested Daniel (Dan. 2), and the wise men of Babylon, concerning the form of his vision: if they could recount it to him, he would infer from this that they could also interpret it. In the second way Elisha tested Gehazi, that he might convict him when he denied it and bring him to repentance (4 Kings 5). In the third way Daniel tested the two elders (Dan. 13), whom he knew to be guilty and who knew themselves guilty, that he might show them guilty also to others.

God also tests in order to teach in two ways, as when he tested Philip [Col. 0193C], saying: “Where shall we buy bread for these to eat?” (John 6). He did not ask because he doubted what should be done, since it is written: “He himself knew what he was going to do”; rather, by this occasion he displayed his power to them and placed before their eyes their own weakness, for they did not believe that he could feed the crowd without bread. A person is likewise tested by a neighbor in order to teach for two reasons: either that he may hold more firmly what he knows, or understand what he does not know—as a pupil is tested by a teacher.

But no one is tested by God in order to be harmed, for as Scripture says, “God is not a tempter of evils,” and no one when tempted ought to say that he is tempted by God (James 1). Therefore the temptation of a human being [Col. 0193D] that is for harm comes either from himself, from his neighbor, or from the devil; and from each of these in two ways, namely in the body and in the soul.

A person is tempted in the body by himself either through the desire of the flesh, as it is written: “For each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (ibid.); or through some bodily affliction by which he is stirred to impatience. In the soul he is tempted by himself through wicked desires, anger, or passions of this kind, arising more from the movement of the mind than from the devil’s prompting. He is also tempted by his neighbor for harm in two ways: either by injury to the body or by disturbance of the mind, so that, offended in either way, he may lose charity. Likewise he is tempted by the devil in two ways: either in the body, as Job [Col. 0194A] was (Job 2), whom Satan asked might be tested, and struck with a grievous sore from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; or in the soul, as Judas was, when the devil entered into him and he began to contemplate the Lord’s destruction (John 13).

Therefore, when we ask not to be led into temptation, it must be understood of this threefold temptation that is for harm. For of the temptation that is for proving, the Psalmist says: “Prove me, O Lord, and test me” (Ps. 25). He prayed to be tested and proved by the Lord, so that either, yielding to temptation, he might recognize his weakness and rise stronger through humility; or, standing firm, might give thanks to God for his virtue; or might establish for others an example of virtue and constancy.

Nor should that testing by one’s neighbor which is for proving always be deprecated or feared, since it often corrects the tested person if he is evil [Col. 0194B], proves him if he is good, and displays him to others as worthy of imitation. Nor should one pray not to be tested by God for teaching, since this would be nothing other than refusing to be taught by him, after the example of those who said: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 2).

Nor does any wise person either fear or deprecate being tested by a neighbor for teaching, since this would be nothing other than obstinately rejecting instruction. It remains, therefore, that this must be understood only of that temptation which is for harm, suffered in body or soul, whether from oneself, one’s neighbor, or the devil; nor do we ask that we should not suffer it at all, but that we should not be led into it by consent. For it is glorious to endure temptation bravely, but shameful and disgraceful—and altogether contrary to salvation—to succumb to temptation.

The effect of this petition [Col. 0194C] is fulfilled in us through the Spirit of understanding, because understanding concerns heavenly things alone and is occupied in contemplating celestial realities. Whoever diligently attends to them easily repels harmful temptations, just as, conversely, whoever despises heavenly things easily succumbs to wicked temptations. Purity of heart also accords with this Spirit and petition, because the purer the heart, the more penetratingly it searches out heavenly things, and the more it despises the alluring or harsh temptations of temporal things. Therefore the vision of God is promised to this virtue, because the person who now beholds God with the eye of a pure heart, in a mirror and enigmatically, will afterward rejoice in the full vision of him. And that we may finally be allowed freely to attain this vision of God [Col. 0194D], there follows the petition that concludes all things:

## CHAPTER IV. The Seventh Petition

**But deliver us from evil.**

Above we distinguished evil into different kinds. From all these we must ask to be delivered in this order. First, that we may not be hardened in sin, which we called hardening evil. Second, that we may not lack justice, which is privative evil. Third, that the soul may not be infected by a corrupt quality in vice, which we chose to call the merit of death. Fourth, that a corrupt quality of mind may not impel us to an evil act, which both is and is called the merit of eternal death. Finally, that, deprived of the divine vision, we may not be assigned to eternal punishments; this is most truly called eternal [Col. 0195A] death.

To be delivered from this final evil alone is the highest happiness and could satisfy every desire; but since it does not follow unless those former things have preceded it, we must pray for the former in their order and for this chiefly.

“Deliver us,” he says, “from evil”: first, from the evil of hardened obstinacy; second, from the deprivation of justice; third, from a perverted mind; fourth, from wicked action; and finally, from eternal condemnation. For you see that frozen earth, unless it is thawed by the warmth of the sun, and, once thawed, renewed by cultivation, and, once renewed, receives seed, and, after receiving seed, produces seed, will neither bear fruit nor ward off the grievous harm of famine.

Something similar is found in the soul, which the Psalmist not inappropriately compares to earth: “My soul is like land without water to you [Col. 0195B]” (Ps. 142). Therefore, unless a human soul hardened in evil is softened from the coldness of its wickedness by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, renewed by justice, and made fruitful with the shoots of virtues, it will never bear fruit in good works or be able to escape eternal hunger, which is nothing other than deprivation of the divine vision.

Therefore we ask to be delivered from these evils in order, so that we may attain true freedom, which the Psalmist sought when he said: “Attend to my soul, and deliver it” (Ps. 68). There is one freedom of the body, another of the soul, and another of both together.

Freedom of the body is a certain right derived from nature, by which each person is permitted to do what he wishes, except what is forbidden by law or custom. By this right all [Col. 0195C] human beings were born free, until in the course of time slavery was introduced, deriving its first origin either from the authority of Holy Scripture or from the law of nations.

According to the authority of Holy Scripture, Noah is read to have condemned to perpetual slavery his son—the father of Canaan—who had laughed at his father’s nakedness, saying: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9). Similarly, Isaac is testified to have subjected his son Esau to the servitude of his other son, Jacob, in these words: “I have appointed him your lord, and have subjected all his brothers to his service” (Gen. 27).

Slavery was also introduced by the law of nations because, whereas previously all those captured in war were killed, humanity seemed [Col. 0195D] better served if some of them, especially those less harmful, were preserved alive and made to serve the victors. Because their lives were preserved, they were called *servi* (“slaves”). From this name *servi* were derived both *servitus* (“slavery”) and *servire* (“to serve”).

This good of bodily freedom is, according to civil laws, so precious that it admits of no valuation; so necessary that one who lacks it is said not even to possess legal personality, but must be regarded as nothing; and so favored that, in order to obtain it, it suffices once to have been in a free womb, even if the mother conceived while a slave and, afterward manumitted into freedom, had again fallen into slavery before giving birth.

How much more must the true freedom of the soul be embraced with every affection of love, be regarded as altogether necessary, and be beyond valuation at any price or [Col. 0196A] time. We called this freedom “true” because the soul has a twofold freedom: one false and destructive, the other salutary and true.
