False freedom of the soul is that by which the unhappy soul exempts itself from the laws of divine service and emancipates itself into a kind of liberty to sin; and through this the miserable person becomes more truly a slave. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Writing to the Romans, the Apostle calls this “freedom from justice,” not because it belongs to the just, but because it despises being subject to the laws and dominion of justice: “When you were slaves of sin,” he says, “you were free from justice” (Rom. 6).

But true freedom of the soul is that which, having taken away from itself the liberty to sin, subjects itself wholly to divine service, and thereby attains full [Col. 0196B] and true freedom. For to serve the Lord is to reign. The Apostle likewise calls this freedom “freedom from sin,” not because it makes us free to sin, but because it does not allow sin to rule over us: “But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (ibid.). Of this it is likewise said: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3).

You see, therefore, that freedom from justice is slavery to sin, and freedom from sin is slavery to justice; and therefore the service of God, which is nothing other than justice, confers true and perfect freedom upon a person.

Freedom of soul and body exists when, in bodily person, we are not subject against our will to anyone’s dominion, nor in soul [Col. 0196C] do wicked desires or destructive demonic suggestions rule over us. Divine Scripture nowhere condemns bodily freedom; yet we do not value it so highly that the Savior would command us to desire and seek it with so great earnestness. Thus the Apostle says: “Were you called while a slave? Do not seek freedom” (1 Cor. 7).

Nevertheless, it is sometimes lawful to seek bodily freedom from God: namely, when we suffer wrongful bonds, imprisonment, or other torments at the hands of Catholics, or when, captured and held by unbelievers, we are prevented from carrying out divine worship. But true freedom of the soul must at all times be desired with every prayer: namely, that by God’s grace we may be delivered in the present age from the first four kinds of [Col. 0196D] evils, and in the age to come from that supreme evil which is the end and sum of them all.

When we have been delivered from the destructive evils mentioned above, the Spirit of wisdom is customarily given: in this life, scantily and variously according to each person’s capacity, where “we see only through a mirror, enigmatically”; but in the life to come most fully, when we shall know by full sight the glory of eternal divinity and the joys of the heavenly mysteries, seeing God face to face, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13).

Wisdom differs from understanding in this: understanding involves the labor of inquiry, while wisdom is the joy of tranquil knowledge. Therefore the virtue joined to this grace of the Holy Spirit makes one peaceful—not only in relation to the tumult [Col. 0197A] of worldly affairs, but also to the labor without which heavenly things cannot be understood. To this virtue is also promised the highest thing, namely the title “sons of God,” as the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5).

You see Christ’s faithful teaching, beginning with the invocation of the Father and ending in the designation of the sons of God. How eager he was to have brothers with whom he might not divide, but share in fellowship, the [Col. 0198A] paternal inheritance. And because by nature there could not be more than one, by grace he labored to make many.

After all the petitions follows the word of confirmation, namely *amen*, which is as though one said: “Undoubtedly,” or “truly,” or even “without defect.” For *a* is interpreted “without,” while *mene* means “defect.”

# BOOK ELEVEN. On the Foregoing Petitions in Reverse Order

[Col. 0197]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0197B]

After that order in which the Savior, in his own words, arranged the form of prayer that he delivered to his disciples, let us also, mindful of our promise, endeavor to continue another exposition: namely, that of those who think that the aforesaid prayer should be discussed in the reverse order of its petitions.

For they say that the heavenly teacher placed first those things which he knew to be foremost and most desirable: for example, our sanctification—not that which we have described, but another which will occur only in the future life—and the coming of the eternal kingdom. Then, by certain intermediate stages, he came to the final petition, in which we ask to be delivered from evil. According to their interpretation, this indeed ought to be first for those advancing toward eternal life.

Accordingly, they also endeavor to apply the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in reverse order to this exposition; likewise the seven virtues which the Lord mentions in the Gospel; and they carefully assign the rewards of those virtues both to the gifts themselves and to the petitions.

They say, then: **Our Father who art in heaven.** This need not be altered, but should be retained under the exposition we have already given, with this addition: that both here and there these petitions are directed not only to the person of the Father, but also to the whole Trinity [Col. 0197C], which itself is most truly the Father of all.

**Deliver us from evil.** The kinds of evil, as we have taught above, are various; to be delivered from them all is good, pleasing, and desirable. But in this place, by the name “evil” should be understood [Col. 0197D] a certain corrupt disposition of mind called love of the world. This love is so evil that it leads to hatred and contempt of God, as it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4).

We are delivered from this evil by the gift of fear, when a person, conscious of his own evils, begins to consider his ways; and, humbly turning to God in fear of Gehenna, voluntarily renounces the pleasures and pomp of the world and embraces voluntary poverty. This spiritual poverty consists not so much in abandoning temporal possessions as in despising them: so that it may exist amid great wealth, if one possesses such wealth with no love or desire for it, but gladly spends it solely [Col. 0198B] upon the necessities of the poor and pious uses.

To this spiritual poverty, which is nothing other than the virtue of humility, the kingdom of heaven is promised, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). He did not say, “theirs shall be,” but “theirs is,” so that those who freely become poor for God’s sake may know themselves already most rich and possessors of the kingdom of heaven.

**And lead us not into temptation.** Often, when people renounce the world, more numerous and more grievous plagues of temptation arise, according to the saying: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). Therefore follows the petition in which we ask God not to lead us into temptation—that is, that, when he abandons us, not through his fault but through our own vice, we may not be led into [Col. 0198C] consenting to temptation.

This occurs through the Spirit of piety, who, when given to us, has compassion upon our weakness and by his goodness preserves and protects us from every temptation of more grievous sin. Through him we also become kindly disposed, meek, and devout, so that we may take pleasure neither in doing nor even in thinking anything that offends God or our neighbor.

To this virtue of piety and meekness possession of the land is promised, when the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5)—not this present land, in which the cruel and ungodly are especially condemned, but that land of which the Psalmist says: “May the Lord be my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141).

**And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.** The third petition follows [Col. 0198D], in which we are commanded to ask God that, just as we forgive sins to those who sin against us, he likewise may forgive our sins. For, as Scripture says, no one is clean from sin, not even an infant of one day, if his life be upon the earth (Job 25).

“Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” Observe the condition: “as we forgive our debtors.” He did not say, “as we forgive you,” because God, whatever he does in a human being, cannot sin or do anything which ought to be forgiven him. Therefore he said, “our debtors,” so that, as we forgive the sins of neighbors who sin against us for the honor of God, God in his goodness may deign to forgive [Col. 0199A] us our sins.

This occurs through the Spirit of knowledge, which concerns earthly things. When a person has received it, seeing that in this present life he cannot possess full and perfect knowledge, he is wholly dissolved into mourning and does not expect consolation in this world, but that consolation which the Savior promised to those who mourn, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 9). This indeed will occur when the misery of the world has ended, our sorrow is turned into joy, and no one takes our joy from us (John 16).

## CHAPTER II

[The supplied source ends here.]

Our daily bread give us today. Amid all these things, we must be sustained by the nourishment of daily bread; and therefore in the fourth petition we ask that God may grant it to us daily—that is, without ceasing [Col. 0199B]. This bread is almost nothing other than the spirit of fortitude; once a person has received it, he is strengthened and confirmed in the love of righteousness, so that in this life he desires nothing besides it, and for its sake suffers, fears, and refuses nothing. To this holy desire, which the Lord calls hunger and thirst, fullness is promised in the future, when the same Savior says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V). This will indeed be then, when all wickedness has ceased and everything is justly ordered in the eternal kingdom of God, as the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

Matthew states this petition thus: “Give us today our supersubstantial bread.” The holy teachers explain this of the body of Christ [Col. 0199C], which in dignity and holiness is above everything that is truly and properly called substance. Yet we do not say that Christ’s body is worthier than his soul; but because it cannot exist without it—lest we seem to receive something lifeless and dead. For “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Therefore, although Christ’s body and soul cannot be separated from one another—for that would be his death—we are nevertheless said to receive the body, not the soul, just as a human being, composed of soul and body, is called by philosophers not “soul” but “body.”

This is the supersubstantial bread which we ask may be given us today, that is, always. It is so necessary [Col. 0199D] that, if we should happen to lack the spiritual refreshment it affords even for a single moment, Christ immediately ceases to be in us and we in him—he himself testifying when he says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Something else may also be said about this supersubstantial bread, if the ears of some do not recoil because of its unfamiliarity. The poor of this world, whose material substance is scanty—such as those to whom the Savior was speaking—are accustomed, I say, to regard it as a great thing if each day, without loss to their resources, they can obtain bread, that is, sustenance. Hence the Lord said to the disciples who were fishing, when they had as yet caught nothing: “Children, have you anything to eat?” And they said: “No” (John XXI). So too we, whose store of virtues is either small, or ought to appear small to us [Col. 0200A], should regard it as a great thing if, without its diminution, we can sustain ourselves day by day, refreshed by the food of spiritual nourishment.

Supersubstantial bread, therefore, may fittingly be called that spiritual grace which God daily adds for us, beyond the measure that was formerly present, as a necessary food for the soul. We therefore ask the heavenly Father for supersubstantial bread—that is, nourishment of spiritual grace—so that, continually refreshed by it, we may make progress in him, “going from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII).

“May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” Thus, delivered from evil, fortified by divine protection against temptations, having also received forgiveness of sins, without which this life is not lived [Col. 0200B], and having received the nourishment of daily bread, nothing remains but that we should strive with all diligence to do the will of him who grants all these things. But because even this cannot be done without his help, in the fifth place we must ask that, with his aid, we may be able faithfully to fulfill his will.

“May your will be done,” he says, “as in heaven, so on earth.” This is not a statement of exact likeness. For it is impossible that we should fulfill his will on earth with the same simplicity and purity with which angels and holy spirits fulfill it in heaven; rather, it indicates some proportion: that, as they fulfill the divine will most perfectly in heaven, so we may fulfill it on earth, insofar as a human being can.

This is accomplished through the spirit of counsel, without which God’s will is not fulfilled by a human being [Col. 0200C]. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your ordinances are my counsel” (Ps. CXVIII), that is, the observance of your commandments. To this fifth petition and to this gift of the Holy Spirit is assigned the virtue of mercy; for one who desires faithfully to fulfill the divine will must be merciful both to himself and to his neighbor. Of mercy toward oneself it was said: “My son, have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX), that is, doing what you know will please him—which is to fulfill his will. Of mercy toward one’s neighbor, the Savior says in the Gospel: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke VI).

To this virtue of mercy, mercy to be obtained in the future is promised [Col. 0200D], the Lord saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V)—that mercy, surely, for which the Psalmist prayed, saying: “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. CXLII). When the night of the present life has ended and the morning of future blessedness has come, he desires to hear that mercy which the Lord will declare to his elect in this manner: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

“May your kingdom come.” Whoever remembers that he has faithfully fulfilled God’s will may confidently desire the coming of his kingdom and say: “May your kingdom come.” This must be understood of the kingdom of eternity [Col. 0201A], whose coming may indeed be desired and sought in this age, but will be fulfilled in the future, when the Lord Jesus “delivers the kingdom to God the Father,” as the Apostle says (I Cor. XV).

Therefore, the spirit of understanding is suited to this petition: illuminated by it, a person, even while placed in this life, understands through contemplation the glory of that kingdom and ardently longs for what he has understood. Since this cannot occur without a pure heart, purity of heart is assigned both to this petition and to this spiritual grace. The vision of God is also promised to this virtue, when the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). In the present, indeed, we see by means of a mirror and in an enigma through the spirit of understanding; but in the future, face to face (I Cor. XIII), when, “with unveiled face” (II Cor. [Col. 0201B] III), “we shall see him as he is” (I John III), as the Apostle says.

## CHAPTER III

“May your name be sanctified.” This sanctification of the name also belongs only to the future age, when all those over whom his name has truly been invoked, and who have it written upon their foreheads, will be sanctified in him, and he in them. This will occur when, as the Apostle testifies, the Son delivers the kingdom to God the Father, “that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV).

God, therefore, will be all in all, because God himself will be the full and perfect blessedness both of all and of each individual. He himself will be the inheritance, life, and refreshment of all the elect; he himself the salvation, rest, and delight of all; he himself the glory and beauty of all. Some also say in another sense [Col. 0201C] that God will be all in all, because we shall be filled with such splendor of his divinity that nothing but the divine will appear in us, just as in glowing iron nothing can be seen except fire, and in a mirror set before the sun nothing but the sun.

To this petition belongs the spirit of wisdom, which consists solely in the apprehension of eternal things: not with some labor of inquiry, as in understanding, but in a full and tranquil knowledge of heavenly secrets. Therefore the virtue which makes peacemakers—that is, tranquility—is most rightly joined both to this seventh petition and to the seventh gift of the Holy Spirit. For when that state has been reached, there will no longer be any disagreement; rather, all things will be composed in peace and tranquility [Col. 0201D]. To this virtue of tranquility is promised the designation “sons of God,” when the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V). We await this in the time when, having been transferred into the lot of the sons, it will be said in wonder concerning us: “See how they have been counted among the sons of God” (Wis. V).

Consider, in both arrangements, the benevolent and faithful teaching of Christ, which, beginning with the name of the Father, advances us to the dignity of the sons of God, so that, made brothers to him by grace, he may admit us as coheirs and companions in the inheritance of the Father—not of one dead, but of one living for ever—as the Apostle says: “And if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, but coheirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

The word of confirmation, “Amen,” should likewise be understood as it is: it is not a petition, but a firm conclusion, as it were, to all the petitions [Col. 0202A]. Having therefore treated at sufficient length and rather leisurely the pattern of prayer given by the Lord—of which much seemed to require saying—both in the order in which he handed it down to his disciples and in the order in which those petitions are fulfilled in us, I wish, before passing to other matters, to add a few words concerning its praise, authority, and reverence.

This collection of seven petitions is customarily called the Lord’s Prayer, not because the Lord himself prayed it, but because he commanded and taught us to pray it. For he would not say to his Father, counting himself among sinners in sin: “Forgive us our sins,” since he never committed sin [Col. 0202B], nor could commit it, nor did anything that could either be forgiven him or ought to be remitted. For he is the one of whom the prophet says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Nor again, as though fearing to be tempted, would he add: “And lead us not into temptation,” he who drove away the devil tempting him with so commanding a voice: “Begone, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. IV).

The Savior certainly had a particular manner of prayer, distinct from that of others, in which he often addressed his heavenly Father, as it is written of him: “He went up the mountain alone to pray; and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke VI). But what he prayed, and in what manner, he himself and the Father to whom he prayed know; we are not permitted to break into the ineffable secrets between them [Col. 0202C]. Yet we can certainly know and say this: in that frequent converse of prayer, our salvation was chiefly at issue; the Son sought it from the Father in prayer in such a way that he himself, together with the Father, at the same time assented to what was requested. It is like the son of some great ruler, pleading his father’s favor for his fellow citizens in such a way that he himself, with his father, grants what is sought.

The Son, therefore, as has been said, had a manner of prayer that was particular, secret, and always effective, as he himself says in one place to the Father: “I know, Father, that you always hear me; but I said it because of the crowd standing around, so that they too may believe that you sent me” (John XI).

But this form of prayer [Col. 0202D], containing everything necessary for us, he first handed down to his disciples and, through them, to all who would believe in him, so that no Christian who is old enough to understand may be permitted to be ignorant of it. Therefore, in very few and plain words, he enclosed great and many mysteries, so that it might be concise because of the fewness of its words, clear because of its fullness, and fruitful because of the scope of its contents.

Hence children, after the first characters of the alphabet, are given this prayer to learn, and after it the creed of the catholic profession. In the former is contained everything that must be sought in prayer; in the latter, those things without which salvation cannot exist. Therefore all priests who preside over congregations ought with every diligence to admonish their subjects, so that they may know by heart and understand wisely these two things [Col. 0203A] so necessary for salvation. This was carefully and faithfully observed in the time of the primitive Church; but now, through the negligence of prelates, it has, like many other things, fallen into contempt and neglect—not without danger to those who ought to have ensured that this did not happen.

There is certainly no doubt that the Savior would not have delivered this pattern of prayer to us with such great care unless he knew how useful, effective, and suited to obtaining requests it is. He knew the disposition of the Father’s mind: namely, by what human vows and prayers he is most readily moved to hear. Therefore he took care to show how we must approach him. It is as though someone especially beloved by a king, who knows all his secrets and knows his character thoroughly, instructs another person who wishes to obtain the same king’s favor: “Thus and thus you are to speak to him; use these words; by this verbal artifice he can easily be persuaded” [Col. 0203B].

Therefore let this Lord’s Prayer always be on our lips and always be held in our heart, for it was uttered and shaped by the most holy lips of Christ. Let it always first meet us when we rise in the morning; let it receive us when we return to our beds in the evening. By it let us hasten to come before the face of the Lord in the confession of true praise; by it let us endeavor to commend to him our thoughts, words, and deeds.

And it is rightly established in our order that the Lord’s Prayer should precede all the offices of both day and night, and bring them to their completion at every time [Col. 0203C]. For it is fitting that those words should frequently sound on our lips in praise of Christ which first sounded on Christ’s lips for our instruction. Yet when it is appropriate, or when we are in private, other expressions of our devotion should be added, such as bendings of the knees, and *palmatae*, that is, beatings of the breast; and, if possible, an abundant outpouring of tears.

Perhaps these things would seem superfluous to someone, if they were not approved by the authority of Holy Scripture and even of the Savior himself. For the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Standing far off, the tax collector beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XIII). Likewise the Lord says through the prophet: “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; rend your hearts, and not your garments” (Joel II). The Apostle also says in one place: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. III), and what follows.

In the bending of the knees is signified the humility of the person praying, when, humbling the whole body, he subjects himself to the divine majesty. In beating the breast, however, the sinner is angry with himself and, in retribution for the evil he has committed, strikes and beats his own heart with the same hand by which a perverse thought, proceeding from that heart, was brought to the completion of a wicked deed [Col. 0203D].

## CHAPTER IV

The causes of tears are diverse, and therefore they are distinguished into different kinds [Col. 0204A]. First, some are called carnal and others spiritual. Carnal tears are those shed for temporal things, such as a lack of earthly goods, some bodily discomfort, injuries inflicted, or some pressure of this kind. Such carnal tears ought not to be entirely excluded from prayer. Indeed, whenever there is great need, God should humbly be asked—with tears and compunction of heart—to come to our aid in all these and similar afflictions.

But there are other tears which may not only accompany us when we pray, especially in this excellent prayer, but are even necessary. I have chosen to call these spiritual, because they are aroused in a person by the power of the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Psalm: “His spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (Ps. CXLVII) [Col. 0204B].

These tears are usually shed for diverse causes: in remembrance of sin; in compassion for one’s neighbor; because of the miseries of this world; through consideration of danger; because of the dispensation of the divine mystery; because of Christ’s sufferings; and from desire for the kingdom. The sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, issuing from one source, distributes these seven kinds of tears into diverse streams, so to speak.

The spirit of fear arouses tears in remembrance of sin, when the sinner, knowing that he has gravely offended God and therefore fearing punishment, has recourse to tears; and he often both merits and receives not only forgiveness but an increase of spiritual grace. Such were the tears of him who said: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch” (Ps. VI).

The spirit of piety moves tears in compassion for one’s neighbor, when we weep in compassionate fellow-feeling for the sins or afflictions of our neighbors, according to the Apostle’s words: “Weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII) [Col. 0204C].

The spirit of knowledge, which concerns earthly things alone, moves tears because of the miseries of this age, when, considering that there is nothing in this world except sin and misery, and being insufficiently certain about eternal things, we melt into tears, attending to the Apostle’s words: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). And in the Psalm: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX).

A person sheds tears in consideration of danger when, seeing himself hemmed in on every side by so many dangers that he can scarcely escape a fall, he wastes away wholly in grief and tears. With these tears the spirit of fortitude is present, strengthening and reminding him that “those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Ps. CXXV) [Col. 0204D].

The spirit of counsel prompts tears because of the dispensation of the divine mystery. Through it, considering God’s goodness toward us and the order of our redemption, and fearing that we may be found ungrateful for such great benefits of God and therefore unworthy, we are dissolved into tears from great devotion, attending to the Apostle’s words: “Because of the exceeding love with which God loved us,” etc. (Eph. II).

The spirit of understanding, which is from above, draws forth tears because of Christ’s sufferings. Through it, understanding that the Son of God is equal in the glory of divinity to God the eternal Father, we marvel that he endured so much for us; and, not believing that we can render him a fitting return—that is, give our life for Christ—we yield to tears, considering the words of the same Apostle: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II) [Col. 0205A].

The spirit of wisdom, which consists in knowledge of eternal things, induces tears from desire for the kingdom. Through it, tasting in some measure the sweetness of heavenly goods, we grieve that they are deferred from us, saying with the Psalmist: “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI).

These kinds of tears—and perhaps more—ought to accompany us in prayer, especially in this Lord’s pattern of prayer, concerning which [Col. 0205B], because we have already said much, let us now briefly continue with the remaining matters.

## CHAPTER V. On the domestic form

A domestic form of prayer is one which each person prescribes for himself at his own discretion: for example, certain prayers or psalms, or even litanies or genuflections, to be performed daily in fulfillment of a vow. This form varies in almost every individual, while each person, with no authority but solely his own devotion, chooses what seems good to him to observe.

### On the monastic form

The monastic form is that established by our elders—such as Basil, Benedict, and the other Fathers—and regularly observed in monasteries, that is, communities of monks [Col. 0205C]. It too varies according to different authors and different kinds of monks, while some add to, alter, or subtract from the customs of others.

### On the canonical form

The canonical form of prayer is that of those who are preeminently called regular canons, although *canon* can be interpreted as nothing other than “regular,” from *canon*, meaning “rule.” Yet this form also, although it ought to be conformed to ecclesiastical canons, is nevertheless sometimes found to differ from them in certain particulars.

### On the ecclesiastical form

[Col. 0205D] The ecclesiastical form is the general form of the Church, and it too usually varies according to different dioceses. Among these forms of prayer, no one should proudly judge his own to be preferred to others, for they are all praiseworthy and good, pleasing to God, and directed toward the one end of blessedness. For just as, as regards the usefulness of the matter, it makes no difference in what order of words you address a king and obtain his favor, so we believe it makes no difference whether, by this, that, or another form of prayer, you attain the prize of eternal recompense. Therefore let each person observe and fulfill his own form with every diligence; and let all, though in different ways, yet with one disposition of devotion, render the service due to God, who is accustomed to regard not so much the words with which he is prayed to as the piety of mind with which one prays.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fifth element of prayer: that is, what befits one who prays

[Col. 0206A]

Now that we have treated the element of prayer concerning what belongs to prayer itself, let us examine the next: that is, what befits one who prays. The following befit one who prays: frugality, chastity, humility, devotion, and compunction.

Frugality is necessary for one who prays, because a filled belly and swollen stomach cannot direct a subtle and pure prayer. It is likewise fitting and beautiful that chastity should accompany the person praying, so that a pure and clean prayer may be presented to God; for nothing is more shameful than to defile the purity of prayer with the foulness of lust. Hence, in the Old Testament, the priest who was about to enter the temple by lot [Col. 0206B] in order to burn incense was commanded to put on linen breeches; and during the entire period of his rotation he was not permitted to look toward house or wife. The Apostle himself also (I Cor. VII) commands even married people to abstain from marital intercourse during the time of prayer, and afterward to return to one another, “lest,” he says, “Satan tempt you.”

But priests and clerics, and monks—indeed all who have taken a vow of continence—must be continually continent, just as they must always pray. Humility also ought to accompany the person praying, so that he may not imitate in public the pride of the Pharisee, but preserve in private the humility of the tax collector (Luke XVIII).

Devotion, as we taught much above, consists in two things: love of God and desire for the kingdom. Both must accompany the person praying: that he may love the God to whom he prays, and ardently desire the heavenly kingdom for which he prays [Col. 0206C]. Compunction likewise consists in two things: hatred of sin and fear of punishment. These two also ought to be at hand for the person praying: that he may hate sins without compromise, and, setting them before his eyes, daily seek forgiveness for each one and beg with the utmost fear and humility to be delivered from the eternal punishment which he has deserved through them.

## CHAPTER VII. On the sixth element of prayer: that is, what results from praying

We shall now attempt to explain the final element of prayer: that is, what results from praying. These are: forgiveness of sins, assurance of rewards, and eternity of joys.

David had merited forgiveness of sins [Col. 0206D] when, after the fiftieth Psalm, in which he had most humbly bewailed his sins, the prophet Nathan was sent to him saying: “God has removed your sin from you” (II Kings X). Assurance of rewards likewise usually results from prayer, when the true and diligent petitioner, through long practice in prayer, begins confidently to expect not only pardon of sins but also the rewards of eternal blessedness. The eternity of joys can indeed be acquired in this life, but cannot be possessed until, finally released from the body, we rejoice to receive the goods long hoped for.

See how useful and effective prayer is: in this life it both receives forgiveness of sins, grants assurance of future blessedness, and at last leads to eternal life.

# BOOK TWELVE. On fasting

[Col. 0207]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0207A]

After the long interruption of this work which necessity of circumstances has caused, the first part of the subject matter—that is, prayer—having been treated, as we believe, with sufficient care, let us now briefly pursue the remaining parts, concerning which less must be said. For we have ceased for a long interval of time: partly because of the charge of souls imposed on me, under which I labored for two years; partly because of the intolerable bodily infirmity that I suffer.

But now, released by God’s will from that office which I had been compelled to undertake, I shall attempt to do violence to my weakness. It is so great that, because of pain in my head and a defect of speech, I can scarcely express to the scribe the words I have conceived. Nevertheless, I shall do what I can, and attempt to put the finishing hand [Col. 0207B] to the work I have begun, lest all the preceding labor come to nothing if this little work, which may perhaps be useful when completed, is left unfinished and mutilated.

## CHAPTER II

Let us first consider fasting: namely, what it is, how many kinds it has, what befits one who fasts, and what the usefulness or effects of fasts are. To fast, as they say, is to abstain; hence *fasting*, that is, abstinence, is derived both in meaning and in word.

There are different kinds of fasting. To consider them briefly in order involves neither very great difficulty nor very little usefulness. There is spiritual fasting and bodily fasting. Spiritual fasting [Col. 0207C] is humbly to abstain from all wicked pleasures of mind and body. Bodily fasting is reasonably to refrain from bodily food and drink for the health of the soul.

Of spiritual fasting, I think nothing truer can be said than that it must be kept and maintained at all times by every person. But concerning bodily fasting, a definite teaching can be arranged according to its various kinds. Some fasts prevailed under the Law: namely, those which Moses commanded to be observed, such as the fast of the first month, the fast of the fourth, the fast of the seventh, the fast of the tenth, and others like them. In their own time these could both be useful and merit reward, just as the other legal observances could. But now, in the time of revealed glory, when observed by the Jews, they neither please God nor merit anything, just as all things done by unbelievers [Col. 0207D] do neither please God nor merit anything.

The fasts received in the Church in the time of grace are either of catholic institution, monastic observance, voluntary devotion, or necessary correction. Fasts of catholic institution are those prescribed for observance by all whom neither age nor illness prevents: such as the fast of the Lord’s Advent, of Lent, of the Ember Days, or of holy vigils. Fasts of monastic observance are those observed by monks or regular clerics, as the Cistercians fast continually throughout one half of the year; while the other monks, who are also called Black Monks, and regular clerics except certain feasts of nine or twelve lessons [Col. 0208A], on which they say they are permitted to relax the fast.

A fast of voluntary devotion is one that a person gladly undertakes of his own will, with no one compelling him: for example, fasting on all Fridays or on some Fridays, either permanently—that is, for as long as he lives—or for a fixed period, such as three, seven, or ten years. A fast of necessary correction is one imposed upon a penitent for graver sins: for example, four Lents, to be fasted each year. The first of these is customarily observed before the Lord’s Nativity, the second before Easter, the third around the summer solstice, and the fourth at the time of the autumnal equinox.

These four forty-day fasts are observed in memory of those fasts of which Moses observed two, Elijah a third, and the Savior a fourth. The last two are known to very few, for almost no one observes them, unless someone, from great devotion or in punishment for some grave crime, either voluntarily promises to observe them or is compelled to do so. The other two are better known: one because they precede the Lord’s Nativity, the other because they precede the resurrection of the same Lord [Col. 0208B]. Since the one preceding Easter is more famous, all are sung and read in it. For it is said of the Savior that, “when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. IV). It is also said of Moses that he fasted forty days and forty nights in order to merit receiving the law of the Lord (Exod. XXXIV). It is further said of Elijah that “he walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, unto Horeb, the mountain of God” (III Kings XIX).

Again, one fast is of strict austerity, another of intermediate character, another of relaxed mildness. A fast of strict austerity is one conducted with bread, water, and raw herbs alone. A fast of intermediate character is conducted with bread and wine or *sicera* [strong drink], and every Lenten food. A fast of relaxed mildness is conducted with milk, cheese, and every kind of food except meat alone, which is granted to no one who fasts [Col. 0208D].

## CHAPTER III

The following befit one who fasts: firmness of mind, purity of body, spiritual joy, cheerfulness of countenance [Col. 0209A], gravity in words and deeds, and sobriety in food and drink.

Firmness of mind is needed in order to trample down and repress the snares of tempting gluttony; purity of body, lest lust and impurity of the flesh harm the faster more than fasting helps him; spiritual joy, by which he may now rejoice and be glad, confident of the reward of future blessedness. There should be cheerfulness of countenance, so that he may not be sad like the hypocrites, lest he appear to human beings to be fasting, but rather to his Father who is in heaven (Matt. VI). There should be gravity in words and deeds, lest one who afflicts his body for his sins do or say anything buffoonish, excessive, or contrary to religion. There should be sobriety in food and drink, lest he exceed the limits of sobriety in any way.

There are five ways in which one is accustomed to act against sobriety: by craving food impatiently [Col. 0209B], by anticipating the proper time, by seeking more luxurious foods, by preparing them with excessive refinement, and by consuming them in excessive quantity.

Esau sinned in the first way in food, when he exchanged his birthright for a meal of lentils (Gen. XXV). David sinned in the same way with drink, when he desired water from the cistern at Bethlehem, which three men brought him at the peril of their own blood (II Kings XXIII). But because the one took food unlawfully, while the other poured out to God the water he had wrongly desired, the former was condemned and the latter obtained mercy.

Jonathan sinned in the second way when, contrary to his father’s prohibition, he tasted honey which he had taken from the ground with his rod (I Kings XIV). But because he had not known of the prohibition, he at last deserved to be rescued from the death with which his father threatened him, by the intervention of the people [Col. 0209C].

Those whom the satirist Juvenal rebukes sinned in the third way, saying (Satire I):

> . . . They consume their patrimonies at one table.

And elsewhere, concerning the same people:

> . . . What costs more tastes better.

Those whom Horace the Flaccan ridicules (Satires, book II, satire IV), under the persona of Catius, whom he introduces as describing numerous kinds of pickled delicacies, sinned in the fourth way [Col. 0210A].

Those against whom the aforesaid Juvenal satirizes in this fashion sinned in the fifth way (Satire I):

> How great is the gluttony that sets whole boars before itself—  
> an animal born for banquets.

See with what hatred even pagan men pursue the vice of gluttony. In this matter it must be known that whatever food you consume which you do not need, you steal in its entirety from the needy. Therefore it is safer to take less than enough than, by consuming superfluities, to make oneself guilty before both God, whom one offends, and the brother from whom one snatches necessities. But we cannot define for each person what is enough, too little, or too much; and therefore we believe this must be left to each person’s own judgment.

The usefulness or effects of fasts are: the expulsion of demons [Col. 0210B], the exclusion of evil thoughts, forgiveness of sins, mortification of vices, certain expectation of future goods, and the attainment of heavenly joys.

The expulsion of demons is not so much from others as from ourselves, because when the malignant spirit sees a person afflicting himself for his sins, it sees itself despised and no longer dares to remain with him. Yet demons are also often expelled by the power of fasting from the bodies of others who are possessed, as the Savior says: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII).

There is exclusion of evil thoughts, because for one fasting on account of his sins it is detestable to think of committing sin. There is forgiveness of sins, because the Lord was appeased toward the fasting Ninevites (Jonah III); and this could not have been the case had their sins not been forgiven. There is mortification of vices, because when the flesh is mortified by continual fasting, the fuel of sin within it is also extinguished [Col. 0210C]. There is a sure expectation of future goods, because one who devoutly and purely afflicts himself for sins cannot fail to hope for the rewards promised to penitents. There is attainment of heavenly joys, because all who afflict their bodies by prolonged fasts for eternal life are brought, as soon as they depart from the flesh, to the banquets of eternal fullness.

# BOOK THIRTEEN. On almsgiving

[Col. 0209]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0209D]

Lastly, let us speak briefly of almsgiving, which is likewise set down as one of the three parts of our subject. Concerning it, we must consider what it is; how many kinds of almsgiving there are; what befits one who gives alms; and what is wont to result from it. “Almsgiving,” a Greek word, is commonly called in Latin misericordia, “mercy.” Human mercy, however, is twofold: one kind toward oneself, the other toward one’s neighbour. It could not be added that there is mercy toward God, because God has mercy on all, and Himself needs no one’s mercy. A person therefore [Col. 0210D] has mercy on himself in two ways: by repenting of evils and by persevering in goods—repenting of evils, by which, if present, he would necessarily be condemned; persevering in goods, without which he could by no means be saved. “My son,” it says, “have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30); that is, by abandoning evils and doing goods, both of which unquestionably please God. We have mercy upon our neighbour in several ways: namely, by compassion, prayer, correction, counsel, assistance, and benefaction.

We have mercy upon our neighbour by compassion when we mercifully grieve either over his sins or over his sufferings. David grieved over the sins of his son Absalom when he persecuted his father (2 Kings 15); [Col. 0211A] and over his sufferings when he lamented his pitiable death (2 Kings 18). Likewise, we have mercy upon our neighbour by prayer in two ways: when we humbly entreat God in prayer either for his sins or for his miseries. Stephen prayed for the sins of his neighbours when he prayed for those who were stoning him (Acts 7); Paul prayed for sufferings when, by prayer, he raised the young man Eutychus, who had been struck down by a miserable fate (Acts 20). We also have mercy upon our neighbour by correction in two ways: either when we rebuke him by reproving evil deeds already committed, or when we mercifully restrain him from deeds yet to be committed. Of this merciful correction the Psalm says: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me” (Ps. 140).

We also have mercy upon our neighbour by counsel when we help with salutary advice one who is wandering and wholly ignorant of himself [Col. 0211B]. We have mercy upon the same neighbour by assistance when we mercifully provide him aid to do or obtain a good which he cannot do or obtain by himself. And we have mercy upon him by benefaction when, from an impulse of piety, we give material support to one in need—for example, food or drink, clothing or money.

In dispensing such benefits, these precautions must be observed: that it not be done from another’s property; that it not be without measure; and that it not be given to one unworthy. It must not be done from another’s property, because “he who gives alms from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in his father’s presence” (Ecclus. 34). It must not be without measure, as when you give one person that by which you could have helped several. Nor should you give to one unworthy if one equally needy and worthy can be found, as it is written: “Let your alms sweat [Col. 0211C] in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may give” (Ecclus. 12). And although elsewhere it is written, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6), nevertheless these benefits of ours ought to be extended more abundantly and more frequently to those of the household of faith, and to our neighbours or familiars.

## Chapter II

These things befit one who gives alms: purity of mind, simplicity, humility, generosity, and cheerfulness. We say that these befit him not as the only things, indeed, but as the chief things. Purity of mind is especially necessary to him, without which whatever he might do would not be almsgiving; for, since almsgiving is nothing other than mercy, no one can be merciful to another who is proved impious and merciless toward himself through impurity of heart [Col. 0211D]. Therefore, if you intend to give alms, you must begin with yourself and proceed to your neighbour.

For what the Saviour says in the Gospel—“Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11)—was not said in the sense that by this act alone you may be cleansed from many great crimes if you give food to the hungry, clothing to the naked, or anything similar. For if this alone sufficed to cleanse many great crimes, the condition of the worst people would be excellent, if they could redeem their wicked deeds merely by an expenditure of temporal things—such as thieves, robbers, and extortioners, who could easily buy impunity for their evils even from an evil portion of their goods. This certainly must not be understood in the Lord’s words; rather, because one who is such that he can truly and worthily give alms, we acknowledge that for him all things are indeed clean [Col. 0212A].

This is like the saying commonly heard: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” It does not mean that a person who has charity may commit thefts, murders, or adulteries, but that, having charity, he cannot do anything that would hinder him from attaining life. Simplicity also befits him, so that, from that which ought to be done for the sole cause of piety, he may not seek human favour—as the Pharisees did, who sounded a trumpet when they gave alms. Of such people the Saviour says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6). “They have received their reward,” he says: namely, the praise from people which they sought under the pretext of false religion; while they still had to receive the punishment due to their pretence [Col. 0212B].

Therefore almsgiving ought either to be done secretly, according to the saying, “Hide alms in the bosom of the poor, and it will pray for you” (Ecclus. 29); or, if it cannot be concealed, it should nevertheless be done with a pure intention, as the Saviour says: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6). That is, mingle no wrongful intention with a good work which ought to be done solely with good intention.

Humility is likewise very necessary, lest what must humbly be done from love of God and neighbour be done arrogantly and proudly. Such are certain utterly depraved people, who lavish upon buffoons and actors what ought to have been distributed to the poor, although it is written: “He who gives to actors sacrifices to demons” [Col. 0212C]. Therefore they are liable to a double punishment: either because they defraud Christ’s poor of their sustenance, or because they lavish upon the most impure class of people, for their buffoonery, goods perhaps violently seized from others. Even if the goods are their own and free from every fault—that is, containing no element of injustice—they nevertheless sin most grievously, because they disgracefully misuse what they ought to have devoted to good purposes. What greater abuse is there than to pour out your resources upon foul people wholly hateful to God, while offering no consolation by any benefit to Christ’s poor, who are also your brothers? “He who sees his brother in need,” it says, “and closes his compassion against him—how does the charity of the Father abide in him?” (1 John 3). Your brother is poor, and perhaps far dearer than you to the common Father, God [Col. 0212D]. He shudders in scant garments, while you shine in purple; yet he is your brother, and you cannot escape your kinship with him. Divide your substance with your brother, lest you grievously provoke both your Father and his.

Generosity also ought to be present in one who gives alms, so that he may not be bloodless and dry in giving, but may willingly share with his brother according to his means—not fearing his own future want so much as attending to the other’s present need. He should remember that He who gave what he presently possesses can, once it has been distributed, supply other things more abundantly. Let each person therefore act according to his means, and for love of Him who gave all things and can give greater things, provide what he can to his needy neighbour. Let him remember the Scripture which says: “If you have much, give abundantly; but if you have little, gladly share even from that” (Tob. 4) [Col. 0213A].

Cheerfulness ought always to be present in one who gives alms, so that he may give what he gives with a joyful spirit; for, as the Apostle says, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). For even among human beings, as the philosopher says, a benefit which has long clung to the giver’s hands and is finally given as though extracted from him is unwelcome. How much more can your gift fail to please God, who has no need at all, unless the cheerfulness of a devout mind commends it. Therefore, when you give alms, you must do so with the utmost cheerfulness of mind and with spiritual joy, knowing with complete certainty that among all your expenditures nothing is invested so happily and profitably as what, when given to the poor, makes God your debtor. “He who has mercy on his neighbour,” it says, “lends to God” (Prov. 19).

Therefore lend, and lay up your treasure in heavenly storehouses, so that Christ may restore it to you a hundredfold when you need it. In this manner he had laid it up who said: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit unto that day” (2 Tim. 1)—the righteous Judge [Col. 0213B]. Consider what the same Judge will say at the last judgment: “What you did for one of my least ones, you did for me” (Matt. 25). A faithful saying and a judgment worthy of God: he professes that he himself received what was bestowed upon his least brothers. Who would doubt to deposit with One who restores what is entrusted to him with such unimpaired faith and with so great an increase? Consider what he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (ibid.), and the other things there set forth concerning works of mercy.

But lest you suppose yourself excused by scarcity of possessions, consider what the prophet says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house; when you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58). Consider what he commands. He does not command you to prepare costly banquets for your hungry neighbour; but, if you have nothing else, to divide a morsel of bread with him. He does not command you to receive the needy and wanderers with elaborate provision, but to bring them into your house, so that at least beneath your roof they may escape the hardships of the night. He does not command you to clothe a naked poor person in precious garments [Col. 0213D], but at least to conceal his nakedness with a worn and old garment. “Do not despise your own flesh,” that is, one who derives with you a common nature from the first earthly father. “No one,” says the Apostle, “has ever hated his own flesh, but cherishes and nourishes it” (Eph. 5). Love your own flesh; love your brother, because he is your flesh and blood. Cherish him with the covering of clothing; nourish him with bodily food.

See what the same Apostle says: “He who gives, let him do so in simplicity; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness” (Rom. 12). By simplicity a wrongful intention is removed; by cheerfulness spiritual joy is enjoined, so that there may be pure simplicity in the intention of a good work and spiritual cheerfulness in its performance. These are the things which seem to befit one who gives alms [Col. 0214A]. Let us now look at its result.

## Chapter III. What comes from almsgiving

Five things result from almsgiving: remission of sins, increase of charity, spiritual joy, sure hope in the promises, and reception of rewards. No one ought to doubt that remission of sins results from almsgiving, since it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3). This, however, must be qualified: almsgiving must be done in the proper way, that is, with those things present which we said a little above ought to be present in one who gives alms. For where purity of mind, humility, and simplicity are present, we believe that no mortal sin can be present at all [Col. 0214B]. Venial sins, however numerous, are easily washed away by almsgiving.

And if any mortal or even grievous sins have indeed been removed through confession, but the satisfaction of works has not yet followed, the generous giving of alms can be very effective also in this regard: the more disposed a person has been to it, the lighter the penance which may be imposed upon him, or the more the penance already imposed may be relaxed. For the faith of the Church holds that, by the bestowal of temporal goods, both sins and penances for sins may be redeemed.

For, as they say, remission of sins is usually effected in three ways. In one way, excellently and properly: when God releases from the liability of hidden fault a guilty person who confesses, or who has the intention of confessing, though the necessity of doing penance remains. If he scorns to do so, then according to some the sin which had been remitted returns; or, according to others, it does not indeed return, but he will be punished as much as for the sin because of his ingratitude and contempt [Col. 0214C]. Of this remission of sin the Psalmist says: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31). And the Lord says through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18).

There is another mode of remission of sin, though less properly so: when the priest, by the power by which he can bind and loose, absolves from sin the sinner who has confessed, imposing upon him the appropriate measure of satisfaction owed. If he does not perform it, neither God’s remission nor the priest’s will benefit him; rather, like the former person—or perhaps more gravely because of his greater contempt—he will be punished. In a third way sin is said to be remitted, quite improperly, when the penance imposed for sin is either entirely remitted or partly relaxed by one who has authority [Col. 0214D].

This is usually done in two ways: through the compassion of charity, and through compensation by a greater good—that is, a good which benefits more people. Through the compassion of charity: as when some part of an imposed penance is relaxed for persons by holy men or by communities of holy men. Through compensation by a greater good: when an imposed bodily penance is exchanged for another thing that can benefit more people—for example, generous distribution of alms to the poor in a time of famine, a contribution of money for the needs of churches, the redemption of captives, or something else that seems similar. In either case, the person whose penance is relaxed or remitted is believed also to be absolved from sin.

Although this is customarily done and accepted among the practices of the Church, I nevertheless believe it safer that no one be so completely absolved from bodily penance in exchange for any temporal thing that he has not either already performed, or is still commanded to perform, some portion of it—for example, the fast of several weekdays out of many, or something else equally burdensome to the body [Col. 0215A]. For we believe no satisfaction for sin is so acceptable to God as that which is commended by bodily affliction and contrition of heart. “Return to me,” he says, “with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2): behold bodily affliction. “And rend your hearts and not your garments” (ibid.): behold contrition of heart. It is fitting that the affliction of the same body should cleanse what has been committed by a bodily act, while the guilt of the mind is washed away by contrition of heart.

Therefore, whatever is expended from our resources, whether granted us by God for good uses or perhaps acquired through sin—whatever, I say, is expended from things external to us upon the aforesaid works of piety—it is nevertheless safer that a penalty of bodily penance be imposed upon the guilty person, both for him who dispenses it and for him who uses that dispensation [Col. 0215B], so that what was committed bodily may be corrected by at least some bodily affliction. For nothing is less to be feared than that someone should repent too purely and perfectly of his sin, especially since there may be many offences which he himself does not understand; and if he has done more than required in penance, the Lord can recompense it with the full reward of repayment.

An increase of charity toward both God and neighbour likewise results from almsgiving. Toward God, in this way: while you presume that your work pleases Him for whose honour you willingly spend what is yours, you burn more strongly in his love in proportion as you hope to be loved more by him in return. The love of God is such that, by its sweetness, so far as lies in itself, it always draws a person more and more to itself; for in God there is nothing, as there is in a human being, by which the mind of one who loves may be offended. “Taste and see,” it says, “that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33) [Col. 0215D]. God’s sweetness and pleasantness are like spices: until tasted, they are unknown; but when you begin to taste them, they become known with a wonderful delight. Saul had not yet tasted this sweetness of God when he was still a blasphemer and persecutor (Acts 8, 9); but Paul had tasted it when he said: “For I am certain that neither death nor life shall be able to separate us from the love of God” (Rom. 8).

Charity toward one’s neighbour also increases through the giving of alms, both because of God, for whose sake you comfort your neighbour, and because you do not doubt that your benefit, being necessary to him, is welcome; and you cannot fail to love one by whom you think you are deservedly loved. Thus as the benefit grows, charity grows also: charity invites the benefit, while the benefit enlarges charity. Therefore, if you do not yet know how to love your neighbour, you can learn this art of loving most effectively by the practice itself: divide your substance with him, and you will begin to love. For in this art practice commonly precedes theory, whereas in other matters theory usually precedes practice. The practice of love is the work of piety; its theory is love itself [Col. 0216A].

Spiritual joy likewise results from the same almsgiving, while a mind conscious of a good work glories that by one and the same deed it has fulfilled God’s will and relieved the need arising from fortune [Col. 0216B]. In the one it rejoices that it has rendered due reverence to the divine majesty; in the other, compassion for a common nature; and in both, that the law of charity has been fulfilled. It is no small joy to have done what pleases God, helps one’s neighbour, and accords with charity. Considering these things, a mind conscious of having done well willingly distributes what is its own for Christ and fears no losses of temporal things, reckoning safe for itself only that which it has spent on such purposes. With earthly resources it fills heavenly treasuries; it places temporary wealth in eternal storehouses, rejoicing to make friends for itself from the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16), by whom, when it fails, it may deserve to be received into eternal dwellings. “It stores up treasures for itself in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6).

In this way that martyr had stored up treasure who, while he was being burned on a gridiron, mocked the most impious tyrant with these words: “It is roasted; turn it now and eat. For the wealth of the Church that you seek has been carried into heavenly treasuries by the hands of the poor” [Col. 0216C].

The sure hope in the promises which likewise usually results from almsgiving rests upon two things: the worthiness of the one who earns them, and the truthfulness of the one who promises them. It rests upon the worthiness of the one who earns them because he who willingly fulfils the divine commandments confidently awaits the promises; and upon the truthfulness of the one who promises, because he most certainly gives what he promises to one who does what he commands. He defrauds no one, deceives no one, and mocks no one with vain expectation. To deposit something with him is nothing other than to put it in a safe place; he restores all things entrusted to him in full faith, returning his own to each person with increase. For power and ability attend his most excellent will, and he has no greater difficulty in doing than in willing [Col. 0216D]. For he is rich toward all who call upon him, as Scripture says (Rom. 5); and however much he gives to one, he has none the less to give to another. Nor must one fear that he who gave grace whereby to merit will deny a reward to one who now merits and is worthy. He who wished you to merit surely wishes to reward one who merits.

Persevere, therefore, in meriting, and gladly give what is yours for the sake of his grace, who restores to you a hundredfold in this world, with persecutions, and will grant eternal life in the world to come. Deposit confidently with him who not only faithfully preserves what is entrusted to him, but returns it multiplied [Col. 0217A]. Deposit confidently with him who neither knows how to commit fraud nor permits anything to perish under his custody. Whatever you entrust to him, you preserve entire; if you entrust nothing, you lose everything, since to have entrusted nothing is to have lost everything.

The final and chief result said to arise from almsgiving is the reception of heavenly joys. These are the joys of eternal blessedness proposed as a reward for all the merits of the elect. This is that good which is the end and completion of all other goods; and if it does not follow, as was said above, the other things have preceded uselessly. To this good every class of elect people runs by diverse paths of merits and hastens by diverse courses of works. Although it is one and simple—for it is eternal life and it is God—it is nevertheless obtained through many causes and the assistance of diverse merits. For all the goods that are either done or possessed by elect people converge upon this, if I may so speak, most certain end [Col. 0217B]. And it is so much the more delightful to the one attaining it as it has been acquired through more causes and greater merits.

Therefore no one should think it absurd that we have said that this same good of eternal blessedness results from any of the three parts of our subject—namely, prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. These three goods, like many others of this kind, are such that, if performed in the right manner, each confers life, while all together attain it more fully; just as several roads meeting at three-way crossroads, both jointly and separately, lead to the same place. Still more, when many roads coming from different directions, both all together and each separately, lead to the same city, much more certainly do all virtues which proceed from the root of charity—both the virtues themselves and their works—direct both together and singly toward the one end of eternal recompense [Col. 0217C].

Thus many hold, or rather judge, that whoever possesses one virtue lacks none, especially if he possesses charity, which is the root of all; just as wherever the root of a tree is found, there the branches joined to it must also be present. For the virtues are arranged in the soul according to the form of a kind of spiritual tree. In it charity is both root and trunk; the greater branches are virtues; the lesser branches, smaller offshoots; the flowers, good thoughts; the leaves, benevolent words; and the fruit, good action.

This resembles the human body itself, which, as physicians say, has the form of a tree—though of an inverted tree, that is, one having its root turned upward and its branches downward. The head is the root because of the nerves proceeding from the brain, by which all the members are joined together and moved; the trunk of the body is the stem; the arms and legs are the greater branches; and the joints of the fingers and toes are the smaller branches. Thus there is, as it were, a tree within a tree: the soul in the body [Col. 0217D].

You will find another tree likewise in wicked souls, but of the contrary kind: not a tree of virtues but of vices. In that pestilential tree, contempt for God is the root; the greater vices are its branches, the lesser its small offshoots; the evil flower is a wrongful thought; the leaf is an idle word; and evil action is the poisoned fruit. Of these two trees—the tree of virtues and the tree of vices—the Lord says in the Gospel: “A good tree cannot bear bad fruits, nor can a bad tree bear good fruits. A good tree bears good fruits, and a bad tree bears bad fruits” (Luke 6; Matt. 7).

The saying may apply literally to that third tree, the human body: when the man born blind was enlightened and the Lord asked whether he saw anything, he said, “I see people like trees walking” (Mark [Col. 0218B] 8). From the interconnection of virtues which we have described, many wish to conclude that they cannot be separated from one another, but that if one is present all are present together. Yet, because it is either impossible or uncommon for all to exercise their acts together, they say that some are present in act, while others are present only in habit. By “habit” we here mean a quality of mind which it acquires by being formed through charity; by “act,” the work of the virtue itself.

Thus Abraham, although married, had continence in habit, because, if he had not been intent upon begetting offspring, he would rather have remained continent than used marriage. But he had marital chastity both in habit and in act, because he consented to it in mind and exercised it in the deed itself [Col. 0218C]. John, however, possessed continence in both modes: he loved it in mind and observed it in bodily act.

It is now sufficiently clear from what has been said that, although all virtues differ in act, all proceed from the one root of charity, and both the virtues themselves and their works tend toward the single end of eternal blessedness. Therefore we could assign to those three things of which we have thus far treated no final result other than that which is common to all goods. There are, however, not a few other things common to them which could aptly and fittingly be attributed to any of them. We preferred to transfer most of these to the treatment of prayer, so that once they had been discussed there, it would not be necessary to take them up a second or third time; and so that the treatment of prayer, which outweighs the other two in dignity, might be richer by their addition [Col. 0218D].

For prayer is conducted with God; fasting, with yourself; almsgiving, with your neighbour. By praying you address God; by fasting you afflict the flesh; by giving alms you comfort your neighbour. In the first the soul is purified; in the second the body is worn down; in the third the neighbour is relieved; but in all God is honoured. For you honour God when you humbly entreat him, when you torment your body in punishment before him, and when you share your possessions with your brother for his love. These three things are good even separately, and all together are especially good; and if other goods are added to them, the more numerous they are, the better they are. For whatever things are naturally good, the more of them come together into one, the more excellent a good they make. Hence the highest good, to which nothing can be lacking, is commonly defined as a state made perfect by the gathering together of all goods [Col. 0219A].

This, indeed, is the supreme blessedness of eternal recompense: namely, God, the end of all goods, their rewarder, and their reward. To this end beyond doubt all goods which are either in a person or done by a person ought finally to be referred and happily consummated in him. For whatever is neither directed to this good by intention nor consummated by attaining it is not even worthy of the name of good.

Among these goods, these three of which we have so far spoken are commonly reckoned by more attentive observers among the chief works of virtue, being more general and more necessary to many people. For to abandon all one’s possessions completely—which the Lord in the Gospel does not command but counsels (Matt. 19)—and to maintain continence—which the same Saviour does not command but left to the Apostle to recommend (1 Cor. 7)—are each great, but rare, and not placed under such necessity, since many attain life without them. But to pray, to fast, and to give alms pertain generally to every Christian, so that if anyone with the means to do so scorns to perform them, he has no charity and is therefore unfit for eternal life [Col. 0219B].

Thus, when the tongue converses with God in prayer, the wantonness of the flesh is restrained by fasting, and the hand is extended for the consolation of one’s neighbour, we surely render service most pleasing to God. This threefold harmony greatly pleases him; he is exceedingly delighted by such a symphony. He hears the person praying, is propitiated toward the afflicted person, and prepares mercy for the person who shows it to his neighbour. Therefore these three kinds of good works must be acquired and maintained with every effort by all the faithful, and especially by us, in whom a greater charity is presumed from the outward religious habit itself; with whatever other goods God may deign to grant being added, so that, aided by them temporarily in this life, we may deserve to attain that highest and incomparable good.

These are the things which seemed necessary to say concerning this three-part subject of ours [Col. 0219D], leaving aside, for brevity’s sake, very many things which, had we not sought to avoid the lengthiness of the work, could usefully and fittingly have been added. Now we wish to make this agreement with the reader: if anything in this little work should appear doubtful, ambiguous, or insufficiently plain, let him not immediately consider what may be objected by contentious argument, but carefully attend to what the author meant; for this is plainly the chief concern in every reading of Scripture, insofar as its meaning is known. It is the part of a discerning and kindly reader faithfully to interpret the words of a writing according to the sense in which they were set down. But one who, disregarding—or rather, failing to know—the writer’s meaning, tries to force resistant wording into another meaning is rightly called not a reader but rather a corrupter and perverter [Col. 0220A]. For although a better sense than the author himself intended may sometimes be drawn from someone’s words, this is not reading another’s work but composing one’s own commentary.

We know, indeed, that in this little work we have touched on some matters quite open to dispute and, as the proverb likewise says, have walked with bare feet over coals hidden beneath ashes. Yet in these matters we took every care to moderate the pen, so that nothing might be committed to the page except what is true and pious, if anyone understands with us rightly. If in this respect some error has perhaps been made by us, it should be attributed either to our weakness or to the difficulty of the matters themselves. But we wish all into whose hands this little book comes to know that this was our intention: both to say something concerning matters which, as we believe, had until now not been discussed, and especially to humbly commend our memory henceforth to fraternal charity on this occasion [Col. 0220B].

For we have no concern to hunt for praise; rather, we have sought the favour of persons of our religious profession, so that for the labour which we have expended on these matters, and especially upon prayer, we may be permitted to hope for their devout prayers. Let this be our reward from this labour, and we shall confess both that we have employed our effort usefully and that we have been treated generously. For after the immense mercy of divine loving-kindness, upon which the whole hope of human salvation rests, the best part of my consolation and confidence lies in the aid of the holy prayers of the entire order [Col. 0220C].

For, considering the multitude of my evils and the poverty of my merits, distrusting my own resources, I am compelled to beg for another’s help. What security, I ask, can there be for me in myself, when I see certain others among those with whom I began to live, who have spent sixty years or more under the discipline of cloistered warfare, burning with such spirit as though they had only now begun; while I, a soldier of the shortest time, grow weary as though at my first entrance into the camp, with my arms only just taken up? Those who either never tasted the world at all or forgot it many years ago repent with such grief and fear as though they had ceased sinning today; while I, who by the grace of conversion have scarcely moved my foot out of the mire of filth and misery [Col. 0220D], languish, deceived by such foolish security, as though I had brought with me nothing to mourn—just as if a monk were made perfect by a change of secular dress and life alone.

Others do whatever they can, heaping merit upon merit; I alone sit among them, as they say, with hands clasped, thinking that nothing else need be done and judging it a great thing to have left the world. How much more excellent and salutary it would have been to offer God the fruit of good works cheerfully, and to devote this very life—which nevertheless must be lived by me in labour—entirely, with spiritual joy, to divine services. For I can say most truly that throughout these seven years now spent by me under the religious habit, I have laboured under bodily discomfort so great and so continual that, except during the time of refreshment or sleep, I cannot remember ever having been well for even one hour [Col. 0221A].

Nor do I now mean by this the austerity of the order, which is dreadful and burdensome to those leaving worldly joys, and which I certainly accept devoutly and reverently according to my strength. I mean a certain intolerable suffering of the head, which I have endured incessantly from my first reception of the habit. Therefore nothing would remain, amid such pressure of circumstances, except to fail under the hand that scourges me, if I did not presume that I am being scourged wholesomely and profitably by the loving disposition of a Father. But now the rod and staff of the Lord themselves comfort me (Ps. 22), as I frequently repeat those words of Scripture: “Whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3; Heb. 12) [Col. 0222A].

Let the wise physician, then, decide what in the sick person ought to be cut or burned; let the best Father determine how far scourges should be used upon his son, and what consolation and joy he intends to give after the scourges.
