As long as it pleases him to strike, I shall try to receive his blows and lashes, with the patience which he himself has given, without any murmuring. This one thing, amid the frequent infliction of wounds, I beg with a great inward cry of heart: that, though punished for a long time, he may at last admit me to a share in the paternal inheritance. Amen.

[Col. 0221] The little work on the three acts of Christians—namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—ends. Printed at Basel by Michael Furter, in the year 1507, on the fifteenth day of March.

[Col. 0221]

GUNTHER THE CISTERCIAN’S HISTORY OF CONSTANTINOPLE TAKEN BY THE LATINS, under Baldwin, about the year 1204. Edited from manuscript parchments in the library of the Academy of Ingolstadt.

(Henry Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, Basnage edition, vol. IV, part i.)

CANISIUS TO THE READER.

In the manuscript codex there was no other title besides this: “Here begins the History of Constantinople.” Moreover, from those words added near the end by someone else, the author’s name is evident. In chapter 24 he indicates quite plainly that he was a monk in the monastery of Pairis, in the diocese of Basel, concerning which more is said in chapter 2. Likewise, when in chapter 1 he says, “the perpetual well-being of this present place of ours,” he expressly testifies to the same thing. This monastery belonged to the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Basel, as is clear from chapters 2 and 4.

That Martin, abbot of Pairis, who took part in the capture of Constantinople and from whose account Gunther derived this History, was still alive when Gunther wrote it, as may be inferred from chapters 5 and 1. How faithfully it was composed is clear even from these words of the first chapter: “The page of our narrative will contain nothing whatever false or ambiguous, but will follow the true and certain sequence of events, as that same man, of whom we shall speak at greater length, related to us the plain and simple history with considerable humility and modesty.”

Nicetas Acominatus Choniates, the Grand Logothete, writes of this same tragedy of Constantinople’s capture in the *Annals of Constantinople*, which, when republished in Greek and Latin in 1593, a certain heretic contaminated with absurdities and heretical scholia. Such men, indeed, are born to foul good books badly.

Since Martin the abbot is mentioned here very frequently, one is reminded of that Martin of the Order of Preachers who flourished under Louis in 1320; Trithemius enumerates his little works in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and adds these words: “There are also others whom either ignorance of the facts or envy has led to suppose should be assigned to the Cistercian Order.” Thus Trithemius. But perhaps Trithemius was deceived here when he read in other authors a reference to Martin, abbot of the Cistercian Order.

Certainly our Martin was a Cistercian; if others remembered him, as a man of the greatest renown, they rightly called him a Cistercian. Yet anyone would err who wished to confuse this Martin of ours, the Cistercian who flourished under Emperor Philip, with that Martin of the Preachers who was distinguished under Louis.

In chapter 24 the year of the Lord 1205 is marked, when Henry was bishop of Strasbourg. “This Henry,” says Bruschius in his fifty-ninth bishop of Strasbourg, “was Count Henry of Veringen, a Swabian; pious and devout, an author and guardian, a most zealous promoter and preserver, of public peace and good tranquillity among all men. He presided wisely and most profitably for twenty-one years. He restored the almost ruined castle of Dagenstein, once the seat and dwelling of Dagobert, king of the Gauls, and built by him as well. He died in the year of the Incarnate Word 1223, on the eleventh of March. He is honourably and magnificently buried in the chapel of St Andrew, which is in the cathedral basilica.” Thus Bruschius.

JACQUES BASNAGE’S OBSERVATION ON GUNTHER’S HISTORY OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

[Col. 0223]

I. One may reasonably doubt whether there were several men named Gunther at the same time. Trithemius does indeed report a certain Gunther, a monk eloquent in verse and prose, flourishing in the time of Emperor Henry IV; but he is plainly different from the man whom we seek, since he preceded him by almost a whole century.

There is another Gunther who bade the Muses, long exiled, return:

> This too, if all else should be lacking, can alone  
> Win me renown: that I prepare to bring forth to the common world  
> The Pierian maidens, hidden now through many ages  
> And not daring to emerge from their shut dwellings,  
> And to restore their ancient brilliance to poetry. . . .

He celebrated the praises of Frederick Barbarossa in ten books. He lived not only under Frederick, but also under Henry VI, Frederick’s son:

> Come first in peace, you who by paternal right  
> Are at once successor and heir  
> To virtues and to the kingdom, and bear the sceptres. . . .

Accordingly, he reached the end of the twelfth century, or even the beginning of the next. To him is attributed a poem called the *Solymarium*, because it described the war of the crusaders.

If what Baronius says were true—that this poet was a Ligurian, that is, a native of Milan—he ought to be distinguished from Gunther who composed the *History of Constantinople*. For this latter man, German by birth, was a monk in the monastery of Pairis near Basel. But Baronius was mistaken in supposing that the title of the poem published by Gunther was the name of his homeland. Gunther called his book the *Ligurine* because he undertook to narrate Frederick’s deeds in Italy, especially at Milan in Liguria. He did not mean to indicate his homeland.

That man did indeed write the *Solymarium*; but the title of that new poem does not fit the *History of Constantinople* published here: for that book was written in verse, this one in prose. Further, the former perhaps recounts the capture of Jerusalem, whereas this one recounts that of Constantinople. The works are therefore different. Let someone else conjecture whether they ought to be attributed to one and the same author—who, in youth, might have sported in verse, and in old age, at the prompting of Abbot Martin, might have described the journey to Constantinople in prose.

II. There is no need for lengthy discussion of the time when he wrote. First, the Constantinopolitan expedition was completed in 1204, when, after the city’s capture, Baldwin, Count of Flanders, was elected emperor of the Greeks. Second, Abbot Martin, who returned from Greece in the following year, urged Gunther to describe that expedition. Gunther is therefore wholly occupied in praising Martin, abbot of Pairis. He thus lived at the beginning of the thirteenth century. Third, he did not complete this little work until after the death of Emperor Philip, who was slain in 1208. For he himself reports that the emperor used to carry, at solemn feasts, a jewel-adorned tablet laden with relics. Philip had therefore died when Gunther wrote these things. Accordingly, the year 1210 has been assigned to this work. For the rest, see Canisius.

III. Some matters here deserve observation. First, not everything Gunther narrates here concerning the Constantinopolitan expedition agrees with historical truth. He trusted Abbot Martin, who sought a herald of his own praises and passed over everything else provided that Gunther flattered him. Therefore, whoever wishes to examine this Constantinopolitan expedition more carefully should consult Bzovius under the year 1204.

Second, I do not know whence he drew certain opinions greatly derogating from the Christian religion: “If any acts committed by our people appear contrary to piety, nevertheless do not doubt that they were performed by the divine will, which is always just.” Certainly God, though omnipotent, can neither approve crimes nor make unjust actions just.

Third, the writer seems to contradict himself when, among the relics transported by the abbot, he lists wood of the Lord’s Cross, although he had written that the venerable wood of the Cross, drenched with Christ’s blood, had been so hidden away that no Christian could know what had been done with it or where it ought to be sought.

IV. I pass over the pope’s hostility toward the Greeks, which is commended; but let the reader beware of Constantine’s Donation and of the tablets attached to it, as also of the pyramid on which Sibylline verses, inscribed long before, promised the Latins victory at sea.

AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0223A] 1. All works of divine power possess the highest degree of wonder, to such an extent that, if any are not wonderful, neither should they be judged divine. Yet we are especially accustomed to marvel at those works which the same divine power deigns to display through humble persons—that is, through persons who, both in their own estimation, through humility, are lowly, and in the eyes of others are thought less fit for such great undertakings.

[Col. 0224A] Thus it is more wonderful that through Moses, a private and humble man, who was accustomed to pasture the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro (Exod. III), the people of the children of Israel were led out from Pharaoh’s tyranny and the iron furnace of Egyptian slavery [Col. 0225A] (Exod. XIV), than if that same people had been rescued by some most mighty king with a strong hand and thousands of armed men.

Likewise, we receive with greater astonishment the fact that the world accepted Christ’s faith—entirely new and unknown—through unlearned and poor fishermen (Matt. IV), rather than if the religion of that same Christian faith had been persuaded and handed down by the authority of Caesar Augustus, the learning of Plato, or the eloquence of Demosthenes or Cicero. For the less God’s works admit human capacity in themselves, the more brightly the loftiness of divine power shines forth in them.

For this reason I have chosen to set forth in a humble and plain style and in accessible language certain very great and arduous things which the Lord deigned in our time to accomplish through a man sufficiently modest and [Col. 0225B] humble: assuredly to the praise and glory of His name; for the devout remembrance of that man; and for the enduring well-being of this present place of ours. Indeed, for the honour and joy of the entire German nation; or, what is truer and greater, for the consolation and protection of the whole Western Church.

The page of our narrative will contain nothing false or ambiguous, but will pursue the true and [Col. 0226A] certain sequence of events, as that same man of whom we shall speak at length related to us the plain and simple history with considerable humility and modesty. We do not dare to write worthily concerning the praise and proclamation of this man, lest he himself—who attributes everything to God and seeks to have nothing ascribed to himself—be offended by his own praises. Yet neither can we be altogether silent, lest we commit manifest wrong against God, through whose agency these deeds were accomplished and who is accustomed to exalt His humble servants.

Therefore we shall take care to temper our pen between the two, so that God’s great works accomplished through him may not remain concealed, while he himself remains unoffended in his humility. Whoever, therefore, brings hand or eye to this little page to read it should also apply the attentive diligence of the mind to closely considering the very matters [Col. 0226B] treated here. For there he will find great and celebrated events, which could in no way either happen or be done unless by divine command. We therefore wish to admonish the reader that, if any actions by our people should appear contrary to piety, he should nevertheless not doubt that they were done by the divine will, which is always just.

HISTORY OF CONSTANTINOPLE TAKEN BY THE LATINS.

[Col. 0225]

[Col. 0225C] 2. At the time when that famous French preacher, named Fulk, but “Leo of Paris,” was stirring up, by his preaching, all the peoples of France, all Flanders, Normandy, and Brittany, and the other provinces, to aid the Holy Land and the pre-eminent city of Jerusalem, long held by barbarians, there was in Upper Germany a man named Martin, abbot of a certain Cistercian monastery situated in the bishopric of Basel and itself called Pairis.

This circumstance seems from its very beginning to possess something miraculous: that both the man who was then publicly preaching the word of the Cross and the man who was soon to become a preacher of the same cause were alike called “of Paris,” just as they were equals in office. The former was so called from the name of his city, from which he had bodily origin; the latter from the monastery over which, as we said, he presided as spiritual father. For both places—the aforesaid monastery, already mentioned a little earlier, and that famous city of the French—are called Paris.

That name has its own etymology in the French language; but in German it seems to have this explanation and cause. The first monks sent from the monastery of Lucelle to inhabit that place found there nothing but a deserted and cold spot and pure ice. [Col. 0226C] But now, by the grace of God, who exalts and advances His poor, it is a celebrated church, enriched with possessions and estates, adorned with buildings, and, more excellent than all these things, devoted night and day to divine services.

The abbot of whom we speak was mature in mind but pleasant in appearance, prudent in counsel, gracious in familiarity, agreeable in speech, gentle and humble among his brethren; so that he was regarded as outstanding in authority among secular persons, and beloved and approachable among both. From the supreme pontiff Innocent—then the third bishop of the Holy Roman Church to bear that name—he received a command both to take the sign of the Cross without hesitation and publicly to preach the same in those regions.

Obeying the papal command in both respects, he confidently and energetically undertook the work of preaching, to everyone’s surprise, because he was a man of [frail] constitution and was thought by all incapable of so great a labour. He delivered an address to clergy and people in his city, which is called in Greek *Basilea*, that is, “royal,” in the famous church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There a great multitude of both orders had assembled, stirred by the new reports. For they had long heard that other provinces round about were being roused to this military service of Christ by notable sermons, while in those regions no one had yet mentioned the matter.

[Col. 0227A] Consequently many of them, inwardly ready to give themselves to Christ’s army, eagerly awaited such an exhortation with all their desire. All stood with ears raised and eyes fixed upon him, most eagerly waiting to hear what he would command or advise concerning this matter, and what he would promise, from divine goodness, to one who obeyed.

3. “A word to you, my lords and my brethren—a word to you: not mine, certainly, but Christ’s. Christ Himself is the author of the words; I am a fragile instrument. Today Christ speaks to you through my mouth in His own words; He laments to you His wrongs.

“Christ has been expelled [Col. 0227B] from His holy place, from His seat; He has been cast down from the city which He Himself consecrated with His own blood. Alas for grief! There, where the Son of God, to come in the flesh, was once promised by the holy prophets; where, once born and an infant, He willed to be presented in the Temple; where, present in the flesh, He preached and taught, repeatedly displayed powers and signs; where, dining with His disciples, He instituted the sacrament of His most holy Body and Blood; where He suffered, died, and was buried; where after three days He rose again; where, before those same disciples’ eyes, He was taken up into heaven; and where on the tenth day He poured out the Holy Spirit upon them in tongues of fire—there the barbarity of a profane people now rules.

“O misery! O lamentation! O utter calamity! The Holy Land, which Christ trod with [Col. 0227C] His footsteps, in which He healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, and raised the dead—that land, I say, has been delivered into the hands of the wicked. The churches have been overthrown; the sanctuary polluted; the seat and dignity of the kingdom transferred to the nations.

“That most sacred and venerable wood of the Cross, drenched with Christ’s blood, has been so suppressed and concealed by those to whom the word of the Cross is foolishness that no Christian can know what has been done with it or where it should be sought. Our people, who were accustomed to inhabit those regions, have almost entirely been consumed by the enemy’s sword or by captivity now long endured. The few who were able to escape that disaster have withdrawn to Acre or other safer places; and there they suffer repeated attacks from the barbarians.

“This is Christ’s need which compels Him today to entreat you through my mouth. Therefore now, mighty warriors, come to Christ’s aid; enrol yourselves in Christian military service; strive to be joined to the blessed army. Today I entrust Christ’s cause to you; I place Him Himself, so to speak, in your hands, that you may strive to restore Him to His inheritance, from which He has been cruelly expelled.

“And lest you be frightened because heathen fury has at this time gained such power over our people, I wish you to recall earlier events. At the time when that celebrated expedition took place under the noble leader Godfrey and the other French and German princes, that unbelieving people had occupied the land, just as now, after all Christians had been killed or captured; and they had securely possessed the Holy City of Jerusalem, Tyre, Sidon, Antioch itself, and other fortified cities—indeed, the whole land as far as Constantinople—for forty years, without any fear.

[Col. 0228A] Yet all these things, by the Lord’s will, were recovered by the same army in the briefest time, as though in passing. Nicaea, Iconium, Antioch, Tripoli, and other cities were captured. The very royal seat of Jerusalem was restored to our people.

“Now, although the impious nation violently occupies that chief seat and the greater part of the land, Acre is ours, Antioch is ours, and some other fortified and strong cities are still ours. By their protection, through divine favour and our strength, illustrious warriors, that glorious seat as well, together with all the rest, can be brought under our power.

“But if you ask what certain reward you ought to hope from God for such labour, I promise you most certainly that whoever receives the sign of the Cross and makes a pure confession will be cleansed entirely from every sin; and wherever, whenever, or by whatever chance he leaves this present life, he shall receive eternal life. I say nothing now of the fact that the land which you will seek is far richer and more fertile than this land; and it can easily happen that many of you may find there a more favourable fortune even in temporal matters than you remember having experienced here.

[Col. 0228B] “See now, brethren, how great is the security in this pilgrimage: the promise of the heavenly kingdom is certain, and the hope of temporal prosperity more abundant. I myself pledge to be your companion in journey and labour; and, as God may please, I desire to share both prosperity and adversity with you. Therefore now, brethren, receive with joyful hearts the triumphant sign [Col. 0228C] of the Cross, so that, faithfully carrying out the cause of the Crucified One, you may receive great and eternal rewards for a brief and modest labour.”

While the venerable man spoke these words, all who were present were deeply moved. One could see tears flowing in greatest abundance down both his face and the faces of all; one could hear groans, sobs, sighs, and other such signs revealing inward compunction. We have therefore related this sermon of the aforesaid abbot in detail because, although he later often exhorted both them and others manfully, we shall say nothing about any other exhortation of his; from this diligence of his it may be judged how energetic he ought also to be believed [Col. 0228D] in other matters.

4. At last the man of God assented to their requests. Having, as we have said, received from the supreme pontiff the care of souls, he was asked to take on the office of external provision as well. Then, exhorting and strengthening them in Christ, whose military service they had professed, he fixed a definite time at which, after arranging their affairs, they should all be ready to meet him at the same place and there undertake with him the journey of the holy pilgrimage.

As they returned to their homes, he carefully admonished them to conduct themselves chastely and innocently during the intervening time and to show themselves fitting soldiers of Christ, the lover of all purity. He himself, with an honourable company, went round the chief and most populous places of the whole region, frequently stopping to preach [Col. 0229A] and converting many to the same military service of Christ. He also took care to enjoin upon them that those able to do so should meet the others at the appointed time in the aforesaid place, intending to depart with them together; while those who, because of the shortness of time, could not free themselves from their affairs should follow the others as quickly as possible.

When the time of departure was now near, Martin, although secure under the authority of the papal command, nevertheless wishing to show reverence to his holy profession, went to Cîteaux, the fountainhead of the whole Order. There he received permission and blessing for the pilgrimage from the abbot of that place himself and from several other eminent abbots; then he returned to his monastery. There, commending himself to his brothers’ prayers and entrusting them to divine mercy in mutual love, he went to Basel, where a great multitude of those signed with the Cross had already gathered and received him most joyfully.

There too, after delivering an exhortatory sermon, he commended himself and his companions to the Blessed Virgin, humbly begging her to reconcile the new army to her Son. Afterwards, taking leave of the clergy and people of that city, by whom he was greatly loved, he undertook with his companions the labour of the holy journey, with a cheerful countenance and an undaunted mind. From this we may conjecture that the man of God had already then conceived in his mind some great design and, by a certain foreboding of the mind, foresaw what God was to accomplish through him.

5. Thus the army of the signed, departing from the city of Basel, left the others and took the road which leads through the narrow bends of the Trentine valley to Verona, a route of less labour and greater brevity. Such a clear and celebrated report of their coming had preceded them that not only those through whose territory they passed, but people also from villages and towns, came out in crowds. Receiving them with much favour and goodwill, they offered necessities for food at fair prices.

[Col. 0229C] They especially marvelled at Martin: a man of religious habit and most spiritual life was leading an armed army and applying himself so energetically to the office of so great a labour. Repeatedly and most famously speaking his name among themselves, they called him “another Martin,” after that Martin of Tours, who is almost first and chief in the catalogue of holy confessors, by a certain likeness between them.

Indeed, if we examine the matter carefully, several similarities, not to say many, coincide in both. First, just as that earlier Martin, while once following armed military service, conducted himself—as has been written of him—so holy and innocently that even then he was thought not so much a soldier as a monk, so this man, a true monk—indeed, the father of monks—led an armed army and lived among men of war in such a way that, as far as the labour of the journey and the care of his imposed office allowed, he relaxed nothing whatever of the strictness of his profession.

Second, just as the former had such compassion for the poor that, in the bitterest cold, he shared with a naked [Col. 0230A] poor man the cloak which was his only possession, so this Martin distributed generous portions to needy companions from what he had brought with him and from what he afterwards, by God’s will, obtained in abundance. Thus, in two days he freely spent one hundred and twenty marks for useful purposes, and seventy marks of silver on the third day.

The third point is that, just as the former, made bishop from being a monk, always maintained himself in the humility of his poverty, so this man, as has been most certainly learned by us, could have accepted, at the request of several persons, either a bishopric or whatever other ecclesiastical dignities he wished—even an immense sum of gold and silver. Yet, out of love for the rule of his monastery, to which God through him, and he through God’s grace, intended solemnly to do good, he refused the offers; and after completing the pilgrimage he returned to his brethren, poor indeed in spirit, yet rich and full in the works of heavenly treasure.

Perhaps there are several other resemblances that might be found in the one Martin by comparison with the other, unless we should seem to a reader less suitable for judgment either to diminish too greatly the most holy confessor or to exalt the worthy man of whom we speak. Therefore it befits us to venerate both with the due measure of honour: the former as a most holy soul now enjoying the fellowship of angels; the latter as a prudent man still living in the flesh, already reckoned of great merit with God and men and, by God’s grace, thereafter to enjoy greater favour with both.

Nor do we think it should be left unsaid that this Martin was born into the world on the holy feast of that St Martin. And therefore he was called Martin, and so forth.

6. When the pilgrim soldiers arrived at Verona with their leader, they were received with the greatest joy both by the people of the city and by another very great multitude of the signed, who had reached the same place before them from various parts of the world. The bishop of that city also devoutly and reverently received Martin into his house and willingly supplied him with support and service for nearly eight weeks.

Afterward they departed for Venice. There they had determined to embark upon ships and sail thence directly toward Alexandria, the Egyptian city, because at that time there was a truce of peace in the overseas regions between our people [Col. 0230D] and the barbarians; our people could not break it without violating the faith which they had pledged.

There were in the army of the signed very many famous and powerful men, both secular and ecclesiastical. Among them Baldwin, Count of Flanders, and Boniface, Marquess of Montferrat, were held pre-eminent in authority, strength, and counsel. All had indeed agreed unanimously to seek Alexandria and besiege it manfully, testing not so much the fortune of war as the power of divine might.

If they had done this, there was sufficient hope that both that magnificent city itself and the greater part of all [Col. 0231A] Egypt could readily have been brought under their power, because almost the whole population of the country had either perished, consumed by famine, or languished in want owing to the barrenness of that land. The Nile, which customarily waters it with fertile streams, had, they say, withheld them for five years already.

But this highly praiseworthy plan of our princes was obstructed by the fraud and wickedness of the Venetians. As masters of the ships and rulers of the Adriatic Sea, they refused them all means of sailing unless they first joined the Venetians in capturing the famous Dalmatian city, under Hungarian jurisdiction, Jafira [variant: Jazira]. They said that it had always been hostile to their interests, to the extent that the citizens of that city had often stripped their ships, laden with merchandise, by piratical attacks.

This appeared cruel and wicked to our princes, as God-fearing men: first because that city belonged to the Christian people, and second because it belonged to the king of Hungary, who had himself received the sign of the Cross and, as is customary, placed himself and his possessions under the protection of the supreme pontiff. Thus, while the Venetians pressed insistently and our people firmly refused, much time passed in this contention and discord. For they thought it utterly detestable and unlawful for Christians that soldiers of Christ’s Cross should ravage Christian people with slaughter, plunder, and fire—things such as often occur in the capture of cities.

Consequently many poor men, who had brought little with them and had consumed it, having no further travelling provision, left the army and retraced their steps homeward. Some powerful and wealthy men likewise turned back unwillingly and almost against their will, not so much oppressed by lack of resources as terrified by the horror of committing the crime. Some of these, going to Rome, could scarcely obtain from the supreme pontiff permission to return, and this only on the condition that they should fulfil the vow of their pilgrimage at least after some years.

The return of these pilgrims not only deprived our army of their presence, but also checked many who were hastening to follow from Germany and other regions in the fervour of mind they had conceived, so that they remained motionless in their own places.

[Col. 0231D] At that time a certain cardinal, Peter of Capua, was sent to our army. The supreme pontiff had sent him to settle the aforesaid controversy and to negotiate with the Venetians, that they might provide timely shipping toward Alexandria for the auspicious expedition (*embola*)—that is, Christ’s military service. When he could in no way extort this from them unless our people fulfilled the condition proposed to them, it seemed to the crusaders more pardonable and less blameworthy to offset a greater good by a lesser evil than to leave their vow of the Cross unfulfilled and return backward to their own people bearing the disgrace of sin.

[Col. 0232A] They therefore promised to do what the Venetians insistently demanded, while receiving from them a most certain pledge that they likewise, armed, would both accompany and carry our men as far as Alexandria.

Seeing, therefore, that not only delays were being woven into the undertaking of the Cross, but that the necessity of shedding Christian blood was also hanging over our whole army, our Martin—knowing neither where to turn nor what to do—shuddered wholly within himself. From among several alternatives, each of which displeased him, he chose that which seemed most suitable in such a crisis.

He therefore approached the aforesaid cardinal and, with every urgency of prayer, humbly begged him to release him from the vow of pilgrimage and permit him to return to the customary quiet of cloistered life. But the cardinal refused him any return at all unless he first completed the pilgrimage. Moreover, imposing a greater burden, by authority of the supreme pontiff he entrusted to Martin all the Germans whom he had brought, found there, or who would later come to the same army. He also directed both him and certain other religious men who were present to accompany their comrades through every contingency and, as far as possible, restrain them from Christian bloodshed.

7. The fleet therefore crossed the Adriatic Sea, which is also called the Dalmatian Sea. It derives one name from the city Adria—or, according to fables, from Adria, daughter of Ion—and the other from Dalmatia, which it washes.

> [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscript corruptly reads “Nunoiis Adringue.” There are those who write, as Eustathius does according to Janus Parrhasius, that Ion the Italian was Adria’s father; from him came the Ionian Gulf, which was soon called Adriatic from his daughter Adria. (CANISIUS.)]

Our soldiers reached the opposite [Col. 0232C] shores of the region at swift pace, though with sad and reluctant minds. So as not to prolong their stay in an undertaking hateful and detestable even to themselves, they besieged the aforesaid city with great terror and clamour. Attacking it for three days not so much as enemies as by threats, they compelled it to surrender without slaughter or bloodshed.

Once the city had been delivered to its victors, the Venetians immediately demolished it from its foundations in implacable hatred. Because our men thereby incurred a sentence of excommunication, for laying hands upon the possessions of the Hungarian king, which he, having received the sign of the Cross, had entrusted to the protection of blessed Peter and the supreme pontiff, our people thought fit to send envoys to that same supreme pontiff, asking him mercifully to make allowance for the compelled offence and absolve them from that sentence [Col. 0232D] of excommunication.

When useful and suitable persons were sought to undertake this embassy, Abbot Martin was chosen; with him went the bishop of Soissons, a man of great holiness and gentle eloquence; and as a third, Master John of Paris, a Frenchman nobly educated and pleasant in speech. Through the intervention of their presence, the favourable case might be more fully supported before the supreme pontiff.

When these three men had arrived in Rome and been admitted, they faithfully explained the case they had brought. They most humbly begged the lord pope to forgive mercifully the forced crime which our soldiers, in Christ’s honour, had committed against Christians, and, having carefully examined the case, to relax that sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 0233A] Moved both by the favour which necessity excused, by our army’s humble supplication, and by the grace and authority of the envoys, he took counsel and kindly assented to the requested pardon. He ordered the form of absolution to be written and carried to our army. For he was a man of great discernment and grace: young in years but grey in wisdom; mature in mind; composed in honourable conduct; illustrious by birth; distinguished in appearance; a lover of equity and goodness, but an enemy of wickedness and malice—so much so that he was called Innocent not so much by fortune as by merit.

8. Now it happened, while our envoys were still at the court [Col. 0233B], that a reliable report was heard: namely, that the young Alexius had arrived in the camp—a Greek by birth, the son of Isaac, emperor of Constantinople—sent by Philip, king of the Germans, with envoys and instructions earnestly requesting the army to endeavor to restore the aforesaid young man to his kingdom. The sequence of this affair is as follows—if a narrative of events conducted so disorderly and cruelly can properly be called a sequence. [Note: [Col. 0233D] Alexius had blinded his brother Isaac and driven him from the throne in 1195. (BASN.)]

Accordingly, while that Isaac of whom we have spoken was ruling among the Greeks, his brother Alexius—the uncle of the younger Alexius, whom we are now mentioning—acting on the counsel of certain utterly wicked men, and especially of one of his own kinsmen, a man noble indeed but treacherous, who among that people was called Murtiphlo, that is, “flower of the heart” [Col. 0233C], deposed his own brother Isaac from the kingdom. Having seized the sovereignty himself, he consigned Isaac’s son—and thus his own nephew, namely this Alexius now under discussion—to prison under close guard.

Yet, finding an opportunity, the young man escaped secretly and made his way by a hidden and swift flight to Germany. There he came to King Philip, who had his sister as his wife, and faithfully laid before him his own and his father’s miseries, and the cruelty of his uncle. Philip received the young man very honorably, kept him with himself for some time in great affection, and supplied him abundantly and generously with provisions and attendance.

But when Philip learned that our army, after taking Jazira, was operating near the borders of Greece, he repeatedly sent the often-mentioned youth, with his envoys and letters [Col. 0233D], to the princes, asking whether, if it could be done, they would undertake to restore him to his father’s kingdom. He laid this matter upon the Germans more confidently and authoritatively, because they seemed to belong to his jurisdiction. He reminded the marquis, his kinsman, of the relationship between them. The Flemings, French, Venetians, and men of other regions he earnestly implored by every means of entreaty, firmly promising that, if the young man recovered his throne by their assistance, a safe and free route through both Germany and all Greece would forever lie open to all pilgrims.

There was added to this the young man’s own most definite promise that, if he were restored by their strength [Col. 0234A], he would give them jointly three hundred thousand marks of silver. As all these reasons converged, the greater part of our army had already begun to incline toward supporting the young man. A few, however, who were more concerned for the success of the Cross, earnestly opposed it. They said—what indeed seemed likely—that the aforesaid young man could by no means be restored without sword and bloodshed. For it appeared to them foolish and wrong that a small body of pilgrims, with nowhere to which they could withdraw, should abandon the purpose of their holy pilgrimage and, at certain peril to themselves and for the advantage of others, declare war upon a city so great, so fortified, and so populous—a war which could not end without great slaughter of one side, or perhaps of both.

But concerning this matter, that is, the restoration of that young man [Col. 0234B], silence must for the present be kept. We shall pursue what follows in its proper place.

Therefore, after this report was heard at Rome, to resume what I had begun to say, the lord pope, together with all his clergy, our envoys, and many others, was greatly alarmed. He feared that the envy of the evil enemy might, on this occasion, contrive either the destruction of our whole army or at least the hindrance of the enterprise of the Cross. The supreme pontiff himself, as also his predecessors for a long time, hated that city, because it had long been rebellious against the Roman Church and differed from the Catholic faith in certain articles of belief—for example, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, whom the Greeks deny to proceed from the Son, and concerning the manner of sacrifice, which they customarily perform with leavened bread.

For they had suspended in the air, feet upward and head downward, a certain cardinal [Col. 0234C] who had once been sent to them by the supreme pontiff to rebuke and instruct them, until, having shared Peter’s fate, he breathed out his spirit. Therefore, as we have said, he hated the city and wished, if possible, that it might be subdued without bloodshed by a Catholic people—unless he feared the destruction of our army. Yet he did not hope that this could be done by our men, saying that the city possessed more vessels merely for fishing than they had in their entire fleet.

For it had sixteen hundred fishing vessels, each of which throughout the year paid the royal treasury, every fourteen days, one gold coin, improperly [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript has *propera*; perhaps *propterea*.] called a *Ferdoni*, equivalent to one quarter [Col. 0234D] of a mark. It possessed, moreover, an innumerable multitude of warships and merchant vessels, and a most secure harbor.

It was also the counsel and judgment of the same supreme pontiff, who was especially anxious over the business of the Cross, that our men should sail directly toward Alexandria. He further permitted them to take, in moderation and without purchase—that is, without payment—from the maritime districts of Romania washed by that sea, food sufficient for them for half a year. Because he feared that this plan might be changed and the progress of the Cross impeded by worldly affairs, he and all the others were rightly disturbed by the new reports.

[Col. 0235A]

9. The abbot therefore pressed with every sort of entreaty and, putting forward all the causes already mentioned and others besides, demanded permission to return. But the pope wholly refused him leave to return unless he had first reached the Holy Land, which he had vowed to seek.

Accordingly Martin left the court with his companions, having received the papal blessing and letters containing the form of absolution to be delivered to our army. He made for Benevento and found there that Peter of Capua whom we mentioned above, wishing to sail directly toward Acre. Martin joined him, but sent the papal letters to the camp through his companions; through them he also took leave, with words of excuse, of the German contingent which he had formerly led, on the second day before the Nones of April, 4 April.

Then, having embarked at Siponto [Col. 0235B], after the labor of a long voyage they reached the harbor of Acre, where they were received with great public celebration by all, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, 25 April. There was there a great multitude of Germans, among them certain noble and powerful men who had formerly known and loved Martin in Germany and received him with deep devotion. Peter of Capua, moreover, entrusted to him, by the authority of the supreme pontiff, all the Germans either then present or expected to arrive afterward.

That same summer, about the days called “dog days” because of the oppressive heat, a most severe plague and corruption of human bodies arose there, so great that more than two thousand corpses are said to have been buried in a single day. The disease was so sudden and unforeseen [Col. 0235C] that whoever began to fall ill could expect death with certainty within three days. Hence many, overtaken by sudden sickness and unable to arrange their affairs, summoned the abbot and entrusted all that they had to him—either to retain as his own or to distribute among needy companions—reserving for themselves whatever portion they chose.

Martin carried this out so faithfully that in two days, as was also stated a little earlier, he spent one hundred and twenty marks for such purposes, and seventy marks on the third. He also generously redeemed at a fair price, without profit to himself, the arms of certain brave men who had pawned them because of want. Moreover, moving actively among the sick in energetic charity, he willingly provided for them both by counsel and at his own expense [Col. 0235D], urging them to make a pure confession and to hold a sure hope of eternity; they were not to fear a brief and momentary death, after which they would immediately receive endless life.

He also exhorted the healthy manfully not to be frightened by that short-lived and swiftly passing calamity, but to be ready in resolute spirit for either outcome: either to prolong this life for a time in God’s honor, or, by following their companions, happily to gain eternal life by a short passage.

10. While this plague thus continued to range for a long time through that city and its territory, the greater part both of the inhabitants and of the pilgrims dwelling there were consumed by the corruption of the same contagion. Of the sixteen persons staying in the abbot’s lodging [Col. 0236A], scarcely he himself, the fourth, escaped death; all the rest succumbed to the danger. Even those who survived, having in effect received death’s sentence, waited for it with certainty at every moment, weak and bloodless.

There came also another misfortune: the truce of peace which had been confirmed by oath between our people and the barbarians was broken by their fraud and wickedness. Two ships of our nation were captured and plundered, and everything carried in them was seized. Our men, however, avenging this injury bravely and swiftly, caught at sea six of their large ships laden with grain, merchandise, and other goods, and made both the vessels and all that they contained their spoil. Thus, through divine power and their own valor, they manfully repaid their treachery [Col. 0236B].

When war was renewed, the enemy’s fury began to press our men more fiercely than usual, both because they were fewer in number and because even those who remained were thought feeble and weak, as though death were near. Therefore those regarded as chief among them thought it advisable to send envoys to the camp of the pilgrims, whom they had learned were in Greece, asking them to bring timely aid to the city of Acre and to that small portion of the Holy Land which our people still held with much labor and danger, and to understand that it could now scarcely be defended much longer.

At their request, Abbot Martin undertook this embassy with another man, namely Conrad, advocate of Swartzenberg. The abbot bears witness to Conrad’s such great integrity [Col. 0236C] that whenever he remembered himself to have lied, whether in jest, earnest, or by accident, he used to seek as many pardons in private. From this it is sufficiently clear that one so scrupulous in slight matters, which almost all others regard as nothing, was by no means negligent in greater ones.

Accordingly, on the third day before the feast of Saint Martin, these two men embarked, and at the Circumcision of the Lord they reached the shore near Constantinople. There our army was then faring far from happily, because it had fallen into great danger through becoming entangled in the affairs of others. It must surely be believed that God so arranged matters that this city, which because of its greatness and power had long been rebellious against the Roman See [Col. 0236D], might by the valor of our men and an unforeseen victory be restored to ecclesiastical unity.

When the envoys of Christ’s transmarine soldiery arrived among us, they were reverently and kindly received by all, especially by those Germans over whom the abbot had been accustomed to preside. Having explained the reason for their arrival, they indeed encountered great compassion, but received from our men no hope whatsoever of counsel or aid, since our men did not seem able sufficiently to assist even themselves.

For they were in such an extremity of adversity that they were not even secure near the city itself, because of the incalculable and hostile multitude of the Greek populace; nor could they depart from it without great labor and danger, because of the countless ships by which [Col. 0237A], if they fled, the Greeks intended to pursue and attack them most fiercely. Thus there came about something rarely seen: our people began to consider laying siege to the very city from which they did not dare flee.

To make this matter clearly understood, it is worthwhile to resume and explain what we recalled having temporarily suppressed above. Whoever considers the matter carefully may come to recognize the hidden judgments of God and the concealed causes of events.

11. The sequence of the events which had brought our men into this narrow extremity of necessity can be gathered as follows. When the royal youth Alexius, as was also said above, had come to the camp with the envoys and letters of King Philip, and had himself greatly moved the princes of our army by his entreaties and immense promises, all gradually began, as we have said, to incline toward his favor and the support of his cause.

This was done for various reasons: partly from regard for King Philip, who earnestly petitioned our men on his behalf; partly because it seemed to them a pious act, if it could be done, to restore to his throne the legitimate heir of the kingdom, cruelly deposed; and partly because of the young man’s own entreaties and promises. If restored, he could render great help to all pilgrims, both then and afterward. There was also the fact that they knew the same city to be rebellious and hateful toward the holy Roman Church, and did not think its subjugation by our men would greatly displease the supreme pontiff—or even God [Col. 0237C].

The Venetians too, whose fleet they were using, particularly urged this course, partly in hope of the promised money, for which that people is especially greedy, and partly because that city, relying on its multitude of ships, claimed for itself supreme dominion over that entire sea.

From the concurrence of all these matters, and perhaps others as well, it resulted that all unanimously consented to favor the young man and promised him their aid. Yet there was, as we believe, another cause, far older and more powerful than all these: namely, the counsel of divine goodness, which ordained that this people, puffed up by abundance of wealth, should be brought down from its pride and recalled to the peace and concord of the holy universal [Col. 0237D] Church.

For it seemed fitting that a people which could not otherwise be corrected should be punished by the slaughter of a few and the loss of the temporal possessions over which it had become inflated: so that the pilgrim people might be enriched with the spoils of the proud; the whole land might pass into our power; and the Western Church, illuminated by the most holy relics of which they had rendered themselves unworthy, might rejoice forever.

There was also this, surely a great consideration: that the often-mentioned city, always unfaithful to pilgrims in the past, would henceforth, God willing, after its inhabitants had been changed, remain faithful and united, and would provide us with aid all the more excellent for subduing the barbarians and gaining and holding the Holy Land [Col. 0238A], because it lay nearer to us. All these things would surely have been thwarted if that people had been conquered by men of another faith, such as pagans or heretics; indeed, what would have been most grievous, it would have passed into their error.

I therefore judge that these causes had preceded in the sight of God—hidden from us, yet manifest to him who foresees all things—by which these great and wondrous events, of which we are about to speak, would be brought by a sure but hidden boundary to their outcome.

12. From this conception of the divine mind, so hidden and inscrutable, which comprehends all things in their forms and which neither the number of grains of sand, nor drops in the sea, nor leaves in forests can escape [Col. 0238B], all things which are accustomed to be done or to occur in time proceed by a certain path and unchangeable course. Hence Greek philosophers commonly call it the archetype, that is, the primary pattern; John in his Gospel, chapter 1, calls it “life”: “What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men.”

For just as, in the mind of a mortal human being, those things in some manner live which that person thinks of in the present, whether they are presently existing or are still hoped for in the future; so, indeed—rather, much more truly—in the divine mind, which the Greeks call *noys* (*nous*, “mind”), wholly alive, or rather itself life, which can neither be ignorant nor forget anything, all things lived even before they came to be: both those later created and those still to be created until the end of the age.

Since this conception of the divine mind contains the ideas—that is, the forms—of all things, even the least, it much more certainly embraced from eternity this event which we propose to describe, so great, so novel, so wonderful, exactly as it was to occur [Col. 0238C]. Therefore it must be believed that it proceeded from that unassailable disposition of God that our army, which, immediately after Jazira had been taken, was hastening toward Alexandria, changed its purpose, declared war on this vast city, entered its territory in hostility with its fleet, and, having pitched camp not far from the city walls, took up its position ready for war.

Alexius, the invader and possessor of his brother’s throne, met them with a great multitude of armed men. Having scarcely tested the soldiers’ courage in a brief engagement [Col. 0238D], he lost confidence in his cause and in the cowardice of his allies, whom he considered insufficiently loyal to himself because of the crimes he had committed, and promptly turned in shameful flight.

13. The citizens of the magnificent [Note: [Col. 0237] This happened in the year 1203, on the first of August; Alexius was in fact suffocated on 5 February, after six months of rule. (BASN.)] city were terrified by the flight of their king, whom many had not previously loved greatly because of his crimes. At the same time they were repeatedly approached through envoys with the promises and entreaties of the younger Alexius, while our men, contrary to their expectation, threatened the city’s destruction unless they received that legitimate heir of the kingdom as king. They opened the gates and peacefully admitted him with the whole army within the walls.

The young man [Col. 0239A], clad in royal garments, was at once duly placed upon the royal throne. He ordered one half of the promised money to be paid out kindly and generously to our princes, hoping to repay the remainder in a very short time. Our men consequently remained in the city for several days and, making moderate use of the service both of the new king and of the citizens themselves, took especial care that they should not seem burdensome guests to anyone.

But since the city, though large and beautiful, could not accommodate two peoples so different in language and customs, not sufficiently united by mutual affection, together with so great a multitude of men and horses, it pleased them to leave the city and withdraw to an open and spacious place. There, having pitched camp [Col. 0239B], they might more conveniently await the king’s promised payment.

After they had left the city, a certain concealed sedition of the citizens against the king began to arise. Many complained that he treated men who were foreigners and alien to their customs with such affection; that he had already transferred to them, almost without cause, the wealth of nearly all Greece; and that he still intended, after despoiling his own kingdom, to bestow upon them as much again, or perhaps more. Since nearly all voiced this complaint, they even dared openly to accuse the king himself. Publicly they forbade him to despoil his kingdom for the advantage of others, to make his own people’s poverty the booty of strangers; rather, they demanded that he pursue and destroy them together with the citizens, as invaders greedily coveting others’ property.

This sedition greatly terrified the new king [Col. 0239C]: both because of the treachery of citizens who had accepted him under compulsion, because of the affection he had for our men, and because of the oath concerning repayment of the money which he had pledged in good faith. One could see him deeply anxious, as though placed between the wickedness of his own people, his love for ours, and his regard for King Philip, whom he greatly feared offending if he either deceived or harmed our men.

Since he could not readily be induced to commit so great a crime, that Murtiphlo, mentioned above—by whose counsel his father had been blinded and he himself shut up in prison—strangled him with his own hand. He said that it was a lesser evil for the young man alone to be removed from this present life than for the wealth of all Greece to be transferred through his folly to certain unknown men [Col. 0239D].

When Alexius had thus been removed, Murtiphlo, as a man of royal lineage and also a blood kinsman, placed the diadem upon himself. Seizing the royal throne as boldly as unwisely, he began cruelly to devise plans concerning the affairs of the kingdom and the destruction of our people. Abhorring more carefully his impiety in this deed, we are compelled to cry out thus.

14. Therefore, after the cruel parricide had strangled the young man, seized the kingdom, and taken possession of it, he ordered that report of this crime be kept silent and suppressed for a time, lest it immediately reach the camp and sound in the ears of our men before he had put the designs of his intended treachery to the test. At once he sent envoys [Col. 0240A] in the name of the younger Alexius, to summon the princes of our army from their camp to him, as though they were to receive the promised money and, besides this, still greater gifts of royal generosity.

When this was reported to them, they, as men of Christian simplicity, suspected no fraud and hastened to enter the city. For nothing was further from their fears than that the new king, whom they themselves had established, should have been removed from the world in so short an interval.

There was, however, there a very prudent man, the doge of the Venetians: blind in face, indeed, but most clear-sighted in mind, who admirably compensated for the blindness of his body by the strength and prudence of his spirit. In doubtful matters the others always consulted him with every diligence and customarily arranged public business at his direction [Col. 0240B]. When the others asked, according to custom, what he thought of this affair, he urged them not, out of love of money, to expose themselves to Greek deceits. He said that he feared precisely what had happened: that the young Alexius had either been killed by his own people or, being Greek by birth, had been corrupted by them and was plotting our ruin with them.

While the princes deliberated for a long time about this and the envoys pressed them more urgently, the report burst out from the heart of the city and shook the whole army with grave terror. They saw that they had been caught in enemy territory, among a most wicked nation, and that he whom they had introduced to them as king by mighty force and with great terror had been snatched from life. Had he lived, he could both have restrained their madness [Col. 0240C] and greatly consoled our men, sending them safely and richly supplied from his kingdom to complete the journey of their pilgrimage.

They now recognized that they were utterly deprived of all these hopes, so that they expected with complete certainty nothing but death from the new king and the citizens. For what could pilgrims do, or what hope could they hold, caught in such a predicament and possessing no safe refuge where they might even briefly catch breath from the enemy’s attack? Should they declare war against them, thus publicly stirring to persecution those whom they knew already to be secretly their enemies? Yet the Greeks’ number was infinite, growing daily through reinforcements, and they were in their own land, where all things were abundantly available to them [Col. 0240D]. Our men, by contrast, were few and destitute among enemies, from whom they could hope for nothing except, so to speak, whatever they could cut down with their own swords.

They were also deeply grieved because they had largely been disappointed of the promised money. In its hope they had delayed their journey and spent the resources for their pilgrimage upon others’ affairs. Nevertheless, they chose what in such a case seemed the best course: concealing the fear which they surely could not be without, they threatened the besieged enemy; and, in vengeance for the strangled king whom they themselves had installed, they demanded the whole city, its citizens, and that execrable parricide—the city for destruction, the citizens for the certain punishment of death.

By thus menacing them [Col. 0241A], they struck such terror into them that they scarcely dared come out from their walls, especially because of our crossbows, whose use, the rarer it was among them, was considered the more terrible and dangerous. Meanwhile our men, with courage strengthened, were ready for either outcome: either to depart, if a worthy and advantageous opportunity presented itself, or to kill the enemy and undergo death at their hands and together with them, should the enemy dare rush out from their positions to fight.

For no hope could smile upon them of defeating so great a multitude or taking the city, because it was exceedingly fortified and the enemy’s incalculable number increased daily. But as eagerly as our army wished to fight and die with the enemy [Col. 0241B], so the enemy shrank from purchasing victory over our men at the price of their own deaths, seeing our men already suffering want in hostile territory while they themselves abounded in every good thing in their own place.

15. Thus our army sat before the imperial city, as has been said, but with no hope at all of taking it. For it abounded not only in an innumerable multitude of citizens but also in every kind of resource, and it was fortified with such care that it could be defended by the hands of a few against countless enemies.

It is a triangular city, according to those who have seen it, having on each side, where it meets the land, a great mile or more, enclosed threefold by a vast earthwork and a very strong wall. Around its circuit it has lofty and sturdy towers [Col. 0241C], so close to one another that a boy of seven can throw an apple from one tower to the next. As for the construction of the buildings in the body of the city—its churches, towers, and houses of great men—hardly anyone can either describe it or believe another’s description unless he has known it by the witness of his own eyes.

On that side where the Hellespontine Sea washes the city—that sea which separates Asia from Europe and is in certain places so narrow that one may look across from one side to the other—on that side, I say, because an earthwork could not be constructed owing to the frequent use of its most safe and famous harbor, there are walls of remarkable thickness and high towers, set so densely together and raised to such a height [Col. 0241D] that anyone recoils from directing his gaze to their summit.

Yet it did not possess from its first origin the great strength and beauty it now has. Long ago it was like each of the other cities and was called *Byzantion* by its Greek name. Thus even today the gold coins formerly minted there are called *Byzantii*, from the name of the city itself. Later, however, because of a certain royal vision, of which we shall say something, it was raised to the splendor and magnificence it now possesses.

Although the vision may seem brief and humble, its subsequent effect showed it to have been the portent of some great matter. For just as very much lesser things are sometimes signified in a vision by greater ones—as, in Joseph’s dream, his father, mother, and eleven brothers were signified by the sun, moon, and eleven stars—so at times great and famous things are found signified by the lowest things, as in Daniel’s vision, where we read that exceedingly powerful kingdoms were foreshown by certain beasts [Col. 0242A]. Therefore those are mistaken who think that among the things which people imagine they see while asleep there is no distinction, that all are vain and contain no mystery whatsoever.

16. The vision which, we are told and read, provided the occasion for the beauty and glory of this great city was of the following kind. After that celebrated donation by which Constantine [Col. 0242B], emperor of Greeks and Romans, having recovered health and been freed from leprosy through a heavenly miracle, royally honored Christ, author of that salvation; the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, who had been its messengers; Sylvester the pope, who had been its minister; indeed, the whole Church of Christ—after this, Constantine left the dignity of the royal seat which he had held at Rome to blessed Peter, proceeded to Greece, and chose above all other places this city, then called Byzantium, as his dwelling. [Note: [Col. 0241] The same account is found in Aldhelm, *On the Praise of Virginity*, book I. (BASN.)]

While one night he rested upon a royal bed, he seemed to see a very old and dead little bird [perhaps *aniculam*, “an old woman,” rather than *aviculam*, “a little bird”]. Blessed Pope Sylvester, who also seemed present, said that Constantine would certainly restore it to life. When the emperor had prayed and restored it to life as a most beautiful young woman [Col. 0242C], and she pleased his eyes with chaste love, he clothed her in a royal mantle and placed his diadem upon her head. Then his mother Helena seemed to say to him: “My son, you shall have this woman as your wife, and she shall remain in this beauty until the end of the age.”

When he had related this vision to many people and one interpreted it one way and another another way, the king resolved not to cease fasting until Christ, through his servant Sylvester, disclosed to him the interpretation of his vision. When, therefore, he had fasted for seven days, blessed Sylvester appeared to him in a vision on the seventh night and said: “That bird [perhaps *anus*, ‘old woman’] which you saw is this city. Now as if dead through neglect and old age, it is to be renewed through you into such beauty that it will be called queen among all the cities of Greece.”

The king, more delighted than frightened by this vision, summoned craftsmen in wood and stone from the whole region and ordered the city to be enlarged in area, strengthened with walls and towers, and adorned with churches and other buildings, until, renewed into the beauty it now has, it should be made like Rome, as they say [Col. 0242D]. Hence the city itself was sometimes called the second Rome, and the land adjoining it is still called Romania. But so that no traces of antiquity might remain, he rejected its former name, which might remind people of its earliest lowliness, and ordered it to be called Constantinople—from his own name and the Greek *polis*, which means “city” [Col. 0243A].

Our men, as stated, besieged it on the landward side, more from resentment at their own circumstances, since for the reasons already given they did not dare do otherwise, than from any hope of winning victory; for the city seemed impregnable. Since they achieved little or nothing on that side, they resolved to test, at great danger to themselves, on the other side—the side enclosed by the sea—not so much fortune as the power of divine strength, without which they knew this could in no way be accomplished.

Accordingly, boarding their ships with something like an impulse of indignation to terrify their enemies, they crossed the sea, narrow at that point [Col. 0243B], and all bravely took position on the shore opposite the city. There, changing their plan, they began more diligently to deliberate on accomplishing their enterprise through death or victory.

17. Moreover, from among those ships, whose number was beyond counting, some lighter and swifter vessels frequently darted forth suddenly to harass them and test their strength. Our men met them with javelins and arrows, and especially with the terror of their crossbows, and easily drove them off. They therefore consulted that Venetian leader whom we mentioned shortly before—a man blind in face, but most clear-sighted in mind—and adopted the plan that upon each ship, beside its mast, they should erect on either side other very long and strong timbers [Col. 0243C], binding them firmly to the hull both to the mast itself and to one another by so massive a joining that they might provide protection like wooden towers or, as it were, battlements. On these timbers, set some distance apart, they also fixed something like the rungs of ladders, by which bold young men, four or six at a time, could swiftly climb and descend in order to defend the ships and attack the enemy from above. This was done; and those towers—or ladders, if one prefers to call them so—were raised to such a height that they surpassed by a great measure all the towers and structures of the Greeks. They fortified both them and the whole ships with such skill on every side that they feared neither missiles nor stones, nor fire, whether ordinary fire or [Col. 0243D] that called Greek fire.

The ships having thus been fitted out and brought up to the city, they resolved first to test God’s favor in attacking the harbor and ships, so that, secure on that side, they might attack those upon the wall and in the towers all the more safely because more easily. That harbor was enclosed by a very secure recess and by iron chains of immense size, stretched from one side of its entrance to the other and holding all ships confined, as though under a single lock. After these chains had been broken by our men with much labor, the Greeks fled, especially in terror of the crossbows, which they could not endure, leaving their ships captive to their conquerors. The latter eagerly seized them and converted them to their own use, as highly welcome spoils of war.

Then, when the tower-bearing ships had been brought as near as possible to the wall, and the bravest men were climbing the ladders, a herald proclaimed that whoever first leapt upon the enemy walls would receive one hundred marks as a reward. One could see all eagerly striving for what was reserved for one alone, not so much from love of the money promised as for God’s honor, the advantage of the common cause, and the swift completion of the undertaking. When they gained the tops of the ladders, others following so hastily as though they would thrust them into the midst of the enemy and then hasten after them, then indeed one could see them pour down from above a hateful rain of lances, javelins, and arrows upon the enemies below. The latter, confused and terrified, having nothing with which to resist, were sorely pressed. Yet the dread and force of the crossbows, because that people is naturally cowardly, especially rendered them helpless. [Col. 0244B]

But after one man was found who first leapt upon the walls, and others followed him with the greatest speed, the citizens, bloodless and trembling, seeing the enemy already let in among them, ran along the wall wherever they could and hurled themselves into flight, as though, after losing the walls, they could remain safe in their city when they had been unable to defend them by its protection. Our men nonetheless ran along the wall and spiritedly occupied their towers. Already they had seized fifteen or more of them; then the enemy, as though recovering their breath, driven alike by shame and danger, began to regain some courage. Encouraging one another, they pressed our men most fiercely with shouts and every kind of weapon. Seeing this, a certain German count ordered the city set on fire in one part, so that the Greeks, suffering the double hardship of war and conflagration, might more easily be conquered. This was done; and, utterly defeated by this stratagem, they turned to flight. Those of our men who had already been admitted within the walls either cut down or broke through the gates—which the Greeks had carefully barricaded with a great mass of timbers and stones—after removing every obstacle, and opened the longed-for entrance to those still aboard the ships. This occurred about Palm Sunday, God, unless we are mistaken, so ordering it that on the day upon which Christ entered the holy city for the triumph of His Passion, Christ’s army should triumphantly burst into this faithless city. [Col. 0244D]

18. Once the gates stood open, those aboard the ships rushed in with joyful cries. They assailed the terrified enemies with lances, swords, crossbows, arrows, and every sort of weapon, seeming to threaten death, but having no wish whatsoever to shed blood. Like scattered sheep, they drove them through every street of the city. So vast was the multitude fleeing that even the spacious breadth of the streets could scarcely suffice for their flight; for our men pressed them with such terror and force that they allowed them neither to catch breath nor look behind them. Although they had as great an opportunity for slaughter as they could never have hoped for, very few were killed by them, [Col. 0245A] since they themselves spared the enemy voluntarily. Indeed, religious men living with them in the camp—Martin, namely, and others—had repeatedly admonished them to keep their hands from bloodshed as far as possible.

Nevertheless, about two thousand citizens fell that day, not at the hands of our men, but by certain Frenchmen, Italians, Venetians, Germans, and men of other nations who had formerly been accustomed to live with them in that very city. During the siege they had been expelled because the citizens suspected them of treachery, and they had attached themselves to our side. Remembering this injury, they cruelly exacted a most severe vengeance upon the Greeks. Of our own men, however, no one at all is reported to have fallen there except a certain exceedingly noble and renowned knight who, while pressing the enemy more vigorously, was himself unwary and, together with the horse he rode, was suddenly swallowed in a pit, bringing great grief to all his companions amid their rejoicing. [Col. 0245B]

When all the enemies had therefore been conquered, put to flight, and driven most miserably from the whole city, and when its doors had also been carefully shut, only then were the victors allowed to run to the plunder. They had previously been forbidden under penalty of death for anyone to presume to think of booty before complete victory. Everywhere and in abundance they found such quantities of gold and silver money, such splendor of jewels and garments, such an overflow of precious merchandise, such abundance of provisions, houses so excellent and filled with every good, that all at once newcomers and poor men alike became the wealthiest citizens. Meanwhile the aforesaid fire had laid waste almost a third of the city. Since everyone, citizens and foreigners alike, was occupied with the more pressing danger, no one was able to extinguish the flames as they spread unchecked.

Women, little children, and feeble old people, unable to flee and left in the city, on meeting our men intertwined finger with finger in the form of a cross and, most piteously, sang: “Holy king marquis” (*hagios basileus marchio*, ἅγιος βασιλεῦς μάρχιο)! This in Latin means “holy king marquis.” They did so because they believed that the marquis—whom the Greeks knew best and therefore considered the greatest among our men—was without doubt king of the captured city; but God had ordained otherwise. [Col. 0245D]

19. While the victors eagerly despoiled the conquered city, which they had made their own by right of war, Abbot Martin began also to consider his own share of booty. Lest, when everyone else had grown rich, he himself should remain empty-handed, he resolved likewise to stretch out his consecrated hands to plunder. Yet, because he thought it unworthy to handle worldly spoils with those hands, he set about gathering for himself some portion of the relics of the saints, of which he knew there was a great abundance there.

Taking with him one of his two chaplains, as though foreseeing something great, he made for a certain church held in high veneration because the mother of the famous Emperor Manuel had a noble tomb there. What seemed important to the Greeks in this matter was accounted as nothing by our men. [Col. 0246A] A great quantity of money from all the surrounding region had been deposited and kept there, as well as precious relics, which a vain hope of security had caused to be gathered in that place from neighboring churches and monasteries. Before the city’s capture, this too had been disclosed to our men by those whom the Greeks had expelled.

Many pilgrims burst into the church together; and while others eagerly occupied themselves in plundering other things—gold, silver, and every precious object—Martin, judging that sacrilege was unworthy unless committed in a sacred matter, sought a more secluded place, where the sanctity of the place itself seemed to promise that what he especially desired might be found. There he found an old man of handsome appearance, with a long gray beard: clearly a priest, though very unlike our priests in his very bodily dress. The abbot therefore considered him a layman and, though calm in spirit, rebuked him fiercely in a terrifying voice: “Come,” he said, “faithless old man, show me the more important relics you keep, or know that you will immediately be punished by death.” [Col. 0246B]

The old man, frightened more by the shouting than by the words—for although he heard the cry, he could not understand the words, knowing that the other had no command of Greek—began to appease him in the Roman language, which he knew in part, and to soften with flatteries an anger which did not exist. The abbot, in reply, could scarcely struggle out a few words of the same language, in order to make clear to the old man what he demanded of him. Then the old man, considering his face and dress, and judging it more tolerable that a religious man should handle the sacred relics with fear and reverence than that secular men perhaps should defile them with bloody hands, opened for him an iron-bound chest. He showed him the desired treasure, which Abbot Martin considered more welcome and desirable to himself than all the treasures of Greece. Seeing it, the abbot eagerly and swiftly plunged in both hands. Girded up as he was for action, he filled the folds of his garment with sacrilege; both he and the chaplain shrewdly concealed whatever seemed most valuable to them and immediately departed. What these relics were, and how great the veneration due to those which this holy plunderer [Col. 0246D] appropriated for himself, shall be explained more suitably later.

As he hurried, so laden, to the ships, those who knew and loved him, hurrying from the ships themselves toward the plunder, cheerfully asked whether he had seized anything and what things he carried so heavily. With the cheerful expression he always wore and with pleasant words, he said, “Things have gone well with us.” When they answered, “Thanks be to God,” he hastened on, impatient of every cause of delay, and returned to his ship. There, in his decent and clean cabin, he placed the votive spoils of his campaign until the tumultuous uproar in the city had subsided. There he also remained for three days in service of great devotion. No one knew of the matter except one of the two chaplains and the old man who had handed over the sacred objects. The old man, seeing that Martin was benevolent and generous, had already attached himself to him quite familiarly. Through his assistance Martin meanwhile prepared for himself in a church of that city a respectable and convenient lodging suited to his profession. [Col. 0247A]

When the aforesaid tumult had subsided, the abbot, taking with him the chaplain mentioned above and keeping his secret to himself, went to the lodging prepared for him. He remained there throughout the summer, ceaselessly embracing those sacred relics and venerating them with a hidden but great devotion, making up by the service of his inward devotion for what was lacking outwardly.
