He stayed there more freely because he had received word that the truce of peace, which the pagans had violated, had been renewed; also because navigation across that sea was not sufficiently safe amid so great and novel a change in affairs; and because he was held by love for his companions, while at the same time awaiting the settled condition of the city and kingdom, so that he might report to those who had sent him the state of these affairs.

Thus, as we have said, that imperial city, the most famous among all Greek cities, was captured, plundered, and occupied by its victors in a very brief space of time. Let others judge how this event ought to be assessed. I confess that, in all that historians or even poets relate, I have read nothing like it or so magnificent. Nor do I think it could have happened without the certain miracle of divine favor: that this most strongly fortified city, to which all Greece was subject, should so suddenly, so publicly, and so easily be delivered into the hands of so few. Here, indeed, I understand that a few brave men accomplished in a single moment more than the ancient poets falsely claim that countless thousands of men achieved at Troy in ten years. [Col. 0247C]

20. The city having been captured and plundered, and its buildings themselves distributed among new citizens, the question of appointing a king began to be discussed, lest they remain without a leader, as though headless. There were two highly distinguished and famous men in our army: Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, and Baldwin, Count of Flanders [Note: [Col. 0247D] This was Baldwin IX, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, who died in 1204, the same year in which he was elected emperor. BASN.]. The circumstances themselves seemed to require, and the whole army demanded, that one or the other should be chosen king. Since both relied upon the support and votes of many, and since one could not easily be preferred to the other because both were considered sufficiently suitable men, all decided to transfer the responsibility and decision for the election to twelve men, who were regarded above all others as men of integrity and sounder judgment. After much deliberation, they named the Count of Flanders. He was placed upon the royal throne, [Col. 0248A] and a diadem was set upon his head.

The provinces of that kingdom were divided into three parts: one belonging in particular to the king’s treasury; another to be held by the Venetians; and the third given to the marquis, namely Thessalonica and its very extensive territories. The marquis also proposed, as we have learned with complete certainty, to take our Martin with him and make him a bishop. Conscious of his vows, Martin declined with thanksgiving, preferring, if God permitted, to return to his brethren as a private and humble man. Then the lesser possessions—castles, villages, towns, and similar places—were distributed among the persons thought more suitable for this purpose. The laws, rights, and other institutions which from ancient times had been considered praiseworthy in both city and province were permitted to remain as they had been; those considered blameworthy were either improved by correction or completely changed. [Col. 0248B]

While these things were being done in the city, meanwhile that pestilent Mortiflo [Note: [Col. 0247D] He was of the noble family of the Ducas. He was called not Mortiflus but Mutzuflus, a man full of crimes. See Du Cange’s notes on the illustrious Hardouin. (ID.)], the perpetrator of a most grievous crime and emperor for a very short time, had fled the city before its capture. Conscious of his evil deeds and fearing punishment, he did not know where to turn or what hope he could place in any man or place. He went to the elder Alexius [Note: [Col. 0248D] This man had ruled Constantinople for seven years and three months, after blinding the brother whose empire he had usurped. But when Constantinople was captured, stripped of all power, he lived most miserably. He fell into the hands of the Marquis of Montferrat, then into those of Lascaris, his son-in-law, by whom he was thrown into prison and ended the rest of his life there. (ID.)]. In the division of the kingdom our princes had granted Alexius, although a wicked man, a small portion of land to hold because he was of royal blood. [Col. 0248C]

Seeing the criminal man come to him, Alexius, though himself not greatly different, was scarcely restrained by his own men from punishing him with the utmost penalty of death. He ordered him blinded and expelled, remembering him as the author of such calamity: he had persuaded Alexius to blind his brother, imprison his nephew, deprive both of the kingdom, and finally, to increase his crime, to suffocate that same nephew with his own hand. The man was disgracefully expelled. Long before blinded in mind, he was now deprived also of bodily sight: poor, miserable, hated by all, and living a wretched fugitive life in those regions. When our men heard of him, they sent people to seize him and bring him before their eyes. Once this was done, all our men and the Greeks remaining in the city [Col. 0248D] began to assail the wretch with insults, abuse, and reproaches, crying out that he was a parricide, a destroyer of his country, and deserving of punishment.

Though all agreed that he should die, there was much debate about the manner of his death. Some thought he should be strangled by a noose, as he himself had killed his lord; others that he should be cast alive into flames, or plunged into the sea with a stone tied to him, or buried in the earth, or stripped nearly of his whole body so that his entrails were exposed, or mutilated in all his limbs, or subjected to whatever other more atrocious punishment someone might devise for a criminal man. What do you suppose the unhappy man then felt when he heard them debating so minutely about his death, except that the pain of his lost sight lessened the fear of approaching death? At last the princes decided that, because although he was a wicked man he was yet of high birth, he should be taken to the top of a very high pyramid and, tied to a long plank, hurled headlong from it. Thus, he who had fallen by sudden overthrow from the lofty position of kingship might likewise, falling from on high, meet a death most miserable indeed, yet not most disgraceful. When this had been done, his whole body shattered, he breathed out his unhappy spirit in pain and misery. [Col. 0249B]

21. Something noteworthy may be said about that pyramid from which he was thrown, which many also call a column. It was constructed of enormous stones, most closely fastened together with iron, beginning with great thickness and gradually tapering into an immense height. At its summit, as they relate, it contained a solitary little retreat belonging to one who, refusing himself earthly habitation and not yet attaining heavenly dwelling, had made for himself a desert midway between the two, in the midst of a most celebrated city. They say that diverse images of things had long ago been carved upon it, representing in various figures the prophecies of the Sibyl and especially those concerning the higher kingdoms or kings [Note: [Col. 0249D] Perhaps read: “concerning the higher kingdoms or kings.”]. Among them were images of ships and what looked like ladders raised from ships, by which armed men climbing upward seemed to attack and capture the city likewise carved there. [Col. 0249C]

Until this time the Greeks had despised this carving, believing nothing less possible than that such a thing could ever happen to their great city. But when they saw ladders raised upon our ships, then at last recalling that carving, they began seriously to fear what they had long scorned. Accordingly, many of them struck those images with stones and iron hammers and disfigured them, believing that by this means they would turn the ill-omened portent against our men. Their hope was altogether vain; the certain outcome of the matter proved that the aforesaid carving was a true sign.

After all these events had occurred and a good part of the intervening time had passed, Martin saw that our army was occupied with immense efforts concerning the affairs of the kingdom, so that for a long time it could not carry out the journey of pilgrimage it had undertaken. The principal cause of the cross was thereby impeded by various contingencies. He therefore turned the whole purpose of his mind toward returning to his brethren and restoring himself to monastic discipline, which amid such a tumult of affairs he could not observe as he wished. Although he could easily sail directly from the place where he then was to Venice, he preferred first to return with what [Col. 0250A] God had bestowed upon him to those who had sent him, so that he might be a faithful messenger to them concerning the state of that kingdom and all that he had heard and seen in person. Then, bidding farewell to all, he would happily begin the course of his own return journey from the Holy Land, which he had sought in fulfillment of a vow.

22. Thus he boarded ship about the Nativity of Saint Mary, both unwilling and willing, confident and fearful, not without much fear and anxiety; and on the first day of October he arrived at Acre. There he was received with the greatest joy by his companions, especially by the Germans, who loved him particularly. He faithfully recounted the state of the kingdom and everything of which he had been an eyewitness or had heard unquestionably from others. Yet he wished to reveal his secret to no one except a most honorable and brave man named Bernher. A German by nation, an Alsatian by homeland, noble by birth, and, most importantly, distinguished in virtue, Bernher had acquired a great name in that land, so that the king’s counsels for the most part rested upon him. [Col. 0250B] He had always been intimate with our abbot, having known and loved him in his own country, and there he cherished him with a still greater affection, above nearly all others.

When the abbot showed him the gifts of God which he had brought with him, Bernher was at once seized by joyful awe and began to marvel greatly at the grace that God had bestowed upon His servant. When he heard of the abbot’s intention to return home, he earnestly tried to dissuade him, saying that it could scarcely ever happen that treasures so great and precious could reach the German land unplundered amid so many dangers by land and sea, so many pirates and robbers, and so many accidents that commonly arise. He advised him rather to honor the Holy Land devoutly and humbly with those same objects. There he might remain with them, and he should not refuse to accept from the king and other princes a bishopric or whatever other ecclesiastical dignities he wished. If he wanted to lead a more secluded life suited to monastic profession, Bernher himself would make complete provision for this at the king’s court, where he was most influential. [Col. 0250C]

For in those regions there is a territory called Mount Carmel, both in present usage and in ancient writings: a place most fertile in every good thing, rich in grain, splendidly clothed with vineyards, olives, and other kinds of trees elegantly planted, and abounding in plentiful pastures. On this mountain are three monasteries of monks, distinct from one another and holding broad estates. He might use one of these monasteries, or all three joined into one, and himself preside as abbot and lord. But if he preferred to preside over brethren of his own order rather than others, those monks could conveniently be transferred elsewhere; and the abbot, taking men of his own order in whatever number he wished, would hold the whole territory of the aforesaid mountain in the freest perpetual dominion, both he and his successors. [Col. 0251A]

Finally, if he accepted none of these offers, he might receive from the king and princes such a quantity of gold and silver money as neither he nor his successors would dare to expect or hope for. He could carry it with him more conveniently, conceal it more secretly, and enrich his church with it at little expense. When the abbot refused all these things, saying that he wished for nothing except faithfully to present to his monastery the sacred objects which God had given, the aforesaid Wernerus, as a most faithful man, kept the secret. He and many others escorted Martin with due honor to the ship prepared in the harbor. Once Martin had boarded it, they exchanged farewells in mutual affection. On the Tuesday before Palm Sunday they returned to their own homes, while Martin, spreading his sails, set out upon the course of his desired voyage. [Col. 0251B]

I am pleased at this point to insert into our narrative certain matters which by themselves, even if all else were lacking, could sufficiently establish that the things which, through Abbot Martin, we have either already related or still have to relate received their order [or origin] from the fount of divine dispensation. On the third night before Martin himself began his return journey, a cleric very intimate with him, named Aegidius and born in Bohemia, saw a vision. The abbot could understand no word spoken by him except in Latin; Aegidius too proposed to return with the abbot in the same ship. He was not asleep but awake and, as he himself most emphatically affirmed, he saw two angels in the place where the sacred relics were kept. There both he and the abbot had customarily had their sleeping quarters: the abbot for the careful guarding of the sacred objects, while Aegidius was wholly unaware what was kept there. [Col. 0251C]

The angels seemed to perform around the chest in which God’s sacred gifts were enclosed an office of wondrous devotion and to praise with every reverence the God who had bestowed these things upon His servant. When this service of divine veneration was completed, they encouraged one another and earnestly prayed to God that He would protect by His defense the man to whom such great goods had been granted, together with all who were attached to him in intimate fellowship. When, the next morning, Aegidius recounted this utterly certain vision to the abbot, he suddenly burst into tears amid his words from profound compunction of heart: “I do not know who you are, whence you have come, or what you keep in that chest of yours; but this I know most truly: the hand of the Lord is with you. Therefore, in this crossing of the sea I shall not depart from the company of your holiness, most firmly believing that I cannot be endangered in the ship in which you are to travel.” [Col. 0251D]

Struck by the miracle of this holy vision, especially because of the faith of the man, whom he knew to be holy and truthful, the abbot related another vision which had occurred to him while he slept that same night. It seemed to him that from Acre, where he then was, as far as the village nearest his monastery, called Sigoltsheim, there was nothing but sea; but it was so safe and shallow that not even the smallest little boat need fear shipwreck upon it. Moreover, from the same place as far as the aforesaid village there seemed to have been made overhead, in a straight line, something like roofed shelters, so that neither wind nor rain nor any other inconvenience of sea or weather could in any way harm the abbot as he sailed. [Col. 0252A]

We may now interpret the abbot’s vision as follows: that from that place to his monastery, although amid many perils of land and sea, he would nevertheless have a safe journey in his return through divine protection; and that the people of the aforesaid village, men and women, would be the first of all to meet the sacred relics at the monastery of Pairis, as the subsequently manifest truth of the event itself confirmed.

23. It is not easy to recount all the mishaps and dangers by which both the abbot himself and those carried with him in the same ship were repeatedly terrified. Yet he feared all the more because he loved more greatly those things which he was afraid to lose. But amid such fear and danger the Lord showed him almost greater grace of protection than he himself could have hoped for. Pirate ships often met him; having despoiled others or desiring to despoil others, when they saw this ship they were suddenly softened into gentleness. Greeting it peacefully with every reverence, they did not so much allow it to depart unharmed as were compelled to allow it. For it was God’s power that could restrain them and bring this vessel to harbor upon a safe course. [Col. 0252B]

After many labors and not a few dangers, that ship of Martin—or rather, of God and of the relics of His saints—was brought to the harbor of Venice on the vigil of Pentecost. When the abbot arrived and discreetly inquired about conditions on land, he learned that no less danger and fear remained on land than had preceded at sea. They said that all Italy, through which he had to pass, was in the heat and tumult of wars. But he knew that the same God is powerful on land and at sea, and that He who had saved him at sea could save him on land also. Horses having been prepared for himself and for carrying his baggage, he confidently, though still not without fear and anxiety, began the journey toward the Alps. [Col. 0252C]

Bands of armed men, who had come for no purpose but plundering and robbery, frequently met him. Yet suddenly compelled by some terror, they timidly recoiled as unworthy from the incalculable booty offered them. Stepping out of the way, they allowed the pack-animal carrying the chests with the sacred relics to pass unharmed through their midst. Thus our Martin crossed all Italy and then the harshest Alps; beyond them he passed many places also dangerous and full of robbers. He entered with great joy the city of Basel, from which he had first begun his pilgrim journey. Seeking before all else the church of the Blessed Virgin, to whom he had devoutly commended himself when setting out abroad, he rendered her all the thanks he could, because she had honored him with the relics of her beloved Son before that same Son, and had brought him back joyful and unharmed from so many and such great dangers. [Col. 0253A] Therefore he adorned her altar, which is especially famous in that church, with a noble hanging. He also bestowed his gifts quite liberally upon the bishop of that city, Lord Luthold, and upon certain other persons and churches of the same place.

He remained there a few days, until his brethren, who had already learned of his return, reverently came to meet him as was fitting. With them, and with very many others from the city who most gladly accompanied him, he proceeded splendidly, though with great humility of devotion, to the monastery of Pairis. There the whole community of brethren humbly hastened to the gate to meet both him and the sacred relics he brought. On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, before the hour of Terce, amid the joy of all and their praises to God in heart and voice, he brought those triumphant trophies of sacred plunder into the church itself and placed them upon the high altar with all the reverence he could offer. [Col. 0253B]

24. Blessed, therefore, be God, who alone works great wonders (Psalm 71), who by His ineffable power and mercy has looked upon and made illustrious the Church of Pairis through certain gifts of His grace which He has deigned to send to us through the venerable man so often mentioned, Abbot Martin. By their presence the Church now rejoices; through their patronage every faithful soul is aided and advanced before God. In order that a more certain faith concerning them may be established for readers, we have thought it proper to set forth some of them under their own titles.

[Col. 0253C] First, and most general—indeed most worthy of all veneration—is a trace of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, shed for the redemption of the whole human race.

Second is wood of the Lord’s Cross, upon which the Son, sacrificed to the Father for us, the new Adam, paid the debt of the old Adam.

Third is no small portion of Saint John, the Forerunner of the Lord.

Fourth is the arm of Saint James the Apostle, whose memorial is held venerable throughout the whole Church.

There are also relics of other saints, whose names follow:

Christopher, martyr. [Col. 0253D] George, martyr. Theodore, martyr. Likewise, the foot of Saint Cosmas, martyr. Likewise, a portion of the head of Cyprian, martyr. Likewise, Pantaleon, martyr. Likewise, a tooth of Saint Lawrence. Likewise, Demetrius, martyr. Likewise, Stephen, the first martyr. Likewise, Vincent, Adjutor, Maurice, and his companions. Chrysanthus and Daria, martyrs. Likewise, Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs. Primus, martyr. Sergius and Bacchus, martyrs. Protus, martyr. John and Paul, martyrs.

[Col. 0254A] Likewise, from the place of the Lord’s Nativity; from the place of Calvary; from the Lord’s Sepulchre; from the Rolled-Away Stone; from the place of the Lord’s Ascension; from the stone on which John stood when he baptized the Lord; from the place where Christ raised Lazarus; from the stone upon which Christ was presented in the Temple; from the stone upon which Jacob slept; from the stone where Christ fasted; from the stone where Christ prayed; from the table upon which Christ supped; from the place where he was taken; from the place where the Lord’s mother passed away; from her sepulchre; from the sepulchre of St. Peter the Apostle; from the relics of the holy Apostles Andrew and Philip; from the place where the Lord gave the Law to Moses; from the holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Likewise, of St. Nicholas, bishop. Likewise, of Bishop Adelehi. Likewise, of Bishop Agricius. [Col. 0254B] Likewise, of John Chrysostom. Likewise, of John the Almsgiver; of the milk of the Lord’s mother. Likewise, of the virgins Margaret, Perpetua, Agatha, Agnes, Lucy, Cecilia, Adelgundis, and Euphemia.

This was done and enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1205, while Philip was reigning as Roman [emperor], Innocent was presiding over the most holy Roman Church as supreme pontiff, and Luthold, bishop of Basel, and Henry, bishop of Strasbourg, were in office.

**25.** Therefore no believer ought either to believe or even to suppose anything other than that this was accomplished through the regard of divine grace: that so many and such great, so celebrated relics, through a man preserving himself in such humility, should have reached our Church amid so many impediments. At their arrival [Col. 0254C] all Germany, as we believe, began to be accounted happier both in itself, more renowned among men, and more blessed before God. Let no one, therefore, judge that this, any more than many other things, happened by chance. For that would be nothing other than maliciously to detract from the great works of God their due splendour. For if we carefully consider the incredible and sudden capture of that greatest city from which all these things were transferred; the sequence of the preceding causes; and the dangerous journey of Abbot Martin by land and sea, yet unharmed in every place through God’s protection—it will appear clearer than light that all these things are not fortuitous accidents but gifts of God. Therefore let all who either see or hear these things [Col. 0254D] venerate and believe in every respect the work of God, by whose agency they were done, and await from him the reward of their faith and devotion.

**26.** From these very gifts of heavenly grace, which the Lord had now bestowed very often upon his servant Abbot Martin and, through him, upon the Church of Pairis, that same Church, for the honour of God and of the whole Roman Empire, presented to the most serene Lord Emperor Philip a most commendable portion: namely, a certain tablet of almost inestimable value, most elaborately adorned with gold and precious gems, and containing, carefully enclosed within it, many kinds of holy relics far more precious than gold and gems. The emperor of the Greeks had customarily worn this tablet, suspended from his neck by a golden chain, at solemn festivals as a certain pledge [Col. 0255A] of empire. Besides gold and many other gems, a jasper of extraordinary size is set in this tablet, with the Passion of the Lord engraved upon it and the figures of the Blessed Virgin and John the Evangelist standing on either side. There is also a sapphire of remarkable size, upon which the divine Majesty—though it cannot properly be represented by any image at all—has nevertheless been artistically engraved in such a manner as this could be done. [Col. 0256A] This gift the most unconquered King Philip, young indeed in age but mature in the fear of God and in every moral virtue, received with such goodwill of heart and thanksgiving that he took the Church of Pairis itself, with all its possessions, under his protection; and by an imperial privilege confirmed to it in perpetual possession all the other relics which Martin had brought.

[Col. 0255] This history was written by a certain Master Gunther, then a monk, but formerly a scholasticus, a man very liberally educated. He, too, warmly applauding the very events which he wrote, had this intention and faith: that from him who had deigned to work these things through his faithful servants, he himself also, as narrator of divine works, might receive everlasting life.

# GUNTHER THE POET, *LIGURINUS*; OR, THE DEEDS OF THE EMPEROR FREDERICK AUGUSTUS, SURNAMED AENOBARBUS, IN TEN BOOKS.

After the repeated labours of Jacob Spiegel, Peter Pithou, Conrad Rittershausen, and Georg Christian Johann, newly edited according to the first Augsburg edition; with selected annotations of the most distinguished men, including Scioppius, Pelugius, Barth, Withof, and others, together with his own; enlarged by historical-literary commentaries, variant readings, and indexes, by Dr. Carl Georg Dumgé, Professor of History at Heidelberg. Prefixed is a historical-literary dissertation on the author, date, fortunes, and editions of the work; and added is a commentary on Frederick I, Emperor Augustus. (Heidelberg: published at the editor’s expense, from the press of Joseph Engelmann, printer, 1812, octavo.)

[Col. 0255]

## [DEDICATORY EPISTLE.]

TO THE ROYAL HIGHNESS OF THE MOST SERENE PRINCE CHARLES LOUIS, HEIR SUCCESSOR IN THE KINGDOM OF BAVARIA; WHOM THE PRESENT AGE ADMIRING, AND POSTERITY SHALL ADMIRE, AS A GRANDSON EQUAL TO THE GLORY OF HIS ROYAL ANCESTORS; A PRINCE UNCONQUERED IN WAR, A FRIEND OF PEACE, AUSPICIOUS TO HIS COUNTRY AND TO THE MUSES BY THE VERY OMEN OF HIS NAME. GIVEN, DEDICATED, AND DEVOTED.

The illustrious deeds of great kings are commended to other mortals by the splendour of the events themselves, but to princes especially by the illustrious examples of deeds. Hence in former times the praises of heroes were celebrated in the courts of nobles, and then, composed into books, were inscribed with august names. The best men were especially delighted by the praises of their own household, and in no matter was favour more certain or approval more abundant. Thus my courage is strengthened while I implore the protection of Your Royal Highness for the *Ligurinus*, that most noble work on the praises of the supreme emperor, intending to adorn this new edition to the best of my powers: so that, crowned with a most glorious name, the book may be carried through the hands of learned men, and authority equal to its subject may enhance the dignity of its theme. Nor, to excuse either ambition or rashness of aspiration, do I put forward anything other than the honourableness of studies in restoring [Col. 0257] an excellent writer, who, circulated in our printing, will be an entertainment to all good men and an ornament to the German name.

For we know your kindness and love of letters; with what zeal you adorn that singular sanctuary of German glory—your centumviral institution; and how there too you have dedicated an altar to the divine Emperor Frederick. For which of the ancient kings can a memory be more sacred to you, or worthier of dutiful favour? Whether you consider in him noble character, martial courage, or, finally, devotion to peace, everywhere you will find one like you and akin to you. Add that this most august hero devoted no small part of his cares to ordering Bavarian affairs, and was sufficiently memorable above all under the distinguished title of king. For it was first under the auspices of Emperor Frederick that the ancient duchy of Noricum, taken from Henry the Saxon, was granted as the reward of valour to your most illustrious house, transferred to Otto the Palatine, renowned in fame, prince of everlasting memory and father of such great princes. This man was indeed the German Achilles: Frederick the emperor’s agent in affairs and the strongest support of the kingdom. Milan feared his spirit unconquered by dangers; the summits of the Alps marvelled at him; Rome itself revered him.

It will not be unpleasant for you to survey the ways in which you compare yourself with so great a prince and your own great ancestor, and to rejoice, from consciousness of your own deeds, that ancestral virtue together with ancient royal dominion has been reborn in new splendour. And while you promise greater things when the time comes, already encircled with the laurels of victory you devote yourself to the arts of peace, cherishing in your breast the seeds of great undertakings. Thus it will come about that, while you now read the deeds of others, others will one day write what you have done—things which will hold the minds of readers in admiration for you, when they observe that true praise of virtue must be pursued all the more in our age because greater exertion is needed to attain it amid such luxury and, to speak freely, amid the zeal for flattery and falsehood and the multitude of the deranged. But let this be the noble subject of the historians of this age and the next. I have one sole endeavour in my prayers: that you receive this gift, however slight, with your customary spirit of humanity and clemency, and admit and preserve me happily beneath your patronage.

Most devoted client of Your Royal Highness,  
C. G. DUMGÉ.

[Col. 0257]

## PREFACE OF THE EDITOR.

Besides the nobility of the work and the excellence of its subject, other causes too, and not slight ones, induced me to undertake this new edition of the *Ligurinus*, nearly a hundred years after the last edition and after the repeated labours of such great men. For when I had set my mind to elucidating the antiquities of medieval Germany, I immediately understood that the studies of young men are scarcely attracted and retained by the importance of events alone: they are for the most part strangers to domestic matters, and to subjects serving only immediate need or certainly amusement. To assist them in some way, I therefore abandoned formulae of abridgment and looked about for a suitable writer of that age, rich in subject matter and agreeable in style, through whose interpretation the principal headings of ancient learning might be introduced, as though incidentally.

The plan itself led to the age of Emperor Frederick I, which enormous political changes and the unanimous testimony of experts point out as the boundary between the two Germanies. That illustrious hero was himself the greatest part of those changes, and, by the rare good fortune of the times, writers worthy of his deeds fell to his lot: the famous names of Bishop Otto of Freising, Radewig of no lesser renown, and then the noble interpreter of both, the poet of the *Ligurinus*. The former are weighty alike in matter and expression; the latter is full of spirit, charming in elegance of speech, and admirable for his age.

Accordingly, eight editions, received with continuous applause for almost three centuries, attest the favour which this one writer enjoyed among his native contemporaries. Yet all these editions, except the very rare one of Rittershausen, share this defect: printed in the larger folio format and mostly joined with other works in a large volume, they appeared inconvenient to carry and handle; now even individually they are less common, and some are absent from the greatest libraries. Moreover, the text, even in the best editions, often suffered a genuine wrong under the title of correction, when, tested by the rules of ancient Roman diction, it was deprived of the marks of its native colouring. Finally, a good part of the annotations are idle and disconnected, displaying their very power; very many things are explained wrongly, and not a few wholly neglected, so that they either confuse the reader or altogether escape him.

Reflecting upon these considerations, I hoped that I should earn the gratitude of young students—and perhaps even of learned persons—if I published this eminent writer in a compact type suited to our times. The principal point of the undertaking seemed to be that, avoiding the inconveniences of previous editions, I should bring together in this new one all their advantages, enlarged as far as I could. I followed the text of Rittershausen in general, since it is the most correct, but carefully employed the authority of the first Augsburg edition, departing from it only under evident necessity and never even then without indication. The conjectures of learned men, so many as I had been able to obtain, I always placed below the text, adding merely marks of judgment—marks not of arrogance but of brevity; I shall give the reasons elsewhere.

I have treated the literary history of the work in a separate dissertation, as no editor before me has done. Finally, I have lightly sketched the first decade of Frederick Augustus, to serve as a kind of introduction to the books of the *Ligurinus*. A following volume of notes will present selected annotations, omitting those that are merely extraneous—such as theological, ethical, technical-political, and other trifles of that sort. In their place I shall supply many things previously neglected, drawn from the more important aids furnished by the historical writings of the age, either wholly new or requiring fuller exposition. Finally, I shall prefix two more dissertations: one shorter, discussing the examples from ancient poets especially familiar to the author; the other longer, discussing the whole constitution of the German commonwealth as it is known in the time of Frederick I.

It remains for me publicly to repay here—though surely not adequately, yet most sincerely and gladly—my thanks to those to whose most generous kindness I remember that I owe the chief and most readily available aids for my labours, gathered in a very short time. For to such and so great services I chiefly attribute the preparation of this edition and my resolve to publish it at my own risk, repaying, as far as such exertion can, the favour granted me.

And first must be named the most illustrious L. B. von Ittner, distinguished no less by the splendour of his lineage than by the highest renown for refined learning: Privy Councillor to the Most Serene Margrave of Baden, plenipotentiary minister at the Swiss Diet, and chief director of the Upper Lake district. His excellent memorial, dedicated in the grave majesty of ancient style to the memory of the divine Charles Frederick, Margrave of Baden, will endure and be celebrated together with the remembrance of that immortal prince.

Next, we received admirable assistance from a man renowned for solid and varied learning and for distinguished services to literature, Jeremias David Reuss, head of the Royal Library at Göttingen, who promptly sent in answer to our requests many and most desirable helps, elegantly copied in his own hand. In Paris, our wishes were fulfilled—indeed, surpassed by the diligence—of a man of profound learning and most cultivated helpfulness, dear and deserving of esteem on many grounds: Charles Hase of Weimar, keeper of the Imperial-Royal Library, recently well known to the learned world through his excellent edition of the still almost unknown writer John Lydus.

At Munich, Bernard Joseph Docen, the highly praised keeper of the Royal Bavarian Library, received my inquiries with the greatest kindness and instructed me with most ready favour: that distinguished restorer of monuments of ancient Germany. Ferdinand Gloeckle of Ingelheim, a writer of the Vatican Library and tireless investigator and defender of German antiquities in that place, most readily answered the requests sent to Rome, and is shortly to be celebrated by many—and notable—titles arising from his industry. Nor should the most friendly zeal of the most noble and learned Sulpiz Boisserée of Cologne be passed over in silence: a most richly furnished and generous possessor of treasures of ancient German art, soon to be extolled among the cultivators of art by a laborious and splendid specimen of his work. Also to be mentioned is Johann Karl Höck, long renowned in his writings for manifold learning, councillor to the government of the most illustrious Count of Limburg-Solms, who delights in devoting the rarer leisure of his office to the advancement of letters. Finally, most grateful toward us was the kindness of the very humane heads of the Albertina Library at Freiburg and the Court Library at Karlsruhe, through which convenient access to nearly all editions of the *Ligurinus* was granted. To these supports for my labours, therefore, and to the more important aids of the times, we owe for the most part whatever progress we may seem to have made in this work. For we seek no little glory other than that of good will, and we are far from the vain persuasion that we have added any weight to the studies of men of the greatest renown.

Finally, we freely avow this chief wish: that the restored image of our once flourishing commonwealth may yet someday find minds not wholly estranged from it. For men live by great examples; and the noblest peoples of every age have stood firm by the precepts and imitation of their ancient fathers, while, scorning ancestral customs, they have declined in weakness. Hence, in accordance with the praiseworthy institution of our forefathers, we find the illustrious monuments of native antiquity diligently presented in schools, and the *Ligurinus* likewise, scarcely yet known through print, read in the most celebrated academies of the fatherland. Perhaps such incentives would be especially fitting in our own times, since very much is accomplished in tender age, and love of country, grown old as it were, can be poured in anew with milk and revived. Certainly our forefathers did not contemplate the examples of Greek and Roman antiquity with idle curiosity or admiration, but, mindful of their own nobility and elevated by comparison with the glory of their race, acting vigorously themselves, they reproduced those examples all the more successfully in deeds and writings.

Heidelberg, on the vigil of the Nativity, 1812.

[Col. 0259]

## PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION OF THE *LIGURINUS*.

Marquard von Stein, provost of the Church of Bamberg; Matthew Marschalk; Bernard and Conrad Adelmann of Adelmannsfelden, canons; Conrad Peutinger and Georg Herwart of Augsburg: greetings to the reader.

In these days Conrad Celtis came to Augsburg, a man then exceptionally learned in the liberal arts and also a most diligent investigator of ancient writers. When, in accordance with our friendship toward him, we had spoken with him, we asked whether, while travelling through Germany, he had discovered any books previously unknown to us, and requested that, according to his kindness toward all, he would make them available to us. He replied that he had found in a certain monastery of Eastern Francia—which our people call Franconia—a certain excellent poet, the *Ligurinus*, concerning the deeds performed by the first Emperor Frederick. When he had given it to us to read and examine at leisure, we judged it certainly worthy to fly abroad upon the lips of men. We therefore urged Conrad to have it printed, and not to allow it to remain concealed any longer.

But since, after some negotiations, he did not come to sufficient agreement with the printer and had resolved to depart from here, we feared that, since only a single copy existed, it might suffer loss or danger under some adverse star. Therefore by our own efforts and at our own expense we finally brought it about that the printer undertook the burden: partly lest the vigils and nocturnal labours of the *Ligurinus* should perish, and partly lest the labours and excellent deeds of our illustrious Emperor Frederick I should be consigned to oblivion. A particular love of country was added to these motives. Since our origin, indeed that of us all, was from Swabia, it seemed most fitting that Frederick, who himself also drew his origin from the Swabian people, should emerge from his dark prison chiefly through the help of Swabians and, after several centuries, come again into the light.

Our Germany certainly owes much to our illustrious Frederick because of the innumerable labours he bore to preserve the honour and majesty of the Roman Empire; but the entire Christian commonwealth owes him far more. For its sake he undertook that notable and most holy expedition to restore the fortunes of Christians in Asia; and in it, after he had happily defeated the Armenians, he also lost his life—befitting a pious emperor devoted to the Christian religion—to the greatest loss of the Christian people. For in that crisis Frederick’s courage and military skill alone could have been safely opposed to the victory and good fortune of King Saladin, and could have raised up the declining Christian commonwealth in Asia. Whoever you are, therefore, who read these things, do not despise this *Ligurinus*, the excellent herald of the virtues of Emperor Frederick, because it comes from Germany; rather, embrace and peruse it in a ready spirit. You will indeed find very many things which you will not merely not regret having read, but which will also be of very great benefit to you.

At the end of Book Ten is subscribed:

> The books of Gunther, most renowned poet of the *Ligurinus*, concerning the deeds of the divine Frederick the First, happily published and printed by the industrious and ingenious Master Erhard Oeglin, citizen of Augsburg, in the year fifteen hundred and seven, in the month of April.

At the end of the edition:

> The *Ligurinus*, happily completed and now known throughout all Germany and its public academies, and offered to German youth for reading and exposition: first at Vienna by Conrad Celtis; at Freiburg by Hieronymus Baldung; at Tübingen by Heinrich Bebel; at Ingolstadt by Jacob Philomusus; at Leipzig by Hermann Bostius [Note: [Col. 0261] Undoubtedly Hermann Buschius, whom Burckhard shows to have taught at Leipzig at that time in his *Life of Hermann Buschius*, p. 164.], who in the aforesaid academies successfully profess Roman letters at public expense.

[Col. 0261]

# FIRST DISSERTATION ON THE *LIGURINUS*. On the Author, Date, Fortunes, and Editions of the Work.

## § I.—On the Author of the *Ligurinus* and His Name.

[Col. 0261A]

There is great debate and controversy among scholars concerning the author of the *Ligurinus*, as commonly happens in doubtful matters. That the first editors transmitted the name with insufficient caution may be understood from this alone: they are not even consistent with themselves. At the beginning of the work they call him “Ligurinus,” and it is not sufficiently clear whether they mean to indicate his homeland or his personal name. Pithou considers the latter more likely. Whatever one accepts, the author himself bears witness that they are mistaken in either case [Note: [Col. 0261A] Preface to the edition.], expressly declaring in plain words that he gave the book the title *Ligurinus*, Book X, verses 615 ff.:

> …May our *Ligurinus* honour  
> the learned men whose affection it will have to defend  
> and foster.

I am therefore all the more surprised that not only those first editors but also later learned men of great name—Melanchthon [Col. 0262A] [Note: [Col. 0261A] *Chronicle*, Book IV.], Giraldi [Note: [Col. 0261A] *History of Poets*, Dialogue 5, p. 307 (Lyon edition, 1696, folio).], Pagi [Note: [Col. 0261A] *Critical Notes on Baronius*, at the year 1160 (Venice edition, 1740, folio, vol. XII, p. 1427). Gerard Vossius unjustly criticizes Baronius himself in *On Latin History*, p. 136 (Amsterdam edition, 1699, folio), as does Schurzfleisch, *On Henry the Lion*, § 1 (*Works*, XLIV, p. 574).], and Joseph Anton Saxius [Note: [Col. 0262A] Notes to Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy* (*Works of Sigonius*, ed. Muratori, vol. II, p. 717 ff., note 16).]—did not notice this manifest error.

Then again, those same first editors added the name Gunther in the subscription to Book Ten; we shall shortly show that this name was newly discovered and sought out while the book was at press. And so Lilius Giraldi, catching this new name “Gunther” from vague report, invented a second writer of the deeds of Frederick I and added him to his *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0262A] In the cited place, Dialogue 5, p. 307.]. All later writers, save Senckenberg alone, settled on the name Gunther, so confidently that their entire controversy appears to concern only two medieval writers bearing that name.

There survive poems of that age inscribed with the name of a certain Gunther, on the Passion of St. Cyriacus [Col. 0263A] and on the customary deeds of Christians. Pithou heard that they had been printed at Basel about the year 1526, but, though he searched long, could not obtain them [Note: [Col. 0263C] Preface cited.]. I remember learning, from I know not what authority, that these same works were printed in the sixteenth century in the monastery of Maulbronn. This Gunther, first mentioned by Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 0263C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 166 (ed. Miraeus, p. 157).] and then by Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0263C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 148 (Cologne edition, 1546, quarto).], was a monk of the monastery of St. Amand at Elnone [Note: [Col. 0263C] Saint-Amand, Belgium, formerly in the diocese of Tournai.], of the Benedictine Order and the Cluniac Congregation. Some writers, especially Belgians [Note: [Col. 0263D] Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 336 (Louvain edition, 1643); Antonius Sanderus, *On the Ecclesiastical Writers of Flanders*, p. 73 (Antwerp edition, 1624); Franciscus Swertius, *Athenæ Belgicæ*, p. 319 (Antwerp edition, 1628).], put forward this man as author of the *Ligurinus*. Others rightly rebuked them, since Sigebert of Gembloux, having died already in 1112, could with the greatest difficulty have known Gunther, forty years before the age of Frederick I, as the herald of his deeds [Note: [Col. 0263D] I am surprised that the most celebrated Pithou himself supports such an opinion in the cited preface.].

[Col. 0263B] Better known was another Gunther, different from that one in date and writings: a monk of the Cistercian Order at the abbey of Pairis [Note: [Col. 0263D] Pairis, or St. Paires, in Upper Alsace near Basel; Schoepflin, *Alsace Illustrated*, vol. I, pp. 73, 451.] in the diocese of Basel [Note: [Col. 0263D] Miraeus, *Supplement to On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 386.]. This is the Gunther who, by the common verdict of scholars, is celebrated as the author of the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0263D] Among many, a few: Gerard Vossius, *On Latin Poets*, p. 254 (Amsterdam edition, 1696, folio); Fabricius, cited place; Christ. Saxius, *Literary Onomasticon*, at the year 1190; Hamberger, *Reliable Notices of Distinguished Writers*, vol. IV, p. 334 ff.]. He wrote a history of Constantinople’s subjugation by the Latins, from the account of his Abbot Martin, who had himself been present at the events [Note: [Col. 0263D] Miraeus, cited place; Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 490 (Geneva edition, 1696, folio); Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 1651 ff.; Fabricius, *Latin Library of the Middle and Later Ages*, vol. III, p. 520 ff.]. Peter Canisius published the book in print [Note: [Col. 0263D] *Antiquarian Readings*, vol. V, p. 358 ff.].

Pithou [Note: [Col. 0264C] Preface cited.] and Cave [Note: [Col. 0264C] Cited place.] were left suspended by doubt, though we do not see either of them setting out the grounds for doubt. In any event, all these learned opinions lack suitable arguments: no medieval writer recognizes the author of the *Ligurinus* as Gunther; indeed, neither the name nor the work itself of the *Ligurinus* is mentioned by contemporaries. [Col. 0263C] Add that Heinrich Bebel, contemporary and companion of the first editors of the *Ligurinus* and its most fervent admirer, calls its author “Christian,” for some reason unknown to me [Note: [Col. 0264C] Letter to Johann Nauclerus: “Which authors ought to be read?” Pforzheim, 1504, folio, signature g. z. b.]. Finally, Johann Nauclerus, a writer of no small distinction in that age, intimate with many persons and a friend of Celtis, who completed his *Chronicle* in 1500, makes mention of the *Ligurinus*, which he had seen [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Universal Chronicle*, XXXIX, p. 759], but knows no author Gunther.

From this silence of the ancients, combined with the carelessness of moderns, Henry Christian Senckenberg, the sole and fiercest adversary of the *Ligurinus*, [Col. 0264A] derived an argument [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Conjectures concerning Gunther, Supposititious Writer of the Ligurinus*, *Göttingen Miscellanies*, vol. I, Book III, p. 149 ff., § 2.] commendable more for appearance than weight. Yet, if such a principle for suspecting origins were admitted, it would be entirely over with very many monuments of the Middle Ages. The *Chronicle of Ursperg*, ascribed by the stable judgment of several centuries to Conrad of Lichtenau, has only in our own age been shown by that outstanding investigator of such matters, Placidus Braun, to be the work of Burkhard of Biberach [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Account of the Manuscripts of St. Ulrich*, vol. II, pp. 93 ff., 232.].

The author of the *Ligurinus* himself furnished the first occasion for discovering the name. For he often mentions a poem written by himself, the *Solymarius* [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Ligurinus*, Book I, vv. 14 and 86; Book X, vv. 648 and 729.], or poem on the expedition to the Holy Land. To those pursuing the clue too hastily and superficially, that Gunther who wrote of the expedition to Constantinople presented himself, and easily led astray [Col. 0264B] men concerned only with the name. Once Gunther had been found, another [mistaken identification] soon joined him by right of association; then the zeal for names removed the next question, favour suppressed it, and credulity neglected it.

Some, to be sure, did not wholly fail to judge that the subject of the *Solymarius* differed from that of the writer published by Canisius [Note: [Col. 0264D] Conrad Rittershausen, notes on the *Ligurinus*, p. 17; Gerard Vossius, cited place.], referring it, on the evidence of the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0264D] Book I, v. 86.], to Jerusalem captured under the leadership of King Conrad:

> We offered written little books concerning the holy seat.

But by far the greater number declared for Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0264D] Miraeus, Cave, Oudin, Andreas, Swertius, Sanderus, etc.], among whom Albert Fabricius alone [Note: [Col. 0264D] Cited place.] came nearer the truth, understanding, at least by an excusable error, the Bouillon expedition [that of Godfrey of Bouillon]. This is the genealogy of the assigned name, whose beginnings compel us to touch upon the first edition, [Col. 0264C] then not yet completed but only begun; for its title leaves the author unnamed, whereas the subsequent epilogue identifies him.

It is pleasant to record a new error arising from Gunther’s name. While I was investigating manuscript codices of the *Ligurinus* and all other literary aids, indexes of Roman censorship came into my hands, listing Gunther under the new forename Peter [Note: [Col. 0264D] *Index of Prohibited Books*, issued at Rome by order of Alexander VII, 1667, folio, p. 64; Innocent XI, Rome, 1704. I was not able to consult more, but learned from elsewhere that Gunther also occurs in others (Clement, *Critical Library*, vol. IX, p. 327).]. After I had paused briefly in astonishment at the matter, an explanation immediately occurred, when elsewhere I saw noted the *Rhetoric* of this same Peter Gunther. By fortunate chance, [Col. 0265A] not long before, the same book had occurred to me in the very extensive catalogue of the Heilsbronn Library [Note: [Col. 0265D] Section 5 of printed books, no. 194, p. 263.], and there I found a note by the most learned Höcker, which I could readily pursue further.

That Peter Gunther had once been an honour and ornament of our Academy. Born at Neustadt an der Haardt and educated at Heidelberg, he taught with distinction in the faculty of philosophy and served as dean in 1508. Then, having embraced jurisprudence, he achieved by the assiduous labour of a few years that, already in 1512, adorned with the highest honours in both laws, he was appointed to replace Nicholas Morsinger, whose health had failed, in expounding the books of the Decretals. He was appointed despite the slanders of a few who reproached him with the defects of his little body—as seats of learning always nourish their own monsters. Subsequently advanced to the professorship of the Code [of Justinian] [Col. 0265B] in 1516 and proclaimed rector of the Academy in 1517, he died by an untimely death in the following year, before old age [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Annals of the Academy*, vol. 4, fols. 175, 247; Schwab, *List of Rectors of Heidelberg Academy*, vol. I, p. 90 ff.].

He was indeed a man of outstanding natural talent, most skilled in the liberal arts, and a laureate poet—whom one might not inappropriately suppose to be the author of the *Ligurinus*, if the many and very weighty considerations of time and place did not wholly dissuade us. For, to say nothing of the marks of antiquity attached both to the manuscript codex and to the work itself, even the time of the first report does not suit our Gunther, who was then still a young man and in no way equal to so great a task. Add that the present author of so notable a work could by no means have remained unknown here, if one knows the customs of learned circles and realizes that such secrets are more safely kept nowhere. The *Rhetoric* he wrote won Peter his reputation: distinguished by the commendation of the leading Musagetes [Note: [Col. 0265D] The manuscript was preserved in the Elector’s Library; Schwab, cited place.], it passed through many hands and, once printed, promptly underwent repeated editions [Note: [Col. 0265D] Mainz, 1521; Basel, 1521.]. The fame of this new book in distant regions, particularly German ones, led the censors of the Roman Curia to prohibit it, whatever it might be. Later, hearing that the author of the *Ligurinus* was Gunther and the herald of Frederick, they convinced themselves that he was the same man—or vice versa.

Given these preliminary points, everyone sees what must finally be decided about the appellation “Gunther.” Nevertheless, I think it should be retained, as accepted by usage and entirely harmless, since no other is available. Moreover, the multitude of writers referring to Gunther advises this; nor do we use the ancient names of others by any greater right. It would certainly be troublesome, not to say something more serious, to wish to disturb the order of things which have acquired the appearance of truth through long-standing use.

## § II. The Author’s Person and Homeland.

It may seem superfluous to inquire into his way of life and homeland when not even his name is certain. Yet it should be observed that the two discussions do not rest on the same [Col. 0266A] principles, and that one or the other is not infrequently discovered from authors’ writings. First, nothing prevents us from suspecting that our author was an ecclesiastic; some points support it. Besides the fact that before the revival of letters almost all writers are known to have belonged to that order, very many passages taken from Holy Scripture are also found in the books of the *Ligurinus*. Rittershausen collected a catalogue [Note: [Col. 0265D] At the end of his edition, pp. 234 ff.], to which we add a few items.

When the author represents the monks of besieged Tortona vainly imploring Frederick’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0266D] Book III, v. 129 ff.], he uses this parable:

> In like manner, at the final end, the judgment of the angry  
> Judge shall hand over to eternal fire those accursed,  
> and with wrath laid bare shall punish those assigned to torments,  
> who, so often warned, so often scorned the one warning them.  
> Thus the wretched citizens returned, groaning, to the closed walls,  
> [Col. 0266B] and lamenting as though to a certain Gehenna.

Setting forth the beginnings of the disastrous conflict between the Roman emperor and the pope, he cautiously and no less modestly adds on his own account [Note: [Col. 0266D] Book VI, v. 518 ff.]:

> Whether the emperor’s or the pope’s party was the more just,  
> let him who could better know judge; but we,  
> ignorant of the facts, should venerate either side.

These and similar passages unmistakably suggest an ecclesiastic, though I would not readily believe him to have been a monk. Nor do those futile inventions about the Gunthers prevent me from subscribing to Pithou’s opinion: “Our author, if we love truth, displays something more polished, urbane, and courtly than monasticism; and near the end of the poem he indicates that he himself at some time adopted this manner of life.” Certainly, anyone who has even cursorily read the books of the *Ligurinus* will perceive the gravity of the author’s utterance.

A far more difficult question arises concerning his native country, and there is no less disagreement of opinion. Yet you may conveniently dismiss many opinions untouched, since they rest upon the traces of the Gunthers. We certainly have nothing here to do with vain appearances, which anyone who wishes may pursue. Since we lack any other certain evidence, the grounds of argument must be drawn from the books of the *Ligurinus* themselves. We have mentioned above that some call him a Ligurian [Note: [Col. 0266D] Cf. § 1, p. 1 sq. c. n.]; nor is that conjecture wholly empty, provided that one does not wish to establish it from the name *Ligurinus*. For Pithou’s doubt [Note: [Col. 0266D] Preface cited]—that a Ligurian would ever have written about his native land in this way—is exceedingly slight. As though an angry spirit of a citizen against fellow citizens were unheard of; indeed, examples of far greater bitterness are not lacking, the greater the injury.

Moreover, one may defend the author’s being Italian with some plausibility, especially if one takes into account the most elegant description of Italy presented in Book II [Note: [Col. 0266D] Vv. 56 ff.]. The poet enlarged it—though for the most part taken from Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0266D] *De rebus gestis Friderici I*, II.13.]—by various and very appropriate details here and there. Likewise, in other passages of the *Ligurinus* he attached epithets to Italian regions and cities such as might persuade one that the man had personally been there.

I had hoped to detect our author in certain obscure, minute, and therefore more difficult points. For the manuscripts of Otto and Radevicus, whose books he rendered into heroic verse, suffered, like very many others, from the customary negligence of copyists. The eminent Antonio Muratori, after comparing the editions with an excellent Viennese manuscript, encountered examples of a corrupted text not infrequently. Among them he noted certain bishops’ names, wrongly written or added, and also the corrupt name of a certain military engine. This occurs in the books of Otto [Note: [Col. 0267D] II.17] and Radevicus [Note: [Col. 0267D] II.47], written *marga* in the former and *manga* in the latter; both forms are erroneous, and the word should be *mangana*, as the distinguished editor teaches, being an Italian and above every exception. But our author omitted not only those bishops’ titles, but also—what is more surprising—the name of that military engine, although elsewhere he freely admitted other technical terms of this sort. I beg you not to suppose this observation idle: what will be said below will show that it was deliberately inserted.

So far as I know, only Caspar Scioppius called the poet of the *Ligurinus* a Frenchman [Note: [Col. 0267D] “Iambics on Gunther, the first poet of France and therefore of Germany,” at the end of Rittershusius’s edition, p. 207.], and he received the assent of none of the rest. I do not equally see on what ground that most learned man did so, unless perhaps he was led by the vain praises of the Gunthers. He may also have been deceived by the shadow of the very word “Gaul,” when the author, recounting the customs and habits of the Lombard people in almost the words of Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0267D] II, v. 153 f.; cf. Otto of Freising, cited passage], adds on his own account:

> “He permits any men from the lowly populace  
> (which Gaul judges shameful) to gird themselves with the knightly sword.”

Otto says nothing about Gaul. Yet it is well known that Germans prohibited commoners of the lowest condition from bearing arms, and nowhere in the world was it considered more disgraceful to summon the populace to arms. What, then, have the French to do with our author, when Germany stood foremost? Indeed, in Frederick’s time Gaul, abandoning its noble custom, had already resorted to the populace as English arms grew more pressing [Col. 0267D], so that the comparison would fail.

What if by the term “Gaul” the author meant Germany itself? You cry that this is a marvel: I shall explain it. Even among the best writers of the twelfth century, all Germany beyond the Rhine was called Gaul. Thus Otto of Freising expressly calls Mainz, the metropolis of Germany, a city of Gaul; and he contrasts Alemannia with the whole province from Mainz to Basel, assigned to Gaul [Note: [Col. 0267D] I.12; cf. ch. 13.]. For all that land beyond the Rhine, once acquired by the victorious arms of the Franks, had, from Clovis to Louis the German, obeyed the Frankish empire together with Germany itself. Thereafter Frankish power was confined to ancient Gaul, except for the three provinces on the Rhine and the rich portion of the old Burgundian kingdom. Consequently, Franks were called Gauls, and Gauls Franks, the peoples’ names being used in the same, mixed sense. The Germans, moreover, delighted everywhere to be exalted by the most noble designation of the Franks; hence the indiscriminate terminology of peoples and kingdoms among medieval writers [Note: [Col. 0267D] Otto of Freising, II.13: “Finally, when the prince [Frederick] returned beyond the Alps, as by his presence he restored peace to the Franks, so by his absence he withdrew it from the Italians.” The term “Franks,” restricted to Germans beyond the Rhine and contrasted with Alemanni or Swabians, occurs at the end of I.13.]. Following these writers here, our author appears to have preferred the word “Gaul,” as the metre required.

Elsewhere, too, he records Frederick’s reply to the ambitions of Roman avarice in these words [Note: [Col. 0268D] III, vv. 458 ff.]:

> “Surely they offer me exchanges far from fair, when they wish to sell us what is ours—as though I should arrive with full purses, as a purchaser, and be about to acquire new honours by payment, honours which Gallic valour has already made its own.”

All who followed the distinct reading of the first edition altered it, putting *Francona* in place of *Gallica*. I myself, carried away by the genuine sense of the word, by the authority of learned men, and by the correction of an old hand in the Freiburg copy, rejected *Gallica*; not indeed by the over-bold emendation *Francona*, but by the milder correction of that same hand, substituting *bellica* (“warlike”). Now, however, I restore *Gallica* with greater confidence.—What remains is this: once these points have been set forth in good faith, the one and only indication for the author’s Gallic homeland has vanished.

That he was German by nationality is the opinion of very many, among whom Caspar Barth stands out as a man of most weighty judgment. Once you have considered the force of their reasons, you will readily concede that they prevail over all the rest. First, Barth noted that the diction abounds in Germanisms in many places; the following volume of notes will supply a catalogue. Next, anyone who gives even cursory attention to the books of the *Ligurinus* will acknowledge that a thoroughly and genuinely German spirit is displayed by frequent and splendid indications.

Moreover, the same most sagacious Barth seized upon a memorable passage of the *Ligurinus*, as though it were the author’s own pointing finger in this matter. When mention has been made of an attempted crime against the life of the Greek emperor, committed by the impious daring of a certain courtier, the author omits Radevicus of Freising’s explanation of the man’s office. Radevicus says [Note: [Col. 0268D] II.27]: “One of the palace servants, namely the *caniclinus*, whom we may call a chancellor, plotted treachery against his prince.” But our author says [Note: [Col. 0269D] VII, vv. 389 f.]:

> “By the usage of the Greek name  
> he was a *caniclinus*; among us he may equally be a *camerarius* [chamberlain].”

Barth rightly observes on this passage [Note: [Col. 0269D] Reuber, *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, ed. Joannis, p. 660]: “It appears quite clearly from this that Gunther was German: for no other nation retained the term *camerarius* for chamberlains.” Yet I think it should not be left unsaid that the author of the *Ligurinus* rendered the meaning of *caniclinus* less aptly than Radevicus, since the most illustrious Du Cange clearly shows that the office of *caniclinus* corresponded more to a chancellor than to a chamberlain [Note: [Col. 0269D] *Glossarium*, s.v. *Caniclinus*.].

Now a few words about the arguments urged against this conclusion. First occurs the most elegant speech delivered for the election of Emperor Frederick at the solemn assembly at Frankfurt. Our author either does not know or conceals the identity of the prince who spoke [Note: [Col. 0269D] I, vv. 226 ff.]:

> “At last the fortune of the realm deigned to reveal through one man what it sought:  
> renowned in name—whether duke, count, or prelate is uncertain—  
> imposing in appearance, powerful in counsel, and skilled in persuasion,  
> he rises.”

The most learned Rittershusius is greatly surprised [Note: [Col. 0269D] Notes on the *Ligurinus*, pp. 22 f.] that the author avoided what was almost universally known: that the first vote in an election belongs to the Archbishop of Mainz. Senckenberg [Note: [Col. 0269D] Cited work, § 8, p. 161] attacks the speech as fictitious, while also reproaching its proposed formulas, on the ground that Frederick attained the empire by the delegation of Emperor Conrad rather than by the support of the princes.

Rittershusius’s observation is indeed of very great importance: if proved, it ought to make the author’s being German more than suspect. But our author is so far from such negligence that he himself states this right of Mainz in the words of Radevicus [Note: [Col. 0269D] VI, vv. 610 ff.; cf. Radevicus of Freising, I.16.]:

> “The election belongs to the magnates, in which, by ancient custom,  
> the bishop of Mainz has the foremost voice.”

That the speech is fictitious may readily be conceded, since no trace of it occurs in Otto of Freising. Indeed, I fear that the very accusation adds to our author’s praise: the speech is excellent, wholly admirable both for the weight of its thoughts and for the elegance of its language. Nor are reasons entirely lacking why the author may have been ignorant of the speaker’s identity. At that very time of the election, Mainz was engaged in a most bitter and serious conflict with its clergy, which was settled only by the prelate’s renunciation [Note: [Col. 0270D] Serrarius, *Rerum Moguntiacarum*, book V (ed. Joannis, vol. I, pp. 556 f.); cf. Otto of Freising, *De Friderico I*, II.9.], so that one might reasonably doubt whether he then enjoyed the prince’s favour. Perhaps too the prudent author considered it a matter of conscience to assign a speech of his own composition to a particular prince, and thus to the primate of the German Church.

Besides, I do not equally understand what Senckenberg means by that delegation of Conrad. For Otto of Freising bears most explicit witness [Note: [Col. 0270D] II.1.] that Frederick was raised by a solemn election and by the votes of the greatest magnates and of all. Conrad’s delegation, moreover, which our author also notices [Note: [Col. 0270D] I, vv. 316 ff.], will be discussed in its proper place. But suppose whatever you please: why should the poet not have followed the unbroken course of events, when Frederick’s voluntary election increased his glory, and when the author himself, disregarding the rules of anxious narration, openly avows that he is merely Frederick’s herald [Note: [Col. 0270D] I, vv. 124 ff.]?

Finally, some persons [Note: [Col. 0270D] Spiegelius, Pithou (prefaces cited), and especially Senckenberg himself, cited work, § 2, p. 153; § 6, p. 157.] seem to have found no small difficulty in believing the author German because of the polish and supreme elegance of the work, infinitely surpassing all efforts of his age and countrymen. By Hercules, our author fares well when excellence makes him suspect, and neither his homeland nor his age has produced his equal. But foreigners, nor even a more recent age, furnish no equal either. Let that most noble exile have as his contemporaries and compatriots whomever he pleases; I would venture no decision. For who can ever attain by the arts of criticism an understanding of what love, joined with gifts of talent, may accomplish in every age and in whatever place?

## § III. Certain indications that the author was either contemporary with Frederick I or at least of a comparable period

Although not even the most perfected criticism can determine what talents any age or land may produce, it is nevertheless both possible and proper to investigate traces of each. We have spoken of his native country; it remains to note, in hurried fashion, certain indications of the period from the books of the *Ligurinus* themselves. Leaving aside the arguments of those who follow their Gunthers, we judge that no weight should be assigned even to the authority of the greatest men when proofs are required.

I often wondered that writers most learned and friendly to sound criticism had been so certain about the date of the *Ligurinus* that, out of many, few had raised even the slightest question. Think of the Conrings, Vosses, Schöpflins, Saxii, Lindenbrogii, Du Canges, Spelmans, Schilters, Scherzes, Haltauses, Wachters, Bunavii, and many other preservers of German law and antiquities, all of whom we read citing the *Ligurinus* as an unquestioned authority. For in the world of letters, no less than elsewhere, it commonly happens that one man leads another.

There is a twofold method of inquiry in ancient writings: it either concerns the so-called external marks, such as the appearance of manuscripts and the signs of handwriting, or it investigates the subject-matter and modes of treatment of books—one pertaining to facts, the other to diction. Now the complete lack of manuscripts throws the whole hinge of our investigation upon the work itself alone; and since, in a later good Latin writer, the character of the diction teaches little, except perhaps whom he has studied, we set aside that less useful inquiry and are constrained, by the narrow limits of these pages, to adhere to more important indications drawn from facts. Above all, we select those matters which seem to have slipped from the author as though unconsciously and in play; for in trifles one most clearly recognizes a mind insufficiently consistent with itself and a poorly concealed pretence. Next, following only what is the author’s own, we omit very many passages in which he merely reproduces his guides, Otto and Radevicus, in their own words.

At the very beginning of the work, in his dedication, he addresses Otto, the third son of Emperor Frederick, saying among other things:

> “Illustrious boy, it is uncertain whether you should be called  
> king or count; for you powerfully rule your mother’s ancient kingdom  
> of the Allobroges, and, worthy of the kingdom’s splendour,  
> derive your name from lofty Otto.”

The most learned Barth, wishing to emend this passage, substituted *duxne* (“or duke”) for *comesne* (“or count”). Observing, of course, the rank of duke midway between count and king, he suspected that our author had passed it over as though by a leap. But the excessively anxious critic supplied a notable example both of his own negligence and of another’s diligence. For Otto, Frederick’s son, was truly Count of Burgundy, not Duke. At no time then was there a Duke of Burgundy, but rather a Rector and a Count of Burgundy.

The rectorship of Burgundy belonged to the dukes of Zähringen, founders of the most august house of Baden. This occurred after that Renaud III, the most powerful Count of Burgundy, who had rebelled against Emperor Lothair, had been outlawed and deprived of his dominions; and his uncle Conrad, Duke of Zähringen, had been appointed in his place, and made rector of all Burgundy and imperial vicar. There followed continual and most savage wars, destined to cease only with the death of the most valiant Prince Renaud. At length Emperor Frederick married Beatrice, the niece of this same Renaud through his brother; and he placed under his son Otto the dotal lands of Beatrice and many other Burgundian lands, unjustly and dishonourably taken from the rector of Burgundy at that time, Berthold IV, Duke of Zähringen, and acquired for Frederick’s own family—while preserving the empire’s supreme lordship [Note: [Col. 0271D] Mascovius, *Dissertation on the Connection of the Burgundian Kingdom with the German Empire*, section 2, § 1, p. 21.]. The Zähringens, however, retained the title of rector, however empty it was.

Thus Otto was Count Palatine of Burgundy, not duke [Note: [Col. 0271D] Barth might have understood this from another passage of the *Ligurinus* itself: V, vv. 284 ff.]; and the passage in the *Ligurinus* is sound, though assailed by foolish criticism. In a small matter, this is all the greater evidence of exact fidelity.

The author calls this same Otto a *puer* (“boy”), and likewise Henry, Frederick’s eldest son [Note: [Col. 0271D] I.59], king of the Romans and husband of Constance of Sicily. Senckenberg vehemently attacks him for this [Note: [Col. 0271D] Cited work, § 7, p. 159], reproaching him with ignorance of the terminology of his age, on the ground that married men and partners with their fathers in royal power do not come under the designation *pueri*. But Senckenberg himself is guilty of the charge he invents, while our author is entirely secure. To say nothing of the fact that words in poets are to be scrutinized less anxiously, being more often excused by metrical requirements, it is plainly false that married young men were not called *pueri*; and Senckenberg is refuted by Du Cange’s own authority [Note: [Col. 0272D] *Glossarium*, s.v. *Puer*.]. For he expressly attests, with examples, that kings’ sons were simply called *pueri*, without any regard to whether they were married, as being *pueri κατ’ ἐξοχήν*—“boys in the pre-eminent sense”—just as we commonly call ours “princes.” This customary formula could easily be proved by many examples, if one were not abusing testimonies in a matter so familiar.

The author describes more fully [Note: [Col. 0272D] I, vv. 375 f.] the regions through which the emperor travelled after his election at Frankfurt, when proceeding thence to Aachen for the rites of coronation. In this description, which the poet furnished almost entirely from his own store, one finds many features especially characteristic of the geography of that age, above all a most careful chorographical description of the territory of Mainz as it still then appeared. Moreover, in even the smallest things one detects the author’s same fidelity, candidly presenting the appearance of matters everywhere; and anyone not wholly ignorant of medieval geography will readily agree that this would have been most difficult for a later writer.

Senckenberg too perceived things which could not be denied and, greatly troubled by them, turns them back against the author by a sufficiently ignoble device. “These passages breathe a learning,” he says, “which recognizes that age” [Note: [Col. 0272D] Cited work, § 6, pp. 157 f.]. At the same time he displays no equally remarkable specimen of learning himself, boldly declaring that the designation “land of Ripuarian [Franks]” was unused at that time. He ought to have recalled this even from Radevicus of Freising alone [Note: [Col. 0272D] I.14.], whom our author follows.

The native simplicity of the age, not yet capable of knowing the causes of fortunate occurrences, is also shown by the author’s candid judgment of the Aachen baths [Note: [Col. 0272D] I, vv. 431 ff.]:

> “Whether hidden nature added those vapours to those places,  
> or the labour of men, let those inquire who inhabit the places they know;  
> through the trustworthy report of their elders, they may have learned the causes and secrets of things.”

Likewise elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0272D] III, vv. 630 ff.]:

> “At nearly midnight, when Titan, shedding his light  
> upon the opposite world—if it is lawful to believe it—  
> equally marks out the middle arc of night.”

Recounting the piety of Emperor Frederick—who, leading an army against the Milanese for the first time, paid compensation from money collected throughout the army for certain robberies committed by his men in sacred buildings under pressure of want, before moving farther—the author, departing from the precise account of the Freisinger, assigns the business of distributing the money, by their own right, to a bishop and a count [Note: [Col. 0273D] II, vv. 24 ff.]:

> “At once he gathers money collected from all the army,  
> and entrusts the funds to faithful men—  
> this one a bishop, that one a count, each approved—  
> ordering that the despoiled be compensated throughout  
> by a just apportionment.”

Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0273D] II.11] assigns this task by name to two bishops, those of Trent and Brixen; and there is no necessity at all for departing from him unless one wishes to suppose that our author was better informed.

Recounting with Otto the arrival of the Lombard people in Italy, he writes, preserving the old spelling:

> “Long ago a barbarian foe, whom Scanzia had sent in war, invaded this land.”

All editions from the Augsburg edition onward printed *Scandia* for *Scanzia*, with no loss indeed of sense but with a real loss of textual integrity. For *Scanzia* must be read, as in many other medieval writers [Note: [Col. 0273D] *Gesta Normannorum in Francia*, in Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol.
