VI, p. 204; *Historia Normannorum*, I.2; II.1; ibid., vol. XI, pp. 623, 626.]; and thus our author’s care in small matters again appears.

Describing Emperor Frederick’s martial pomp after the ceremonies of his Roman inauguration [Note: [Col. 0273D] IV, vv. 54 ff.], and representing him seated upon a horse adorned as splendidly as possible, he says, almost playfully, of that horse:

> “A shining carbuncle hangs from the middle of its brow;  
> its bright breast is adorned with many-sounding bells.”

Who does not know that these *bullae*, or little bells, were very common ornaments of nobles especially in Frederick’s age [Note: [Col. 0273D] J. G. von Eckhart, *Explanation of an Old Jewel Casket*, etc., § 9, p. 14.]? Later they became obsolete; and at last, when the fifteenth century was nearly mature, they were left as badges of madness to fools and buffoons [Note: [Col. 0274D] J. C. H. Dreyer, *On the Usefulness of the Excellent Poem Reinke de Voss*, § 2, note 2, pp. 24 ff.].

The author furnished a striking proof of being a contemporary when accusing the deed of the Veronese, who surrounded Emperor Frederick with an ambush as he was returning from Italy. The instigator of the fatal crime was Alberic, a knight, a Veronese noble, together with a summoned band of young men. Of them our author says [Note: [Col. 0274D] IV, vv. 449 ff.]:

> “Alberic, greedy for crimes and greedy for plunder,  
> terrible, keen, fierce, born of the knightly order,  
> was your citizen, Verona; and youth, sworn to shameful  
> service and summoned by new monstrosities,  
> was to perish with its master.”

These verses are, if anything is, evidence of the genuine temper of the age, when it was most shameful for men of knightly rank to earn the pay of cities. For who does not see that the poet measures an example by no means unusual in Italian lands with a German mind? At that time German nobles, even of the lowest rank, most vehemently disdained alliances of that kind with cities. Matters changed greatly a little later, when the wealth of cities increased while that of nobles declined, and dire necessity not infrequently compelled knights to enter either the jurisdiction or the pay of cities. Yet even then that ancient pride was not allowed without penalty: the customs of knightly tournaments barred from those games every knight enrolled either in the pay or under the jurisdiction of any city, until he had abandoned both.

The author is entirely consistent with himself in the various addresses which, in Emperor Frederick’s name, he either composed or embellished [Note: [Col. 0274D] Examples: I, vv. 175 ff.; VI, vv. 314 ff.; vv. 610 ff.; VII, vv. 325 ff.]. In them one principle is carefully emphasized: that the election of the king of the Romans belongs to the princes, and indeed to all of them. Although this is directed not obscurely against the pretensions and designs of the Roman pontiff, it also states an important point of German constitutional law neglected by many: namely, that the election of the king of the Romans was not confined to the seven electors [Note: [Col. 0274D] Nicolaus Cisnerus’s cited dissertation is wholly occupied in proving this. Cf. Pütter, *Reichshistorie*, I, 264.]. This stable consistency of his assertions seems not a little to establish that he was a contemporary and exceptionally well informed.

Recounting the death of Count Ekbert before the walls of Milan [Note: [Col. 0274D] VII, vv. 483 f.], he incidentally mentions the very ancient German custom of celebrating the downfall and funerals of heroes in songs:

> “And, weaving sorrowful strains over his death,  
> Fame lamented him in tearful song through Teutonic cities.”

Aventinus too affirms [Note: [Col. 0274D] In the *List of Bavarian Affairs*.] that the premature fate of this Ekbert, a most valiant prince, was grievously received by all Germany.

Soon afterward, describing from Radevicus the siege of Milan by the emperor’s army and the arrangement of its forces [Note: [Col. 0274D] Ibid., vv. 496 ff.], the author clearly renders the ancient German battle array, still preserved at that time, through the substitution of one word:

> “And dividing all the forces into seven companies,  
> he prudently assigned to each wedge  
> its own commander.”

Radevicus says nothing about wedges, since, affected by a foreign term, he speaks of legions and obscures the actual disposition by an ambiguous word.

Following the same Radevicus, the author recounts the military regulations promulgated by the emperor with the agreement of the magnates in the fields of Milan, omitting the last four. One runs as follows [Note: [Col. 0275D] Radevicus, I.26.]: “A soldier who has robbed a merchant shall restore double what he took, and shall swear that he did not know him to be a merchant. If he is a servant, he shall be shorn and branded on the cheek; or his master shall make restitution for the robbery.” Our author gives it thus [Note: [Col. 0275D] VII, vv. 273 ff.]:

> “The merchant robbed by our soldier shall receive all things doubled;  
> the servant, with his cheek burned and head shorn,  
> shall lay his back beneath the lash,  
> or be redeemed by his master in the prescribed manner.”

Radevicus says nothing about lashes; but do not suppose the addition false. Shaving and branding were at that time always accompanied by flogging, which, though not expressed, is understood in the sentences of that age [Note: [Col. 0275D] Ch. Ulr. Gruppen, *Observations on German Matters and Antiquities*, Halle, 1763, pp. 128 f.].

And so much for indications of the date: the limits of these pages bid me lay down my pen, reserving more points, each to be discussed in its proper place and with greater weight, for the following volume of notes.

## § IV. At what date the work was written, as it itself indicates; and whether the author is to be judged to have taken part in the events

The manifest testimony of the books clearly shows that the *Ligurinus* was not composed before the thirty-fourth year of Emperor Frederick. At the very outset, addressing Frederick’s sons, it calls Henry king of the Romans and of Italy [Note: [Col. 0275D] I, vv. 56 ff.]; elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0275D] V, vv. 416 ff.] it mentions his marriage to Constance of Sicily; and finally it laments the death of Beatrice of Burgundy, Emperor Frederick’s wife, which most writers place in 1184 or 1185, whereas the inscription on her monument at Speyer [Note: [Col. 0275D] Lehmann, *Chronicle of Speyer*, VII.11, p. 648.] states that it occurred in 1190.

Henry, indeed, had been elected king of the Romans at Bamberg in 1169, through the agency of his father Frederick [Note: [Col. 0275D] Otto of St Blasien, *Chronicle*, ch. 21; *Chronicle of Reichersberg*, under 1169.], while still a boy of four; but he was not crowned king of Italy until 1184 [Note: [Col. 0275D] Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, with notes by A. Saxius, XIV (*Works*, vol. II, p. 823, Muratori edition)], and married Constance in the following year [Note: [Col. 0275D] Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, for that year, § 11; Pagi on Baronius for that year, §§ 14, 15, 17], or, in the view of others, in 1186 [Note: [Col. 0276D] Sigonius, cited passage, p. 827; cf. Saxius’s note (3). The apparently divergent testimonies may readily be reconciled if the betrothal is assigned to the earlier year and the marriage to the following one.].

Many other considerations agree excellently with this dating, which one may not inappropriately relax a little, so that the author proves wholly consistent with himself. Thus, concerning the marriage of King Henry [Note: [Col. 0276D] V, v. 416. The author pursues this Henry with particular favour, industriously seeking material for praise, so that one might not without reason suppose him to have been Henry’s client.]:

> “[Lacuna.] So that at last in our own time,  
> destined to impose an everlasting end upon the ancient quarrel,  
> there might come to you, King Henry, a noble bride  
> from the Sicilian house: peace and concord of the two kingdoms.”

Concerning Zurich in Switzerland, which still adhered too stubbornly to the doctrines of Arnold of Brescia after that man’s execution [Note: [Col. 0276D] III, vv. 310 ff.]:

> “Whence that people, long corrupted by poisoned flavour  
> and adhering too strongly to the teaching of a false prophet,  
> still preserves the taste of its ancestral grape.”

Arnold had taught at Zurich about the years 1140–1145, and the great interval of time, together with the force of the words, supports the conclusion.

Likewise, concerning the laws of fiefs, which the emperor had enacted at Roncaglia in 1158 with the common consent of the magnates of both realms [Note: [Col. 0276D] VIII, vv. 590 ff.]:

> “Then, concerning the common law of fiefs, which that age  
> had not yet set out in clear writings,  
> he gave these laws and ordered them to be made known in writing.”

Senckenberg, indeed, finds a twofold argument for spuriousness in this very passage [Note: [Col. 0276D] Cited work, § 10, pp. 162 f.]. First, in the expression “common law of fiefs,” which he maintains is a mode of speech much later than Frederick’s time; secondly, in the words “that age.” “For who,” he asks, “ever spoke of his own time as ‘that age’?” He plainly failed to see the interval of thirty years. As for the word “common,” the objection is utterly futile. What has a poet to do with the formulas of the courts? And what indication of spuriousness is there if he adopted one of its formulas after it had entered legal usage? Finally, by what other word ought that law to have been denoted, established by the votes of the magnates of both realms and binding both together in a common bond?

Accordingly, the author must be understood only figuratively when, near the end of the work [Note: [Col. 0276D] X, vv. 604 ff.], after Emperor Frederick’s second expedition against the Milanese, he writes:

> “And now let the few songs which we have ordained for the sacred court suffice,  
> and let the poet be permitted to take breath for a while,  
> while the standards of war are at rest  
> and the soldier, dismissed from war, enjoys welcome leisure.”

For the year of this expedition falls in the eighth year of Emperor Frederick and plainly conflicts with what has just been indicated to us. I will say what the fact is: Radevicus of Freising also concludes and ends at precisely that point; and our author, deprived of his guide, withdraws with dignity, disguising his lack by a fictitious interruption. Yet, lest one should find him lacking in candour and integrity, he adds, by a sufficiently ingenious device, the purpose of continuing; he quite clearly acknowledges when he wrote and proves wholly consistent with himself:

> “But when, recalled with anxious care, he returns to arms,  
> we too shall resume our interrupted undertaking with new labour—  
> the battle lines and camps marching to war;  
> and, provided only that life remains, we shall draw the subsequent events,  
> undertaken in one continuous thread, down to our own times,  
> mindful of our purpose.”

Finally, one may infer that Emperor Frederick survived the *Ligurinus* from the fact that the author addresses him as present [Note: [Col. 0277D] I, vv. 19 ff.; X, vv. 60 ff.] and that the work contains nothing later than his lifetime. Combining these and other indications, one can assign the *Ligurinus* only to the final years of the reign, that is, 1186–1190. The same must be said of the *Solymarius*, which, on the poet’s own testimony [Note: [Col. 0277D] X.650.], we learn was published scarcely five months before the *Ligurinus*. Thus one may all the more marvel at the man’s supreme eloquence and ease of style, which completed such great and excellent labours in so brief a space.

The question raised by some whether the author himself took part in the events may be denied partly from the evidence already given and partly from another singular declaration of his own, since near the end he says expressly [Note: [Col. 0277D] X, vv. 576 ff. Passages cited by some from IV, vv. 607 f. are merely taken from Otto of Freising, II.27. Senckenberg either did not notice this or shrewdly suppressed it while attempting to charge the author with negligence; cited work, § 8, p. 160.]:

> “I too followed the camp, not with arms but with song.”

Nor should Philip Melanchthon be heard at all, for he rashly imagines, along with nearly everything else, that the poet attended Emperor Frederick at the siege of Milan as Ennius attended the elder Scipio and Polybius the younger Scipio at Carthage.

## § V. The character of the work; the writer’s authority

He would certainly make no slight error who, misled either by the appearance of its form or by the praises of learned men, persuaded himself that the *Ligurinus* is properly an epic poem. The entire work is nothing else than a poetic paraphrase (*periphrasis*) of the books of Otto and Radevicus of Freising, *On the Deeds of Frederick I Augustus*. It begins with Frederick’s election, that is, with Book II of Otto of Freising, and ends with the penultimate chapter of Radevicus, that is, with Frederick’s second expedition against the Milanese; it embraces in ten books the events of eight years.

Although the author generally follows those guides closely, he does not proceed with excessive anxiety. Removing here and there what seemed not to serve his purpose, he compensates for it with various representations and images of events. The historians of Freising had inserted verbatim certain documents, especially on ecclesiastical matters; excellent in their own place, they do not suit heroic verse. These and some other minor matters our author omitted, intent only upon Frederick’s praises and, as it were, impatient of delay. He himself clearly explains these principles of composition [Note: [Col. 0278D] I, v. 125.]:

> “Those who wrote before, wishing to preserve faithfully  
> the ordered sequence of history, appear to have inserted into their pages  
> not a few things—if I may say so—  
> which neither greatly increase Caesar’s honours  
> nor cohere with the texture of the narrative, but cling like sewn-on patches.  
> But we, voluntarily leaving aside anything less beautiful or outstanding,  
> or anything which does not greatly concern  
> the emperor’s distinguished deeds and adds no ornament to truth,  
> shall follow only the more important matters.  
> From many things we shall strive to compose a moderate compendium  
> and to close the little book in a briefer form,  
> forging it to charm the ears of readers,  
> and, as if from a full garden after flowers have been plucked—”

To weave into a brief garland worthy of its prince. It follows that the author intended to offer neither different nor new material, but only to reduce the books of Otto and Radevicus, as it were, to a compendium; apart from elegance of form, he claimed no merit for himself. Indeed, he modestly adds [Note: [Col. 0278D] In the cited passage, v. 152 ff.]:

> So that, if anyone is perhaps little moved by my poorly cultivated speech,  
> Let at least the arrangement of the feet and the melodious verses  
> Hold him fast, and let this be something praiseworthy in us.

[Col. 0278B] These words ought, if anything ever could, to have restrained Senkenberg; yet he proceeded to such impertinence that, through an excessive zeal for censure, he even charged the author himself with bad faith, mingling falsehoods with truths [Note: [Col. 0278D] Ibid., § 5, p. 156.]. “Everywhere,” he says, “he walks with Otto of Freising and Radevicus. Where they are brief, our author is more concise than usual. Where they spread themselves more widely, nothing prevents him from wandering equally far. Where they begin, he begins too; where they end, our author has no further matter for writing. And yet this fictitious Gunther writes that, after the marriage of the later Henry VI with Constance, he offered this little book of his to Emperor Frederick and to the royal house. Certainly he would earn high favor from that great emperor, a connoisseur of refined learning, who had himself ordered his life to be committed to letters or had supplied his own memoirs for that purpose, if he had merely rendered Otto and Radevicus in verse—and indeed, as he himself admits and the facts show, with no few omissions—and had done so twenty years after their books had already been read and approved. At the time of Henry VI’s marriage to Constance, deeds of Frederick more illustrious than those our author describes certainly existed—above all the destruction of Milan, which, if one considers the city’s power, is surely memorable for all posterity. Hence no one would doubtless have gained favor by attempting to reheat things adequately described already, while omitting newer and more illustrious events. I recall, indeed, that the impostor himself says [Note: [Col. 0278D] Book X, v. 613.]:

> With the affairs undertaken carried on in an unbroken thread,  
> Mindful of our purpose, we shall draw them down to our own times.

[Col. 0278D] But this is precisely what was meant to conceal the imposture. It does so quite unsuccessfully, since “our own times” can scarcely be said by a writer of the same age who describes events while their actors are living and breathing, and does not profess to have been born only later.

So he speaks. But how little truth itself is aided by dialectical traps of this kind, everyone sees. First, comparison of the copies and the number of the books can show anyone, as we have also demonstrated by other examples, that it is plainly false [Col. 0279A] that the author everywhere either begins or ends with Otto and Radevicus. Then there is the utterly empty and foolish quibble that the author of the *Ligurinus* could not have earned the favor of Emperor Frederick and the royal family by doing nothing but recounting deeds. For, leaving aside the wholly different character of the work and the judgments of the most learned men of every age, what if at last our author had accommodated the *Ligurinus* to the wishes of the royal family—or rather, of the court? That Emperor Frederick was certainly most desirous of praise and fame is shown even by his letter addressed to Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0279D] Prefixed to Book I of Otto of Freising’s *De rebus gestis Friderici*], to whom he had transmitted the chief documents concerning his own achievements. After the death of that most holy man, that he pressed the services of Radevicus, canon of Freising, is likewise indicated by that writer’s letter addressed to the two officials of the palace [Note: [Col. 0279D] The same letter is prefixed to Radevicus’s books.]. Their splendid books testify plainly that both satisfied the prince’s desire and also the duty of prudent and upright men.

Yet those works, written in a weightier style, recommend themselves more by the substance of things and words than by artistic elegance or charm of expression. Moreover, the frankness of these worthy men does not everywhere favor Frederick’s praises, nor indeed could it do so consistently with the course of events. For who ever, like Homer, does not love his own heroes and hate truth when it is too sacred? What wonder if Frederick himself, or his friends, desired a more accommodating herald of his deeds? And behold: the exceptionally industrious author of Solymar was at hand, approved by the praises of his uncle Conrad and devoted to the Augustan house. The material was ready, and not raw, but arranged for style and compliant in the hands of one who took it up. Our author himself, I think, seems to indicate a not dissimilar literary intention when, with a certain cheerful simplicity, he reveals his purpose of flattery as though about to beg pardon for it. And indeed the dedicatory formulas, the very brief time, the frequent traces of haste and weariness, and finally his failure to proceed beyond the bounds of prepared material, may be thought to agree excellently with this.

This passage itself and the course of the discussion prompt a brief treatment of the arguments for the individual books of the *Ligurinus*, which the first Augsburg edition prints together in one place [Col. 0279D] before the work. They are each composed in as many verses as the entire work has books: namely, ten-line poems (*dekasticha*, δεκάστιχα). Such a jeu d’esprit certainly suited the twelfth century, and the thing itself lacks no precedents. Thus, already in the third century, we read that the jurist Herennius Modestinus prefixed ten-line arguments (*argumenta dekasticha*) to the individual books of Virgil’s *Aeneid*; arguments were also supplied for their books by Gualterus, Joseph of Exeter, Devonius, and William the Breton, nearly contemporaries in the twelfth century.

But among the *Ligurinus* arguments there is a striking disparity. The first seven agree sufficiently well both with the narrated events and with the author’s diction; the remainder, by contrast, are extremely corrupt, not owing merely to scribes and incapable of restoration by any art [Note: [Col. 0279D] Withofius had indeed promised a restoration, but the man’s boastfulness was altogether remarkable. The distinguished Vonckius attempted something, with wholly adverse fortune.]. Whether one considers the sequence of events, the vocabulary, or finally the manner of expression, one would certainly nowhere recognize the author of the *Ligurinus*. The earlier arguments always set the action, as they should, in the present tense; a faithful sequence of events appears, together with metrical congruity and elegance. In the latter appear grossly false factual details [Note: [Col. 0279D] Arguments to Books VIII and IX.], monstrous vocabulary, a frequent joining of past tense with present, and finally the author addressed by the name *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0279D] Argument to Book X, final verse.].

This last error of a foolish versifier—whoever he was—had aroused the suspicion of the distinguished Pithoeus [Note: [Col. 0279D] Preface cited above], though it occurs only in the Augsburg edition [Note: [Col. 0280D] Spiegel ingeniously rather than correctly altered the reading; the later editors followed him.]. I am surprised that the very learned Rittershusius pretended not to notice this [Note: [Col. 0280D] *Notes on Gunther’s Ligurinus*, p. 9; he does not hesitate to declare: “What prevents us from regarding Gunther himself as the author, I do not see.”], and consequently did not adhere to his stated purpose of restoring the arguments in accordance with the first edition. All other editions assigned the individual arguments to their respective books. Therefore I should regard the first seven *dekasticha* as genuinely the author’s, since there is no evidence of spuriousness (*notheia*, νοθεία), indeed there is a double confirmation. For from them the doubtful passage of the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0280D] Book V, verse—], from the argument to Book V, is very conveniently restored; and their very discontinuance seems not obscurely to prove that our author was either carried off by fate or prevented in some other way.

## § VI. Testimonies of the learned concerning the *Ligurinus*

[Col. 0280C]

You will admit that the best testimony for the *Ligurinus* is a work thoroughly examined; nevertheless, I think it part of my task to report the judgments of several eminent scholars. For not a few men of letters are guided by others’ opinions, and it is not unpleasant to survey the sentiments of men differing in age and country. It must, however, be noted that in such judgments account must be taken both of period and homeland, and that some allowance must be made for each writer’s style and talent.

Thus among the first is Conrad Celtis [Note: [Col. 0280D] “To the poem *Ligurinus*, after the Preface of the Augsburg edition”]:

> Gladly I yield to your writings, most learned *Ligurinus*;  
> I, Celtis, adore both your knees and your soles.  
> O Frederick, happy to have gained so great a poet,  
> [Col. 0280D] who thunders forth your deeds in grandiloquent song.  
> He stands next to the poet whom learned Mantua produced,  
> And who sings of the arms of Pompey and Caesar.  
> Not Stilicho alone, nor Honorius or Majorian,  
> Nor he who celebrates Scipiads and Sporiads;  
> Nor he who sings how swollen Jason crossed the seas,  
> Nor the Aeacid, nor he who recounts the *Thebaid*;  
> Let him too who cultivates the deeds of the Macedonian leader,  
> Proclaimed throughout the whole world, yield to your heroic poems.  
> [Col. 0281A] Let warlike Germany rejoice in this poet of ours,  
> Who sings Teutonic glory with so mighty a voice.

Jacques Cujas and François Hotman, the most celebrated jurists of the sixteenth century—and rivals of each other in nearly every other matter—nevertheless join amicably in praising the *Ligurinus*. Cujas relies upon its authority in more than twenty places, and somewhere declares that it explains certain heads of feudal law better than the whole muddy troop of feudal lawyers [Note: [Col. 0281D] Comparison shows, however, that this praise belongs to the Freising historians.]. Hotman repeatedly extols our author as a most noble and excellent poet.

Gerard Vossius [Note: [Col. 0281D] *On Latin Poets*, p. 254, cited edition; *On Latin Historians*, p. 136, same work.] calls him altogether a poet of great talent for his age, elegant as well, and an Apollonian bird. Justus Lipsius calls him a poet of spirit and talent not to be despised, indeed remarkable for that age. Marquard Freher, replying to Conrad Rittershusius’s plan to edit the *Ligurinus*, writes [Note: [Col. 0281D] Reuber, *Writers of German Affairs*, Johannes edition, p. 414.]:

> I understand your undertaking, my Rittershusius, of revising and elucidating Gunther, and warmly approve it. Certainly he is an author elegant beyond that age—indeed beyond his nation—and worthy of more cheerful fame than he has hitherto received.

Rittershusius himself, the savior of the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0281D] Preface to his edition.], writes:

> Among the few writers of the Middle Ages who survive, Gunther stands out with especial distinction. In a poem more elegant than his age could bear, and sound and learned, he described the deeds bravely, wisely, and magnanimously performed at home and abroad in his own age by Frederick I, the greatest, best, and most powerful emperor of the German name, who from the color of his beard received the surname Ahenobarbus, or Barbarossa; he followed the thread of Otto, bishop of Freising, and of Otto’s continuator Radevicus, canon of the same church. To these men, as to sources, he himself somewhere not obscurely directs the readers of his work. . . . Since the dignity and excellence of a work are commonly assessed either from its subject or from its manner and form of treatment—and since this work concerns the deeds of Frederick Ahenobarbus, a prince so great and such a man, so renowned in peace and war that under him a golden age may rightly seem, as it were, to have returned; and since it treats them not in a common fashion but with every ornament and illumination of speech—can it be obscure to anyone how highly our Gunther deserves to be valued by all?

Gaspar Scioppius [Note: [Col. 0281D] At the end of Rittershusius’s edition, p. 207.] greets him as “the poet of poets, the prince of the Franks” [Note: [Col. 0281D] See above, § 2, col. 267.], through whom “France is compelled to acknowledge that poetry owes its beginning to Germany.” Janus Dousa [Note: [Col. 0281D] In the second preface to his verse *Annals of the Batavians*.], in approximately these words [Col. 0282A] [Note: [Col. 0281D] That is, in Baillet’s translation, since the original cannot be consulted.], says:

> Critics agree that Guntherus is a poet of great genius and much fire, who did too much honor to an age insufficiently refined to discern his merit.

Caspar Barthius [Note: [Col. 0281D] *Adversaria*, pp. 2340 f.] says: “He is unquestionably a better poet and possesses a truly remarkable spirit, of which the others of that kind—that is, of the Middle Ages—are devoid; so much so that, when compared with him, they seem to display more labor than talent.” The same writer elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0281D] In manuscript notes collected by Feller and communicated by Georg Christoph Johannis; see Reuber, *Writers of German Affairs*, Johannes’s Preface, pp. 411, 414.] says: “All poets of the Middle Ages stand very far below this German. Walter was praised above the rest: compare a single page, and you will see bronze in this man, wolfish stuff in the other.”

Pedro de Mexía, a Spanish knight, at the end of his account of Frederick Barbarossa: “Gunther, an eminent poet, who wrote of him in heroic verse.” Henri Estienne [Col. 0282B] [Note: [Col. 0282D] On Saxo Grammaticus’s *Danish History*, Book II.] calls him “a most noble and excellent poet.” Hermann Conring [Note: [Col. 0282D] *Letters*, p. 303; *Dissertation on Academic Antiquities*, 6.] calls him “the most successful poet of the twelfth century, worthy of the age of Emperor Frederick.” Johann Friedrich Gronovius [Note: [Col. 0282D] To Nicolaus Heinsius, *Collection of Letters Written by Illustrious Men*, ed. Burman, vol. III, p. 4.] says: “Gunther is the foremost poet among those Germans whom we know to have brought back from Helicon a crown of evergreen foliage.” Meric Casaubon [Note: [Col. 0282D] Notes on Polybius, p. 171.] calls him “a most elegant poet, considering the capacity of a barbarous age.” Olaus Borrichius [Note: [Col. 0282D] *On Latin Poets*, Dissertation 2, p. 88.] writes: “Considering the age in which Gunther wrote, his diction is altogether magnificent and his composition learned.” Adrien Baillet [Note: [Col. 0282D] *Judgments of the Learned*, vol. III, part II, no. 1209, p. 336, Amsterdam edition.] says:

> He is a marvelous poet for the time, and I do not know upon what basis those who say that he was a monk proceed. . . . Besides his great talent for poetry, he took care to cultivate his style and render it sufficiently elegant [Col. 0282C] to make his verses pleasing.

Finally, Hieronymus Gundling [Note: [Col. 0282D] *Gundlingiana*, Fascicle VI, observation 2, § 27, p. 185.] says: “Gunther described the ancient order of electing a king both fully and clearly. It is to be wished that all students of German affairs read this poem repeatedly.”

Against these unanimous votes of the learned, Lilius Gyraldus alone raises an objection. “The work,” he says [Note: [Col. 0282D] *History of Poets*, dialogue 4, p. 247, Lyons, 1696, folio], “is such as that age could produce—melodious and fluent, but inelegant and diffuse, and bearing the native flavor of both writer and writing.” A weighty judge indeed—if only he had read the book. But, by Hercules, the truth is that he had not even seen it. For the same man shortly afterwards says [Note: [Col. 0282D] Ibid., dialogue 5, p. 307.]:

> There is also a *Ligurinus* concerning Henry Ahenobarbus, that is, Barbarossa. There is likewise a work by the German Gunther, arranged in twelve books of heroic verse [Col. 0282D], containing the deeds of Emperor Frederick. If at times you have leisure to read them, in order to alleviate your heats, [Col. 0283A] you will seem to see certain breaths, as it were, of the poet Lucan under the Scythian sky: namely, swollen and inflated ones. This man also wrote a *Life of Saint Cyriacus* in nearly the same verse around the year of Christ 1100.

Behold the man’s ridiculous drowsiness and virtual delirium: a *Ligurinus* on Henry Barbarossa; Gunther’s twelve books on the deeds of Emperor Frederick; and, finally, the writer of these works placed around the year 1100. He was, evidently, dealing with a medieval writer and therefore a German—hence “Scythian”; Gyraldus composed these things, more or less, in a pagan spirit of arrogance.

## § VII. The lack of manuscript copies of the *Ligurinus* and its probable cause

[Col. 0283B]

My first and chief concern in preparing this edition was to investigate whether manuscript codices of the *Ligurinus* existed anywhere. I often wondered why this matter, of the greatest importance, had not troubled even a single earlier editor. The principal circumstances of the time promised happy auspices for such researches: namely, many public libraries, and those exceedingly rich; an immense multitude of manuscript codices, roused and, as it were, redeemed from their age-old stagnation by recent transformations; and, further, the most humane liberality of their owners and custodians and their remarkable favor toward letters. Without delay I approached the most celebrated libraries: the old Vatican library at Rome, Vienna, Paris, Munich, and finally St Gall and Zurich in Switzerland. Here above all I must renew public thanks to men greater than my praise, by whose most upright services, although I did not obtain what I had hoped, I nevertheless acquired the certain knowledge that a manuscript codex of the *Ligurinus* is sought in vain everywhere.

I would not venture to affirm this with respect to Vienna, while I still must rely upon silence rather than a definite reply from Friedrich Schlegel, a man otherwise most praised for his devotion to ancient German letters, whom I found less accommodating. Yet, after hope had been disappointed, a better hope has dawned, in which I may rest more safely; nor will an opportunity be lacking to contribute to public use whatever may someday come to hand.

Meanwhile, while awaiting friendly letters from those places, I myself turned through every catalogue of manuscripts that I could obtain: those of Lambecius, Labbe, Montfaucon, Reiser, Sinner, and many others, together with certain treasures of distinguished private libraries. Long searching in vain, I finally came upon the *Catalogues of the Manuscript Books of England and Ireland Collected into One* [Note: [Col. 0283D] Oxford, 1595, 2 folio volumes.], and there [Note: [Col. 0283D] Vol. II, p. 227.] the *Catalogue of the Manuscript Books of Edward Bernard*, showing [Note: [Col. 0283D] Nos. 1507, 155.] under the heading “Latin books collated with old copies”: “Gunther’s poem on Barbarossa”—an item, so far as I know, noticed by no one until now.

Immediately various thoughts came into my mind, enhancing the value of the discovery. I believed the author of the *Ligurinus* to have been English by nationality, persuaded by the very notice in the first edition. What is more, I suspected a touch of pious vanity in that magnificent inscription of Conrad Celtis: “among the Franks, in the Hercynian Forest, and in the Druidic monastery of Eberacum.” That great man might have added those words from his own invention, to create favor or value; for splendor of titles was not especially uncommon in that age and is excusable on many grounds. Indeed, Conrad Celtis might have been led by the very words “Druidic monastery of Eberacum,” perhaps visible on the front of the codex. For the English monastery of Eboracum [Note: [Col. 0283D] York.] might not inappropriately enjoy the designation “Druidic,” since, on the most weighty testimony of Julius Caesar, we learn that the Druids first came from Britain [Note: [Col. 0283D] *The Gallic War*, Book VI, chapter 13.]; while the Frankish land was anciently celebrated as the principal seat of the Druids in Germany.

Then Senkenberg’s not wholly groundless doubt concerning the place where the codex was discovered could conveniently be answered at the same time: he wonders that Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the neighboring monastery of St James at Würzburg and a most diligent investigator of Franconian libraries, did not see it. There was further the notable passage in the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0283D] Book VI, v. 168 ff.], which describes and adorns with manifest care the letters and gifts sent by the English king to Emperor Frederick. Finally, another passage of the *Ligurinus*, likewise by far the most difficult of all, was explained—provided one admits a foreign and thus distant writer. I greatly wonder that this point entirely escaped all the learned men who have published anything on the *Ligurinus*.

The writer of the *Ligurinus* explicitly designates the year in which Frederick assumed the kingship as 1154 [Note: [Col. 0284D] *Ligurinus*, Book I, vv. 167 ff.]. But anyone even slightly familiar with German history knows from the common testimony of writers that this year is plainly false and must be reduced by an interval of two years. How could this escape a contemporary or near-contemporary writer? How could it escape a German, or even an Italian? I do not, indeed, ignore the chronological difficulties of that age and the extreme disagreement of contemporaries in reckoning years, conspicuously evident even in the history of Emperor Frederick—for example, concerning the famous court of Mainz, which hailed Henry, Emperor Frederick’s eldest son and king of the Germans, as emperor [Note: [Col. 0284D] Some contemporaries assign that solemn and exceedingly crowded court to 1181, others to 1182, and others finally to 1184; de Bünau, *Life and Deeds of Frederick I*, p. 285.]. Nor do I ignore that some foreigners date the first year of King Frederick to 1153, as does even the domestic writer Johann Nauclerus [Note: [Col. 0284D] *Chronicle*, cited place.]. But no writer whatever gives the year 1154 [Col. 0285A], except a single Viennese manuscript codex of Otto of Freising’s *De rebus gestis Friderici I Augusti* [Note: [Col. 0285D] Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. VI, p. 699, note 1.]. It can scarcely be doubted that the writer of the *Ligurinus* had before his eyes a codex of this kind—if not this very one—and in good faith followed a copyist’s error.

If anyone compares these points with that epilogue of the first edition [Note: [Col. 0285D] See above, p. 261.], “the *Ligurinus* . . . first presented at Vienna to German youth by Conrad Celtis,” and if he knows the man, easily the foremost poet of his age, then he will with the utmost difficulty withstand the onset of a very grave suspicion. I freely confess that I was somewhat troubled; but the ancient appearance of the codex itself called me back from hesitation: “a copy worn away by age and almost by decay.” Thus the first editors expressly testify [Note: [Col. 0285D] At the end of the edition, before the list of corrections.]. Who could believe that those most celebrated men, illustrious in reputation and highly praised for integrity of character, conspired together in fraud?

You have, then, reasons that render a contemporary German or Italian suspect, and a recent author less probable; reasons that can recommend a foreigner, indeed an Englishman, and thus the intervening testimony of an apparently English codex. But that codex—if you regard it as such—is not yet to be assigned great weight. Apart from its not yet having been seen and examined, it is especially held back by the name Gunther inscribed upon it, which indicates a date later than the first edition; nevertheless it is not on that account rashly to be condemned.

Moreover, the cause of the great scarcity of manuscripts may readily be defended by the many instances of copies that have perished, especially [Col. 0285C] if one applies to it, and with better right, what we read that the illustrious Rittershusius had applied to the rarity of editions [Note: [Col. 0285D] Preface to the *Ligurinus*.]: namely, that a good author was suppressed by those who cannot in any respect, small or great, endure the light of truth shining into their eyes, and who, insofar as they can, strive to erase from all human memory whatever may oppose their desires and domination. But whatever explanation of the deficiency one accepts, one certainly seeks evidence of spuriousness (*notheia*, νοθεία) from it in vain.

And do not attribute too much to Senkenberg’s note, which is not worth enough to make you deny outright that the codex was found at Eboracum rather than among the Franks. What is more, Trithemius himself did not become abbot at Würzburg until 1506, and therefore several years after the codex’s discovery; he also survived the publication of the *Ligurinus* by twelve years and was very well placed to investigate the truth, yet thereafter nowhere raised a doubt, much less openly contradicted it. Why he did not include the author in his catalogues is not so difficult to understand. Perhaps he understood the word *Ligurinus*, and, not knowing the person designated by it, could include him neither in his book *On Illustrious Men* nor in that *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. And is Trithemius’s silence in catalogues of such consequence? Did he not also pass over Thietmar of Merseburg, a most celebrated writer? And where now is that most excellent Antwerp manuscript of Thietmar’s chronicle, once delivered to Leibniz, of which not even a trace could in our time be pointed out to Johann August Wagner, the most diligent editor of Thietmar’s chronicle [Note: [Col. 0286D] Preface cited above.]?

Finally, I cannot grasp by conjecture alone why not a word about the *Ligurinus* occurs in the learned correspondence of that age. Whatever the judgments of scholars may have been, one would at least expect some indication of them. Above all, I was troubled by the deep silence in the correspondence of the highly renowned jurist Ulrich Zasius with leading men of the same age, and thus with those bound to him by acquaintance, who either had published the *Ligurinus* [Col. 0286B] or illuminated it in their own lectures: Hieronymus Baldung, Heinrich Bebel, Jacob Philomusus, Conrad Peutinger, and Jacob Spiegel. I read through its otherwise excellent entirety [Note: [Col. 0286D] *Letters of Ulrich Zasius to the Most Learned Men of His Age*, ed. Joseph Anton Riegger, knight and jurist, Freiburg and Ulm, 1774, octavo.], and learned much about every other memorable matter of his age, but nothing whatever about the *Ligurinus*. Whoever can reconcile this with scholarly habits and the character of the age will be a great Apollo!

Whatever, finally, you decide concerning the scarcity of manuscripts, you cannot yet determine it conclusively. Until fortune’s favor brings such a thing to light somewhere, better hope rests upon England; and, given the present condition of public affairs there, it will rest there for some time.

## VIII. Editions

[Col. 0286C]

We shall describe more fully the first and principal Augsburg edition, the preserver of the *Ligurinus*, a copy of which should be reckoned among the rarest treasures of libraries.

The title inscription is not given on a separate leaf, as is usual in books, but, in the manner of manuscripts, precedes the preface. On the opening page one reads:

> Ten books of the *Ligurinus*, concerning the deeds of the Emperor Caesar Frederick the First Augustus, composed in heroic verse, recently discovered among the Franks in the Hercynian Forest and in the Druidic monastery of Eberacum by Conrad Celtis, and restored after return from exile.  
>
> Dedicated by the same man to eternity and to love of country.

Immediately follows the editors’ preface, or letter to the reader [Col. 0286D], which we printed above. On the other page of the leaf, at its head, is read: “A poem to the *Ligurinus* (by Conrad Celtis),” namely the same poem presented by us [Note: [Col. 0286D] See § 6, col. 280.]. Then follow the “Arguments for the ten books of the *Ligurinus*,” occupying this page and both pages of the second leaf, except that, after the arguments for Book II are finished, one again reads: “Epigram to Johann Rymann, bookseller and book-dealer throughout all Germany, by C. [Conrad] C. [Celtis], a poem”:

[Col. 0287A]

> “Through your zeal, cultured Rymann, Latin and Greek letters  
> Have now come into our lands;  
> For this Germany gives you fitting thanks,  
> And here and everywhere will return praise to you.”

Only with the third leaf does the work of the *Ligurinus* itself begin, headed in two lines of large capital letters: “Here begins the first book of the *Ligurinus* concerning the deeds of the Emperor Caesar Frederick the First Augustus.” The same heading is prefixed to each following book; nowhere is an end indicated by the word *explicit* or anything similar. The whole is completed in seventy-five leaves and ends precisely on the second page of leaf LXXV, with the appended indications of printer, place, and year, which we likewise transcribed in the appropriate place. This subscription, however, was placed only at the end of the work of the *Ligurinus*, not at the end of the whole edition, and was therefore overlooked by some; it produced several errors.

First, all editions of the *Ligurinus* mentioned here and there without place and year must be considered Augsburg editions, since that evidence could not have appeared to writers seeking it at the end of the final leaf of the edition. Likewise, editions recorded by some under the year 1567 [Note: [Col. 0287D] I warn also against Oudin in both cited places. Oudin further invents Strasbourg as the place from his own imagination. This double error also crept upon the distinguished Maittaire (*Annals of Printing*, vol. I, p. 742, Amsterdam edition, 1733) and made even the very diligent G. Panzer hesitate (*Annals of Printing*, vol. I, p. 67), who appeals to Maittaire.] must be considered Augsburg editions: a writer, in a moment of inattention, changed the third zero in the number into a six, and others rashly followed him. Finally, in Rittershusius’s edition the printer’s name is read in error as “Veglinus,” corrupted from “Vegelinus.”

The first page of leaf LXXVI is entirely blank. The leaf appears to have been printed separately, for it is attached to the rest by glue. On its second page is read Conrad Peutinger’s dedicatory letter, with the heading: “Conrad Peutinger of Augsburg wishes prosperity to the Lord Emperor Caesar Maximilian Augustus.” It ends exactly on the second page of leaf LXXVI. Then, beginning with the first page of the following leaf, LXXVII, there follows in an unbroken sequence the entire letter of Emperor Frederick I to Otto of Freising, such as the prologue to Otto’s books *On the Deeds of Frederick I* presents. Thus leaf LXXVI seems to have been printed solely for the sake of Peutinger’s dedication, perhaps written later. The emperor’s letter ends near the top of the first page of leaf LXXVIII and is followed by: “Conrad Peutinger of Augsburg to the reader, on the birth, lineage, and descendants of the Emperor Caesar Frederick the First Augustus.” When the very brief dissertation ends halfway down leaf LXXIX, there follows a list of corrections under the heading: “Errors of the first book of the *Ligurinus*, partly through the carelessness of the printers, partly through the age, near-decay, and damage of the worn-out copy. Let the diligent reader observe the orthography.”

This list of errors fills two and a half full leaves and is itself marred by many mistakes, so that everywhere one sees the infancy of the printing art, against which the editors’ and correctors’ diligence is understood to have struggled in vain. Otherwise, for the period the type is very elegant: letters neither too heavy nor too thin, ink of lively color, paper dense in texture, well finished and smoothed, and altogether beautifully white; the format, called folio, is of the most proper proportions. Finally, in accordance with the practice of the age, there are nowhere page numbers, catchwords, or signatures; but the running title observes only the number of the books, so that on one page of the leaf one constantly finds the word “Book,” and on the other the book number.

In the copy which the generosity of the custodians of the Freiburg library kindly placed at our disposal for this edition, the first page after the preface bears the subscription: “Conrad Peutinger of Augsburg sends this as a gift to Master Jacob Heinrichmann” [Note: [Col. 0287D] On this Jacob Heinrichmann, a celebrated grammarian and teacher at the Tübingen Gymnasium, who in 1560 was still living at Augsburg, a venerable old man nearly a hundred years of age, after his labors in the school, see Burckhard, *On the Fate of Latin Learning in Germany*, vol. I, p. 299; vol. II, pp. 415, 417, 419, 421.]. This testimony from the first and principal editor greatly increases the value of this most handsome copy. One might think it had been taken from the press only a few days before, had not this very page—perhaps more exposed—acquired a slight rust-stain, while all the others remain untouched.

Besides, one hand, not unlearned, has written very many annotations; yet they should not be considered Peutinger’s, as the different formation of the letters and the plainly different ink show. Peutinger’s hand is very heavy, whereas that of the annotations is thin, and their strokes are altogether unlike. Only on the first page of leaf LXXVIII did Peutinger supply an omitted word in his own dissertation on Frederick’s birth, lineage, and so forth, using precisely the same letters and ink as on the opening page. These annotations [Col. 0288C], whether Heinrichmann’s or another’s, are especially copious in Books I and II, fewer in the following books, and cease in Book VI. The same hand also wrote above the title of the *Ligurinus*, in capital letters as though imitating print: “Of Gunther the German, most illustrious poet.” The printed title *Ligurinus* then follows in a single, as it were, continuous phrase, so that one sees the annotator understood entirely correctly the meaning of the name *Ligurinus*. Finally, I judge it worth noting that quite a few of these annotations anticipate Rittershusius’s conjectures. Rittershusius declares that he used another Augsburg copy furnished with annotations by the Augsburg physician Henisch [Note: [Col. 0288D] Preface, fol. 6b].

The second edition appeared at Strasbourg, from Johann Schott’s press, together with Bartholomeus’s *Austriad*, under the title:

[Col. 0288D]

> *Gunther, most illustrious poet: Ligurinus, or a work concerning the deeds of the Emperor Caesar Frederick I Augustus, completed in ten books. The *Austriad* of Richard Bartholinus of Perugia, in twelve books, dedicated to Emperor Maximilian Augustus. With scholia by Jacob Spiegel of Sélestat, distinguished man. 1531. Folio.*

Some falsely date it 1551, an error arising from writers’ carelessness; Sélestat, Spiegel’s birthplace, is also mistakenly given as the place of printing. Spiegel supplied both books with copious annotations: historical, geographical, ethical-political, theological, and grammatical-philological. Nevertheless, he neglected the text of the *Ligurinus* itself beyond what one could believe possible, leaving errors altogether manifest. He was the first to append separate arguments to the individual books, a practice scarcely worthy of recommendation but imitated by later editors. The type is sufficiently elegant for the period, and the edition itself is to be numbered among the rarer ones.

The third edition is that of Peter Perna, bookseller of Basel, published in 1569 with a preface by Philip Melanchthon.

I have not yet seen this edition, and have therefore so far searched for it in vain, since it is not found even in the excellent Göttingen library. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that it exists, persuaded by the weightiest testimony of witnesses. For it was evidently seen and handled by the most learned Rittershusius, who expressly records that it had been given him as a gift by Joachim Camerarius, physician of Nuremberg [Note: [Col. 0289D] Preface, fol. 6 b]. David Clement states that it was bound together with the books of Otto of Freising and Rahewin [Note: [Col. 0289D] Loc. cit., p. 326]. Yet how it differs from the following edition I nowhere discover, unless it be that, according to that same witness, the books of the Freising authors appear to have been added after the *Ligurinus*. I should indeed consider the two one and the same edition, the bookseller having divided copies either through enterprise or accommodation, so that they might be recommended the more effectively to differing preferences among men; or perhaps, as a mark of honour, which he could render to both parties without injury to his own advantage.

The fourth edition, issued in the same year from the same press, appears under the following title:

*The Chronicle of Otto, bishop of Freising, son of Leopold the Pious, Margrave of Austria; or, eight books of events from the creation of the world down to his own times. By the same author, two books on the deeds of Frederick I, Emperor Augustus. Two books by Rahewin, canon of Freising, on the deeds of the same Frederick, added to the former. The Ligurinus of Gunther, the poet, or ten books On the Deeds of Frederick. Other works too have been added, relating both to the history of Frederick and to that of later emperors; their catalogue is set out on the following page. Some of these are now published for the first time, the rest far more complete than before [Col. 0289D], with notes also added and an accurate index. Basel, Peter Perna, 1569. With the privilege of His Imperial Majesty. Folio.*

After the index displayed on the verso of the title-page follows P. Pithou’s letter to Jacques Cujas, jurist; after it, Pithou’s own judgment on Otto, Rahewin, and Gunther, placed in the position of a preface and called by us this encomium. Then comes the index of chapters for Otto and Rahewin; after a blank leaf, their works follow, together with the appendix of an ancient writer upon Radewin—that is, Rahewin—by which that volume is concluded. After another blank leaf [Col. 0290A] come seven printed leaves, not, however, marked with page numbers. They contain certain supplements and variant readings for Otto and Rahewin, taken from manuscripts sent by Matthias Flacius to P. Pithou. One of these, a very ancient manuscript, supplies an altogether notable addition to the history of the Counts of Scheyern, especially the Ottos of Wittelsbach, with a most learned annotation by Pithou. When these are finished, there are presented a very few corrections by the distinguished man on the *Ligurinus*, and certain notes on Albert of Strasbourg. There follows a brief apology concerning the fuller annotations on the *Ligurinus* which had been promised but not supplied. In their stead, in order to fill the quire left to them by the bookseller, Conrad’s ancient and well-known [Col. 0290B] *Chronicle of the Affairs of Mainz* is substituted. Finally, after yet another blank leaf, follows the *Ligurinus*, bearing no title, after the chronicle of Albert of Strasbourg, with Cuspinian’s letter appended to it; lastly comes an index of subjects and words, which in fact pertains in vain to the *Ligurinus* and Albert of Strasbourg. These two form, as it were, a separate volume, distinguished also by a separate sequence of page numbers.

Concerning the promised annotations Pithou himself writes:

> We had resolved to add fuller notes—or rather collections of observations—in which certain matters of ancient French and German law not sufficiently well known to the public, but especially the origins and developments of dignities, offices, and military institutions, should be explained as briefly as lay within our power. But since, on the one hand, the haste of the press already running, while we were engaged upon I know not what else, pressed us, and, on the other, a certain private and more necessary occupation that had arisen called us away, we were compelled to postpone until another time a task already wholly conceived in our mind.

It is indeed to be regretted that a man so highly skilled, drawn away by other concerns, was unable to elucidate matters of the greatest importance—provided only that it were established that he had seriously undertaken the matter. From his own words, however, it is not obscurely understood that Pithou, regarding what he had conceived in his mind as easier in execution, indulged his announced plans and promises beyond measure, in a manner not unusual among learned men. You may see, indeed, an entire quire, left at the bookseller’s trust for the promised material, afterwards filled by other matter. What is more [Col. 0290D], although he survived the edition by twenty-seven years, he did not redeem his pledge.

The fifth printing of the *Ligurinus* was published by Justus Reuber, Palatine councillor, in the *Collection of German Historical Writers*, Frankfurt, heirs of Andreas Wechel, 1584, folio.

This edition contains nothing except the entire volume of Jacob Spiegel, adopted word for word along with every one of its faults. Know that this Reuber edition, otherwise most handsome, which we call the first, is dated by some falsely to 1582 [Note: [Col. 0289D] Christian Neuhof, *Mentissa* to Degory Wheare’s *Winter Lectures*, section 110, p. 130. Leyser, *History of Medieval Poetry*, p. 790], being deceived, evidently, by Rittershusius’s indication. Some persons [Col. 0291A] [Note: [Col. 0291D] Valerius Andreas, Casimir Oudin, locc. citt.] invent a third volume of Reuber’s collection, which never appeared.

The sixth, and by far the best of all editions, was prepared by Conrad Rittershusius. Its title is as follows:

*Gunther’s Ligurinus, or ten books on the deeds of the Emperor Caesar Frederick the First, P. P. Augustus, surnamed Ahenobarbus, or Barbarossa. A work pleasant to read not only for poets, but also useful and especially necessary for historians, statesmen, and courtiers, as an example for deliberations, counsels, embassies, speeches, and letters; and for jurists also, for the knowledge of feudal law. Conrad Rittershusius, jurist, has revised it: after collating five editions with one another, he has removed very many and very serious errors scattered throughout, both of readings and of punctuation [Col. 0291B]; he has illustrated it with notes; and for the first time enriched it with an accurate index of memorable matters and words. Tübingen, Georg Gruppenbach, 1598, octavo.*

A separate volume of annotations appeared the year before, bearing this title:

*Notes on Gunther’s Ligurinus, by Conrad Rittershusius, jurist and professor, a Nuremberger. To the most noble and learned Johann von Bredow, knight of the March. Tübingen, printed by Georg Gruppenbach, 1597, octavo.*

Let us hear the words of that most celebrated editor himself concerning the causes and principles of this edition [Note: [Col. 0291D] Dedicatory letter, fol. 2 b ff.; Preface, fols. 4 a–b, 7 a]:

[Col. 0291C]

> For my part—to say a few words about myself and about the occasion by which I was led to prepare this edition—when as a young man I had several times heard this Gunther, of whom I have spoken, praised in the schools of elegant jurists (for the others have as much to do with good authors and letters as a dog with a bath), during their exposition of feudal doctrine; and when several of his elegant verses were also adduced to embellish and illuminate certain points in that law of fiefs, otherwise described rather barbarously and unsuccessfully: I often felt myself inflamed with a great desire to see and read the entire author. How good he was could readily be judged from those little passages which were quoted—one recognizes the lion, as the saying goes, from his claw. But because he had never been published in a convenient format, and because the form in which he had been published was nowhere found for sale, copies of Gunther were then sought in vain by myself and my fellow students.
>
> At length, when a few years ago I came upon him, I read him with such eagerness and care as one who wished to quench a long thirst. During my reading, I noted in the margin of my book many matters that happened to occur to me and seemed relevant either to correcting or to elucidating this writer. Those things which I had noted down thus casually, as each came under the point of my pen, I afterwards enlarged, while copying them out, by continually adding new material. At length, especially as the exhortations of very distinguished men were added, and an additional incentive was furnished by the most noble and learned Christoph Pflug, knight of Meissen [Col. 0292A], I began to consider arranging a new edition of Gunther—one, indeed, that might be useful to more persons and might have attached to it those little annotations of mine which several great men judged neither useless nor contemptible. . . . . . .

The same author says in his Preface:

> This writer, then, so great and so distinguished, ought to have been carried perpetually in one’s bosom, worn by handling, and repeatedly read by all, because of the abundant and varied benefit which can flow from him to every class of men, especially those who acknowledge the Roman—or rather German—Empire. Yet he was treated and handled so badly [Col. 0292B] that I was moved to pity at his fate. For not only did he lie hidden and unknown for many centuries, but even later, when a generous hand championed him and brought his poem forth from the filth and darkness of its prison into the light, it was disfigured by a great many errors, and the author was almost endangered in his very name. For when a manuscript codex had been brought to Augsburg by Conrad Celtes Protucius, who was the first poet in Germany after the revival of good letters, and when, through the kindness of the jurist Conrad Peutinger and the generosity of certain other noble and learned men, it had been arranged that it should be printed, then the writer himself was called *Ligurinus*, the name which the author had given to his work. Many learned men afterwards fell into the same error, praising Ligurinus [Col. 0292C] instead of Gunther. . . . I could no longer endure this unworthy fortune of Gunther; and after those first two Conrads, to whom he owes life and light, I myself came as a third, that I might be his defender and champion, especially at the exhortation of certain great men, whom I wished to be able to satisfy. . . .
>
> Finally, since I had observed the author’s very deliberate intention, namely that he wished himself to fashion
>
> > A little book, to be shut in the hands in a shorter form,
>
> that is, to write an *enchiridion* or handbook, I judged that I ought to follow this intention and advised the printer at last to reprint this author in a smaller format. But because of the very many errors which had persisted in all earlier editions down to this time [Col. 0292D], I considered another edition altogether necessary, by which these might, so far as possible, be washed away. Although most of the errors which I have removed were of such a kind that any reader neither inattentive nor unlearned could have detected them, and although I do not claim from this any great praise for either intelligence or acuteness, still I could not bear or overlook the continued circulation of this writer in so corrupted a state. Thus I was fired by I know not what desire to prepare this new edition, to which I added a special book of Notes, in which not only the grounds of the corrections might be given, but certain matters [Col. 0293A], and notable expressions and sentiments, might also be elucidated.

This is what he says, and with good reason. For he was the first, in the common judgment of scholars, to restore to the books of the *Ligurinus* something like their ancient brightness; and by his many annotations, full of learning, he increased the benefit of the undertaking, setting a rare and noble example of careful criticism to later ages. Everywhere weighty in his judgments, rich in examples, and an outstanding observer, he is nevertheless stronger in grammatical matters. In other fields he excels less; some matters, though most learned, are disconnected. He is especially extensive in theological questions and in ethical and political rules, according to the fashion of his age. Moreover, being too zealous an advocate of Roman jurisprudence, he wrongly confuses many features of German customs with it, not being equally versed in the ancient native system. At times he neglects the sources of the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0293D] A notable example of this kind of carelessness may be found in the note on Book IX, verse 35 ff. Compare Rahewin of Freising, Book II, chapter 9]. Finally, the arrangement (*οἰκονομία*, “organization”) of the edition itself is not very convenient. The reader making frequent searches is troubled by the division of the notes into chapters, for which one can perceive no rationale at all; then by their frequent disagreement with the text of the work, with the result that one very often reads in the notes a correction which one looks for in vain in the text. We have already spoken above about the summaries of the books [Note: [Col. 0293D] Col. 279]. Rittershusius himself, however, says in the preface to the volume of notes: “The summaries which in other editions are prefixed to the individual books, we took care to print together in one place at the very beginning before Gunther’s work itself, following the authority of the first and most ancient Augsburg edition.” Quite right, of course—provided that one could find it actually done. These and other matters, especially the spelling of names, contrary not only to the Augsburg edition but also to the authorities, can only with great difficulty be reconciled with the man’s diligence unless one admits that distinct editions of the text and the annotations are at issue—and thus that Rittershusius was distracted by other business while putting the *Ligurinus* to press. For it is not permissible to believe that in so many instances he changed his mind or carelessly contradicted himself, since not even a trace of an abandoned view is found in the preface.

The seventh printing of the *Ligurinus* is found in the reprinted *Collection of German Writers* of Justus Reuber, Hanover, from the Wechel press, at the expense of Daniel and David Aubry and Clement Schleich, 1619, folio [Note: [Col. 0293D] Preface to the following edition, p. 2].

It is merely a reprint of the fifth edition, neither enlarged nor corrected. In the annotations it is called the second edition.

[Col. 0293D]

We come to the eighth and, so far, final edition of the *Ligurinus*: the same Reuberian collection, again reprinted under the supervision of Georg Christian Joannis, Frankfurt am Main, 1726, folio. There, on p. 407:

*The Ligurinus of the most distinguished poet Gunther, or ten books On the Deeds of Caesar Frederick I Augustus. With the scholia and annotations of Jacob Spiegel, Conrad Rittershusius, and Caspar Barth.*

[Col. 0294A]

Georg Christian Joannis himself says of his labours on the *Ligurinus* [Note: [Col. 0293D] Preface, p. 413 ff.]:

> I shall briefly set forth what has been accomplished by my labour in this new edition. When I undertook the revision of these books of Gunther, I followed Rittershusius’s edition, since it is the best. Yet, as regards the summaries of the books, which he had arranged to be printed together and at the beginning of the work, I followed in the footsteps of Spiegel and Reuber, who prefixed individual summaries to individual books. Then, at the urging of certain men, as distinguished in learning as in the glory of their offices and merits, I inserted Rittershusius’s notes among Spiegel’s, both because they are very rarely found and because they are altogether brilliant. Accordingly they are rightly called learned by Vossius [Note: [Col. 0294D] *On Latin Historians*, cited edition, p. 254] and Sagittarius [Note: [Col. 0294D] *Introduction to Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24, §39, p. 629], and most learned by Struve [Note: [Col. 0294D] *Historical Library*, chapter 7, §14]. I inserted not only those [Col. 0294B] which that most learned author formerly appended to Gunther and published at Tübingen in 1597, but also those which he later added in the margin of his own copy; these the most judicious Eucharius Gottlieb Rinck, a man deserving in many respects not only of the University of Altdorf, where with great renown he teaches canon and public law, but also of the whole republic of letters, kindly shared with me. Moreover, I added the manuscript notes of Caspar Barth, which the most noble Feller had formerly collated for this purpose: few in number and very brief, to be sure, but sometimes correcting the author and sometimes casting some light upon him. So that you may know what belongs to each writer, I have everywhere marked Spiegel’s with the letter Sp., Rittershusius’s with R., and Barth’s with B.

Everything that this celebrated man here says of his labours on the *Ligurinus* is entirely true, nor will anyone deny that this Reuberian edition was thereby made far superior. If only he had not thought every annotation of Spiegel and Rittershusius of such value as to add them in full. The bulk of the volume was thereby enlarged without benefit, to the reader’s inconvenience. For the text floats amid notes as a little boat in the Ocean; it burdens the reader rather than assists him. Furthermore, Joannis added little or rather nothing of his own, although he certainly devoted his whole life and learning with singular zeal to purging other men’s dregs and exalting their name. How, however, he can say that he used Rittershusius’s text [Col. 0294D], I do not easily understand [Note: [Col. 0294D] Yet one may understand that he had it before his eyes even from this: he censures the corrupted name of the printer Oeglin], since he states that Rittershusius prefixed the summaries in a single sequence and together at the beginning of the *Ligurinus*, which we have plainly demonstrated to be false. Finally, I have discovered that this distinguished man transferred in the same good faith both Rittershusius’s own observations and those taken from elsewhere; as a result, he reproduced also several of Rittershusius’s errors and even printers’ mistakes.

[Col. 0295A]

It is pleasing to append to this catalogue of editions a few remarks about two others which never saw the light. The first of these had been seriously planned by the man renowned by his name alone, Johann Friedrich Gronovius, the celebrated professor of history and eloquence at Leiden. Let us hear from his own words why it did not succeed [Note: [Col. 0295D] Letter to Nicolaus Heinsius, in the collection of letters written by distinguished men, edited by Burman, vol. III, p. 4]:

> C. Rittershusius published him—the same *Ligurinus*—with notes at Tübingen nearly forty years ago. I too had once resolved, in honour of our nation, to do so, because, although he did not escape the faults of his age, there nevertheless appear in him both strength of genius and imitation of the best poets; not to mention the history, in which, together with Otto of Freising and Rahewin, he is unique; not to mention that he most beautifully exposes the devices of the papal court [Col. 0295B] and asserts the majesty and right of Caesar, so that it is not in the public interest that this writer should perish. Yet he is still most corrupt, and we had already noted a great many things, particularly when he was available to me at Amsterdam. But it was well that I abandoned that plan. For what mockeries of judgment concerning this writer and my own labour would there have been among those for whom Silius and Statius, after we had done fairly well by them, became worthless! At this price let us keep our hands entirely off all authors, lest, after we have edited them, we be thought deservedly unworthy of being edited ourselves.

See what immense damage was inflicted upon the advancement of the *Ligurinus* and the republic of letters by the arrogance of a few persons!

The other edition, and indeed an attractive one, had often been announced [Col. 0295C] [Note: [Col. 0295D] *Leipzig New Journals of Learned Matters*, year 1730, no. 23, p. 203 ff.—*Duisburg Miscellanies*, fascicle I, p. 142. Withof’s *Specimen on Gunther’s Ligurinus*, Duisburg, 1731, quarto; 1755, quarto, passim] by Johann Hildebrand Withof, famous professor of eloquence at the University of Duisburg. I transcribe its title:

*Gunther’s Ligurinus with commentary, notes, and corrections. There are added the complete observations of Rittershusius and Pithou; selections from Spiegel; and selected observations of Barth, Lipsius, Casaubon, Heinsius, and others.*

Although ready for the press as early as 1730, why it had not been published forty years later—years during which Withof himself survived for nearly the whole period—you would not easily say, indeed not even comprehend. Certainly the published specimen proves that Withof contributed a great deal to this undertaking. That specimen, moreover, was reprinted twenty-four years later, in the remarkable circumstance that not a single letter [Col. 0295D] was added—indeed, it was repeated with the very same list of errors. If now you consider that specimen and the author’s manner of commenting, which always wanders into every other subject, you will grasp the cause of the omen. Evidently individual books of the *Ligurinus*, encumbered by that method, would have had to swell into thick volumes, so that one would have found the *Ligurinus* in the *Ligurinus* [Col. 0296A] only with the greatest difficulty. This prediction, not very difficult to make, undoubtedly seems to have alienated the booksellers—and even the favour of scholars—although at that time they fostered large volumes of works. Thus those huge threats came to rest in empty praises, and we saw only the title of the Daedalian work.

## § IX. On the scattered labours of various scholars upon the *Ligurinus*

There can be no doubt that this writer, so dear to our forefathers, read not only by learned persons and in universities but also, by an entirely praiseworthy practice, in German grammar schools, printed eight times over a period of almost two centuries, received many and varied attentions from scholars. This almost astonishing example of favour, when we know that most men spoke of nothing but Greek or Roman matters [Col. 0296B], should also be considered the chief reason why the greater part of such labours remained within private papers.

Among those labours which we have learned were either supplied or intended for public use, the first place belongs to the annotations of Caspar Barth, the most learned polymath of the seventeenth century. The sixty books of *Adversaria* which have so far seen the light offer only a small part of them, and that part serves less to illuminate the *Ligurinus* than to elucidate other writers by means of it. We also owe a very few others to Feller’s noble service to Georg Christian Joannis, who placed them in their proper locations. But we have learned from competent witnesses that a very rich harvest lay concealed in the withdrawn manuscript one hundred and twenty books of *Adversaria* [Col. 0296C]. Chief among these witnesses is Christian Daumius, Barth’s contemporary and intimate acquaintance, who spoke of them as follows [Note: [Col. 0296D] Letter to Reinesius, in Thomas Reinesius’s *Letters to Christian Daumius*, edited by J. A. Bosius, Jena, 1670, quarto, pp. 77–78]:

> He had long ago filled the whole of the poet Gunther with marginal notes, though he had not yet copied everything into those “three” volumes beyond what he observed on Book I. The entire “one hundred and eightieth book of the *Adversaria*” was devoted to Gunther’s second book, beginning with these words, which I shall copy out in order to satisfy both my garrulity and no less my fidelity: “Having begun to edit Gunther, a writer of German stock and name and by far the most outstanding poet of all the later age, we have advanced to his second book.”

Afterwards all memory of Barth’s papers was entirely lost; in our own times it was revived by the accidental inquiry of a learned Frenchman [Col. 0296D] [Note: [Col. 0296D] *General Literary Advertiser*, 1797, no. 151, p. 1557 ff.]. This occurred under favourable auspices indeed, since the highly regretted literary correspondence established shortly afterwards by the Leipzig bookseller Friedrich Roch pursued the inquiry vigorously once more [Note: [Col. 0296D] *General Literary Advertiser*, 1798, no. 74, p. 763 ff.; 1799, no. 182, p. 1815 col., no. 199, p. 2016 ff.; 1800, no. 203, p. 2016 ff.; 1801, no. 180, p. 1729 ff.]. There is no doubt that the counsels of many would eventually have brought the matter to certain evidence [Col. 0297A], had not that excellent undertaking collapsed through the death of its originator under adverse fate. For matters had already reached such a point that the method of further inquiry seemed, as it were, pointed out with the fingers; and I strongly suspect that the reputation of some scholar of great name would have been seriously imperilled had the affair proceeded further. Finally, Friedrich Roch himself supplied evidence of the greatest weight, with noble and at the same time restrained candour. For how eagerly, and no less shamelessly, certain scholars coveted Barth’s posthumous writings was observed immediately upon the death of that distinguished man. Notable in this regard is the passage in Daumius [Note: [Col. 0297C] Loc. cit., p. 223]:

> Hands, if not keen-scented, at least grasping, have long hung over the *Adversaria* of Barth, *τοῦ μακαρίτου*—“of the blessed deceased,” who is to be buried tomorrow—against the will of his most noble widow. Matthias von der Lage claimed them for himself, but was compelled publicly to restore them; he did not fulfil the wish of correcting my hastily composed funeral poem, afterwards sent in a somewhat improved form.

The loss of Caspar Barth’s annotations must therefore still be lamented, apart from those few published ones. A smaller part was in the *Adversaria*, which we understand were continued only as far as Book 180, and that book was at last devoted to the second book of the *Ligurinus*; the very much larger remainder was in papers, unless perhaps one or the other may someday be brought forth. All those which we have seen are very brief, usually bare, often bold, not rarely fortunate, at times rash, and almost extemporaneous. [Note: [Col. 0297C] An example occurs in *Adversaria*, p. 1259, where on “Gunther, no inept poet,” Book III, verse 220:

> [lacuna] scarcely inspired by the whole Apollo  
> Either Virgil or great Homer could equal these things by their fates.

He says that *factis* (“by deeds”) should be read, since it is wrongly printed *fatis* (“by fates”). Yet in no edition whatever is there either *factis* or *fatis*; all have *verbis* (“by words”), as Barth himself gives elsewhere (*Adversaria*, p. 2529).] Barth, evidently, owes all his best work to the acuteness of his natural talent [Col. 0297C] and judgment and to his immense learning, but little to sustained reflection. Hence he is an example not for others, but only for himself; he is altogether to be counted among those men whom one would more properly admire than imitate.

There are also reported corrections of the *Ligurinus* by Lipsius, Casaubon, and Heinsius, men of the highest rank, though it has not yet been my lot to see any of them. Withof alone, so far as I know, mentions them in the title of his announced edition. His frequent intercourse with learned Dutchmen, especially with his teacher Burman, and his familiarity with their studies, may have afforded him access to annotations of this kind, both published and unpublished; and I fear that he may have anticipated certain conjectures of distinguished men, as well as those of others.
