For my own part, that I too might at some time be permitted to use them, I should very much wish for a guiding hand from some scholar favourable to our labours.

We have already spoken of Withof’s specimen on the *Ligurinus* with regard to its forms and editions. There are also other conjectures by that most learned man on the *Ligurinus*, published by him here and there almost playfully. Thus we read a passage in the *Ligurinus* most happily corrected and appended to the *Oration in Memory of the Augsburg Confession* [Note: [Col. 0297C] Duisburg, 1727, folio]. Very many others, however, which, according to his own testimony, he published separately [Note: [Col. 0298C] *Emperor Frederick’s Invented Treading upon Heads, Quite New Proofs, Together with a Passage from Gunther: Four Pieces*, Duisburg *Intelligence Gazette*, 1737, no. 5 ff. *Fifteen Discourses on the Most Distinguished Deeds and Achievements of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, together with the Correction of Many Remarkable Passages in Gunther’s Ligurinus*, ibid., 1747], we have so far requested in vain through public appeals [Col. 0298B]. In conjectural criticism Withof is not seldom fortunate, so far as he was able to achieve it by acuteness or recollection of the ancients. Yet he was not very knowledgeable about medieval Latin and had occupied himself with the sources of the *Ligurinus* to no avail. Hence it happened that he sometimes attributed to the author matters contrary to the character of that age, since he recalled almost everything to the standard of ancient elegance. We have observed this fault of criticism exceeding its proper bounds in others too, and for that reason may judge that his excessive complaints about the extremely corrupt text of the *Ligurinus* were in large part unfounded. Further, he showed great arrogance, insolent boldness [Note: [Col. 0298C] Van Staveren calls him “a most audacious critic” in his *New Miscellaneous Critical Observations*], and shameless rashness in judging others. Finally, we have found not a few corrections anticipated by Pithou, Rittershusius, and Barth, and judged that these should be restored to their respective authors. For the eighth edition had long since become known in Withof’s time, and it can neither be proved nor reasonably believed that he encountered it merely by chance.

The most recent conjectures on the *Ligurinus* known to us are those of Cornelius Valerius Vonck. Their number is small, however, and their acuteness rarer; so that, apart from three or four, the rest corrupt the text rather than assist it. Nor can I wholly subscribe to the judgment of that most learned author and of the eminent Saxius with him, that no fewer blemishes had been wiped from the books of the *Ligurinus*.

[Note: [Col. 0299] Two daughters died before marriage, having been betrothed to Soldanus of Iconium and Richard, Count of Poitou.]

[Col. 0299]

# DISSERTATION II ON THE *LIGURINUS*

## On the origin, lineage, and deeds of Frederick I Augustus, especially during the first decade of his reign

“To extend fame by deeds.” (VIRGIL.)

## § I. The ancient seat of the Hohenstaufens and the first growth of the family

[Col. 0299A]

Among the illustrious families of the Germans which, with fortune as the companion of valour, possessed the height of royal power for a long time, the renowned line of the Hohenstaufens won for itself by far the foremost distinction. For from the first, as it were, auspices of fame down to the final fate of its descendants, it stood bravely for the rights of the Caesars and of the Empire; and, preserving the majesty of royal power in an unbroken course of deeds, it fell in a most glorious death. The more ancient seat of the Hohenstaufens, however, may not implausibly be sought in the eastern parts of Swabia, near the town long since an imperial free city, Schwäbisch Gmünd, and specifically at the place called Buren [Note: [Col. 0301D] An excellent description of those regions, and especially of the Hohenstaufen castle together with the adjacent monuments, is supplied from the sixteenth century by Martin Crusius, *Swabian Annals*, part III, Book XII, chapter 35, and passim; for its most recent appearance see “The Pilgrimage to Hohenstaufen,” in the highly valuable little book entitled *Herda; Tales and Pictures from the German Past*, etc., by J. G. Pahl, part II, Freiburg, 1812, p. 151 ff.—There, p. 175, is the conjecture concerning Buren, to which we wholly subscribe on the most weighty evidence of Wibald, Letter 384 (Martène and Durand, vol. II, p. 557). Compare Schöpflin, *Alsatia Illustrated*, vol. II, p. 557 ff.]. Traces of ancient remembrance still remain in that district: namely, the village named Wäschenbeuren and, in the neighbouring area, a stretch of meadows still today designated by the name Buren. Frederick I either built the castle of Hohenstaufen upon, or at least restored it upon, the adjoining mountain about the middle of the eleventh century; and, according to the solemn custom of the time, adopted thence the surname of his family. This Frederick was a count on the side of Emperor Henry IV against Rudolf, the anti-Caesar; a good man, vigorous in war, steadfast in spirit and loyalty. Therefore, most acceptable to the Emperor and established in these regions as the author and defender of his interests, he obtained the rich duchy of Swabia, taken from the rebel Rudolf, and as wife the king’s only daughter Agnes [Col. 0301B].

## § II. Frederick II, surnamed Cocles or Monoculus, candidate for the Empire; his deeds on the Rhine

The wealth of the Hohenstaufens was immediately increased, Henry V, their maternal uncle, also favouring the aspirations of his nephews. Thus, when the emperor finally died, Frederick II, son of Frederick I and heir of the Swabian duchy [Note: [Col. 0301D] At that time a certain Count Frederick, taking his surname from the noblest counts of Swabia, had established a colony in the castle called Stoyphe. Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick I*, Book I, chapter 8], rose to hope for the Empire—and would have obtained his desire, had he not had the Archbishop of Mainz as an adversary. For this man, the bitterest enemy of the Hohenstaufens, cleverly forestalled Frederick’s plans and hastened the votes of the Saxon nobles in favour of Lothair [Note: [Col. 0302D] Anonymous, *Narrative of the Election of Lothair*, in Pez, *Writers on Austrian Affairs*, vol. I, p. 570 ff.]. This was, of course, that same Archbishop of Mainz who had once been chancellor to Emperor Henry V and, raised by his special favour to the primacy of Germany [Col. 0301C], acted as a traitor, forgetful of his benefits. Accordingly, having been committed to custody and shortly afterwards restored by the armed action of the citizens, he omitted nothing that might be attempted against the absent emperor in a hostile spirit, everywhere mingling the lowest with the highest. Then Duke Frederick of Swabia crossed the Rhine with an army and checked every disturbance by his powerful authority [Note: [Col. 0302D] He fortified many castles along the whole bank of the Rhine, so that it passed into a proverb: “Duke Frederick always drags a castle behind the tail of his horse.” Otto of Freising, loc. cit., chapter 12]. Soon afterwards he attacked Mainz itself, the workshop of disturbances, with war and enclosed it in a siege, restraining his soldiers, as best he could, from devastation. Then, when the exceedingly crafty prelate sought a truce, Frederick generously granted it, intending himself to return home with a few companions after dismissing the army. The bishop immediately pursued him with a large force of soldiers, contrary to the faith of his oath, and prepared to destroy him when surrounded on every side [Col. 0301D]. But Frederick, suddenly [Col. 0302A] disturbed by the treachery to no purpose and greater than his dangers, gathered a band of his few companions and charged the men of Mainz. Having inflicted immense slaughter, he routed the attackers and continued cutting down the fugitives even to the gates, so that only very few escaped the avenging sword. Then the greatest danger threatened the bishop himself. Barely received within the walls, he almost turned upon himself the curses—and indeed the arms—of the citizens, who with fierce outcry cursed the bishop as author of the deadly deed and the homes bereft of parents [Note: [Col. 0302D] Ibid., chapter 13]. From this came that man’s most hostile disposition toward the Swabian, and the stealthily won favour of the princes for Lothair. For what is more bitter than cowardice when offended? What is more vehement than the hatred of a priest?

## § III. The quarrels of the Hohenstaufen brothers with the new king, Lothair

[Col. 0302B]

Frederick, bearing most indignantly the loss of the kingdom wrested from him, only at last, on the third day after the election, prevailed upon by the prayers of many, greeted the king in the assembly; he wholly rejected the 200 marks offered to him as a benefice. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Anonymous narrative cited above, § 7, p. 573.] Hence the duke’s disposition appeared doubtful, as the beginnings of a new reign are seldom free from suspicions. Soon a decree was made in the assembly at Regensburg: fiefs taken from the unworthy were to be reclaimed not for the king’s patrimony but for the goods of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Dodechin, Appendix to Marianus Scotus, under the year 1125.] Lothair, indeed, carried this out with excessive eagerness, plainly directing it against the Staufen possessions and reclaiming for the kingdom very many holdings retained by the Swabian brothers. Frederick was declared an enemy in the next assembly at Strasbourg; in the following spring the king marched against the duke.

By chance his brother Conrad, duke of Eastern Franconia, was then absent, having recently set out for Palestine with a chosen body of soldiers to aid the Christians in their distress. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Chronicle of Ursperg, under the year 1124.] Thus the whole weight of the war fell upon Frederick. By prudent counsel, avoiding the hazard of battle and keeping himself within the fortified strongholds of Alsace, he safely frustrated every attempt of his enemies. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Saxon Annals, under the year 1126.] Meanwhile Conrad returned from the expedition, suddenly united his forces with his brother’s, and prosecuted their common cause—an enemy no less hostile and more dangerous. The brothers occupied the castle of Nuremberg and furnished it with a strong garrison against sudden contingencies. In response Lothair won over Duke Henry of Bavaria, the Staufens’ brother-in-law, having given him his only daughter Gertrude in marriage. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Same source, under the year 1127.—Frederick had married Henry’s sister Judith, who had died the preceding year. Koeler, *Familia Augusta Stauffensis*, p. 9.] This added great weight to the king’s side, not merely because the two families’ interests were divided, but because they were now directly opposed. [Col. 0302D]

[Col. 0303A] Yet the king pressed his new fortune too importunately, immediately attacking Nuremberg with his forces. When the Swabians approached, he abandoned the siege and, not even daring to risk battle, withdrew in disgrace. The victors, returning in turn and gathering an army as though they meant to undertake something substantial, easily captured the town of Speyer, expelling its bishop in a facile triumph.

## § IV. Conrad seeks the kingdom

With the Staufens’ arms thus flourishing, the support of many began to converge upon them. Elated in spirit, they planned ever greater enterprises and returned to the hope of empire. Conrad, now assuming the royal title at the urging of his brother Frederick and his friends, hastened to Italy. There [Col. 0303B] he was received above all with immense applause by the Milanese, and was crowned king of Italy by Archbishop Anselm, first at Monza and then at Milan. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Landulf the Younger, *History of Milan*, ch. 39 (in Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. V, pp. 510 ff.).] Travelling through the Lombard cities, he drew very many to his side by gifts or arms, except those held back by hatred of the Milanese rather than by hostility to his cause. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Lithifrid of Novara, Letter to Lothair (in Eccard, *Corpus Historiae Medii Aevi*, vol. II, p. 364, no. 354); cf. Landulf, cited work, p. 512.]

But Pope Honorius soon gravely disturbed the hitherto auspicious course of events. Attached to King Lothair, whose election he had approved, he awaited his coronation. Thus, in an unusual instance for those times, unconcerned by the Roman populace, he feared nothing from Conrad as he approached through Tuscany: he barred him from the city and solemnly consigned him, together with his brother Frederick, to curses. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 17; Saxon Annals, under the year 1128.] More than anything else, the political situation made the blow of the thunderbolt fatal: on the one hand certain most noble cities hated Milan; on the other, fear of Roger of Sicily threatened; and on both sides the weight supporting the Roman party increased. Conrad’s fortunes accordingly declined, and his companions deserted as his money was exhausted. He remained for the most part at Parma, languishing in enforced idleness.

That he was heavily indebted to the city and, as it were, detained there captive may be understood from this: he handed over to the Parmesans as a hostage, for the debt he had contracted, Archbishop Meginher of Trier, whom he had seized while returning from Rome. This Meginher, while he was in Germany, had been suspect because of his attachment to the Swabians; perhaps he received the pallium in order to support Lothair. Certainly, he had now been sent by Honorius to proclaim the anathema. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Saxius’s notes on Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book XI, p. 659 (Muratori ed.). Mascov should therefore be corrected in his *Commentary on Lothair II*, etc., p. 23.] At last [Col. 0303D], with King Lothair approaching and all hope abandoned, Conrad secretly departed from Italy. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Otto of Freising, cited work, ch. 18.] [Col. 0304A] I do not know whether he was not released by means of the Trier hostage, since the chronology fits exactly.

## § V. War with the Swabians in Germany

While this was occurring among the Italians, Frederick at home sustained the attacks of his enemies, aided manfully by his wife. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Namely his second wife, Agnes, daughter of the count of Saarbrücken and niece of Albert, archbishop of Mainz, whom Frederick had defeated.] They achieved nothing so long as they fought separately. Henry, unable even to endure the sight of Frederick, fled shamefully. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick I*, book I, ch. 18.] Having vainly resorted to deception, he incurred still greater disgrace. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Ibid., ch. 19.] The king, meanwhile, was induced to withdraw from Speyer, which he had besieged, after arranging a truce. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Saxon Annals, under the year 1128.]

Then the two brothers joined their forces and again attacked Speyer, which could be taken only after a long siege and not without an agreement. Frederick’s wife, it seems, defended the town stoutly and, when matters were finally desperate, yielded more to hunger than to arms. [Col. 0304B] She herself was received with the highest admiration by the men; she and her people were allowed to depart freely, and the king made her gifts, though she lacked nearly everything. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Chronicle of Ursperg, p. 277 (Basel ed., 1569).] From this point the Staufens’ power began to waver, especially under the pressure of Henry of Bavaria, who overran almost the whole duchy of Swabia as far as Staufen Castle, devastating it with fire and sword. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Ibid., same passage.] Soon Nuremberg too surrendered when Lothair attacked it. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Saxon Annals, under the year 1130.] Further curses were pronounced through Innocent’s legate in the assembly at Würzburg, before sixteen bishops. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Ibid.] Nevertheless Frederick, still unbroken in spirit, continued to resist the king. When the king attacked the duke with an army, and Frederick did not offer battle, he departed without accomplishing anything.

## § VI. The Staufens, as suppliants, are received into favour

[Col. 0304C]

The king set out for Italy with a small force. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Mascov, cited work, ch. 27, p. 43.] He vigorously conducted the exiled Pope Innocent to Rome, restored him to his see, and was crowned emperor of the Romans by him in the Lateran palace. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Saxon Annals, under the year 1133.] The basilica of St Peter was held by the antipope Anacletus, relying on the resources of his faction. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, end of ch. 18.] Thereafter, having successfully conducted many affairs throughout Italy, he secured for himself great admiration among both peoples and was received in Germany with the strongest support of his adherents. Milan alone still upheld Conrad’s cause, Lothair not venturing anything against so powerful a city. [Note: [Col. 0304D] Mascov, cited work, note 3 at the end, pp. 329 ff.]

Pope Honorius had earlier deprived Archbishop Anselm of sacred functions, after convening a council at Pavia following Conrad’s departure, [Note: [Col. 0304D] Landulf the Younger, *History of Milan*, cited passage, and the learned Saxius’s note there, p. 512.] and Anselm was soon to leave his see. Thus [Col. 0304D] the Staufen dukes, abandoning their cause, came to their senses, Frederick taking the lead in the assembly at Fulda. For Henry of Bavaria, after a war against the Swabians had recently been decreed, forestalled the emperor’s final resources: he took the very strongly fortified city of Ulm at the first assault and destroyed it by fire. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Saxon Annals, under the year 1134.] Thus, when the emperor arrived, Frederick received back only his dependants after they had pledged faith.

Then the duke, reduced to extremity, came as a suppliant to Empress Richenza at Fulda. He was not admitted to the emperor’s presence, but was summoned to the next assembly and immediately released from the curses by the apostolic legate. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Same source, under the year 1135.] In the following year, Lothair the emperor saw the most valiant Duke Frederick standing before him as a suppliant in the very crowded assembly held at Bamberg. Certainly this was a hard lot for the man, though not altogether undeserved. Nor is it easy to say whether, by an example of such severity, the emperor aimed more at the dignity of the empire and the interests of the commonwealth [Col. 0305B] than at the impulses of his own mind.

Frederick, however, aside from his humiliation and the obedience sworn to Caesar, was dismissed unharmed and promised his forces for the Italian expedition. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Ibid.] He might perhaps have suffered more severely had not the pope, who in fear of Roger of Sicily pressed the expedition with all his strength, devoted every effort to reconciling the princes. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Same source, under the year 1136.] Conrad followed his brother Frederick after an interval of five months, and appears not to have received precisely the same terms of pardon or the same treatment. He too came as a suppliant before the king in the full assembly at Mühlhausen; he was released in their presence from the curses by Conrad, archbishop of Magdeburg. Yet he was received back into favour far more readily and experienced something like the favour of his former distinction. [Col. 0305C] Lothair assigned him first place among the dukes, restored all his possessions, and, having entrusted him with the imperial standard, admitted him to a position next to the royal person. [Note: [Col. 0305D] Bosau Annals, under the year 1135 (in Eccard, *Corpus Historiae Medii Aevi*, vol. I, p. 1011); Godfrey of Viterbo, *Pantheon*, part XVII (in Muratori, cited work, vol. VII, p. 459); Landulf of Milan, cited work, ch. 41. The Saxon Annalist, under this year, must not be heard, since he maliciously defiles the course of events in his annotation, as is manifest from his recognized partiality for the Swabians.]

Moreover, Conrad promised assistance for the proposed Italian expedition, brought it in full, and very bravely aided the emperor with both the counsel and arms of the greatest princes. These services should therefore be attributed wholly to the impulses of a noble spirit rather than to conscience. Thus the monstrous wars of nine years, ended on sufficiently equitable terms, at last subsided—wars all the more disastrous to the German commonwealth because of the greater power of the contestants and the more ruinous example the men set for public peace.

## § VII. Death of Lothair; Conrad, king of the Germans

[Col. 0305D]

The most pious emperor did not long enjoy the fruits of his labours [Col. 0306A] and his victory. Soon, having put Germany’s affairs in some order, he set out again for Italy, never to see his home again. Burdened by old age, he was struck by illness on the return journey; nevertheless, hastening onward in longing for his homeland, he succumbed to the strength of the disease in an obscure village of the Trentine valley. [Note: [Col. 0305D] 3 December 1137. Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 20; Saxon Annals under this year; Chronicle of Ursperg, p. 278, middle.] He left all men with the greatest longing for him.

Lothair having died without sons, Henry of Bavaria both entertained and pursued the highest hope of empire. In addition to his blood relationship and the renown gained by his deeds in Italy, he was distinguished by extraordinary power and displayed the deceased emperor’s favour and the insignia of the kingdom entrusted to him. [Note: [Col. 0306D] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick I*, book I, ch. 22.] But this same Henry, inflated with the utmost arrogance, had provoked everyone’s envy during the Italian expedition [Note: [Col. 0306D] Mascov, cited work, book II, ch. 2, p. 115.] and was still regarded with suspicion because of his very power.

Conrad, on the contrary, was commended by pity for the dignity taken from him, by his most generous services to equals and inferiors, and especially by the influence of the bishop of Trier, his close friend. [Col. 0306B] For at that time the see of Mainz was vacant, since Albert, that most hostile enemy of the Staufens, had died shortly before; authority was consequently in the hands of the bishop of Trier. [Note: [Col. 0306D] Ibid.] The most upright support of his brother Frederick also aided him, [Note: [Col. 0306D] Otto of Freising, cited work.] as did Conrad’s own skill in conducting affairs. Taking the most opportune advantage of the growing hostility between Henry of Bavaria and Albert the Bear of Brandenburg, he had roused a formidable opponent against his rival.

Accordingly, when the assembly was convened by the bishop of Trier at Koblenz [Note: [Col. 0306D] 22 February 1138.], in the presence of the bishops of Trier and Worms [Col. 0306C] and of Conrad himself with his most faithful brother Frederick, Conrad was unanimously proclaimed king of the Germans. [Note: [Col. 0306D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 22.] Theodwin the cardinal, a Swabian by birth [Note: [Col. 0306D] Chronicle of Lüneburg in Mascov, cited work, p. 117, no. 4.], legate of Pope Innocent II, supported this by every means. [Note: [Col. 0306D] Otto of Freising, cited work.] He was soon brought to Aachen and, in the seat of Saint Charles, raised according to ancient rite. [Note: [Col. 0306D] 6 March.] The aforementioned Theodwin performed the sacred ceremonies, since the archbishop of Cologne had not yet received the pallium. Thus at last, after varied reversals of fortune and immense labours, the most noble Conrad attained his desire and inaugurated the august Staufen line under happy auspices.

## § VIII. The election is attacked in vain

The news struck Henry of Saxony and Bavaria and his friends with the greatest consternation, as was natural. [Col. 0306D] All loudly declared the election illegitimate and surreptitious, [Note: [Col. 0306D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 22; Saxon Annals under the year 1138.] while many leading men throughout Bavaria, above all the venerable aged bishop of Salzburg, disapproved what had been done, as the disturbances of war increased throughout Saxony. King Conrad, however, vigorously exercising imperial authority, appointed a date at Bamberg and there held an assembly on the feast of Pentecost. Very many Saxon princes came with Empress Richenza herself and, from fear, greeted the king. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Otto of Freising, cited work, ch. 23; Bosau Annals under this year, p. 1012; cf. Mascov, cited work, p. 119, note *.]

Proud Henry and most of the Bavarian nobles, by contrast, were still absent. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Dodechin, under the year 1138, p. 472.] Conrad therefore fixed a further date in the heart of Bavaria, to be held at Regensburg. There the archbishop of Salzburg, consulting for the peace of the realm, came to King Conrad, together with other princes who followed the man’s example. When Duke Conrad of Zähringen voluntarily pressed him in the full assembly to render homage to the king, he received this reply:

> “See, my lord duke: if you were a wagon, you would not hesitate to run before the oxen. The matter between myself and my lord king will be decided in such a way that you will find no concern of yours in it.”

The king, fearing harsher abuse from the men, restrained the agitated duke from replying by amicably covering his mouth with his turned hand; at the same time he publicly declared that he desired nothing from the bishop except goodwill. [Note: [Col. 0307D] *Life of Conrad, Bishop of Salzburg*, ch. 4.] This restraint of the king won him considerable favour with the whole assembly, particularly turning the clergy’s minds toward him. Henry of Bavaria also appeared in person, now wholly anxious about his own position, having abandoned hope of the kingdom; enticed by great promises, he surrendered the insignia. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Otto of Freising, cited work.] But because agreement could not be reached on the varying terms proposed on each side, [Col. 0307C] the assembly was dissolved and the date postponed to Augsburg. For Conrad, once he had received the royal insignia, which were always held to be of great importance, seems to have turned his mind to entirely different matters and to have thought little about peace.

## § IX. Negotiations abandoned; Henry proscribed

The very nature of affairs foretold that an agreement would be uncertain and dangerous; recent memory of calamities made it a perpetual spark of war. Henry of Bavaria followed the king to Augsburg with a substantial force of soldiers and encamped on the river Lech not far from the city; the king conducted himself peacefully within the walls. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Chronicle of Ursperg, p. 279.] Messengers and mediators passed frequently in both directions, neither party to the negotiations yielding anything to the other. Conrad demanded back certain fiefs of the duke granted by Lothair; when Henry imperiously refused, the king, distrusting the man’s intentions and the character of the place and alarmed by his brother’s example, broke off the affair and left the city by night. [Col. 0308A] With a few loyal followers he made for Franconia.

Soon, after an assembly had been held at Würzburg, Henry was suddenly proscribed—certainly by a judgment far too hasty and unworthy of that king. Conrad, setting aside both the majesty and safety of the realm and indulging only his anger, immediately assigned the duchy of Saxony in the next assembly at Goslar to Albert of Brandenburg, Henry’s bitterest enemy. Then, going to Bavaria, he awarded the duchy of that land to his uterine brother, Leopold V, margrave of Austria. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 23.] Very few princes had joined in this violence of the king; the assemblies especially at Goslar and Quedlinburg were therefore regarded as almost private. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Saxon Annals under the year 1139. There was, of course, a notable difference between a private assembly and a full or solemn one, and the authority of each was altogether different. The former accompanied the king; in the latter public business was transacted and fixed functions were assigned to the princes.]

## § X. The Saxon-Bavarian war; the battle of Weinsberg

[Col. 0308B] Leopold of Austria [Note: [Col. 0307D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 25.] and Albert of Brandenburg lost no time in taking possession of the duchies entrusted to them. Albert, greedily eager for his new dignity, ranged widely through Saxony under arms, intending to assert to his authority not only the rights he had undertaken but every adherent of Lothair. [Note: [Col. 0308D] Helmold, *Chronicle of the Slavs*, book I, ch. 54.] Immediately after the emperor’s death, he had disputed the duchy of Saxony with Henry of Bavaria on hereditary grounds. Attacked by the united forces of many of Henry’s friends and of Empress Richenza herself, he had emerged victorious from battle. [Note: [Col. 0308D] Saxon Annals under the year 1138.]

Now far fiercer disturbances boiled throughout Germany, and Henry’s courage, less conspicuous in prosperity, shone in adversity. Of the few who stood by his fortunes, he took only four with him into Saxony; the rest followed by various routes under the pretext of pilgrimage. With these men he suddenly attacked Albert of Brandenburg, plundered very many of his strongholds, and in a short time drove him from the whole duchy, compelling him to flee to the king. Then he confronted Conrad himself as he arrived with an army and, displaying courage in battle, brought him to agree to a truce. [Note: [Col. 0308D] Chronicle of Ursperg, pp. 279 ff.; Otto of Freising, ch. 25; Helmold, ch. 56.]

The authority of the bishop of Trier was paramount in this affair, together with the clever resourcefulness of a man shrewd in the ways of his time and people. He had promised to attend the king with twenty thousand men, but brought only five hundred, along with innumerable dishes of food and thirty cartloads of wine. Distributing these liberally to the princes, he easily brought the affair to a settlement and subdued it without bloodshed. [Col. 0308D] For he judged that an abundance of wine and other provisions contributed more to victory and to inflaming men’s courage than many thousands of hungry men. [Note: [Col. 0308D] *Deeds of the Archbishops of Trier*, in Martène and Durand, vol. IV, p. 200.]

Henry, having restored affairs in Saxony and planning from there to move into Bavaria, was cut off by sudden death. [Note: [Col. 0308D] The Saxon Annalist, under the year 1139, hints at poisoning; but no contemporary corroborates this suspect testimony. The *Chronicle of Petersberg*, nearly two centuries later and of no greater authority, is the source on which Hahnius relies from Fabricius’s notes (*Reichshist.* III, 210).] [Col. 0309A] He left among the Saxons an illustrious memory of himself and the highest goodwill toward his little son. The vain and frivolous efforts of the Brandenburg margrave counted for little against the people’s affection and the most prudent alliances of the archbishop of Magdeburg. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Mascov, cited work, p. 125, note *.]

Bavaria, moreover, had been entrusted to Henry’s brother, that most noble Welf, renowned among princes for military glory and virtues: count palatine of Tübingen, and powerful in lands throughout Swabia and on the Rhine by marital title, as heir of Uta, daughter of Godfrey, count of Calw and count palatine of Tübingen. Welf successfully defeated Leopold of Austria [Note: [Col. 0309D] Monk of Weingarten, ch. 13.] and stoutly maintained the war, aided especially by Roger of Sicily’s money and by Géza, king of Pannonia—each of whom intended to entangle Conrad at home. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Godfrey of Viterbo, cited work; Monk of Weingarten, cited work.]

He even took the offensive against the king, who was besieging Weinsberg Castle; [Col. 0309B] but, under ill-omened auspices, he fought, was defeated, and put to flight in that most celebrated battle, memorable in the annals of Germany for the hereditary party emblems. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Twice cited. On the feast of St Thomas, that is, 21 December 1140. Otto of Freising, cited work; Trithemius, cited work.] These names, through a corruption of their meaning, had become established as labels for utterly different factions, long disastrous to the peace of the commonwealth. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Mascov, cited work, p. 141.] No less famous was the ensuing surrender of the castle itself, when the noble action of the women outwitted the king’s anger. Conrad’s celebrated answer is also praised: “The faith of kings is unchangeable.” [Note: [Col. 0309D] Chronicle of St Pantaleon, cited work, p. 931.] That is, it befits a king publicly to do what might be neglected privately.

## § XI. Saxony secured for the Welfs; the Italian expedition impeded; alliance with the Byzantines; Staufen-Zähringen war

[Col. 0309C] This victory brought little benefit against the Saxons, whom the king had hitherto laboured in vain to bring to his wishes; [the damaged phrase concerning the count of Würzburg is uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Mascov, cited work.] For what can arms or stratagems accomplish against a united people? The death of the Austrian duke was therefore opportune, since he left no offspring. [Note: [Col. 0309D] October 1141. Chronicle of Melk under this year.] The duchy was given to Henry, his brother, and a marriage was arranged with Gertrude, widow of Henry the Proud.

Saxony was secured by agreement for young Henry, son of Henry the Proud, afterwards distinguished by the epithet “the Lion.” At his mother’s persuasion, he renounced his claims to Bavaria. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Otto of Freising, cited work; Dodechin under the year 1142; Chronicle of St Pantaleon, cited work.] Albert of Brandenburg, persuaded by the archbishop of Mainz, laid aside the title duke of Saxony and was restored to the old March, receiving at the same time what he had lost in war. The marriage was celebrated immediately in the presence of the assembly, with royal expense and magnificence; public joy was all the greater [Col. 0309D] because the long discord of the two houses had been so much sadder. Not so with Welf, who stubbornly asserted his hereditary right to Bavaria and, carrying war and seditions now here, now there, persisted in stirring up perpetual disturbances in martial zeal. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Otto of Freising, cited work; Trithemius, cited work, under the year 1142, p. 410.]

The king, seriously considering the assumption of the imperial crown and invited by the Italians themselves, especially the Venetians, through their fear of Roger, was deterred by the pope’s equivocal settlement with that Sicilian. Yet the pope did not delay to appease the man by a solemn embassy. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Trithemius, cited work, p. 411.] Among the envoys were Theodwin, dear to the king for his proven loyalty, and the celebrated Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. The king then resumed his plan and sent envoys to the pope to agree upon the arrangements. An alliance with John of Byzantium, formerly concluded by Lothair, was also renewed. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Saxon Annals under the year 1135.] At the same time the queen’s sister was betrothed to Manuel Comnenus, son of John.

This was Bertha, daughter of the count of Sulzbach, most beloved by King Conrad and regarded altogether as his daughter. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Letter of Abbot Guibald, no. 188, cited work, p. 375.] The Greeks called her Irene. [Col. 0310B] Moreover, she was highly praised by Greek writers for the beauty of her appearance, her exceptional gifts of mind, and even her learning in Greek letters. Accordingly, while she lived, German affairs enjoyed great prosperity and most abundant advantages at Byzantium, since she always pursued her homeland with uncorrupted goodwill and fostered the friendship of the two courts with most noble devotion.

Meanwhile the affairs of the Italians were increasingly disturbed, as very many cities fought each other and the city of Rome, after Innocent’s death, was agitated by factions. The chief leader and author of these was Arnold of Brescia, the famous pupil of Abelard: a man of subtle intellect, excellently learned, and of blameless—indeed, austere—conduct. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Bernard of Clairvaux, Letter 195 (Mabillon ed., Paris, 1690).] [Col. 0310C] Attacking the dissolute morals of clerics and the luxury of monks, he was received everywhere with immense applause from crowds. Delighted by popular favour, he advanced the following propositions: that the clergy should possess nothing of their own according to the rule of Holy Scripture; that they should have no secular power, no fixed revenues, much less abundant ones; that after completing sacred duties they should live chastely on the alms of the devout, avoid the ambition for honours, and wholly abstain from earthly things.

Then he urged the people to assert their own rights, appoint magistrates, and administer affairs in the ancient order; to remove the Church’s rulers, and thereby restrict the imperial regalian rights. From this came an astonishing reversal of affairs: hatreds of the clergy, persecutions, and killings, [Note: [Col. 0310D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book VII, ch. 31; same author, *Deeds of Frederick I*, book II, ch. 28; cf. Guibald, letters nos. 211, 212, 213, and passim, pp. 396 ff.] and, at last, insofar as their resources allowed, the ridiculous revival of ancient Rome. [Note: [Col. 0310D] I find the learned Simonde de Sismondi treating these matters far too seriously in *History of the Italian Republics*, vol. II, pp. 34 ff.]

Solicited by frequent letters from both pope and people, [Col. 0310D] [Note: [Col. 0310D] See no. 1.] who competed in accusing one another, the king prudently held himself in the middle, declaring the majesty of the kingdom by letters, envoys, and royal diplomas. [Col. 0311A] For neither was the faith of the popes secure, nor were the people’s complaints wholly empty; even Abbot Bernard’s unwelcome eloquence showed this. [Note: [Col. 0311C] For he indulged too greatly the authority of the popes and his own affections, being accustomed rashly to condemn and inconsiderately to assail whatever displeased him. A most bitter enemy of Abelard and Arnold, see Peter Abelard’s *Apology against Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux* (*Works of Abelard and Heloise*, Paris, 1616, quarto, p. 302 ff.); cf. William Godellus, *Chronicle*, under the year 1137, in Bouquet, vol. XIII, p. 675; Bernard of Clairvaux, letters nos. 189, 195, 196. Cf. Letter to Caesar, no. 244, which the learned Mascov, cited work, p. 156, understands less aptly as written against Roger of Sicily.] Nevertheless, after a brief suspension of the assembly, the privileges of the Roman see were confirmed in their established form, chiefly through the bishops’ assistance.

Domestic disturbances and neighbouring affairs also detained the king from setting out: a fierce war between the bishop of Trier and Henry, count of Namur; serious disputes among the princes of Hungary and Poland; and the kings of both countries, exiles, seeking refuge in the empire. Amid these conflicts came also a hereditary war against Conrad, duke of Zähringen. The ancient hostility of the princes grew stronger, dating from the time when the duchy of Swabia, first fraudulently seized by violence from the Zähringens and afterwards torn from them by war, had fallen to the fortunes of the Staufens. [Col. 0311B] Their neighbouring power was mutually hateful; the Zähringens’ manifest attachment to the Welfs, recently displayed against Conrad, was equally so. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Schoepflin, *History of Zähringen-Baden*, vol. I, p. 167.]

Now the younger Frederick, duke of Swabia and later emperor, having taken the knightly belt and burning with desire to win renown, had not long before displayed a brilliant first campaign in Bavaria. He attacked Conrad, duke of Zähringen, a prince most valiant and wealthy in a double dominion; after storming the strongest bulwarks of war and the hereditary castle itself, he compelled him to implore the king’s mercy. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chs. 25–26.] The principal cause is unclear, [Note: [Col. 0311D] The date is also unclear. But Mascov rightly notes Schoepflin’s error: deceived by a marginal note, he records the year 1138. Schoepflin, cited work; cf. Mascov, cited work, p. 175.] nor should it be investigated too anxiously in view of the character of the time, when a bare desire to fight very often moved men to war. [Note: [Col. 0311D] Thus we read that this same Frederick joined Welf in arms against his own uncle, the king. Chronicle of St Pantaleon under the year 1143, pp. 931 ff.]

## § XII. Conrad’s crusade

[Col. 0311C]

At that time sudden terror had spread through the Christian world because of the most cruel destruction of the city of Edessa in Palestine. [Note: [Col. 0311D] William of Tyre, *History of the Sacred War*, book XVI, chs. 4–5; [Col. 0312C] Supplement to Gembloux, under the year 1146 (in Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol. XIII, p. 273).] This was the beginning of the Turks’ growing power throughout Asia and of their recently expanded empire reaching the borders of the Latins. The kingdom of Jerusalem now seemed at its last extremity, though it had been won by the noble blood and labours of so many thousands. Report, distance, and the lack of aid had, as usual, magnified the enemy’s terror. Hence came immense universal fear and pity for the situation, and trembling expectation of the last day. [Note: [Col. 0312C] Bosau Annals, under the year 1147 (cited work, p. 1013).]

Then the Franks were the first [Col. 0312A] to make vows for military service, [Note: [Col. 0312C] Letter of Abbot Suger, in Mascov, p. 185.] in keeping with the noble ardour of their nation; the king himself was also prompted by private devotion. No less ardent was Pope Eugenius, who stirred up princes everywhere by letters and envoys, while domestic disorders prevented him from personally urging them. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Chronicle of William of Nangis, under the year 1143 [1145], in d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, latest ed., vol. III.]

The central figure in the affair was Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of the greatest authority throughout the West and singularly fitted to stir and lead men’s minds. [Note: [Col. 0312D] I should not without reason call him an orator, whom rhetoricians define as “a good man skilled in speaking.” For that good man, worn down by the prolonged squalor of the wilderness, by fasts and pallor, reduced to a certain thinness of spiritual form, persuades first by his appearance, then by his speech, etc. Guibald, abbot, Letter 147 (cited work, p. 339).]

Having wonderfully dispatched matters in Gaul, Bernard, full of a loftier plan, came up into Germany. There he first met the king secretly at Frankfurt. [Note: [Col. 0312D] This first meeting led some writers falsely to report that the king took the cross at Frankfurt—for example Bernard Gui, *On the Origin of the Kings of the Franks*, and the *Chronicle of Tours* (Bouquet, cited work, vol. XII, pp. 231, 473).] Perceiving that the king was disinclined, he prudently concealed his purpose, saying that it was not for one of his lowliness to press the royal majesty too importunately. Thereupon [Col. 0312B] he departed, remained for some time at Constance, then suddenly changed his route and again confronted Conrad at Speyer. Conrad resisted as though with some presentiment of the coming disaster, but Bernard compelled him with spiritual arms to answer that he would deliberate with the princes.

A few days later, in the midst of the solemnities of the Mass, Bernard burst forth as if by sudden impulse. Straining every sinew of his eloquence, he so overwhelmed the minds of those present that the king, bursting into tears, immediately made his vow. The abbot extended a banner to him before the altar, and he was immediately marked with the cross, together with his nephew Frederick—later emperor of the Romans—and a most numerous train of princes and nobles who followed the king’s example. [Note: [Col. 0312D] *Life of Saint Bernard*, book VI, *On Miracles*, no. 15 (in Bouquet, vol. XIV, p. 378); cf. Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, book I, ch. 39; Robert of Monte, appendix to Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 1146.]

[Col. 0312C] The most valiant Welf was not present at the assembly; on the very night of Christ’s Nativity he had taken the cross with certain other nobles at his own castle of Bitengau. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Otto of Freising, ch. 40.] Throughout Germany an innumerable multitude flocked together, upon hearing the report, to receive the cross from the abbot of York, to whom Bernard had delegated this task. Frederick, duke of Swabia and the king’s brother, took it most grievously that his son had received the cross: the young man was the sole comfort of his feeble old age and the strength of his family. Bernard visited him and filled him with blessing; yet, unable to bear the grief of bereavement, [Col. 0313A] he soon died. [Note: [Col. 0313D] Otto of Freising, ch. 39.]

The pope’s notable arts are also apparent. When he learned of the king’s devotion and was secure regarding the Germans, he rebuked the man in friendly fashion for having undertaken so great a matter without consulting him—[Note: [Col. 0313D] Bernard pressed the expedition by the pope’s command. *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes* (d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 754).]—[Note: [Col. 0313D] Guibald, Letter 20, p. 205.] thus gaining an opportunity either for unpunished arrogance or at least for avoiding blame.

Finally, the Saxons, as always hostile to the Franks, abstained from the enterprise. So as not to yield the glory of zeal, they themselves marched against the nearest enemies of the Christians, the Obotrites and Liutici—that is, Slavs—[Note: [Col. 0313D] Helmold, *Chronicle of the Slavs*, ch. 63.] and used an emblem different from that of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 0313D] They displayed a cross not sewn on, with a wheel beneath it. Otto of Freising, ch. 40.]

Before setting out, Conrad arranged for his son Henry to be made king, no prince opposing; shortly afterwards, at Aachen, he had him crowned and made him his partner in the Empire [Col. 0313B] [Note: [Col. 0313D] Ibid., ch. 43.], thus providing for the kingdom both publicly and privately. Since the youth was not yet fit for the task, Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, was associated with him, according to custom, as counsellor and authority, together with Guibald, Abbot of Corvey [Note: [Col. 0313D] Guibald of Corvey, letters 99, 30, 31, loc. cit., pp. 268, 212.], a most celebrated man of the age, who had been an arbiter in affairs of the realm under four emperors, from Henry V onward. The expedition itself was most disastrous, although the forces of the kings were immense: each army was reckoned at as many as seventy thousand armoured men, apart from the multitudes of infantry and camp-followers [Note: [Col. 0313D] William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, bk. XVI, ch. 22.], of whom very few returned. Conrad spent most of his time at Constantinople, whether ashamed of his diminished army, or because of the princes’ repeated dissensions, and also because his health had failed [Note: [Col. 0313D] Letter of King Conrad to Abbot Guibald, loc. cit., p. 252 ff.].

[Col. 0313C] Yet the king performed a noble deed and striking proof of courage at Damascus: breaking with his Germans through the struggling midst of the Frankish ranks into the Turkish line, he threw the terrified enemy into flight. In that battle he carried off, as a sign of victory, the head of a barbarian soldier, severed together with the right shoulder by a single stroke [Note: [Col. 0313D] *Deeds of King Louis*, ch. 22 (in Mascovius, loc. cit., p. 225).]. Otherwise the undertaking was wholly abandoned, and the departure was disgraceful. Hence arose no small odium against Bernard, who in turn pointed to the pope [Note: [Col. 0314D] Otto of Freising, ch. 60; Geoffrey, *Life of St Bernard*, bk. III, ch. 4, §9.]. Nor was the suspicion altogether groundless that Pope Eugenius, aided by Bernard’s efforts, had sought glory for the Cistercian order. For both belonged to the same rule, long before restored through Bernard’s efforts [Note: [Col. 0314D] *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, loc. cit.]; and the Cistercians themselves afterwards opposed with all their strength the proposal for a new expedition [Note: [Col. 0314D] Otto of Freising, chs. 29, 42.]. The sole and unique consolation amid such great losses was that the favour of very many princes and of the expedition caused men to refrain from arms, [Col. 0313D] so that the sad storms of battle were sometimes stilled by a remedy sadder still [Col. 0314A].

## § XIII. Conrad’s return, final deeds, and death

Hardly had the king returned home when most serious disputes met him. That Bavarian Welf, his companion and intimate during the expedition, and accordingly heaped with gifts [Note: [Col. 0314D] *Chronicle of Ursberg*, loc. cit., p. 280 ff.; King Conrad’s letter to the Greek emperor, among Guibald’s letters, no. 188, p. 377.], was contriving injury in return for favour. He had left the king at Jerusalem while the latter was preparing for Damascus; returning home under the pretext of illness, he visited the Sicilian king on his journey, was honourably received and supplied with money, in order to conspire against the king. Having therefore gone to Rome, he hastened into Germany, intending to demonstrate his treachery in action.

Servants intercepted at Rome by adherents of senatorial rank [Col. 0314B] supplied clear evidence of the plot. Letters of Roger were found, commending Welf to Duke Frederick of Swabia, Henry of Saxony, Duke Conrad of Zähringen, and his son Berthold (IV), as men privy to his purpose [Note: [Col. 0314D] Letter of John, notary of King Conrad, who was then by chance staying at Rome, to Guibald, no. 239, p. 423.]. The plans had not entirely escaped the king, though still detained in Greece: he had sent ahead to Germany his nephew Duke Frederick, to whom he entrusted much, to protect the public peace against Welf’s attempts [Note: [Col. 0314D] Otto of Freising, loc. cit., ch. 59.]. Perhaps he had discerned Frederick himself and was testing the young man’s mind by an honourable commission. Certainly this affair urgently required Conrad’s return [Note: [Col. 0314D] Conrad’s cited letter], since the issue seemed to concern not peace alone but also the kingdom.

Welf did not long postpone hostilities: in a sudden attack he assailed [Col. 0314C] Eger, the king’s particular castle. But, having seized his opportunity badly, he was gloriously defeated by Henry, Conrad’s son and king of Germany. By Guibald’s counsel he was to be proscribed, had not Duke Frederick of Swabia offered equivocal assistance in settling the dispute [Note: [Col. 0314D] *Chronicle of Ursberg*, p. 281.].

The revived dispute concerning the duchy of Bavaria also seemed to touch the king more directly. Immediately after the death of his mother Gertrude, Henry of Saxony had begun to demand Bavaria back; it had been ceded by agreement to her Austrian husband. When the holy expedition was then pressing, Conrad had courteously addressed him and induced him to defer the matter [Note: [Col. 0314D] Otto of Freising, loc. cit., ch. 43.]. Now, pressing the claim afresh, Henry had entered Swabia, relying upon the power of his father-in-law Conrad, Duke of Zähringen [Note: [Col. 0314D] Mascovius, loc. cit., p. 280.]. The king, on the other hand, forbade violence and appointed a day for hearing the case; [Col. 0314D] the outcome is unclear. But shortly afterwards, advancing into Saxony on the advice of Albert of Brandenburg, the king compelled Henry to withdraw to his own lands, being in no way likely to attain his aim while Conrad lived [Col. 0315A].

Even after Welf’s defeat and the Saxon’s repulse, however, arms in Bavaria did not finally fall silent. A serious conflict arose between the Bavarian counts palatine, the Ottos, and the bishop of Regensburg, whom the father together with his sons was pressing with hostile arms. The very ancient line of the Ottos is traced back to Arnulf, at the time when Emperors Henry I and Otto the Great held the duchy of Bavaria. It is reported that, in that period, a certain Count of Scheyern in Bavaria summoned the savage people of the Huns into the Empire [Note: [Col. 0315D] The reference appears to be to Hermann, surnamed the Little, son of Arnulf, whose wife is commonly believed to have been the Hungarian Agnes, sister of King Géza. Tolner, *History of the Palatinate*, p. 197.]; they were destroyed by Otto the Great’s most noble victory. The count was killed by the Huns in revenge for the defeat. His goods were then plundered and taken into the fisc; some were divided among churches, and some left to his heirs [Col. 0315B] together with the castle of Scheyern. Subsequently, from Wittelsbach castle, built in the eleventh century by Otto III of Scheyern [Note: [Col. 0315D] Tolner, loc. cit., p. 267.], the family acquired a new surname, in accordance with the custom of the age; its related hostility toward the clergy remained [Note: [Col. 0315D] Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, bk. VI, ch. 20. A remarkable alteration of the wording in this passage of the chronicle was pointed out by the learned Pithou. The common editions of the *Chronicle* display nothing but the author’s fierce denunciations of the Scheyern family; whereas, according to the Pithou manuscript examined, in a remarkable divergence of tenor, splendid praises of the contemporary counts palatine were added.].

Now the king embraced the bishop’s cause. The count palatine, proscribed and frightened by the siege of Kelheim castle, gave his other son Otto as a hostage and appealed to Conrad’s good faith [Note: [Col. 0316D] Otto of Freising, *The Deeds of Frederick I*, bk. I, ch. 63.]. This is that Otto, Count Palatine of Bavaria, who adorned the reign of Emperor Frederick I with the highest virtues, and who at last, on receiving the duchy of Bavaria, transmitted through an enduring line the memory of a most celebrated name to the most august kings of Bavaria.

Among Conrad’s greatest concerns at last was an Italian expedition, hitherto delayed by various affairs and especially by the holy expedition [Col. 0315C]. But while he was pressing forward the plan by letters, embassies, and every diligent effort, the unexpected death of the king deprived the kingdom of its double hope. He had gone to Bamberg to hold a court there, awaiting envoys returning from Italy; as they were just entering Speyer, they encountered the most sorrowful news. Although his bones were intended for burial in the ancestral sepulchre at Lorch, Bamberg retained them and laid them with royal ceremony beside the tomb of the Emperor St Henry [Note: [Col. 0316D] Otto of Freising, ch. 63.].

Conrad was a straightforward and upright man, not without a certain native keenness, but wholly untrained in letters, and therefore less powerful in counsel than in arms. Yet he possessed the highest affability and a bearing which widely displayed the king [Col. 0315D] [Note: [Col. 0316D] *Deeds of Louis VII, King of the Franks*, ch. 27; William of Tyre, bk. XVII, ch. 8.]. His son Henry, king of the Germans, had already died; the sole son surviving his father was the young Frederick, soon Duke of Swabia and distinguished among the princes, called “of Rothenburg” from the castle chosen as his seat. While he was in Tuscany as a companion in the Italian expedition, he was carried off and died at Rome in a pestilential contagion, together with many nobles [Col. 0316A] [Note: [Col. 0316D] A.D. 1167. Otto of St Blasien, ch. 20.], and was buried at Ebrach in Franconia [Note: [Col. 0316D] Gropp, *Sepulchral Monuments of the Church of Ebrach*, p. 67.]. By his wife Richenza, the only daughter of Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony, he had likewise had an only son, who died in the cradle; so that Conrad’s entire progeny failed in him.

We have related these earlier fortunes of the Staufen family somewhat more fully, because they had to be told once for all; the remainder we shall pursue in a more concise style, with the proofs arranged in a volume of notes.

## § XIV. Frederick, Duke of Swabia, king of the Germans: his election, character, and the beginnings of his reign

When Conrad was already near death, despairing, as it were, after considering the state of the Empire, of his little son, he summoned his nephew Duke Frederick and, handing over the royal insignia before [Col. 0316B] those present, commended him as successor. Nor did the influence of his wish fail: about the sixteenth day after his death Frederick was elected king at Frankfurt by the unanimous votes of all. Two days later, the court having been dismissed and the homages of the nobles received, he went to Aachen and was raised, as a most worthy successor, to the august seat of St Charles.

Many things besides aided the peaceful and swift election: the fresh affection felt for the dead Conrad; Frederick’s double kinship with the most powerful families of the realm, and the consequent happy omens of peace; also his private ties with Welf and the Saxon, the most powerful efforts of Abbot Guibald, and finally the duke’s exceptional qualities. For his deeds were certainly renowned; he had vigour of mind, spirit, and body; prudence exceeding his age in public affairs [Col. 0316C]; beauty and dignity of person; charm of manner and remarkable gravity. Everything promised imperial glory in this youthful hero.

Indeed, since Charlemagne neither Germany nor any land had yet seen a greater man. In the very first decade of his reign, measuring out the life of others, he made the majesty of the Empire formidable to all nations of the world through his virtues. Whereas earlier emperors had often followed only a shifting rule of conduct, according to circumstances as they arose, he directed the steady course of his reign through the greatest perils of obstacles with an unmoved mind. He must therefore be compared with the most exalted examples; perhaps he should in this respect be preferred to them, because he encountered far more difficult adversaries, who had to be overcome not merely by war and courage but by skill and prudence [Col. 0316D]. The chief objects of his policy seem to have been these four: the supreme and absolute majesty of the Empire, perhaps even its hereditary character; a just arrangement between royal and priestly power; Italy vindicated for the Empire; and finally the public peace of Germany, with the licence of arms forcibly restrained [Col. 0317A].

## § XV. The new king’s concern for his country

Frederick’s most ancient care was to win the goodwill of the princes, settle the old disputes of his forebears, and reconcile the minds of the powerful by extinguishing the sparks of war. He therefore first applied his attention to Bavarian affairs, summoning Henry of Austria on an appointed day. When, even after a third summons, he stubbornly refused, the duchy was adjudged to Henry the Lion of Saxony after the man’s persistent solicitations; Regensburg was soon delivered to him, and many nobles were compelled to acknowledge his rights. Yet the Austrian did not yield, confident in Frederick—namely, relying on the deference of his august nephew. And he had not judged wrongly [Col. 0317B]. For when the business was soon resumed, Frederick voluntarily advanced to meet him and, by granting the amplest privileges [Note: [Col. 0317D] Senckenberg removed Bunau’s unjust doubts about the authenticity of the document (*Life and Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, pp. 64 f.). (*Thoughts on the Use of Ancient German [Col. 0318D] Civic and Constitutional Law*, p. 113.)] and the honours of a new duchy, finally settled a most weighty matter amid the great rejoicing of the court.

A settlement between the rivals Henry the Lion and Albert of Brandenburg had preceded; another followed between the Austrian and Otto, Bishop of Freising. Hence came Henry the Lion’s highly welcome goodwill, since he was to assist the king’s Italian expedition with exceptional strength. The king also showed reciprocal liberality by voluntarily granting Henry the whole county of Uto. By contrast, immediate punishment for disturbers of the peace was demonstrated by the disgrace of Arnold, Archbishop of Mainz, and Count Palatine Hermann. The terrified nobles watched the count palatine carry a dog with his companions [Col. 0317C], while the bishop was spared only with difficulty. Moreover, the king’s continual journeys through the realm, and his eye watching over peace everywhere; the plundering of the castles of robber-nobles; severe punishments inflicted on many. Finally, the abolition of unlawfully assumed tolls markedly increased the benefits of trade.

## § XVI. The state of Italy; Frederick’s plans

The whole strength of the king was thereafter occupied with the kingdom of Italy, scarcely still to be called a kingdom except in name. The pope ruled; the cities ruled; the Sicilian was to rule. Through emperors’ long absence, neglect, and weakness, this threefold power had grown up; though for the most part rivals of one another, they nevertheless conspired together against the kingdom. The chief rights of the Empire had slipped away, fiscal regalia had been usurped, and nearly all had become obsolete, surviving only in faint recollection [Col. 0317D].

Frederick’s first designs were directed against the Sicilian and the city of Milan. But detained by domestic business, he sent envoys to the Greek emperor to arrange an alliance against the Sicilian, while also proposing a marriage between the king and Manuel’s daughter. He had long discerned Roger’s designs; and from Roger’s letters we know that Welf had formerly been commended to Frederick. Already faithful subjects of the Empire, witnesses of violence, had complained of their injuries at Würzburg and stirred indignation; nor did the situation change when Roger died in the meantime, while his successor William was pursuing the same schemes [Col. 0318A].

Then the disorders of the Milanese especially offended him; and events later proved that the king’s wrath, once precipitated, was betrayed at Constance. A slight disagreement arose with Pope Eugenius III over the rights of the kingdom, guarded too resolutely in the election at Magdeburg; it was soon annulled by an agreement. Afterwards, at the pope’s instigation, the Archbishop of Mainz was removed, and shortly the bishops of Minden and Eichstätt—up to this point with the king’s consent. But when the papal envoys acted too freely and even attempted to reopen the Magdeburg affair, they were immediately forbidden and ordered to leave the realm. By chance the pope died; Anastasius, a Roman by birth, succeeded him. With him relations were wholly peaceful, but also very brief [Col. 0318B]. After fourteen months he died, and Adrian, an Englishman, fourth of that name, succeeded. An elevated character had raised him from the humblest beginnings to the summit of honours: great in intellect, greater in spirit, but hard, gloomy, and puffed up by fortune.

Now Frederick, as the agreed time approached—in the third year of his reign, around the beginning of October, a season especially convenient for Germans—assembled an army at Augsburg and marched into Italy. He was to act more from counsels supplied by events than from a premeditated plan, though his general aims were fixed. At once upon his arrival, meeting the injuries of the cities, he displayed only arms and anger toward the powerful, mercy toward the afflicted lesser cities [Col. 0318C]. He directed himself chiefly to arriving victorious and made famous by some notable deed at Rome. Having punished the insolence of certain cities on the way and imposed order on the army’s discipline, he attacked Tortona, ally of the Ligurians [Note: [Col. 0318D] Henceforth we shall call the Milanese “Ligurians,” using this shorter and more elegant term.], powerful in wealth, fortified by walls and alliance.

Chiefly through the efforts of Pavia, he reduced it after a most vigorous defence, and not without heavy losses to the besiegers. As an example of severity more terrible than honourable, he gave the city over to the soldiers for plunder—its most wretched citizens scarcely being granted life—and afterwards to be destroyed by fire. Proceeding thence to Pavia, he celebrated for three days a splendid triumph, displayed by that rival city more for Tortona’s ruin and the injury of the Ligurians than for the king himself [Col. 0318D]. The king abandoned the siege he had undertaken of Piacenza, difficult because of Ligurian assistance; impatient of delay, he now turned mind and strength toward the city of Rome and the imperial crown, as spring had already advanced.

Alarmed by his sudden arrival, the pope sent envoys to meet him and sound out the king’s mind; himself, distrustful of the Romans’ intentions, he had withdrawn to Orvieto. Arnold of Brescia was the cause. We have mentioned that he returned to Rome after Innocent’s death. Protected by popular favour against Eugenius and Anastasius, Arnold had formerly been expelled by Adrian through a most opportune measure. For when worship was interdicted during Holy Week, the religion of the populace had trembled; Arnold, abandoned in order to appease the pope, fled the city [Col. 0319A]. Captured by the plots of a certain cardinal and handed over to custody, he was soon freed by the aid of certain Campanian counts and lay hidden in the neighbourhood.

Now the pope’s fear grew more vehement from his very victory: a secret enemy, an uncertain populace, and a new and crafty king advancing with an army. Hence, before all else, his instructions concerned Arnold’s punishment. Frederick readily agreed, himself hating the man as hostile to the rights of the kingdom. The unfortunate Arnold was torn from his defender and surrendered to the clergy’s vengeance; they, indeed abstaining from bloodshed, had him burned through the prefect of the city. Yet there was no mutual trust as yet, until envoys had been received on both sides. At last the pope advanced to Viterbo and visited the king in his camp [Col. 0319B]. Though received reverently with due honour, he is said to have quarrelled over the stirrup; the affair nearly caused a breach, had Frederick not yielded to the impulses of his desire for the crown.

They proceeded together to Sutri. The Romans uttered lofty words: it pleased the Quirites to admit the king; the fasces of the Empire had been decreed; let him swear obedience to the City; let him distribute five thousand to the crowd acclaiming upon the Capitol. The reply was ready, carefully refuting each point and, so far, beneath a king’s dignity. One may perceive that he was somewhat daunted by the appearance of the Roman name and the astonishment of the event. Indeed, from the threatening departure of the envoys he was almost anxious and at a loss for counsel, so that he, commander of the army, entrusted the whole conduct of the affair to the pope. Adrian’s loyalty then appeared truly praiseworthy: chiefly by his aid Frederick was brought to Rome, and, disregarding the danger of entering it, was crowned emperor [Col. 0319C].

For the sudden and most savage battle that followed the completion of the ceremonies showed the immense fury of the populace when it learned what had happened. In it, Roman women materially assisted the Germans’ long-doubtful victory: enamoured of the appearance of the young men, they restrained their own men from arms by exhortation and entreaty. Henry the Lion’s valour for Caesar was at the same time displayed, as was the pope’s generous goodwill toward both men. The pope had steadfastly refused the investiture of the bishop of Altenburg, appointed through Henry against the wishes of the Archbishop of Bremen, Frederick’s most powerful friend; now, as a reward for devotion, he voluntarily confirmed it at once by ordination, offered in Henry’s presence [Col. 0319D].

Yet the victory brought no advantages; indeed, scarcity of provisions compelled departure from Rome. The emperor subdued the Tiburtines, who came to meet him with the city’s keys, much to the pope’s displeasure, although he preserved the Empire’s rights. Soon, to restore soldiers afflicted by the unhealthiness of the air, he moved camp into the neighbouring Apennines, where they might enjoy life-giving air and advantages of every kind. When the Spoletans fraudulently withheld the contribution of fodder that had been imposed, their city was destroyed in a single assault, the emperor himself rushing in with his soldiers. Shortly afterwards, with the spoils collected from the pyre, the army advanced to Ancona. There Caesar heard Greek envoys seeking promised auxiliaries and a large sum of money for war against the Sicilian [Col. 0320A]; although he himself was wholly ready, opposition from the princes compelled him to defer the plan. Envoys were sent in return with tokens of friendship, among them the most distinguished Guibald, Abbot of Corvey.

With the greater part of the army now dismissed, Caesar proceeded with the rest toward Verona. There, in contempt for his small numbers, the citizens not only excluded him from the city but also sought to ambush him. Yet again the fortune attending the man and the courage of Count Palatine Otto happily defeated their attempt, not without serious injury to the enemy.

After three years had passed amid domestic concerns, Frederick returned, well acquainted with places and men, with a premeditated plan and an army of one hundred thousand armed men. The chief cause of this immense preparation was Milan, a city long rebellious, which had provoked the emperor by the unbridled wantonness of its power [Col. 0320B]. Conscious of its guilt, foreseeing the weight of war, and scorning obedience, it had placed its sole hope in its most fortified walls, the courage of its citizens, and its immense riches. These were vain consolations of pride. At the emperor’s very first arrival, the city of Brescia, distressed by its alliance with the Ligurians, offered an evil omen.

Milan itself was immediately enclosed in the closest siege, with the allied assistance of the Italians; after the citizens’ most obstinate efforts, it was compelled by hunger rather than arms to surrender. It was fined nine thousand marks, and subjected, beyond doubt, to the harsher spectacle of its suppliants. But the triumph was exceedingly short. Caesar had scarcely departed with his army to attend to Italian affairs when the Ligurians rose again; and that revolt, far more troublesome, was avenged only after the greatest hazards of war by the destruction of the city [Col. 0320C].

The next concern in pacifying Italy was to identify and recover the imperial regalia. Count Palatine Otto and Chancellor Rainald, with a chosen band of soldiers, went ahead of Caesar’s return; almost by the authority of the imperial name alone they brought very many cities back to allegiance to the kingdom. After Milan’s surrender, an investigation was held with the cities into usurpations; thirty thousand talents per year were thereby secured for the fisc. At that time the fiefs of the famous Matilda were reclaimed for the Empire and granted by the emperor to Duke Welf, thereby confirming a bond of favour with a powerful friend and providing a very strong defence against the Sicilian [Col. 0320D].

The Roman pontiff bore this zeal more bitterly than anyone, having long been hostile to Caesar because Frederick had repelled the man’s arrogance. The pope’s very first letter had incautiously represented the Empire as a *beneficium* (“benefice,” favour conferred); it aroused such tumult throughout the court that they scarcely refrained from killing the envoys, Count Palatine Otto already standing over them with drawn sword. The envoys returned to Rome in disgrace, their route prescribed and guards added. Other measures of the pope followed, especially the alliance concluded with the Sicilian; the maintenance at Rome of the calumnious painting; and the condemnation of Caesar’s marriage to Beatrice, if the writers report truly [Col. 0321A].

A milder letter, sent to Augsburg at the princes’ request, did little good, because fresh papal arrogance followed. For the pope shamelessly attacked the emperor then present in Italy with accusations concerning the elected archbishop of Ravenna; and he wholly exceeded every measure in that most insolent invective against Frederick, addressed to the two archbishops, the joint rulers of Germany [Note: [Col. 0321D] S. F. Hahn, *Collection of Monuments*, vol. I, p. 122 ff.]. What wonder, then, if the emperor, enraged by the calumnies of the Roman see, not only reclaimed indisputable rights of the kingdom but also laid unjust hands upon the discipline of the Church itself? It was indeed a most grievous excuse for enormous evils—an anger more righteous than prudent. From that time Frederick’s fortune was shaken, and destruction was prepared for the Staufen family. For it was Caesar’s contest, not the Empire’s, with the Roman see; among the German princes were traitors to the German cause; hence the victories of the popes . . . [Col. 0321B]

## § XVII. Frederick’s authority over the German Church

At first Frederick vigorously and moderately defended the remaining rights of the kingdom over the German Church; but as hostilities with the Roman see grew fiercer, he sometimes acted violently and arbitrarily, opposing his own cunning and power to the pope’s cunning and curses. He needed the wealthy clergy for the high counsels of the kingdom, and needed the Church’s support against the pope’s settled designs. Accordingly he was cautious and just in the election at Magdeburg, and afterwards in the similar case of Cologne; nor was he without satisfaction in the removal by the pope of Henry of Mainz, since Arnold, Frederick’s chancellor, was appointed in his place [Col. 0321C].

When about to set out again for Italy, he distributed alms, especially to churches, and carefully took bishops into counsel; he notably enlarged the archbishop of Trier’s privileges. When Arnold of Mainz had been cruelly killed, he rejected Rudolph, Duke of Zähringen, elected by unlawful votes; he also prohibited his own friend Christian, who had been rashly appointed, and installed Conrad of Bavaria, full brother of Count Palatine Otto. These actions were done by his own authority, but also with the pope’s consent.

But once quarrels with Alexander arose, Frederick most severely punished bishops’ obedience to the Roman see; he despoiled, expelled, and afflicted in every manner the pope’s adherents. Conrad of Mainz, suspected on account of his attachment to Alexander and afterwards a fugitive at Rome, was immediately proscribed, notwithstanding his brother’s favour; Frederick restored the previously rejected Christian in his place. Even at the eventual agreement with Alexander at Venice, though made on unfavourable terms, he did not receive Conrad, but placed him at Salzburg; only after Christian’s death did he finally restore him to Mainz [Col. 0321D].

For much the same reason he proscribed Folmar of Trier, who had solicited papal help for his fraudulent election. Rudolph of Zähringen—the man formerly deposed from Mainz—was put in his place; and, despising Folmar’s papal ordination, he was [Col. 0322A] invested by Caesar’s arms, while King Henry harshly punished his opponents. The Archbishop of Salzburg, Eberhard, and his successor Conrad were likewise proscribed; Albert, appointed without consultation, was not admitted. Some, struck by fear, voluntarily abandoned their sees, among them Henry of Passau and Berthold of Metz. Frederick long had a serious quarrel with Philip of Cologne; it was finally allayed by payment of money and Philip’s renunciation of any intention to harm him.

At last matters reached the point that bishops appointed by the emperor, with Roman investitures prohibited, were consecrated by the Archbishop of Mainz, and punishment was decreed against those who resisted. Bitter complaints of the bishops followed, and they were not unjust; but they had little effect. The emperor persisted with a resolute mind, supported by the most powerful strength of King Henry [Col. 0322B]. Thus the authority of the Roman see was greatly diminished, and was scarcely vindicated even in appearance when the Archbishops of Mainz and Cologne renounced it on their own initiative.

## § XVIII. The kingdom’s majesty abroad

The far-reaching vigour of the Empire and the Italian wars chiefly made Frederick’s august name extend far and wide. His arms were more displayed to foreign peoples than used against them, because the efforts of princes, domestic disturbances, and at last the very storms in Italy diverted the emperor from his designs. Under the first auspices of the reign, the minds of the nobles opposed action against Géza, king of Hungary, and Roger of Sicily. There can scarcely be doubt that this was chiefly due to the counsels of Henry of Saxony, the dukes of Zähringen, and Welf [Col. 0322C], since we know of Roger’s letters and of the money by which Welf was supported by both men in injuries against the kingdom.

Géza had deprived Boris, the lawful king of Hungary and son of King Coloman, of the kingdom. After vain attempts to recover it, Boris fled to Conrad and asked for the Empire’s aid, supported by the recommendations of Vladislaus, Duke of Bohemia, and of his wife Gertrude, Conrad’s sister. Conrad granted the request; but when the holy expedition was decreed, the king’s intention remained merely an intention, since he was distracted by other cares and needed Géza, through whose dominion he was to pass. For the same reason Boris’s petitions to Louis, king of France, who was following with an army, were abandoned [Col. 0322D]: he received only safe passage in the king’s company.

At last, received at Constantinople with the highest favour, to Géza’s resentment, he served as a commander of the Greeks against the Hungarians and was killed in an expedition by the treachery of one of his own soldiers. Frederick had inherited Conrad’s promise, while Boris was still alive and the Empire’s friendship with the Byzantine court remained intact. But Géza, changing his policy according to changed circumstances, sought to win Frederick over by services, sending a chosen body of soldiers against the Italians. He also promised future assistance and thus bound the emperor so closely that Frederick sent Géza’s brother Stephen to Constantinople, suspending the case, although Stephen complained of his brother’s tyranny; he set aside an uncertain cause for assured advantages, less honourably than prudently [Col. 0323A].

Against Roger, king of Sicily, the princes’ minds had been stirred not only by an old injury and recent ambition, but by immediate compassion for the Apulian nobles despoiled because of loyalty to the kingdom.
