It was agreed that an expedition was to be undertaken jointly with the Roman one within two years. But when action was required, the sad miseries from the Roman war, the unhealthiness of the climate, and an army diminished by exhaustion supplied pretexts; the emperor pressed in vain, though the pope too had inflamed his anger for his own reasons.

[Col. 0323B] Roger was the grandson, through his brother Roger, of the celebrated Robert Guiscard, founder of the Sicilian kingdom. He succeeded his father as Count of Sicily in 1101 under the guardianship of his mother Adelaide of Burgundy. When the related line of the dukes of Apulia failed in 1127, Roger seized that land, and Pope Honorius II, opposing the deed, declared war. But after the province was received as a fief, the pope recognized him as duke. When the schism then arose between Innocent and Anacletus Pierleoni, Roger embraced the latter’s party, married Anacletus’s sister, and was crowned king of Sicily by his pontiff father-in-law. Afterwards, cursed by Innocent, he was utterly defeated throughout Apulia by Rainulf, Count of Campania; Emperor Lothair granted the duchy to Rainulf. When Rainulf died, Roger returned; having quickly recovered the whole province, he compelled Pope Innocent himself, captured at Benevento, unwillingly to place the crown upon him and conclude an agreement on his terms [Col. 0323C].

Now rising to greater things and planning Italy, Roger died in the second year of King Frederick’s reign, amid the highest objects of his ambition. This is the same Roger whose notable exploit against Constantinople is celebrated by the poet of the *Ligurinus*. On his return he rescued Louis, king of France, returning from Palestine, from Greek plots, and was for the third time crowned with a diadem by him through a sufficiently ingenious festive device. By his first marriage, with Joanna of England, Roger had a son William I, who succeeded his father; by his third marriage he had a daughter Constance, married in 1186 to King Henry, the firstborn of Emperor Frederick and afterwards emperor of the Germans. When William II, son of William I, died childless in 1193, Henry obtained the kingdom of Sicily [Col. 0323D]. Thus the continual injuries suffered from the father by the Empire and its Staufen emperors at last came to rest in a most splendid expiation.

The cause of the expedition decreed against the Poles was an old one. After Duke Boleslaus III of Poland, who died in 1138, had divided his lands among his sons, the eldest, Vladislaus, dissatisfied with his allotted Silesia and Cracow, first brought complaints and then openly deprived his brothers by war. When they united against him, he was defeated and put to flight in a sudden battle; fleeing to King Conrad, he sought aid against his brothers, relying on kinship despite consciousness of the injustice of his cause, for Conrad’s queen was his half-sister. Conrad sent envoys, who received an ambiguous answer [Col. 0324A], since the brothers knew that the king was preparing for Palestine. Conrad himself effected nothing except to commend the exile to Pope Eugenius, meanwhile granting Vladislaus refuge at Altenburg.

After returning, Conrad, together with his son King Henry, made every effort, with Pope Eugenius also assisting by placing religious observances under interdict throughout Poland. But since the bishops paid little attention to this, Frederick found the business unresolved. The enthusiasm for the expedition was so great that the second Italian campaign was set aside; the German soldier, reaching the Oder and unexpectedly finding a bridge-crossing, rushed eagerly upon the enemy. The Poles, who had ravaged their own land far and wide, tried in vain to hold them back and were compelled to submit. Yet, apart from payment of a sum of money and the restoration of Silesia to Vladislaus, the remaining conditions of peace were disregarded [Col. 0324B].

Imperial authority was recognized in the kingdom of Denmark when Sweyn and Canute—grandsons, through sons, of the great Sweyn, king of England and Denmark—submitted their long and violent dispute concerning the crown to the Empire’s judgment. The matter was handled at Merseburg among the first affairs of the reign, both parties to the dispute having been summoned and being present. The court judged that the kingdom belonged to Sweyn, while Zealand with certain dependent territories was to be assigned to Canute. Sweyn was therefore immediately girded with the diadem and, after swearing fealty to King Frederick, was invested with the sword according to custom. In the solemn procession, the vassal bore the sword before his crowned lord, the king, and went before him to church.

[Col. 0324C] Emperor Frederick endowed Vladislaus, otherwise called Boleslaus, Duke of Bohemia—who had earned great merit against the Poles in the king’s army—with royal dignity; the same man was also to give notable military support against the Ligurians. Afterwards, deprived once more of that dignity for disregarding Frederick’s commands, he did not transmit the reward won by valour to his heirs.

With the kings of England and France he maintained, for the most part, friendly relations, though never a trustworthy friendship with the Frenchman. For first Burgundy had been recovered, and then also the efforts of Pope Alexander gave rise to mutual suspicions and at times slight injuries. Finally, in Frederick’s last years, there was a brief and irregular war on account of the Count of Flanders—though the emperor himself was not present, having delegated the expedition. At last, when the king of France sought the emperor’s assistance against the Englishman, a treaty was concluded; once this had been done, the Englishman too abstained from arms.

With the Byzantine court, while Irene remained alive, there was at least an appearance of concord, declarations of goodwill, and proposed alliances. But soon, once Greek deceits had been discovered, there were injuries done to envoys, arrogance, and hostilities. At length there was irreconcilable hatred, after it became known that the Byzantines and Pope Alexander were sharing counsels against the Empire.

Moreover, the emperor’s court was by far the most magnificent of its age: a continual multitude of princes paying their respects; a private court constantly presenting the appearance of a solemn assembly; an inexhaustible throng of embassies flowing in from every quarter; innumerable gifts, unusual alike in cost and workmanship, and worthy of the man. In the midst stood Frederick, displaying the emperor in face and bearing; by the fame of his exploits he won admiration, by his dignity reverence, and by his graciousness and eloquence the affection of all. Most shrewd in affairs and in men, he never dismissed those who approached him—having heard and received them according to the substance of their proposals and the rank of their orders—without an even-handed reply.

## XIX. His Aspiration to World Empire

The energy of emperors, repeatedly delayed and broken by the designs of princes, must, from the Carolingian period onward, be judged less by what it accomplished than by what it could have accomplished. For the greatest unity of counsel in conducting affairs, and a sure capacity for arrangement, are suited to great undertakings and especially become lofty minds. But, Cicero says, “what is objectionable is that, in this elevation and greatness of spirit, stubbornness and an excessive desire for rule most readily arise.” [Note: [Col. 0325C] *On Duties*, I.19.] We observe that this happened also in Frederick’s case. For he not only bore most indignantly the dissension of his own men, and generally repressed it with more than equitable severity, but, begrudging even foreign kingdoms their independence of his authority, aspired to the summit of universal empire.

He displayed the example of Charlemagne in word and deed. Charlemagne’s bones, too, he raised at Aachen with immense pomp and deposited with remarkable veneration in a new tomb, the most august hero being enrolled among the gods. Frederick himself allowed himself to be called by the title of “the divine,” [Note: [Col. 0325C] The books of Radewig of Freising, written at the emperor’s urging, are witnesses.] after the manner of the Roman Caesars. Replying to the envoys of the City, he boasted of ancient Rome’s dominion and of kings subject to it; and at the conference of Laon he asserted unrestricted authority in ecclesiastical matters over Louis, king of France.

The chief fuel for these commotions came from Roman law, long since becoming powerful and promoted by the favor of the emperors Henry V and Lothair. New formulas were already employed in summoning the Milanese; at Roncaglia the rights of the Italian kingdom were defined from Roman law, as were also the Lombard fiefs. Thus there finally arose that monstrous formula of universal empire, the long-standing mockery of German jurists.

## XX. His Policies toward His Family

Frederick devoted such care to enlarging his family’s hereditary resources and to the splendor of the august house as no emperor before him had done. Yet this desire was not altogether blameworthy, since, as the hereditary character of fiefs grew stronger, little prospect remained for nephews to achieve distinction through merit or fortune. That he sought the inheritance of the Empire itself for his family is shown both by many clear indications in his acts and especially by the open efforts of his son Henry, who followed in his father’s footsteps.

Immediately upon his elevation to the kingship, Frederick resigned to Frederick, son of Conrad, the ancestral duchy of Swabia and Alsace—that is, Alemannia—whether by compact or favor is uncertain. Soon afterward he substituted Conrad, his brother by the same father, for Hermann, Count Palatine of the Rhine, who died without issue. He caused his eldest son Henry, still of very tender age, to be created king of Germany. He afterward loved this youth, most like his father in natural ability and aims, so intensely that he intended to have him crowned king of Italy, crowned also emperor, and made partner in the kingdom and future heir of Sicily.

To another son, Frederick, after the death of his cousin of Rothenburg, which left the office vacant, he granted the duchy of Alemannia while still in the cradle. Otto, his third-born, likewise babbling in the cradle, he proclaimed Count Palatine of Burgundy, having by agreement deprived Berthold, Duke of Zähringen, of the governorship of Burgundy. This indeed seemed rather unjust toward a prince who had deserved extremely well of Frederick; yet it is not without excuse. For Frederick held Burgundy, as it were, by a double right: through the authority of the Empire, though that authority had become quite obsolete, and as the richest prince in Burgundy through his marriage with Beatrice, which increased him by very extensive dowry lands; while nothing had long remained to Berthold beyond the title of honor.

He set his fourth son Conrad over Würzburg as duke of Franconia, after the death in Palestine of his unmarried brother Frederick, intending him to become duke of Swabia. Finally Philip, the youngest by birth, perhaps at first intended for ecclesiastical eminence, he made lord of Tuscany and of the land of Matilda, redeemed from Duke Welf. Yet in all these grants the emperor did nothing other than secure to his family most of the ancestral benefices, in accordance with the hereditary custom then gaining strength; accordingly these policies should be regarded as the result of the times rather than of greed.

[Col. 0327]

# Gunther the Poet’s *Ligurinus, or On the Deeds of the Emperor Caesar Frederick Augustus, Surnamed Aenobarbus*, in Ten Books

You, young man, deserter and enemy of your country’s glory,  
and needy pursuer of foreign renown,  
look up at the most joyous heights of the Teutonic kingdom,  
at the lord of lands and glory of his race.  
And now, worthy offspring of an ancient line of fathers,  
gather virtues: the time has come to bring them forth.

## Abbreviations in the Notes

A. First Augsburg edition, 1507, folio.  
Sp. Spiegellian edition, Strasbourg, 1531, folio.  
P. Pithoean, or Perna’s edition, Basel, 1569, folio.  
R. First Reuber edition, Frankfurt am Main, 1584.  
Rs. Rittershusian edition, Tübingen, 1598, octavo; and its notes, Tübingen, 1597, octavo.  
R. Third Reuber edition, edited by Georg Christoph Johann, Frankfurt, 1726, folio.  
B. Barth’s brief strictures on Gunther in his *Adversaria*.  
Pfl. Pflug’s observations, cited by Rittershusius.  
SC. Scioppius’s observations, in the same place.  
V. Vonck’s *Emendations in the Reading of Latin*, II.4, pp. 124–132.  
W. Withof’s specimen on Gunther’s *Ligurinus*, and notes occurring elsewhere.  
m. “prefers.”  
pp. “proposed.”  
r. “restored.”  
rr. “the remaining editions.”  
s. “follows.”  
ss. “follow.”  
v. “the following editions.”  
c. A correction added in handwriting, especially in the excellent copy of the Augsburg edition in the Academic Library of Freiburg.  
* A reading apparently wholly sound, yet one which there is no urgent need to receive into the text against the authority of the first Augsburg edition.  
(*) A reading or passage indicating that the author was a contemporary of Emperor Frederick I.  
+ A reading or emendation not to be accepted.  
++ An extremely bad reading foisted off as an emendation.  
(+) A reading in the prefixed arguments of the books showing a later author, alien to Gunther; but insofar as the sign occurs beneath the text of the *Ligurinus* itself, it indicates a reading or passage not equally suited to the author’s supposed date.  
o. A printer’s error in the first Augsburg edition, which seems either to have led subsequent editors into error or to have exercised them in vain.  
Readings or notes to which no sign either of assent or dissent is attached I have considered of no great importance; those to which no author’s name is added are to be considered as published at the editor’s own risk.

# Arguments Prefixed to the Books of the *Ligurinus* by an Uncertain Hand

[Col. 0329]

The **FIRST** book contains the first honors of the elected king.

At Aachen he bears the sceptre in his hand  
and the first sacred crown upon his head. His deserved wrath  
straightway turns toward Maastricht; from there the boy king visits great cities.  
He gives laws to peoples and reforms their ancient rights.  
And, once the kinsmen’s dispute has been settled, he grants  
the sceptre of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0329] (+).] to Peter to possess.  
Wishing to declare war upon the Pannonians,  
he is dissuaded by the numerous and loyal entreaties of the nobles.  
He restores to you, Saxon, the duchy taken from your uncle—  
the cause and seed of a great war.

The **SECOND** leads the royal standards across the Alps.  
When the Caesar is established at Roncaglia, the Italian people rejoice,  
as though illumined by the rising of a new star,  
and all hasten to bring forward complaints long suppressed.  
Above all, Cuma, suppliant, praises him and denounces  
the crimes of the Ligurians. Having discovered their fraud,  
the king captures their noble garrison and destroys Rosate.  
He lays the guilty waste with slaughter, burns towers and bridges,  
takes the Ligurians’ forts, and overturns Cairo and Asti;  
he encircles the walls of Tortona with a heavy siege.

The **THIRD** gives the besieged city over to the conquerors;  
its citizens expelled, its walls are ravaged by flames.  
Devoted Pavia displays triumphs deserved by the victor.  
Then Frederick turns toward the Tuscan shores.  
He praises the Pisans bearing gifts and commands them  
to equip powerful ships for Sicily.  
The Roman bishop meets him and complains of the impious deeds  
of his own populace; and the insolent Arnold perished  
[Note: [Col. 0329] “perishes by fire,” W. *].  
To the king about to enter the City, the commanding mandates  
of the eloquent fatherland bring imperious demands,  
and carry back harsh answers.

The **FOURTH** advances the king to empire and supreme titles;  
in the sacred seat of Italy he puts on the consecrated crown.  
Then unhealthy camps suffer the heat and rage of a violent sky,  
and are afflicted with a dreadful pestilence.  
Soon, as avenger, he devastates Spoleto with sword and fire,  
for having dared to defraud the treasury with false coin  
[Note: [Col. 0329] W; A and subsequent editions: “faithful”; printer’s error.].  
He prepares to invade Apulia and the Calabrian territories,  
but changes his intended undertaking at the nobles’ dissuasion.  
Having dismissed his army and revisited the lands of his birth,  
he puts savage brigands to a fitting death.

The **FIFTH** sends cities out to meet the returning prince;  
the towns rejoice, their gates flung open.  
He avenges the clamor of wars, conflagrations, losses, and plunder,  
and consumes the guilty with deserved destruction.  
With the Count Palatine he compels ten powerful counts  
to bear hounds upon their shoulders, a most shameful burden.  
When all things have been restored to order by firm peace,  
he shares the covenant of a chaste bed with Beatrice.  
The gentle man preserves for his uncle the honor of his ancient name  
and commands Austrian lands to become a new duchy.

The **SIXTH** raises royal standards against the untamed Poles;  
after battles, he returns victorious to Würzburg.  
He despised the deceitful messages borne by the Greeks  
[Note: [Col. 0329] “despises?”].  
The Englishman sends an outstanding gift of tents.  
A papal letter, suspicious because of its ambiguous wording, moves him while he is stationed at Chrysopolis  
[Note: [Col. 0329] Rs.; A: *positis* (“situated”); perhaps *positos*.];  
soon the prince seeks the lands of Nuremberg  
[Col. 0331] and compels his uncles into their ancient covenant;  
first he creates Ladislaus king from a duke.  
Peace having been made at home, he hastens to invade the Ligurians in war  
and recalls his cohorts to camp.

The **SEVENTH** summons an assembly at Augsburg; then he enters Italy  
to receive the highest honors.  
There he recounts Greek frauds, the pope’s embassy,  
the counts seized, and the replies.  
The sceptre is granted to the king of the Danes; nations gather from the North,  
and he advances upon the city of the Ligurians.  
Laws are written; he exhorts the nobles; in wrath  
the most valiant hero burns wholly against the Ligurians [Note: [Col. 0331] (+).].  
A fierce battle is fought at Trezzo; with siege  
he shakes all its walls and breaks gates and towers.

In the **EIGHTH**, the provident Caesar surveys the Ligurians’ city  
and sees from afar the citadel of the ancient theatre [Note: [Col. 0331] (+).].  
Pavia [Note: [Col. 0331] (+).] and strong Cremona wage mutual war.  
Thereupon famine and fierce pestilence raged in the Ligurian city  
[Note: [Col. 0331] “raged?”].  
Guido of Bladerenza [Note: [Col. 0331] (+).] conducted the business, but that of peace;  
and the Caesar had soon given the citizens a condition of peace  
[Note: [Col. 0331] P, Rs.: *Ut* (“as/when”) and *dederit* (“may have given”); perhaps *conditiones* (“conditions”).],  
and according to custom celebrated a splendid triumph.  
He dismisses the nobles, restores Tisuidum and the camp;  
a court is appointed at Roncaglia and he lays out the camp.  
He holds a council [Note: [Col. 0331] “assembly?”]; feudal laws are given.  
The Placentine condemns the Cremonese to a payment  
[Note: [Col. 0331] Either corrupt or false; perhaps “the Cremonese [condemn] the Placentines?”],  
and then Caesar held the borders of Sardinia and Genoa  
[Note: [Col. 0331] false.].  
Otto of Freising dies; soon the pope grows arrogant.  
The Ligurians defect; envoys come; and the defeated Ligurian restores  
the pope’s former rights.  
A battle is joined, with great slaughter of his own men.  
The Ligurian lays waste the fields and is surrounded by siege;  
his walls suffer immense ruin.  
And now pestilence comes with famine; and, in a great crime,  
plots against the king are laid, after the Ligurians’ manner.

In the **TENTH**, Beatrice, august wife of the great Caesar,  
comes escorted by her princes to Italian shores; and Crema groans.  
He establishes camp and hears his Rome more mercifully.  
Then he returns victorious to the Ligurians and creates a pope.  
Crema seeks peace, and the Ligurians are again attacked.  
At last the prince burned with conceived wrath;  
the Ligurian city falls [Note: [Col. 0331] false—“and conquered Crema lies low,” P and subsequent editions, + (+).], twenty thousand are captured;  
the city itself melts into ashes [Note: [Col. 0331] “The city melts into ashes,” P and subsequent editions, + (+).]. Caesar gives gifts and thanks,  
dismisses the camp, and the author of the *Ligurinus* writes poems  
[Note: [Col. 0331] “The author of the *Ligurinus* walks about the court,” Sp. and subsequent editions, + (+).].

# Book One

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331A] Lofty deeds, memorable for ages, I sing in anxious verse;  
and I prepare to publish abroad, Frederick, your triumphs to the world,  
and Fortune, who so often tried in vain to mock you,  
and the ambiguous faces of the two-formed monster,  
[5] its shifting movements; the world restrained by your valor;  
and adverse chances endured with the same bearing of mind  
as prosperous ones.

A burdensome task indeed, not to be undertaken by a lesser talent,  
[Col. 0332A] and formidable even to great poets.  
[10] Yet love and devotion will supply my slender strength;  
great hope will support the frail vigor of my spirit,  
and Fortune will favor dutiful affection.

And now, if in that former pursuit we could do anything of worth,  
and if our *Solymarius* dares to be read,  
[15] and perhaps even gives pleasure—before it I rejoice  
[Col. 0333A] that it penetrated royal houses and touched  
the noble hands of the powerful boy—that work was a kind of prelude,  
the first attempt of a new Muse,  
and a boyish offering. Now we offer other gifts  
[20] to the supreme man: little books written in his own praise;  
and, singing father and offspring together,  
we dedicate these jointly to all by a shared right.

Receive them, greatest ruler of all kings;  
receive them, light of the world, before or beside whom  
[25] no equal head breathes in the world. The world rejoices in you as prince;  
peoples and kingdoms fear you; from the rising  
to the setting of the sun, all look up at you  
[Col. 0333B] with bowed heads, and acknowledge you at once as lord and king.

And not only do you surpass in valor all men, greatest of men,  
[30] of our own age: all the names of kings of the past  
yield to you—let me speak with the leave of the ancients.  
You alone rejoice in a shared honor with Augustus,  
and Charlemagne admits you as companion in his famous deeds.

Surely it is the certain madness of a poet to have sung rustic verse  
[35] concerning so great a man; but spare my dutiful frenzy,  
great prince. Let not our presumption  
trouble you; poets alone may be mad.  
You see [Note: [Col. 0333] Rs: “you see”; A: “certain”; printer’s error; Sp., P, R: “stag,” ++.] how, by the gentle breath of the summer sun,  
both herds and humankind rejoice; so too the little creatures  
[40] [Col. 0333C] of the shady ground and green lizards commonly delight.  
And as birds soothe heaven with their song,  
so light cicadas shake the leafy shrubs.  
Indeed, it is even their custom to strive to sing more,  
the worse they sing; and stammerers speak more  
[Note: [Col. 0333] “may speak,” preferred by m.; Rs., +.].

[45] Thus I, whom famous poets wish to praise  
but are unable to praise worthily, rash in precipitous daring,  
prepare to celebrate in a slender song.  
Grant assent, most gentle prince, to your anxious poet,  
and turn your favorable regard toward his dutiful devotion.

[50] [Col. 0333D] You too, young Caesars, whom on this side paternal nobility,  
derived from the ancient stock of kings,  
and on that side your mother’s distinction and the succession  
[Note: [Col. 0333] Rs.: “on this side”; A and subsequent editions: “now”; printer’s error.]  
of ancient blood, and Rainald, founder of an illustrious lineage, commend—  
grant assent, and receive alike praises of yourselves  
[Note: [Col. 0333] Rs.: “your”; A and subsequent editions: “our”; printer’s error.]  
[55] and of your great father—for this is a common sacred service.

[Col. 0334A] First, come graciously, you who by paternal right,  
heir and successor alike of his virtues and kingdom,  
bear the sceptre. You equal your father in great virtues,  
boy king; already you press upon the Po and Tiber,  
a terror to Italians and Tuscans. Perhaps we shall sing  
[60] of these deeds of your nature, and of those which you yourself  
will add by your valor in succeeding years,  
if life is granted and I may please beneath your sceptre, Henry.

O happy fortune, that divine power has established  
[65] such a king, imbued with honorable pursuits,  
who knows how to distinguish the learned from the foolish rabble,  
and already long arouses the silent Muses, accustomed to be mute,  
[Col. 0334B] to their ancient labor by worthy reward.

You too, Frederick, duke of dukes, whom the Rhine, revered through your father’s name,  
and Swabia, feared by other lands, holds in awe,  
receive the little gift of our care. Kindly do not scorn  
the memorials of a small labor; stretch out your hand  
[70] and raise the poet—staggering beneath a great burden  
and overwhelmed by fear—if you can.

But [Note: [Col. 0333] “But”; “And,” SC, *] to you, for whom the entire Rhône serves from its source  
to its mouth, and whose whole course flows until, exhausted in its current,  
it at last mingles with the swollen waters of Ocean—  
[Col. 0334C] may these things be pleasing, illustrious boy. It is uncertain whether you wish  
to be called king or count [Note: [Col. 0333] “or duke,” B, + (*)]; for you powerfully rule  
[80] your mother’s kingdom of the ancient Allobroges, and, worthy  
of the kingdom’s splendor, derive your name from lofty Otto.

Nor are you to be passed over, Conrad, famous by a king-making name  
and true grandson in valor: succeeding by a sure covenant  
of name and right, you rule Frankish lands and Würzburg.  
[85] To you we offered the gifts of our first Muse,  
little books written about the sacred place;  
but here also we wish you to have a name,  
and dedicate [Note: [Col. 0333] “say,” Sp., + (*)] to you a share of this new honor.

[Col. 0334D] Last offspring of a magnificent prince, yet no less illustrious,  
[90] receive with childish hand this offered gift;  
rejoice in these little books and play with them, Philip.  
By what name of future honor may I rightly promise you?  
Shall I call you count, king, duke,  
or rather pontiff? For such, it is said, is your father’s dread intention,  
[95] [Col. 0335A] whose presages fate or the hidden order of things  
is never accustomed to disappoint.

Whatever you shall be, already you are great and venerable to us.  
Already I imagine you not as a boy, but your sacred temples  
veiled by a mitre and you seated upon a lofty chair.

[100] O noble offspring of a truly great father!  
O truly fortunate fruit from a sweet stock!  
O truly famous house, beneath which the whole world  
is laid from the rising sun to the western waves!  
Who knows it loves it; those who do not know it fear it.  
[105] At the hearing of it [Note: [Col. 0335] A, Rs.: “unheard of”; printer’s error.], enemies melt away in confusion  
and confess that they can do nothing against it.  
For the father, strong and sound despite weakened age  
[Note: [Col. 0335] Rs.: “in strong”; *],  
[Col. 0335B] urges on and leads his tender offspring through difficult ways.  
That offspring, rival follower of its fatherland’s glory,  
[110] hastens on; it thinks delay a loss  
[Note: [Col. 0335] A, Rs.: “the slow [thing]”; remaining editions: “the slow [person],” *],  
and outstrips its years by its merits.

What poet, then, could sufficiently celebrate with worthy praise  
such a father together with such offspring?  
Yet I shall undertake it, if only I may recount the brave deeds  
[115] of an extraordinary man—not all, but the fairer ones.  
For what book could contain them all if I pursued them all?  
Or what reader could run through them?

Those deeds are sufficiently illustrious through the service of great men;  
and I fear that, while striving to be helpful,  
[120] [Col. 0335C] I may be found to have done more harm,  
and as a mad poet be accused of drawing darkness over bright events.

Yet there is an argument which perhaps may dare to defend  
our undertaking, grant pardon, and wipe away the fault.  
Those who wrote before, desiring to preserve faithfully  
[125] the order of history, seem to have inserted not a few things  
into their pages which—if I may say so—  
neither greatly increase Caesar’s honor  
nor cohere with the narrative, but cling to it as though sewn on.

But we, voluntarily omitting whatever may be less beautiful and extraordinary,  
[130] or does not greatly pertain to Caesar’s outstanding deeds—  
adding no embellishment to truth—shall follow only the more important matters,  
[Col. 0335D] and shall strive to make a modest sum from many things,  
to close a shorter book within the hand  
[135] and fashion it to charm the ears of readers,  
and, as from a full garden after flowers have been gathered,  
briefly weave garlands worthy of their prince.

If, therefore, anyone is pleased by a fuller order of events and uncorrupted truth,  
let him consult the writings of learned men  
[140] and drink streams drawn from the very source.  
[Col. 0336A] But if anyone thinks it sufficient merely to gather the matter in summary  
[Note: [Col. 0335] “merely,” Rs.],  
let him set his eye upon our work  
and drink a slender draught from the middle [Note: [Col. 0335] “moderate,” B, +.] of the stream.

Moreover, relying on the splendor of the matters recounted  
[145] and at the same time on their artful language and deep meaning,  
they rejected applying metrical laws to such distinguished material;  
and, I think, they were ashamed to sport  
in childish games and weave empty trifles.

But we, crude in speech and small in spirit,  
[150] calling individual words beneath number by fixed method,  
will veil them with a coating of superimposed color.  
Thus, if our ill-adorned speech happens insufficiently to move someone,  
at least the structure of the feet and the musical verses  
may hold him, and this may be something praiseworthy in our work.

[155] Now then, having prefaced what either the matter itself required  
[Col. 0336B] or the devoted love of the poet, for the assured consolation  
of the prince and young men, let us address what remains of the subject.

Let the present narrative therefore begin from that time, Frederick,  
when you first bore the sacred sceptre in your hand—  
[160] though indeed you had performed not a few deeds worthy of narration  
bravely even from tender youth.  
For we have no leisure to recount the first memorials of your youth,  
nor all that you accomplished, worthy of remembrance,  
under your father or uncle as your years increased.

[165] Those deeds are splendid in their proper places. We shall follow only  
the royal deeds with a light pen and with a certain brevity.

The thousandth year from the new-founded City was passing, and, to mark  
the event as precisely as speech can, the eight-hundredth:  
[Col. 0336C] or rather, that you may distinguish time from the birth  
[170] of Christ, who created time, add one hundred to the thousand,  
and then join four years to fifty  
[Note: [Col. 0335] The same year, though falsely, is indicated in a manuscript of Otto of Freising, as Muratori testifies, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, VI, p. 699, note 1.].

This span of time had elapsed, and the bereft seat  
of the Teutonic kingdom stood vacant through Conrad’s death.  
The nobles, the living substance of the whole realm,  
[175] gather to act concerning the successor to the sacred crown  
at a well-known place, close to the swift Main,  
famous for its situation, populous and adorned with walls,  
but bearing a rude name. For the Teutonic inhabitant called it  
“Franconefurt”; let us in Latin speech call it  
[180] “the Ford of the Franks,” because Charles, attacking  
[Col. 0336D] the Saxons, rebels in their excessive untamed savagery,  
is believed to have crossed the broadest waters of the rushing Main  
at an unknown ford and sent his cohorts through the middle  
of the river, neglecting a bridge.  
[185] Hence the permanent name adhered to the place.

Here sacred and illustrious men, whom mitre or sword  
makes revered in the world by bright renown, flow together  
from every region for the public advantage of the kingdom.  
They prepare, with exact deliberation, to act and decide  
[190] [Col. 0337A] upon the highest affairs, and with eager devotion seek  
to place over themselves from among all one man  
who alone may be worthy to succeed to so great an honor.

So, when a ship runs over the night-wandering sea by starlight,  
and perchance an envious cloud presses upon it the harmful darkness  
[195] by which its course is guided,  
interrupts its route, the sailor seeks his way by another star,  
alters the handling of rudder and trim of sail,  
and skillfully adjusts the vessel to the rays.

Thus [Note: [Col. 0337] “here,” B.] after the leaders had taken their seats and debated in uncertain minds  
[200] to whom the honors of so great a kingdom should be entrusted,  
the Saxons gathered, as did those governing the land called Ripuarian,  
the cities of Westphalia and the lands of Nuremberg;  
the dukes of the Allobroges also, and fierce Cimbrians,  
[Col. 0337B] whom warlike Germany, bathed in her Rhine,  
[205] sent forth, and the land marked by great Luther;  
the Vindelicians and Raetians hasten in, whom Swabia nourishes,  
and those whom Austria bounds with the Carinthian fields,  
whom the Lech and the Danube glide past in swollen waters;  
and those who directed their powerful cities here—  
[Note: [Col. 0337] “who,” Rs.]  
[210] the famous names of the Teutonic kingdom assembled.

Nor had the fame of these new events drawn here fewer men  
from the Italians and the Latin race.  
They desired to see the assembly and the new king,  
to behold the venerable faces of the leaders  
[215] and learn their famous names, then report accurately to their peoples.

Therefore, when the fathers had heard of affairs so great, they took their seats  
[Col. 0337C] in a fitting place and, weighing great matters with differing favor,  
look now upon these men, now immediately upon those.  
For long they consider character and lineage,  
[220] ability, reputation, the use of untroubled fortune,  
the outcome and the end alike; what benefits may flow from him to the kingdom,  
what injuries to themselves; whether he will be a stern  
or gentle judge, dutiful or fierce, an honorable giver  
or rapacious; whether he promises peace  
[Note: [Col. 0337] “shares out peace,” (*)] or threatens war.  
[225] They weigh all things in the anxious balance of their cares.

At last Fortune deigned to reveal through one man what the kingdom sought.  
A man famous in name—whether duke, count, or bishop was uncertain—  
venerable in appearance, powerful in counsel  
[Col. 0337D] and skilled in persuasion, rose. When he had composed his voice  
[230] to a matter commensurate with his great frame,  
the eloquent elder opened his lips thus,  
and with persuasive speech soothed every heart:

“Nobles of the Franks, whom it can never shame to call  
the famous strength and firm columns of the kingdom,  
[235] you know how Conrad, alas, was taken from our midst  
by bitter death and left behind life and kingdom.  
Now therefore, just as when dice are being played,  
if something has fallen badly, the prudent player corrects it by skill,  
[Col. 0338A] so let us, whom the dice of human lot have played with,  
[240] hasten by counsel to correct the calamity of hostile fate  
and bring consolation for so great a grief.

“The kingdom is in your hands; for by its custom  
that power always returns to you when it is bereft.  
For other kings there is the sure assurance of succession by paternal right,  
[245] and a new heir receives his father’s sceptre.  
We, whose liberty is better, possess by ancient right, whenever  
the illustrious seat stands empty of its own prince,  
complete freedom to appoint whatever king we choose.

“Since, by our valor, Rome was redeemed and its enemies expelled,  
[250] the most just order transferred the Empire to us.  
The glory of the Roman kingdom belongs to us;  
[Col. 0338B] whomsoever Germany appoints as king over herself,  
wealthy Rome receives him with bowed head,  
and the Rhine rules the Tiber in a reversed order.

“Deliberate together; from so great a multitude of mighty men  
[255] choose one worthy to succeed so great a king,  
worthy to bear the Italian crown.

“But if, with the leave of your judgment, I may advise what my mind thinks—  
you should weigh the matter more closely—I shall declare  
the direction toward which the weight of our counsel inclines.

[260] “Here is a young man of exceptional worth, illustrious through the lofty  
name of his ancestors, but more illustrious by his own deeds:  
Frederick, heir to his father’s name,  
[Col. 0338C] a Swabian and not far in blood from the kings of old.  
While his royal uncle still enjoyed the light of life,  
[265] he rejoiced to have this nephew as one worthy of him;  
he was accustomed to entrust him with many affairs  
of the kindred kingdom and to associate him in its highest concerns.

“What need is there for me to speak of the young man’s distinction? Of the brave  
deeds of his first youth? Or how, following the foreign  
army of God, he performed as a famous novice in arms  
[Note: [Col. 0337] P, Rs: “as a famous novice”; A and remaining editions: “first”; W emends “for himself.”]  
[270] and endured such great labors with unconquered courage?  
If I unfold them, I fear that by saying much  
I shall be found to have said too little. The matter is very well known:  
whoever happens to deny it may say that he has never seen  
the daily rays of Phoebus, nor flowers in spring,  
[275] nor heard thunder in the middle of summer.

“I urge that this man be summoned as ruler with favorable acclamation,  
[Col. 0338D] that his shining hair be encircled with the sacred diadem;  
and I confess I shall never be ashamed to have given this advice.

“If I know him sufficiently, and if my omens do not deceive me,  
he flourishes in nobility and, through illustrious blood, reaches kings  
[280] on one side and dukes on the other as ancestors. He possesses sweet eloquence,  
a radiant appearance, a discerning spirit, an active hand, skill  
in counsel, fierceness in war and moderation in peace;  
old in mind, young in age, prudent in affairs,  
[Col. 0339A] steadfast in affection, robust in loyalty, firm in spirit—  
not to be broken by misfortunes nor lifted up by prosperity;  
loving praise, generous with wealth, terrible to the cruel,  
[290] calm toward the peaceful, fierce and untamed toward the proud,  
kind to suppliants, pious toward the just, harsh toward the unjust,  
brave amid present dangers, prudent for the future,  
mindful of the past, good to allies, relentless to enemies.

“These, nobles, these are the qualities accustomed to preserve  
[295] and fortify kingdoms. By these arts the lowly rise  
and the greatest are maintained. Unless we are mistaken, by these arts  
he will govern himself and his own. For he will not abandon, once reward is received,  
the qualities he has hitherto cultivated freely and without payment.

[Col. 0339B] “For the saying that supreme power changes good character  
[300] I think derives rather from another cause.  
If someone conscious of a depraved craft  
and an evil disposition secretly seeks office,  
he dissembles for a time; when he has gained what he desired,  
he returns to vice and his former habits. Then honors, though undeserving,  
[305] seem to have changed and corrupted the man,  
whereas he himself rather corrupts and pollutes them by evil use.

“But whoever has been given by nature a good disposition, inviolable by any chance,  
if he happily receives an honor of which he was worthy,  
then, once the time of concealment has been removed,  
[310] that hidden integrity begins to ripen in joyful fruit,  
and the shoots of virtues show themselves.

[Col. 0339C] “Thus the boy who from tender age flourishes in chaste habits  
and turns this natural disposition into practice—  
what kind of man, how great a man, do you suppose he will become?  
What glory of kingdom,  
[315] what splendor of empire will arise beneath so great a prince?

“That Conrad himself wished him to succeed to his realms, joined to him by blood,  
the fact itself proves: dying, and expecting nothing from his own young offspring,  
he lately left him the royal insignia as though to an heir.  
For if God had wished the kingdom to stand long  
[320] in that house, he could have preserved the elder offspring,  
who, after entering into the covenant of a shared kingdom,  
went before his father in lamentable and undeserved death.

“Now, since one brother has died by hostile fate  
[325] and by bitter mischance deprived the kingdom,  
while the other is still a boy, weak in his tender years—  
[Col. 0339D] who can better succeed his uncle, if only your will approves,  
than one whom his uncle himself seems almost to have designated as heir,  
being near to him in affection and flesh?

[330] “He knew the strength of this noble mind;  
he knew it, and therefore, so far as lay in his power,  
transferred the kingdom and wished to prefer his nephew to his son.

“He will not be an outsider. There will be no transfer of the kingdom here;  
we shall not be reduced beneath the laws of an unknown tyrant.

[335] “Add that, having been reared in the ancient court of kings,  
he knows how prudently to manage royal business.  
[Col. 0340A] Add also that he will be able to reconcile the two houses  
of kings and dukes—this one through his father, that one through the illustrious  
blood of his mother—which an impatient rivalry for shared glory  
frequently rouses to discord.

[340] “If anyone, from envy and love of hidden ambition,  
secretly and uselessly obstructs so many good qualities by his counsels,  
he proves himself either foolish or faithless.”

Thus, when whoever he was had ended his speech in honeyed  
[345] and eloquent words, all immediately assented with one accord.  
The young duke is summoned as king with joyful acclaim;  
the whole court sings Frederick’s name,  
extols his honorable character and brave deeds,  
and declares him worthy of the sceptre, to be sought voluntarily  
[350] [Col. 0340B] or compelled to accept it. Some recall the famous  
names of his ancestors and his mingled descent from kings and dukes;  
others his zeal, the vigor of his great spirit,  
and his gentle yet weighty character.  
Some proclaim the titles of his achievements, deeds performed in lesser age  
[355] scarcely to be matched by men in their full strength and years.

I think it safer to pass over this matter altogether than to say only a little about it.  
I do not have such confidence in my poem that, writing a full account,  
I should wish to equal everything. This matter requires a great poet;  
in small matters we have courage enough.

[Col. 0340C] Soon, when the nobles had duly bound their faith by sacred oath  
and completed all that order required,  
they departed, leaving a few men with the new king,  
and gladly returned to their own cities.

[365] So, when the stars that rule worldly affairs—if those who delight  
to hand down such doctrines speak truth—after many ages  
meet in a favorable sign and swear by a harmonious compact  
some greater benefit for the world: peace for lands,  
salvation for humankind,  
[370] moderation of the sky, faithful fields for their cultivators,  
or something similar; then they again depart by their own courses  
and returning revolution, dissolve their choir, and return home,  
[Col. 0340D] not to meet again until after long labors.

[375] But the king, making his first move after this matter had been happily accomplished,  
seeks by ship, across the traversed waters of the river mentioned,  
a celebrated city of famous name,  
where the Main mingles its waters with the swelling Rhine.  
Though it loses its own name in that current,  
[380] it nevertheless gives the first element of its name to the distinguished city;  
and that city, though it stands upon a greater and more populous river,
It disregards this and deigns to be called by its guest, the river.

For, overwhelming the Rhine—if we are to believe everything that report tells—Mainz takes its name from the Main poured into it.

[385] This city of the Franks, set in the midst of their territories, rich in fields, vines, orchards, and a populous people,

[Col. 0341A] touches the Rhine on this side at its station, while on the other it stretches its borders far out to the swift Moselle,

which, scarcely smaller, as it passes through peaceful country,

[390] fertile in crops, fruits, and sweet grapes, retains its name and its waters under its own authority as far as the place named from the confluence of the two rivers. Then the conquering Rhine carries both away and, stronger, rules the mingled waters.

[395] This same city, once proud in its towers and walls, was throughout the whole realm a seat of great renown,

[Col. 0341B] until, laid low because of an unspeakable and detestable frenzy, it paid the deserved penalty for the murder of its bishop.

Thereafter, ugly and dreadful in its ruined walls,

[400] it bears witness to the just anger of an offended prince.

Lest Germany should celebrate this as her principal seat, Cologne envies it and holds the prior place.

Both are metropolitan sees: this one rules by ancient right those cities which the river, higher toward its source—Basel alone excepted—or placed laterally on either side, looks upon;

[405] the other those which it possesses upon the same bank of the Rhine, far or near, until it mingles with the waters of the sea.

Thus the Rhine is divided in equal portions and serves each mistress alone.

[410] Then, as far as he pleased [Note: [Col. 0341] “was permitted,” Rs. +], he made his way down the same river by oar; many great and powerful men came to meet him and greeted the new king and lord.

When it seemed sufficient, leaving Rhine and boats, he exchanged his river journey for a ride on horseback.

[415] Thence through the woodland passes of the Ardennes he came as far as that place to which the ancients gave its name from its waters.

To one inquiring into the reason for this fact, or the cause of this name, I can offer only this [Note: [Col. 0341] “these?”]:

there are there hidden and dark channels within the earth,

[420] [Col. 0341D] which, concealed in the silent ground in differing ways, shoot forth waters. Some, boiling with living sulphur, are said to burst out amid billowing smoke;

but others issue as streams as though from an icy spring; then the water, led through hollow channels,

[425] flows together by a remarkable contrivance into a certain pool.

Thus royal baths [Note: [Col. 0341] “cold baths,” m. Rs. *] are mingled with hot thermal baths;

and the skill of ancient craftsmen set marble steps around them, by which one may descend into the water

[Col. 0342A] as far as one wishes: here one finds cold waters, there hot, and tempers the waters for oneself at will.

Whether hidden nature has added these vapours to those places, or human labour [Note: [Col. 0341] (*)], let those inquire who inhabit the familiar locality; their elders [Note: [Col. 0341] “of a greater man,” or “of greater men,” V. *] may have learned the causes and secrets of things by trustworthy report.

[435] Charles, wishing this place to be, as it were, the cradle of his realm, when both Frankias were subject to the great king, ordered the first crown to be borne there and kings to be installed in that sacred seat.

And when Gaul at the same time withdrew from our kingdom [Note: [Col. 0341] “but,” Rs. +],

[440] we preserve the ancient custom of the realm; but she enjoys her own law, now ignorant of ours.

Therefore, in the presence of a crowd of many magnates—not only Germans, but also those whom Flanders had sent, and Gaul, admiring the fame she had heard, and those upon whose sacred head

[445] Arnold, the bishop under whose pastoral care rich Cologne then rejoiced—for that place claims this honour as its ancient right—had placed the royal insignia—

then Frederick, seated in the sacred chair, ascended the throne of his ancient forefathers.

[450] Nor do I wish to pass over certain manifest pledges of stern justice and examples of strict severity.

[Col. 0342C] For one of his household servants, while Frederick was still a private man, in a mad frenzy had dared by a dreadful crime to strike down a distinguished and illustrious duke; and, terrified by the just anger of the man which he knew, he fled from the image of his own deed.

This man too, deceived by the empty hope of pardon,

[455] was present among the people, his face hidden [Note: [Col. 0341] Rs. A; “with face uncovered,” o.], concealing himself beneath humble clothing and disguising his identity.

Therefore, when the bishops had according to custom placed the sacred crown on the man, he threw himself down full-length,

clasped the royal feet, and, pitiful in groaning voice and tears, began to beg pardon.

[460] All were moved, and with devout prayers earnestly asked that he spare and deign to pardon the afflicted dependant.

But Frederick, wishing to establish fear of himself among all,

[Col. 0342D] and to terrify the wicked, steadfastly refused to hear the men, though they had pleaded long and much.

And lest the magnates should perhaps be shaken by this harsh refusal,

[470] he openly declared that he had acted thus not from hatred of the wretched man, but from love of strict justice and as an example.

The prudent man removed all odium from his action and established powerful precedents.

Perhaps others will blame this; I praise the noble deed of the man and call him worthy to bear the mighty sceptre in his hand,

[475] [Col. 0343A] who thus restrained his spirit, though pity was suppressed, and gave all certain proofs of his vigour [Note: [Col. 0343] “strictness,” m. Rs. +].

For a king’s wisdom often harms more than severity: the latter harms a few; the former encourages all,

[480] while they hope to bear their own offences with impunity.

Perhaps the noble youth had heard how of old Romulus, first ruler of his city of Rome and founder of its empire,

wishing to establish the foundations of an everlasting kingdom, ordered his brother—who had dared to violate the tender laws and leap across the lowly ditches—to fall to avenging death.

[485] And now the boy-king, having attained the full height of his honour, prepares with a manly hand to drive childish things from his mind and direct his youthful capacity to great affairs.

For he was not unaware of himself, nor of how great a burden attends honour; he had begun to feel this formerly from the death of his illustrious father.

[490] But now he feels himself pressed by a weight heavier than usual and perceives that his labour has greatly increased.

[Col. 0343B] As when, after many unwearied labours, Alcides was ordered to take the place of weary Atlas,

and, amazed to bear great Olympus with so many stars, sweated under its unfamiliar weight.

[495] Therefore he associates with himself men to whom famous prudence and long experience of many affairs had given renown,

men accustomed often to participate in secret matters;

[Col. 0343C] diligently managing the hidden business of the great kingdom, he takes counsel concerning everything to be done and with studious mind inquires what is honourable, just, or useful,

[500] what is fitting and what is not.

Without delay he orders envoys bearing commands to hasten to the supreme pontiff, and proclaims throughout all the cities of Italy his own accession to honours.

He preferred these to be the first fruits of his actions as prince:

[505] that he might immediately crush the manifest enemies of the realm and cleanse its scandals with the just sword.

Without delay he attacked Utrecht, which, while his uncle was reigning, had proudly cast off the yoke from its neck

[Col. 0343D] and had lately dared to offend the pious man by cruel deeds;

[510] in hostile fervour he prepared to level its walls to the ground, overthrow its captured towers, and, with an avenging hand, fully satisfy the anger of his uncle and the kingdom’s grief by punishment of the guilty—O great piety and judgment of the nephew!

[515] Thus the first and greatest monarch of the august ones, the distinguished grandson, a pious and most brave avenger, after his enemies had been destroyed, immediately expiated the cruel wrongs done to Caesar of old when he received the diadem.

[Col. 0344A] At last, scarcely yielding to the prayers of many great dukes, after they had first been redeemed for much money,

[520] he spared them, and the anger of the just prince’s sword subsided.

Nor could the madness and pride of the foolish populace have been punished better than by taking away the wealth that had been the cause of so great an arrogance;

[525] and poverty might bring back to themselves those whom abundance of possessions had made proud [Note: [Col. 0343] “and that,” Ps. +].

Then he turned his steps back, bearing his standards before the welcoming waves of the Rhine.

Fair Cologne, he entered you more joyful while you rejoiced;

[530] there the pious man celebrated with worthy honour that day on which Christ, having resumed the flesh,

[Col. 0344B] returned in radiant victory from the shades below and, death overcome, brought back his glorious triumphs.

Afterwards, entering the territories of Saxony, he summoned to the city which the German inhabitant calls Martinopolis an assembly of magnates from the whole body of the realm,

[535] so that the court might be celebrated by a worthy gathering at the solemn season when the gracious Spirit, coming from on high with a sound, poured fiery lights in divided tongues into the holy breasts of the devout.

He also summoned there Peter and Guy, two Danish magnates, whom a dispute stirred by disagreement over the same kingdom had set at variance, though they were joined by blood;

[540] and he settled and decided their case on these terms: that an entire province should fall to Guy, but Peter should retain the kingdom with its name.

Therefore, when the former received from him the portion which we have mentioned by the standard, and the latter the kingdom by the sword—

[545] for our court preserves this custom observed for a long time—Peter, laying aside the royal diadem, took in his right hand the sword of the high prince,

and the diadem fell somewhat short of the sacred crown.

There also parties from the Virgin City—if I may speak thus, for my page admits no barbarian name,

[Col. 0344D] nor does it seem possible to say it better without a name—brought a dispute concerning two elected bishops.

[550] While the ruler had long endeavoured vainly to reconcile them peacefully and bring them into one,

at last, both candidates being rejected, a third pastor was given by the prince against their wishes.

For the court testifies that this right was conferred upon it by the supreme bishop in the reign of King Henry V:

[555] that if a see should happen to contend over a new bishop and the complaint cannot be stilled by an imposed settlement,

the ruler himself ought then to intervene and appoint a pastor to the see by his own judgment.

[Col. 0345A] Nor is anyone elected to be consecrated by right before the prince grants him the regalia with his ivory sceptre.

Then at Regensburg—whose old name derives either from its suitability for boats, or because sailors were accustomed there to moor their vessels, and in which city the duchy of Noricum has its principal distinction—

[560] a solemn court was appointed for a fixed time, a short interval after these events, at the season when the whole world rejoices in the twofold splendour of the apostolic triumph.

[565] And now the men whom the prince had long before sent returned from the Italian cities and also from the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See, bringing back all happy news.

As soon as the king had handled the matters laid before him in their proper order and settled all things in peaceful accord,

[570] desiring great seeds of glory to be won and powerful means of enlarging the realm, he was preparing, if his allies also approved, to enter the Hungarian borders with an armed force.

He would have done so, nor would the prince’s design have been unprofitable; he could have brought the affair to his desired conclusion.

[575] But certain dukes, whether with good intention and faithful advice, or through deceit and hidden guile—which we rather believe—dissuaded him.

And lest he should seem to oppose them or, in this matter, to pursue private rather than public advantage,

[Col. 0345C] he reluctantly abandoned his lofty design. Thus the intention, not indeed removed but still deferred through their dissuasion,

[580] is hoped to be fulfilled either by the valour of his great father or by the auspices of his exalted blood, when circumstances find their proper time.

For I shall not suppose that he wished in vain, or ever conceived empty forebodings of the future in his sacred breast, or rashly hoped for anything.

[585] Yet, set amid so great a splendour of affairs—so utterly is no human enjoyment unalloyed—the ruler does not possess full joys in a tranquil breast,

[Col. 0345D] whom the anxious discord of a kinsman’s quarrel torments, though affairs have been well ordered by divine gift.

For two magnificent magnates, each named Henry [Note: [Col. 0345D] “both,” Rs.], equal in distinguished deeds and in the titles of their ancestors, were waging a grievous and doubtful war, threatening the realm with much ruin.

[590] Of these, the Austrian, this very uncle of the ruler, had been begotten by Margrave Leopold, the king’s grandfather through his grandmother;

[Col. 0346A] the other, the duke of Noricum and likewise the king’s maternal uncle, the noble Henry, was born of noble stock.

These drew the melancholy causes of war and the first seeds of rage from the following reasons:

[595] the father of one of them, duke of the Noricans, expelled long ago on account of cruel envy and proud conduct, while retaining only the bare right to Saxony,

had felt the avenging wrath of Prince Conrad.

And the duchy taken from him, by grant of the realm, was held first by Leopold and now by his brother, the warlike Henry, who was also the ruler’s uncle.

[600] So that this single pestilence might at last depart from the healthy body, like a hateful cloud from the middle of a clear sky,

[Col. 0346B] the powerful peers of the whole realm were ordered to assemble at Würzburg under their illustrious prince.

The Saxon was present; the Austrian was absent, as one avoiding judgment and fearing to lose the rights to the duchy long possessed.

For in every case, he who has been dispossessed loves judgment; he who possesses hates it.

[605] The court of the whole realm decreed by three edicts that the absent man must be summoned to law.

No less were there present magnates of high birth from Apulia and the Calabrian territories; Roger, invader of those places, had ordered them to leave their native shores

[Col. 0346C] and had driven them as fugitives from the whole region.

Lamenting with tears the many cruel deeds of the tyrant, their expulsion from their native soil, their proscription from their goods, and the many indignities they had suffered—

[610] condemned to death, exile, or long confinement in prison—they added wretched complaints broken by groaning, and justly sought aid from our prince and the kingdom’s vengeance for their condition.

The assembly of magnates was moved, and all faithfully begged the king to avenge such manifest scandals of the entire realm and so great a ruin of law and morals.

[615] The prince gladly accepted this and rejoiced at being asked, finding material for new glory to pursue;

[Col. 0346D] he resolved by the common oath of the magnates to bear his standards across the Alps after the first two years,

so that at the same time he might receive the crown from the sacred seat of empire and correct the savage acts of unjust Roger.

[620] This man, as report has it, Normandy once produced together with his brother Robert, who, on account of his quick wits and vigour of spirit, bore the byname Guiscard.

They were of middling fortune in possessions or birth, but far outstanding among their own in heart and mind,

[Col. 0347A] strong in hand and handsome in appearance, lovers of glory, seeking the seeds of great enterprises and eager to become known by their deeds;

[625] they claimed descent more from the illustrious blood of kings than from a private people of the Franks.

While still under tender and growing years, conceiving I know not what noble design in their vigorous [Note: [Col. 0347] “warm,” m. Rs. +] hearts,

as Fortune herself, surely, urged the men with hidden voice and with enticing hand promised some very great thing [Note: [Col. 0347] “each?”],

[630] already drawing the future to themselves in hope, they judged every land to be a homeland for the brave [Note: [Col. 0347] “for each,” Sp. P. R. Rs, +].

Daring, with their native fields wholly despised, they migrated from home, desiring to win for themselves a name, a people, and a homeland;

nor did they merely cross the fields of Gaul, but with hasty step passed the Alps, broken by lofty crags.

[635] At last the men sought Apulia and Calabrian homes through the cities of Italy and Latin dwellings, as though these were lands owed to them.

So the royal bird, when it feels its first feathers growing on its limbs and its tender claws becoming hard, follows the course of nature.

[640] Already it disdains to be fed by its parents’ care, leaves its nest, and is ashamed to have lain hidden in a small shelter;

soon, trusting in itself and safe in confident flight,

[Col. 0347C] it hunts a hare in the fields or snatches a swan from the sky; upon a sharp cliff it builds a dwelling of its own and prepares to produce offspring like itself.

[645] That land indeed, lacking no gift, shone exceedingly rich in tree-fruits, vines, fields, cities, fortresses, and every adornment.

But its people were foolish, corrupt, uncultivated, fickle, vain,

accustomed to pursue prolonged idleness and flee labour, sluggish in mind and hand, useful neither in peace nor in war.

[650] Therefore the men, weighing the character of the inhabitants, the condition of the region, and their own talent with the shrewdness of an industrious mind,

and judging that bold enterprises ever befit brave men, seized in their hearts the hope of gaining those territories.

[Col. 0347D] Sending trusted agents, they gathered to themselves all Franks whom either their parents’ humble fortune, love of novelty, or great boldness of spirit had called from their native lands to great rewards;

[655] and in a short time, by force, skill, treachery, and much labour, they held the whole land, subdued and with its inhabitants expelled, by an unjust title.

And Robert left you, Bohemond, as an heir worthy of your country’s glory and exalted name.

[Col. 0348A] You, victor under your father’s auspices, soon captured with your own hand the walls of Antioch destined for you and gave them to be preserved by your race.

But the other begot a namesake and like-minded Roger, who, never falling short of his father’s deeds, added many things to the Sicilian realms by his own warfare.

[660] Indeed, carried as far as Byzantium in warlike ships, he himself bravely sent gilded arrows with his youthful bow into the royal palace, and left memorials of eternal fame.

Yet most people confuse this course of history in their account and alter it after their own fashion,

[Col. 0348B] delighting to assign the glory of the great deed to Robert alone.

They assert that he begot this brave Roger together with Bohemond and that the father formed both sons in his own virtues,

not only in those matters which fortune had already granted, but in those which the lofty mind of a man, foreknowing the future, promised [Note: [Col. 0347] “promised,” plural, Sp. P. R. +].

[665] They say that he trained heirs prepared to succeed him in great expectation, gave the boys, at his last end, strong instructions suited to their noble disposition,

and with lavish hand bestowed whatever either an enemy, a timid man, or a less worthy possessor held.

[Col. 0348C] Hence our historian of Jerusalem reports, following the common rumour, that he assigned to Bohemond Libya under foreign rule, Sicilian homes, and the famous city of Antioch, which Bohemond had not yet seen.

[670] Whether rumour or the historical order is more reliable, let the reader determine; and let him pardon a poet writing great matters in doubtful verse.

For that lineage and the succession of the Sicilian court have not yet become sufficiently known to us,

from which the greatest world rejoices that a bride of noble blood has touched the august womb and entered the chaste bed of a mighty king.

[675] After this, Worms first saw, at the king’s command, an assembly of magnates gather.

Both dukes came there; but even then the court could not quell the old quarrel of the magnates.

At another time, the assembly of powerful men was again summoned to Regensburg and vainly attempted, after peace had been restored, to restrain the prolonged dispute.

[680] Next came the gathering of magnates at Speyer. They strove long and greatly to bring the two dukes back to peaceful dispositions and a firm peace,

[Col. 0349A] but spent their prolonged labour in vain.

From here the ruler also ordered envoys to hasten to Manuel, in whose time the imperial seat then rejoiced in a purple-born prince [Note: [Col. 0349] “Porphyrogenitus,” B. *],

[685] bearing words concerning a treaty of peace, the common good, and the safety of both realms.

He urged him to declare war, on account of Roger’s deeds, upon William, who now held the sceptre of his dead father and his plundered wealth.

[Col. 0350A] And because the pope had recently ordered William, his kinship by treaty having been discovered, to separate from his first wife, so that, deprived of the lot of marriage, he lacked a spouse,

[690] Manuel sought a consort worthy both of the realm and of the marriage-bed, from the same stock, in order to bind him more firmly in strong knots of peace.

At last, as the pious Saxon pressed the king strongly and demanded back his duchy without end,

which the king himself was preparing to add to his own dominions, he summoned the magnates and both parties in the dispute to Goslar.

[695] There, since the uncle fled the suit, he restored the duchy, won by judgment and with law preserved, to the nephew.

## BOOK II

[Col. 0349]

[Col. 0349B] The third year from the illustrious beginning of your happy reign, Frederick, had come, and the appointed day for moving the camp was at hand.

Then, leaving the territories of Saxony and making for the upper parts of his realm with a great army, where the Lech, now gentler in its quiet waters, washes the lands of Noricum,

[5] the ruler himself encamped not far from the city of Augsburg.

The nearest camps reached Brixen, a city of famous name; others reached rocky Trent.

[10] Then he made his way through rough winding paths, narrow places made dreadful by stony ridges, and treacherous defiles.

At last, after great and prolonged labour in overcoming the Alps, he saw the fields and plains of low-lying Italy,

[Col. 0349C] and set up his tents in the plains near the lake, at your Verona.

But because, driven by lack of food while crossing a harsh valley by a hard route, the soldiers had despoiled holy buildings by unlawful plunder in places fertile neither in Ceres nor hospitable to Bacchus,

[15] before the king was willing to advance the marching camp and deal with the affairs of the human realm,

he resolved to appease God and humbly subject himself and his men to the heavenly king in devout prayers.

[20] At once he collected the coins gathered from the whole army and, entrusting the money to faithful men—this bishop and that count, both approved—

[Col. 0349D] ordered it distributed in just proportion among all who had been robbed, and made compensation for the losses of the lawful plunder [Note: [Col. 0349] “unlawful,” B. +].

A noble deed of the king, although scarcity might excuse the act, as it once did that of holy David.

[25] Yet in this matter he did not attend to excuses, but to the deed; not to what was lawful, but to what was honourable.

For it is characteristic of a good mind to acknowledge fault where no fault is present [Note: [Col. 0349] *est* is lacking in A, Sp., and R.].

Then at last, striking camp, he hastened to reach Roncaglia with his swift forces.

[30] There is a place in Italy, a little apart from the city which, because it is pleasing in its beautiful situation, is therefore named Piacenza:

flat, adjoining the gentle river Po, it spreads wide plains over a spacious expanse.

[35] Whenever the German ruler makes for the famous city to receive in due form the Italian crown, he customarily pitches camp here.

A shield is hung high on a raised pole;

[Col. 0350C] then the royal herald summons all who hold feudal rights from their lords.

By the ancient custom of their forefathers, faithful men must keep the king’s watch on the first night.

[40] But whoever, left at home without his lord’s permission, fails to appear, the court decrees that he be deprived of his fief.

At that time also some lost possessions long held through this charge, by the vindicating judgment of the realm.

[45] Indeed, the bishop of Halberstadt and he under whom Bremen stood lost their regalian rights by the same sentence:

that is, the persons themselves, not the Church; for it is not right that what a pastor has unjustly done should be repaid to the Church’s detriment.

[Col. 0350D] Now come: as we are about to recount many things worthy of sacred remembrance concerning the land, we shall sing of its situation, the seat of its regions, the peoples, its given names, and ancient customs—as ancient report has made them known.

[50] This land, bounded and hemmed in on one side by the rugged cliffs of the Apennines and on the other by the airy Alps,

[Col. 0351A] long but allotted the narrow shape of a belt, is enclosed on this side by the Tyrrhenian Sea and on that by Venetian waters.

For the Apennine barrier of your mountain moderates for itself the swift heat of Notus and the blasts of Auster.

[55] But the Alps, with their opposing peaks, come to the aid of those who fear the swift north wind [Note: [Col. 0351] A reads *rigidum*, “stiff/harsh,” for *rapidum*, “swift” +] and the icy Bear.

The Tyrrhenian is beaten by Zephyr, the wandering Adriatic by Eurus [Note: [Col. 0351] P: “barrier,” *objice*].

Perhaps someone joins these mountains as though they were one body, and, as two arms are joined to a single head, says that the whole is truly called by the name Pyrenaeus, while the Apennines and Alps are parts of the whole.

[60] Yet this opinion has seized some minds for the following reason: where Genoa, so often tried by the martial ships of the Tyrrhenian surge, is struck by the tide,

there are seen two mountains touching each other and, as though faithfully embracing with arms spread on either side, enclosing peoples and walls in a broad bosom.

[65] The Po, great and not unknown in the western world, much indebted to ancient poets, divides this land with its stream running through the middle;

it makes two lesser zones from one and divides the peoples in two.

Flowing from both sides, it enriches them and enters the Adriatic waters with greater abundance.

[Col. 0351C] In this one land three provinces are divided among three peoples: Venetians, Ligurians, and Aemilians inhabit it;

each province takes its name from its people and contains many cities.

[70] This land, therefore, rejoicing in sweet moisture, so fertile in Ceres, Bacchus, the gentle olive-tree, cattle, and every kind of produce,

lacks the distinction of no crop and complains of no delayed gift.

We have learned that Aquileia is the foremost city of Aemilia in renown, rightly so called because it derives its famous name from the eagle, sovereign of all birds.

[75] They call Milan the metropolis and supreme seat of the Ligurians:

[Col. 0351D] either because in some central core of the land it abounds most richly in every noble thing [Note: [Col. 0351] “most abundantly,” B. +],

or because it derives its name from a discovered pig which bore woolly fleece upon the middle of its back.

But the seat which the Venetian inhabits as foremost is called by no name other than that of the land itself:

[80] a city exceedingly wealthy, though the sea roars around it and a mound heaped against Adriatic waves, beaten by the waters, has allowed it but a small site.

Ancient speech calls this Italy “outer,” because, divided off by the intervening ridge of the Tuscan mountain, it lies farther from lovely Rome, the Roman colony, and is in some sense a boundary of the Ausonian world.

[85] But the land enclosed by the great Apennine, containing Etruscan homes and the famous city, has by ancient custom been called “inner.”

Then that region which stretches to the Sicilian deep, embracing Apulia, the Calabrian bays, and Campanian fields,

[Col. 0352B] was formerly called either Nearer Italy or Greater Greece; yet many also count it as central and place the two under one name.

[90] In former times a barbarian enemy, whom Scanzia [Note: [Col. 0351] A reads *Scanzia*; other witnesses, *Scandia* +] had sent in war, invaded this country.

After its males had been slain in battle, their hair pressed under grim helmets down to the chin, and their blue hair imitating a manly beard,

the women are said to have armed themselves in bands and supplied the loss of men with their weak hand; and thus, victorious, to have held these places by female triumph.

[95] For this reason too the land is said to be called Lombardy, from the long beards.

Then, gradually mingling blood with the natives,

[Col. 0352C] the barbarian people, contrary to the custom usual among nations, passed into a partner people after adopting its name.

A shrewd, sagacious, prudent, industrious, skilful people, provident in counsel and learned in laws and legal right;

strong in body and mind, alert in spirit, handsome in face, vigorous in the agility of their limbs, patient of labour,

[100] prompt in hand, fluent in speech, exceedingly eager for praise, refined in arts and in the pursuit of new works,

temperate, fearing the future, modest in expenditure, watchful over wealth, carefully preserving what has been acquired,

[Col. 0352D] content with little food, delighting to equip their bodies with shining arms and bright clothing;

loving liberty, for which they rejoice to dread neither grievous losses nor death itself;

[105] not willingly bowing their necks beneath the yoke of king or lord. They delight to entrust the highest authority to consuls,

and to change them annually, chosen from a threefold order, lest prolonged office breed arrogance.

They compel each person to live subject to the laws of his own city and bind even powerful outsiders under the same law;

[Col. 0353A] so that scarcely a count, or anyone else free from civic jurisdiction, can be found in that land.

And so that they may expel every enemy from their borders and defend their country by the strength of arms,

they permit any men from the humble populace—something Gaul judges shameful—to gird themselves with a knight’s sword.

[110] Yet that people, prudent in laws and devoted to the love of legal right, violates laws and rights by an impious deed [Note: [Col. 0353] Rs. and A c.; other witnesses, “by law”],

and voluntarily stains itself with heavy guilt.

For it never receives, except under terror, the king whom it ought to venerate with particular love and at the same time fear;

[Col. 0353B] and it abandons him once received through ready deceit.

It refuses all the more to submit to the king imposed upon it because victorious Germany often summons back her kings:

for Germany loves these realms in their presence with as great an affection as Italy trembles before them in fear.

[115] Thus it happens that this wicked people harms itself by a double loss, while in faithlessness it oppresses the king with undeserved trouble and suffers deserved penalties from the just prince.

Thus it feels cruel the man whom it despises when gentle: he punishes her as guilty whom he would prefer to have faithful.

[120] One Ligurian city had risen higher than all Italy in power of title and glory of name, lifting its lofty summit to strike the starry heaven.

[Col. 0353C] It lies at nearly equal distances between the Alps and the Po, bounded here by the Adda and there by the Ticino.

Both rise from neighbouring Alps and seek the famous lakes of the greater Po;

[125] they enclosed this city and two others, Como and Lodi, within their ample embrace.

But this one, stronger than the other two, prevailed and oppressed its conquered neighbours beneath harsh dominion.

So greatly did being greater harm the neighbouring cities; indeed, proximity has harmed many.

[130] And it had not merely oppressed peoples and other cities less powerful than itself; raised up by success and, as it were, drawing the first impulses of its own ruin,

it dared to provoke the powerful anger of the prince [Note: [Col. 0353] Rs. transposes this line; A and the other witnesses place it before line 184.].

[Col. 0353D] Therefore, that the cause of such great evils may be known, I shall review a few points concerning the ancient right of kingdoms.

[135] A custom handed down from the old time of ancient kings provides that whenever the German ruler crosses the Alps and intends to visit the Italian lands,

he must first send faithful officers through all his cities to demand the fiscal dues belonging to the treasury.

But whatever city has made itself guilty by faithless sacrilegious daring and denied its dues to its king,

[140] [Col. 0354A] laid low, must pay the deserved penalties for defrauding its prince.

Hence it is that even now, throughout the whole land, you may see many places hideously disfigured by shattered walls.

The German ruler also has this right in every city—not merely German cities, but those situated here and everywhere:

[145] that, present as supreme judge, he ought to conclude all lawsuits by his hand and settle every dispute; and that every judge, every authority, and every magistrate must be inactive in his presence.

The sanction of ancient laws and the enduring force of custom also declare this honour for the king:

[Col. 0354B] that every crop which Italian soil produces—after retaining only what the cultivation of the land demands—
