the cultivator must supply to the treasury at the prince’s command, for the expenses of the realm and use of the army.

[150] Therefore, when Caesar had remained at Roncaglia for a few days, talkative Rumour spread abroad among cities and peoples the news that, after gloomy clouds, the bright star and avenger of violated law was present [Note: [Col. 0353] P, Rs., A c.: “to cities”; other witnesses, “by forces”].

From every side many gathered and hastened to set forth their cases

[155] and bring out in mournful complaints the unpunished deeds of many whom the king’s absence had long made safe and eager for crimes.

So when fiery Phoebus begins, after the darkness and wintry cold of night, to cross the Ethiopian mountains and show his shining face to the lands,

[Col. 0354C] the ship distressed by storms at sea rejoices and gladly receives the rising of the desired light [Note: [Col. 0353] “receives?”].

[160] Neither the moon before this nor the other stars could save it, weary amid the nocturnal darkness.

Bright hope returns with the sun; the sailor now skillfully steadies the ship and guides the helm; all mutiny subsides, and the sea’s roar rests with the night.

I am reluctant to recount, and to attach to great affairs,

[165] [Col. 0354D] towns or castles threatening from lofty battlements, overthrown by the assault of a few and by easy victory,

because of the penalties of their crimes and in honour of the realm’s avenger.

Among the many serious complaints laid before him, royal Lodi together with suppliant Como implored the aid of its king.

[170] Both cities, sending their faithful consuls and elders, bewailed in plaintive Ligurian voices the cruel deeds of the city of Milan,

their own miseries, and their experience of prolonged tyranny;

[Col. 0355A] though speaking eloquently and mournfully, they groaned in the presence of the Ligurian consuls, who stood ready to defend their city with ornate words.

[175] But because a journey still remained for him who was making for the highest places of Italy through Ligurian territory, he preferred to defer the complaint, to be heard between them a little later in their own region,

as needing a weightier deliberation and a longer interval alike.

And, since he retained the Ligurians as guides of the route and pointers-out of places, he ordered them, now on the point of returning, to go before his camp.

[180] And now young men were present, bringing the foreign gifts which lofty Genoa had sent in joy at the new triumph.

For it had recently, after crushing its enemies, devastated barbarian cities with its own arms,

and had won for itself a memorable name by the deed [Note: [Col. 0355] “deeds,” m. Rs.], bringing home great plunder with exceptional praise.

[185] It had therefore sent the king new gifts from its spoils: barbarian garments, ostriches and lions, and a parrot matching the sounds of human speech.

At last, moving camp, Frederick made for the Ligurian coast and pitched his tents in the midst of the fields.

[190] But when he learned that the men commanded to precede the royal standards, the guides of the route, were leading them through hard and dry places, through barren regions lacking crops,

[Col. 0355C] he recognized the deceit. Then, blazing with anger, he ordered the condemned men to depart from his camp

[195] and sent them back to their city without honour.

Fortune added other incentives to anger to this righteous grief: for the soldiers, having endured bitter cold and been battered by the storms of winter weather, were distressed alike by hunger and rain.

[270] Hence rage and savagery add to the men’s furious anger grave goads; and there was this further cause: the city of the Ligurians pressed hard upon, and with severe terror kept down, whatever towns it had previously overthrown in war, lest they perhaps rise again; and it was making many payments to bend, if it could, the mind of the unconquered prince into complicity with its crime (for what cannot the favor of gold obtain?).

[275] Therefore, leaving the barren places and hungry fields, the most unconquered king pitched his royal tents not far from the lofty city, in fertile plains, and refreshed his cohorts, worn down by hunger and hard labor, with more abundant food and peaceful rest.

Rosate, conspicuous from afar for its towers and strong wall, lay a short distance from the faithless city: a secure dwelling and safe refuge for its citizens—if anything could be sufficiently safe from a German incursion and could disregard the threats of the kingdom.

[285] The Ligurians had fortified it, leaving five hundred men in that place, well supplied with provisions and stout weapons (but what defenses can stand against the auspices of empire?). The soldiers were driven from the fortress and compelled, without bloodshed, into the faithless city. At once the king ordered everything which the enemy had provided there for itself to be plundered, all the defenses to be burned with fire, and the fortress to be overthrown after its walls were broken.

[295] No less boldly, the young men pouring out from the camp rushed more swiftly to the walls and even to the city gates. The enemy met them, and with a mighty uproar began battles that would burn for many years, [Note: A. “Ausura”; Rs.: “what if *mansura*, ‘enduring’?”] and would yield only after long, unwearied labors and finally the utter ruin of the place. Besides those captured—whom we can neither count nor care to count—countless men returned bloodied by their own wounds, half-dead; many lay slain.

[305] The populace, stunned by this disaster and terrified by the first beginnings of its coming ruin, already condemning the present and fearing what was to come, in a roaring and rapid tumult destroyed the house of the consul Giraldus [Note: A.: “the house”], for he had been the chief author and instigator of this notorious crime. By this means it hoped to appease the just anger of the violated prince; but the prince, judging the display of the foolish populace empty and as it were vain, despised it, and, hastening to add other disasters to these, immediately made for the swift waters of the Ticino.

[315] This river, deriving its source from the cold Alps, flows after a short course into the Po not far from fair Pavia; some call the city by the river’s name. And it, a boundary in the midst of these places, separates you, little Novara, from the plains of the Ligurians.

[320] Here the Ligurians had added two bridges, and towers on the bridges themselves, with a strong defensive work, so that whenever Novara or Pavia wished to ravage their territories, they might cross and return in safety. The king seized both bridges; after conveying his men across, he burned the wooden defenses and towers, and divided the river by breaking the bridges.

[325] Immediately, in immense pride, the ruler powerfully destroyed three forts founded by them on hostile ground; he freed the wretched citizens from long fear, and snatched away from the victors the fields they had seized.

Prince Henry had long before utterly overthrown this city as rebellious through the inherited treachery of its people. But later, when the prince’s anger had been satisfied, antiquity—now taught to serve its masters—raised its ruins again, enjoying kinder fates: a small city indeed, but safe behind a new and handsome wall [Note: V.: *spaciosaque*, “and spacious,” marked +], and a moat drawn around it with a sufficiently broad embankment.

[335] Guido of Blandrate held its county, almost alone among the Italian counties freed from exactions by the Ligurians. They hoped, as they had swallowed up many cities by force, to swallow this one too in their jaws.

[340] The prince then passes Vercelli and the walls of Turin; and, as [Note: Rs., Jo.: *usque*, “as far as,” marked ++] he reaches the farther bank after bringing his army across where the Po approaches nearer to its source, he immediately turns his march toward the borders and countryside of fair Pavia, glad to visit faithful land.

There was a city which usage had called Asti from ancient times, possessing broad and very populous towns within its territory; its people called one of them Chieri. William, marquis of Montferrat, had humbly complained, while the king was conducting the public affairs at Roncaglia, that this city denied him his due rights and the respect owed him; mourning the arrogance of the proud people, the wicked deeds of the unyielding mob, [355] his own insults, and the repeated contempt shown for royal edicts, he had long stirred the noble anger of the unconquered prince by much speaking.

There was also a blood relationship between the two houses: the woman who had taken this man as husband rejoiced in having the king as her nephew. Therefore the prince resolved at last to punish with unconquerable penalty these peoples, guilty of injured majesty for so long, so often and vainly summoned under the laws, [Note: “*indicta*?”] and he hastened with rapid step toward their towns.

[365] Terrified by the new enemy but not corrected, the people had gone out in trembling fear to the high hills. He rushed in; and the army gladly found towns full of every good thing [Note: variants *omni* (“every”) and *omnis* (“all”): Rs., A., c.; A., Sp., R., Jo.], cellars with foaming nectar, granaries with grain, and jars fragrant with oil [Note: B.: *spirare*, “to breathe/fragrance,” marked +].

[370] They spent a few days there, while they filled their sacks with great quantities of grain and their skins, casks, and bulging jars with oil and wine. Then, without delay, after plundering the choicest goods, they consigned the towns to flames and utterly overthrew the strong fortresses.

[375] Departing thence, they attacked Asti with hostile terror—not only guilty under an earthly king of this crime, but, by divine law, condemned for contempt of its own bishop. With the citizens fled, it received the victors, itself full of every good thing, with a cheerful abundance; it supplied plentiful food for many days; at last, plundered and given over to fires, the innocent seat bore an undeserved punishment for the perverse crime and double guilt.

[385] But because the young soldiers, accustomed to the frequent plundering of camp life, had made it a habit to quarrel and even to fight with the sword, the provident king ordered this frenzy of depraved desire to be checked by such a law: if anyone from the army of the camp should strike another, or savagely attack a comrade with unjust weapons, the executioner should cut off either his head or right hand for such an offense, and the axe should strike the capital crime.

[390] Without delay they resolved to attack and destroy Terdona with captured standards—a city which, in wicked alliance with the Ligurians, had lent support to their counsels and unspeakable crime; madly preferring to give such favor against its own king, it had not yet returned, though so often recalled. For this city, hostile to faithful Pavia and harassing it repeatedly, oppressed it even more than the Ligurians did.

[400] Although the Ligurian city is separated from it by only a short distance, the stream of the Ticino lies between and divides the two tumults. But on the side where Terdona looks toward tower-bearing Pavia, everything lies open: there is no mountain, forest, or river there capable of restraining their mutual rage.

[405] The March of Busca, as it is called in common speech, saw the nearest tents of the magnificent king. From there he ordered Conrad, his brother, rejoicing in the honor of the Palatine right and united with him in purpose; Otto, his standard-bearer, sent by the land of Noricum, a man often proved in great dangers; and Berthold, leader of the Allobroges, under whose jurisdiction the gentle Saône pours its quiet waters into the Rhône [Note: A.: “Rhine,” marked °], to advance with many soldiers, carefully reconnoiter the position of the said city, and discover what the enemy was doing and planning. He promised that he himself would follow with the whole strength of the camp and bring aid to the men. But they hastened ahead and, having crossed the rapacious Tanaro [Note: A.: *Tancramque*; another reading: *Tanarumque*], made their way as far as the city’s walls and gates.

[420] They surveyed with their eyes and discerning minds the nature and site of the place, weighed the task, and awaited the royal standards after the camp had been established.

On the third day, behold, the warrior Frederick arrived with all his forces. He pitched his tents on the farther bank; a river swollen by rain prevented the forces from immediately joining. But when the river subsided and, its fury laid aside, began to be fordable—before its waters had fully settled—the soldiers crossed, or rather swam, its waters upon their vigorous horses, [Note: *validorum*: “strong”; variants *validore*, *validiore*] and the united companies took up their positions in the allied camp [Note: W.’s emendation: *junctaque*, “joined”; editions: *cunctaque*, “all”].

[430] On the rocky summit of a steep mountain stood the site of a fortress; there a rounded rocky knob had risen high from the ridge, neighboring both mountains where the Apennines and Alps meet at their boundaries. That place looked down from above not only upon your homes, Terdona, but, as from a watchtower, upon the Ligurians, the plains of Pavia, and other Italian cities, like limbs set beneath its head; no shadows obstructed those looking out [Note: A. and other manuscripts: *sectantibus*; A., Sp., c.: *spectantibus*].

[440] Here, besides strong towers which made the site seem secure on every side, the renowned tower, gleaming with a red wall, had brick instead of stone. Rumor had it that Tarquinius Superbus had once founded it there; retaining the place’s name, it had long been called the Proud Tower. Below this ridge rose walls, most secure with a strong wall, towers, and lofty battlements, and they adorned their city with high-roofed buildings.

[450] A small torrent, leaping from the neighboring mountain and ready to assume fierce anger after a modest rainfall, cut through it and separated the walls into two parts.

The first day added great weight to the mighty undertaking and depressed the scales of doubtful fate [Note: *dubii*?]. For on that very day, after the first assault, the suburbs were taken; the enemy were beaten back, and the populace withdrew in greater numbers into the fortress, in order to fortify their narrow [Note: P.: *angustam*, “narrow,” marked +] position on every side.

[460] Besides the citizens and their own standards, many Ligurians were present, whom the Ligurian city, the common cause of so great a disaster, had sent a few days earlier as vain support to the distressed city. Moreover Opitius [Note: P., Rs.; other manuscripts: *Apicius*] the marquis, surrounded by many armed men, had voluntarily joined himself as an ally in their desperate cause. Because of his harsh character, if I am not mistaken, common report called him “Evil Thorn” (*Spina mala*) with sufficient truth [Note: A.: *quam* (“which”); perhaps *eum* (“him”)?]—for, rebellious against morality and the ordinances of law, what can be found more bitter in human affairs than to provoke and sting a pious king with cruelty?

[470] Trusting in these forces and in the strong defense of the place, the ill-fated citizens neither surrendered the walls nor deigned, after so many calamities, to submit themselves to their king. Foolish fury persists in its undertaking, tends toward ruin, and the lost people hasten toward certain destruction.

[475] Then indeed, when royal nobility gathered itself into just anger and savage rage, forced at last, came to arms, it no longer strove to spare the ungrateful or offered pardon to those still hoping for it. It was now ashamed to have recalled the guilty citizens so often and invited them by salutary counsel to sweet compacts.

[480] Like a lion which had long been made gentle by peaceful habit and for a long time had put off its savage ways [Note: variants: *exueritque*], if someone equipped [Note: P., Rs.: *perditus*, “ruined/lost,” marked *] with javelins—or approaching close with naked sword [Note: R., Jo.: *eum*, “him,” marked *]—provokes it, it conceals and long restrains the anger of its noble heart; it disdains to stain its cheeks with a lesser slaughter or feed upon base blood. But if the condemned and wicked enemy persists and adds threats, then, stirred by the lash, it rouses itself, springs upon the wretch with a violent blow from its breast, and cruelly breaks his mangled limbs.

[490] So the long-suppressed anger of the noble prince blazed up, and his high-minded spirit seized a new fury. In order that the wicked populace might know by a sufficiently certain sign what reward it ought to expect for its deeds, he ordered instruments of torture and crosses to be raised immediately before the gates of the wretched and certain culprits, in their very sight. And lest anyone, cautiously escaping the disaster, should be able to slip away in fearful flight, the prince enclosed them on every side in this disposition:

[500] Where the west wind touches the fortress shut in behind by two obstructing mountains with its gentle breath, the royal standards gleam and block every approach, having attacked [Note: V.: *egressus*, “having gone out,” marked *] the enclosed enemy. Where winged Apennine receives the south winds and whistles back to the hot southeast winds, proud Henry stations the untamed Saxons and the Norican camp, and threatens the walls doomed to perish. But where the plains lie open and free passage and access are afforded to the east wind, the people’s standards and fair Pavia place their forces with a numerous army.

[510] At once the prince ordered great siege engines to be raised, whose powerful stroke would hurl huge stones against the walls; and an engine which, advancing, might overlook the enemy towers and entangle them from above with cast javelins [Note: A.: *implicat*; Rs.: *impluat*, “rain down,” marked *]; others, mounted on light wheels, might by hidden contrivance undermine strong walls or batter them with a blow.

Then the air shrieks with javelins, the bolt launched by the whirling force of the ballista whistles among light arrows, and the sling cuts the yielding air with deadly lead.

[520] No less do the ill-fated enemy roll great stones from the tops of their towers, hurl iron and fire, take courage, and exhort one another to arms: fear presses them, and dangers make men brave. Often, trusting in their own strength, they leap out in attack, throw the men into confusion, and escape in swift retreat, returning again to their fortress.

[525] Yet not without cost: besides the many deaths of their own men, which were mournfully kept secret in the city, many, while returning to the walls with retreating step, were captured and hung upon crosses, and perished by a pitiable fate.

Nor do I wish to pass over something sad and memorable, previously unknown. A stone hurled with swift force against the walls was shattered by a violent blow; dividing into three parts, it gave three bodies of young men to cruel death as they stood in close formation and deliberated upon their chief affairs in the middle of the fortress.

[535] But the excellent king, finally setting pity aside and adding threats, exhorts his allies and himself gives courage to his men; he attacks and assails the enemy. Often he himself rouses a strong hand with a light javelin and swift arrow; present in person, he equips the engines of war and directs sure blows against the walls. He leaves nothing undone or neglected which practical necessity demands; ordering much and everywhere, and fighting with his own hand, he fulfills both the role of a finished soldier and the duty of a discerning prince.

[545] On that side from which the walls look toward Pavia there was one spring, sufficient for the whole garrison while it remained free. But now the hostile enemy controls the waters, and Pavia’s hostile standards bar the ill-fated enemy from their own springs.

[550] Thus thirst compels them continually to endure the hard labors of fighting and always to remain in rigid armor; and therefore the spirited youth, while pouring out their own blood for a forbidden spring, do not fear to drink waters mingled with a stream of blood. The bitter thirst which breaks their bodies also increases their courage. No boldness is greater than that to which necessity—thirst and hunger—supplies the material of nature: one who thirsts or hungers can fear no evils. The violence of a wretched affliction forces fear away, while present torments distress more than future ones alarm.

[560] The prince saw the extreme crisis and that the whole struggle hinged on this point. He added the marquis of Montferrat with men as a guard, that he might share the danger with his allies, protect the pools, and terrify the enemy.

Moreover, they throw in filth and everything harmful to the spring; before their eyes they dare to pollute the clear waters with carrion and foul corruption, and plunge sulphur-smeared torches into them, so that their natural taste may be violated by bitter flavor.

[570] No less eagerly does the thirsty youth, lacking liquid, desire these waters and fight for certain death, exchanging foul waters for them at the cost of spilled blood. For the little stream which ran through the middle of the city, the enemy themselves having wantonly disturbed its scanty waters with a mass of ruins, many stones, and dust [Note: *ultra*: “in addition, moreover”], flowed muddy, filthy, and putrid.

[580] Nor, I think, should the courage—or rather the headlong madness of an incautious mind—of a certain man be passed over in silence. He was a groom, indeed of the common people and not of a much-known name, earning a modest wage in the camp.

[585] As though enraged by the war, weary of its length, indignant at delay, and therefore crueler toward the enemy, while he pressed the fortress in a fierce assault more violent than usual, and stones, firebrands, and weapons flew from here and there like Iberian hail, he—without helmet over his temples, without a woven cuirass protecting his breast, scarcely protected by sword and light shield—strove to climb the high hill on which Tarquin’s royal tower, founded there, shone.

[590] With a small axe—the kind which men of this class carry tied beneath the saddle for servile purposes—he cut footholds for himself in the high rock, while his comrades called him back and the enemy stood astonished, marveling at the man’s foolish exploit. Neither stones, nor the iron shower of missiles, nor the rocks which assailed the tower in a violent storm, could turn him back. Amid the cries of his own men and the enemy’s threats, he gained the fortress.

[600] Immediately, unarmed, he engaged an armed man; stronger, he hurled him headlong from the high cliff to the ground. Then, with Fortune accompanying him, he turned his steps back victorious and returned unhurt in all his body to his comrades and the royal standards; he withdrew himself alike into the camp and into a secure state of mind [Note: B.: *tota*, marked +], himself marveling, once his breath had returned, at what he had done.

[610] For this brilliant deed the king wished to grant him rewards worthy of praise: titles and the rank of knight, arms, fierce warhorses, and splendid attire. But the commoner was ashamed to rise so high and to transcend the bounds of his birth; he preferred to remain in his former station, accepting the prince’s generous gifts.

[615] But the king, troubled in mind that the undertaking proceeded with sluggish pace—for he was hastening to receive the crown and the monarchy of the whole world—considered in his discerning heart everything that might drive forward the slow war and hasten its tardy delays. He saw that the walls were everywhere strong by native strength and protected by the natural defense of the site.

[620] Yet on one side, where the royal tower stood, art and the labor of craftsmen [Note: B.: *artificemque*, “and the craftsman,” uncertain] had supplied what nature had given less abundantly. At last an enterprise memorable and remarkable to tell, though not sufficiently useful in result, occurred to his mind: by digging out the inner parts of the solid earth, hollowing out the depths and leading tunnels to the foundations, he would overthrow the tower itself by inclining its wall and open the walls for himself by its sudden fall.

[630] The crafty enemy forestalled the king’s plan and cleverly resolved to oppose art with art. Accordingly, when the royal digger had entered by a hidden route into the dark interior of the earth, the enemy immediately came upon the men trapped by the earth in the open mouth of the pit; cutting off their return and leaving them aghast, he suffocated them in the middle of the trench’s earthen bank.

[635] Thus the wretches regretted having dug their own grave; enclosed by the hollow mouth of the earth, the black abyss did not restore them any further to the sky [Note: *ulterior*: variants *ulterius*; Sc., A., c.: same].

Bold Fortune also dared to display to the king other angry faces, although he was accustomed to despise all chance events.

[640] Not far from the boundaries of the same city shone a fortress of the Ligurians, visible from far away. Frederick sought to put into action the desire, long conceived in his heart, to take it. At once he constructed in the camp ladders and the other devices by which walls may be scaled without the enemy’s knowledge. The men guarding the town thought these were made for use against themselves and wondered at their purpose.

[650] Without delay the ruler entrusted picked young men from the knightly order, brave and of outstanding bodily strength, to the leader of the Allobroges and to Otto the Palatine. He ordered the men to go there at the time when the first night mingles its cold shadows with the last light of day.

[655] He obeyed, and the soldiers, trusting in each leader [Note: Rs.: *utroque*, “each of the two,” marked +], set out for the safe position. When all were overcome by sleep, they secretly brought up ladders [Note: Rs. and Sp.: *allatis*; A. and other manuscripts: *ablatis*, “taken away,” marked °] and climbed to the topmost height of the wall. And, had the young men not through a chance cry given information of the deed more hastily than was fitting, the fortress would shortly have been snatched from the garrison and carried off by a fine stratagem.

[660] Roused by the clatter of arms and sudden shout, the garrison leapt from their beds and took flight. But when greater courage came to the frightened men and valor glowed after they took up weapons, they began battle; they drove back and repelled from the captured wall the enemy who had almost gained possession of their walls [Note: Sc.: *castro muroque*, “from the fort and wall,” marked +].

## Book Three

[Col. 0363]

The day had now come on which Christ, instituting for His disciples the mystical feast, wished, after the flesh of the lamb—the ancient offerings of the law—to satisfy us with the eating of His own body and the drinking of His sacred blood, setting before our eyes a true figure of bread and liquid, [5] but imparting to our senses the nourishment of certain life [Note: readings: *certe*, “certainly”; A.: *quidem sed eadem et: vite*—uncertain OCR]. When the practice of the old rite had now ceased, the new priest is believed to have established the new ordinances of the altar, first handed down and received in one manner, which the ecclesiastical order observes.

The noble prince resolved to celebrate this day and the three other days closely following it, in devotion and unarmed, because of the honor of the sacred season.

[10] When this day too had passed and the following dawn had risen, on which God hung upon the wood in true flesh, behold: a pitiable multitude, driven from the fortress [Note: readings *proculcata*, “trampled down”; *flagellata*, “scourged”; Rs.: *et profugus alta*; Pfl.: *profligata*, “routed”], clergy, and a shapeless throng of monks, the walls having been opened, hurried to the tents of the gentle king. Wasted with emaciation from enduring long fasts, with thirst producing hunger, they covered their squalid faces with sacred garments, setting their steps with bare feet. Then they bore aloft the signs of the cross and caskets containing the guardians of pious ashes, making them fragrant with offered incense.

[25] When the venerable prince saw them coming peaceably in a dense procession, he ordered prudent men to go out to meet them and ask why they had come and what that strange spectacle meant. Immediately one of them, squalid in pale face, adapting his words to his fortune, yet speaking with eloquent speech, began thus in a voice sufficiently sorrowful:

“Our intention was to fall at the feet of the unconquered king and lament the hardships which, though undeserved, we suffer. Since we are now prevented by our wretched repulse from approaching him, at least carry our complaints to him.

[35] What penalty do we wretches pay? What have we done worthy of your anger, unconquered king? What cause stirred such rage that you seek, by so great an effort, to destroy the unarmed clergy together with the guilty people—a clergy accustomed faithfully to sing hymns to God for Christ’s people and often for you yourself, if you believe it?

[40] What is our crime here, unless it is considered a crime to have placed our dwelling amid a guilty people? We have neither aided these monstrous plans by counsel nor their deeds [Note: variants *actis*, “deeds”; *actu*, “action”]; all this happens against our will. They are accustomed to discuss civil causes and matters of state among themselves; we are an unarmed crowd, an abject band, admitted to none of their counsels. We only join night-long to day-long devotions, accustomed to utter unceasing psalms and knock upon God with prayers; but in such disasters war does not allow them to practice these observances.

[50] We are shaken by war on every side; the churches are battered by the throwing of stones; a priest, standing at the holy altar, is pierced with missiles and breathes out his life in death.

[55] Shall the pious man, then, perish equally with the wicked, and shall it not profit him before a just judge to have lived piously? If [Note: Sp., P., R., o.: “Thus … have you come?”] you have come as avenger of crimes and comforter of the righteous; if you restore law and legislation to your peoples and labor to recall them to their proper force, spare the good and destroy the wicked. Set justice before every person according to merits, matching rewards to causes.

[60] Although—if it is permitted to use truthful speech, with your leave, prince—when the matter is weighed in its balance, Terdona is not so guilty toward fair Pavia as fair Pavia is guilty toward Terdona and toward you. For, besides the other cities which it has either subjected by forcing them to serve or captured and utterly destroyed, consider the noble fortress of Lunelli, shamefully treated. It had overturned that seat and the faithful household of the Palatine by treachery; the faithless city summoned the count and citizens to a conference on peace, and, by wicked fraud, compelled the unsuspecting men—fearing nothing hostile—into harsh chains.

[70] It left the fortress itself overthrown not by arms or by the law of war, but by trickery—or rather by treachery. And now that count, a loyal man, and that powerful prince of the royal court, under whom the Roman axe ought by ancient custom to punish offenders in Italy, is compelled to serve the unjustly victorious city [Note: A. expressly: *injustae* (“unjust”); Rs. manuscript: *injuste* (“unjustly”), marked +] as a humble client, and, with no right left to him, fears the commands of his proud mistress.

[80] This savagery of the city of the Ligurians, which alone does not fear Pavia, joined us to it, prince, in an unhappy alliance: not from hatred of the kingdom, not from rebellious sedition; indeed, to speak truth, we do not follow it even out of love for that city itself, but lest Pavia with its devouring mouth swallow us up—Pavia, which devours all cities. Yet amid such great gains from crimes, it rejoices and, behold, happily possesses the omen of your favor.

[90] But this does not concern us. It concerns you, most just prince, long since to investigate Italian customs, avenge the injuries of crimes, punish offenders, raise up the oppressed by your hand, and restrain the proud. We are content only to weep for our own hardships.

[95] We pray you: now spare the devout, and remember men joined by the bond of nature and the mark of faith. Look upon bodies languishing with pestilential disease; look upon misshapen faces and mouths parched by long thirst. These throats scarcely can open a path for the words of a voiced utterance—throats which sulphurous water, long continued, burns rather than soothes [Note: B.: *quas*, “which [feminine]”]. We drink polluted waters corrupted by pus and cups infected with putrefaction, scarcely won with the sword from the midst of our enemies.

[100] Our entrails harden with accumulated mud; our throats are constricted [Note: A., approved by Rs.: *arctantur*]; our lungs, hot with mad fever in the breast, tighten their alternating passages. Nor do we wish to relieve the plague with food or strengthen languishing limbs with nourishment: we have ordered hunger to be solace for our wretched sickness. Thus we relieve plague by plague.

[110] Alas for a life wretched and heavier than every death: to live and not know the welcome reasons for living! But by the shared sacraments of faith, by Him whom this day reminds us drank gall upon the wood of the cross, stretched forth His pious hands, whose pierced side dripped with a shower of sacred blood, and underwent death—spare us, most excellent man; do not, though pious, afflict the innocent further. Allow us, death being left behind (a form of death), to lead a poor life wherever you command, stripped of everything else; [Note: Rs.: *aliis quaecunque*, uncertain variant] and do not wish to return us again to our wretched enclosure. That place, once a pleasing home, is now sadder than every prison and more dreadful than Stygian Avernus.”

[120] Thus he spoke; and all, with palms raised toward the stars, struck the absent prince’s ears with wailing cries. Yet the prince, moved by hidden pity, concealing the distress of his mind and wishing to establish weighty lessons and an example of himself, ordered them to return to safety [Note: B.: *tecta*, “roofs/dwellings”] and compelled the wretches back into the enclosed fortress.

[125] So the final judgment of an angry judge will hand over to eternal fire those accursed men who, though so often warned, so often despised their adviser, and will punish them with punishment through wrath laid bare. Thus the wretched citizens, groaning, returned to the closed walls, as though complainingly returning to a certain hell.

[135] At last, hope abandoned and compelled already to despair, enclosed as it were in a prison of uncertain death, the enemy gathered great courage from their very disasters. During the interval of granted peace, they constructed a Balearic engine of marvelous size, capable of piercing the air far off with a powerful cast.

[140] Therefore, when the time granted to divine honor had passed, they again tried every method of attack—with missiles and the rolling of stones. Then that massive structure, supported by immense weight, was raised and rose higher over the lofty towers; hurling great stones, it compelled our men to stand far off and broke the strength of the very engine which had more often afflicted the besieged enemy.

[145] This gave courage to the enemy; and by as much pain as it brought to our side, by so much did that savage foe exult. Threats resound on both sides; when the course of fighting is somewhat relaxed, the struggle begins again with renewed force, a crash arises, and the walls are shaken by fierce war.

[150] No less do the besieged hasten whatever fear and headlong anger suggest: they hurl iron and fire and launch stones driven by a terrifying engine. They do not hesitate to break down the very walls for battle, and, if weapons fail, threaten to cast themselves against the enemy.

[155] At last, after many struggles of war on either side, the ruin and numerous deaths of the wretched populace, walls more taken by assault than surrendered [Note: Rs.: *dedita*, “surrendered”], yielded to our men. Only this greatest favor was granted to the guilty—indeed only with difficulty, through the prayers and much entreaty of the nobles—namely, safety; everything else became the spoil and reward of all for their long labor. The walls themselves, broken down everywhere by the enemy, sank beneath a dusty ruin.

[165] Who could recount the squalor of the wretched populace, their bodies wasting in diseased decay, and their loathsome color, when by the king’s permission there emerged from the fortress as though from a tomb not a man, but the pale image of a man?

[170] Then the wretches were able by their own experience to judge how miserable it is to be oppressed by a long siege.

The joyful people of Pavia urged the victorious king, about to depart for his own walls, to turn aside to their city. They would display splendid triumphs to their leader in the ancient manner. “There is no place within Italy,” they say, “better suited to so great an honor, nor one which you might wish more to distinguish with your triumph, than the city which has remained faithful to you through prosperity and adversity alike and has failed at no time.

[180] Add that this toil of yours serves our interests, and that you have waged these wars for your Pavia. You have utterly overthrown a hostile city, ready to gape after our misfortunes and bound by a tight alliance to cruel enemies. What return can we make for this? We are not ungrateful: only let Pavia be permitted to render thanks and rejoice at her king’s entry.”

[185] He obeyed; not disdaining the honor offered, the victor approached the walls. What joy, what a great concourse of people from the city, cannot be expressed by sense or eloquence: with what ceremonial the chaste bishop and clergy, rejoicing in their bishop, came forth dressed in shining garments, bearing precious signs of the cross, sacred texts, and the smoke of incense; how a caparisoned horseman, spreading glittering standards far and wide and mounted upon warhorses draped everywhere in purple cloth, champed the foaming mouths restrained by bits and compelled their swift courses to halt;

[195] how daughters-in-law and mothers together with gentle maidens, their white bodies veiled in Sidonian cloth, wearing pearl necklaces upon their shining necks and girding their golden temples with jeweled circlets, stood in dense ranks along both sides of the city and shouted favorable cries, greeting their lord; how every house steamed with fragrant things and rich incense, hung wide with curtains, and how the streets were spread with pictured carpets;

[205] how the trumpet with terrible breath, the gentle flute, horns with windy clamor, hollow drums with rough sound, or the lyre with the sweet melody of struck strings, soothed astonished ears with gentle murmur; how boys and the lesser people spread spoils beneath the horses of those coming forth and sang the joyful paean and “Io, triumph!”—all this, and more, should have been remembered by us, if only our strength had sufficed.

[215] My talent fails; my mind has not such confidence that I should wish fully to recall these things and pursue their splendor in words. Even Virgil or great Homer, if stirred by all Apollo, could scarcely equal them in speech.

What, madman, did I mean to do—attempting [Note: other manuscripts: *tentare*, “to attempt”] with rustic sound and a slender Muse the weight of matters so great? The work succumbs to its material. With my poor vein words flow; this matter demands a great poet.

[225] Having been graciously received, they conduct him to St Michael’s, where the ancient palaces of the old kings gleam; his shining head is encircled with a jeweled crown, and his right hand is adorned with the sacred sceptre. The devoted people rendered this honor to the king for three days, heaping new joys with lavish expenditure.

[230] Then he crossed the territories of Piacenza, the countryside of Cremona, and the fields of Modena; and having taken possession of the city—
Bologna, so called as though “full of good things,” celebrated the coming of the sacred breath (*flamen*) with fitting honour.

[235] Soon he crosses the Apennines by their rocky pass and enters your borders, warlike Tuscany. The nobles whom Pisa, famed Pisa, most renowned for triumphs on the sea, Pisa well known as a harbour for foreign ships, had sent, come to meet the leader. He orders them, at an appointed time, to assemble warships for the Sicilian king and to equip the vessels.

Then he seeks Rome, the head of the world, and reaches Viterbo, a city no farther removed from that lofty city than a slow traveller can go in two days.

[245] [Col. 0369C] The bishop of the Apostolic See and supreme priest was then Adrian. Rejoicing at this report, he immediately came out, attended by an eminent company of clergy, and laid before the man great and grievous complaints, recounting many cruel deeds of his city. He reported that he himself was treated with contempt, and that he often endured the furious people’s quarrels, insults, threats, mockery, abuse, and violence; that his clergy, as though exposed to insults with no avenger, suffered continual plundering. They were beaten by violent hands and attacked with the sword.

[255] Thus a feeble father, when his son has returned after a long absence, whether from camp or from a distant region—the son in whose hands lie authority over affairs and the whole responsibility for governing the house—recounts the wrongs, insolent deeds, and contempt of his household, the hardships he endured while the son was absent, the house laid waste, and countless losses; and he keenly inflames the avenger’s threats.

[260] [Col. 0369D] The originator of this evil and author of so vast a gulf was Arnold, whom Brescia produced in his ruinous birth. Gaul maintained and nourished him at its expense,

[265] and instructed him for a long time. At last, restored to his native land, he assumed the appearance of a wise man and deceived the ignorant with beguiling speech; attacking the clergy with shameless hatred, the bitterest enemy of monks, the flatterer of the populace, delighting in popular applause,

[Col. 0370A] he dared to assail pontiffs, and even the pope himself, with his biting tongue; spreading criminal doctrines among the crowd, he filled their ears with diverse words. [Note: “vain” in manuscript Rs.]

[270] He declared that the clergy ought to possess nothing of their own; that monks had no right to estates or lands; that fiscal rights belonged to no pontiffs, and that no abbot should be granted the honour of public charge or the right to issue sacred laws. [Note: “court,” *curiae*, in manuscripts Rs.]

[275] All things, he said, were subject to earthly rulers and were to be entrusted to, and governed by, men of the people. To these he assigned first-fruits, offerings made by popular devotion, and tithes for chaste bodily needs—not for luxury or the pleasures of the flesh, soft foods, splendid apparel,

[280] [Col. 0370B] unlawful games, or the wanton delights of clergy. He utterly condemned the pride of pontiffs, the lax morals of abbots, and arrogant monks.

Indeed, unless our own times reject faithful warnings, he taught many true things mingled with falsehood. [Note: “but mingled” in manuscripts Rs.] And I confess: he knew well the handsome art of deceiving, proving falsehoods by truths; for no one can deceive merely by speaking falsehoods. Beneath the appearance of truth falsehood enters and secretly takes possession of deceived ears.

[290] He also, in his folly, did not uphold the articles and settled course of the faith with sufficiently exact devotion, mingling impious poison with honeyed words.

[Col. 0370C] This madman had so stirred up against the clergy and pontiff his own city and many others that the sacred clergy, they say, were already held in mockery and extreme disgrace—a harm which, unless I am mistaken, still afflicts that people and greatly diminishes sacred honour.

[300] Soon condemned in a council at Rome by that bishop whose honourable name derives from his blameless life, Innocent—he who was forbidden to enter our poetic metres—Arnold, terrified and confounded by the spectacle of his wretched guilt, fled from his city. Received beyond the Alps,

[305] where Germany looks upon the neighbouring Alps, he settled at famous Zürich, so report says, a name derived from Alpine Lake Leman, under the false title of teacher; and in a short time the faithless man corrupted the whole land with the breath of his impure doctrine. [Note: “impure” in A., Sp., R., P.; “of impure” in Rs., RJo.; A corrected to “impure.”]

[310] Therefore that people, long corrupted by poisonous savour and adhering too strongly to the teaching of the false prophet, still retains the taste of its ancestral grape. [Note: “teaching” in manuscript Rs.]

But when the supreme bishop was removed from the midst, Eugenius assumed the rights of the sacred chair. Arnold, wishing to shake Peter’s solid rock,

[315] [Col. 0371A] so that, as an infirm head spreads pain through the remaining limbs, he rashly assailed Rome’s walls with sacrilegious daring and wickedly infected the whole city with the corrupt seed of his impure word. [Note: “spreads,” *diffundit*, in the manuscripts.]

[320] He stirred up such anger among the people against the clergy that they rendered absolutely no honour to the supreme pontiff and harassed the clergy with unjust hatred. And if anyone possessed a more equitable and reverent mind, and his heart burned with a pious desire for better things,

[325] and happened to dare to oppose or dissuade their madness and set himself against these new monsters, then, stripped of all possessions, his house utterly destroyed, his body afflicted, or finally his blood shed, whether cleric or layman, he paid for the deed.

[330] [Col. 0371B] Moreover, he urged the people to renew the city’s ancient titles, restore patrician men and the ancient Quirites, distinguish the equestrian rank from the plebeian name, restore the rights of tribunes and the sacred senate, and reinstate laws worn out and mute with age;

[335] to restore the ancient Capitols, fallen with ruinous walls and still hanging in decay, to their primeval splendour; to manage at their own discretion, by counsel and arms, the supreme direction of their commonwealth, granting no authority in this matter to the supreme pontiff and little to the king. Thus, foolishly offending both majesties, [Note: “both,” *utraque*, in Rs. and A corrected; manuscripts: “each,” *uterque*.] he made himself guilty before the two powers.

[340] Therefore at last—and I do not think this should be passed over,

[Col. 0371C] nor will the account return later to this fatal matter—having been convicted by the judgement of our clergy under the prince, he was hanged on a cross; and, consumed by burning flame and reduced to ashes, was scattered, O Tiber, upon your waters.

[345] This was done so that the error which the wicked man had created among the foolish populace might not cherish a martyr’s bones or ashes with a new honour.

And now, with the bishop of the see of Ravenna dead, the king conferred that see upon Anselm, returned from the Greek land, as a welcome reward for completed service; for the curia often transfers its own pupils to a bishop’s chair.

[350] Thus the two nobles, like the two greatest lights of the world, united their camps for some time: here the father, there the devoted son of the kindly father;

[355] [Col. 0371D] the one most famous among priests, the other among rulers; this one feared by the sword of empire, that one by the heavenly sword. Having at last obtained the sweet fellowship of conversation, they enjoyed joys which their pious desire could not satisfy.

When the ruler, now approaching Rome, had left behind Sutri’s small walls and was nearing the great city,

[360] men came to meet him, bearing their country’s proposals: outwardly adorned with impressive speech, but crafty and entangled in secret deceits. [Col. 0372A] They did not at once dare speak, unless a covenant of royal peace were first granted, permitting them to say without penalty whatever they might bring forward.

[365] Then one of them, arranging his words with pretended moderation, set forth plans long premeditated:

“Powerful, unconquered prince, Rome rejoices with blessed gladness at your arrival, and, devoted to you, opens her walls and her motherly bosom to the mighty man whom she chose as her ruler; she rejoices in a friendly lord.

[370] She freely promises you empire and the dignity of the name Augustus, than which nothing is greater on earth—if only you come in peace, and preserve inviolate for your faithful and well-deserving mother her ancient rights.

[375] What was the city’s glory at its height under the ancient kings; what the people’s freedom; how great the majesty of the senate;

[Col. 0372B] the dignity of the praetor and of the two annual consuls; the protection of the people by the two tribunes; the grace of customs; the sanction of chaste laws; the orderly course of law in peace; courage in just wars; how great the love of praise and endurance of labour—

[380] these were what raised our city, through long advancement, [Note: “advancements,” *provectibus*, in manuscript Rs.] from the humble origin of its nascent destiny, from its small homes, its first king’s asylum, straw-thatched huts, and furrow sprinkled with blood, to famous titles and the summit of such honour,

[385] that it saw nothing above itself but the stars alone. [Note: “they raised,” *extulerunt*, in manuscripts Rs.] Rejoicing in these things, it subjected nations and kings throughout the world to itself by counsel and mighty arms.

Then the people gave commands to the king concerning war and domestic affairs, not the king to the people; and this city would endure no king except one whom it ordered to reign,

[390] so that it seemed no hardship for the gentle fatherland to give commands to nations and to kings of the great world. [Note: B: “to kings of the great world”; A: “to kings of the great city”; manuscripts: “to kings of the great city.”] Then the land encircled by the eastern and western deep, and Boreas beneath the pole of the cold world, feared this people’s commands and threats.

[400] But when, through Fortune’s fault and the negligence of a fearful people, the marks of its ancient dignity perished, and when laws, suppressed by a long suspension of justice, fell silent, Rome sank back by so great a decline that she scarcely dared extend the shadow of her name to the tenth milestone and the neighbouring bounds.

[405] [Col. 0372D] She is despised among nations, insecure in herself, supported by none of her own strength; frequent sedition and discord tear her apart in civil wars. There is no love of law, no reverence for moral conduct;

[410] no freedom now remains, nor even an image of freedom. Nowhere are patricians, nowhere the sacred order of the senate,

[Col. 0373A] nowhere a consul with his colleague, or a praetor, or tribune. And while the walls fall in ruin, [Note: “fall,” *procumbunt*, in the manuscripts.] we suffer and lament a greater ruin of morals.

[415] This, excellent prince, has therefore happened to us: this people has no power to order the government of the realm and rule the whole world by ancient laws. Royal majesty long ago took it away and mutilated the people’s former honour, from the time when Rome admitted Teutonic tyrants.

[420] You are far away from us, absent in a distant world; you are seldom in Italy, and most seldom in this city; and you are more familiar to me as a guest than as my king. [Note: “is” or “are,” B.]

Thus neither do we sufficiently attend to ourselves, nor do you, illustrious ruler, attend to us; [Col. 0373B] and we are defrauded of both kinds of care, exposed to every fate with no avenger.

[425] At last look upon us with kindly mind and countenance, and imagine Rome herself weeping and speaking thus to you: ‘If concern for me touches you, [Note: Rs., R., J.: “touches”; W: “for herself arrogates”; manuscripts: “may touch.”] if any favour owed to a mother moves you, if rejoicing I placed you, summoned from the Teutonic people, in the supreme seat of empire,

[430] repay service with service and gratefully render deserved honours. Drive away long decay; let the ancient age flourish anew; let the old insignia of ancestral customs return. Summon back patricians, citizens, and ancient Quirites; let the noble order be separated from the plebeian name.

[435] [Col. 0373C] Grant freedom; restore the sacred senate. Let the senior [Note: perhaps “censor,” Rs.] now return; let the praetor return with the consul; and let the two tribunes return with the dictator. Let the curia breathe again; let the fallen Capitols rise again; let the fair insignia of ancient customs return.

[440] Rejoice that the glory of so great a deed has been preserved until your times. May you arrive happier than Augustus, whose name and place alike you assume; be gentler than Trajan.

And whatever treaties other kings made with me by oath down to your time, swear to them also;

[445] do not wish to curtail or abolish what was granted me by the gift of ancient kings. [Col. 0373D] Do not shun dangers for my safety and for my people; render generous gifts to the Roman people, so that, devoted to you, it may celebrate your festive triumph.’

He spoke. But the emperor discovered the deceits and words infected with poison; roused by royal anger, he scorned to conceal his deep pain in speech:

[455] ‘How greatly Rome—not Rome, but a resident of Rome—rejoices at my arrival, your words, consonant with your secret mind, have openly shown sufficiently.

[Col. 0374A] You certainly do not offer me an equitable bargain, when you wish to sell me what is ours, as though I came with full money-bags to purchase, at a price, new honours which Gallic valour has already made its own. [Note: A: “Gallic”; manuscripts: “Franconian”; A corrected: “warlike.”]

[460] We do not buy offices of state. Nor, if we believed them purchasable, do we possess a price to offer besides virtue. On these terms—or none at all—will I enter into dealings. Our purses do not bulge with money stuffed into them;

[465] we come burdened not with many riches but with glory. The Teuton’s heart is not heaped with money; he seeks not wealth for himself, but the honours of fair renown.

[Col. 0374B] He does not possess gold himself, but commands those who do. By as much as the most covetous Roman eagerly amasses bronze and watches over his great heap, by so much—or by still more—the Teuton scatters riches once acquired and considers it a shameful crime for bright hands to be stained with foul rust.

[470] Let the greedy keep watch over their riches: power alone is enough for me, and the ability to give laws to all lands. Why should I need wealth, I to whom the glory of the world is subject, whom the possessor of riches worships, though he be rich, together with the poor man?

[475] Whatever the wealthy man has, whatever the miser guards, whatever the earth conceals in hidden caverns—though it is ours by right, we grant its use to the people.

[Col. 0374C] The king’s image on coinage makes clear that it is the king’s; beneath Caesar, the image of Caesar shines for its lord. Why should I need wealth, when kings and peoples never cease to send the finest things as frequent gifts? The court always has old envoys and always sees new ones, sent from every region and every prince; new gifts always come from unknown lands.

[490] Therefore I am ashamed to be compelled to pay, as though a debt, to a greedy people, when great kings pay it what is not owed. I wonder that a city famous from antiquity for its morals should have hoped for so foul a crime [Note: “breathed,” *spirasse*, in manuscript Rs.] as to extort payment from a constrained king, as though it had already enclosed him in a vast prison and bound him with harsh chains.

[495] Would Rome, then, impose a law on her king? When rather it is fitting that you submit yourself to your king’s law. You demand five thousand pounds as a debt; I deny that I owe it to one demanding it. A gift, not extorted payment, befits kings. Such a fate presses captives and defendants: let them redeem their time with money wrung from them.

[500] The gifts of great kings wish to be cheerful and spontaneous, so that the giver may rejoice more than the recipient. This alone I can call free, [Note: A and manuscripts: “I can”; variant: “I am able.”]

[Col. 0375A] in which the giver rejoices more in giving than the recipient in receiving. My munificent ancestors left me this custom; I wish to preserve it. I do not refuse to gladden your people with a generous gift, but I reject a bargain. This hand knows how to give only freely and of its own accord.

[510] You demand oaths? I deem it disgraceful for a king to swear to one beneath him. The king’s bare word ordinarily has force and reverence greater than any oath. It does not become a king that slippery words should pass over his lips; it does not become a king to forge lies with his sacred mouth.

[515] [Col. 0375B] Royal words are sacred and full of their own weight: once spoken, they justly admit no reversal. Therefore cease to fear what you urge me to settle by a sworn compact; [Note: W restores the previously faulty punctuation.] I shall care for it even unsworn.

Moreover, what you seek is itself useful to our affairs and is something we must do without anyone’s urging. Shall I uphold ancient laws? [Note: W: “rub out,” *teram*.] Rather I am ready to supplement than diminish anything among the city’s good customs.

[520] Shall I not preserve you even at the greatest peril to myself? While you were not mine, I commanded, at the greatest danger, that you should become mine; now that you have become mine, shall I abandon you?

[525] For as to the empire which, you say, I received at Rome’s invitation, and for which you proclaim the praises of so great a service,

[Col. 0375C] I do not choose to reckon it a great matter. I confess that I came when summoned; but you must consider what cause you had for summoning me, lest perhaps you think yourself to have deserved too much.

Pressed on every side by hostile enemies and the turmoil of war, no longer able to defend yourself by your own strength or those forces which you had tried to summon by prayers to aid you, long despairing and abandoned by all, you lay helpless.

[530] Where now, Rome, are your own powers? Where is that faithless little Greek and arbiter of the Sicilian court, your avenger, whom you regard as your guardian, though you fear to confess it openly? Perhaps, Rome, your avenger will feel—when circumstances offer a fitting time—

[535] [Col. 0375D] the strength and weight of the Teutonic realm.

At last, as is evident, using sound counsel, you sought the power and unconquered standards of the Franks. Charles, bravest tamer of the immense world, came and redeemed you in your misery by great valour.

[540] Having rescued you from enemies’ hands, he transferred the empire to himself and, having recovered you by the course of war, joined these your walls to the Frankish kingdom.

Come now: recount in splendid language your grant to us of the fasces, and your supposed original invitation out of gratuitous kindness; but in truth it was a plea. Thus a poor man repeatedly crying at closed doors calls a powerful man with a plaintive voice.

[550] For who does not know that Berengar and Desiderius, your tyrants—beneath whom, pitiable Rome, you had bowed your terrified head and subjected neck—were defeated and captured by Frankish arms, suffered perpetual exile, served their conqueror in our realm for many years,

[555] and at last in slow old age pressed the earth with their servile corpses?

That day, by a single triumph, transferred to the Franks your ancient rights, insofar as the fortune of the Greek city had left any to you. They were not extinguished, but survive,

[Col. 0376B] following their own empire; for an empire, drawing after itself the honours due to it, could not pass over stripped and empty of its dignity.

Look upon my camp: all things whose removal you have long lamented you will see living here in the same form under a changed name—here the knight, here the praetor, here the authoritative dignity of consul and tribune, and the public care of the senate.

[565] Look upon the Teutonic nobles and troops of knights: recognize these as your patricians, these as your Quirites, this as your senate ruling you by perpetual right.

[Col. 0376C] These, Rome, govern you by their laws, though you yourself may be unwilling; they conduct the business of peace and war.

But you recall titles of freedom and ancient times of laws. What laws, wicked woman, do you seek besides Teutonic laws? What rights besides mine? What greater freedom could happen to you than to serve your king?’

[575] Thus he spoke, and royally stirred fierce anger in his noble countenance. [Note: critical mark on *regaliter* (“royally”).] The men heard him, their hearts oppressed by stunned fear. When many asked whether they wished to speak further, they dared add nothing to their former words, grieving only that they had said so much.

[580] So great was their terror at seeing the angry prince’s grim face that they would rather have been silent and never undertaken the business of their Rome;

[Col. 0376D] they seek a safe return to the protected walls, intending to report to the city the utterances of the formidable prince.

But the king, holding conference privately with the bishop and noblemen, carefully consulted what remained for him to do and what stratagem he could oppose to the crafty artifice of the deceitful people. [Note: manuscripts read “apply,” *apposuisse*, rather than “oppose,” *opposuisse*.] At the same time he seethed with inward anger.

[590] [Col. 0377A] The eminent father, wishing to add gentle consolation to his offended mind, [Note: Henisch’s copy of A reads “offended,” *laesae*; manuscripts: “to the offended man,” *laeso*.] said:

“My excellent son, it is neither new among this people nor surprising that they suavely stroke the powerful with hidden frauds and show a cunning fox to their rulers.

[595] This national vice possesses them: this is how men live there. You already grieve that you have partly experienced it; but henceforth you will understand it more truly and see still greater things.

When I had not been resident long, it assailed me too with many deceits, and this wicked populace inflicted many things unworthy of telling upon me and upon the sacred clergy.

[600] But contempt and injury against us are less serious:

[Col. 0377B] an unwarlike hand, armed with no power of blood but supported only by fear of God, exposes us to be scorned with impunity by wicked men. But that it should labour to entangle you, whom the fearful power of an earthly kingdom and the avenging sword against crimes make an object of fear to Romans—[Note: variant: “feared, the Roman …,” etc., in Rs.]—is sufficiently astonishing.

[610] Yet spare just grief, and, by God’s agency, let this wicked people pay due penalties to us and to you at a fitting time.

Only send forward secretly chosen brave men, in martial array, equipped with missiles and every weapon. Let them fearlessly seize the sacred thresholds of blessed Peter and the fortifications of the Leonine City.

[615] [Col. 0378A] There are there, under my name, young men of outstanding courage for the purpose of the garrison; they will surrender the walls and admit your men. There will be one to order the walls delivered up: an eminent son of Roman stock, companion of the Apostolic See, and excellent priest—this Octavius, most faithful to you above all.”

The bishop had ended. The praiseworthy plan, sincere loyalty, and open intention pleased all. About five thousand men are sent swiftly, [Note: A: “are sent swiftly”; variant: “strive properly.”]

[625] [Col. 0378B] almost at midnight, when Titan, presenting his light to the world opposite—if one may believe it—equally divides the middle arc of night.

There is no delay. The men, when ordered, hasten; entering through open gates, and having first instructed those who held the foremost thresholds, [Note: A: “instructed,” *edoctis*; manuscripts: “led out,” *eductis*.] they silently seize the fortifications of Saint Peter and the Leonine City in hostile fashion.

[630] A messenger returns to the nobles, tells them of the swiftly accomplished deed, and the troops throughout the whole camp grow joyful.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377C] Now, when sleep-bringing night had run its course, golden Phoebus began to bring his lamp, raised from the hidden sky, into our heaven. At no other time did he lift up brighter dawns, cleanse the sky, and remove all clouds more completely.

[5] A fortunate day arose, brighter than almost all other days, to confer upon you, Frederick, the first honours of empire and diffuse public rejoicing through the whole world with serene rays.

The prince, now arriving down the slope of the mountain opposite, sees the famous city which he had not yet seen. The people’s joyful delight gave the place its festive name, because those who approach the bright walls from that direction

[10] [Col. 0377D] first see the city from that height and greet you, sacred Rome.

The Golden Gate, rejoicing, first admitted the leader to the Leonine City. Then the supreme priest, clad in sacred vestments after the divine rites had duly been performed, met him seeking the holy threshold of the Apostolic See; leading him to the high altars of sacred Peter,

[15] [Col. 0378C] leading him with fingers entwined, he set upon his head the honour of the whole world and pressed the sacred diadem upon his hair. Performing in due manner the solemn rites of Mass, he secured the noble deed by a heavenly covenant.

All rejoiced exceedingly, and the entire company acclaimed the man with the auspicious cry, “May it be fortunate!”

[25] This armed favour and this applause of the mounted crowd delighted the ears of the August prince more sweetly than a venal honour and the hired rejoicing of the mob. Here there was sincere love, rejoicing in loyal obedience, and devoted faith; there, only glory painted over with lying deceit and costly display.

We too ought to have acclaimed your honour, most valiant Caesar, in songs,

[30] [Col. 0378D] and celebrated your fasces and the splendour of events, filling them out in speech and their proper verse. But I fear that, speaking more and labouring much, I shall be found to have said too little and be charged with great fault for casting clouds over distinguished deeds.

[35] [Col. 0379A] Therefore I hasten to run briefly through not every individual event, but the substance of the deeds accomplished. Indeed, following the true abridgment of the deed, I think this itself enough. For that season of serene rejoicing and the signs of so great applause did not last long.

Fearing the plots and tumult of the furious people, armed cavalry stands everywhere, guards the temple doors and thresholds,

[40] blocks the house of Crescentius and the narrow approach to the bridge, and holds all the streets with a dense guard.

[45] The fourth year after his accession to the realms conferred upon the king these titles and this famous name of honour; and more than half the month of June had passed, as the fourteenth rising of July was appearing.

Then, joyfully bearing the gem-studded crown upon his head, he mounted his horse. Purple cloth covers the whole animal, with embroidered coverings of figured designs.

[50] A shining golden saddle, with jewels radiating in marvellous order, encloses the king in its painted arch. The horse disdains golden reins with interwoven chains; it chews jewelled wolves and yellow gold. A bright carbuncle hangs from the middle of its brow; its shining breast is adorned with many-sounding bosses.

[55] [Col. 0379C] Fierce, he multiplies uncertain steps in wandering motion, sometimes strikes the thin air with his hoofs, and the warhorse is proud of so great a rider.

Riding thus, with a crowd of footmen accompanying him, he rejoices to have powerful men at either rein, conspicuous by birth and rulers of the world’s laws.

[60] Thus escorted, with the applause of his followers resounding, he himself returned to the nearest tents by the towered walls. But the eminent bishop, dismissing the prince, remained in the Leonine City and his own seat.

As the soldiery, burning with thirst and wearied by much heat and time, lay spread in the desired shade of camp, preparing to restore their exhausted bodies with food,

[65] behold: a sudden cry sounds from the neighbouring city, and the deadly signs of a sudden tumult.

[Col. 0379D] Now the furious people, indignant that their ancient right had been denied and that the prince had assumed the fasces without their command, had rushed across the bridge in a headlong throng; they had routed a few of our men, left too careless and without alarm.

[70] But others, swift in the pressing danger, sought the camp, their comrades, and the king himself, calling him by name, for his valour was well known to all.

Caesar shuddered with the goads of anger and righteous fury, and compelled his allies to resume their unwelcome labour, leading out all the troops from camp.

[75] He hastened all the more because sharp fear drove him: lest the impious rabble, raging in its customary madness, should dare some cruel act against the eminent Father. Anger deferred food; they preferred to satisfy their postponed hunger with hostile blood. Terrible as lions in their roar, they return to the city and take up arms.

[80] The enemy did not yield, but received battle with steadfast breast. The war is joined with hurled spears, light javelins, and arrows which the air rained down. [Note: V reads, “and arrows which anger carried.”]

[Col. 0380B] But when anger at fiercer provocations grew hot, they joined hand to hand and brought weapons close. They wished now to fight not with missiles and flying iron, but with swords.

[85] You might hear helmets ring beneath resounding blows, [Note: Rs. and A corrected: “blows”; A and others: “blow,” with “resounding” altered in the preceding verse.] arms struck by weapons, and light shields bellowing under heavy crash. You could see men scattered everywhere, then pressing on again with strength recovered, as fortune shifted from side to side.

The greatest mass of the fighting was at the entrance to the bridge before Crescentius’ house.

[90] The royal side could easily have fallen into certain destruction, overwhelmed by the easy rolling of stones or by spears sent from above, had not mothers stationed on the tower battlements for the sake of watching begged the young men, already preparing to cast their weapons, to spare the strong and fair company rather than join their madness to that of the foolish mob.

[95] [Col. 0380C] Thus the favour of chaste mothers aided our side, preventing innocent hands from bloodshed.

This raging battle continued, prolonged and unbroken, from the tenth hour until the first darkness after the sun had set. No one, though they had endured long fasting—for the soldiers had spent the entire day fasting—could now feel hunger or the burden of labour, forgetful of himself.

[100] So great an ardour for shedding the blood of a more criminal enemy and satisfying anger with just slaughter seized the avengers.

And one man, rejoicing amid so great a slaughter of the guilty, exulted over their misfortunes: “Rome,” he said, “let these be your rewards for ancient right. Such payment is rendered you by a just prince; thus are kingdoms gained for us, thus do we buy the fasces, thus does he order you to acclaim his triumphs. Such treaties does Caesar strike with you; such oaths does he confirm with your blood.”

[110] [Col. 0380D] Only at last, late in the evening, did flight and night drive away the wretched citizens, long battered by war. Clear signs of heavenly justice appeared, revealing various outcomes in accordance with the merits of events.

For, with only one man slain on our side,

[115] [Col. 0381A] they report that a thousand of the hostile populace either perished by arms or were drowned in the Tiber, and that two hundred captives submitted their necks to the chains imposed upon them.

Soon the victors return joyfully to camp with praise to God, and restore their limbs with welcome food and sweet sleep, [Note: Sp. and R read “savour,” *saporem*.] enjoying rest in the secure camp.

[120] Hardly had day risen when Caesar moved his royal standards away from the suspect city—for the soldier in his distress did not expect necessary supplies from an enemy—and pitched his fine tents in fertile fields near the mountain where once Sylvester hid, fearing the cruel commands of a tyrant, before you, Constantine, had been reborn.

[125] They call it Soracte. He crosses the ancient Albula by its placid ford,

[Col. 0381B] Albula, whose waters made the Tiber take its name. He first pitches camp near the walls of Rome, between the Greek-built citadels of famous Tibur.

As fame relates, three men from Greek stock founded these homes: Coras [Note: A: “Corax.”] with his brother Catillus, young men of Argive lineage, and Tiburtus, elder than them both, from whose name noble Tibur is said to take its name, if poets speak true.

[135] Now the venerable day was at hand, bright with apostolic triumph, festive indeed throughout the world, but especially for the city of Romulus. Its fathers had consecrated its walls by their martyrdom while they despised the sceptre of cruel Nero.

[Col. 0381C] The army received that day with whatever honour it could; [Note: Rs. reads “could,” singular; manuscript: “could,” plural.] the supreme bishop celebrated devoted prayers of Mass, and Caesar piously bore the sacred crown of empire on his head.

For on that day the pope, standing at the sacred altars, loosed and cleansed from pardoned guilt everyone who, under a just prince, had girded the avenging sword in war against Roman slaughter, relying on the heavenly keys and Peter’s honour.

[145] And with reason: whoever defends the rights of the Church or the dignity of the realm, should he happen to shed human blood, is not a murderer but an avenger. For war undertaken by a soldier compelled by love of justice is called merit, not fault.

Then he sought the lofty city called Tusculum, secure in its high walls, and took up his position there.

[150] Now the Dog of Erigone, rising fiercely from its dreaded high ascent, began to irradiate the world with its heat-bearing lamp. Sad Orion, seeing him approach to bark at him and bite at his tracks with rabid bite,

[Col. 0382A] seethed with eternal rage. Each flame is harmful, but far more grievous is that one at whose rising the sky, corrupted with clouds, glows hot and the air burns with mournful fires.

The squalid earth lies torpid; pools and lakes are infected with corrupted waters; black vapours rise from sluggish marshes; by the hot breath of heaven, languid bodies waste away with deadly sickness.

[160] Thus it happens that every year the Roman populace is compelled to leave its own homes and, while that Dog rages, inhabit mountains near the city.

Add that Rome, grim with ancient ruins and uncultivated, lies empty over its greater part; it conceals in monstrous caverns very many living creatures of a harmful kind:

[165] [Col. 0382B] here green snakes and black toads; here winged dragons have made their dens. As their carcasses rot, the air is corrupted, and bodies dissolved by heat decay.

Therefore the people, forbidden by fear of war to change their homes, begin suddenly to waste away with disease in their own city, seized by a violent pestilence.

[170] Nor does the vigorous Frankish youth suffer the air any better; [Note: Rs. reads “chosen,” *lecta*.] overcome by so great heat, they languish and waste away, squalid with an unfamiliar disease. Thirst seizes their mouths, foulness infects their disfigured limbs, and their bodies waste away in jaundiced heat. [Note: Rs. reads “colour,” *colore*.]

[175] [Col. 0382C] Immediately the wretched men burn with their vital parts inflamed, drawing pestilential air as though from a furnace.

If our men could have borne the oppressive air and kept the camp fixed for a short time, there is no doubt that the Roman people would have submitted themselves and their city to their pontiff and king.

[180] But now the foul plague and unfamiliar disease had so devastated the royal camp and troops that everywhere frail men, exhausted by long labours, breathed out their lives; others, weak though fate still survived, dragged out a wretched life with death postponed, often cheated of the death they desired.

[185] Therefore the ruler, compassionate toward his own camp and its shared hardship, though many urged him to leave that place, unwilling and almost compelled to do so, left their bodies captive to the sacred pontiff;

[Col. 0382D] moving his sorrowful standards and surmounting the ascent and crags of the Tuscan mountain, subject to a better climate, he pitched camp beside the cool waters of the nearby Nar.

[190] Here, with every care and the aid of the healing art, he diligently sought to drive the sacred disease away and cleanse the harmful contagions of the evil air.

And when, for the use of the troops, fiscal dues began to be demanded from Etruscan cities,

[Col. 0383A] Spoleto, under the name of the treasury, was assessed eight hundred—
By the prince’s edict, he was ordered to render the talents [Note: “of a talent,” A., Sp., and P. o.];

[235] Yet he did not fear to defraud the king with counterfeit coin.

Moreover, Count Guido, of Tuscan stock—

Than whom no one had earlier dwelt on the Etruscan shores;

His surname was Guerra—had borne the king’s commands

To the cities of Apulia; and, on his return,

[240] While enjoying treacherous lodging in the place of hospitality,

He had been seized and was kept shut in a harsh prison.

And although the prince ordered that he be released, unbound,

And the man sent forth, the people, proud in their contempt for the king,

Persisted in their crime, laughing at the royal

[245] Commands; though they themselves, after a short time, would weep for their calamities

And render the just expiations of their crime.

For when by so many cruel and proud deeds

They had both deserved and stirred the prince’s righteous wrath:

Caesar, preparing to avenge uncorrected crimes [Note: “Indirecta,” Pfl. +.],

[250] Though he would rather pardon offenders when corrected [Note: Rs.—A. and the rest: “directa.” o.], turned his march toward the city. Its people, rash in sacrilegious daring,

Meeting him before its very gates, scarcely safe within the closed city,

Began the first battle with sling and light arrows

[Note: “met him,” Rs. *], [Note: Bartholomew reads “they begin.” *], and with spears hurled from afar,
