[255] He laughed and said: “Here are boys, unarmed [Note: In A., Sp., P., and R., the Greek article *to* before *inermes* is lacking, damaging the metre; P. noted this but supplied nothing. Rs., together with Jo., reads: “He laughed at this, and thus: ‘Boys,’” etc. A. c. adds *inermes*, ‘unarmed,’ which I have judged preferable to all the other readings.],

Not brave men fit to fight. Thus cowardly fathers

Have taught their offspring to play. Charge with all

Your strength, comrades; let the enemy forestall the citizen turned toward the walls

And seize the open gates before him.”

[260] [Col. 0383C] So he spoke; and, rejoicing at the signal received from the prince,

The German rushed with his fellow-soldiers upon the hostile city.

At once the suburbs were set aflame by torches brought near;

They fell into ashes [Note: “rush down,” manuscript reading, Rs. *], and neither the desire for rich plunder nor royal commands—

[265] Not yet heard by the soldiers [Note: P., Rs., and Jo.: “nor”; the rest: “not.” *]—could restrain their furious spirits.

Though stripped bare, the city, glittering with many treasures,

Was delivered to the flames without awaiting a signal.

Stunned by so great a whirlwind of wretched events,

The unhappy citizens—not now a pitiable mob,

[270] But rather one deserving hatred—seized in terror the co[lacuna]endia—perhaps “shortcuts”—of the lofty mountain,

Bearing back a fitting recompense for their arrogant deceit. There those who,

By puffed-up fraud, had falsely denied to their king his fiscal rights

[Note: “as,” Rs. +],

[Col. 0383D] Grieved, poor and wretched, having lost everything.

There stood upon a lofty and more strongly fortified citadel

The best part of the city, sufficiently raised upon a secure hill;

There its leading men had placed their lofty dwellings

And safe homes; there stood the episcopal seat,

[280] And the high structure of its conspicuous church rose up.

There a good part of the people, trusting in the fortification of the site

[Note: Pfl. and Rs.—A. and the rest: “Thus.” o.],

[Col. 0384A] In their extremity strove to defend themselves and the place,

And, wielding the sword and hurling stones,

Prepared either to hold the place or meet their fate.

But the unconquered king, thinking that he had done nothing memorable,

[285] Nothing worthy, while anything remained,

Burningly encouraged his men by voice and hand, often adding threats;

He restored their courage and supplied their anger.

He himself, despite his companions’ efforts to restrain him, explored every chance

And was the first to encounter every danger,

[290] Forgetful alike of his kingdom and himself,

Desiring to complete his undertaking even at the utmost peril.

Compelled by the prince’s example, the soldier dared bravely;

And under a bold king it was shameful to be afraid.

There was neither pause nor rest, until with a final shout

[295] [Col. 0384B] The broken citadels lay open to their conquerors.

But because, with the time for escape cut off, a great part

Of the populace had been consumed in the sudden fire,

And because the air was corrupted, while they drew in the foul smell

And the place exhaled a savage pestilence,

[300] Although much household property, by no means to be despised,

Could have been snatched from the fire, and necessity pressed our men,

Unable to endure the air, he withdrew, leaving the plunder behind;

Not far from the ruined city, the victor made camp

Under a better sky and in more gently breathing air.

[305] Soon, when the savage stench subsided as the flame died down,

And the attenuated reek dispersed into the empty air,

[Col. 0384C] The camp-following crowd at once returned to the plunder;

Whatever perhaps still remained unharmed by the flames

They snatched away, fearing neither to tread hot ashes underfoot

[310] Nor to burn their soles on glowing embers,

Hastening to rescue from the flames half-burnt booty.

They found wines carefully stored in full cellars,

And no small heaps of preserved grain [Note: Rs. and A. c.: “nor”; the rest: “not.” o.];

They found chests full of precious garments,

[315] And riches which the people had amassed by frugal use

And eagerly guarded; the victor seized all things,

And the camp grew rich with trophies half consumed by fire.

Without delay, where Ancona is beaten by the waves of the Dalmatian sea

[Col. 0384D] And makes an end of the great Apennine,

[320] The prince bore forward his standards and pitched his tents

Not far from the walls of the lovely city, in the middle of the plain.

There two great men, come from the Greek nation,

Met him [Note: Rs., RJo.: “the man”], bearing the king’s commands

And great gifts from their lord. One was called Mardochus,

[325] [Col. 0385A] The other Palologus [Note: “Palalogus,” A. o.; “Palaeologus,” Sp. and R. ++.];

Receiving them with gracious countenance, he heaped upon them fitting honour.

Having heard the reason for their journey, he ordered Guibald—

Distinguished in merits and sprung from illustrious stock

(He was abbot of Stablo [Note: “Stapulensis,” Sp., R., RJo. +.])—to go and give an answer

[Note: A.: “Gribaldus.” o.].

[330] Meanwhile Andrew, exiled from his native land,

And the other nobles whom that Sicilian tyrant

Had long ago proscribed throughout all the regions of Apulia,

As though returned by the Roman prince’s right of postliminy,

Had laid hands upon the territories and rights long taken from them

[335] And held the fortified cities and castles.

All were astonished and thought that the king himself

Was following behind, ready at any moment to invade their lands.

[Col. 0385B] And indeed he was about to do so, and eagerly prepared

To transfer Caesar’s avenging cohorts thither.

[340] But the heat of the sky, the oppression of the sultry weather,

The weakness of his companions, and the multitude exhausted

By long labour, together with the camps gleaming with innumerable funerals

[Note: “enormous,” manuscript reading, Rs. *],

Prevented him; and the German nobles, by faithful counsel,

Compelled him—though unwilling and planning great enterprises—

[345] To return beyond the Alps.

Therefore, when at last, laying down their arms, the royal grace

Granted the warlike troops leave to grow peaceful

And by a wished-for return to visit their native lands:

At once you might have seen them sorrowful at departure, beating their breasts

[350] With deep groans and faces wet with copious tears

[Note: “wetting,” manuscript reading, Rs.],

[Col. 0385C] So sweet had it been for the men under a gentle prince to endure every toil.

He too solemnly praised the veteran [Note: “veteran,” feminine, manuscript reading, Rs.] cohorts with grateful speech

And commended them with fitting honour;

Then he dismissed the men. One part, carried by the vast gulf

[355] And the Venetian sea, reached their native fields

And gladly beheld their ancestral homes.

But others returned in more than one column to the boundaries

And farthest barriers of Italy, to the Alps,

Terrible with harsh cliffs;

[360] Not by precisely the same route, but following the confined turns of places,

Difficult roads, and grim passes,

At last, with difficulty, long labour brought them to their native fields.

But those who were present from Tuscan or other Italian

Cities, numerous as they were,

[365] [Col. 0385D] Returned to their own walls with easy effort and in less time.

So, when a stream divides its manifold channels from one source

And produces different rivers in separate courses—

Some winding in a gentle flow across level plains,

Others roaring among hollow rocks—

[370] The sea receives them, after their long struggle in different regions,

Sooner or later according to the length of the current.

Yet neither the prince was left empty when so great a multitude of men had been dismissed,

Nor was the court left alone.

It is not for great kings to live with few attendants:

[375] [Col. 0386A] However many it dismisses, the court retains more.

Nor does a prince seek hiding-places, nor the sun shadows.

Let him hide the sun who wishes to hide the king.

Whether new men arrive or those who have arrived depart,

The court is always thronged by an inexhaustible multitude,

[380] Like the sea, which, although it scatters abundant waves throughout the world,

Ever swells fertile with inexhaustible waters.

Therefore, though a good part of his men had been dismissed,

The prince nonetheless moved a great camp, worthy of Caesar alone,

And hastened through the region now called Senogallia—

[385] Because the Gallic Senones are thought to have held it

When they oppressed trembling Rome with foreign soldiery—

[Col. 0386B] To reach your hills, Apennine.

Having crossed these too, Bologna received him in its level territory,

Watered by the little Reno,

And, as though full of good things, derives its name from a happy omen

[Note: “good things,” Rs. +].

[390] Departing thence [Note: “thence,” Rs. *], and crossing you, Po, ruler of Italian waters,

He reached the plains of mighty Verona and pitched his tents

In familiar fields, where the torrent-force of the Adige drives its swift waters.

A custom, handed down from the age of ancient kings

And preserved by fixed law through many years, required

[395] That whether the German ruler sought the Latin City

Or, returning as the consecrated one from the City, bore home his standards

[Note: “sacra,” manuscript reading, Rs. +],

[Col. 0386C] Verona should build a broad bridge of joined vessels

Stretched across the middle of the waters of the Adige,

So that the mighty prince might pass with the city walls untouched

And duly convey his companies across [Note: “and,” A., Sp., P. o.].

Then too, with vessels joined in a fragile structure,

[405] That faithless people had thrown timbers lightly across them above,

Building a bridge that would give way under an easy weight,

So that when our cavalryman, secure upon the sounding planks,

And the vessels rocking under uncertain weight,

Had already pressed upon them, the treacherous series, its fastening undone,

[410] Might yield and the soldier be borne into the swift waters.

Moreover, having cut down the willows at the river-bank’s edge,

They had piled the branches into many bundles of brushwood

[Note: “had bound,” Pfl. *],

Which, as if swept away by the current coming by chance

[Note: “by chance,” manuscript reading, Rs. +],

[Col. 0386D] The descending wave, driving them against the chained vessels,

Might release the treacherous bridge and deceive the soldiers.

Thus, when part of the German cohort had crossed,

With the river blocking the way, the impious enemy might attack the rest

And sate its dreadful sword with blood.

This infamous contrivance of deceit brought misery upon them,

[420] And, destined for great evil, by divine will

The wicked enemy fell into the pit which he had dug.

For as soon as the columns crossed in harmless passage over known dangers,

Forgetful of the deceit,

[Col. 0387A] And certain men of the fierce populace began from behind

[425] To assail them with tricks and suddenly provoke battle,

The soldiers prepared to cross back with retreating step;

But they found the bridge broken apart and undone,

Themselves cut off and shut in by a sudden abyss,

And they saw in astonishment the planking yawning with a new collapse.

[430] The avenging German soon slaughtered those caught there,

Without resource and stunned by disaster.

They had reached the narrow throat and confined barriers of the roads,

Where the terrible Alps, with cloud-bearing cliffs,

Offer themselves to be penetrated only by a narrow passage,

[435] And the confined path, with rocky track, opens footing

For a struggling multitude only one at a time.

[Col. 0387B] There [Note: Rs.: “There”; A. and the rest: “Thence.” o.], where broken ridges form a precipitous, dark chasm,

An empty chaos opens, a horror like the abyss of hell,

Able to render men lifeless; and it receives beneath their feet the Adige

[Note: “the Adige,” R. +], contending among shattered rocks

[440] With hoarse murmur—a river the astonished traveller hears but does not see.

From there a cliff rises above the sky with its cloud-bearing summit

And broadly covers the region with enormous shadow.

And from the brow of its rocky peak one man,

With easy effort, by dislodging falling stones,

[445] Can drive back a thousand men and close the approaches of the roads,

Or destroy the unwary [Note: Rs.—A. and the rest: “the wary there”; A. c.: “those shut in there”; Henisch also has this reading written in his copy.] by hurled stones.

To this place had withdrawn the fierce and infamous retainer

Albricus, greedy for crime and greedy for plunder,

[Col. 0387C] Horrible, keen, savage, born of the equestrian order.

[450] He was your citizen, Verona; and a band of youth,

Bound by oath to shameful service and enlisted in new monstrosities,

Was destined to perish with its master

And to make wretched the homes of its parents by bereavement.

They guarded, from a hidden station, the seat of an inaccessible cliff,

[455] Reached by long labour, and prepared a dreadful [Note: Rs.—the rest: “hard.” o.] and shameful crime.

Their desire was to despoil the columns by compulsory payments,

Or block the passage by hurling stones.

They did not choose to attempt their tricks or reveal their crime

Until the unsuspecting cohorts, wholly ignorant of the treachery,

[460] Had fallen into the narrow throat and confined pass.

Therefore, allowing a few to go safely ahead,

They held back hands prepared for great atrocities.

So a hunter seeking wild boars and tawny lions

Disregards timid hares and fleeing deer:

[465] He is ashamed to pursue lesser prey.

He hides under the great arch of a high [Note: “high,” P.] cliff,

[Col. 0388A] And restrains his noisy dogs [Note: P. and Rs.—A. and the rest: “has”; here.],

Checking his eager mastiffs so that they do not shake the air [Note: “their mouths,” B. *] with barking,

Until antlered stags come into the nets,

[470] Fierce lions, savage boars, the leopard beautiful in spotted hide,

And shaggy bears together with swift tigers.

Yet the concealed instruments of deceit could not deceive the king:

Nothing can pass unnoticed by heavenly minds;

This is what the Wise Man declares:

[475] “My son, do not secretly curse a ruler;

A bird of the air carries hidden curses to the king.”

Therefore Caesar had learned long before and perceived their rage,

And did not choose to expose his camp to certain danger

Or subject the fate of the Roman king to sacrilegious men.

[480] At once, sending a few men in advance from our column,

He ordered them to desist from their infamous design,

To leave their occupied post and their arrogant purpose.

The mad band roared and, by rolling stones,

Drove away the men bearing the imperious commands.

[485] At that same time there were in our camp

Two young men born of the Veronese populace—

Verona called one Isaac, the other Carzabanus—

Who for a long time, following the royal standards,

[490] [Col. 0388C] Had striven to commend themselves to the king by faithful service

And to please him through zealous, loyal favour.

The nobles ordered these men, as fellow citizens who might therefore speak more safely

To their associates for Caesar by right of fellowship,

To go and break the fierce hearts and savage minds

[495] Of the violent men by admonition [Note: B.: “arrogance,” W.; editions: “mind,” o.; Rs., pp.: “deserts.”].

But the impious crowd, refusing to hear them no less as though they were strangers,

Drove them away as avowed enemies.

And unless our people redeemed themselves by a fixed tribute

Of a coat of mail or a horse, left beforehand for each man,

[500] And unless the king himself freed his own head with much money,

They swore that they would never grant safe passage [Note: “departures,” manuscript reading, Rs. +],

Never allow the columns to pass through the pressing defiles.

[Col. 0388D] This condition seemed pitiable and shameful to the king;

Touched by deep anger, he began thus:

[505] “Comrades and nobles, comforts of my fortunes,

Whom the glory of the Roman empire makes masters of the world

And rulers by a sure and mighty right:

You see to what disgrace royal majesty has at last come,

After so many affairs of the kingdom,

[510] After cities stormed by victorious arms

And the crown received according to the sacred custom of empire,

[Col. 0389A] After many punishments of crimes and disasters of the guilty.

Now, when we prepare on our return to enter the threshold of our native land,

Our first ancestral homes and longed-for dwellings

[Note: A: “we prepare”; the rest: “we are preparing.”],

[515] Shame! We are prevented by a few cowardly men

From proceeding farther on the royal road; honour and shame do not permit us

To turn our course. Nor may we proceed farther,

Because the savagery of criminals prevents it. A few robbers

Demand shameful tribute from the Roman king,

[520] At whose discretion every tribute is imposed;

And they compel the Capitoline head to pay a sum

[Note: “And the illicit head,” Pfl. +]

Than which there is none nobler in all the world.

It does not befit us to be redeemed from a cowardly robber with money—

From one by whom the guilty often receive their own lives,

[525] Though redeemed by no payment, when their crime is pardoned.

It is not loss that moves me, but grievous covenants that alarm me;

I flee foul dealings that would leave a lasting stain upon our fame.

Yet we shall pay a just tribute, we shall one day pay

Such as befits a king to render and a robber to bear.

[530] Stand firm, brave men; it pleases me to storm these criminals.

Either here or nowhere shall we cross the cold Alps.”

So he spoke, and ordered the column to halt after pitching camp,

Eager to punish the cowardly robbers.

[Col. 0389C] As he considered all things, a plan plainly apparent [Note: “hidden,” manuscript reading, Rs. +]

[535] Came into his mind: just as the criminal crowd had climbed before,

So his own men might by some means make their way over the steep cliff.

He entrusted two hundred young men of bravest heart to standard-bearing Otto,

Ordering them to seek out, on every side, secret ascending paths.

They obeyed; armed lightly, but secure in stout hearts,

[540] The high-minded young men searched woods and shattered cliffs

On every side by winding routes.

At last, scarcely amid the rocks and sharp crags,

They saw a place by which there seemed at last to be great opportunity

For accomplishing their undertaking.

[Col. 0389D] At once they exerted themselves upward along a narrow path;

[545] Their nails broke against the crags, and if some root,

Already decayed upon its ancient stem, projected from a cliff,

They seized it with straining hand. The man following raised and supported the one before him by the shoulder;

The first drew up those behind, and they supplied one another

With alternating assistance in their efforts.

[550] But if by chance no path, cut off by the cliff,

Lay open to the men, they joined their spears in customary [Note: “solid,” B. +] bindings

[Note: B.: “to themselves,” W.; A. and the rest: “huge.” o.]

To imitate the rungs of ladders, and did not hesitate

To carry their suspended feet high into the air.

Thus, when exhausting labour had scarcely been struggled through

[555] [Note: Rs. and RJo.: “with the utmost [labour].” +]

The warlike young men stood upon the summit of the cliff,

Mighty Otto raised the royal standards which he had secretly carried beneath his garment,

And dreadful trumpets sounded with fierce clamour.

The rocks, amazed at hitherto unknown cries of men, echoed back—

[560] Rocks known before only to wild beasts and wearied birds,

Scarcely ever touched even by windy storms.

The doomed troop was stunned when it saw the royal standards

And the enemies standing on the highest rocks.

What could the wretches do? Steep cliffs barred their flight;

[565] [Col. 0390B] Their evil cause and fear prevented battle, as did their trembling confidence in their feeble right hands.

The royal soldier attacked them, stunned and utterly bereft of reason [Note: “all,” B. *],

And, when the rest had been slain and their leader captured,

Reserved twice ten bodies for shameful punishment,

[570] Presenting all these to the king as a welcome gift—

Except, of course, one man,

Who, ordered to hang his companions with his own hand,

Obtained his wretched life by the king’s gift.

He was a Gaul, recently drawn unwittingly into these wicked schemes;

[575] Sparing him, the most just avenger commanded the throats of the others

To be crushed by the dreadful [Note: W.—editions: “hard.” o.] noose.

[Col. 0390C] Thus they say that five hundred underwent the final fates of death by cross or sword:

All free-born young men of the equestrian order, who, having suffered royal wounds

[Note: “shameful,” W.; I doubt whether this is appropriate.],

And being destined by their punishment to provide an example to all,

[580] Were piled by the German soldier in great heaps.

Extinguished in their own bodies and in bloody slaughter,

They blocked the road which, while alive, they had vainly attempted by arrogant deceit

To shut against their righteous king.

But the king, passing through the Italian throat and narrow defiles,

[585] Reached peaceful Trent at his first halt. There, dismissing many

Who were seeking their native lands, the most gracious guest went to the nearby

Walls of Brixen; soon the land of Noricum received him,

Returning after a year, in its joyful bosom.

[Col. 0390D] These deeds, among so many acts of the noble prince [Note: Rs.—the rest: “Nor.” o.],

[590] We have thought fit to attempt in our slender song;

As from a tree laden with flowers we pluck a few rare blossoms,

And count a few flames in the sky.

For if one wished to record in uninterrupted course

All that, on his journey to Italy or return from it,

[595] Or wherever he was stationed, he so bravely

[Col. 0391A] And wisely accomplished—what book, pray, could contain it all?

What writer could record it with hurrying hand?

It is no task for a slight poet to write of so great a prince:

He demands a magnificent poet.

[600] We, small in spirit and sustained by no strength,

Sweat beneath a great burden at an easy labour.

[Col. 0392A] Add that, being absent, it is enough for us to report a few things out of many,

And lightly touch upon the matter with modest hand.

Those can describe deeds solidly

[605] Whom eyewitness assurance and the presence of the event itself instruct,

And whom the known sequence of events does not permit to err.

We, unworthy to behold from afar the royal deeds of Caesar,

Have received with a slight ear a few things out of many,

As public report survived.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0391]

[Col. 0391B] Therefore Germany, rejoicing in the return of her king

And seeing him return more great than she herself had sent him out—

Burdened with the fasces and the surname of highest praise—

Summoned nobles and faithful peoples to meet him,

[5] Ordered entire cities gladly to open their devoted walls

[Note: P., from the argument; corrected by Rs. and RJo.—A. and the rest: “obey.” o.]

And bestowed grateful honour.

Thus, after many perils of harsh war,

You once saw Cecropian Athens rejoice in Theseus returning,

Bearing back the standards of Thermodonian triumph

[10] And adding many regions to his realm.

In the prince’s uncle there still breathed that old hostility,

Born from the seizure of the duchy of Bavaria.

The most gentle nephew, wishing to calm this anger,

Met him in the city of Regensburg with persuasive words

[15] And laboured much and long;

Yet he could not quell the old grievance

Between the two men and restore firm peace.

Therefore he appointed another conference between the men concerning the same matters,

Where the Bohemian lands touch the first boundaries

[20] Of Bavaria by a common border.

While the prince, lest there should be any delay through him,

Was making for the place of conference and approaching those boundaries,

Behold, Labezlaus, then duke of Bohemia,

And Herrmann, the illustrious count of the sacred court,

[25] [Col. 0391D] Whose land was encircled by the swelling Rhine,

And Albert, mighty margrave of Saxon land,

Came to meet him and greeted his return, whether from fear or love.

For so great a fear had seized all the nobles

Who had refused to follow his standards and leave their native lands,

[30] So great a terror held them trembling,

That each man, conscious of guilt and considering himself already worthy of Caesar’s wrath as judge,

[Col. 0392B] Strove by every service to appease the injured leader,

Whom rumour proclaimed glorious in praise,

Distinguished in merits, adorned with every virtue,

[35] And terrible to the guilty.

For the ambassadors made plain how great a terror the ruler had left behind

[Note: Rs.—A. corrected: “had left.” o.]

In fearful Italy, and how much fear he had inspired, departing,

In the Italian cities: ambassadors whom Verona, conscious and afraid of her own guilt,

Had humbly sent, after a short time, to the German city

[40] [Note: “to the German world”? Compare below, line 76, and Book X, lines 2–3.]

Their humble flatteries and tearful words—

To be remembered hereafter in their proper place—I now pass over.

Indeed, royal majesty possesses in itself this power of just terror:

[45] Whether far or near, present or absent,

It is ever terrible, ever to be feared, and remains full of its own strength.

It is believed that none may oppress it with impunity,

And it is always feared by all and everywhere.

At this conference too, the nobles on either side,

[50] Searching with shrewd mind into the cause at Caesar’s command

And long attempting to calm such great disturbances,

At last gave up their undertaking in vain.

For whatever form of peace the men tried to forge

[Col. 0392D] To bring an agreement that might end the dispute [Note: Rs.—the rest: “hence.” o.],

[55] The Norican rejected it and remained in his customary anger,

Departing angrily after greeting the king.

Then the assembly of mighty men, summoned again to Regensburg

At the prince’s command, convened.

There, when by the judgment of the nobles and according to legal rule

[60] He had established the Saxon prince in the seat of his ancestors,

All the fathers of Bavaria first ratified a treaty of loyal oath

With their new leader [Note: “all,” P. and Rs.].

But the people, possessors and inhabitants of the famous seat,

Were compelled not merely to swear allegiance to their leader

[Col. 0393A] But also to guarantee secure faith by many hostages;

[65] They obeyed. For the treaty was demanded of the greater leader with greater care,

Because the people might appear loyal to the former lord

And suspect to the new one.

They say that many complaints also arose amid uncertain litigation;

Among these, almost the greatest was this:

[70] Arnold, your bishop, Mainz, and Count Herrmann,

The great court official under the supreme prince,

Were fiercely conducting a contest of litigation with one another

[Note: Rs.—the rest: “with one another.” o.].

For while the ruler had been removed from German lands

[75] And was pressing Italian cities by war or law,

So great a fury of war had blazed in the northern world

[Col. 0393B] That Germany, thoroughly shaken, bewailed her disasters

And zealously called back her absent king.

This cause too, with many others but stronger than all,

Brought Frederick back from the Italian lands.

[80] Yet in so great a storm of the whole kingdom,

Warlike Germany had felt the force and anger of these men

With disaster so much greater

As their power was greater and more exalted.

[85] While the king with tranquil mind was settling these tumults of the nobles

And the clamorous business of the realm,

Behold, your citizens, Isaac, well known at court,

And Carzabanus together—of whom, if we are not mistaken, mention was made before,

[Col. 0393C] When they bore the petitions of their timid bishop to Caesar’s gentle ears

[90] And the commands of your people, Verona.

And when the men had been granted access and opportunity to speak before him,

The bishop began in eloquent speech:

“I bring to you the commands of your Verona,

And the words and prayers of its faithful people,

[95] Greatest ruler of the Roman name—

I, scarcely worthy bishop of that same city.

Nor did they prevail upon me to take up this task

Before the entire people of the greater church, gathered with one mind,

Promised before God and His saints

[100] To observe in deed and in full faith all things

[Col. 0393D] Which they had entrusted to us to report to you. Who would have believed that there was room for deceit?

Had they wished to deceive, they could surely have exposed another’s reputation to shame,

Entrusted their tricks to another, and spared their own fatherland.

But because pure faith, adorned by no false colour,

[105] Was in their instructions, they chose to entrust them to us.

Therefore they added as companions men tested by gravity of character,

Whom you yourself have been able to recognize as faithful

Through long experience of camp and time.

[Col. 0394A] You have heard, and grieved, that arrogant robbers—not your citizens, Verona—

[110] Laid snares for you as you prepared to cross. Who would dare call them citizens,

When they wickedly plotted against their own king?

He who violates a citizen ceases to be a fellow citizen;

He who violates a king—who could call him a citizen [Note: “can,” ?]?

But it is well that the impious band underwent deserved punishment,

[115] And their cast-out corpses feed wild beasts and birds.

Verona condemns the bones of the slain by denying them tombs,

As well as the savage spirits and cruel [Note: “sinister,” manuscript reading, Rs. +] names of the criminals;

Their enraged parents hate their offspring.

And lest you perhaps think that the counsel of this deceit proceeded from our city,

[120] [Col. 0394B] Verona promises and offers herself for purgation wherever

Royal nobility shall command; she pledges the surest proofs

Of her loyalty and innocent intention.

Is Verona not bound to you by a sacred covenant

[Note: P. and Rs.—the rest: “And is Verona not?” o.]?

[125] Did she not first receive your cohorts

When you sought mighty Rome with fortunate soldiery?

Did we not joyfully see your return and returning columns,

And send them onward from our native land?

A city seen so often rejoicing to meet your camp,

[130] Do not call faithless in vain.

Cease, I pray, to transfer the diseased contagion of a few

To the whole flock, and to equate those free from fault with the guilty.

Let not the innocent be dragged down by the guilt of criminals;

Under a just judge let each receive from his own deeds

[135] The rewards or punishments of his deserts.

We are innocent; the criminal band has received the just wrath it deserved.

Now spare a people loyal and devoted to you,

And instead turn with all your strength against Rome, rebellious and long faithless to her own people

[Note: Rs., manuscript: “your [Rome]” *],

[140] Or against the arrogant city of the Ligurians.

Do not hesitate to enlist Verona in your just wars

And make her bring her forces to bear. Whatever city has deserved Caesar’s anger

Will feel our anger also.”

He had spoken, and both companions added their support with complete assent,

[145] Seeking to appease Caesar [Note: “while appeasing Caesar,” Rs.—“Caesar being appeased,” A. c. +].

But the king, by counsel of the nobles, stipulated under a definite condition

[Col. 0394D] That they swear to pay a sum to the fisc

And follow the royal camp with all their forces against the Ligurian city.

Thus at last peace having been obtained,

They joyfully turned their steps toward their native borders.

[150] The venerable day was drawing near on which Christ,

Equal to the Father in a single divinity, without beginning in time,

Begotten from eternity, author of time, chose in time

To be born from a virgin through divinely infused power:

There without a mother, here receiving nothing from a father,

[155] [Col. 0395A] Thus a child in the cradle, that as God he might reign among the stars.

Caesar, intending to celebrate this day with fitting honour,

Made for Worms, choosing there for his court a distinguished seat

[Note: “as,” Rs. +],

One able to feed so many thousands from its full horn.

[160] Situated midway on the stream of the Rhine, it sets Gallic lands

Against German settlers;

Each land is most fruitful in fertile fields,

Each abounds in vineyards, each in fruits,

Fish, wild game, and every kind of food.

[165] There, after the prince had passed the sacred season with devout heart,

Great affairs of the realm at last began to be handled under the highest judge.

You might see men pour out manifold complaints from every side

And bring uncertain cases into collision.

Whatever they had endured at one another’s hands during the king’s absence,

[170] [Col. 0395B] They complained of with mingled outcry.

So servants, when their master returns home after a long time abroad,

Are accustomed to recount their tearful affairs,

Their oppressions and the blows of unjust quarrels,

Mutual deceits, hidden crimes of theft,

[175] The injuries of wicked deeds, and whatever wickedness has been done;

They tell all they can in blazing hatred.

To all these the prince’s constancy lent calm ears

And, with tranquil mind, moderated violent tumults,

Disdaining to be moved without some reason.

[180] He relieved the oppressed and struck down the proud with heavier punishment—

[Col. 0395C] Kind to the afflicted and formidable to the unjust.

Then the two aforementioned nobles, Arnold and that other courtly count,

Convicted by judgment of deeds cruelly done in manifold guilt,

Many accusations being fiercely kindled against them and provoking the king’s deep anger,

Received the wounds of capital punishment.

[185] And had not grave age and sacred order protected the bishop,

He would either have paid the penalty in blood

Or suffered the disgrace of utter shame.

For it is an ancient custom that if anyone, while the king is absent,

Dares to harass the kingdom by bloodshed, fire,

[190] The open tumult of rebellion, or repeated plundering,

Before he undergoes the severe penalty of shed blood,

If he is free-born, he is compelled by ancient custom

[Col. 0395D] To carry a dog laid upon his shoulders through the borderlands

Of the adjacent county; if of another status, a saddle.

The guardian of the most celebrated Palatine court,

That count, could not escape the humiliation of this penalty;

[195] In the sight of all, he bore the barking dog upon his shoulders for more than a thousand paces.

Ten other counts suffered this same punishment for a like crime,

And an equal number were compelled to bear foul dogs,

A shameful weight upon their noble necks.

[Col. 0396A] The deep fear of this unheard-of penalty rushed upon all,

[200] So that none of the nobles thereafter presumed to contend by armed hand;

Instead, under the arbitrament of a just judge, each sought his own claims in peace.

Add that the unconquered Caesar, ranging everywhere,

Eagerly hastened to storm with his own hand the robber-barons’ castles

Bristling on the highest ridges [Note: “clinging,” manuscript reading, Rs. +],

[205] And citadels scarcely visible upon lofty cliffs;

To overthrow them after their walls had been scattered,

Or burn them with flames. He rejoiced to destroy the very makers of crimes—

Those who disturbed the peace of the realm

And were accustomed to despoil the wretched with repeated plundering—

[210] By cross, sword, or long imprisonment,

An avenger not to be entreated.

Thus, after the darkness and the sad clouds of savage war,

[Col. 0396B] The turmoil of the German kingdom having been calmed,

The prince’s arrival had begun, like a new image of the sun,

[215] To pour forth the rays of wished-for peace

[Note: Rs., manuscript: “spread forth.” *].

Only the Norican land, agitated by the efforts of dukes,

Was still without this peace and impatient of salvation.

And the day had now come again in swift returning course

[220] Which the Holy Spirit himself made venerable to his world by his advent,

When, marking mystical gifts, he distinguished tongues in fire poured down from above.

Frederick, relieved of cares, was spending leisure

In the castle of Palatine Otto.

When three days had passed in this secluded abode,

[225] He once again turned his mind, dispelling sloth, to his usual cares

And public business of the realm [Note: Rs.—the rest: “turned back.”].

Therefore, at Regensburg, his uncle concerning the covenant of peace—
He addresses and sways the man, perhaps having taken an example from those whom, because of their quarrels and unjust wars, he had heard had experienced the king’s threats.

[240] And when, with the peace of so great men restored, public rejoicings flourished throughout the whole kingdom, so that, with affairs well ordered, the glory of perfect splendour might be present, lacking no part, it remained for the king to join his widowed bedchamber, in desire for noble offspring, to the chaste Beatrice. Recently brought to him through certain loyal persons, she was already, by the prince’s summons, queen in hope, passing through German cities and the lands of her future husband.

For she who had first married the mighty man, but was not to remain with him, having been ordered to withdraw from the unlawful bed of her kinsman, had yielded both place and cause to the second marriage. This separation too may have arisen from the hidden counsel of Him who governs all things, so that perhaps that blessed Beatrice might succeed to the prince’s bedchamber—worthy of so great a husband and destined to bear blessed offspring.

[255] Count Rainald, sprung from the ancient stock of kings among the Allobroges, and himself made more illustrious by his deeds, begot her; and, dying, he left you, Burgundy, your borders bereft while she was still in tender and orphaned years, together with strong cities and fortified castles.

This land begins from those regions where Basel washes its walls with the neighbouring river and gladly welcomes the approaching Rhine. Thence it embraces innumerable peoples and borders upon the lands of Gaul; on this side it is enclosed by the rocky cliffs of the harsh Alps, and extends in equal breadth as far as where swift Rhône enters the first waves of the sea, and where Arles is said to have been the capital and seat of the ancient kingdom, the court of former kings. Joining Provence to itself by equal right, it bore among the ancients the name and title of a kingdom. Arles was said to be its seat and boundary on that side, until the final will of King Rudolf ordered it to be added to our realms and stripped it of the name of its ancient dignity, so that it is now no longer a kingdom but a fine portion of the kingdom.

[275] There we know these as its metropolitan and chief cities: tranquil Chrysopolis, Lyons, or Vienne, and Arles, which Provence closes against your borders with its foaming sea, exposed to strong winds. The Doubs flows past Chrysopolis; the Rhône, greatest river of the Allobroges and lord of waters, flows past the others.

A certain William, called “the Boy” by report, came from an ancient royal lineage and possessed this country. He had been born of distinguished stock, the son of the sister of Duke Conrad. When, as the ancients report, he was removed from human affairs through the treachery of his own people, Count Rainald, his nearest kinsman and lawful heir, obtained the government of so great a dominion. Relying, naturally, upon his right and illustrious blood, he frequently spurned the German kings and their edicts. Thinking it unworthy that the Allobroges should be subject to other kings, he was excessively mindful of their ancient liberty and proudly played the king.

[295] At last, because of his countless acts of arrogance, the royal judgment brought its avenging power against him; and, under the judgment of the king, took the land from the man and granted it to Conrad to hold in the name of the fisc. Thus, as though a rebel despiser of the kingdom had been outlawed, Conrad was to succeed his extinguished nephew as nearest heir.

Conrad soon invaded the territory granted him with an armed force, attempting to defend the royal gift for himself and secure it by a strong hand. But Rainald, striving to protect what he had received from his fathers, fought many battles with varying fortune. In our own time the royal power finally calmed these hostilities by this skilful settlement: Berthold was to govern the two cities in those territories—Lausanne and Geneva, situated upon its cold rock—while Rainald held the rest. For this reason, I think, Berthold preferred to be called ruler of the former kingdom of the Allobroges rather than count; Rainald remained under his customary title.

[314] When Berthold too died, his only child by so great a father, noble Beatrice, inherited by right the honour due to her paternal estate and assumed the government of great affairs while still in tender years, destined to marry an exceptional husband.

Accordingly, when word was spread through various cities that the day had come on which the prince would deign, amid festive torches, to join to himself a companion of his sacred bed and inaugurate a better marriage under new destinies, magnificent nobles summoned from every side assembled and made for the city whose name, they think, is derived from herbs in the common tongue. Thus that illustrious work, as though at the heart of the kingdom’s middle, might be celebrated, and that famous seat might offer a place worthy of so great an honour.

[325] Whoever wishes to measure in explicit words how many bishops and great men attended, what was the appearance of the nobles, what the honour and magnificence of the occasion, what popular favour and devotion of the clergy, I confess could count the sands along the shore or the shining stars in the vast sky.

In this splendour of events the queen came into the sacred embraces of her husband, destined to bear, for a fortunate throne, counts, kings, and dukes: above all, you, Henry, who now by ruling the Italian cities bravely first acquire a great name in your earliest age; and you, Frederick, leader of the Swabians and most worthy heir of your father’s name, as your deeds prove; and you also, Conrad, illustrious boy with great Otto, of renowned praise; and Philip, younger than them all but not unlike them in excellence of character.

[344] The princely woman indeed bore these in happy childbirth, and perhaps would have borne from her noble womb still more lords of lands, mighty far and wide, had the envious Fates not cut the deceptive threads during their flourishing youth. Alas for me: how swiftly did the illustrious mistress fall by fate, leaving behind a widowed husband and offspring.

Yet she had seen her sons ruling with their father Augustus, and the crown placed upon your head, Henry, in your own time, when the court of Mainz beheld its fathers summoned from the whole world in a gathering greater than any before and believed never to be equalled in the future.

[355] The prince had not yet permitted the magnates, assembled for such great rejoicings, to return to their own homes and native lands. The court still sang wedding songs worthy of the sacred marriage-bed, with solemn applause, a happy omen, and votive celebrations, when Guibald returned from the Greek city of Stabulum, together with envoys bearing the king’s commands.

Yet, because of the fraud of others whom that same distinguished envoy of the Emperor Manuel had earlier sent, they were ordered to stand far off, unworthy to approach the ears and presence of so great a prince at so joyful a time; and they trembled, fearing the emperor’s grave anger.

[367] For those who had brought to you, Frederick, then holding the Italian cities and Etruscan lands, the earlier commands of the aforesaid tyrant, had employed national tricks: falsely using the king’s name, they had produced for themselves lying documents stamped with a forged seal. After the king had honourably received them, heaped honours and gifts upon them, entrusted them with favourable words to report to their master, and offered the terms of peaceful friendship, he dismissed them. But when they heard that the royal standards had returned beyond the Rhaetian Alps, they immediately filled the peoples and towns of Apulia and Campania with false reports deceitfully obtained. They alleged that coastal cities and towns neighbouring the sea had received beneficent documents from the prince.

[380] With these frauds and Greek gold they wickedly corrupted the ignorant minds of the populace. Count Andrew of Capua joined them, as did a band recently returned from exile under our king, and one Robert of Caivano, a count of exceptional valour. Whether the favour of our prince, hatred of the Sicilian, or very great reward had impelled them, they supported the undertaking with all their strength.

Moreover, the populace—faithless and fickle toward its lords, desiring to cast off the burdens of servitude and the yoke of Sicilian tyranny—rejoiced to assist the crime and to follow the movement of revolution. Trusting in these resources, they attacked Bari, a place fortified by the Sicilian with a strong citadel and no small garrison. In contest of arms they took it by force and transferred its captured walls, won in war, into their own jurisdiction and to new destinies.

[399] Not, however, without loss: for Palologus, a man of greatest promise among them, disturbed their rejoicings by a bitter death. His sorrowful comrades conveyed his body, embalmed with aromatic fragrance, to his ancestral tomb.

By then the report had spread through the Italian cities and reached the prince’s noble ears: William had either ended his life or, weighed down by illness, been deprived of the use of his own senses; and every city in those regions had been shamefully deceived by Greek frauds. Caesar judged this sufficiently disgraceful and utterly shameful, and shuddered in immense anger.

[411] For although he grieved that cities of the Roman name and mutilated kingdoms had hitherto been seized by the Sicilian, he thought it still more disgraceful and foul that cities should be captured by trickery, seduced shamefully by cunning, and that he himself should be mocked by the false shadow of his own name.

Who can doubt that there were hidden and wholly concealed reasons why he had borne so patiently the Sicilian’s enjoyment of such prolonged plunder and restrained his righteous anger until then? At last, in our time, a bride was to come to you, King Henry, from the Sicilian royal house, to bring an everlasting end to the old grievance and peace and harmony between the two kingdoms.

[423] Perhaps he would then have atoned for the crime, the contrivances of unjust deceit, and the tricks of the Greek-born by the death of the Greeks; or he would have compelled them, dishonoured and subjected to the gravest reproaches, shamefully to return to the Argive city—had not a good part of the nobles advised the king to spare the envoys and to prefer a good reputation to resentment.

Thus at last an opportunity of approaching the king was assigned to the Greeks, under a fixed arrangement of time and place. Yet the fierce wrath of the unconquered prince did not subside until the nobles swore to follow the avenging standards of the realm into Apulia at the appointed time.

[434] Avenging Germany had already stirred its grave anger and hastened great preparations amid terrifying tumult, when a new report from Italy, better than the first, announced that, their enemies destroyed and the Sicilian victorious, the cities which they had deceitfully subjected to themselves had been recovered.

Therefore the prince turned the weight of such great affairs elsewhere and hastened to direct war against the Ligurians. He sent innumerable documents bearing his name to the nobles, conveying these royal commands:

“If your loyalty had not been made known by clear signs, and if your labours, with much sweat, had not long ago furnished manifest pledges of a sincere heart, we should not so confidently seek your aid in all the changing circumstances that time brings. But because we know you to be devoted to us, as dutiful members ought to be to their supreme head, we now entrust one task and now another to your zeal as circumstances change: thus the order of affairs demands; thus Fortune varies her turns. For the honour of the Empire, we do not fear to associate you with any labours.

[454] “The war in Apulia, which we decreed a few days ago at Würzburg, I remit without penalty to you. For Fortune has forestalled our efforts, and great concerns have perished when their causes were removed. Other wars now await our arms—an excellent task of valour and noble labour: to fulfil the Empire’s threats and, after the Ligurian city has been utterly overthrown as is fitting, to establish our terror among all nations and peoples throughout the world.

“For that city, ever deceitful, faithless, and rebellious toward the Italian kings, obedient to serve no powerful ruler, now swells especially against our reins. It despises us as degenerate, timid, and lacking intelligence; it thinks that he whom it sees too ready to pardon and slow to punish crimes cannot punish offenders. It takes our patience as proof of fear. You do not know, alas, ruined city, you do not know what man you provoke to your destruction! You too ought to have learned what unhappy Tortona, partner and accomplice in your guilt, experienced. As it fell, so you too, conquered, shall fall; and with a ruin so much heavier as you now seem yourself stronger than others.

[475] “Small things fall more lightly: they are not weighed down by a great mass. Great things are broken by the fall of an immense weight. Come then, magnificent nobles: bring fearless hands to great deeds, and, bearing just arms, come with me to aid the distressed realm. It is safer now to cut away rotten limbs with the sword than for the whole body to waste away through the corruption of one part.

“This is that guilty city which, stronger than all others, persecutes every city and continually oppresses our Pavia. It pursues nearby Como and Lodi with lasting hatred, cruelly presses them both, terrifies them with threats, and violently overturns other cities by arms. Holding them crushed in the dust, it does not allow the conquered to raise their heads again. Proudly it scorns and mocks the threats of the realm. It loves the cities we hate and hates those we have loved.

[491] “Despite our prohibitions, it raises the old fortresses of Tortona and dares to repair forbidden ruins. It neither fears the angry king, whom it knows is far away, nor thinks that it will feel our return any more. It is deceived and draws comfort from a vain wish. Sooner than it expects, we shall press Ligurian walls with our camp; we have fixed the war for the completed year. Then it will be compelled to pay us the penalties it deserves; and it which now protects and raises other cities will lie prostrate, not to be restored until after a long time.

“Therefore, brave men, enlist for yourselves whatever resources each of you can, so that, when the year has turned, the entire army may assemble at our Ulm and, under my command, cross the harsh Alps safe and unharmed, then swiftly seize the sufficiently guilty city. And lest, under this pretext, you suppose you are being called to greater things or perhaps led across the Apennines, let that fear be far from you. By the royal name I swear that no one shall be compelled farther than the Ligurian city.”

[511] Meanwhile, the city of the Ligurians, seething with the accustomed tumult of war after learning that the royal forces had conquered the Alpine passes and occupied their native country, began to encircle the river Ticino with two bridges, threatening fearful Pavia with its habitual ferocity. It ravaged the surrounding fields with fire and plunder, stabbed human bodies with the sword or bound captives in harsh chains; it restored Lunello, hastily raised the walls of Tortona, and hurried to repair new ruins.

Not far from the safe walls of Pavia, castles shone from a high site. Tradition has handed down nothing certain about their name (the text calls them Vigevano). At that time William, marquis of Montferrat, guarded these walls, together with Pavia’s young men assigned to the place as a garrison. But the stronger enemy eventually stormed the fortifications after a long siege, seized them victoriously, and, granting life only with great difficulty to the captives under many hostages, imposed terms at his own pleasure.

[530] Pavia then rejected these terms and this unjust form of peace, cast off the burden, and broke away. When the festive celebrations had ended, the king immediately made for the Norican camps, leaving part of the nobles at Würzburg, and stayed there for a time.

Here, as they had been ordered, the envoys of the king of the Achaeans came to meet him and communicated the royal commands, whose tenor—unless we are mistaken—was as follows. They promised him a wife from the illustrious family of their kings and proposed to bind new marriage ties and a perpetual peace by a firm bond.

[541] There was also another reason for this undertaking. The ruler of the proud Achaeans had recently sent a great army against Hungary under the command of Boricius. When a large part of it perished in bloody war, cut down with its commander by a Scythian arrow, the ruler was too weak to avenge the disaster by his own strength. He therefore begged our king, whom he knew capable of everything, to declare war upon the savage peoples and attempted to enlist him as avenger of his actions. But each hope deceived the man: he had already joined himself to better marriage alliances, while private concern, more urgently pressing, and war prevented him for a short time.

[554] From there the prince summons the nobles to Regensburg, called by the public business of the kingdom and news of new events. Here the king’s uncle and the king’s nephew prepare at last to make public and proclaim the settlement of peace which had until then been concealed. The following order of events will adequately show what it was.

The king’s uncle formally resigned the duchy through seven banners, which he handed to his nephew. Of these, the nephew resigned two to be handed back to his uncle, leaving the rights of Austria to pass with them to that man. This land was then a march, but is now a duchy. For the king, wishing to preserve for his uncle the name of ancient honour when he held three counties, joined them as though compacted into one body and, with the counsel of the nobles, made them into a renowned duchy. Lest subsequent kings should overturn or revoke the deed, he left the duke documents secured by the royal seal and certain records.

[572] So that this land too might enjoy the royal gift while the benefit of peace flourished through all cities, Norica was the last to receive the sworn peace. Thus, as though the age of antiquity had returned, a golden age revived beneath a peace-making king. But as much peaceful repose as the king’s presence, after peace was secured, had bestowed upon our realm, so much disaster had his absence inflicted upon the Italian peoples and released the fury previously held in check. Thus, while the sun’s absence darkens half the world with shadows, its presence pours light upon the other half and divides the sky with alternating radiance.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0403D] Thus noble Germany, smiling with a joyful countenance after many times of restored peace, enjoyed sweet rejoicings, putting anxieties aside. Men gladly believed that they themselves and the age had changed; even the air of heaven breathed more gently, and the earth bestowed better gifts.

[5] Yet amid so great a peace the prince did not idly enjoy leisure, believing that he lost whatever time added nothing to the kingdom’s revenues; and the peace which he had given others he voluntarily denied himself. Therefore, having found a new cause to attempt bold deeds, he resolved to declare war upon the savage Poles.

Report holds that the Vistula, binding with its rushing waters the peoples beginning from the quarter of the rising sun and the summer dawn of Phoebus’ lamp, encircles them; while the Oder flows rapidly past the region that sees Phoebus sink into the steaming sea. On the side turned toward the rain-bearing south, it touches the Bohemian lands, dreadful with ancient forests; on the northern shore of the Scythian sea its waves swell, and the untamed Ruthenians have established their home.

[20] This region includes the Slavs, the Poles, and other peoples whose barbarous names and harsh customs cannot become known to us. The land is fortified by its position, scarcely to be assailed by any enemy’s armed hand. The people are uncouth in culture, terrible in appearance, to be feared for the savagery of their customs; violent in horrible speech, cruel and threatening, ready with the hand, lacking reason, accustomed to plunder, scarcely conducting themselves after the manner of men, more savage than a beast in their ferocity, impatient of laws, most eager for slaughter, mobile, inconstant, fierce, slippery, deceitful, accustomed neither to keep faith with rulers nor to love relatives nor to be moved by an affection of compassion.

[35] Nature has given them this in part; in part the harmful contagion of a pestilential people makes them corrupt. For whatever short island lies in the Scythian sea, the people who inhabit it neither plough the soil, sterile through perpetual cold, with a ploughshare, nor turn its barren fields with the hard hoe, nor marry vine to elm, nor gather autumn’s fruit from trees. They seek sustenance only by hunting and frequent plundering, and grow old as pirates upon continual waves.

[44] But if at any time prolonged lack of food sharpens hunger—horrible to tell, and scarcely credible even to me, yet so report has it—the wretched are said in turn to tear one another’s limbs with pestilential bites. Neither father knows how to spare son nor brother brother, and a daughter restores herself with her mother boiled.

Nevertheless, neither the invincible harshness of the land nor the fierceness of its people could restrain the king’s mind from advancing with confidence toward his appointed labours and feeding his righteous anger with vengeance.

[54] For this land had once fallen by the common law of inheritance under the lot of three brothers of distinguished lineage; but their barbarous names cannot properly find their way into our books. One of them, who had preceded the others in birth, was duke and had as his wife Gertrude, the king’s kinswoman, daughter of Leopold. Out of jealousy of her, the brothers, with rebellious necks, cast off the yoke and forced him, driven from his paternal seat, to depart as an exile from the whole land.

He likewise fled with his wife and sought King Conrad, lamenting to his kinsman and king the criminal acts of his brothers, his own miseries, and the rights of the duchy taken from him. The king sent sufficiently imperious commands and threats, ordering that the stolen honours be restored.

[70] They swelled with pride, savage men; they cared neither to heed the royal commands nor the stern threats, nor now to obey his orders. Messengers were sent and sent again, but in their pride they despised them and held their brother’s rights. Thus under the aforesaid prince the duke long lamented in vain and remained an old exile at the perpetual court.

But when Frederick happily held the royal sceptre and undertook, in place of his uncle, whatever that uncle had left unfinished or uncertain, the brothers—often admonished, yet even then refusing the king’s command to restore what they had seized from their brother—did not dare to despise the king. Nor did they care to swear allegiance or to pay, as was ancient custom, five hundred marks of annual tribute. An ominous course: for after noble patience had often been rebuffed, righteous anger roared forth.

[84] Quickly leading his forces through difficult roads and hard places, whose approaches the enemy had blocked with great obstacles, he reached the point where the Oder divides Germans from Poles. Neither Conrad nor any king of earlier times had attempted to cross it with an armed force, broad between its banks and swollen with devouring waters. But the unconquered king, allowing nothing to prevent the undertaking he had begun, aflame with keen intelligence, attempted to conquer nature herself, who commands all.

He immediately ordered countless vessels to be constructed by his allies, so that the whole army might cross the rushing river at once and transport men and horses alike.

[97] They were astonished at the event when they saw the man occupying their lands and the bank untouched by all previous kings, and royal standards shining over their fields. In fear they shamefully turned their fleeing backs in flight, though that camp contained Poles, Pomeranians, Prussians, Parthians, Ruthenians, and fierce peoples from all Scythia. Lest the land provide food or refuge for those who followed, they burned farmsteads, secure towns, and fortresses scarcely conquerable even by long labours, leaving the countryside despoiled.

Nor did the prince less devastate whatever remained unharmed behind him, judging it unworthy to spare those who had refused in fierce spirit to spare him.

[112] At last the other of the proud brothers, who unjustly held the territory of his exiled brother, saw that certain and grievous destruction had come upon his affairs through the wrathful prince. Secretly and openly, sending his men and sending them again, he began repeatedly to address the summoned nobles in suppliant speech and to negotiate, at the prince’s discretion, the terms of open surrender and pardon.

He finally obtained it on these terms: he was to pay the king two thousand marks of tested silver, and the ministers two hundred; the nobles were to receive another thousand marks as rewards for their services, and the officials of the sacred court two hundred. To you, royal wife, who shone worthy of glittering metal, he was to give twenty great marks of gold of noble quality for the adornment of your person.

[128] He was to swear allegiance to the king and a fitting degree of favour, and to attest by oath, as a dishonour under the law of the kingdom, that he had not expelled his brother from his paternal throne. Finally he was to present himself in the virgin city [place-name uncertain], to stand before the supreme judge of the kingdom on behalf of his brother, and, as a loyal royal soldier, follow the standards beyond the Alps to the faith-breaking city of the Ligurians.

When he had confirmed these things by oath and many hostages, he returned again to his foul conduct and vice, broke his promises, and gave them to be carried away uselessly by Aeolian storms. For he neither wished to follow the army nor came to the city which the king had appointed for the dispute between brothers.

[140] Victorious, the prince brought his standards back to the famous walls of Würzburg. There, they say, other envoys of the ruler of the Achaeans met him, bearing gifts in Greek magnificence and words sufficiently inflated with proud commands. The gracious ruler endured with unoffended ear, and for a long time in civil speech, those who spoke windily and boasted too greatly of their king. He might have despised them and allowed them, mocked by insults, to be provoked—pretending not to notice—had the arrogant and foolish men not confessed their fault and moved the noble heart of the mighty king by tears and groans.

[150] At the same time they swore that they would never bring such things into their own kingdoms, would hang up Greek trifles at home, and leave their florid words beneath their ancestral roofs if chance ever recalled them to our city. Thus, at last safe, having received the whole speech in their hearts, they asked the supreme man—and his willingness was not slow—to order that the boy Frederick be formally girded with a sword in their presence.

They reported that this had been commanded and often requested by the boy’s aunt, Irene, consort of the Argive king, with her husband’s support because of the great affection with which he had embraced the boy’s father. The queen had indeed sent the boy generous gifts of exceptional beauty, both then and often before, and had instructed the men not to return until they could report to their mistress the joy they had seen.

[168] There were also present envoys of King Henry, under whom wealthy England then flourished. They likewise bore eloquent commands in carefully composed words and precious gifts from their land. The chief of these, remarkable for its marvellous beauty, was a stage or pavilion; earlier generations had seen nothing like it, nor, I think, will any future age see its equal.

“What was its material?” you ask. It is believed to have been woven from foreign thread. “What was the workmanship?” It had wonderful figures. “Its weight?” Human hands and effort could not lift it from the ground. Yet skill raised it; and it occupied more than five broad acres, spacious enough to contain many people.

[180] The royal letter accompanied these gifts shining with so great a splendour in honey-sweet words:

“The English king wishes Augustus, the true monarch, great and true joys, and the blessed joys of eternal life. May true salvation, best of kings, always be yours from Him who by His goodness gives kings their salvation and inspires every heavenly good in your heart, He in whose enclosed hand the devout hearts of kings are said to be held.

[188] “I congratulate you and rightly rejoice with our kingdom, because although you are the greatest of all kings whom the stars behold and yield to none in the whole world, nevertheless you do not despise in friendly affection our treaty and the resources of a lesser kingdom. By frequent gifts and letters, mighty ruler, you honour us. The gifts are welcome indeed, but far more welcome is the goodwill that makes your gifts welcome: it bends itself down to us from so lofty a height of affairs and seeks partnership in our peace.

“Therefore, with devoted mind and willing purpose, we promise and gladly consecrate to your honour whatever it is permitted to promise or do for our kingdoms. I pray that peace and concord may exist among our peoples: one love, sincere faith, and safe commerce. May it often please you to employ our services and faithful zeal, and seldom happen that you need them.

[205] “Whenever circumstance or time requires assistance, may we mutually render welcome support according to our resources. Yet so that you, who excel me and all kings throughout the world, may possess, as is fitting, the right and authority to command, while it is necessary for me to obey. May it please you as much to command what we ought to do as it pleases us to have done it. We seek no interest from flattering obedience and do not covertly seek great rewards for small services. Let the supreme king receive thanks.

“We preserve our resources intact; we lack no one’s aid. Our kingdoms flourish, Fortune favours us, and we are feared by many nations and peoples. Under my rule Aquitaine is ours, and England calls the count of Anjou its king.

[218] “We do not ask help against other kings or unexpected wars, enjoying tranquil peace; yet even amid peace we desire faithful friends. And among these, whom could I hope might be a more useful or greater friend to me than you, whom Roman power has placed as lord over the whole world and whom the whole world beholds with awe?

“I have taken care to send you small gifts, but such as I thought would please you. Receive kindly what we bring; and I pray you always keep for your use this pavilion which we have sent, that it may protect you, best leader, who protect the whole world with outspread arms.”

[230] The hasty reader had not yet finished producing the recent commands when other men entered the royal palace—those sent by the king of Spain, by Gaul, by the Dane, and by the Pannonian who rules the Hungarian fields; others were sent by great men who hold kingdoms scattered throughout the world and rule in distant lands.

Indeed, you will never find that household without a great multitude from every land and nation. Whoever wishes to learn languages, local customs, and whatever rare thing occurs in the whole world could nowhere learn them more completely. Thus on that occasion too a great throng was present, diverse in speech and unequal in customs. They vied in bringing gifts and joyful commands, and rejoiced to submit their kingdoms to the pious king.

[245] The mild prince, filling them with gracious addresses, dismissed them happy with his replies and burdened with gifts.

Then the man resolved to visit his wife’s dowry lands and the homes of the Allobroges, moving camp. When report, running ahead of his arrival, spread through the cities and performed great announcements of the event, the nobles of the Allobroges immediately came swiftly to Chrysopolis, together with many powerful Italians, Venetians, Tuscans, Latins, Gascons, Spaniards, and those sent by rich Provence and Gaul adjoining the boundaries of the Allobroges. There they chose to await the royal camp and the German companies of dukes.

[257] Two distinguished envoys sent by the Roman pontiff also came: Bernard and that Roland who afterwards, when installed in the chair, was called Alexander after changing his name and endured many great disturbances of the Church. In his time the long schism burned for almost forty-eight years.

Besides the Roman court’s customary love of immense revenues, with which it inflames its citizens, this too had been a reason for their journey: recently, as a certain English bishop, greatly beloved in the apostolic court, was returning from that see, he had been shamefully treated and despoiled in German lands; and the prince had not yet punished the cruel and recent outrage with fitting anger.

A document concerning this matter was delivered to the magnificent king,

Textual and editorial notes

- [Col. 0395], on “perfect splendour”: B reads *decori* (“of adornment”), perhaps.
- [Col. 0395], “through certain loyal persons”: Pfl. and Rs., with `+` on the exact word, read *quosdam*, “certain men,” for *quasdam*.
- [Col. 0395], “the lands of her future husband”: Pfl. and the remaining witnesses read *arma*, “arms,” for *arva*, “lands.”
- [Col. 0395], “by the prince’s summons”: Pfl. and the remaining witnesses read *a coitu*, “from intercourse,” for *accitu*, “summons.”
- [Col. 0395], “already queen in hope”: Pfl. and the remaining witnesses read *spem*, “hope” (accusative), for *spe*, “in hope.”
- [Col. 0395], “This separation”: P., R., and Rs. read *dissidium* for *discidium*; both mean “division/separation.”
- [Col. 0395], “so that perhaps”: Sp., with `+` on *vi*, reads *vi*, “by force”; R., with `+` on *ni*, reads *ni*, “unless,” for *ut*.
- [Col. 0397], “washes”: manuscript Rs., marked `*`, reads *abluit* for *alluit*.
- [Col. 0397], “metropolitan and chief cities”: A., c., and W. read *et primas nominis* (“and cities of the foremost rank”); the editions read *et primas nominis*, omitted in one witness; Rs., marked `+`, reads *primi nominis* (“of the first rank”).
- [Col. 0397], “Relying, naturally”: Rs. reads *nimium* (“excessively”) for *nimirum* (“naturally”), against metre in A. and the remaining witnesses.
- [Col. 0397], “Thus”: P., ss., Rs., and RJo., marked `*`, read *ut* for *et*.
- [Col. 0397], “rather than count”: A. alone correctly places the punctuation after *comes* (“count”).
- [Col. 0399], “summoned from the whole world”: Rs. and RJo. read plural *vocatos*; A. and the remaining witnesses omit it and read singular *vocatus*.
- [Col. 0399], on Guibald and Manuel: B., marked `+`, reads *Egregio Manuel monocrator, etc.*; A., c., reads *Rex Graiae Manuel oratum, etc.* The editor proposes either *E Graia Manuel orator miserat urbe* (“Manuel had sent an envoy from the Greek city”) or *Et Graiae Manuel orator miserat urbis*, or wholly *Egregiae Manuel, etc.* Rs. judges that nothing should be changed, uncertainly. The transmitted wording is therefore retained as uncertain.
- [Col. 0399], “lying documents”: B reads singular *mendaci* (“lying”) for plural *mendaces*.
- [Col. 0399], “ignorant minds”: manuscript Rs., marked `+`, reads *ignaraque* (“unknowing”) for *ignavaque* (“sluggish”).
- [Col. 0399], “a place fortified”: B., marked `+`, reads *qua* (“where/by which”) for *quam* (“which”).
- [Col. 0399], “shamefully deceived”: W. reads *foedere* (“by a treaty”) for *foede* (“shamefully”); the editions omit the latter reading.
- [Col. 0399], “until then”: Rs., marked `+`, reads *uti* for *ubi*.
- [Col. 0401], “degenerate, timid”: Rs. reads *tumidumque* (“swollen/proud”) for *timidumque* (“timid”); A. and the remaining witnesses omit it.
- [Col. 0401], “proof of fear”: W., marked `+`, reads *stante* for *teste*.
- [Col. 0401], “alas”: W. reads *ha* for *heu*; the editions omit the variant.
- [Col. 0401], “ought to have learned”: the editor queries *decebit?* (“will it be fitting?”) for *decebat* (“it was fitting”).
- [Col. 0401], “as you now seem”: A., c., P., ss., Rs., and RJo. read *nunc* (“now”); the remaining witnesses omit it and read *nec* (“and not”).
- [Col. 0401], “by the fall of an immense weight”: W. and R., marked `+`, read *pondere lapsa* (“having fallen by weight”) for *pondera lapsu*.
- [Col. 0401], “great deeds”: Rs., marked `*`, reads *ausis* (“bold enterprises”) for *actis* (“deeds”).
- [Col. 0401], “the powerful city”: Pfl., marked `*`, reads *sontem* (“guilty”) for *fortem* (“strong/powerful”).
- [Col. 0401], “human bodies”: Pfl., marked `*`, reads *mortali* for *mortalia*.
- [Col. 0403], “Vigevano”: so the text from Otto of Freising; A. reads *Vigenum*, A., c. *Vigevum*, and the editions *Vingevum*.
- [Col. 0403], “Pavia then”: R., ss., Rs., and Jo. read *tunc* (“then”); the remaining witnesses omit it and read *tum* (“then”).
- [Col. 0403], on the sequence of the embassy: the editions put verse 536 after 537. W. had noticed, but not perceived, the defect; Rs. and B. report this.
- [Col. 0403], “cut down”: B reads *pereunte* (“perishing”) for *perimente* (“killing”); the editions omit the variant.
- [Col. 0403], “but private concern”: Rs. reads *at* (“but”) for *ad* (“to/toward”); the remaining witnesses omit it.
- [Col. 0405], “had as his wife”: B reads *nuptum* (“married [masculine]”) for *nuptam* (“a wife”).
- [Col. 0405], “jealousy of her”: Sp. and R., marked `+`, read *infidiam* (“treachery”) for *invidiam* (“jealousy”).
- [Col. 0405], “had forced”: manuscript Rs., marked `+`, reads *compulerunt* (“they forced”) for *compulerant* (“they had forced”).
- [Col. 0405], “their brother’s rights”: manuscript Rs., marked `+`, reads *rura* (“lands”) for *jura* (“rights”).
- [Col. 0405], “obstacles”: Rs. reads *obicimus* (“we oppose”) for *objicibus* (“obstacles”).
- [Col. 0405], “in flight”: the reading *fuga?* is queried.
- [Col. 0405], “Prussians”: B., marked `+`, reads *Prussos*; the Radevicus manuscript reads *Pruschos*, for *Bruscos*.
- [Col. 0407], on the indemnity: either the poet has erred or the passage is corrupt. Radevicus, book 1, chapter 5, reads: “Two thousand marks to the emperor and one thousand to the princes; twenty marks of gold to the empress; two hundred marks of silver to the court.”
- [Col. 0407], “To you”: P., s., and Rs. read *quae* (“who,” feminine) for *qui* (“who,” masculine); the remaining witnesses omit it.
- [Col. 0407], “our city”: B., marked `*`, reads *nostrum ad orbem* (“to our world”) for *nostram ... urbem* (“our city”).
- [Col. 0407], “Irene”: A. reads *Herenam* for *Irenen*.
- [Col. 0407], “great and true joys”: A., with Rs.’ support, reads *grandia*; the remaining witnesses read *gaudia* (“joys”), and W., marked `+`, *gaudens* (“rejoicing”).
- [Col. 0407], “letters”: W. reads *sceptrisque* (“and sceptres”) for *scriptisque* (“and letters”); the editions omit the variant.
- [Col. 0409], “the Pannonian who rules the Hungarian fields”: Sp. and R., marked `+`, read *Hungaricus* for *Hungaricis*; A. reads *armis* (“arms”) for *arvis* (“fields”), and the editions omit it.
- [Col. 0409], “Whoever wishes”: the Greek word `το` and Latin *ut* are absent from Sp.; R., marked `+`, reads *qui* (“who”) for *ut qui* (“whoever”).
- [Col. 0409], “whatever rare thing”: Pfl. reads *rerum* (“of things”) for *rarum* (“rare”).
- [Col. 0409], “Gascons”: A. reads *Guascones*; Sp. *Vascones*; the remaining witnesses *Wascones*.
- [Col. 0409], “came swiftly”: Pfl., marked `+`, glosses *celeres* as *celebres*, that is, “numerous/frequent.”
- [Col. 0409], “endured many great disturbances of the Church”: Sp., P., and R., marked `+`, punctuate *Pertulit, Ecclesiae* instead of *Pertulit Ecclesiae*.

[Col. 0403]

Of many empty things indeed, yet this too he is thought to have urged:

That Caesar should remember so great an honour bestowed upon him, and the crown received through the Pope’s gift;

[275] that the pontiff should never repent of the gift conferred upon so eminent a man, nor—had he bestowed even greater rewards—should he thereafter become a burden or a cause of grief.

The prince believed that these things, therefore, were conveyed in letters not to be disregarded and not without weight, because earlier, while he was staying in the Italian lands,

[Col. 0410D] he had heard it spread abroad among the Latin populace, and commonly said: that no man attained the Italian realms unless the Roman bishop, in Peter’s name, delivered them to him with friendly hand.

[285] This too was vainly proclaimed by the image standing in the halls of the Roman court, in so far as an image could speak. Here a lying painter had depicted Luther, receiving the rights of empire from the Roman bishop,

[Col. 0411A] standing with bent knee; and, equally deceitfully, had added inscriptions above it corresponding to the fictitious scene.

Adrian had undertaken utterly to erase this representation, lest the contrived affair furnish seeds of genuine disaster; but he had still deferred the fulfilment of his promise, a very slight task, and the image, the tinder of evil, remained alive.

[295] Therefore, when the letter couched in magnificent language arrived and admonished the man, the prince, sufficiently indignant, denied that he had received the Empire from him. When the envoys tried to object and argue in reply, and advanced falsehoods on their own side [Note: thus A; the editions read “stirred up”]:

[300] the princes roared with anger. Otto, that courtly count, went before them all in fury and, drawing his sword fiercely, hastened to exact bloody punishment.

[Col. 0411B] But the king, mindful of his reputation even in the midst of anger, seized and restrained the men and checked their rage. Having dismissed them with sufficient implacability, he ordered them to retrace their steps safely by the same route by which they had come:

[305] yet they were not to be permitted to turn their course either to the right or to the left, nor to remain one night longer in any single place, until they had returned to the city.
