And so that the cause of his anger might be known to all, he immediately indicated it in countless letters sent abroad and hastened to dictate the following complaints:

“When divine power, with your agreement, granted me to restrain the Empire with my hand and to establish Italian dread among all nations throughout the world,

[315] if anything more grievous than expected or worthy of complaint should occur, I do not fear to strike your ears with justified grievances: by whose favour I glory that I both first received the realm and now retain it when received; nor shall it ever grieve me to be mindful and grateful.

[320] Hence it follows that I am compelled to reveal to you the unjust arrogance of the supreme pontiff—if it is permitted to say so.

“For recently at Chrysopolis, when I held a council concerning the highest affairs with a great assembly of magnates,

[325] two false prophets arrived from the Roman see, who, professing that they brought us salutary commands of peace and measures beneficial to the entire kingdom,

[Col. 0411D] had mixed sweet honey with secret poison [Note: manuscript R and Rs read “mixed”].

For, although in its first part the letter begun and sent to us by the bishop had the savour of peace,

[330] it immediately dared to add in express words that the kingdom bestowed upon us, the imperial fasces and the rights of the sceptre, had been granted by his favour; and that he rejoiced in what he had given, and that the pontiff would never repent of the act or the gift even had he bestowed greater things.

[335] When the envoys reinforced this madness also by spoken words, the court blazed with such flames that, unless our presence had helped by calming the swelling disturbance, they would have perished in a lamentable catastrophe.

[Col. 0412A] “Behold paternal fidelity, the gracious integrity of the great bishop, following the humble footsteps of Peter! He now delights not in bearing the Lord’s cross but in handing over kingdoms, and prefers to be regarded as Augustus rather than bishop.

[340] He rends the peace of the Church, which rightly employs two swords and is never firmly established if either is removed, and turns the twin swords against one another. While he tries to join king to priest, not content to injure one alone, he harms both.

[Col. 0412B] “What did the two swords mean, which Peter declares to be in that world, unless they are the two titles of supreme authority in the Church? Although they once render mutual assistance to one another through the bond of reciprocal covenant,

[350] yet they are distinct; nor do they appear able, when joined, to meet in one head. Nor are they often to be exercised in the same manner, although each authority under heaven has one author from whom it takes its name.

One dignity requires the consent of the clergy; the other is obtained by the decision of the magnates and the favour of the realm.

[355] Therefore, I ask, what concerns the pontiff in the supreme right of the kingdom?

[360] [Col. 0412C] This authority recognizes no head above itself, except the King of Heaven. Let him govern his own Church and regulate divine law; let him leave the Empire and the fasces to us.

“Add that the bearers of the letters and agents of the commands, cherishing an unspeakable design in their hearts, were preparing to plunder the houses of God, carry off sacred vessels, strip crosses of their coverings, tear gold from textiles,

[365] and greedily scrape together with cruel claws whatever they could, in order to take it away with them.

[370] And so that they might the more readily harass the unwary with lies and terrify them by documents, among them a sheet of blank parchment was discovered, bearing many impressed seals,

[Col. 0412D] ready to receive whatever new forms they might wish.

But we, wishing to spare the German kingdom and at the same time to prevent the clergy’s unjust plundering, ordered them to turn back their pestilential steps at the very threshold and return cheated, with empty purse [Note: Pflugk reads “return trembling”].

[375] “Come now, magnates, through whose agency I govern this court and the Empire: I ask that this present injury stir you and that you urge on with me my just indignation.”

[Col. 0413A] Meanwhile wealthy Burgundy had of its own accord set its great magnates and bishops in motion from their seats to meet the king. Throughout the land, towns and cities fortified with strong towers received him reverently with their gates opened;

[385] and every region that had been enjoying its ancient liberty, left to itself, recognized as master the man who came with a small force, and humbly acknowledged him as king.

Louis himself, governor and arbiter of the Parisian court, approached the king with a large force—whether peacefully or as an enemy is uncertain—for the purpose of a conference.

[390] But when he learned that, after arranging the dotal estates, the latter had turned his march back to the German cities, he sent a magnificent embassy under the appearance of peace and received equitable commands in return.

[Col. 0413B] And now Caesar, traversing your plains, Germany, had entered the borders and famous city of Saxony, which he had previously appointed for the faithless Poles. When their absence, undefended before all, proved that they intended deceit and made light of their sworn faith,

[400] he moved his standards to Regensburg, where a great assembly of the fathers was convening for a solemn council.

An embassy also came there from the Pannonian lands, bringing words and prayers in the name of King Géza [Note: A reads “Garza”; editions “Geisa”].

[405] He had a brother, Stephen, a youth vigorous enough for his tender years, whom King Béla, at the prompting of an adviser, accused of deceitfully aspiring to the summit of kingship.

[Col. 0413C] Béla had reared the boy with gentle care, since he was a good and prudent man and uncle to them both. But the king harassed his brother with unjust hatred, treating him as suspect to the kingdom and as preparing impious deeds;

[410] and, charging him with a deadly plot, he was preparing to condemn the youth through witnesses and false evidence [Note: Pflugk reads “judgements”], while his raging mind brooded upon murderous hatred.

But the boy, placing his hope and aid for his affairs only in the mighty Caesar, believing him to be the sole man beneath the stars who either would or could restrain swollen tyrants,

[415] approached him. Lamenting the heavy wrath he had endured from his haughty brother,

[Col. 0413D] his reputation stained by an unworthy accusation, and his exile, he finally moved the illustrious heart of the great man by repeated complaints to write commands and threats to his cruel brother, ordering that the youth, injured by a false report, be restored to his good name and paternal house.

[425] The other, raging in hatred and rejoicing at his brother’s removal—for the innocence of his brother’s mind was suspect to a wrongdoer—ordered faithful men to convey these instructions to the king, wishing to excuse his own fault by accusing his brother [Note: P, Rs, and RJo read *fraternae*, “of brotherly [guilt”]],

[Col. 0414A] and to soften the odium incurred by his own fury:

“That, so long as his brother did nothing cruel and his plots remained hidden, he had regarded him as a partner in the common bond of right and in no way inferior except in name, sharing what no one can divide;

[435] but after a dreadful crime came to light [Note: Rs reads “hard”], he could not endure it amicably; nor had he then acted with any greater severity than by prudently withdrawing himself from an unfaithful friend once the deceit was discovered.

[Col. 0414B] “The brother, though able to remain safely, had voluntarily feigned a compelled flight; and the cause of his grief was that he could not accomplish the acts of madness he had undertaken.”

But since the king could not put an end to this dispute while concerns greater than private care pressed upon him, he postponed the matter and prudently sent the youth through the lagoons of the deep Venetian sea to the Greek city for safe keeping.

[445] At this assembly of magnates, too, that Bohemian duke—whom report calls Vladislaus because of his deeds lately displayed bravely in the Polish war—earned elevation from duke to king, wielded the sceptre in a mighty hand,

[450] [Col. 0414C] and encircled his hair with a new diadem.

The new king immediately returned his steps to the cities of his homeland, having pledged his forces for the Italian war.

We think it no less noble and beautiful to relate that the duke of Austria and Otto, bishop of the see of Freising, the king’s uncles, were reconciled through zeal and care for their nephew.

[455] Previously the goads of anger and their brotherly quarrel had tormented them with bloody hatred, when the duke attempted forcibly to sever certain things of his brother from the Church, while the latter strove to defend the ancient rights of his see.

[Col. 0414D] With these matters satisfactorily settled, Caesar proceeded into the fields of Ripuaria and hastened to traverse the furthest borders of the Rhine, restoring peace and law to the peoples. He joyfully put this before all other concerns,

[465] so that, when he moved his standards to Italian enterprises, he would not leave any part of his realms wavering.

Again he revisited the fields of the Vangiones and Lautern, and occupied for a few days, with mind at peace, the royal residences he himself had built.

[470] [Col. 0415A] Believing that all business should properly be conducted with the counsel of holy men, he bestowed generous gifts upon neighbouring churches and kindly distributed wealth to the needy crowd. In this he found an adviser in Hermann, weighty in merits, handsome in appearance, distinguished in blood,

[475] who at that time was bishop of Brixen, pre-eminent in the fame of his illustrious name above all whom the German land then possessed.

Therefore, following the counsels of this man in great affairs, the prince sought by gentle efforts to turn divine wrath away from himself and his camp.

[480] And now, when the soft west winds had removed the stormy north winds from the air and driven away the chill of old age,

[Col. 0415B] the welcome season of pleasant weather grew green again: every field flourished, and the earth, resuming its beauty, rejoiced to grow young in flowers and green grass.

Then the farmer’s toil compels the oxen, long unused after their prolonged rest, to bear the yoke [Note: Rs and RJo read singular “the unused ox …”];

[485] the sailor launches into the uncertain sea the ship that had long occupied a safe berth; and kings about to wage great battles for their realms summon warlike companies back to their camps.

Caesar now prepared himself for the Italian war and called strong cohorts to his camp.

[490] Yet, lest any taint of fault should cloud the purity of his cause, he preferred to summon holy fathers

[Col. 0415C] and explain the grounds of his just wrath. When they had added fresh spurs to one long desiring war, declaring that the war carried on under the ruler’s name for the kingdom was just and pious,

[500] his anger burned more fiercely under these goads, and, secure in the hope of pardon obtained, the prince girded on his sword for punishment of the Ligurians [Note: Sp., P., and R read “sword”].

Meanwhile our lord’s envoys, having returned without honour to Rome, lamented to you, Adrian, the terrible wrath of the prince,

[505] the dangers which they had tremblingly endured to their lives, and all the insults and reproaches;

[Col. 0415D] and by their mournful account sharpened the bishop’s excessive anger against the king.

Already then dissension divided the Roman clergy into parties, and the schism split into a twofold fury. Some followed the side of the envoys and the Pope;

[510] but others defended the king’s fair and praiseworthy deed, calling it brave and worthy of a crown. They blamed the others as arrogant and excessively swollen, declaring that they had given the cause and first fuel of the dispute.

[515] [Col. 0416A] That day furnished the cause and first beginnings of evils, and of a plague destined to survive for a long time [Note: Rs and RJo read “of long duration”].

Whether the prince’s or the Pope’s party was more just, let one who has been better able to know decide; but we, ignorant of the facts, should revere both parties.

But the bishop, excessively ardent in sudden wrath [Note: Pflugk reads “suddenly”], hastening to lament with mournful complaints before the bishops the cruel outrages inflicted upon our kingdom and the contempt shown to himself, ordered letters of this kind to be carried everywhere:

[525] “If you are sufficiently united brethren in Christ’s name and the most sure offspring of the same mother, we believe that contempt for us and scandals against the holy Church will cause you great grief.

[Col. 0416B] “How badly royal majesty received our envoys, and how great was the fury into which it blazed, deceived by the false interpretation of a single word, either those who were present saw, or anyone absent could hear through reliable reports.

[530] But we, God being witness, said that the sceptre and rights of the kingdom had been conferred upon him by us—not indeed given, but rather handed over to our ministry, or entrusted to him through it; and we believed that this could quite correctly be expressed by that word.

[535] “Ought a son, because of the dubious terms of an ambiguous expression, to be inflamed into such great anger and oppose harsh words to his father’s commands?

Add that he endured the famous guardians of our side, men of distinguished name,

[Col. 0416C] to be attacked with such ferocity that they scarcely escaped swords and the cruel dangers of death, and shamefully sent them back, sorrowful and terrified, to the sacred threshold, forbidden to proceed farther.

[545] And it is said that he has stationed guards and blocked the passes and narrow defiles of the roads even in the middle of the Alps, so that no one from the whole body of the kingdom may dare bring any of his affairs to our see.

But you, bishops, strong and mighty pillars of the Church—for it is not permissible to believe that this was done by your counsel—let this injury touch you;

[550] and do not fear to oppose a firm and steadfast wall for God’s house, which, founded upon solid rock with Christ as its ruler,

[Col. 0416D] although it feels storms when shaken, nevertheless knows neither overthrow nor collapse.

And let your first concern be to bend the young king by admonitions [Note: Pflugk reads “the proud king”], so that he may hasten to purge so great an offence and correct and openly punish with fitting wrath the authors of evil, Otto and Rainald,

[560] men of rabid violence: one a courtly count, the other now falsely holding the pontifical summit in the Church’s name.

[565] [Col. 0417A] Let him render obedience to God and honour to us; let him leave them hope of pardon [Note: manuscript R and Rs read “to no one”], and examples to all.”

Upon receiving such letters from the supreme bishop, the bishops replied in one and the same tenor:

“We know and hold by undoubting faith the firm promise of the Lord that the Church, which Peter protects, commanded to stand upon the solid rock of faith under its rightful ruler, shall never be moved from her seat.

[570] Yet when the Roman see is shaken by unaccustomed storms, the distress of the head is shared by the whole body, and the pain of one is transferred to all.

[575] Hence it was, gracious Father, when that recent letter had lately troubled royal hearts with ambiguous words, and the magnates of the kingdom raged and with fierce uproar

[Col. 0417B] stopped ears stupefied by unfamiliar utterances, that we were unable either to provoke the prince’s thunderous wrath and cruel threats against you, or, on the other hand, to provide defences against him for your party.

[580] Just as, if the wondering stars should behold the moon rushing against the new sun by an impulse of heaven, terrified they would perhaps dare to withdraw to neither side of the conflict and would sympathize with both.

[585] They would dread this one because of its innate and proper heat; to that one, gentler and accustomed by shared labour to dispel thick darkness, they would offer silent favour, venturing nothing further.

[Col. 0417C] “Thus we feared Caesar’s anger, while a secret will favoured you so far as was possible. Yet, amid so great a roaring of magnates, in the midst of fury, with all hostile, we did not dare undertake to defend words of ambiguous meaning.

We read the commands which, in addition, you gave us to read; and, eager to obey paternal admonitions, we immediately soothed the royal heart with gentle exhortation

[595] and had already softened its anger, lulled to sleep by prayers.

That you may recognize its exact words, suppose that it replied thus in sweet address:

‘The Empire is administered by a twofold rein, by laws and by observance of the established path of ancient customs.

[600] [Col. 0417D] Content with these, I neither wish nor can pass beyond the boundaries of my fathers; nor do I desire, through superfluous glory, to be thought wiser or greater than they.

Due reverence should be shown to the pontiff; let the kingdom be governed by ancient laws and ancestral custom.

[605] The granting of it proceeds only from the eternal King; election belongs to the magnates, in which, according to ancient custom, the bishop of Mainz has the principal voice.

[Col. 0418A] The first anointing of the newly elected king is granted to your shepherd of Cologne; it is the right of the supreme pontiff to consecrate the splendid imperial crown, so that in truth he may be called not giver of the Empire but its confirmer.

[615] “These are the rights I received from great forefathers; these I wish to retain. If anyone tries to add anything further, I reject it altogether as invalid and void [Note: Rs and RJo read “if anyone … anything whatever”; A reads “if anyone anyone whatever”].

Let the father have his own rights: let him govern the world by divine laws and rule the churches according to the right that belongs to him.

[620] Let him consider the ancient years of the earliest age, review days gone by and turn over the ages of old. Did Peter, or Clement, or the rest of the earlier company [Note: Pflugk reads “the pious”]

[625] [Col. 0418B] bestow Italian sceptres? In ancient times the Roman bishop was poor; he grew through royal benefaction. Yet not so that he might presume either to grant the fasces and rights of the Italian kingdom or to take them from anyone.

The gifts of great kings exceeded measure if they gave anyone such a right over their own realms.

[630] But the grant was not so great, nor can anyone give what he himself lacks. The granting of this kingdom, having God as its author, can by no right belong to any human being; God is the giver of this gift, and this kingdom is conferred from the highest heavens.

[635] Yet in our time the Roman bishop claims this prerogative, produces empty proofs in images,

[Col. 0418C] and gives proud letters grand words. Let the empty paintings now, I warn you, be removed; let the letter be cautiously softened with modest language.

Now it is fitting to deal with realities; let the dumb or loquacious lying image yield and be removed from the midst.

[640] Before his heedless or rejected hand touches royal persons, let him strive to weigh what his words convey, if he desires peace between Church and kings.

Nor are we ignorant of what honour a son owes his father, or he in turn owes me by right.

[645] We ordered the envoys, whom we did not permit to proceed, to turn their steps back to the City not in contempt or hatred of the divine Father [Note: Rs and RJo, with P, read “fatherland”],

[650] but because they were carrying with them many contrivances of new deceit, either already written under seals or still to be written, wishing to oppress and suck dry the wretched clergy, despoil the houses of God, and carry away with them gold,

[655] for which Roman thirst is never satisfied.

“Is it sufficiently honourable and worthy of the supreme bishop to issue blank sheets stamped with a seal,

[Col. 0419A] upon which the bearer may write various trifles whenever he wishes and attach false charges to miserable persons [Note: manuscript R and Rs read “affix”], in order to carry off a real prey on a fabricated accusation?

For as to his complaint that I have blocked all roads by posting guards: I shall not deny it, nor shall I confess it was done except after mature reflection [Note: manuscript R and Rs read “carefully considered”].

[660] If anyone, a foreigner or otherwise, approaches the sacred threshold with a case established by law, the road shall duly lie open; but if anyone, a disturber of peace, wishes to bring empty trifles there, he shall be allowed to pass nowhere.

[665] “These things, best Father, we think should be written to you concerning the replies of the divine king, with your peace preserved.

For what he added besides—namely, certain secret clauses of agreements made without the prince’s knowledge,

[Col. 0419B] new contracts, and alliances secretly plotted with the Sicilians—

[Col. 0420A] seems better left unmentioned.

That royal count palatine, Otto, had not then been sent ahead by our prince as a forerunner to the Italian cities; and Rainald, preparing to hasten to the same place, proved before many persons as witnesses that he had protected the men from blame and from the anger of the raging populace.

[680] “Now then, most holy lover of tranquil peace, mirror of justice, guardian of gentle conduct: now, setting aside whatever anger grief has brought, turn your mind to better things and take counsel for us and for yourself.

Let not the grave discord of Church and kingdom be able to disturb the peaceful quiet of the world.

[685] [Col. 0420B] A gentler letter, restraining such great agitations of mind, seems one that should be sent to Augustus’ ears.”

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0419]

[Col. 0419C] And now the prince, holding the Rhaetian countryside with a great army, had pitched his camp near the Vindelician city, where the swift Lech waters Augsburg with its gentle stream.

[5] Here he chose to wait seven days for forces arriving from the various regions of the world.

When the Roman bishop learned through reliable report of his arrival, seized at last by genuine fear in so great an anger, he ordered Henry and Hyacinth to go ahead,

[10] soothe the man with gentle words, and render the writing of the letters less harsh with conciliatory language.

[Col. 0419D] For prudent Rainald, together with valiant Otto, already held Italy and your borders, Verona. At their first entrance Rivoli, an unconquered fortress, not to be overcome by any force,

[15] built at the first gorge of the lofty Alps, was delivered to them; Verona held it within her dominion.

This contributed much to their cause [Note: B reads “this”] and rendered grateful service to those following, enabling the troops to pass safely.

[20] Then whatever cities or great towns it befell the men to enter adorned the gladly received visitors of their own accord with the joyful observances of honour.

Then magnates, illustrious men, and the eager multitude of lesser folk, devoted in loyal zeal,

[25] [Col. 0420C] gave oaths to be observed throughout all the cities: that they would not injure the right, reputation, person, or honour of the Italian prince, and that, should anyone attempt injury, they would resist with all their strength even to death.

Then they quickly crossed your territory, Mantua—Mantua celebrated by the Muse of the famous poet—and made for neighbouring Cremona, where they were to perform great deeds, and which the Po gently washes with its spreading waters.

[30] A vast company of bishops and magnates had gathered there from the Italian cities, reverently to receive the fresh commands of their king.

[35] When the eloquent men had expounded these commands with the splendour fitting to them, and the venerable fathers had received them with attentive ear, to be fulfilled with great goodwill,

[Col. 0420D] they turned their steps through Emilia and made for you, Ravenna, to intercept the envoys of the Greek king, whom they had heard were at Ancona devising certain hostile measures—one of them was that Palaeologus, the other Logothete.

[40] These men, while outwardly moving arms against the Sicilian, concealed their frenzied designs beneath the pretext of war. For they were preparing, by craft, deceit, fear of war, or payment, to win over the cities standing along the coast to their side and sever them from our kingdom;

[45] and with much gold sent by Greece they were raising mercenary forces and municipal garrisons.

Ravenna, shamefully, had sent them a warlike band of youths, to earn payment by hired arms;

[50] [Col. 0421A] for that rabble judges nothing unjust where there is hope of wages, and nothing is abhorrent when gold is offered.

As they were returning, already safe within their own walls and preparing to enter the gates of neighbouring cities, men came out, seized them in deserved anger, and raised a fierce tumult around them.

[55] Their leader was a certain young man named William, a wicked turncoat, perhaps called by his true surname because, as though by wicked deceit, he turned everything upside down.

[60] Although he stood before the city gates amid the ranks of his men, Otto, an energetic avenger of the royal offence, burning not with the size of his following but with anger for the kingdom,

[65] rushed upon him and perhaps would have pierced him through with his bloody sword, had he not at last been prevailed upon by the great weeping of the cowardly populace together with the entreaties of his own men,

[Col. 0421B] and granted, as a great gift, wretched life to the frightened man who confessed that he had sinned [Note: Rs and the common readings have “wretched man”].

Having also dismissed these men, the brave men established camp near Ancona and ordered the Greeks, summoned powerfully from the city and made to endure threats and rebukes from the kingdom because, without the Roman prince’s command,

[70] they had dared to set in motion undertakings suspect for their dubious deceits [Note: V reads “to set in motion”],

[75] to disclose swiftly the schemes of their Greek fraud and withdraw from the entire kingdom.

After they expelled the scandals of Greek pestilence, they turned their course back and sought the walls of Modena.

[Col. 0421C] To this place Ferrara, washed by the Po, sent your envoys, Adrian, toward the royal camp. When the leaders recognized that they were peaceable, bore instructions for peace, and had come as mediators to restore peace,

[80] they sent them safely on to their business and allowed them to complete their peaceful task.

They passed safely with the bishop of the see of Trent through the harsh Alps, with their narrow passes;

[85] yet he was unable to provide the men uninjured and safe roads all the way to Caesar’s royal camp. For two warlike counts, accustomed to repeated robberies—one named the combative Henry, the other, according to common report, Frederick—

[90] [Col. 0421D] fiercely stripped them of their possessions and threw into harsh chains both the man who was leading them and those who considered themselves safe under that leader.

[95] Nor were they released until Hyacinth, after giving his own brother as hostage, ransomed himself and his fellow labourer, the bishop held captive, from their lamentable lot.

But soon, by divine prompting, the bishop and hostage, with the help of Henry the Saxon—under whose command the Norican land then lay—

[100] [Col. 0422A] cast off the necks’ clanging chains, for the honour of the Roman see; the abductors having been severely punished and compelled to return what they had carried off and pay just penalties.

Therefore, while Augustus was delaying not far from the walls of the Vindelician city, the Italian envoys entered the royal camp. It was prudent first to say a few words aloud, by which whatever anger remained in the venerable king might be softened.

[105] “To you, most august of all kings, the supreme successor of Peter in the Church, and at the same time a father devoted to you in mind and a faithful worshipper, sends words prefaced by apostolic greeting;

[110] and now the entire greatest court of the Roman clergy greets you as its exceptional king and lord.

[Col. 0422B] The following matters which we bring—and which we now deliver in bare words (and they delivered them at the same time [Note: manuscript R and Rs read “delivered”])—the page will relate.”

Immediately, when the heading of the papal letter had been unfolded, it appended the following words in continuous account:

[115] “How great has been the zeal of diligent loving service, how great my paternal fidelity toward you, most gentle son, ever since I first received, through divine gift, the see and duties of pastoral care,

I deem to be undoubted pledges of my devoted mind toward you: because I gladly received the first commands concerning your honour,

[120] [Col. 0422C] and often performed with joyful services everything commanded by you; because I placed upon you with rejoicing hand the sacred crown and imperial fasces bestowed on you by divine favour, and joyfully witnessed your honours;

[125] because for your sake I endured the conflicts of the Roman populace and suffered many labours, as you yourself know.

Amid so many most certain tokens of genuine affection, if our letter, compelled by circumstances, has perhaps brought to your ears anything insufficiently exact or harsh,

[130] it is not fitting for you immediately to be stirred into sudden anger. Whoever wishes to judge truly should consider causes and occasions in all things [Note: perhaps “distinguish”].

[135] That son is considered wise and his father’s glory who willingly receives both his father’s caresses and threats in an even mind and friendly hearing.

Indeed—to speak with your permission—he who endures sparing the rod is said to hate his son.

[Col. 0422D] It was neither fitting for a king, worthy of so great a prince, nor civilized, that, when my letter lately added the avenging wrath of the injured bishop,

[140] it should cause you to blaze into such great anger at a few words which the writer had set down with insufficient care, when it intended not at all to reproach you with my service

[Col. 0423A] but to remind you by reporting certain signs: so that you allowed the associates of our side, always faithful to you also, as you yourself bear witness, to be assailed with such ferocity and suffer such thunderbolts from the angry kingdom,

[145] and forced the men, their opportunity of completing their undertaking blocked, to return mocked to the sacred threshold.

If you had observed anything monstrous in their deeds, unworthy of you or intolerable in your realms,

[150] your letter could have made it known to us in three words, and reserved the offence for correction.

Now, once gently admonished, I ask that you not attempt anything of the kind further; correct what is past by what follows, preserving the honour of the Roman see.

[155] [Col. 0423B] We too lay aside whatever complaint there was in a disturbed heart and share sweet affection with you.

Receive, most excellent son, the bearers of the letters and ministers of the commands which you read, with the honour due to their exceptional piety; and believe that what we say through them to your ears proceeds from the inward affection of a sincere heart.

[160] At least send these men back safe and kindly treated, rejoicing, to the sacred threshold.”

That Freising Otto, whose grief in this dispute was greater insofar as the court was bound to him by closer ties—he was the king’s uncle—

[165] [Col. 0423C] then expounded these new commands of the pastor. And as he himself piously added his own contribution to the terms of peace set down by the supreme bishop,

[170] the dread in the prince’s noble heart at once subsided, and, with the prince calmed, brightness returned to his face.

As when a storm has beaten down roses and white lilies and struck away their shining beauty with its rods:

[175] shapeless thorns bristle, and flowers vainly sought disappoint one seeking them among bared stems.

But soon, when the gentler breeze of the tranquil west wind begins to blow more kindly after the south wind is expelled,

[180] branches immediately put forth their shoots at the peaceful breath, and shrubs shine in their usual beauty.

Apart from the anger of the disturbed prince mentioned above,

[Col. 0423D] other complaints remained as fuel for dispute. When Caesar set these out to the envoys in order, and those sent for their bishop carefully gave excellent answers in reply,

[185] he immediately granted them, in the presence of all, the kisses of the desired peace; conveyed greetings to the Pope and clergy, and dismissed them gladly to the City.

And now envoys were present from the king of the Danes, newly elected and created by the people’s favour, seeking the rights of the sceptre at the prince’s discretion.

[190] [Col. 0424A] The king agreed on this condition: after his return from the wars, the little king should carefully hasten to visit him before forty days had passed, to receive the kingdom from him and swear the oath of obedience.

And now Alemannia had stirred up her forces in a mighty movement, and fierce peoples flowed from every side in burning excitement toward the royal camp:

[195] Saxons; the rigid settlers who occupy the Norican lands and Westphalia; those whom Ripuaria holds; Francia, divided with German settlers by the Rhine; or the land that took its name from great Lothar;

[200] then the Allobroges joyfully took up their dowry arms, the light Celts and fierce Cimbri,

[Col. 0424B] Vindelicians, Swabians, Slavs, and Bohemians, Pannonians, those whom Austria rears in its happy plains [Note: B reads “broad”], and the people dwelling in Carinthian regions.

I could not enumerate the peoples or the illustrious names of all the powerful men whom rough Boreas, loosed from the icy Arctic, lashes from the quarter of the world until one comes to the cloud-bearing Alps.

[205] The peoples bear arms: there are none to guard the walls, none to cultivate the fields [Notes: B reads “scarcely”; Rs reads subjunctive “may guard”; “cultivate?”]. Camps everywhere boil with men sent ahead, to learn from the great prince by which routes he might order them to cross;

[210] [Col. 0424C] for the multitude of common soldiers was so great that the cloud-bearing crags of the Alps could not be crossed if the forces were united in one camp.

And when the ruler had assigned suitable places to all the leaders,
And he assigned the routes; soon, with the host divided, some made for Canale and the Forum of Julius, and many for Chiavenna and Lake Como; many sought Trento.

The ruler himself, taking with him the king of the Bohemians, many mighty men of the Allobroges, the duke of the Suebi, and you, Frederick, his loyal kinsman, made king by King Conrad, hastened to cross those heights which the ancient inhabitant called Mount Jove. And now, seeing the homes and fields of prostrate Italy, and the loyal cities that he knew, he gladly greeted Pavia, his own Lodi, and Como, and conceived a fierce anger against the Ligurians.

Brescia, secure in its position and trusting too much in the strength both of the Ligurians and its own, first received the savage motions of war and the fury of the kingdom, to its ruin. After it had resisted the king’s attempted arms beyond its power, it was at last crushed; its walls having been broken down, it received as lord him whom it had made its enemy, and, scarcely redeemed, paid heavily in money for its arrogance.

When the entire forces had entered the leader’s camp, lest that barbarous multitude, divided in languages and customs, should with impunity stir up anything inhuman in the camp, the following laws, framed by the emperor with the agreement of the nobles, were promulgated as the firm law of the camp:

No one shall dare to quarrel with the sword or provoke a fight in the camp; nor, when summoned because of a dispute that has arisen, shall he come armed, protected by a breastplate [variant: “unclothed,” V.], and carrying anything except a staff with which to settle the contest of the quarrel.

Nor shall anyone raise the signal for war, unless perhaps he is summoning his own household troop. If a soldier does these things, he shall be expelled from the camp, suffer very many shameful penalties, and lose all his camp equipment. An armed attendant shall depart after his forehead has been branded with glowing metal, his hair cut off, and he has been beaten; or he may be redeemed by the goods and all the arms of his master.

A man convicted of wounding or killing on the testimony of two persons who have not themselves been implicated in the shedding of blood shall lose his head in one case, his hand in the other. If one party lacks a witness, and the accused wishes, through fear of punishment, to deny the crime on oath, anyone willing may lawfully challenge him by offering judicial combat, and, if defeated while the charge has not been proved, shall suffer a like punishment. [Variant: “he may swear,” editions; added reading.]

A soldier without a riding horse, shield, or spear, even if he belongs to the opposing side, may safely enter the royal camp; whoever violates him shall be held to have violated peace in the case of an ally as well. If it is a war-horse, shield, or spear, he shall not be guilty or deserve any punishment. [Variant: “If it is a warrior, a horse,” manuscript tradition.]

A merchant despoiled by one of our soldiers shall receive everything doubled; a servant shall have his cheek branded, his head shaved, and his back subjected to lashes; or he shall be redeemed by his master in the manner stated above.

Whoever sees someone plundering a sacred building shall strive to prevent the crime if he can; if he cannot prevent it, he shall remain unharmed. But the offender shall pay the penalty for his crime at the judge’s discretion.

Whoever attacks a city or castle protected under our name may be deemed a violator of peace. No woman shall be in our camp with us; if anyone is found guilty in this matter, he shall depart stripped of his goods, and she shall be shamefully mutilated by the cutting off of her nose.

A servant convicted of the detected crime of theft, if he had formerly been a thief, shall die a disgraceful death. Otherwise, marked by the shaving of his head, he shall endure harsh blows upon his forehead and be expelled from the camp, unless redeemed by the goods and arms of his master.

If anyone happens to find a riderless horse and does not know its owner, he shall not shear it in order to render it unrecognizable, nor deceitfully keep it shut up; but he shall report it to our stable-master, and then, if the owner is found, he may enjoy it as his own, no one forbidding him.

If the owner catches it burdened with a new load, he shall not be permitted to take away the seized burden after throwing it down; he shall patiently follow the bearer into camp, and, when the service is completed, may reclaim it.

If anyone burns the villages or homes of peaceful people, his face shall be marked by the shaving of his hair, and after many lashes he shall depart expelled from camp.

The same lesser penalty prescribed for this offense is laid down for a German who sells more dearly in the camp. Yet with this addition: whatever he had offered for sale shall be seized by the officer of the treasury as a shameful usurious gain.

No German soldier shall take as his companion a man of the Latin people unless he knows the German tongue; if he presumes to do so, let him lose everything.

Let the discoverer of a pit enjoy what is found there, no one hindering him; but if any wicked man uses violence against him, let our stable-master correct it with fitting indignation.

Let no one, by acting too carelessly or too violently, break vessels of wine after their contents have been drawn off, vessels which can be useful for the camp.

These laws, and others proclaimed by the sacred mouth of the prince, the nobles agreed to observe in every respect.

Then the king, wishing to arm his warlike troops and instill avenging anger in his brave men, stood in a higher place, conspicuous in his gracious expression yet awe-inspiring in the weight of his noble voice, and filled attentive ears with these words:

“Although I am an earthly king, I could deservedly repay the most exalted proclamations of praise to the heavenly King, if only I had the power of voice and office to do so, when I see such a company of nobles stand before me in devotion—a company by whose gift I rejoice to have received kingdoms, and by whose zeal I strive to retain them.

“For my own glory will never make me forgetful of so great a gift; and, as long as I can live, whether in war or peace, I shall acknowledge that I need your favor. Your support is imprinted upon the marrow of my bones; and the more I recall it, the more it seems worthy of remembrance. He who has been forgetful of a kindness has not been sufficiently mindful of his duty; nor has he been truly grateful who ceases to be grateful. [Variant: ‘our favor,’ manuscript tradition.]

“What has gone before has given me hope for the future; gratitude is owed for past services, hope must be applied to those to come. But now the time has come when your loyalty may shine forth by a sure pledge. We have come to great affairs; we have conceived mighty anger for war.

“The matter is not undertaken for my own private interest, nor do I voluntarily enter upon predetermined labors. I receive the causes and anger of war under compulsion, and vengeance stirs justified resentments. You see to what shameful arrogance the city of the Ligurians exalts itself: it mocks the threats of our kingdom and our commands, and the laws issued by ancient kings—laws which Charles established together with the venerable lawgiver Otto. Alas for shame! In our own time it has at last rejected them; proudly cast off the imperial yoke from its neck; and openly confesses war.

“If I tolerate this, I shall be judged to bear the sword in a feeble hand without cause, and to show myself a degenerate and less worthy descendant of former kings. Are my times, then, chosen for such abominable cruelty that they cannot punish outrages so great? The judgment of an idle populace is mistaken, unless I am mistaken. Whatever is committed against the empire in our age finds an avenger. That impious city shall pay—ah, it shall pay—the penalty; by grievous destruction it shall atone for its criminal deeds, if I know you well, if the image of your valor so often proved does not deceive my heart.

“For the shared loss does not permit you not to be partners in my grief. The enemy, unless you come to aid me, takes away against my will the gifts that you voluntarily gave; he prepares to wrest your gifts from me and in one deed despises both you and me, his allies. And while he thinks that in war he need not seek our judgment, he takes from you the power of decision, and from me the fruit of your gift. [Variant: ‘me,’ Sp. R.]

“Come now, strongest strength of the German kingdom, forces of the empire, glory of the whole world, magnificent nobles: set your hearts upon great undertakings. Let it be plain that under the bounds of the great heaven there is no city that can safely withstand our power or with impunity kick against Latin law.

“If love of your native homes and chaste marriage-beds, service to our kingdom, and the claim of a just grievance have brought you here; if you have willingly left sweet pledges—your children—and your weeping maidens at home, then for these same causes fiercely pour forth avenging anger upon the swollen enemies of the Latin name. Wipe away in our age that disgrace: let not the city of the Ligurians, feared by Rome, be said to have scorned our threats with impunity. Neither law nor any statute forbids this. Whenever injury troubles the kingdom and the empire’s peace is harassed by a sudden enemy, most just wars are waged by the prince’s decree. [Variant: ‘are waged?’]

“That people is guilty; we defend the rights of the kingdom. Following the avenging eagles and the public standards, we shall surely carry back triumphs marked by exceptional glory.” [Variant: “certain,” manuscript reading.]

The valor of his men was inflamed by the emperor’s speech. Threats roared; fierce anger set hands upon drawn sword-hilts; all spoke with one voice. They approved his words and praised the man, urged on one who delayed with their goads, and strengthened their loyal right hands for battle.

But lest royal prudence, in precipitate movement, should presume anything while neglecting the order of law, legal experts advised that the enemies should first be summoned by public edicts according to law.

When the Ligurians saw certain destruction hanging over them and the offended prince’s anger deferred, they began, now more hopeful, to demand heavier penalties for their crimes. They sent to the camp chosen men of their own people, learned in the laws, to persuade the powerful ruler by flattering methods; and it was thought that their eloquent speech might soften the prince’s anger.

But when they saw themselves hard pressed by serious penal charges under Italian laws and strict justice, and that no support lay in artfully colored speeches or in the great money they had promised, their business uncompleted, after much useless entreaty of the princes, they returned with sorrowful faces to their walls and filled their city with great terrors.

The king, hastening with his army drawn up against the walls, had now reached the place where the Adda, a more definite boundary, cuts the fields of great Cremona from the territory of the Ligurians. Although it cast its waters between the two peoples, it could not restrain hostile fury from often foaming with each other’s blood. Then, fuller than usual, the stream ran more violently; the melting Alps had swollen its turbid waters, and, having neither bridge, ford, nor boat, it gave no hope that warlike bands could cross it.

No less did the Ligurian soldiers stand ready upon the opposite bank: high-spirited young men prepared, even if safe fords lay open, to receive the invaders under arms and drive them back. Thus, repelled by the double obstacle of river and war, the angry army stood halted amid the waters, and a heavy terror possessed horses and men alike.

Yet, standing on opposite banks, they hurled missiles at one another in rivalry with mighty arms, until the Bohemian, with the Dalmatian leader, cast themselves of their own accord into the rushing fords from the outer edge of the bank. The whole army followed them. Horseman pressed infantryman; but the river, more violent to many, undermined slippery footsteps with treacherous water [variant: “swept away,” *surpuit*], and, enfolding arms, men, and horses of swift fierceness in hollow whirlpools, dragged everything it had seized downward. Thus almost two hundred men perished.

Others, relying less on transport than on their horses as oarsmen, at last planted their feet upon solid bank. The enemy, frightened into shameful flight, sought his familiar walls and brought to the citizens a baleful omen and signs foretelling their future ruin.

On the descending bank of the same river stood a castle, remarkable for its towers and strong wall. Its name was Trezzo; until then it had been secure under Ligurian control and untouched by any war through the ages. One side was surrounded everywhere by lofty towers; the other was defended by the river’s water and encircled by the rapacious Adda and its great bridge, which an imposing tower guarded with stationed watchmen.

The king judged that place very suitable for our camp, because of the advantages of the bridge and the great benefit it would bring, and ordered the troops to storm it. The eager young men obeyed and surrounded the secure fortress with warlike tumult. But the soldier who guarded the garrison and town, after vainly attempting to defend the walls by force of arms, and realizing that no help could come to him from the city, bargained only for the miserable gift of life and opened all the gates of the walls. Leaving arms and the fortress full to the victor, he was driven naked and pitiably toward the hostile city.

Yet envious Fortune disturbed these happy events and rejoicings by an adverse chance. For some men, seeking the seeds of new glory and desiring to win a famous name for themselves, approached the Ligurian walls with terrifying noise, summoned the enemy from their safe dwellings, and stirred up savage battle in a harsh encounter.

Foremost among them was Ekbert, a count indeed, but one who would yield to no royal honor in nobility of blood and who equaled great kings in courage of soul. While he sought to raise one of his men who had fallen and been rolled down by the swift rush of his horse, the spear hurled by a Ligurian youth passed through the great man and found his life in its deep hiding-place.

Some nevertheless assert that he was captured alive and sound in body, dragged by hostile hands into the city, and suffered cruel death after his limbs had been torn apart. German nobles, Italian magnates, and a great part of the Ligurians are said to have mourned him bitterly. And Fame, weaving sorrow around his death in tearful song, lamented him through the German cities.

Many also of Caesar’s troops perished there. John, whom renowned Ravenna had sent from home as a mighty leader, fell in the lamentable disaster. Some endured rigid chains about their necks; others returned to camp with their bridles turned back. The prince sharply rebuked these men with bitter words, and perhaps they would have paid the penalty for their conduct had not the nobles, by gentle prayers and much entreaty, speaking of Fortune’s changes and uncertain fates, scarcely at last calmed the prince’s just anger.

Soon, with anger mingled with so much grief, he eagerly hastened to avenge his allies and planned to shut up the guilty city in a close siege. Dividing the whole army into seven divisions, he prudently assigned to each wedge of troops its own commander. Now the horn-blowers and the sound of trumpets began the first combats with terrifying tumult, and he distributed throughout every battle-line the standard-bearers who would first endure either prosperous or adverse events. [Variant: “divided,” *dispertit*.]

But where the royal bird, the Latin standard of Caesar’s troops, shone, he massed dense companies of mighty men, as though they were the vital organs of the great kingdom. From this point a compact band of servants and common infantry carried enormous burdens loaded upon pack-animals, and such things as were thought suitable for storming walls. Last came a hired company, engaged for a small payment and ready for desperate service, and the soldier accustomed to barter his loyalty for payment, who, having received both gift and war-service, held as enemy the man whom the giver of his wage commanded him to regard as such.

Thus the fortunate battle-line, splendidly ordered, sought divine aid for itself with martial song and hymns sounding afar, and slowly advanced with fearless step toward the Ligurian walls.

But the anxious citizen who had come out from the city and occupied the foremost gates and rampart stood neither frivolously amid noise—whether he did this in honor of the king or because his heart already drew certain forebodings of great ruin—nor proudly with shouting; instead he watched the notable enemy attentively. [Variants: “hearts,” for “heart”; “blind,” for “certain.”]

The king, with his camp arrayed in sufficiently fine order, besieged the enormous city with more than a hundred thousand men. A plain, striking in its broad extent and more than a hundred stadia in circuit, surrounded it. A wall built of squared stones enclosed the city; and a huge ditch had still further girded it, prepared in that same year at great cost against sudden alarms of war and expected attacks, with towers, battlements, and engines for hurling missiles. [Variants: “but this” or “and this” for “still”; “undertaken,” “unripe,” or “made” for “expected.”]

They had applied themselves less to this because they thought that a city full of so many citizens could not be pressed by any siege. Therefore they took no care to show themselves loyal to the empire, and that populace, luxuriating long in proud spirits, had often spurned the yoke with rebellious neck and safely despised the anger of the kingdom. [Variant: “of the king” for “of the kingdom.”]

Accordingly, when German nobles, after the enormous city’s gates had been divided among them by the whole plan of war, surrounded it on every side, the Ligurians saw the royal standards and Ausonian birds sporting upon their fields, and their lands covered with soldiers. Their first concern was to encircle the men’s tents with a deep ditch, thicken the stakes, draw a rampart, and fortify the recesses of the camp, lest a crowd confined within should break out by hidden treachery or openly trembling in daytime battle, disturb men and camp in sudden fury, and assail the unwary with unforeseen destruction.

For they did not think that the populous walls could be taken by engines or swift assault. It seemed better to await hunger—for hunger is accustomed to conquer all these things by mighty force—or, if the fierce enemy, trusting in arms, should leap forth and willingly join battle, to test fortune by the sword and win easy triumphs.

At one of the gates stood, united in allied valor, two related young men. One was the courtly count Conrad, brother of the king; Frederick loved the other, Conrad’s namesake, whom his father Conrad had left as leader of the Suebi. [The manuscript inserts a particle after *Chunrado*.] Both were prompt in battle, both impressive in appearance, equal in nobility, and of the same generation.

Whether because the Ligurians believed them less watchful by reason of their tender years, or because, closer to the city and frightening it, they saw them besieging it at a distance from their allies, they prepared first to attack these men. Under cover of night, when frost-filled darkness was restoring shadows to the world and the first dew of sleep bathes limbs worn out by the day’s hardships, they silently led their troops from the walls. They attacked the men still weighed down by the first stupor of sleep, threw them into confusion, and assaulted the camp.

The men sprang up in bewilderment from their beds; scarcely did night or fear allow them to take up weapons. A dreadful shout struck the air and multiplied their alarm: fears are more grievous than realities. Yet, not devoid of courage or forgetful of themselves in so great a crisis, the young men stirred up anger by powerful exhortations; bravely taking such arms as time and chance provided, they began a fierce struggle, striving with sword, volleys of stones, and every weapon available to drive from the camp the enemy raised up in swollen strength.

The shout and the clamor of arms had already reached the nearby tents of the Bohemians through the dark silence of night. They immediately gave their allies notice by the trembling blare of trumpets and by shaking hoarse drums with terrible strokes. Soon they held the camp; soon they had joined their own arms to the German troops. The unhappy citizens, stunned by sudden terror, sought disgraceful flight and, in shameful retreat, made for their familiar walls. But night, the gate, and fear impeded their entrance; the crushed crowd struggled.

Thus a large part fell prostrate beneath the bloody sword or bore captive chains thrown about their necks. Others returned half-dead and suffering many wounds; only a few came back wholly unwounded. They gave their people an example and sure warning not to dare place hope in nocturnal stealth. [Variant: “bonds,” for “wounds.”]

But because the situation of the besieged place prevented the war from advancing rapidly, and the great undertaking required much time and slow stages, the valor of many men, unable to grow numb, could not endure delay and hated long quiet and the barren hours of idleness.

Therefore that Palatine Otto, with his two brothers—men of exceptional valor, firmest supports of our soldiery—burning with love of glory and seeking by force of hand to accomplish something great and worthy of commemoration among the most celebrated deeds of great men, when evening was almost bringing the twilight of night, led their forces from camp to the walls. [Variant: “full,” for “almost.”] They secretly brought burning torches to the gate and bridge. A stronger wind swiftly supplied the planking with material and fuel for flame. [The editors and manuscript tradition do not distinguish between *materiam*, “material,” and *fomenta*, “fuel.”]

Immediately people rushed together from the whole city. All desired to extinguish the hostile flames; for, apart from danger to the bridge, the whole Ligurian city lay exposed to fire unless the flames were checked. Without delay, a great contest was fought on both sides. These men prepared to prevent the bridge from burning; those opposed sought to prevent those who were trying to prevent it. Missiles flew, stones whistled, and the air, thick with arrows, both overcame and aided the shadows of night.

At last, after the flame had been extinguished at much risk, they were scarcely separated late in the night, with almost equal fortune, having suffered reciprocal slaughter and mutual wounds. The one side went beneath the walls, the other returned to its camp.

Nor did the Ligurians wish to be slower, less daring, or less high-spirited than our men. On their recent success they thought it noble and praiseworthy voluntarily to return the stroke. They often rejoiced to sally out from their besieged walls, to trouble unwary men with javelin, light sling, or swift arrow, and to harass the camp with frequent raids. They broke out most often through the gate which the Austrian leader had blockaded with powerful arms.

At last anger, burning with more violent goads, drove the men to lead their troops out from the whole camp and approach the walls in joined battle. But the Ligurians no longer hastened merely to defend the walls; instead they advanced to bear arms against the men who came to meet them and joined in the hard contest of battle.

The first fighting was entrusted to flying arrows; then, once the spears had been hurled, they rushed eagerly together. But when courage grew hot for swords and drawn rage at close quarters, then indeed there was dreadful shouting everywhere, and weapons clashed utterly with immense crash. You could hear hollow helmets ring under blows of swords, shields struck by trembling spears roar with heavy sound, and the falling men meet death with groans and lay their stiff trunks upon the ground.

The men of the camp pressed on, tore hostile breasts with cruel wounds, and were angered that resistance was offered. Nor did the Ligurians yield or abandon their position; steadfast, they killed and were killed alike. Until at last, scarcely driven back by great valor, leaving our men victorious but splashed with much slaughter, they reached their walls in retreating flight.

Among the many, that utterly foolish Statius fell—the man whom the Ligurians had wished to set over themselves as their ill-starred king and for whom they were preparing to dedicate a scepter. His corpse, redeemed from our men for much money and exchanged for a numerous throng of captives, was buried with the customary honor of kings. Foolish superstition and stupid error granted in death what just Fortune had denied him in life. [Variant: “would deny,” for “had denied.”]

The wickedness of a certain Ligurian, and the fierce madness of his foolish mind, seem to me not to be passed over in silence. Mounted on a swift, snorting horse, conspicuous from afar in shining armor, he delighted to mock our camp, to call the Germans untrained in warfare and ignorant of the art of riding, and to cast out many reproaches in shameful words. Proudly displaying his empty skill, now borne in the swift whirl of his four-footed horse, now with reins drawn by certain art twisting sinuous circles about, he repeatedly demanded that one man out of many—or rather one out of all—be chosen as worthy to meet him, and laughed at men supposedly seized with empty fear.

Like that Philistine, proud and destined once to perish by a sling-stone [variant: “by praise,” *laude*], who hurled reproaches and threats at the trembling people until his swelling forehead was struck by the wound dealt by the Hebrew shepherd and he fell.

Count Albert of Tyrol could not endure the display of this arrogant mind. He prepared to curb the Ligurian’s vain folly by fitting punishment and remove the shame of the German people. Yet he took no care to protect his temples with helmet, gird his loins with sword, cover his breast with iron [variant: perhaps “to cover,” *texi?*], or use the service of the riding horse upon which he always fought. Content with shield and spear, pressing the flanks of an inferior horse, he drove it forward with a shaken lance and, unarmed himself, cast the armed man to the ground.

But he did not deem the sword worthy of staining with base blood, nor did he choose to adorn his victorious hands with spoils won without risk. He left the man lying on the earth; and, though others counted the deed great, he himself disregarded it and measured the act by modest honor. [Variant: “to burden,” *onerare*, for “to adorn.”]

## Book Eight

Amid these praises and brave deeds of men, Frederick devoted himself especially to the concern [variant: “pure concern,” *puram*] that he might bring his undertakings to their desired end without great loss or disaster among his own men.

Sometimes with a few companions, sometimes surrounded by a dense body of soldiers, he examined the difficult walls with anxious step. He inspected the walls, the strength of the rampart, and the ditches that encircled the place with their huge earthworks. Wherever Fortune seemed safely likely to make a path easy for his undertaking, he keenly directed sagacious care and attention there, marking it with eyes and mind.

This vigilance so disturbed the frightened citizens that whenever they saw him go around the walls, the whole city seemed to shake with heavy uproar, just as if he were already preparing to smash their strong gates or hurl stones against their lofty towers. Then varied shouting and noise sounded through the whole city; bells were anxiously rung in the sacred buildings, and women’s wailing and mournful lamentations resounded.

But the trumpet with dreadful blast summoned the plumed young men to the tops of the walls; they gathered everywhere in close array and guarded the defenses.

Not far from the besieged city—no farther than an arrow shot from a drawn bow can travel—stood an unfamiliar structure built in the Roman manner from squared stone. Surviving report commonly called it the Roman Arch. Supported upon four strong columns, it rose so harmoniously that no discerning observer could separate a single stone from the others. [Variant: “this,” for “it.”]

It had the shape of a tower, with vaulted chambers, floors at many places within [variant: “inner”], and high windows, from which there was a view over all the fields and missiles could readily be hurled. They said that some Roman king had once raised it as a most certain monument of his triumph, or that at some later time angry kings had subjected conquered walls to themselves by means of it. [Variant: “once,” for “some.”]

That populace had stationed a garrison there and laid in provisions for the duration and long needs of war. They thought that they had acted prudently: whatever the enemy did outside could be seen from there by watchers and could easily be made known to their allies by signal.

Frederick planned to transfer this advantage to his own camp. He ordered young men skilled at striking even far-distant bodies with javelin or swift arrow to stand opposite and direct sure shots, so that, if anyone dared to shoot missiles from the open windows or even put forth his face to look out, they might transfix his face with opposing arrows. [Variant: “here,” for “this.”]

He himself prepared to shatter the battered structure with engines and utterly break it with hard iron. The men stood stunned and surrendered their fortification to the king’s powerful hands, having bargained for life. After he had sent them safely into the allied city, he stationed his own loyal men in the secure position.

Yet in this war the fierce young men of Pavia and Cremona did not forget their old anger, but raged more fiercely against the Ligurians as hatred swelled. For whenever any Ligurian, driven by cruel fate, happened to fall into their hands and hostile weapons, they gave him terrible memorials of their fury to behold: before his eyes they plunged swords into his throat, or, binding him to a hard stake, competed in piercing him from every side with hurled missiles.

And no less, if any of their own men by evil fortune came into the hands of the Ligurians, they scattered his severed limbs and mutilated remains from the top of the wall. Such fury and discord had always breathed between the neighboring cities from ancient causes.

Now the hunger of the Ligurians, desired by our men, had begun to crush their proud minds with an unfamiliar affliction; and, I think, a foul pestilence, proceeding from the anger of the highest Judge, had corrupted the deadly air. Yet the air, an avenger pursuing the guilty and sparing the innocent, kept the nobles’ camp apart from the city. The camp flourished; it suffered neither the plague of hunger nor that of the sky. The city was in want and languished weakly beneath an uncertain atmosphere. Many now planned flight from their own city, and their native home harassed its own children.

There are men to whom it seems sweet, in an unflinching resolve, to promise death in the last extremity for the defense of liberty; to endure hunger, sky, and the hardships of war, provided that these things may be borne for their country’s safety. [Variant: “are,” for “may be.”]

But those in whose troubled minds amid wretched circumstances there is more judgment and deeper reflection urge that arms be cast aside, a treaty of peace be sought, and whatever laws the prince wishes be accepted.

The foremost advocate of proposing a treaty was Guy of Blandrate, who advanced this useful counsel. He was an eminent count, a fellow citizen of the Ligurians, and at the same time dear to the king, yet not therefore suspected in the city. Glorious report had made such a character of the man widely known. [Variant: singular “such.”]

We learn that, in the midst of the trembling crowd, when the question concerned their highest interests, he spoke thus in prudent language concerning both favor toward Caesar and devotion to his country:

“If my diligence has never been sluggish in your affairs; if I have always willingly performed your commands; if, at this very time, I am pleased to suffer hardship with you and share your sorrowful fortunes—consider with discerning mind not only what I advise, citizens, but with what affection and what loyalty I advise it. [Variant: “to consider,” for “consider.”]

“You yourselves know, more than sufficiently, the face of affairs, the likeness of this time, the condition and form of our miseries; clear examples of adverse Fortune stand manifest. We have experienced, as many others have, Fortune’s rule over all mortal things; perhaps we are not without fault. [Variant: “nor,” for “perhaps not.”]

“We know that this people once created kings and drove some whom it had created from power by its own valor. We know that Italian laws and legal rights flowed into the cities from this place. But our domination has been harsher than is just—may I say it without offense. We have terrified neighboring cities with excessive laws. Como knows what this is; royal Lodi knows. We have laid low, or compelled to serve by force of arms, cities and towns throughout the Italian territories. [Variants: “indeed,” for “what”; “whom” for “which.”]

“Fortune has changed her loyalty and withdrawn her right hand; she repays a long season of favor with new disaster. The Ligurian city must now no longer establish or expel its own kings, but serve the ruler of Latium. And the matter proceeds in right order, if only it is permitted to speak truth: Germany is accustomed lawfully to send us kings who will give laws and rights to the Italian cities, ever since Charles and the kingdom of great Otto arose from those regions and German kings began to wear the Ausonian crown.

“We safely despised and rejected their yoke before; now Frederick the warrior is here, an avenger in just arms, made dreadful to his enemies by a mind and hand that know not defeat. Tortona can testify to its own ruin as an example. There is no small fear that our city may vainly be forbidden to rise again from the forbidden dust with rebuilt walls. Spoleto, destroyed by the just anger of an avenger, ought to have been an example, as should the towns throughout Italy that tried in vain to resist and were overthrown by victorious German arms.

“Nor do I fear, allies, I confess, that I am thought to offer false counsel because of affection for the king. My loyalty, long well known to you, has been able to show itself by sure signs. For I urge this not under the pretext of any private cause, nor because favor or hatred—which often obstruct public advantage—commands it, but because sure loyalty and pure purpose do. God, searcher of the deep heart, knows it, and my own mind is well conscious of its purpose. Considering everything in my heart, I judge that there is no salvation unless Caesar’s anger is first appeased.

“Do you wish to take up arms and provoke bare battle? [Variants: ‘timid’ or ‘cruel’ for ‘open.’] Yet we can scarcely keep the enemy out with our blocked walls. Shall we preserve secure peace by shutting ourselves within the city walls? Yet fierce hunger prevents it, pestilence wears out the wretched, and the air fights for Caesar against us. Shall we endure everything confidently for liberty’s sake? But no sane man loves liberty after despising safety; for devotion to liberty, when it is an acceptance of certain ruin that might be avoided without abandoning safety, is reckoned not love of liberty but empty glory.”

[160] Do we not see that this right exists even among brute and untamed beasts: that the greater wish of their own accord to rule the lesser, while the inferior yield to the greater?

For these reasons—provided only that you are willing—I confess that the chief and sure remedy is to seek Caesar’s feet and request terms of peace. Nor will it shame us, once conquered, to obey a gracious king; for no honour or glory of a people is greater than to serve a devout lord.” The crowd received the speaker’s final words with a mixed uproar.

[170] Most approve the counsel and the terms of peace to be sought; nor are there lacking others who speak against the assembly, judging it shameful and disgraceful: that one ought rather to die for one’s country and liberty. At last, when the murmuring of the raging populace had been restrained, reason prevailed. Powerful men of the city were sent, and that mighty Austrian leader together with the Bohemian king was summoned. Through them the Ligurians wished to convey their commands and prayers to the powerful man.

[180] When asked, he showed himself neither difficult nor harsh; rejoicing that the guilty city, together with its citizens, had repented of its conduct, he prudently reduced the laws and treaties of peace to writing in the following form.

[Col. 0438D] First, the Ligurians shall swear to maintain faith and peace. Every person of middle age shall swear who is neither of underage nor has reached his seventieth year. Under the heading of a fiscal penalty, they shall pledge nine thousand marks, struck from pure metal.

[190] Moreover, they shall restore the neglected palaces of the former kings and repair the buildings fallen into ruin, so that whenever either the king or a royal procurator happens, for some cause, to enter the great city, he may have a worthy place in which to transact important business. They shall allow oppressed Como and Lodi, released from their laws and wholly removed from their long domination, to breathe again; they shall demand no former tribute, except the ancient honour due by divine right, through which the illustrious Ligurians’ see holds sway over these cities.

[199] They shall secure the faithful fulfilment of all these provisions with three hundred hostages, chosen from every rank. A mild guard, at the prince’s discretion, shall keep these hostages in Italian cities; and wherever these young men are entrusted, they shall swear, once the agreement has been fulfilled, to restore these cherished pledges—the sons—to their fathers.

[205] Once the consuls have been appointed and peace established, they may remain for one full year. Afterwards no one shall be elected except one approved by the king himself and chosen by the people. When those called to this office are selected, if the prince is dwelling in Italian lands, the greater part of the electors shall reverently approach him; but two shall suffice if he is beyond the Alps. They shall swear fealty to the king and seek from him the gifts of the realm—that is, fitting favour—for themselves and their associates. [Note: “and,” V. ++.] [Note: “thinking,” B. ++.]

[215] No less, when absent, having received the king’s grant, they shall before their people and the city’s leading men undertake the same sworn obligations of office. [Note: Perhaps “of the absent king.”] If, however, a royal legate is in Italian lands, he shall possess this same authority in the king’s stead and may make all arrangements concerning the consuls.

[221] Before the victor departs from the closed city, the Ligurians shall entrust all captives, old and new, to the Bohemian; he shall immediately restore them to their ancestral homes, if by the prince’s command the cities have been joined in concord with the people of Liguria. In return the Ligurians shall receive their own captured men, and the cities that support them in allied undertakings. Otherwise, they shall retain the prisoners in their customary confinement, yet shall suffer no anger from Caesar on that account.

[230] When hostages have been given and captives duly released, the following day shall see the king’s army depart. The Ligurians may raise from their subject inhabitants the sum in silver to be paid for peace, provided they leave Lodi and Como exempt. [Note: “At,” P. ++; o?] [Note: “poterunt” (“may be able”), P. s. Rs.–rr. and o.] They shall not seize shipping, ports, customs duties, coinage, or whatever other revenues belong to the fisc; nor, if anyone should perhaps wish by wicked invasion to seize such things, shall they allow him to go unpunished.

[239] Once the rebellious populace had gratefully accepted these laws and terms, long made lighter by hope, all poured out at once from the whole circuit of the walls. First came the clergy with their bishop, resplendent in sacred dress, barefoot, with supplicating countenances and bowed heads, bearing before them the memorials of our salvation, the signs of the Cross. Then followed the unhappy citizens in dark wool, their bare feet treading the ground, carrying naked swords pressed to their bare throats as a sign and punishment of their guilt; their faces, touched by deep shame, they bathed in tears. [Note: “an indication,” MS. Rs. +.] [Note: “carrying at their necks,” Pfl., from Radevicus.] [Note: “covered,” Pfl. *.]

[250] Immediately soldiers flowed from the whole camp to the spectacle, and a narrow boundary divided the dense crowds standing on either side. Through it the groaning multitude could scarcely reach the imperial countenance of Caesar. With calm brow and serenity he received their contrite hearts and their confession that they had sinned; and joyfully gave thanks to the supreme King for so great a benefit—who had crushed the rebels in his stern purpose and at last compelled the proud to come to their senses. [Note: “timid,” o, for “swollen/proud,” Rs.–rr.]

[259] But the foremost Ligurians, prostrate bodily before Caesar’s feet, uttered a few words in confused and trembling complaints, begging pardon for their transgressions. This alone they sounded and spoke: “Pardon, pardon.” They had not made war from hatred of the realm, but had been unable calmly to bear the injuries which neighbouring cities had repeatedly inflicted upon them. Now, having obtained pardon, they would apply care and effort to redeem old offences by new deeds, and their former acts by those to come.

[268] Soon, when the written document of the prescribed agreement had been read aloud and approved by the men, they received the pledges of the desired peace, joining right hands in a binding compact. No less, captives—enemies formerly taken from various cities—were released from the Ligurians’ long imprisonment, having endured harsh dungeons for many years. [Note: “enemy,” Rs. +.] In a scattered line around the great leader’s feet they sat, their wasted bodies covered in filthy clothing. Foul emaciation born of neglect possessed their pitiable limbs; a sickly and ugly complexion disfigured their faces; dry skin clung to their compressed members, preserving only traces of human form and retaining nature’s former outline.

[280] And, if you wish to apply the true names to things, each seemed not a man but a living image of a man. [Note: “Or perhaps ‘As.’”] [Note: “livid,” B. +, for “living.”] Yet they rejoiced that they had escaped the long labours of prison and cast off their harsh chains once for all. Gladly, after gloomy clouds, they looked upon the sun, long unknown to them, and still more gladly upon the king himself, by whose power they remembered that they had been restored from exile, as though drawn from Stygian darkness.

[Col. 0441A] Who could recount the tears and tearful joys of so great a people, and the griefs stirred by inward affection? [Note: “drawn,” pp. Rs.–rr.; “silent,” V. ++, for “touched.”] When, after the long exile of a dreadful prison, bodies long held captive were at last restored to rejoicing citizens, parents scarcely recognised their sons, now white-haired with age, whom the last hour had sent to war in the first bloom of youth under unhappy auspices, condemned to bear long chains. Not time alone had made the wretches unknown, but also their squalor, rough clothing, neglect, emaciation, and the uncombed hair flowing on either side almost prevented recognition.

[301] Then Frederick departed from the conquered city and went to Modena. Deeming it worthy of its ancient honour, he adorned the place by putting the sacred diadem upon his head and wielding the sceptre in his powerful right hand. For a long time fortune and the rich power of the Ligurians had oppressed this exceptional seat of the realm in the age of his forefathers and held it in prolonged subjection.
