But the gracious prince, judging that all things ought to be restored to their original splendour, freed it from unjust laws and renewed the place’s ancient honour. At his own expense he ordered its old ruins repaired and its aged destiny to cast off decrepitude.

[313] Then, his enterprise having succeeded and all things being settled in peace, while the whole land was quiet before Caesar, he decided to dismiss part of the army from the camp. The Austrian duke departed with the duke of the Allobroges and the Bohemian king, as well as the Pannonian cohorts under that same king, and many nobles with the bishop of Mainz. Having saluted the king, splendid in their merits and praise, they left the camp, turned their standards, crossed the Alps, and returned to German cities. He himself retained many men in the camp, as though none had departed, and was drawn onward to the fixed affairs of the kingdom and noble labours with an unconquered mind.

[325] Yet amid such honour of the illustrious victor and terror of Italy, the madness of a foolish people did not lie altogether quiet, repressed by the Ligurians’ example. For there was a citizen—yours, Verona—named Tusuidus, as they say, surrounded by a wicked retinue. [Note: “named,” Pfl.] From the faithless city he drew motives and secret incitements of fury. He seized and captured by treachery the royal fortress, which they commonly call Garda. [Note: “common,” Pfl. +.] Though repeatedly ordered to desist from those mad enterprises and leave it, [Note: “and again,” o, for “ordered” Rs.–rr.] the madman scorned to obey the king’s command.

[336] At last the prince grew angry; and, disregarding the river Adige in flood, he crossed it neither by boat nor by the customary bridges—for the burning summer had already made the river fordable. He ravaged the territory of the proud city, destroyed certain fortresses of the guilty, and crossed back over the despised waters unpunished. [Note: “crossed,” P.–rr., despite the metre.]

[342] No less remarkable a deed was then performed by that courtly count Otto. Preparing by the king’s command to approach you, Ferrara, he is said, fearing nothing, to have first broken the untouched waters of the Po by a ford and crossed the swollen river.

This event likewise added great concern and rightful fear to Italian cities, and great renown to our camp under its illustrious prince: [Note: “sorrowful,” Pfl. ++, for “rightful.”] nature herself was thought rightly to fear a man who attempted nothing in vain; the elements, subject to his endeavours in a new manner, freely favoured him.

[353] Therefore the Count Palatine, received with great fear by the astonished populace and with equal honour, carried out the royal commands with diligent zeal. Having received forty hostages as pledges for maintaining faith and peace, he turned back toward the royal camp, all things accomplished with fitting praise.

[359] I judge this also fitting, worthy of so great a prince, memorable among Caesar’s chaste deeds, and deserving to be written: at that same time the ruler purged his camp of seductive scandals and indignantly expelled from his company camp-followers, prostitutes, and a harmful and wanton rabble.

[365] Unable to endure delay or to indulge idle days of repose, having excluded from his sacred heart the concerns of war, he considers how to make good use of peace and labours to benefit the world unarmed. Lest the Ligurians’ inconstancy, after the treaty had been reconsidered, should withdraw from it and, raging in their customary hatred, threaten the people of Lodi, he hastened and pressed to transfer the entire household of the city and change its old site. He marked out a place which the rushing Adda wholly surrounds in its winding currents, leaving a short approach, [Note: “Abdua,” P. +, for “Adda.”] so that a modest effort of skilled construction might provide secure fortifications.

[377] The ruler commanded them to transfer their homes there and abandon the old walls; under the realm’s authority, he himself founded the new Lodi at great expense, with his father as patron. [Note: “father,” Sp. P. R. R. Jo. +.]

[380] Thereupon it was ordered that the famous assembly at Roncaglia be held at a fixed time, attended by the powerful men of Italian cities, in order that laws of peace, public rights, and those matters which practice applies to the fiscal revenues might all be brought forward for common consideration and strictly observed.

[385] It is pleasant to recall an event which may perhaps benefit a later people as an example, lest anyone believe that whatever he has dared or intended to commit against august kings will go unpunished. [Note: “will intend,” P. s. Rs. *.] At that time a servant of the king of the Argives—called Caniclinus in Greek usage, though for us he may equally be called Camerarius (“Chamberlain”)—was secretly plotting his lord’s murder. [Note: “Camiclinus,” Sp. R. Rs. +; “Calinicus,” B. ++.] He had added to himself three companions in this crime, men made ready for great evils by abandoned audacity and sacrilegious arms. [Note: “joys,” o, for “evils,” Rs.–rr.]

[395] Having wickedly instructed them in carrying out the unjust fraud, he entrusted to them the unspeakable deed. Once the murder was done, he planned to seize the diadem with bloodstained hands and, desiring to invade the desolated realm, ignorantly pursued vain imaginings of his own fate. But when the affair was discovered, the executioner first gouged out his eyes, then pierced his exposed throat, with his tongue thrust out; together with his companions, he perished under prolonged torture and wrath. [Note: “Than,” Pfl. ++.] [Note: “under long … wrath,” B. +.]

[403] From every land, in obedience to the prince’s edict, a distinguished assembly had gathered at the appointed place. So great a multitude of eminent men flowed to Roncaglia that earlier generations believed they had never seen its equal, nor could later generations hope ever to see one. They pitched their tents beside the swelling Po, in the manner prescribed by ancient Roman military practice.

[410] The Roman soldier always seeks to pitch camp on level ground, if the nature of the place allows, and labours upon a plain. But if the site lies on a difficult slope or the soil is rougher, he usually first levels it by work, then throws up an embankment, digs a ditch, and surrounds the fortifications with a great rampart. Immediately he places the tents in a square or circular formation, according to the nature of the ground. In the middle the prince’s camp gleams in worthy splendour, resembling a lofty temple. Around it the nobles stand nearer or farther away, with the due distinction of rank granted to each. Gate leads to gate through immense streets, broad-fronted after the manner of a great city. [Note: “fountains,” P. s. Rs.–rr.; “bridges,” Pfl. ++.]

[425] Before the very entrances, craftsmen and those carrying goods for sale, following the royal camp, establish smaller camps and make something like suburbs. Thus, as though a colony hastily built with sudden dwellings, there appears the new image of a city raised at once.

[430] Then also the royal forces, their camps arranged, took their positions in accordance with the prescribed compact. The Ligurians, and other citizens as well, occupied joined tents on the opposite bank. Brescia had produced some, Bergamo sent others, and many other Italian cities in those regions sent still others. The prince prepared to connect these camps with his own by extending a bridge across the river; and, after two days spent on the work, a passable bridge enclosed the middle of the waters.

[439] To recall the names of the great fathers whom the assembly then saw, to report their number and nation, is neither easy nor very relevant. [Note: “Nor,” MS. Rs. *.] Rather, we must carefully consider what was well arranged, what they successfully accomplished, what new laws were issued under so great a prince, and what statutes the most famous assembly revised.

[446] Therefore Frederick, associating with private discussions only holy fathers, experts in law, and a few princes in whom he knew there was fear of God, investigated secret matters for three whole days and consulted them concerning the applications of law and the tenor of the statutes. He gladly imposed this duty upon them: that by wholesome counsel and the advice of men they should labour to formulate matters concerning the rights of Church and realm. [Note: “adopting?”] [Note: “inform,” MS. Rs.]

[454] At last, after long silence, with face revealed, conspicuous in the midst of the assembly of nobles, the prince opened his eloquent lips in the following manner:

“If, whenever three or even two are gathered in Christ’s name with equal agreement in their love of justice, Christ declares that he is present among them, who can doubt that Christ, according to his custom, is present among such great men called together for such great benefits? Far be it that Christ’s presence should ever wish to abandon us fathers, by whom the order of the Church, the laws of the Empire, and public rights are governed.

[465] “Therefore now, nobles, let us bring forward in common fellowship of law, with Christ present, whatever properly pertains to the benefit of Church or realm. Although indeed I am held by divine gift to be the highest prince in the world, exempt and free from the laws—not compelled to serve the law but permitted to establish laws—I nevertheless desire to arrange everything according to your counsels; by our command [Note: perhaps “your command”] I willingly promise either to enact new laws or to employ the old.

[474] “For, to confess the truth, I think nothing more fitting or more kingly than that a king, though released by right from the law, should nevertheless voluntarily subject himself to law. Thanks be to the great King who governs all things: we have suppressed on every side the swelling storms of war; warlike Germany is silent now that arms have been laid down, and the old fury of Italian rage has cooled.

[481] “But the old laws and royal edicts, which Charles once promulgated and which our Otto published, have been silenced by a long suspension of justice; the fisc recognises few traces of its right in Italian lands. Deliberate among yourselves which laws you wish me either to introduce anew or to renew after they have suffered old age. And first I urge that whatever you decide ought to be useful, just, suited to nature and customs, adapted to time and place, and wholly honourable.

[490] “Whatever it may be, I am prepared to defend and enact it with all my strength; and while I reign, no one shall be permitted with impunity to assail these laws of ours. If any proud man presumes to oppose them, immediate punishment and manifest penalty shall teach that I am no less invincible in laws than in war.”

[496] The assembly watched in astonished admiration as he spoke these things royally with eloquent mouth: he had not been steeped in scholarly studies and was almost a boy in age, yet he surpassed grey-haired men and experts in Scripture in understanding and in the pleasing art of speech.

Immediately some men, exhausting their eloquent mouths in native speech according to their people’s custom, whether wishing to display their zeal for the king or rather demonstrate their own capacity for speaking, spent that day upon him with the service of their tongues and copious studies. Among them one was more distinguished—the bishop of the Ligurians—and he uttered in eloquent speech the joys of all, scarcely to be equalled in narration:

[509] “Of all the days we have seen from our earliest age,” he said, “this deserves to be happier and more brilliant, since the Italian land rejoices to see you, most gracious prince, sitting peacefully among your people [Note: perhaps “among your own people”], reviving laws hitherto extinct. This is that salvation which the shipwrecked lot of a wretched land, tossed amid so many storms, is accustomed to await.

[515] “We know from ancient times how great and what kinds of tyrants the most unhappy fortune of the Italian people has endured: when, so often deprived of their goods and delivered over to the sword, they fed their rage with plunder, leaving men naked, or with blood. [Note: “swollen,” pp. Rs. +.] Reason did not establish law, but the sole will of kings; power delighted in the sword, not in justice. Nor did this faithless people, oppressed by hostile tyrants and often attempting resistance to its own ruin, favour them joyfully from love so much as it did under the pressure of fear.

[525] “Hence came hatred among the peoples, seditious rivalry, and the fury of Italy which raged for many years; dissension made two parties, and cities supported partly their country, partly the rulers. Long battered by the savage din of wars, their walls experienced alternating destruction. Who could recount the slaughter of the Ligurians, the cruel wounds of Pavia, the losses of Crema, the mournful devastation of Cremona? Amid these cities, with laws overthrown in various ways, frenzy blazed and the licence of the sword endured long.

[535] “But you, like an exceptional star at last appearing after gloomy clouds, drive war away and restore peace. You establish new laws and rights; with you governing affairs, a welcome aspect returns and a sure order is reborn. Come now: whatever the judgment of your divine mind dictates to be just, command. For the prince’s will is customarily taken as law; whatever he decrees to be valid is right and possesses the force of law. [Note: “whatever,” o, for “whatever thing,” P. s. Rs.–rr.] [Note: “is lawful,” V. +, for “is custom.”]

[543] “Use your right: whatever you judge right or pious, command to be observed. We willingly accept all things; our greatest freedom is to obey so gracious a man.” [Note: “truly,” o, for “we,” P. s. Rs.–rr.]

Thus the eloquent bishop brought all the more readily to agreement with the king and struck their hearts with great favour. Then some also sang, in composed and resounding verse, royal songs of praise for Caesar.

[551] The following day had arrived. The venerable judge sat upon his lofty throne. Many were present from every city and village; in complaint they brought forward innumerable “crosses” with clamour—for this is the customary manner in which they set forth their grievances. The king lent his ears to all, and likewise, as judge, was fairly present to the complainants’ cries, settling disputes by a certain examination.

[558] But because the assembly then present could not give an end to so many cases, the noble leader determined upon something both useful and fine. In every city he appointed men learned in law and followers of truth, to investigate all legal business by an impartial standard. He chose them not from the same cities, lest favour or hatred corrupt their judgement, but summoned them from elsewhere to these honourable offices, or delegated them from his sacred court.

[567] Afterwards a careful inquiry was begun into the ancient right of the realm, obscured by the old error of a neglected age through long disuse. First the Ligurians were questioned by the king concerning this. They surrendered to the sacred fisc tolls, ports, the right of coining money, mills, customs stations, rivers, bridges, the contribution commonly called *fodrum*, and the fixed-time tax called the *capitolitiŭm*. These things, and whatever else was subject to like right, prelates, nobles, and cities through their powerful envoys left wholly free to the Roman realm.

[579] Yet so great was the illustrious king’s indulgence that whoever had hitherto held these things in good faith by grants of former kings, and could prove this by lawful documents or demonstrate it by charters, should, with the prince’s consent, continue to possess them, enjoying the same title; the rest having been restored to royal rights, an annual revenue of thirty thousand pounds of pure silver was customarily added to the fisc. [Note: “grant,” Sp. P. R. RJo. +.] [Note: “possesses,” o, for “had possessed,” P. s. Rs.–rr.]

[587] Then the ruler ordered the nobles to bind themselves by oath to a stable peace and, with a specified penalty added, to promulgate it widely through Italian cities.

[590] Next, concerning the common law of fiefs, which that age had not yet set out in clear writing, he gave these laws and ordered them made known in writing:

[593] “If anyone holding a fief wishes to sell it, either wholly or in part, for money, without the lord’s permission; or considers giving it away or placing it in pledge, he who gave it shall lose it, and he who received it shall not keep it. No prescription, even of long time, shall prevent the transferred property from returning to its former lord. A good-faith purchaser shall have an action against the seller compelling repayment of the price paid. [Note: ‘Praetorique,’ o, for ‘Emptorique,’ P. Rs. and RJo.–rr.]

[601] “The great Lothair forbade this to be done; but we wish acts already done to be rescinded and future acts prevented. If the successor to a fief, after reaching the first age of puberty, whether through deceit, negligence, or proud intent, neglects for a whole year and a day to seek the feudal rights from his lord, he shall lose them, and the lord shall take them for his own use.

[608] “A vassal shall not refuse the public duties of rightful military service; when willingly summoned to his lord’s camp, he shall either go or send another in his place, at the lord’s discretion; or he shall compensate and redeem his own service with such payment as the lord approves. [Note: ‘is compelled,’ o, for ‘considers,’ Rs.–rr.] [Note: ‘by which,’ pp. Rs.]

[613] “If the son of a vassal injures his father’s lord by a serious offence, the father shall promptly seek to reconcile him. If he neglects to do this, he shall be deprived of his grant; but if the son, with unruly ear, neglects to heed his admonishing father, he shall not be a suitable successor to that fief until he has first appeased his lord’s inflamed anger. [Note: ‘that,’ B. *.]

[620] “If your vassal has granted that same fief to someone else and made him his own vassal by your grant, and if that third successor has incurred your anger through atrocious deeds, and does not make satisfaction to you, his lord, for the offence through the intermediate second vassal, then, once that third successor has been repudiated, the feudal rights shall immediately return to the second lord.

[626] “If that vassal of yours refuses to reconcile his own dependent to you, and is proved sluggish or faithless, both being rejected, your rights shall return to you.

[630] “Whenever a dispute concerning a fief is litigated between vassals of one lord, they shall contend before the same lord whose fief they hold, with him as judge. If a vassal perhaps initiates a suit against you concerning a fief which he admits that he received from you but you deny, not you but the court shall hear the case as judge and determine it by a fixed procedure.

[637] “A margraviate, a count’s possession, or a duchy shall remain whole; other fiefs may be shared by many, provided that each promises loyal service to the lord and gives the sworn pledges. Yet no vassal of a fief shall be compelled to have several lords under the same title. Moreover, whenever a vassal, having received a fief by feudal right, swears his oath of fealty to his lord, the Roman prince shall be excepted by name.”

[646] Caesar wished to attach laws of peace to all these provisions, so that, set at the end of his speech, these words might penetrate the listeners’ minds more deeply:

[649] “To all peoples and nations in our realm, which is pre-eminent over the whole world, we issue an edict by our authority, [Note: “patent authority,” B. *, for “authority.”] that all men may now begin, once the ruin of war has been removed, to maintain in our age the repose of peace. We further impose penalties upon wrongdoers and set forth the just anger of the laws.

[655] “All nobles—count, duke, margrave, consul—together with judges, the venerable body of captains, knights, rural inhabitants, citizens, and peasants, [Note: “and,” Pfl. *, for “or.”] and the noble order together with the common multitude: all, I say, whom neither minority nor their seventieth year exempts, shall swear this thoroughly in a united compact. [Note: “and … nor,” MS. Rs., for “neither … nor.”] And lest forgetfulness of the sacred peace arise, every five years they shall renew the form of the oath.

[664] “Let all pursue their rights through the office of a judge and restrain their hands. Let the sword, returned to its sheath, lie idle, and let iron grow red with rust, not blood. But if anything is rashly done in contempt of the laws and the reverence of sacred peace is violated, a city shall be fined one hundred pounds of pure gold, towns twenty; a margrave, count, or duke shall pay fifty talents for the broken peace; great men, twenty; lesser men, six. [Note: Hotmanus, from Radevicus; editions read ‘twenty each.’]

[673] “Wounds, violence, killings, assault, mutilation of a limb, plots, frauds, injuries, thefts, robberies, and damages shall be punished by the lawful penalties assigned to them. A higher judge convicted of refusing to punish offences against the peace shall pay ten pounds of yellow metal and make good all loss according to the law’s determination. A lesser and local judge shall be condemned to three [pounds]. If his impoverished means cannot pay the pecuniary penalties in gold, bound in chains and having endured more severe lashes, the fiftieth milestone shall remove him from his native home for five years; then he may return and reach his country’s desired boundaries.

[685] “We forbid, under this law, any conventicle, conspiracy, brotherhood, or league by ties of blood to arise in our cities. Whoever is convicted shall be fined one pound of gold.

[690] “Let bishops and holy fathers fearlessly strike with sacred anathema those who despise peace and dare what the laws condemn; and let them labour to establish human laws by heavenly laws and a righteous fear. Let the exaction, hitherto customarily made in Italian cities and daring even frequently to harass sacred houses by forced services and the clergy with its demands, cease; or we order that more than double what has been exacted be restored.” [Note: “the clergy,” W.–Edd.; “usually,” o, without sense.]

[698] “Whoever wickedly refuses to swear the prescribed peace and keep its form, all that he possesses shall be open to public plunder and his household to destruction. Whoever supports and harbours a violator of the peace has deserved a share in the penalty through participation in the offence. Oaths extorted by fear or pain of death—especially lest anyone should publish by speaking matters harmful to many or complain of cruelty done to himself—we decree to be of no value or weight.”

## Book Nine

[Col. 0449C] Amid the very frequent disputes of the complaining crowd and quarrels brought from every city, a great conflict troubled the citizens of Piacenza and fair Cremona, and that old rivalry still lived and drove the men with bitter goads. Though the Po, scarcely dividing the cities with its channel between them, joined the former to Pavia and the latter to the city of the Ligurians by an allied compact, they had hitherto been accustomed to stir up alternating hostilities and the grievous incitements of hatred.

[11] But this further cause had then been added to the old ones. As Frederick was making for Roncaglia and the war standards of the Cremonese force followed him, hostile licence sent out the insolent citizens and, provoking the men, instituted a real battle as though by some mock contest. The fighting was not without slaughter or wholly bloodless; men were killed on either side, and each found consolation in the reciprocal disaster of the other.

[20] Therefore the Cremonese, having the better case and relying also upon the unfeigned praises of an eloquent speech, heap resentment and the prince’s anger upon their enemies—for the latter did not adequately excuse their unlawful deeds—until at last, only with difficulty and after much money had been paid, favour was restored to the accused on this condition: that, their towers cast down throughout the city, the mournful walls should be torn by their ruined structures; and that the open ditches which they had begun to dig from fear of the king should again be filled with earth heaped into them.

[30] With Italian affairs thus arranged in sufficiently fine order, Caesar, wishing to extend his hand to all that lay beyond, [Note: The reading is thus in A; the other editions read “further.”] prepared forcibly to reconcile and add to his realms the boundaries of Sardinia, enclosed by the Tyrrhenian sea, and the lands of Corsica. For this purpose he decided to send ahead two nobles, one a count and the other a bishop, to test the suspicious dispositions of those peoples—whether they wished peace or war, whether they must be compelled or would follow voluntarily. Genoa and lofty Pisa were ordered to provide the envoys with safe access.

[40] Both were greatly to be feared far across the Tyrrhenian waters; both were widely renowned for famous victories. Yet we may infer from what follows why this embassy did not attain its purpose: each of these states was accustomed to derive very great advantages from its long dominion over those regions. Hence they may clearly seem to have obstructed the business entrusted by the realm through concealed treachery.

[48] But neither the trickery of the crafty Genoese populace, nor the Tyrrhenian sea, nor the mountains which nature had placed before them—barely approachable through narrow passes and only with much toil—availed to escape the fierce threats of the enraged prince. Having sought pardon, Genoa scarcely redeemed its treachery by a payment of one thousand marks.

[Col. 0451A] Yet with this addition: the people were ordered to desist from the wall they had begun, lest they continue to close in the city. Winter was now advancing upon the sluggish summer camp as the season turned, and the mighty leader, rich in many resources, resolved to occupy, with troops dispersed widely and his camps spread abroad, the boundaries of a better and more fertile land, previously untouched.

[61] Without delay he occupied wealthy Alba in its fruitful territory, walls well suited to winter quarters. Here the earthly prince celebrated, with all the honour he could, the approaching nativity of the heavenly King. From there he sent envoys through Etruscan cities, the towns of Campania, and those washed by the wave of the sea’s salt on the curving shore, to demand the ancient rights due to the fisc, establish magistrates and every civic authority in each city.

[70] Moreover, the king reclaimed into his own rights the revenues from all those territories which beautiful Matilda had formerly possessed and which several persons had seized. Then, having gathered them together and brought them back, as it were, into one body from many parts by some force of weight, the prince granted them with accumulated gift to Catulus, who desired to hold some ancient right as though he were an heir. Catulus, the king’s uncle, was at that time a powerful duke and aided his nephew’s prosperous camp with no small force of soldiers and vigour of mind.

[80] Him, illustrious by descent and name from the Roman blood of the Catuli—if report does not deceive—the German language, deceived by the resemblance of an ambiguous sound, called Guelpho after altering the name.

[84] Amid joyful successes and great prosperity, a sudden loss struck the king with grief and disturbed the joys of his tranquil mind. For many nobles, whether those who followed the camp beneath the illustrious prince or those who, in quiet peace, inhabited German cities and their native fields, closed their final day. At that time Bishop Otto of Freising, by his death learned of, became a cause of greater grief to his noble nephew.

Here this uncle of the king, skilled in both branches of learning,

[Col. 0451D] had always been accustomed to follow the royal standards; but now, I believe, at God’s recalling, weakened by illness, he had remained behind, so that amid the mournful hymns of his brothers and of the grieving clergy chanting psalms, rather than amid the din of camps and the clash of iron, he might breathe out the sacred breath of the divine gift of light [Note: [Col. 0451] “of light,” B (?)] and at last render his soul to the heavenly King.

Meanwhile the supreme pontiff, stirred by evil advisers, began to renew his old anger and grievances extinguished in his mind; and Adrian, anxious over the great honour of the powerful man, felt the pricks of envy. Especially after he learned that, with the assent of the nobles, his rights had been acknowledged to the fisc throughout all the cities, he was grieved by the deed; and as much honour as he saw had accrued to the man, so much, the pope himself believed, had been taken from him. Then everything that had previously seemed to have been done with special harshness—the contempt shown to his envoys and to himself, threats against his realm, and commands more severe than their harsh terms—he added, as it were, as fuel for the flame and as torches of envy, freely feeding the swift heat of the furnace.

[Col. 0452B] A further recent cause was also at hand: while the king’s agents, sent to investigate royal rights, were carrying out the public commands of the supreme pontiff through his castles and districts more faithfully than was fair, they oppressed the wretched citizens with an unfamiliar burden through excessive severity intended to inspire fear.

Therefore, with a new cause stimulating his old pain, he rejoiced to accuse the king in repeated complaints, calling him unjust, cruel, arrogant in his kingdom, and ungrateful to him, who had of his own accord bestowed upon him the name and highest honour of so great an eminence and of empire.

[Col. 0452C] At first he sought by gentler letters and paternal speech to persuade the man; then he rebuked him more sharply and pressed him too insistently with vexatious words. Nor did the latter, rejoicing to return abuse for abuse, fail to send back offensive words in proud letters.

Thus, bearing in turn the quarrels of opposing parties, correspondence more keenly stimulated their inflamed minds; and the most illustrious names of the whole world shook in grievous conflict, amid struggles over great affairs. Nor was it doubtful that the Ligurians, induced by the letters and frequent solicitations of the supreme pontiff—as many say, if it is permissible to believe them—had again, with rebellious neck, broken off the sacred laws, despising the treaty.

[Col. 0452D] Therefore, when Bishop Rainald, together with the distinguished Otto—this prudent standard-bearer and that chancellor—and Count Gozwin, a man of exceptional renown, came to the city to transact great business of the realm, the mob roared and began to rage together. The Ligurians hastened to demolish with a savage shower of stones the house in which the famous bishop had been received (for the two counts, prudently avoiding the walls and the suspected fortifications, were staying outside), and eagerly sought to deliver to cruel death the legate of the great Caesar himself, the pontiff feared for his high reputation and strength of mind.

[Col. 0453A] Not even the nobility itself, more devoted to the king, could restrain them, nor Guido of Blandrate, who had an eminent name as a fellow citizen in that allied city. At last, only with difficulty, aided by the bishop of the same see, the bishop escaped their raging threats and left the walls and treacherous dwellings of the pestilential city.

The royal legates, their business frustrated, immediately made for the camp and the allied troops with hasty step.

Meanwhile faithful embassies from powerful kings brought to the ears of the great Caesar fresh messages from various kingdoms, prompted by different concerns. Certain men bearing the commands of the Greek ruler came safely into the camp and sought peace. For they had long heard that, since the death of Guibald of Stabulum [Note: [Col. 0453] Later editions: “of Astabulum.”], whom his final day had overcome in Greek lands [Note: [Col. 0453] P., ss., Rs., and RJo: “whom the final day had overwhelmed in Greek lands”; rr.: “whom a duke …”; Pfl.: “whom a cross …”], they themselves were held in deep suspicion by the king, and they were preparing to clear their nation.

Nor less did the ruler of Hungary, having learned of the Ligurians’ recent treachery, write faithful offers of peace to Augustus; and, as punishment for their crime, he promised to send him forces greater than the former ones. The English king and the king who then ruled the urban Gauls both sent faithful men to the royal camp, competing to seek the pledge of peace and the favour of the great Caesar by gifts offered.

[Col. 0453C] An old and serious hostility was said to have arisen between these kings, because the wife of the French ruler, after leaving her husband, had married the English ruler. Hence fierce hatred and anger, burning with goads, and savage wars fought over disputed borders, afflicted them; and therefore each hastened to enlist Caesar’s arms for the injury of the other.

The most prudent man praised them all with cheerful countenance and dismissed them laden with his gifts. Meanwhile the returning legates entered the camp, bringing reports of the foul deeds ventured by the Ligurians. The affair, once known, shook them all and the king himself with fierce goads, and his anger again flared up.

Yet, lest anything be done without due order under Augustus, experts in the law advised that the Ligurians be summoned again by three edicts.

[Col. 0453D] When those proud men despised these with haughty mind, the court declared them condemned enemies of the realm. Then, in order that he might again inflame the men with stronger incentives of just anger for military exertions, Frederick spoke these words in the midst of the assembly of nobles and the crowd of the people, with honeyed speech:

“Indeed, the repeated wickedness and the frequent injury inflicted by the Ligurians often compel me to summon your strength to battle and employ your faithful hands. It is a burdensome undertaking; and, even if your loyalty were welcome [Note: [Col. 0453] Pfl.: “certain.”], I should not dare so often to ask for hands slow and reluctant for great enterprises. But because this is a common labour, and I do not suppose that what is being done concerns you less than it concerns me, whenever the time requires your help and assured support, and recent fortune assails the realm, I flee confidently [Note: [Col. 0453] A: “secure”; Rs. is silent; rr.: “wholly.”] to the unconquered devotion of your valour and appeal with confidence to your faithful hands.

[Col. 0454A] “You know—and I do not doubt that it seems terrible and harsh [Note: [Col. 0453] Perhaps “dreadful.”] to you as to me—the monstrous crime of that repeatedly perjured city. Though only lately, through our favour, it obtained pardon for its offence and the benefit of safety, its relapse into savagery now rouses its accustomed frenzies. What hope can now remain for keeping faith and peace, when oaths, pledged faith, and so many sureties throughout the Italian cities under our rule cannot restrain the rage of the faithless populace? Let the perjured city pay heavy penalties, at last expiate its cruel deeds, and deservedly fall, since it refuses to stand [Note: [Col. 0453] pp., Rs.: “because.”].”

They had heard him, and, competing in zeal, each outstripped the other and urged the men with still greater incentives. But the king, believing that so great an undertaking, requiring such labour, could be accomplished only by Teutonic strength, summoned to himself from beyond the Alps the German nobles, the standards of his kinsman the duke of Bavaria, many other powerful men, and you, noble Beatrice, companion of his sacred marriage-bed.

[Col. 0454C] He himself, attended by few men, ranged everywhere through the Italian regions, hastening whatever he believed would benefit him or harm the enemy in the coming war. He supplied castles with men, arms, and provisions, and surrounded Lodi with a strong new fortification, to bear the burden of the nearby war [Note: [Col. 0453] W; editions: “of Ticinum,” without sense.].

When he had reached the walls of faithful Como, seeking martial forces and auxiliary troops, he received more than he had requested, offered freely; and he rejoiced in the love of that loyal people.

There lies an island surrounded by the lake of Como, rich in warriors, which by an ancient treaty had allied itself with the faithless city of the Ligurians. Powerful at sea and engaged in piratical war, it rejoiced to trouble the lake with frequent plunder. The king, wisely provident for the various uses of war, considered how to win it over to his arms.

[Col. 0455A] Nor was this in vain. For when a fleet had been built and the man was preparing an assault and war, that people, conveyed in ships into the middle of the lake, yielded when the victor was received; and from that noble time onward it remained faithful to the king and kept faith with pure devotion.

Then too Piacenza could not restrain itself from vomiting forth the poison it had conceived and concealed. While the imperial legates were carrying through the territory of that unjust city the money which it had paid as a penalty for the gate [or toll], robbers quickly came out from the city itself; they did not fear to plunder the men and disgracefully lay their hands upon the royal money.

Therefore the prince, roused to fierce anger also by this, confident in the majesty of his name, entered the trembling city of his own accord, attended by few men. Instilling royal threats and fearful words into the proud citizens [Note: [Col. 0455] Perhaps “proud” singular.], he was scarcely persuaded by them to accept, peace having been granted, the sum they had brought.

The venerable day was at hand on which Christ, raising his desired face from the depths of the earth to the faithful throng, returned as victor from the infernal dwelling, leading back the captives.

[Col. 0455C] Caesar celebrated that day with all the honour he could in the city of Modena [Note: [Col. 0455] Rs.; rr.: “this day.”], and entered, O Bologna devoted to learning, your territory. There he had long before left his camp and troops, not seen for a long time, in the charge of the eminent Eberhard in great affairs.

Therefore, when he saw that the Ligurians, often summoned by lawful edicts, had despised them and had planted their foot in an excessively obstinate purpose, he did not act hastily in any way. From the famous city he summoned leading men learned in law and asked what penalty was due for contempt. After prolonged discussion, this was at last prescribed by the judgment of all: plundering of their property, enslavement of the people, and destruction of the city from its foundations.

[Col. 0455D] Present in the camp were prudent and distinguished men sent by the supreme pontiff: William, and that man who, a rebel in schismatic savagery, persisted for a long time until the tomb and left it to his successor. After the agreeable beginnings of their speech and the soothing of ears by eloquent words, they brought propositions harsh and unacceptable to Frederick’s tranquil mind, formulated in definite terms:

“It is not lawful for Augustus to send legates to the sacred city except with the consent of the supreme pontiff, in which Peter alone rightfully holds every jurisdiction.

[Col. 0456A] “Nor is it lawful for the fisc to oppress the pope’s castles or towns by collecting its dues, save only at the time when the ruler rejoices to wear the first crown at Rome and to receive the new honours of empire.

“It is not expedient that Italian pontiffs be men of the ruler, called merely to oaths of fealty [Note: [Col. 0455] W and editions: “all,” without sense.].

“Nor is it lawful for anyone bearing the king’s commands to harass the dwellings of pontiffs; by ancient custom the ruler alone rightly defends this honour for himself.

“Whatever of old rightly belonged to the patrimonies of the eminent Peter, whether possession or tribute, shall be restored to him: the land of Countess Matilda and, under the same jurisdiction, the duchy of Spoleto. Whatever separates the hanging waters [the waterfall] from the lofty walls of the Roman city—Ferrara, Massa, and fertile Corsica with its Sardinian fields—

[Col. 0456B] shall pay tribute to the supreme pontiff according to ancient custom and remain under the ancient laws by a just rule.”

The prince, sufficiently weakening all these claims by subtle arguments, refuted each point in learned words. He opposed his own complaint concerning the broken peace, which, he said, had been confirmed with him by this law: that the pontiff should not enter into allied treaties with the Romans, the Sicilian, or the Greek ruler without his permission.

Finally, he promised that he would either abide by strict law and legal rigour, or submit to the judgment of wise men, and would do enough and undertake whatever was required under an equal condition. But they said that they had indeed come prepared to receive, but not to render, such a judgment—an absurd thing.

[Col. 0456C] For they denied that the pope, who exercised the office of judge on earth under no judge, could submit himself to judgment. After making many proposals in vain, Caesar added this also: that six men chosen by the supreme pontiff, and as many men from his own side, who should judge all things to be set beneath truth by sound reasoning, should undertake to settle every dispute with careful concern and carry it out in the certain fear of God [Note: [Col. 0455] A: “by the tenor [of God].”]. But the pontiff did not agree even to this; desiring that everything should proceed according to his own will, he refused to submit himself to just law, as though seeking causes for great anger.

But the Ligurians prepared to put into action the designs of their secret treachery with violence. They threatened to capture by terrible assault and strong hand Trezzo, which the ruler had long before fortified with a strong garrison after taking it from them. They secretly made engines of war by deceit, carried them apart on wagons with great skill [Note: [Col. 0455] B; editions: “in war.”], quickly assembled them into a great mass, and pressed the castle with new assaults.

[Col. 0457A] Some aimed missiles and swift arrows at the high walls; a sling spun smaller stones; a Balearic engine struck great walls with great stones [Note: [Col. 0457] “with great [stones],” Rs.; another reading: “with great … walls.”] and battered the defences with a hard blow [Note: [Col. 0457] Perhaps “struck.”]. Others, joining shields in a dense tortoise formation, hastened either to fill the pits of the ditches, undermine the walls by hidden craft, break them by the blow of hard timber, or fiercely climb the towers by ladders and seize the high battlements. They pressed this effort the more because the royal standards were in the neighbouring territory and they feared Caesar’s great anger.

No less courageously did the defenders roll stones from the highest towers and break up their own walls for use in battle.

[Col. 0457B] Weapons rain from every side; the bolt discharged by the ballista whistles, and the air echoes with long shrieks. The first and following day gave great impetus to the work begun; the third exposed the conquered walls. For our men, already exhausted in their whole bodies, had no opportunity either to withdraw their hands [Note: [Col. 0457] Pfl.: “spirit.”], to breathe, or to change the place which each had first undertaken to defend. But the Ligurians’ standards repeatedly relieved one another, changed shifts, and their number always seemed to grow and their strength continually to increase.

Valour yielded to numbers; in the savage tumult the broken gates lay open, and the fighting youths either stained hostile swords with their miserable blood or bore chains thrown upon neck and hands.

[Col. 0457C] Yet this distinction was observed amid these harsh circumstances [Note: [Col. 0457] Rs.: “this”; manuscript: “here”]: all whom the victor found there of Latin stock he struck down, fierce and inexorable, and fed the sword with the blood of their nation. But those whom their language clearly showed to be of Teutonic blood he judged should be treated more mildly; sparing them from slaughter, he preserved the captives. Of those whom true report declared to be retainers of the realm, eighty [literally, “twice forty”] were forced into harsh chains; all the others perished in unspeakable slaughter. The fortifications of the little castle itself, its walls broken down, were overthrown and given to devouring flame [Note: [Col. 0457] Pfl.: “yielded.”].

When Caesar learned of the wound of this great disaster, he grieved, moved by heavy sorrow and anger; yet he restrained his groan and held his pain within his heart, offering the princes a brave example of mourning. He did not choose to exact the deserved penalties for their crimes [lacuna].

[Col. 0458A] or avenge his own men, or wage war, before the court long summoned at Roncaglia had met. There, to the astonishment of all, he set forth the Ligurians’ frauds, broken treaties, and offences against himself; while all condemned with just speech the perfidy of the proud populace, he rallied forces to his cause.

Immediately he burst into the hostile territory with an attacking army and devastated the broad fields with sword, fire, and plunder. He cut down fig trees [Note: [Col. 0457] P., ss., Rs., and RJo: “fig trees”; rr.: “boundaries.”] and vineyards with the sword, and stripped the bark from tree-trunks, leaving them no longer fit to bear fruit. He judged it more useful to deter the guilty and crush their proud minds by losses than by shed blood; or, if perhaps even so the fierce people would not repent, that they should perish consumed by famine, their food supplies quickly exhausted [Note: [Col. 0457] W and editions transpose verse 399 before verse 398.], or be compelled at last by surrender

[Col. 0458B] to deliver themselves and their walls together. Moreover, after posting guards throughout every quarter [Note: [Col. 0457] A: “quarters”; rr.: “gates.”], he cut off trade in useful goods from those shut in. So that no one might carry wares to the hostile city, he fixed punishment for the one who dared and rewards for the informer.

Often, attended by a strong force, he approached the city gates in order to lure the enemy out from the safety of their walls. After more than once allowing them to go out unpunished and return again, Frederick finally deceived them by an excellent stratagem. Drawing the Ligurians a short distance from their city and then ordering his allies, turning in flight, to run ahead, he trapped them in a narrow pass; denying them entrance through the gates, he captured or killed many with the sword, and returned scarcely a few unharmed to the city.

[Col. 0458C] When he had penetrated far into the Ligurians’ territory and, devastating their fields, added great strength to the war, five hundred young cavalrymen, brave in spirit and arms, came swiftly from the enemy city to the royal walls of transferred Lodi. Finding herds and cattle in the broad fields, they drove them at full speed toward their own walls.

Duke Guarnerius of Ancona, quickly taking up arms, and another man under whose bishopric wealthy Mantua then flourished, one deserving the praise of exceptional fame, pressed them from behind with a strong troop of young men and a terrible shout. They recovered the spoil; after sixteen Ligurians had been killed, the sorrowing city scarcely received the rest, terrified, within its walls.

[Col. 0458D] By now the illustrious ruler had for forty days devastated the enemy fields with sword and flame, and captured towns and strongholds fortified with mighty towers. Among them a certain fortress, previously yielding to no king, however unconquered, surrendered; the populace calls it Mount Saint John.

[Col. 0459A] He had now mutilated the faithless and reprobate head almost everywhere in all its limbs, and, having subdued the rest, left only two fortresses. To these fresh fortune added another fine success and heaped up the gifts of abundant favour.

For rich Cremona and Brescia sent out their knights and plundering squadrons [Note: [Col. 0459] Rs.: “richly”; A: “Brisia.”]. When they began to range widely through the invaded territory and took no precaution through fear of what was coming, enemies, long forewarned and concealed in ambushes, sprang forth, terrified the men, routed and put them to flight,

[Col. 0459B] killed them in their dismay, and fed the sword with blood. Thus the sword struck down sixty knights and three hundred foot soldiers, or chains bound them. But Caesar, having ravaged the territory of the wicked city, returned as victor to the faithful fortifications of Lodi.

There, having dismissed the Italians, he chose to await the standards of his wife and the transalpine troops. Meanwhile, as time passed, the Ligurians’ calamity grew; the evil, gaining strength with the passing days, had become urgent, and famine had taken possession of the whole city. Yet such great evils did not teach the doomed people to repent; desperation had made them secure, banishing fear of certain ruin.

[Col. 0459C] Hence they did not fear to prepare ambushes and hidden devices of infamous death against the sacred king [Note: [Col. 0459] B: “to direct”; B, second hand: “to hand over.”]. At once they incited with money a certain man of terrifying size, to whom it came easily to feign genuine madness [Note: [Col. 0459] Rs.; rr.: “favour.”], so that, pretending madness in words and gestures, he might enter the royal camp and, once admitted by deceit, kill the king at a suitable time by whatever means possible.

Nor was he slow to obey the evil plan. Disguised beyond recognition, he entered the enemy tents near Lodi, conspicuous as those of the great king. Once admitted, he delighted in becoming the mockery of the whole camp, making easy jokes and provoking laughter, a clever imitator of foolishness:

[Col. 0459D] filthy, with unwashed face, horrible with beard and uncombed hair, ragged and scaly in torn clothing, with a gleam in his eyes and a foul, foaming mouth; now fearful in expression, now savage; now gentle, now fierce; now speaking sweetly, now stringing together insults;

[Col. 0460A] now humble, now threatening in speech and burning with anger; now swift in his gait, now slower; now pale, now with a face inflamed by a dreadful blaze. Now he broke into tears through laughter, now into joy through groaning. He often delighted in offering his cheeks to slaps and his neck to blows, a knowing imitator of a foolish man.

So once did that deceitful Sinon, equipped with Greek trickery, approach Priam and doomed Troy. For a long time he deceived the wretched Trojans and wished to mock them, devising treacheries in his wicked mind.

And so that, by the surest signs of counterfeit madness, he might cease to be suspected by everyone in the camp [Note: [Col. 0459] Rs.: “ceased.”], the deadly man even began to ingratiate himself with the king by foolish jokes, until, when he had seized his opportunity, the feigned madness disclosed itself as real madness.

[Col. 0460B] For when the king, as was his custom at first light, had energetically risen from his neglected bed for the morning offices of divine praise, while everyone in the camp was breathing heavy air, weighed down by the torpor of morning sleep [Note: [Col. 0459] pp., Rs.: “sluggish.”], that most savage satellite, prompted by a demon and judging the moment favourable for accomplishing his treachery, resolved either to submit himself to death or to commit the crime. He seized the unsuspecting king in strong arms and, crushing him beneath his powerful body,

[Col. 0460C] dragged him out of the camp and prepared to hurl the king from the ledge of a high bank and plunge him into the river. And he would, I think, have done so, had not Caesar, recognizing the treachery and struggling greatly, at the far edge of the camp clung with both hands to ropes which he had grasped and called his companions with a loud cry.

They promptly rushed up, shaking off the torpor of sleep, and surrounded the monster on every side, laying hands upon him. First they tried to loosen the rigid grip of his arms and carefully draw out the unharmed leader. Then, flogged and receiving the fitting reward for his treachery, he was swallowed by the torrent’s river waters.

[Col. 0460D] Yet when the end of this crime became known, the crafty wicked populace did not rest or refrain from its deceits. They incited eight of their own men, hired at great price, to set Lodi on fire by stealth. The first of these who attempted the crime was caught in the very act, after fire had been applied, and was compelled to pay upon the gallows the penalty he deserved. He left his accomplices a clear example of punishment, lest they suppose that they could henceforth dare anything of the kind with impunity.

[Col. 0461A] Another, in order to be able to enter the enemy camp as a scout and put on the appearance of an innocent mind, had dressed as a monk; but he too was caught and underwent death and shameful fate by the same punishment.

Nor should it be passed over that at the same time Caesar received salutary warnings, written by an uncertain author, that a certain man would come to the royal camp: a man powerful in poisons and magical madness, deformed in appearance, having suffered the loss of much time, deprived of the use of one eye [Note: [Col. 0461] Rs., s. RJo; rr.: “use.”];

[Col. 0461B] a despiser of death, accustomed to regard all threats of powerful men as nothing, having twenty and more followers in the same error [Note: [Col. 0461] Perhaps “or more”; B: “terror.”]. This man, a pagan Arab, would bring to the king, as though they were little gifts, bridles, spurs, belts, clasps, golden finger-rings and golden neck-rings. All these were so smeared with sulphurous poisons

[Col. 0462A] that, if the ruler should happen to touch them with bare hand, the poison, mingled with infected blood, would boil and the pestilence would dominate his whole body. But if the holy hand should more cautiously refrain from the harmful touch, a dagger hidden beneath his garment would pierce the royal breast, or he would stab the royal breast with a thrust knife.

Therefore, when that poisoner bearing the predicted tokens approached the camp of the great leader, readily recognizable, he was captured and his limbs bound in chains. The man was shown a promise of pardon if he told the truth; but, though asked long and earnestly what he sought and at whose instigation he had undertaken these things, he scorned the offer and declared that he did not fear feeble, fragile threats. If anything severe should be inflicted upon him, he said, the king—condemned by his spell—

[Col. 0462B] would immediately give him satisfaction for the penalty by death, and would be his companion in the very same destruction. Such things might perhaps have seemed fearful to others; but Caesar laughed at the fraudulently invented fabrications and threats, and, as a most just avenger, hanged him on the gallows and killed him by a fitting death, his throat crushed.

## Book Ten

[Col. 0461C] Meanwhile Beatrice, august consort of the great ruler, gathering strong cohorts from the Teutonic world under the command of her husband and bravely crossing the Alps—for love and the bond of marriage made her strong—had entered and occupied Italian territory.

Besides other nobles and men of lesser renown from the German nation, that most faithful Saxon youth, grandson of a king and kinsman of the king, commanding the standards of the Saxons [Note: [Col. 0461] “of the Saxon” or “Saxon,” pp., Rs.] and of the land of Noricum lately restored to him [Note: [Col. 0461] A: “commanding”; rr.: “bearing.”], had joined her with the forces of the two peoples.

The arrival of all these men brought great joy to the entire camp and shook the Ligurians with bitter fear.

[Col. 0461D] A little later there arrived that renowned uncle [Note: [Col. 0461] P., ss., Rs., and CJo: “renowned uncle”; rr.: “renowned to all,” rejected on metrical grounds.] of Caesar, lord and margrave of the Etruscan land, powerful in the Teutonic region and a duke feared on its shore: Welf. He brought increased joy to our side and filled up the camp with a strong force.

[Col. 0462C] Crema itself had been made a place neighbouring great Cremona and had long remained subject to it under the same ancient laws [Note: [Col. 0461] P., Rs., RJo: “under the same”; editions: “at the same time.”]. But now, shaking off the yoke and released from restraint, it had dared to follow the proud fury of the Ligurians; often summoned already by the king, it had despised his edict and would not submit to law.

Moved by these provocations and by a hundred thousand talents—which wealthy Cremona itself gave freely—Caesar planned to overthrow proud Crema by war. Dividing his army into two parts, he led one with himself to ravage the Ligurians’ fields; to the other, he entrusted the arms of great Cremona [Note: [Col. 0461] A, Sp., R: “another”; P: “others … had occupied Cremona’s fields.”] and ordered it to attack the hated city in war.

The forces obeyed, each soldier attacked the secure defences with strong assault, and suddenly fell upon the enemy. Yet the enemy, undaunted and accustomed to hard warfare, met them and joined battle. Men fell slain by the sword on either side; among them the great Marquis Garnerus, worthy of special lamentation, died [Note: [Col. 0463] A: “Garnerus”; rr.: “Warnerus”; Radevicus: “Guarnerus.”], and left both war and life.

[Col. 0463A] Others pitched camp, watched the enemies shut within the walls, and hastened with great care to devise what they thought suitable for taking the walls. The enemies enclosed in the besieged city no less hurriedly made engines of war with anxious labour, content to fortify only the side facing the enemy; for on a great part of its circuit the walls were enclosed by marshy mud, and the muddy bogs, unable to support footprints in the soft slime, defended the walls in safety.

Then an embassy came from the city of Romulus, citizens mighty in lineage and distinguished in name; it bore the humble petitions of the Roman people to Caesar’s ears,

[Col. 0463B] and the cautious proposals of the senators: namely, that, finally setting aside his anger, the most august king might spare his own city and not, as avenger, extend to all its citizens the crime that had arisen from a foolish, nameless mob.

Caesar received this with calm ears and gentle heart. Remembering the disaster by which, at the beginning of his reign, he had crushed the wretched people in his own city and afflicted the guilty, compelled by compassion of spirit he changed his course for the better. In return he gave a gracious answer, filled the hearts of those desirous of it with great gifts, and, as they returned, added two men who would carry royal words to the magnificent city: Otto the Palatine, famed for his praise,

[Col. 0463C] and the prudent Haribert, who had long served the realm with faithful zeal and care as first [official] in the Church of Aachen, now provost as the worthy reward of his labour, and soon to be bishop in the city of Chrysopolis, by the pleasing gift of the illustrious king. So profitable is it to serve great leaders.

He gave them instructions, with the consent of the bishop and the whole people, to renew the ancient senate, restore the rights of the prefect to their original force, and, if those treaties should please the supreme pontiff, bring all things, corrected, back to the ancient peace.

He himself ranged in every direction across enemy fields with a numerous army, carrying out every hostile operation, mixing all things with fear [Note: [Col. 0463] Pfl.: “hand”; W: “reaps.”], sword, flames, and blood. He had already forced all the Ligurians into their secure walls,

[Col. 0463D] and, lest the closed fortifications should make safe those whom neither wall nor any [other barrier] prevented from being conquered in war, he devised a stratagem. Wisely, he ordered the Pavians, foremost enemies of the Ligurian name, to advance ahead and, with conspicuously driven-off booty, draw the deceived enemy out from their closed walls.

He secretly stationed his own men in ambush with him and ordered them, while the enemy pressed, to turn their course here [Note: [Col. 0463] Rs.: “him.”]. Nor did expectation deceive the king. For after the cautious men had feigned flight, turning their backs in retreating dust, the unsuspecting enemy fell into the hidden ambushes and, surrounded by uproar, recoiled in horror. As swift stags often fall into nets, their horns clash with a loud crash, and the hunter sets barking dogs upon them and joyfully strikes down the bellowing creatures without danger,

[Col. 0464A] so, after the men had fallen into the midst, hemmed in on all sides by hostile missiles, they could neither use their weapons nor retreat; they were slaughtered at close quarters without resistance and suffered, confined in too narrow a space.

There, one hundred and fifty were killed by the sword, and six hundred submitted their necks to harsh chains. But it is neither brief nor easy to ascertain by a definite number those whom the nearby stream swept away and submerged in its rapid fords [Note: [Col. 0463] Pfl.: “waves”], or those who, suffering mortal wounds, the sorrowing city at last received trembling within itself.

The victorious Augustus returned to the faithful fortifications of new Lodi and the city made glad by his successes.

[Col. 0464C] During the same period, before those whom Frederick had sent to the city of Romulus had returned, Anagni, neighbouring and closely connected to great Rome, saw the funeral rites of the Roman shepherd. The clergy, however, transported him thence to their city and faithfully buried him with honour in Peter’s holy see.

But before the bishop committed his bloodless limbs to the tomb, a schism had already arisen; he left behind two parties and a dispute over the see that would last long. For when the clergy considered the succession to so great a man, Rolland, formerly chancellor and distinguished by lineage, was sought out by the party of sounder judgment. Changing his former name, he became Alexander and survived for many years,

[Col. 0464D] at last seeing the Church’s peace when the schism had been calmed, and then finally resting in his desired end. The other sacred party, deceived by its own omens and ignorant of the judgment from above, set you, Octavian, in the see and falsely called you Victor by name.

Again Caesar energetically moved his standards to devastate the enemy fields. Extending war far through every countryside, he overthrew whatever had remained untouched by the new disasters, adding heavier afflictions to the earlier ones.

[Col. 0465A] But when the land, continually stripped by frequent plunder, could now provide neither food for its master nor fodder for the horse [Note: [Col. 0465] Pfl.: “not for a man.”], he changed course and moved with swift force toward the trembling walls of besieged Crema.

Indeed, immense fear had already taken Crema from the beginning of the siege; but now, when they saw Caesar’s royal standards, the Latin eagles fluttering in the wind over their fields, and Caesar himself encouraging his companies to battle with awe-inspiring majesty, fear shook their bones and foreboding clouds of coming disaster threw their troubled minds into confusion.

Yet even now it did not occur to the ill-fated people to repent, submit themselves and their walls to the merciful victor, avoid avenging threats,

[Col. 0465B] and earn pardon. They persisted in crime and preferred to perish rather than live by the leader’s gift: free death was deemed worth more than salvation bestowed and life granted.

Therefore the citizens and our young warriors alike chose arms and rejected peace, raising engines and heavy structures. A machine was constructed for various uses: one to hurl stones, one to cast spears, and one to scatter against walls or rival lofty towers flames of quick-burning sulphur; the printed reading “extinguished flames” (exstinctas flammas) is uncertain. Weapons, firebrands, and stones fly; a black cloud darkens the air, and the breeze is interwoven with launched arrows.

[Col. 0465C] Fury burns on both sides; the sky is broken by savage shouting, and anger seethes under stronger incentives. These men, wishing to appear equal in courage to those shut within, think it shameful and disgraceful and fiercely delight in trampling upon threats; those others strive not to be inferior, return like for like, and pay back greater things. Certain death makes them bold, and hopeless safety banishes fear; then, if by hostile chance—
They seize and hold those whom they have caught; hostile frenzy rages against them, and, before the eyes of their companions, they cut their necks with the sword, play with them in their hands as the neck is spun round like a ball, or cruelly tear their wretched limbs to pieces.

[Col. 0465D] Not far removed from the savage tumult of war, the royal wife was keeping watch in a neighbouring fortress, lest she should see the pitiable slaughter and many unspeakable deeds, and pollute her chaste eyes with the cruel sight.

While her husband was watching her, the enemy burst forth through the gate guarded by the royal standards, from their secure positions; with a great din they assault the king’s tents, kill many, stain the ground with enemy and their own blood, and alternately strike down and fall. Throughout the whole day they could not be driven off by any force, until Phoebus, his lamp sunk, poured darkness over the shadowy world.

[180] A most reliable messenger brought everything to the absent king. [Note: “most sorrowful,” Pfl. +.] Shaken deeply by the grievous news, he hastens to the camp and sees the standards still bloody from the recent slaughter. In sight of the captive city he compels certain prisoners to put their throats beneath the noose and hangs them high in the air from a tree.

Then some men were also dragging into the camp six bound men of the Ligurian people. Bearing the commands of the Ligurian populace to the people of Piacenza, they had fallen into enemy hands. One of these, who seemed to be the foremost, took pride in being the bishop’s nephew and was distinguished by the standing of his family and by wealth. The prince inflicted the same punishment on these also, disregarding the considerable sum of money which they promised to pay to the treasury as ransom for their lives.

[195] No less did the besieged hang every captive whom they held, rejoicing soon to repay in kind what had been done. Then the wrath of the noble Caesar burned fiercely: the defeated dared, as though equal to him, to contend with him, and still refused to acknowledge their wretched plight or confess their condition even in death.

[Col. 0466C] At once he orders the besieged to be warned by the herald’s voice that they are to place no hope of any relief or salvation in his goodness, lest anyone wish to flee to him in expectation of pardon. Let each contend for his own blood, he says, and know that he must secure his own safety by his own hand, placing hope only in strong arms.

Then he orders forty men—sure hostages and pledges for keeping faith and peace, whom that faithless populace had formerly given to him—to be fastened to structures and lofty towers, so that they might receive upon their wretched bodies the missiles and torches of their own people, and the stones violently hurled from the city by engines, shielding the wooden structures. [Note: Rs.—other manuscripts: “and which these bundles,” without sense.]

How great was the mourning, what a spectacle of wretched grief, what groans throughout the whole city walls, when miserable parents saw their sons hanging with outstretched bodies, exposed to the missiles.

[215] Their breasts heave with sobbing; their cries break forth in grief; tears stream beneath every helmet. Yet they do not therefore think the towers should be spared, nor do they take care to divert their own missiles.

And one man, hanging with his whole body stretched out, seeing his wretched father hurling stones at him, calls out in mournful lament; thus the son speaks:

[Col. 0467A] “What are you doing, unhappy, cruel, and pitiable father? At last look here; check the revolutions of your stones; hold back the missiles in your hand. You are not crushing an enemy: it is your son whom you seek to kill. Or, if Fortune forbids a father to spare his son, grant me some brief span of life, and let my most miserable mother come and first see hanging and prepared for death the one whom she bore.”

Thus that wretched man may have bewailed his fate to his father; and thus his anxious father may have answered him:

“Your image does not deceive me, son; nor, though I know you, do I unknowingly crush you with my hand. Wretched myself, I recognize you as wretched and hear you calling.

[Col. 0467B] Alas for natural affection! Yet I do not spare you. But cease to accuse your cruel father: it is not you, pitiable one, but the enemy—and towers erected for my destruction—that I attack with this storm of missiles. Love of country compels me. I would rather stand, torn to pieces, in your place, exposing my body to your stones.

“Your lot is less harsh: the engine will immediately shatter you with a blow of stone. We, a most miserable multitude, fear Teutonic arrogance, the king’s threats, and the anguish of a long death, now that liberty has already been lost.”

[245] Hardly had he spoken when a mass, discharged by the swift engine, struck the hanging man with a mighty blow and shattered him. Thus several boys underwent death; but all, exposed to fate, endured a terror harsher than death, hanging long in their pitiable condition.

Meanwhile the Ligurians, thinking the king so occupied by these great enterprises at the walls that he could give no help elsewhere or relieve his allies’ hardships, gather a host greater than before and prepare to overthrow Manerbio, a fortress not far from Cumae, scarcely capable of being taken by assault, in a sudden war.

[255] Gozwin, then acting as count by the emperor’s command, learned of these movements. A soldier long ago of Teutonic stock, summoned to imperial service, he had earned in those regions a noble name by his merits. He reports to the king the Ligurians’ purpose and their great preparations, prudently requests reinforcements from the prince for his own camp, gathers all whom that land possessed fit for such affairs, takes up arms, and attacks the men who threatened either to overthrow the now-besieged walls or bring death or chains upon the garrison. He throws them into confusion and, by a swift retreat, turns, bends back, and deceives their pursuit.

[Col. 0467D] Thus again and often the energetic count, by his own stratagem, outwits the Ligurians and delays their great undertaking, thinking this enough until the standards of the allied cohort and the soldiers bringing assistance from the prince should arrive.

Therefore, when the swift cavalry arrived in conspicuous armour—five hundred young men, the strongest strength of war—and reinforced his forces with their powerful aid, the Ligurians, imagining that more men, and Caesar himself as well, were present, fled headlong. In fear, abandoning the siege, they hurry to reach their own walls.

[275] The victor presses upon the terrified men; retaining their spoils, killing many and compelling others to bear chains, he did not refrain from the sword until, with the pivot turned and the enemy shut out, the gate received the fugitives.

Piacenza, already faithless through frequent deceits and malignant craft, had dared to provoke the pious king. For mad Piacenza was unwilling even to refrain from secret conferences among the Ligurians, and treacherously sent welcome supplies of food and arms to the condemned populace.

[Col. 0468B] Therefore Caesar, repeatedly offended by the people of Piacenza, declares them open enemies of the Empire. He judges this preferable to their concealing wicked poisons beneath honey and setting every hostile action in motion. No plague indeed is more industrious in doing harm than feigned affection and an enemy too intimate.

Crema too, the rebel city, its fear overcome, crushed by past evils and fearing future ones, had begun to return to itself after heavy punishment. Now, fearful and sad, its people acknowledge themselves less able to continue and no longer dare harass the men with their customary sallies.

[295] Yet, lest they should be entirely without harmful deceit, like mousetraps they spread snares and tenacious nets and stealthy devices of astonishing, invisible fraud—by a new art, and, I think, one hitherto less familiar—along every path and around the walls. [Note: Rs.—other manuscripts: “so that,” for “as if.”] Thus, if anyone incautiously places a foot insufficiently wary into the snare, before he can free himself the enemy is at hand, to cut him down or hold him captive.

Moreover, having hollowed out the ground with dense pits, they dug precipitous traps and covered hidden ditches with a light layer of earth, so that an unsuspecting enemy might fall into them and suddenly be exposed to the peril of death. [Note: “might perish by a sudden peril of death,” Pfl. +.]

[310] Provoked at last to avenging anger by these and other tricks which the crafty populace had accustomed itself to lay, Frederick hastens to put the finishing hand to the work. For the sixth month of winter cold had already passed while he kept the city shut in. Since all were exhausted and had long desired an end to the wars, he prepares by whatever means of war to storm the fortifications. It seems too slow to him to await famine, when he has prudently gathered abundant supplies from all the fields for the city’s prolonged needs.

[Col. 0469A] At once he brings up on wheels towers fortified on every side and made firm by their great weight, and stations them high upon the enemy embankment. Their upper levels are occupied by men whom either crossbow or bow, sending death from afar, makes dreadful to the enemy—men who have learned to hurl the javelin far with strong arms and to shoot an arrow with even greater force.

[325] Chosen brave men from the whole host, ready of hand, guard the lower platforms. While these assault the walls across open trenches with an extended bridge and attempt to break them, those occupying the high places harass the wretched citizens through the battlements with javelins and light arrows, lest they be able to come to the aid of the walls being broken down.

Then there is an easy downward view upon the towers below, and a light attack from on high upon the trembling enemy. [Note: “attempts,” B. +.] If they inadvertently try to turn their faces upward toward their own men, they are struck in the face by violent arrows. Nor is it possible, nor permitted, to know or see the author of the wound, whom the wooden platforms conceal safely in hiding. [Note: “heavy,” V. *.] From the hollow structures an air of arrows rains down from above, and deaths are poured forth from the whole sky.

[340] But missiles flying from the walls against our moving towers fly weakly and, their force slackened by the distance, barely graze the upper timbers with their iron. [Note: perhaps “and by the force of their course.”]

If engines happen to hurl swift firebrands against the wooden structures and fire clings to the towers, that blaze is immediately quenched by water poured down from above, or dies when sprinkled with wine. [Note: “vinegar,” B. ++.] Or, if it cannot be quenched and the hot flame rages with living sulphur, the smoking members are cut away with an axe, and the whole structure is saved by severing the affected part.

[350] The engines strike great millstones against the walls with thunderbolt-like violence, battering walls and roofs. The sling pierces the air with twisted lead, and missiles burn amid the yielding air.

[Col. 0469D] Others fill the ditches with earth thrown in and advance against the enemy walls beneath a dense tortoise-formation. Others undermine the towers and hollow out the strong foundations below; or, striking with hard timber, they drive against the walls and shake the weakened fortifications; or, having shifted stones from their place and broken the wall’s structure, they strive to remove the tightly packed stones with wedges. Or, as though making certain footsteps upon level ground, they struggle to reach the lofty battlements by the rungs of ladders, and fight at the same time. [Note: All editions: *apprehendere*, rejected by the metre.]

[365] Nor is the enemy less active: running everywhere, he receives now these men, now those who approach him; he thrusts the clinging ladders down from the high edge of the walls; strikes close adversaries with the sword, or crushes their temples with a hard pole; buries more distant assailants beneath a torrent of falling stones, or wounds them with javelins and a sure bow.

Anger boils with threats; on both sides the savage uproar grows fiercer; exhorting voices inflame their hearts. And as, when winds agitate the stormy sea, it assails a ship destined to perish in a wretched fate, the south winds tear its sails, a cloud mingled with hail rushes down, and afflicts the wretched sailors from the sky:

[Col. 0470B] waves leap upon it; the water, driven by mighty storms, beats the side; the loosened joints make the broken planking groan, and, drinking in the sea, its cracks gape open. The wretched sailors stand where the fiercer force presses and, thinking to bring aid there, attempt it with greater effort.

One, trembling, pours the salt water into the bilges and hastens to mend the gaping opening of a crack. Another supports the reeling ship as the waves toss it, by rowing and practised hand; contending with the sea itself, he breaks the waves with his oar. The sail resounds under the south wind, the men shout, the rigging creaks, the ship crashes in its shaking, and the water resounds with lamentations—

[390] until at last the tenth wave leaps upon it from the violent gulf and, overwhelming it, swallows the conquered vessel. [Note: “absorbs,” manuscript Rs.] For scarcely a brief time can you see its scattered fragments and planks floating upon the surface of the waters: one part perishes swallowed by the shipwreck; another, restored to the sky, swims out, and naked sailors come to shore.

So the unhappy populace, unaware of the approaching disaster, is brave in adversity and still resists unconquered. Now the towers had been brought as close as possible to the walls, long bridges had extended toward the fortifications, and the war-frenzied, courageous youth had planted their feet upon the very edge of the wall’s summit.
