[Col. 0470D] The defenders meet them and hurl darts, stones, and firebrands; they drive the men back with spears and stakes, throw them down to the ground, and cut down with the sword certain men who had bravely dared to leap onto the trembling walls with a light jump. Among them the fates of two men were as excessively bitter as they were pitiable.

One of them, while terrifying the frightened citizens by attacking them across their own walls—report called him Berctold [Note: Thus A.; other manuscripts: Bertolf.]—was the first to have thrown himself by a leap among the astonished enemy. [Note: P, ss. Rs., and RJo.: “enemies”; other manuscripts: “enemy.”]

[Col. 0471A] While all fled from one man and their fearful courage failed, an axe, stealthily swung from behind, struck his temples covered with yellow hair; [Note: P, ss. Rs., and RJo.: “with hairs”; other manuscripts: “with hair.”] the whole scalp was stripped from the severed head and placed upon the bright spear of his killer. Shading the enemy helmet with its hanging locks, it offered a cruel sign of unspeakable triumph.

The other, with hands and feet cut off by the sword—his name is not preserved, but his memorable disaster remains—rolled shamefully as a trunk upon enemy ground, quivering and providing a spectacle for his wretched fate. [Note: Sp. and R.: “in turn,” for “of the other.”]

[420] Yet the citizen did not go unpunished, nor did he enjoy his wicked joy long: on that same day he suffered the losses of a great disaster and fought for a long time in battle, but then, driven back in fear, withdrew into the inner citadel.

At last he had begun to distrust the assured success of his own affairs. He resolved to adopt measures of safety often previously neglected and to prefer the useful counsel of seeking peace to certain ruin. Without delay he requests a conference with the Saxon and with Peregrinus, whom wealthy Aquileia then possessed as a patriarch of exceptional and illustrious renown.

[Col. 0471C] The gentleness of their eloquent words soothes his ears; with polished speech he seeks pardon and excuses his offences in learned words: he had not taken arms from hatred of the kingdom or in rebellious sedition, but lest he should lament that his fate was subjected to proud enemies and arrogant Cremona. So long as possible, he had kept in faithful observance the treaties sworn with the Ligurian people; now, since the king commands it, he would at last sever that bond. [Note: Rs.—other manuscripts: “join himself,” for “sever.”] He would make no further delay. He asks only that the victor punish the guilty as he pleased and inflict whatever penalty he chose, provided that the defeated populace not be made a mockery for Cremona through the corruption of the prince.

When these terms were brought to the leader, the fierce anger of his mind subsided, and the familiar, domestic clemency well known to the great man moved his heart deeply. [Note: “terms,” Sp. and R. ++.]

[445] At once, with the assent of the nobles, he adopts a course so tempered that the unfortunate citizens need not grieve that pardon and life had been denied them, while punishment more lenient than was right should not encourage many others to a similar course. [Note: “fury,” pp. Rs. +.]

They are allowed to depart safely and unharmed from the abandoned walls, carrying on their shoulders whatever they can carry at one time; [Note: “together,” manuscript Rs. +.] they are ordered to leave everything else behind for the victor to seize.

[Col. 0472A] What mourning, I ask, was there? What clamour throughout all the town? What groans of the people, while the miserable citizens, burdened with few possessions and leaving much behind, bade farewell with their last words to their own walls, to the homes about to burn, and to beloved thresholds; while twenty thousand of the lamenting crowd left the sweet cradles in which their stock had begun and the dwellings cultivated by their parents.

But those whom either the Ligurian people or Brescia had sent as assistance to the besieged, stripped of all possessions and arms, were sent back in disgrace and sadness to their own cities, having scarcely received life alone from the prince. [Note: “at last,” manuscript Rs. +.]

[465] Immediately there is a rush for booty and the plundering of the walls, and the soldier grows rich with abundant spoil. Once every possession of the garrison had been seized, the towns collapse into ashes under flames; their towers overthrown and shattered, they pay for their former pride with destruction. [Note: Rs.—other manuscripts add “of the garrison,” etc.]

The victor turns his march toward the faithful fortifications of lofty Pavia and enters in his victorious camp the beautiful city accustomed to rejoice in his triumphs. It would require a poet to describe the joys of the people of Ticinum, Caesar’s celebrated triumphs, and the spectacle of the great applause; but I think that both this and much else must be omitted, sparing my cautious and feeble Muse.

[Col. 0472C] Elsewhere we have already described similar honours of devoted praise displayed to the king in the same city after your disasters, Tortona; therefore the present events seem to require passing over, lest the same matter be treated twice.

The Ligurian city still stood fast, clinging to its wicked purposes; it was not yet willing to desist from its undertaking, instructed neither by its own many disasters, nor by Crema’s recent fate, nor by your ruin, Tortona.

But since the land was now exhausted by two years of war and flourished less in crops and its customary abundance, since the enemy territory had been repeatedly drained by plundering, and since the needs of the immense multitude compelled the king still to spare his allies, he resolved, after dismissing the soldiers, to spare the despoiled land until the hungry field should again behold the returning sun, until the soil, sown with seed, should swell joyfully, until Bacchus should fill and swell the brimming cask, and his gifts return upon the branches of trees. [Note: P, ss. Rs., and RJo.: “return”; other manuscripts: “returns.”]

[Col. 0472D] Therefore, when the warlike companies stood gathered from every quarter, ears raised to receive his words, he stood in the midst of the assembly, handsome of face and serene, commanded silence with his hand and tranquil expression, and began to speak from on high in learned, eloquent words. His customary charm was present, and grace accompanied his noble voice, capable of great weight:

[Col. 0473A] “Comrades, I do not undertake to recount praises worthy enough of you, nor, even if the wisdom of great Nestor or the eloquence of Ithaca’s tongue were at my command, would I ever hope that praises conceived in my breast could equal your immense merits.

Yet, lest you perhaps judge me forgetful and ungrateful, I gladly offer you such thanks as the present occasion allows, however slight they may be; and I bid you expect greater rewards, if only life is granted me. Their proper times will come, and honour will be rendered to merit. You have given your anxious shoulders to bear the arduous burdens of the realm.

[515] You have often crossed the icy Alps with me and think it a small matter, now made customary by your action, to leave wives, native home, and children. Why should I recount the labours undertaken with ready spirit: those which Tortona gave, those at Asti, those of the earlier siege of the Ligurians, and the rebellion of the arrogant populace?

You have secured for me the supreme title of Empire and the diadem drenched in much bloodshed. Enduring pestilential air and pitiable deaths, you have experienced with united lot the hardships of your companions.

[525] And now, what sufferings have you endured for me at Crema, besieged in winter cold—whether from heaven or from the enemy? I gratefully remember these things and more, which no passage of time shall make me forget; and I rejoice to be debtor for an immense recompense, which I shall repay with full and accumulated interest.

We know, and retain inscribed in our remembering heart, those who have repeatedly stood forth at certain perils at our command: those whom it pleased to endure wars and harsh labours, and to maintain a cheerful countenance along with a cheerful heart amid the utmost evils; those who first dared to attempt the battles or bravely climb the wall. We have seen many such deeds with these present eyes and are ourselves true witnesses.

[Col. 0473D] I pray great thanks to the supreme King, who has deigned to sustain me by the devotion of my men. Others attract mercenary camps and hired companies for a fixed payment; [Note: manuscript Rs.: “may attract.”] I, trusting in unpaid aid freely and voluntarily offered, go safely to great enterprises, leading faithful bands into war.

[545] But now, because the land refuses sustenance, its enemy fields having been devastated on every side, and the ally who supplies provisions to the camps suffers more from his zeal than the enemy does from war, it is pleasing to take breath, disband the extended camp, send the companies back across the Alps, and spare the populace oppressed by constant expenditure—until the fields promise better, and the Ligurian new-ploughed lands, restored by cultivation, yield joyful crops.

When the year has been completed, at our summons, you shall all return to camp, if your loyalty remains as well known as it is now. Nor shall we renew war from the enemy city until, having experienced just threats and been overcome in war, it is handed over to your hands for plundering, mournful because its inhabitants have been proscribed; it shall lie utterly destroyed.”

[555] When he had delivered these words, full of royal force—or better ones—he praises all alike with gracious speech and magnifies the titles of their outstanding deeds. Then, if he recalls that any have done something illustrious or deserving lofty praise by their own hand, he addresses them royally, makes each man mindful of his own deeds, and declares himself mindful of them likewise.

[Col. 0474B] With generous hand he lavishly bestows great gifts upon the deserving: much silver and gold, goblets, basins, dishes, and large drinking-bowls. He adds swift horses, helmets, breastplates, and swords; woven fabrics laboriously embroidered with many kinds of images; and stamped coinage bearing the king’s broad image. He distributes the royal money among his companies.

Thus, after suspending one part of the camp’s labour, he dismisses them—happy with gifts, laden with distinctions, and promising ready strength for whatever should follow.

[Col. 0474C] I too, who have followed the camp not with weapons but with song, having thus far completed my share of this excellent labour, hope—if I have deserved the rewards of a soldier in the camp—that the great king’s favour will dismiss me neither without praise nor without gifts.

My services in this warfare are not to be despised—if only I may speak the truth. I do not think it more illustrious to have performed a few deeds well by hand than to recount many; nor is this labour less than that. What many have bravely done individually, I alone pursue in its entirety.

This alone also can win me fame, should other things be lacking: I prepare to make public the Pierian Muses, which for many ages have lain hidden and have not dared emerge from enclosed homes; to restore ancient brilliance to poetry and spur the slow poets.

[590] Indeed, by the splendid undertaking concerning the venerable Caesar and the imperial house, I seem to have earned their favour. From the broad sea of great affairs I have eagerly selected those deeds of his name which I preferred to write, lest darkness obscure deeds worthy of becoming known and splendid actions remain hidden.

Therefore, while this new Muse and this work of mine are read—unless eager hope deceives the poet—the world, Frederick, will admire your virtues.

[Col. 0475A] Perhaps someday, if Fame favours it, both the father and the noble offspring of the great parent will take this little book in hand, lend a kindly ear to its readers, and admit their own praises.

And now let these few poems which we have composed for the sacred court suffice; let the poet be permitted to breathe for a time while the standards of war are at rest and the soldier, dismissed from war, enjoys grateful leisure.

But when he is anxiously recalled and returns to camp, we too shall resume our interrupted undertaking with new labour, following the warlike battle-lines and camps. If life remains, we shall draw all the enterprises undertaken, in an unbroken thread and mindful of our purpose, down to our own times.

[Col. 0475B] Meanwhile let our Ligurinus hear silently what the court thinks of him, and let him honour the learned men, by whose affection he must be protected and fostered. Nor should he wish to hold his head high, even though one or two should find fault and mock his merit with hooked nose.

Each man ought to remember himself: we are not of lofty name; the court scarcely receives distinguished poets. Yet in this assembly there will perhaps be one, or two, or more, who will judge you, Ligurinus, worth reading and, once they have read you, and read you again, will favour you more. At last they may wish to carry your name and authorship, the distinctions you bear, and what you seek, to the prince’s attentive ears, and speak as friends. [Note: Rs.—same manuscript conjectures *putes*, i.e. *exputes*, “what you reckon/seek”; A and other manuscripts: “what you think.”]

[625] Whoever he may be who proves so gracious toward us, I pray that he may always rejoice in greater blessings and be upheld by the eternal love of the king.

Thus, when at last you stand as a new guest in the illustrious court and see the pious ruler’s offspring, like so many stars with the shining sun, these words will not seem foolish for you to utter:

“May that house rejoice, whose ruler makes the world rejoice; may the fortunate offspring rejoice with its August father; may it rejoice and command our father to rejoice. Nor may it suffer its poet to have ploughed his native shore in vain, to have broken useless new fields with deceived furrows, or to have cultivated in this service, through so many wakeful nights, light webs which the spider has woven.

[Col. 0476B] But whoever, through your testimony, reads the splendour of the deeds which he has written, may also know the reward of this noble work and that the labour has been gratefully and happily undertaken. For I am impelled to spread through the whole world the great deeds of Caesar and the praises of his sacred offspring.”

Having thus spoken beforehand, you may offer yourself to all for reading and spread your wings openly and fully. Then you will seek out that Solymarius of ours, to whom we earlier gave a slight gift as to a noble pupil. He will wonder that you, created scarcely in the fifth month after him, and as though cast forth by a miscarriage from the middle of the womb, have come to him as a brother in this new order.

[Col. 0476C] It is enough to have given these instructions. Go now; proceed cautiously; may fortune and a happy outcome attend your ventures.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1212: HELINAND, MONK OF FROIDMONT

[Col. 0477]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE

*(Oudin, On Ecclesiastical Writers, III.19)*

[Col. 0477A] Helinand, monk of Froidmont, was born to Herman, a noble Fleming who had fled into France. Helinand himself indicates this in his Chronicle under the year 1127, where he explains the cause: the death of Charles, count of Flanders, [Note: Surnamed “the Good.” See his Acts in *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, col. 943.] was avenged by the king of France; in that vengeance many innocent persons paid for what they had not taken. “Among them,” he says, “were my father Herman and his brother Elleband, noble and very handsome boys, who, having lost great inheritances, fled from Flanders into France.”

Helinand, therefore, noble by birth, keen and quick in intellect, handsome in face, elegant in body, and so richly endowed with every good of nature and fortune that no one in France was his superior and scarcely anyone his equal, was nevertheless exceedingly frivolous and inconstant. At last he professed as a monk at Froidmont.

[Col. 0477B] Writing under the name William to Walter, he describes himself as follows, in Vincent of Beauvais’s *Speculum historiale*, book XXIX, chapter 107, in *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, and in volume VII of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 318:

“To say nothing of myself, how many can I show you who have passed from a most luxurious life into this order, which you call most harsh, and yet have not fallen back from it, although they are younger than you in age, more delicate by nature, and weaker in strength? To take one from among so many thousands, I will put before you one man who certainly suffices by himself as an example to all.

“He became a spectacle to angels and men through the wonder of his sudden change, though formerly he had been a spectacle to them through the marvel of his frivolity: no stage, circus, theatre, amphitheatre, forum, street, gymnasium, or arena resounded without him. You know Helinand—if anyone knows a man, if indeed he is a man.

[Col. 0477C] “For he was no more born for labour than a bird for flying, going about the earth and walking through it, seeking whom he might devour either by flattery or by abuse. Behold: he is shut up in a cloister, he for whom the whole world once used to be not merely like a cloister but like a prison. How then can you not do what he can do?

“For he himself was no more frivolous than frivolity itself. Hence such great frivolity, so lightly changed, is thought by many to be nothing other than frivolity. Thus his conduct, now five years old, scarcely gives anyone confidence for the future: for in proportion as he gave proof of inconstancy in himself, so now he weakens the evidence for perseverance in constancy.”

Vincent of Beauvais, in the same place, chapter 108, under the year 1208, speaks words tending so greatly to Helinand’s praise that I cannot omit them here:

[Col. 0478A] “At this time, in the territory of Beauvais, there was Helinand, monk of Froidmont, a religious man and eloquent in speech. He composed, with elegance and usefulness—as is clearer than daylight—those verses *On Death* in our vernacular, which are publicly read. He also diligently arranged a Chronicle, from the beginning of the world to his own time, in a certain very large volume.

“This work has been broken up and dispersed, so that it is nowhere found complete. For it is said that Helinand lent some quires of that work to a close associate of his, namely Lord Guarin, bishop of Senlis, of blessed memory, and thus lost them entirely, whether through forgetfulness, negligence, or some other cause.

“Nevertheless, according to what I have been able to find, I have inserted many things from that work in different places in this work of ours also. Here I wished further to insert certain noteworthy matters from that work which have nowhere been set out above, and likewise matters from some of his other writings, from which I have extracted flowers.

[Col. 0478B] “For, as is read, he wrote an epistle entitled *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, sent to Walter, a cleric who had been a novice in the Cistercian order and a canon in the Premonstratensian order. Yet, considering himself free from the vow because he had not professed at all, he returned to secular life and married a woman named Rixenda.

“Asked concerning these matters by William, namely the brother of that same Walter, the companion and fellow-cloistered monk of Helinand himself, Helinand wrote a letter to Walter in the person of William himself, so that it appears to be William’s letter.

“Helinand also wrote certain excellent sermons. These, then, are the extracts I made from his aforesaid little works and have assembled here in one place,” etc.

John Tynemouth, an Englishman, says the same in his History, which he took word for word from Vincent of Beauvais, as William Cave records in his *Historia litteraria*, under the year 1212, p. 707.

[Col. 0479A] Moreover, in the *Library of Ancient Writers of the Cistercian Order*, which Bertrand Tissier, prior of Bonnefont in Thiérache, arranged to have printed in several folio volumes and which is sold in Paris by Louis Billaine, there appear in volume VII, p. 73, the following works of Helinand:

*A Chronicle from the year 635 to the year 1202.* Bertrand Tissier, in the preliminaries to the works of Helinand which he published, laments that only the final part of this Chronicle survives, and that this is merely the fourteenth part of the Chronicle which once existed. I think this is not true, but that Helinand’s Chronicle has reached us intact.

For this History, which still survives in the original manuscript—which was once sent to me from Froidmont and remained in my cell for three weeks while I was staying at Bucilly—is nothing other than some tables of various successions, such as patriarchs, kings of Israel, Persians, Medes, Assyrians, Romans, and others of that sort, from the beginning of the world. These contain almost nothing but names, and nothing historical; owing to the smallness and abrasion of the script, they can scarcely be read even by the sharpest and most attentive eyes.

[Col. 0479C] Hence, if this Chronicle contained forty-eight books, each book must have been very small and scarcely equal in size to the proper extent of the chapters of one and the same modern book. Add that such bare tables of names, or transcribed lists of successions, are today of no use or of only slight use.

But when I examined at leisure and carefully the original *History of Helinand the Monk*, which extends to the year 1203, I judged that it had been written in forty-eight books. Its first part, in sixteen books, would have treated summarily, as we said above and almost solely by lists of names, matters from the creation of the world to the times of Darius Nothus. The second, in the same number of books, would have treated the following periods somewhat more fully down to Christ’s birth. The third, in twelve books, would have extended from Christ’s birth to the year 636; the fourth, concerning the latest times, in four books, etc. Only this latter part, judged useful, was published.

[Col. 0479D] This, at least, was my conclusion from the original of Helinand himself, brought to me from the abbey of Froidmont to Bucilly in Thiérache of the Premonstratensian order. But after reading the catalogues of manuscripts in English libraries, published at Oxford in two folio volumes in 1696 and 1698, I became afraid that my conjecture on this point was false or uncertain.

For in the catalogue of manuscripts in the Cottonian Library, p. 40, col. 2, under the letter Claudius B., manuscript IX, no. 1, one reads: “First part of the Chronicles of Helinand, monk of the Cistercian order, from the creation of the world to the times of Darius Nothus and Archelaus, in sixteen books.” The manuscript appears to be of excellent authority and to have been written not long after Helinand’s lifetime.

Sermons by the same Helinand, ibid., p. 206, no. XXVIII, on various feasts and subjects. Several of these sermons, which you also have in manuscript at Froidmont together with his complete Chronicle, likewise survive in manuscript in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, shelf-mark R. R. 3. From this manuscript it is evident that Helinand remained for some time at Toulouse after his conversion, and there delivered sermons to certain scholars.

The little work *On Self-Knowledge*, ibid., p. 306, upon that oracle of Apollo, “Know thyself,” which Vincent of Beauvais transcribed in its entirety, as he himself admits above [Col. 0480B].

Helinand’s letter to the cleric Walter, written in the name of William, Walter’s brother, entitled *The Book on the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*, ibid., p. 316. Vincent of Beauvais also speaks of it; in manuscripts it is likewise called *The Book in Praise of the Cloistered Life*. In it, by praising the advantages of the cloistered and celibate life, he attempts to bring back Walter, a canon of the Premonstratensian Order, to the profession he had made, despite his scorned and abandoned wife Rixenda, whom he had openly married after his canonical profession.

Moreover, Anthony Loisel, in his *History of Beauvais*, published in French, writes that in 1594 he arranged for the printing [Col. 0480C] of Helinand’s French verses *On Death*. He extols and praises them highly in a prefatory letter to Lord Fouchet, First President of the Mint, containing Helinand’s life; from it he inserted several particulars into his aforementioned *Histories of Beauvais*. From these verses *On Death*, Anthony Loisel concludes that their author was very familiar with princes and various bishops because of his charming and lively wit—specifically Philip of Dreux, bishop of Beauvais; Henry of Dreux, his brother, bishop of Orléans; likewise Reginald, bishop of Noyon and count of Boulogne; and Geoffrey, bishop of Senlis.

Also extant under Helinand’s name are: *The Contest, or Martyrdom, of Saint Gereon and His Companions*, which [Col. 0480D] Surius published in volume V, under 10 October. [Note: [Col. 0479] It was subsequently reprinted and annotated in the Bollandist *Acts of the Saints*, October, vol. V.] It is quite worthy of reading because of its style, far more distinguished than that of the legends of other saints. Moreover, that Helinand was the author of this *Martyrdom* is also acknowledged by Caesar Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 10 October, in these words: “Of Gereon and his companions, whose Acts, excerpted from ancient tablets by Helinand, Surius has in vol. V.” So much for printed works; now for manuscripts.

He wrote a notable Commentary on the Apocalypse of John, drawn from the writings of earlier doctors. I have seen it twice in manuscript, bearing the author’s own name, in the library of Longpont, as [Col. 0481A] I said above. It is also found in the library of Morimond, of the same Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Langres; I have also seen it anonymously in the Royal Library of France.

Helinand sang most sweetly; hence the king of France frequently ordered him to recline at his table, as we learn from certain French verses cited by the Fourth Century of the University of Paris, p. 746, in its catalogue of distinguished academics. Therefore, being exceedingly dear to Philip Augustus, he also wrote at that king’s request a treatise or book *On the Government of Kings*, preserved in manuscript in certain Belgian libraries, as Charles Vischius reports. An anonymous copy exists in the Royal Library of France, manuscript 6608, at the beginning of which a few verses begin thus:

[Col. 0481B]

Every ministry that holds precedence in the wearied world  
Must be governed by skill; the gifts of skill are many, etc.

But the little work beginning, “After a Christian ruler has assumed the royal sceptre and the reins of the kingdom,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0481B] That the little work *On the Education of a King* contained in royal manuscript 6608 is wholly different from that which Vincent of Beauvais transmitted to us in part or in full is attested by M. Brial (*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XVIII, p. 99). He says that, at the head of the manuscript, these words are found, doubtfully written in a recent hand: [Col. 0482B] “Perhaps [the work] of Helinand, monk of Froidmont.”] Concerning this little work, the Chronicle of William of Nangis, under the year 1210, says: “Helinand . . . wrote . . . a book *On the Government of Princes*.”

[Col. 0482A]

Helinand died, as he had lived, most holy, in the year 1227. [Note: [Col. 0482B] Nothing certain can be determined concerning the year of Helinand’s death. Fabricius follows Oudin, but he does not say on what authority. Bulaeus gives the year 1212; Tissier, 1204. M. Brial conjectures that he was still alive in 1229 in the *Histoire littéraire de la France* (XVIII, 92).] Bellarmine and Labbe both discuss him in their respective books *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Anthony Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. I, fol. 721; and Charles Vischius in the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, pp. 140 and 142. It should be noted, however, that Gerard John Vossius made two men out of one Helinand, and fell into much the same error as Charles Vischius in his *Library*. Thus, in book II of *On Latin Historians*, ch. 54, p. 441, Vossius calls one “Elimand, monk of Froidmont in the district of Beauvais,” to whom he attributes a Chronicle composed in forty-eight books, after Vincent of Beauvais. Then in ch. 55, p. 445, he calls another “Helinard, monk of Froidmont,” [Col. 0482B] to whom, forgetting himself, he attributes a work of Histories in forty-eight books, beginning from the creation of the world. There is no one who would fail to recognize the error there—an error that may be frequent in a man attending to very many matters. Caesar Egassius Bulaeus, in the Fourth Century of the *History of the University of Paris*, fol. 746, and others mention him.

[Col. 0481]

# SERMONS OF HELINAND, MONK OF FROIDMONT

(D. Tissier, *Library of the Cistercian Fathers*, vol. VII, p. 206; Bonofonte, 1664, folio.)

## FIRST SERMON: ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0481C]

“His coming forth is prepared as the dawn, and he shall come to us as the early and the latter rain upon the earth” (Hos. VI).

The Catholic faith is accustomed, in these holy days, to celebrate and commemorate with annual devotion the four comings of the Savior to humankind, which are signified by the Sundays of this season: in the flesh, especially to the Jews; on the mountain, to the elect; in death, to individuals; and at the end, to all. The first is for redemption; the second for justification; the third for recompense; the fourth for judging the world by fire.

Of the first you have: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV)—that is, not as much as they have. [Col. 0481D] Of the second: “We shall come and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). Of the third: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. [Col. 0482C] XXVII). Of the fourth: “The Lord will come and bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (I Cor. IV). Of all alike is the text which we have set before us: “His coming forth is prepared as the dawn,” etc.

For of these four comings, the two outer ones—the first and the last—are bodily and visible; the two middle ones—the second and third—are spiritual and invisible. Therefore the outer two are not improperly called “comings forth,” and the middle two “rain.” For to go forth, as it were, from secrecy into public view is either to appear in passible flesh as passible, gentle, and humble, or visibly to present oneself in immortal flesh as judge. Yet the first of these two is called hidden because of the gentleness of humility in which incarnate divinity lay concealed; [Col. 0482D] whereas the other is manifest because of the judicial power of that same flesh, which the Son of Man will visibly exercise.

Concerning the concealment of the first advent, you have: “He is also a man; and who shall know him?”—that is, who shall recognize God in the man? Concerning the manifestation of the last, it is written: “God shall come openly; our God, and he shall not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX); again: “Every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. I). Therefore, as I have said, each advent is called a coming forth.

Of the first: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ” (Hab. III); again: “The sower went out to sow his seed” (Luke VIII). Of the other it is written: “The Lord shall go forth from his holy place” (Isa. XXVI). God’s place is mercy; his place is peace, according to the text: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV). From this place the Lord shall go forth in judgment, because God shall forget to show mercy and spare no one, when the Lord is roused as one asleep, [Col. 0483A] “like a mighty man overcome with wine,” to strike his enemies on the back and give them everlasting reproach (Ps. LXXVI). He shall come in fury and wrath; “fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. XLIX).

The saying here, “His coming forth is prepared as the dawn,” can be understood of either coming forth. Why “as the dawn”? Because dawn ordinarily drives away the darkness of night. What are the darknesses of night? In Sacred Scripture, night is taken in three senses: for ignorance, for guilt, and for misery. The first night has the darkness of error; the second, the darkness of wickedness; the third, the darkness of calamity. Of the first: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII). Of the second: “Those who sleep, sleep by night” (I Thess. V). [Col. 0483C] Of the third: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX).

Of all three alike is the saying: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the sanctuary, and bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII). That is to say: in the night of ignorance, against the darkness of error, seek the light of wisdom; in the night of guilt, against the darkness of wickedness, seek the light of righteousness; in the night of misery, against the darkness of calamity, seek the light of peace and spiritual joy. All this is Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God the Father. Since he is wisdom, he can enlighten your ignorance; since he is power, he can heal your weakness—that is, remit guilt and confer grace; since [Col. 0483D] he is Christ, that is, Anointed and Sweet, he can anoint you with the oil of gladness with his companions and utterly wipe every tear from your eyes.

Christ drove away the first darkness of these three nights at his first Advent by his word, preaching truth; the second, by pouring charity into the hearts of believers; the third, by bringing peace to all. Of the first: “It is the time to seek the Lord, when he comes, who will teach us righteousness” (Hos. X). Of the second and third: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Ps. CXXI). To all of them belongs: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John VIII).

And this light is rightly compared with dawn, [Col. 0484A] because, just as dawn gradually increases until it advances into brightness and reaches heat, so faith in the Lord’s Incarnation first became known to very few; then it spread more broadly through the world; finally, it grew warm even to the ardor of martyrdom. Dawn has three stages: the rising of the emerging aurora, which is the rising of Lucifer; the brightness of morning; and the heat of noon. Of the first:

> Now the star of light has risen.

Of the second and third:

> With morning brightness you instruct,  
> And noon with fires.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Church hymn.]

Thus faith in the Lord’s Incarnation, with all its sacraments, was first proclaimed, then proved, [Col. 0484B] and thirdly defended. First it was proclaimed by simple preaching; then proved by reason; thirdly defended even by blood. It was proclaimed by fishermen; proved by converted philosophers and rhetoricians; defended by martyrs of both sexes and every age. It was proclaimed against those erring through ignorance; proved against those who resisted deliberately; defended against those persecuting out of envy. In the first stage it was like the rising of emerging dawn; in the second, like morning brightness; in the third, like the heat of noon.

The final Advent of Christ will also illumine these three nights and expel their darkness. For when Christ comes for judgment, he will drive away the night of ignorance [Col. 0484C] when the book is opened—that is, the secrets of hearts; the night of guilt, when all workers of wickedness are cast into the lake of burning fire and sulfur (Rev. XX); and the night of misery, when God wipes every tear from the eyes of the saints (Rev. XXI). This dawn too will increase through its stages. It will be like the rising of emerging dawn when bodies are raised from the dust; like morning brightness when good and evil are separated to the right and left; like burning noon when these are taken up and those left behind.

Therefore he says: “His coming forth is prepared as the dawn,” as though he openly said: Just as, in the natural and established course of times, it is impossible that dawn should not follow night, [Col. 0484D] so, in the order of divine disposition, it is impossible that the Son of God, to be incarnate for our redemption and for the judgment of humankind, should not come.

It follows: “And he shall come to us as the early and latter rain upon the earth” (ibid.). Just as what precedes, the comparison with dawn, signifies the two bodily advents, so what follows, the comparison with early and latter rain, designates the two spiritual ones. For Christ is like the early rain when he justifies the ungodly; like the latter rain when he rewards the righteous. For, as Jerome says, literally the early rain makes the seeds that have been sown take root; [Col. 0485A] the latter rain brings fruits to maturity. Faith working through love makes the sown seeds take root; righteousness rewarding the righteous brings fruit to maturity: the fruit of righteousness in eternal life, the fruit of corruption in everlasting death.

But if the coming forth of the Savior who is to come and save us is prepared, how much more must we prepare ourselves to meet him! As it is written: “Be prepared, Israel, to meet your Lord, for he comes” (Amos IV). Let us therefore prepare, as John says, the way of the Lord; let us make straight the paths of our God (Matt. III). For to be prepared to meet the Lord and already to have prepared the way for the coming Lord are one and precisely the same thing.

Yet it is not written, “Prepare a way for the Lord,” [Col. 0485B] but “the way of the Lord.” Every way by which God comes to a human being is God’s way, not a human being’s. And what are the ways of the Lord? “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). The first two advents, which occur in flesh and mind, are in the way of mercy; the second two, occurring in death and at the end, are in the way of truth. To redeem souls held captive under the devil and to justify the ungodly from sin are works of immeasurable mercy, and of divine mercy alone. But to render to each according to merits and judge the world through the conflagration of material fire are works of truth and judgment, and of almighty God alone.

These two ways must be prepared. Do you wish to prepare for yourself the way of mercy? [Col. 0485C] Be merciful yourself. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Do you wish to prepare the way for judgment? Judge yourself justly. For if we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged. “With the judgment,” he says, “with which you have judged, you shall be judged” (Luke VI), before the supreme Judge.

Mercy is never without truth, nor truth without mercy. Therefore, if his mercy and truth are to save you, let mercy and truth not abandon you: mercy toward your neighbor, truth toward yourself. Mercy, that you may spare your neighbor; truth, that you may punish yourself. For if you punish yourself, you will show mercy to yourself, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX).

There are four obstacles [Col. 0485D] that make roads difficult: mud, stones, hills, and pits. Mud defiles; stone injures; hill wearies; pit throws down. By stones and mud are signified crime and disgraceful vice; by hills and pit, pride and hypocrisy. Against the first two it is written: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” (Prov. III): beautiful, without defilement; peaceful, without stumbling-block. Beautiful, that they may not be defiled; peaceful, that they may not be injured. Holy wisdom does not give itself to dogs, nor pearls to swine. It hates the garment of the body that is stained, and does not enter into a malicious soul. Therefore blessed Benedict commands us to return the vessels of our ministry to the cellarer clean and sound: clean from disgraceful vice, sound from crime.

Of the final two, Truth says in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens [Col. 0486A] and birds of the air nests” (Luke IX). Foxes are the deceitful, hypocritical, and crafty; birds, the frivolous and proud. Unless we cleanse our hearts and bodies of these four things, the Son of Man will find in us nowhere either to place his foot or to lay his head.

## SERMON II. I. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV).

Truly blessed is the earth from which Truth has sprung; and more blessed than heaven itself, from which falsehood once sprang—namely, when that false Lucifer descended from heaven, he who rose in the morning and already threatened ruin because he meditated pride, saying in his heart: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne. I shall sit [Col. 0486B] upon the mountain of the Testament, on the sides of the North; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

Truly a false Lucifer, when wickedness thus lied to itself, promising itself what was false and impossible. For “who among the clouds shall be made equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII). “O God, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God,” from casting down this Lucifer, who in the presence of your majesty produces so many and such bombastic, foot-and-a-half words; who sings not Priam’s fortune, but the glory of his own beginning, and declares noble war upon you. “I shall be like the Most High,” he says. Wickedly desirous, he sought likeness to divinity in honor and glory, not in goodness and righteousness.

Most wretched one, why do you not say, “I shall be like the most righteous,” or “the most holy,” as you say “the Most High”? [Col. 0486C] You would not unjustly usurp that likeness, but would rightly and happily seek it. Indeed, the Most High commands it to every rational spirit, saying: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” “I shall ascend into heaven,” he says (Lev. II). Yet you were in heaven when you said this. Why did you disdain that height of heaven and seek a higher height? Because the saying is true:

> “This is peculiar to all ambition: it does not look to the end. No one gives thanks for the tribunate; rather, he complains that he has not been advanced as far as the prefecture.”  
> —Seneca

But you, most miserable one, had been created in a prefecture and did not give thanks for it; instead, insatiable even in the depths, you sought the monarchy of your own Creator. “I shall ascend into heaven,” he says; “above [Col. 0486D] the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne; I shall sit upon the mountain of the Testament, on the sides of the North; I shall be like the Most High.” What outcome worthy of so gaping a promiser will this produce?

> Mountains shall be in labor; there shall be born a laughable—not a mouse, but a dragon—to be fashioned to mock him.

Truly a false Lucifer, who is a liar and the father of lies. He sins from the beginning and did not stand in truth. Though he is wholly dark, he is nevertheless called Lucifer by antiphrasis, just as a grove (*lucus*) is so called from shining (*lucendo*) because it shines least of all. Or perhaps, so that his name may be derived from the thing itself, he is called Lucifer as one inflicting violence upon light, taking light away, ever hostile to light. For he inflicted violence on light—that is, tried to inflict it—when he wished to make himself equal to the Creator. He took away, or rather stole, light when, through envy, he harmed humankind. He is ever hostile to light [Col. 0487A] because he struck a covenant with death and made a pact with hell: that he might not return to the light, but, having fallen once, might never rise again.

For, blinded by the smoke of ambition rising high but falling back upon him, as though finding no place to which it might rise further, he was unable to foresee his own ruin. Suddenly his own iniquities seized him and he could not see; at his very rising he was compelled to experience that Davidic saying: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up.” A wholly just downfall for the presumptuous one, who, despising the privilege of angelic rank and impatient of divine subjection, would not be subject to every created spirit unless he were equal to the Creator himself. A new Caesar against God, a Pompey against the angel, as in the line:

[Col. 0487B]

> Nor can Caesar now endure any predecessor,  
> Nor Pompey any equal.

Therefore, having fallen under the excessive weight of his presumption, he fell from heaven like lightning, Truth saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X). By saying “I saw” and “falling,” joining the present time to the past imperfect, he indicates that the devil has not yet fallen completely but is still falling until the day of judgment; then, weighed down by the mass of his crimes, he is to be submerged like lead in the violent waters of the hellish abyss.

Thus he is said to have fallen like lightning: that is, unexpectedly and swiftly, violently, heavily, with excessive heat, stench, and smoke. These three are evident signs of lightning and most familiar traces of the dragon. For the fire-breathing dragon exhales fire with his breath, corrupts the air, and darkens the light, like that smoke-producing serpent of whom the poet says:

> Tearing open its greedy jaws, it gives forth smoking vapors.

Likewise the devil, before he was cast from heaven like lightning, was cast down as a dragon. With a threefold pestilence he breathed upon the whole world: namely, by instilling through his viperous mouth into the first parents desire for evil, like excessive heat and stench; and ignorance of good, as though scattering dust, mist, and smoke. This smoke and mist later increased so greatly that at the Savior’s birth they covered the whole earth, as the prophet says: “Looking from afar, behold, I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth.” [Note: [Col. 0487D] Words of the Church.]

And truly a cloud had covered the whole earth at the rising of Truth, when almost the entire world still did not know the true and living God, but worshipped false and dead gods, revered deaf and mute idols, neither sought true and eternal goods nor fled evils, did not believe that the world was governed by providence, and attributed even all voluntary human acts, on false grounds, either to fate or to fortune.

Hence came Plato’s and Pythagoras’s error concerning the revolutions of souls; that of Trismegistus and Mima, Socrates and Porphyry, concerning association with demons; that of Zeno and Chrysippus concerning voluntary death; that of Aristotle concerning limited providence—namely, extending as far as the lunar region [Col. 0488A] but no lower; that of Epicurus, concerning no providence at all and the supreme good of bodily pleasure; that of Ptolemy, concerning fate; and that of almost all alike, especially Cicero and Seneca, concerning the claim that punishment of souls after death is not to be feared.

These are those who say in Ezekiel: “The Lord has abandoned the earth, and the Lord does not see” (Ezek. VIII); and in Zephaniah: “The Lord will do neither good nor evil” (Zeph. I); and in Isaiah: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII). Hence comes that complaint of Boethius in the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> Governing all things by a fixed end,  
> You reject human acts alone.  
> Why then does fickle Fortune  
> Turn such great changes?

[Col. 0488B]

For this reason Hosea cries out: “There is no mercy, no truth, no knowledge of God in the land” (Hos. IV). And the Psalmist, as though suffering violence: “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished among the children of men” (Ps. II).

Therefore, to remove from the earth the clouds, errors, and smoke of ignorance; the heats of anger and fires of avarice; the stench of lust and the filth of idolatry, today Truth has sprung from the earth and righteousness has looked down from heaven. As a sign of this, all the images of Egypt fell together at the approach of the infant Jesus fleeing there, as Isaiah had long before prophesied: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and all the images [Col. 0488C] of Egypt shall be moved” (Isa. XIX).

This collapse began today in Rome with Romulus’s palace, the image of the city of Rome, and the Temple of Peace: three things which fell in Rome on this day. The collapse of Romulus’s palace was a sign that worldly glory was to fall through Christ. The collapse of the image of the city of Rome, which took the form of a certain enormous and very corpulent woman, was a sign that avarice was to be destroyed through Christ. For the corpulence of this bronze image signified the avarice of the Romans, long reigning already, which, like some unfillable abyss and insatiable gulf, had swallowed up the riches of the whole world and could not be filled even when the entire world had been registered under one census.

Nor is it surprising that Romans reared on wolf’s milk should either formerly have been, or still be, so rapacious. As the common saying goes, [Col. 0488D] foxes change their coats, not their habits. And:

> Drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will always return.

But this avarice began to be destroyed through Christ when, through him, the poor began to receive the Gospel. The same image had signified this when it was first erected. For when some criticized its legs as too slender and insufficient for sustaining the weight of so great a bronze mass, it is reported to have replied through magical art: “I shall not fall until a virgin gives birth.” Romulus is likewise said to have declared this of his palace when it was first built; he too was a magician. Because of these two utterances of demons, treated as gods, [Col. 0489A] Rome was formerly called eternal.

Moreover, the collapse of the Temple of Peace signified that the pleasure of the flesh—in which alone the world’s peace consists—was to fall through him who says: “I came not to bring peace upon earth, but a sword” (Matt. X). As a sign of the same thing, today a young virgin appeared seated in the sun, holding an infant in her lap, signifying that celibates alone will reign in heaven and that today, from the womb of the Virgin, has arisen the teacher of celibacy, to teach human beings to castrate themselves with the iron of the fear of the Lord for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore the collapse of the temple, image, and palace, by and for which false gods were worshipped, signified that today Truth has sprung from the earth; while the virgin seated in the sun signified that today righteousness has looked down from heaven. For what is more just than that each person [Col. 0489B] should possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God?

“Truth,” he says, “has sprung from the earth.” What is truth? This was once Pilate’s question (John XIX), though he did not deserve to hear the solution to his question because he did not wait for the answer; after putting the question and not awaiting the answer, he immediately went out to the Jews.

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to learn from Truth itself what truth is, let us not go outside—that is, let us not seek external and transitory goods—but remain within the praetorium of the heart, listening to what the Lord God speaks within us. For the word is near, in our heart and in our mouth:

> Do not seek yourself outside.  
> We seek to live well by ships and chariots; what you seek [Col. 0489C] is here.  
> —Persius

Let us not go outside like Satan, who went forth from the face of the Lord (Job I); or Cain, first a farmer and afterwards a fratricide (Gen. IV); or Ishmael, who was a wild man and an archer, deprived and exiled from his father’s inheritance; or Esau, a hunter and persecutor of his simple brother. Rather, let us remain within—that is, let us guard our heart with all vigilance—first seeking the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all externally necessary things shall be added to us in abundance (Matt. VI). Woe to the foolish virgins, who must be left outside, and for no other reason than that they abandoned the guarding of their heart (Matt. XXV).

What is truth? Truth is called, as it were, the word of a thing that exists, understood in the way in which it is spoken. [Col. 0489D] For the truth of any thing is nothing other than the equality of its existence: when the mind comprehends a thing as it is, neither falling short nor overflowing beyond it. Whoever speaks truth says only and entirely what is in the thing, neither more nor less. For if one said more or less, one would not speak truth but falsehood, because one would say what did not belong to the thing’s existence and therefore not to its truth.

Truth, then, is the equality of the existence of things: that is, the measure below or beyond which nothing at all can subsist. But this equality of the existence of things is nothing other than the equality of unity. For equality, as also unity, is in individual [Col. 0490A] things the form and cause of being, through which each thing subsists.

For just as whatever exists truly exists because it is one—for if it were not one, it would not be something; and if it were not something, it would be nothing—so whatever exists truly exists because it is equal to the one. For if it were not equal to the one, it would not be one. Therefore truth, that is, equality, is in individual things the form of being and the cause through which each thing subsists.

But if truth is the cause of the existence of things, and every cause is prior to that of which it is the cause, then truth is prior to every creature; therefore it is eternal; therefore it is the principle of things; therefore it is God. Unity, then, and its equality are one cause of all things, one principle of things, and one God, Creator of all; [Col. 0490B] of altogether the same power and wisdom, therefore of the same substance.

But the Father’s unity is the Son, who is also the Word, Truth, Splendor, and Figure of God’s substance. He is not improperly called the Word because he decrees to be whatever truly is; Truth, because whatever he says once, he confirms and establishes, as it is written: “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time” (Job XXXIII); Splendor, because through him the name of the Father is made manifest—that is, knowledge of the Father is obtained—as the Psalmist says: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). Hence he himself says: “Father, I have made manifest your name to the people whom you gave me” (John XVII). He is called the Figure and Image of the Father because he perfectly represents the Father’s beauty.

For he is the Father’s face, into which angels always desire to look [Col. 0490C] (I Pet. I)—that is, to behold from afar, for from nearby they could not do so because of the immensity of his brightness. Therefore he is also said to inhabit light. He is called Son because he is truly begotten. But if you ask how: certainly in the way equality proceeds from unity, splendor from light, the truth of the Word from the Father, and the word of the heart from the heart, by equality of existence.

For unity generates from itself and from its own substance nothing other than equality; into equality, however, through the other numbers. For one times one is nothing other than one. All these are coeval and coequal with those who beget them; they differ not in substances but in properties. Therefore the Son is in every respect equal [Col. 0490D] and coeternal to the Father.

Where, then, is the foolish disputation of unhappy Arius, asserting that the Son is less than the Father and failing to attend to the implications of its own arguments? Moreover, since this very truth is the equality of the existence of things, and the measure below or beyond which nothing can subsist, it is therefore righteousness. For righteousness is nothing other than steadfastness of measure and equality established between more and less, suffering no deficiency at all and producing no excess. And what is this righteousness itself other than supreme blessedness, or the highest good?

For Boethius defines supreme blessedness as a state perfected by the aggregation of all goods. But this state cannot be contained outside the bounds of justice. [Col. 0491A] The same Boethius proves that two distinct supreme goods cannot exist. For if one has less than the other, it will not be supreme. Therefore one of the two must either be imperfect or superfluous. Supreme blessedness may therefore be defined otherwise in this way: the totality of goods comprehended under one reality, the vision of which, once attained, produces in the beholder every sufficiency of delight and fullness of joy, surpassing every desire without diminution, satisfying without weariness, renewing and inflaming without anxiety.

Truth, therefore, is the supreme good, and likewise justice. Thus the supreme good sprang up from the earth when “Truth sprang up from the earth”; and the supreme good came from heaven when “Justice looked down from heaven.” But [Col. 0491B] Christ calls himself Truth in the Gospel (John 14), not Justice. He did this, I think, because the name justice suggests something of severity and vengeance; and because Christ had come to be judged, not to judge; to minister, not to be ministered to (Matt. 20); to spare, not to strike; to show mercy, not to exact vengeance; to soothe, not to terrify. Therefore he chose to attribute to himself nothing that sounded harsh, but that which was wholly of peace and forgiveness, sweetness, gentleness, and loving-kindness: thus he called himself not Justice, but the Way and the Life. Yet the Apostle says that he was made for us by God wisdom, justice, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1); and he expounds this thus: wisdom in preaching, justice in conduct, [Col. 0491C] sanctification in the remission of sins, redemption in death.

But the Psalmist, knowing that it belongs properly to justice both to merit and to render, and that both our merit and our reward come from Christ alone, called him Justice. Christ, however, in place of that single name set these two, Way and Life, saying: “I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life” (John 14). The Way because of merit, Life because of reward, Truth because it embraces both: the way of justice, the truth of doctrine, the life of joy; the way of virtue, the truth of speech, the life of blessedness; a way without stumbling-block, truth without cloud, life without weariness; a way neither impeded nor defiled; truth neither deceiving nor deceived; life neither injured nor ended. The way directs, truth corrects, life governs. It directs actions, [Col. 0491D] corrects excesses, governs affections. It is a way for the righteous by example, truth for the wicked by judgment, life for angels through itself. For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself; and gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man (John 5).

Therefore Christ is the Way in this world, Life in the world to come, Truth in both; here promising, there giving; here threatening, there striking. Let this suffice concerning Truth which sprang up from the earth. Now let us consider the earth from which it sprang. “Truth,” he says, “sprang up from the earth.” O how true is the common saying: “Good comes from the earth!” But what is this earth? For we read in Scripture of two kinds of earth. There is earth that is cursed, desert, and barren; and earth that is blessed, [Col. 0492A] fruitful, and rich. Of the first it is said: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3); of the second: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land” (Ps. 88).

The first kind is threefold: among cursed lands, one is the earth we fear, another that which we tread upon, another that which we carry. The first is hell, which the prophet calls “the furthest land” (Ezek. 26), that is, beyond which there is none. Truly cursed earth, full of sins and torments, guilt and suffering: all its guilt unremissible, all its punishment endless, all its weeping inconsolable, all its stench intolerable, all its gnashing implacable, all its burning unquenchable, all its worms immortal. This is the land of the dead, in which everything is contrary to life.

The second [Col. 0492B] earth is the common earth which we tread: cursed in Adam’s work. Every fruit of it is naturally cursed, as Truth testifies in the parable of the sower, where he says: “What fell among thorns are those who hear; and, going their way, they are choked by the riches and pleasures of this life, and bear no fruit” (Luke 8). Now it is evident that all earthly riches come from the fruits of the earth: wheat, wine, oil, gold, silver, precious stones, and things of that kind. If, then, earthly goods are thorns, what must evils themselves be? How indeed are they not thorns, when in coming they sting sharply, in remaining more sharply, and in departing most sharply? For they are acquired with much anxiety and great labor, guarded with fear, [Col. 0492C] and lost with grief.

And because a curse is originally inherent in all earthly fruits on account of Adam’s sin, the holy and catholic Church—having this institution from the Lord himself—has wisely and beneficially ordained that whenever we approach the table to refresh ourselves with earthly fruits, we should first give thanks to God; invoke his holy name over them; and, making the sign of the life-giving cross, as of the tree of life against the forbidden tree, drive away the curse by blessing. Then, with fear of the Lord, we may safely take them, now cleansed and sanctified, afterwards giving thanks to their Giver for the divine gifts received.

For those who, without blessing and preceding prayer, apply themselves to devouring earthly fruits like [Col. 0492D] beasts of burden or cattle often find in them the occasion of death for body and soul. So that holy woman who, biting a lettuce, bit the devil sitting upon it, and from that bite at once became mad, as blessed Gregory testifies in the book of the *Dialogues*. So too that Tarquinius who had ordered blessed Sylvester to be imprisoned was choked by a fishbone caught in his throat. And so also that rich man who sat at the table of the king of England, whom the king suspected of the death of his brother: holding a morsel in his hand, he said to the king, “My lord king, if I am guilty of, or privy to, the murder of your brother, may I never be able to swallow this morsel without being choked by it.” Having said this, he put the morsel into his mouth; [Col. 0493A] when it reached his throat, it stuck fast, and he immediately rolled his eyes and fell dead upon the table.

Therefore blessed Benedict commands in the *Rule* [Note: [Col. 0493D], ch. 43] that no one presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour. This that unhappy monk did not observe well. While carrying certain fritters into the refectory, drawn away and enticed by his own appetite for gluttony, he quickly devoured one of them like a rabid dog. At once he felt so great an itch of lust in his flesh that, since he could not otherwise fulfill the foul desire—something shameful even to speak of—he shed the seed of his genitals by manual act; something which had never happened to him before. Truly, to this wretch the unhappy Judas’s saying is aptly applied: “And after the morsel Satan entered into him” [Col. 0493B] (John 12). Nor is it surprising. If the first-created humans, through disobedience, found in the fruit of paradise—which certainly was not cursed but only forbidden—the occasion of death of body and soul, how much more must we fear that the fruits of the cursed earth, all of which are originally cursed, may become for us, through our misuse, an occasion of both deaths?

Further, the third earth, namely that which we carry, is our flesh; and it too is certainly originally cursed, because of the words, “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3). This curse is to be understood allegorically not only of the earth that we tread, but also of that which we carry, thus: “Cursed,” he says, “is the earth in your work,” that is, cursed is the earth in which and from which you will work, seeking in it either [Col. 0493C] the sustenance of life or the heir of your death. The earth in which Adam was to work in seeking an heir was the flesh of his own wife; the earth from which he was to work in it was his own flesh. Thus the flesh both of male and female was mortally wounded by one dart of curse when it was said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work.”

What is this work to be understood as but sexual intercourse? Even in marital union it did not escape this curse which follows: “When you have worked the earth, it shall not give you its fruits” (ibid.), that is, such fruits as it would have given had you remained obedient. For every flesh born from you would have been born holy, not resisting the spirit nor desiring against [Col. 0493D] it, but rather wholly following it in whatever things are holy, praiseworthy, and of good report. But now it shall produce thorns and thistles for you, because with the goad of the flesh and the burning of lust, with the preface of shame and the irreparable loss of virginity, you and your descendants shall bring forth. And “in the sweat of your face”—that is, in the resistance of your strong spirit desiring against your flesh—“you shall eat your bread”: you shall keep my commandments, perfect justice, fulfill my will; you shall be fed with the bread of tears, and eat the bread of angels in heaven.

Thus the earth that we carry is necessarily subject to a curse, according to the Apostle: [Col. 0494A] “For good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7). And again: “The prudence of the flesh is death” (Rom. 8). And: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (ibid.). Therefore the saying, “Truth sprang up from the earth,” cannot be understood of any of these three earths: neither of the earth of the dead, which is hell; nor of the earth of the dying, called earth, ground, soil, or dust; nor of the earth of mortals, which is the mortal body. Rather it is understood of the blessed earth of which it is written: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land” (Ps. 98), which itself is to be understood threefold: namely, as the desirable earth, the entreatable earth, or the adorable earth.

The desirable earth is that heaven—whatever it may be—to which the Apostle was caught up, [Col. 0494B] where true unutterable things are heard and unspeakable joys are hidden. This earth truly is blessed earth, lacking every curse—that is, punishment and sin—the land of the living, into which whoever enters once lives forever. It is fruitful earth, from which manifold fruit has descended to us: the sweet consolations of angels appearing visibly; the most health-giving commandments of the divine law; Christ’s visitation; the Father’s testimony; the anointing of the Holy Spirit. Angels appeared in order that the law might be ordained, as it is written: “The law was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 5). The law was written so that sin might be put to death. “For through the law comes knowledge of sin.” Christ visited us so that sin might be taken away, as [Col. 0494C] it is written: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The Father bore testimony so that people might believe in the Son, as it is written: “But I have testimony greater than John’s” (John 5). The Holy Spirit was sent so that, in place of the Lord’s bodily absence, another Paraclete might be given to believers, to remain with them forever, as it is written: “I shall ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14).

Woe to those who account this desirable earth as nothing. And who are they but those who think much of this barren earth that we tread or carry? If contempt and rejection of this desirable earth is reckoned a most grievous sin to the Jews, to whom these earthly, fleeting, [Col. 0494D] and transitory goods had been specially promised, what will become of us, who have been commanded to despise earthly things and desire heavenly ones? Let us therefore desire, desire, I beseech you, the desirable earth, which surpasses every desire, transcends every prayer, exceeds every merit, and shows every price to be nothing in comparison with itself.

Further, the entreatable earth—that is, worthy to be prayed to and easy to entreat—is the Virgin Mary: blessed earth, sanctified from the womb, impregnated by the Holy Spirit, lacking every curse; conceiving without loss of modesty, giving birth without pain, dying without fear, living without sin. This is the promised land flowing with milk and honey: that is, bringing forth for [Col. 0495A] us the promised Savior, milky in his humanity and heavenly in his life; white in innocence, sweet in forgiveness, abundant in mercy, outstanding in justice, little in humility, sublime in power; a tiny child in the manger and most lovable, great in heaven and most praiseworthy.

This earth, drinking upon itself the coming rain of the Holy Spirit—the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance (Ps. 67)—was filled with every spiritual blessing in heavenly things in Christ. Watered like the paradise of God, it brought forth for us every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food: the price of our redemption weighed in the balance of the cross; the threefold fruit, namely the pattern of all justice and exemplar of perfection, like [Col. 0495B] the tree of life in the midst of paradise; and the greatly necessary aid of most powerful intercession, like a fountain divided into four places or times: first, in the fall into sin, that we may immediately rise again through repentance; second, in the state of innocence, that we may not fall again through sin; third, at the departure of the soul, that we may be delivered from those roaring and prepared for prey; fourth, at the pronouncement of judgment, that we may experience a less long or severe punishment of purgatory than we have deserved.

O truly fertile earth, which bears such great and such excellent fruits! This is the land of the living, that is, of penitents. For just as sin, when consummated, produces death, so repentance, when consummated, restores life. “For on whatever day the sinner groans, he shall be saved.” And just as “the soul that sins, it shall die,” so: “When the wicked man turns from his wickedness which he has done, and performs judgment and justice, he shall live and shall not die.” “I do not will the death of the sinner,” he says, “but that he be converted and live” [Col. 0495C] (Ezek. 8). Blessed are the living who have been planted in this earth and will thereafter suffer neither hunger nor want; but more blessed are those who have been made fruitful from this earth and have now been sent into its possession, who will thereafter hear no accusations, whether from human beings or demons.

The Cistercians are planted in this earth: they render homage to this great lady and profess her perpetual service. For our Order has chosen her alone as its advocate, and decreed that all its churches be entitled in her name. Those who die in our Order with a good conscience receive this earth as a fief and are sent into its possession. And as we provide this queen security of our service in our profession, so she provides us security for our fief in her charter—that is, in the briefs made for the dead—where the sweet name of Mary and the confirmation of her same inviolable seal are recited thus: “On that day died brother N., monk or lay brother of Saint Mary of Froidmont.” [Col. 0496A] The recitation of this instrument alone restrains every wickedness of an accuser, shuts every mouth that speaks iniquity, settles every lawsuit, and establishes every possession.

And it should be known that this earth from which Truth sprang can also be understood as that heaven from which Justice looked down upon us: heaven through loftiness of life; through cleanness and purity of body and soul; through serenity of conscience; through the two great lights, that is, great examples of each life, namely the active and the contemplative; an exalted throne through the arduous newness of vowed virginity; raised high through the uniqueness of the spiritual gift, that is, the fruitfulness of the womb; starred with as many stars as it is illumined by virtues, adorned with as many gifts of grace. But now let us consider the adorable earth. This is Christ’s humanity, which I call adorable because of [Col. 0496B] the Psalmist’s words: “Adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Ps. 98). This is earth free from every curse of sin, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). This is earth full of every blessing, “from whose fullness we all receive” (John 1). To it the Spirit was given, not by measure, as to those adopted, but in overflowing abundance, as to the Only-begotten. The whole casket of paternal anointing was poured out upon him, according to the words: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1).

O fragrant name, steeped in the entire abundance of heavenly balm! O most fetid nostrils, blocked by deadly nasal polyp, which do not perceive the sweetness of this fragrance so lavishly poured out! Whoever truly perceives it runs after him—or rather, into it—as do those women who say: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” [Col. 0496C] (ibid.). This is the land of promise promised to us from the beginning of the world.

This is the land of the living, that is, of the righteous, in which a threefold fruit, most great and necessary, is received by those to whom no land except this alone could ever offer it: namely, abolition of guilt, bestowal of justice, and a pledge and earnest of eternal happiness. The first was bestowed on us by the shedding of Christ’s blood; the second by the infusion of the Holy Spirit; the third is bestowed on us by participation in the Lord’s body and blood. Of the first you have: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). Of the second: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0496D] who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). For charity itself is justice, rendering to each what is his; seeking not what is useful to itself but what is useful to another; seeking not its own things but those of Jesus Christ. Hence: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. 13); and: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (ibid.). But if the law, then justice. Of the third is the saying: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6).

Yet all are found in each, and each in all: for neither is blood without body, nor body without blood, nor Christ’s anointing without both, nor either one without the anointing. This threefold truth therefore sprang up from the true humanity of Christ as from earth: namely, the truth of remission of sins, [Col. 0497A] the truth of the justification of the wicked, and the truth of the glorification of the wretched. For “the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). The law foreshadowed, prefigured, and proclaimed all these things, but bestowed none of them. For it was impossible for sins to be remitted or blotted out through the blood of goats or calves; likewise, justice could not be fulfilled through works of the law, “for the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). It is equally evident that the glory of the Mosaic law is wholly eclipsed in comparison with the glory of the Gospel. For “what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory.”

But what is cleansed by Christ’s blood is perfectly washed. What most inveterate stains would he not cleanse who split rocks, opened tombs, shook the earth, and darkened the sun? And what is anointed by the Holy Spirit is perfectly sanctified. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him [Col. 0497B] (Rom. 6). From that resurrection his face shines as the sun when it shines in its strength, and his garments became white as snow (Matt. 17), such as no fuller can make on earth. Therefore he could give us no greater earnest of eternal brightness, no more precious pledge that blessed immortality is to be completed in our flesh, than immortal flesh, daily received by us mortals as food unto immortality.

That this is altogether true the devil himself confessed in Apulia, invisibly compelled by Truth itself, through the mouth of a possessed woman freed from the demon through the merits and prayers of Saint Bernard. [Col. 0497C] But who is that rich man, so happy and blessed, who gathers these three fruits of truth from this earth, except the one whose earth brings forth truth, so that what is written may come to pass: “Truth sprang up from the earth”?

Brothers, the Lord has blessed our earth. Therefore truth may now also arise from our earth, which could be personally assumed by Truth itself. Let true compunction arise from the earth of our heart; true confession from the earth of our mouth; true satisfaction from the earth of our body. Contrary to this threefold truth is a threefold lie: the perversity of voluntary consent, falsity of speech, [Col. 0497D] and the craftiness of pretence. Each of these lies, however, is committed in two ways.

Consent to perversity occurs whenever either another’s good displeases us or another’s evil does not displease us. The former ought to please us so much that we give every possible help; the latter ought to displease us so much that we resist it according to our strength. Likewise, falsity of speech is twofold: either falsehood is spoken, or truth that ought to be spoken is kept silent. For an error which is not resisted is approved. Even that pagan comic poet understood this keenly when he said: “He who keeps silent often swears falsely”; for to keep silent about truth is as grave as to speak falsehood. Likewise, [Col. 0498A] pretence is twofold: when either the health of the mind or the weakness of the flesh is feigned. Both fictions are most evil; for no lie is greater than that which is affirmed not only with the mouth but with the whole body.

The first kind of hypocrisy abounds among cloistered persons, the second among secular persons, although among the former it is very easy to find some spiritual hypocrites, and among the latter very many carnal ones. In both kinds “iniquity lies to itself” (Ps. 26): to itself, I say, not to another. For “if you are wise, you shall be wise for yourself; but if you are a scoffer, you alone shall bear the evil.” Truth will destroy all who speak lies, but even more those who commit iniquity: those who, against conscience, either pretend to be what they are not or conceal what they are.
