Pretenders and crafty people provoke God’s wrath.

Moreover, threefold justice from heaven will look down upon this threefold truth from the earth. Eternal glorification of the body will behold and receive true satisfaction; eternal song—that is, the everlasting exultation of the mind breaking forth in divine praise—will behold and receive true confession; blessed and eternal knowledge of the Trinity will behold and receive true expectation. Of the first you have: “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” [Col. 0498B] (Phil. 3). Of the second: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). Of the third: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). May Truth, which today sprang up from the earth, deign to bring us to that [Col. 0498C] vision through the merits and prayers of his mother Mary. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD, II. To the Clergy

“And he rained manna upon them to eat” (Ps. 77). Very fittingly, after so long a fast, the Lord rains manna upon us to eat. He rains in abundance manna—that is, the heavenly grace of the incarnate Word, his sweet and saving presence—to eat, that is, to perform justice. For this is the true eating of the hidden manna, that is, of the incarnate Word: the delightful and sweet exercise of justice, according to Augustine’s saying [Note: [Col. 0497D], St Augustine, on John, ch. 6]: “Believe, [Col. 0498D] and you have eaten.” That is to say: have the faith that works through love, and thus the power of the sacrament will be eaten by you.

Blessed, then, are those who hear the Word made flesh as Word and eat him as flesh. For this is why he is Word: that he may be heard to our salvation; and why he became flesh: that he may be sweetly eaten, as the Word himself says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). Flesh is surely delightful food, and therefore by flesh is signified delight in work. For just as flesh when eaten passes into the body with a certain pleasure and is incorporated into flesh and blood, so a work of justice voluntarily and perseveringly [Col. 0499A] fulfilled is in some manner incorporated into the Spirit, so that it cannot be separated from it even after death, as it is written: “Their works follow them” (Rev. 14).

Hence it is that when God’s incarnate Wisdom suffered a new hunger in the foreign lodging of the flesh and was tempted by the devil to turn a stone into bread, he answered: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). In saying not simply “by the word,” but adding “by every,” he signifies that many kinds of dishes are contained under the single nourishment of the word. For there is a word as bread, strengthening; there is a word as flesh, fortifying; and there is a word as wine, gladdening the heart and intoxicating the mind of the hearer. In commandments it is bread; in counsels, flesh; in promises, [Col. 0499B] wine. In the first is necessity, in the second free choice, in the third delight.

Without bread every table is poor; without the observance of commandments salvation is not secure. Without flesh, however, a meal can indeed be served, although it is much more splendid with it. Likewise, salvation can indeed be attained without embracing the counsels, but it is attained much more abundantly with them.

The hundredfold, besides eternal life, is promised only to those who embrace the counsels; this is like a certain richness of flesh. Further, the wine of promises is that of which the common proverb says: “Every religious life tastes better with good wine,” because everyone truly religious desires that best wine. Of it the steward says to the bridegroom: “But you have kept the good wine until now” [Col. 0499C] (John 2). And of it the Psalmist says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall make them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35).

Since, then, the word of God is that true food by which the soul is nourished, strengthened, and lives, it is certainly evident that no one obtains life from hearing the word alone. The word must without question be eaten, as incarnate Truth himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6). This is that manna which is given us today to eat. To eat, I say: not to waste, not to gaze at, not to carry, not to sell, not to store away. The forgetful hearer wastes it; the curious reader gazes at it; the overly scrupulous doer carries it; the ambitious reporter sells it; the lazy and fastidious worker stores it away. [Col. 0499D] Whatever is kept from manna for the next day breeds worms from itself, because whatever is left unfinished from the Lord’s commandments in the present through negligence will torment the conscience in the future.

Hence it is written that not one iota or one stroke shall pass away from the law until all things are fulfilled (Matt. 5)—understand: either by granting life to those who do them or by inflicting punishment on those who despise them. Hence, when the Lord sent his disciples to preach, saying, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” he added: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded [Col. 0500A] you” (Matt. 28). “All,” he says, not a part or a half.

Since whatever is done with manna profits the doer nothing unless he eats it, woe to all who gather much and do not eat; woe to those who behold the face of their birth in a mirror, and on departing immediately forget what they have seen themselves to be. Woe to those who today approach the Anointed One dry and depart dry: remaining dry in rain, blind in sunlight, rough in dew, fasting at the table; and amid the angelic foods which today the honey-flowing—or rather manna-flowing—heaven has rained down, miserable people perish from hunger and are consumed by starvation. But blessed are those who collect the heavenly manna so as to eat it; blessed are those who eat the bread of angels; blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11).

[Col. 0500B] They keep it as bread, which is never better kept than when it is eaten. For it is subject to many dangers before it is eaten; but once received into the eater’s stomach, it is immediately safe from every danger. There is then nothing for it to fear from thief or mouse, dog or age: from a thief, lest it be stolen; from a mouse, lest it be gnawed; from a dog, lest it be torn apart; from age, lest it be spoiled with mould. The thief is the cunning of the tempter; the mouse, the wickedness of fleshly desire; the dog, distressing and afflicting adversity; age that consumes is pride and envy.

Not without reason have I expressed these two vices under the name of age, since among other evils none is more ancient in origin or more destructive in corruption. These are the firstborn of Egypt, that is, the first vices of the devil, prince of darkness: the first arose in heaven against the Creator himself, the second in paradise against the first human. Of the first the philosopher elegantly says: “Pride takes pleasure in receiving nothing from you; whatever you give, it corrupts” (Seneca). And the poet:

> Pride, when joined to them, stains excellent morals.  
> *(Claudian)*

Of the second Solomon says: “The life of the flesh is sweetness of heart; envy is rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14). Therefore, in order that all of today’s manna may be eaten, and each *gomor*—that is, each word of the Lord—may be well kept by the hearers, a fourfold remedy against the four aforesaid dangers is necessary: [Col. 0500D] against the thief, watchful prudence; against the mouse, restraining temperance; against the dog, strong patience or patient fortitude; against the twofold age, perfection of charity, which is neither puffed up against pride nor envious against envy, but being kind and humble kills both the one and the other.

But now let us turn what we have gathered, God giving it, from this manna into lay loaves. The common saying is: “A fasting stomach is not fastidious,” which the poet expresses thus:

> A fasting stomach rarely despises common fare.  
> *(Horace, Satires 2.2.38)*

For, as Cicero says, “All foods and drinks are seasoned by desire.” When Ptolemy was travelling through Egypt and his companions had not caught up with him, a common loaf offered to him in a basket when he was hungry seemed to him more delightful than anything. When Darius, in flight, had drunk water muddy and polluted with corpses, he said that he had never drunk anything more pleasant. The Lacedaemonians used to season their food with hunger and labor. These are the seasonings of our Order.

For this reason the holy and universal Church, taught by the Holy Spirit, has beneficially and wisely ordained that fasts be observed through the whole of Advent before the Nativity of the Lord, wishing us to bring empty stomachs to the table of heavenly feasts prepared for us today. For if we brought full stomachs to it, we would either reject those delicacies or, taking them with distaste, lose the flavor they bring; because, as the saying goes, the third morsel tastes of paste. Brothers, when God had made angel and human being, [Col. 0501B] he loved the human being so greatly that he intended to nourish him upon angelic fare. But because wisdom acts wisely, he did not wish from the beginning to give him food so solid: for human frailty in its newness, still almost toothless, had not yet received senses trained to chew it.

God himself did not delay to prove this by experience. When he had given the human being an exceedingly easy commandment to carry, the man, intoxicated by the newness of his happiness, could not carry it. He set his wife’s will before the divine will, obedience to which is the food of angels; nor was he recalled from such folly by the dreadful threats of death. By a just judgment, therefore, the Lord deprived the human being of the delights of paradise. Great though these were, he had set higher delights before them: namely, doing the divine will.

Yet when he had been expelled from the mountain of delights into this valley of misery, the merciful Lord permitted him to use worldly pleasures as solace for miseries, though at times he mercifully sprinkled them with much salt of calamities. Hence, at last wearied by his iniquities, the human being to be redeemed began to desire justice, crying out for it everywhere through the mouths of the prophets with unwearied longing. This is signified by our boys, when in their nightly shouts they caper as they cry out the Nativity of the Lord. At length, roused by their cries, the Father of mercies sent the bread of angels at the fitting time: namely, when the world had begun to grow weary of earthly bread. For long ago, in the wilderness, the children of Israel did not deserve to receive the dewy rain [Col. 0501D] of angelic bread until the Egyptian foods which they had brought with them had failed (Exod. 16). But after they reached the promised land, as soon as they began to eat the fruits of the land, the bread of heaven failed them.

Blessed is he for whom earthly bread fails, lest the bread of angels fail. Blessed are those emptied of earthly fare, that they may deserve to be filled with heavenly food. For nothing so merits the filling of heaven as the voluntary emptying of earthly things undertaken for its sake. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5); but, conversely: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation” (Luke 6). This is also shown by ecclesiastical practice [Col. 0502A], which permits no one to approach the sacrament of the altar except fasting, unless perhaps he is burdened by the sudden danger of some illness. For our Elisha too pours forth the abundance of spiritual oil only into empty vessels; and the Psalmist promises the fullness of angelic bread only to the poor, saying: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21). “The poor,” that is, “those who despise the world,” says the interlinear gloss. Therefore, whoever has emptied himself of carnal desires through this Advent fast may confidently approach the delights of the angelic bread that flows abundantly for us today. For this is that manna, hitherto hidden but today made manifest in flesh: namely, the divine Word, by whose exceedingly delightful eating—that is, most sweet working—those blessed spirits [Col. 0502B] obtain both life and blessedness. Strengthened by such food lest they fall, fortified lest they languish, animated lest they grow lukewarm, and satisfied lest they hunger any longer.

Yet this manna has a twofold rain: one under the form of the pure word uttered bodily by a human being; the other beneath the royal robe of human flesh. In this latter manner it came forth for us today, from the more secret bridal chamber of the virginal palace, as a rain of manna. The divine Word is beautifully called manna, receiving an interrogative—or rather an exclamatory—name in place of a proper or common name, from the event of sudden astonishment. For when the children of Israel first saw the dewy frost, or frosty dew, they said, “Manhu?” which is interpreted, “What is this?” (Exod. 16). This [Col. 0502C] name is very fittingly applied to the divine Word, both as uttered by a man and as born of the Virgin, because never did a man speak as either of them speaks. For he is a Galilean, and thus makes both natures manifest by his speech; and therefore he is well called manna because of the astonishment caused by his singular power and unheard-of newness.

Hear the singular power: “Your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). And: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148). And: “Are not my words like fire, and like a hammer breaking the rock?” (Jer. 23). Hear the unheard-of newness: “Blessed are the poor; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger; blessed are those who suffer persecution” (Matt. 5). “Manhu?” [Col. 0502D] “What is this?” (Exod. 16). Who has ever heard such things? He gives the names of blessedness to forms of misery. Truly, never did a man speak as this man speaks (John 7). The world says that the poor fall everywhere; but he says that the poor are kings—and kings of heaven. The world says that the meek will lose their land; he says that they shall possess it. The world says mourning is contrary to consolation; he says it merits everlasting comfort. The world says hunger can never accord with fullness; he says that the hungry alone shall be filled. The world says that suffering persecution, even for righteousness, is the height of misery; but he says that by such endurance one comes to everlasting blessedness. “Manhu?” What is this? Never did a man speak as this man speaks.

[Col. 0503A] Only three kinds of speech are known to human beings: the speech of the world, of the flesh, and of the devil. The first suggests lofty things, the second pleasant things, the third evil things. Against the first speech the Word of God says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14). Against the second: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3). Against the third: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5). Against all of them together: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2). “Manhu?” What is this? The voice of the world is like the voice of a Python speaking from the earth. But this voice is truly like the voice of God thundering from heaven. For “he who is of the earth speaks of the earth; but he who comes from heaven is above all, and testifies to what he has seen and heard.” Therefore [Col. 0503B] the divine Word is rightly called manna: it speaks contrary to flesh and world alike. Let it therefore be said: “And he rained manna upon them to eat.”

Brothers, do not let this name, full of wonder, frighten you. This manna is sweeter to eat than it is easy to understand. Indeed, before the Word of God became flesh, it was audible, but not edible—except perhaps to a very few, because most perfect, who had senses trained to receive solid food and no longer needed milky juices like infants at the breast. Such was Jeremiah: a boy in age but an elder in understanding, who said, “Your words were found by me, and I ate them” (Jer. 15). So too Ezekiel, to whom the word came, saying: “Son of man, your belly shall eat and your inward parts shall be filled with this scroll which I give you.” “And I opened,” he says, “my mouth, and he fed me with that scroll; and it became sweet as honey in my mouth” (Ezek. 3).

Nevertheless, Ezekiel’s eating may, without prejudice to other mystical interpretations, signify the hardness of the Jews, who, gnawing only the bark of the letter, never deserved to reach the marrow of the spirit: always chewing the word written on parchment, but raw—as a shell without a kernel, chaff without grain, skin without flesh. They eat the word with its bark, not the fleshy Word; a word that puffs up, not the infant Word. A word that strikes, not the Word that heals, as it is written: “He sent his Word and healed them” (Ps. 106).

What wonder, then, that they are always bloodless and pale, fed on such dry food? Such food was the law [Col. 0503D] without grace, knowing only how to describe guilt, not how to remove it; powerful to punish, powerless to justify and pardon. But after the little Son of God was born for us—knowing how to pardon and easy to appease, not knowing how to strike and slow to anger, swift to give grace and slow to exact vengeance—“grace and truth came through Jesus,” and “the Word was made flesh” (John 1). Truly it was made edible, because through flesh it is sweet and pleasant, gentle and placable; and now not only edible for adults, but also drinkable—indeed, if one may say so, suckable for newborn infants—freeing them from the guilt which they did not voluntarily contract, through grace which they do not voluntarily receive.

Therefore let us eat, most beloved brothers, [Col. 0504A] the manna of the Lord’s Word, which the Lord rains down for us to eat. Let us eat it eagerly, as hungry persons; sweetly, as the bread of heaven; reserving none of it for worm and decay, but consuming it all—or destroying it by fire—as is commanded concerning the Paschal lamb: that nothing of it be left until morning, but either a neighbor invited in should eat it all, or fire should consume what remains (Exod. 12). Blessed is he who has so wholly eaten the bread of angels that the enemy steals none of it through his imprudence, gnaws none of it through his lack of self-control, bites none of it through impatience, puts none of it to decay through the poison of envy, and corrupts none of it through the leaven of pride. Blessed are the gates of heaven, whose opening pours forth so precious a rain! How glorious [Col. 0504B] are those clouds to which divine wrath commands that they not rain this shower upon the unworthy!

These are the gates which are also clouds: namely, the doctors of the Church and any holy preachers. They are called gates from the commendable example of their lives, and clouds from the suspended moisture of the word. These gates are opened when an abundant grace of teaching is bestowed upon them, as Scripture testifies concerning the very fountain of graces: “And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit,” and so forth (Matt. 5). But they are closed when, because the gates of righteousness have not first been opened, the rain of doctrine either flows elsewhere contemptibly or does not flow at all; for when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is despised.

But these things have been said concerning the first rain of heavenly manna, insofar as it signifies the life-giving dew of the divine Word ministered through human service. Now [Col. 0504C] let us consider the second, by which is signified the longed-for presence of the incarnate Word, coming today from the virginal womb like a rain of dew falling from heaven, as it is written: “In the morning dew lay round about the camp; and when it had covered the surface of the ground, there appeared in the wilderness something small and white, like frost, like coriander seed, and as though pounded with a pestle” (Exod. 16).

See how rightly the incarnate Word was called manna, since he was set as a sign against which almost all would speak. For Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when Mary, the mother [Col. 0504D] of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph and was found by him to have conceived in her womb of the Holy Spirit, Joseph himself said: “What is this? I know her virginity; whence then does she have this in her womb?” Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary, and all the world said: “What is this? How can this woman be both virgin and mother? Who shall recount this generation?” Hence the Church sings: “When you were born ineffably from the Virgin” (*Office of the Church*). The same Savior, now born, was announced by an angel to the shepherds with this sign: “You shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger.” “And all who heard wondered at the things which were told them by the shepherds” (Luke 2); and they said: “What is this? How can he who lies in a manger be the Savior of the world?” A [Col. 0505A] star indicated him to be King of the Jews, and the Magi sought him as their king; and Herod said: “What is this? Am not I King of the Jews?” He was circumcised on the eighth day, as though he had brought something superfluous with him from his mother’s womb; and the devil said: “What is this? What has the remedy of circumcision to do with the Son of a virgin—indeed, with the Son of God?” He was redeemed on the fortieth day by the offering of birds, as though he too, in Adam with the rest, had been sold under sin; and again the devil said: “What is this? How is he the Redeemer, as Simeon says, when like other infants he is redeemed by an offering?”

In this sentence, however, the manifold commendation of manna should be carefully noted: from the timeliness of the hour, the generosity of the gift, the sweetness of the dew, and the usefulness of eating it. “In the morning,” he says, “dew lay” (Exod. 16). Morning: that is, at the beginning of a new light after the darkness of former ignorance and wickedness, yet not in full light, while the Jewish people still limped. Hence: “His going forth is prepared as the dawn” (Hos. 6). At dawn there is, as it were, a mingling of darkness and light; therefore the Savior’s coming is beautifully compared to dawn. For although he brought a new light to believers, night did not depart from unbelievers, according to Isaiah: “The morning comes, and also the night” (Isa. 21). Morning and night came together, as it were, when the Gentiles came to the light of faith and unbelieving Jews remained in their darkness. For the light shines in darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it.

In this morning, then, he lay, [Col. 0505C] that is, he came poor and despised; for the poor lie everywhere. Truly he lay: he chose for his mother at his birth a poor virgin, not a queen or princess; the severity of cold and winter’s horror, not the mildness of spring or the heat of summer; the silent middle of nightly rest, not the public tumult of daytime activity; little Bethlehem among the thousands of Judah, not a royal city in Judah’s tribe. Truly he lay, wrapped in swaddling clothes rather than silks; reclined in a manger rather than a palace; content with earth for a mattress, hay for down, a stable for a hall, and heaven for a canopy. “Dew lay,” he says: that is, Jesus the Son of God was born in lowliness, gentle and sweet, kind and gracious, meek and patient, [Col. 0505D] merciful and compassionate. Dew: that is, wholly anointed with the unction of the Holy Spirit, anointed above his fellows with the oil of gladness.

Thus he showed that among the *christs*, or anointed ones, he was called Christ by antonomasia, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61)—understand: preeminently above all others, dew. In dew three things are to be considered: coldness, brightness, and sweetness: coldness in its sensation, brightness in its appearance, sweetness in taste and touch. These serve to extinguish heat, repel darkness, mitigate pain, remove disgust, and provoke appetite. This dew had, in the first respect, the appearance of frost; in the second, whiteness; in the third, the taste of fine flour with honey, or of oiled bread. Of the first it is said: “Dew will cool every burning heat” [Col. 0506A] (Ecclus. 18). Of the second: “Your dew is the dew of light” (Isa. 26). Of the third: “I shall be as dew; Israel shall blossom as the lily” (Hos. 14).

Dew descends at night: Christ was born at night. Night signifies the sins of the human race, which deserved the Judge’s wrath more than the Savior’s mercy. Therefore, by Christ’s birth is signified that the grace of the divine calling is given not from merits but gratuitously, and is bestowed upon the undeserving, according to the saying: “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Ps. 102). Again, dew descends quietly and without noise. Likewise the almighty Word of God came from the royal thrones “when all things held the middle of silence.” This signifies that God’s grace tolerates no contradiction, suffers no impediment, can be repelled by no barrier, and can be delayed by no obstacle. Again, dew descends scattered abroad. Likewise Christ’s birth was, as it were, scattered through the world: Christ was born in Judea according to the flesh, but was not born there according to faith. In the East, however, he was announced to the Magi by a star, as though born there by faith while unknown in the flesh. Hence it is written concerning this scattered rain of dew: “I rained upon one city and did not rain upon another; one part was rained upon, and the part upon which I did not rain withered” (Amos 4). Similar are the sayings: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1), and “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9).

Thus dew falls in tiny drops, because the saving mystery of our redemption [Col. 0506C] was revealed neither wholly nor all at once even to the patriarchs and prophets, but in portions. Hence John the forerunner and Baptist, whom Truth itself called more than a prophet, after pointing to him with his finger and saying, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1), later asks, as if doubting the outcome of that redemption: “Are you he who is to come, or should we await another?” (Matt. 11). Nor did the Redeemer’s grace ever bestow itself wholly and all at once upon anyone; rather, it is accustomed to descend upon the elect through certain stages of daily progress, as it is written: “The path of the righteous is like a shining light: it goes forth and increases unto the perfect day” (Prov. 4). [Col. 0506D] “For no one becomes supreme suddenly: these things come through numbers and their proper stages.” Hence Paul: “He who supplies seed to the sower will also provide bread to eat, and will increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Cor. 9).

This dew is beautifully called by Isaiah “dew of light”: dew, that it may cool; of light, that it may illuminate—cooling the desire for evil and illuminating ignorance of good. Dew of light, watering and shining upon, enriching and enlightening: watering dryness, shining upon blindness, enriching affection, enlightening understanding. It follows: “Round about the camp” (Exod. 16), that is, around those who live chastely, soberly, and piously. For a camp is called *castrum* from castration; and the phrase “round about” suggests what is said elsewhere: “The Lord is sweet to all” [Col. 0507A] (Ps. 144); and again: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him” (ibid.); and: “Mountains are round about him, and the Lord is round about his people” (Ps. 124). For with God there is no respect of persons (Rom. 2), but in every nation the one who fears God is acceptable to him. Thus in “morning” is shown the haste of aid; in “lay,” the highly useful but despised accessibility of the example; in “dew,” the sweetness of the remedy; and in “round about the camp,” the giver’s generosity and the recipient’s worthiness.

Of the first you have: “The medicine of all is in the swift passing of the cloud” (Ecclus. 43). Of the second: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich” (Job 12). Of the third: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). Of the fourth: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach” (Jas. 1). Again: “This shall be the covenant between me and you, and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised,” and so forth (Gen. 17).

We are invited to the first when it is said: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I shall give,’ when you can give at once” (Prov. 3). “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day.” He who is not ready today will be less fit tomorrow. “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). Yet today the fruitful poverty of virtues is fled from: this is manna lying upon the face of the earth. To the third we are invited when it is said: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6). Again: [Col. 0507C] “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). Again: “Have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9). From this sweetness of anointing all are called Christians. Moreover, to the fourth he invites us who says: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9). Again: “Not from sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver” (ibid.).

Brothers, the Father of mercies, in giving us his only-begotten Son, showed himself in this gift almost extravagantly generous, since he made a rain of him, pouring it out not upon Bethlehem alone but round about the camp—that is, the Church militant. For Christ, insofar as he is man, was born in Bethlehem; insofar as he is God, he begins to be born everywhere that he begins to be adored, as we said above concerning [Col. 0507D] the Magi.

Finally, by this rain of manna the Catholic faith concerning the sacrament of the altar is especially commended. For the same Lamb who is immolated in this place is sacrificed throughout the world. The same bread which is eaten here by the people is the very bread which is nonetheless eaten by them today and will likewise be eaten tomorrow. For he himself said: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6). Because it is bread, it can be eaten and refresh the eater; but because it is living bread, it cannot fail by refreshing, nor be consumed by being eaten. Thus blessed Andrew says of this Lamb that, after being eaten by the people, it nevertheless remains whole and living. And blessed Ambrose, in the prayer said while the Mass is sung, by the priest seated at the altar [Col. 0508A]:

> “Beautiful bread, pure bread, living bread, holy bread, most white bread, possessing every delight and every flavor of sweetness: you who always refresh us and never fail in yourself—let my heart eat you.”
>
> (*Prayer of Ambrose before Mass*)

This prayer is falsely ascribed in certain missals to blessed Augustine. For in the copy belonging to the lord pope it is entitled with the name of blessed Ambrose, whose flourishing style it most aptly breathes. By this bread upon the altar must be understood that offering of which the prophet says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name” (Mal. 1).

[Col. 0508B] This offering is also called Lamb, from its supreme innocence, its sacrifice most acceptable to God, and its perfect expiation of sins; and it is called bread, from its refreshment of the pilgrim on the road and the citizen in his homeland. It is called flesh not only because of the reality of human flesh, but also because of the ineffable love for humankind. Therefore, in this bread the Word is contained and hidden like an inner crumb, while animated flesh surrounds and contains it like an outer crust. The appearance of bread, indeed, is true without substance, like a kind of flower of fine flour; yet it appears scattered abroad—not to be extinguished, as something hindering taste, but rather to be desired, as something reviving appetite and rekindling desire. When the figures pass away, it is concealed not because of lowliness but because of excessive brightness.

Blessed is everyone [Col. 0508C] who is both enlightened by this dew of light, so as to believe thus; and enriched, so as to love, revere, and fear what he believes; and who, by working through love, eats, and by eating lives. For demons believe but do not love; but no one loves who does not believe. Whoever does not believe the power, brighter than light, of so great a union of the divine Word with human flesh; whoever does not love the good will of so great a divine charity toward humankind—is both blind and dry, without light and without dew; nor shall he escape either the everlasting darkness of blindness or the eternal miseries of blindness and hunger.

For who, if capable even slightly of reason, does not see that the almighty Word, inseparably [Col. 0508D] united to human flesh, as it is in itself both non-spatial and impassible, existing everywhere not merely potentially but substantially, could also confer this upon the flesh which it assumed: that it might both exist sacramentally in many places at once and refresh those who eat it, yet not fail when eaten, but remain living and incorrupt? As it is said in the canon of the Mass: “Humbly we beseech you, almighty God: command these things to be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high, before the sight of your divine majesty, that all of us who, by this participation at the altar, receive the most sacred body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.”

Behold: we ask that the flesh of the Word, by his omnipotence, be borne even into heaven, and yet we in no way doubt that we shall be refreshed by that same flesh [Col. 0509A]. For this is not, as some wrongly understand, to be interpreted concerning the devotion of those praying alone, but also concerning the flesh of him who says: “Does this scandalize you?”—namely, what I said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” (John 6). Understand: then you will be able not to be scandalized by this saying of mine, but rather to be edified; and to ask my Father that my flesh, as viaticum, by the almighty power of the Word, both be borne by an angel into heaven and nevertheless be changed for you in the sacrament into food. Food, I say, not of the body but of the soul; not of mortal but of immortal life.

But this rain [Col. 0509B], my most beloved brothers, made from the Only-Begotten, what else does it suggest to us than that no one should be greedy in giving or sparing in sowing, when he can make an abundant rain even from one penny or one farthing? “For no person’s means are small whose spirit is great,” says Pope Leo; “nor does the measure of devotion depend upon the size of one’s estate.” [Note: [Col. 0509D] Leo, sermon for Lent.] For God does not consider how much is given, but from how much it is given. Therefore the poor widow, casting two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12), was preferred to the rich who cast in from their abundance—giving, but retaining more—whereas she, in giving all, kept nothing for herself.

Woe to those who have gone in the way of Cain, that is, after greed: making their offerings rightly indeed, but not dividing rightly [Col. 0509C], because they give God their little and worse possessions while reserving the better and greater things—indeed, themselves wholly—for Mammon. Therefore God does not look upon them or their gifts, but curses them together with their gifts. “Cursed,” he says, “is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. 48). Again: “Cursed is the deceitful man who has a male in his flock and, making a vow, sacrifices to the Lord a weak thing” (Mal. 1).

Brothers, every generosity prevails; every greed produces dryness and hunger. I tell you that if there were no greed, there would be no famine on earth. “Bring,” he says, “every tithe into my storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me” (Mal. 2), whether I shall not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out for you a blessing even unto abundance. What [Col. 0509D] will the sons of Cain say here—our pseudo-Christians—who not only refuse, even when asked, to render the tithes they owe, but even presume to retain them when excommunicated? When do these wretches suppose that God accepts their voluntary gifts, when by not returning what is owed they violently seize what belongs to him? For the first part of justice is to render what you owe; the second is to give generously from what you possess. And if robbery committed against human property is detestable, how much more is that committed against divine property! The former is simple robbery; the latter is sacrilege. Blessed therefore is he who, with the widow of Zarephath, makes bread rain down from a handful of flour by generous action, and makes an anointing flow from a flask of oil [Col. 0510A] by generous will (3 Kings 17). But let these things be said because manna is said to have rained around the camp.

I say, around the camp, not around prostitutes. The chaste, spiritually, like eunuchs naturally, are cold. Therefore this dew is likened to frost, because by its work the evil heat is quenched—a heat that is twofold: carnal desire and hatred. This dew restrains the first fire when it says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Hence Jerome: “Woe to us, who commit fornication as often as we desire.” It restrains the second when it says: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you: everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable [Col. 0510B] to judgment” (ibid.). Here too Jerome might have said: “Woe to us, who commit homicide as often as we grow angry”—anger, I mean, when it has become ingrained: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3).

Certainly every worldly heat can be extinguished; infernal heat cannot. Therefore whoever is not restrained from carnal love or hatred by such warnings of the incarnate Word is already kindled with the fires of Gehenna. But let us now run through the remaining points concerning this bright dew. It follows: “Something small, like coriander seed, and as though pounded with a pestle, appeared in the wilderness” (Exod. 16). It is called *minutum*, “made small,” as though diminished: that is, made less from being great, according to: “You made him a little lower than the angels” [Col. 0510C] (Ps. 8); and again: “A little child is born to us” (Isa. 9); and again: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2).

Coriander is a kind of vegetable; and vegetables are food for the weak, according to: “He who is weak may eat vegetables” (Rom. 14). Therefore, by coriander seed is understood the weakness of human flesh, and the flower which soon withers, as it is written: “Do not emulate evildoers, for they shall quickly fall as the vegetables of the herbs” (Ps. 36). Thus by diminution is signified the emptying of majesty; by coriander seed, the assumption of our weakness; and by being pounded with a pestle, the passion of the cross. This most excellent example is set before all [Col. 0510D] so that he who is great in rank, birth, life, or learning may arm himself with humanity; he who is strong in bodily power or mighty in wealth may condescend to the weak through compassion; and he who is righteous or innocent may not refuse to suffer persecution for righteousness, even from inferiors.

Such dew, and in such a manner, appeared in the wilderness. He appeared who was formerly hidden; he who was terrifying appeared kindly; he who was God appeared human and a man. He appeared not in a city but in a wilderness; not in a town but in a desert. This wilderness is Judea, which, drawing near to the Lord only with its mouth and honoring him with lips alone, was far from his worship [Col. 0511A] in heart and deed. Or the wilderness is the Church of the Gentiles, uncultivated in its manners, “that the children of the desolate woman might be more numerous than those of her who had a husband”—that is, she who bore the yoke of the law. “For a woman is bound to the law while her husband lives” (1 Cor. 7). Therefore the cultivator of souls appeared in the wilderness, to teach the slothful person to cultivate his field and the foolish person not to leave his vineyard deserted, but to uproot from it whatever is harmful, lest the earth, often drinking the rain that comes upon it and producing thorns and briars, become near to a curse and its end be burning.

## SERMON IV. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD, I

“The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared” [Col. 0511B] (Titus 3). As Isidore testifies, there are two Epiphanies—that is, appearances or manifestations—of the Lord. The first was made to Jewish shepherds through an angel; the second to Gentile Magi through a star. Hence in ancient times all the days from the Nativity of the Lord to the octave of Epiphany were called the days of the Epiphanies. But the name of the former Epiphany has now become obsolete, both because the title “Nativity of the Lord” is more honorable and because of the preeminence of today’s manifestation. For the assumption of human flesh is expressed more distinctly by the name Nativity, while the personal union of divine majesty is manifested today by the name Appearance, or Epiphany.

On the day of Christ’s Nativity from the Virgin Mary the weakness of assumed flesh appeared; but the majesty of the Word assuming it did not appear as plainly [Col. 0511C] as today. The angel indeed announced the Savior’s birth much more clearly to the shepherds than the star did to the Magi: he by sweet speech, it in silence. Nevertheless, the Magi believed much more devoutly and perfectly on lesser testimony than the shepherds did on greater. The shepherds came from nearby to the newborn king before the Magi came from afar. Yet, contrary to the commandment of the law, they appeared empty before their Lord, offering him nothing at all: no gift from the hand, no gift from the tongue, no gift of service. What good, then, was it to them that they came hastily and found first the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger, when they departed with their business unfinished [Col. 0511D] and the Savior unadored?

How apt is the proverbial saying: “What does a rustic seek at court?” What did these rustics seek at the court of the new king? “Let us pass on,” they say, “as far as Bethlehem” (Luke 2): that is, let us go quickly, in passing, and return; let us not linger there, but run to see the new infant and run back to our flock. “Let us pass and see”: that is, let us do nothing else but look, and immediately return. O unhappy men! Today the whole matter is to pass and see the infant—but are you not also going to see the Savior? And if you are going to see him, why not worship him also? Why not offer gifts? “But,” they say, “we are poor. We have nothing in our purse to offer him.” Yet the Savior does not seek silver and does not need gold: he desires you, not your possessions. No one is so poor or needy that he cannot offer faith from the heart, praise from the mouth, and service from a body prostrate upon the ground.

These are the gifts which the Saviour, rich in mercy, begs from our poverty. If, then, you sought the Saviour, why do you not worship him when found? If you did not seek him, why did you run so eagerly to this child, as though to one differing in no respect from others? For what great thing is it to see a child wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger? Yet these tokens were given you as a sign of the Saviour, not merely as a matter for reasoning. For thus it was said to you: “You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger” (ibid.). Surely, even from this alone you ought to have recognized [Col. 0512B] that this child possessed something beyond the human, since the messengers of his birth were above human beings.

From these things it is plainly inferred that those shepherds either did not believe, or did not fully understand, the announcement of the Saviour’s birth made to them by the angel. For if they had fully understood, they would undoubtedly have worshipped him, as the Magi did; and they would have received him in every way as the true Saviour—as the Gospel indicates briefly when the Evangelist says: “And when they saw, they made known concerning the word that had been spoken to them concerning this child” (ibid.). “They made known concerning the word,” he says; he does not say “the word,” but “concerning the word”: that is, a part of the word, not the whole word—namely, this part: “You will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger”; but not that part of the message which the angel had first announced, [Col. 0512C] saying: “There is born to you today a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord” (Isa. IX).

Or, certainly, if they believed him to be the Creator, they did not believe him to be the author of eternal salvation, but only of temporal and earthly salvation. Thus the Pharisees answered the Lord when he questioned them, saying: “What do you think concerning Christ? Whose son is he?” They say to him: “David’s.” He says to them: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’?” (Matt. XXII). From this it follows that the Jews of the present day do not believe that the Messiah for whom they still wait will be God, but a mere human being; and therefore, likewise, not a Saviour—or, if a Saviour, of bodies only, [Col. 0512D] not of souls; for a time, not for eternity.

Yet they may reasonably be excused in this respect. For this manifestation of the Saviour was made to shepherds in winter, and their devotion was exceedingly cold: since, when he appeared only to the shepherds, it is said that they returned, “glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, as had been told them” (Luke II). Their lukewarmness in not advancing to worship him, whom they had hurried to see, may be excused by the simplicity of their age and the rusticity of their life: for they were still children, had always been reared in the country, and therefore had not yet learned the language of worship or the offering of reverence.

Mystically, however, it must be believed that, to signify the outward knowledge of Christ which could discern in him nothing beyond a human being, the fact that they did not worship him indicated the future unbelief and hardness of the Jews. These would see—not, I say, an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger, but a young man commanding demons and raising the dead from the tomb—yet would not believe. For even now the Jews find the child Jesus wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger: that is, they read him as foretold in the Old Testament in simple and rustic words, wrapped in the ragged mysteries of figurative types. Under these they believe that nothing else lies hidden than the infancy of weak flesh, ignorant that the power and wisdom of the incarnate Word are wrapped in such little cloths of mysteries.

Accordingly, they first find him in the manger, like irrational [Col. 0513B] beasts finding hay or barley; but we, with the centurion and the thief, recognize him on the cross as the ransom of the world; with the two disciples, at table, as the living bread and food of rational beings; with the apostles in the city-bearing woman [the Latin *urbe bajula* is uncertain], as true God. The Magi, therefore, were taught better by the silent star than the shepherds by the speaking angel. As it is written: “The Magi saw the star and said to one another: ‘This is the sign of a great king’” (Matt. II). They recognized this, certainly, by the anointing alone as their teacher, not by astrological art; and we prove this briefly.

All the stars whose courses are reduced to rule were made together at the beginning on the fourth day; but this star was newly created then. Therefore its significance could not be inferred from the rules governing the others. Again, if the new and unprecedented birth of the Saviour could have been recognized by astrological art, then there was no need for a new star to be created to demonstrate it. But the new star was created for this purpose; therefore either its creation was superfluous, or it was altogether impossible for his birth to be comprehended by already established canons.

Thus, just as the anomalous eclipse of the sun which occurred at the Lord’s Passion confounded the calculation of every canon, and could not be found in all the rules of Ptolemy, Alcander, or the other astrologers—how this could happen, though it did happen—so neither could it be discovered how a new star might point out God born of a Virgin, though it did point him out. And just as Apollophanes, fellow-disciple and fellow-student of Dionysius the Areopagite in Egypt, when they spoke together and considered the eclipse that had occurred, uttered not an astrological but an almost prophetic saying: “Either the God of nature suffers, or the elements deceive”; so the Magi spoke not as mathematicians but as prophets—that is, not by human reason but by divine inspiration—when they said: “This is the sign of a great King.”

Nevertheless, they could also have known this through the conjectures of astrological art—that is, have held it with strong probability—because, just as that star had been newly created, so the child to whom it belonged had been born in a new manner. And just as that star was naturally more excellent than all others, so that child excelled all other mortals.

[Col. 0514A] There were, moreover, five notable features in that star: its time, place, motion, brightness, and magnitude. Its time: because it shone by day, not by night, as was useful for travellers. Its place: because it was not fixed in the firmament with the other stars, nor did it wander near the firmament with the planets; rather, in the sublunar region, close to the earth, it travelled the path assigned to it. Its motion: because it did not move with the firmament from east to west, nor with the planets in the contrary movement from west to east; but by a singular and proper movement from east to south, according to the position of Persia in relation to Jerusalem. Its brightness: because its daylight was not obscured by the sun’s light, but it shone alone with the sun. Its magnitude: because it was higher—and appeared higher—than all the other stars except the sun and moon.

[Col. 0514B] Therefore, its brightness signified that this child would be brighter, that is, more renowned, than all mortals. Its time signified that he would make a name for himself by other causes and merits than those of other mortals. Its magnitude signified that he would be higher than all people, not in body but in power; not in stature but in might. Its place signified that he would be the humblest of human beings. Its motion signified that he would conquer all sinners in a contrary manner and teach a contrary way of life.

But that this child was born of a Virgin and without male seed; that he was Son of God and son of man; that he was impassible according to the nature of the Word which assumed, and passible and mortal according to the assumed [Col. 0514C] human nature—none of this could at all have been known through that star unless, as I have said, the Holy Spirit taught it, or unless that star spoke, as Saint Gregory seems to affirm. But if it spoke and had the form of a child bearing a cross upon its head—as Chrysostom seems to suggest, though he himself does not affirm that it was so—it is evident that this singular miracle must be attributed not to astrological art but to divine power.

Thus divinely instructed, the Magi come to seek the child, already ready to die for him whom they could not yet behold. For what do they cry through the streets of Jerusalem? “Where,” they say, “is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. II). The shepherds, instructed by an angel, saw the child but said nothing and did not worship him; they merely looked in silence, signifying that the Jews would be mute and tongueless in confessing Christ’s praise. But these men, while still seeking the Lord, had already found him by faith, whom they sought with such full faith and honoured by public confession—especially in a place and at a time so dangerous.

Certainly neither the cruelty of King Herod the parricide nor the severity of Roman law was unknown to them; Roman law condemns by a capital sentence anyone guilty of treason against majesty. And who is so guilty of injured majesty as one who, in a king’s presence, confesses another king? How well these blessed Magi observed that most salutary counsel of the prophet: “If you seek, seek; turn back and come” (Isa. XXI). They truly sought the Saviour, and in seeking continued to seek him: placed amid so many dangers, [Col. 0515A] they did not cease from the eagerness of their search.

Therefore, after the instruction of the star, they deserved also to be taught by the testimony of the holy Scriptures. They come, then, with the star going before them, as far as the place where the child was, and enter the house. It is not said that they knocked at the door or called the doorkeeper, but that they entered at once. Hence it is conjectured either that there was no door there, as in a common lodging which yielded to whoever occupied it first; or certainly that, if there was a door, Mary kept it open throughout the day so that any who wished might enter to see the Saviour. Or perhaps it was then divinely arranged that it should stand open, lest such devout messengers should encounter a closed door, into which the Lord of the house had already entered.

It is also very credible [Col. 0515B] that the child himself, by his crying, invited to himself those still standing outside, that he might more quickly fulfil their desire. Entering, therefore, they found the child and his mother Mary. Of the shepherds it is written that they found Mary and Joseph and the infant lying in the manger. These words covertly suggest that those shepherds, through the fault of human curiosity, first looked around to see who was in the house with the child before seeing who the child himself was, for whose sake alone they had come.

But why was it necessary that they should find Joseph? Certainly, lest, as Jews and rustics—that is, unbelieving and talkative persons—they should suspect the child of having been born in adultery and, by blaspheming, injure the mother’s modesty if they found her alone with the child and without a husband; especially since they had not been persuaded [Col. 0515C] that the child was God. But the Magi, whom full faith had brought, were to find the Virgin alone with the child, since they doubted nothing about the child’s divinity.

And see how full was the faith that brought them. For it immediately follows: “And falling down, they worshipped him” (Matt. II). Truly these men did not come to the court of the great King as rustics, but as noble men, refined and liberally educated, bringing every kind of gift: a gift of service, in the worship of their prostrate bodies; a gift of the tongue, in the prayer of their devout hearts; a gift of the hand, in the offering of gold, myrrh, and frankincense. With these mystical gifts, worshipping they honour, and honouring they worship: divinity in flesh; power in weakness; majesty in swaddling clothes; wisdom in simplicity; might in humility; the Word of God in an infant; true God in a human being.

[Col. 0515D] “And opening their treasures,” he says, “they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. II), confessing in the gold the supreme ruler to whom tribute must be paid by every mortal; in the frankincense the true God to whom every human being must pray; in the myrrh the true Redeemer, for love of whom every flesh must contend even to death, since he first tasted death for his friends. Gold signified that he would be the true and just judge of the world; frankincense, that he would remit sins to penitents; myrrh, that he would suffer death for sinners, [Col. 0516A] and be glorified through the penitence of sinners together with the death of martyrs.

From this it is plainly inferred that the kindness and humanity of our Saviour appeared more excellently to the Magi than to the shepherds: teaching the former by inward anointing, the latter only by the angelic word and the outward sight of the child.

But now let us draw, with lips meeting upon the surface, the milky sweetness from the Apostle’s words which we have set forth, leaving their more solid food to the more practised and perfect. “The kindness and humanity of the Saviour appeared,” he says. To appear is to be seen suddenly and unexpectedly; and the term properly applies to invisible forms showing themselves in visible form. Hence Ambrose says: “Angels are said to appear because they are seen suddenly and cannot be foreseen.”

[Col. 0516B] Therefore the Saviour’s birth and his manifestation today are called an appearance, because where, when, how, and to whom he appeared lay in the will of the one appearing, not in the power of those seeing. The word “appearing,” therefore, plainly signifies that Christ existed before he appeared visibly. For angels do not begin to exist when they begin to appear.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Something appears to be missing.]

This is also signified by the common custom in which ordinary people, and even the wealthy, every year on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity place in the fireplace to be consumed a great log uprooted from the ground; its remains they preserve throughout the year, rekindling them in summer to ward off thunder. They call this log *transfocalis*, “crossing the hearth,” because it extends beyond the fireplace on either side. It signifies him who says of himself: “I am the light of the world; I am Alpha and Omega” (John VIII; Rev. I).

[Col. 0516C] The hearth—that is, the place of the fire—signifies the world, which lies wholly in the evil one; for whatever is in it is “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John II). All this is nothing other than that threefold fire which Satan, falling from heaven like lightning, sent down to earth.

Perhaps this is also signified by the lightning bolt’s threefold ray: it stinks, burns, and splits. Likewise lust stinks, avarice burns, and pride splits—that is, divides unity and breaks the bond of charity. The rekindled remains of this log avail against lightning, because the devout faith of the saints, the unconquered hope of believers, and the perfect charity of Christ overcome the prince of the world, according to the Apostle’s saying: “In all things taking the shield of faith, whereby you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0516D] This is against the Paulianists and Photinians, or Ebionites, who, poorer in understanding than in name, say that Christ had his beginning from his birth in the flesh. If that is so, then he was not said by the Apostle to have appeared, nor was he truly and properly said by the prophet to be going to appear, who says: “He will appear at the end, and will not lie” (Hab. II).

“The kindness appeared,” he says. It appeared so as to be seen by the eyes; it did not merely sound so as to be heard by the ears. Thus kindness seen might please more and affect more deeply than kindness heard, because:

> Things received through the ear stir the mind more slowly  
> than things set before faithful eyes.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 180)

It appeared, I say, by acting so as to be seen; it did not merely sound by commanding so as to be heard, lest that most biting—yet most true—saying could now be thrown in its face: “It is delicate teaching for one who fights to prescribe blows from the wall; and, while you yourself are anointed with perfumes, to accuse a bloodied soldier of cowardice.”

Indeed, before the Son of God appeared in flesh, while he gave the world commandments alone and not examples, he was like a delicate teacher, as though content with the leisure of blessedness. But after becoming man, he put his hand to hard tasks: hungry among the hungry, thirsty among the thirsty, and labouring with the labouring. Then his command began plainly [Col. 0517B] to be as persuasive as his way of life was commendable, fulfilling that saying of David: “Arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment which you have commanded; and the assembly of peoples shall surround you” (Ps. VII). That is to say: O Lord, first fulfil the command of humility and patience which you have given; immediately you will find many who follow you.

Indeed, the meaning of this verse is nowhere better explained than by these verses of the poet:

> If you command anything to be held in common and maintained,  
> first submit yourself to what you command. Then the people  
> become more observant of justice, and do not refuse to bear it  
> when they see the author himself obeying it. The world is shaped  
> by its ruler’s example; edicts cannot bend human minds as greatly  
> as the life of the one who rules.  
> The noble populace is always changed with its prince.  
> (Claudian, *Fourth Consulship of Honorius*, 295)

[Col. 0517C] “The kindness appeared.” This is what Lucan says of Cato:

> … He shows how to endure labours;  
> he does not command it.

Indeed, before the Son of God was born of the Virgin, he did nothing but command. But now, an infant, lying and crying wordlessly in a manger, he did nothing but show. “The kindness appeared.” Angels, both good and evil, are accustomed to appear to human beings: the former in order to teach, the latter in order to deceive; the former in order to help, the latter in order to harm. The appearance of the former brings consolation; that of the latter, fear.

The maker of all things and restorer of human beings, in order to show himself not only kind but kindness itself, appeared most kindly, made in the form of all things made: [Col. 0517D] that is, in the form of a newly born child, unable to harm and ignorant of how to strike. And it should be noted that neither a good nor an evil angel is ever recorded to have appeared in such a form, either before or afterward. Nor without reason. For in either case such an appearance would be useless: one appearing in this way could neither comfort if good nor deceive if evil; the latter would not achieve the aim of malice, nor the former fulfil the office of charity.

But the Angel of great counsel, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, could, even in such a form, retain the power to comfort and the knowledge to teach. For the Word of God did not cease to be the Word because of the infancy of the flesh, nor did he become less power. Therefore, long ago the kindness of the deceiver, the devil, appeared in the form of a serpent standing erect, so as to overthrow; speaking, so as to trip up humankind. For before the curse the serpent moved upright—a fact still observed in the *parea*, of which the poet says:

> And content to furrow its path with its tail, the *pareas*.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX.721)

[Col. 0518A] But now kindness has appeared in the form of a child lying down, that it may raise up; silent, that it may teach; suffering, that it may conquer—already crying out in silence what it will later cry in words: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). And in Isaiah: “The cultivation of righteousness is silence” (Isa. III). And again: “In silence … is your strength” (Isa. XXX).

For Eve, the mother of all living, preserved innocence as long as she kept silence. Her entire posterity is still naturally compelled, by the privilege of age, to observe this. Every infancy remains innocent as long as it lacks the power of speech; but once it begins to speak, its innocence at once becomes mute. For the tongue, a small member placed in the human body, just as it first breaks silence on the face, so it first removes the merit of innocence—as all of us learn by experience.

Divine compassion acted most mercifully toward humankind when it punished guilt through silence and healed the rash audacity of presumption by the helplessness of weakness, as with a medicinal antidote. In later grace it crowns the fullness of this mercy by himself also drinking the antidote—he who had not drunk the poison—in order to confer greater authority and efficacy upon this same antidote for others. Hence he says: “Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls”; and adds: “My yoke is sweet” (Matt. XI), and so forth. It is as though he said: Do not fear to be gentle or humble after my example, because, by drinking it, I have made sweet the ancient bitterness of this antidote.

[Col. 0518C] And truly, who, on hearing that God became an infant, would not shrink more from being exalted by human pride than from being humbled by the example of God? O unbearable pride and intolerable obstinacy! There the disciple wishes to reign where the master serves; the slave to rest where the lord labours; the guilty person to be honoured where the judge is wronged.

Thus kindness appeared. Long ago the severity and divinity of the Judge appeared to the Jews, when voices and thunder were heard, the trumpet sounded, they saw lamps and lightning flashes and the smoking mountain, so that they might receive the spirit of slavery in fear. But the kindness and humanity of the Saviour appeared to us, when whoever wished could see the Word as an infant and God as a little child, so that we might receive the spirit of adoption in love. Oh, how much sweeter is the fruit of this appearance than of that one!

God frightened and threatened, saying: “I am the Lord; keep my laws. I am the Lord” (Lev. XIX). Yet amid terrors and frequent, dreadful punishments, his laws were despised. But now he is silent and does not frighten; he spares and does not punish; he entreats and does not rebuke; he suffers and does not take vengeance—and people run to martyrdom for his [Col. 0519A] love.

Let all who are placed in positions of authority hear this: those who command the people with harshness and power and domineer over the clergy with arrogance; arrogant in their rule, grim-faced in their silence, idle in their business. Let them hear and understand that whatever is commanded proudly is very easily despised and most difficult to keep. If God’s own commands could not be kept so long as they were given with terror, how much less can human commands be kept!

The moral fable of Boreas and the Sun offers us a most beautiful example. Having placed a wager between themselves, they began to contend over which could take the cloak from a traveller. In that contest the violence of Boreas’s blast yielded to the graciousness of the sun, signifying that the rule of gentleness is much more powerful than the rule of terror.

That most gentle emperor Julius Caesar knew this, of whom it is recorded that he never called his soldiers anything but “fellow-soldiers,” nor ever said to them, “Go there,” but always, “Come here”—showing how to endure labours rather than commanding. For he knew that nothing is more powerful for persuading hearers to obedience than the humility of rule, supported by the greatness of example. Hence our Bernard [Note: [Col. 0519D] St Bernard, Sermon 2 for Easter]: “The example of a good work is a living and effective word, easily persuading what is said by showing that what is taught can be done.”

Thus, so long as the Lord ruled mortals without the example of humility, he blew like Boreas; but once he himself first offered the traveller an example of humility and patience, he took the cloak, as *Laxias* [the reading is uncertain]. This is what it means for the kindness and humanity of God to have appeared.

[Col. 0519C] O kindness—an appearance as powerful as it is wondrous! In it power lies down, wisdom is silent, justice is mute, abundance is needy, blessedness suffers, weakness prevails, infancy persuades, injustice seemingly triumphs: for the guilty person does not suffer, but guilt is forgiven; poverty reigns, affliction exults. Kindness appeared. O mighty kindness! What is more powerful than this weakness? What wiser than this infant—who, crying in the cradle, is mighty in heaven; silent in flesh, speaks in the star; mute to ears, clamorous to minds; makes foolish the wisdom of the Chaldeans; humbles the pride of kings; draws humble nations from afar; repels indignant Jews from nearby; frustrates Herod’s and Satan’s plot; shatters their assault; dazzles the eye; binds the mind; provokes weapons; mocks hatreds; escapes wrath; invades the homeland; converts the people; overthrows the kingdom?

[Col. 0519D] The Saviour could have appeared in another form, if he had wished; but he could not have appeared in a kinder one. From any material whatever, he could suddenly have created a new man of perfect stature, voice, and strength, who might even sustain life without food. But in order to redeem Adam’s posterity, he had to come from that posterity. Moreover, if such a man had been made, he would have confirmed error more than instructed faith. For who would believe that he had true flesh when he saw no weakness of flesh in him, since John the Baptist himself was believed to have a demon because of his incredible abstinence? “Thus,” as Augustine says, “while doing everything miraculously, he would remove what he did mercifully.”

Therefore he could assume no form more fitting than that of human infancy, in which he might conceal the power of divinity, exalt ordinary things by extraordinary ones, and temper extraordinary things by ordinary ones. The second cause of this appearance is that already stated: the open manifestation of divine kindness, so that no one, however guilty, might fear to approach the gentlest infant; no one, however oppressed by debt, might hesitate to ask from one who possesses all things and denies nothing.

[Col. 0520B] Therefore the kindness of the Saviour wished to appear in an infant—indeed, wished to be an infant. For kindness is liberality in giving and readiness in forgiving. This virtue is so natural in an infant that it can neither put a petitioner to shame nor wish harm upon one who harms it. Therefore the now-grown Saviour, an infant for the salvation of adults, preached thus to adults: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII). He explained this, as it were, when he said: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke VI). To forgive is not to desire vengeance; to give is to give oneself to everyone who asks. These two things belong naturally to infants and voluntarily to saints. Therefore heaven is promised only to those resembling little children.

The third reason for this appearance [Col. 0520C] was, as we have already said, that God might teach humanity, by assuming infancy, to triumph over every enemy through silence and childlikeness. For, as the distinguished orator says, there are two forms of injustice by which all who harm us do us harm: deceit and violence. But deceit, he says, is more deserving of our hatred. In the first respect the devil is called a dragon; in the second, a lion. Under deceit are contained all alluring tricks of flatteries; under violence, all troublesome stings of adversities. This is the double battle-line which the world brings out against us: flattering in order to deceive, frightening in order to break us.

But deceit does not deceive silence, and violence does not conquer patience. By silence I mean not merely silence of tongues but also of affections. For, as the philosopher says: “What profit is there in the silence of an entire region, if the affections make noise?” The affections are silent when they desire nothing beyond necessity, nothing beyond reason. In this silence is peace for human beings of good will. In such silence innocence is preserved, when the tongue is restrained from evil speech and the heart from wicked desire. But in patience justice is perfected, when through it both peace of heart is gained and the soul is possessed.

Perhaps these are the two secrets of which the prophet says: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isa. XXIV). Hence, when a certain holy man was suffering at the point of death and his abbot asked him, “What do you see, son?” he replied: “Nothing is better than keeping silence, Father.”

[Col. 0521A] A fourth reason may be given for the divine appearance in the form of a little child: it was altogether most just that the age which had first borne another’s sin through God’s justice should first receive, through his mercy, the joy of redemption; and that the second Adam should restore another’s salvation in the same order in which the first had violated it. The fifth reason is that which we placed first above, namely the privilege of the New Testament. Since the Lord wished to confer more abundant grace upon it than upon the Old, he wished to appear in the form of a little child, not of fire, thunder, cloud, or smoke.

Let these remarks suffice concerning these two words, “Kindness appeared”; and since we have already prolonged the discourse, let us leave the rest for another time.

## SERMON V. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD, II

[Col. 0521B]

“Today the Church has been joined to her heavenly Bridegroom.” [Note: [Col. 0521D] From an antiphon of the Church.]

Among the solemn holidays instituted by Roman law, the birthday of the emperor, the birthday of his empire, and the birthday of his city were customarily celebrated more solemnly than the others. By a certain divine providence, under Caesar Augustus these three solemnities flowed together on this day as if into one channel of celebration—not according to the beginnings of the celebrations, but according to their expansions.

For Caesar Augustus was first called *imperator* on this day, and thus he himself was in some fashion born emperor today. When he returned from the city of Apollonia after the slaughter of his uncle Julius’s killers, as he entered Rome, a golden circle, with the radiance of a heavenly rainbow, encircled the orb of the sun. The augurs and haruspices, when consulted about it, replied that on this day an empire was being born that would have no end, and that the emperor of this empire would be foretold by heaven and the stars. The Roman senate and people interpreted this response as referring to Augustus and called him emperor.

Afterward, when he had defeated Antony—who ruled the East with Cleopatra and had repudiated Augustus’s sister for Cleopatra’s sake—in naval and land battle, and had forced them to voluntary death, he struck such terror into the whole East that no nation dared take up arms against him. Therefore, today—that is, on the sixth day of January—returning from the Actian victory, he entered Rome victorious in a triumphal chariot. Twenty-five kings, bound like captives with their hands behind their backs, went before his chariot; fifteen kings, his allies, rode behind and around him.

[Col. 0521D] Moreover, among the captives the children of Antony and Cleopatra, Sun and Moon, were dragged along. He himself sat in a golden chair, something no triumphant commander before him had presumed to do; all had stood in the triumphal chariot itself, at its golden rail. He also ordered the temple of Janus shut, in which the weapons of the republic were stored, signifying that he had secured profound peace and respite from every war for the Roman people. He decreed that this day be celebrated throughout the Roman world with perpetual religious observance; this feast lasted until Constantine.

[Col. 0522A] Thus today the Roman empire was born, not according to its beginning but according to its expansion; from this expansion Augustus himself received the name Augustus, which he was the first of Roman emperors to bear. From the joy of this celebration came the decree of Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered (Luke II). From this registration it came about that the City was as great as the world. For anyone who paid tribute to the Romans was a Roman citizen. Hence the whole world is called, in the laws, the Roman world. Thus Virgil says in the epitaph of Julius Caesar:

> Caesar, you were as great as the world;  
> but now you are enclosed in a tiny urn.  
>   
> After you, let everyone know that he too will fall,  
> and let no glory any longer remove death.

[Note: [Col. 0521D] You will search these verses in Virgil in vain: they are by Marbod, bishop of Rennes (d. 1123), *Patrologia* edition.]

Thus today the Roman city too was born, not with regard to the building of its walls, but with regard to the universal registration of its citizens throughout the whole world. Thus these three greatest festivals came together on one and the same day, not according to their beginnings, as we have said, but according to their expansions.

Among us likewise these solemnities in some fashion converge today upon the same day. The birthday of the emperor is Christ’s nativity; the birthday of his empire is the nativity of faith; the birthday of the City is the nativity of the Church. There are, however, three births. The first is eternal, according to which God is born from God; the second temporal, according to which, at the end of time, he was born from the Virgin; the third mystical, according to which in the mystery the head and body are one Christ.

In the first, Light is born from Light, and as the Father is, so is the Son. In the second, man is born from woman and flesh from flesh, and as the mother is, so is the son. On earth, a human being is born though he is old; and what is born is from the Holy Spirit. There are naturally three positions in which those born into temporal life come forth. Either they are born feet first, with their arms arranged similarly alongside them; or with the head coming first, the arms similarly arranged; or, indeed, with arms crossed over the head which comes first.

But holy Jacob, so that through his singular birth the author of nature might signify something beyond nature, was born with his arm extended before [Col. 0522D] his head, grasping in his hand the sole of his elder brother’s foot.
