Hence Jacob signifies Christ according to the sense in which head and body are one Christ, not according to Christ’s individual person. The arm raised before the head signifies the earlier people of the elect, forestalled by grace before the temporal birth of the Saviour, embracing Christ through the five ages of the world, as through the five fingers of a hand; or binding that same people by the five books of Moses. But the remaining body is joined together on either side by the fullness of the Gentiles together with the few Israelites who believe.

[Col. 0523A] The head is born in the middle; yet, once it has been born, the arm which had gone forth before it is assigned to its proper place with the remaining members, so that He may be recognized as the head of the whole Church—to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth. This mystical birth of Christ is celebrated from the beginning of the world until its end; and, just as Paul testifies that he supplied in his own body what was lacking of Christ’s sufferings, Christ has not yet been wholly born. For Christ is born as often as anyone becomes a Christian. For Christians, as Jerome says, are made, not born. But today the faith of Christ was first born among the Gentiles, whose first fruits were the Magi. Today it was also first born among the Jews, whose first fruits were the apostles, who, at the miracle of water made into wine at the wedding, today first believed in Christ, as the Evangelist testifies (John 2); for today Christian faith was born in the human heart, through which Christ reigns in us.

Today, therefore, is not inappropriately called the birthday of Christ’s empire. For today the Magi first confessed Him to be King, saying: “Where is He who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. 2.) Moreover, the city of this great King is the Church itself, gathered from Jews and Gentiles and joined together in Him, the cornerstone. Today this city was built through the faith of believers in both walls; and thus today is not inappropriately called the birthday of the City which is mistress of the whole world—not that city of which it was said, “Her first walls were drenched with a brother’s blood,” although this too may not unfittingly be applied to the Church, in which Cain slew his brother Abel and the Jews slew Christ.

Certainly, that circle of golden colour which surrounded the disk of the sun when Augustus entered Rome signified the birthday of this empire. For the faith of Christ is coeval with the world, beginning from the world’s beginning and destined to endure to its end. The children of Antony and Cleopatra, called Sun and Moon because they represented the fullness of the two sexes, more properly signify Christ than Augustus, who rules heaven and the stars. The census of the whole world made under the governor Quirinius more truly designates the Church than Rome, which will reign without end. Further, Quirinius, whose name is interpreted “heir,” openly points to Christ, to whom the Father says: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2).

The twenty-five kings who were led captive before Augustus’s chariot, their hands bound behind their backs, signify the kingdom of sin, of the world, and of the senses of the flesh, which is to be subjected to Christ and taken captive by Him through the victory of the resurrection and the triumph of the ascension, as it is written: “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Eph. 4). This number, namely twenty-five, which arises from the square of five, signifies the circuit of worldly things, which returns into itself, as it is written: “What is it that has been? The very thing which shall be” (Eccl. 1). It also signifies the circuit of the ungodly, concerning which it is said:

[Col. 0524A] “The ungodly walk in a circle” (Ps. 11).

And again: “My God, make them like a wheel” (Ps. 82).

For this reason this number is called circular, because it always returns to five, whether it be squared or cubed. And perhaps these are those twenty-five men of whom it is written in Ezekiel, who had their backs turned to the Temple and worshipped toward the rising of the sun (Ezek. 8). The Apostle almost explains this when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5).

But if there were twenty-two kings, they signify the kingdom—or rather, the tyranny—of pride, which transgresses natural and written law, and which, therefore, being designated by twice eleven kings, is to be destroyed through Christ’s cross, as the Apostle says: “He removed from the midst the bond of the decree which was against us, fastening it to the cross” (Col. 2).

Moreover, the fifteen kings who were Augustus’s friends, riding beside the triumphant emperor as companions, signify the fulfillers of both Testaments, that is, of the whole Law, through the single commandment of charity. For “the whole Law is fulfilled in this word: You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Rom. 13). This charity, however, comprised by the Apostle in fifteen members, plainly shows that it contains the heptad of the Jewish Law and the evangelical ogdoad, concerning which it is said: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11).

The philosopher says: “You will be king over many kings, if reason rules you; and, they say, king over playing children, if you act rightly.” But what is more right, or more suited to reason, than that you should not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself, and should not delay to do for another what you wish done for yourself? In these two precepts the whole natural law is contained. Written law, moreover, is nothing but the full recollection, with exposition, of the natural law effaced in sinners. Therefore, since to be king is to live rightly and to govern oneself according to the rule of faith, those who obey the divine commands are fittingly signified by kings. These are those friends of the great Augustus of whom it is written: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honoured; their rule is exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. 138).

Augustus seated in the chariot signifies Christ, who is our peace and the rest of the saints; the golden chariot signifies evangelical teaching, shining with the splendour of heavenly wisdom. Thus the golden circle surrounding the sun’s orb signifies Christ’s birth according to the flesh; Augustus’s triumph signifies His spiritual birth according to faith. The census of the whole world prefigures the birthday of the city—that is, the Church—to which it is said: “You shall spread abroad to east and west, north and south” (Isa. 54); and again, of which it is said: “Mount Zion is founded in the joy of the whole earth, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. 47).

This city is also a bride: a city by its capacity, a bride by its charity; a city because it is gathered together, a bride because it is loved; a city by number, a bride by merit. Therefore it is said of her:

[Col. 0525A] “Today the Church has been joined to the heavenly Bridegroom.”

She was drawn from the distant boundaries of misery by the cords of mercy, so that Jeremiah’s saying might be fulfilled: “I have loved you with everlasting love, having had mercy on you” (Jer. 31). Similar is Isaiah’s saying: “I have taken hold of you from the ends of the earth, and called you from its remote regions” (Isa. 41). The remote regions of the earth are lesser sins; its ends are greater ones. Those at the ends of the earth are farther from God than those in its remote regions. These are called; those are seized. To be seized is more than to be called, because where sin abounded, grace abounded still more. The apostles were called; tax collectors and prostitutes were seized. We are called through commandments; we are seized through chastisements. Hence it is written: “Lay hold of discipline” (Ps. 2). As if to say: Lay hold of Him who lays hold of you; embrace Him who embraces you.

For the grasping of discipline is nothing other than the holy and delightful embrace of wisdom and the bond of charity. Hence Hosea’s saying: “I shall draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of charity” (Hos. 2). The cords of Adam—that is, of human beings—must be understood according to their threefold use. For we use cords to bind, to draw, and to measure. Necessity binds; desire draws; mortality measures.

Necessity is threefold: natural, voluntary, and accidental. Natural necessity consists in hunger and thirst, sleep and wakefulness, labour and rest. These are wholly involuntary by nature. Voluntary necessity is sin, without which mortal life cannot be lived. For every sin is voluntary; but because it cannot altogether be avoided, it is called necessity. Accidental necessity is tribulation inflicted upon us by God, by a neighbour, or by the ancient enemy. The first two are inward; the third comes from without.

Of natural necessities it is said: “Does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it away to water?” (Luke 13.) For in the same way we satisfy natural necessities on feast days as on ordinary days. Of voluntary necessities it is said: “The cords of sinners have wrapped themselves around me” (Ps. 118). Again: “The ungodly man is bound fast by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5). Of accidental necessities it is said: “Should not this woman, whom Satan has bound now for eighteen years, be loosed on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13.) For accidental necessity afflicts more painfully than natural necessity; and therefore it is no less lawful to seek a remedy for the former than for the latter. Of all together it is said: “The troubles of my heart have been multiplied; deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24).

This is concerning cords which bind. But concerning cords which draw, it is said: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1); and: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 5). For God draws, and the devil draws: the former upward, the latter downward; the former to heaven, the latter to hell; the former to glory, the latter to punishment. God alone draws; but with the devil the flesh draws, and the world draws: the flesh through hunger for gluttony and lust, the world through thirst for money and honour. Worldly fear draws one back from good; desire for temporal things draws one toward evil. These are the two cords by which the dragon’s tail draws a third part of the stars to itself—

[Col. 0526A] and that part alone. For it does not prevail against the other two: those who either preserve innocence or practise repentance. But it prevails against those who, neither cold through fear nor fervent through charity, languish in deadly lukewarmness; who neither consider the song of the angels nor dread the woe of the reprobate. This concerns the individual cords which draw.

Concerning cords which measure, however, it is said: “He divided the land among them with the cord of apportionment” (Ps. 77); and elsewhere: “He measured two cords, one for putting to death, the other for keeping alive” (2 Sam. 8). These two cords signify either God’s election and reprobation, or that twofold and differing judicial sentence: “Come, you blessed”; “Depart, you cursed” (Matt. 25); or death and judgment, concerning which the Apostle says: “It is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment” (Heb. 9). The cord of death measures the present life; the cord of judgment, the future life. That death has a fixed boundary is attested by Job, who says: “You have established his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job 14).

These two measuring cords may also signify the good represented by the Pythagorean figure, which divides the choice of human discernment into two branches. Its right branch may be called the life-giving cord, its left the killing cord. Of these the poet says:

> And the letter which leads you along sound branches  
> Marks the path rising by the right-hand way.

Therefore the Word made flesh bound Himself with Adam’s cords, in order to loose us who were bound; He made Himself like us so that, through the likeness of such great condescension, He might draw our affections more powerfully to Himself. He measured Himself by our mortality, so that He might make us participants in His immortality. In all these things His condescension in becoming like us is commended.

For how like us He chose to become—He who, except for sin and ignorance, assumed our nature; bound and measured by the cord of passibility! And why, except that by the most gracious likeness He might draw us to love Himself, whom we were unwilling to love so long as He was unwilling to make Himself like us? For it is written: “Every living creature loves its like; so every human being is joined to his neighbour; all flesh is joined to what is like itself; so every human being [is joined to] his like” (Ecclus. 13).

Hence comes the prophet’s most powerful consolation to his own soul:

[Col. 0526D] “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God” (Ps. 41).

That is to say: O my soul, do not fear to draw near to my God. He bears my countenance, being like me; in Him my salvation has also been made—that is, my Saviour Himself is a man like me; passible like me; hungry and thirsty like me; worn out by vigils and labour like me; not hating His flesh, nor loving death, just as I do not. O likeness most worthy of every love! Divine compassion clothed it in charity; only the condescension of highest dignity assumed it.

And see how graciously He was made “in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2). For, in assuming humanity, He did not disdain to become grass, clay, and a corpse. For the Word became all this when He became flesh. Every flesh is grass, every flesh is clay, and every flesh is a corpse: grass by its beauty, clay by its origin, a corpse by its death; grass by its passing away, clay by its entrance, a corpse by its fall; grass by its form, clay by its material, a corpse by its ruin.

Of the first it is said: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40), and: “Human beings: their days are like grass; they flourish like the flower of the field” (Ps. 102). Of the second: “Remember, I pray, that you made me as clay” (Job 10). Of the third: “Wherever the corpse may be, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24). Origen, most learned in the Hebrew language, thus translated the passage in Matthew.

Therefore, when God became man, He became grass, clay, and a corpse—but grass ever flowering, clay never filthy, and a corpse never decaying. Grass, that He might nourish; clay, that He might cleanse; a corpse, that He might feed. For there is a kind of clay suited to removing stains from garments and washing away dirt. Christ became grass in His flower, clay in His blood, and a corpse in His flesh. His life and teaching flourished and will flourish for ever; His passion washed and will always wash; His flesh fed, feeds, and will feed for ever without end.

In this grass the holy confessors made their nests; in this clay the glorious martyrs made their robes white; to this corpse the flying eagles were gathered—that is, the souls of the saints, now released from the prisons of their bodies, who ascended from the valley of tears to the mountain of the Lord and rest securely beneath God’s altar. On this mountain they find prepared a banquet of rich things, a banquet of vintage wine: rich things full of marrow, vintage wine clarified of its lees. The rich things full of marrow are those orders of blessed spirits who continually feed upon the inmost vision of God, because they always behold the Father’s face. Their banquet is the most glorious flesh of the Son of God, seated at the right hand of the Father’s majesty, into which angels desire to look. The clarified vintage is His most blessed and surpassingly excellent soul, established among the chief goods of divine blessedness.

How truly, then, the Apostle says: “The kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3). God’s kindness appeared especially in His humanity—that is, in His most gracious assumption of humanity. For God could never have shown better how kind He was toward humanity and how greatly He loved it than by assuming flesh, as we have already shown.

Therefore our necessities, which Christ took upon Himself; our iniquities, which He blotted out like a cloud; the innumerable sufferings which He endured for us; and the immeasurable compassions which He showed us from His heart—these are the cords of Adam by which today He drew the Church to Himself, as a bridegroom draws a bride: though heavenly, [He drew] one earthly; though noble, one ignoble; though rich, one poor; though beautiful, one ugly. Clearly men do not ordinarily choose wives in this way. For, as Isidore says, four things are sought in choosing a wife: lineage, beauty, character, and wealth. But before Christ’s bride was joined to Him, she was called Canaanite because of the lowliness of her lineage, Ethiopian because of her ugliness, naked because of her poverty, and bloodstained because of her foulness—that is, full of crimes and shameful deeds.

[Col. 0528A] Moreover, in choosing a husband, according to the aforesaid Isidore, four things are usually sought: virtue, lineage, character, and wisdom. It should be noted that in both choices character is placed near the end, because among the lovers of this world scarcely any inquiry is made into character—and would that it were made even last! For with most people no inquiry is made at all.

But Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, has such power that at His touch the sick regain strength, at His fragrance the dead revive, and at His cry the buried leap forth. He is noble as the Son of the Most High; wise as the Angel of Great Counsel; beautiful as the Son of God; rich and affluent as the Creator of the world. O how rich He is, whose is “the earth and its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it”! The streets of His city are paved with pure gold. O how beautiful He is, whose beauty sun and moon admire, and into whom angels desire to look! O how wise He is, who catches the wise in their own craftiness, who destroys the wisdom of the wise and rejects the prudence of the prudent; whose wisdom founded the earth, whose understanding established the heavens; whose foolishness is wiser than human beings! His nobility cannot be related any more than His generation itself: “Who shall declare his generation?” he says (Isa. 51); much less, then, His nobility. O how great is His power—He conquered sin by living, the world by preaching, the devil by dying, and hell by rising again!

But who can explain the sweetness of His character? Certainly He could not have explained it better or more fully than when He said: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8). What do you say to this, O bride—not ugly but beautiful; not ignoble but noble; not poor but wealthy; not unhappy but blessed? Behold, you have a Bridegroom answering every desire: when you love Him, you are chaste; when you touch Him, you are clean; when you receive Him, you are a virgin; when you marry Him, you are blessed. Surely He could not have taken a wife more humbly, nor could you have married more gloriously.

Therefore let us run, brothers, let us run, I beg you, especially to the royal wedding; but let us run like the Magi—that is, as wise men—with gifts. For it is foolish to make a request with empty hands. To run is to seek, ask, and knock. “Everyone,” Scripture says, “who seeks finds, and whoever asks receives, and to the one who knocks it is opened” (Luke 11). Many seek but do not find because they seek foolishly; many ask but do not receive because they ask foolishly; many knock but do not enter because they knock foolishly. We must seek, but with a light; ask, but with a gift; knock, but with a cry.

The light with which we must seek is repentance, which burns through contrition and shines through confession. This is the lamp which the woman lights in order to sweep the house and find the lost drachma (Luke 15). To sweep the house is to change one’s way of life; to find the drachma is to restore in the conscience the dignity of the divine likeness. That likeness is contained in the ten commandments, as in ten drachmas. Whoever loses one loses all; whoever offends in one point becomes guilty of all; and whoever finds one finds all, for whoever possesses one virtue possesses all.

We must ask, but with a gift, because, according to the common proverb, “an empty hand makes a fruitless request.” Therefore let us offer the Saviour gifts which He first offered us, as a lord offering them like a servant. He offered us gold in words of grace, incense in deeds of power, and myrrh in the bitterness of patience: gold in commandments, incense in miracles, myrrh in afflictions. Let us, therefore, offer Him the gold of almsgiving, the incense of prayer, and the myrrh of continence, which is customarily signified by fasting; or the gold of faith, the incense of desire, and the myrrh of martyrdom.

[Col. 0529B] We must knock with the key, with persistence and perseverance. This alone enters, because it alone saves; it alone obtains, because it alone crowns. Persistent labour conquers all things. Nothing is so closed that the importunate knocker cannot enter it.

Blessed are those to whom, by thus running and knocking, it is granted to enter the wedding of the Lamb, so that the guests may rejoice at water made into wine—that is, fear wholly transformed into love, or rather swallowed up by love; for “there is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear.” Or water made into wine is rest after labour, abundance after poverty, fullness after hunger, joy after sorrow. As it is written: “Sorrow in the heart of a man shall humble him, but by a good word he shall be made glad” (Prov. 12)—namely, by this word: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6). This is the good wine which the Bridegroom of the Church still keeps for us, as it is written: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30). May He bring us to it, who lives and reigns without end.

## SERMON VI. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY, I

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Ps. 47).

This mercy is received in two ways: mentally, so to speak, in the Word; sacramentally, in the flesh. The first pertains to Simeon, the second to Anna. That is, Simeon bears in himself the mystery of the first reception; Anna the widow contains the sacrament of the second reception. Simeon is interpreted “hearing of sorrow.” The word of God announces to us a twofold sorrow: the eternal misery of Gehenna and the temporal discipline of repentance. For “all discipline at the present time seems not to be joyful but sorrowful” (Heb. 12).

The first sorrow is announced by him who says: “Which of you can dwell with devouring fire? Or which of you can live with everlasting burnings?” (Isa. 33.) And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Fear Him who, after He has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna” (Matt. 10). Gehenna is twofold, of heat and of cold, according to the saying: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8). How fearful and dreadful that Gehenna is, the Lord shows when He so often repeats its eternity, saying:

[Col. 0530A] “It is better for you to enter into life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the Gehenna of fire” (Matt. 18). “Where their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched” (Isa. 66).

Repetition confirms the saying, so that He may terrify us from eternal damnation, which will most certainly come. Whoever hears this sorrow believes most certainly in the future judgment and always fears it. Whatever the poets have invented about infernal punishments is believed by philosophers to be fable. But charity cannot deceive, truth cannot invent, and Scripture cannot be dissolved.

Therefore whatever is written in Scripture about hell must be believed to be true, because it is undoubtedly true. These things were not spoken by the Holy Spirit merely to frighten us, as they were invented by poets, as the Origenists falsely assert; rather, they are as Scripture says. Otherwise, if the punishment of the wicked is not eternal, neither should the rewards of the righteous be believed eternal. But it is true what is written: “The righteous shall go into eternal life” (Matt. 25). Therefore that which precedes is also true: “And these shall go into eternal punishment” (ibid.).

Jerome reports that Zeno, leader of the Stoics, believed in the underworld and in immortal souls. Juvenal likewise, the satirist, contrary to the general opinion of the Gentiles, affirms that this should be believed, saying:

> That there are shades and subterranean realms,  
> And a pole, and black frogs in the Stygian whirlpool,  
> And that so many thousands cross one channel in a single boat—  
> Things even boys do not believe, except those not yet washed for a coin;  
> But you, hold them true.  
> *(Juvenal, Satires 2.45.)*

[Col. 0530C] Therefore, as we have said, to hear the sorrow of Gehenna is firmly to believe that Gehenna exists and always to fear it. Those hear this sorrow but do not heed it who merely hold such an opinion and do not believe it firmly. But no one who believes firmly fails effectively to heed this sorrow; and because of such heeding he is designated by Simeon’s name.

Moreover, heeding the second sorrow is the undertaking of repentance and the persevering performance of what has been undertaken. He divides by injustice, but does not heed, who has accepted an imposed penance but casts away what he accepted. Therefore neither of these two sorrows can be heeded without the other: Gehenna cannot be feared healthfully without carrying out repentance, nor can repentance be completed without fear of Gehenna. These two joined together make Simeon—that is, the good hearer of twofold sorrow.

This is the old man, that is, the wise man, because wisdom is found among the ancients. For it is written: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28). Hence this same Simeon is called righteous and God-fearing: God-fearing because of his continual fear of the Lord; righteous because of his unceasing zeal for justice. Nothing is more just than for us all to fear continually the Judge of all.

This Simeon always dwells in Jerusalem and awaits the consolation of Israel, because justice is allied with peace and consolation is promised to the mourning. “Justice and peace,” it says, “have kissed” (Ps. 84); and: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). He received an answer from the Holy Spirit—that is, from his conscience responding well to him by spiritual testimony—that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ: that is, before his sins had first been forgiven and their yoke had decayed before the oil, that is, before the rich mercy of God.

Therefore he came in the spirit into the Temple. “In the spirit,” that is, with a spiritual will: intending to hear the word of God, retain it in memory, keep it faithfully, and fulfill it effectively, knowing truly that it is written: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11). No one can profit in the Temple who does not know how to come into the Temple in the spirit. No one, moreover, comes in the spirit unless a spiritual will leads him.

There are those whom wantonness leads into the Temple; there are those whom greed brings there; there are those whom ambition introduces; there are those whom curiosity admits. The thief comes only to steal; the wanton person only to be seen or to see, to be touched or to touch; the ambitious person to be honoured; the curious person to pry. The Temple is a house of prayer; but the first make this house a den of thieves, the second a brothel of prostitutes, the third a marketplace, the fourth a forum for lawsuits. For even among those who hear God’s word, some hear it merely to be praised; others, in order to criticize; few, in order to receive it; fewer still, in order to keep it. Yet to criticize is evil, to praise is insufficient, to receive is necessary, while to preserve and keep is best and perfect. Would that whenever we come to the Temple, we came in the spirit; would that devotion to hear God’s word led us there, rather than a desire to disparage led us astray!

[Col. 0531C] Yet the reception itself shows in what spirit each person comes. How devoted Simeon was, that most devout affection showed well, by which he embraced the child presented. Indeed, his most impatient longing did not wait until Mary, carrying God’s incarnate mercy in her arms, had reached the altar; but while His parents were still bringing in the child Jesus, he met them in the middle of the Temple and received the child there—indeed, with a certain eager haste he snatched Him from Mary’s arms into his own, embraced Him, and kissed Him.

Certainly this is how the word of God must be kept. The hearer must meet the preacher with a lively mind, willing spirit, and ready heart, so that he may say with the Prophet: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 107). He should not wait until the preacher brings forth keen sayings and penetrating—that is, persuasive—words. Rather, as soon as God begins to speak through him, he should open to Him the door of his heart and, as Augustine says, make a nest for the Lord’s word, where it may lay and warm its young. For the proper dwelling of the Lord’s discourse is nothing other than the human heart: this is its proper house, its abode, its lodging, its nest. God’s word seeks this lodging from us. Hence it says: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23).

If a little child stood outside at the door of your house and, for the love of God, asked you for lodging, would not anyone who failed to take him in be cruel and inhuman? But it is all the more cruel and unhappy to turn away this child, called Jesus Christ, when He asks for lodging, because He is worthier and sweeter, and because His condescension is greater in asking lodging from human beings, without whom human beings cannot fare well.

And what is sweeter than mercy, or worthier than wisdom? What is sweeter than salvation, or worthier than the Saviour? Yet what is worthier than His condescension in lodging among the misery of our unworthiness? “If anyone loves me,” He says, “he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3). O happy is the human being with so great a guest!

[Col. 0532B] The Lord knocks at your door whenever He offers you, through a preacher, the word of salvation. Therefore receive it in the midst of the Temple—that is, in the midst of your heart—as it is written: “That I might do your will, O God, and [have] your law in the midst of my heart” (Ps. 39). For if, according to the Apostle, our bodies are the Temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 6), what else is the midst of this Temple but our heart? For the heart of an animal is in its midst.

Moreover, this child must not only be received as a guest, but also carried in the hands. What is it to carry the child Jesus in one’s hands except to fulfill the word of salvation by works? Yet fewer things can be carried in the hands than embraced with the arms; therefore He must not merely be carried, but embraced and sweetly clasped to the breast. What we are accustomed merely to carry often burdens us as we carry it.

But what we embrace and press to our breast always delights us without doubt. Therefore, to carry the child Jesus in the hands is to do what is commanded; to embrace Him is to fulfill more than is commanded. Prohibitions belong to reception; commandments, to carrying; counsels, to embracing. The two arms with which He must be embraced are cheerful obedience and strong patience; or temperance in prosperity and patience in adversity. These are the ambidextrous, who fight with the left hand as with the right; whom neither prosperity deceives nor adversity crushes.

Woe to those who are maimed in both arms for embracing this child: luxurious in prosperity, grumbling in adversity; unrestrained in pleasures, impatient in calamities; unable—or rather unwilling—to do good or endure evil. The embrace and pressing to the breast of this child signify devotion in good work and glorying in tribulation. We cannot walk for long with burdened arms unless we take care to clasp the very burdens of our arms to our breasts. For the farther laden arms are held from the breast, the more easily they grow weary with labour. Likewise, no one can long remain either eager in obedience or long-suffering in patience unless he is willing and devoted to both. For what we do unwillingly, we soon abandon; and what we bear unwillingly, we cease to bear as quickly as we can.

[Col. 0533A] Therefore devotion alone completes an undertaking; sloth alone destroys it. Devotion lightens even heavy labours; sloth makes light ones heavy, according to the saying of the comic poet: “Nothing is so easy that it is not difficult if you do it unwillingly.” Conversely one may add: nothing is so difficult that it is not easy if you do it willingly and devoutly. This is the libation which must always accompany sacrifice, according to that prophetic saying: “Sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God” (Joel 2). Sacrifice without a libation is a vain work without devotion.

Next, the child must be kissed—not on His own lips, but only upon the traces of His feet. For that highest kiss must be reserved by the privilege of a singular gift. This child is never read to have been kissed upon His mouth except by His mother or by a traitor. It is the height of presumption for a polluted mouth to wish to offer itself to the lips of the Highest. Yet to whom does that prophetic woe not apply, so that he may say that he is of unclean lips? “Every human being is a liar” (Rom. 3). Shall he then kiss the lips of Truth itself with his own unclean lips?

Let the kiss of His feet suffice us sinners. To kiss above them is something which not even that holy Simeon presumed to do. Is this not a great thing? For who could be considered higher than one who kisses the feet of Him seated in heaven? O truly a man of gigantic height, to whom it was granted to kiss the footprints of so exalted a majesty! But what is it to kiss the soles of the Lord’s Word except to despise all our good deeds in our own sight and reckon them as nothing, as it is written: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: We are useless servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17)?

[Col. 0533C] He truly kisses the Lord’s feet who always considers himself less than others and, praising and magnifying the good deeds and words of others, judges that he himself has done nothing by comparison with them, and thinks himself to be nothing.

He kisses the feet of God who attributes every good thing not to his own exertion but to God’s grace, while imputing and ascribing his evils to himself alone. He kisses the Lord’s feet who casts his good deeds from his sight and always remembers his evils with tears. Blessed Bernard invites us to this by a most beautiful comparison: we should act as poor and sick persons seated beside main roads or in the porticoes of churches, asking alms from passers-by or those entering the church. For what is healthy and strong in them they conceal rather than display; but what is ulcerated and decayed, foul and pitiable to look upon, they strive to exhibit rather than hide, so that those who see them may be moved more readily to compassion and induced to give. So too, in God’s sight, we ought not boast of and magnify whatever good things are ours, as that Pharisee did, but rather uncover our wounds, like the humble tax collector. Humility alone, therefore, deserves to kiss the Lord’s feet. Pride, however, always standing arrogantly upon the heights and lifting and raising itself beyond its proper measure in swollen self-exaltation, approaches fracture and ruin all the more closely insofar as it presumes to claim for itself a familiar kiss wholly undeserved in the presence of the lover of the humble.

To kiss the soles of the Lord is also to render heart-felt thanks, with the most devout affections, for the Lord’s Incarnation. See, then, how the Word of God must be received. Yet it truly belongs to God himself that the Word offered may be rightly received. And as we have learned from St Simeon the manner of receiving, so we must learn from the Blessed Virgin Mary the manner of offering. In her offering three things especially must be considered: time, manner, and place—when, how, and where. For this Word was not offered immediately after his birth from his mother, but only when the days of Mary’s purification had been fulfilled. He was offered neither in terrifying majesty nor in contemptible nakedness, but clothed in tender limbs and wrapped in the purest swaddling-clothes. He was offered not outside the Temple, nor at its doors, but in its very midst.

Likewise, the future preacher, who is the spiritual mother of the divine Word, ought not, as soon as he has lightly and superficially touched upon certain mysteries of Holy Scripture, preach publicly in church; rather, he should first do so when his conscience has been cleansed and his former way of life wholly purified. “For who shall be cleansed from the unclean?” Then let him offer the Word, neither in philosophical majesty nor in rustic simplicity, but adorned with most moving thoughts and clothed in most sweet discourse. His tongue must not merely make a noise outside at the people’s ears, as though offering Jesus at the doors of the Temple; rather, it must penetrate inwardly to the depths of the heart, as though offering Jesus in the midst of the Temple, so that hearers may say: “We have received thy mercy, O God, in the midst of thy temple” (Ps. 47). Thus preachers are commanded: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem” (Isa. 40). As though he said: Do not speak to purses, tongues, or ears, but rather to the people’s hearts.

There are indeed four kinds of preachers: preachers to purses, preachers to tongues, preachers to ears, and preachers to hearts. Of the last there is a very great scarcity; of the others, a harmful multitude. The first seek nothing but money; the second desire nothing but fame; the third do not know what to seek; the fourth wish to lose nothing. Therefore, having rejected the first three kinds, let us strive to attain the fourth. I say, “let us strive,” because this is work; this is labor. For such effectiveness in speech as not only pricks but pierces the human heart requires in every way a *eucharis* tongue, which can abound only in a good person.

For the most holy eucharist of salutary and persuasive speech, just as it is prepared only upon the altar of a pure heart, is likewise administered only through a *eucharis* tongue. As a woman who conceives in sin gives birth in sin through natural generation, so undoubtedly one who is unclean when conceiving the divine Word is necessarily both an unworthy sower of so holy a seed and a useless steward. Holiness of life alone is not enough unless fertility of doctrine is also present; and doctrine is always barren unless the eloquence of the tongue makes it fruitful. Nor is the *eucharis* tongue one that skilfully teaches falsehood and easily persuades people to anything unlawful. For since the Greek name *eucharis* means in Latin either “good grace” or “well-graced,” it is clear that no tongue deserves so gracious a designation unless it is manifestly gracious toward what is good.

Thus, as though a new offering of the child Jesus were being made by the Virgin Mary—mother and full of graces—in the midst of the Temple, pleasing to those who come to meet it and most welcome to those who receive it, so it is when an ecclesiastical preacher, pure in life, fruitful in knowledge, and most eloquent in speech, persuades people to proceed along the way of salvation and walk in salvation. He uses speech that is pure and simple, honorable and useful, holy and life-giving, gracious and sweet, as it is written concerning this child: “Grace is poured out upon thy lips” (Ps. 44). Certainly, if there is one who offers him thus, there will be one who receives the offering well. For no one now comes, like Simeon, to receive the child Jesus, because no one proceeds, like Mary, to offer him.

## SERMON VII. ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY, II

“But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4).

This sentence of Paul, writing to the Galatians, is customarily referred to the Nativity of the Lord because of the words, “God sent his Son, made from a woman”; but it also belongs to today’s solemnity because of what follows: “made under the law.” For this brief saying nevertheless fully embraces everything that today’s reading from the holy Gospel says concerning the Purification of the Blessed Mary and the bringing of the child Jesus by his parents into the Temple, that they might do for him according to the custom of the law. Accordingly, today at the sixth hour in our order a short chapter was made from this sentence. Perhaps this very child Jesus was also presented in the Temple on this day.

Because today’s feast wholly depends upon the grace of this text, we have therefore proposed to your charity to explain the entire sentence of Paul briefly and plainly, insofar as God grants and time permits. Five matters must be considered in its explanation: time, author, work, cause, and manner. These are: the time of fullness; the author of all things; the work of the divine Incarnation; the cause, namely our redemption; and the manner of the work—that is, the formation of the Redeemer from a woman and his subjection under the law. Let us explain each in order more fully: “When the fullness of time came,” and so forth.

All time before the Savior’s coming remained as though empty and void, a time of want and need, since in it there could never and nowhere be found that by which even one man could redeem his soul from the hand of hell. Yet the redemption of a man’s soul is his own true wealth. But that time was truly most full in which the Savior brought the full gift of salvation, namely the price of abundant redemption, as the Church sings throughout the whole world today: “According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 47). The Lord’s name is Jesus Christ: Jesus from salvation; Christ from anointing. The work of Jesus is salvation—true salvation—who “worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” The work of Christ is redemption—abundant redemption—which redeemed the world from everlasting death. Therefore, because his work corresponds to his name, his praise likewise corresponds to his name unto the ends of the earth: that everywhere he may be praised as the true Savior and Redeemer—Savior from sins, Redeemer from punishments, restorer of innocence, rewarder of righteousness.

Hence it follows: “Thy right hand is full of righteousness” (ibid.). Your righteousness, Jesus: you who are wholly right-handed, with nothing left-handed; wholly prosperous, with nothing adverse; wholly strong, with nothing weak. For “what is weak in thee is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1). You are altogether nothing other than mercy justifying the ungodly, and justice rewarding the just, exalting the humble and casting down the proud. Your work is an abundance of mercy and a fullness of justice.

Indeed, he in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” and in whom are hidden “the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2), could not come except with the fullness and abundance of salvation. He is the fountain of goodness, the fountain of light, the fountain of life, the river of peace, and the torrent of glory, as it is written: “Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66). Hence he formerly said to the Jews: “The world is mine, and its fullness” (Ps. 49). “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am full” (Isa. 1). O how full is he who has no need of our goods; who alone suffices to himself; from whose fullness we all have received (John 1), whatever good we possess; from whom all good things proceed and to whom all return, like rivers to the place from which they flow, that they may flow again.

Thus John says that he is full of grace and truth (ibid.): full of grace, so that through abundant grace he might fulfill the commandments of the law and enable others to fulfill them; full of truth, so that by the truth brought to fulfillment he might fulfill whatever the law had prophesied. Hence he says: “I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). Augustine, against Faustus, says on this passage: “He fulfills the law who lives as the law commands; for the fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. 13). It is fulfilled when what is commanded is done, or when what was prophesied therein is accomplished. When this was fulfilled, grace and truth came to be. Grace pertains to the fullness of charity, truth to the fulfillment of prophecies; and both occur through Jesus. Hence: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1) [Col. 0537A]. This is his praise unto the ends of the earth.

Augustine, to Volusianus [Note: [Col. 0537D] Augustine, Letter III]: “In Christ Jesus, at that time which he knew to be most fitting and had ordained before the ages, instruction and assistance for attaining everlasting salvation came to humankind. For he brought us instruction in charity, as the Angel of Great Counsel or Wonderful Counselor, as God’s Wisdom and teacher of righteousness; and assistance, as Mighty God or God’s Power and giver of grace, forgiving sins and granting merits. His wisdom enlightens our ignorance; his power helps and strengthens our weakness.”

For this reason the Apostle called the Savior’s coming in the flesh “the fullness of time,” that is, the time of fullness, by hypallage; or “fullness,” that is, the completion of the time promised in the law. Therefore, when this fullness of time came, God sent his Son.

Behold the author; behold the work. The author is most excellent; the work most excellent. The author is the Father of mercies and God of all consolation; the work is the Son of God, sent for the salvation of human beings and the consolation of the miserable, as he himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to heal the broken-hearted, and to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those who are shut in” (Isa. 61).

“He sent,” he says, “his Son.” He sent him not that he might be where he had not previously been, but that he might appear where he had been hidden. He sent him as an ambassador and as a gift: as an ambassador to enemies and as a gift to friends; to reconcile the former and honor the latter. Of this embassy Obadiah says: “We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an ambassador among the nations” (Obad. 1). And Paul says more plainly: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their offenses to them; and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we perform an embassy for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5). What could be sweeter than this entreaty? What more exalted than this embassy? What easier than this reconciliation? We should have done this even without being asked; how much more when God asks us so sweetly! He asks us when he sends ambassadors to ask us.

Of the gift we have in Isaiah: “A little child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isa. 95 [probably 9]). And in the Gospel: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3), namely to the world, as price and food: as a price for captives, that they might be redeemed from everlasting death; as food for the hungry, that they might be nourished unto everlasting life. For we were bought at a great price by him who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 5). O most precious price, by which the entire world was redeemed! O most delightful food, which is the food of angels!

Hence Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0537D] More correctly, Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, [Col. 0538D] Patristic Edition] says in praise of the Cross:

> Blessed is she upon whose arms  
> The price of the world hung,  
> And bore away the prey of Tartarus.

And the Psalmist says: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 87 [probably 78]). What do you say here, O human ingratitude, ungrateful toward so great a giver and gift? Who hastens, with the shepherds, to see this most magnificent gift; eagerly desires, with the Magi, to adore it; ardently waits and seeks, with Simeon who came to meet it, to receive it in his hands and embrace it in joyful arms? Finally, who gladly and cheerfully, with the widow Anna, gives thanks to the Lord for the happy reception of so great a gift, offering from the depths of the heart a holocaust of thanksgiving to the freely bestowed liberality of so great a giver?

Ten lepers are cleansed by the Lord, but nine ungrateful persons are unrecognized by him (Luke 17). They wrongly join the fourfold grace of him who became for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption from God, to the fivefold number of the senses; they cannot wisely seek or happily find the tenth drachma; nor can they attain, through the one thing necessary, the reward of the eternal denarius. Thus only one is grateful—and he is a foreigner, making himself a stranger to worldly affairs; like a pilgrim and sojourner who has no abiding city here but seeks the one to come, striving toward one thing and seeking one thing; not anxious about many things, because one thing is necessary, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Ingratitude alone makes us remain in the deficiency of the number nine, short of the perfection of ten. It hinders our conversion from growth in eagerness and fervor of spirit, extinguishing the first warmth of our faith by a certain deadly lukewarmness and torpor. Therefore, to the one leper who returned and gave thanks to his cleanser for his cleansing, the same cleanser says: “Go, because thy faith has made thee whole” (Luke 17)—that is, the devotion of faith.

Our fathers once advanced from day to day; today, among us who had the same beginnings of conversion, a person would be considered great if he preserved even the very beginnings of his religious life. Has the Lord’s hand been shortened, or have the treasures of grace failed? Has his will to save us changed, or has his power diminished? Far be it! Rather, our ingratitude has kept the increase of his grace far from us who are lukewarm. Such ingratitude makes the favorable time of grace most disastrous for the ungrateful, because living in the time of grace is not as great a happiness as refusing grace when it is offered, or failing to keep it when it has been received, is a misfortune.

Yet it is also an act of mercy, as Blessed Bernard maintains [Note: [Col. 0538D] Sermon against the vice of ingratitude], to withdraw grace from the ungrateful; just as, conversely, it is an act of indignation and wrath to show mercy to such persons, according to the saying: “Let us have mercy on the ungodly, and he will not learn to do righteousness” (Isa. 26; printed “John 26”).

But let us now consider the remainder. “God sent his Son, made from a woman.” Behold the manner of working. For the sending of the Son is his Incarnation, and the manner of this Incarnation is that he was made from a woman.

But you will say: Were not other human beings also made from a woman? Certainly not in this manner; rather, principally from male seed. For just as no human being is said to consist of soul or flesh alone, but of flesh and soul, so no human being can properly be said simply to be made from a woman, without qualification, since he is made from man and woman. This kind of making, therefore, belongs to Christ alone. Nor could the Apostle have described more briefly or plainly the making of such a human being—one made in righteousness and holiness of truth—than by saying, “made from a woman.” The first man was made from earth; the first woman was made from a rib; all other men and women from man and woman; Christ alone from a mother alone.

This is that noble making of which the Psalmist says: “Thou hast made me glad, O Lord, in thy making” (Ps. 91). Truly, we should delight in this making alone. For the first and second making of humankind fell through sin; in the third we are begotten from the ruin of sin, naturally destined for the ruin of death. But in this fourth making we are reborn from the ruin of sin unto righteousness and raised from the ruin of death unto life. Therefore, in this making we should delight with the Psalmist and at the same time tremble with Habakkuk, saying: “I considered thy works and was afraid” (Hab. 3). We should delight at the manifestation of such gentleness and tremble at the self-emptying of such majesty. For as great as the weight of blessedness which this grace will confer upon those who receive it, so great is the burden of calamity which that same majesty will bring upon those who despise it.

Augustine, in a homily on the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0539D] Augustine, vol. X], says: “Human pride weighed you down so greatly that nothing could lift you up except divine humility.” In another homily on the same subject he says: “From this we understand how grave our God judges the causes of human crimes to be, for which he sent to earth not an angel, not an archangel, but God.” And he adds: “The magnitude of the remedy reveals how grievous sin is and how harsh its condition; the concern by which they are redeemed shows what a great overthrow of evils there will be when they are condemned.”

What do you say here, O human ingratitude? Why do you not receive so great a benefit graciously? Instead, ungrateful toward so great a benefit and benefactor, you raise, contrary to Solomon’s counsel, a foolish complaint about the present, saying: “What is the reason that former times were better than the present?” “Such a question,” he says, “is foolish” (Eccl. 7). It is truly foolish because such speech is false. For times are better now under the light Church and sweet yoke of Christ than they were formerly under the exceedingly heavy burden of Moses’ law, which, as Peter says, neither our fathers nor we were able to bear (Acts 15). They are better even than the times before the law, in the age of the patriarchs, when the world flourished with an abundance of temporal goods; when life was long, health uninterrupted, possessions plentiful, offspring abundant, and prolonged peace tranquil.

None of these things made the time good any more than they made a person good. “The Sabbath,” says Truth in the Gospel, “was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Matt. 2 [probably Mark 2]). If this is true of the Sabbath, it is true of every other day as well. Other days were made for human work; the Sabbath for human rest.

If, then, time was made for humankind, the goodness or badness of time must be assessed by the badness or goodness of human beings. For nothing makes a person’s time good except what makes the person good. Hence Jerome on Ecclesiastes: “Virtues make days good for one who lives; vices make them bad.” Therefore, he says, we must live in such a way that the days always present are better than those past, lest, when we begin to decline, the Apostle’s saying be addressed to us: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. 1 [probably 5]). And: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being completed in the flesh?” (ibid.).

A person’s good time, therefore, is not produced by abundance of temporal goods but rather of spiritual goods, such as fullness of faith and uprightness of conduct. The Son of God, sent to us, made from a woman and made under the law, brought us this goodness of time, as was said above. That he was made from a mother was a miracle of divine power, according to the words: “Behold the miracle of the Lord’s mother” [Note: [Col. 0539D] Responsory of the Church]. That he was made under the law was a lesson in supreme humility, according to the words: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 2 [probably 11]).

He was under the law of Moses until the thirtieth year of his life; under the law of the Lord until the end of his life. Hence Chrysostom says [Note: [Col. 0540D] Chrysostom, Homily 10 on the Nativity]: “After thirty years Jesus came to baptism, about to abolish the old law.” And further on: “For thirty years he had fulfilled the righteousness of the law; and then he came to baptism, about to teach the Gospel and place the crowning fulfillment upon all the observances of the law.” Thus he was under Moses’ law until the thirtieth year of his life, but under the Lord’s law throughout his life—the law of which the Psalmist says: “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls” (Ps. 18).

Blessed Bernard says of this law in his Letter to the Carthusians [Note: [Col. 0540D] Bernard, Letter 11]:

> There is one who confesses to the Lord because he is powerful; there is one who confesses to the Lord because he is good to him; and there is one who confesses to the Lord because he is simply good. The first is a servant and fears for himself; the second is a hireling and desires for himself; the third is a son and pays honor to the Father. Thus both he who fears and he who desires act for themselves; charity alone, which exists in a son, does not seek its own things. This is the spotless law of the Lord, converting souls, which alone can turn the mind away from love of the world and direct it toward God. For neither private love nor private fear converts the mind: sometimes they change one’s face or conduct, never one’s affection. The servant sometimes does God’s work, but not willingly; the hireling does it too, but not freely. Where there is possession, there is singularity; where there is singularity, there is a corner; where there is a corner, there is filth or rust. Thus neither the law of the servant—that is, fear—nor the law of the hireling—that is, desire—is spotless or able to convert souls. But charity is a spotless law because it retains nothing for itself from its own possession: indeed, it has nothing as its own, but everything it has belongs to God. And what belongs to God cannot be unclean. Therefore charity is a spotless law, because it does not seek what is useful to itself but what is useful to many. It is the law of the Lord because he himself lives by it, or because no one possesses it except by his gift. Charity holds and binds the Trinity itself in unity through the bond of peace. Charity, moreover, is not a quality or accident, but substance. For “charity,” “God,” and “gift of God” are rightly said. Thus charity gives charity: substance gives an accidental quality. Where the name signifies the giver, it is the name of substance; where it signifies the gift, it is a quality.

Again, in the same letter:

> The servant and the hireling have a law not from the Lord, but one they have made for themselves: the former by not loving God, the latter by loving something else.

And shortly afterward:

> Those who do what the Apostle says, “Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Rom. 13), are indeed, as God is, in this world; and they are neither servants nor hirelings, but sons.

And shortly afterward:

> For these no law has been imposed, but it has been freely given to those who are willing, because it has been sweetly inspired. Hence the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matt. 2 [probably 11]). It is as though he said: I do not impose it on the unwilling; take it, if you wish. Otherwise you will find not rest but labor for your souls. Charity, then, is a good and sweet law: it is not only borne gently and sweetly, but also makes the laws of servants and hirelings bearable and light. It does not abolish them, but causes them to be fulfilled, as the Lord says: “I came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). It moderates the one, orders the other, lightens both, and nullifies neither. Charity will never be without fear, but it is chaste fear; never without desire, but it is ordered desire. Charity therefore fulfills the servant’s law when it infuses devotion; it fulfills the hireling’s law when it orders desire. Devotion mixed with fear does not abolish fear but makes it chaste. Desire is rightly ordered when evil things are wholly rejected, better things are preferred to good things, and good things are sought only for the sake of better things. When this happens, and through God’s grace one becomes accustomed to acting thus, a person loves the body and all bodily goods for the soul’s sake; the soul for God’s sake; and God for his own sake. At the first stage, therefore, a person loves himself for his own sake; at the second, God for his own sake; at the third, God for God’s sake. At this stage one remains. Whether the fourth can be perfectly attained in this life—namely, that a person love himself for God’s sake—I do not know. But this will happen when the good servant has been brought into the joy of his lord.

This is what St Bernard says about the spotless law of God, which is charity. Charity is a law to itself and an eternal law, because God is charity, God is eternal, and charity is eternal. This law made Christ do everything that he did and suffer everything that he suffered. It made him become human though he was God; poor though he was rich; a servant though he was Lord; circumcised though he had nothing superfluous; redeemed by an offering though he had nothing sold under sin; baptized though he had nothing unclean; accused, scourged, and mocked without fault; condemned without cause. He did all this in order to redeem those who were under the law—that is, under the yoke and burden of the law.

Accordingly, Christ redeemed us from the burden of Moses’ law when he removed the ritual of its legal ceremonies and instituted the sacraments of the new law, greater in power, better in usefulness, easier in performance, and fewer in number, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0541D] Augustine, Book XIX against Faustus, ch. 13], “once the righteousness of faith had been revealed.” Good God, how burdensome were those legal sacraments: in various washings and fleshly purifications; in the circumcision of infants; in slaughtering animals; in flaying skins; in cutting limbs apart! This is the work of executioners, not priests. Indeed, all the priests of the old law were lictors, executioners, and cooks.

Thanks be to him who redeemed us from this curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. He redeemed us from the burdensome law of Moses by instituting the sacraments of the new law, and from the most burdensome law of death and sin by dying for us and rising from the dead. O how fittingly has the sacrament of circumcision been changed into the sacrament of baptism! The former grievously injured males; the latter injures no one. It washes both sexes and every age, immediately opens the gate of paradise, and admits the baptized person if he dies immediately thereafter. How fittingly has the sacrament of victims been changed into the sacrifice of the immortal Lamb under the species of bread and wine, established with most honorable ease and no less mighty power.

That old sacrifice polluted, bloodied, smoked over, and covered with ashes the very priests who were supposed to cleanse others. Everywhere bodily pollution was encountered; nowhere cleansing of the soul. For, as the Apostle testifies, it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of goats and bulls (Heb. 10). But in this new sacrifice the cleansing of souls is most effective; no pollution of bodies occurs; rather, there is a holy and sober refreshment of both the inner and outer human being.

Thus we have been redeemed from the unbearable yoke of Moses’ law by the sacraments of the new law, or evangelical Truth, Christian faith; and through this same law from the law of sin and death. For it is the law of the Spirit of life—that is, the law of spiritual and life-giving grace—which is in Christ Jesus: namely, faith in Christ’s Incarnation with its sacraments, which makes the dead alive by justifying the ungodly. Whoever therefore wishes to be redeemed from this condemnable law of sin and death must come under the law of the Redeemer, just as he himself was made under the law. For if he had not redeemed us—that is, if he had not become under the law—how could we have been redeemed by him, so as to receive his faith, keep his commandments, and hope for his promises? “The righteous person lives by faith” (Gal. 3).

As faith is the life of the soul, so love working is the life of faith. “For faith without works is dead” (Isa. 2; printed citation). The life of love is humility, which considers itself nothing, for “charity is not puffed up” (1 Cor. 13). Further, the life of humility is ready and cheerful obedience, not in agreeable things pleasing to the flesh but in laborious and difficult things; and therefore the life of obedience is patience, in which the soul is possessed; the life of patience is perseverance, to which alone eternal salvation is promised and given.

The whole sacrament of today’s feast, therefore, is the virtue of humility. Mary was purified though she had no need of purification, and an offering was made for Christ according to the law though he owed the law nothing, in order that the mystery of human redemption might be concealed from the devil and an example of humility might be consecrated for the world in mother and son. Humility, insofar as it can, hides its good deeds; it reveals its evils, if it has them, through humble confession; but if it does not have them and is believed to have them, it does not refuse to undergo legal purification.

The two daughters of this humility are obedience and patience. They are, as it were, the two arms of charity by which the child Jesus must today be received from the Virgin Mary. Thus that most blessed old man Simeon received him today: righteous and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel. He was righteous through obedience, fulfilling the commandments; God-fearing through humility, dreading all his works; awaiting the consolation of Israel through patience, rejecting worldly and temporal consolations and hanging in most eager expectation upon eternal and heavenly ones. For the Holy Spirit was in him as charity, sustaining him in this expectation through the answer given to him as he prayed.

The whole sum of human salvation lies in humility. It makes one God-fearing—that is, constant in fear—and “blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. 28). For one who fears, and fears God, neglects nothing, neither great nor small. Would that we had as much humility in our sins as saints and perfect persons have in their righteous deeds!

Augustine, to Dioscorus [Note: [Col. 0543D] Augustine, Letter 56, after the middle], says: “When we rejoice in some good deed, pride tears everything from our hand. For the other vices are to be feared in sins; pride is to be feared in good deeds.” Later he says that a most distinguished rhetorician, when asked what he considered the first thing to be observed among the rules of eloquence, replied, “Delivery”; when asked what was second, gave the same reply; and when asked what was third, again the same reply. So, he says, must one answer concerning humility: in all the precepts of the Christian religion it is necessary first, second, and third. For it is the beginning, progress, and perfection of virtues. Whoever has it has everything.

May the teacher of humility and gentleness, the child Jesus, deign to grant it to us through the intercession of his most humble mother, the Virgin Mary, and of righteous Simeon, whose desire he himself—desired by all nations—fulfilled today. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON PALM BRANCHES, I

[Note: [Col. 0543D] This sermon was delivered entirely in French and was the author’s last, as the autograph states.]

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16).

The common saying is: “Let one who is well off not stir himself.” But who is well off while he is in the world, which is wholly set in the evil one—that is, in the power of the evil one—so that he cannot fail to be tempted by him? How will he refrain from tempting, when he did not refrain even from the Savior? The days too are evil, and each succeeding day grows worse. Hence the Lord says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow. [Col. 0544B] For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6), that is, its own affliction. Hence too the saying of the son of Sirach: “The number of a man’s days, at most, is a hundred years; and they are reckoned like drops of seawater, small and full of bitterness” (Ecclus. 18). And Jacob says to Pharaoh: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life upon earth are a hundred and thirty years, few and evil” (Gen. 47). Therefore, if even the place where we are is set in the evil one, our days are evil, and the time most wicked, who here is well off? The saying, then, “Let one who stands well not stir himself,” does not apply to us. Rather, we shall truly—and for the first time—be well off when we have been brought into the joy of our Lord, so that thereafter we may not be moved. Meanwhile, we must move, because we must pass [Col. 0544C] from toil to rest, from war to peace. Hence Micah says: “Arise and go, because you have no rest here” (Mic. 2). As though he said: You are not well here. “It shall be well with the man who fears the Lord in the end; and on the day of his death he shall be blessed” (Ecclus. 1).

The present life is a road. “In this way in which I walked, they set a snare for me” (Ps. 141). From the moment we are born, we go: for who stands still? Who, once he has entered life, is not compelled to walk? The infant is born and walks by growing. This road is dangerous, because “there are ways that seem right to men, whose end plunges down to the depths of hell.” “Be imitators of me,” says the Apostle, “and observe those who walk thus, as you have our example” (Phil. 3). As though he said: Have the prudence of the wolf, which ordinarily follows [Col. 0544D] the tracks of men, not of wolves; for it has persuaded itself that in doubtful places a man knows better how to protect himself than a wolf does. Therefore the Apostle continues: “For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction,” etc. (ibid.). He who lives well goes well, because he goes to the kingdom of heaven; and blessedness exists nowhere else. But he who lives badly goes badly, because he goes to the prison of hell, where supreme and eternal misery is found.

What is it to live well? As Blessed Bernard says [Note: [Col. 0544D] Bernard, sermon for the feast of Peter and Paul.], to live well is to do good things and endure bad ones. The iniquity of those who say that people live well when they feed themselves well and indulge their pleasures has lied [Col. 0545A] to itself, in accordance with the Terentian passage in the *Hecyra*:

> “What did our cousin Phania leave behind?” says Laches.  
> Pamphilus replies:
>
> “He was a man devoted to pleasure while he lived; and people such as he do not greatly assist an heir.  
> But they leave themselves this praise: ‘He lived well while he lived.’”

(TERENCE, *Hecyra*, act 3, scene 5.)

Hence Sidonius, speaking of a certain parasite, whom his own bread fed less than another’s bread, offers [Col. 0545B] a commendatory judgment not about one who lived well, but about one who fed well. Therefore those who do good things and endure bad ones truly live well, go well, and walk rightly.

For there are only two roads: one leading to heaven, the other to hell. Whoever is not on the first is on the second. The first is the straight road, which leads a person to his homeland—not the one in which he was born, but that for which he was created, and for which he was reborn in baptism. For, as Jerome says, we are born for the present age and reborn for the age to come. Of this road the Psalmist says: “And he led them in the straight way, so that they might go to the city of habitation” (Ps. 106). The road leading to hell, though it leads straight to it, cannot be called straight, because it makes a man wander and fall into the hands of robbers, according to the Gospel saying: [Col. 0545C] “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers” (Luke 10).

Each road has its own leader and standard-bearer. The leader of the infernal road is the devil, who first discovered it; he is “king over all the children of pride.” His standard is pride, which makes a person despise God in scourges, though God is wise in his commands and gracious and sweet in his benefits. The first contempt makes one fearless, and therefore unhappy. “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). But he who is hard of mind—that is, fearless—shall fall into evil. The second contempt makes one disobedient; the third, ungrateful. And who is more unhappy than one fearless before dangers, disobedient to commands, and ungrateful for benefits? For it follows that he is shameless concerning shameful things, [Col. 0545D] inhuman concerning human concerns, and unbelieving toward counsels and exhortations. Hence it is written of the devil: “His heart shall be hardened like a stone; he shall esteem the hammer as straw; an archer shall not make him flee; the stones of the sling are turned for him into straw” (Job 41).

Certainly, when holy Job said these things, the devil’s heart had already been hardened like a stone—indeed, more than a stone. Yet he used the future tense, saying “shall be hardened,” not “has been hardened,” in order to show that he was speaking not only of the head, the devil, but also of his members.

For the heart of the devil is anyone who knowingly does and accomplishes his will. The devil’s will is evil, pleasing to evil, and set upon evil: namely, that the sinner may never turn from his evil way, and so become with him an heir [Col. 0546A] of eternal damnation. A stony heart is one—which may God in his mercy remove from us—that does not fear the threat of the future judgment. To have no fear of it, or to regard it lightly, is to consider the hammer of the judicial sentence as straw.

God punishes sinners in three ways: with a rod, a staff, and a hammer. By the rod, sons are instructed in the present life; by the staff, servants are struck in purgatorial punishments; by the hammer, enemies are crushed in the punishment of Gehenna. He considers this hammer as straw who either believes eternal damnation will never come, or thinks it will be slight. “The archer”—that is, the ecclesiastical preacher—will never drive such a man from his place. The place of this sinner is rightly situated in the very line of fire of the stone-throwing engine, that is, [Col. 0546B] of the divine threat that foretells eternal death. For this threat casts from afar and strikes terribly, like a siege-engine and like a hammer crushing all things. Whoever, therefore, after often hearing the divine word is not corrected, has his heart hardened like the devil’s heart, like a stone.

This threefold contempt, then, is the mark of the beast of which the Apocalypse speaks: “And a fierce and most grievous wound came upon the men who had the mark of the beast” (Rev. 16). The mark of the beast—that is, of Antichrist or the devil—is pride; the fierce and most grievous wound is disobedience and impenitence. Disobedience is like the cutting off of the ears; impenitence, like the branding of a red-hot iron; contempt for God’s commandments is like the gouging out of the eyes.

[Col. 0546C] Such marks are customarily made upon robbers caught for the first time, when they are spared hanging, so that, if they are caught again, they may more justly be hanged. So the Lord deals with sinners who, when warned, refuse to repent, though he himself waits for them patiently so that at last they may someday be converted. By a just but terrible and hidden judgment he permits them to have their ears cut off through disobedience, to be branded through shamelessness, and to be blinded through contempt. For Augustine says: “He who begins to believe begins to fear judgment.” Without doubt, therefore, he who does not fear does not believe. Hence: “To rebel is like the sin of divination; and unwillingness to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). But he who does not believe does not see. For as [Col. 0546D] faith is light, so unbelief is night. Hence the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Such men are most justly to be hanged when, at the judgment, they have all been caught as in the Lord’s net, according to the saying: “Sinners shall fall into his net” (Ps. 40). “For the day of the Lord shall come like a thief in the night”; and therefore, as fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so human beings shall be caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them.

Therefore this standard-bearer must not be followed, nor must his mark be received. Rather, let us follow Christ as he goes to his Father, who is in heaven, carrying the sign of the cross—indeed, bearing the cross itself—and saying: “If anyone wishes,” etc. (Matt. 16). He is our standard-bearer, [Col. 0547A] who, like a good shepherd, when he has sent out his sheep, goes before them. His sign is the cross. He brought that sign from heaven; he did not first take it up on earth.

For in the cross a twofold form is displayed: the form of man and the form of God—the human visibly, the divine invisibly. The form of man appears in the twofold division of length and breadth, on account of the double substance of soul and body, which without a mediator could not attain conformity with the Trinity. When man was fashioned from the clay of earth in the form of a cross by the hand of the craftsman, he was long and broad, in order that he might live forever and happily like God. For the Mediator himself bore witness to this when he said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). He stood as mediator among men, though the Jews did not recognize him. Therefore they remained in the duality of division: broad, in whom ruin was multiplied; long, so that their misery might be eternal. For they are the people with whom the Lord is angry forever.

The form of God is understood in that fourfold dimension of which the Apostle spoke: [Col. 0547B] “Rooted and founded in charity, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3).
