The Father is the root of nature; Christ is the foundation of the Church. To believe in the charity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is to strive with most steadfast love toward God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus one comprehends the breadth of divine love, the length of eternity, the height of power, and the depth of wisdom.

The first of these appeared most especially in the Lord’s Passion, when he stretched out his hands on the cross; the second in the Resurrection; the third in the Ascension; the fourth in the sending of the Holy Spirit. Of the first: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children, and you would not!” (Matt. 23). Of the second: “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6). Of the third: “God, whose Son in the heights of heaven powerfully carried our captivity captive by his own might” [Note: [Col. 0547D] Prayer of the Church.]. Of the fourth: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all truth” (John 14). Hence Pope Leo: “Oh, how swift is the word of wisdom; and where God is teacher, how quickly what is taught is learned!” [Note: [Col. 0548D] Leo, sermon on Pentecost.]

Yet the Holy Spirit [Col. 0547D] would not have been sent unless Christ had bodily ascended into heaven, according to the saying: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16). Likewise, he would never have ascended into heaven with his glorified body unless he had first risen after death. Hence John, indicating that the Resurrection and Ascension were the cause of the Spirit’s mission, says: “The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7). Moreover, he would never have risen from the dead unless he had first died. But by no kind of death could he have shown better the breadth of his love than by dying on the cross with outstretched arms. Therefore the Apostle [Col. 0548A] named breadth first.

Our standard-bearer, therefore, having been made before us this sign of eternal blessedness, thus invites us to battle: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). He compels no one, but leaves it to each person’s will whether he wishes to follow him. For God does not accept compelled service; so great is the freedom of the human will that no one can be evil or good unwillingly.

Indeed, at that time no one wished to accomplish this. For he who had earlier said, “Let us go and die with him” (John 11), and he who had promised, saying, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26), when the matter came to the test, were unwilling. Yet it was not necessary for anyone to die with him. His death alone was sufficient for the redemption [Col. 0548B] of all; hence: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140), and “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. 63). No man was prepared to die with him; but one woman, his mother, was prepared. Yet although her death was then offered in desire, it was not received as a fellow-servant in the Passion, as unnecessary in the mystery of redemption.

He did not say, “If anyone comes after me,” but, “If anyone wishes to come after me,” in order to show that the resolve of good will must be fully paid to God and not fulfilled by the substitution of any lesser good. Hence Gregory says: “Whoever has resolved upon some greater good has made unlawful for himself the lesser good which had formerly been permitted.”

When the foundations of our Order were first being laid, there was in the church of Lyons an upright and honorable cleric, John, who, moved by the good and fragrant reputation of our Order, quietly resolved within himself to join our fellowship. [Col. 0548C] After a few days, however, he changed that resolution when another thought entered him, and, as a kind of compensation, undertook a pilgrimage to Saint James. When he had devoutly completed it and returned, he was joyfully welcomed by his household; but, weary from his journey, he withdrew to his chamber.

As he rested, God and our Lord Jesus Christ immediately appeared to him, accompanied by the two blessed apostles Peter and James. Peter held a book in his hand, which the Lord commanded to be opened. It was written in golden letters and contained the names of the predestined. The apostle, being commanded, began to read; and when he read there the name of that John, the Lord said: “Take it away; erase him—erase him who promised that he would be mine and recoiled from his promise.” Then Saint James came nearer and, beseeching him, said: “Lord, he is my pilgrim; I beg you, do not erase his name.” The Lord replied: “He ought not to have been my pilgrim, [Col. 0548D] but my citizen. Is it not greater to be my citizen than your pilgrim?” But the Apostle James persisted in his supplication: “Do not erase him, most merciful Lord; I beg you, do not erase him. I stand surety to you for him that he will do what he promised.” And the Lord said to him: “When will he do it?” [Col. 0549A] The Apostle replied: “Within fifteen days.”

Awakened by these words, John threw himself to the ground and, shedding an abundant flood of tears, thanked his guarantor, saying: “I shall certainly do it, holy Apostle; I shall do what you have so mercifully promised on my behalf.” Not long after his great weeping he fell asleep again. Again the Lord appeared with the aforementioned apostles and ordered the book opened again. In it the same John heard Blessed Peter reading: “We shall make you little chains of gold, adorned with silver” (Song 1). John immediately arose and, before the appointed day, fulfilled his vow. He became the first abbot of the monastery of Bonneval and afterward bishop of the Church of Valence; his life and death were distinguished by many merits and miracles. It is certainly with good reason that the Israelites are reproached [Col. 0549B] for returning in heart to Egypt, when this John, because in his heart he recoiled from Cîteaux, was ordered to be erased from the book of life.

We must at the same time consider with what devotion we ought to implore the aid of the saints, who so lovingly give surety for us and intercede so effectively. Therefore let the Albigensian dogs be ashamed, who, barking against the truth, lie in saying that the saints’ prayer does us no good. They ought not only, like wicked and importunate dogs, to be driven away with stones and clubs, but also, like rabid dogs, to be pierced with swords or burned with fire.

Therefore, to wish to come after Jesus is to resolve to live according to his example. Whoever [Col. 0549C] makes this resolution, in order to fulfill the vow, must deny himself: that is, he must reckon himself to be nothing, able to do nothing, worth nothing, except insofar as he fears God and keeps his commandments. For this is the whole of man: a human being is something only insofar as he does that for which he was created. Otherwise, “he who thinks himself something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Jas. 1).

In baptism a person renounces the devil; in religious life he must renounce himself. He renounces the devil who firmly believes that the devil can do nothing, knows nothing, and is worth nothing—that is, wills no good—because he has become nothing and shall be nothing forever. Likewise, he renounces himself who reckons whatever power, wisdom, or grace he has to be nothing as regards his own merit, but only something insofar as it is God’s gratuitous gift. “For what have you that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4). Thus he denied himself who said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

This self-denial is produced by the knowledge of human weakness, which consists in four stages: two in considering evil and two in considering good. Thus we know that by our own power we can avoid no evil, and that after falling we can rise from no evil by our own power; and we recognize that by our own effort alone we can attain no good. Hence Abraham says to the Lord: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Dust is shaken from its place by every disturbance, and, wherever it is cast down, is never raised except by another. [Col. 0550A] Behold, in these two lies the pattern of human deficiency with respect to the consideration of good: of itself it produces absolutely no grain, and it is insufficient to nourish by any richness what it has received from elsewhere. Behold the pattern of human deficiency with respect to the consideration of good. He easily denies himself who rightly considers his deficiency.

The Son of God had no deficiency in himself, yet in a certain manner denied himself when, though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as plunder, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2). How much more ought one to deny himself who wholly fails in himself and is sufficient for no good from himself?

[Col. 0550B] Moreover, self-denial consists in three stages. First one denies one’s possessions; then one’s own people; then oneself. He denies his possessions who sells all that he has and gives it to the poor. He denies his own people who leaves all things—house, father and mother, brothers and sisters, and other relatives, fields and vineyards and other possessions—in order to receive a hundredfold in spiritual things and possess eternal life in the end (Matt. 19).

Many people are unhappy in religious life. Though in professing religion they have renounced all their possessions, they cannot renounce their relatives; rather, on their account they commit thefts and sacrileges, giving them whatever they can from monastic property. To deny oneself is to chastise one’s body, not to embrace the delights of this world but rather to reject them [Col. 0550C] and withdraw from one’s body all unnecessary pleasures. To deny oneself is to hate one’s own will.

Charity denies its own possessions, because it “does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 13). Chastity denies itself, because it chastises its body and brings it into servitude (1 Cor. 9). Obedient humility denies itself, because it does not do its own will, but the will of him who sent it (John 6), that is, of the one who presides over it. Thus the Apostle denied himself, saying: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). So too did the man who replied to a woman once wrongly known to him, when she said, “It is I”: “Even if you are you, I am not I.” Thus, when all our former vices, now expelled from us by God’s grace, again knock at us wickedly and importunately, we ought to reply: “I am no longer I.”

It follows: “And let him take up his cross” (Matt. 16). It was said above that to live well is to do good things and endure bad ones. The first part is contained in self-denial, which makes one generous and a lover of poverty, chaste and sober, obedient and humble. The second part is contained in what follows: “Let him take up his cross.” In the time when Christ suffered, the cross was the most disgraceful and most bitter kind of punishment, and was very commonly used among Jews and Romans. Hence the poet:

> “If a slave should say to me, ‘I have committed no theft, nor fled,’  
> I say: ‘You have your price; you shall not be burned with thongs.  
> [Col. 0551A] You shall not feed ravens on a cross.’”

(HORACE, *Epistles*, book 1, epistle 16.)

Therefore, to take up the cross after Christ is to endure all insults, injuries, and troubles for Christ. Not all who are tortured bear their own cross. One carries a cross, but not his own, as Simon of Cyrene did. Another suffers his own cross—that is, the cross he has found by sinning—but does not take it up, because he does not receive his torment with equanimity, does not repent of his evil deed, but murmurs against the just judgment and kicks against the goad, like that most wicked, impenitent, blaspheming thief.

Another takes up his own cross because he receives the suffering, as it were, with equanimity and lightens it by accusing himself and confessing that he has been justly condemned. Such was that blessed, penitent, and restrained thief [Col. 0551B] who accused himself, rebuked his blaspheming companion, suffered with the innocent Christ, and feared him. Though an accused man, he entreated the judge; though a servant, he addressed the king, saying: “We indeed receive the due reward of our deeds; but what has this man done?” (Luke 23). “Why then, wretch, do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation as I?” And turning to the Lord, who hung in the middle as though weighing the merits of both in a central balance, he said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (ibid.).

Wonderful was this thief’s confession, and wonderful his petition. Jesus was held fast to the gallows by nails, just as that thief and the other hanging with him were. Yet all were going somewhere; Jesus alone was going through punishment to the kingdom. For “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18). [Col. 0551C] Though fixed with nails, he ran to glory. The others, however, went through punishment to judgment: the blaspheming thief to judgment without mercy, because he had shown no mercy even to himself by having pity on his own soul and pleasing God, so that, judging himself, he might not be judged; but to the confessing thief, who judged himself, mercy was granted as to one humble and lowly. Therefore he immediately heard from the mouth of Mercy: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

There is also one who takes up his own cross—not, I say, the cross he himself deserved, but that which he imposed upon himself, as Christ did, paying for others what he had not stolen. Likewise the martyrs bore their own cross in order to follow the Lamb wherever he goes, preserving both innocence and patience. [Col. 0551D] Again, another deserves the cross but does not suffer it: such was Barabbas, released at the unjust request of the Jews and by Pilate’s unjust judgment. Such is every unpunished sinner, than whom nothing is more unhappy. For, as Augustine says, nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners. This prosperity of fools destroys them.

These are Barabbases—that is, sons of the master—because they have the devil as master in wickedness; Barabbases—that is, sons of the father—because they have that same devil as father in their inheritance, most unhappy of all. Or they are Simons of Cyrene, that is, hypocrites, who carry another’s cross under compulsion, doing a good work from the pursuit of vanity and performing the deed [Col. 0552A] of a just person without the fruit of justice. They appear obedient but are not; they appear about to receive an inheritance but will not receive it, because they receive their reward here.

Let us therefore take up our cross: either suffering persecution with Christ for righteousness, or, with the blessed thief, vindicating God against ourselves through patience. Gregory says that the cross is taken up in two ways [Note: [Col. 0551D] Gregory, Homily 32 on the Gospels.]: “Either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the mind is afflicted through compassion.” Augustine, writing to Laetus, says among other things [Note: [Col. 0552D] Augustine, Letter 38.]:

> “What else ought we understand by our cross, which we are commanded by the Lord to bear, than the mortality of this flesh? It troubles us until death is swallowed up by victory. Therefore this very cross must be crucified and transfixed with the nails of the fear of the Lord, lest, while its members remain sound and free, you be unable to carry it as it resists. But you cannot follow the Lord at all unless you bear it. For how do you follow him if you are not his? But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5).

These are Augustine’s words. “Let him take up,” he says, “his cross and follow me”; that is, let him persevere in following me. Let him follow so that he may attain. For one is not said to follow someone when he goes after him now and then withdraws from him. But someone may say: It is difficult to follow one crucified. What is man that he can follow his king and maker?

Brothers, Christ not only invites us to follow him; he also helps us. He is the good shepherd, not a hireling; he does not flee from wolves, but puts wolves to flight. He calls his sheep by name [Col. 0552C] and sends them out; and when he has sent them out, he goes before them as guide of the road. He also comes behind them as guardian of the flock and surrounds them as their defender, according to the saying: “The mountains are around it, and the Lord is around his people” (Ps. 124). He walks in their midst as the helper of all, according to the saying: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18). He is “a helper in opportunities, in tribulation,” doing the will of those who fear him; he will hear their prayer and save them. Who has hoped in him and been confounded? “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 123). Without him we can do nothing, and we can do all things [Col. 0552D] in him who strengthens us.

At the beginning of our Order, there was a cleric from Vandœuvre studying at school near Lyons. In a vision of the night he saw a level valley beneath a certain mountain. Upon that mountain stood a city of such beauty that no one could be satisfied with its sight; and whoever saw it strove by every means to discover how he might reach it.

Meanwhile the cleric saw a river flowing around the foot of the mountain. As he went about it seeking some way to cross it, he saw on the riverbank twelve or fourteen poor men washing their tunics [Col. 0553A] in the river. Among them was a man clothed in a most white garment, very unlike the others and far surpassing them all, who helped them wash their tunics. After helping one, he went to help another, and so passed through them all in turn.

Then the cleric who saw these things went to the one helping the others and said to him: “What people are you?” He replied: “These poor men are people doing penance, who wash and cleanse themselves from their sins. I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Without whose help neither these nor others can do good. I deny my help to none who ask for it, but gladly grant it to all. This most beautiful city that you see is paradise, where I dwell; it is much more beautiful within than it appears outwardly. [Col. 0553B] Those who have already washed their tunics—that is, who have completely cleansed themselves from every sin—dwell there with me. Whenever any one of these has washed his tunic, that is, has done penance, he shall enter that city. There is no other road leading to it except penance. You yourself have long enough sought a way by which you might arrive there; but neither you nor anyone else will ever find another than the way of penance, that is, of washing one’s tunic.”

Awakened from sleep by these words, the cleric began to rejoice in the vision and to marvel with a certain fear at its meaning. Not long afterward, when he had returned from school to his homeland, he recounted the vision to the bishop of Chalon, with whom he was familiar. On hearing it, [Col. 0553C] the bishop urged him to leave the world, saying that the most merciful Lord was calling him to religious life; and above all Orders he commended to him the Cistercian Order, which had recently begun.

He therefore came to Cîteaux and found the place uncultivated and deserted, with the brothers living among wild beasts. At the gate of the monastery, which was made of wicker, hung an iron hammer, by whose sound the porter was summoned. Called by this sound, he came outside to the cleric and bowed in greeting. Looking at him, the cleric immediately recognized that he had seen him among those poor men who were washing their tunics in the river. The cleric asked him to bring the abbot to him. The porter replied: “He will soon go out to work with the others, and you will be able to see them all.” Not long afterward [Col. 0553D] the abbot came out with the convent. Looking at them all, the cleric recognized that they were the poor men whom he had seen washing their tunics in the river.

He immediately fell at the abbot’s feet, begging with tears to be received into their fellowship. When the abbot answered that the Order was most difficult to bear, the cleric said: “You have a good helper, and I hope in God that he will help me as he helps the others.” Recounting the vision, he greatly strengthened them all, and was thus received; not long afterward he became prior.

Therefore, brothers, do not—do not, I beg you—become fainthearted. Do not fear to follow our crucified standard-bearer and to take up your cross after him, because truly we have the same helper as leader, [Col. 0554A] Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Helinand died after this sermon.

SERMON IX. ON PALM SUNDAY II.

“Your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3). Today the most dutiful simplicity of the children and the most obedient multitude of the crowds received with wonderfully eager joy the Saviour’s coming from the Mount of Olives into the city of David—an advent as marvellous as it was marvellously humble. What could be more wonderful than that, at the arrival of this poor man seated on an ass, the road is eagerly strewn by children with both branches of trees and their own garments, while to this same poor man, as to the true Saviour, the Davidic *Hosanna* is cried out with festal and unanimous applause? O truly new and unusual riding of a King—and of such a King! He who sits above the cherubim, seated with the Father, assessor of equity, possessor of heaven, deigned to become the rider of a little ass! O again new and astonishing salvation wrought by a King riding thus: when one poor man seated upon an ass, as though lowly, rejected, and fit to be laughed at, is honoured as an emperor, adored as Redeemer, and received as Saviour!

Truly great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills (Psalm 110). Truly Wisdom always acts wisely. The King of glory and teacher of humility could not have been received more gloriously, nor have arrived more humbly. Already then, in the pattern of that example, that judicial rule of heavenly wisdom was being fashioned: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14). The more God humbled himself, the more he was exalted by the people; and in a most beautiful contest, the more ready humility was to flee glory, the swifter glory was to pursue humility.

We indeed read that certain glorious men of the earth were formerly received with the greatest ambition by some royal cities. But what wonder is that, when they themselves came to those cities with still greater ambition? For they did not sit on asses, but proceeded pompously upon horses and in chariots, four-horse carriages, and ships; displaying much dust before them, very little valour, no salvation, a great deal of destruction, and vanity in its entirety. Thus Holofernes was once received by the Syrians; Antiochus by Jason; Cecilianus by the high priests of the temples. Thus Alexander Philopompus was once received by the Jerusalemites [Col. 0554D], Plato the philosopher by the Syracusans, and Julius Caesar by the Romans. The first was received because of the terror of his power, the second for the honour of his wisdom, and the third not only because of the favour arising from his victory over the Gauls, but also because of the love inspired by the kindness and leniency with which he was accustomed to treat his soldiers, whom he called his fellow-soldiers. He was the first commander of all to employ that designation for his troops in a public address.

But behold, here is one greater than Alexander, because more powerful; behold, one greater than Plato, because wiser; behold, one greater than Caesar, because kinder. If, therefore, those most wretched sinners and perpetual heirs of infernal misery were received in such glory, how gloriously ought my Jesus today to be received by us—true God and Son of God, conceived without sin, carried without weariness, born without pain to his mother! As the true sun of righteousness, by his rising he illuminated the world; by poverty he enriched it; by his word he healed it; by example he taught it; by death he redeemed it. With how much justice, therefore, does the Prophet cry out to him: “Your riding is salvation.” Thus it is read in the ancient translation, where we have: “Your chariots are salvation.” Without prejudice to other sound and Catholic interpretations, we may fittingly understand this riding here as the Lord’s present seating upon an ass.

For *equus*, “horse,” is indeed a particular term, whereas *equitare*, “to ride,” is a general word for any similar manner of travelling, according to Flaccus:

> [Col. 0555B] “To play with equal mate, to ride upon a long reed.”

Therefore he says, in the person of the crowd coming out to meet the Lord: “Your riding is salvation.” And it should be known that today the Lord was surrounded by more abundant honour upon earth than ever before. When he was announced by angels, the shepherds alone heard it; when he was sought by the shepherds, no others went with them; when he was announced by the star, the three Magi alone understood it; when he was adored by the Magi, none adored with them; when he was offered in the Temple by his parents, none then went with them; when he was received by Simeon and Anna, they alone offered him the devotion of faith. But today the great crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: [Col. 0555C] “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21).

The question therefore arises why, arriving so humbly, he was received so gloriously; or why, being to be received so gloriously, he arrived so humbly. He himself resolves the first question for us, saying: “For this reason the crowd went out to meet him, because it had heard that he had done this sign”—namely, that of which it had been said: “The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead bore witness” (John 12). Above all, the Lord had recalled from the tomb to life, by the power of his most mighty word, a man dead for four days and already stinking. The renowned report of this most renowned miracle, sounding about human ears delighted by novelty with the clear ringing of a new wonder, spurred the envious to hatred and the humble to service. Hence the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council in order to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. They also planned to kill Lazarus, because many of the Jews were leaving on account of him and believing in Jesus. But because the crowds had heard that he had performed this sign, they ran out to meet the Saviour with flowers and palms.

O envy, most unhappy kind of disease! It has as its cause of death a sweet odour which is for others a cause of life. O kind of disease that tortures its sufferer with every kind of torment! To it, itself is a nail in the eye, a spear in the side, consumption in the lung, cancer in the heart, erysipelas in the liver, jaundice in the face, and *noli me tangere* (“touch-me-not,” an ulcerous disease) throughout the whole body, according to this saying:

> [Col. 0556A] “The Sicilian tyrants found no torment greater than envy.”
>
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.2.48

This is the tree universally evil and eternally accursed. Its root is pride; its trunk, ill will; its branches, rancour and hatred; its leaves, detraction and lying; its flowers, pallor and emaciation; its fruit, grief and joy—yet grief that is not produced except by another’s joy, and joy that is not produced except by another’s grief—as in the saying:

> “To exult in evils and grieve at happy circumstances.”

And again:

> “There is no laughter except that stirred by the sight of pains.”
>
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.727

What is envy? That most powerful fraud which despoiled heaven, enriched hell, inherited the world, cast down Satan, laid Eve low, infected Cain, killed Abel, sold Joseph, destroyed Saul, shook Joab, struck Abner, excluded Hilary, enclosed Daniel, pierced Judaism through, and crucified the Son of God, according to the saying: “For he knew that the chief priests had handed him over through envy” (Mark 15).

What is envy? A worst and most pestilential beast; a most deadly and most ferocious plague. Every good belonging to another which it hears, it hates; which it sees, it envies; which it looks upon, it despises; which it touches, it extinguishes; which it infects, it kills; which it corrects, it corrupts. What is envy? The strength of malice, the power of wickedness, the sowing of vices, the rust of virtues, the plague of secular people, the wasting disease of cloistered people, the life of the devil, the death of the Christian, [Col. 0556C] according to the saying: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wisdom 2).

What is envy? The strongest and unconquerable fortress of iniquity, furnished with every device for harming and armed with every weapon of malignity. With its tooth it threatens like a boar; with its tongue, like a serpent; with its horn, like a bull; with its brow, like a ram; with its foot, like a horse; with its tail, like a scorpion; by its gaze it takes away one’s voice like a wolf, and one’s life like a basilisk, according to the saying:

> “[The lambs] first see the Maenalian wolves.”
>
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* IX.54

And again:

> “I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs.”
>
> —Virgil, *Eclogues* III.103

O how bewitching were the eyes of him who said of our Jesus: [Col. 0556D] “He is grievous even to behold” (Wisdom 2). Thus, indeed, the sight of the sun of righteousness, and the same ray acting differently upon different materials, hardened the mud of envy into hatred and softened the wax of piety into the service of devotion. For while the Pharisees were devising Christ’s death, the crowds that came to meet him received him with most eager devotion, so that “let him who is filthy be filthy still, and let the righteous still be justified” (Revelation 22).

But again the question arises why, though he was to be received so gloriously, he came so ingloriously—riding, namely, upon an ass. For what is this, that he who yesterday raised Lazarus as the power of God now sits upon an ass like some Lazarus? For this is how a leper rides. Perhaps therefore it was said: “And we thought him as it were a leper” (Isaiah 51). The answer is this: in this coming the Lord wished to prove two things, namely, that he was the King of glory and the teacher of humility.

He proves the first by the testimony of children, who cannot lie or flatter. For, as that eminent orator says, nothing is more certain than a child as witness—one who has reached the years in which he understands, but not yet those in which he invents. He proved the second by the manner of riding, most unbecoming to a royal person. No way of appearing in public was less suitable for a king than riding thus. He proceeds more lowly and contemptibly in this manner than if he walked on foot. For walking on foot is common to noble and ignoble alike; but riding an ass, according to worldly custom, belongs only to the lowly and despised.

Therefore, foreseeing that the crowd would come to meet him honourably and greet him by the name of King, the Lord did not wish to mount a horse or chariot, because he was not accustomed to do so; nor was it fitting for him to use such a vehicle, lest he seem to seek the haughtiness and exaltation of rank. Neither did he wish to go to them on foot, as he was accustomed, lest he perhaps seem to have given them an opportunity to seize him and raise him, even against his will, to royal honour. For they had wished to do this before. But you will say: “He could have fled, as he had done before.” Certainly; but at that time he intended to be honoured as a king, though not to appear as a king, just as, conversely, in his Passion he wished to appear as a king, though not to be honoured as a king.

Therefore, [Col. 0557C] in order to cut off from himself every sign of arrogance and pride, he voluntarily chose the manner of riding proper to the humble, lest perhaps he be forced to mount higher. And he mounted an ass in order to show that his kingdom was not of this world. For it is not characteristic of royal majesty to ride a she-ass or an ass, but a fierce horse, a triumphal chariot, or some solemn badge of pride. Here the Pharisees might say: “O most wretched man! He does not know how to live.” But Christians may answer here: “O gentlest Lord! He does not know how to be fierce. O most humble King! He does not know how to be proud.” In this act, therefore, he cries out what he had earlier said in words: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 2).

What does our pride say here—we who, I do not say, are unwilling to use asses and mules, for who would dare that?—who now do not even think ourselves worthy to use ordinary horses? One may see certain prelates of the Church shamelessly made effeminate, even to the delicacy of the most delicate queens, by a softness of luxury; they reject every horse’s gait except that one which moves softly and quietly with even steps, without stirring so much as a hair of the head, so greatly do they wish there to be no difference between travelling and sailing. Others, who ought to be “not as lording it over the clergy, but made an example to the flock,” do not think even gently walking palfreys worthy of their seat unless the horses resemble Bucephaluses, athletes in shape and beauty, displaying, of course, the nobility of their lineage so that they may seem sprinkled with Alexandrian blood. O pride, [Col. 0558A] how far have you ascended! Yet “if you set your nest in heaven, thence I will bring you down,” says the Lord.

What shall I say of trappings and superfluous ornament? Today clerics proceed more pompously than soldiers, bishops than dukes, while Christ is cold and hungry at their doors. Their horses, in the middle of the streets, are covered in silken cloths from the patrimony of the Crucified, and chew yellow gold beneath their teeth. Tell me, bishops: what does gold do on a bridle, breastplate, saddle, or spur? Can your horses not feel the spur unless it shines with gold? Or can they not be controlled by the bridle unless they chew gold under their teeth? Spare, I beg you, spare the riches that you love. If, according to Plautus’ judgment, it is better to carry such people out than to injure them, let us return to the mystery of the Lord’s riding.

Therefore, as the Lord was about to enter the royal city, he was to be touched by the flash of honour before the hailstorm of humiliation, according to the saying: “Before the hail comes lightning” (Ecclesiasticus 32). Thus, since we must contend with the twofold enemy of honour and insult, he provided us with a twofold aid: the example of humility and patience. He wished to sanctify this by mounting an ass, a gentle and humble beast, bearing burdens and quiet, in order to show us thereby that humility must be preserved in prosperity and patience in adversity. For this is the double battle-line which the world deploys against us: it flatters in order to deceive; it terrifies in order to break us.

These are the sun and the north wind, who, according to the parable of the wise man, make a wager and contend with one another to take the traveller’s cloak. In this contest the sun is said to have been stronger than Boreas, because prosperity truly overthrows us more powerfully, easily, and frequently than adversity; and misfortune harms a person less than success. Hence that preacher of Clairvaux, in sermon 29: “You will more easily find one who has retained wisdom amid adverse fortune than one who has not lost it in favourable fortune.”

This riding of the Lord also signifies the chastisement of the body. For the ass signifies the human body, which ought to be subjected to our rational nature as a beast of burden to a human being; hence Sallust: “We make greater use of the rule of the mind and the service of the body.” Hence the saying in the Song of Deborah: “You who ride upon shining asses, bless the Lord” [Col. 0558D] (Judges 5). To mount a shining ass is to find a body delicately nourished from childhood, solid, full of juice, and surrounded by splendour, according to the comic poet; and to govern it by natural love with the bridle of temperance, and tame it under the laws of chastity.

This ass is untied when our outward person is released from the bonds of its former way of life. For it is written: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Proverbs 5). Two disciples untie this ass, that is, faith and hope. Faith unties the she-ass, that is, the flesh, from the bond of corrupt pleasure. For the first step of faith is fear of the coming judgment: as Augustine says, “He who begins to believe begins to fear judgment.” Hope unties the colt, that is, one’s action, from the habit of sinning. Thus untied, they are brought [Col. 0559A] to Jesus—that is, to any teacher of salutary observance. The apostles lay their garments upon them, that is, examples of holy conduct. For as a garment is related to the body, so bodily conduct is related to the soul. Jesus sits upon these, that is, salvation rests upon them. The procession that we make through the cloister shows his journey toward the heavenly Jerusalem.

But first we must consider what it means that the crowd went out to meet him. One part of it scatters flowers beneath the feet of this ass; another throws down branches; a third spreads garments underneath. It is certain that flowers do not hurt the ass’s feet but make its steps shorter. The branches impede its progress, and the garments entangle it. The crowd coming out to meet it therefore signifies turbulent thoughts that confront the beginnings of our religious life. These are the promptings made through evil angels.

At first the devil sets before us the pleasures that we have left behind, and the honour and glory of the world in which we formerly flourished. The intrusion of such thoughts is like the scattering of sweet and sweet-smelling flowers. But it is easy to despise these things if we consider that, by despising temporal glory and present pleasures, we purchase eternal blessedness. When the devil sees that he gains nothing by suggestions of this sort, he adds temptations concerning the hardships of keeping the Rule: the austerity of food, the continuance of fasts, the length of vigils, the coarseness and cheapness of clothing, the urgency of labour, the discipline of silence, the weariness of the cloister, the patience necessary against the envious and detractors, and the vow of obedience, scarcely or never fulfilled. To suggest these and similar things is like strewing branches in the road and placing obstacles before the feet of one who is passing through. Such are also the examples of those who, overcome by so many hardships, were unable to persevere but, like a dog returning to its vomit, returned to the world.

Yet the fear induced by considering temporal hardships is easily overcome if the mind looks to the bitterness and duration of eternal ones. Nor does the small number of those who leave have much force for discouragement if the multitude of those who persevere is considered. O most unhappy beast, which, either enticed by flowers, impeded by branches, or entangled in garments, [Col. 0559D] throws off the Saviour whom it bore! Our Jesus is able in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, to remove every obstacle from the path of his beast. Only let it not cast off that most light burden, which relieves rather than weighs down its bearer.

Thus the Saviour leads his beast into the heavenly Jerusalem. The first stopping-place of the procession is before the chapter-house and before the dormitory. In the chapter-house we confess; in the dormitory we rest; in the auditorium we listen silently to what the prior or abbot commands us, according to the saying: “You will hear more quickly if you are silent.” It is called an auditorium from the office of the disciple, and a speaking-room from the office of the teacher—not because all ought indiscriminately to speak there, but because there the prior and abbot make provision concerning necessary matters. As it is fitting for the disciple to be silent and listen, so it is fitting for the teacher prudently and justly to arrange all things.

Therefore confession is the first stall necessary for the sinner, according to the saying: “Let us anticipate his face in confession”; or, according to another heading: “Begin to the Lord in confession.” Confession is twofold: private, concerning hidden sins; and public, concerning manifest ones. After confession there ought first to follow cessation from sins, according to the saying: “You have sinned: cease.” This is the first part of the penance to be imposed upon a sinner. Hence the dormitory follows immediately after the chapter-house, signifying rest from evil works.

But if we are to rest pleasantly and healthfully, the eyes must be closed, because the first law of modesty ought to be imposed upon the eyes. This is the first and greatest window of our house, through which access to the soul is immediately easy. Therefore it is prescribed that in the dormitory we always wear hoods deeply lowered over our eyes. There are five things concerning which we especially ought to keep silence: lying, swearing, detraction, flattery, and a scurrilous or idle word.

There is a certain chapter-house like a blacksmith’s workshop, in which that noble horse, belonging to the king’s stable, is shod. For the ass is now worthy of the name “horse,” after, having been brought to the Saviour, it deserved to become the vehicle of so great a king. The four shoes which it receives on its feet are the four austerities of more severe penance: vigils, fasts, restraint of speech, and prolonged chanting of psalms. The nails are the manifold pricks of sorrow that torment the heart of the penitent. The red colour of modesty, moreover, is like the purple covering with which the royal palfrey is covered. The discipline of regular silence is like the bridle of the same palfrey, adorned with the gold of wisdom, which becomes known in words that are few, reasonable, timely, and uttered without laughter or a loud voice. In this gold, as though jewels, are set those five virtues which we have just expounded.

After guarding the eyes and tongue follows the guarding of the belly and hands, signified by the second stopping-place, before the lavatory and refectory. In the lavatory we wash our hands; in the refectory we restore the belly. Washing the hands signifies that every impurity must be repelled from every bodily touch. [Col. 0560D] This is the third line of defence, containing also the two that follow. For all the blandishments of love consist in sight, speech, and touch.

Touch is twofold: touch at close range and touch at a distance. Touch at close range is effected member to member; touch at a distance is effected by the mutual sending and receiving of gifts. Our hands must be washed from the impurity of both kinds of touch. She is not modest who permits herself to be touched by another flesh; and, as St Jerome says, “The matron who accepts gifts is not chaste.”

In sobriety and refreshment four things must be considered: the appointed time, so that we do not eat before the hour or outside it; the quality of foods, so that we do not take things too costly or delicate; the quantity to be taken, [Col. 0561A] so that we do not stretch the belly by the burden of food; and their preparation, so that we do not have ordinary foods prepared in a conspicuous fashion. By this abstinence and sobriety our horse must be restrained; and by the twofold continence of touch mentioned above it must be bound as by two most powerful straps.

After this follows the third stopping-place, which is not made on the third side of the cloister but on the fourth. For we do not stop at the third side, but pass through it; nor is this without reason. The third side of the cloister, beside the public road, signifies the way of the world, which we have left and to which we ought not return, but from which we must depart in body and heart. Therefore we do not stop there but at the fourth side. There monks are more commonly engaged than elsewhere in reading and meditation, by which we proceed to Jerusalem, signified by the oratory, into which we enter after the third stopping-place.

All the stopping-places are arranged in relation to the oratory. At the first the abbot stands by the oratory; at the second the lay people who follow the procession; at the third the monks who make the procession. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says, we cannot of ourselves either do or even think anything good, but all our sufficiency is from God (2 Corinthians 3), let us ask God to make us walk and advance in his commandments in such a way that, proceeding in good order, from virtue to virtue and from good things to better, we may be brought with joy to the heavenly Jerusalem. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON PALM BRANCHES III

[Col. 0561C]

“Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem; and mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations done in its midst” (Ezekiel 9). The Lord says this to the man clothed in linen—that is, the Father says it to the Son, surrounded by the manifold pressure of most pure flesh, and yet to be surrounded in many ways further.

For just as flax, which springs from the earth, must first be worn down by many beatings before it attains the purity of perfect whiteness, so, as Truth himself testifies, Christ had first to suffer before entering into his glory (Luke 24). By “Christ,” however, I mean the whole Christ: head together with body, Christ together with the Church. For head and body are one Christ. Thus the Apostle expounds it when he says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” [Col. 0561D] (Acts 14). Hence in the Apocalypse the same Lamb of God is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13), because from that time he began to be slain in his members. For the same reason he may be said to be slain until the end of the world, just as he confessed in Peter that he was going to Rome to be crucified again. Finally, Paul too says that he fills up in his own body what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings (Colossians 1). By this he clearly shows that Christ has not yet suffered wholly, but will suffer in his members until the end of the age. For all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution (2 Timothy 3); and because he has not yet suffered wholly, he has not yet wholly entered into his glory. He must first suffer before he is glorified.

Force must be given to the word “must,” because it is altogether necessary, and it is impossible in any other way for anyone to enter the kingdom of God than through many tribulations. “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it” (Matthew 7). And to all it is said: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13).

It should be noted that whiteness is of two kinds: natural and artificial. Natural whiteness is found in the lily; artificial whiteness, in flax. The first whiteness belongs to Christ; the second to the Christian. Christ always possessed perfect purity of heart and body without effort, because he felt none of the impulses of the flesh which we, begotten from the seed of corruption, experience; through the punishment of original sin we always endure the natural opposition of flesh and spirit in the exercise of spiritual combat. But Christ, conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, came to an undefiled body, in which Wisdom built herself a house (Proverbs 9) worthy of so great an inhabitant, and an ark of shittim wood worthy of so great a treasure. Therefore he says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2).

The artificial whiteness of linen garments, however, signifies the twofold whiteness of souls: laborious holiness and eternal brightness. The former is meritorious; the latter recompensing. Neither can be acquired without great labours; neither can be attained without great difficulties. For who among mortals has ever attained the virtue of chastity without chastising the body? Who has attained humility without insult, meekness without injury, poverty without want, or, finally, even the smallest share of righteousness without discipline?

What will the unhappy and wretched say here—those to whom the Holy Spirit pronounces woe because they “enter the earth by two ways”? These are people who wish to attain virtues without labours: to leave everything and lack nothing; to possess chastity and eat enough; to be called poor and wear soft garments; to be accounted humble and suffer no insult; to flourish with the world in the present and reign with Christ eternally; to feed the mind there and the belly here; to pass from luxuries to luxuries and appear glorious in both ages. These are those who, against the Law, wear a garment woven of wool and linen: pursuing soft things while professing rough ones. [Col. 0562D] Not so James, the brother of the Lord, who used no linen garments or baths, seeking no carnal rest in anything; but, together with the blessed Baptist, utterly rejecting soft clothing in all things.

If their head—he who entered the world without sin, lived in the world without sin, and departed the world without sin—although he was Lord of virtues and King of glory, nevertheless did not enter into his glory without sufferings, that is, into the glory which was his before he entered it, how do we sinners and impious people, mercifully drawn out from perdition and separated from it, suppose that we sinners can come to it without the observances of discipline and the purifications of suffering? “My glory,” he says, “I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42): “another,” that is, one unlike me, who does not walk in my paths.

[Col. 0563A] Priestly garments are linen garments. By this it is shown that above all ecclesiastical shepherds and teachers ought to labour more than others to acquire purity of flesh and spirit. For “who shall be cleansed from one who is unclean?” (Ecclesiasticus 34). Thieves too, when they are led to torture, are customarily stripped of all their garments before being hanged and left only in linen, so that their nakedness may not violate the reverence due to public sight, but modesty may remain even in the condemned and the dignity of shame not itself be condemned.

Therefore, by this man’s appearing in linen it is signified that Christ was indeed always prepared to endure the cross, but awaited the time which he himself foresaw as more suitable for this purpose and which the Father had predestined from eternity: “A time to be born, and a time to die” (Ecclesiastes 3). Of this time of dying he himself says: “My time has not yet come” (John 7). For just as it was within his power by what kind of death to lay down his life, so also was it within his power when to do so. Therefore, until today he fled death; but today he ran toward it.

For many times before this day the Jews had wished to seize him, but no one laid hands upon him because his hour had not yet come. On one occasion they had even led him to the brow of the mountain in order to cast him down; but he, passing through their midst, went away. From the beginning of his life Herod also had sought to destroy him; but on the very night on whose following day he was to be destroyed, the angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt” [Col. 0563C] (Matthew 2).

These flights and concealments of the Lord seem to me to be signified by the crosses and crucifixes which, throughout Lent, are covered by the hanging of veils. For what is Christ’s concealment—and its twofold form—but first, concealment from the faces of those persecuting him, and second, concealment from the knowledge of those looking at him? They saw him and yet did not know him, as had been prophesied concerning them: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see” (Psalm 68). And again: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm 34); that is, through the visible weaknesses of my assumed humanity I frustrated their troublesome, treacherous, and crafty investigations into my divinity, so that they believed not merely that I had the likeness of sinful flesh, but sinful flesh itself.

Hence comes that saying of St Jeremiah the prophet: “You will give them a shield for the heart: your labour” (Lamentations 3). For the manifold labour through which Christ administered the mystery of assumed humanity before the eyes of the Jews—hungering after fasting, thirsting after heat, sleeping after vigil, weary after labour, drenched in reproaches, surrounded also by insults, afflicted with wrongs, exposed to scourges—these things, I say, and others like them covered the hearts of the Jews as with a shield of ignorance sevenfold thicker. The thickness and hardness of this shield repelled every dart of divine words and every flash of miracles, so that they did not penetrate to their inmost parts.

Yet the aforesaid hanging of veils before crosses and crucifixes in Lent may signify [Col. 0564A] the same thing signified by the two curtains. The first of these hangs between lay people and clerics; the second between clerics and the altar. The first signifies the obscurity of the Jewish Law, which before the Lord’s Passion could never be fully revealed, and whose figures and ceremonies had necessarily to be removed from the midst after “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5). To signify this, as soon as Christ breathed out his spirit upon the cross, the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom.

Why, then, was it torn rather than rolled up into one place or drawn aside to some part, when either would have been equally easy for divine power, just as tearing it was—unless because by this the Holy Spirit plainly signified that the legal ceremonies were to be removed from the midst [Col. 0564B] as now useful for nothing, once all usefulness had been fulfilled in that single sacrifice in which Christ, priest and victim, offered himself? In signification of this, we do not draw back the curtains but remove them entirely on the Wednesday of the sorrowful week. Moreover, the second curtain, which hangs between choir and presbytery, between clergy and altar, signifies the obstacle of our flesh, which hinders us from beholding eternal things, so that for the present we do not see either the glory of the saints or the punishment of the reprobate. Therefore, on Sundays and feasts of saints we draw back the curtains, signifying that in the general resurrection those things now hidden will be naked and open to us; and that the souls of the saints, stripped of their bodies, now see [Col. 0564C] what they had believed, hold what they had hoped for, and already possess what they had desired. They cleave to Christ, whom they had loved, with neither danger nor end: without obstacle to their cleaving, without danger of falling back, without end to their enjoyment.

In signification of this same matter, on Good Friday we uncover all crosses, draw back the curtain for the Mass of a person presently deceased, and carry an unveiled cross to that person’s funeral rites: signifying, assuredly, that the soul of the deceased has now passed through the wall of flesh and sees the place assigned to it according to the merit of its life. Hence the words in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice” (Song 2). He himself, that is, personally and not merely through a messenger, [Col. 0564D] stands ready to help and awaiting the penitent; he is immediately behind the wall, that is, to be found after death. Thus Ezekiel saw him standing in the gate (Ezek. 40), that is, neither wholly outside nor wholly inside. “Looking through the windows,” that is, knowing fully; “gazing through the lattice,” that is, attending carefully. For the ear of zeal hears all things, and likewise the eye of zeal sees all things. Through the windows, present things; through the lattices, future things. Through the windows he sees future deeds; through the intricate lattices, tangled thoughts or perplexed utterances. He sees some things with a latticed gaze: “Woe to the rich, and to those who now laugh; blessed are the poor, and those who now mourn.” Hence: “You received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16). Thus Jacob [Col. 0565A] blessed Joseph’s sons with crossed hands; the thief runs to paradise, Judas to hell. Nor does he see only through the lattice, but also through the wall—he who enters when the doors are shut. In vain, therefore, will they say: “Walls are everywhere; who will see us?” Or, by the windows understand the apostles; by the lattices, the prophets.

Happy is the person for whom the Lord stands only beyond one wall, whom only the law of sin in the members separates from him. For one who adds consent, act, habit, and contempt has the Lord standing beyond five walls, and he comes to that person’s aid late—if the wall of the body is first broken down and he is not beforehand snatched away by the roaring beasts prepared for prey. Therefore, the covering of veils before the crosses and crucifixes sets forth a threefold meaning: the veil of the figures of the Jewish law, the veil of the darkness of mortal life, and the veil of the Lord’s hidden concealment [Col. 0565B]. To signify the revelation of this concealment, today we carry the uncovered cross in procession.

For he who had avoided the face of death until today now runs toward it with no less eagerness than humility, showing that he had hitherto declined battle neither from fear of death nor would henceforth display his endurance from love of praise. Therefore, knowing that the time of human redemption had come, the Father says to his Son: “Pass through the midst of the city, and mark Tau,” and so forth; that is, draw near to Jerusalem, to the jealous Jews whom you have hitherto avoided, since they sought to kill you. For you must pass through [Col. 0565C] the midst of their hands, all the way to death and hell. It is enough that until now you have given the weaker an example of fleeing persecution while they can flee it with a safe conscience; now you must give the more perfect an example of contending for righteousness unto death. Pass, therefore, through the midst of the city. I will lead you to the city of hell, so that I may bring you back safe and unharmed; but you must pass through the midst of death and through the hands of the Jews who seek your life. Yet I will that you go to hell alone, but I do not will that you return alone from there. Indeed, I will that all who from the beginning of the world have borne the standard of your triumphant cross return triumphantly from hell with you. Pass, therefore, through the midst of the city; that is, henceforth do not seek hiding places [Col. 0565D] against death, nor conceal your divinity from the faithless Jews. Rather, reveal yourself to them as you pass through, so that today they may receive you as the true Savior, whom later they will hang as a thief.

And this is what he adds: “In the midst of Jerusalem”; that is, let that unhappy city receive you today openly and publicly, not merely peacefully as a friend, but also ceremonially as Lord, so that the preliminary flash of passing honor before the coming hailstorm of the Passion may both increase for you the weight of endurance and make heavier for them the burden of vengeance. For as joys sent beforehand intensify unexpected sorrows, so every insult is intensified by the greatness of preceding honor. It follows: “And mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan,” and so forth. It is the custom of kings [Col. 0566A] that royal standards go before each king proceeding to war, so that terrified enemies may flee and secure soldiers may not retreat. Thus the Father, sending the Son to battle, commands him to bring his own sign and to place or imprint it upon each of his people, so that it may be known who are his.

What, then, is this sign except that of which the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5)? “Mark Tau”: that is, mark the sign, for *Tau* is interpreted “sign”; but a sign in the eminent and antonomastic sense—a principal, royal, or imperial sign, singular and excellent, the sign of signs. For as the king to whom this sign belongs is called “King of kings and Lord of lords,” so [Col. 0566B] his sign is the sign of signs. What is more powerful than this sign, which by its appearance alone puts the adversary to flight and grants victory to its standard-bearer? This is so not only when it is borne by a citizen, but even by an enemy. Thus it is read of a Jew outwardly marked with the sign of the cross: when demons, enemies of the cross, wished to harm him but could not, they fled in terror, saying: “A vessel empty, but marked.” As if they said: “We could dwell in this vessel as in an empty vessel, had it not, closed on every side and strongly defended by a dreadful sign as by an impenetrable wall, denied us every entrance.”

Thus demons who had held a chapter concerning sins not to be erased but written down, because at the end of the chapter we are accustomed to say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 123), were compelled to cry out: “Our destruction is in the sign of the Lord.” O sign of singular power and more-than-human virtue, which is not only a sign, but also shield and sword, tree and scepter! A sign, to distinguish; a shield, to protect; a sword, to kill; a tree, to nourish; a scepter, to rule. The sign of faith, the shield of help, the sword of vengeance, the tree of life, the scepter of justice, the pledge and earnest of eternal blessedness.

Hence it is read of Constantine’s standard-bearer, who by the office of his lawful rank bore before him in battle a golden sign of the cross, that he was never wounded, never captured in battle or led into captivity, and suffered no kind of misfortune. For the sign of victory cannot be borne by anyone without an auspice of blessedness [Col. 0566D]. And of this sign it had earlier been said to King Constantine: “In this, conquer.” The sign of the holy cross still lay buried in the earth in a most ignoble fashion, yet the power of that same sign was already shining forth from heaven most wonderfully, when the sign of the cross, as though in a ray of the sun, appeared to Constantine with most beautiful letters containing only this inscription:

> Ἐν τούτῳ νίκα — “By this, conquer.”

Therefore Wisdom, always acting wisely, wished first to have the sign of the holy cross worshipped before the wood itself, lest only that wood on which his body had been stretched should be thought worshipful, and not the sign which the extension of his body had divinely consecrated for the salvation of believers. For just as in geometric art the power and truth of figures are considered more according to [Col. 0567A] abstract quantity than according to concrete quantity, so the power and dimension of the holy cross must be estimated more according to its form than according to its material. Demons are not frightened at the sight of stone, wood, or metal—of whatever material a cross may be made—but rather by the invisible power of its invisible form, invisibly expressed in art from the body of the Crucified, visibly in the cross.

And it must be known that the sign Tau never possessed such power while it had only three dimensions: length, breadth, and depth. It first began to possess the fourth dimension, height, when the Son of the Most High was crucified upon the wood. Pilate added this to its three ancient dimensions when he inscribed upon it, in three languages, the triumphal title of imperial majesty and royal victory [Col. 0567B]. The sign of the cross was fittingly denoted by the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which set an end to the legal figures and confirmed the power of charity that contains the whole law. For the entire mystery of human redemption, hidden in the twenty-two books of the Old Testament, was revealed and fully completed on the cross. Hence the Lord, placed on the cross, when he had received the vinegar, said: “It is finished” (John 19).

There is another mystery which lay more secretly hidden in this mystical number of twenty-two letters. For this number, containing two elevens, signifies a double transgression: of the natural law and of the written law. Humankind [Col. 0567C], made in the image and likeness of God—after the image in wisdom, after the likeness in justice; after the image in reason, after the likeness in choosing good and rejecting evil—received the Decalogue of the law, to be preserved in indelible memory upon the fleshy tablets of the heart, reduced to this brief form: “Do not do to another the evil that you do not wish done to yourself; and do to another the good that you wish done to yourself” (Matt. 7). But Adam, transgressing the Lord’s command, was the first of all to borrow from the usurer, the devil, eleven for twelve in the game of vanity. For just as eleven signifies transgression of the command, so twelve signifies the punishment of sin. For it contains the number six doubled, which is the number [Col. 0567D] of work and labor, according to the saying: “There are six days on which one must work” (Luke 13). What, then, is six doubled except labor doubled?

When, therefore, the sinner passes after the labor of this life not to rest but to the labor of the life to come, he does not pass from six to seven, as though from Friday to Sabbath, but rather returns to another six—that is, to labor repeated. Thus he pays twelve for eleven: punishment for the transgression of the command, penalty for fault, judgment for injustice. Therefore, as has been shown, the first eleven borrowed from the devil—that is, lent to us—was transgression of the natural law; the second, violation of the written law. For this reason its alphabet contains twenty-two letters [Col. 0568A], the last of which is Tau, the figure of the Lord’s cross: because Christ, placed on the cross, paid what he had not taken, but what we had taken.

Indeed, in the ancient books of the Samaritans, as blessed Jerome testifies, Tau is accustomed to represent the figure of the cross; but in the newer Hebrew books which Ezra found, it lacks the fourth dimension, that is, height, which was discovered and added in Christ’s Passion. For the punishment of the cross, especially customary among Romans and Jews, was formed of two pieces of wood: one fixed in the earth and raised on high, the other laid crosswise, so that the suspended person’s head had no support. In this punishment the upright wood represented length and the transverse wood breadth. But that in which the upright wood was fixed—whatever it was, whether stone, wood, or the earth itself—was called depth [Col. 0568B]. Yet the Son of the Most High, raised on the cross, could not but raise his cross also, completing in it the dimension of height from the height of his divinity.

This was signified by the charge written above his head: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27). The plain sense of this writing is: this man, named Jesus, a Nazarene by homeland and a Jew by race, was crucified for no other reason than because he said that he was king of the Jews—as indeed he truly is. This is what the judge’s affirmation means: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). From that time the sign of the cross, complete in all its parts, began to be as terrible to the hosts of demons, as venerable to the choirs of angels, and as saving to the children of humankind [Col. 0568C]. For then humanity first began to understand how beneficial to the human race was the crucifixion of that man.

For the whole human race was marked with the cross when the Word was made flesh. The form of divinity is nothing other than the form of the cross. For the form of divinity is most simple and indivisible, as it is invisible: long in eternity, broad in charity, lofty in power, deep in wisdom. What is longer than eternity, broader than charity, deeper than wisdom, loftier than power? Because of eternity it is said: “I will satisfy him with length of days” (Ps. 90). Because of charity: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 113). Because of wisdom: “O the depth of the riches [Col. 0568D] of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments!” (Rom. 11), and so forth. In this passage “height” is used for “depth,” as when one says, “The well is deep.” Because of power it is said: “For the Lord Most High is terrible over all the earth” (Ps. 46).

Within these four dimensions are contained six kinds of linear motion. In length there are forward and backward; in breadth, right and left; in depth and height, upward and downward. Eternity is long forward because it lacks an end; long backward because it lacks a beginning. These two are denoted in the Apocalypse by α and ω. This length of the cross contains the two regions of the world, east and west. For the east is before us, the west behind. Charity is broad on the right and on the left [Col. 0569A]: on the right through friendship, on the left through patience. These two are noted there: “Charity is patient, is kind” (2 Cor. 13); that is, immeasurably broad on either side, giving all things and enduring all things. This breadth of the cross contains the two regions of the world, north and south, denoted by Aquilo and Auster, of which the former is left and the latter right.

The lowest power is that which draws strength only from another’s weakness. Such is the power of demons, whom our sins alone make powerful. For the devil has only as much power against you as you have consented to give him, and no more. Why, then, should a Christian fear the devil, when the adversary can do absolutely nothing against him if he does not consent? Finally, every power [Col. 0569B] has only as much height as it has justice. For the ability to do evil and not good is not power but weakness, not strength but impotence. Why then do the rulers of this world pride themselves on a power to harm which is common to beasts and serpents, flies and fleas, and proper to demons? It is of no benefit that the same person cannot harm; but not conversely. To be able and not to benefit, and not to will, is altogether as nothing as that which benefits not at all. Therefore, as I have said, every power is as lofty as its will is just. But because the human will, even when just, often lacks effect, all human power is small and low; the power of an angel is great and high; God’s is supreme; the devil’s is none. Hence it is said to him: “You have become nothing” (Ezek. 28).

[Col. 0569C] God’s wisdom is as deep as it reaches everywhere because of its purity. “The heart of man is deep; who can know it,” except God, who alone knows the hearts of the children of humankind? O that deep wisdom which reaches even to this depth of the human heart and to the depth of hell. Because of these four dimensions the sign of the cross was made, reaching mightily from end to end through the length of eternity, and therefore terrible to fleeing demons; ordering all things sweetly through the breadth of charity, and therefore saving to miserable humans; drawing upward to heaven through the loftiness of power, and therefore venerable to angelic powers; penetrating [Col. 0569D] downward to hell through the depth of wisdom, and therefore again intolerable to unclean spirits. Their flight has perished, for there is nowhere for them to flee from the face of the length of the Lord’s cross. In vain does their envy burn: by the height of divine charity they have no way to find an entrance for harming. In vain does their pride swell: they have no place to ascend from the lofty power pressing them down. In vain do their fear and cowardice lurk: they have nowhere to hide from the depth of wisdom reaching everywhere.

By this, then, as it were by a faith-shaped form of divinity, human nature was figured when God’s Wisdom was incarnate. But the wondrous mystery of that form would never have been revealed to humankind except through Christ’s cross, although in Christ’s manner of life [Col. 0570A]—in which he deigned to live among humans as a human—there appeared a certain superficial trace of this form in obedience, charity, patience, and justice. His obedience unto death displayed the length of the cross; his love of his own unto the end, its breadth; his endurance unto the cross, its depth; his zeal for justice unto blood, its height. Thus, by living and then dying, Christ showed the human race how they ought to be marked with the seal of the cross: namely, by obeying, enduring, and zealously acting.

Now the first command that he, as man among human beings, commanded on earth is this: “Repent” (Matt. 3). This is the length of our cross, if it is long forward and backward. Behind are past sins; before are future ones. Therefore perfect sorrow for past sin and perfect caution concerning the future make us long forward and backward [Col. 0570B].

One who grieves over past wrongdoing but does not take care not to sin again is long backward but short forward. Therefore he must fall into the hands of the enemies of Christ’s cross, because he is not commensurate with its length. Such was that wretched man near the city of Avranches, who grieved that he was tempted by a spirit of fornication but, taking no care against its assault, went to Rome nine times for prayer, as though making satisfaction to God for his repeated fall. When he returned from his ninth pilgrimage, made more secure by so many labors, he returned to his vomit—that is, to sexual intercourse—and in the very emission of seed breathed out his spirit.

One who takes care not to seize what belongs to another, but nevertheless retains another’s property, is long forward but short backward. Thus that German count, who otherwise had been most just, was nevertheless seen burning in hell for this alone: that he unjustly held a certain right belonging to the Church of Metz of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, which his ancestors had appropriated to themselves by prescription of long duration [Col. 0570C].

Charity makes us broad on the right and on the left: on the right by giving, on the left by forgiving. With these two arms we embrace Christ on the cross, crying out to us by voice and deed: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; and it will be given to you” (Luke 6). Forgive the sinner; give to the needy. But he said “Forgive” before “Give,” because one who asks forgiveness ought first to forgive fault, according to the saying: “A man preserves anger against a man and seeks healing from God” (Ecclus. 28). Those who know how to give but not how to forgive are broad on the right but narrow on the left; those who know how to forgive but not how to give are the reverse. Hatred and envy make us narrow on the left, greed and stinginess on the right: greed for another’s goods, stinginess with one’s own. Envy forgives nothing; stinginess gives nothing. Both are enemies of Christ’s breadth.

The depth of Christ’s cross is humility enduring all things, even to death and death itself; its height is justice zealous even to blood. As everyone baptized is washed through water, so each is tested by the judgment of water; in this kind of trial those who float are condemned, those who sink are saved.

Water is tribulation. In this water the person floats who either [Col. 0571A] rebels or murmurs silently; but the person sinks who endures all things with equanimity, and this person alone is saved—provided that he has the fourth dimension, namely zeal for justice even to shedding blood. Thus it is written: “Mark Tau upon the foreheads of the men groaning over the abominations that are done in the midst of Jerusalem” (Ezek. 9). These words show that those to be marked already abstained from their own sins, since they grieved over those of others. Thus they already had the length of the cross through caution against sin, breadth through compassion, and depth through the humility of concealment. But since they did not have height through zeal in rebuking, they still had to be marked with the sign Tau upon their foreheads.

Woe to those who do not bear this sign of victory and honor [Col. 0571B] upon their foreheads but hide it under their feet. Woe to prelates who do not wear upon their foreheads the woolen plate on which the tetragrammaton, the name of the Lord, is written, but trample it beneath their feet. These are hireling shepherds who, when they see the wolf coming, leave the sheep and flee. The six men carrying the axe are the six orders of messengers whom God sent into the world through the six ages: “men,” that is, speaking manfully. The vessel of destruction, which the Seventy Interpreters call an axe, signifies the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; it is a vessel of destruction for one who is only a hearer and not a doer.

Observe that these men are not said to bear a lyre or cithara, but an axe, because a preacher of God’s word ought not [Col. 0571C] to flatter sins, but strike and pierce, as it is written: “The words of the wise are like goads and like nails driven firmly in” (Ecclus. 12). No one will be able to escape the axes of those men, which are already laid at the roots of the trees, unless he sets the sign Tau upon his forehead. Thus marked, the Lord comes today to Jerusalem, not only to approach the Jews but also to provoke them, driving sellers and buyers from the temple, overturning the money-changers’ tables and pouring out their coins; sharply rebuking his enemies, whom he knew could in no way be corrected. Thus John the Baptist rebuked Herod for adultery, though he did not doubt in the least that Herod would not dismiss the adulterous woman.

Nor should anyone think that all these dimensions of the cross are too harsh or burdensome to bear. For just as the cross, once terrible to behold, has now become delightful in appearance because it received a singular beauty from the limbs of the Lord, so it has become light to bear because it gained gentleness from the burden of charity, anointing from the sign, and sweetness from the anointing. Nothing is gentler than Christ, who bears the person bearing him; nothing sweeter than the anointing, which not only softens what is rough but also refreshes the weary. Charity was wholly stretched out upon the cross, and its anointing was poured over the entire cross, the most precious blood of the Redeemer flowing in most abundant streams through each of its dimensions. The depth of the cross was anointed by blood flowing from Christ’s feet; its breadth, from his hands [Col. 0572A]; its height, from the wounds of his head through the crown of thorns; its length, from the spring made in his side by the lance.
