O how poor are the judges of things who consider Christ’s cross, so light and so sweet, harsh or heavy! Truly, those who do not sense its sweetness have a most infirm palate. Of this sweetness that most holy Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, had happily drunk his fill when he sang in metre:

> Faithful cross, among all  
> the one noble tree;  
> no forest brings forth such a one  
> in leaf, flower, or seed:  
> sweet wood, sweet nails,  
> bearing a sweet burden.

Surely, one who has tasted this sweetness is not ashamed to bear the cross upon his forehead—that is, to contend for justice unto death [Col. 0572B]. This is the chief mark of the servants of the Crucified, according to the words: “Do not harm the earth, the sea, or the trees, until we have marked the servants of God upon their foreheads” (Rev. 7). May God and our Lord Jesus Christ deign to mark us all thus, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON PALM BRANCHES IV

“Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel! Hosanna in the highest!” (Matt. 21; Luke 19).

People commonly say, “All honors are due to the lord”—that is, they are due. This proverb is true, but it must not be understood universally. For not every honor is due to every lord. Yet how many lords there are today who deserve either no honor or little honor! There is one Lord alone to whom this proverb applies. Who is he? He who is King of kings and Lord of lords: our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God and son of David. Son of God according to divinity; son of David according to humanity. As Son of God he is creator of all things; as son of David, redeemer of human beings—not, however, of all, but only of the faithful. To this Lord every honor is due, because every honor proceeds from him, as it is written: “To the place from which [Col. 0572D] the rivers flow, they return, that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1).

That every honor is due to him is attested today by the Hebrew children, not only playing in the street, but also hanging at their mothers’ breasts. Their childish grace today uttered a devout “Hosanna” to the Lord seated upon an ass and passing along the road. They did not, however, utter this praise from natural understanding—nor did the older generation, which uttered the same words—but rather from the gift of the Holy Spirit, who today made infants’ tongues eloquent in Christ’s praise. Thus they say: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” that is, “May salvation be to the Son of David.” Thus Jerome glosses Mark. It is like the passage in the Apocalypse: “Salvation to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. 7). When we say this, we do not wish that our God [Col. 0573A], or the Son of David—which is the same—may be safe; rather, its meaning is: whoever hopes or waits for salvation ought to hope and wait for it from the Son of David as Savior. For he is Savior in the depths and in the heights, in heaven and on earth, of angels and humans, of souls and bodies.

Jesus was called Son of David before he was born. Thus the angel says to Mary: “He shall be great and shall be called Son of the Most High. And the Lord shall give him the throne of David his father, and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1). None of David’s sons could reign eternally except Christ, of whom Daniel says: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be corrupted” (Dan. 7); and of whom the Apostle says: “Who was made for him from the seed [Col. 0573B] of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1).

Of all the patriarchs, Abraham and David alone are called Christ’s fathers according to the flesh, because to them alone was specially made the promise that Christ would be born from their seed. Therefore he is called their son at the beginning when it is said: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). David is placed first because he was nearer to Christ than Abraham. Yet the promise was first made to Abraham rather than David, because in Christ’s inheritance the righteous receive first place and penitents second. Nevertheless, Christ is read to be called son of Abraham only once in the Gospel (Matt. 1), but Son of David very often, because very few preserve righteousness most perfectly after their first calling, whereas very many return by repentance to their former grace after falling.

Therefore, in Christ’s being called Son of David more often than son of Abraham, great hope of pardon is set before sinners—not merely of pardon but of recovering all grace, even grace fuller than they ever possessed. This is evident in David after his threefold fall of adultery, homicide, and betrayal; and in the Apostle Peter after the abyss of his threefold denial. For both, by repentance, recovered fuller grace than they had lost by sinning. Indeed, David’s sins were so wholly removed through repentance that he is even said not to have sinned. Thus one reads in the book of Jesus son of Sirach [Col. 0573D]: “Except for David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all sinned” (Ecclus. 49).

What is this, Lord? Then David did not sin—David, who did this and that? Here God would plainly answer: “I do not remember what he did; and who can prove it to me? What has been completely erased does not exist at all. I am witness and judge of all sins; who can testify to what I do not remember, or rewrite what I have erased? If the wicked person, having turned, does penance, I shall not remember any of the iniquities he has committed.” Therefore David did not sin: for he is not the one who sinned, but another, according to the saying, “Turn the wicked man, and he shall not be” (Prov. 12)—supply, “wicked,” but rather “righteous,” because he has been turned from wickedness to righteousness.

Hence Solomon’s saying: “Such is the way [Col. 0574A] of an adulterous woman, who, eating and wiping her mouth, says: ‘I have done no evil’” (Prov. 30). The adulterous woman is the sinful soul, cleaving to someone other than her true Bridegroom. This adulterous woman eats when she fulfils the desires of the flesh; for she feeds the barren woman who does not bear, and does no good to herself, who is a widow. But she wipes her mouth when she confesses her sin. O what refinement it is to wipe one’s mouth after eating—that is, to repent after sinning! The mouth of the heart must be wiped by true contrition; the mouth of the body by pure and complete confession; and, so to speak, the mouth of one’s deed by worthy and fitting satisfaction.

Blessed is the person who wipes his mouth thus, so that, once the Lord has been made propitious to him, he may already deserve to be received into the kiss of peace: the eternal love of human souls, a lover not fastidious but readily forgiving and receiving the beloved after faults, not reproaching her for having offended, according to Jeremiah’s words: “If a man dismisses his wife, and she departs from him and takes another husband, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have committed fornication with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you” (Jer. 3). O incomparable kindness! Thus the adulterous woman says—now no longer adulterous, but another woman, after wiping her mouth after eating—“I have done no evil.”

On this passage Ambrose aptly says: “She does not say, ‘I have been released, I have been dismissed, I have been covered, I have been washed’; but she speaks confidently: ‘I have done no evil. I am not the woman I was, made another by you, who turn the wicked and he shall not be’” [Col. 0574C]. Certainly this is like the saying: “Except for David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all sinned” (Ecclus. 49).

For this David is not the one who sinned, but another, undoubtedly made through Him who “turns the ungodly man, and he shall not be.” Nor is David merely counted among those who did not sin, but is even set before them, so that he may in some sense be shown worthier. Thus too, in invocations of the saints, Mary Magdalene is not merely numbered among virgins, but is set before them all, precisely because she wiped her mouth so elegantly that it is evident both to God and to human beings that she had never eaten before. O how well [Col. 0574D] she wiped her mouth when she kissed the Lord’s feet, watered them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment! (Luke 7.) This is why the Son of God preferred in Scripture to be called more often Son of David than Son of Abraham: namely, so that sinners might conceive from this designation the most certain hope of obtaining the fullest pardon. Therefore he is rightly called Son of David, and received as King and Saviour, not only by childlike innocence, but also by a crowd of both sexes and every age, crying out in prophetic voices: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

Every king is a lord, but not every lord is a king. Yet every lord ought to be a saviour to the same extent that he is a ruler. For every [Col. 0575A] lord is appointed, according to his ability, to save those, male or female, over whom he rules—except, however, in the kingdom of Satan, in which all who are set over others and all their attendants are established for destruction. For, as Tertullian says, “the operation of demons is the overthrow of man.” Spiritual wickedness, from its beginning, has aimed at humanity’s ruin. And the more they oppose us, the more they oppose themselves also; for as great as is their effort at human deception, so great is their advance in their own damnation. Yet such is their rage against the Judge that they count any burden of punishment, however great, as little, provided they see human beings driven onward to like punishments. Thus their desperate condition, by reason of their prior condemnation, counts as a consolation the opportunity for enjoying malice meanwhile [Col. 0575B] through the delay of punishment. Yet even meanwhile they are not without punishment, and that punishment is manifold and most grievous; but they deem light whatever they suffer, provided that they may range about at will to deceive people.

Therefore all people who injure those subject to them belong to Satan’s kingdom. “There is no authority except from God; and those which exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13). But every divine ordering in human affairs is a provision for human salvation; for He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth. God commands no one to act impiously. Yet he does at times make—that is, permit—a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people: either because subjects such as these deserve such a king, or because such perverse persons deserve such a kingdom. Therefore every lord is appointed by God over human beings for saving them, [Col. 0575C] that is, for ordering the salvation of his subjects.

But woe to those who misuse their dominion over others for their destruction or their own, like Alexander, who knew how to save nothing but to destroy everything. The most certain omen of his birth itself foreshadowed this. For on the night when he was born, not only was the earth shaken and great thunder heard, but actual stones also fell from heaven, signifying, of course, that the boy then born had come to stone human beings. Many who rule today among the clergy or among the people are of this sort: disturbers of peace, enemies of justice, plunderers of property, stoners of men. They rage through the provinces as though Satan had gone out from the presence of the Lord [Col. 0575D] to scourge Job. They conduct themselves among those over whom they are set as though Tisiphone or Megaera had been sent up from hell to kindle torches for crime. Among such men judgment is nothing but a public bribe, and they can scarcely restrain their tears when they see nothing that calls for tears.

Indeed, the name of every lord would be venerable among the people if it were exercised with as much solicitude as it is sought with ambition; if they judged justly; if they preferred being useful to presiding; if they were sparing in exactions; if they cast away avarice gained through false accusation, shook their hands free from every gift, and did not consider every profit to be godliness. Every lord ought to save and preserve both the property and the bodies of his subjects. Yet where among mortals [Col. 0576A] will a lord be found who can always preserve even these?

> Neither house nor estate, nor a heap of bronze and gold,  
> has driven fevers from the sick body of its master.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.48

But suppose that these two things, namely body and possession, are safe for every person: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers loss to his own soul?” (Matt. 16). Therefore he alone is the true Lord who is the true Saviour—that is, who can preserve souls, bodies, and possessions for eternity. For if this is established concerning souls, then it is so also concerning bodies and possessions. “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” He who can do the greater can surely do the less.

Christ preserves the souls of Elijah and Enoch, lest they leave their bodies; [Col. 0576B] for they have already lived for so many thousands of years in those same bodies without any disturbance. Long ago in the wilderness He preserved the bodies and garments of the Jews for forty years; and through so long a period there was no sick person in their tribes, nor were their garments worn out. But he has brought us not temporal but eternal salvation, and has taught us how our souls are saved through faith and obedience to the commandments; our bodies, through the mortification of the members; our possessions, through the support of the poor.

Of the first: “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 18). And: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19). Of the second: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12); and the Apostle: “Mortify your members which are upon [Col. 0576C] the earth” (Col. 3); and again: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15). Augustine: “If you keep grain, you lose it; if you sow it, you renew it.” Of the third: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not dig through or steal” (Matt. 6). Likewise Augustine: “The hands of the poor are Christ’s treasury.”

The soul lives through faith; the body rises again through the sowing of penitence; possessions do not perish through the liberality of almsgiving. Blessed is that Lord who has taught us thus to save ourselves and what is ours. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” This name *Dominus* signifies, as it were, “one giving a gift.” What gift, or how great a gift, does this Lord give? Every good thing, and the highest good. “I,” he says, “will show you every good thing” [Col. 0576D] (Exod. 33). “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. 1). Therefore, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

On this passage Augustine, writing on John, says: “What great thing is it for Christ, King of angels, to be king of the Jews?” Christ is not king in order to exact taxes, gather armies, and defeat enemies; but he is King of Israel because he rules minds and brings believers, those who hope, and those who love, into the kingdoms of heaven. Therefore, that the Son of God, equal to the Father, was willing to be King of Israel was condescension, not promotion; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power.

It should nevertheless be noted that in [Col. 0577A] the Gospel Christ is called King in three places, especially where, by human standards, the insignia of this royal majesty were least apparent. To gather everything briefly: he was called King lying in a manger, sitting on an ass, and hanging on a gallows. What have all these to do with a king, good God? What has a king to do with a manger? A prince with a beast of burden? An emperor with a cross? Is not the first ordinarily prepared for beasts, the second for the lowly, the third for criminals? Yet everywhere, for anyone who considers well, the true insignia of royal majesty are shown.

Above we said that every lord and king ought to be the saviour of those things established under his rule, because he is appointed by right for their preservation. Let us now see what signs of a Saviour were present in one lying [Col. 0577B] in a manger, sitting on an ass, and hanging upon the gallows. Of the first sign the angel says to the shepherds: “For a Saviour has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. You will find an infant laid in a manger” (Luke 2). Behold what a sign of the Saviour: infancy in a manger. Infant silence accuses no one; infant weakness strikes no one; hay in a manger refreshes beasts. Therefore this infant, placed in a manger, signified that he had not come to accuse or punish sinners, but to endure them and spare them, and to refresh the souls of penitents with the hay of his flesh. And this is to be a Saviour: truly to rule, and to be lord.

The Magi, however, put forward another sign of his royal majesty, saying: “Where is he who has been born King [Col. 0577C] of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east” (Luke 2). And to show how great a King he was, they continue and say: “We have come to worship him” (ibid.). For a star newly created, with new brightness and royal magnitude, truly signified a new man and a new King—not only ruler of human beings but also creator of the stars, and therefore worthy of worship by all people, even kings.

But the greatest sign of clemency lay in his sitting upon the ass, according to that prophetic saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem. Behold, your King comes to you, righteous and himself a Saviour, poor, and riding upon a she-ass and upon a colt, the foal of a beast of burden” (Zech. 9). Hence this Ambrosian saying [Note: [Col. 0577D] Ambrose, in a hymn]:

[Col. 0577D]

> O how astounding is this loving-kindness!  
> Wondrous the clemency of God:  
> the Creator of the age deigns  
> to become the rider of a little ass.

Certainly this riding signified both the gentleness of the rider-King and the salvation of the gentle. For this purpose he came: to become the rider of the gentle and humble; to lay his sweet yoke and light burden upon the gentle, so that those who had formerly bent unhappily under the devil’s yoke might walk uprightly and pleasantly under Christ’s yoke, as it is written: “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51). Blessed indeed is the one who can say with the Psalmist: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72).

Blessed [Col. 0578A] is the beast of burden that carries the Saviour, upon which Jesus rides, upon which Christ sits, which bears the Messiah, which breathes forth the anointing of sweetness and healing, which is covered with the garments of the apostles, before whose feet flowers are strewn, which has cast off from its bondage to very many masters the yoke of sin, whose bonds of sin the apostolic hand has now loosed, which subjects itself to the one God, and which is brought to the vision of eternal peace.

That sudden, prophetic cry was likewise a sign of ruling power: the Saviour, perfecting praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children, made their tongues eloquent in praise of our King—not through human teaching or natural skill, but through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Through the grace of the Holy Spirit, which by their credible testimony destroyed the hostile venom and wonderfully confounded the avenger—that is, the Scribes and Pharisees— who had become enemies of truth and foes of justice, as though in vengeance for the Jewish law. Finally, the great sign of omnipotence that had shortly before been wrought in the raising of Lazarus, dead for four days, marvelously recalled from the tomb to life, was the chief reason why the crowd came to meet Christ with reverence and devotion. For thus the Evangelist says: “Therefore the crowd also came to meet him, because they heard that he had performed this sign” [Col. 0578B] (John 12).

O truly a sign of great penitence: to restore suddenly, not merely to life but even to perfect health, one lying dead in the tomb and remaining for four days amid the stench of his own putrefaction; and this by the power of this voice alone, with which he cried in [Col. 0578C] a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth from the enclosure of the tomb, where human beings have placed you”; and immediately, he says, “he who had been dead came forth, bound hand and foot with bands” (John 2 [citation as printed]). But what wonder, when he gave the command who held the keys of death and hell?

Behold what signs of royal power, what insignia of royal majesty, he bore with him as he came so gentle and humble upon an ass. For he did not conceal that he was the Lord of majesty, when he called himself Lord of the temple, saying: “It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Luke 19). And having made a whip of cords, he drove all buyers and sellers from the temple, signifying that every person must be bound by the cords of his own [Col. 0578D] sins, and cast out from the company of the saints by no whip other than the merit of his own sins.

On this passage Jerome says: “Among all the signs this seems more wonderful: that one man, with the blows of a whip, drove out so great a multitude of those who, because he was destroying their profits, were raging against him.” And he adds: “For something fiery and star-like shone from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity gleamed in his face.”

Moreover, on the day of his Passion he was three times called “Lord King,” and three times kings’ honour was bestowed upon him: once mockingly and twice affirmatively. Mockingly by the soldiers of Pilate the governor, who with mockery rendered him royal honour; affirmatively by Pilate himself, writing [Col. 0579A] the title, and by the penitent and confessing thief: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (John 19). For both Pilate and the thief bore witness that Christ was king: Pilate by writing the triumphal title and confirming the inscription, saying, “What I have written, I have written” (Luke 23); the thief by confessing and imploring royal clemency, saying, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.”

It should nevertheless be known that the soldiers’ mockery bore a threefold testimony to this same truth, though unknowingly. For in that mockery the soldiers unwittingly signified two very great matters, altogether necessary for our instruction: namely, that the honour of the world is vain and that Christ’s honour is true. Every kingdom and empire of this world is transient [Col. 0579B] and fragile because of the shortness of time, piercing and sorrowful because of the burden of anxiety, fiery and terrible because of the expectation of a graver judgment.

Of the first it is written: “Every dominion is of brief life” (Ecclus. 10). Behold, truly a reed sceptre, easily broken. Of the second: “The weight of office does not allow kings and princes of this age to be moderately wicked.” Behold, truly a crown of thorns, with which the head of its wearer is most painfully pierced. Of the third: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments, and a stronger torture awaits the stronger” (Wis. 6). Behold, truly a scarlet cloak and a fiery garment, by which the whole body of its wearer is burned.

Yet all these things truly expressed Christ’s royal honour. For the reed sceptre signified [Col. 0579C] that he is the one who wrote the law of justice in human hearts and who will render to each according to his works (Matt. 16), since we customarily write and measure with a reed. The crown of thorns signified that Christ is the one who had perfectly conquered sin and had won a perfect victory over sins. For “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Nor does the Lord triumph only over sins, but always also over sinners: either by mercifully converting them or by justly punishing them eternally.

Moreover, his purple garment signified three things: the supreme beauty of immortality; the royal honour of highest power, with which his flesh was adorned when it rose from the dead; and the common participation in similar beauty, with which the holy Church is to be adorned round about on the day of judgment. It signified especially [Col. 0579D] the rosy washing-bath of his most precious blood, by which she was redeemed and washed on the day of his Passion, as had been foretold in Jacob’s splendid prophecy, in the blessing of his son Judah: “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Gen. 49).

The robe, they say, a matronly ornament, signifies the body of Christ, namely the Church; and this is also denoted by the cloak, because the Church is Christ’s ornament and garment. Hence it is written: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with an ornament” (Isa. 49). But the blood of grapes signifies Christ’s blood: according to his humanity he is the true vine, in whom branches that abide bear much fruit; according to [Col. 0580A] his divinity, he is the husbandman, not applying cultivation externally but giving growth within. Christ’s blood is aptly called both wine and a washing-bath: wine, because it gladdens; a washing-bath, because it cleanses, washes, and sanctifies; as in the saying: “He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). Elsewhere it is said: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion and wash the blood of Jerusalem” (Isa. 4), and so forth. Here sin is signified by blood.

O blood of exceptional efficacy, of unique power! Every other blood defiles and stains; this alone washes away filth and cleanses stains. O new kind of fuller, who washes blood with blood! What will not the blood of the Creator of all things be able to do, if the blood of certain animals can do so much? We read of three most powerful kinds [Col. 0580B] of blood: that of a goat, of a menstruating woman, and of a murex-shellfish. The first splits the diamond, the hardest stone; the second dissolves bitumen, the most tenacious glue; the third dyes purple, the finest colour. Surely the blood of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world ought to possess no less than these, indeed far more; according to the Apostle’s saying: “If the blood of goats and calves sanctifies the defiled, etc., how much more the blood of Christ!” (Heb. 9).

Therefore, when this blood was shed, to signify its power to wash and sanctify, the earth shook, hell burst open, the sun was afraid, and rocks were split. And, so that these bloods may yield us some moral instruction, it should be known that by the power of Christ’s blood the diamond is split as often as an obstinate sinner is softened to penitence; bitumen is dissolved when an inveterate habit of unjust desire is violently broken; purple is dyed when one contends for justice, even unto death, amid tribulations and persecutions. The diamond was split in the conversion of magicians, such as Cyprian and Daria; bitumen was dissolved in the continence of fornicators, such as Boniface and Pelagia; purple was dyed in the constancy of martyrs, such as Lawrence and our Thomas.

## SERMON XII. ON PALM SUNDAY V

“For you have been bought at a great price: glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6).

The outstanding preacher, like one skilled in law, most fittingly brings an action against us according to our own law; knowing, of course, that it is customary among all people for a servant to be more diligent in his master’s work according as he has been acquired for a higher price. Therefore, about to exhort us to glorify God by keeping the commandment, and to bear him under the discipline of the scourge, he wished first to remind us of the ever-to-be-considered greatness of the price by which we have been redeemed through the Lord’s mercy, saying: “For you have been bought at a great price.” Thus Peter: “You have not been redeemed with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Christ Jesus” (1 Pet. 1). Isaiah: “You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed” (Isa. 52). He does not say, “And you shall be redeemed for nothing,” but “without silver”: that is, not with corruptible money, never pleasing to God, but with the saving sacrifice of the gentle [Col. 0581A] Lamb, uniquely acceptable to him.

“You have been bought at a great price.” Paul says, “bought”; Peter, “redeemed.” Both are true. We were redeemed from the enemy’s hand; bought from God’s hand. We were redeemed from our vain manner of life, so that we might not remain in it; we were bought by the Lord, that we might serve righteousness. We were redeemed because we had first been sold; we were bought lest we be sold any longer. For he whom the Son, who is Truth, frees is truly free.

Adam first sold us when, through the fault of his disobedience, he made us all children of wrath, as it is written: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death” (Rom. 3 [citation as printed]). Then we sold ourselves when we willingly consented to the devil, as the Lord says through Isaiah: “Who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold in your iniquities; in your crimes I dismissed your mother” (Isa. 50). It is aptly said: “You were sold for nothing” (Isa. 52), that is, without any price or gain. For by sinning we gain nothing but bondage and death, which is sin’s wage, reward, and fruit.

The devil has nothing else that he can give. He is so poor and destitute that he lacks every good; so miserable that he abounds in every evil. O what folly, what misery, to sell oneself to such a lord, who can help neither himself nor another, benefit neither himself nor another. But once sold under sin, no one can redeem himself, because he has made himself sin’s slave, as it is written: “He who commits sin [Col. 0581C] is the slave of sin” (John 8). He is so much a slave that, even if his mind consents to God’s law, his flesh nevertheless resists. Therefore he cannot escape the slavery of sin—that is, concupiscence—nor sin’s wage, that is, death and Gehenna.

Hence Augustine, on that passage: “But the strength of sin is the law. Prohibition, he says, increases the desire for the unlawful deed when justice is not so loved that the desire to sin is overcome by delight in justice. But for justice truly to be so loved and to delight, only divine grace comes to aid. Therefore he alone could redeem us whom no other could sell: namely, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, into whom sin could not enter, and who thus alone fulfilled all righteousness [Col. 0581D] that, though he could not be convicted of sin, he did not refuse to die for sinners.” The same Augustine, in a homily *On the Incarnation of the Lord*: “Human pride pressed you down so greatly that only divine humility could raise you up.”

Therefore we were bought by the devil for no price, but redeemed by Christ at a great price. He gave himself for us as the price—not to the devil, who had bought us for nothing and possessed us for nothing, but to God his Father, who had justly sold us, that is, permitted us to be sold; as in the Psalmist’s words: “You sold your people without a price” (Ps. 43), that is, you permitted them to be sold. And Moses: “Was it not because their God sold them and the Lord shut them up?” (Deut. 3 [citation as printed]). Thus God is said to have sold us, just as he is said to have hardened Pharaoh and turned the heart of the Egyptians so that they hated his people.

And as we were sold by flesh and blood—that is, by the fleshly pleasure of the first human being—so we were redeemed by flesh and blood—that is, by the loving offering of the second human being. For this reason he assumed the nature of our mortality, that he might have something to offer to the Father on our behalf. “Every high priest,” as the Apostle says, “is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices” (Heb. 8); and therefore it is necessary that this one have something to offer.

But the heretic says: What does the offering of flesh and blood have to do with the redemption of a soul, a spiritual substance? For what is any flesh and blood but flesh and blood? Listen, wretch: not every flesh is the same flesh. One is the flesh of birds, another the flesh of fishes, another of beasts of burden, [Col. 0582B] another of cattle, another of wild beasts, another of creeping things (1 Cor. 15). All human flesh, conceived from impure seed, is naturally impure and defiled. But Christ’s flesh, because it was taken without male seed and from a virgin, is naturally most pure; and because it is personally united with God, it is also most pure.

Hence Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0581D] Ambrose, in a hymn]:

> Flesh is at fault;  
> flesh cleanses;  
> God reigns;  
> God’s flesh.

“Who can make clean what is conceived from impure seed? Is it not you alone?” (Job 14). Understand: conceived without seed. For he who makes something from nothing can make what is clean from what is impure. Every human blood, simply because it is a bloody fluid, defiles and pollutes. But Christ’s blood, because it is God’s blood, most powerfully cleanses and washes—not, I say, stains on garments or bodies, but, incomparably more, those of souls. For it is the blood of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Hence John in the Apocalypse: “He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” [Col. 0582C] (Rev. 1).

Thus the Apostle to the Hebrews argues most aptly from the lesser, saying: “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of a heifer’s ashes, sanctifies those who are defiled for the purification of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself spotless to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” (Heb. 9).

And lest such power in flesh and blood perhaps seem incredible to anyone, let him consider, I beg, the flesh of the *tiri* serpent [term uncertain] and the blood of a goat. Is not theriac made from the flesh of the *tirus*, driving the destruction of poison out of human flesh? Then could not a medicine be made from God’s flesh which might drive out from every soul the venom of the ancient serpent, that is, the putrefaction of sin? Hence it is written: “A medicine for all things in the hastening mist” (Ecclus. 43), that is, the antidote of human salvation was truly prepared in Christ’s death of three days. Its darkness, quickly passing and swiftly vanishing through the splendid miracle of his hastened resurrection, was powerfully blown away from the hearts of the faithful, leaving tangible darkness of denser ignorance in the hearts of the proud.

For this mist was so thick that even in the hearts of the disciples, at the time of the Passion, it almost extinguished the whole light of faith. Hence they said: “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” [Col. 0583A] (Luke 24). But, as I said, this darkness quickly passed when the Lord appeared to them after the resurrection, and remained only in the hearts of the proud, who refuse to believe the holy Scriptures and therefore cannot come to the knowledge of truth. As it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7).

Does not the unconquerable hardness of diamond break through the blood of a goat? Then cannot the blood of Christ, the Son of God, dissolve however hardened the ice of our sins may be? Hence: “And as ice in fair weather, your sins are melted” (Ecclus. 3). For this reason the Lord himself wished to be signified through the bronze serpent and the scapegoat. The serpent, raised upon a pole and looked upon by the crowd, healed in those bitten the bites of serpents; but the goat, in the high priest’s prayer, bore the people’s sins into the wilderness.

The bronze serpent had no destructive venom whatever, but only the serpent’s form and image. So too Christ had no corruption of sin, but only the likeness of sinful flesh. His flesh also was bronze, because it always remained incorrupt: before the Passion, without the corruption of fault; after the Passion, without the corruption [Col. 0583C] of punishment. For this reason Job said: “Neither is my strength the strength of stone, nor is my flesh bronze” (Job 12 [citation as printed]). If the figure of Christ’s Passion could accomplish so much in the bronze serpent, how much will the reality accomplish in the blood poured out by the sufferer? Looking upon that serpent healed serpent-bites; looking upon this one heals the sins of those who confess and opens paradise to them, as was said to the thief who confessed simultaneously his own guilt and Christ’s innocence and power: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

Let the Apostle therefore say: “For you have been bought at a great price” (1 Cor. 6). It is as though he openly said: Let no one make little of the greatness of this price, because the more high the solicitude with which we were redeemed by the gentleness of Christ hanging [Col. 0583D] upon the gallows, the more exacting the judgment to which we shall be subject from his majesty now reigning in heaven.

Hence Augustine, in a homily “On the Incarnation of the Lord”: “From this we understand how grave God considers the causes of human crimes, for which he sent to earth not an angel, not an archangel, but God the Son of God.” And he adds: “The greatness of the remedy reveals how grave and hard the condition of sin is; the solicitude with which people are redeemed indicates how great will be the examination of evils by which they are condemned.”

The Apostle also proves this terribly by an argument from the lesser in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses; how much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered unclean the blood of the covenant in which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” Therefore let us not trample underfoot the Son of God, nor consider unclean the blood of the covenant in which we have been sanctified, nor insult the Spirit of grace by sinning deliberately and selling ourselves once again to the devil. Rather, let us glorify and bear God in our body.

God is to be glorified in three ways: in heart, mouth, and deed. In heart, by believing; in mouth, by confessing; in deed, by overcoming. Of the first kind of glorification the Lord said to Moses: “Because you did not believe me, so as to glorify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I shall give them” (Num. 20).

There is a twofold confession: of sin and of praise. Hence: “We will confess [Col. 0584B] to you, O God; we will confess to you” (Ps. 74). We shall confess our sins; we shall confess your benefits. For through both God is glorified. Thus Joshua said to Achan, who had committed theft from what was devoted to destruction: “My son, give glory to God, and confess what you have done” (Josh. 7). This concerns confession of sin. The angelic hymn, “Glory to God in the highest,” concerns confession of praise.

Of glorification by deed the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let them see your good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). And the Apostle: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10). Without this third glorification by deed, the other two are nothing; for faith without works is idle and dead, and praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner who blasphemes by deed. Of such praisers the Lord says to the Pharisees: “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied concerning you, saying: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15).

Similar is Jeremiah’s saying: “You are near to their mouth, but far from their reins” (Jer. 12)—those who delight in lust or money. Nothing is more shameful than one who praises God.

For what is it to praise God with one’s mouth as though one were celibate, while dragging one’s reins over the earth like a toad? What is it to proclaim the heavenly homeland in loud voices while gathering earthly money with all one’s strength? Clerics do the former with the outermost lips, but the latter with the deepest marrow. Therefore, lest anyone should suppose that glorification by voice—this being done in loud [Col. 0584D] speech, while the other is done with all one’s strength—were sufficient, the Apostle added: “And bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 5 [citation as printed]).

To glorify God, as we said above, concerns the keeping of the commandment; but to bear him concerns the discipline of the scourge. For to bear God is to receive his scourges and fatherly corrections not only patiently but willingly, and through them to correct one’s blameworthy conduct. For those who are scourged by the Lord and do not correct themselves do not receive his discipline. Hence the Lord complains of such people through Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your children; they did not receive discipline” (Jer. 2). Hence the Apostle’s saying to the Hebrews: “Persevere in discipline: God offers himself to you as to sons. For what son is there whom his father does not correct?” [Col. 0585A] and so forth (Heb. 12).

Then, showing by a most beautiful argument why we receive this discipline willingly, he adds: “We have had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” (ibid.). And a little later: “Every discipline at present seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; but afterward it yields to those trained by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness” (ibid.).

As Blessed Cyprian says [Note: [Col. 0585D] *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*], the twelfth degree of abuse is a people without discipline, which he himself describes thus: “Discipline is the ordered correction of conduct and the observance of the rules handed down by preceding elders.” And he adds: “The tunic of Christ’s body is the discipline of the Church. Whoever is outside it is alien to the body of Christ. Let us not tear it; rather, let us cast lots to determine whose it is. Let us not relax anything of Christ’s commandments; rather, let each person remain in that state in which he was called.”

Christ’s tunic is most aptly called the discipline of the Church; for Christ was always clothed in the tunic of discipline, and, so to speak, wholly wrapped in it. Hence he is called a boy and servant of the Lord. For boys and servants are always under discipline. Thus St Benedict commands that boys be kept under supervision and discipline until they reach the age of understanding. And of a servant it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Fodder and a rod and a burden for an ass; bread and discipline and work for a servant” (Ecclus. 33). But of the Lord it is written: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen: [Col. 0585C] I have placed my Spirit upon him” (Isa. 42). Likewise: “You are my servant, because in you I shall be glorified” (ibid.). Likewise: “It is too little that you should be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob,” etc. (Isa. 49).

For an ill-disposed servant there are torture and shackles. No servant was better, more well-disposed, or more obedient than this one; yet, questioned under insult and torment, he was condemned beyond all servants to a death most shameful and unjust. “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is fitting shall receive many blows.” This servant did everything fitting; he did nothing wrongly, nothing unworthy; yet no one else received so many blows. For he was beaten not only, like a servant, under interrogation, but also—as the common saying has it—like an ass at a bridge. Although he most willingly crossed that bridge, namely the [Col. 0585D] narrow passage of death, he did so step by step, because his flesh, passible and weak by nature, shrank from death; but his ready spirit most wisely led it, like a very gentle ass, and one heavily laden with the burden of our sins, across the bridge at measured steps. From this slowness—that is, this deliberateness—it came about that this ass was more grievously burdened in his body, so that we might be better relieved of our burden.

The fodder of this ass, or the bread of this servant, was obedience. Hence: “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me, and to complete his work” (John 4). The rod of discipline was patience. Hence: “The chastisement of our peace was upon [Col. 0586A] him, and by his bruise we are healed” (Isa. 51 [apparently Isa. 53]). His burden and work were the bearing of our iniquities; hence: “God laid upon him the iniquities of us all” (Isa. 53).

Finally, this is why today the King of powers, the King of glory, drawing near to the place of his Passion, whose time was approaching, deigned to come riding upon an ass: showing that by this gentleness he would display to his servants not so much the severity of a lord as the service and usefulness of a domestic beast of burden. For he is that Samaritan who, taking pity on the man wounded by robbers, bound up his wounds by pouring in wine and oil, placed him upon his own beast, and brought him to an inn (Luke 10). The ass is an exceedingly brutish beast; and therefore the most humble of men, coming to our aid [Col. 0586B] against the King of the proud, chose to ride this kind of animal, intending to overthrow him by gentleness and obedience, by the weakness of the flesh and the folly of the cross. Its weakness and folly are wiser and stronger not only than human beings but than all demons as well.

Therefore our servant, our ass, came to offer his back to the scourges, to undergo discipline for us. He received seven disciplines for us: in the scourges; in the blows while his face was veiled; in the spittings; in the thorns; in the nails; in the piercing of his side; and in the taste of gall and vinegar, when he said: “It is finished” (John 19)—that is, what had been foretold concerning the endurance of my sufferings is completed; the bodily disciplines imposed upon me for my brothers [Col. 0586C] are completed.

Thus Christ, as a beast of burden, bore our yoke and our burden, himself first fulfilling the command which he gave through his Apostle: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 5). What great thing, then, is it if we bear Christ in our body, when he first bore us in his own? Yet he counts it a great thing if we deign to bear him as rider, like beasts under a yoke, him whom we first had as yoked beneath us—that is, as the bearer of our yoke and burden. Our yoke is penal mortality and the necessity of dying.

Hence: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their return to the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). Our burden is our [Col. 0586D] iniquity; hence: “My iniquities, like a heavy burden, have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37). Christ bore both: made mortal for us, and dead for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God; wounded for our sins and crushed for our crimes. Therefore he wishes us also to bear his yoke and burden. “Take,” he says, “my yoke upon yourselves, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). “Take my yoke,” he says, “as I bore yours; bear my burden, as I bore yours. Your yoke was most harsh, your burden most heavy. [Col. 0587A] Indeed, beneath your yoke and burden I sweated blood with my whole body, endured the cross, poured out blood, made my flesh bloody, and breathed out my soul. But my yoke,” he says, “is sweet and my burden light.”

My yoke is my law; my burden is my cross; my law is love. A yoke is so called from joining; a law from binding; love is, as it were, the binding of two. For every love exists between at least two. Charity binds not only person to person and angel to angel, but also God to angel and human being, and angel and human being to God. It bound God to humanity through the mystery of the Incarnation; it binds humanity to God through the sacrament of true faith and the sweet bond of cheerful obedience. For whatever cheerfulness does is sweet. Hence Jerome: “Nothing is hard for one who loves; no labour is difficult for one who desires.” Therefore charity is called by the angel “the bond of perfection,” because it binds perfectly—that is, strongly and sweetly. Other bonds, the stronger they are, the less sweet they are; the sweeter they are, the less strong. Iron binds strongly but not sweetly; thread sweetly but not strongly. But the more strongly charity binds, the more sweetly it binds; and the more sweetly, the more strongly. Therefore it is the bond of perfection, because it binds most perfectly—that is, most strongly and most sweetly.

“Who,” he says, “shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8). As though he said: no one. “I am certain that neither death nor life,” etc., “nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God” (ibid.). Behold the inseparable strength of the bond; behold also its incomparable delight. “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth besides you? [Col. 0587C] It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72): good beyond every desirable good, since he is desirable as the highest good.

The law of charity is rightly called a yoke and a bond, because it binds and joins the created spirit to its Creator. It is also called a burden and a cross, because it presses and afflicts rebellious flesh, and subjects and yokes it to its spirit. Yet it does all this gently and sweetly, like a light burden and a sweet cross, being joined throughout by the ointment of holy liquid—that is, the rosy blood of Christ, which flowed forth in most abundant streams through all the dimensions of the cross. The cross anointed by the holy blood poured from the Lamb’s body cannot be harsh or heavy to bear. At the dedication of churches, crosses are anointed with chrism, [Col. 0587D] because the Spirit helps our weakness, so that we may suffer even the greatest torments for Christ with joy. What is joy or glorying in tribulation but an anointing upon the cross? Consider the twelve crosses anointed with chrism. “The apostles went away rejoicing,” etc. (Acts 5).

The breadth of this cross is generosity in giving and readiness in forgiving: that one give oneself to everyone who asks and forgive every injury to the penitent. With these two arms Christ embraces us, and desires to be embraced by us. “For God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. How shall he not also with him have given us all things?” Behold generosity in giving. Of readiness in forgiving there is this: “Forgiving yourselves, as the Lord also forgave you” (Col. 3). “Come to me, all who labour and are [Col. 0588A] burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matt. 11). He draws everyone; he repels no one. He forgives every injury; he reserves nothing for vengeance. Therefore he cries to us: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and you shall be forgiven. For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6).

The length of the cross is long-suffering expectation, bearing all things and enduring all things. For charity bears all that is cruelly inflicted; it endures all that is faithfully promised. Hence: “The patient person shall endure until the end, and afterward there is a return of joy” (Ecclus. 1). “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end. Behold, we call blessed those who endured. Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Jas. 5). The height of this cross is heavenly desire, raising our hearts upward; its depth is chaste fear, penetrating [Col. 0588B] our hearts and always preserving us in humility.

Therefore we shall bear God in our body if we fulfil that apostolic command: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 5). May he deign to grant this to us—Jesus Christ our Lord, who, first fulfilling this law, deigned to bear our burdens. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON EASTER

“Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre: I shall awake at dawn” (Ps. 51, 107).

Let us therefore at last arise, as Scripture exhorts us and says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep; for our salvation is nearer now than when we believed” (Rom. 13). Truly it is nearer: for now the way has been shown us, the door opened, the table prepared, and the voice of the turtledove heard. The way has been shown to pilgrims; the door opened to beggars; the table prepared for the hungry; the voice of the turtledove made known to friends. The way of discipline, or obedience, has been shown; the door of mercy, or pardon, opened; the table of Wisdom, who feasts and invites to the feast, prepared; the voice of the turtledove heard, that we may rejoice.

The way of three days is the profession of the order, in which we profess three things: stability in one place, conversion—that is, amendment of conduct—and obedience according to the Rule. Stability in one place is not to move from one’s place without the superior’s command; for one who changes place at command does not lose stability, because he preserves obedience. Conversion of conduct is the overthrow of vices and the planting of virtues. Obedience according to the Rule is not slow, not timid, not murmuring, not lukewarm, but swift, tranquil, cheerful, and fervent; and this is especially in hard and contrary matters that do not please the flesh. For in pleasant matters, which contain nothing in themselves of penitential bitterness, obedience should be slow and lukewarm if the matter itself can be done without sin.

But if it cannot be carried out without sin, one must obey God rather than human beings. For a person owes another person nothing except with innocence preserved. This, then, is the way: walk in it—a way narrow and steep at its beginning, but after its beginnings broad and spacious, easy and level; yet in both respects beautiful and [Col. 0589A] straight (Isa. 30). For, as our lawgiver says [Note: Col. 0589D, St Benedict, Prologue to the Rule], “the way of life must be begun only through a narrow entrance”; but afterward, when the heart has been enlarged, one runs with ineffable sweetness, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118).

Moreover, a narrow way does not carry an animal grown excessively fat; a steep one does not advance a traveller weighed down with baggage; a beautiful way admits nothing defiled; a straight one does not allow a wanderer to pass through. A fat horse soon kicks back; a burdened traveller, soon wearied by the toil of the journey, stops. An unclean person pollutes whatever he touches and, like a diseased sheep, infects the whole flock; but the erring person never agrees with reason. Gluttons grow fat, the greedy are burdened, the lustful are defiled, wanderers go astray; and all heretics and those of unstable mind wander as errants. This way was shown us in the itinerary of Jesus Christ in two ways, by word and example.

The narrow way was shown to us by word when he said: “See to it that your hearts are not weighed down with revelry and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). It was shown by example when he fasted forty days and forty nights, and when his disciples were so pressed by hunger that, walking through the fields, they plucked ears of grain and ate them, plucked and rubbed in their hands as they went. The steep way was shown to us by word when he said: “If anyone does not renounce all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14); and again: “If anyone does not carry his cross daily and follow me, he is not my disciple” (ibid.). Behold, we are commanded to bear the cross alone, and forbidden to possess anything else.

A demon was once asked, speaking through a possessed man, what it thought of a monk who possessed property. It answered: “The monk who has one obol is not worth one obol.” A certain philosopher says, “No one swims out with baggage.” But I say that still more certainly no one flies with baggage. All money, every earthly possession, whatever is possessed beyond food and clothing—of which we are commanded to be content—is a burden.

The beautiful way was shown to us through the Word when incarnate Wisdom of God gave the world the counsel of perpetual virginity, the Lord saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God; let the one who can accept it accept it” (Matt. 19); and the chief Apostle: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7). This same way was shown us by Christ when the Son of God himself deigned to be born of a Virgin, and, dying upon the cross, to entrust his beloved mother, a Virgin, to his beloved virgin disciple. This beauty of the way suffers nothing unclean. Therefore, if under the law of Moses every unclean person is cast out of the holy camp, how rightly, under the severity of our Fathers, is every impurity commanded to be bodily removed from the assembly of saints—not only in deed, but even in any sign or word.

The straight way was shown to us by word when it was said: “These things have been written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that, believing, you may have life in his name” (John 20). It was shown us by example when he who had thus lived and thus taught was lifted up before his disciples’ eyes, and a cloud received him from their sight. This, then, is the way: walk in it. “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118). Here, under the name “stain,” every impediment is included: namely, fatness and burden, impurity and error. “Blessed,” he says, “are the undefiled in the way.” He explained which way he meant when he added: “Who walk in the law of the Lord.” Therefore those undefiled in the way are those who neither grow fat [Col. 0590B] through gluttony, nor are burdened through greed, nor defiled through lust, nor wander as errants through heresy.

As the way has been shown to us, so the door has been opened to us. To whom has it been opened? To the thief, the denier, the sinful woman, the murderer, the apostate, the woman subject to seven demons—but to the confessing thief, the apostate weeping in love, and the sinful woman loving greatly. In the thief confession is commended; in Peter contrition; in the sinful woman a loving satisfaction, or love that makes satisfaction. I have deliberately numbered these three greatest sinners most prominently, so that no sinner, however great, may despair that the door of mercy will be opened to him.

The table too has been prepared for us, namely the most holy altar, at which we may eat the Paschal lamb. But it must be eaten thus: “You shall gird your loins, have shoes upon your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste. For it is the Phase”—that is, “the passing-over”—“of the Lord” (Exod. 12). “You shall devour its head with its feet and entrails.” In girded loins is chastisement of the flesh; in shod feet, a desire for death, or the fortification of our affections; in staffs held in the hands, rectitude of action, or at least continual meditation on eternal judgment. That judgment is like a staff because it rules and strikes, supports and casts down. In both respects the staff is straight, because to each person what is right shall be rendered. The head of this lamb is the sublimity of divine power; the feet, the humility of his human dispensation; the entrails, the bowels of compassion in both natures. All these [Col. 0590D] must be devoured—that is, firmly believed, simply adored, and devoutly honoured from the heart.

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land,” namely this: “Awake, my glory,” etc. The voice of the turtledove is the voice of the Father, like that of one mourning and speaking to his equal—that is, to his coequal Son: “My Son, my glory, you have fallen into dishonour: arise into honour. My Son, my psaltery—that is, sounding my praise from above—you have fallen into shame: arise into glory. My Son, my lyre—that is, sounding my praise from below—you have fallen into suffering and death: arise into impassible immortality. Young lion of Judah, you have gone up for prey, [Col. 0591A] my Son: who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49). Which of the angels or archangels? Not Michael, not Gabriel, not Raphael, nor any other. Yet he could raise himself at the Father’s command and word: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre”; while he himself answered: “I shall awake at dawn.” Therefore he spoke and acted, because for him to speak is to act.

Behold, he has risen; and he is still not only with the Father but also with us, his brothers, and he will be with us all days until the consummation of the age. These words of the Father can also be understood not only of his only-begotten Son but also of his last-born son. For he has three sons: one only-begotten, another first-born, and a third last-born. The only-begotten is our Lord Jesus Christ; the first-born is the Israelite people in the elect Fathers; the last-born is the Christian people. Therefore he speaks to us, saying: “O my Son, Christian people, my glory through the free remission of sins; my psaltery, by proclaiming my praise; my lyre, by confessing your iniquity.” “All,” says the Apostle, “have sinned and need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3).

Or: “my glory,” by living wisely, because “a wise son is the glory of his father”; “my psaltery,” by living harmoniously, for they hold the highest peace; “my lyre,” by acting courageously and enduring patiently. Or: “my glory,” through redemption; “my psaltery,” through love; “my lyre,” through the mortification of the flesh. For we have been redeemed for his glory and praise. We play the ten-stringed psaltery when we love our neighbour. For “the whole law is fulfilled in this saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Rom. 13). Thus the one-stringed instrument of love is worth the ten-stringed instrument of the law. We play the lyre when we mortify the flesh.

“Awake”—that is, rise from earth unto heaven: seeking the things above, setting your mind on the things above. The Christian answers: “I shall awake at dawn”—that is, as soon as the sun of righteousness has risen for me and breathed upon my mind with the rays of his grace: so that he may suspend me from the earth, draw me after himself, draw me onward to heaven, and finally receive me to himself. Thus he promised his disciples, saying: “I shall come to you and receive you to myself, so that where [Col. 0591D] I am, you also may be” (John 14). May he deign to grant this to us all—he who today, the new author of resurrection, rose from the dead. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD, I

“In the shelter of your wings I shall rejoice” (Ps. 62).

Good Jesus, who protect me beneath the shadow of your wings, who shade me with your shoulders, who draw me in the fragrance of your ointments, who receive me with hands outstretched and in your arms: today you teach me to fly loftily after you into heaven, you who first taught me humbly to walk after you on earth. “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child” (1 Cor. 13); but now, growing through the advance of wisdom, age, and grace, [Col. 0592A] I speak and hear wisdom among the perfect.

Lord, you instructed us in both: then as a hen, now as an eagle. Then, a little one among little ones, you spoke of little ones: “Let the little children come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10). You set a child—yourself—in the midst; and thus you came to seek what had been lost, so solicitous for me. The devil sought me, found me, and ensnared me. Christ sought me, found me, and helped me. The devil sought me through a serpent—not the devil, but unknowingly filled with the devil—and found me in the light and deceived me. God sought me through an angel—not God, but God’s good messenger—and found me in the shadow, but did not bring me back.

Afterward God sought me through a man, not God but a mere human being, though a great prophet—namely Moses—and [Col. 0592B] found me labouring in mud and brick: serving the devil through soft, effeminate luxury and hard, obstinate malice. He found me and led me out, but did not bring me to rest. At last God sought me through the God-man, that is, Jesus Christ; he found me, led me, and brought me into the mountain of his sanctification.

But he led me as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings and warms them; he sought me by scratching and overturning the house and turning over all its bedding in sickness—like an abbot searching the beds of monks, not as they already were, but as they ought to be, on account of some special task, so that what was sought might be found. Thus, bent over her chicks, the hen taught us to live soberly, justly, and devoutly upon earth under her wings, which are the example of life and the word of teaching, both humble. As a little one he associated with little ones; as a little one he spoke with little ones, teaching earthly things—that is, the use of sacraments to be practised only on earth—not yet setting before those to whom he said, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16), the sublime fruit of the earth to be received in heaven.

Thus in dust he sought dust, and in dust a pearl: dust, which appeared; a pearl, which was hidden. At last he whom he sought found him “in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude”: that is, in corrupt flesh, subject to the unavoidable necessity of death, and in the corruption of the inward senses. Truly it was a vast solitude, in which the human being alone was laid waste: alone without truth, without good, without himself, without God; knowing neither whence he came nor where he went, ignorant alike of his beginning and his end. Hence his counsel was made foolish, his judgment reprobate or falsified, and his desire corrupted. Counsel discerns good and evil, expedient and inexpedient; judgment, the just and unjust, true and false, as light and darkness; desire, pleasant and sad things, bitter and sweet. Thus in himself he turned back the prophetic threefold woe: “Woe to those who call evil good,” etc. (Isa. 5).

Thus, ignorant of himself, he went after the flock of his companions, attending to present things rather than extending himself toward those to come; putting the best wine first, not prudently measuring the outcome of things, because according as one’s end is good or greater, so the thing itself is good or evil. In these things God, who is man, found man who is not God; and, in the manner of a hen, he led him around, taught him, and guarded him as the pupil of his eye. He led him around, purifying nature on every side, cutting off and circumcising what is superfluous, as though it were merely adjectival; going about and sacrificing the vices of the flesh, and effacing the footsteps of the ungodly who walk round about. For Wisdom encompasses not only the earth but also the circuit of heaven. He led him around, taught him to be led around, and guarded the flesh as a hen and the mind as an eagle.

But fire goes before him and sets his enemies aflame round about: namely, the fire of fear, which always causes the mind to think of God’s watchfulness. Charity casts this fear outside for safekeeping, so that charity itself may rest securely within upon the bed with [Col. 0593B] its Solomon. In this manner he led him around through fear, taught him through hope, and guarded him through faith. He teaches that death is not to be feared, but rather that through it one must pass to life, so that the just person may rejoice exceedingly when he finds the grave, because when he thinks himself consumed, he shall arise like the morning star. How sweet a sleep, when the Lord’s inheritance is transferred in royal fashion from chariot to chariot, from beneath a hen’s wings onto an eagle’s shoulders! He shall go forth from the battle of death, wounded by pain and destined to die even to death itself, and shall return into his kingdom, according to the words: “You shall go out in joy and be led forth in peace” (Isa. 55).

In this hope God teaches the human being knowledge, whom he finally guards through faith as the pupil of his eye. Without faith, virtues have eyes but have no pupil: [Col. 0593C] they do not know to what they should direct intention, devotion, or prayer; but they run as though uncertain and fight as though striking the air. Idols have eyes but do not see, because they have no pupil. Thus God through faith guards and directs counsels, judgments, and desires, lest they stray and go beyond good and truth, both of which are delightful.

Thus—yes, thus—our hen turned for her chicks the desert land, in which the Apostle found not good but a land overgrown with thorns and briars, into a garden of delights, according to the words: “That desolate land has become like a garden of delight” (Ezek. 36). He turned the place of horror into a harbour of salvation, where Christ stands upon the shore. Then your death shall be precious, and “to die is gain” (Phil. 1), [Col. 0593D] when holy angels receive you as you return from the sea. Having first rejoiced at your conversion, they will lay out before the Lord the rare and most precious goods from your hand, acquired amid the waves; they will establish them in the sight of him whose money you have multiplied, and because of a few things he will set you over many.

This ship is regular discipline. Thus the Lord, in humility, led us around, taught us, and guarded us, as though saying: “I have spoken earthly things to you as to little children; henceforth I shall speak heavenly things to you, and you shall believe and say: ‘Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus’” (2 Cor. 5). Hence it follows: “Like an eagle provoking her young to fly and hovering over you” (Deut. 31 [apparently Deut. 32]). This eagle has children, concerning whom it is said: “The eye that mocks its father and despises [Col. 0594A] its mother’s childbirth, let ravens of the torrent pluck it out, and let the young of the eagle eat it” (Prov. 30).

This eye is self-will, perverse and obstinate against God; for it neither fears God nor respects man. Through it custom enters and goes out, bewitching and making foolish others through it, and it through others. It mocks its father, despising the humble and laborious life of Christ and the precious death of the saints; and it despises the childbirth of the Church, which has sorrow when she gives birth. Let ravens of the torrents—that is, saints who mortify their bodies and drink from the torrent in the way with Christ, bearing the marks of Jesus in their bodies—pluck it out and drive it from its place, from its purpose. Such ravens feed Elijah at the torrent with bread and flesh [Col. 0594B] (3 Kings 17): that is, with devotion of heart and mortification of flesh, in the morning and evening, at the beginning and end of conversion.

The young of the eagle are the souls of the saints, whom the Sun of righteousness blackens outwardly but illumines and adorns inwardly. Thus the righteous correct sinners by the example of authority and pierce them with the zeal of charity. Today Christ the eagle provokes these his children to fly, so that they may direct their attention where he is going. He hovers over them—indeed, over the cherubim and the wings of the winds, beyond all the merits of saints and all orders of angels—far surpassing their life, glory, and knowledge. It belongs to a prelate to fly above his young, surpassing all in merit as in rank. He hovers alongside them if his life is equal to that of his subjects; below them if his life is inferior to theirs; above them if it is greater.

Christ spreads his wings, which are forgiveness, releasing us from lower things, and sending us onward to strive toward higher things. In the shelter of these wings we must rejoice, as did the one who said: “My soul has clung after you” (Ps. 62). Let the greedy, covetous, and earthly person—indeed, earth and dust—cling to his own dust, that is, to his earthly riches, whose soul has been humbled in the dust. For what are earthly riches but dust: light, unstable, uncertain? “Command,” he says, “the rich of this age not to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6). Let the carnal and lustful person cling to his harlot—indeed, to his dung. “For every woman who is a harlot shall be trodden under foot like dung [Col. 0594D] in the way.”

Whoever, therefore, clings to a harlot becomes not only one body with her, but one dung. Let the sensual and slothful person say: “My soul has clung to the pavement” (Ps. 118), which is hardness and insensibility, a disgust with good; as the following words explain: “My soul has slumbered from weariness” (ibid.). But not so the spiritual person, who says: “My soul has clung after you with the glue of holy love. It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72). “Who shall separate me from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8). “Your right hand has received me” (Ps. 17).

The hand of Christ is Christ’s operation; his left hand is the operation of his humility, raising my head, which I could by no means raise without it, even if I were just. O beautiful passage by the left hand: dishonour that glorifies, poverty that enriches, pain that gives joy, folly that makes wise, weakness that strengthens, thirst that intoxicates, misery that makes blessed, and finally death itself, enlivening and giving life to souls! This left hand raises us from this captivity to the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For it sends roots downward and bears fruit upward. The left hand raises to the right; his right hand embraces us, receiving us into grace and glory.

This right hand is the operation of the Trinity, which receives us in three ways, according to the words: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength,” delivering me; “the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. 117), enlightening, strengthening, and assisting me to understand and accomplish lofty things; “the right hand of the Lord has wrought strength,” making me blessed. It delivered from Egypt, gave light on holy Sinai, and glorified in the kingdom.

The first operation of power receives us in the sacrament of holiness; then the operation of wisdom in the instruction of truth; finally the operation of kindness and goodwill in the experience of blessedness. From this third reception none can be snatched from God’s hand; for even the elect, if that were possible, can be torn away from the first two. For even after the sacrament, holy persons are sometimes profaned; and after instruction, wise persons are sometimes made foolish, according to the words: “If Jeconiah, son of Joakim king of Judah, were a signet on my right hand, I would tear him from there” (Jer. 12 [apparently Jer. 22]). This means: if one is righteous in the operation of the sacrament and of divine instruction, like a seal distinguishing and shaping others [Col. 0595C] by example and word, and departs from righteousness and commits iniquity, I shall tear him away from there; for neither the washing of baptism nor the word of faith will profit him.

But in the inheritance of the Lord all things are fixed (Ezek. 48), and the one who dwells in that Jerusalem called *Adonai shammah*, “the Lord is there,” shall not be moved for ever. Jesus himself is my God and my salvation; I shall not be moved any more. Thus the Lord Jesus changed earth into a garden of delight, the place of horror into a harbour of salvation, and the waste of solitude into a city of habitation. That fortified city is power and sanctification. Receive me, Lord Jesus, after this merit and grace, into that joy of your power, which shall be a sufficient reward for yours and fullness of joy for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD, II

Delivered at Toulouse to student clerics in the church of St James.

[Col. 0595D]

“Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and clean of heart” (Ps. 23).

Since I have been compelled to make this sermon, exposed to so just a criticism and not shaped by proper prior meditation, there comes to mind that poetic saying:

> Criticize the poem which neither  
> Many a day nor many an erasure has restrained,  
> And which has not been perfected by ten corrections to the fingernail.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 292)

Quintilian agrees with this judgment in his book of *Oratorical Constitutions* [*Institutio oratoria*], saying: “Let the style only be slower, so long as it is careful. For nature has not willed that anything great should be accomplished quickly, and has set difficulty before every great work.”

But I often incur this danger through the rash judgment of the populace, which, as Sallust says of Fortune, celebrates and obscures all things more according to whim than according to truth; and causes someone to have the reputation of being alive when he is dead, or of discoursing elegantly upon every subject when he stammers. Hence your praiseworthy devotion hastens to me as though toward a pleasant voice and the poem of the friendly *Thebaid*, whose author was Statius, surnamed Surculus, a native of this city. There, as Jerome asserts, he pleased the Romans so greatly by the sweetness of his recitation that, as the satirist testifies, [Col. 0596B] he broke the benches of his listeners.

Yet we read that many other authors, worthy of distinguished praise, survived in obscurity so far as recognition was concerned and were almost universally unknown, as though they had never been born. So slight, frivolous, and accidental is pleasing human beings that, as that eminent orator says, even virtues themselves win favour in some persons, while in others the vices themselves delight.

Woe, then, to human favour born of rash judgment: when, without testing the strength of a person’s powers, it often lays a most grievous burden upon weak shoulders, and demands that a task of great exertion and much labour be completed by the infirm and in a short time. But let this lesson now speak: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” etc.

[Col. 0596C] “It is pleasant to climb lofty heights; it is shameful to descend from heights,” says one man (Horace); and another:

“There is one sole honour about which men are anxious.”

For every rational spirit, as though naturally striving upward and desiring honour, sufficiently indicates both the nobility of its origin and the dignity of its former estate. Of the first, the poet Aratus says:

“For we too are his offspring.”

Of the second, the Psalmist says: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand” (Ps. XLIX [49]). Hence man finds no rest in a lowly earthly place, because he draws his beginning from on high, that is, from the heavenly region.
