For his Maker is in heaven, according to the words: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI). Therefore he must return thither, that there he may find true rest. Hence Micah: “Arise and depart, for you have no rest here” (Mic. II). And the Apostle: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is,” etc. (Col. III).

Certainly, whatever is in God is on high; for nothing is higher than God. Therefore our faith, salvation, peace, and rest are on high. Hence, when the Hebrew children came to meet the Saviour, they asked to be saved “in the highest,” knowing that there, and there alone, are true and full rest for souls, health for bodies, peace for both, and the place and city of all who are to be saved. Thus Christ, when about to ascend into heaven, promised his disciples, saying: “I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I shall come again to [Col. 0597A] you and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV).

Therefore every person is invited to this assumption, or to the preparation for this assumption, when it is said: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” etc. “He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart” (Ps. XXIII [24]). Let the children of Adam who desire ascent hear: hunters after glory, fowlers after power, lovers of heights. Let them hear and rejoice that they are not merely not forbidden to ascend, but are now rather summoned to ascend, according to Ambrose:

> Now, our deeds being summoned forth,  
> It befits us to await Christ,  
> And to live such a life  
> As can climb the heavens.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Hymn for the Ascension.]

And lest anyone perhaps should complain that the way to heaven is either wholly impossible for man or too arduous: behold, the climber of heaven—being the way, the truth, and the life—today plainly showed himself to be the way to heaven by the example of innocence, the truth of the way by the word of teaching, and the life of truth by the joyful spectacle of his Ascension. Woe to those who, summoned by example, do not come; summoned by the word, do not listen; summoned by miracle, do not hasten. For no excuse is left to one who remains behind, when so great a reward for innocence is displayed.

Certainly innocence ought to have been preserved by us even if no reward for innocence were hoped for and no punishment for wickedness feared. It was enough that the servant should act because the lord commanded—especially such a Lord, whose nature is goodness, whose will is [Col. 0597C] power, and whose work is mercy. But now, since so great a weight of glory is promised to the innocent and so great a burden of misery is laid up for the guilty—so that the former surpasses every desire and the latter exceeds every fear—most justly indeed, but most strictly, will anyone who has not ascended be convicted concerning sin, justice, and judgment: concerning the sin he committed, by not preserving innocence; concerning the justice he omitted, by not desiring the reward of justice; concerning the judgment he did not fear, though not ignorant of the devil’s condemnation.

He will come indeed, he will come: the teacher of innocence, the avenger of guilt. He will come to judgment as he went into heaven: as desirable on the right hand as he will be intolerable on the left; that is, he will render ineffable rewards to the innocent and [Col. 0597D] torments to the guilty—those ascending to the palaces of heaven, these plunging into Tartarus.

But someone says: “Who can ascend into heaven?” Hear who: “He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.” Heaven is called the mountain of the Lord because “no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III): understand, whole and entire—that is, head together with body. For head and body are one Christ. Therefore heaven is called the mountain of the Lord, either because of dwelling there, according to the words: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in heaven” (Ps. CXXII [123]); or because of ascent, according to the words: “He built his ascent in heaven: the Lord is his name” [Col. 0598A] (Amos IX).

Christ dwelt in heaven before he ascended into heaven, because he was first God dwelling in heaven before he was man raising himself from earth to heaven. But for us, ascent precedes dwelling, which is called standing in a place. The Prophet first asks concerning ascent and afterwards concerning standing, saying: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” He asks this as though standing and praying in the sanctuary of his heart. And an answer is given him from the inner courts of the temple, and as if from the horns of the altar this voice is sent forth to him: “He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.”

Innocence is sometimes understood narrowly and sometimes broadly. Narrowly, as in Seneca: “Innocence,” he says, [Col. 0598B] “is not a perfect virtue, but abstinence from what belongs to another.” Likewise Jerome, on the passage, “Thou wilt not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence” (Ps. LXXXIII [84]), says: “In the Hebrew, ‘in perfection’ is better; for innocence is not a perfect virtue.” Innocence is also sometimes used for simplicity, as in Solomon’s Proverbs: “The simple man believes every word; the prudent man considers his steps” (Prov. XIV). But innocence is understood broadly when it denotes the perfection of justice, as in Augustine [Note: [Col. 0597D] Hymn for the Ascension.] on the passage, “I walked in the innocence of my heart”: “Possess innocence,” he says, “and you have perfected justice.”

This innocence has two parts: not to make a person miserable, and not to abandon one who is miserable. We make someone miserable by word, deed, or consent alone. By word, in three ways: by detraction, flattery, or insult. You detract in three ways: as an originator, as a reporter, or as a listener not unwilling to hear. For if there is no one to hear, there is no one to speak. As it is the detractor’s part to diminish good things and enlarge evil ones, so the flatterer does the contrary. Thus in Terence, when Thraso asks:

> “Does Thais really give me great thanks?”

Gnatho answers:

> “Enormous ones.”  
> (Terence, *Eunuchus*, III.1.1.)

“It would have been enough,” says Cicero, “to have said ‘great’; but it is the flatterer’s way always to enlarge what the man whom he flatters wishes to hear.”

Of this the Satirist says:

> [Col. 0598D] What of the most ingenious race of flatterers, who praises  
> The speech of an uneducated man, the face of an ugly friend,  
> And matches the long neck of the weakling to the shoulders  
> Of Hercules holding Antaeus far from the earth?  
> (Juvenal, III.89.)

The insult of speech is twofold: against God, blasphemy; against one’s neighbour, anger. Blasphemy against God is twofold: that of heretical opinion or that of unlawful swearing. An oath is unlawful whenever there is no sufficient cause—for example, the clearing of an accusation, covenants of peace, or the persuasion of virtue. An insult against one’s neighbour occurs in two ways: by an expression without meaning, such as *raca*; or by one with meaning, such as “fool.”

Likewise, [Col. 0599A] we make either ourselves or others miserable both by speaking falsehood and by withholding truth. A lie, broadly understood, is a false signification; strictly understood, it is false signification with the intention of deceiving. It is called signification not only of the voice, but also of writing or gesture. To lie, broadly understood, is to say what is false; strictly and properly, it is to go against one’s mind. It is defined thus: to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind, whether that thing be true or false. Therefore everyone who utters a lie lies, but the converse does not hold.

There are three kinds of lying. The first is a lie of kindness or utility, made for a neighbour’s sake, and it is venial. The second is a jesting lie, likewise venial unless it is made habitual. The third is a lie of deception, and that is a crime. Augustine [Note: [Col. 0599D] Augustine, *On Lying*.] describes eight kinds of lies. The first [Col. 0599B] concerns religion, as in the articles of faith. The second is injurious: it benefits no one and harms someone. The third is likewise injurious in kind: it benefits one person and harms another. The fourth is one of desire, namely the mere will to lie. The fifth is flattery, made from the desire to please by pleasant speech. The remaining three concern utility alone, but differ: the sixth is told to avoid loss of money; the seventh, to avoid harm to a person; the eighth, to avoid the loss of chastity. Among these eight kinds, one sins less in proportion as one is farther removed from the first.

Truth is twofold: there is the truth of a thing and the truth of a statement (*veritas dicti*). The truth of a thing is considered in the adherence of predicate to subject; the truth of a statement, in the steadfastness [Col. 0599C] of the speaker. From the truth or falsity of a thing one is called true or false; from the truth of a statement one is called truthful or deceptive. Accordingly, if the terms are rearranged, someone can be at once true and truthful, and then both are from God; false and deceptive, and then both are from man; truthful and false; deceptive and true—and then one quality is from God, the other from man.

We also make a person miserable by deed in two ways: by bodily injury or by loss of property. Each is committed in two ways: by one’s own hand or by that of another; as when David killed Uriah by the sword of the sons of Ammon. Again, each of these is carried out in two ways: either by a direct act or indirectly, as if sinning “with a long hand.” Directly, when we ourselves do it, or urge that it be done. [Col. 0599D] Indirectly, in two ways: causally or by occasion. Causally, when one person is punished for another’s sin, as often happens either through a judge’s ignorance or through the anger of the injured party seeking vengeance. In this case, I think that the person who first sinned is bound to intervene, in order to free the innocent person by offering his own body, saying with Virgil:

> “Me, me—for I am here, the one who did it—turn the sword against me . . .”  
> (*Aeneid* IX.427.)

Thus David did when the angel was striking the people for the sin which he himself had committed, saying: “I am he who has sinned; turn, I beseech thee, thy sword [Col. 0600A] against me,” etc. (II Kings XXIV).

We make someone miserable by occasion when we say or do something from which another takes an occasion to sin, although we did not say or do it for this purpose. Such was the case when David received from Abimelech the loaves of offering and Goliath’s sword in the presence of Doeg the Edomite. Therefore he said to Abimelech’s son, who had fled to him: “I am guilty concerning all the lives of thy father’s house” (I Kings XXII). Such also was the case when, in the presence of his three mightiest men, he desired water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which could not be brought without danger. When it was brought, reproaching himself for such a saying, he would not drink it but poured it out as a libation to the Lord, saying: “Far be it from me that I should drink the blood of these men” (II Kings XXIII). [Col. 0600B] Yet this occasion is more immediate than the former and makes one more guilty.

We likewise make a person miserable by consent alone in two ways: either expressly by words or by any sign that it be done—and this consent is very immediate and equivalent to the deed, deserving equal punishment—or silently and remotely: when we do not give counsel, but nevertheless wish it to be done; or rejoice if it is done; or at least do not grieve. Or silently and more remotely: when we grieve at the deed but do not prevent its being done, although we could prevent it. For one who does not resist when able to resist consents.

Likewise, we abandon the miserable person in the six works of mercy which the Lord enumerates in the Gospel, saying: [Col. 0600C] “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. (Matt. XXV); and in the seventh, namely burial of the dead, of which we read in Tobit and Ecclesiasticus: “Do not withhold kindness from the dead” (Ecclus. VII)—that is, the kindness of burial. Although the loss of a tomb is easily borne, and nature buries those left behind, and the awareness of such a loss cannot reach the dead person, yet, so far as lies in us, we leave him miserable if we leave him unburied. Yet we leave ourselves more miserable, since we do not fulfil a work of mercy.

Likewise, we abandon the miserable person by omitting not only bodily alms but also spiritual ones, which are much greater than bodily alms and are neglected more dangerously and more destructively: for example, when we do not instruct one who errs or rebuke one who sins. But since every act of mercy ought to begin with ourselves, according to the saying: “Have mercy on thy soul, pleasing God,” [Col. 0600D] we abandon ourselves most dangerously in misery whenever we do not immediately repent of sin. For every sin not immediately washed away by repentance draws by its own weight toward another sin.

Behold how many and how great are the ways in which innocence is lost: while not only one’s own or another’s misery is brought about, but even merely abandoned and not relieved. Therefore the greatest effort is necessary, and much care must be employed, if innocence is to be preserved. Hence Augustine in *The City of God*: “Just as it is not beneficence to assist [Col. 0601A] in such a way that a greater good is omitted, so it is not innocence to spare severity in such a way that one falls into a graver evil.”

Therefore it belongs to the disposition of an innocent person not only not to do evil, but also to assist or punish the sinner lest evil be done, so that the person rebuked may be corrected by punishment or others may be frightened by the example. Purity of heart is necessary for preserving innocence, because it is written: “Hand in hand, the evil person shall not be innocent” (Prov. XI). For the will to do wrong alone, or negligent guarding of the heart, suffices to destroy the treasure of innocence; because if the opportunity to sin is removed, the will alone is reckoned as the deed. Even if you will never achieve the effect of a wicked act, nevertheless you already cast [Col. 0601B] yourself into the guilt of intention.

Therefore guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it. This complete guarding of the heart is its purity, which above all is wrought by fear of the Lord. “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. XXVIII). The fear of the Lord expels sin like a doorkeeper, who constantly sits at the door of the heart in order to admit no one except one worthy of entry. Since every arrogant person is unclean before God, humility and a firm contempt for empty glory are especially necessary for obtaining purity of heart. Hence Augustine in *The City of God*: “The more like God a person is, the cleaner he is from the uncleanness of empty glory. But this purity of heart is never born except from the chaste and holy fear of God, concerning which [Col. 0601C] it is written: ‘He who fears God neglects nothing’” (Eccles. VII)—that is, neither great things nor small; neither the things which ought to be done nor those which ought to be omitted.

Accordingly, purity of heart is that simplicity of the eye of which it is written: “The lamp of thy body is thine eye. If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” (Matt. V). Only such an eye shall see God, as it is written: “Blessed are the clean in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid.). But where shall it see him? Where he dwells, as it is written: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in heaven” (Ps. CXXII [123]).

Therefore the two parts of innocence—not making a person miserable and not abandoning one who is miserable—are the two rungs of the ladder by which one climbs to heaven. Purity of heart is the brightness of the eye by which God is seen. Hence, to the question, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” the answer is: “He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.” O answer brief but not slight, plain but full of truth, penetrating and effective, divine and deifying: “He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.” Hear, children of Adam, how easily one ascends—not, I say, upon a horse or a royal throne, but above heaven itself.

Hence the wise philosopher, set above heaven, understands, when he mounts a chair or tribunal, how low a place he occupies. No one is wise unless he is innocent; he alone is a climber of heaven and an ascender to knowledge of the heavenly one. “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord [Col. 0602A] or who shall stand in his holy place? He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.”

Behold, dearest brothers, divine Wisdom has discovered an art by which men may fly above birds, tread upon demons, leap over clouds, ascend above the heavens, exalt their throne above the stars of heaven, and place their nest among the very orders of angels. What is more subtle than this art? What knowledge more useful? What capacity more salutary? What power more sublime? “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV [4]) Why do you neglect so great an art and so great a mastership?

That obscure Lucifer did not know this art, though he is himself an artificer: he who fell from heaven like lightning. That proud king Alexander did not know it, who perished through his own power. That pestilent prince of sorcerers, Simon Magus, did not know it, who fell in his presumptuous flight. The philosophers did not know it, who failed while searching with inquiry: probing heavenly things, falling back to earthly things because they fell back upon them; setting their mouth in heaven while their tongue passed over the earth and they themselves licked the earth; calling their own lands by their own names, so that disciples might be designated Pythagoreans or Platonists, Epicureans or Stoics, and the like.

The poet of falsehood falsely calls these men blessed, saying:

> “Happy the souls whose first concern it was  
> To know these things and climb into the dwellings above.”  
> (Ovid, *Fasti* I.297)

And shortly afterwards:

> [Col. 0602C] “They brought the distant stars close to our eyes  
> And placed the heavens beneath their intellect.”

You are deceived, wretch; you are deceived. This curiosity is not happiness. Rather, nothing is more unhappy than to climb to heaven through knowledge of heavenly things and then immediately fall from heaven through the pride of one’s mind. “The horse is deceitful for safety” (Ps. XXXII [33]). Such people are not climbers of heaven, but climbers of horses, of whom it is written: “At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell asleep” (Ps. LXXV [76]).

Horses signify proud and rebellious men, sons of Belial—that is, without a yoke—who do not bear the Lord’s yoke, kick against the goad of discipline, burn for intercourse, and leap up for battle; for this is the horse’s nature. Woe to thee, ever-blind ambition of mortals; [Col. 0602D] woe to thee, ruinous lust of domination! Why, by exalting thyself, dost thou cast thyself down; by magnifying thyself, diminish thyself; by multiplying thyself, annihilate thyself; by expanding thyself, burst thyself apart; by raising thyself, hurl thyself down?

For behold: in order to ascend either the bed of pleasure, the step of dignity, the judgment-seat of equity, or the chair of honour, you lose innocence, abandon humility, and defile purity. Without their vehicle, every ascent is a fall, every height a precipice, every elevation a ruin. For the rule of truth declares: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XVIII).

> High things fall; inflated things burst; swollen things are pressed down.  
> . . . . . God crushes every proud person.

“Not so, the wicked, not so” (Ps. I). This is not how one ascends [Col. 0603A] the mountain of the Lord. But how? Listen: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He that is innocent in hands and clean in heart.”

But now let us speak a few simple words to simple people, so that they too, about to ascend with us, may by God’s grace find in our discourse a way and vehicle, lamp and provision for the journey: a way amid error, a vehicle amid weariness, a lamp amid darkness, provision amid hunger—lest they either turn aside from the way or fail upon it. Men travel far to learn. Many endure many things for gain. Students commonly go around cities and the world, that through much learning they may become mad. For what else can learning that saves nothing contribute, except to make people “always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of truth” (II Tim. III), unless perhaps at times it leads them into madness?

> A wise man will bear the name of madman, a just man that of unjust,  
> If he himself pursues virtue beyond what is sufficient.

They seek learning beyond what is sufficient who acquire it at the cost of their morals. Hence the Apostle: “Do not be wise beyond what is proper, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII); or, as the Greek has it, “unto chastity.” “It is better,” says Jerome, “not to know something than to learn it at peril.” Thus Blessed Benedict, seeing many in the schools of liberal arts rushing headlong down the precipices of vices, withdrew the foot which he had already set in the world. He departed unlearned, yet wisely unlearned.

Behold, clerics seek the liberal arts at Paris; authors at Orléans; legal codices at Bologna; medicine-chests at Salerno; [Col. 0603C] demons at Toledo; and nowhere morals. For no question is raised about morals—not even a final question, but none at all. Knowledge is sought everywhere and life nowhere; without life, knowledge not only profits nothing but is itself nothing. Therefore knowledge itself is not found, because it is not sought where it is: namely, in the book of life, which is also the book of knowledge, that is, the wisdom of God, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II).

But today this book withdrew into its own cupboard, because it lifted itself into heaven. Therefore one must ascend there if one wishes to attain true knowledge, as Blessed Bernard showed, on the night when he passed from this world to the Father, to William, his beloved and loving friend. William had been lord of Montpellier and was then living as a monk in the monastery of Grand-Selve, in the region of Toulouse. In a vision of the night he seemed to see that holy man soothing him greatly with conversation. Then, giving him his hand, Bernard led him from the dormitory toward a very high mountain near Jerusalem and said that he had to climb that mountain. Then William said: “For what purpose, lord?” He replied: “That I may learn.” And when William said that he thought him wiser than all mortals, Bernard said: “Only when I have climbed there shall I first be wise.” Immediately he ascended with great speed. While William, wondering, followed the climber with attentive eyes, the striking of the clock for Vigils, waking him with the brothers, ended the vision.

Just as in this [Col. 0604A] book are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, so in this treasury are stored all the treasures of sufficiency. For this book is wisdom to those who read it, sufficiency to those who see it, and life to those who taste it. O how much men do, and how weighty and hard things they endure, in order to become rich! How often, for uncertain gain, merchants, soldiers, athletes, and thieves incur certain dangers and suffer losses! Far more sweat is expended in acquiring riches than in learning letters. For the person who wishes to become rich wishes to become rich quickly.

Yet both labour in vain: those who strive to acquire deceitful riches and those who strive to acquire learning falsely so called. “There is no wealth above the health of the body.” True knowledge is saving wisdom, properly called the knowledge of the saints. [Col. 0604B] Hence: “He gave him the knowledge of the saints” (Wis. X). The knowledge of the saints is to live piously; to know how to abound and endure want; to know how to fear God; to know how to turn from evil and do good; to know how to save one’s soul; to know, for the avoidance of eternal evils and the acquisition of goods, how to despise present goods and endure evils. The first wisdom is to be free from folly. “You first owe me the goods of the mind.” For what profits a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his soul? (Matt. XVI).

The true health of the soul is justice; the true health of the body is the glory of immortality. Of justice also it is read that it is perpetual and immortal. Learning that makes no sound contributes nothing to this salvation of the soul. The riches of this age contribute nothing to this salvation of the body. [Col. 0604C] “Treasures shall not profit in the day of vengeance; but justice delivers from death.” The soul cannot be healed unless it cleaves to Christ its Saviour. The body likewise cannot be saved unless it remains in heaven, as in the proper place of salvation for human bodies. Attend briefly to this.

All the elements of this world destroy the human body, though they compose it. Whether decay dissolves corpses or the pyre does so makes no difference. Our bodies decay in water, earth, or air; they are reduced to ashes in fire. Therefore, if bodies are to remain safe, they must be raised above all the elements. Thus, just as the Saviour of souls is none other than Christ, who today ascended into the heavens with glorified flesh, [Col. 0604D] so, if I may say it, the place of salvation for bodies is none other than heaven, which received Christ ascending and keeps him whom it received.

For this is what he himself signified when he said: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John XIV), as though saying: I go to prepare a repository in which I shall store you; I go to adorn the casket into which I shall transfer you; I go to prepare the lodging in which I shall receive you: a repository-vessel for clean fish, a precious casket for holy bodies, a royal lodging for citizens to be received. Woe to evil and unclean fish, to be cast into the sulphurous lake. Woe to putrid and lustful bodies, to be thrown upon the dung-heap. Woe to those who reject grace, to be thrust back into hell.

Christ’s net now gathers fish of every kind. But when it has been filled, it shall be drawn out; the good fish shall be selected and placed in heavenly vessels—namely, those dwelling-places of which it is written: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John XIV). [Col. 0605A] But the evil fish shall be cast out into the lake of fire and sulphur, prepared for them not so that they may play there amid delights, but groan amid pains.

The good fish, according to the Law, have scales and fins: strong and armoured to endure evils; cheerful and trained to perform good works; eager and swift to leap over—that is, to despise—present goods; keen and ardent in desiring future goods. Moreover, the heavenly casket in which the bodies of the saints, as true and heavenly relics, are to be placed, is signified by those golden and silver caskets in which they are now kept. [Col. 0605B] Their threefold adornment—gold, silver, and precious stones—signifies both the external adornment of heaven in the sun, moon, and stars, and its internal adornment in the three hierarchies. For the sun glows like finest gold, the moon shines like silver, and the stars gleam and radiate like gems. Precious stones signify the highest hierarchy; gold, the middle; silver, the lowest.

For the first three orders are like incomparable jewels crowning the King of heaven or clinging more closely to him. The middle three are like his golden garment; the lowest three are like the bells of that same garment, through whose message, as through a silver ringing, heavenly secrets are often reported to mortals. More properly, however, the adornment of the holy [Col. 0605C] caskets in which the relics of the saints are kept signifies the saints’ remains, virtues, and precious miracles, through which they deserved to be exalted from the earth. For the virtues of the saints and works of justice are like certain most beautiful and precious buildings, to be built by all believers upon the foundation of faith, according to the Apostle’s words: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones,” etc. (I Cor. III).

Should one believe that the heavenly city, which God prepared for his saints and which he himself built, contains houses of wood or hay? Far be it! So rich a homeland does not receive such cheap dwellings. No corruptible or combustible material has a place there. Whatever has been built upon the precious foundation of faith from wood, hay, or straw shall be burned by fire. These three signify venial sins, without which life is not lived. Mortal sins, however, are not wood, hay, and straw, but copper, bronze, and iron. Sins of this sort not only defile the foundation but destroy it altogether. “For faith without works is dead” (Jas. II).

One venial sin is more venial than another, just as one mortal sin is more mortal than another. Wood signifies those more rigid than is just; hay, those softer and more self-indulgent; straw, those more frivolous. He builds wood who is slower to forgive and more sparing in giving; hay, who is slower to chastise the body and more inclined to indulge [Col. 0606A] it; straw, who is readier for laughter, roaming about, or idle speech, and less restrained in the discipline of silence or the gravity of stillness.

Here, however, a question of no small importance arises. For if wood, hay, and straw signify venial sins without which this present life is not lived, why are the saints likewise not said to build wood, hay, and straw as others do, since they do not pass their lives without such sins? For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us (I John I). “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. III).

To this I reply that the word “building” signifies a multitude of venial sins. A building cannot be constructed from one piece of wood, hay, or straw, but from many such things gathered together. [Col. 0606B] But saints and all perfect persons, so far as they can, abstain not only from every mortal sin but even from every venial sin. Therefore they do not accumulate from these such a multitude as can be called a building. The name “building” also signifies lingering and persistence in any venial sin. But the saints redeem their daily offences by the daily sacrifices of good works; therefore they construct no building out of those offences. Yet because they gather many good works, they build gold, silver, and precious stones: gold in the redness of patience, modesty, and shame; silver in good repute and in the word of teaching; precious stones in the brightness of chastity, the ardour of charity, the purity of conscience, the firmness of perseverance, and the radiance [Col. 0606C] of miracles.

The saints’ works are raised from earth because it would be quite unworthy that those who have not performed works of corruption should rot in corruptible decay. Rather, it was fitting that signs should show they await the reward of incorruption, and that, although their earthly habitation is dissolved, they have “a house from God, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V). The Lord himself signified this house when he said: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John XIV).

This place has been prepared from the origin of the world by predestination and is prepared daily by justification. Of the first manner of preparation it is said: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). Of the second, [Col. 0606D] it is said here: “I go to prepare a place for you.” For, as Augustine says, the Lord prepares dwelling-places in heaven when he prepares dwellers for those same dwelling-places, withdrawing his bodily presence from them on earth so that they may desire to be with him in heaven. Thus Christ, ascending on high, became, in Leo the Pope’s striking phrase, more present in his divinity and more distant in his humanity.

The heavenly city was prepared for its future earthly citizens from the time when the devil fell from heaven. He had occupied that land like a dead and useless tree. “Thy throne was prepared from then” (Ps. XCII [93]), that is, from the time when Satan, with his apostate angels, fell from it like uprooted trees, twice dead. Or “from then” means from the day before the Sabbath, from which day that psalm received its title: when man was made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. I). In man, Wisdom also made a seat for itself—a seat whose place is the soul of the just person, and likewise the humility of the penitent person resting from past sins and tremblingly guarding against future ones, according to the words: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). [Col. 0607A] “Justice,” he says, “and judgment are the preparation of thy throne” (Ps. LXXXVIII [89]). Justice preserves innocence; judgment recovers lost innocence through repentance.

O singular dignity of the human condition, whose hostelry is prepared by the One who ascended into heaven, and whose place is cleansed by the Maker of the world! O how noble a creature is the pure human being, for whose sake the God-man, his servant, hastened beforehand into heaven to prepare a lodging for him, carrying with him letters to the Father commending us and pleading for us—letters as powerful in obtaining their request as they are delightful to read. For making these letters on our behalf, the virginal womb supplied the parchment; the Holy Spirit prepared the parchment supplied; the Son of the Most High inscribed it when prepared, writing in golden letters, from the earth of his body, with the finger of God and with the stylus or pen of wisdom, the works of human redemption. He rubricated these same letters with the precious vermilion of rosy blood, by which virginal cheeks are adorned, according to that saying of Agnes, bride of the Lamb: “And his blood adorned my cheeks.”

Moreover, in order to establish the authority of the letters, so that it might remain unshaken and be preserved with eternal stability, kept inviolate, the royal seal of the cross was affixed on the outside, most firmly stamped with the marks of the nails and lance. The entire certainty of a seal consists in its impression. It is not a true seal that lacks a bulla; nor is that truly a cross which has no nails and lance. The cross is outward affliction and bodily exercise, which is useful for a little; the nails and lance are piety, powerful for all things. The nails are the fear of the Lord, which pierces hands and feet when it puts to death the works of the flesh and humbles the affection of the mind, according to the saying: “Fasten my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118 [119]). The lance is charity, which opens the side when it wounds the very heart, according to the saying: “I am wounded by charity.”

Here perhaps someone may ask: How did he carry the cross, the nails, and the lance with him into heaven? I answer that he carried with him the form of the cross in his uplifted hands, and the marks of the nails and lance in his scars. For when, as a man setting out on a journey, he had first held a solemn and familiar meal, and when this was completed, he led them out to Bethany and, with uplifted hands, blessed them, so that the people who were to serve him might increase both in merit and in number. Then, in the same posture, with his hands thus uplifted, while they watched, he was raised up, carrying that same form of the cross as far as his seat with the Father. For our Jesus was not wearied by holding his shield thus aloft, when the Father said to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109 [110]).

A ship has the form of a cross while it sails; a man while he swims; a bird while it flies; a priest while he sings Mass. Thus Christ ascended into heaven, as though leading sailors to port, fish to safety, birds to their nest, and peoples to God. Blessed are those who shared in Jesus’ meal at his departure. Blessed also—indeed, more blessed—are those who will share in his meal at his return.

The first is given us for the sustenance of the way; the second is reserved for the fullest refreshment of our homeland. At the first the apostles were present; at the second the angels are continually present. Thus, as we have said, Christ prepares lodging for us by standing before the face of God on our behalf, singing out that verse of the Psalmist in the person of the Church, which sent him ahead into heaven—not so much by raising its voice as by raising his body and displaying his wounds:

> “Look, O God our protector, and look upon the face of your Christ”  
> (Ps. 83 [84]).

Certainly, the meaning of this verse is written very legibly and wholly indelibly upon the body of the Savior. It says, therefore: “Look, O God our protector,” that is, behold before you the bent-down wisdom of your Son, whom you sent to us for our deliverance. “And look again,” or “look once more,” upon the exalted humanity of that same Son, standing before your face for us. See how fervently he fulfilled your command, how eagerly he ran to us, how wisely he conducted our cause, how bravely he alone overcame our most powerful enemy, how lavishly he shed his blood for us, how mightily he shattered the bars of hell, and how, bringing back from there our captivity—captive and free—he led it back to you; how liberally he shared his dignity with us, so as to make us reign with him in heaven, and has already placed us most sublimely at your right hand in his body, which is our head.

Look upon your Christ, so that you may hear him, as he intercedes with you for us, out of reverence for himself. Look again upon his body, which we are, still journeying in the valley of tears and misery, so that in your mercy you may join and unite it to its head. Look upon your Christ, whom you sent to us to journey with us. Look again upon us wretches, who have sent that same one back to you to prepare lodging for us. Brothers, blessed is he who prepares himself for the lodging already prepared in heaven, lest, unprepared, he fall into the punishment prepared in hell. For just as joys are already prepared for the righteous, so torments are already prepared for the wicked, according to the saying: “Judgments are prepared for mockers, and hammers that strike the bodies of fools” (Prov. 19:29).

For just as the kingdom has already been prepared from the origin of the world for the blessed, so eternal fire has also been prepared for the cursed—the same fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.

That fire, already prepared, was encountered by a certain prince of Mâcon. While he sat in his own palace at a solemn feast, surrounded by many soldiers of differing rank, suddenly an unknown man, mounted on horseback, entered through the palace door and, in sight of all, who marveled, rode straight up to him. He said that he wished to speak with him and insisted that he rise and follow him. Bound already by an invisible power and unable to resist, the prince immediately rose and proceeded to the palace door. There he found a horse ready; at once, as commanded, he mounted it. The rider who had summoned him took the reins and began, in sight of all, to carry him at the swiftest pace through the air. But the miserable man cried out in a pitiable and horrible voice: “Help, citizens, help!” and threw the whole city into commotion. All watched him flying through the air for a very long time, as long as they could follow him with the natural sight of their eyes. And so at last, withdrawn from human sight, he became an eternal companion of demons.

He went out with his companion through a gateway in the wall near the palace; because of the horror of so great an event, the citizens blocked that gate with stones. More recently William Ogerius, provost of Count William, wishing to restore this gate for certain purposes that seemed necessary for private or public use, hired workmen one day and removed the stones from the entrance. While he was occupied there, behold, he was invisibly snatched away by the devil; shortly afterwards he was released and fell down, his whole body grievously bruised and his arm broken. When his companions saw this, they blocked the gate again.

O how much better a lodging had Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, prepared for himself! When the day of the Lord’s Ascension was at hand, after the vigils had been completed, he remained alone in the church, as was his custom, for prayer. And behold, an innumerable multitude of white-robed beings, wearing golden crowns upon their heads which flashed with inestimable brilliance, burst in through the church door, gathered together before him, and greeted him in these words: “Hail, our Dunstan, hail! The Son of God, whom you lovingly desire, commands you that, if you are ready, you should come and celebrate with us this day, for whose joy you long.”

Remaining undaunted, he asked who they were. “We are Cherubim and Seraphim,” they said; “answer what you desire.” Then he said: “Today is a most solemn day, and it is incumbent upon me to refresh the people with the bread of God’s word and to show them how they may attain to this joy. For this reason many have assembled, and I ought not deceive them; therefore I cannot come today.” They said: “Come then, make ready, so that on the Sabbath day you may be ready to come hence with us to Rome, and before the supreme pontiff sing eternally, ‘Holy, holy, holy.’” He assented, and they departed.

Therefore, after the Gospel had been read at Mass that day, he spoke to the people as he had never spoken before. Returning to the altar, he celebrated the mysteries. But when the time came for the blessing over the people, he again came back from the altar to preach, so that you would have thought not a man but an angel was speaking. Again he returned to the altar, and, after giving the blessing, returned a third time to the people, while all marveled. As soon as he opened his mouth to speak, such brightness shone from his face that no one could [lacuna: a verb ending in “-ere”]; and he foretold that his death was at hand, promising that he would never afterwards be absent from them.

After this he returned to the table of the Body. When he had risen from the table after taking food, he went to the oratory and marked out the place in which he wished to be buried. Immediately illness seized him. On Friday he took to his bed. He invited all who came to him to follow in Christ’s footsteps. On Saturday he received communion again. And as he awaited his hour, suddenly he was lifted up with the bed on which he lay as far as the upper beams; the beams resisting, he was gently lowered to the ground. When he had been lowered, those who had fled returned to him as though he were resting; again he was snatched up with his bed to the beams as before, and again lowered. This also happened a third time.

Then he said to those standing around: “You see where I am called. If you wish to come with me, go by the way in which I have walked. May the God who calls me himself direct your hearts and bodies to do his will in peace.” When all answered, “Amen,” he passed happily to the Lord. Truly happily: for so many and such great messengers, of such dignity and excellence, were sent from heaven by the gracious King of heaven to make him blessed in view of his most nearly impending happy assumption. They were sent not only to gladden him, but also to confirm in faith the people standing around.

For why was he taken up with his little bed, unless it was to show clearly that that blessed soul, which was then taken up alone without the body, would someday also be taken up with the body itself? For the time will come when, in all the elect, what was fulfilled historically in that paralytic will be fulfilled anagogically. To him, once healed, that great physician said: “Arise, take up your bed, and go into your house” (Matt. 9:6). Every soul lies, as it were, paralytic in its bed as long as the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind. But after the sack of mortality has been torn apart, then we shall truly take up our bed and go to the house of our eternity. In the hope already conceived of this journey, the Church rejoices in the Lord, arranging ascents in its heart and saying: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” (Ps. 121 [122]).

This will happen when we are all together caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air (1 Thess. 4:17). This was signified by that cloud of witnesses, that is, the company to which the most delightful spectacle of the Lord’s Ascension was displayed today. For they numbered one hundred and twenty, a number consisting of fifteen arranged as a triangle—that is, fifteen aggregated together with all its units. This number is composed of seven and eight. Seven signifies all the elect of the Old Testament; eight, all those of the New. But we who remain at the coming of the Lord shall not precede those who have slept, but shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air (ibid.), so that, as it were, one hundred and twenty gathered from two parts of fifteen, we may all ascend together with the Lord; that in the mystery of the Ascension we may be as many as those who today were, in number, spectators of the Lord’s Ascension. May Jesus Christ grant this to us—he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST I

“Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing spirit,” etc. (Acts 2:2).

May the subject matter appropriate by solemn custom to today’s festival—burning and fiery, a torrent and fervent—have so warmed me, numb with the double cold of conduct and speech, of life and eloquence, as much as it has made me tremble; and as much as it has made me tremble and frightened me, so much may it have scorched me. For whom would not the flaming—indeed, lightning-like—coming of this fiery torrent, boiling from its fountain, terrify, a coming which can be expounded only in fiery—indeed, lightning-like—words? To speak of divine fire, indeed of fire which is God, every tongue is unworthy and ineffective unless it is fiery; every discourse incongruous and useless unless it is fiery. For this reason the Holy Spirit was seen on this day to descend upon the disciples assembled together in divided forms of tongues: to show that his fiery law can properly and rightly be preached only in fiery words and through fiery tongues.

For it is, as it were, a certain barbarism in doctrine to offer a cold thought concerning the fiery law, and to utter a dead discourse about a life-giving reality. Every cold or dead discourse is reckoned to be one which slips out, as they say, from the very lips; which does not come from a full breast nor bubble up from the fountain of the heart. Every discourse, I say, is to be reckoned cold and dead if it does not live in the hidden place of conscience and shine forth in the mirror of life.

“Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing spirit.” And a little later: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire,” etc. Therefore three things are especially to be considered here: namely, those three companions whom the Holy Spirit brought with him—sound, fire, and tongue. Without prejudice to a better opinion, it seems to me that these three have a triple significance.

First, I judge that these three signify the knowledge of the Holy Trinity, which was first conveyed to the world today. Second, the threefold grace bestowed upon the disciples today. Third, the form of our conversion, which is briefly expressed in these three things. Let us consider each in order.

First, it must be known that the mystery of the Holy Trinity became known to the world not all at once, but in parts and in successive periods of time. For before the Son assumed flesh, only the person of the Father was known to the world, even by those who believed, as we do, that there is only one God. But even that person was not fully known, because the world did not yet know what in God should be called person and what substance. They believed only that God was the author, creator, and Father of all creatures—but Father by creation, not by generation—because the world did not yet know that he had a Son. Therefore no one yet had knowledge either of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, except a very few perfect persons, such as the prophets and chief patriarchs, who possessed the same knowledge of the Trinity as we do, indeed a more perfect knowledge than ours; for God had revealed himself to them. The Father had strengthened them by patience against the powers of this world; the Son had enlightened them by wisdom against errors; the Holy Spirit had armed them with love against enmities.

With these exceptions, as I have said, all the remaining multitude still had knowledge of the Father alone, and that very slight. But after the Son was incarnate and presented himself to the world to be known, and now taught with his own mouth, rather than through the mouth of prophets, that he was God, then the world began to have knowledge of two persons, the Father and the Son. It learned that the Father is not without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, but that the eternal Father has an eternal Son, and conversely. Yet it still knew nothing of the Holy Spirit.

But after the Holy Spirit appeared to the world in fiery tongues and manifested the power of his divinity, then for the first time the mystery of the Holy Trinity became known; and then the world believed that there are three unconfused persons in the Godhead, just as there is one undivided substance. Hence, in the Old Law the Father alone is introduced as speaking, when it is said, “Thus says the Lord.” But in the Gospel the Son himself speaks in his own person, saying: “You have heard that it was said to those of old. But I say to you,” etc. (Matt. 5:21–22). As though he said: “I have the same authority to hand down the Gospel as my Father had to hand down the Old Testament to the ancients.”

But in the writings and Acts of the apostles, which are the third part of the whole canon of sacred Scripture, the entire authority of speech is referred to the Holy Spirit, as to the author of that part, and of the same authority as the first two; as when it is said: “The Holy Spirit said” (Acts 13:2). Thus, although the Holy Trinity has no degrees in itself, it came to human knowledge through certain degrees, so to speak: first the Father alone was known; second, the Son with the Father; third, the Holy Spirit with both.

It should also be noted that this knowledge of the Trinity proceeded not only through succession of times, but also through distinctions among its works. God performed three great and principal works: the first was the creation of the world; the second, redemption; the third, the strengthening of the redeemed in virtue and, as it were, their earnest toward love. First, man was created, that one who did not exist might exist; second, he was redeemed, that one who had fallen might rise; third, he was strengthened, that one who had risen might stand. These three works are equal.

For it belongs to the same power and might, goodness and wisdom, not only to make things from nothing, but to make them good; to restore what has been lost; and to preserve restored things so that they do not perish. Each of these works is assigned to one of the persons. The creation of the world is assigned to the Father, the redemption of the redeemed to the Son, preservation to the Spirit. For the Father created, the Son redeemed, and the Holy Spirit preserves and guards.

Yet the individual works are assigned to the individual persons in such a way that all the persons work in every work. For in each of these works the marks of all the persons are evident. The world, indeed, was created great, beautiful, and useful. In its greatness the Father showed himself; in its beauty, the Son; in its usefulness, the Holy Spirit. For it belongs to power to make great things, to wisdom to make beautiful things, and to goodness to make useful things. Thus, in the proper operation of the Father, one finds the trace of the whole Trinity.

Likewise, in the proper work of the Son—that is, in the redemption of the world, accomplished by the dispensation of the incarnate Word—the whole Trinity made itself known. For when the Lord was baptized by John, the Father became known in the voice, the Son appeared in the flesh, and the Holy Spirit descended in a dove (Matt. 3).

Therefore a trace of the Trinity likewise had to be found in the operation of the Holy Spirit. For this reason, on this day the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples with a certain sign of the Trinity: with sound, fire, and tongue—with terrifying sound, visible fire, and flashing tongue. Sound came from heaven; fire from sound; tongue from fire. The sound was sudden; the fire brilliant and harmless; the tongue fiery. The sound was to be heard, the fire to be seen, the tongue to speak. The sound was for terror; the fire for brightness; the fiery tongue for heat and brightness together. The terrifying sound was the sign of strength and power; the brilliant and harmless fire, the sign of wisdom and justice; the fiery tongue, the sign of love and teaching.

Thus the Father resounded in the sound, for he is power; the Son shone forth in the fire, for he is wisdom and the source of all justice; the Holy Spirit, who is the love of Father and Son and teaches every human being knowledge, flashed forth in fiery tongues. The Father terrified, so that he might be feared; the Son shone, so that he might be believed; the Holy Spirit kindled, so that he might be loved. Who is more rightly to be feared than he who can do all things? Whom should we trust more than him who knows all things? Who is more to be loved than he who gives all things?

Therefore let us fear the Father’s power, because he can condemn us; let us believe the Son’s wisdom, because it cannot deceive; let us love the Holy Spirit’s goodness, because it cannot harm. Truly, power must be feared because it strikes powerfully; wisdom must be believed because it never errs and deceives no one; charity must be loved because it never hates but always loves. Let us fear the Almighty; let us believe him who knows all things; let us love him who gives all things. God must first be feared, then believed, and thirdly loved. Salvation begins from fear, advances through faith, and is perfected in love. The beginning of saving knowledge is fear of the Lord; faith is its increase; love its end. We begin from fear, walk through faith, and by love arrive where we are tending. Fear is nothing without faith; faith is nothing without love.

But sound, fire, and tongue will be discussed more fully below. Meanwhile, it must be known that the Holy Trinity wished to manifest itself in the individual works of the individual persons in order to show that their operation is undivided and inseparable, and that whatever one of them does, the others do also. This is shown to us by a sufficiently elegant comparison: in sacred Scripture the Son is called the hand of the Father, and the Holy Spirit the finger of that hand; or the Son is called the mouth of the Father, and the Holy Spirit the tongue of that mouth.

For an artisan works through his hands in everything he does, and whatever hands do, they do through fingers. Yet a human being, his hand, and his fingers are not three arts, artisans, or workers, but one. Similarly, whatever a human being says, he says through his mouth; and whatever the mouth says, it says through the tongue. Yet the human being, his mouth, and his tongue are not three speakers, but one speaker. Accordingly, under this likeness, whatever the Father does or says, he does and says through the Son; and whatever the Son does or says, he does and says through the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). And these three are not three workers or speakers, but one.

Thus whatever the Son does or says, the Father and the Holy Spirit also do and say; and whatever the Holy Spirit does or says, the Father and Son also say and do. So whatever a man’s hand does, the man and his finger do; and what the fingers of the hands do, the man himself and his hands do. Likewise, whatever a man’s mouth says, the man and his tongue say; and what the tongue says, the man and his mouth say. But because for God doing and speaking are the same—for in speaking he does, and in doing he speaks, according to the saying: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148 [147]:5)—the Son is called not only the Father’s hand but also his mouth; and the Holy Spirit not only his finger but also his tongue.

This is one reason why the Holy Spirit came in sound, fire, and tongue: namely, that his proper work might give some trace of the Trinity, just as the works of the Father and Son had previously done; especially since knowledge of the Trinity itself was first to be acquired chiefly in this third work.

The second significance is the threefold grace bestowed upon the disciples in this coming. Sound was made over them to signify the great power granted them. Fire shone over them to indicate their justice and wisdom. Divided tongues came over them to signify their burning charity and fiery teaching. The terrifying sound was the sign of their great and marvelous power in performing signs; the brilliant and harmless fire, the sign of wisdom in understanding the Lord’s commands and justice in keeping them. The fiery tongues were the sign of most ardent charity in loving their neighbors and most effective preaching in converting peoples.

They received the first grace in order to terrify the world; the second, to enlighten it; the third, to set it on fire. Power made them terrifying; wisdom and justice made them shining and worthy of esteem; charity, as fruitful as it was eloquent, made them as eloquent as they were ardent. They received the first properly for fighting against powers of the air; the second against fleshly allurements; the third against worldly deceits. By the first they became terrifying even to demons; by the second honorable to human beings; by the third lovable to all.

Therefore these three signs were made over the disciples so that, through them, the self-confident might be terrified, the blind enlightened, teachers instructed, converts admonished, the admonished rebuked, the rebuked corrected, and the kindled set over others. The disciples had indeed previously received these graces from the Father and the Son. But at the Holy Spirit’s coming today they began to receive them more fully.

For the power of performing signs had been given by the Son when he said to them: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke 10:19). In baptism, too, they had been justified and cleansed, as was said to Peter: “He who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet” (John 13:10). Moreover, the Lord testifies that they had already received both wisdom and charity when he says to them: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15). And again: “For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed in me” (John 16:27).

They had also already received the Holy Spirit himself from the Lord when it was said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them,” etc. (John 20:22–23). Yet what they already possessed from the Father and Son, they began today to possess more fully from the Holy Spirit—not because the Holy Spirit possesses these things more fully than the Father and Son, but because he who was to be made known after them was to be honored with more abundant gifts. For it was fitting that what had seemed lacking in the knowledge of the Holy Spirit should be made good by the greater abundance of gifts at the final time; and that the world should know that, although the Holy Spirit came later into knowledge than the Father and Son, he nevertheless possessed no lesser power or glory than they.

The Holy Spirit demonstrated this most beautifully at a certain council presided over by Pope Hildebrand, otherwise called Gregory VII.

> [Note: [Col. 0615] Hildebrand was not yet pope, but the pope’s legate.]

At that council, a certain archdeacon accused of the Macedonian heresy—which maintains that the Holy Spirit is a creature and denies that he is Creator—was ordered by the pontiff to appear, and he came. Asked concerning his faith, he answered that he was Catholic. The pope said to him: “Do you believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?” He replied: “I believe.” “Do you believe,” he asked, “that these three persons are of the same power, majesty, and glory?” He replied: “I believe.”

“Then,” said the pope, “so that I may believe that you speak truly, say this verse to me: ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’” At first the man blushed, thinking that the supreme pontiff considered him like a layman, ignorant of letters. “Lord,” he said, “I am not a layman, but I know letters.” The pope replied: “I am not concerned with your learning, but with your faith; and therefore I command you by the power of the Holy Spirit: if you rightly believe in the Holy Spirit, say this verse to me; but if you do not rightly believe in the Holy Spirit, may you be unable to say it.”

Then he began tremblingly: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son,” and immediately fell silent; nor could he complete: “and to the Holy Spirit.” The pope repeatedly made him repeat the entire verse from the beginning, but he could by no means finish it, always becoming silent after “Father and Son.” Seeing this, the pope said to him: “Behold, wretch, how the Holy Spirit has shown through your silence that he possesses glory coeternal and coequal with the Father, which you, in your folly, were trying to take away from him.” And he deposed him from every ecclesiastical office and honor.

Thus, as we have said, the Holy Spirit became known to the world with greater glory than the Father and Son had previously become known, because he brought more abundant gifts of manifold glory than they had previously given; so that it might be known by this that, although he became known later, he was nevertheless not inferior to them. For those who had previously known the Father alone received the spirit of servitude in fear, so that they might fear the Father’s power. But at the coming of the Son, the Holy Spirit of knowledge and understanding was given to the apostles in their preaching, that they might understand the Son’s wisdom. At the coming of the Holy Spirit, however, the spirit of love was given in the likeness of fiery tongues, that they might both love and preach the benevolence of the Holy Spirit himself.

Thus, just as knowledge of the Trinity came through certain degrees, so its grace increased through certain degrees. But let this suffice concerning the second significance of the three signs—sound, fire, and tongue. Now let us consider the third, which is the form of our conversion briefly expressed in these three things.

When a sinner returns into himself in order to be converted to God, first a sound comes to him from heaven; then fire from the sound; third, a tongue is formed from the fire. For first a human being is terrified by God, so that he may fear him reverently; then he is ardently pierced, so that he may grieve intensely; he is wisely consumed, so that he may disclose his sins. Sound pertains to terror, which converts the sinner; fire to sorrow, which burns the penitent; tongue to confession, which, just as the tongue of a dog heals a wound while licking it, also heals the sinner by making his sins manifest.

It must be known, moreover, that each of these three things takes place in three ways. For by a threefold threat God threatens us in order to terrify us: eternal fire, purgatory, and sudden death; eternal punishments, purgatorial punishments, and the perils of sudden death. He threatens the first to those who do not fear him, the second to those who fear him little, the third to those who do not fear him always.

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is very necessary and useful that we should not only fear God, but fear him greatly and fear him always. Let us fear him as sinners ought; let us fear him greatly, as the righteous are accustomed to do; let us fear him always, as the perfect fear him. Of the first it is said: “Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being” (Eccl. 12:13). Of the second: “Always,” he says, “I feared God as I would swelling waves” (Job 31:23). Of the third: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14).

God must be feared because of eternal punishment; he must also be greatly feared because of purgatorial punishment after death; and he must always be feared because of unforeseen death and the uncertainty of the hour of death. Those who do not fear God must descend into hell and not come out of it. Those who do not fear greatly must pass through fire after death.

The ways of hell are mortal sins; and as many such sins as there are, so many are the ways leading to hell: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the ways of hell.” Good God, who will guard himself from these ways, so as not to remain in them, pass through them, fall into them, or tend toward them? It is dangerous to tend toward them, wretched to fall into them, more wretched to pass through them, and most wretched to remain in them. Blessed indeed is he who has not sat in the seat of pestilence; but more blessed is he who has not stood in the way of sinners; yet most blessed is he who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked. For this is the one who has not even directed his step toward the ways of hell—that is, who has not even deliberated about committing mortal sin.

For one who even merely contemplates such a sin already has his steps turned toward hell. But one who carries out what he has deliberated has already run into the ways of hell. One who repeats what he has done passes through the way of hell—or rather, runs along it. And one who does not abandon what he has repeated remains in the ways of hell. Such a one must someday arrive in hell, because he never turns aside from the way of hell and always hastens to run through it.

Therefore it pleases one to cry out with the Prophet: “Who is the man that lives and shall not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” (Ps. 83 [89]:49). For who is there that does not merely go, but actually run, to the lower regions? Who, I say, is the human being who does not see death—that is, who does not at some time incur mortal sin?

Murder is mortal sin; hatred is mortal sin, for “he who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). A single word spoken against one’s neighbor from bitterness of soul, swelling pride, or burning anger is mortal sin. For “whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22). Yet who does not at some time sin in such a word?

A single adultery is mortal sin. I say more: a single lustful glance is mortal sin, for Christ says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (ibid.). I say still more: a single movement of lust, confirmed in intention, is mortal sin. For whoever takes delight in thought alone even to consent to the act commits adultery not only by looking but even by thinking. Likewise, whoever looks at any possession of his neighbor in order to steal it has already stolen it in his heart.

Therefore among the commandments not to kill, not to steal, and so forth, the commandment not to covet is placed, so that Scripture might show that when the opportunity is removed from one who covets, will alone is reckoned as the deed. Let us therefore flee the ways of hell: that is, the act, desire, and consent of every mortal sin.

One must also beware of purgatorial fire, because no magnitude of present punishment can be compared with that burning; for that fire is as much more grievous than temporal fire as a fire blazing in a furnace is more grievous than one painted on a wall. But he avoids purgatorial fire who avoids venial sin. For every venial sin not purged in this life must necessarily be purged in that fire. Good God, who can guard against so many paths and disentangle himself [Col. 0618B] from so many snares? Who can avoid paths which he cannot enumerate? Venial sins are infinite, and all the more dangerous because they are committed more easily. For many evils are thought to be goods. Hence the poet:

> And evils lie close beside goods, beneath error itself;  
> Virtue has often borne accusations in place of vice.

Many mortal sins likewise are regarded as venial. Hence the Prophet: “Who understands transgressions?” (Ps. XVIII). Moreover, blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0617D] Sermon 41, *On the Saints*.], enumerating certain lesser sins, says that they include cases in which someone takes more food or drink than is necessary. And certainly this is often a mortal sin. But Augustine must be understood to have said this [Col. 0618C] of a slight excess, not an excessive one, which is gluttony or drunkenness. Finally, he adds: “Whenever someone speaks more than is necessary, or is silent more than is expedient.”

Yet in the examples given by Augustine, he does not determine below what limits the sin is venial, or beyond what limits it is mortal. Perhaps he meant this: however much such things may be minimized, they are at least venial sins. Finally, many things are venial in the imperfect which are reckoned mortal in those who have professed perfection. Hence blessed Bernard [Note: [Col. 0618D] St. Bernard, Book II, *On Consideration*, at the end.]: “You have consecrated your mouth to the Gospel: to open it for trifles is unlawful; to become accustomed to this is sacrilege.” I can scarcely, therefore, be brought to believe that a monk or priest accustomed to trifles does not sin mortally. For if all human beings must render an account on the day of judgment for words of this sort [Col. 0618D], with how great a strictness, do we suppose, will this account be demanded from those who have professed perfection by order or habit?

Who, moreover, would not be terrified by the example of a certain Cluniac monk who, as a testimony to his religious life, was not only made abbot but was even raised to the episcopal chair of Toulouse? Although he was circumspect in other matters, he nevertheless too often indulged in words provoking laughter, more than befitted a monk. For this vice he was often reproved by St. Hugh. When he was repeatedly corrected and did not amend, Hugh foretold that he would repent too late: namely, when after death he should appear, suffering and anxious, with foam upon his lips [Col. 0619A]. And so it came to pass. For, when dead, he appeared to a chaplain of the aforesaid Abbot Hugh, with foam upon his lips as had been foretold, asking the chaplain to go to St. Hugh so that he might free him by his prayers from the punishment he had foretold.

Having summoned seven brethren, Hugh enjoined them to keep silence for seven days on behalf of that man’s soul. While six brethren diligently observed the command, the seventh broke it and did not maintain the silence imposed. Therefore the aforesaid bishop again appeared to the same chaplain, bitterly complaining of that brother who had not properly kept silence and had thus interrupted his salvation. The chaplain reported this to the abbot. Summoning the transgressing brother, he imposed a penance on him and ordered that the silence broken should be repaired by seven days of silence [Col. 0619B]. When these had been completed, the deceased bishop appeared with a cheerful countenance and in episcopal vestments to the abbot who had delivered him, giving thanks for his release.

Clearly, he could have been condemned for trifling alone, had not so many other virtues in which he had abounded come to his aid. Let us therefore avoid purgatorial fire by avoiding, as far as we can, the deed, desire, and consent of every venial sin, and by washing away daily sins with daily repentance. But we must not merely fear God: we must fear him greatly and always; so that we may avoid not only eternal punishment and the punishment of purgatory, but also sudden death. This is never properly guarded against unless it is always feared, always kept before one’s eyes, and always contemplated.

[Col. 0619C] Forgetfulness of our mortality, delight of the flesh, and security concerning death drive us into these three dangers. Against the first stands the saying: “Remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII). Against the second: “Your laughter shall be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. IV). Against the third: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII). Likewise: “Not slothful in diligence” (Rom. XII).

Someone will say to me here: “Who can always think about death without continual sadness and grief? For the memory of death is sad and bitter.” This is true, but for those who do not trust in God, for whom eternal things have no savor, and to whom temporal things are sweet. For those who by present faith foresee the rewards of the righteous, by hope catch their fragrance beforehand, and by love and longing [Col. 0619D] taste them in advance—for these, the remembrance of death is truly not bitter, but rather sweet and pleasant. They do not fear death, but desire to be released, saying with the Prophet: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged! When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. CXIX).

Although in the Gospel of the Nazarenes [Note: [Col. 0619D] An apocryphal book.] the Lord is read to have said to the disciples: “Never be joyful except when you see your brother in charity.” This, then, is what the Apostle says: “As sorrowful in the world, yet always rejoicing in the Lord” (II Cor. VI). He said “as sorrowful,” and not “sorrowful”; and “rejoicing,” but not “as rejoicing”: for in this world there is no true sadness or joy except [Col. 0620A] from a conscience that accuses or defends. Finally, as the Apostle says: “There is a sorrow that works salvation” (II Cor. VII). Nothing is more useful for victory over future sin than sorrow over past sin. Hence among poets Victory is said to be the daughter of Styx, which is interpreted “sadness,” because vices are conquered through sadness, but conquer through joy. Hence one poet says:

> While she was not joyful, Ilium was defended by arms;  
> Joyful, she received the horse pregnant with soldiers.

These, then, are the three threats from the Lord, like three thunderclaps from heaven, intended to frighten us away from sin. The Lord threatens us with hell through himself, saying: “These shall go into eternal punishment” (Matt. XXV); with purgatorial fire through the Apostle, when he says: “He himself shall be saved, yet so as through [Col. 0620B] fire” (I Cor. III); and with sudden death when he says: “The master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know” (Matt. XXIV).

This, then, is the threefold sound that comes from heaven upon the sinner in order to terrify him. Sound comes from heaven in two ways: either with some preceding sign, as when the air is disturbed or clouds converge; or unexpectedly and suddenly, with no preceding signs, as when under a clear sky and calm air we suddenly hear thunder roar. So too, a sound of terror from the Lord is sometimes made with preceding signs, and sometimes with none. It is made with preceding signs when a sinner is scourged by God, whether by loss of property, injury to his own body, or the death of a relative, before he is terrified. But a sudden sound comes from heaven [Col. 0620C] when the sinner, by a sudden inspiration of divine grace and with no preceding adversities, returns into himself and is terrified by his own conscience.

A sound from heaven was made with a preceding sign over the Apostle Paul, who was struck with blindness before he was frightened by the voice. But a sudden sound from heaven was made over Mary Magdalene: divine grace humbled her after suddenly changing her inwardly, not after outwardly scourging her with punishments. The same happened to the brother mentioned in the *Lives of the Fathers*: when he entered a church miserably bound by demons, with a most hideous and dreadful face, he was suddenly converted there to God; the demon was put to flight, and he was seen surrounded by angels. Truly, over him there was made [Col. 0620D] a sudden sound from heaven—“sudden,” that is, with no preceding sign. But this is enough concerning the sound. Concerning the fire and the tongue, with God’s help, we shall explain in the following sermon.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY, II

The fire produced from the sound, like the sound from heaven, signifies a certain brightness of divine grace together with the ardor that follows in the mind of the sinner disturbed by fear of the Lord. For as the sound preceded in order to strike and disturb the sinner, so fire follows in order both to illuminate and [Col. 0621A] to brighten the mind.

The sinner is illuminated in three ways, that he may know, if possible, the weight, nature, and measure of his sins: that is, how, how greatly, and how often he has sinned. Weight refers to the quality of sin, measure to its quantity, and number to the habitual practice of sinning. Quality is considered in the substance of the sin, quantity in its circumstances, and habit in relapses. Thus, after the sound from heaven, fire is produced from the sound: because, after the sinner, struck by fear of the Lord, returns into himself, he is immediately compelled to consider how he offended God by sinning—how, how grievously, and how frequently. This is the threefold illumination concerning the evils he has committed.

He is likewise illuminated in three ways to consider the evils he has deserved: namely, the worm [Col. 0621B] that does not die, the fire that is not extinguished, and the death that does not end. He is also illuminated in three ways in considering good things: because he considers the good he did not do; the good he did do, but not as he ought to have done it; and the good he lost—that is, what he would have deserved if he had done what he ought, as he ought.
