There is a threefold consideration in each case, because he did not do the three goods which he ought to have done. He did not love God, his neighbor, or himself. He did not render to each what belonged to it: obedience to God, justice to his neighbor, and temperance to himself, according to the saying: “Let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this world” (Tit. II). Likewise, he did not do in three respects the good he did do [Col. 0621C] as he ought: because he did not do it with the purity of intention or the perseverance of long-suffering which he ought to have had. And, as St. Benedict says: “Every righteousness that is lukewarm, transitory, and sold into oblivion will stand before God.”

Therefore, a person would have deserved three greatest goods if he had done as he ought: the glorification of the body, the blessedness of the soul, and the vision of the blessed. But he who considers all these things closely heaps up material for sorrow; and the more penetratingly he directs the gaze of his mind to each, the more ardently he will weep over each. For it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. I). No one, therefore, can be kindled by this fire unless he has first been illuminated by it; because no one can weep for his sins or spiritual losses unless he first knows them and wisely evaluates them once known.

[Col. 0621D] What is remarkable in this fire is that ardor proceeds from brightness, whereas elsewhere brightness is usually thought to follow from ardor. Yet this is so in the very substance of fire. For fire is bright because of heat, and not hot because of brightness. But in participation in fire it is otherwise. Those previously remote from fire, when they begin to approach it as it burns and shines, must necessarily be illuminated by it before they are warmed, and become participants in its brightness before its heat. For the brightness of fire extends farther than its heat, and therefore makes itself shared first. This is evident in the sunbeam, which shines equally everywhere but does not warm equally everywhere; indeed, it illuminates many persons to whom it gives little or no heat. Finally, the sun shines upon us at its very rising, but does not burn within us at that moment; rather, in the morning it attends us with brightness, and at noon with heat [Col. 0622A].

Similarly, then, the sinner must see his sins before grieving for them. And who has grieved so worthily as he ought? “More easily,” says blessed Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0621D] Ambrose, Book II, *On Repentance*, ch. 10.], “have I found persons who preserved innocence than persons who performed repentance worthy of it.” Nor is this surprising, since we must repent not only for our evil acts, but also for our good ones, when we turn those very goods into evils by not doing them well. Therefore Isaiah says: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV). If our righteousnesses are such, what are our unrighteousnesses? If the light that is in us is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?

Behold, God compares men to women—and not only soft and effeminate men, but strong and robust ones; and not merely to women, but to menstruating women. Woe to all of us because of the frailty of corruption and the corruption of frailty, we who are called women! Woe to us for shameful softness! Woe to us for virtues which are compared even to an unclean cloth!

How much must we weep for injustices if we must grieve even for righteousnesses! “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently,” and still more he who does it deceitfully (Jer. XLVIII). For each departs from your commandments, you who commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly (Ps. CXVIII). He does God’s work [Col. 0622C] negligently who does it lukewarmly, or who does not burn fervently in work once begun, or does not persevere in the fervor of work. But he does the Lord’s work deceitfully who either trusts in his own strength, or is wholly devoted to his own praise; who attributes the work itself to someone other than God; who seeks a reward other than God; who assigns another price to his work than God himself; who considers someone other than God alone to be the author of his good works, or expects someone other than God as their rewarder.

After that fire has thus enlightened a person to understand sins and inflamed him to grieve, it will immediately form from itself a tongue for confession. For he does not grieve worthily for his sin whose sin does not yet displease him perfectly. But no sin perfectly displeases someone [Col. 0622D] who still keeps and possesses it as a treasure, while he conceals and retains it. For one who perfectly hates sin immediately spits and vomits it out from himself as most harmful poison. Therefore, after recollection and contrition one hastens at once to confession, so that the visitation of the Holy Spirit may be complete in all its parts: as sound is sent out from heaven and fire comes forth from sound, so a tongue may be formed from fire.

Every tongue formed from fire is necessarily fiery. Therefore confession ought to be fiery. Nothing is purer, or more purifying, than fire; nothing clearer, brighter, more gleaming, or redder. Fire is a most pure, most bright, and most richly colored thing, because it is most ruddy; it has nothing mixed with it of rust, dirt, or obscurity, nothing pale or dead in color. Likewise confession must be pure, clear, and ruddy: pure, so that one confesses only one’s own sins—that is, neither one’s own virtues nor another’s sins; complete, so that one reveals all sins and their circumstances and conceals nothing from the confessor; ruddy, so that it makes the face of the penitent blush.

A confession complete in all its parts is pure through humility: it has not learned to publish others’ evils and does not know how to boast of its own goods. It is clear through simplicity, which does not know how to hide truth or fabricate a lie. And it is ruddy through modesty, which has learned to adorn [Col. 0623B] the penitent’s face with a rosy color, so that by this, as by an inward allurement, it may please its beholder more.

There are people who hide their sins in their bosom as gold. There are people who, selling such a possession, dispense it avariciously like Ananias and Sapphira, disclosing some things and retaining others, and lying to the Holy Spirit. There are those who recount not only their own sins but also others’. There are those who recite only their own, but as though it were a tale or some history—without shame or modesty, without blushing or sorrow, without tears or groaning, without contrition or grief. There are those who, while confessing, sigh and groan only superficially, lest they seem to do nothing. There are those who enumerate their virtues, boasting like Nebuchadnezzar of their dreams, the fantastic visions of their heads [Col. 0623C], or sophistical apparitions of demons. There are those who groan and weep while confessing their sins, yet seek praise for that very thing.

Not so the man who says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’” (Ps. XXXI). “I said,” he says—that is, I firmly resolved in my heart that I would do it. What? What follows:

“I will confess”—I myself, before another accuses me; but freely and willingly I shall speak against myself, not against another; my injustices, not my righteousnesses. “I will confess to the Lord”: that is, for the praise and honor of the Lord, not for my own honor or praise, imputing my sins to myself but glory to God.

Therefore, wherever the Holy Spirit is to lodge, all these signs must necessarily go before, because through these three he is accustomed to prepare lodging for himself in the hearts of the elect. Fear of the Lord, which is produced from the sudden sound and holds primacy throughout the whole house, orders the house to be swept and its dirt and rubbish diligently sought out. Knowledge of sin and remembrance of loss, like most obedient servants, diligently sweep the house and gather its dirt and rubbish into one place. The violence of sorrow, like a most devouring flame, burns what has been gathered; confession, like a broom, casts out what has been burned. This is the broom that empties and cleans the lodging of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit therefore sends these servants before himself.

But when he remains, what companions will he retain? Certainly the same ones. He remains with us [Col. 0624A] with the same companions with whom he enters us: that is, with sound, fire, and tongue; with terror, light, and ardor; with fear, sorrow, and confession—but in different ways. He who came with servile and initial fear remains with chaste and filial fear. He who came with sorrow for sin committed remains with sorrow for the reward delayed. And he who came with confession of sin remains with confession of praise: that is, with thanksgiving for benefits received and hope for those yet to be received.

For as at first we feared lest we be damned, so now, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, we still fear, but no longer lest we be condemned by the Judge; rather, lest we be less praised by him. Hence the Apostle: “Do you wish not to fear? Do good, and you shall have praise from her” (Rom. XIII). A maid fears her mistress in one way, a wife her husband in another. The former fears lest she be entirely expelled; the latter, lest she be loved too little. Likewise, now made joyful in the Holy Spirit, we still grieve—not for a guilt already washed away, but for a gift delayed—like one who says: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXIX).

We also confess to the Lord, not indeed our sins, which have already been confessed and forgiven, but divine benefits freely given to us, as did the one who spoke thus: “I will confess to you, O Lord and King, and praise you, O God my Savior; I will confess to your name, because you have become my helper and protector, and have delivered my body from destruction” [Col. 0624C] (Ecclus. LI).

Fire of this kind does not wear down our mind by making it sad, but fattens it by making it joyful. This appeared in that brother who, sustained on bread and water for a year, appeared after the year fat and cheerful, as though strengthened in the Lord. For without interruption, in his cell, with much gladness and exultation, he had given thanks to God because God had recalled him from the world, joined him to the fellowship of the saints, and rescued him from hell. So also it often occurs in our communities: there are young men who, although nourished on the driest foods, are nevertheless more robust and better colored than when formerly in the world they ate the most delicate foods. This was prefigured long ago in Daniel and his companions, who exchanged royal foods [Col. 0624D] for vegetables and water (Dan. I).

We also have a fiery tongue when we do not wish to be saved alone, but are concerned for the salvation of others, laboring fervently in teaching or effectively in exhorting on behalf of others. Both functions of the tongue must be fiery, because a cold prayer does not rise to heaven, nor does a lukewarm exhortation kindle the mind. This was also the third reason why the Holy Spirit came with sound, fire, and tongue.

A fourth reason may also be adduced: he came with these three signs in order to signify that, in the same order in which he has now come to confer his grace upon us, he will come to judgment to demand an account of the gifts he has bestowed. For it is read concerning the second coming of the Lord Jesus: “He [Col. 0625A] who is to come in the Holy Spirit to judge the living and the dead, and to judge the world by fire” [Note: [Col. 0625D] Ecclesiastical Office.]. But if he will come in the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit too will come with him. The Holy Spirit himself, I say, will effect judicial discrimination in the Son, because he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. He will come with the Son—that is, in the person of the Son, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily; that is, he who is most perfectly full of God’s power, wisdom, holiness, and goodness. For as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Son is in the Holy Spirit and the Holy Spirit in the Son.

Therefore he will come to judgment with sound, fire, and tongue. The sound at judgment will be sudden, because calamity will be sudden. For as in the days of Noah [Col. 0625B] people were eating and drinking, and so forth, until the day Noah entered the ark and all were taken away, so will the coming of the Son of Man be (Matt. XXIV). “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ calamity will come suddenly, because the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (I Thess. V). Therefore the sound will be sudden—that is, terror sudden—and an immense fire will come with the sound, not upon only one hundred and twenty persons but upon the whole world. It will not only be bright but also most burning.

Perhaps it will be harmful to the unjust and harmless to the just, as the Babylonian fire was to the three youths in the furnace: it did them no harm at all, yet burned the Chaldeans standing nearest the furnace. Moreover, the fiery tongue is nothing other than [Col. 0625C] the Judge’s definitive sentence, by which he will say to the reprobate: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire,” and so forth (Matt. XXV); but to the elect: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and so forth (ibid.). The former will be fiery—that is, most grievous—to the reprobate; but fiery—that is, most bright, dear, and beneficial—to those to whom it is said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

May Jesus Christ our Lord, the Judge of the living and the dead, bring us to that kingdom: he who comes and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST, III

“Divine fire has come” [Note: [Col. 0626D] Ecclesiastical Office.]. There is good fire and bad fire; divine fire and diabolical fire. [Col. 0625D] Bad and diabolical fire is of one kind the fire of guilt, namely concupiscence; of another kind the fire of punishment, namely Gehenna. Neither fire ever says, “Enough”; each is insatiable. In contrast to this evil fire, the fire which came today upon Christ’s disciples is called divine.

The word “has come,” however, declares the fire of grace, not the fire of glory, which has not yet come. Therefore this time is called the time of grace, not the time of glory. Divine fire—that is, the fire of divine grace—has now come, that is, has come to us abundantly, so that where sin has abounded, grace may superabound. Behold, dearest brethren, God’s grace offers itself to all. It lies within us either to receive it or [Col. 0626A] to reject it. It knocks at the doors of each person; if anyone opens to it, it will enter that person—not merely one person, but every individual.

For it is fire; it is not diminished by being distributed, but rather increased. I say increased, not in its own substance, but in participation. Let no one excuse himself by impossibility, saying that he cannot receive it. For it is fire, which all can feel either as burning them or warming them. Those who approach fire kindly are warmed, but those who vigorously repel it are burned. So God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (I Pet. V). “The valleys abound in grain” (Ps. LXIV), and “waters pass through the midst of the mountains” (Ps. CIII); but “lightnings strike the highest mountains” (Horace, Book II, Ode 10).

[Col. 0626B] This fire shines in some, but in others is hidden. It shines in the elect who are already acting well; it is hidden in elect persons who are still erring and still need correction, like fire in dead coals that must still be rekindled.

Let him who has received this fire see that he does not lose what he has received, but preserves it forever. For this, fuel to feed it is necessary. Therefore, as is read in the Law: “Wood must be placed upon it each day, so that this fire may burn continually upon the altar” (Lev. LXII). By the wood which is the fuel of fire I understand examples of saints, counsels of teachers, or the reading of divine commandments; or certainly the continual remembrance of grievous sins [Col. 0626C] built upon the foundation of faith and to be purged through the fire of most severe repentance. These things must be laid on every morning—that is, considered at the beginning of every temptation drawing one toward vain glory—and likewise in the evening, that is, in every temptation suggesting useless sadness. Thus the fire, that is, the fervor of good work, will always burn upon the altar of the heart.

Let no one despair that he cannot be cleansed by God’s grace as though too filthy, or illumined as though overshadowed by thickest darkness. For it is fire which subdues all things, and by which a spark is struck even from the hardest stones. Likewise, let no one think that he has deserved it by his works or can preserve it by his merits. For it is fire, which moves of itself, moves another by itself, and is always in motion. Likewise, “the Spirit breathes where he wills, and we do not know whence it comes” (John III)—that is, for what merits of ours it comes to us when it comes—“nor whither it goes” [Col. 0626D], that is, why it leaves us when it leaves for a time. This often happens even to the righteous, though they are conscious of nothing against themselves.

But because fire is always in motion, it either increases or diminishes; so too God’s grace. We either progress in it or decline; there is no middle state, because fire cannot remain in the same condition. Let no one, then, neglect God’s grace. It is fire, and neglected fire is extinguished. Hence: “Do not neglect the grace of God which is in you” (I Tim. IV). And elsewhere: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” [Col. 0627A] (I Thess. V). Not to neglect God’s grace is to exercise oneself in the grace given with every fervor of devotion.

Likewise, let no one complain that he has received little grace. It is fire, and fire grows from a little thing into immensity. Similarly, anyone can make the grace received great from small beginnings, if he does not neglect it. But fire does not pass to things too far away; it imparts itself to those who draw near. So God’s grace does not go to those who distance themselves, but distances itself from them, as it is written: “He did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Ps. CXVIII). Therefore the Prophet invites us, saying: “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII).

Nothing is so contrary to fire as water, and nothing more opposes God’s grace than lust, as the Apostle says: “Corruption shall not possess incorruption” (I Cor. XV). Fire is neither cold nor lukewarm nor slightly hot, but fervent and blazing. So God’s grace does not remain in the cold or lukewarm, but in those fervent in spirit. Hence in the Apocalypse: “Would that you were hot or cold; but because you are lukewarm, I shall vomit you from my mouth” (Apoc. III). This means: Would that you either burned with Christianity or were faithless; for then I would not taste you, being food or drink unknown to me, and thus you would not cause me nausea. But because you bear the name of Christian, I cannot help testing what you taste like; and because I find you lukewarm, you provoke nausea and vomiting in me.

This should be understood generally concerning all Christians, but especially [Col. 0627C] concerning us monks: for us, who have professed the fervor of righteousness, it is worse to be found lukewarm after the vow than to have been cold before the vow. Are not those lukewarm who immerse themselves in earthly consolations, seek no heavenly things, and do not aspire to heaven? What have such people of divine fire—of fire which is always borne upward and moves and raises things upward? Certainly, those not moved upward are not led by the Spirit of God; indeed, not even by the human spirit, but by the spirit of a beast, which always follows the flesh and is borne downward.

Divine fire also signifies the effective ardor from which the order of Seraphim was created. St. Dionysius describes it as follows [Note: [Col. 0627D] *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.]:

> “For their perpetual motion about divine things—unceasing, hot, keen, and most fervent; intensely directed by a self-sufficient and ever inflexible motion; drawing those subject to them upward and actively assimilating them, reheating them and reviving them to like warmth; heavenly, fiery, and purifying as a whole burnt offering; unconfined, inextinguishable, and ever possessed of a light-bearing and illuminating property—these characteristics teach the names or manifestations of the Seraphim: investigating, or dispelling, and making manifest every darkening unholiness.”

These are the words of blessed Dionysius—indeed, thunderclaps—which bring more astonishment and admiration than knowledge. Yet they seem to refer to the nature of love. For the entire life, activity, and every affection of the Seraphim is love for God and neighbor, which is signified by the foregoing words. Let us say a few things about them, passing over them rather than expounding them, and divining rather than disputing.

The construction must be begun from the end, thus: “The names or manifestations of the Seraphim teach their motion.” That is, the interpretation and explanation of the name *seraphim*, which is plural in number. He said “names” or “manifestations” in the plural because the interpretation of the name *seraphim* is not single but multiple. *Seraphim* is interpreted as “the beginning of their mouth,” or “burning ones,” or “those who set on fire.” The first interpretation signifies that these spirits hold the first place around God and are first to speak God’s secrets and praises; the second signifies how they burn with love of God; the third [Col. 0628B] how they set others aflame with love of neighbor.

He therefore says: “The names or manifestations of the Seraphim”—that is, the multiple interpretation of this name *seraphim*, which manifests its meaning—“teach their perpetual motion,” and so forth; that is, it demonstrates that those spirits always and unceasingly move about divine things; “hot,” that is, that they are warm; “keen,” that is, that they penetrate; and “most fervent,” that is, that by penetrating they are rendered more fervent for further penetration. “It teaches,” he says, “motion,” that is, the mobility of their movement, that is, their affection—an intense movement, that is, an affection tending toward God, and perhaps inward. For it is thus read later in another translation: namely, perhaps entering into God himself [Col. 0628C].

What he said, “perhaps,” was not intended so much to express doubt as to temper the statement: as though he were saying, “I mean an affection perhaps inward,” that is, not utterly inward, yet nevertheless inward. For whatever enters into God is truly inward, but not utterly inward; because not all his secrets are penetrable by created spirits, nor can he be known within except by himself alone, as the Apostle says: “No one knows the things of a human being except the human spirit which is in him; so also no one has known the things of God”—supply, fully and completely—“except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). Hence he had also said beforehand, “around divine things.” He did not say “in divine things,” but “around divine things.” However far these most blessed spirits enter into the knowledge of God [Col. 0628D], they are always, as it were, around, not as it were, within. They are indeed within, with regard to what they grasp; but they are around, with regard to what they do not perceive. Hence he says “around divine things” in the plural, not “around God,” because in God there are many things knowable by blessed spirits, but also many incomprehensible things. This, then, is “perhaps inward”: that is, not unto the fullness, so to speak, of divine inwardness. Or, if it is read “not in need,” it means an affection not frustrated of its desire, but wholly fulfilling its desire; and “unbending,” that is, not turning back upon itself in weariness. And this is, as it were, an explanation of what he had said, “intent”: that is, always tending toward God [Col. 0629A] and never turning itself away from him.

Therefore “mobile” signifies the swiftness of their affection. For their motion—or rather, mobility—is nothing other than the supreme agility, rapidity, swiftness, or rather flight, of their will or affection, longing, or desire. Hence they are depicted not only with feet but also with feathers and wings; because, just as a bird’s feather is light, pleasant, bright, and carries upward, so too is their affection. Our affections, however, are called the feet or steps of the soul. Thus the Prophet says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out” (Ps. 72), that is, my affections almost slipped into an evil deed. And Gregory well says [Note: [Col. 0629D] Homily on the Gospels]: “To will to do something is already to go there in the mind.” But if our affections, which through the conflict of flesh and spirit suffer much slowness, are sometimes called wings even in saints still placed in the flesh [Col. 0629B], how much more rightly are the affections of those who are wholly spirit!

The swiftness of their affection, therefore, is signified by this word “mobile”; but their purity and holiness by what follows, “around divine things.” For they desire nothing but God. Their perseverance is signified by what is added, “and unceasing”; the fervour of this perseverance is marked when it is said, “and hot.” For something may move always and yet languidly; as the river Arar, which always runs, but so slowly that those watching doubt in which direction it runs. But because there is a certain fervour without effectiveness, “and sharp” follows: [Col. 0629C] that is, penetrating and penetrative, which signifies attainment of the thing desired. But because attainment of a desired thing usually diminishes the desire of one attaining it with respect to the thing possessed, he adds, “and super-fervent,” which signifies a kind of bubbling-over of heavenly fervour. It fills them to satiety and in some manner flows out again into desire, as we see in a pot constantly boiling: through continual heat it is filled to the brim and emptied to the bottom; and in being filled it is emptied, and in being emptied it is filled.

But because the liquid that boils in those spirits is inexhaustible, the heat from which that boiling proceeds is unquenchable, and the boiling itself cannot diminish, therefore in them there are always “sharp” and “super-fervent.” And because they always penetrate into God [Col. 0629D] and always desire to penetrate, because, as a certain holy man says, spiritual delights increase desire in the mind while satisfying it, according to that saying: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24).

Thus both thirst and satiety are delightfully impressed upon them together. For they desire without labour, because satiety accompanies desire; and they are satisfied without weariness, because satiety itself is always kindled from desire. Necessity is far from their thirst; weariness is far from their satiety: for those thirsting are satisfied, and those satisfied thirst. This, therefore, is what he calls “super-fervent”: superabundant from fervour, and from abundance [Col. 0630A] boiling over. For this “super-fervent” signifies that immeasurable sea of divine joy into which their “sharpness” penetrates and plunges itself. The ineffably knowable overflow of that joy does not blunt or dull that most powerful sharpness of the liquid, so as to recoil in weariness; rather, it animates and renews it to penetrate in desire.

For that vast heat of vehement fire which ever boils over in the highest furnace of that order is nothing other than the holy vehemence of divine love. The liquid, however, which in the best and most tested vessels of that furnace boils over and bubbles from the burning of that heat, is nothing other than the torrent of divine delight, overflowing through the most capacious hearts of those spirits: that river of joy and stream of peace which surpasses [Col. 0630B] all understanding and not only transcends but also kindles the burning desire of those blessed spirits. The indescribable fineness, inexplicable subtlety, and ineffable sweetness of this liquid are signified in those supercelestial waters which are said to be suspended there in order to pour the dew of sweetness upon lower things.

Yet that joy, that delight, is called water, wine, torrent, river, and sea. Water, because it cleanses and sanctifies; wine, because it delights and gladdens; torrent, because it rekindles and renews desire; river, because it abounds and satisfies; sea, because in its immensity it transcends and surpasses every desire. By these words the Lord seems to promise Dionysius’s “super-fervent” quality: “They shall give into your bosoms a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, [Col. 0630C] and running over” (Luke 6). Elsewhere, however, he says: “With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7).

The sense of this latter passage, however, is this: if you give a small measure, you will receive a small one; if a large one, a large one. Yet you will always receive more than you give, because “they shall give into your bosoms a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.” This is also what the Apostle says: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9).

Fear of threats is a good measure; hope of promises, a pressed-down measure; observance of commandments, a shaken-together measure. The running-over measure [Col. 0630D] may be called the addition to those three things which are read in Deuteronomy: “You shall love the Lord with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6); for “with all your mind” is not added there. Yet, when the lawyer was asked by the Lord what was written in the Law, he said: “You shall love the Lord,” etc., “with all your mind” (Luke 10). The Lord not only did not rebuke this answer but confirmed it, saying: “You have answered rightly.”

Either, then, it was written in Hebrew as the lawyer answered, or in some translation, or at least an equivalent expression was present. For where our translation says thirdly, “and with all your strength,” I think “and with all your mind” is also included [Col. 0631A], because the whole strength of a human being does not consist in bodily powers alone, but also in the powers of the mind. In Deuteronomy a twofold strength is included under one member; in Luke it is divided into two members. Therefore, whatever we measure is either of the first degree, or “much” of the second, or “perfect” of the third; but overflow belongs only to rewards, not to merits.

You see, then, how Dionysius’s “super-fervent” and the Lord’s “running over” designate reward. The Lord measures back to us a good measure when he delivers us from everlasting condemnation; a pressed-down measure, when he clothes us with the first robe, in which he singularly establishes us in hope and entirely draws us out of fear; he will render a shaken-together measure when the second robe, of immortality, clothes us; but he will heap upon us the running-over measure when he grants us the eternal blessedness of his vision, which surpasses every desire [Col. 0631B].

Nor does the Lord’s measure exceed ours only in this respect, but also in every one of these degrees. For whatever we give or do is temporal and passing; whatever we are to receive is immortal and eternal. Therefore, as we cast our seeds in good works and in tears, let us not grow weary; for in its time we shall reap, if we do not fail. Woe to those who sow sparingly through avarice; woe to those who sow nothing through sloth; woe to those who sow evil through folly; woe to those who sow good things in faithlessness. The first reap sparingly; the second reap nothing; the third reap evil; the fourth also reap nothing, because [Col. 0631C] they lose their seed. Woe, I say, to the lukewarm, the lazy, the carnal, the hypocritical. But of these elsewhere.

Thus Dionysius described the burning of the seraphim toward God when he said: “Their mobility around divine things,” etc. What follows demonstrates their kindling of their neighbour; of that we say nothing at present, although it pertains sufficiently to our subject, since we are treating the fire of charity. We have said these few things in order to show, at least in part, how we ought to burn with the fire of charity. For, so that the hammer of Dionysius’s words may strike out for us some sparks of holy fervour from that furnace of the heavenly Jerusalem, let us understand the “mobile” of our love around divine things to be the purity of our affections and works, by which [Col. 0631D] we climb toward God. For our affections are our feet; the works of these feet are their steps; moreover, the “unceasing” of this mobility is perseverance in both.

The “hot” of this unceasingness is fervour in work, the most burning zeal for righteousness, and the most fervent desire for our homeland. The “sharp” of this heat is either the hope of that desire itself, which through its sharpness advances, like an anchor, after Christ the high priest even into the inner place behind the veil; or certainly our whatever-small ecstasy in contemplation. For this is the sharpness of our love in this age. By it alone, through loving, we penetrate into God. The “super-fervent” of this sharpness is the overflowing joy of contemplation itself in apprehension, as well as the overflowing astonishment from wonder. “Mobile” here [Col. 0632A] seems to signify aptitude rather than act, so that “mobile” means capable of being moved; while “unceasing” means the absence of cessation. “Mobile,” therefore, pertains to their subtle and simple nature; “unceasing,” to their perfect diligence.

Further, “hot,” “sharp,” and “super-fervent” signify both prevenient and subsequent grace. For without “hot,” not even “mobile” would be present. There is no motion without heat, nor heat without motion; but heat accelerates motion, and motion increases heat; great heat makes motion swift, and swift motion produces great heat. “Hot,” therefore, signifies preceding grace, which gave them mobility around divine things—that is, a nature fitted [Col. 0632B] to desire divine things. “Unceasing,” however, signifies that their free will has never departed from this divine grace.

“Sharp” and “super-fervent,” moreover, signify that divine grace has confirmed this steadfastness in them, so that they can no longer be unfit to understand God or only slightly fervent in loving, but are always sharp to penetrate and super-fervent to be super-fervent: that is, not merely always to enjoy, but to enjoy beyond others—namely, to enjoy more blessedly than others, as the highest angels do. To compare the whole measure of the Lord with the measure of Dionysius, we may say that the mobility of our love always being around divine things—that is, our natural aptitude to desire good things—if it is unceasing, that is, if it perseveres in good desire, is a good measure. If it not only possesses this motion unceasingly, but also glows and burns in it perseveringly, it is a pressed-down measure. If this “hot” advances as far as the “sharp” of penetrating and most joy-giving hope, it is a shaken-together measure. But if this “sharp” boils over as far as the ecstasy of contemplation, it is in some way a running-over measure. For this ecstasy exceeds nature by the gift of grace and therefore in some manner overflows.

Woe to those who always have mobility around divine things and yet never move around them. These are those who receive from God the talent of understanding and hide it in the earth or wrap it in a napkin, entangling themselves in secular business [Col. 0632D] or sweating at the works of the flesh (2 Tim. 4). Woe also to those who have sharpness around divine things but not unceasingness. These are those who believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away (Luke 8). Woe also to those who have unceasingness but do not have heat: always living in religion, yet always lax and lukewarm in their manner of life, and not fervent in spirit. For they ought not to have eaten the Paschal lamb not only raw, but not even boiled in water, but only roasted with fire (Exod. 12).

There are some who have the “hot” of this love but do not have the “sharp.” These are the good, simple, unlearned persons, who have much devotion and love but little knowledge. “But it is much better,” as Saint Jerome says, “to possess holy rusticity than sinful learning or eloquence” [Col. 0633A]. The sharpness of persons such as these is not the sharpness of heat but of cold; not the sharpness of fire, but the sharpness of iron, which always lies useless and ineffective if it lacks the force of that which burns. Its very usefulness and effectiveness, moreover, are more often employed in the service of death than in the aid of salvation.

Not so the sharpness of fire, which is always useful and effective in itself. It will not be idle if the assistance of an alien power is lacking, but will always accomplish by its own strength what belongs to it. The sharpness of such talent is not merely idle but utterly pernicious if the sharpness of divine love is absent. For what then? Will it not lie dull and consumed with rust, unless it is set, as it were, to some whetstone and sharpened by the constant practice of study and exercise? But if diligent exercise is devoted to unfruitful arts and to letters that signify nothing, what profit, what gain comes of it? Every subtler sharpness of knowledge is like an ear of grain: nothing is finer, nothing more useless. So too there is much subtlety in the liberal disciplines, and if it is not directed to the love of God, there is no usefulness.

But if someone applies himself to the divine Scriptures and does not fulfil the commands of Scripture itself, what salvation comes to him from that—or rather, what destruction does not come? Will those who are mighty in the Scriptures, if they are not also mighty in good works, therefore not suffer torments mightily? And certainly these especially, as Jeremiah says, “have broken the yoke, burst the bonds” (Jer. 5).

Who now is corrected even through knowledge of the Scriptures? [Col. 0633C] Who uses his learning for salvation? Rather, who does not use it for his own ruin? Whom will you find, even among those who have attained knowledge of the divine Scriptures and belch forth sacred letters, whom an unlearned and licentious person does not conquer more by licentiousness than he himself conquers by learning? Which of all the salaried soldiers of the Church does not serve his own belly or appetite more than Jesus Christ, bridegroom of the Church, from whose inheritance he lives?

Alas! How rarely virtue and learning meet today! By I know not what bond of a new faction, lusts and letters have clung together. This companionship is no less monstrous than destructive. For what have the former to do with the latter, since the latter profess the good of virtue in order to teach it, while the former unteach and detest it? Yet when has this monstrosity not reigned? From ancient days the most celebrated philosophers had concubines—not secretly, but, as Jerome says, publicly. This monstrosity still reigns, when owls fly by day and horned owls no longer flee the sun.

What cleric is ashamed to appear in public elaborately groomed? Who is ashamed to walk with a soft and womanish gait—indeed, who is ashamed to be a woman? You may see those who ought to have given others an example of humility, modesty, gravity, and penitence, dressed with excessive care: hair parted at the crown, locks curled, face closely shaven, skin polished with pumice, head uncovered, shoulders bared, sleeves flowing loose, arms tattooed, hands shod, feet gloved, groins slit open. And all day they search before a mirror for what still may be lacking to the adornment of their appearance and to the dishonour of their order and body [Col. 0634A]; and thus they proceed in public in brightest green clothing, with foulest mind, rings gleaming from their fingers, and eyes laughing from their souls.

Finally, they are compelled to wear on the very crown of their head that tonsure as though it were Christ’s stigma; yet, lest a larger circle of hair should diminish its coiffure or make it rough, they trim it into so tiny a circle that it looks more like the mark of a body for sale than of clerical order. And do these men dare publicly to profess doctrine concerning the most sacred mysteries of the holy Scriptures, with reddened cheeks, puffed-up jaws, swollen throat, protruding belly, and words choked off? What could these men persuade me about voluntary poverty and Christian abstinence, when they show themselves to know the harshness of the cross and the squalor of apostolic poverty as little as they show themselves to despise them? Or what can these rosy teachers, pretty by art rather than nature, say at length about chastity among the unchaste—men whose unchastity, I do not say is marked, but openly proclaimed by reputation, face and eye, countenance and dress, speech and gait, food and company? Yet they are all too ready to talk, sufficiently thorny in disputation, and keen in learning:

> But if the boy of Virgil lacked  
> a tolerable lodging, all would fall from their hair.

[The quoted verse is textually corrupt or incomplete as supplied.]

What is more, they even profess that their intellect is sharpened by this kind of canine pleasure. I lie if I have not myself heard this from some of them. Yet plainly they had not read that saying of the wisest of men: “Nothing is so deadly to intellectual powers as luxury.” But perhaps the one who said this was a Stoic: did they draw this opinion, of muddy teaching, from some pig out of Epicurus’s herd? Yet Epicurus himself, the advocate of pleasure, is read to have commended nothing more, beyond the easy pleasure gained from letters, than sobriety and continence, even to the point of refraining from taking a wife.

Certainly Marcus Cato thus defines an orator for his son: “An orator, Marcus my son, is a good man skilled in speaking.” “Go now,” says Seneca, “and seek an orator among these dissolute and exposed men, who are never men except in shamefulness.” Go, and seek theologians and preachers among the same men. Or does it belong to an orator in the court [Col. 0634D] to be a good man, while an orator in the Church is to be a lustful man? To such lustful theologian-preachers the Lord cries out: “Why do you recount my righteous ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49).

Woe to boys and youths entrusted to teachers of this kind, from whom every sort of honourableness must first be unlearned before one letter is learned. Pliny did not speak so to someone concerning his son: “Entrust him,” he says, “to a teacher so that he may first learn character, then eloquence, which is badly learned without character.” And Quintilian, this Pliny’s teacher, says that pupils must beware not only of the charge of indecency but even of the suspicion of such a charge. For this reason he by no means permitted adolescents [Col. 0635A] to learn in school mixed together with boys.

But now, though the disgrace of unchastity is condemned by both human and divine laws, and the title of chastity shines everywhere through the Son of the Virgin, nevertheless, I know not how, lusts and vices have entered into alliance, as though a conspiracy had been made against it. So much so that among very many people it has now become a rule that a person of keen intellect can scarcely become continent. See how dangerous it is for us to be sharp and not found hot: that is, clever in evil and not fervent in good, according to the saying: “They are wise to do evil, but do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4); and the Lord in the Gospel: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16).

For many today are eloquent against justice and learned in favour of falsehood: wise to do evil, eloquent to attack truth. These are they who have turned the crafty knowledge of civil and ecclesiastical law into an art of fishing and bird-catching: with their tangled nets they ensnare the poor and bait the rich. And this is enough concerning the sharpness of cunning. Since above we said that the gift of natural talent is signified by “mobile,” it is better to say that the sharpness of cold signifies fear and reverence. That cold is sharp is clear from this:

> And the blood congeals cold with fear.

And the Prophet says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). Therefore to have the sharpness of fear without the sharpness of heat is dangerous—indeed most pernicious—because [Col. 0635C] to fear without hope is nothing other than to despair. The sharpness of fear always looks, as it were, downward; the sharpness of love always stretches upward, because it is the sharpness of fire. Fear looks toward judgment; hope toward mercy. Unless the sharpness of hope, which stretches upward, draws along with it the sharpness of fear, which looks downward, the sharpness of fear must fasten the sinner’s mind downward and thus crush it in despair. Although someone who does not love may be able to hope, no one who does not love can possess the sharpness of hope. For this sharpness never proceeds except from the heat of fervour.

Therefore, lest the sharpness of fear prevail, let us sing mercy to the Lord; and lest hope presume vainly, let us reflect upon the Lord’s judgment. Let this be said concerning “sharp.” Further, those have “super-fervent” but not “sharp” who burn for this world and have neither hope in the Lord nor fear of hell. Such joy may indeed be called “super-fervent,” that is, bubbling up superfluously and vainly in the hearts of fools. But to us it is said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, that you will weep and lament, while the world will rejoice” (John 16). Yet consolation immediately follows when it is added: “But your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (ibid.).

Take from me, Lord, vain and worldly joy, so that at last I may someday attain that heavenly, secure, solid, and truly super-fervent joy; and may see with my eyes that seraphic mobility—ever mobile around you, and unceasing [Col. 0636A], hot, sharp, and super-fervent. And grant me meanwhile mobility for seeking, sharpness for finding happily, and super-fervour for cleaving eternally. Amen.

## SERMON XIX ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, I

“Hear me, divine fruits; and bear fruit like a rose planted by streams of water” (Ecclus. 39). A rose is commonly praised for two goods, beauty and usefulness. Its beauty is considered in two respects, colour and form. The rose’s colour is then outstanding when its petals are kindled with flaming redness into loveliness, except that below, near the roots of the petals, a little most delicate and somewhat shadowed whiteness shines through. Yet five short [Col. 0636B] green pointed sepals above conceal this from without by their protection, like little pyramids constructed around it.

The form of the rose is of most perfect beauty when its petals do not shrink from view by remaining entirely closed, nor grow lax through drooping backward; but when the globular roundness of its moderately budded, spreading cluster expands and rises with manly firmness, so that the modestly smiling little cup-like [*calathil abellula*, uncertain as supplied] seems to seek a kiss from above. Moreover, the greater the number of petals with which the cup is packed, the more it approaches the glory of the eyes, and their number adds to the charm of the sight. Such is the material beauty of the rose; now let us consider its mystical meaning.

That delicate whiteness near the roots of the rose-petals is the perpetual purity of heart in the Virgin Mary, proceeding from the very birth, so to speak, of her affections, as from the roots of the petals. The fivefold guarding of the bodily senses, like an impregnable outer defence, covered and protected it; she always preserved it perfectly whole and advanced it to the purity of perpetual sinlessness [Col. 0636C]. And therefore it is so delicate and shadowed that, even today, some theologians of our time can neither see, understand, nor believe it. They perversely interpret Augustine’s authority, though he clearly asserts it, saying [Note: [Col. 0635D] *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 20]: “When sins are under discussion, I do not wish any question whatsoever to be raised concerning the Blessed Mary, Mother of the Lord, on account of the honour of the Lord.”

And as though someone asked him why he said this, he gives the reason, saying: “For from this we know that more grace was bestowed upon her for conquering sin in every respect, because she merited to conceive him who could have no sin.” Whenever sins are under discussion, he says—that is, whether the sins of the young or old are discussed, whether the sins of adolescents or boys, whether those of infants or of mothers giving birth, whatever sins of any human age are discussed—Mary must always be excepted. But if she had any personal sin, she did not conquer sin in every respect. But she did conquer sin in every respect. Therefore, she never had personal sin.

What could be stated more plainly? Yet our theologians imagine that Augustine meant this only from [Col. 0637A] the time when Blessed Mary conceived the Lord. But Blessed Bernard understood it more truly and better, saying [Note: [Col. 0637D] Sermon 4 on the Assumption]: “Far be it from us to believe that the house of the Virgin ever had anything of personal defilement!” And he adds: “But if she drew the stain of original sin from her parents, Christian piety forbids us to believe that she was less sanctified in the womb than Jeremiah, or less filled with the Holy Spirit than Saint John.”

Whom should we believe more: Augustine and Bernard, men full of holiness and learning, most noble doctors of the Church; or modern teachers? Therefore I do not approve that opinion which Peter Lombard sets down in his *Sentences*, saying [Note: [Col. 0638D] In the Third Book of the *Sentences*, distinction 3]: “The flesh of Christ was always bound to sin before it was united to the Word, just as the Virgin’s remaining flesh was.” Is this the honour which Augustine commands us to render to the Mother of God: that when sins are discussed, we should entertain no question about her? Therefore I most firmly believe, do not doubt in any way, and confidently declare that Holy Scripture by no means includes Mary the Lord’s mother.

For it is written: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3)—that is, says Blessed Jerome, as long as the seed of God remains in him. But the seed, which is the Holy Spirit, always remained in Mary from her first sanctification, preserving her not at the same degree of holiness but always sanctifying her more and more. Hence in the Song of Songs she is said to advance by being born, namely, “like the dawn rising,” whose brightness is never diminished from its first rising [Col. 0637C], but always grows. Therefore, just as Mary was born holy and without sin, so she remained always holy and without sin, always advancing in holiness and brightness.

To what sin, therefore, was Christ’s flesh bound before it was assumed by the Word, or the Virgin’s remaining flesh? Every sin is either original or actual. Original sin had already been remitted; she had committed no actual sin, since the seed of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—remained in her and preserved her holy. For how could he desert that temple which he had once dedicated to divine use? Thus the Holy Spirit is said to have come upon her to bring about the conception of the Word, as one who had never previously departed from her, who by always remaining in her had kept her immune from sin and [Col. 0637D] made her abound in progress of holiness. But then he came upon her more abundantly than upon any saint ever.

Jerome, in Book 3 of the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*: “We too say that a human being can be without sin, if he wills, for a time, according to place, according to bodily weakness, as long as the mind is attentive, as long as no string in the lyre is loosened by any vice. But if he relaxes himself even a little, like one who draws a skiff against the current, if he lets go his hands, he immediately slips backward and is carried by the flowing waters where he does not wish to go. Thus human nature, if it relaxes itself even a little, learns its fragility and recognizes that it cannot do many things.”

According to this comparison of Jerome [Col. 0638A], I say that the grace of the Holy Spirit always kept Mary’s heart attentive and, as it were, drew the skiff against the current, so that what she could not do by nature she could do by grace.

What Jerome says afterward, therefore—“We must reserve perpetual sinlessness for God alone”—is true. For he alone can possess this through himself, without another’s assistance. But Mary could possess it not from herself but through preserving grace. For, as Jerome says in the same book: “Whatever depends upon the will of another does not belong to the one whom you maintain can do it, but to the one without whom it cannot exist.” Was it therefore impossible for the Word of God to cleanse from every sin, before assuming it, the flesh which he was to take from the Virgin? [Col. 0638B] Or perhaps he willed it but was unable? But this is the same question concerning the Virgin’s remaining flesh, which they say was all bound to sin until that time.

Where, then, is the Lord’s saying, “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20)? For he did not honour her as he ought if, from the time he could do so, he did not cleanse her from sin—her from whom he would begin to be a human being in flesh and soul. What, then, had the Holy Spirit done when he sanctified her in the womb? Had he perhaps sanctified her in part, not wholly—that is, in her soul alone, not in her flesh? But what could be more absurd? It remains, therefore, that from that time she was wholly sanctified in flesh and soul. Therefore from that time her flesh ceased to be bound to sin.

[Col. 0638C] But they say that Jeremiah and John also were sanctified in the womb, and yet afterward the flesh of each was bound to sin. What comparison is either of them to Mary, to the Lady? Are we then to believe that the Holy Spirit bestowed equal grace upon them and upon her? Far from it! “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). The same may be said of Mary: Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lady, the mother of the King of angels? I do not mean her as already existing as mother, but as yet to be mother: she who from eternity was predestined, as it were, to be the spouse of the Father of spirits, that she might have a son in common with him and be mother of the Son of God, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, temple of the whole Trinity, the proper house of Wisdom [Col. 0638D], as it is written: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9).

Wisdom always acts wisely, as Jerome says; therefore it always kept its house clean. For what wise person, building a house for himself to inhabit, would not wish from the very beginning of construction, if he could, that it should lack every defect? Certainly, just as it was fitting that Blessed Mary should remain always clean from every sin after the conception, because she had conceived the cleanser of the world, so it was fitting that she should remain always clean from every sin even before the conception of her Son, so that she might be made worthy of such a conception.

In the Book of Kings (3 Kings 6) it is read that, while the house of God was being built, no hammer or axe was heard in it. In this passage, besides the historical sense concerning the stone house and the anagogical sense concerning the pilgrim Church to be raised to heaven, there is a third, allegorical sense concerning the Virgin Mary. While she was being built into God’s house—that is, throughout the period in which she was nurtured by the Holy Spirit before the Lord’s conception—no hammer or axe was heard in her by human, angelic, or divine ears [Col. 0639A]: that is, no sins of act or thought.

For by the hammer, with which we strike outwardly, is understood the external sin of deed, including speech; by the axe, which is also set to the root of the tree—that is, to the intention of the heart—is understood the sin of thought, which is always the root of wrongful action. Hence Isaiah says (ch. 1): “Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes.” Therefore, while Mary, the house of God, was being built—that is, while she was still being prepared so that God made human, made in her and from her, might dwell in her not only spiritually but also bodily—no hammer and axe were heard in her. For throughout the whole period in which this virgin was being built into the most exalted house, to be set above all the heavens, after the first sanctification which she received in her mother’s womb, there was no sin in her, either outward or inward.

Wisdom, therefore, in building her house left no work of folly remaining. And what is the work of folly but sin? Thus Wisdom also hewed out seven pillars; that is, she placed in her every necessary support of spiritual [Col. 0639C] grace, for the avoidance of every sin and the increase of every virtue. To what fault, then, shall we say that the walls of this house were subject after the first sanctification? That is, to what sin was the body of this most holy Virgin bound? Good God! To what sin could the flesh of this Virgin have been bound—she whom from eternity you had chosen as your mother; whom in her mother’s womb you had wholly sanctified and filled with the Holy Spirit more than John, your forerunner; whom, before you assumed flesh from her and in her, you had always cherished and nourished with your Holy Spirit; whom you had wholly anticipated with blessings of sweetness, wholly instructed with heavenly disciplines, wholly adorned inwardly and outwardly with the gold of chastity and of every spiritual wisdom [Col. 0639D], and wholly filled with the treasure of humility? By what avenue, then, could sin enter a garden so enclosed, a fountain so sealed?

For she is not called an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain, or a closed gate merely on account of chastity, but because of her perfect guardianship of holiness and righteousness, and because she was free from every offence. Thus both her body and her heart were guarded with every vigilance, so that from the time of her first sanctification no stain of sin could ever enter her in any respect. Hence in the Song of Songs she is called, by antonomasia, “beautiful.” For, as the eminent orator says: “She is not beautiful whose leg or arm is praised, but she whose whole face has taken away admiration from its individual parts.” Those five little pouches surrounding the rose at its lower part, shaped like pyramids, signify this perfection and the unceasing guardianship of heart and body, as is said in praise of her in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like a tower of ivory.”

For by the neck the head is joined to the body; and that neck fittingly and beautifully signifies Mary, who, after Christ—the head of the same body, which is the Church—is its most eminent member, and our mediatrix, through whom we deserved to receive the Author of life, through whom Christ became the mediator of God and human beings. And how fittingly is that neck compared with a tower of ivory! Such a neck was suited to such a head, which upholds all things by the word [Col. 0640B] of its power; whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, and upon whom angels continually desire to look. For as it is written of this head, “The Lord has reigned; he has put on splendour; he has put on strength” (Ps. 92 [93]), so also of the neck: “Strength and beauty are her clothing” (Prov. 32). This strong woman was indeed difficult to find, but was nevertheless at last found: so strong that she, a woman among the mightiest, alone among countless persons, always triumphed over her enemies; so beautiful that she never had either spot or wrinkle of sin; and therefore the Author of all beauty loved her in a singular manner.

Rightly, therefore, is the most prudent Virgin called a tower of ivory: a woman most beautiful and at once most strong—lofty in vow, pre-eminent in merit, strong in resolve, upright in counsel, raised in desire, unconquerable by the enemy; white in virginity, pure in affection, steadfast in purity, armed with zeal for chastity; set before all as an example of holiness, placed above all as a refuge of mercy, placed around each individual as a defence in battle, and laid up for all who strive as the prize of the crown. Certainly, nothing is more beautiful or more precious than such a building because of the whiteness of ivory; nothing is stronger or more useful because of the fortification of the tower. From her very birth she was built into a tower of ivory; but thereafter she continually grew upward, until she ascended into heaven and attained that state beyond which she could not ascend.

Therefore those five pyramids of the rose signify the same thing: namely, the strength [Col. 0640D] of this ivory tower—that is, Mary, immune from every sin. Finally, no victory over sin is higher than to resist sin unto blood; and many saints, of both sexes and every age, even boys and infants, attained that perfection. The seven Maccabean brothers suffered under Antiochus Epiphanes; likewise the seven sons of St Felicity in childhood. Blessed Agnes was thirteen years old, Eulalia twelve, Justus and Pantaleo nine, Tryphon seven—to pass over many others. Since, then, it is certain that even at younger ages, where this might have seemed less credible, boys and girls have not been lacking who received from God such great grace that they shed their blood for love of him—a victory over sin than which none can be higher—how much more must this most blessed and singular Virgin be believed already to have received from God in all those earlier years what she deserved to receive more highly than all others, whatever others received, and unquestionably did receive? Otherwise, how could she deserve to become the mother of him whose servant to be is the whole merit of holiness?

It is therefore necessary that at every time of her life she should have been holier, better, more perfect, and purer than all her contemporaries—not only those living with her, but also those who had lived before her or would live after her. If, then, from the day on which a human being is born upon earth until the day on which Blessed Mary conceived the Lord, persons of both sexes are found who resisted sin unto blood, than which victory none can be greater; and if it is certain that Blessed Mary [Col. 0641B], on every day until she conceived the Lord, conquered sin more strongly than anyone else: then it is shown by incontrovertible reasoning that she always conquered sin most perfectly. Therefore throughout that whole period she was without personal sin. And from another’s sin, if she had ever had it, she had already been cleansed. To what sin, then, was that most holy flesh bound?

Just as baptized infants are without sin for some period, so the blessed Virgin was without sin at every time; and what nature could not do, grace could do. Did not St Nicholas, in infancy, by grace and not by nature, suck at the breast only once on the fourth and sixth days of the week? Did not St John leap in his mother’s womb at the greeting of the Virgin Mary, filled with the Holy Spirit? If, therefore, the Holy Spirit came so abundantly upon Mary that her greeting filled both mother and child with that same Spirit, how much more abundantly must that Spirit be thought to have come earlier into her, while she herself was still in her mother’s womb! John was already an infant of six months when he was filled with the Holy Spirit. Therefore Mary must be believed to have been filled with the Holy Spirit earlier and more fully than John.

Certainly, when Gabriel greeted her, saying, “Hail, full of grace,” she was already without every sin. For she could not be full of grace unless she were empty of every sin. For although other saints are said to have been full of the Holy Spirit, they were not wholly without sin, as James says: “In many things we all offend” (Jas. 3); [Col. 0641D] and John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1). We have already said that Mary, according to Augustine’s testimony, must always be excepted whenever sin is under discussion.

> [Note: Col. 0641D, *On Nature and Grace*.]

But not all fullnesses are equal, for not all vessels have the same capacity. The Holy Spirit fills different persons with his grace, but in different measure; for the souls of the saints are like different vessels, some more capacious than others. Therefore, when someone is said to be filled with the Holy Spirit or with God’s grace, this must be understood according to that person’s capacity, not according to an absolute fullness of measure. Now among all created spirits, both angelic and [Col. 0642A] human, excepting the soul of Christ, none was ever so capable of the fullness of divine grace as the soul of blessed Mary. Thus no one was so full of grace as she.

Finally, when saints are said to be filled with the Holy Spirit, that filling should be understood as intermittent, not continuous. For the Holy Spirit comes to assist us and sometimes withdraws to test us. Therefore David prayed: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50 [51]); and elsewhere: “Do not utterly forsake me” (Ps. 118 [119]). But blessed Mary must be believed to have been filled with divine grace not at intervals but continuously; yet not always with equal fullness, but according to the progress of age. The fullness of grace continually increased in her, so that she always became better than herself, as is written of David that he continually advanced and became stronger than himself. Yet the Holy Spirit did not remain upon her in the same proportion as upon the Lord. Rather, the Holy Spirit remained upon her to the extent that he continually sanctified her inwardly and outwardly, and kept her holy, so that from that point onward sin could enter her in no respect.

Although, therefore, she was always perfect according to her age, she nevertheless became more perfect than herself from day to day. For she was not always equally perfect; this belonged to Christ alone, who, at once a wayfarer and one who had attained, possessed an always equal perfection—equally perfect in his mother’s womb and on the scaffold of the cross—according to that prophecy of Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). He was called a man even while enclosed in the womb of the Virgin who enclosed him, because there he possessed as great a perfection as he did afterward when encompassed by the Synagogue. For from the time when the spirit of the Lord—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and so forth—rested upon him, which occurred at his conception, he immediately stood upon such a summit of perfection that he could neither fall from it nor rise higher; he neither desired progress nor feared decline.

But Mary always progressed, like the rising dawn; and she never lost anything of her first sanctification, nor after it did she contract a stain of sin in soul or body, as blessed Bernard truly affirms. This is signified by that most subtle and somewhat obscure whiteness lying below near [Col. 0642D] the roots of the rose’s leaves, enclosed, as we have said, by the green and black grouping of five pyramids as an outward guard. For the heart can never be kept inwardly under its own guard unless the guarding of the bodily senses keeps watch outwardly. For, as the prophet laments, “Death enters through our windows.” Hence Isaiah: “He who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil—he shall dwell on high” (Isa. 33).

Let us now turn to the rose colour. In Mary the rose colour signifies three things: the blush of modesty, the ardour of charity, and zeal for righteousness. The first, modesty, fearing to displease the inward Inspector, always and everywhere turned most perfectly away from every evil. The second, in charity desiring to please the eternal Lover of human souls, always and everywhere sought to do good. The third, knowing that she must stand before the supreme Knower, always and everywhere resisted sin and freely yet discreetly rebuked the sinner, as befitted virginal modesty; most ready, if necessary, to shed her own blood and lay down her life in defence of justice. By this threefold endeavour Mary always portrayed herself according to the mirror of Scripture and the testimony of conscience, and thus became, before all mortals, beautiful and delightful in her delights, pleasing to God and angels.

Because of modesty she always loved solitude; because of charity’s ardour she always persisted in prayer; because of [Col. 0643B] zeal for justice, while she was still a little girl being brought up in the Temple, as is read in the book of her Nativity, she watched lest her fellow virgins should sin even in speech. Each of these three virtues contains perfection; and whoever has one has all three. For modesty, as Augustine says, is nothing other than a certain fear of displeasing. But what is fear of displeasing except fear of offending and of giving offence to God? Worldly modesty fears to displease people; the modesty of saints fears God more than human beings, conscience more than reputation. Yet it neglects neither, but attends to both. This modesty may be defined specifically as follows: modesty is a conscience that fears to displease its Creator and truly desires to please him.

This is the righteous fear of the Lord, enduring for ever and ever, containing all virtues. For through fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil, which is the effect of modesty; and the one who fears God will do good, which is the effect of charity, for the proof of love is the performance of a deed. And the one who fears God neglects nothing—that is, neither great nor small things, neither what ought to be done nor what ought to be omitted—and this is the effect of zeal for justice. In modesty alone, when praiseworthy, as in charity, the whole old and new Law is contained, all sacred teaching is embraced, every divine command is fulfilled, and all righteousness is perfected. To sum everything up briefly, modesty is the virtue in which resides all beauty of the soul: [Col. 0643D] like the redness of roses, the whiteness of lilies, the purple of violets, the transparency of crystal, the clearness of sapphire, the greenness of emerald, the beauty of pearl, the splendour of topaz, and the radiance of carbuncle.

What shall certain utterly black professors of modesty in speech, destroyers of it in deed, say here—shameless toward indecencies, fearless in dangers, inhuman toward human things, brazen in sinning, slow in repenting, foxes in deceiving, dogs in slandering, horses in wantonness? So much for the colour of the rose.

But the shape of the same flower, spreading into the circle of its narrower calyx, and shining round about with a natural diadem as the sign of royal eminence which it possesses above all flowers, plainly signifies that the Virgin Mary was born of royal lineage and chosen from eternity to bear the King of heaven and to be called and to be the Queen of Heaven. For as the rose is the most beautiful of flowers, so Mary is the most beautiful of women. And because among all women she obtained the singular crown of perfect beauty, she also had to obtain among all women the ornament of royal dignity. Morally, moreover, the circle of the rose signifies the rounded completeness of perfect chastity and immovable perseverance in every holiness.

The righteous person who turns away from righteousness has nothing of the rose’s circle: he draws an alpha without an omega and presents a head without a tail. For every praise is sung at the end, and every contestant is crowned not for the contest but for victory. Or again, the rose colour signifies the merit of this present life, that is, righteousness and holiness; while the little crown of its shape indicates the reward of the life to come, that is, the crown of righteousness. To this crown the rose invites us when it says: “Hear me, divine offspring, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water” (Ecclus. 39). This is the voice of Wisdom in the person of Mary. Previously it had said: “I was exalted like a palm tree in Kadesh, and like a planting of roses in Jericho” (Ecclus. 24).

Mary is not undeservedly called a rose and a planting of roses. She was a rose: martyr and Virgin, whose whole life was martyrdom and an example of perpetual chastity. Indeed, more than a virgin and more than a martyr: more than a virgin because a fruitful mother, virgin in conceiving and virgin in giving birth; more than a martyr because she suffered not in her flesh but in her mind the suffering in the flesh of her Son, not bodily but mentally—and this was a martyrdom more bitter to her [Col. 0644C] than bodily martyrdom. She was a planting of roses because she bore the rose and flower of the world, Christ, who is called “I am the flower of the field”; and truly a rose—that is, a virgin and martyr, king of virgins and martyrs.

Therefore she says: “Hear me, divine fruits.” O minds of the elect, whom divine grace regenerated through me, whom the tree of life springing from the paradise of my womb has graciously incorporated into itself and suspended upon the arms of its cross: hear me—or, as the true text has it, “obey me”—that is, always and in all things obey me. Hear me as mother, as teacher, as queen: as mother I love, as teacher I instruct, as queen I command; and I, the queen of the world, honour and exalt those who obey me. Hear me, and bear fruit like a rose planted beside streams of water; that is, by living well produce fruits worthy of martyrdom. For, as St Bernard says, to live well is to do good and endure evil.

> [Note: Col. 0643D, *Sermon on the Feast of the Apostles*.]

Bear fruit like a rose—that is, as I do, planted beside streams of water, that is, always nourished in the fullness of graces and now at last exalted above the choirs of angels. For you too are like roses planted beside streams of water, because, transferred from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of God, you were made conformed to the likeness of his death when you were buried with him through baptism into death—through [Col. 0645A] baptism, I say, reddened by Christ’s blood. Therefore all souls so planted ought to bear fruit like roses, because they received the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit in the font of baptism, sanctified in the womb of their mother Anna, whose name means “grace.” “Bear fruit like a rose.”

How does a rose bear fruit? What is this fruit of the rose? In this place the fruit of the rose is nothing other than that by which a rose can be useful or pleasing: namely, colour, fragrance, taste, and medicine. Its colour is most beautiful, its fragrance most sweet, its taste best, its medicine most effective. By colour is signified conduct; by fragrance, reputation; by taste, intention together with devotion; and by medicine, instruction. Therefore, whoever has blameless conduct, praiseworthy reputation, chaste intention, continual devotion, and instruction that is useful, effective, salutary, and sweet, truly bears fruit like a rose.

The Apostle invites us to the first, saying: “Abstain from every appearance of evil” (1 Thess. 5). To the second, he who says: “Take care of a good name; for a good name is better than precious ointments” (Ecclus. 14). To the third, Christ saying: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 5). Likewise: “In every sacrifice of the Lord you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2), that is, the savour of devotion mixed with the reverence of fear. To the fourth, he who says: “Let him who hears say: Come” (Rev., final chapter), that is, whoever already obeys should exhort others to obedience.

But the distinctive thing about a rose is that it always bears fruit among thorns. For it bears fruit where it grows and is born, that is, among thorns; not where it is already gathered and stored, that is, among roses. In this world, as in a great rose-garden, neither are roses without thorns nor thorns without roses. The shrub that produces both is tribulation, which produces patience for the endurance of thorns, and patience in turn produces hope for the fragrance of roses. In the shrub of our heart, the flowers of roses ought always to overcome the prickles of thorns, as they do in every rose-garden.

Some have thorns without flowers, that is, tribulation without consolation. Some have flowers without thorns, and this in two ways, for good or for evil. For good: the elect, to whom every bitter thing is sweet for Christ’s sake. For evil: those who spend their days in prosperity and in a moment go down to hell. Some [Col. 0645D] have both flowers and thorns, who say: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [94]). Many also who live pleasurably have these, because, according to the poet:

> No pleasure is unalloyed.

Hence he adds:

> Something troubling intrudes upon happy things.

Some have neither: namely, those who, like Ephraim, a heifer trained to love threshing, find even tribulations mixed with sins sweet, because their feeling has grown callous through habit. In this fourfold distinction, then, the name “thorn” means tribulation, while “rose” means any kind of consolation, whether carnal [Col. 0646A] or spiritual: carnal because of its beauty for a brief time, spiritual because of both fragrance and taste, and because of its position above the thorns. But in this passage it is better to take thorns and roses as representing the persons of sinners and righteous persons.

According to this sense, then, there are no thorns without roses except in hell: here the thorns are gathered, but in hell they are burned. There are no roses without thorns except in heaven: here they are gathered, there they are stored. But in this mortal life, full of scandals, on this cursed earth that brings forth thorns and thistles, thorns must be mingled with roses and roses with thorns; because, as Jerome says, in every condition and sex the worst are mixed with the best. Thus, as pleasures are mixed with pains and virtues with vices, so the righteous are mixed with sinners, as grain with chaff in the barn and wheat with tares in the field. “Let both grow until the harvest,” and until the winnowing separates them by the harvesting sickle and the judicial fan.

Therefore, in different communities, according to the various characters of people, two kinds of thorns and as many kinds of roses are found.
