A thorn among thorns is an evil person among evil persons. A thorn among roses is an evil person among good: Satan among angels, Judas among apostles. A rose among thorns is a good person among evil persons: like Noah among giants, Lot among Sodomites, and in general all Christ’s disciples, sent by him like lambs among wolves. To be a thorn among thorns is very evil; to be a thorn [Col. 0646C] among roses is worst of all. To be a rose among roses is a great good; but to be a rose among thorns is best of all, for this belongs to consummate virtue and exceptional praise. Therefore our thorns must neither be utterly uprooted, since they produce, test, and commend roses, nor embraced too dearly, since they prick and tear; and, what is most miserable, they await fire . . . . . The rest is missing.

## SERMON XX ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY, II

“Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31.) Truly, a strong woman is difficult to find. Certainly, “woman” (*mulier*) is said to derive from softness (*mollities*), while “strong” derives from strength (*fortitudo*). Hence strength in a woman seems almost to be a contradiction in terms. But not every softness is contrary [Col. 0646D] to strength, nor is every strength contrary to softness. There is a softness that falls short of strength; a softness suited to virtue; and a softness indifferent, capable of tending either way. There is blameworthy softness, praiseworthy softness, and neutral softness. The first is called softness of life, the second of grace, the third of nature.

Of the first is the saying of the Satirist:

> There are also great wearinesses in a soft life;  
> rarer use makes pleasures more welcome.

Of the second is the saying of the holy man: “God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me” (Job 23). Of the third, the saying of Isidore: “Woman (*mulier*) is so called from softness (*mollities*), as though *mollier*.”

> [Note: Col. 0645D, Isidore, *Etymologies*.]

The first kind of softness is comprised, and is reproved, in three matters: softness of clothing, speech, and gesture. The first the Lord reproves indirectly where he praises John for harsh and rough clothing. For praise of rough clothing is blame of soft clothing. “What,” he says, “did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11). It is a severe reproach to royal houses that they nourish the soft, teach softness, and know nothing of a hard life. Hence a certain wise man says: “I was nurtured amid great wrappings and anxieties. For no king had any other beginning of birth” (Wis. 7).

Solomon reproves the second, saying: “That you may be delivered from the strange woman and the foreign woman, who makes her words soft” (Prov. 2). And the Psalmist: “His words are softer [Col. 0647B] than oil, yet they are darts” (Ps. 54 [55]). For nothing is softer to hear, or more penetrating in its power to please, than the blandishments of flattery. As Seneca says, they have this natural quality: even when they are not accepted, they please. “Let not this oil make fat my head.” These are those soft garments with which John was not mystically clothed, because he flattered no one, reproved sinners most sharply, and did not know how to spare even a king when he sinned. Woe to the houses of the rich that abound in such softnesses. For this is the worst poverty of the rich: that the rich person does not find someone who will tell him the truth.

The third softness, which lies in gesture or action, is noted in the *Saturnalia* in Quintus Hortensius, a man soft by profession, who arranged himself before a mirror. To this too should be referred everything belonging to the practice of a more dissolute life: play, jesting, sloth, and sleepiness; a soft gait, affected carriage, and other things; also wanton touching, from which those called “soft” received their name, whom the Apostle joins to male concubitors and excludes from the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6).

The softness of grace is divided threefold: into fear of judgment, compassion for one’s neighbour, and devotion of love for God. Of the first is the saying: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender.” Likewise: “God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me” (Job 9; 23). “Blessed is the person who is always fearful, but whoever is hard of heart shall fall into evil” (Prov. 28), as Solomon says. [Col. 0647D] Of the second softness, it is said in praise of Augustus:

> Since by force he cannot be overcome by anyone,  
> he is gentle toward the prayers of the fearful.

He was full of this softness who said: “From the beginning mercy grew up with me, and from my mother’s womb it went forth with me” (Job 31). “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” says the Lord (Matt. 5). In the description of the iniquity of Sodom, it is set down as almost its most grievous sin that she did not stretch out her hand to the needy and poor (Ezek. 16).

Of the third softness it is written in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke; I sought him,” and so forth (Song 5). O what violence of a word, by which the soul is so melted! Swift is the word’s passage, but it has no little force, leaving the soul melted, that it may run and seek, and so forth. Of this threefold softness God says: “I will take from you a heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11), that is, a soft and pliant heart, easily penetrated by the threefold sword of fear, sorrow, and love.

By this threefold sword the most gentle Mary was transfixed, as that most blessed old man foretold to her: “A sword passed through your soul” (Luke 2)—the sword of fear in nursing the little child, of sorrow in seeing her Son crucified, and of love in receiving back from death her own Son in the resurrection, and especially in longing to ascend after him. Softness of nature is twofold: that of sex and that of age—of sex in a woman, of age in a little child. For a child’s age is soft and apt to be guided; a woman likewise is quickly softened by a man’s prayers and bent from the firmness of her purpose; [Col. 0648B] she is quickly changed from the judgment of her counsel, according to Virgil’s saying:

> Woman is ever variable and changeable.

She also quickly softens a hard heart, bends a rigid heart, and tames a heart of iron. Because of this softness and power of softening, “woman” (*mulier*) and “hammer” (*malleus*) have the same origin of name. For as a hammer (*malleus*) is said to derive from softening (*mollire*), because it softens iron, so woman is so called because she softens man.

> Iron hearts grow soft beneath wanton arrows,

says Claudian. “Lust subdues iron minds,” says Jerome. This is the hammer of the whole earth, by which that great hammerer, the devil, hammers, softens, and almost wholly demolishes the world. He hammers by suggestions, softens by enticements, and demolishes by evil [Col. 0648C] desires, shameful acts, and crimes. The force of this hammer often makes Solomons foolish, so that they worship idols; enfeebles Samsons, so that they serve the Philistines; inflames Herculeans, so that they burn alive; changes Jupiters into bulls, so that they bellow after Europa; and chains Marses, so that they yield to Venus.

Thus woman is named from the softness of nature. Caesar too was called by a certain most biting critic “the woman of all men and the man of all women.” But Mary is called woman from the softness of grace: she who, beyond all mortals, feared God, grieved for God, and loved God; especially because she is easily softened by holy prayers into mercy, and is powerful to soften others toward conversion. For she is the mother of mercy, and therefore is quickly softened by the tears of penitents, quickly bent by the prayers of the humble, and quickly moved to petition her Son, the judge, on their behalf. She is also the mother of grace, and therefore has power quickly to soften the sinner, quickly to bend the judge, and also quickly to punish the obstinate when necessary. She softens the sinner so that he may repent, bends the judge so that he may spare, and punishes the obstinate so that he may cease blaspheming. In the first two respects she is a hammer of mercy; in the third, a hammer of justice.

She was a hammer of mercy when she converted the Egyptian woman and Theophilus; a hammer of justice when she crushed Julian the Apostate. Indeed, in this hammer one may see Christ’s wisdom against the devil’s cunning and his clemency against cruelty. For as the devil uses a woman as a hammer to soften the hearts of the proud [Col. 0649A] toward lust, so Christ uses this woman as a hammer to soften the hearts of the humble toward repentance. Hence, when the sweetest name of Mary is heard in church, the stony hearts of laypeople, struck as if by a hammer of mercy, immediately shake themselves, lift hands and eyes to heaven, and ask Mary for aid; and, like sailors in danger, look more frequently to the star known to them. So much concerning “woman”; let us now consider “strong.”

“Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31.) Here Solomon does not speak of that womanly strength of which the Satirist says:

> They show a strong spirit in deeds which they dare shamefully.

It is not strength to be strong in crimes, just as it is not wisdom to know how to do evil. Jeremiah reproves such wisdom, saying: “They are wise to do evil, but they did not know how to do good” (Jer. 4). Isaiah likewise reproves such strength: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5). Catiline, a noble young man, was strong with such strength. Though he was a workshop of every shameful act and crime, he was nevertheless, as Sallust says, able to endure vigils, labour, and hunger beyond human measure.

Strength of body more often harms the spirit than it benefits it. For the spirit is willing when the flesh is weak. Hence the Apostle: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12). Hence Gregory’s saying: “The flesh when glad draws one to fault; when afflicted it calls one back to pardon.” Strength that is a virtue belongs to the mind, not the body. Yet not every strength of mind is a virtue, but only that which accords with reason, according to Augustine’s statement defining virtue as “an equality of life agreeing with reason in every respect.” But if virtue is equality, a circle resembles it more than a plane figure. Hence Horace:

> The wise man is wholly smooth and round.  
> (*Horace, Satires* II.7.85.)

For reason is, as it were, the centre of a circle, and equality of life the circumference of the same figure. Therefore a man’s life, consonant with reason in every respect, is like the circumference of a circle harmonious on all sides: on all sides, that is, in thought, speech, and [Col. 0649D] deed. For by these three human life is revolved and carried round. Thus, for Horace, the wise man is wholly smooth and rounded.

Nothing is stronger than the human mind, which has such strength that it cannot be overcome except by itself. For the devil or a human being can persuade, entice, terrify, and kill; but cannot compel at all. True strength, therefore—the true vigour of the mind—is equality of life agreeing with reason in every respect: that is, the perfect preservation of innocence, so that you never do what you know to be unlawful; never will what you know to be contrary to reason; never subject yourself to a human being or a demon for the sake of sin. By this strength the saints were strong, who through faith conquered [Col. 0650A] kingdoms; but Mary was strong above all women and above all men. Hence Christ always calls himself the Son of Man, never the Son of Woman. For Mary, most beautiful of women, was stronger also than men, because by the help of heavenly grace she conquered sin in every respect, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0649D] *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 36.]. And blessed Bernard says [Note: [Col. 0649D] Sermon 4 on the Assumption]: “Far be it that the house of the Blessed Virgin should ever be said to have had any defilement of its own!” And shortly afterwards [Note: [Col. 0650D] Ibid.]: “Therefore, as it is pious to believe, Mary never had a sin of her own; and thus repentance, as unnecessary, was far removed from that most innocent heart.”

Mary was plainly strong in faith, believing things impossible; strong in hope, hoping for unheard-of things; strong in charity, desiring only the promised things of heaven [Col. 0650B] and despising all earthly things. She was strong, I say, in conquering the devil, the world, the flesh, and death. But above all she conquered death in that, though destined to die, she did not fear; in dying she felt no pain; dead, she saw no corruption. And we also, dearest brethren, ought to be strong in faith, strong in hope, strong in charity: strong in faith through obedience; strong in hope through endurance; strong in charity through the intensity of holy desires and the forceful contempt of worldly things, concerning which it is written: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). Of strength in faith is Peter’s saying: “Resist the devil, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 3). Of strength in hope Paul says: “We glory in tribulations, [Col. 0650C] knowing that tribulation produces patience, and patience hope; and hope does not put to shame,” etc. (Rom. 5). Of strength in charity there is that saying in the Song of Songs: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” (Song 8).

As death separates the soul from the flesh, so love separates it from the pleasure of the flesh. No place endures what hell endures: such heat, such cold, such stench, and so forth. So too charity, which is patient, bears all things and endures all things. It bears what is cruelly inflicted; it endures what is faithfully promised, as it is written: “The patient person will endure until the appointed time, and afterwards there will be a return of joy” (Ecclus. 1). Therefore love is strong as death, and jealousy hard as hell, because as death prevails over all and no one prevails over it, so love always conquers and is never conquered. And as hell receives much and gives back nothing, so charity gains much and loses nothing.

We must also be strong in overcoming the devil: that is, in attacking, resisting, and overcoming him. In attacking, so that we may rouse Leviathan, sleeping in the reprobate, as it is written: “Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse Leviathan” (Job 3). In resisting, so that we may put him to flight, as it is written: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from us” (Jas. 4). In overcoming, so that we may be crowned for victory, as [Col. 0651A] it is written: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2). He who fights in this manner overcomes.

He attacks the devil who willingly removes from himself an occasion of sin. He resists him who, without compulsion, rejects his suggestions. But he overcomes him who perseveres in the good he has received: who advances more profitably the good which he had begun and brings it to the best completion. For the end does not fight, but crowns. All virtues run; perseverance alone receives the prize. We must also be strong in rising again, if perhaps we have fallen, as it is written: “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. 24). The common saying is: strong is he who has struck another down, but stronger is he who rises again. Hence this reading is read on the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene; it is not read at any feast of Mary [Col. 0651B] the Mother of God, because Magdalene, who fell in weakness, rose in strength. But Mary the Mother of God, because she never fell through sin, never needed to rise through repentance.

We must also be strong in overcoming the world, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0651D] Sermon on St Vincent]: “The world brings forth a twofold battle-line against Christ’s soldiers. It flatters in order to deceive; it terrifies in order to break them. Let not our own will hold us; let not another’s cruelty terrify us: and the world is conquered.” Again, we must be strong in overcoming the flesh, as the Apostle says: “So I fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9). Those delicate teachers indeed fight, but as though beating the air, who dispute about [Col. 0651C] fasts with full bellies; who, yielding their hands to unchastity, preach chastity; who, reclining upon amassed wealth, clad in foreign cloth and wrapped in silver, crammed with gold, commend poverty. Such preaching is nothing other than bark without sap, a wedding without a bridegroom, food without seasoning, a lamp without oil; and therefore before God it is reprobate, as the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (ibid.).

Concerning such people there is Chrysostom’s elegant saying: “He who lives well and teaches the people well instructs them how they ought to live; but he who lives badly and teaches well instructs God how He ought to condemn him.” Certainly no one can conquer the world or the devil unless he has first conquered his own body. Why? Because the devil’s strength is in his loins [Col. 0651D] and his power in the navel of his belly; for the weakness of human flesh affords great assistance to demonic power. Therefore the greatest part of that weakness is in men’s loins and in women’s navel. For this reason loins and navel of this sort are called the devil’s, because through them they persecute our souls.

We must also be strong in overcoming death, not by fearing the hour of death, but rather by awaiting it eagerly with the testimony of a good conscience, so that, when the Lord comes and knocks, we may immediately open to him. Indeed, even before he knocks, let us hasten to open the door to him, as he hastened who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with [Col. 0652A] Christ” (Phil. 1). And another: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41). Such strength brings about that violence of which it is written: “Death has been swallowed up in force” (1 Cor. 15). Thus death, the necessity of dying, and the weakness of corruption were swallowed up in the resurrection of the Virgin Mary and in her Assumption; and so indeed it will be in the resurrection of our bodies, if we have imitated her in the strength of so many victories.

Moreover, we have her not only as an example of victory, but also as aid in battle, as is plainly shown by the secret prayer in yesterday’s Mass, which reads thus [Note: [Col. 0651D] The Church, in the vigil of the Assumption]: “Great, O Lord, in the presence of thy mercy is the prayer of the Mother of God, whom thou hast therefore taken from the present age, that she may confidently intercede with thee for our sins [Col. 0652B].” And certainly it was fitting that she should thus become mediator for all. For every hammer strikes more strongly from above than from below; therefore this hammer of mercy had to be raised on high. Its powerful blow is efficacious prayer, never to be frustrated of the effect of showing mercy before the presence of the divine majesty. May Christ, her Son, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages, Amen, bring us to that presence through the protection of the same Virgin and Mother.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. I

“A star has risen out of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0652D] Words of the Church from Num. 24]. The frequent solemnities [Col. 0652C] of the perpetual Virgin offer us frequent occasions for solemn rejoicing; and they imprint the sweet and delightful memory of her abundant sweetness upon receptive hearts all the more deeply the more frequently they attach it. Whom would not our sweet advocate, blessed among women—ever to be invoked for aid whenever recalled to mind—make glad: a most mighty Lady, no less merciful; queen of virgins, empress of angels, mediator of humankind, Mother of God, Mother of mercy, nurse of wisdom, cultivator of justice, discoverer of grace, restorer of glory? As it is written: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord” (Luke 1). And in Proverbs: “A gracious woman shall find glory” (Prov. 11).

Certainly, upon this gracious woman, this glorious queen, the Lord bestowed grace [Col. 0652D] and glory in such abundance that, anticipated by him with blessings of sweetness, she was made blessed in her going in and coming out; for the Lord guarded both her entrance and her departure, and in guarding them blessed them. Blessed was her entrance, through which light and life entered in to us; blessed was her departure, she who opened to us all the gate of paradise which the first-created humans had shut. Hence angels rejoice and praise the Son of God not only over her Assumption, by which she was taken up into heaven, but also over her Nativity, by which she entered the world. Why should angels not rejoice over the Nativity of the Mother of God, when they rejoiced so greatly over the birth of the virgin Geneviève [Col. 0653A]?

Yet a more particular cause for joy is furnished to human beings today than to angels. For in Mary there was born to us an example of most perfect holiness and an aid of most powerful intercession; and from her there rose for us the price of most necessary redemption—things for which the perfection and happiness of angels had no need. Therefore there is no one among all mortals who should not rejoice and be glad at the most joyful birth of the Mother of God, unless perhaps he does not know how greatly one ought to rejoice in her birth. For her virgin birth, salutary and necessary to the whole world, makes the Virgin’s birth joyful for all the faithful; and not only the Virgin’s birth, but also the birth of the Forerunner. For as she was born to bear the Saviour, so he was sent by God to prepare the Lord’s way, to bear witness concerning the light, so that all might believe through him.

But the Church does not celebrate the birthdays of other saints—the days, that is, on which they entered weeping into this valley of tears. Rather, it celebrates those days on which they joyfully ascended from this valley to the mountain of the Lord, went gladly into the house of the Lord, [Col. 0653B] and entered into the joy of their Lord. Truly it is written: “The day of death is better than the day of birth” (Eccl. 7). For it is better to leave prison than to enter prison. Every human being is born for labour—indeed, for prison as well—although he is born from prison, with prison, and in prison. He is born from the prison of his mother’s womb, with the prison of his mortal little body, and in the prison of this world; but alas, also for the prison of hell! For by nature he is born a child of wrath, heir of perdition, offspring of corruption, inseparable companion of calamity and misery, as though guilty of an eternal transgression.

Who, then, would regard and celebrate so mournful and grievous a day as a festival, except one wholly devoid of reason and ignorant of the human condition? Therefore the saints do not celebrate their birthdays, because they hate their souls in this world. They do not desire the day of humanity; rather, they desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. They curse the day on which they were born, ready to rouse Leviathan, sleeping in those who love this world. But unhappy Herod, who did not reflect that he would die, did not grieve that he had been born in prison; rather, he rejoiced that he had found straw there in abundance, in which he unhappily surpassed his fellow captives in abundance. And alas, how deadly was that joy to him, in which the drunken adulterer attempted to extinguish—and, so far as he could, did extinguish—the Forerunner of the Lord, namely the burning and shining lamp which the Father had prepared for his Christ, which scattered everywhere rays of holiness and justice, sobriety and chastity, [Col. 0653D] when he set before his guests on a dish, as if it were a wedding-course, that most holy head which even the angels revere and to which the Lord of majesty had graciously bowed himself.

Thus, thus, dearest brethren, they extinguish within themselves the Spirit whom the Apostle (1 Thess. 5) forbids us to extinguish, [Col. 0654A] that is, spiritual grace—who, forgetful of future things, cling to things present, and, with their whole soul dissolved, delight in things that pass away: not using temporal things but enjoying them. These behead the grace of God, putting far from themselves the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom. The head—that is, the beginning—of this beginning is fear of the coming judgment, according to Augustine’s saying: “He who begins to believe begins to fear judgment.” O how deep was the night when almost the entire world lay amid such darkness of ignorance, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0653D] Words of the Church]: “Looking from afar, behold I see the power of God coming and a cloud covering the whole earth.”

But who, amid great darkness, would not look toward the rising of a new and great star? According to Balaam’s prophecy [Col. 0654B], today a star has risen out of Jacob. But why is it that the prophecy of Balaam—a man who was a magician and evildoer, augur and diviner, enchanter and soothsayer, and whom Holy Scripture reproves in many places—was confirmed by the authority of the Holy Spirit? It was because the Holy Spirit spoke through him, as through Caiaphas and the Sibyl. For he who deigned to open the mouth of the she-ass to rebuke the prophet’s folly—or rather madness, as sacred Scripture testifies—why should he not also deign to open the mouth of a madman, to prophesy the hidden wisdom of human redemption, concealed in mystery from ages past, which none of the rulers of this world knew?

At the same time, a twofold benefit must be considered in this divine mystery. First, it is no great thing to have from God the gift [Col. 0654C] of speaking well without doing good, as Balaam did, in whose mouth, not in whose heart, the Lord had placed his word. Secondly, the word of the Lord is always precious and must be heard with all reverence, whoever the human speaker may be. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit caused the prophecy of the soothsayer Balaam to be committed to writing by the prophet Moses, and the prophecy of the high priest Caiaphas by the evangelist John.

See also God’s goodness. Balaam was hired for pay to curse Israel, but he could only bless (Num. 24). So good is the Lord whom we have, and so kindly the Father: merciful comforter, wise reconciler, prudent governor, mighty helper, a wall and outer rampart for us, [Col. 0654D] so that no one may harm us, if we are zealous for good. “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21). Balaam fittingly concluded the sum of his blessings by prophesying the birth of the Blessed Virgin, who would bear the blessed Son of God, whom all generations rightly bless; for she acquired for all generations such an abundance of blessing—namely, the blessed fruit of her womb. He is blessed by God, so that whoever blesses him may be filled with blessings, provided that he blesses not under compulsion or unwillingly, nor only on the surface of words as Balaam did, but willingly and with the pattern of a good life.

For many bless with their mouths but [Col. 0655A] curse with their hearts—that is, by the perverse desire of their hearts—saying, “Lord! Lord!” while not at all doing what the Lord commands. But not everyone who says to him, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of his Father who is in heaven (Matt. 7). Therefore Balaam says of himself in the person of such people: “Balaam son of Beor says; the man whose eye is closed says; the hearer of God’s utterances, who knows the doctrine of the Most High, says; he who falls and has open eyes” (Num. 24).

Balaam means “vain people”; Beor, “driving on.” Of the vain people are those who speak and do not act, or who hear the word of God and do not keep it. For what do they pursue [Col. 0655B] but words of faith, not works? Whoever pursues words alone will have nothing. These are sons of the devil, who drives them into sin. The inner eye of this Balaam is closed: though he sees visions of the Almighty—that is, understands his judgments and commandments—he does not live according to what he understands, but falls with open eyes; that is, he sins knowingly and descends alive into hell, a hearer of God’s words and not a doer. Understanding is indeed good for all who practise it; but for those who do not practise it, it is not good, because it is not reckoned to them for good but rather as a greater testimony to their condemnation. For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes; and it would have been better for him not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back [Col. 0655C] from the holy commandment delivered to him.

Blessed indeed are those who hear the word of God, but only if they keep it; otherwise no one is blessed by hearing alone. For just as a word heard but not mixed with faith is of no benefit, so faith itself is of no benefit without obedience. Therefore it is written: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” For as faith comes from hearing, so obedience comes from heeding. It is of no use to hear unless you believe; of no use to believe unless you obey. These are the twin, spiritual, holy ears of the heart which the Holy Spirit requires from us: namely, to believe and to obey. Of the first: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isa. 53). Of the second: “The Lord opened my ear” (Ps. 17); “but I do not resist; I have not gone backward” (Ps. 39). Again: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me.” Of both: “But you have perfected ears for me” [Col. 0655D].

Although in this place perfected ears may be understood as obedience to commandments and endurance of insults; or as fear of threats and desire for promises. And “he who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11) means: let him who hears believe; let him who believes obey. Let him believe threats, believe promises, believe sacraments. Let him believe threats so as to avoid them; promises so as to desire them; sacraments so as not to doubt their sanctification and invisible power. Let him obey commandments so as faithfully to fulfil and firmly preserve them, lest he be, like Balaam, a hearer of God’s words and not a doer. But let these remarks about Balaam suffice. Now let us return to the star: “A star has risen out of Jacob.”

A marvellous thing: the human race was made from mud, [Col. 0656A] and this before Christ’s birth. Whence then, from a muddy race, does there now come a star after Christ’s birth? How could heavenly offspring be born from human stock, from unclean seed? For what is cleaner than a star, what more unclean than mud? Who can make clean one conceived from unclean seed? Hear who can: “Is it not you, who alone are?” (Job 14). Therefore that power, that wisdom, which at the beginning of time formed man from the mud of the earth in its own image and likeness, began at the end of the ages to make stars from human beings and human beings from stars, to restore in them its own image, making the homeland of earth and sky one commonwealth, so that heaven might have human beings and earth stars.

For what else [Col. 0656B] are the righteous but stars shining on earth, according to the Apostle’s saying: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the firmament of heaven?” (Phil. 2). And what are the righteous reigning in heaven but stars shining in their own dwelling and human beings living in their own house? Hence the Apostle himself says: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5).

But this work—namely, making stars from human beings—belongs to the work of grace, not to the work of nature or of justice. For nature produces like from like: human beings from human beings, beasts from beasts, birds from birds, fish from fish, [Col. 0656C] and so forth in this manner. Justice, however, often destroys what nature had built, making sick people from the healthy, blind from the sighted, deaf from the hearing, mute from the speaking, lame from the walking, leprous from the clean, dead from the living; and, more terribly, it ordains that sinners should be born from saints and righteous persons. Grace, on the other hand, often rebuilds what justice had destroyed and perfects what nature had left imperfect, making healthy persons from the sick, living persons from the dead, righteous persons from the ungodly, blessed persons from the wretched. This kind of work most of all proves God almighty, according to the saying: “O God, who chiefly manifestest thy omnipotence by sparing and showing mercy, multiply thy grace upon us,” etc.

Thus grace, [Col. 0656D] by justifying the ungodly, in one and the same work makes a star from a human being and heaven from earth. And certainly, dearest brethren, such offspring and such a dwelling—that is, heavenly and starry—had long ago been promised to holy Abraham, when it was said to him: “Look at heaven and number the stars, if you can. So shall your seed be” (Gen. 15). From the words “number the stars, if you can,” the vain presumption of certain astrologers is manifestly refuted, who boasted that they had comprehended and recorded the entire number of stars, such as Aratus and Eudoxus. For when, says Augustine, can they all be numbered, when they cannot all be seen? Certainly, he alone who could create them can also number them, and call them by their own names, according to the saying: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by names” (Ps. 146).

Hence a certain learned man says [Col. 0657A]: where we have the adverb *sic* (“so”), the Hebrew has the adverb *quo*, which is both comparative and locative. The most expert Hebrew scholars say that the same adverb occurs in that passage of Exodus where it is written of Moses: “When he had looked this way and that, and saw no one, he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand” (Exod. 2). For where we have “this way and that,” the Hebrew has *quo et quo*. Jerome therefore translated this passage better by saying “so” than if he had said “there.” For a locative adverb could signify only the height of the place; but an adverb of comparison signifies both the height of the place, the multitude of stars, their numerous greatness, and the brightness of the heavenly [Col. 0657B] reward. He therefore says: “So shall your seed be”: that is, so numerous, so bright, so steadfast—so numerous in number, so bright in merit, so lofty in reward, so firm in place. Yet I say “so” and “so,” not to indicate equality but likeness. For in all these respects your seed will surpass the glory of the stars: it will be more numerous, brighter, loftier, and firmer.

Of its number you have in the Psalm: “I shall number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138). Of its brightness: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (1 Cor. 12). Of its loftiness: “I know a man in Christ caught up even to the third heaven.” Of its firmness, and of all the rest, you have in Daniel: “Those who have understanding shall shine like the splendour of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12). Therefore he says: “So shall your seed be”: that is, so clean and pure—so pure in conscience, bright and radiant in celibate life and heavenly teaching, firm and steadfast in perseverance, lofty and sublime in the heavenly homeland, glorious and noble in the glory of eternal resurrection.

For insofar as concerns the life of righteousness which we live in the present [Col. 0657C], the light of the stars here signifies illumination; their heat, the fervour of holy desire; their standing, steadfastness of purpose. For a star is said to be so called from standing, shining, and burning. But insofar as concerns the life of glory which we shall live in the future, the light of the stars [Col. 0657D] signifies the brightness of the glorified body; their heat, the ineffable joy of the heart; their standing, security, eternity, and in both the security of eternity. Therefore he says: “So shall your seed be.” As if he said: Thus shall your offspring possess heaven; thus shall heavenly brightness shine in it; thus shall its charity rejoice securely; thus shall its happiness have no end. So shall your seed be. Thus shall heaven be starred by your progeny; thus shall flesh, never to fall, be planted on high; thus shall flesh, destined to reign, be enthroned. The glory of flesh will be changed, not its nature.

Behold, brethren, what kind of stars were promised to St Abraham. But the first and chief of these stars is this singular star which rose today, surpassing in merit and reward not only all human stars but angelic ones as well, [Col. 0658A] as it is written: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. 31). For never did any star so shine by example or so stand firm in purpose.

Let us therefore learn from this star to shine by the example of chastity, to burn with desire for blessedness, and to stand firm and steadfast in the purpose of holiness. Nothing is brighter than chastity; but chastity is called from chastisement of the body, without which the virtue of chastity cannot be perfectly attained. Hence the Apostle: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). The body must be chastised by fasts, vigils, manual labour, continual silence and solitude of place, hunger and thirst, cold and the stroke of the lash, [Col. 0658B] holy meditations, and devout prayers. For much meditation of the flesh is affliction.

Nothing burns more than charity; nothing is firmer than constancy of mind. What profit is there in seeming to shine and burn in heaven for an hour, only briefly to fall from it eternally? “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14)—that is, who had begun to rise. How aptly the prophet used here the imperfect past tense, which signifies a thing begun but not yet completed. By this is signified in the falling devil a certain beginning of light, but no progress, no completion. For he did not stand in truth. The Lord says: “I was seeing Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). He said “I was seeing” and “falling,” joining an imperfect-past verb [Col. 0658C] to a present participle, indicating that the devil had begun to fall but had not yet fallen wholly; for he still falls daily in his members. For as the Lord Jesus Christ has not yet wholly ascended into heaven, but, lifted up from the earth, draws all things to himself—not all at once, but part by part—so the devil, falling from heaven, draws after himself a third part of the stars; and would that even two parts might remain! Woe to stars that do not stand but fall from heaven, which allow themselves to be dragged by the dragon’s venomous tail! Woe to the stars that follow her whose name is Wormwood, so that they may be filled with everlasting bitterness! What profit is it to find wisdom and then immediately lose what has been found? “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom,” but only if he keeps what he has found, [Col. 0658D] and he who holds it does not let it go. For Wisdom cries in the streets: “If anyone loves wisdom, let him come to me and he will find it; and when he has found it, he is blessed if he holds it” (Prov. 8). To find wisdom is to do penance; to hold it is to persevere in penance, which is to remain in wisdom, as it is written: “Blessed is the man who will remain in wisdom” (Ecclus. 14).

There are three things which prevent a person from remaining in wisdom and drive him away from what he has found: pride of heart, the enticement of flesh, and inconstancy of mind. The first drove away the philosophers who, although they had found God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but became vain in their thoughts and, professing themselves wise, became fools (Rom. 1:21–22). The second [Col. 0659A] drove away Solomon, who, after finding wisdom, bent his knees to women and brought a stain upon his glory. The third drove away Demas, who loved this world and abandoned the Apostle, although earlier, for the Apostle’s sake, he had despised and abandoned this world (2 Tim. 4). The same thing drives away apostates from religious life, making them return like utterly unclean dogs to their vomit, recoil from their good purpose, and say, “Anathema to Jesus.”

Concerning them is Augustine’s terrible statement in his letter to the clergy and people of Hippo: “Just as I have found, by experience, persons who have advanced in monasteries sometimes better than others, so I have never found persons worse than those who have failed in monasteries.” And he adds [Col. 0659B]: “Hence I think it is written in the Apocalypse: ‘Let the holy one be made holy still; and let him who is in filth grow still more filthy’” [Note: [Col. 0659D] St Augustine, Epistle 153.]. Explaining this, as it were, he continues: “For just as those who live worthily of their vows go before others in the kingdom, so those who withdraw from their vow are worse in the world and lower in hell.”

Thus the same Augustine, in his letter to Armentarius and Paulina, says: “Before you were bound by a vow, it was free for you to be inferior; although it is not a freedom to rejoice in, by which one does not owe what is repaid with gain. But now, because your promise is held by God, I do not invite you to great righteousness but deter you from great wickedness. For if you do not do what you vowed, you will not be as you would have remained had you vowed nothing of the sort. You would then have been less, not worse; [Col. 0659C] but now, God forbid, you will be as much more wretched if you break faith with God as you will be happier if you fulfil it. Nor should you regret having made your vow; indeed rejoice that what would have been permitted to you to your harm is now not permitted to you. Therefore undertake it fearlessly. He who demands your vows will help you. Happy necessity, which compels one to better things” [Note: [Col. 0659D] Ibid., 45.]. Thus Augustine.

Apostates of this kind belong to the third part of the stars, which is dragged by the dragon’s tail from heaven to hell (Apoc. 8). For the two parts over which that tail does not prevail are those who preserve their innocence intact by never committing mortal sin, and those who recover lost innocence by bringing to completion the penance they have vigorously and eagerly undertaken. The first kind is indeed most rare and precious, although [Col. 0659D] Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0660D] St Ambrose, *On Penance*, book 2, ch. 5.] that he had more easily found those who preserved innocence than those who performed true penance.

What then is the third part of the stars following the dragon’s tail, that is, falling into the devil’s judgment, except those who begin to repent of lost innocence but, through inconstancy of mind and instability of soul, do not persist in their penance once begun? For those who do not even begin to repent are unworthy of the name of stars, showing no beginning of light. Therefore Mary received by divine appointment such a name, namely *stella maris*, “star of the sea”: that is, illuminator of the world, which swells like a sea in the proud, boils in the wrathful and envious, [Col. 0660A] and stinks in the lustful, drunken, and gluttonous. For who, placed in any danger whatever, has looked toward the ray of this star and not immediately felt help?

Yet she is especially called the star of the sea—that is, consoler of the sorrowful, illuminator of penitents, namely of those who recall all their years in the bitterness of their soul. Their contrition is great like the sea, that is, broad and deep, so that the bitterness of confession may bring all the circumstances of sins into the light; the bitterness of satisfaction may run through every member of the body; and the bitterness of compunction may always bubble up from the depth of the heart. Mary is not the star of seas or fountains, of sweet waters, but the star of the sea, because the earth of those who live pleasantly does not deserve to receive her consolation. Thus the foreheads of those laughing and rejoicing do not deserve to be marked with the sign Tau, but those of men who groan and grieve because of the abominations done in their midst [Col. 0660B].

Let us beware, therefore, brethren—let us beware, I beseech you—of those signs which the Lord foretold would be in the sun, moon, and stars: that is, in the prelates of the Church, the rulers of the earth, and the subjects of both, clergy and laity alike. For very many of both sexes and of both ranks seem indeed to stand in the Church, but are about to fall from it, or even are already falling—not so much in position as in merit—through those three dangers mentioned above: pride of heart, enticement of flesh, and inconstancy of mind.

[Col. 0660C] No fall delights the devil as much as that of apostates from religious life (Job 40). For he “swallows up a river and does not marvel”: that is, he does not regard it as a great thing if he draws many from the world after himself; but he is confident that Jordan will flow into his mouth—that is, the descent of those who humble themselves to perform penance, so that there they may learn from Christ to become meek and humble in heart. These especially the devil desires to swallow up, because “he eats hay like an ox”; “his food is choice”; “he lies in wait for the soul of the righteous.” Therefore let those who are already being chewed by Christ’s favour beware the jaws of the devil, according to the words: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). How wretched, how unhappy, is the person who, vomited out of Christ’s mouth, is swallowed again by the devil’s mouth—by him who had first swallowed him up. For that infernal dog desires nothing so greedily as to lick up his own vomit [Col. 0660D] and swallow it all again; since he never vomits out the sinner whom he has swallowed willingly, but only under compulsion, as it is written: “He shall vomit forth the riches which he swallowed, and God shall draw them out of his belly” (Job 21). As much as the fall of such people delights Leviathan, so much does it grieve Mary.

Therefore let us stand, brethren, with our loins girded in truth; let us stand, I say, unwavering and immovable in our holy resolve, like the blessed martyr Genesius. When he had been hung on the rack at Rome, scraped with iron claws, and burning plates had been placed against his sides [Col. 0661A], he stood unmoved and cried out: “There is no king except Christ. Though I should be killed a thousand times for him, you will not be able to take him from my mouth or from my heart.” O strongest pillar in the house of God! O most steadfast star, most firmly fixed in the firmament of heaven! When could the dragon’s suggestion prevail against one whom the cutting of iron and the burning of fire could not overcome? Certainly this star had Christ impressed upon it; from him it could by no means be separated.

For it is related of another martyr in Greece, named Nimias and Nehemias, that when he was similarly tortured and gave similar answers, the tyrant ordered his belly to be cut through the middle, and his heart to be torn out whole and split open, in order to see whether Christ was in it, as the martyr had said. When this had been done, there appeared in the very middle of the cleft heart a most beautiful likeness of Christ, extending over the whole length and breadth of the heart. At this sight the tyrant, confounded, blushed; but the people of the faithful, greatly gladdened by so great a miracle, with hands stretched out to heaven and knees fixed upon the ground, cried aloud to the Lord in joy and said: “Glory to you, Lord, who make us experience so magnificently that the saying of your Apostle is true: that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts.” Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY, II

The most joyful Nativity of the glorious Virgin Mary—longed for by the prayers of the ancients, awaited with sighs, sought with tears, and foretold in prophetic song—deserved to be celebrated with public rejoicing by the whole world, because after the long sadness of the age it introduced the firstfruits of public joy. It is as though, with the first cry of your infancy, you brought forth to all the children of humankind that evangelical consolation, saying: “Look up and lift up your heads: behold, your redemption draws near” (Luke 21).

This is as though it were said in other words: “Behold, Wisdom has now prepared for herself an ivory throne, suited to the devising of thoughts of peace”; so that, charmed by the most holy songs of those thoughts, mercy and truth may meet one another in the midst of this throne, and justice and peace, kissing one another, may be bound in mutual embraces. For until now the Wisdom of God, like a wanderer and exile upon [Col. 0661D] earth, had found no fitting place in which to rest because of the flood of human filth. But now, thanks be to God, King Solomon “made for her a great throne of ivory.”

A throne is a royal or judicial seat. It is royal, as in: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of equity is the sceptre of your kingdom” (Ps. 44). It is judicial, as in: “You sat upon the throne, judging righteousness” (Ps. 9). And in the Gospel: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). But since “the honour of a king loves judgment,” while the honour of a judge does not respect persons and leaves no evil unpunished, it was necessary that our king and judge—who is called the God of avengings and Counsellor—should first offer mortals a counsel of peace before [Col. 0662A] he imposed upon sinners a judgment of vengeance: that he should first act as a dove in the role of ambassador, before acting in the role of executioner.

Of the first it is written that it returned to the ark bearing in its mouth an olive branch with green leaves. Of the second: “Flee from the face of the sword of the dove” (Jer. 46), that is, from the impending infliction of a capital sentence: first to be announced by a meek and humble ambassador, and finally to be pronounced by that same Judge of the living and the dead; yet a judge who is angry without gall, judges with calmness, and always exalts mercy above judgment.

The throne of Solomon belongs to the gentleness of the ambassador; the throne of Artaxerxes to the angry judge. Of the latter it is written in the book of Esther that he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, clothed in royal garments shining with gold and precious stones, and was terrible in appearance (Esther 15). Woe to the nations that desire wars, for they shall be scattered; woe to the Jews who abandoned the counsel of peace, rejecting peaceful Solomon and choosing warlike Caesar, for they shall be left to fall before their own Caesar. For the work of Solomon corresponds to his name, and likewise that of Caesar to his.

For the devil, not undeservedly, is called Caesar from slaughter, blood, and the weapons of wickedness in which he always abounds; and he always strives to fill out the measure of this name with a measure of cruelty, according to the poetic line:

> Caesar, raging into arms, rejoices in no paths  
> unless blood has been shed.

But our Solomon, in accordance with his name, is truly peaceful. As a most wise craftsman, he made [Col. 0662C] a great throne of ivory as, so to speak, the first and chief work of peace: when Christ, who is our peace, who made both one in order to reconcile things in heaven and things on earth, as Prince of Peace and King of Righteousness chose the most innocent of virgins and humblest of women as his own mother, as a mediatrix in the seat of peace.

For a throne, as has been said, is both a royal and a judicial seat. Rest belongs to a seat; honour, to a king; fear, to a judge. Innocence belongs to rest, justice to honour, humility to fear. Of the first you have: “You have sinned; be at rest” (Gen. 4, LXX). Of the second: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of Wisdom”—a seat, that is, the rest which Wisdom seeks in all things, but says that it finds for itself only in the humble, according to that saying. Of the third: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66).

It belongs to innocence to avoid what is forbidden; to justice, to keep the commandments; to humility, to fear judgments and to reckon all one’s merits as nothing, according to the saying: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17). Yet the description of this throne cannot be referred to just any innocent or humble person. For when it is said later of the same throne, “No such work has been made in all the kingdoms” (3 Kings 10), it is clear that it can be understood only of the humblest woman.

The humblest of human beings is he who was assumed in person by Wisdom itself, of whom [Col. 0663A] Daniel says in the third vision: “Until the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomsoever he will, and sets over it the humblest of men” (Dan. 4).

The humblest of women is she from whom that same man—that is, Christ—was born. For Wisdom, which always acts wisely, could not have assumed a body from elsewhere more fittingly or more wisely than from the humblest woman. For she is the one more innocent and more sacred than all others, yet who accounted herself more lowly than everyone. Therefore to the angelic greeting, the magnificent praise, and the wondrous promise, she replied: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). And because she always rested in humility, she caused God to rest in herself not only spiritually [Col. 0663B] but also bodily, as Wisdom says in her person: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. 24).

Therefore what Solomon is said to have done in making a throne, the Psalmist seems to have expounded when he says: “He bowed the heavens and came down” (Ps. 17). For a throne entails sitting, and sitting entails both bending down and rest.

What, then, is God’s sitting but the emptying of majesty and the assumption of a servant’s form? As it is written: “You have known my sitting” (Ps. 138), that is, you approved my condescension by eternal judgment. Unless he had sat upon the throne by bending himself down, no one would have had access to him, according to the words: “And when he had sat down, his disciples came to him” [Col. 0663C] (Matt. 5).

But what kind of throne is that? An ivory one. “Solomon,” it says, “made a throne of ivory.” Woe to kings who make a throne of dung. For what else is a mind resting in lust but a king sitting on dung? For, as Sallust says: “We employ the rule of the mind and the service of the body.” Flesh given over to lust, therefore, is a seat made of dung. As far as an ivory throne differs from a dunghill, so far does a chaste body differ from a lustful one.

Ivory is so called because it comes *e barro*, that is, from the elephant, which in Greek is called *barrus* from its strength; hence its cry is called *barritus*, “trumpeting.” The elephant is an animal surpassing other beasts in bulk and height. Thus its name in the Greek and Indian languages signifies “mountain.” It excels not only in size but also in strength [Col. 0663D]; hence it is accustomed to carry wooden towers containing thirty armed men. It is also very strong in perception, discerning differences of routes and the ambushes of dragons, with which it has continual conflict and inexorable enmity. It is naturally merciful, loves chastity, and lives a very long time—until the third age of Nestor, that is, to three hundred years, as they say.

All these things morally suit no one more than the Virgin Mary. For by keenness of perception prudence is signified; by love of chastity, temperance; by strength, fortitude itself; by mercy, justice—for, as a certain philosopher says, “true [Col. 0664A] justice is that which is preserved toward inferiors”; by greatness, magnanimity; by height, sublimity of merits; by long-suffering, perseverance; and by the three hundred years, faith and imitation of the Lord’s Passion are expressed, because the letter Tau among the Greeks has the form of a cross and signifies the number three hundred.

Ivory, moreover, is the elephant’s tooth: bone naturally cold, stripped of flesh, solid in substance, white in colour, and reddish with age. By its natural coldness is signified the fear of the Lord; by its bareness, contempt of the world; by its whiteness, purity of flesh; by its solidity, constancy of mind; and by the redness of age, fervour prolonged over much time. For true chastity is naturally fearful—but with fear of the Lord, not fear of the world. The fear of the Lord cools the minds of believers from the heat of carnal vices. This is the angel of the Lord who descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace and drove the flame of fire out of the furnace (Dan. 3): that is, the burning of temptation out of the flesh, though first out of the heart, which the breath of the tempter had set on fire.

The fear of the Lord drives out sin: not only sin which still stands outside, knocking very insistently at the heart’s door, but also that which has already entered the soul through consent. Worldly fear, however, never cools the mind; it always burns inwardly with hidden desire. Thus it does not drive out sin but cherishes and conceals it until a time comes for it to break forth outwardly. Hence the Philosopher: “Because the vices of many are weak [Col. 0664C], they lie hidden; they would venture no less, once their strength became apparent to them, than those vices which opportunity has already exposed.” [Note: [Col. 0663D] Seneca.]

A venomous serpent is sluggish when it is stiff with cold; it does not then lack poison, but its poison is numb. Hence someone wishing to distinguish true from false chastity said elegantly:

> She alone is chaste who remains chaste when fear is removed;  
> she who does not act because she could not, does act.

(Ovid, *Elegies* IV.)

Likewise, true chastity is solid: inwardly such as it is outwardly; in private such as it is in public; while engaged in the battle of temptation such as it is when free from temptation. Not so those who are temporary and hollow: who “believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8); like reeds and hemlocks, outwardly glossy, inwardly [Col. 0664D] empty; green from a distance, foul-smelling at close range. When nothing pricks inwardly, they are celibate; when nothing attracts outwardly, continent. But if some desirable appearance should perhaps present itself to their gaze, immediately, as wax melts before fire, so sinners perish before the face of God.

Either they clutch at the desired corpse with the hands of Briareus and the claws of sphinxes; or, if worldly fear prevents them from doing this, at least they direct the eyes of Argus there with roaming looks, that by passive sight they may feed the hunger of their heart and, with the breakfast of concealed delight, foreshadow the fast of lust’s hunger. Thus perished the man who said:

> When I saw her, I perished: thus evil error carried me away.

[Col. 0665A] And another:

> Assuredly, here I am sufficiently strong among thousands;  
> but when something better and more richly anointed comes my way, I am the same.

Likewise, every true chastity is bare; that is, it is a friend of voluntary poverty, shaking its hands free from every gift. For, as our Jerome says, “No married woman who accepts gifts is chaste.” And according to Quintilian: “Avarice is the foundation of women’s vices.”

Indeed, the chastity of many men and women has stood unmoved and intact when assailed by the missiles of words, but has fallen when battered by gifts. To touch briefly upon stories from fable: gold broke into the fortifications of Acrisius’ tower; and upon the foolish virgin who had seemed to triumph over lust on earth, incest rained down from heaven in golden form. Thus one whom a lowly suitor does not seduce is deceived by an exalted one. Thus the north wind uproots the tree which a gentle breeze did not move. Thus too a rose-garden is always stripped of its purple by some storm; but by none more easily than by the golden wind—that is, the brilliance of a monetary gift—according to the verses:

> I do not come as teacher of love to the rich;  
> he who is going to give needs none of my art.  
> He has genius with him who, when he can, has said, “Take”;  
> we yield—he is stronger than my devices when gifts are found.

(Ovid.) And again:

> Believe me, gifts win over both men and gods.

Of the chastity of such persons the Satirist says aptly:

> Thus Penelope is virtuous for you; but if, only once, she tastes  
> of one old man and shares with you some little gain,  
> like a dog from a greased hide she will never be driven away.

(Horace, *Satires* II.5.101.) [Col. 0665C]

But what does it mean that ivory is said to be the elephant’s tooth, except that chastity ought to be toothed: offering the tempter a bite rather than a kiss; displaying a sad rather than cheerful face; answering with hard rather than soft words; more ready to reject than to receive sticky—indeed poisonous—little gifts and letters, as deceptive as they are sweet? For, as Jerome says, “holy love has no flattering little gifts or sweet letters.”

The elephant is toothless who gently refuses consent to shameful conduct. For a gentle refusal to a first request is a certain prognostic of consent to a second. Eve’s soft answer made her penetrable and accessible to poison. Eve’s daughters still retain this manner [Col. 0665D] of replying gently:

> Of many women, scarcely one will refuse you.

“She will refuse,” that is, she will refuse outright—and none refuses outright. For what woman decisively cuts off the petitioner’s words? Who has grieved her suitor with a permanent refusal? Rather, the negative concession, or concessive refusal, of some women has a certain savour of favour. However harshly they answer, somewhere in some corner of their words he will always find a spark of his request still entangled there, as though deliberately and intentionally left. This happens because each woman seems to herself lovable:

> The worst woman becomes so; no one fails to be pleased by her own beauty.

[Col. 0666A]

> Those who grant and those who refuse alike rejoice to be asked.

Hence Jerome: “Even if you do not yield when asked, you nevertheless consider it testimony to your beauty if you are asked.” Therefore they take another’s amorous pursuit as proof of their attractiveness; and from seeing that they please others even a little, they begin already to please themselves too much, according to the line:

> The praises of beauty delight even chaste women.

But in truth she is not chaste who delights in such praise, being already corrupted by the exaltation of her mind. The feeling of corruption commonly accompanies, as a prelude, hidden self-exaltation; and an ulcer of this kind is often healed by a most foul plaster, as it is written: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” (Job 12). Hence Augustine: “I dare to say that it is often useful for the proud to fall into some open and manifest sin, by which they may become displeased with themselves—having already fallen through being pleased with themselves.” [Col. 0666B] Peter found it more salutary to be displeased with himself when he wept than to be pleased with himself when he presumed.

Therefore the elephant is well toothed when, against the importunate grunts of suitors—or rather, swine—it not only bars the way with very harsh words, but with its toothed mouth bites back and repels them in indignant spirit; and with the horned brow of resolute refusal drives and lashes away the suitor once for all, so that there is no need for a second time. Thus blessed Agnes answered, saying: “Depart from me, fuel of sin, food of death, nourishment of crime.” [Note: [Col. 0665D] St Ambrose, Sermon on St Agnes.] Thus the philosopher teaches one to answer, saying: “Let a married woman raise eyes fixed upon the ground, and toward an official greeter be inhuman rather than immodest; let her defend her chastity with her expression long before she does so with a word; for no one who sings loudly is asked a second time.” [Note: [Col. 0665D] Seneca.]

Thus that most unconquered martyr answered: because his hands and feet were bound and he could not otherwise defend himself, he thrust his crushed tongue into the mouth of an immodest woman. Thus our Benedict—blessed both by grace and by name—answered the hidden tempter, vigorously rubbing the enticing but evil itch by rolling most painfully among nettles and thorns.

Thus Mary was, through humility and innocence, a throne; through chastity and constancy of mind, an ivory throne; through perfect charity, a great throne; through fruitfulness, a royal throne and Solomon’s throne. In the throne are shown rest and tranquillity; in ivory, whiteness and solidity; in greatness, capacity; in Solomon, the fruitfulness of peace. Nothing is more tranquil than a conscience that does not reproach itself; nothing more solid than firmness of mind; nothing more capacious than charity. Of the first you have: “A secure mind is a continual feast” (Prov. 15). Of the second: “They can be killed, but they cannot be bent.” [Note: [Col. 0666D] St Gregory.] Of the third: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118). For charity is broader than the ocean and more capacious than heaven itself: it gathers enemies as guests and embraces foes as friends—something neither heaven nor ocean can do.

Truly she was a great throne, who could contain wholly him “whom the whole world cannot contain” [Note: [Col. 0666D] Office of the Church], as the pagan [Col. 0667A] poet also beautifully pursued her praise in Christian verses, saying:

> The virgin womb swelled; the untouched mother marvelled  
> that her hidden entrails were filled with childbirth,  
> about to bear her own Creator. Mortal hearts concealed the Maker of heaven.  
> The Repairer of the world became part of the human race  
> and lay hidden beneath one breast—he who broadly embraces the whole world.  
> He whom neither earth’s expanse, nor ocean’s wave,  
> nor heaven can contain, was gathered into tiny limbs.

But as nothing is more capacious than charity, so nothing is more fruitful than peace, according to the words: “Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent, the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66). Truly she was a great throne, who is also a tower, as is said of her in praise of the bride: “Your neck is like an ivory tower” (Song 7).

We know that by the neck the head is joined to the body and the body fitted to the head. The neck is also the body’s most prominent member, and through the neck, as through a channel, the stomach draws life-giving nourishment to itself. What then is signified by the neck except our mediatrix, the blessed Virgin Mary? She stands uniquely eminent in the body which is the Church; through her we deserved to receive the Author of life, namely the bread of life that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. Through Mary Christ was made Head and Bridegroom of the Church, when the Word, made flesh and coming forth from the virginal womb like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, joined that same Church to himself in a permanent marriage and consecrated her as his own.

This neck is aptly compared [Col. 0667C] to an ivory tower: a tower because of its height, strength, straightness, and gravity. In its height is signified sublimity of vow and loftiness of merit; in its strength, firmness of purpose and the security of human refuge; in the straightness of its desire, holiness and purity of intention; in its gravity, every maturity of character. Mary was truly a tower: sublime and lofty in vow, most exalted in merit, strong in purpose, upright in counsel, erect in desire. Truly an ivory tower: white in virginity, solid in integrity of mind, cold in chaste fear, bare in contempt of the world, armed with zeal for chastity.

Still more, she is truly an ivory tower: set before all as an example of holiness; placed around each person as a protection in battle; placed above all as a spectacle of glory; laid up for all who contend lawfully as the prize of a crown. Indeed, such a neck ought to be placed upon such a head, one wholly fitting to it. What is stronger than a tower, what more beautiful than ivory? Therefore, as it is written of the head: “The Lord reigns; he has put on splendour; the Lord has put on strength and girded himself with power” (Ps. 92), so also of the neck: “Strength and splendour are her clothing” (Prov. 31).

O most beautiful structure, which is both throne and tower: an ivory throne and an ivory tower; a throne for God’s sake, a tower for human beings’ sake. A throne to receive the judge turned toward mercy; a tower to receive the sinner turned toward repentance. A throne capable of containing [Col. 0668A] the God of majesty and immensity, refreshing him when weary, and appeasing him when angry; a tower which protects, defends, and saves those who flee to it.

Let us imitate, I beseech you, beloved ones, the gravity of this tower in our actions, its whiteness in our effects, its sweetness in our conduct, and its holiness in avoiding transgressions. Certainly, if we knew how inflexible the rod of justice is and how unyielding the equity of judgment, we would fear to forfeit innocence so often and to transgress order. For a certain holy man saw most severe punishments inflicted on the souls of the dead for transgressions which we foolishly consider very slight: for immoderate laughter, the harshest blows; for idle words, blows to the face almost to the point of knocking out the eyes; for useless and excessively wandering thoughts, varied harshness of the air; for unrestrained gesture, most severe and often fiery bonds; for a superfluity of gestures by which they conveyed to one another foolish and idle matters, the fingers of the negligent were either stripped of skin down to the palm or battered with hammer-blows upon anvils.

Those who had sought useless wandering, without necessity, outside the cloister or cell—even though in that wandering they had behaved properly—were nevertheless punished by a most severe tossing from place to place, like stones shot from a sling, with a most painful battering of all their limbs. For they had done this from weariness of cloistral silence and regular observance, preferring such comforts to monastic quiet. A discourse stained by any impurity, irreligion, or other disgrace [Col. 0668C] was punished, especially in men of sacred orders, as though it were a capital crime.

Therefore, brethren, let us flee to the strongest and impregnable refuge of this ivory tower: loving quiet, avoiding wandering, immovable before every frivolity like a tower, moving no bodily member without cause. Thus the blessed Bernard commends Saint Malachy: no one, even if he watched attentively, ever saw him move foot or hand in vain. [Note: [Col. 0667D] St Bernard, *Life of St Malachy.*] Let this suffice concerning the words: “Solomon made a great throne of ivory” (2 Kings 10). We leave the remaining part of the description untouched for the present.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS, I

[Col. 0668D]

“The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0668D] Office of the Church.] They rejoice, I say, with exceedingly great joy, because, returning from this world by the right of postliminy, they have deserved to recover the heavenly palace as though recovering gold, an estate, and their paternal possession. Indeed, their possession generally consists in three things: possession of the heavens; fellowship with the angels and with the Queen of angels herself, the glorious Mother of God and Virgin Mary; and finally the most blessed vision of Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts and King of glory.

O what most swift torrents of delight arise, as from fountains of joys, from each of these things! For, to say nothing for the moment of the other two [Col. 0669A], how great a source of joy is the possession of heaven alone! “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” Why should not those rejoice who now dwell in heaven? But in what heavens? What are the heavens, and how many are there?

The Jews say that there are seven heavens. They so extol the number seven that they even maintain that seven heavens were created from the beginning. Pagan philosophers likewise make distinct heavens from each of the spheres of the planets within that well-known heaven in which the fixed stars are found. There have been those who asserted that worlds and heavens alike are innumerable. Some, however, have said that there is, or can be, only one heaven. For they say that the work of one heaven is so great that a second could not be made. As though all great works were unique, when we see so many and such great rivers and seas spread here and there, so many broad and spacious lands, so many dragons of immense length, so many whales of immense breadth, so many elephants of immense bulk.

But what do Jewish tales or philosophers’ dreams matter to us? Scripture of truth plainly asserts that there are several heavens, saying: “The heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you shall remain; and all shall grow old like a garment” (Ps. 101). But the question is how many there are. Let us therefore bring forward the most truthful witness, the Apostle Paul, who said that he was caught up as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12). He thus most plainly declares that there are three heavens. Yet, while he did not affirm that there are more than three, neither did he deny it. And certainly, whether there are more, I do not know; this one thing I know: that there are three.

For, leaving intact every mystical interpretation according to which this saying of Paul is customarily expounded, it seems to me that it can be understood literally also of three material heavens. There are indeed three heavens of which Scripture speaks openly: the aerial heaven, the starry heaven, and the empyrean heaven. The aerial heaven is nearest the earth and filled with its birds. The starry heaven is remote from the earth and studded with its stars. The empyrean heaven is raised far above both and adorned with its blessed spirits. Of the first you have: “Birds of heaven and fish of the sea” (Dan. 3). Of the second: “Stars of heaven, bless the Lord” (ibid.). Of the third: “Heavens and the powers of heaven, and blessed seraphim.” [Note: [Col. 0669D] Office of the Church.]

The first heaven, [Col. 0669D] the aerial heaven, does not belong to the blessedness of souls, for it too is subject to many miseries and shaken by storms and tempests, according to the poetic line:

> Air, nearer to the earth, is kindled by thunderbolts.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book II.)

Finally, that heaven has been assigned as a dwelling-place not only to birds but also to demons. They have been placed there not to adorn the air, as philosophers falsely claim, but are confined there as in a prison until the day of judgment. From the other two heavens, however—the starry and the empyrean—together with their, so to speak, appendages, is constituted that heavenly house [Col. 0670A] of which it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). Yet the starry heaven is, as it were, the pavement or foundation of this house, while the empyrean heaven is its upper structure.

This house is called by many names in Holy Scripture: heaven, earth, bridal chamber, desert, homeland, city, court, bedchamber, and temple. It is called heaven from its serenity; earth from the firmness of its place and the fertility of every good thing; desert from its capacity for all who are saved in comparison with the multitude of the lost; homeland from the native sweetness of its soil, which draws minds toward itself as the natural land of all, according to the line:

> By some sweetness, I know not what, one’s native soil draws all,  
> nor does it allow them to forget it.

[Col. 0670B] (Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book I.)

Even those who are not citizens of that homeland long for it, because although it belongs to few by grace, it ought to have belonged to all by nature. For God is Father of all by creation, though Father of few by adoption. It is called a city from the harmonious multitude of citizens joining together into one commonwealth; a court, as Augustine says, because care for us is conducted there; a palace because of the surpassing nobility of that royal building; a hall because of the great nobility of the persons standing there; a region because of the magnitude of its place; a kingdom because of the justice which chiefly reigns there; and a house because of the sacred and stable dwelling of its inhabitants, and because of the multitude of dwellings, according to the words: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). For there is no campaigning there, as in a tent; rather, there is dwelling, as in a house.

It is called an atrium because of the solemn throng who there praise together and lead choirs, according to the words: “In his courts confess to him with hymns” (Ps. 99), by metonymy, the container being put for what it contains. It is called a bridal chamber from the marital union of Christ and the Church; a mountain from eminence and loftiness; a bedchamber from the highest and most secret pleasure of those resting there; and a temple from the holiness of those who minister there to Christ with untiring diligence, and from their unwearied cry as they sing praises to the divine majesty.

O temple of holiness! O bed of delight; bridal chamber of nuptials, courts of those at play! O house [Col. 0670D] of God, eternal kingdom, region of light! O hall of nobles, royal palace! O court of angels, glorious city, sweet homeland, fertile desert! O land flowing with milk and honey, serene and cloudless heaven! O mountain exceedingly high, curdled mountain, rich mountain; mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell (Ps. 67); mountain upon which has been prepared a feast of rich things, a feast of vintage wine: rich things full of marrow, vintage wine well clarified!

Thus in the name “temple” is signified holiness; lest it be thought sad and burdensome, the temple itself is called a bedchamber, in which pleasure is signified; lest that pleasure be thought common, it is denoted as hidden and innermost through the bridal chamber, according to the words: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isa. 24). In the atrium solemn joy is signified; for an atrium is nothing other than a public square, and games are customarily held in public squares.
