In the house, stability; in the kingdom, power; in the region, abundance and spaciousness; in the hall, nobility; in the palace, beauty; in the court, ordered dominion; in the city, peace and concord; in the homeland, the sweetness of possession; in the desert, the precious scarcity of possessors. For it is called a desert not because the place is uncultivated, but because of the foolish multitude who abandon it. In earth is the firmness of blessedness; in heaven, the serenity of brightness; in the mountain, the loftiness of habitation.

In that temple none minister except the holy; in that chamber [Col. 0671B] none sleep except the chaste; in that bridal room none lie except virgins; in that court none play except the innocent; in that house none dwell except those of one mind, according to the saying: “God, who makes those of one manner to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67).

In that kingdom none reign except the poor, according to: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Yet in that region there are none except exceedingly rich and powerful merchants, according to: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls,” etc. (Matt. 13). Likewise: “God does not reject the mighty, since he himself is mighty” (Job 36). In that hall none stand except those who serve Christ the King in humility. For this is the highest nobility [Col. 0671C]: that in which service of Christ is approved. In that palace none shall reign except those clothed in spiritual softness, as in the purple of modesty and the fine linen of chastity. “For those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11). Into that court none shall enter except those who seek and care for not what is their own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), and what is useful to others rather than to themselves. In that city none remain except the harmonious and peaceable. To that homeland none return except those who groan and weep because their sojourn has been prolonged (Ps. 119), and who therefore hasten to return home and desire it with their whole heart. For this is the speech that reveals the native-born citizens of that homeland; this is their idiom: weeping and sighing out of a longing [Col. 0671D] to return.

Through that wilderness none walk except deserters of the multitude and lovers of solitude, according to the Pythagorean saying: “Do not walk upon the public road”; and the Gospel saying: “Lord, are there few who are saved?” To this the answer is: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13)—as though it said: Learn to be few. Upon that mountain none rests except one “innocent in hands and clean of heart” (Ps. 23); except one ascending from strength to strength; except one transcending the common life of others.

In that heaven none rejoices except one who keeps his conscience, who flees—and indeed drives away—darkness, and who loves the light. For that heaven always enjoys its own day and is always illuminated by the sun. Finally, none possess that land except the gentle and meek. [Col. 0672A] “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5). And again: “The meek shall inherit the land” (Ps. 36). But what land? Certainly not the land of the dying, but that of the living, of which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). For hell is the land of the dead; this world, or the corruptible human body, is the land of the dying. But the land of the living is the immortal body which we shall possess, or that heavenly dwelling in which we shall dwell. And truly blessed are those who are to possess that land.

What land? Not land which brings forth thorns and thistles (Gen. 3); not land subject to a curse or struck with anathema; not barren and unfruitful land, but fertile and rich land, which [Col. 0672B] “devours its inhabitants” through its delights and riches (Num. 13): a land of promise and possession—of promise in relation to us, to whom it is still promised and not yet given; of possession in relation to those by whom it is already possessed—the land that flows with milk and honey.

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5). What then? If this land of the dying—subject to a curse, struck with anathema, and bringing forth thorns and thistles for those who cultivate it—nevertheless produces for its inhabitants so many and such great kinds of pleasures, how much more numerous and greater things must that land of the living be believed to produce for its possessors? If this accursed earth delights miserable mortals so greatly—whether by the colors of its flowers, the flavors of its fruits, the fragrances of its spices, or the sweetness of various harmonies—how much more must that land, filled with every blessing, be believed to delight the blessed and immortal? Must we suppose that there are lacking there most beautiful colors, unusual fragrances, most delicate flavors, or the sweetest harmonies of voices? “But,” you will say, “these are bodily goods.” Certainly spiritual counterparts can exist. For even bodily goods cannot delight any bodies except living ones; inanimate things do not perceive them.

Moreover, if the soul, imprisoned in a body, enjoys its delights, does it lose all pleasures when it leaves the body? But if it cannot rejoice except in a body, then by the same reasoning it cannot suffer except [Col. 0672D] in a body. Thus it cannot perceive except in a body, nor live except in a body. For just as there is no joy without perception, so there is no pain. Where there is no perception, there is plainly no mode or kind of living, and in general no life whatsoever. Therefore the soul does not live at all without a body, nor perceive without a body. But if this is granted concerning one sense, it must necessarily be granted concerning all. It remains, then, that the soul, even when placed outside the body, can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch. Otherwise one would have to say that neither angel nor God does any of these things, since they are not bodily.

“What then,” you ask, “does an incorporeal spirit have eyes, ears, and its other members?” I answer: no. These are necessary to the body, so that by means of the instruments of such members it may perform the functions of its senses. But they are not necessary to the spirit, which, because it is simple, can perceive without them just as it can live without them. Therefore the soul sees and hears wholly through itself, just as it touches wholly through itself. For not only is the general sense of touch exercised through the whole soul; all the other senses are exercised through the whole soul as well. It does not see through one member and hear through another, since it has no members; nor does it see with one part and not see with another, since it is not divided into parts. Rather, it is wholly capable of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching.

If this seems strange to anyone, let that person consider something greater concerning the soul, and this lesser thing will not seem strange. For if, while it is in [Col. 0673B] the body, the soul is wholly in each individual part of the body, what wonder is it if, when it is outside the body, it is wholly present in each of its senses? It therefore perceives more effectively outside the body than in the body. For then whatever it perceives, as people commonly say, it perceives in the manner of a spirit. Then it perceives whatever it does perceive wholly, and not in part, since it has nothing about it by which it could do otherwise. Therefore it sees more clearly, hears more keenly, smells more powerfully, tastes more inwardly, and touches more strongly and, in some manner, more closely. Hence it rejoices or suffers more intensely.

When, however, it receives its body again—not an animate but a spiritual body, not heavy but light, not a burden but an honor to it—it will not lose this power of perception, but will retain it all the more powerfully and wholly. Thus, as I have said, the soul, already stripped of its body, has its own colors, fragrances, and flavors, either suited to it, by which it is delighted, or opposed to it, by which it is tormented. As we have shown this by arguments, so we shall now show it by examples.

We read that at the bodies of many saints much heavenly light has shone forth, that many heavenly assemblies have been present, that they have uttered many sweetest songs, and that by their presence they have sprinkled those present with many most sweet fragrances. O how great must be the abundance of all these things in heaven, if their foretaste on earth is so great! Philosophers also testify—if their testimony is true—that the motion of the heavenly sphere produces a most sweet harmony. But whatever may be the case concerning heaven’s harmony, I believe without doubt that the voice [Col. 0673D] of a single angel is sweeter than the swiftest motion of the firmament. What an angel’s voice is, I believe, cannot be known by a mortal human being, unless perhaps by one who, with Paul, has been caught up to the third heaven and there heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12).

“O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession!” (Baruch 3). What, then, do we suppose to be the breadth of that royal palace, whose pavement is so wonderfully embossed, so thickly studded with stars, illumined by radiance, raised to such a height, set apart in breadth, extended in length, founded in firmness, and adorned most beautifully? O you who seek beautiful houses on earth, why do you despise so beautiful a house in heaven? Why do you spend your riches upon such worthless buildings? For however fine they may be, they must be destroyed, and “not one stone shall be left upon another” in them (Matt. 24). Where are David’s cedar house, Solomon’s stone house, Ahab’s ivory house, Khosrow’s silver house, Nero’s golden house, Ahasuerus’s jewelled house? All have fallen and shall not rise again. Even if they could be rebuilt, they would have to be destroyed again.

Happy is the person who has exchanged a collapsing and lowly house for the eternal dwelling of angels! For “every human being shall go to the house of his eternity” (Eccl. 12): his own house, that is, which he has acquired by his merit—good if by good merit, evil if by evil. Yet an evil and eternal house is worse than an evil and collapsing one, or than no house at all. For nothing is more unhappy than immortal evil. Therefore I called happy the one who exchanged a collapsing house not merely for an eternal one, but for one both eternal and glorious. There are two eternal houses: the worst and the best, hell and paradise. The first is wholly subterranean; the second heavenly. No building is more glorious than heaven, none more enduring, none more delightful.

Why do you marvel at the beautiful yet perishable buildings of the rich? You ought rather to observe and marvel that their houses, the more beautiful they are, have been built all the more shamefully: because they have been built with more sins, greater wickedness, and more cruel plunder. The lesser part of the expense comes from the builder’s own property; the greater from another’s. For the rich have learned such a habit of using what belongs to others that they do not know how to make even a little house out of their own resources. From their own they are most miserly; with another’s goods they are generous—yet with a generosity as ungrateful as it is arrogant and self-seeking. For they give nothing freely; though they grant little, they count it as much, reckoning whatever they receive as little, however much it may be.

But this is most shameful in them: although they are not in need, they nevertheless, as though needy, very shamelessly beg much under the pretext of friendship, obtain more by fear, extort the greatest part, and seize everything by force. They shamelessly seek building materials from abbeys; they collect, with the utmost injustice, from those whom they set over their affairs the money needed for these materials; like harpies, they inhumanely exact unpaid labor from their subjects. Thus, though they build beautiful buildings out of what belongs to others, they boast as if they had built from their own. Yet I wonder whether anyone can consider beautiful a building known to have been built so shamefully.

One should ask such builders why they work so hard to construct beautiful houses. Is it so that they may delight in looking at them? As if anything could be more beautiful than heaven or more adorned than the firmament! Miserable person, if the beauty of a building delights you, why does the beauty of heaven not delight you? Certainly, if you wished, you could possess heaven more easily than you could build yourself a palace. For in the purchase of heaven, will alone is the price; in building a palace, great wealth is necessary.

Most truly, then, did blessed Pope Gregory say: “Nothing is cheaper than the kingdom of heaven when it is bought; nothing more costly [Col. 0675A] when it is possessed.” This kingdom, this possession, belongs principally and properly to the poor—namely, to those who desire to possess nothing in this world; secondarily, it belongs to the rich who are rich in good works and bind the poor to themselves, so that the poor may become intercessors for them before God. O how happy an exchange: to receive a poor person in this hut for a brief time, and to be received by that person in heaven eternally! O what glory: to become poor for your sake, good Jesus, and soon thereafter to become with you the advocate of a rich person! Hence the Gospel saying: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven; and blessed are the meek, because they shall possess the land (Matt. 5). [Col. 0675B] For the former, possessing heaven, can distribute it to their friends; and the latter can share with others the land they possess. O how unhappy and foolish is the rich person from whose gate a poor person is excluded, when that rich person is himself to be excluded from the gate of paradise unless he is introduced by a poor person as by a doorkeeper! This is why the poor, and indeed all the perfect, make no house of their own for themselves on earth: they know that God has prepared for them an eternal house in heaven, as Paul also teaches. Thus the poor man sings: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” (Ps. 121). And again: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (ibid.).

In preparation for this house, the ancient saints before the flood, and many afterward, are recorded as having possessed no houses, but as living in tabernacles [Col. 0675C] and tents—mobile houses, as it were, which can be carried here and there. By this they signified that they had no lasting city or house in this world, but sought the future one. Therefore Christ too was born not in a house but in a lodging-place, in order to show that every one of his disciples is not a citizen of this world but a pilgrim. In agreement with this is Cato’s saying, cited by Cicero: “I depart from life as from an inn, not as from a home. For nature gave us a lodging-place for staying, not a house for dwelling.”

Cain, the first fratricide, is recorded to have built a city (Gen. 4), and from this it is understood that he was also the first to build a house. After the flood, however, the tower of Babylon was constructed.

[Col. 0675D] The first covering of the human being was innocence; the second, woven fig leaves; the third, a garment of skins; the fourth, an earthen house; the sixth, wooden, iron, and stone houses. Thus humanity gradually advanced to more precious material for these coverings, or fortifications. The first may be called of nature; the second, of fault; the third, of misery; the fourth, of shame; the fifth, of fear; the sixth and those following, of pride. For when humanity lost innocence, it was stripped, as it were, of its natural garment and robbed of the protection of glory. When it saw itself naked and unarmed, it quickly wove for itself, from whatever material first came to hand, some sort of covering and fortification at once.

But the covering made of leaves concealed, as it were, fault alone; it did not drive away misery. I say “as it were,” not truly concealed, because by a kind of presage it made the human being appear covered and protected, though in reality naked and left exposed to every misery. But when God determined to punish humanity for sin, even in punishment he had mercy on it because of the weakness of the flesh, so that even then he might fulfil that prophetic saying: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3). Therefore he made a garment of skins, by which he might both cover nakedness and in large measure protect weakness.

In the course of time, when innocence among humankind began not merely to be stripped off but utterly extinguished, and clothing was no longer sufficient to cover lust, houses began to be built to protect shamefulness, as it is written: “The beginning of human life is water and bread, clothing, and a house protecting shamefulness” (Ecclus. 29)—that is, protecting against the violence of shameful people. Shamefulness, in respect of human eyes, is as well covered by reed as by gold; but chastity, against the behavior of the shameful, is not as well protected by hay as by wood. As wickedness increased, it became necessary not only to cover lust, but to protect chastity and to defend against iniquity. Thus huts began to develop into palaces, hedges into walls, estates into towns, hamlets into cities: first from necessity, then from excessive wickedness and fear.

Yet traces of ancient sobriety still remain among certain peoples. Some Scythians have no houses, but travel in wagons covered with hides against rain and heat. The Gymnosophists in India’s wildernesses philosophize naked, not only without houses but even without clothing. Sallust testifies concerning the people of the Mundas that they have low houses resembling the hull of a ship. And indeed, how great is the madness for one human being to labor so greatly over the spaciousness of great houses and of a bodily multitude, when so small a dwelling of the body contains him! What good will costly buildings made for the body do him when the soul leaves the body itself? Why this waste? Such things could and should have been left aside, and the expenses given to the poor.

But our rich people, as was said of the citizens of Megara, live [Col. 0676D] as though they were to die tomorrow; they build as though they were to live forever. O what a most perverse order! For the worst course is to build [houses: the printed “virtues” appears corrupt] as though we were always going to die, and to live as though we were always going to live. Thus provision would be made for bodily health and expenses would be spared. Certainly a collapsing house was sufficient for a collapsing guest, just as a mortal body was made for a dying human being. How great is the madness for a human being soon to collapse to build as though he were to live forever! “The form of this world passes away,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 7); yet people wish to dwell in this world as though they would never pass away.

“But here,” someone will say, “why then do you Cistercians, although you have left everything and professed sobriety and poverty, construct buildings so costly and superfluous? You could—indeed, you should—have left these things aside and distributed the expense to the poor.” As though these things were not made for the poor!

For they are made not only for the poor of the present time but also for those who will come long afterward. “But,” one says, “they could have been made simpler.” What if things so costly were necessary? For whatever is costly is not immediately superfluous. After all, what is ornate in them? What paintings, sculptures, or columns supporting nothing are there? Indeed, what in them is not necessary? They are large so that the expected abundance of produce may be stored together rather than scattered among many buildings and many guards. They are of stone so that they may more easily resist collapse, fire, and other dangerous accidents. I say this only of buildings [Col. 0677B] which are storehouses for provisions and do not exceed a suitable measure, and in which provisions are stored not only for monks but also for the poor and pilgrims.

Otherwise, this excuse of ours—though cautious—will have no weight and offer no defense to those of our profession who, as though fighting against wealth, build with inexhaustible and hidden springs of money: palaces in place of guesthouses, ramparts in place of walls, towers in place of refectories, castles in place of dormitories, churches in place of chapter houses, fortresses in place of churches, estates in place of granges. They are rightly mocked by secular people for these excesses. A meal could be eaten in a refectory without such things; a poor person could be received in a guesthouse; grain gathered in a barn; sleep taken in a dormitory; pardon sought in a chapter house; the divine office celebrated in a church.

“But,” they say, “we do not make these things for ourselves alone, but for the religious who will be among us in the future.” As though the evil of the present day were not sufficient unto itself unless anxiety were added concerning not merely tomorrow but a day a hundred years hence. Clearly we ought to live in our own time, not another’s. It is misery enough that we should be anxious about necessities sufficient for our own age; why do we lay upon ourselves the burdens of those to come? It is great enough charity to bear one another’s burdens, which can be understood only of contemporaries: for one who does not exist is not “another” in relation to me. Whoever does not yet exist, does not exist.

We are not, therefore, commanded to bear the burdens of the future, but only those of the present and of those living with us—and would that we did even these! Certainly, one who did so would, according to the Apostle’s testimony, fulfil the law (Gal. 6). What sort of charity is it not to heed a poor person now crying at the door, but to construct a building for one who will cry out later; to give nothing to one now hungry, but to reserve alms for one who does not yet exist, though, when that person does exist, perhaps he will receive nothing from what you prepare? By your present example of foolish thrift you train the ears of your successors not to listen to those crying out, and you sharpen the claws of the greedy to seize what is yours.

Finally, if we are poor and wish to be believed poor, why do we make ourselves seem rich? Although such great [Col. 0678A] buildings are made by us poor people for the poor, people nevertheless find it difficult to believe that those who spend so much on buildings are poor. Still more difficult is it to believe that these things are made for the poor, since they will benefit not so much the sustenance of the poor as the plundering of the rich. For although these buildings themselves are truly holy, both because of the religion of their inhabitants and because of the celebration of divine worship, nevertheless, because they are excessively costly, they win among secular people not as much reverence as envy at the excessive scale of their expense.

Certainly Solomon’s Temple was holy and venerable; yet because it was built at such cost and possessed vessels so desirable, it provoked the nations more to plunder its riches than to observe its rites. But let this be said against the esteem of great and beautiful buildings, which greatly hinder their lovers from attaining the eternal house not made by hands in heaven, where the souls of the saints now rejoice. They rejoice, I say, first, as we have already said, in their threefold deliverance; then in their threefold possession, the first part of which is their possession, now secured, of this eternal house. Let what has been said thus far suffice concerning it. To avoid weariness, we have judged that what remains should be assigned to another sermon.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS, II

“The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0677D] Ecclesiastical Office.]

People commonly say: “He who saves something from his dinner has the better of it when he eats supper.” You know that on this very day of the preceding year, from this same antiphon, filled with the sweet melody of a special chant, I prepared for you a spiritual dinner—perhaps neither as useful nor as pleasing as it ought to have been, but certainly as useful as I was able to prepare. Yet at that little dinner I did not wish to set before you the small remainder that I could have offered. Since nearly half was abundantly sufficient for the occasion and time, I judged that it was not useful to serve the whole. For that small portion then served was multiplied by so abundant a blessing of the Lord that, after the diners had been filled, fragments remained, like those of the Gospel feeding. [Note: [Col. 0678D] He alludes to Christ’s deed, John 6.]

In accordance with the Lord’s command I have now endeavored to collect these with utmost care and thanksgiving, so that from [Col. 0678D] them I might prepare for you today a supper no smaller than the dinner which preceded it. In reverence for this supper, lest you approach it as though with unwashed hands, I have thought it proper first to pour out a few words as a kind of hand-washing. “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven,” etc.

I told you, and you have already heard, that from this antiphon there resounded for us two songs of the heavenly harpists: the song of the way and the song of the homeland; the song of exile and the song of the kingdom; the song of those fighting for the kingdom of heaven and the song of those already reigning in heaven. Of these two, I had first to expound to you the first, the song of the way, because by nature it must always come first.

[Col. 0679A] It follows, therefore, that I should redeem my promise with a word concerning the second, that is, the song of the homeland, since I am already bound to fulfil it by the bond of my promise. And certainly, to confess it with shame, it would have been wiser for me to promise nothing. For since, as one saint says, [Note: [Col. 0679D] St Bernard.] no one can belch forth what he has not tasted, and, according to another, [Note: [Col. 0679D] St Jerome.] small talents cannot bear great subjects, what mortal human being—and especially a sinner of slight knowledge and weightier conscience—can discourse on the immortal joy of the saints? Therefore I must have recourse to that saving counsel of blessed Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0680D] In the Prologue of the Rule.] namely, that for what nature possesses too little ability, we should ask God to deign to supply the help of his grace. He must be asked, moreover, not only by me but also by you, [Col. 0679B] because I speak not so much for myself as for you.

Indeed, this is said to have been the custom of blessed Augustine: whenever he preached to the people, if a difficult passage arose, he would first ask for the people’s prayers in order to obtain a fitting transition. Therefore, in a similar situation, raise the cry of your prayers and call upon for me the merciful power and powerful mercy of him who made the deaf hear and the mute speak, that by the most powerful key of his word he may release the bond of my tongue for grace, open the door of your heart for understanding, and at the same time draw back the bolt of the will of us all for obedience.

Otherwise, the one who refuses to obey the command of the heavenly King hears or speaks in vain about heavenly joy, according to that promise of the Lord joined with a threat: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling,” etc., “the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1). Here it is plainly shown that no one can better—indeed, no one can otherwise—either purchase or earn the feast of heavenly goods except through obedience to the commandments. Otherwise he will be devoured by the sword of God’s word; that is, he will be eternally enveloped in the sentence of condemnation and inseparably incorporated into the mass of the lost, so that thereafter he can no more escape condemnation than food incorporated into a body can leave it.

The word “devour,” moreover, signifies the total destruction of body and soul. For what is devoured is swallowed whole, not bitten piece by piece: as a herring is swallowed by a whale, or a frog by a pike; as the reprobate have been swallowed whole by hell. The reason given, “the mouth of the Lord has spoken,” is excellent—as though it said: Not the mouth of a human being, which is often despised with impunity, but the mouth of the Lord, for whom to speak is to do; whose curse is everlasting condemnation and whose blessing is eternal salvation.

Any Catholic preacher may rightly be called the mouth of the Lord, because he is a proclaimer of the divine word. Hence the Lord says to him: “If you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15). Of such persons it is also said: “Whoever hears you hears me, [Col. 0680A] and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). Therefore the mouth of the Lord speaks to you when we speak to you. Do not be deceived: we shall not be despised with impunity, nor heard without consequence. Through hearing us, you are either to be saved or, through contempt, condemned.

“The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” There are three sources of joy in heaven for the souls of the saints. They rejoice in their deliverance; they rejoice in their possession; they rejoice in their expectation. They rejoice in what they have been rescued from, in what they have gained, and in what they know with complete certainty that they will attain. They rejoice in the evil they no longer have, in the good which they foresee that they will possess. Let us consider each in turn.

The souls of the saints, stripped of their bodies, have none of the three evils in which all human misery is contained. They now have no sin, suffer no pain, and fear no danger. They are freed from every bond of fault, every sensation of punishment, and every fear and danger belonging to both. Yet while they were in their bodies, they could never lack these three evils. For no human being lives without the first and third, and no saint without the second. Concerning the first, you have: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Concerning the third: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10). If all who stand can fall, then all are in danger. Concerning the second, Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, that you shall weep and lament, but the world [Col. 0680C] shall rejoice,” etc. (John 16). This is said properly of the saints, from whose salutary and temporal sorrow this world is exempted and is therefore excluded from their everlasting joy.

“The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9)—that is, thinks various and changeable things. This proves that we are not without sin, because we do not always think upon the one thing necessary. But the fact that “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3), and that “while we are in the body we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5), shows that we ought not to be without pain. And the saying, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—understand, not only—“but also against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6), [Col. 0680D] signifies that we cannot be without danger and must always fear for ourselves. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28).

Otherwise, one who has sin and does not grieve over it does not have even the beginning of righteousness. But one who sees danger and does not fear it does not have even the beginning of wisdom. For sorrow over fault is the gate of righteousness, and “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). And as sin is a most just cause of sorrow, so danger is a cause of fear.

These three evils, which accompany all the saints while they are soldiers in the body, signify three sacraments of the Church, [Col. 0681A] instituted at once to signify them and to guard against them: the washing of feet, the imposition of ashes, and sprinkling with holy water. The first of these was instituted by the Lord; the following two by the Church. In the washing of feet is signified that, so long as we live upon the earth, we contract something of the dust of sin, from which we need to be cleansed. Hence this observance is more frequent among monks than among others: namely, to signify that, although they have left the world, although they have renounced all things, although they have transcended the common life of others, yet, while they are in the body, they cannot be wholly without sin. Therefore, if they wish to be washed by the Lord, they must wash one another: that is, each must forgive the other what he has against him. Otherwise, according to the parable of the wicked servant (Matt. 18), so also will the heavenly Father do to them unless each forgives his brother from his heart.

This sacrament, then, was instituted for three purposes: for mystery, for remedy, and for example. It signifies sin by the filth of the feet, which is scarcely washed from the feet; it provides the remedy of brotherly love through mutual washing; and it leaves us the example of humility from the Lord, which is also shown in the bending of the knees. I call this washing of feet a sacrament because it is a sign of a sacred thing. For it signifies the two greatest virtues, the first and the last: humility and love, which are the alpha and omega, the beginning and end, of all good things. For every good begins from humility [Col. 0681C] and is perfected in love. Thus this sacramental washing of feet is not inappropriately called, by antonomasia, “the commandment”: that is, as though it were the commandment of commandments. Hence it is also the completion of the rest, delivered by the Lord after all the others, given not by word alone but commended by his own example. In it the humility of the divine majesty and the compassion of the Father are, in a manner, visibly expressed.

That blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, knew very well the sweetness and efficacy of this commandment. Every night, kneeling, he washed and dried with his own hands the feet of twelve brethren; weeping for each one, he sought from each prayers in return for such service. But whoever washes another’s feet, or is washed by another, and does not from his heart forgive the brother who asks pardon, is among his brethren as Judas was among the apostles. Not even the Master’s own love and humility could move Judas to lay aside the resentment previously conceived in his heart.

Then, by the imposition of ashes, is signified what wage is due to sin: namely, the necessity of dying and the burning of fire. For just as useless wood is destined for fire, so sin is destined for burning; and just as fire necessarily ends in ash, so sin ends in death. Hence: “The wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6). Ashes are therefore imposed upon the sinner, so that he may remember death and continually turn over in his breast [Col. 0682A] the avenging fire of Gehenna. Thus it is said to him: “Remember, man, that you are ashes, and to ashes you shall return” (Job 34). Therefore also among philosophers, as Basil says, the first definition of philosophy is meditation upon death.

Job gave us the first example of this sacrament, when he did penance in dust and ashes. Moreover, he who said the following most briefly and fully defined the usefulness of remembering death:

> “He easily despises all things who always reflects that he is going to die.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0681D] Jerome, Epistle to Cyprian.]

Therefore blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, in order to keep this remembrance continually in his heart, ate ashes and slept in ashes, so that he might fulfil even literally that saying of David: “I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. [Col. 0682B] 101).

What will Christians of our age say here—especially priests and clerics—who do not cover themselves with ashes but perfume themselves; who do not mourn but applaud; who do not sleep in sackcloth and haircloth but luxuriate in purple and fine linen? O glory of the Christian people, where are you?

In the sprinkling of holy water is signified that invisible enemies always come to meet us. Hence, on entering church for Prime, and on leaving it after Compline, we sprinkle ourselves, signifying that, whether we wake or sleep, we always and everywhere encounter our adversaries ready to harm us. What do the sons of distrust say here, who neither fear God nor reverence man; who are always in foolish security, as though they possessed the works of the saints; who think all things safe while enemies everywhere lie hidden in ambush? O foolish and blind children of this age, who set a table for Fortune, thinking themselves fortunate if they always have at their head a wine-vessel with a cup ready, rather than a little vessel of holy water with an aspergillum; who do not see imminent dangers, or, if they see them, do not fear or avoid them; who sleep dangerously among serpents and perniciously make a pact with enemies.

For this is why those careless and secure persons are so often bitten: now by the *hypnale* of lust, now by the *prester* of pride, now by the *haemorrhois* of anger, now by the *pareas* of arrogance, now by the scorpion of detraction, now by the deadly basilisk of hatred. Against the bites of such serpents, against the assaults [Col. 0682D] of these enemies, the sprinkling of holy water has been given to us not only as a mystery but also as an aid. Demons greatly fear holy water—not because it is water, but because it is blessed: because the invocation of the divine Name has been pronounced over it, together with the dreadful remembrance of the judgment that is to come upon them.

Yet they fear even more the virtues themselves signified by holy water, in the signification of which the water itself is exorcised. For in holy water there are three things: water, salt, and the invocation of the divine Name. Water signifies fear, salt discretion, and the invocation faith or prayer. Fear cools the heat of desire; discretion gives savour together with the other virtues; faith or prayer obtains what is asked. Water without salt is fear without discretion. Fear is indiscreet when a human being is feared more than God, or when one fears without hope. For one ought to fear in hope and hope with fear. But neither fear nor hope benefits, nor can accomplish anything, without faith. Faith, however, can do whatever it can do in God’s name; and therefore the invocation of the divine Name is joined to the two things already mentioned.

These are weapons mighty through God, by which the devil must be resisted while we are still placed in the contest and in an uncertain struggle, with victory hanging in doubt and hope inclining now this way, now that. But the souls of the saints, stripped of their bodies, no longer need these weapons, for they fear no danger. Rightly, therefore, [Col. 0683B] they rejoice in heaven, freed not only from every evil but also from the causes of evils. Every stain has been cleansed from them, every affliction wiped away, every fear shut out, every danger passed beyond; temptations have been torn away from them, nor can the enemy hurl against them the missiles of his malice.

Therefore, rejoicing, they say to God: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65). That is to say: O Lord, with your help we escaped every kind of temptation. We crossed the water of fear, tribulation, and corruption while you guided our passage; we leapt over the fire of desire and the fire of punishment while you breathed upon us; and we were brought out into refreshment, that is, into a most secure place, where neither guilt now stains, [Col. 0683C] nor punishment wounds, nor danger frightens or disturbs.

The Psalmist declares this threefold joy of souls in their threefold deliverance in these words: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you. For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from slipping” (Ps. 114). It is the voice of a holy soul brought out from the prison-house of the flesh, as though saying to itself: “My soul, consider and measure your rest—your own, I say, not that which you acquired by your merit, but that which you merited by God’s gift.” And this is what follows: “Because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you”: that is, because the Lord gave you this rest.

What rest he gave it is explained when he says, “For he has delivered my soul,” and so forth. He delivered my soul from death—that is, from sin, which is the cause of the soul’s dying; my eyes from tears—that is, my senses from every affliction, which causes the eyes to languish; my feet from slipping—that is, my affections from the dangerous companionship of slippery flesh, which causes the affections to fall again. Or thus: “He delivered my soul from death,” that is, from eternal damnation; “my eyes from tears,” that is, from the punishments of purgatory, which wash away sins in the future age as tears do in the present, though more severely; “my feet from slipping,” that is, from every danger and fear of falling again.

And if we wish to attain this first joy of souls through threefold deliverance, we must strive in the present life to be delivered from the death of sins, from the tears of sorrows, and from the danger of falls. The first deliverance is obtained through confession and penance; the second [Col. 0684A] through security of conscience and patience; the third through fear and caution. For all things are washed in confession, and penance frees from death. The former is the washing away of sins; the latter is the first resurrection of the dead.

Moreover, a secure mind is like a continual feast, and patience is a remedy for every pain. There are two kinds of pain: pain of the heart and pain of the body. A secure conscience delivers from the first, patience from the second. A secure conscience consists in two things: cleansing of past sin and firmness of purpose regarding the future. One who cleanses past sins but does not resolve and strive to avoid future ones is secure behind, but not before. But one who has a firm purpose to avoid future sins, yet does not grieve for those committed, is, as it were, armed and secure in front but left unarmed behind. But one who breaks his heart over sins committed, afflicts his body, and moreover has a firm purpose to avoid future sins is secure on every side.

Patience is like an iron wall, impenetrable by the sword of any pain. But one who is fearful and cautious cannot easily encounter danger. Yet we can avoid danger in no way better than by fleeing the dangerous place—that is, the world. But how can we flee the world while we are in the world? Hear how: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). Hear also another way of fleeing the world: “Do not love [Col. 0684C] the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 3).

There are, then, three kinds of fleeing the world. The first renounce worldly things, but not desires; the second renounce desires, but not things; the third renounce both things and desires. The first flee the world bodily; the second mentally; the third in both ways, that is, in mind and body. The first are false religious; the second good secular people; the third good religious. The first flee fire and hide fire in their bosom. The second stand at a precarious height with wavering step, like tightrope-walkers. The third proceed on the straight and royal road, unburdened and secure.

Because of this twofold flight, I believe that, according to blessed Gregory, the word “flee” is placed twice in the Song of Songs where it says: “Flee, my beloved, flee” (Song 8). It is as though it said: Flee in heart, flee in body; flee inwardly, flee outwardly. Hence the Philosopher says: “Flee the multitude; flee the few; flee even one.” And the voice addressed to Arsenius says: “Arsenius, flee human beings and you will be saved.” Moreover, as the Wise Man says, one who thinks of flight ought not to doze.

I say this because of certain persons known to me, who resolved long ago indeed to flee, not knowing, miserable men, that death coming unexpectedly grants no one a reprieve for flight. Chrysaurius bears witness: as he was dying, he asked and repeatedly asked for a reprieve even until morning, but did not receive it.

Let these remarks suffice concerning the first joy of holy souls, which they have from their deliverance. Now our pen must turn to the second joy that they have from their possession; [Col. 0685A] but because the hour has now passed, let us reserve this for another time.

## SERMON XXV. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS, III

> The saints’ devout faith,  
> The believers’ unconquered hope,  
> Christ’s perfect love  
> Triumphs over the prince of the world.  
> [Note: [Col. 0685D] Church Hymn.]

Every rational creature was created finally in order to reign, formally in order to fight. For the Lord, like a warrior—whose name is Almighty; the Lord strong and mighty in battle—created it in his image and likeness, that it might fight, conquer, and reign. For it cannot reign unless it first conquers, nor conquer unless it fights. For without conflict there is no victory, and without victory no crown. “For he shall not be crowned unless [Col. 0685B] he has competed lawfully.”

Hence the name *militia*, military service, is common to every rational creature, both angelic and human. “There was, with the angel, a multitude of the heavenly host praising God” (Luke 2). This concerns the good angels. Of the evil angels Scripture says: “They worshipped all the host of heaven” (2 Kings 21), that is, every aerial power. Of human beings Scripture says: “The life of man upon earth is military service” (Job 7), or, according to another reading, “temptation,” which comes to the same meaning. For where there is temptation, there is attack; where there is attack, there is conflict—at least on the part of the attacker. Where there is conflict, there is military service: that is, service in fighting. For to serve as a soldier is to serve in order to fight.

There is good servitude, and there is bad servitude. No servitude is better than serving God, to whom to serve is to reign. He serves God who serves righteousness, who commanded righteousness to be kept, reserving eternal rewards for those who keep it and punishments for those who do not. No servitude is worse or more shameful than the servitude of sin, to which to serve is to perish. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). No servitude is more miserable than serving the devil, whom everyone who serves sin serves. “He who commits sin is the servant of sin.” “For whoever is overcome by anyone, to him he is also enslaved.”

Hence God is called the God of Sabaoth, that is, of hosts or armies, because all the holy orders of blessed spirits in heaven and all the choirs and battle-lines of the elect on earth serve in his army. Thus: “What will you see in the Shunammite [better, the Shulammite], except the choirs [Col. 0685D] of camps?” (Song 7).

There are two things that make a lawful soldier, whether bodily or spiritual: election and an oath, namely. For one who, not having been chosen, thrusts himself into military service provokes against himself the sword which he presumptuously usurps; and, as that greatest author of Roman eloquence says, he is rightly called not a soldier but a cutthroat. In the writings of the ancients, all who bear arms without the law’s command are called robbers and cutthroats. For arms which the law does not employ attack the law. Cato does not call anyone a soldier unless he has already been consecrated to military service by the oath. Hence in a letter he warns his son not to enter battle. For he denies that one who is not a soldier—that is, chosen and consecrated—has the right to fight the enemy.

For one who is to serve as a soldier must first be chosen, then, once chosen, be bound to military service by an oath. Julius Frontinus says that in the consulship of Lucius Plancus and Gaius Varro soldiers were first made such by the *iusiurandum* (sworn oath); previously they had been bound only by the *sacramentum* administered by the tribunes. The formula of the oath, as Vegetius says, is this: “Soldiers swear by God the Father, and Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the emperor—which, after God, must be loved and honoured by humankind—that they will vigorously do all things commanded by the emperor; that they will never desert military service or refuse death for the republic whose soldiers they are.”

Therefore, to describe lawful military service briefly: it is the voluntary selection of young men and sworn service, undertaken permanently for the defence of the commonwealth. This description of military service applies both to angels and to human beings. For all were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world; all are also young, more by the vigour of their office than by bodily age. All serve voluntarily, not under compulsion, inclining by grace the freedom of their will to serve righteousness. Their service is also sworn, that is, confirmed by an inviolable purpose. I say inviolable in angels, because it cannot be violated; in human beings, because it ought not to be violated.

The holy angels publicly swore this service in the presence of God and his adversary Satan when that one, with his followers, proudly rebelled against God and abandoned his most just and blessed service and obedience by a voluntary, not compelled, falling away. They themselves voluntarily remained firm in their purpose of humble obedience, and were immediately confirmed in it, God rewarding them happily. For they feared, and, terrified, were purified.

All Christians swear this same service when they receive the sacrament of baptism. How, then, can the prince of this world trust those soldiers whom he sees not keeping the faith owed to their lord, to whom—to say nothing of the rest—they are bound even by the oath of military service? There is no direction in which the ungodly person can turn who prefers a human being to God. One who has made the first faith void will by no means keep the second. [Col. 0686D]

The defence of the commonwealth is the defence of righteousness. A commonwealth is the affair of a people. But that is most truly a public affair which is commonly necessary to the whole people and ought to be loved in common by all the people and, if possible, equally. What is as necessary to every people as righteousness? This is the thing which all must use in the present and enjoy in the future. We use it through the practice of virtues and through longing for righteousness to be fulfilled; we shall enjoy it through the satisfaction of righteousness fulfilled. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5). Truly they, and they alone. For righteousness is an everlasting and immortal food [Col. 0687A] which alone can fill the infernal abyss of human desire—that is, the broad, deep chasm opening out without measure.

The public enemies are the enemies of righteousness: all demons who attack human beings, and all human beings who assist demons in sin. All these have become an aid to the sons of Lot.

This service must be undertaken permanently and never abandoned, as not only the Church’s profession of faith teaches, but also the formula of the oath of this particular military service and the solemn custom of ordination as a soldier. It is as follows. On the day when a man serving as a soldier is adorned with the belt, he solemnly enters the church, hears Mass, and, with a sword placed upon and brought forward, as though having made a public profession, devotes himself to the service of the altar and promises God the service of the sword—that is, the yoke of his office. Henceforth such a man may do much for the Church, but nothing against it. For he does no less than a monk, abbot, or bishop who offers a written profession.

The proper use of ordered military service, therefore, is to protect the Church, attack unbelief, venerate the priesthood, repel injuries to the poor, pacify the province, shed blood for one’s brethren, as the formula of the oath teaches, and, if need be, lay down one’s life. Thus among human beings the name *militia* is a name alike of labour and honour; among demons it is a name only of labour; among holy angels, only of honour. Their military service is nothing but triumph: [Col. 0687C] for they serve without labour, fight without difficulty, minister without weariness. They are burdened by no weight of corruption and rejoice continually in the vision of God, whom to see is to live, flourish, conquer, and triumph.

“There was a battle in heaven,” it says. “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was their place found in heaven” (Rev. 12): namely, so that they might conquer the elect, although they do not cease to attack them. For even if the elect sometimes fall into sin, this very thing benefits them by making them cautious. Well, therefore, was it said: “The life of man upon earth is military service,” because so long as we are in the body and are away from the Lord, we cannot be without this adversary. It is fixed: God spoke once to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3). These enmities are immortal and irreconcilable conflicts.

O how grievously Carpocrates the heretic erred long ago—the leader of the Cathari who are called Gnostics! He said that no human being who wished to attain the perfection of his mystery, or rather his crime, could otherwise escape or avoid such rulers, namely demons, unless they were appeased through certain evil deeds which he himself prescribed. Certain philosophers had earlier spread the darkness of this error. Following them, the Platonist Porphyry said that the good god or genius could not be found in a human being unless the evil one had first been appeased. [Col. 0688A] Yet he himself, contradicting himself, testifies that association with demons must be avoided—fluctuating between alternating opinions, apparently torn between the vice of sacrilegious curiosity and the profession of philosophy, to which he recognizes such association to be contrary.

But holy Peter should be heard saying: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5). And James: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4). He says, “Resist,” not “appease him” or “consent to him”; for if you consent to him, you will be conquered. Therefore, since the devil always opposes us without reconciliation, we must always resist him and never appease him by doing his will. That is to make cakes for the queen of heaven, as in Jeremiah (ch. 7). For the more we appease him in that manner, the more we displease God and the heavier punishments we shall pay.

But how shall we resist him? “Resist him in faith,” Peter says. Nothing is stronger than faith, by which the devil is conquered. “What is the victory that conquers the world except our faith? And who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (1 John 5). Through this faith the saints conquered kingdoms (Heb. 11).

> The saints’ devout faith,  
> The believers’ unconquered hope,  
> Christ’s perfect love  
> Triumphs over the prince of the world.

Faith, however, without works is idle. [Col. 0688C] Idle faith conquers nothing because it does nothing. Indeed, it is not only idle but dead. The life of faith is love at work. God’s love is never idle. If it exists, it works great things; but if it refuses to work, it is not love. Faith without love at work, being idle and dead, does not conquer because it does not fight; or, if it fights, it is like one beating the air, not wounding an enemy, nor freeing itself from the enemy.

The Pharisees fight as those who beat the air: they speak but do not act. So do delicate teachers who dispute about fasting with full bellies, and who, while yielding their hands to impurity, preach chastity. Likewise fight diligent hearers of God’s word who are not vigorous doers. In such persons the strong man armed guards his courtyard, and therefore all that he possesses is at peace, because no one resists him so long as the sinner, whom he has cast down by consent alone, does not add the further act of rising again. If the sinner did this, he would be stronger than that enemy.

We have often seen the victor overcome by one who was overcome. The common saying is: “Strong is he who throws down; but stronger is he who rises again.” Hence blessed Jerome says:

> “Nothing is stronger than the Christian who conquers the devil; nothing weaker than the one overcome by the flesh.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0687D] Epistle to Rusticus.]

Therefore the Apostle calls the struggle between us and the devil wrestling, saying: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). That elegant comparison of the Wise Man comes from the art of wrestling:

> “Just as,” he says, “a great wrestler is not one who unravels every hold, which is seldom useful, but one who has diligently practised one or two holds; for it makes no difference how many things he knows, provided that he knows as much as victory requires: so it is more beneficial to hold fast a few precepts of wisdom, provided they are ready and in use for you, than to have learned many things but not have them at hand.” [Col. 0689A]

Nothing truer could be said. Indeed, the devil learned from himself the wrestling-holds of vices struggling against virtues, because he invented them all. Hence he is said to possess a thousand arts of doing harm. Yet he is especially accustomed to exercise himself in three things: “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). Everything that is in the world—that is, whatever is loved by lovers of the world—is one or another of these. For there are many tribulations and distresses in the world, but they are not loved.

See the wrestling-holds in which the prince of the world exercises himself: lust, avarice or curiosity, and pride. For “the desire of the eyes” denotes both avarice and curiosity. In Genesis pride is indicated by the serpent’s breast, lust by its belly according to the Septuagint, which, where we have “you shall go upon your breast,” says, “you shall crawl upon breast and belly” (Gen. 3). Curiosity or avarice is signified in what follows: “You shall eat earth.” For one who eats earth penetrates deep and dark places: so does the curious person. And one who eats earth always has something left that he can eat: so the avaricious person is never filled with money, but

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Ovid)

Sometimes all these things are designated simply by the name of covetousness, as when the Apostle says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6); sometimes by the name of pride, as when it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). Hence Rabanus, on Ecclesiasticus: “Covetousness and pride are not two evils but one, from which all things take their beginning.”

The tempter tempted the first Adam in all these matters and conquered; he tempted the second and was conquered. In the first hold he is strong, in the second stronger, in the third strongest. Of the first it is said: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). The loins and navel of the lustful are called the devil’s because they act for the devil against themselves and throw down their souls by the bond of illicit delight. Nothing is weaker than the Christian who is thus overcome by his own flesh. In that wrestling-match Antaeus conquers Hercules: that is, desire conquers a mind otherwise strong. O how great is the devil’s strength in this wrestling-hold! For this hold makes Samsons effeminate, renders Solomons foolish, inflames Herculeses, binds Marses in chains, and changes Joves into oxen. Hence Jerome says: “Never trust in past chastity. You cannot be stronger than Samson, holier than David, or wiser than Solomon.”

Of the second hold, avarice, the Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptations and into the snare of the devil,” and so forth; and shortly afterwards: “For covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6). The devil’s strength [Col. 0690A] is very great in this hold, which is his snare and the root of all evils. Many have proved victors in the first hold who were conquered in this one. This hold suspended Judas by a noose, stoned Achan, and slew Ananias and Sapphira by the sword of the apostolic word.

Avarice has two teeth with which it devours everything: an excessively immoderate desire for another’s property and an excessively tenacious keeping of one’s own. He desires too immoderately who demands what he lacks beyond the law of necessity and use. Things are held too greedily when they are withheld from use. Covetousness, as the saints say, is love for things which a person may unwillingly lose.

O how widely this snare is spread! How many does this hold enfold and entangle! Today all run after riches as though there the rest from labours and solace for pains could be found; as though shipwrecked persons could more easily rise out of the depths and escape if they were burdened with an enormous load. What ulcerated person ever piled up thorns so as to rest more softly upon them?

Yet this snare especially ensnares tax collectors and officials. Their whole body, from the greatest to the least, attends to extortion rather than justice; and they rage so against the people that what one leaves behind, the others do not delay in taking away—as though established for this purpose, that the *bruchus* should eat what the locust leaves. Hence they heap up several offices in themselves, so that, although they do not receive from one, they may draw from another.

The *bruchus* is a locust before it has wings; when its wings grow and it begins to flutter, it is called an *athelebs*; but when it has flown fully, it becomes again a locust. So among officials the *bruchus*, the *athelebs*, and the locust are the same, because the *publicanus*, that is, the public servant, harms both those near and those far away. Every official of a court may be called thus.

Lawrence, bishop of Milan, describes him in this way: “The publican is the head of plunder, the law of violence, a shameless robber, a destructive physician, more savage than thieves. For a thief sins fearfully; this man confidently. A thief fears the snares of the law; this man calls whatever he does ‘law.’ Who, then, is more unjust? He who condemns justice with words of justice, and with the weapons of innocence despoils, wounds, and kills the innocent—this man kills law by law; and while he presses others toward the law, he himself is lawless. For just as a praetor, even when he decides unjustly, is said to pronounce the law, because regard is had not to what he does but to what he ought to do, so public officials, even when they do wrong, say that they are fulfilling justice.”

O how venerable the name and office of prelates and rulers would be if they were fulfilled with as much conscientious care as they are sought with ambition! Certainly they would be loved as fathers, feared as God, and honoured as saints, if they spared exactions, cast from their minds whatever proceeds from calumny, and did not reckon every gain to be godliness. But who has handled money—whether gold or silver—for long without soiling his fingers? Yet from it the hand is less soiled than the mind.

The devil’s third hold is pride. He too is “king over all the children of pride,” as Job says (ch. 41). Pride is love of one’s own excellence. Folly always accompanies it, as it also accompanies covetousness; folly advises one to love and seek what cannot be possessed. Folly, as Augustine says, is a blameworthy ignorance of things that ought to be known. Ambition—that is, desire for power and honour—is born from pride. Whom can you give me who does not wish to surpass even one person in power? Above all, in the courts of the powerful are usually found hunters after offices and suitors for honours. Often even in monasteries, under the tunic of a penitent, there is a kingly spirit.

Long ago messengers of the king of Babylon came to King Hezekiah with gifts, and the pious King Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival: “And he showed them the house of spices, the gold and silver, the various spices, the ointments also, and all that he could have in his treasuries” (2 Kings [Col. 0691B] 20). Then everyone rejoices imprudently when he is approached by messengers of the king of Babel—that is, of confusion—for they must be regarded and feared as suspicious enemies even when they bring gifts.

> [Note: [Col. 0691D] Vergil, *Aeneid* II, v. 49.]

Therefore, whoever displays the spices of good works, the gold of virtue, the silver of eloquence, the spices of prayers, and whatever good things are stored in the treasuries of a good conscience, should know for certain that all things which appear to serve glory will receive the wages of confusion and death. For whatever is done for the sake of display leads to death. Just as the honey of pleasure, so also the leaven of pride is forbidden to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice.

Therefore three other bonds, those of virtues, must be learned by us against these three bonds of vices, so that, freed and released from them, we may escape. Against the bond [Col. 0691C] of lust is that saying of the Lord: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). Against the second is: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5); and: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6); and the Apostle’s saying: “We brought nothing into this world; without doubt neither can we carry anything out” (1 Tim. 6). Against the third is: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11).

To gird the loins is to mortify the flesh. For without chastisement of the flesh no one can long possess the vessel of his body in sanctification and honour. Therefore mortification of the flesh is called the girding of the loins, because it is always the precursor of chastity, just as lust is the precursor of gluttony. Poverty of spirit is a love of voluntary poverty, conceived in the heart and undertaken in deed for the sake of eternal life [Col. 0691D]. Humility of heart is a love of one’s own subjection, not desiring dominion over another, according to Peter’s saying: “Servants, be subject to your masters” (I Pet. II). Blessed are those who rejoice in continual subjection and refuse to be set over anyone in this life.

The first belongs to the devout faith of the saints; the second to their unconquered hope; the third to their perfect charity. Devout faith is that which mortifies the flesh more than it is commanded to do. For he is scarcely devout who does not fast, pray, or labour more than is prescribed for him. From the age of fifteen the virgin Geneviève consented to break her fast only twice a week, namely on Sunday and Thursday. Throughout her life she abstained from wine and every intoxicating drink [Col. 0692A]. She lived thus for fifty years. Thereafter, at the bishops’ persuasion, she began to eat fish and milk, but always with weeping. Her devout faith had imposed this penance upon her.

Blessed Arsenius said that one hour of sleep was enough for a monk. The monk Publius, as is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, stood in prayer for ten continuous days and did not permit the familiar demon, whom Julian the Apostate was sending into the West, to pass. Our holy lawgiver Benedict threw himself naked among nettles and brambles, where he rolled for a very long time and most painfully, in order to scratch flesh that itched badly. Thus devotion of faith always does more than can be commanded of it.

The unconquered hope of the saints, firmly and securely awaiting eternal goods and ardently desiring them [Col. 0692B], despises and abandons all temporal goods as easily as it regards them as nothing in comparison with eternal things, to whose desire it has already attached itself. Perfect charity toward Christ lays down the soul for Christ or for the brethren, and judges nothing intolerable to itself except deprivation of Christ. “Charity is patient, is kind.” Many have been crushed in the torments of the flesh through lack of charity toward God, though they could not be crushed by the first two assaults of lust or avarice. But “love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” (Song VIII). It is called hard as hell because it bears all things and endures all things. It bears all things cruelly inflicted; it endures all things faithfully promised: “The patient man shall endure until the appointed time [Col. 0692C], and afterward gladness shall be restored” (Ecclus. I).

The first—that is, to mortify the flesh—belongs to virgins; the second—that is, to leave all things—to holy confessors; the third to holy martyrs—that is, tirelessly to endure all things for Christ. O how devout was the faith of the holy virgins, who so manfully resisted pleasures of the flesh! How unconquered was the hope of the holy confessors, when they regarded as nothing the world and all that is in the world! How perfect was the charity of the holy martyrs, who, tortured by such great punishments, stood so steadfastly in the contest of battle! Thus therefore:

> The devout faith of the saints,  
> The unconquered hope of believers,  
> The perfect charity of Christ  
> Triumphs over the prince of the world.

May God bring us to that triumph through the merits and intercessions of those same saints—Jesus Christ our God, the portion, crown, and reward of His soldiers. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI  
### Delivered at the Synod of Toulouse, in the Church of St James

“Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI).

This prophetic admonition, dearest brethren, applies fittingly not only to us, who are called priests of the Lord, ministers of our God, but also to the entire assembly of the faithful, to whom it is said by the voice of the Prince of the Apostles: “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (I Pet. II) [Col. 0693A].

The peoples of the faithful are called a chosen generation, whom these apostles begot through the Gospel in Christ—not they alone, but Christ Himself also, as James says: “Of His own will He begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some first-fruits of His creature” (Jas. I). “A chosen generation,” he says, not a reprobate generation; such as those to whom it was said: “Ye are of your father the devil, and ye will do the desires of your father” (John VIII). A chosen generation: that is, separated from the mass of unbelievers, according to that saying of the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song V).

This may be understood in two ways: of Christ our Head, who is the Bridegroom and Beloved of the Church; and of the individual members of that same Head. For Christ in His own person is beloved of the Father [Col. 0693B], who says of Him: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke III). Likewise He is beloved of the Holy Spirit, who rested upon Him and anointed Him; and of His blessed mother Mary with singular love; and of the universal Church, which here calls the Bridegroom Himself white and ruddy: white in His divine nature, in which He is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. VII), and the splendour and express image of the Father’s substance (Heb. I); ruddy according to His human nature, in which He was conceived from the most pure blood of the Virgin Mary, as Damascene says.

Or the whole may be referred to the divine nature: white and ruddy—that is, sweet and upright, merciful and just, gentle toward the righteous, terrible toward the ungodly, as it is written: “The Most High is a patient requiter” [Col. 0693C] (Ecclus. V). For, as blessed Gregory says, He bears our sins and repays them.

In signification of this, the angel who appeared at His resurrection had a countenance like lightning and raiment like snow: the former to terrify the guards, the latter to soothe the women. Or certainly both belong to His humanity: He is called white because born of the Virgin; ruddy because He suffered on the cross. Or white by righteousness, than which nothing is purer—whence it is written: “The righteous shall blossom like the lily” (Hos. XIV); ruddy by charity, than which nothing is more ardent—as it is written: “A fiery law is in His right hand” (Deut. XXXIII). “Chosen out of thousands”: that is, surpassing all the chosen in incomparable holiness. For He is the Holy of Holies [Col. 0693D], sanctified not by any human being but Himself sanctifying others, as it is written: “Of His fulness have all we received” (John I). He is therefore called chosen out of thousands, that is, out of all, as alone undefiled and separated from sinners, He who committed no sin.

But if this is understood of His members, understand it thus: separated from the mass of those who perish, “who are multiplied beyond number.” It follows: “A royal priesthood” (I Pet. II), that is, chosen for this purpose, that you may be a royal priesthood, or kings in priestly holiness, like Christ from whom you are called Christians. Raised to the summit of both dignities and born according to the flesh from both tribes, priestly as well as royal, He showed Himself to be the true King of righteousness and High Priest of holy souls [Col. 0694A].

For, to establish His royal dignity, when Pilate asked whether He was a king, He answered that He was a king and had come into the world to bear witness to the truth. He also wore royal insignia in His mockery: sceptre, diadem, and cloak—the first of reed, the second of thorns, the third scarlet. By these the ungodly, though unknowingly, signified that every kingdom of this world is falling and fragile through the shortness of time, piercing and sorrowful through the burden of care. But the kingdom of truth or righteousness, which, as the Lord says, is not of this world, was established in eternal stability by the triumphal title of the venerable cross, in a trilingual and altogether indelible inscription, confirmed by Pilate the judge in these words: “What I have written, I have written” (John XIX).

But the priestly dignity according to the order of Melchizedek, which is far better than the order of Aaron, or the legal order, was confirmed in this: that the Apostle says, “Christ, being come a high priest of good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, and through His own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. IX) [Col. 0694B]. Behold how He was both priest and victim.

It follows in Peter’s words: “A holy nation,” that is, a nation washed from sins by the grace of baptism and consecrated for divine worship. Or holy, that is, supremely anointed. Hence it is immediately called “a people of acquisition,” that is, a people whom Christ acquired for Himself and which by His grace acquires eternal life here. Of the first acquisition there is this: “Take heed unto yourselves and to the whole flock, wherein the Holy Spirit hath placed you bishops, to rule the Church of God, which He acquired by His blood” (Acts XX) [Col. 0694C]. Of the second there is this: “Unless ye eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, ye shall not have life in you” (John VI).

This kingdom and priesthood are shown more clearly in the Apocalypse in these words: “Who loved us, and washed us from our sins in His blood, and made us a kingdom and priests unto our God” (Apoc. I). In this statement four things are to be noted: the author, the work, the cause, and the manner. The author: God and man. The work: washing from sins and conferral of the twofold royal and priestly dignity. The cause: love. The manner: in His blood. The author’s divinity commends glory; His humanity, grace. The former exalts our affections [Col. 0694D], the latter enlarges them; the former demands fear from us, the latter love.

The work is an excellent, chief, singular work, possible to omnipotence alone. For who can forgive sins but God alone? Certainly no one can forgive sins except He alone who cannot sin. Yet He not only washed us from our sins; He also made us a kingdom and priests. A kingdom of righteousness, so that righteousness, not sin, may reign in our mortal body. He said “kingdom,” not “kings,” so that we may present our members as serving righteousness unto sanctification. But because to serve God is to reign, this kingdom may also be understood actively: that we may reign; priests, that we may offer sacrifice. That we may reign—that is, govern ourselves by the rule of reason; priests, that we may offer [Col. 0695A] ourselves by mortification of the flesh. And all this unto God, by holding the true faith as Catholics; not as unbelievers, who sacrifice whatever they sacrifice to demons; nor as heretics, worse than pagans through apostasy, who sacrifice themselves to demons whenever, through the blasphemy of their error, they teach in word and example alike abstinence from foods which God created.

Therefore let us be kings, ruling ourselves by reason; let us be priests of God, not of the devil, sacrificing ourselves through abstinence in the Catholic faith. Of the first there is the saying of the philosopher: “You have many kings, if reason rules you.” And the poet:

> You will be king, they say,  
> If you act rightly.

Of the second there is the Apostle’s saying: “I beseech you that ye present [Col. 0695B] your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. XII).

The cause of this work was none other than love. “Who loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins, and made us a kingdom and priests unto our God” (Apoc. I). O love sublime and sweet, great and strong! No one possessed a greater love than this. It was truly excessive, in comparison of the thing bought and the price paid. “Ye were bought with a great price” (I Cor. VI). He spoke truly when he said “great”; he would equally truly have said “excessive,” just as earlier he called the Father’s charity not great but excessive—not reproving it for being excessive, but commending its greatness as much as possible.
