And as it is truly excessive love to deliver up the Son so that the slave may be redeemed, so it was an excessive price [Col. 0695C] to shed the utterly innocent blood of that same Son so that the guilty person might be acquitted.

Hence Peter says: “Ye were not redeemed with corruptible gold or silver from your vain manner of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless and undefiled Lamb” (I Pet. I). Therefore the Psalmist, marvelling at the wonderful bargain of this purchase, says: “Lord, what is man, that Thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that Thou visitest him?” (Ps. VIII). And again: “What is man, that Thou hast made Thyself known to him? or the son of man, that Thou accountest him worthy?” (Ps. CXLIII). That is: why dost Thou value him so highly as to pour out Thy blood for him?

“Who loved us,” he says, “and washed us from our sins in His blood” (Apoc. I). A wonderful thing: washing in blood [Col. 0695D]. For what is more defiled than human blood? Thus elsewhere it is read: “When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Sion, and washed away the blood of Jerusalem,” etc. (Isa. IV). He first said “filth,” then repeated it as “blood.” For blood often signifies sin in Scripture. Therefore, when Christ washed us from our sins in His blood, He washed us from our blood in His blood. O wondrous fuller, who washes blood with blood! O marvellous whitening wisdom, what a remarkable lye Thou hast prepared in Thy blood! In it Thy flesh served as ashes, the cross as a pile of wood, charity as fire, water from Thy side to wash, blood to whiten; our souls as linen garments, our bodies as woollen ones. Hence in the Apocalypse: “These are they who came [Col. 0696A] out of great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Apoc. VII).

O blood of extraordinary power, wondrous might, singular efficacy! What will not the blood of the Creator of all things be able to do, if the blood of certain animals can do so much? We read of three most powerful kinds of blood: the blood of a goat, that of a menstruating woman, and that of the murex. The first splits the diamond, a most hard stone; the second dissolves bitumen, a most tenacious glue; the third dyes purple, the finest colour. Certainly the blood of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world ought to have possessed nothing less than these. Therefore, at its shedding, hell burst open, the earth trembled, the sun grew afraid, rocks were split, tombs opened, and many bodies of saints who had slept [Col. 0696B] arose.

Morally, by the power of this blood, the diamond is split as often as an obstinate or hardened sinner is softened unto repentance; bitumen is dissolved as often as an inveterate habit of enticed lust is abandoned; purple is dyed as often as invincible patience is maintained even unto death in whatever tribulations are endured for righteousness. The diamond was split in the repentance and conversion of magicians, such as Cyprian and Daria; bitumen was dissolved in the continence of fornicators, such as Boniface and Pelagia; purple was dyed in the suffering of martyrs, such as Lawrence and our Thomas. This is the power of that blood which washes away the filth of our sins and made us a kingdom and priests unto God.

To them it is now said [Col. 0696C]: “Let Thy priests be clothed with righteousness.” A priest is called, as it were, one who gives sacred things. What sacred thing? First, certainly, a sacred example; second, a sacred word; third, sacred food; fourth, sacred judgment. For doing comes before teaching. “He,” it says, “was a burning and shining lamp” (John V): burning in love, shining in speech; burning in life, shining in doctrine; burning in conscience, shining in reputation. First pomegranates are described on the priestly robe, then bells. First the apostles are told: “Ye are the salt of the earth”; then, “Ye are the light of the world” (Matt. V). The first of the apostles is Peter, that is, God’s steadfastness; the second, Paul, that is, doctrine of the word. The former was indeed privileged in doing; the latter in teaching [Col. 0696D], and was therefore called the Doctor of the Gentiles.

But as doing comes before teaching, so teaching comes before communicating. For Christ first established the Gospel, then gave His body as a sacrament, signifying that no one is rightly ordained priest unless he is already able to build up the neighbour subject to him by fitting and appropriate speech of exhortation. Hence the Apostle to Timothy: “Let the elders who rule well be held worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and doctrine” (I Tim. V). And as teaching comes before communicating, so communication precedes judgment—that is, priestly ordination, a rank of honour. For judgment properly belongs to prelates, namely archbishops, bishops, and supreme judges [Col. 0697A].

Each of these sacred things is twofold. A sacred example is continence or temperance in prosperity, and patience in adversity. One cannot suffice without the other, because prosperity without temperance corrupts, and adversity without patience breaks a person. Likewise every priest ought to give the sacred word in two ways: prayer to God and preaching to the people, if perhaps he has undertaken the care of others. Likewise sacred food in two ways: holy communion at the altar, and daily refreshment of the poor at his own table. The same judgment applies to sacred judgment: he ought to absolve the penitent and humble, but bind the rebellious and obstinate.

The first sacred thing must be given with a strong hand; the second with a discerning hand; the third [Col. 0697B] with a clean hand; the fourth with a hand both outstretched and shaken free. A strong hand is needed so that one subject may not succumb beneath the burden of temptation, neither enticed by flatteries nor frightened by dangers. For this is, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0697D] Sermon on St Vincent.], “that twofold battle-line which the world draws up against us.” It terrifies, in order to break us; it flatters, in order to deceive us. Therefore let not your own will hold you fast, nor another’s cruelty frighten you, and the world is conquered.

The second sacred thing must be given with a discerning hand, because the priest ought not always to devote himself to prayer and silence, nor always to preach. There is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak”; a time for labour and a time for rest. Hence blessed Benedict says in the Rule [Note: [Col. 0698D] ch. 48.] that at fixed hours one must give oneself to divine reading and at fixed hours to manual labour. The word must also be given to the people with a discerning hand [Col. 0697C], because neither should the great depth of mysteries be related to those less capable, nor concealed from those capable of receiving it. For some, through ignorance, offer milky juices to adults; and through arrogance, solid food to those still at the breast. Not so he who said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect”; and again: “As unto little children, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. II). Thus the Lord’s measure of wheat ought to be given: the more perfect, who have their senses exercised, should be refreshed with solid food, and little children nourished with milk.

But sacred food must be given with a clean hand, lest either holy communion be received unto judgment or refreshment of the poor become robbery offered as a burnt sacrifice. Of the first: “Whosoever of the seed of Aaron has uncleanness in him shall not approach those things which have been sanctified” (Lev. XXII) [Col. 0697D]. Of the second: “I the Lord love judgment, and hate robbery in burnt offering” (Isa. LXI). Hence Augustine: the poor are not to be fed through theft, just as children are not to be sought through adultery.

For judgment to be secure, it must be given with an outstretched hand, that is, without respect of persons, and likewise with a hand altogether shaken free of every gift. “Let Thy priests,” he says, “be clothed with righteousness.” His saying “Thy” distinguishes them from the priests of the devil, who were formerly called priests of idols, or who are still bishops of heretics, or their elect. Though in them no truth of righteousness is found [Col. 0698A], yet much cloaked semblance of holiness and truth is found.

Jerome reports in his book *Against Jovinianus* that the Stoic Chenon wrote concerning the priests of ancient Egypt that they displayed astonishing abstinence in food, continence in sexual intercourse, poverty in clothing, humility in diet, and gravity in their gait. Finally, once they had been devoted to the worship of false gods, they never afterward visited their parents, nor allowed even their children to come before their sight. They always abstained from wine and flesh, and never joined themselves to women; indeed, they shuddered not only at flesh but also at eggs and cheese. They called the former liquid flesh and the latter blood changed in colour. They lay on bare ground, placing a footstool beneath their heads as a pillow [Col. 0698B].

Euripides says that the priests of Jupiter in Crete always abstained from certain foods. Porphyry, in his letter to the Egyptian Anelontes, asks not without reason why priests of idols are forbidden contact with sexual intercourse, while they do not fear to lead anyone whatsoever into indiscriminate intercourse; why they are commanded to abstain from animals, while their sacrifices are celebrated with the blood of cattle and the fumes of flesh. “Behold,” he says, “I ask a third question: why are they forbidden to wear rings on their fingers, though they are permitted to have treasures in their caskets?” It is evident, therefore, that priests of idols were forbidden these practices for no other end than that, through their pretended holiness, they might more easily be believed.

Exactly the same pretence exists among the heretics of our time [Col. 0698C]. For their elect appear to abstain, and perhaps are commanded to abstain, from eating flesh and from intercourse with women; yet they try to persuade their believers that every sexual union with a woman is indifferent, and that one need no more abstain from a sister, daughter, or mother than from one’s own wife. O infernal doctrine, from what darkness have you emerged? It is therefore evident that the same spirits of error—that is, unclean demons—now speak in the world through teachers of heretics who then spoke in Egypt through priests of idols.

Therefore it is said: “Let Thy priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI), as though it said: not with a pretence of righteousness, as formerly the priests of falsehood were clothed and teachers of error are still clothed, but with that very truth of righteousness with which priests of truth ought truly to be clothed: “Let Thy priests [Col. 0698D] be clothed with righteousness.”

O garment most beautiful and most precious: the garment of righteousness, which is not merely a single clothing to cover nakedness, but also double to repel cold; an adornment to beautify and honour, and an impregnable armour to protect. It is a child’s garment, like a white robe; a man’s garment, like a cloak; a royal garment, like purple; and a soldier’s garment, like a breastplate. It covers like a white robe, warms like a cloak, adorns like purple, and covers and defends like a breastplate. It covers so long as it preserves innocence, or restores innocence once lost through repentance. For repentance is the rank nearest to innocence [Col. 0699A]. It warms when it helps the needy through mercy, according to the saying: “If his sides have not blessed me, and if he has not been warmed with the fleece of my sheep” (Job XXXI). It adorns and honours when it bears all things through patience and endures all things through long-suffering. It defends and protects on every side when it renders to each person what is his, while preserving the common good.

Of the first garment there is this: “Blessed is he who keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked” (Apoc. XVI). And again: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI). The first covering belongs to the innocent, the second to the penitent. Of the second, that is, warming, there is this: “She shall not fear the cold of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed with double garments” (Prov. XXXI) [Col. 0699B]. Of the third is the statement that Christ wore a crown of thorns and a purple garment. This is that purple ascent which is in Solomon’s litter. Of the fourth is the Apostle’s saying: “Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness” (Eph. VI). Righteousness, insofar as it gives each person what is his, is compared to a breastplate covering the whole body round about and leaving nothing uncovered.

We owe God three things: fear, honour, and love. Of the first two there is this: “If I am a Father, where is My honour? If I am a Lord, where is My fear?” (Mal. I). Of the third there is the command to love God with the whole heart—that is, sweetly, against enticements of the flesh; with the whole soul—that is, wisely, against errors; with the whole mind, perseveringly; with all one’s strength [Col. 0699C], bravely, against afflictions.

We must also render the neighbour what is his. He is threefold: superior, inferior, or equal. To the first you owe obedience and reverence; to the second, discipline and goodwill; to the third, as it were, two breasts: rejoicing with him in prosperity and compassion in adversity, according to the saying: “Rejoice with them that rejoice, weep with them that weep” (Rom. XII). But to the devil we owe absolutely nothing except combat, according to the saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. IV). And again: “Be strong in battle, and fight with the ancient serpent.”

We fight him effectively when, as Sixtus the Pythagorean says, we advance as though in a square battle-array of virtues, so that the fourfold body of virtues may be ordered like a battle-line of camps [Col. 0699D]. In the first rank prudence—or faith—should advance against ignorance and errors, according to Prudentius:

> First to seek the field beneath the uncertain lot of battle,  
> Faith goes forth to fight.

In the second place temperance should be stationed, as though on the right wing, against the enticements of the flesh and pleasures of the world. Third, fortitude should be stationed on the left wing against all troubles and adversities. Some are sufficiently strong and vigorous in enduring adversities, yet exceedingly weak and feeble in rejecting pleasures. David, who had struck down Goliath, was struck down by a single sight of Bathsheba. Judas Maccabaeus, who had overthrown Bacchides’ right wing, was crushed by the left wing [Col. 0700A] (I Macc. IX). But justice must be stationed in the rear against vain glories and exaltations. For the battle-line of pride is first to attack and last to be defeated, according to the verse:

> When you have fought well, when you think all things subdued,  
> Pride, which most fiercely assails, remains yet to be conquered.

Thus must the devil be resisted; thus must the ancient serpent be fought.

But we owe ourselves four things: a rose, a lily, fire, and a sword. The rose of modesty, the lily of chastity, the fire of fervour, the sword of mortification, which the prophet called “the sword of great slaughter.” The sword of small slaughter is present when an evil habit is abandoned and an evil act, though less frequent than before, is restrained. The sword of great slaughter is that of which the same prophet says: “Let the sword be doubled [Col. 0700B] and tripled” (Ezek. XXI). It is doubled when an evil habit and a wicked action are abandoned. It is tripled when even the original root of evil will is cut off. Then we are truly priests of God, when by such a sword we slay our body and soul.

## SERMON XXVII  
### On the Dedication

“If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” (I Cor. III).

Brethren, the terrible blast and saving cry of the apostolic trumpet has sounded. Let all who hear it fear and beware: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him,” etc. I shall not be silent, because [Col. 0700C] my soul has heard the voice of the trumpet, the cry of battle. If anyone hears the sound of this trumpet and henceforth does not guard himself, his blood shall be upon his own head. “If anyone violates the temple,” etc.

Hence the little interlinear gloss says: “Take heed unto yourselves: the voice of the apostles is not like the voice of other men, and our enemies are judges,” just as an enemy bears witness concerning a certain apostle, saying: “His voice is like a mighty trumpet.” Certainly this testimony suits Paul, who trumpets into the ears of all: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.” For Paul himself was Bartholomew by interpretation, though not in person or name. For he was the son of Him who suspends the waters—that is, of God—the adopted son of our Lord Jesus Christ, who [Col. 0700D] has been established by God as judge of the living and the dead: a just judge, strong and patient; who is not angry every day, nor quickly pronounces sentence upon offenders, but, as the Most High, patient requiter, reserves vengeance for the final judgment, as waters held suspended in a cloud.

But it will come, and without doubt will come, when the waters that are suspended, with the clouds of heaven burst and the sluices of heaven opened on every side, are poured out upon the ungodly. Then He shall rain snares upon sinners: fire and brimstone and a tempestuous wind, the portions of their cup (Ps. X); then the Lord shall rain from the Lord fire and brimstone upon the whole Pentapolis—that is, upon all who have devoted themselves to the five senses of their flesh, corrupters of the Lord’s temple. Hence the Psalmist says: “Unless ye be converted, He hath brandished His sword, bent His bow, and made it ready” (Ps. VII) [Col. 0701A]. For He signifies the same thing by the bow bent in the clouds as by the waters held suspended. For the red colour of the heavenly bow not only prefigures, but also holds suspended, that universal fiery rain, of which the poet says:

A common pyre will rain upon the world. Therefore Paul, like a son of him who suspends the waters, forearming and warning us meanwhile against the flood of this fiery deluge held in suspension, thunders and flashes with trumpet-like voice, saying: “If anyone [violates] the temple of God,” etc. O truly mighty trumpet, a voice so powerfully terrifying! But why do I call it a trumpet? It is certainly thunder. For, as the most learned Jerome says: “Each of Paul’s words should be called not so much words as thunders” [Col. 0701B]—and truly thunders: for they are heavenly and terrible alike. The sons of Zebedee are not more rightly called Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder, than our Paul, caught up into the third heaven—that is, into the heavenly paradise—where he heard ineffable words, which it is not lawful for a human being to utter: like thunders which it is not lawful to write, according to that saying in the Apocalypse: “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it” (Rev. 10).

“Thunder” is so called as if meaning a sound that terrifies. And what is more terrible than this threat: “God will destroy him”? People fear the threats of human beings—corruptible, mortal, weak, and powerless human beings—who, after killing the body, have nothing further that they can do; whose whole power is bounded by the body’s brief life, death, and a moment of time [Col. 0701C]. How much more are the threats of almighty God to be feared, who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna; whose power is without limit, whose majesty is incorruptible, whose strength insuperable, whose justice inflexible, whose wrath in judgment implacable, terror intolerable, vengeance immortal! “Yes, I tell you,” he himself says of himself, “fear him” (Luke 12).

Paul therefore thunders to us from his heaven when he sounds the trumpet from his throat, fulfilling that prophetic saying: “Let a trumpet be in your throat.” Certainly he has a trumpet in his throat whose mind savors of the fear of the Lord. He has a trumpet in his throat who humbly fears and avoids what he teaches others to fear and avoid. He has a trumpet in his throat who keeps what he commands others; fulfills what he orders [Col. 0701D]; observes what he enjoins; performs what he speaks. Paul had a trumpet in his throat when he not only roused others to battle, but himself fought with them and before them, saying: “So I run, not as though uncertainly; but I chastise my body, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). These words did not come merely from the lips, but from the depths of the throat. These utterances had, as the philosopher says, a foundation. They were not like the utterances of those of whom Truth says: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens upon people’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. 23).

Their trumpet is not in their own throat [Col. 0702A], who speak and do not act; for what they say has no savor for them. A trumpet of this kind indeed gives some sound, but a wholly uncertain one. “If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound,” says the Apostle, “who will prepare himself for battle?” (1 Cor. 9). And what is more uncertain than a voice reproving life, than a word unsuited to life, than one person building while another destroys, than one praying while another curses? Whose works will the Lord regard? Whose voices will God hear? But if even such voices, though uncertain, are nevertheless to be heard, according to the wholly certain testimony of Truth, who says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23), then woe once, woe again, and woe a third time to hearers of God’s word who do not perform it: woe for drowsiness, sloth, and madness!

Woe for drowsiness, to those whom the crash of such great thunder does not awaken from the sleep of sin; for sloth, to those whom so certain a trumpet-blast does not prepare for the Lord’s battle; for madness, to those whom this archer does not drive from before the sword, according to what is written of the devil: “The archer will not put him to flight; the stones of the sling are turned for him into stubble” (Job 41) [Col. 0702B]. Of such people it is written: “I shall heap evils upon them, and spend my arrows upon them” (Deut. 32). That is: I shall not only pronounce threatening and terrible judgments against them, so that they may be afraid; I shall also issue fatal and capital judgments against them, so that they may be crushed.

But, dearest brothers, after pouring these things out before you learned hearers as a washing of your hands, I must offer the same bread that I have set before you to satisfy the toothless hunger of little children, breaking it into smaller pieces for them. Every church teacher is especially bound to do this: to break for them the Lord’s bread, since the more learned have no need of teeth for breaking it. “If anyone defiles the temple of God”—which temple you are from the time of baptism, as the interlinear Gloss says, and says truly. For then we first begin to be the holy temple of God: when the Holy Spirit of God, who sanctifies every holy thing, begins to dwell in us and in a sense consecrate us. For just as every material temple is built before it is sanctified, and established before it is preserved, so every human being must first be born bodily before being reborn spiritually. Natural things underlie gratuitous gifts and necessarily always precede them. For “that which is spiritual” is not first, “but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual” [Col. 0702D]. No one is conceived holy; no one is born a Christian. Hence Jerome: “Christians are made, not born.”

For by a most high counsel God, the creator of all things, willed that nothing should be sanctified in the first creation; he reserved this second grace for another time. He did not wish to bestow all his gifts at once, but preferred to distribute them in portions and at different times, so as to make his gifts more welcome and to commend his love more abundantly in us, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “If you want to make something welcome, make it rare.” Hence it is that in the canon of the Mass, where we say:

> [Note: [Col. 0701D] Words of the canon of the Mass.]

> “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things, sanctify them,” etc. [Col. 0703A]

At the word “create” we do not make the sign of the cross, but we do so at the three following words. Thus we signify that creation alone, although it is the work of the thrice-holy Trinity, nevertheless sanctifies nothing by itself; rather, it reserves all the grace of sanctification for the power of the holy cross and the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion.

Therefore, in bodily birth we are built into a house; in spiritual regeneration we are consecrated into a temple. Yet this consecration is temporal, not eternal; conditional, not absolute. Unless each person keeps whole and inviolate that condition—that is, the promise of faith—he will perish. For, as people commonly say, an agreement overrides the law; and thus whoever does not keep the baptismal covenant alienates himself from baptismal grace. This grace indeed causes past sins not to be imputed [Col. 0703B], but it does not wholly cut off future sins. It removes all unrighteousness for a time, but does not yet confer all righteousness. It immediately opens Paradise’s gate to the baptized person, but does not at once bring him inside. Through it every iniquity is forgiven, so that we may be freely sanctified by grace’s gift; but with it there remains the weakness of the flesh, so that we may still be exercised toward merit.

Hence Jerome, on the passage “Not a neophyte”:

> [Note: [Col. 0703D] Jerome, on 1 Timothy 3.]

> “Those whom we see today chosen for the highest righteousness,” he says, “if baptism made a person righteous immediately, the Apostle would by no means reject a neophyte. But baptism forgives old sins; it does not bestow new virtues. It releases from prison, and promises rewards to the released person if he labors” [Col. 0703C].

I therefore wonder how some learned persons are accustomed to ask why God does not transfer a person to immortality as soon as he is baptized, when they know that even Adam himself, before he sinned, was made such that he could not die and could be received into the fellowship of angels without testing. Thus they wish more to be given to one who was born in sin and afterward has done no good than to his father, who was born without sin and afterward, deceived, fell into sin, yet immediately repented when he understood his sin. This certainly does not accord with that supreme justice which is God.

For it is certain that God is supreme justice and supreme goodness. It belongs to supreme justice that one who has already merited a reward should receive it rather than one who has not yet merited it. The baptized person has as yet merited nothing, and nevertheless has already freely received many things above merit and even contrary to merit. It is therefore more just that some subsequent merit be awaited from him than that the highest reward be immediately bestowed upon him without any merit whatsoever. Likewise, it better accords with supreme goodness to grant two great things rather than only one. But the merit of eternal life and the eternity of life are two great goods. Therefore more is given to the one who receives merit together with the reward than to the one who receives reward without merit.

To the human being, composed of a double nature, his Creator prepared from the beginning two goods: one visible, the other invisible [Col. 0704A]; one bodily, the other spiritual; one passing, the other eternal; one for the mortal flesh, the other for the immortal spirit. One was for the flesh’s comfort, the other for the spirit’s joy. He gave one immediately; the other he promised. The first was to be possessed freely; the second sought through merits. He freely gave the visible; he set the invisible before us as something to be sought, so that the excellence of the promise and the faithfulness of the promiser might be proved from the gratuitous gift. For if that which he gave freely is of such kind and greatness, what kind and greatness is that for which he asks service? Again, if such goodness was in him that he gave so much without merits, how could malice be in him, so that he would not reward those who have served him well and merited it?

The human being, once created, was immediately made lord of the world; by serving faithfully [Col. 0704B], he was to be made lord of heaven. For this reason, as I have said, God did not give everything at once: because it was more fitting for supreme goodness to give both merit and reward than reward alone without merit. Yet at that time he did not require service in return for temporal and passing things, lest the dignity of the human condition be reduced to baseness if a human being were compelled to serve in return for things subject to him.

For this reason Jesus too became human: so that, for a time, he might have need of certain things, and thereby recognize his own need, and understand that the good which he himself gives was not sufficiently good for him unless he also deserved to possess that good from whom it came. Yet this very fact—that a good short of the supreme Good was not sufficient for him—was itself good for him. For it was a great dignity of the human being that he was made so that no good except the highest could suffice for him [Col. 0704C]. And again, it was great generosity that he was left to such freedom of choice that he could not be compelled even to the supreme Good.

For this reason the person seeking baptism is asked: “Do you wish to be baptized?” It is as though the saying of blessed James were addressed to him: “It is not our discipline that anyone should be converted unwillingly.” Just as the devil could not compel you to submit to him, so I shall not compel you to submit to me. The bishop’s knocking at the closed door of a church being consecrated signifies the same thing: as if he openly said, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I shall enter in to him, and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3). I do violence to no one, because I do not accept forced service.

The thief who entered first, although he is a breaker-in, may go about, persuade, and entice; he cannot compel at all, nor enter unless the door is opened to him, however much he may shout or knock [Col. 0704D]. Therefore, from one desiring baptism, renunciation of the devil and faith in God—which works through love—are required. No one will do this unless willing, because, as Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 0704D] Tractate 26 on John.]

> A person may go unwillingly to church, take part in the mysteries unwillingly, fast, keep vigil, and labor unwillingly; but he absolutely cannot believe unless willing.

O sweet and delightful condition, in which nothing burdensome or difficult is required of me! Nothing except what is wholesome, pleasant, useful, and what I ought to have done even without being asked. Yet I could not have done this without help from another; for human nature, which fell by itself, does not rise without divine help. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God—that is, the grace of him who forgives sins—and because of this he is always rightly to be glorified by all.

To renounce the devil is to detest and abjure every sin; knowingly to do, say, or desire nothing that conscience reproves. For whatever is done against conscience builds toward Gehenna. Note that we are commanded to renounce all the devil’s works, not two or three, or half, or even the greater part, but universally all of them. For there is no fellowship of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. 6), nor of righteousness with iniquity; “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” [Col. 0705B] (1 Cor. 5), and whoever offends in one point becomes guilty of all and loses many good things (James 2).

All works of the devil fall under two kinds: disgraceful vice (*flagitium*) and criminal wrongdoing (*facinus*). Hence the devil himself is called an unclean spirit because of disgraceful vices; malignant and wicked because of crimes. It is not enough to renounce his works unless one also renounces all his pomps: that is, love for every kind of worldly and temporal glory, whether in riches, honor, praise, or any gift intended to please. The church to be consecrated signifies these two renunciations by being clean and empty. Likewise, the soul of the candidate for baptism is cleansed by renouncing diabolical works; it is emptied by renouncing worldly pomps.

The novice abjures these two things on the day of his consecration and dedication, that is, of his profession [Col. 0705C]: namely, his own will, which is the root of all evil works; and property, under which name every worldly pomp is contained. By the first renunciation he is cleansed of all uncleanness; by the second he is emptied of all hindrances. But since every person renouncing the devil rouses Leviathan against himself—Leviathan who previously slept within him, as in the shadow and hiding-place of reeds and moist places, through love of vanity and desire for pleasure—the priest arms the candidate for baptism against him by signing him with consecrated oil on the breast and between the shoulders, so that he may be fortified before and behind [Col. 0705D] by saving arms. He is signed on the breast so that he may not yield shamefully, but resist bravely, as it is written: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4).

For the devil behaves like a crocodile: he pursues the one fleeing and flees the one pursuing; timid against the bold, bold against the timid. The candidate is signed between the shoulders so that he may know how to bear the breastplate of righteousness; so that he may take upon himself the sweet yoke and light burden of Christ, charity, which is patient so as to bear the one who inflicts evil, and kind so as even to love the one it bears. Understand the cross in patience and consecrated oil in kindness. Therefore the candidate is signed with consecrated oil on the breast so that he may know how cheerfully to do good; between the shoulders, so that he may know how joyfully to endure evil [Col. 0706A]. In these two crosses all righteousness is contained. These are the two timbers from which our high priest constructed for us a bridge by which we might cross from death to life. Neither suffices without the other.

For in patience alone the soul is possessed, but patience endured because of unrighteousness merits no grace with God. Hence Peter: “For what grace is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, while doing good, you suffer patiently, this is grace with God” (1 Pet. 2). After this the candidate is asked whether he believes in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit: that is, in him who can do all things, in him who knows all things, and in him who hates every evil and loves every good. The devil is wholly opposed to these three [Col. 0706B], for he can do absolutely nothing, knows nothing, and loves no good but every evil. “He who is nothing can do nothing at all”; and the devil is told: “You have become nothing” (Ezek. 28).

The devil can do no good because he cannot even will it. Yet he does many good things unknowingly or unwillingly; these are not to be imputed to him, but to him from whom all good things proceed, who knows how to use even the devil’s evils well through his wisdom. Just as a physician, in order to draw superfluous and harmful blood from a person, often uses a leech, so divine mercy uses the wickedness of our enemy to remove from us harmful fleshly desire. And just as a leech does not care for a person’s health but for drinking blood, so the devil does not care for the healing of the sinner, but rejoices only in affliction [Col. 0706C].

Therefore the devil can do no good, nor indeed any evil unless he is permitted. Whatever depends upon another’s decision belongs not to the one acting below, but to the one permitting from above. But whoever can do neither good nor evil can do nothing at all. Therefore the priest breathes upon the child’s face, to show that the devil can do no more than dust, a feather, or straw. For the devil is dust not cohering with itself, wholly dried up from God’s grace, cast from the face of the land of the living by the wind of his own puffing-up and the whirlwind of divine indignation. He is also a feather because pride has borne him aloft; straw because he is to be burned in eternal fire. O how easy it is to fight against so weak an adversary [Col. 0706D], especially for one whom almighty God supports.

Likewise, the devil knows nothing. For all wisdom is defined as being in the fear of the Lord, which makes one avoid every evil. Therefore the devil, who has become such that he fears nothing, not even God himself, is empty of all wisdom, foolish, and tasteless. Hence in the second catechism blessed salt is placed in the child’s mouth, so that through the salt of the fear of the Lord he may know how to drive out the foul suggestions of the tasteless demon. This is the salt of the Lord’s covenant, which must be put on every sacrifice, according to Job’s saying: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender” (Job 9).

Let us therefore always remember this salt which we have eaten in the lower palace of the great King. Woe to those who know all lands and have lost remembrance of this salt: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12) [Col. 0707A]. Therefore nothing is more miserable than the devil, who knows the Lord’s will very well and nevertheless always does the opposite, not unwillingly or unknowingly, but from malice clings to evil and abhors good. For as a toad cannot bear the good scent of a flowering vineyard, and a pig cannot help loving the stench of a dungheap, so Satan, though he has the golden ring of discernment in his nostrils, nevertheless delights always to thrust the snout of choice into the dungheap of sins.

Therefore in the third catechism the priest anoints the ears and nostrils of the candidate for baptism with his saliva and with the sign of the cross, so that he may know how by desire to reject evil through its odor and choose good—not like that most wretched person who condemns himself in what he approves, according to that poetic saying:

> … I see the better things and approve them;  
> I follow the worse. …  
> (Ovid)

This question, then—“Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” etc.—is as it were a test of the question in which he was asked: “Do you renounce Satan and all his works?” For no one can serve these two masters, so contrary to one another. He renounces the devil, therefore, who always fears God’s supreme power, which created us. And whoever believes that the devil can do nothing renounces all his works. Whoever always honors God’s wisdom, which redeemed us, and believes that the devil knows nothing [Col. 0707C]—that is, possesses no useful knowledge—renounces all his pomps. Whoever always loves God’s justice, which adopted us as children, also believes that the devil can confer no good on anyone. And this is to believe in God the Father, in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit.

The further words, “Do you believe in the holy Church?” must be understood thus: Do you believe that there is one Church spread throughout the whole world, working through faith in love, joined to God by an eternal and inseparable marriage? For he himself said: “I will betroth you to myself in faith; and I will betroth you to myself in righteousness” (Hos. 2). It is as though he said: I shall make you my bride; but you shall give me as dowry faith and righteousness. But because the Church could not give even this to her bridegroom unless she first received it from him [Col. 0707D], he adds: “I will betroth you to myself in mercy and compassions” (ibid.): in mercy, by forgiving sins; in compassions, by bestowing merits.

The meaning, therefore, is this: “Do you believe in the holy Church?” that is, do you believe that no one can be saved unless he faithfully remains in the unity of the body of the Church? Blessed Augustine adds the preposition “in”; but we customarily say, “Do you believe the holy Church?” The Church’s unity is fourfold: in faith against heresies; in charity against schisms; in communion of sacraments; and in the enlivening power of the Holy Spirit. The communion of saints comprises three things: sharing in sacraments, participation in the Holy Spirit, and fellowship in prayers. Thus, when the candidate for baptism is asked, “Do you believe in the communion of saints?” the meaning is: Do you believe in the mutual fellowship of prayers and good things among believers?

Just as the one answering “I believe” signifies that he renounces Satan’s works, so he declares that he renounces Satan’s pomps when, being questioned, he affirms that he believes in forgiveness of sins, resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life [Col. 0708A]. For these are the Christian’s pomps, wholly contrary to the devil’s pomps. All the Christian’s ambition and glory consist in these. Nothing else ought at all to be sought, because nothing greater or better can be possessed. Behold the condition under which each believer remembers himself baptized and dedicated as God’s temple. Whoever does not keep this condition will perish; but whoever keeps it, just as he is now anointed to fight in conflict against the enemy, so at his second dedication he will be anointed for comfort and refreshment, like a traveler returning from a laborious road and fatigued by the journey; and at the third, he will be anointed for a kingdom in which he shall reign with Christ without end.

As a type of this, David was first anointed at Bethlehem among his brothers; secondly at Hebron over Judah alone; thirdly at Jerusalem over all Israel. At Bethlehem is anointed the person who hungers for righteousness, the true food of the soul. At Hebron, where Abraham was buried, is anointed the person who now sleeps in peace and, buried in Abraham’s bosom, rests especially in hope of receiving the twofold robe, already clothed with the first white robe [Col. 0708C]. At Jerusalem is anointed the person who now sees eternal peace close at hand, who now possesses what he hoped for. Among his brothers is anointed the person who still remains in the battle-line of brothers. Over Judah alone is anointed the person who now returns into his rest and confesses the Lord over his deliverance, singing David’s words: “Return, O my soul, into your rest,” etc. (Ps. 114). Over all Israel is anointed the person who, now joined to the angelic assemblies, sees the glory of Christ’s humanity with the eyes of the glorified body and the glory of divinity with the eyes of the purified heart.

The first dedication may be violated; the second and third are inviolable, because they are exempt from every adversity and danger. In the first, immunity from past sins is given; in the second, immunity from all dangers; in the third, fullness in every good. But, leaving the others aside, let us pursue what we began concerning the first.

To dedicate is to assign the newness of some house to sacred and most solemn use. In baptism we are made new when, stripping off the old human being with his deeds, we put on the new, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. The newness of our house is consecrated to these uses of holiness and righteousness, peace and sanctity. To signify this, the baptized person is immediately clothed in white garments and anointed with sacred oil upon the crown of his head, as if Solomon’s words were spoken to him: “Let your garments always be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9): that is, let your body be full of the purity of holiness, and let the sweetness of peace not perish from your mind [Col. 0709A].

If you keep this command well, in the future you shall be clothed with the robe of immortality and glory, prefigured for you by the new white garment; you shall be anointed with the oil of gladness and endowed with the honor of a kingdom, prefigured for you by the sacred anointing of the head. But what shall we do? What shall we say about those terrible threats which Paul declares when he says: “If anyone defiles this temple, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3)? And who is there who has not defiled God’s temple after the first dedication, unless he can say with Paul, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4), and with blessed Job, “My conscience does not rebuke me in my whole life” (Job 27)? To how many does the precious rarity of so blessed a declaration fall?

What then? Will all the others perish? Far from it! For we hold the certain promise of God, who says: “When the wicked person turns away from his wickedness,” etc., “he shall give life to his own soul” (Ezek. 18) [Col. 0709B]. And blessed John says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with God, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). Paul himself forgave, in the person of Christ, the sin of one who had defiled God’s temple and exposed his father’s shame, because of the repentance that followed.

Where is it then, O blessed Apostle, that you had previously thundered universally: “If anyone defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him”? Behold: to this defiler you promise forgiveness. Therefore it is not the case that if anyone defiles God’s temple and afterward repents, God will destroy him. Why? Because he has restored what he defiled; and thus he is not said to have defiled it. Hence the Lord says of the wicked person converted to righteousness: “I shall not remember any of his iniquities” (Heb. 2). Thus all the iniquities of the penitent wicked person are as though they had never existed. Hence he says again: “Turn, and do penance, and iniquity shall not be your ruin” (Ezek. 18). Certainly, if it will not be a ruin, it will not be one; for it cannot both be and not be a ruin. Again: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. 43). What was written, once blotted out, is not.

Hence Ambrose:

> [Note: [Col. 0709D] Book on Solomon, at the end.]

On the passage, “Such is the way of an adulterous woman,” etc. (Prov. 30), he says: “‘I have not done evil.’ She does not say, ‘I have been freed, dismissed, washed,’ but confidently says: ‘I have not done evil. I am not what I was: made another by you, who turn the wicked person, and he shall not be.’”

Likewise Jerome on Hosea:

> [Note: [Col. 0710D] On Hosea, chapter 2.]

> “This is the difference between human marriage and God’s marriage: a human being makes a mother out of a virgin; God makes a virgin out of one corrupted.”

Many things are said to be what they once were, rather than what they are: for example, Simon was called “the leper” after he had been healed. And Aaron’s rod swallowed the rods—that is, the dragons—of the magicians. So in Zechariah: “What is his goodness, and what is his beauty? Is it not the grain of the elect and wine that makes virgins flourish?” (Zech. 9). In these virgins not only bodily corruption but every memory and every trace of corruption perishes. Therefore the Apostle said [Col. 0710A]: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 2). O how many among them had defiled God’s temple, yet are said as though not to have done so after they were changed through repentance.

Since, therefore, our dedication is exposed to many dangers and is frequently violated by the enemy’s snares and violence, our merciful, compassionate, and just God suspends the judgment of vengeance for a time, so that, if what was violated through guilt should perhaps be restored through repentance, what was threatened for warning may not be inflicted for vengeance. The sacred and most solemn practice of the dedicated Church signifies this restoration through repentance. For two works are chiefly celebrated in the Church: prayers and offerings. Hear the most beautiful reason why [Col. 0710B].

Because God is supremely good and hates every evil, he is angry with us on account of our iniquities. Because he is supremely just and leaves no evil unpunished, he opposes us when we sin. Therefore, because he is angry with us, he must be entreated by prayer; because he opposes us, he must be appeased by offering. These are the two most powerful forms of assistance required in secular lawsuits: an eloquent advocate and an eminent procurator. The first wins the judge’s favor; the second calms the anger of the indignant party. Prayer performs the advocate’s role; offering, that of the procurator. Under the name “offering” I also include sacrifices. Every sacrifice is offered, but not every offering is sacrificed. Sacrifice properly pertains to living things [Col. 0710C]; offering properly to inanimate things, though Leviticus uses one term for the other.

A judge is customarily appeased in two ways: by a gift and by punishment. Of the first you have: “A hidden gift turns away anger, and a present in the bosom the greatest indignation” (Prov. 21). Again: “A person’s gift broadens his way and makes room for him before princes” (Ps. 105). Of the second: “Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased” (ibid., 18). And the Apostle: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 2). Here, then, offering signifies fasting and almsgiving: fasting in place of sacrifice or punishment; almsgiving in place of gift or present.

Prayer is every holy affection of the heart toward God, expressed in mind or even in voice. Almsgiving is every good will or beneficent act bestowed for God’s sake to help one’s neighbor. Fasting is every voluntary chastisement of the body undertaken for God’s sake in punishment for sin [Col. 0710D]. Prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, therefore, are most effective and powerful for appeasing God. Blessed is the debtor, and wise, who redeems so great a debt at so small a price. These are the three gifts of the Magi: the gold of almsgiving, the incense of prayer, and the myrrh of fasting—always to be brought to the temple of the Lord’s body, which we are, because the faithful must always practice these things.

But take care, brothers, that you are not deceived by presenting these gifts without peace and holiness—the two most solemn practices of which we spoke earlier, and to which our house has been specially dedicated by the Son of the Virgin as acceptable. For sins cannot be redeemed by any price, not even by Christ’s own blood, unless they are abandoned. For, as Solomon says: “He will not consent to anyone’s prayers, nor accept very many gifts for redemption” (Prov. 6). And Job says: “Let him not, deceived by vain error, believe that he is to be redeemed at some price” (Job 15). Hence Gregory: “Because he gives alms in such a way as not to abandon guilt, he does not redeem the soul, which he does not restrain from vices.”

Likewise, fasting from food profits absolutely nothing unless one also fasts from vice, according to Isaiah’s words: “Why have we fasted and you have not seen; we have humbled our souls and you have not known?” (Isa. 58). Hear why: “Because on the day of your fast your own will is found” [Col. 0711B]. “Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and strike wickedly with the fist” (ibid.). “Is this not the fast that I have chosen? Loosen the bonds of wickedness; undo the bundles that oppress” (ibid.). Here he openly says that neither bodily chastisement nor the giving of alms profits anything unless sins are first abandoned.

Whoever, therefore, does not abstain from sin but trusts in fasting, almsgiving, or prayer is like the Jews who trusted in lying words, saying: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this” (Jer. 7). They said this while vainly trusting in the outward adornment of walls, in the empty clamor of wordy prayers, and in the legal rite of sacrifices. It was as though they said to the prophets: “You prophesy to us in vain that this temple is to be destroyed [Col. 0711C]. It will not be destroyed, because the temple of the Lord is holy, and in it such great prayers are offered daily by the people. It will not be destroyed because the temple of the Lord is also to be revered by the Gentiles, and it alone is the place in which sacrifices are daily offered.”

The remainder of this sermon is lacking, apparently a small amount.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE POWER AND VIRTUE OF THE CHURCH.

A heavy yoke lies upon the children of Adam. Recognizing in himself, humbly, the grievous misery of the human condition, and lamenting it, the Apostle says: “I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish what is good” [Col. 0711D] (Rom. 7). And a little later: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid.). And below: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God; indeed, it cannot be” (Rom. 8). Here one asks why it cannot. I answer: because it was originally cursed in Adam. “Cursed is the earth in your work,” God says to Adam (Gen. 7). This curse of the earth was also a curse upon human flesh, which was taken from earth, throughout all Adam’s posterity. God, who is merciful and just, inflicted this curse mercifully and justly, so that, while the flesh desires against the spirit, it might train that same spirit for warfare.

For this warfare the Apostle groaned, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). It is as though he said more plainly: Until I depart from this body of death, I shall find no rest from labor, because I shall not have peace with my flesh. If, then, our earth—through the humbling of the pride of the first transgression, though we are unprofitable—does not cease to produce only thorns and thistles for those who cultivate it, what, do you suppose, will it do if through our negligence it remains uncultivated and we do not work it? Precisely what Solomon says: “I passed through the field of the sluggard, and through the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface” (Prov. 24).

The nettle is so called from burning, as in the line:

> A mole digs up gardens; a nettle burns the fingers.

Nettles are the itching desires of the flesh. While they touch bodily pleasures through the bodily senses, and, by scratching the itching of flesh wantonly lusting after the alluring stings of pleasure, as it were burn the fingers of the human mind through the superfluous handling of their nettles’ mass. That itching was most excellently answered by our Benedict—blessed both by grace and by name—when the devil inflamed him with a new and unfamiliar itch of the flesh, scratched by his own thoughts: he preferred that his flesh be wounded by thorns and brambles rather than that his soul be wounded by fleshly pleasures. Thorns are the piercing anxieties of worldly cares, which prick and tear, rend and make bloody.

But wretches whose senses are softened toward love do not feel their own pricks; and therefore they do not grieve at being bloodied, but reckon it a delight to be among thorns. They choke the seed of God’s word in their hearts; they feed the barren woman and do not do good to the widow; and thus, sowing in their flesh, they now sow thorns and will gather fire at judgment. Behold the fruit of earth that is not cultivated, but, left deserted, is reduced to a wilderness.

To remove this danger from the earth of the Church, that great master of the household has not ceased, from the morning of the age until our evening, to send laborers into his vineyard, that they may hasten to cut off at the root the thorns and brambles growing up in it, as soon as they begin to arise. This is what is said to Jeremiah, in the person of all cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard: “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, that you may uproot and destroy, lay waste, build, and plant” (Jer. 1). Every ecclesiastical prelate [Col. 0712D] is appointed by the Lord over nations and kingdoms, because he is set by the Lord above the multitude of laypeople and above the authority of kings and princes. For from the beginning the Lord so ordained that every secular dignity and worldly power should be subject to ecclesiastical dignity, and should be governed by it, as an inferior by a superior and a less worthy by one more worthy.

For he who blesses is greater than he who is blessed, because he who blesses holds the place of the Creator, who at the beginning of the world blessed living creatures, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1). A priest is not blessed by a prince, but a prince by a priest, just as Melchizedek, the high priest of God, blessed Abraham, the supreme patriarch and most holy man. Finally, not only among Jews and Christians but also among pagans it is always found to have been the custom and law that the high priesthood should take precedence over every grade of honor. Augustus Caesar, greatest of emperors, remained subject to the pontiffs of sacred rites until he himself was made by the senate pontiff of Vesta, lest anyone be held more honored than he.

Plutarch the philosopher, tutor and teacher of Prince Trajan, says that the commonwealth is like a body animated by the benefit of a divine gift, guided by the motion of highest equity and governed by the moderation of reason. The prince is the head of this body. But those who preside over divine worship and religion are to be received and honored as the soul of that same body. From this it is plainly concluded that, by as much as the soul surpasses the body, by so much does a priest surpass a king.

Therefore let the kings of the earth, the princes of the world, and all powers of the age hear, and hear with impartial ears, that the Lord has so ordained that priests should preside over them: “Behold,” he says, “today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms.” But let priests and prelates hear for what they have been appointed: “that you may uproot and destroy,” and so forth. That you may uproot evil which has taken root; destroy evil already built up; lay waste evil already amassed; scatter evil strongly fortified. Rooting belongs to the intention of pleasure; building to the carrying out of the deed; gathering to the practice of habit; fortification to the hard obstinacy which defends its sin, glories in it, or corrupts others by example.

He says therefore: “I have appointed you that you may uproot the vice which has already fixed its roots; destroy that which the perpetration of an evil deed has already built; and lay waste that which has already grown strong through a perverse habit.” An evil will is uprooted by a good will; an evil deed is destroyed by a good deed; an evil habit is overcome and destroyed by a good habit; the evil obstinacy of vices is scattered by the good perseverance of virtue. Teach, therefore, and preach that contrition uproots evils badly rooted; confession destroys evils badly built; satisfaction destroys evils badly amassed; and the strength of perseverance scatters evils badly fortified. These are the four parts of penitence, without which there is no return from evil to good, from the devil to God.

And perhaps these are the four “Returns” by which the Shunammite is recalled in the Song of Songs [Col. 0713D] (ch. 6). First, we return to the heart through reflection and contrition, as if from a certain wild place and the solitude of the wilderness to the house in which Jacob, the simple man, is said to have dwelt. Second, we return from the heart to the mouth through confession, as if from a house to a temple, so that there we may confess to God, bless the Lord, and give him glory, accusing ourselves and justifying him; for it is written: “In his temple all will speak glory” (Ps. 28). Likewise: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). “My mouth shall proclaim your righteousness” (Ps. 70).

Third, through satisfaction we return from the mouth to the body, from speech to deed, as if from the temple to the field, so that we may fulfill in deed what we promised with the mouth [Col. 0714A], and pay our vows, which our lips have uttered (Ps. 65). Of this field it is written: “Diligently cultivate your field, that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24). Or it is as if from the temple to battle, so that we may fight bravely against the vices of the flesh. Hence: “I caused the stench of your camps to rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me” (Joel 2). The stench of camps is the stench of bodies nourished in lust and the disgrace of criminals. Fourth, through perseverance in satisfaction and watchfulness we return from the body to death, as if from labor to rest, from work to reward, from battle to peace, from camp to the city.

Of the first return it is written: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 26). Of the second, in the Gospel: “Having returned, he said: ‘I will rise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you’” (Luke 15). Of the third: “If you return and are at rest, you shall be saved” (Isa. 30). Of the fourth: “Virgin Israel, return to your cities” (Jer. 31). As there is one Church and many churches, so there is one heavenly city and many cities, because of the many orders of saints. Of all these together it is said: “The four living creatures went and returned like flashing lightning” (Ezek. 1). Nothing is swifter than flashing lightning. So are all these returns. Swift reflection produces swift contrition; swift contrition, swift confession; swift confession, swift satisfaction; swift satisfaction, swift perseverance. And although this perseverance may perhaps be long in duration, yet it must be reckoned short, in the humility of the mind, in comparison with the endless reward to be received, according to the saying: “The days seemed few to him because of the greatness of his love” (Gen. 29). And: “The momentary and light affliction of our present time will work in us, beyond all measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4).

It follows:

“That you may build and plant.” Build, indeed, with gold and silver and many precious stones. You will find a natural foundation: a mind prepared and disposed to receive the good. This material does not fear fire. Wood, hay, and stubble ought not to be built, because they must pass through fire and perish in the fire. These are venial sins. Mortal sins [Col. 0714D] are not wood, hay, and stubble, but lead, bronze, and iron; and sins of this kind not only disfigure but also destroy the foundation of faith. For there is a double impiety, that is, unbelief: not believing and not obeying. Hence Samuel: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). And the Apostle: “He who does not provide for his own, and especially those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

Wood here signifies a certain hardness of heart; hay, the softness of the flesh, because “all flesh is hay” (Isa. 40); stubble, the lightness of the mind. He builds wood who is too rigid of heart in forgiving resentment, too hard in showing mercy, too sparing in giving; yet he does forgive, show mercy, and give, but more slowly and with greater difficulty than he should. For one who does not forgive at all builds not wood but iron. He sins not venially but mortally. He builds hay who is too reluctant to discipline the body and too inclined to indulge it. He builds stubble who is insufficiently practiced in the seriousness of silence and too ready and eager for laughter and idle words.

But he builds gold who perfectly loves God and neighbor, whose perfect charity casts out fear; whose faith is tested through temptation as gold through fire, and who, tested and proved, can say with blessed Lawrence: “You tested me by fire, and no iniquity was found in me” (Ps. 16). Anyone builds gold to whom is given a word of wisdom concerning divine things, for the instruction of faith and the edification of morals. He builds silver [Col. 0715B] to whom is given a word of knowledge concerning earthly things, for prudent provision in worldly affairs for the benefit of the neighbor. But he builds silver better who shines in chastity; who keeps God’s chaste utterances chastely and teaches them chastely; who diligently exercises himself in God’s praises, in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and chanting in the night and day offices.

Precious stones are bright and solid. Their brightness signifies purity of conscience; their solidity, firmness in patience. Therefore he builds precious stones who keeps his heart with every vigilance, losing neither purity of conscience in prosperity nor firmness of patience in adversity. But here an important question arises. If wood, hay, and stubble signify venial sins, without which this present life is not lived, why are saints not likewise said to build wood, hay, and stubble, as others do, since they do not live without such things? But the word *building* signifies a multitude of venial sins. A building is not made from a single piece of wood or one stalk of stubble, but from many gathered together. Saints and the perfect, however, avoid even venial sins as far as they can; and therefore they do not gather from them so great a multitude that it may be called a building. Likewise, the righteous redeem their daily offenses by the daily sacrifices of good works, and therefore construct no building out of those offenses. But because they gather many good works, they build gold, silver, and precious stones.

“Build,” he says, “and plant”: namely, in the soil [Col. 0715D] of heart and body, prepared, cleansed, and enriched. There plant the plant of faith, the shoots and plantings of virtues, so that in the house of the Lord there may be a garden of delights in the sweet joy of those living together; a garden of nuts in the hardness and austerity of penitents; a garden of spices in the fervent thought of those who love God; a lily of the valleys in the shining chastity of the humble; a paradise of every fruit in the sweetness of those who taste beforehand eternal spiritual things and breathe forth the fragrance of a good reputation.

For as God planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, in which he placed the man to dwell and delight there, so a human being ought to plant within himself a garden of delight in which God may continually abide as amid his delights. Thus he says: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8). And in the Apocalypse (ch. 3) he is said to knock at the door, that he may enter and dine with the human being. But what is it that he considers a delight in dwelling with us? Hear Zechariah: “What is his goodness, and what is his beauty, except the grain of the elect and wine producing virgins?” (Zech. 9). The grain of the elect is Christ, who calls himself grain; the wine producing virgins is the Holy Spirit, who produces virgins when he pours into hearts the love of chastity, holiness, and purity.

Grain is so called from enjoyment (*frui*). But how do the elect enjoy Christ? Through the charity of brotherhood, if they render it to one another in chaste love. For they cannot enjoy the grain unless they also enjoy this wine which proceeds from Christ the vine. “When the Paraclete comes,” he says, “whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” [Col. 0716B] (John 14), and so forth. Bread is made from grain; from charity the fruit of bread is produced. Hence: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6). Nothing dead, tasteless, or insipid comes down from heaven. Peace without holiness is bread, but dead, tasteless, insipid bread: bread from the world, not from heaven. “I do not give to you as the world gives” (John 14). The world gives peace without salt; I do not do so, but say to you: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9). Therefore the grain of the elect cannot exist without the wine that produces virgins. For if it exists without it, it will be the grain of the reprobate, not of the elect.

Paul to Philemon: “May I enjoy you in the Lord” (Philem. 20). Not in this way do those enjoy one another of whom it is written: “There is great concord among the effeminate.” O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity! This is God’s goodness; this is God’s beauty: chaste charity and cherished chastity. “His place was made in peace” (Ps. 75); and likewise in holiness. God is called the author and lover of peace. “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11). “But you dwell in holiness, O praise of Israel” (Ps. 21). And again: “O God, your way is in holiness” (Ps. 76). “My God, his way is undefiled” (Ps. 17). Nothing is pleasing without peace. Therefore the Apostle says: “Have peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you” (1 Cor. 13). But he made clear of what peace he spoke when he said: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” [Col. 0716D] (Heb. 12). For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification; he is not a God of dissension but of peace. God will present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle of disgrace or crime, nor anything of that kind (Eph. 5).

Therefore God’s delights are nothing other than purity of bodies and peace of souls. Thus that prelate or preacher plants for God a garden of pleasure and delights who by word and example plants peace and holiness in the hearts and bodies of his hearers. Behold, this is the work of an evangelist; behold why legates from the side of the lord pope are so often sent to us: namely, that they may uproot and destroy, build and plant.

But why does the prophet add four sorrowful things and only two joyful ones, except because, as the flood of iniquity daily overflows and the charity of many grows ever colder, a double labor is now necessary in cutting down vices compared with planting virtues? “The earth is filled with iniquity; there is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the earth; cursing and lying, murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.” Whence comes this, except because, as the poet says:

> When fields are neglected, the fern destined for burning grows up.  
> (Horace, *Satires* 1.3.37)

Virtues cannot be planted or grafted except where vices have first been uprooted. Hence Boethius, *Consolation* 3.1:

> Whoever wishes to sow a noble field  
> first frees the land from shrubs,  
> and with the sickle cuts down brambles and fern, etc.

Does not Scripture say the same? “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). And again: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1). “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96)—that is, begin from this degree of love. For the first degree of love for God is hatred of sin. This degree is divided into three parts: penitence for past sin; uprooting present—that is, reborn—sin; and avoidance of future sin.

None of these can be done without the hoe of discipline, of which Isaiah says: “All the mountains which shall be hoed with a hoe, there shall not come upon them the terror of thorns and brambles” (Isa. 7). This hoe is discipline, to which Paul beautifully invites us: “Persevere,” he says, “in discipline. God presents himself to you as to sons. For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, in which all have become participants, then you are illegitimate children and not sons” [Col. 0717C] (Heb. 12), and so forth.

From these words of the Apostle discipline may be described thus: discipline is a child’s acceptance of paternal correction; it consists in two things, the discreet and natural ordering of those who preside, and the voluntary and humble obedience of those subject to them. Of these matters there is that elegant saying of Plautus: “There are two kinds of power: one commands, the other obeys; thus all things are governed.” And he adds: “The former is more distinguished, that of the greater; but often the favor of the lesser is greater. Therefore, while avoiding envy and expense, place your hope in those below.”

Behold, this most eloquent man calls obedience and subjection a power; and truly it is a power, and the greatest. For to obey and be subject is far more powerful than to command and rule—indeed, by as much as doing is harder than speaking. Nothing is easier than speech. Therefore every wise person, every truly Christian person, is accustomed to seek humble service in subjection rather than the lofty rank of prelation, because humble subjection truly makes one more powerful than lofty prelation. He therefore beautifully bids us hope in those below, where there is greater rest [Col. 0718A], greater favor, less expense, and less envy.

Blessed Cyprian describes discipline thus: “Discipline is the orderly correction of conduct and the greater observance of preceding rules. ‘This,’ he says, ‘is the tunic of Christ; whoever is outside it is alien to Christ’s body’” [Note: [Col. 0717D] Cyprian, tractate *On the Twelve Abuses*.] Let us not tear it, but cast lots for whose it may be; that is, let us relax nothing from the Lord’s commandments, nor from the commandments of the Church’s superiors established by him, to whom he himself says: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Hence the same blessed martyr says that the final and worst degree of abuse is a people without discipline. But what is a people without discipline except a people which does not permit itself to be ruled by the command of its superiors, but is carried away unbridled and wandering through byways; when, abandoned to its own will, like some wild and untamed animal, it rushes headlong and roams through the fields of license in harmful freedom? Hence it is written: “A vain man is lifted up in pride, and thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild ass” (Job 11).

Such was that tribune of the people, Durio, whom the censors Lucius Flaccus and his colleague expelled from the senate, because he had repealed the law enacted to restrain expenditure, using these words: “A tight bridle has been put upon us, citizens; it must by no means be endured. We are bound and constrained by the miserly chain of slavery. For a law has been passed commanding us to be frugal. Let us repeal this authority, coated with the rust of grim antiquity. And what need have we of liberty, if we are not permitted to perish when we wish?” O man worthy of a thousand deaths, to be removed not merely from the senatorial order but from the whole human race!

Do not, brothers, do not, I beseech you, be among such people. Do not be without discipline, like the sons of Belial—that is, without a yoke—who, according to Jeremiah (ch. 2), “broke the yoke” of obedience and “burst the bonds” of discipline and said, “We will not serve.” Rather, as the Psalmist says: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2). Lay hold of discipline as a spiritual defense, as a singular refuge. Lay hold of the one who lays hold of you. “I took hold of you,” he says, “from the ends of the earth, and called you from its farthest places” (Isa. 41). The ends of the earth are greater crimes; the distant places are lesser ones. Those at the ends of the earth are farther from God than those in the distant places; and to take hold is more than to call. We are taken hold of by a hand, called by a command, taken hold of by a scourge. Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.

What then is the laying hold of discipline, except the most delightful embrace of wisdom? “Because,” he says, “I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and there was no one who looked” (Prov. 1). Augustine, to Docelinus: “Those whom Wisdom has first bound and tamed by certain training labors, she will afterward release and, once released, give them herself to enjoy; and those whom she has first instructed by temporal bonds, she will afterward bind with eternal embraces—a bond than which nothing more delightful [Col. 0719A] or more secure can be conceived. I confess that these first things are somewhat hard; but those final things I would call neither hard, because they are most delightful, nor fragile, because they are most firm. What then are they, except something which cannot be spoken, but can only be believed, hoped for, and loved? Yet the bonds of this world possess harshness, never pleasure except false pleasure; certain pain, uncertain delight; hard labor, uncertain rest; a thing full of misery, and an empty hope of blessedness.” And he adds: “Do you put into these both hands, neck, and feet, when you desire to be subjected to earthly honors—where you ought to go not only uninvited, but not even compelled?”

Behold, Augustine agrees with Plautus: he calls prelation a yoke, and subjection and discipline a liberty that happily binds. Therefore lay hold of discipline—that is, receive Wisdom knocking at the door and saying: “Behold, I stand at the door” (Rev. 3), and so forth. O delight of delights: to have God as companion and fellow traveler, guest and table companion! Do not take away his delights, lest he take away yours. His delight is to be with you. And he will be with you if you lay hold of discipline: “My son, do not cast aside the Lord’s discipline, nor turn away when you are corrected by him; for the Lord corrects whom he loves, and, as a father, delights in a son” (Prov. 3). O how delightfully a father dwells with a son!

But the Apostle briefly indicates what it is to lay hold of discipline when he says: “Obey your superiors and be subject to them” (Heb. 13) in those matters which they order concerning you. Behold, the superior sent by the lord pope, this new legate who has brought us a new hoe of discipline, has issued new and many rules of command. Yet no one will complain of the multitude of rules who patiently permits the multitude of his thorns to be cut down. For in all of us there have grown up [Col. 0720A] many things not only superfluous but even harmful. All these must be cut away if we wish to bear fruit; nor can they all be cut away by the sickle of one command, but by many. Otherwise, what benefit is it to cut down one thorn and leave many?

> What benefit does it give you to remove one thorn from among many?  
> (Ovid)

One disregarded spark has often kindled a great fire. One neglected thorn has sometimes grown into a great thorn-brake. Hence Isaiah: “It was kindled like fire, and shall be kindled in the thickness of the forest” (Isa. 9). He spoke of thorn and bramble in the singular, then added in the plural sense “the thickness of the forest,” clearly indicating that the neglect of one thorn sometimes grows wild [Col. 0720B] into a dense forest of wickedness.
