Therefore let us patiently endure the not-new multitude of our vices being cut down by a new multitude of commandments. For, among other things, the modesty of the commander himself ought greatly to move us to show due reverence to this legate and obedience to his commands. He does not go about pompously; he does not pursue greed; he does not run after gifts; he seeks not what is ours but us. In short, he is not like many: that is, he does not go after gold, nor put his hope in monetary treasures. He is a lover of justice, zealous for souls, a despiser of money, keeping in memory that poetic saying:

> Dare, stranger, to despise wealth, and imagine yourself also worthy of God.

And that saying of Seneca: “No one is more worthy of God than the person who despises wealth.” I therefore urge you now humbly and devoutly to hear the commands which he has conveyed to you for the salvation of souls, and to be obedient according to my counsel. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to you.

[Col. 0721]

# Flowers of Helinand, Monk of Froidmont, Collected by Vincent of Beauvais

(D. Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, VII, 306.)

## Notice

The *Flowers* of Helinand concern three subjects. The first is “On Self-Knowledge”; the second, “On the Good Government of a Prince”; the third seeks by means of a letter or book—usually entitled *On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*—to recall a novice who had departed from the monastery. Vincent of Beauvais divided it into chapters, but here we have restored it to its earlier form.

# Preface of Vincent of Beauvais

[Col. 0721]

In these times there was in the territory of Beauvais Helinand, monk of Froidmont, a religious man and eloquent in speech. He composed, with such elegance and usefulness as is clearer than daylight, those verses *On Death* in our vernacular which are publicly read. He also carefully arranged in a very large volume a chronicle from the beginning of the world to his own time. This work, however, has been broken up and dispersed, so that it can nowhere be found complete. For it is said that this same Helinand lent certain quires of the work to one of his friends, namely Lord Garin, bishop of Senlis, of good memory; and that thus, whether through forgetfulness, negligence, or another cause, he lost them entirely.

Nevertheless, so far as I could find it, I have inserted much from this work in various places in this work of ours. Here, however, I wished also to insert certain notable matters from the same work which have nowhere above been placed, and likewise selections from certain other writings of his. For, as is recorded, he wrote a letter entitled *On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*, sent to Walter, a cleric who had been a novice in the Cistercian order and a canon in the Premonstratensian order, and who at last, considering himself free from his vow because he had not made profession, returned to secular life and married a woman named Rixenda.

At the request of William, brother of this Walter, who was Helinand’s companion and fellow-cloistered monk, Helinand wrote a letter to Walter in the person of that same William, so that it appears to be William’s own. This same Helinand also wrote several excellent sermons. These, then, are the things which I have excerpted from the aforesaid small works and placed together here.

# On Self-Knowledge

[Col. 0721]

## Chapter One. Visitors are admonished to visit and examine themselves.

[Col. 0721A]

In the *Chronicles*, book 8, I set out more fully the errors of philosophers concerning the entry of souls into bodies, their return from bodies, and the places of the lower world, so that, being better understood, they may be avoided. Therefore, concerning Apollo’s oracle, by which Macrobius attempts to confirm his error—namely, “from heaven descended *gnōthi seauton*” [Note: [Col. 0721] **Γνῶθι σεαυτόν** (*Know yourself*), a saying of Chilon, inscribed in the temple of Apollo, from Pliny, book 7.]—I remember that I delivered a sermon in an assembly of brothers in this manner.

It is read in the book of Job, chapter 5: “Visiting your countenance, you shall not sin.” A timely word is best. What is a timely word? A timely word is one suited to time, place, and person, according to the saying of Wisdom: “Nothing is so characteristic of wisdom as fitting words to places and times.” The time of which we speak is a time of visitation. The place in which we are gathered was established for this purpose. The persons to whom we speak are visitors and those to be visited.

O you, whoever you are, visitor of others: if you first visit yourself, afterward you will not sin in visiting your neighbor; for within yourself you will be able to read how you ought to judge the errors of others. And indeed, what is more just or fitting than that spiritual physicians, who visit those spiritually sick, should dare first to visit themselves, question with the fingers of discernment their inward condition, and feel the throbbing veins of their affections—lest it happen to them, still unvisited and already visiting, that is, still uncorrected and already correcting others, to hear this proverb from the sick as they murmur: “Physician, heal yourself” [Col. 0723A] (Luke 4).

## Chapter Two. On that oracle of Apollo, *gnōthi seauton*, that is, “Know yourself.”

Long ago at Delphi there was, it is read, inscribed upon the most ancient tripod of Apollo the most famous oracle, given to one consulting how he might attain blessedness: *gnōthi seauton*, that is, “Know yourself.” Yet Apollo ought not to be believed the author or inventor of this saying, but rather its thief. For he stole it from the present passage. To know oneself is the same as to visit one’s countenance. Or, certainly, he stole it from that passage in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and depart,” and so forth [Col. 0723B] (Song 1).

Our satirist Juvenal calls this saying—or rather this theft of Apollo—a divine and heavenly saying, because of the supreme usefulness contained within it. For he says:

> Him I should rightly despise  
> who knows by how much Atlas rises higher  
> than all the mountains of Libya, yet does not know  
> how much an iron-bound thing differs from a chest—
*Sacculus* (“little bag”): “From heaven descended, *Know thyself*.” (Juvenal, *Satires* XIV.)

That is to say: it is foolish learning and useless, senseless wisdom to know superfluous things while remaining ignorant of what is necessary. For what profit is there in knowing how to measure the world, and not knowing oneself? Without this knowledge nothing is useful to mortals, nothing saving to human beings. This knowledge is necessary above all things; even by itself it is sufficient. For it teaches a person to fear God, avoid sin, love the neighbour, despise earthly things, and love heavenly things.

I say that the most deceitful spirit gave this response, not from any desire to teach, but with the intention of deceiving. For he thought he could persuade people to believe themselves sprung from the race of the gods—gods whom they heard had been human beings—and so incite them to mutual rivalry, ambition for honour, and the desire to rule under the guise of liberty. Indeed, when the sages of Greece were consulted by kings about this oracle, they replied with nothing other than that a human being ought to know that he belonged to the race of the gods. Hence Macrobius, in his commentary on Scipio’s dream, says that souls fell from heaven into bodies, and that this is the soul’s perfect wisdom while it uses the body: to recognize whence it arose. For he thinks that in this way the soul puts on the virtues themselves through consciousness of its nobility, so that, when lifted beyond the body, it may be carried back to the place from which it descended.

But this interpretation broadly encouraged every licence to sin in accordance with civil theology, since people seemed to be imitating those whose innumerable outrages and crimes they heard represented in the theatres. Yet demons often utter truth and give good counsel to people, not willingly but unwillingly, compelled by necessity—namely when those above them desire it: the saints, or angels, or God. Thus we read of the demon dwelling in a demoniac, whom blessed Bridget questioned, saying: “Tell me a word of the Lord.” Through the possessed person the demon immediately replied, in the hearing of the people: “Bridget, fear God, and you will be feared by all. Love God, and you will be loved by all.” Can the devil become a voluntary preacher of the fear and love of God? He said these things under compulsion and against his will. Likewise, whenever the Gospels and lives of saints report that the devil uttered some saving word, we must believe that he did so under compulsion. Such things are recorded not only in Holy Scripture but also in pagan histories. We must therefore believe that Apollo gave this answer not voluntarily but unwillingly, declaring what he knew would benefit human beings; or else that he willingly uttered an ambiguous saying which he did not expect to be taken in a good sense—that is, as an argument for humility.

## Chapter III. On knowledge of the outer human being

But let us also consider the usefulness of this prophetic and truly divine, rather than Delphic, saying: “By examining your appearance, you will not sin” (Job 5). For the human appearance is twofold, because the human being himself is twofold, according to the testimony of the Apostle: “Though our outer human being is decaying, yet our inner one is renewed from day to day” (2 Cor. 4). The outer human being is the body; the inner is the mind.

In the outward appearance four things are to be examined—that is, pondered more frequently: the lowliness of its material, the dignity of its form, the painfulness of its life, and the inevitability of its ruin. Of the first it is said: “God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. 2). Of the second:

> While the other animals look downward upon the earth,  
> He gave the human being an exalted face,  
> And commanded him to gaze upon heaven  
> And raise his upright countenance toward the stars.  
> —Ovid

Of the third: “Man is born for labour” (Job 5). Of the fourth: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3). Hence this couplet:

> Why is man proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> Whose birth is punishment, whose life labour, whose death inevitable?

Persius the satirist explains this more fully:

> Learn, unhappy people, and know the causes of things:  
> What we are, for what manner of life we are born, what order  
> Is given us, how gently we must turn around the goal, and whence [we come].

This consideration produces a fourfold fruit: a sense of one’s own lowliness, desire for the heavenly kingdom, love of one’s neighbour, and fear of judgment. The first arises from the lowliness of the material; the second, from the dignity of the form; the third, from the painfulness of life; the fourth, from the inevitability of ruin.

For a human being, born of woman and living for a short time, is filled with many miseries (Job 14), both of body and soul. Therefore we have our eyes raised to heaven: that, despising earth, we may desire heaven; and that we may love above all things God, who formed us in so elegant a shape and so ennobled the human form among all other animals. Therefore Plato gave thanks to nature that he had been born a human being.

Once some brothers were conversing together in a lecture-room. When one said to his companions that he saw nothing from which he did not derive edification—[Note: This was Saint Bernard’s brother, concerning whom see the *Great Exordium*.]—another, quite ready with speech, replied: “What edification, I ask you, does the sight of a toad provide?” He immediately said: “Certainly, very much. Since I had deserved nothing by which God should form me a human being rather than a toad, whenever I see a toad I call to mind this gratuitous benefit of God and give him thanks, because, although I deserved nothing, he did not give me so execrable a form, but granted me a most beautiful appearance and a royal figure.

“Further, the sight of a toad benefits me thus: whenever I see it so horrible in shape, so savage in nature, so slow in movement, so harmful in venom, so hostile to humankind, I greatly fear lest, made like it in my morals, crawling upon breast and belly, I may someday—may God avert it from me!—be handed over to be devoured by such most evil worms: not these earthly worms, which are soon crushed, but those dreadful worms in Gehenna, living from Gehenna, which never die.”

Confounded by this most wise reply of the brother, the critic fell silent. Thus the dignity of the human form alone, even if we say nothing of God’s other benefits to humankind, is a great occasion in us for love of God. The painfulness of life, however, which is common to all, contains a great cause for brotherly love. For, as someone aptly said, since calamity is complaint and prosperity pride, if we were not mutually miserable, one person would long ago have become hateful to another.

Yet he is utterly foolish whom the necessity of death does not bring fear of judgment, when it is written: “It is appointed for human beings once to die, and after this, judgment” (Heb. 9). This has been said about the outward appearance; let us now consider the inward.

## Chapter IV. On knowledge of the inner human being with respect to natural appearance

The appearance of the inner human being is twofold: natural and voluntary. The natural appearance is common to all; the voluntary is peculiar to each individual. The natural is considered according to condition, the voluntary according to will.

In the natural appearance four things must be considered: that the soul is rational, immortal, invisible, and not localized. The first consideration forbids a human being luxury; the second, avarice; the third, boasting; the fourth, envy and every injury to a brother.

Among all the monsters in this world, nothing seems to me more monstrous than that in certain human bodies we see brutish minds and affections more bestial than those of beasts. Aristotle and Sallust hold that persons devoted to gluttony and lust should be counted not among human beings but among animals. What can those who are Christian in name and bestial in life say here—those who rot in their own filth?

The office of reason is threefold: to discern, reject, and choose. It discerns between opposites, rejects the worse things, and chooses the better. Demons naturally possess the first office, but are deprived of the second and third, not naturally but voluntarily. Therefore those who knowingly choose evils and reject goods must be counted among demons, not human beings; they wrap themselves in that prophetic cloak of malediction: “Woe to those who call evil good, and conversely” (Isa. 5), and so forth.

The second consideration, as we said above, teaches us to abstain from avarice. For nothing is further from reason than for a human being, immortal in soul, to desire mortal things with an immortal desire, when what is desired must altogether soon be left behind by the one who desires it.

The third consideration ought to persuade us to flee boasting, all arrogance, and love of praise. Since our mind is invisible, this is a strong argument that every good thing we do or say should, so far as lies within us, be done or said invisibly and in secret, so that our Father, who sees in secret, may reward us. Otherwise, it is indeed a great perversion, almost comparable to magical practices, to parade before human eyes an author who is hidden and invisible in his good deeds or words through the vice of boasting. The most effective and swift remedy for this vice is for our mind to examine its evils more frequently than its goods.

The fourth examination—that is, consideration of the inward human being, namely how the soul vivifies the entire body without being localized and gives itself wholly to every one of its parts, leaving none without the faculty of sensation—is surely a marvellous invitation and persuasion toward brotherly love. Thus the Apostle showed by a most beautiful example that every body, however large the congregation, ought to be animated by one and the same spirit when he said: “If one member suffers, all suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12), and so forth.

What will slanderers and the envious say here? They regard every honour of a brother as their own dishonour, thinking that whatever accrues to another’s glory has been subtracted from theirs, whereas they ought rather to have judged the opposite: that whatever accrued to another’s glory had been added to their own. “Are you jealous for my sake?” asks Moses. “Would that all might prophesy” (Num. 11). O most unhappy of all mortals, who prosper only through their neighbours’ misery and to whom the prosperity of their brothers alone is adversity! This is that evil eye; and, if you believe Aesop or Anianus, you will see one who wishes to have one of his own eyes plucked out so that his neighbour may be deprived of both.

## Chapter V. On knowledge of the same human being with respect to voluntary appearance

We have spoken of the natural appearance of the inner human being; now let us consider the other, which we shall call voluntary. This appearance lies within a human being’s choice and is therefore called voluntary, because, as was said above, it is considered according to the will of free choice.

Its beauty consists in two things: willing what we know God wills, and refusing what we do not doubt that he refuses. For, as a certain holy man says, the will of God is the rule to which we ought certainly to correct and govern our own will.

Indeed, the beauty of the soul is holiness; and holiness is a holy affection, constant and firm in a holy resolve. It is twofold: holy hatred and holy love—hatred of evil and desire for good. Evil is nothing but sin and an occasion for sin; good is nothing but God and imitation of God. The first two must always be fled; the second two embraced. For purity of heart consists in these two affections. Hence it is said: “Your eyes are those of doves” (Song 1). The dove is a bird greatly fearful and exceedingly loving. Hence the poet’s words:

> …the most timid flock, the doves.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.506

The two eyes of doves, therefore, are nothing other than holy fear and holy love.

“These excerpts from that discourse are sufficient to prove that Apollo’s oracle was wrongly understood by Macrobius and certain other philosophers.” [Note: Words of Vincent.]

## Chapter VI. On the seven likenesses of the soul to God; first, the first three

Concerning this same oracle, I remember that I once wrote a certain letter to Drogo, canon of Noyon, part of which I have taken care to insert here.

Knowledge of the human being consists in the same things as composition; and composition consists in two things, or rather is made from two things: soul and body. Knowledge of the soul, however, is obtained from its archetype, in whose image and likeness it was made. Therefore, if we are to convict Apollo of falsehood, God must be known before the human being. For naturally the idea is prior to the *eidos*, the seal to what is sealed, the model to the work.

God is spirit, and so is the soul; God is simple, and so is the soul; God is immortal, and so is the soul; God is invisible, and so is the soul. God is one in substance and three in persons; the soul is one in essence and three in powers. God is wholly everywhere in his substance; the soul, though not everywhere, is wholly diffused through each part of its body. Finally, God is rational—or rather, Reason itself; likewise, the soul is rational.

Here are seven likenesses of the soul to God. The first six also belong to the souls of brute animals; for the spirit of animals, as some falsely claim, is not bodily, although it is mortal, but incorporeal. The seventh likeness alone is proper to the human soul—indeed to every human soul, though not to it alone.

Nevertheless, knowledge of the first properties brings it much benefit. Because the human soul knows itself to be spirit, it can know another life of spirits, separate from the life of the flesh. It can also know that it ought to walk more according to the spirit than according to the flesh, according to the saying: “Walk by the Spirit” (Gal. 5), and so forth. From its simplicity it is shown that it ought to walk simply and flee every pretence. From its immortality it can know that mortal joys must be fled and immortal ones always sought; and by the same reasoning, that mortal punishments should not be feared, but immortal ones.

## Chapter VII. On the last four

Because the soul is invisible, it can know that every good it does in this world ought, so far as lies within it, to be done in secret. Because it is one in substance, it ought to know that it must always maintain one and the same form of innocence and justice, “for the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27).

Because it is threefold in powers, it is instructed not to seek a solitary authority; but a further and deeper meaning is also indicated in this triad. Three is the first number that possesses a bond. For two, which has no middle, has no bond and signifies division. But three, which has a middle, is a sign of concord and union. It is the first of the odd numbers and the first wholly odd number, and therefore is, as it were, wholly concord: for each of its parts is in the middle between the other two. Thus it fittingly signifies the indivisible substance and inseparable operation of the Trinity, and indissoluble love.

And because every odd number is bound by a certain bond of mediation, I think the Mantuan poet signified peace and concord by an odd number when he said:

> God delights in an odd number.

This is as though he had said: God loves peace and love, because he himself is peace and love. Therefore, through its three powers, so firmly and naturally joined to one another, the soul is admonished to flee every division and schism, and to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Because it communicates itself wholly and equally to all the members, the human being is admonished, according to his ability, to communicate to every neighbour—that is, to every human being—the service owed by humanity, according to the saying: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6).

Finally, the soul is rational, as God is—except that God ought not so much to be called rational as Reason itself. Hence Seneca says: “God is wholly reason.” By this likeness the human being is admonished to flee things not to be sought and not to seek things to be fled, but, with the eye of reason, to discern between both and choose the better among what has been distinguished. For discernment between good and evil, or good and better, or evil and worse, is useless unless choice of the better and rejection of the worse follow. So too the will chooses in vain what reason has not first judged ought to be chosen.

Beasts have choice without discernment; demons have discernment without choice. To descend living into hell is to sin knowingly; it is to fall with eyes open, as Balaam fell (Num. 24), and as the speaker who said:

> I see and approve the better things;  
> I follow the worse.  
> —Ovid

Finally, just as in the Trinity which is God, two persons proceed from one, so in the trinity of the soul’s powers its irascible and concupiscible faculties ought always to proceed from reason: so that the former flees nothing, and the latter desires nothing, except what reason has prescribed to be fled or desired. For without reason either one is nothing other than rage and madness.

Therefore, what a halter is to an ass, a bridle to a horse, a driver to a chariot, and a tamer to a lion, that is reason to anger and love. Accordingly, both must inevitably be carried into the precipice unless reason provides guidance for both. Let this suffice for the present concerning knowledge of the inner human being; now let us consider the outer.

## Chapter VIII. On knowledge of the human body

Knowledge of the human body consists in two things: material and form. I leave complexion or constitution to physicians. Its material is from mud or mire, but its form from heaven. Hence someone says: “I possess this from heaven” (2 Macc. 7).

Therefore the Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth. Having formed him, he commanded him to look upon his form in heaven, so that he might know that his maker dwells in heaven. From these two things a human being draws a double obligation: from form, to be holy; from material, to be humble.

For although human form has always excelled all animal forms from the creation of the world itself, it acquired a far greater preeminence of dignity from the incarnation of the Word and from the form of humanity assumed by God. The Apostle did not without reason call excessive that love by which God loved us; he certainly understood that so great a benefit, as no greatness of worldly justice could deserve it, so no weighing or estimation could weigh its worth. Our devotion estimates it better than our reasoning; thanksgiving better than disputation; and poverty of spirit obtains it more readily than any heap of riches.

Before the incarnation of the Word, only the inner form was like God; but from the incarnation of the Word, the outward human form itself was also made God’s form. Therefore, at every suggestion of the serpent, we ought to consider the single dignity of this double form; and we shall immediately be ashamed even to have thought anything shameful. For each form is too dignified to be conformed to so shameful a garment. Certainly of both forms it can—indeed must—be said:

> Let not so good a form produce evil morals.

Otherwise, what punishment do you think he will suffer who has dishonoured the form of God?

Knowledge of the human body can also be gathered by another reasoning. Three things must be considered in the human body: its filthy origin, its miserable life, and necessary—that is, inevitable—death. Our outer human being is conceived from impure seed, born for labour, and destined to die whether it wills or not. Most certain death, and the most uncertain hour of death, cry out to us that death always hangs before the eyes of all and therefore ought always to be held before everyone’s eyes and continually pondered, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). Plato, Pythagoras, and Basil—our philosopher among Christians—placed wisdom in this meditation.

## Chapter IX. Further on the misery of the same human being

To these three points may be referred the definition of a human being given by a certain wise man to one asking, “What is man?” “Vile sperm,” he said, “a vessel of excrement, food for worms.” He was vile sperm in conception, a vessel of excrement in the remaining course of life, and food for worms in his end.

But I say that every human being is food for worms not only after death, but also before it. Though one changes and changes again one’s clothing, one cannot altogether avoid the bites of moths, fleas, or such creatures. What profit did Nero gain from never wearing the same garment twice? Or what harm did Hilarion suffer from not changing his hair-shirt?

This place calls for a story. Hear, then, not a story but an event involving your own Helinand. Philip, bishop of Beauvais, once lodged with us, not—as some do—for devouring, but for devotion. For by now the shared hospitality of our order finds more people to devour it than its distinctive holiness finds to honour it. The aforesaid bishop ordered me to have him hear the morning Mass.

When, on the following day, after Prime had already been sung, I came to him, I found him still sleeping; and none of his household or familiar attendants dared wake him. But I went closer and woke him, as though joking, saying: “It has long been time for the sparrows to rise and bless the Lord, while our bishops are still snoring in their beds.”

Awakened and embarrassed by these words, he grew angry with me because I had reproved him so freely. Indignantly he said: “Go away, wretch, and kill your lice.” Turning his irritation into a joke, I replied at once: “See to it, Father, that your worms do not kill you; for I have already killed my worms.”

Know, then, that this is the difference between the worms of the rich and those of the poor: the worms of the rich kill the rich, whereas the worms of the poor are killed by the poor. Read the histories of the Maccabees, Josephus, and the Acts of the Apostles, and you will find the most powerful kings Antiochus and Herod Agrippa consumed by worms. Overcome at once by the argument and its authority, he immediately fell silent.

## Chapter X. Further on knowledge of the human being, and souls appearing after death

But let what has been said for the present concerning knowledge of the human being suffice. I have set it down for you, brother, lest you think that true knowledge of the human being can be had from the crafty saying of an unclean spirit, rather than from the saving teaching of the Holy Spirit alone.

If you desire to know a more perfect treatment of the same knowledge, read the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory, poured forth from the mouth of the Holy Spirit himself, according to the testimony of Peter the Deacon, who saw a dove suggesting into blessed Gregory’s ear the words that he should write. Read also the most beautiful book of Blessed Bernard, *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius. From its most noble style and almost more-than-human thoughts, you will be able to know not only what a human being is but also what God is; and you will understand that the author of this book was wiser than Apollo, more eloquent than Demosthenes, subtler than Aristotle, more moral than Socrates, and more discerning than Plato.

These things have been said because Macrobius cites the authority of the Delphic response, *gnōthi seauton*, “Know thyself,” to prove that souls fell from heaven; and he says this is the human being’s self-knowledge. But he looked back to their first beginnings, so that, conscious of its noble origin, the soul might put on virtues by which it could ascend again to the place from which it descended.

In the same place, Virgil’s authority concerning the heroes is to be understood. He relegated them to the underworld and says that they know their own sun and their own stars; he also testifies that after death they perform the lighter pursuits which they had practiced while living, saying:

> The delight they had in chariots and arms while alive,  
> The care they had to pasture shining horses,  
> Follows them when they are laid beneath the earth.

This falsehood of opinion—or opinion of falsehood—took its beginning, unless I am mistaken, from the fact that the souls of deceased sinners, lamenting their punishments, often appear to many people in the dress in which they formerly lived: peasants in rustic garb, soldiers in military dress. Thus common report tells of Hellequin’s company, concerning which Henry, bishop of Orléans and brother of our bishop of Beauvais, used to relate a most remarkable event which he himself had heard from one who had seen it—namely John, canon of the Church of Orléans. This John, speaking of the matter to the aforesaid bishop, said:

## Chapter XI. An example concerning this: Hellequin’s company

Burchard, the archdeacon called “of Pissac,” was about to go to Rome. He asked me to give him as a companion a certain cleric named Natalis, the steward of my household. He was so capable in managing domestic affairs, so good a manager, prudent, and faithful—qualities very rarely found in stewards. Burchard wanted him as companion on the journey, not so much because he loved him as because, being extremely avaricious, he was very afraid for his money.

I could not refuse so noble a person and my archdeacon. Therefore I ordered the cleric Natalis to go with him and obey him in all things as he would obey me. Natalis reluctantly agreed, fearing Burchard’s character, whose avarice he knew well.

Natalis and I had entered into a most secret pact: whichever of us died first should, if possible, return to the other within thirty days, causing no terror by his appearance but gently warning him and assuring him concerning his condition.

When they were already near Rome, one day Burchard and the cleric Natalis were reckoning the daily expenses. From a large sum Burchard exacted an account, coin by coin and obol by obol, of where and for what uses they had gone. Natalis, unused to rendering such minute accounts to me, since I trusted him as I trusted myself, became angry at the nobleman’s most sordid thriftiness. When he failed in giving the account, he commended himself to demons—horrible even to hear!

That same day, as Burchard and Natalis were crossing some water, Natalis was drowned. On the next following night, as I lay awake resting in my bed, with a lamp shining before me because I have always been accustomed to dread darkness at night, behold: the cleric Natalis stood before me, wearing a rain-cloak, as it seemed to me, of a most beautiful leaden-grey colour.

I was not at all frightened, recognized him perfectly, and, as though rejoicing at his swift return from beyond the Alps, began to say: “Natalis, welcome. Has the archdeacon returned already?”

“No, lord,” he replied, “but I have returned alone according to our agreement. For I am dead. Do not be afraid; I shall cause you no fear. But I beg you to help me, for I am in great torments.”

“Why?” I asked. “You lived honourably enough with me.”

“Lord,” he said, “that is true. I would indeed be well, had I not today been overtaken by sudden anger and commended myself to demons. I ask you to warn everyone you can that they must never do this. Whoever commends himself to demons gives them power over himself, as I, most wretchedly, did. Therefore they had power immediately to drown me, and for this alone I am tormented. For I had confessed well all my sins and had fallen back into none of them.”

Then I said: “How can you have so beautiful a cloak if you are in torments?”

“Lord,” he replied, “this cloak, which seems to you so beautiful, is heavier and more burdensome to me than the tower of Parma would be if it were laid upon me. Its beauty is the hope of pardon that I possess because of the confession I made—provided help is given to me.”

I said: “Certainly I shall help you as much as I can; but I beg you to tell me whether you have been assigned to that company which they call Hellequin’s.”

“No, lord,” he said. “That company no longer travels, but recently ceased to go because it completed its penance. The common people corruptly call it Hellequin for Karlequin. For there was a Charles V who performed a long penance for his sins and was at last recently liberated through the intercession of blessed Dionysius. But I beg you, have mercy upon me.”

Saying this with tears, he vanished.

## Chapter XII. Another example on the same subject

I have said this in order to make clear from what source the Virgilian error concerning deceased souls arose: he calls them heroes and says that after death they have the same care for horses, chariots, and arms as they had while living.

My uncle Hellebaud, chamberlain of the late Henry, archbishop of Reims, used to report a most certain example concerning this matter. He said: “My lord the archbishop was sending me to Arras. When, around noon, we had approached a certain wood, my servant, who rode ahead of me quickly to prepare lodging for me, heard a great tumult in the wood: as though there were many varied neighings of horses, clashing of arms, and voices of a multitude rushing violently into battle.

“Terrified, he and his horse immediately returned to me. When I asked him why he had come back, he answered: ‘My horse cannot be compelled by stick or even by spurs to go forward. I too am so frightened that I do not dare proceed at all. For I have seen and heard marvellous things. This wood is full of the souls of the dead and demons. I heard them cry out and say: “We already have the provost of Arca; shortly we shall have the archbishop of Reims.”’

“To this I replied: ‘Let us make the sign of the cross upon our foreheads and go forward securely.’ When I proceeded and came to the wood, the shades had already gone on; yet I heard certain confused voices, clashing arms, and the neighing of horses. But I could neither see the shades nor understand the voices.

“When we returned, we found the archbishop already at the point of death, and he did not survive fifteen days after those voices. Hence it is conjectured that he was carried off by those spirits by whom he had been heard to be about to be carried off.”

From this it is apparent what kind of horses those are on which the souls of the dead are sometimes seen riding. They are demons transformed into horses; their riders are most wretched souls burdened with sins as though with arms and shields—though in truth disfigured and burdened by their own crimes. As the prophet says: “They went down to hell with their weapons” (Ezek. 32)—that is, with their members, which they made weapons of iniquity for sin, refusing to make them weapons of righteousness for God.

Now it is certain that the horse is a proud and stubborn animal, desirous of contention and war, ardent for mating, and exceedingly powerful in lust. Therefore demons transformed into horses signify that their riders delighted in crimes of this kind.

## Chapter XIII. Further on the same subject
Such was the horse which a charcoal-burner showed to a certain count of Nevers. This charcoal-burner was a poor man in worldly terms, but rich in God, devout and God-fearing. For this reason he was on familiar terms with the aforesaid count. One night, as he was keeping watch and carefully tending his blazing charcoal-pit, behold, a certain naked woman appeared running, and after her a horseman rode swiftly upon a black horse, with sword drawn, in order to seize the fleeing woman. As she fled around the pit, he caught her, pierced her with his sword, and she became as if dead. He threw her into the fire and, having burned her, drew her out again; and [Col. 0734B] placed her before him upon the horse and departed. This vision was shown to him on many nights.

One day, therefore, as he was exceedingly troubled while thinking of this vision, which recurred so often, the count met him as he went thus absorbed and sorrowful. Astonished, the count drew him aside and privately asked what troubled him, saying: “If anyone has wronged you or done you some harm, do not hide it from me; for I shall avenge you well. If you are in need, I shall assist you.” He replied: “I need nothing and complain of no one; but I have seen this and this so many times—and would that you yourselves had seen it.” “Certainly,” the count said to him, “I shall go with you and see this great vision.”

Accordingly, the count confessed all his sins, changed his clothing, took the charcoal-burner with him, and went alone with him into [Col. 0734C] the wood. As they kept watch about midnight, they heard someone sounding a trumpet loudly, and he made the sign of the cross over himself. And behold, that wretched woman came running naked, as before, and began to flee around the pit. The horseman pursued and seized her, killed her with his sword, threw her into the fire, and drew her out again. When he had placed her before him upon the horse and was about to flee, the count adjured him in the name of the Lord to stop and tell him who he was and why he did this.

Then he halted and said: “I am that knight of yours; and this is that noblewoman, the wife of the knight whom she killed for love of me, so that she might enjoy my intercourse more freely and more often. We both died in this sin—except that, alas, too late, we repented in that very death. Now [Col. 0734D] she suffers such a punishment that every night she is killed and burned by me. For she suffers in the stroke of the sword with which I strike her such pain as no one has ever suffered in death, and far greater pain in the burning.”

To this the count said: “Who is that horse upon which you ride?”

“A certain devil,” he replied, “who torments us with unspeakable affliction.”

“Could anyone help you?”

“He could,” he replied, “if you caused prayers to be offered for us in all the congregations subject to you, masses to be celebrated by priests, and psalms to be sung by clerics.”

Such was the horse upon which that unhappy man of Mâcon mounted, concerning whom Peter, Abbot of Cluny, relates in the *Book of Miracles* that, when [Col. 0735A] one day of festival he was sitting in his own palace at Mâcon, attended by many knights of different ranks, suddenly an unknown man riding on horseback entered through the palace door. Before all who saw and wondered, he came up to him, saying that he wished to speak with him and commanding him to rise and follow him. Unable to resist the invisible power, the man rose and went as far as the door of the house. There he found a horse ready, which he was immediately commanded to mount. [Col. 0736A] The man who had come for him took its reins and began to carry him at the swiftest pace through the air, in the sight of all. The unhappy man cried out miserably, “Help, citizens, help!” and stirred the whole city. All saw him flying through the air as long as their natural eyesight could follow him; and thus, at last withdrawn from human sight, he became an eternal companion of demons.

## ON THE GOOD GOVERNMENT OF A PRINCE

[Col. 0735]

## CHAPTER XIV. On appointing a king, and first on his character

[Col. 0735B]

“You shall appoint as king,” he says (Deut. XVII), “him whom the Lord your God shall choose from among your brethren.” The question is asked why the people displeased God when, under Samuel, they desired that a king should be made for them, although this is found to have been permitted. The answer is that it displeased Him because He had not commanded that this be done, but allowed them to do it when they desired it.

“And when he has been appointed, he shall not multiply horses for himself,” so as to burden his subjects by their number. To multiply horses is to gather more than necessity requires, for the sake of vain glory or some other error. Much less, therefore, may he multiply dogs, birds of prey, savage beasts, or whatever monstrosities of nature there may be. There was no need for the law to mention actors and mimes, buffoons and procurers, prostitutes, and such monstrous specimens of humankind, [Col. 0735C] whom a prince ought rather to expel than to foster.

It follows: “Nor shall he lead the people back into Egypt”—that is, he must not corrupt his inferiors by his example. For:

> The world takes its pattern from the king;  
> nor can decrees so bend  
> human minds as can the ruler’s life.  
> The fickle crowd always changes with its prince.

It follows: “Nor shall he have many wives, who may entice away his soul.” Although, in the cases of Abraham and Jacob, one man was permitted to have several wives, for the sake of producing offspring and enlarging the faithful people, among kings it is perpetually established that one woman should belong to one man. Much less, therefore, may he commit fornication, adultery, [Col. 0735D] or any sexual outrage. For how shall he punish these crimes in others when he is himself subject to them?

It follows: “Nor shall he possess immense weights of gold and silver.” What then are those to say who, despite the Lord’s prohibition, heap up gold and silver for themselves, making profit from calumny and seeking exceptional abundance out of the poverty of many, riches out of plunder, and blessedness out of calamity? For he shall not possess riches which he owns in another’s name; and fiscal possessions, which he acknowledges to be public, were private for himself. Nor is it strange that a king may not have private fiscal possessions, since he himself does not belong to himself, but to his subjects.

## CHAPTER XV. On his learning and wisdom

[Col. 0736B]

“And after he has sat,” he says (Deut. XVII), “upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write out for himself in a book the Deuteronomy of this law.” Therefore a prince ought not to be ignorant of law, even though he enjoys many privileges; nor is he permitted, under the pretext of military service, to be ignorant of the law of God. Indeed, the most Christian prince himself decrees in his laws: “Let not the prince disdain to imitate the sacred canons. For every enactment of a prince is useless if it is not conformed to ecclesiastical discipline.”

It follows: “And he shall have it with him and shall read it all the days of his life.” Knowledge of letters is therefore necessary to a prince, who is commanded to read the law of God every day. For any day on which he has not read the law is not for him a day of life, but a day of death. Hence, in a letter which the king of the Romans is recorded to have sent to the king of the Franks, he urges him to have his children instructed in the liberal [Col. 0736C] arts; and among other things he added: “An unlettered king is like a crowned ass.” But if he happens to be unlettered, he must at least be governed by the counsel of learned men.

Hence a copy of the law is commanded to be obtained from the priests of the Levitical tribe—that is, from Catholic and learned men. For Plato, as Boethius testifies, said that commonwealths would be happy if either wise men ruled them or their rulers devoted themselves to wisdom. For Wisdom herself says: “By me kings reign, and the makers of laws decree what is just” (Prov. VIII). The Gentiles worshipped wisdom as a god, without whose divine prompting they believed nothing should be done. Thus the ancient philosophers decreed that an image of Wisdom should be painted before the doors of all temples, with this inscription:

[Col. 0736D]

> Practice begot me, memory gave me birth;  
> the Greeks call me *Sophia*, you call me Wisdom.

They also commanded this to be written:

> I hate men idle in work and in philosophical knowledge.

Wisdom is the chief knowledge of divine and human things, and of things to be done and avoided; and to devote oneself to it is to practise philosophy.

Concerning his humility and piety it follows: “Let not his heart be lifted up in pride above his brethren.” What is especially necessary is repeatedly emphasized; for humility never seems sufficiently commended to princes, because it is most difficult for a degree of honour not to produce swelling in the mind of the one who presides. Pride cast Tarquin from his kingdom.

Roman law, however, provides that the man who administers justice should make himself readily accessible, while not allowing himself to be despised. Princes, like physicians, should never employ severe remedies except when the desired health is despaired of through the benefit of milder ones. Hence Lucius says: “A prince ought not to be savage in character, but should follow more moderate counsels” [Note: [Col. 0737D] Seneca.]; and they should take the place of physicians, who treat diseases—now by depletion in those who are overfull, now by nourishment in those who are empty—and who relieve pain now by cautery, now by poultices.

If cithara-players and other musicians take great care to correct the fault of a discordant string and restore harmony with the others, with what solicitude must a prince govern [Col. 0737B] so as to make his subjects, as it were, of one mind and dwelling in one house with one disposition? It is certainly safer to slacken strings too much than to stretch them too tightly; for the tightening of slack strings is restored by the craftsman’s skill, whereas a string once broken is repaired by no skill.

> Let the prince be slow to punish, swift to reward;  
> and let him grieve whenever he is compelled to be stern.  
> —OVID

The one belongs to justice, the other to piety. Of these Solomon says: “Let not mercy and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck, and write them upon the tablets of your heart. And you shall find favour and good instruction before God and men” (Prov. III). Favour, indeed, belongs to mercy, and discipline to justice. He who lacks the former is hateful to all; he who lacks the latter is contemptible to all.

Plutarch also wrote a book *On the Moderation of Magistrates*. When magistrates oppress their subjects, Plato says, “it is as though the head of a body should swell so that it cannot be borne by the limbs, either at all or without immense distress.” Again: “When power rages against subjects, it is as though a guardian persecuted his ward, or as though you cut down with your own sword the man who gave you that sword for his defence.” Hence Claudian:

> Be merciful above all; for though we are surpassed in every  
> office, mercy alone makes us equal to the gods.  
> Though you rule widely over the farthest Indians,  
> though the Mede, the soft Arab, and the Seres worship you,  
> if you fear, if you desire petty things, if anger carries you away,  
> [Col. 0737D] you will bear the yoke of slavery and endure  
> unjust laws within yourself. Then you will hold every right  
> when you can be king of yourself. Use tends more readily  
> toward worse things, and licence urges luxury;  
> it favours unbridled passions. Then it is harder to live chastely  
> when Venus is at hand; then anger is restrained with greater difficulty  
> when punishment lies open. But check these impulses.  
> Let not what is permitted to you, but what it would be fitting  
> to have done, occur to you; and let regard for honourable conduct  
> subdue your mind.

## CHAPTER XVI. On his equity

It follows: “Nor shall he turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deut. XVII). To turn aside to the right is to wish that what is right should be attributed not to God’s grace, but to oneself. Or, to turn aside to the right or to the left [Col. 0738A] is to sin through the truth of those things which are shunned. Again, to turn aside to the right is to pursue virtues themselves with excessive intensity, and to exceed, in works of virtue—which consists in measure—the proper measure. Hence Juvenal:

> The wise man will bear the name of madman, the just man that of unjust,  
> if he pursues virtue itself beyond what is enough.

And the philosopher says: “Beware of excess; for if this very caution abandons moderation, by that very fact it departs from virtue.” All intensity is inimical to health; every excess is blameworthy; and excessive familiarity even with good things is very bad. Hence Solomon says: “Do not be excessively just” (Eccles. VII). What good, then, is too much, if the queen of virtues harms by her own excess? Excessive humility likewise is a very great part of pride.

Again, he turns aside to the left who is too prone to vengeance in punishing the faults of subjects; but to the right, he who indulges gentleness too greatly. Again: “Let him not turn aside to the right or left.” For equity, to which a judge owes obedience, knows neither the right hand of love nor the left hand of hatred. To carry it out justly is to seek nothing but justice—neither more harshly than is equitable, nor too remissly, in asserting or enforcing justice.

Courtiers may nevertheless accept gifts freely, provided they do not extort them shamelessly. Whoever asks sets aside shame and, indeed, buys twice over; for he sells his modesty for the price of the thing or of the expectation. But a gift offered by the devotion of generosity, not extorted by the shamelessness of one who asks, bears no mark of an unjust request. Yet he must not [Col. 0738C] accept the gifts of wicked men, lest, if he does not favour them after accepting a gift, he be ungrateful; or, if he does favour them, be judged unjust. Account must be taken both of the cause and of the person, so that a gift be received neither from a shameful source nor shamefully. For gifts often shine or become sordid by the hand, the cause, the time, the place, or the manner.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the reward of royal justice in the king himself and in his heir

It follows: “That he and his son may reign for a long time over Israel” (Deut. XVII). For the succession of children is often prolonged because of the virtue of their parents, and the prosperity of successors is cut short through the wickedness of their predecessors, according to the saying: “But the unjust shall perish together; the remnant of the impious shall perish” (Ps. XXXVI). [Col. 0738D] Again: “The kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, wrongs, insults, and various deceits.”

Injustice, according to the Stoics, is a disposition of mind that banishes equity from the region of morals. Justice is not to harm and, from the duty of humanity, to prevent those who harm. To harm is not to prevent those doing injury. Injustice is insult when a manifest act of injury follows the swelling of the mind. Deceit, as Aquilius defines it, occurs when one thing is done and another pretended; it is wicked when it is done with the intention of harming, and harms as though by ambush. Deceit, therefore, because it arises from fear, is opposed to courage; but insult to prudence, [Col. 0739A] which says to itself: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. X). Temperance does not admit injury, because it is unwilling to inflict upon another what it would not wish another to inflict upon itself. Justice excludes injustice by doing to others what it would wish done to itself in a good and honourable manner.

As for the addition “various,” I think it must be referred generally to all these things: not only to the various kinds of vices, but also to different persons and to all the ways in which these vices are committed by anyone whatsoever. For the prince is answerable for all, and is even regarded as author of all; because, since he can correct everything, he rightly shares in those things which he refused, though able, to amend. For, since power is public, it drains the strength of all [reading uncertain: *vites*]; and, lest it fail in itself, it must provide for the safety of all the members.

But just as [Col. 0739B] “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI) if they depart from justice, so they shall enjoy the rewards of justice more abundantly if they have exercised power rightly; and in the life to come they shall possess glory over their subjects in proportion to the virtue by which they surpassed them amid great licence to sin. Hence it is said: “He was able to transgress, and did not transgress” (Ecclus. XXXI). For even when princes refrain from wrongs, this is counted to them as justice; their ability to sin is material for merit. To turn away from evil is a great thing in them, even if they do great good, provided they do not destroy their subjects through indulgence.

Therefore a son succeeds his father if he imitates his father’s justice. But charity is by no means preserved when a father transfers to his children the love chiefly owed to country and parents, and filial affection alone drains the chamber of his fatherly breast. Yet today the vices of children are preferred to the safety of the commonwealth, although the people’s safety ought to be preferred before all children. For in the book *Regnum* Saul is covertly reproved because, in the matter of the vow concerning the day’s fast, he spared Jonathan contrary to the vow of religion itself, by whose violation the people fell (I Kings XIV). Eli likewise, although holy in himself, perished because he spared his sons (I Kings IV). And, not to mention others, how greatly did God the Father love the commonwealth, who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all?

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the four things necessary to a prince, and the body of the commonwealth

[Col. 0739D]

Plutarch strives to impress four things upon princes: reverence for God, cultivation of oneself, discipline of officials and mastery of the passions, and protection of subjects. For he elegantly described what a prince ought to be in that very beautiful book entitled *The Education of Trajan*, the beginning of which we have given above in its proper place.

“Finally,” he says, “you will conduct everything most rightly if you do not depart from yourself. If you first order yourself toward virtue, all things will proceed rightly. For I have excluded from you the greater powers of the political constitution [reading uncertain: *exclusi*]; if you obey him, you have Plutarch as an author for your way of life. Otherwise I call this present letter as witness that, with Plutarch as your authority, you are proceeding to the ruin [Col. 0740A] of the empire.”

The chapters of the political constitution follow afterwards. A commonwealth, then, according to Plutarch, is a kind of body animated by the benefit of divine gift, guided by the will of highest equity, and governed by a certain moderation of reason. Those things which pertain to religion occupy the place of the soul. The prince is the head of this body, a man subject to God and to those who perform God’s offices on earth. The senate occupies the place of the heart. Judges and governors of provinces claim for themselves the offices of eyes, ears, and tongue. Officials and soldiers are fitted to the hands. Those who always attend the prince are likened to the sides. Quaestors and record-keepers—not those who preside over prisons, but the companions responsible for private affairs—bear the image of the belly and intestines. Farmers are the feet. Thus, among these four are the things Plutarch seeks to impress upon princes: reverence for God, and the other matters mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XIX. On reverence for God and the cultivation of oneself

God wonderfully infuses understanding of Himself by withdrawing it, and withdraws it by infusing it. For He shines forth in many ways and manifoldly. He is wonderful in majesty, venerable in wisdom, lovable in goodness. This is the threefold cord between Creator and creature, which is not easily broken: that He may be feared, honoured, and loved.

He is worshipped in two ways: by the affection of the mind and by outward bodily observance. Reverence outwardly displayed consists either in persons or in things. In persons it arises from nature, office, character, condition, or fortune. Nature includes parents, kinsmen, and relatives by marriage. Office is the obligation to perform what, according to institutions or customs, each person must do; and among such duties some pertain to the public and others to each person’s own station. For some offices are called public and others private. Private offices are as numerous as persons. Public offices derive either from divine or from human law. To a public office reverence is owed in proportion to the eminence of each magistracy.

Character is a disposition of mind from which the continual practice of individual actions flows. It embraces virtues and vices alike. Hence we speak of good and bad character; we call persons well-behaved or compliant from the good, ill-tempered from the bad. Condition is the accidental state of a person, in which one lives either amid adversity or prosperity.

In those who administer divine laws, God is especially either honoured or despised, since He regards their honour and contempt as His own, saying: “He who despises you despises me, and he who receives you receives me” (Luke X). Reverence consisting in things is found either in bodily objects, buildings and holy places, sacrifices, or spiritual things, such as the laws belonging to sacred matters. To violate these is sacrilege, to be expiated by death. To overthrow the immunities of sacred things is to rise up against God.

The cultivation of oneself consists especially in temperance. They relate that Marcus Cato was content with the same wine as the rowers. Gaius Curius, conqueror of the Sabines, unwilling to have his lands enlarged by decree of the senate, was content with the portion of an ordinary citizen, saying that he was a bad citizen for whom what sufficed the other citizens was not enough.

## CHAPTER XX. On the discipline of officials

It follows concerning authority and the discipline of officials. Nothing is more destructive than the unjust adviser of a rich man. Hence in Proverbs: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV). Care must therefore be taken that those in authority do not lack advisers, and that they do not desire the possessions of others too immoderately. Nothing is more wicked than to love money, and so forth.

This principle must be observed not only in the heart—that is, in the adviser—but also in [Col. 0741B] the belly and intestines of the commonwealth—that is, in quaestors and record-keepers. It must also be observed in the sides, that is, in those who always attend the prince. For character is changed by companionship: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII), and a grape, seen or touched, takes its dark colour from another grape (Juv.).

Thus certain legates of the Apostolic See rage in the provinces as though Satan had gone forth from the presence of the Lord to scourge the Church: acceptors of persons and, as it were, hammers against good men. Hence Juvenal:

> Every vice of the mind has in itself a crime so much more conspicuous  
> as the person who sins is held to be greater.

The name and office of bishops would be venerable if fulfilled with as much solicitude as it is sometimes sought with ambition; and they would be loved as fathers, feared as lords, and revered as saints, if they spared exactions, cast out of their minds everything arising from calumny, and did not regard every profit as piety.

In the households of prelates and princes, everything today is for sale. In vain, among courtiers, do you trust in the witness of conscience, the grace of character, or a torrent of eloquence unless money intervenes.

> Though you come attended by the Muses, Homer,  
> if you bring nothing, Homer, you will go out. 

I myself believe that I have seen doorkeepers harsher than Cerberus. Yet among the dead, as they say, there is only one Cerberus. But as many side-entrances as there are in courts, so many Cerberuses there are. For the whole household either bites or barks. [Col. 0741D] It is an old proverb: “An empty hand makes a rash petition.”

Even among advocates, silence itself is for sale. Perhaps they learned this from Demosthenes, who asked Aristodium, a producer of plays, what fee he had received to act, and he answered, “A talent.” “But I,” Demosthenes said, “received more to keep silent.” The tongue of legal pleaders is ruinous unless, as the saying goes, you bind it with silver cords. Nothing, says Seneca, is more needy than mercy that is for sale. It is wholly unjust to sell either mercy or justice.

But the law says: “You shall execute what is just justly” (Deut. XVI). The Julian law concerning extortion also binds anyone who, having some authority to judge [Col. 0742A] or determine, receives money in order that he may do more or less than his office requires. These are the words of the law. Again, all assessors and judges must keep their hands from money and patronage. They must not think another person’s lawsuit their own prey. A plebiscite likewise provides that no governor may accept a gift or present, except food or drink, and that indeed only when offered during the immediately following days; nor may guest-gifts be extended to the value of presents.

Concerning such gifts, an epistle of the Emperor Severus says: “It is an old proverb: neither everything, nor always, nor from everyone. For to receive from no one at all is very inhumane; to receive indiscriminately is very base; to receive in every circumstance is very avaricious.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On public tax-collectors and their violence

[Col. 0742B]

Lawrence, bishop of Milan, speaks excellently about such men when he describes public tax-collectors:

“A tax-collector is the head of robbery, the law of violence, a shameless plunderer, a physician of destruction, more savage than thieves. For a thief sins in fear, but this man confidently. A thief fears the snares of the law; this man calls whatever he does ‘law.’ Who is more unjust than the man who condemns justice by the word of justice, and with the arms of innocence despoils, wounds, and kills the innocent? He destroys law by law; and while he presses others toward the law, he casts them down from the law.

“Moreover, the company of tax-collectors, from the greatest to the least, occupies itself with extortion rather than justice. They rage so against the people that what one leaves behind, the others do not fail to take away—as though they had been established for the purpose that the locust’s remainder might be eaten by the caterpillar. Unless you comply in everything with Caesar’s official, you oppose Caesar. Whatever he dictates, unless it is so and stands so, is an offence against the king’s person and against the crown. Whatever he says has force as though it were found in the official records. And though, in other circumstances and under the moderation of blameless self-defence, it is lawful to repel force by force, one may not even murmur against officials who extort, plunder, and torture.”

All these things, however, redound to the prince. Individuals are answerable for individual matters; upon the prince rest all burdens together. A prince is said to be released from the bonds of laws not because injustice is permitted to him, but because he ought to be one who cultivates equity not through fear of punishment but through love of justice. For in public affairs he may will nothing except what law or equity [Col. 0742D] persuades, or what the reason of common utility induces.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the equity of judgment

Equity in law, as experts maintain, is the fitting relation of things, which makes all things equal by reason and requires equal laws in equal cases. Law is its interpreter. Whatever is equitable, however, is just only if it is voluntary.

In no matter do the powers of this age offend so greatly as in judgments, failing to heed what is written: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. VII). And likewise the text quoted above: “You shall execute what is just justly” (Deut. XVI): that is, without respect of persons or gifts, as soon as the case is clear to you, you shall deliver a just sentence for each side.

When a case is doubtful, judgment must be deferred, because hasty judgments bring repentance. Therefore, if danger cannot be avoided in judging, nothing is more useful than delay. But if the interest of one or the other litigant is endangered and the difficulty of the matter allows no delay, it is most unjust to defer judgment.

The law itself provides that the awe-inspiring writings of the holy Gospels be laid before the judge’s seat, and remain there from beginning to end, not to be removed until the sentence has been pronounced, so that the whole extent of the court may be filled with the presence of God Himself, instilling fear and reverence for the sacred Scriptures in all, and driving every iniquity from the investigation of truth.

[Col. 0743B] As it is said in the second book of the Code, the laws incline more readily to defence than to attack, and are more easily drawn toward an exception than toward an action. Hence, while not all are admitted to make an accusation, all are admitted to a defence—unless someone is to be condemned in absence.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the selection of soldiers and their duty

We have considered the other members of the commonwealth; now let us consider the soldiers, who are called its hands. According to Vegetius Renatus, there is no one who ought to know better things than a prince. A Christian prince should choose soldiers more for faith and character than for strength. Yet today our soldiers go to war white-clad as though to a wedding. In camp their talk is of banquets; at a banquet, of arms.

Two things make a soldier, whether bodily or spiritual: selection and the oath. Long peace selects a soldier less carefully. Under the consulship of Lucius Flaccus and Gaius Varro, soldiers were first made by an oath. Previously they had merely been required to take the military oath by the tribunes.

According to the testimony of Vegetius, the formula of the oath is this: soldiers swear by God, by His Christ, by the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the prince—which, after God, ought to be loved and revered by the human race—that they will courageously do everything the prince commands, never desert military service, and never refuse death for the commonwealth in whose army they have enrolled.

Cato does not call a man a soldier unless he has already been consecrated to military service by the oath. Therefore a soldier belongs both to labour and to honour. “No one takes honour to himself unless he is called by the Lord” (Heb. V). He who, not being selected, thrusts himself into military service calls down upon himself the sword which he usurps through his own rashness.

The purpose of ordered military service is to protect the Church, attack unbelief, venerate the priesthood, repel wrongs against the poor, pacify the province, and—as the formula of the oath teaches—shed blood for brethren. Yet I wonder how a prince can trust men whom he sees not keeping faith owed to their God, to whom, besides other obligations, they are bound by the military oath. He who makes the first pledge void will by no means keep the second.

Finally, the consecration of a soldier is this. [Col. 0744A] It is a solemn custom that, on the day when someone is adorned with the military belt, he should solemnly enter a church and, placing his sword upon the altar and offering it—as though making a public profession—devote himself to the service of the altar and promise God the continual service of the sword, namely of his own office. They may therefore do very much for the Church, but nothing against the Church. For in their profession they do either more, or no less, than bishops and abbots who offer a written schedule of profession.

In certain places it is also customary that a soldier to be consecrated on the following day spend the entire preceding night awake in prayers, having no permission either to lie down or sit, unless perhaps the necessity of sudden illness compels it, but praying throughout the night while standing.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That they ought to obey the prince, but God more

[Col. 0744B]

First homage is owed to God, to whom man belongs by creation and redemption. The second is owed to a human being, yet with God’s lordship safeguarded, for God requires innocence from all His human beings. No one, therefore, owes faith to anyone else at the risk of innocence: neither a monk to an abbot, nor a son to a father, a slave to his master, nor a wife to her husband.

It is therefore the prince’s first duty to ensure that his soldier does not lose innocence in defending the commonwealth; without innocence, the commonwealth cannot be safe. For only that prince is good and that judge incorruptible whose judgment, through constant contemplation, is an image of equity. He is the public defender and servant of equity, and he bears a public person in this: that he corrects the wrongs [Col. 0744C] and losses of all, and punishes all crimes with impartial equity. His office is to oppose especially those who are able to do the greatest good and who desire to do harm.

Hence in Sacred Scripture he is called “the sword of the dove” (Jer. XLVI), because he contends without gall, strikes without anger, and receives no bitterness when he fights. For, as Cicero, the outstanding orator, says: “As the law pursues faults without hatred of persons, so ought the prince to act.” David was called a man of blood not because of his wars, as Augustine says, but because of Uriah. For neither Samuel nor Elijah nor Phinehas was called a man of blood, although each of them shed blood.

According to the Stoics, moreover, an executioner is aptly called a *lictor*, as though a “striker of the law,” because it belongs to his office to strike the person whom the law judges should be struck. Hence in ancient times, to the man by whose hand a blameless judge punished the guilty, as the sword hung over him, it was said: “Obey the judgment of the law,” or “Fulfil the law,” so that even in this way the gentleness of the words might lessen the sorrow of punishing the offender.

Since, therefore, soldiers are the hands of the body of public authority, that prince’s hands are full of blood whose officials and soldiers either shed the blood of innocents or oppress the innocent. The prayer of such a prince is never to be heard; his alms are never to be accepted by God.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the mutual affection of prince and subjects

The last of the things which Plutarch commands a [Col. 0745A] prince to possess is love for his subjects. Codrus, king of the Athenians, gave himself over to death for the victory of his people. For, having changed his kingly clothing and gathered brushwood, he entered the enemy camp and was killed by a soldier whom he had easily provoked in a quarrel. Hence also that poetic line:

> . . . . . . . and the quarrels of Codrus.  
> —VIRGIL
Decius, commander of the Romans, is famously said to have devoted himself to death for his armies. Julius Caesar too used to say: “A commander who does not strive to be dear to his soldiers does not know how to love a soldier; he does not know what the humility of a commander ought to be in the army and against the enemy.” He also threw his baker into chains because he had set before him at table better bread than that given to the other soldiers [Col. 0745B]. When Alexander saw one of his Macedonian soldiers, worn out by age and numbed by excessive cold, while he himself was sitting on a raised seat near the fire, he immediately stepped down and placed the body, doubled up by cold, upon his own seat. When Plato saw Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, surrounded by guards for the protection of his person, he said: “What great evil have you done, that you must needs be guarded by so many guards?” [Col. 0746A]

For a prince ought so to win the affections of all by acts of service that every subject, when dangers threaten him, will offer his own head in his behalf. Thus too, when nature presses, the other members are accustomed to interpose themselves for the head. Hence Claudian:

> Not watches nor weapons standing around  
> Protect as love does: you will not compel a man to be loved.  
> This mutual loyalty, this single-hearted favour, bestows it.

Thus far let what has been said suffice concerning the training of kings and princes: how they ought to conduct themselves, whether at home or in war, according not only to divine laws but also to human ones, which have force only insofar as they do not depart from the divine [Col. 0746B]. Otherwise the statement written in the law is false: “What pleases the prince has the force of law.” For some believe that no laws are to be preferred to civil laws; but Anacharsis the Scythian compared these to spiders’ webs, which catch flies and gnats but let larger flying creatures pass through.

## Helinand’s Letter to Walter the Clerk

Written in the name of William, brother of the same Walter. It is entitled: *The Book of the Restoration of the Fallen.*

[Col. 0745]

[Col. 0745C] Because of lamentations and woe, I send you nothing of song. [Note: [Col. 0745] This alludes to the book in which were “lamentations, song, and woe,” in Ezekiel 2.] For song is owed to those for whom it is good to confess to the Lord and sing praise to the name of the Most High. Song is owed to those in whose hearts the Lord is sung, with whose spirit psalmody is made, whose mind rejoices; whose activity makes music for Christ upon the harp, whose thought plays the organ, whose prayer plays the psaltery, and whose devotion plays the lyre. For you have nothing to do with song. You are not able to sing the Lord’s song in a strange land. You have nothing to do with *ave*—“hail”—who do not change the name of Eve; nothing to do with *salve*—“be well”—who do not keep what has been entrusted to you, while you do not keep the commandments; while you do not prepare yourself for judgment, nor procure the aid of your Advocate, Christ, but prepare a second cross for your Saviour and for yourself the torment of a second death. You have nothing to do with *vale*—“farewell”—who live only badly [Col. 0745D], who do not seek to be well because you refuse to repent.

Therefore, my soul, send and send again lamentations and woes to my brother, who waits and waits again: a little in the world, excessively in sin. For, having surveyed with every care the entire mass of the present subject, I could find nothing to send in place of song; but, full of bitterness and full of anxiety, what I have written, I have written. A greeting of health sent to one who is not healthy is trifling; sent to one unwilling, it is superfluous. For what good is any greeting of health directed to one to whom [Col. 0746C] no salvation is welcome? Clearly, one is greeted in vain by one who does not desire salvation.

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep abundantly for my brother’s deserved ruin?” (Jer. 9.) You are righteous, O Lord, even if I dispute with you. Yet I shall speak justly to you—not as disputing with you, but as reckoning with you what I calculate within myself and charge to my brother. For my brother still begs for the husks of swine in that country where famine arises but does not die, where want begins but does not end; nor does the unhappy man remember how many loaves not merely the sons but even the hired servants have in abundance in his father’s house (Luke 15).

Yet he is neither shaken by grief nor confounded by shame that he perish through hunger, burn with thirst [Col. 0746D], be wearied by labour, and be crushed by slavery. O how easily he would pass beyond all these things! With only two steps he would leap back from so grievous an exile: by the first he would return to himself; by the second he would turn to you, Father. But you commanded me to love not only him, but every neighbour, as myself. And who is nearer to me than my brother? Nowhere am I wholly present where my brother is absent, that is, one half of my soul. Do you not, Lord, command that you be loved with the whole soul? How then will the whole soul love you unless both its halves love you? For you are not well loved by halves.

Therefore, that I may love you wholly, grant, I pray, that both I and my brother may love you. If you will that I follow you, grant, I beseech you, that my brother follow too; for I cannot follow you by halves. That you may make me entirely whole, make my brother whole also—you who made the whole man well on the Sabbath. Indeed, you do nothing by halves, but whatever you do, you complete. Otherwise that could not be said of your works: that they were all very good. And in Deuteronomy: “The works of God are perfect” (Deut. 32), etc.

“Because of lamentation and woe.” Lamentation concerns the present; song and woe, the future. I set woe before you that you might flee from it; I set lamentations before you that you might flee to them [Col. 0747B].
