But I did not set forth song, so that, with every memory of joyful things removed, you might set your heart upon no passing beauty; rather, as long as you know that you sit by the rivers of Babylon, you might weep, lament, groan, hang your instruments upon its willows (Ps. 136), and give yourself wholly, utterly, to the very marrow, over to grief. No mention of song shall be made to you until you fulfil the command: “Go out from Babylon; flee from the Chaldeans.”

But now I shall speak to you. Lamentation itself, namely that which has hitherto spoken on your behalf: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14)—you who rejoiced in the Lord with the morning stars, when, in the assembly of novices, in the weeping of monks, in the fear of converts, in the sight of angels, you sang psalms to the Most High. How did that drawing tail of the dragon, with its third part of the stars, draw you also along with it—you to whom God had given the light of wisdom, the splendour of knowledge, and the radiance of understanding, so that you might shine, if you wished, with the steadfast stars through everlasting ages? [Col. 0747C]

I do not spare you, dearest brother, so that God may spare both me and you. You have fallen: “Will not he who has fallen add to it that he may rise again?” (Isa. 24.) “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. 24), that is, as often as he falls, so often he rises. You who fall throughout the whole day and fall again every day—why do you not rise even on one day?

But as for your accusing our order of intolerable harshness, the fault assuredly belongs not to the order but to its accuser. For it is not so harsh as to be inaccessible [Col. 0747D], or unbearable contrary to nature; otherwise it would not be an order. But you are unstable and enervated. Moreover, what is more in accordance with nature than to live in an ordered fashion? Yet no life is more ordered than ours. There all things are arranged in number, weight, and measure (Wis. 11). There food, rest, and sleep are granted in accordance with natural sufficiency. Fasts, labours, and vigils are imposed upon no one beyond his strength; all things are done in due measure.

For life is sustained by simple food and clothing, nature is nourished, and health preserved. Finally, what is more natural, what healthier, than the sort of food and drink for whose appetite nature alone is both cook and physician? Who cannot drive away hunger with wheaten bread and well-cooked legumes?

> A fasting stomach rarely disdains common fare.  
> —Horace, *Satires* II.2.38

“The satisfied soul will tread honeycomb underfoot, but to the hungry soul even bitter things will be sweet.” Seneca says: “What nature desires is reasonable; one labours for superfluities.” I pass over the fact that nothing is more effective for preserving health than maintaining sameness in food and drink. For diverse dishes have diverse natures. Every such diversity produces conflict among the humours, and every conflict of humours opposes health.

Hence one of our young men answered most elegantly and wisely when the bishop of Beauvais asked why he was healthier and more handsome in the cloister than he had been in the world. “Because,” he said, [Col. 0748B] “I live uniformly and fittingly. From the first I gain health; from the second, good looks. But in the world I lived as ugly as I did variously; from the first arises ugliness, even bodily ugliness, and from the second sickness.”

The bishop continued to inquire: “What, then, did you eat today?” “Enough,” he replied. “What yesterday?” “Likewise enough.” “I do not ask,” he said, “about the quantity, but the quality: what did you eat yesterday, and what today?” “Yesterday,” he said, “I ate peas and vegetables; today, vegetables and peas; tomorrow I shall eat peas with vegetables, and the day after tomorrow vegetables with peas.” See then with what pleasing circuit he brought the same statement round, displaying in various ways that he always used the same diet, which gives health and beauty to the body.

Thus every accusation of difficulty which you advanced against the order, and every excuse of impossibility which you offered on your own behalf, has been refuted [Col. 0748C]. For the order is not so difficult that it fails to receive the infirm, since it satisfies even them carefully and delicately; nor are you so infirm or weak that you are wholly unequal to bearing it, when I—both more infirm and weaker than you—do not fail. And, not to speak of myself, how many can I show you who have passed from a most luxurious life to this order, which you call very harsh and very difficult, and have not yet recoiled from it, although they are younger than you in age, more tender by nature, and weaker in strength?

And, to take one from so many thousands, I shall take one for you—a single man certainly sufficient as an example for all. He became a spectacle to angels and men by the lightness of the miracle, who before had been a spectacle to them by the miracle of his frivolity: for no stage, circus, theatre, amphitheatre, circular amphitheatre, forum, street, gymnasium, or arena resounded without him [Col. 0748D].

You know Helinand, if anyone knows the man—if indeed he is a man. For he was no more born for labour than a bird for flight (Job 7), going about the earth and walking through it, seeking whom he might devour (1 Pet. 5), whether by flattery or rebuke. Behold, he has been shut up in a cloister, he for whom the whole world once used to be not merely as a cloister but even as a prison. How then can you not do what he does? His change—the right hand of the Most High (Ps. 76)—has brought as much astonishment upon the world and shame upon the devil as it has brought honour to the Lord himself.

For he had not been so frivolous as frivolity itself. Hence so great a frivolity, changed so lightly, is thought by many to be nothing other than frivolity. Thus his manner of life, now in its fifth year, scarcely causes anyone to believe in its future continuance. Doubtless, the degree to which he gave proof in himself of inconstancy weakens the evidence now for the constancy that will persevere. Blush, therefore, most wretched man, that you do not at least follow this man who goes before you, though he is younger, more infirm, weaker, more delicate. For who, observing from what a state this man rose, could fail to rise?

[Col. 0749B] Therefore rise, and do not turn aside into words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins (Ps. 140), attributing to nature what belongs to an impure mind, to necessity what belongs to the will; making the order more difficult than it is, yourself softer than you ought to be, and weaker than you can be. For no one can fall into such infirmity that the rigour of the order, yielding in mercy and sympathizing in charity, cannot provide an appropriate remedy of consolation. If through infirmity he cannot fast, he will not only be permitted but even compelled to eat. If he is unequal to labour, rest will not fail him. If vigils weigh him down, sleep restores him. Are you infirm? Do not flee: you will not carry the order, but the order will carry you.

Yet many deceive others—and not so much deceive as are deceived—by faintness of heart, saying that they cannot do what they could do if they tried. They judge before they examine, and therefore fail at the first threshold; before the trumpet sounds, trembling seizes their limbs. Such faint-hearted people commonly say: “Today I fasted, and already my head aches. If, therefore, I fast tomorrow, I shall become frenzied, lethargic, melancholic, epileptic, mad, or possessed by a demon.” Clearly this does not follow:

> A weak beginning will be followed by better fortune.

Many things not attempted seem difficult at first approach, but practice makes them easy. Thus our infirm man says: “Today I fasted and therefore my head already aches.” You plainly lie—or rather, it is because you have fasted for only one day. For your head does not ache because you fasted even once, but because you are not accustomed to fasting [Col. 0749D]. Finally, how do you know whether this came upon you from fasting? Perhaps yesterday you ate or drank something immoderately that naturally weighs down the head. Therefore not everything is to be ascribed either to the difficulty of the commandments or to the impossibility of one’s powers.

Rise, then, brother. For to rise is not impossible, though it is difficult—as difficult as falling is easy. Aristotle says, “It is easier to destroy than to build.”

> …The descent to Avernus is easy, says the poet;  
> But to retrace one’s steps and escape to the upper air—  
> This is the task, this is the labour. …  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI

He did not say, “This is impossible,” but, “This,” he says, [Col. 0750A] “is the task, this the labour”: that is, it is possible, although difficult; possible if effort is applied, works are undertaken, and labour expended. Hasten, then, to rise, for if rising is difficult today, it will be more difficult tomorrow.

> He who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love* 94

Every length of time added before death is also added to the fall. The longer you lie, the deeper you fall. For lying there itself is falling. I grant that falling is human; but rising again is no less human, according to the saying: “Will not he who has fallen rise again?” (Ps. 40.) That is: can one who was able to fall not be able to rise? Therefore failure to rise must by no means be called human, but diabolical; the whole life of the devil is ruin.

We should therefore note a fourfold distinction here. There are four states: standing, falling, rising, and not rising. The two middle states belong to man. For man falls and rises; then falls again and rises again. But to stand without falling belongs to the angel alone; not to rise belongs to the devil alone. Therefore, he who stands and does not fall is an angel; he who falls and rises is a man; but he who falls and after falling does not rise—not because he cannot, but because he will not—is truly a devil, even if he is a man. Hence it was said of such a man: “One of you is a devil” (John 6). And it is said to human beings: “Let no temptation take you except a human one” (1 Cor. 10).

Here, clearly, diabolical temptation is excluded: namely, the threefold temptation above oneself, beneath oneself, and against oneself [Col. 0750C]. A person is tempted above himself when he exalts himself beyond himself. He is tempted below himself when he desires to live lower, more foully, and more basely than the dignity of his nature requires. Temptation against oneself is when someone knowingly sins, even unto death, and yet afterwards does not repent: either despairing, or hoping too little, or neither hoping nor despairing, but unable through unbelief either to hope or to fear—that is, neither believing that mercy will avail nor that damnation will harm, believing that neither will come to pass, but thinking that all judgment will fail, saying with Epicurus: “Nothing after death, and death itself is nothing.”

Above I had enumerated four stages of your calamity: namely, that you did not stand, that you fell, that you lie there, and that you do not rise. That you did not stand was due to frivolity; that you fell, to weakness; that you lie there, to pleasure; that you do not rise, to habit. Frivolity impels, weakness throws down, pleasure kills, habit buries. First you were a reed shaken by the wind; second, a leaf falling from a tree; third, you became a paralytic fastened to a bed. For what difference is there between a dead man and one always lying down? Fourth, you are Lazarus, four days dead, stinking in the tomb, wrapped in grave-cloths and buried.

You were a reed when you bent at the serpent’s lightest hiss. You were a leaf when, “the spirit having power” came up over you, you left your place. Paralysis is dissolution, and nothing dissolves a man more than pleasure [Col. 0751A]. By adding habit to these three stages—frivolity, weakness, and pleasure—you made yourself a four-days-dead man; you were buried and crushed by obstinacy. For this is the tomb laid over the corpses of dead souls.

Therefore I greatly fear that you hope too much, although you have no more grounds for excessive hope than for despair. For as Cain, who despaired, was cursed, so everyone who sins in hope is cursed. But Christians, having experienced God’s mercy more frequently than his wrath—that is, his vengeance, for now is not its time—find the mind more easily inclined to this right hand than to that left, as though God possessed more mercy than justice, although he is both: mercy and justice, and cannot be greater than himself.

Therefore, if you think of God as very merciful, think of him as equally just, according to the saying: “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100). This thought will produce in you fear, which is the beginning of wisdom, the key of righteousness; and that key alone opens the tombs of souls. For it is the angel who rolls the stone from the door of the tomb, whose appearance is like lightning and his clothing like snow (Matt. 28). The appearance of fear is to think and understand terrible things.

There are especially four things which must always be set before the eyes of our mind: the truth of judgment, the severity of the judge, the eternity of torments, and the enormity of sins. When these four are carefully considered, they make the mind of the one considering them like lightning: that is, burning and reddening, or in other words grieving and wise [Col. 0751C]. Again, when these four are carefully considered, they make the garments of the one considering them like snow. For when the sinner attentively considers what he deserves if he does not repent, he immediately puts on the sackcloth of repentance, stiff with the cold of continence and shining with the whiteness of chastity. Whiteness and stiffness are the two properties of snow.

For he did not say, “His clothing was like white wool” or “like milk,” but “like snow,” plainly intending to signify that, although repentance is bitter, constraining, and severe, it is nonetheless white and quickly melts, because it is brief, however long its duration may be. Jesus cries to you in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11); for you must come out, though still bound. Whoever is buried in this way brings even his habit with him to confession, but not obstinacy; otherwise he would not come to confession. How then shall we free you from these bonds?

We must have recourse to the origin of habit, which must first be rooted out, so that, once its root has been wholly pulled up, its branches may not sprout again. Augustine says in the *Confessions*: “From the will comes lust; while lust is served, a perverse habit is made; and when habit is not resisted, necessity then arises.” These are like certain little loops interlinked with each other, making a chain by which the sinner is bound. Of this chain, or cord, Isaiah says: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” (Isa. 5)—that is, adding sin [Col. 0752A] to sin, as thread is added to thread to make a rope. This is the threefold cord which is difficult to break.

The first twisting of this cord is made from two threads: perverse will and lust. And within this cord, lust is a threefold, twice-twisted thread. The third twist is made from habit and necessity. What is perverse will? It is a perverse movement of the mind to desire something other than God for its own sake. From this perverse movement, as a punishment for sin, a person deserves that what he perversely moved himself to desire should please him—that is, become agreeable to him—and thus lust follows, both as sin and as punishment for the first sin. For *libido*, lust, is so called from *libendo*, “pleasing.”

But whatever pleases us readily compels us, through a certain alluring violence of its own, to use it. For what we gladly do, we do if we can—and often; indeed, if we could, we would never cease doing it. Thus habit arises from lust, because those who eat this food will still hunger. The human belly can never be filled with the husks of swine. Why necessity is born from habit is manifest: habit is a second nature. O violence of habit, how great is your power! From freedom you make slavery, from disease a constitution, from will necessity, from accidental things natural things, and from contingent things impossibilities.

Do you wish to escape this cord as subtly as swiftly? Return, then, to the first knot, formed from perverse will and lust, and be assured that, when this knot is untied, the later ones will be untied, because when the cause ceases, the effect must cease. Indeed, here the whole force of this cord resides. In other cases the last knot must first be untied and the first last; here the reverse is true.

Let the things that attract the bodily senses be removed from those senses, and perverse affection will easily be removed from the mind; once it is removed, lust will immediately be removed. Hence Seneca says: “We must act,” he says, “so as to flee as far as possible from the stimuli of vices.” For who can live chastely beside a brothel? Who can live abstinently near a tavern? Who can live silently amid the quarrels of the law courts? Indeed, who can live wisely in the world? “He who is a companion of a fool becomes like him” (Prov. 13). “He who touches pitch—will he not be defiled by it?” (Ecclus. 13.) He who throws himself into flame—will he not be set ablaze?

Do you wish, then, to extinguish lust? Set enmity between yourself and woman; let it suffice that, deceived by the serpent, she has hitherto deceived you. Do not give the leech blood to suck; instead, pull it from your skin, whether it will or no, even though it be half-full. Do you wish to extinguish lust? Remove the wood from the fire, even if the blaze crackles. “What,” you ask, “is this wood which should not be piled upon the fire of this quarrelsome man?” It is innumerable; nevertheless, I shall enumerate a few, in which you may recognize all the rest. These, then, are:

> Idleness, overly long sleep, flesh, woman, wine,  
> Prosperity, play, songs, beauty, a boy.

[Col. 0753A] On the first you have:

> Idleness nourishes the body; the mind too is fed by it.

And Lucan:

> …Idleness gives the mind its changing moods.

And one of our own says: “Every idle person is ruled by desires.” And that Rule of Benedict says: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.” And one of the Fathers says: “May the devil never find you idle.”

On the second you have:

> The question is asked: why did Aegisthus become an adulterer?  
> The cause is ready to hand: he was idle.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love* 161

On the third there is this in Cato’s *Ethics*:

> Always keep more watch; do not be given over to sleep.  
> For prolonged rest supplies nourishment to vices.

Finally, those first two always accompany this third. No one can be sleepy without also being idle and slothful. Of the fourth the Apostle says: “It is good not to eat flesh and not to drink wine,” etc. (Rom. 14; John 6.)

On the fifth, since examples are infinite, it suffices to give woman’s etymology alone: “Woman,” Varro says, “is called from softness, as though *mollier*.” This *mollier* must be understood in two ways, active and passive, as if it meant “capable of softening,” that is, both quick to soften and quick to be softened. But I do not want you to be ignorant that a hammer likewise is called from softening, because it softens iron. “Lust itself,” says Jerome, “subdues iron minds.” And Claudian:

> Hearts of iron grow soft beneath wanton arrows.

[Col. 0753C] You see, then, how the reasoning of the etymologies agrees with that of the natures. What does a hammer not soften? Whom does a woman not soften? Therefore woman is a hammer. Truly she is the hammer of the whole earth, by which the devil both softens and hammers the whole world. How did you not guard yourself against this hammer? Is that not the hammer which beat the mass of your body out into sheets of lead—indeed, which, striking continuously upon you, made you its own anvil out of yourself?

Therefore, if you wish to flee from this hammer, leave the iron furnace of Babylon—unless, God forbid, you do not dread the incessant blows of this great and heavy hammer, which, unlike the nature of other hammers, can join nothing together and knows how to make nothing solid, but breaks all things, crushes everything, and dissolves the whole.

Return, therefore, return to bear the cross of the Lord; and do not place your portion with Pilate, whose name is interpreted “hammerer.” But let us pass to the remaining stimulants of vice. Concerning wine, which I placed after woman, there is that wine “in which is lust.” And the poet says:

> Venus rages in wines, fire in fire.

Hence Jerome aptly says [Note: [Col. 0753D] Jerome, *On Virginity* and on Ephesians 5.]: “To drink wine in youth is to add oil to the furnace and a sword to poison.” Of prosperity you read in Ovid:

> Minds commonly run to excess in favourable circumstances;  
> It is not easy to receive advantages with an even mind.

[Col. 0754A] Hence Augustine says of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0754D] Book XVII, *City of God*, ch. 20.]: “Prosperous circumstances, which weary the minds of wise men, harmed Solomon more than wisdom itself helped him—wisdom praiseworthy then and still remembered far and wide.” Solomon himself says in Proverbs: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them” (Prov. 1). Hence Juvenal:

> Filthy money first brought foreign ways among us,  
> And soft riches broke the ages with shameful luxury.

But as prosperity draws one toward sin, adversity often draws one back from sin. Hence Gregory says: “At one time the world draws us back from God; now it is so full of adversities that it sends us to God. For behold, the Lord, as he promised through the prophet, has hedged your ways with thorns, so that you may not find your paths and may not run after your lovers” (Hos. 2).

Why then do you not say: “I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now”? Why do you not summon the devil concerning the agreement he made with you and the covenant he struck with you, and put this alternative before him: “Either give me the riches and pleasures which you covenanted to give me if I served you, or I will go to such a Lord as will give them to me—not merely to satiety, but even to overflowing”?

O how fittingly you would put this before him! For he promises these things not only to you but to everyone willing to submit himself to his dominion, according to the words: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4). Behold: you worshipped by falling down, and in worshipping him you fell. For he is worshipped only by falling, whom one serves only by sinning. But he did not give what he promised you: for he lied. Did you think that he could speak truth? Is he not a liar, who did not stand in the truth from the beginning? (John 8.) How do you tolerate the intolerable slavery imposed by this covenant-breaking lord, this most savage exactor?

Yet I wonder greatly how the expenses of such slavery can be supplied:

> Poverty has not the means to sustain its own love;  
> You, madman, have not the means to sustain your frenzy.

Consider that, since you began to serve this lord, nothing has ever turned out prosperously for you: every kind of poverty followed, adversity came upon you, calamity was added, and misfortune exceeded all measure. Now gather briefly how unhappily you serve him:

> Poor, needy, destitute, pale, bloodless, empty—  
> Of money, food, rest; through cold, plague, and hunger.

O burdensome slavery! O bitter subjection! To serve and be in want; to be a servant and be afflicted; to be humbled and trampled underfoot. Good God, what is more bitter, what more burdensome, than poverty full of sins? Hear, then, my counsel. Deceive him who deceived you; lie to him who lied to you. Cease serving him who not only does not serve you as he promised, but even acts against you. Thus let art be outwitted by art.

Next comes play, by which term I mean every sort of jest. Every jest is a fuel of lust; hence Venus is called playful [Col. 0755A], and her intimate companion plays thus concerning her:

> She is not accustomed to come among mournful choirs.  
> —Ovid

After play I also placed songs, by which term I include every kind of musical melody, whether made by instrument or human voice. Hence Isaiah says: “Harp and lyre, drum and flute, and wine are at your feasts, but you do not regard the work of the Lord” (Isa. 5). For how can those who not only behold but practise so many works of vanity regard the work of the Lord—that is, truth? And Ovid says:

> For many, their own sweet voice was an advantage in beauty.

Physicians say that nothing is more powerful in weakening the mind than the seduction of melody. Thus even certain demons are captured by it, as is said of Saul when possessed and David playing the harp: Saul was better when David himself played psalms. Musical contests were also found for Delphic Apollo; and Orpheus, that excellent physician, theologian, poet, and harpist, pursued his lust by harp-playing even to hell.

Receive further evidence of this matter: it is difficult to find someone with a light voice and a serious life, since lightness of voice desires singing, but seriousness of life demands lamentation. I have seen countless men and women whose lives were worse in proportion as their voices were better. But, to spare our own times, let Nero be brought forward. Suetonius relates in his book *The Lives of the Caesars* that Nero so delighted in singing that not even an unexpected earthquake would make him cease singing before he had finished what he had begun. Suetonius also relates that Nero often lay upon his back and placed a sheet of lead upon his chest, for the preservation of his voice; that he abstained from apples and harmful foods; and that he never summoned anyone except through another person or in a subdued voice. Hence Juvenal’s saying:

> A sweet voice has wicked fingers.

Behold, we have found a man with the sweetest voice and the worst life. And since examples are overabundant, let us proceed to other matters. Next is beauty, always attended by two dangers, the same two that attend a sweet voice: pride and lust. Hence Ovid says in the *Fasti*:

> Arrogance is in the beautiful, and pride follows beauty.

And Juvenal:

> …Rare is the harmony of beauty  
> And chastity.

And Ovid again:

> Great beauty is the enemy of chastity.

I do not condemn nature’s gifts, but curiosity and vanity, which beauty carries along with it as inseparable, almost natural companions. Next comes the boy, whom I have also called a fuel of sin, on the same grounds as woman. For as much danger as sex brings in woman, so much does age bring in a boy. Of the former Varro says, “Woman, as though *mollier*”; of the latter Ovid says, “A boy’s age is soft.” Of the former Virgil says:

> …Woman, ever varying and changeable.

Of the latter Horace says:

> Wax, to be moulded into vice. …

[Col. 0756A] For a boy’s age is dangerous, companionship with him more dangerous, and familiarity most dangerous. Thus it is read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that one should not have intimacy with a woman or a boy; and it adds: “or with a heretic.” All these things, therefore, are stimulants of vices, incitements to pleasure, and torments of chastity. With this oil, this pitch, this tow, this naphtha, these firebrands, and these twigs, the furnace of Babylon is kindled.

Would you flee the fire of pleasure? Flee every kind of this fuel. But where will you flee from the face of these things? Look round upon the whole world: everywhere the devil baits the hook of sin with some fuel of delight. Therefore the world must be fled, in order that its desires may be fled. Otherwise, if you wish to remain in the world, even with hands cut off, feet mutilated, and eyes gouged out because they have caused you to stumble, you will not be without scandal [Col. 0756B]. Something will still remain for the ears and nostrils to make them, and through them the mind, stumble.

Accordingly, since we can neither live without the bodily members that serve us nor live well while they give scandal, we must necessarily seek a place healthy not so much for bodies as for morals: a place where, though not lacking the functions of the bodily senses, we may be free from their scandals. And what place is fit for this except the cloister, where peace is enclosed, decency shut in, pleasure shut out, and lust secluded? Of this place it is written: “It is better to sit in a corner of the house than with a quarrelsome woman” (Prov. 21). [Col. 0756C] The corner is the harmonious cohabitation of those in the cloister. Into it they themselves, converging from different kinds of men as from different walls, and dwelling in the house of one manner of life and unity, pursuing the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, learn by happy experience how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Ps. 132).

For the quarrelsome woman is, literally, either every woman; or the flesh itself; or womanly life; or companionship with lovers of soft and womanly living. Each of these always provokes quarrelling in spiritual men. How fittingly, as they say, was that captive little woman called Rixanda, “Quarrel-maker,” who draws you captive! For she is the devil, who is called [Col. 0756D] Rixoaldus, “Quarrel-ruler,” who always nourishes strife. Indeed, this name too is read as the proper name of a certain demon.

Flee therefore, dearest brother; flee the strife which this Rixoaldus stirs up against you through that Rixanda; and return to your cloister, the place of peace and rest, the lover of silence and persecutor of strife. Return, brother; return from the circuit of the world in which the wicked walk, which the roaring lion continually prowls, seeking whom he may devour, to the cloistral square. There, by the wondrous workmanship of prudence, the columns of justice, most firmly founded on bases of fortitude and cemented with temperance, tirelessly sustain the architraves of hope; and the sides of charity, set at intervals in the courses of discretion, or rather their breadth, are brought in straight lines to the angles—that is, the narrow limits—of humility, beginning from those same angles. Thus they establish the most beautiful square of a life perfectly ordered. In the midst of the square, smiling to complete its beauty, is the meadow of the divine Scriptures, most richly filled with the healing, unfading little flowers of delightful sayings. [Col. 0757A] Return therefore, brother; return from the iron furnace to the coolness of the cloister, so that in that most pleasant place, under the most gracious Lord, the most merciful Jesus Christ, you may delightfully pass through the calamity of this present misery.

But you say: “Is there no life other than the cloistered life that leads to God?” Certainly there is—but not for you. Before you chose this life, many others lay open to you. But when, out of many, you chose this life for yourself, you made one out of them all. “What then,” you ask, [Col. 0757B] “are cloistered persons alone saved, or do all secular persons perish?” Surely neither. But these alone are saved easily; all those with difficulty. Why is this, except because one removed from fire is safer from burning than one close to the fire?

Brother, let no deceitful thought persuade you that you need not fulfill what you vowed, because you did not complete a year of probation under Saint Benedict, nor even spend half your days under Saint Augustine, but said, “In the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38). Question your conscience. Do you not know with what merchant you entered into a contract? Namely, with him who cannot deceive because he is most just; who cannot be deceived because he is most wise; whom no one can resist because he is most strong; whom no one can corrupt because he is most good. You had first contracted with the devil, when you had sold yourself to him under sin. But then you contracted with the Lord, in a wondrous way selling to him what had been his before the sale and was to become yours afterwards. For no one will be his own—that is, under his own legal power—until he has sold himself to him by whom he has already been redeemed.

Do you wish to know what that contract between you and the Lord was like? You sold yourself to the Lord: withdrawing yourself from the world, drawing yourself back from sin, taking yourself away from hell, drawing yourself out of the mire, drawing yourself together in the cloister; drawing the devil after you, drawing the Lord toward yourself, and thereafter to be drawn by him to heaven. Moreover, as the price of this sale—that is, this transfer—the Lord secured for you eternal blessedness [Col. 0757D] on this condition: that you should persevere for him. Did the price you were to receive seem small to you? Yet “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

Why then, brother, do you not faithfully abide by this contract, so wholesome, useful, and delightful for you? If you wish to deny it, all who were then present at that chapter meeting will be witnesses against you, whether you wish it or not. “I do not deny,” you say, “that I vowed; but was willing in such a way the same as vowing solemnly, rather than simply?” By no means. For if a distinction is made between simple and solemn vows, that vow is made simply which is made [Col. 0758A] in silence—when deliberation is content with its own bounds, that is, does not break outward into speech—or, if it does break forth, is made with no one present or with only a few present, outside a church, and before one’s former habit has been changed. Such a vow is said to have been made simply, uttered simply, or merely simple.

But a vow is called solemn when it is made before many people; or, if before few, before persons of weight and in a church; or into the hands of a priest even outside a church; or over relics. Or, to say it more briefly: two things especially make a vow solemn—the holiness of the place and the authority of the person; by authority here I mean the dignity of rank. A vow is made solemnly in any church, even without a priest, provided only that some persons are present [Col. 0758B] whose testimony does not permit sex, weakness, age, or ill repute to cast it into doubt. A vow is also made solemnly before any priest, even outside every church.

But you vowed before many and weighty persons, that is, before a very numerous and devout community, and also before an abbot and in a church, because it was in chapter. For the chapter house is not not a part of the church; nor is what is done in chapter not done in church. In the whole body of the church, apart from the place where the altar stands, there is no place holier than the chapter house, none more worthy of reverence, none farther from the devil, none nearer to God. There the devil loses whatever he gains elsewhere; there obedience restores to God whatever negligence or contempt has elsewhere taken away from him. [Col. 0758C]

You see, then, that whatever factors cooperate in making a vow solemn concurred in the vow which you made as a novice in the Cistercian Order. I do not yet come to that vow which you made in the Premonstratensian Order. In the time of blessed Benedict, however, there was a different custom for receiving and testing novices than there is now. For novices then neither changed their own clothing nor received the monk’s tonsure until they became monks; and this is still prescribed in the canons. Hence I wonder with what face the abbots of our time have dared to change this custom. Yet I suppose it was to inspire fear and shame. For a man is more ashamed to return to the world in secular dress with his hair cut off than if he had retained neither [Col. 0758D] of these things.

That novices did not change their clothing in the time of blessed Benedict before they were to become monks I prove from the text of his Rule. For in the chapter entitled “The manner of receiving brothers,” its conclusion reads thus: “At once let him be stripped in the oratory of the possessions with which he is clothed, and let him be clothed in the possessions of the monastery.” And afterwards: “But let the clothes of which he has been stripped be put away in the wardrobe, so that, if at any time, at the devil’s persuasion, he consents to leave the monastery—which God forbid—then, stripped of the possessions of the monastery, he may be cast out.”

Thus it could then freely be said to the novice: “Depart free,” since, his former dress not having been changed and the tonsure not having been received, [Col. 0759A] he was bound by no vow before the Church, but only before God. For when it was said there, “Depart free,” it must be understood with respect to us; but with respect to God, he did not depart free.

A cloistered fugitive, by laying aside his habit, scandalizes more people than by breaking his profession. By breaking his profession, he scandalizes only those to whom he had joined himself by profession. But by laying aside his habit, he scandalizes all those from whom he had separated himself by receiving it: the whole world, therefore. What courage have you now, brother—more a brother in name than in reality? What courage have you now? For if consolation is hidden from Christ’s eyes because hell will divide among the brethren, how much more must it be hidden from the eyes of the brethren themselves, lest perhaps it divide among them! [Col. 0760A]

I beseech you therefore, dearest brother, by the tender mercies of our God, “whereby the Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1), to labor together with me, lest hell divide us. For why should we, born from one fleshly womb and reborn from one spiritual womb, be halved by one hell? Or rather, to put it better, lest it divide us from Christ, because we have been redeemed by his precious blood.

> **[Note: Cols. 0759A, 0760A]** The ending appears to be missing, since the author indicates that he will treat of the vow made among the Premonstratensians by Galter, to whom he writes, but says absolutely nothing about it.

[Col. 0759] Here end the *Flowers* of Helinand, a good, religious, honorable, and holy man, distinguished also in life. (These are the words of Vincent of Beauvais, in the *Speculum Historiale*, book 29, chapter 148.)

[Col. 0759]

# PASSION OF THE HOLY THEBAN MARTYRS GEREON, VICTOR, CASSIUS, AND FLORENTIUS, WRITTEN BY HELINAND

(*Acta Sanctorum Bollandiana*, October, vol. V, 10 October, Brussels, 1852, p. 14; from the manuscript of the author’s own museum, shelfmark P. M. S 159, collated with the Saint-Omer manuscript and Surius’s edition.)

## PROLOGUE. The author explains on what principle he will treat of the martyrs here presented.

[Col. 0759B]

1. On this day we are exhorted to extol with festal praises the most sacred legion of Theban martyrs,

> **[Note: Col. 0759C]** We have already dealt principally with this legion under 22 September, the day on which Saint Maurice and his companions suffered martyrdom at Agaunum and are commemorated in today’s Roman Martyrology.

on which we venerate the most precious pledges of that holy fellowship—Gereon, Victor, Cassius, and Florentius—with their companions. For those who had in no way differed in the glorious constancy of their passion are not separated in the joy of their recompense.

2. For although they did not receive the glory of martyrdom on one day or in the same place, nevertheless, according to the Apostle, they had “one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all, God blessed for ever” [Col. 0759C]

> **[Note: Col. 0760C]** Eph. 4:5–6.

To him all alike clung with one purpose, one devotion, and happy perseverance, fulfilling in deed the words of the Psalmist: “But for me it is good to cling to God; to place my hope in the Lord God” [Col. 0760B]

> **[Note: Col. 0760C]** Ps. 72:28.

Firmly and unanimously believing in their hearts unto righteousness, and confessing with their mouths unto salvation, in that highest charity which is God, they diligently meditated in will and conduct upon this apostolic steadfastness: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?”

> **[Note: Col. 0760C]** Rom. 8:35.

They also added the sure ground of their confidence: “But in all these things,” they say, “we conquer through him who loved us.”

> **[Note: Col. 0760C]** Ibid., v. 37.

3. Nor should anyone be troubled that in this account of our Thebaid we do not set out, with full detail and in the customary manner of historians, the deeds of the blessed martyrs and their most holy contests for Christ’s faith. For our purpose in this discourse is to stir the hearts of our hearers, together with ourselves, toward spiritual joy, [Col. 0760C] so that, kindled with longing for heavenly things, they may desire more to advance by charity that builds up into fellowship with the martyrs than [Col. 0761A] to fall away from delight in eternal joy through knowledge that puffs up.

4. But because it is the custom of the slowness of human understanding to seek from outward knowledge that which may be impressed upon the hidden place of the heart—as though it could not otherwise rise to rational understanding except by the guidance of sensible and imaginable things—this is what the Apostle says: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual.”

> **[Note: Col. 0761D]** 1 Cor. 15:46.

Let us also relate, according to what we have heard, something like a history: not indeed embracing each matter in order, but briefly touching upon some of the more necessary matters in the manner of a chronicle, concerning the most holy angelic recruits of this legion—Gereon, Victor, Cassius, Florentius, and their companions—who are deservedly venerated throughout the whole world and who, by the victory of their death, so to speak, procured the most delightful fruits [Col. 0761B] of security and peace.

5. After the most victorious passion of blessed Maurice, the wonderful and provident dispensation of almighty God preserved these notable victors for the delay he willed, so far as human inquiry may conjecture, rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation. Thus, the more they sowed in tears, the more joyfully they might reap the fruit of everlasting gladness; and the more widely they extended, in confessing Christ, examples of the labor they had undertaken for his name, the more people they might kindle to imitate their constancy and greatness of soul. Yet they themselves, with hearts fixed on things above, burned with that apostolic desire expressed in the words: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is far better.”

> **[Note: Col. 0761D]** Approximately Phil. 1:23.

For shortly after their martyrdom had been accomplished, very few remained in the province in which they suffered who did not ardently seek the very thing which, when their hearts had long been obstinate, they had dreaded—just as though the narrow way itself had not previously been passable, when it had been worn by the footsteps of so many who had gone before.

## CHAPTER I. The saints’ constancy in faith and martyrdom

6. Therefore, when approximately the two hundred and ninety-first year after the Lord’s Incarnation was turning, Diocletian—thirty-third emperor from the first, Octavian Augustus, in the forty-second year of whose reign that unique birth was accomplished through Mary, the perpetual Virgin—made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, first Caesar [Col. 0761D] and then his associate in the whole empire; he exalted him together with himself in the name and power of Augustus.

> **[Note: Col. 0761D]** The beginning of Maximian Herculius’s rule is here placed later than truth permits. For he was created Caesar not only in 291, but already in 285, and then Augustus in 286. See Pagi’s *Critica* under both years.

Their cruelty against Christians flamed up so fiercely that Diocletian in the East and Maximian in the West ravaged the churches of God everywhere, spared no one of the Lord’s flock, and strove utterly to root out the Christian name. But by divine direction, what had then been endured in the seed later became manifest in the shoot.

7. This persecution, said to have been the tenth from Nero, was more savage and longer-lasting than the rest, continuing in the cruelty it had begun for as much as ten years. It was immediately followed by the violent ruin and lasting destruction of idols, when peace was restored throughout the world to the churches of God, [Col. 0762B] and it subjected even those whom it had lately endured as bitterest enemies to the yoke of the Catholic faith. It resembled the tenth Egyptian plague, which, by the sudden and most terrible death of all the firstborn—being also the last plague—not only allowed the Lord’s people to depart free, but even compelled them most urgently to hasten away enriched with money. If anything after this persecution of Christians was modelled upon that event, it may still be seen among us in ancient church buildings.

8. Therefore, when a destructive uprising against the Roman Empire had grown in Gaul,

> **[Note: Col. 0761D]** That the uprising spoken of here is the one stirred up in Gaul by the Bagaudae under the leaders Aelianus and Amandus in the year 286, as most hold, is clear from what follows in no. 10. For the Bagaudae, see vol. 6 of our work for September, p. 346 ff., in the annotations to letter b.

Maximian, having assembled an army in Italy, summoned for assistance Theban soldiers—Maurice, Gereon, Victor, and other men [Col. 0762C] of the same order—already initiated by a bishop of Jerusalem into the sacraments of the true faith and saving baptism.

> **[Note: Col. 0761D]** Some judge this bishop to have been Zabdā; but whether rightly or otherwise you will decide from what is said in vol. 6 of our work just cited, p. 347, in the annotation to letter C, and also in vol. 2 for October, in the commentary prefixed to the Acts of Saints Thyrsus and the other Trier martyrs, no. 108.

They at once, trained as they were in military courage and obedient to imperial commands, each equipped with his followers in weapons of war and fortified by divine counsel, joined that expedition unanimously. Then, seeking an audience with blessed Marcellinus, Roman pontiff—twenty-eighth after the blessed apostle Peter and fourth before Saint Sylvester, bishop of the same see, who steered the ship of holy Church amid the waves tossed by the stormy world—they learned from him how, while under arms in the Roman military service, the innocence required by the Christian religion ought to be preserved.

> **[Note: Col. 0762D]** If, as our biographer states clearly below, Saints Maurice, Gereon, Cassius, Florentius, and their companions suffered martyrdom during the war against the Bagaudae—which arose in Gaul in 285, or at least was concluded no later than 286—then what is here recalled about their consultation of Marcellinus, Roman pontiff, cannot accord with truth, since he did not occupy Saint Peter’s chair before 296.

They preserved the manifest truth of his teaching, in the invincible justice of faith, to the end of the good contest.

9. O blessed and holy assembly of soldiers ready [Col. 0763A] for campaign! They contemplated war outwardly through obedience, but peace inwardly through innocence. They bore arms to conquer the enemies of Roman peace; to resist premeditated wrongs, they prepared not weapons of iron but the most firm weapons of faith. For they dedicated this concord of theirs universally to the Lord: against public enemies they would obey imperial decrees; against the religion of the faith they had embraced, they would recognize no emperor. They would rather lose temporal life for Christ than live temporally by denying Christ, God, and thereby lose eternal life.

Surely, taught by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, they recalled the words of Truth, who speaks to the Father about his disciples: “And this is eternal life: that they may know [Col. 0763B] you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

> **[Note: Col. 0763C]** John 17:3.

With breathless longing they also desired that the Lord’s prayer might soon be fulfilled in them: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may my servant be.”

10. Then Maximian Augustus—

> **[Note: Col. 0763C]** Maximian is correctly called “Augustus” here if the war against the Bagaudae was concluded in 286; but not so, unless perhaps by anticipation, if this occurred as early as 285, for Maximian was then only Caesar, not Augustus.

—having united his army, although it was a mixed body of believers and unbelievers, hurried across the Alpine passes and approached Gaul. By his arrival alone he terrified the leaders Amandus and Aelianus; he easily suppressed, without loss to his army, the storm of their stubbornly aroused sedition.

> **[Note: Col. 0763D]** Our biographer appears here to indicate that Aelianus and Amandus were subdued by fear of Maximian’s approach alone; but Eutropius teaches in book 9 of the *Breviarium* that this was done not without battles, however slight.

But when he learned that a certain nobleman named Carausius was plotting treachery against the frontiers of the Roman Empire—

> **[Note: Col. 0763D]** It is here indicated, but incorrectly, that Carausius’s rebellion occurred no later than the point at which Maximian’s expedition against the Bagaudae, or Aelianus and Amandus, was already prepared; for, as I showed from Eutropius in no. 77 of the preliminary commentary, the latter preceded the former by one or two years.

—although he had been appointed procurator of the province [Col. 0763C] by the Ocean, where the Franks, expelled for the second time from their own settlements, had settled near the borders of the Gauls and Saxons, Maximian sent there through the channel of the Rhine part of his army,

> **[Note: Col. 0763D]** It is not at all contrary to truth that Maximian, while still remaining in the Alps, sent some companies of soldiers, and thus also Thebans, ahead into Gaul to protect against enemies the region bordering the Rhine.

so that this impious undertaking might be thwarted by its military courage.

11. On this journey the happy companies of Christian soldiers followed the principal commanders of the Lord’s army, Gereon, Victor, Cassius, and Florentius. [Col. 0764A] Meanwhile Maximian, the fiercest persecutor of the Christian name and most unworthy leader of such a host, set up an idol of zeal near the foot of the Alps, in the place called Octodurum.

> **[Note: Col. 0763D]** The situation of Octodurum, and likewise of Agaunum, the arena of Saint Maurice and those who suffered martyrdom with him, is explained in vol. 6 for September, in the preliminary commentary on the Acts of Saints Maurice and his companions, nos. 1–2.

He ordered the whole army, man by man, to assemble with eager solemnity, and that no one, as a follower of another religion, should withdraw himself from the act of supplication to the gods, whom Maximian called immortal, and the common rejoicing.

> **[Note: Cols. 0764C–D]** The following narrative indicates that Saint Maurice and his companions, and then also our saints, were slain because they refused to obey this command of Maximian. This is expressly asserted, concerning Maurice and his companions slain at Agaunum, in the interpolated Acts of these saints, reprinted in vol. 6 for September, pp. 345, 346, 348, and 349. But in the older Acts of Saint Maurice and his fellow martyrs of Agaunum, written by Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, printed in the same volume, p. 342 ff., an altogether different reason is given in no. 3 for their martyrdom: namely, that, “when [lacuna] like the other soldiers, they were assigned to drag away” (two manuscripts in Ruinart read “to tear apart”) “the multitude of Christians,” they alone dared to refuse the service of unbelief and declared that they would not obey commands of this kind.

Now Gereon’s troop had gone ahead and, by its bodily absence, left the fellowship of its most faithful comrades. Thus it happened that Gereon did not hear of the most wicked sacrilege and preserved himself with his most holy bodies for our everlasting joy.

[Col. 0764B] 12. They came to the place of the appointed crime. There, while the numerous army of Roman valor bowed as if in religion before deaf and mute idols, Saint Maurice was absent with his legion, because meanwhile he had withdrawn to a place of spiritual exercise in order to strengthen his fellow soldiers for their coming contests. When the king, greedy for the destruction of good men, learned this from the herald, and could not bend the divine battle-line by crafty persuasion, he ordered it to be decimated once and twice.

> **[Note: Col. 0764D]** That decimation was used among the Romans in punishing mutinous soldiers is shown by Baronius in his notes on today’s Roman Martyrology for 22 September, from Polybius, Julius Capitolinus, Livy, and others. Let anyone who seeks more on this matter consult him.

And if those who remained still preferred death to surrender, Maximian decreed that that entire most blessed legion, wherever it was dispersed, should be slaughtered by soldiers sent out for the purpose. He made the work of the executioners worth the price by ensuring that the more persons each man killed, the richer he would rejoice to have become in plunder. [Col. 0764C]

13. These things were first done at the town of Agaunum, where the largest body of the holy army was stationed. Then, following the tracks of those who had gone before, they found the leading soldiers Cassius and Florentius, with seven other men of similar constancy, settled beside the city of Verona on the bank of the Rhine, together with very many other followers [Col. 0765A] of the same force but not of the same purpose.

> **[Note: Col. 0765C]** From this it appears that not all who had been sent ahead into Gaul by Maximian together with Saints Cassius and Florentius were Thebans.

> **[Note: Cols. 0764D–0765C]** By Verona here is meant not the Dutch city of that name, formerly situated not far from Alkmaar and now destroyed, but Bonn. This I demonstrated against Miraeus in nos. 7–8 of the preliminary commentary; and I there added, in no. 10, evidence proving that this German city was also called “Verona” in the eleventh century. One may add the inscription cited by Gelenius in *On the Greatness of Cologne Agrippina*, book 3, syntagma 12, p. 363. In it Volcmar, archbishop of Cologne from 966 to 969, is praised, and Bonn too is called “Verona.” If, as appears likely, that inscription was made during Volcmar’s lifetime or not long after his death, it is evidence that Bonn was called “Verona” also in the tenth century.

When the persecutors recognized them as belonging to the eastern garrison, they raged against them and questioned them about their profession of faith. Since they differed from those above them neither in the will of their hearts nor in the judgment of their reply, they bowed their heads and were killed in that same place for Christ’s name.

14. Soon the persecutor—or perhaps rumour still more swiftly—reached blessed Gereon and his 318 companions, likewise armed with him in the faith of truth. They nevertheless advanced a little way ahead of the executioners who followed, and in the fields of the great city of Agrippina awaited the glory of martyrdom, encouraging one another. Those sent by the judge immediately came upon them and found in them no plea for defense, no will to depart from their purpose, but the most steadfast confession of Christ’s name. [Col. 0765B] There blessed Gereon, an eminent leader and martyr, having subdued everything that might entice toward the pleasure of this life, freely offered himself as a living sacrifice to God with those servants of the eternal King. The mad torturers stained the saints’ bodies with blood, dragged them across the level ground of that field, and threw them into a great pit.

> **[Note: Cols. 0765C–D]** At least in the age of Gregory of Tours it was believed that fifty soldiers of the Theban legion, whom Gregory mentions in book 1 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 62, had been treated in this way, as may there be seen in that author.

To this day a sight of Gereon’s blood is shown at the place where Saint Gereon was slaughtered,

> **[Note: Cols. 0765D–0766C]** Here a column, probably the one said to have been splashed with the blood of the holy Theban and Moorish martyrs, is likely meant. Gelenius, *On the Greatness of Cologne*, p. 260, writes: “They further relate that a remnant of a column survives from the slaughterhouse of the holy Theban and Moorish martyrs, sprinkled with their blood; on its upper portion it has a plate bearing this inscription:
>
> ‘Add faith: this same blood was once poured out here;
>
> If I give myself wickedly to the stone, that same blood punishes.’
>
> But if Saint Gereon had his arena in the *Theatre*, how can it be true, as the sequence of Helinand’s narrative indicates, that he was killed in an open field?”

and the place itself retains from its inhabitants the name “At the Martyrs.”

[Col. 0766A] 15. While these things were taking place, the cohort accompanying blessed Victor, hurrying to the place to which it had been assigned, came to a town of the Franks which they called Troy or Xanten from the settlements of their ancestors.

> **[Note: Col. 0766C]** The town in question was first called *Vetera*, then *Bertinum*, and finally, after Saint Victor and his companions who suffered and were venerated there, *Sancti* or *Sanctum*. Later, because the basis of this latter name was not adequately known, some persons—and Helinand in particular—who believed in the Trojan origin of the Franks, and who, carried away by an ill-judged love of excessive antiquity, wished this town to have been founded by Trojans, called it “Xanthus” and “Lesser Troy.”

There, with its leader, it pitched camp in green meadows. Nor were those bold and bloody soldiers absent. Having killed there Victor, the most valiant soldier of Christ, with 330 martyrs, they submerged their holy bodies in marshy places.

16. At length, enriched with the plunder they desired, they returned rejoicing in their crime by the way they had come with the rest of the army, because that Carausius had fled and crossed over to Britain. At the same time soldiers from Mauretania, a part of Africa, and neighboring regions, summoned by the emperor because of the frequent uprisings of the Gauls, came into Gaul. There 360 of them [Col. 0766B] were slaughtered for the Catholic faith and chose, with blessed Gereon and his companions, the rest and perpetual veneration of blessed bodies.

> **[Note: Col. 0766C]** Surius reads “fifty”; but the Saint-Omer manuscript, Peter de Natalibus, and Mombritius’s compendium of the Passion of our saints also read “sixty.” Since this is so, and since 360 Moors are also counted in the Life of Saint Anno, cited more than once in the preliminary commentary, the reading of our manuscript should here be maintained.

## CHAPTER II. A church erected in honor of Saint Gereon and his companions and made illustrious by miracles

17. After these events, Maximian Augustus returned to Italy. At Diocletian’s urging, that he might retire with him into private life, Maximian, though unwilling, laid down both purple and empire, but not the practice of tyranny.

> **[Note: Cols. 0766D–0767C]** It seems to be indicated here that Maximian renounced the empire and purple not long after the martyrdom of our saints. But this cannot be true if, as the whole preceding course of the narrative likewise indicates, our saints died for the faith while the war against the Bagaudae was imminent. As I have explained above, that war was concluded no later than 286 and therefore long before 305, the year in which, as is now agreed among scholars, Maximian and Diocletian renounced empire and purple. Nor did Maximian—who, though after 286 he often left Gaul for Italy after repeated stays in Gaul—renounce the empire in Italy, as is again indicated here, but at Nicomedia in Bithynia. Nor is it rightly asserted here that, after laying down the empire, he retained the practice of tyranny. For although the Acts of Saint Victor of Marseilles, from which this might in some way be proved, report that this saint was killed for the faith at Marseilles by Maximian’s command when Maximian came there in 310, intending to put an end alike to his life and crimes, nevertheless those Acts are not to be followed in this matter, as the material adduced by Cuperus in no. 24 of the commentary prefixed to that saint’s Acts sufficiently shows.

[Col. 0767A] In his place he appointed Constantius, a most mild man, as Augustus over Italy, Africa, and Gaul; the remaining provinces were assigned to Galerius. But Constantius, content with Gaul and Spain, governed them with great mildness and harassed the churches of God with no troubles.

> **[Note: Col. 0767C]** How these statements about Constantius are to be understood is explained in more than one place in our work, and especially under 4 October, in no. 94 of the commentary prefixed to the Acts of Saints Thyrsus and his fellow martyrs.

When he died in Britain, while Maximian was still alive, he left those same provinces to be governed by his son Constantine, a most eminent devotee of the Christian religion.

> **[Note: Col. 0767C]** Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 24, relates that this occurred, as Pagi places it in his *Critica* under the year 306, when Constantius Chlorus was already suffering from the illness by which he died.

18. After he had been strengthened in his rule and had obtained the monarchy of the Roman empire through very great wars [Note: Surius inserts between this word and the next: “Having been initiated into the laws of the Christian religion by blessed Pope Sylvester.” From these words—which, however, do not occur in our manuscript and perhaps therefore are not Helinand’s—the author appears to accept the baptism of Constantine the Great by Pope Sylvester. But whether Constantine was truly initiated by baptism by St Sylvester is discussed in the historical Commentary on that emperor, chapter 2, inserted in our work under 21 May, the day on which he is commemorated in certain sacred calendars, and composed by Papebroch.], he granted to his most blessed mother Helena the right and authority to honour and exalt the burial places of the holy martyrs, while he himself, occupied with the same endeavour almost throughout the whole world, did likewise [Note: St Helena has already been treated by us under 18 August, the day on which she is entered in the present Roman Martyrology. Whether what is here related—that Constantine the Great granted this holy mother of his authority to raise the bodies of the holy martyrs, and himself exercised it throughout the whole world—certainly agrees with the truth may be determined from the discussion there in the Commentary prefixed to the Acts of St Helena, and likewise in the historical Commentary on Constantine the Great cited in the preceding note.]. In the monastery of blessed Gereon, very many memorials of this matron worthy of God [Note: The collegiate church of St Gereon at Cologne—or, if one prefers, the college of canons attached to it—was formerly a monastery, as Gelenius teaches in *On the Greatness of Cologne Agrippina*, syntagma 2, §1, and the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 722. Hence it is doubtless so called here as well. But the memorials of which discussion is made here do not prove that it was founded by St Helena, since they could have been placed there only some centuries after Helena’s time had passed.] are still preserved; and frequent miracles, repeatedly performed there at her memorial, testify what sort of woman she was.

19. Among the many remarkable works of her devotion, she indeed constructed over the bodies of that same holy martyr and his companions—where the aforesaid holy martyrs [Note: The word “Mauri” is inserted between this word and the next in the Audomarus manuscript and in Surius.] also rest, for the singular consolation of mourners and the sick—a distinguished church, utterly incapable of being explained by any expression of speech or imitated by artistic workmanship: a structure wondrous and lofty. She adorned it so with the brilliance of metals and variety of craftsmanship, and strengthened it with walls so massive and high, that common report declares that nothing greater has existed or will exist in all those regions.

20. It is said that it contained no wooden material, or any material so readily yielding to age or neglect, since there was such abundance there of solid marble that the entire work was supported by columns of that kind, strong and beautiful. Such a golden splendour shone from it that, gleaming within and without with the elegance of mosaic work, it received from its inhabitants the name “At the Golden Saints” (*Ad Aureos sanctos*) [Note: Concerning the name by which the church or basilica of St Gereon at Cologne was called, Gregory of Tours writes thus in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, book 1, chapter 62: “The inhabitants chose to call the basilica itself ‘the Golden Saints.’”]. Since this could not of itself please the supreme Maker of all things, it was furnished, so as to shine still more richly and worthily, with many suitable heralds and ministers of divine praise, fitting for it [Note: What is reported here, without saying by whom it was done, is attributed by Gelenius to St Helena, but without any ancient authority.].

21. Thus St Maternus, bishop of Trier, as first shepherd directed the church of Cologne Agrippina with worthy governance [Note: St Maternus, bishop of Trier, has already been treated by us under 14 September, the day on which he appears in the present Roman Martyrology; and it is clear from what is said there that what Helinand here records about him is true.]. The writings concerning his deeds recount that his life shone with many virtues. The third bishop of this see known to us, successor of St Severinus, confessor of Christ, was named Evergislus [Note: Between St Maternus and St Severinus, Euphratas sat at Cologne Agrippina. Thus St Evergislus, who immediately succeeded St Severinus in the see of Cologne, was not the third but the fourth bishop of this see. Yet Helinand perhaps calls him “the third known to him,” because Euphratas, infected with the Arian heresy, was, according to some, deposed from the episcopate. See the writers of the enlarged *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 622 ff. Moreover, the bishop of Cologne discussed here is called “Evergisilus” in our Audomarus manuscript and by Surius, in agreement with most other literary monuments that speak of him. But since in our codex he is called “Evergisilus,” why might Gregory of Tours, *The Glory of the Martyrs*, book 1, chapter 62, have called him “Eberegisilus,” given only a slight difference between the two names?]. One day, suffering severely from a headache, he came to pray at the memorial of the blessed martyrs Gereon and his companions; and while no raised monument of that holy treasure yet stood out to mark it [Note: This indicates, I think, that at that time there was not yet in that church any monument projecting from the earth to indicate at what place in the church of Gereon St Gereon and his companions lay buried.], he entered the church and began the verse customarily sung in praise of the saints: “The saints shall exult in glory.” Immediately an answer came from that venerable resting-place of the saints’ bodies: “They shall rejoice in their dwellings.” When the bishop heard this in amazement, he at once cried aloud praise to God with all who were present. Drawing near, he applied to his head, as a healing remedy, dust from that place; and, having marked the place with the utmost reverence, withdrew [Note: What Helinand here relates about St Evergislus corresponds to what his biographer recounts, except that Helinand presents only obscurely the latter of the two miracles plainly related by that biographer. But did all the circumstances recounted by Helinand and St Evergislus’s biographer really accompany this latter miracle? If the cited biographer and Helinand are to be trusted, it happened to St Evergislus while he was in the church of St Gereon at Cologne Agrippina. But if credence is to be given to Gregory of Tours, *The Glory of the Martyrs*, book 1, chapter 62, the miracle occurred to Evergislus not in Cologne Agrippina, but while he was staying in a village near that city; and he was miraculously cured of his headache not by dust which he himself had taken from the Cologne church of St Gereon, as the aforesaid biographer says, but by dust taken thence and brought to him by a deacon.

But what are we to do here? Gregory, being a sixth-century writer, is much older than Helinand and St Evergislus’s biographer—the latter of whom flourished most probably no earlier than the ninth century, the former only in the thirteenth—and consequently is much less distant than they from the fifth century, when this miracle most probably occurred. Therefore Gregory is here to be preferred to those two writers. Further, since the first of the two miracles which, as stated, the biographer of St Evergislus and Helinand recount must certainly, as reflection will show, have happened to St Evergislus nowhere other than in the church of St Gereon at Cologne, it follows that it occurred not when St Evergislus was miraculously healed of the headache, but either before or after, contrary to the teaching of Helinand and the cited biographer. Gelenius most probably observed this. For in his work entitled *On the Greatness of Cologne Agrippina*, book III, syntagma 2, §1, he writes:

> Among their number [the miracles by which the church of St Gereon and his companions was made illustrious] is that which befell Bishop Blessed Evergislus . . . . When he was afflicted by sharp pains of the head, or cephalalgia, he calmed them with dust gathered at the memorials of the saints of this place, as Blessed Gregory of Tours testifies in *Miracles*, book I, chapter 62. Evergislus also at another time recognized there the help of angels, when, reverently approaching these thresholds and greeting the saints with the verse of Psalm 148, “The saints shall exult in glory,” he heard the angels reply: “They shall rejoice in their dwellings.”

Further, Fisenus, in his *History of the Church of Liège* under the year 450, no. 38, commenting on this passage of Helinand, writes of St Evergislus:

> While on one occasion, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, he was prayerfully visiting the holier places of the city of Cologne, he entered the church of St Gereon and, kneeling, greeted the blessed martyrs by reciting this verse: “The saints shall exult in glory.” Immediately this reply was divinely returned, to the great astonishment of the crowd standing by: “They shall rejoice in their dwellings.” At the same time he perceived himself divinely instructed that there was there a burial-place of the holy martyrs, whence the voice appeared to proceed, and that it was the very day of their martyrdom. Both facts had been unknown until that time.

So he writes. But what determinate place in the church of Gereon could be meant, in which St Evergislus was divinely taught that the holy martyrs’ burial-place lay? In Gregory of Tours’s time, we learn from that writer’s words that there still survived in the middle of the church of Gereon a well—or, more probably, at least part of a well—into which, as report then had it, fifty Theban martyrs had been cast after martyrdom. Yet it is rendered unlikely by the veneration of the earliest Christians for martyrs that the bodies of those fifty saints were still deposited there in St Evergislus’s time. That veneration most probably—indeed, one might say certainly—caused them not long after the martyrdom to draw the Thebans’ bodies from the well and grant them honourable burial, as was fitting, together with the other bodies of our other martyrs killed with St Gereon. Nor is it at all contrary to the truth that Christians then did this in the vicinity or circumference of that well, on the very site where the church of Gereon is now seen. But even if this were so, no one who considers what Rudolph, abbot of Saint-Trond, records in his letter—soon to be transferred here at the end of the posthumous glory of our saints—about the bodies of martyrs discovered in the church of Gereon at Cologne by St Norbert, one of which most people believed to be St Gereon’s, will readily believe that all these bodies lay there separately and scattered about, but rather that they were heaped together in one and the same place and enclosed as though in one tomb.

That being so, I do not sufficiently see what Helinand and Fisenus mean, in the words transcribed above, by the place which could have been revealed as the common burial-place, as it were, of St Gereon and his companions, and marked with utmost reverence by St Evergislus. And it is certainly clear that St Gereon’s body was not found by St Evergislus, contrary to what this later writer also notes in the margin, since, as will become evident below, it was not discovered before the year 1121.].

22. Very many such things could indeed be recounted upon trustworthy report, if concern for the brevity promised did not prevent it. For works of power were not, and are not, rare there; they are almost daily occurrences. Whoever converses with any religious devotee of that church marvels alike at their number and greatness. For whoever asks there for any healing with faith that does not sleep never doubts that the health desired is always present for him there. SS Victor, Cassius, and Florentius with their fellow-soldiers likewise never cease frequently to give such indications of their merits—things which surely no one could recount fully in words, still less in writing. Yet in their own places, where they are miraculously much frequented, they are celebrated more abundantly in reports and trustworthy testimonies, although the things published as occurring individually should rightly be ascribed to the merits of all together.

23. But through the intercessions of the holy martyrs, whose bodies it deserved to receive and cherish in its bosom, the holy church of Cologne does not cease to cultivate even to this day the unviolated faith which it remembers having received from Maternus, its first bishop. A famous custom has grown up there: the blessed martyrs Gereon, Victor, Cassius, Florentius, and their companions—crowned by a threefold martyrdom and reverently buried in three places—are honoured on one day, namely the sixth day before the Ides of October, with an appropriate feast. Yet it is doubtful whether their martyrdom was completed on one day or two, because Verona, the furthest place of the aforesaid martyrdom, lies no fewer than twenty-six miles from the most splendid basilica of St Victor; and it is hard to believe that this could have been done in one day, except by the hasty assault of excessive fury, especially because delays were necessary at each individual place [Note: Regarding the twenty-six thousand, or miles, by which Helinand here measures the distance from Verona—or, from what has been said above, Bonn—to the church of St Victor or the town of Xanten, he most probably understands Gallic leagues by the “miles” of which he speaks. In any case he cannot be understood to mean German leagues, since between Bonn and Cologne Agrippina there are at most four, or indeed only three, ordinary German leagues, and between that latter city and Xanten scarcely more than twelve.].

24. Therefore, brothers, let us celebrate the yearly joys of this day in such a way that through their intercession they may become continual for us. Let us rejoice in their glory in such a way that, by words of instruction and examples of good works, we may gain with us, in unfeigned charity, as many as we can. For, as a certain sage of this world said, to will the same things and not to will the same things is the firmest friendship. And if the holy martyrs, our patrons, find us calling to them and speaking of them in the disposition in which they themselves were, they will certainly not disdain to look upon us as strangers, but as their own and members of their household; and, by that love in which they never cease to burn forever, they will judge our cause to be their own. Thus it will come about that we shall not lack the necessary aid in this present age, and in the age to come shall be joined to their everlasting fellowship, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, being God, lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0771]

# Chronicle of Helinand, Monk of Froidmont

## Book Forty-Five

[Note: The beginning is missing. “For in the author’s autograph, preserved among the monks of Froidmont,” says Dom Tissier (*Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, VII, 73), “this final part begins with quire 79 and ends with 84; therefore quire 78 is missing and only six remain.” — On the various sources from which Helinand drew, see *Patrologia*, vol. CLX, from col. 120.]

[Note: In this final part of Helinand’s *Chronicles* which we have published, he normally follows Duke Sigebert, reporting his words and making them, as it were, his own. Whenever he adds his own material, he prefixes in the autograph the word “Author.” But since it is often uncertain how far Helinand’s own words extend, whether he continues the discourse or begins a new text of Sigebert, I have very frequently omitted that word “Author,” otherwise itself intrusive. Yet where I judged it necessary, I have supplied it.]

**The year of Christ 634.**

Romans and Saracens fight with varying outcome. Oswald and Oswin, successors of Edwin, are slain by Cædwalla after becoming apostates. Dagobert defeats the Slavs in war.

635. Pope Severinus died on the fourth day before the Nones of August; and the episcopal see was vacant for four months and twenty-four days. After him John, the seventy-fourth pope and the fourth of that name, a Dalmatian by nation, son of Venantius the *scholasticus*, held the see for one year, nine months, and twenty-eight days. He sent much money through Istria and Dalmatia to redeem captives. He built a church for the holy martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, Maurus, and others, whose relics he caused to be brought from Dalmatia. He ordained eighteen bishops. After Abu Bakr, Umar reigned for twelve years. When the Saracens invaded Syria, Heraclius transferred the Lord’s cross from Jerusalem to Constantinople. Oswald, son of King Æthelfrith, having received the kingdom of the Northumbrians, slew Cædwalla, king of the Britons; and because he held firmly to the faith of Christ, he surpassed all the kings of Britain. He became a Christian among the Scots and brought under his dominion peoples of four languages: Picts, Scots, Britons, and Angles. He reigned eight years.
