At that time the worship of idols in England grew cold to ashes. Bishop Aidan, disciple of St Columba, coming from Scotland, shone among the Angles in holiness and teaching. When he preached to the people in the Scottish language and an interpreter was lacking, King Oswald himself, clothed in royal dress, performed the interpreter’s office. The same king also deprived himself of food for the sake of the poor.

Dagobert defeated the Gascons in war. 636. Pope John died on the third day before the Ides of October; and the episcopal see was vacant one month and ten days. After him Theodore, the seventy-fifth pope, a Greek by nation and son of Theodore, bishop of the city of Jerusalem, held the see for six years, five months, and twenty-five days. He was a lover of the poor, generous and kindly beyond all others, and very merciful. In his time Mauritius the *cartularius* was killed by the soldiers of Isaac; his head was placed on a stake in a place at Ravenna as an example. Not long afterward Isaac died, and Theodore the patrician was sent as exarch in his place to govern Italy. Then Pyrrhus came from Africa to the thresholds of the Apostles; he had been patriarch of Constantinople. He offered a document in which he condemned the things written by himself or his predecessors against the Catholic faith. Pope Theodore restored him to his see; but afterward, returning to his vomit and condemned by the same Theodore, he returned to the East. Then the bodies of the saints Primus and Felicianus were raised from the sand-pit on the Nomentan Way and placed in the church of Blessed Stephen. He also made an oratory for St Eupillus the martyr, deposed Paul, the heretic of Constantinople, and ordained forty-six bishops. Having captured Damascus, the Saracens occupy Phoenicia and Egypt.

637. At this time three brothers flourished in Francia: Ado, Rado, and Dado, also called Audoenus. Each founded a monastery; Dado was the referendary of King Dagobert. A referendary was so called because public documents were referred to him, in order that they might be sealed by the king’s ring through him. Eligius the goldsmith, long famous at the court of King Lothair, had encouraged them to this; from King Dagobert’s gift he also built the monastery of Solignac. There St Remaclus, coming from Aquitaine, gave himself to be trained under him in Christ’s service. St Audoenus built a monastery within the forest of Brie, called Resbatis; there St Aurea flourished, and St Eligius set her over a monastery of virgins which he had built in Paris.

**638.**

The Saracens capture Jerusalem, which they had besieged for two years. St Amandus, having later obtained the bishopric of Tongeren, labours in the ministry of the word. Under him St Laudoaldus flourished; instructing from boyhood Lambert, son of Aper, an illustrious man, he led him into the way of God. Abbot Romaric and Goeric, bishop of Metz, flourish.

639. The Saracens occupy Syria. The Jews in Spain become Christians. For Sisebut, most glorious king of the Visigoths, subjected to himself by warfare many provinces in Spain and many military cities, and converted the Jews in his kingdom to the faith of Christ. The Saracens capture Antioch.

**640.**

Dagobert sends his son Sigibert as king to the Austrasians, under the guardianship of Pippin and Bishop Cunibert. St Arnulf, formerly mayor of the palace at Metz and then bishop of Metz, and after being bishop a solitary, falls asleep in Christ. “This Arnulf,” says Peter Damian, “was father of Pippin and grandfather of Charlemagne.” He held a duchy not far from Flanders in Lotharingia. When, putting aside affection for wife and children, he sought the wilderness, it happened that he had to cross the river Moselle. Coming to the middle of the bridge, where the river is deeper, he threw his ring into it under this bond of covenant: “When I find this ring,” he said, “then I shall undoubtedly trust that I have been loosed from the bonds of my sins.” Having done this, he sought the wilderness, where, dead to the world, he lived to God for no small time. Meanwhile, when the bishop of Metz died, he was elected. Since he abstained from flesh-meat as he had been accustomed to do in the wilderness, a fish was presented to him. When the cook opened it, he found the ring and joyfully offered it to his master, who immediately recognized it. There is a journey of two days from the bridge into which the ring had been thrown to the place where the fish was presented to the bishop. Then the man of God was more deeply awestruck and judged himself all the more indebted to God the more he experienced His goodness. Choosing a successor for himself, he again sought the wilderness, and died there. His son Clodulf, later bishop of Metz, imitated his father’s holiness. Doda, Clodulf’s mother, was enclosed at Trier.

When Eadbald, king of the Angles, who had reigned twenty-five years, died, his son Combert, born of Emma, daughter of the king of the Franks, reigned twenty-four, or according to others twenty-five, years. Religious toward God, devoted to his country, and just toward all, he razed to the ground all temples and shrines of the gods, and commanded the Lenten fast to be observed throughout his kingdom. His daughter Etagota lived as a nun and a holy woman at the monastery of Kala in Gaul.

641. The Persians again fight the Saracens and are defeated; their king Hormizd having fled, the Saracens subjugate all Persia.

**642.**

Emperor Heraclius dies, and after him his son Constantine rules. In the fourth month of his reign he was killed by poison by Martina, his stepmother, and Pyrrhus the patriarch; and Martina seized the empire with her son Heraclonas. Under them Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, renewed the heresy and established one operation in Christ’s divinity and humanity. Bede places Heraclonas immediately after Heraclius, together with his mother Martina; after them, Constantine, Heraclius’s brother, whom he says reigned seven months. Under these rulers, Paul, Pyrrhus’s successor, afflicted Catholics by open persecution, some with prisons, some with exiles, and some with beatings. After Constantine, the same Bede says that his son Constantine reigned twenty-eight years.

When Sisebut, king of the Visigoths, had died, Svinthila reigned two years. Because the Saxons helped Dagobert against the Wends, he remitted to them an annual tribute of five hundred marks. Heraclonas, after his nose was cut off, and his mother, after her tongue was cut out, were exiled. After them Constans, also called Constantine, son of Constantine, reigned twenty-six years.

643. King Oswald is killed by Penda, king of the Mercians. His right hand, lavish in many alms, lies incorrupt with arm, skin, and sinews, while all the rest of the body has dissolved into ashes. When King Penda of the Mercians stirred up rebellion, Oswald himself, bearing brotherly goodwill in his heart, prayed to God for the souls of his faithful people. After his death, the fury of the insatiable victor cut off his arms with his hands and his head and hung them upon a stake. The arm with the hands remains unharmed. It was placed by his brother Oswiu at the city of Bamburgh in a shrine and is displayed as a miracle. His head, buried at Lindisfarne by his brother, is now said to be at Durham, between the arms of St Cuthbert.

When Queen Ostryth, wife of Æthelred king of the Mercians and daughter of King Oswiu, moved by affection for her paternal uncle, wished to place the bones of the rest of his body in her monastery of Bardney in Mercia, not far from the city of Lincoln, the monks expelled her. They begrudged the dead man the repose of his bones because he had obtained the kingdom over them by the law of war. But in the dead of night, by a lamp sent from heaven over the relics, they of their own accord asked for what they had earlier rejected. There, from the falling blood, turf grew green again; by it a horse was healed, and when it was affixed, a consuming fire avoided it by winding turns. A little powder (*pulviculus*) from the washing of his relics heals those out of their minds. The stake that had received innocent blood grants healing to the desperate by its washing. His son Oswin reigned after him for twenty-seven years. Judicael, king of the Britons, purchases for himself Dagobert’s favour.

**644.**

Umar the *Amir* builds his temple in Jerusalem. Since the structure could not stand in any way, at the suggestion of Jews he orders the cross removed from Mount Olivet above it; and then the structure could stand. In Spain, after Svinthila was rejected by the Visigoths for his cruelty, Sisenand, raised to kingship through Dagobert’s assistance, reigned twenty years.

645. King Dagobert dies at the estate of Épinay in the district of Paris and is buried in the basilica of St Denis. In certain chronicles it is said that Dagobert died in the year of the Lord 641. By a vision it was revealed concerning him to someone that, when his soul was brought to judgment and many saints cried out against it for despoiling their churches, and evil angels wished to drag him to the punishments of hell, he was delivered through the intervention of St Denis, to whom he had been especially devoted. After him his son Clovis reigned seventeen years, while his brother Sigibert was already reigning in Austrasia. This Clovis’s mayor of the palace was Erchinoald. Clovis had a wife of Saxon stock named Balthild.

646. St Remaclus becomes bishop of Maastricht. Rodoald, brother of Itta and maternal uncle of St Gertrude, archbishop of Trier, shines in that city in holiness and teaching; his sister Severa was an abbess. After Rothari, his son Rodoald reigns among the Lombards for five years. Pippin, mayor of the palace, dies; his son Grimoald succeeds him at the court of King Sigibert.

647. A Persian, pretending that he wished to worship Umar, kills him by plunging a sword into his belly. After him Uthman reigns for ten years.

**648.**
Pope Theodore died on 14 May; and the see was vacant for five months and eighteen days. After him Martin, the seventy-sixth pope, a native of the city of Tuder in the province of Tuscia, sat for six years, one month, and twenty-seven days. The Saracens occupy Africa. King Sigebert engages in war with Radulf, duke of the Thuringians. Saint Furseus flourished in [Col. 0776B] Ireland. Having gone abroad for Christ’s sake, he was honourably received in Gaul by King Clovis, son of Dagobert, and founded the monastery of Lagny. Not long afterwards his brothers Foillanus and Vultánus, following him with the same resolve of pilgrimage, became renowned throughout Gaul. Foillanus subsequently founded, through the gift of the virgin Gertrude, the monastery of Fosses, where he also rests, crowned with martyrdom. 

Once Furseus fell ill, and, when he saw himself surrounded by the darkness of a deep gloom, he beheld four hands stretched down towards him from above, holding him by the arms and flying beneath wings—for they were beneath wings. He also saw a third angel, armed with a white shield, distinguished by splendour, sword, and brightness. These three sang, one beginning: “The saints shall go from strength to strength; [Col. 0776C] the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. VIII [as cited]). There was a rising movement in the chant, and a settling at its close. He also heard another chant, as though unfamiliar, of many thousands of angels, from which he could scarcely understand a few words. They went forth to meet Christ.

Then one of those from heaven commanded the armed angel who went before to restore the man to his body, saying that he must carry back with him his concern. As they returned, Furseus, then for the first time recognizing himself to be stripped of his body, did not wish to return or to be separated from them. The angel answered him: “When the concern foretold for you has been fulfilled, we shall return.” He had been dead from evening until cockcrow. But on reviving, he immediately requested and received holy communion, and remained ill on that day and the following one. At midnight, on the third day, [Col. 0776D] he died with his hands stretched out in prayer; and he saw those same three angels, two at his sides and the third, armed, at his head.

As the angels raised him up, he heard one of the demons saying: “Let us go before him, and stir up battles before his face.” Then the devil began to accuse him most subtly, saying: “It is written: ‘Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to them, are worthy of death’” (Rom. I [as cited]). “This man consented as often as he failed to resist.”

The angel: “He resisted when he could, and when he judged that resistance was called for.”

The devil: “He often uttered idle words.”

The angel: “Unless you bring forward principal crimes, he shall not perish because of trifling ones.”

The devil: “It is written: ‘Unless you forgive men their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive [Col. 0777A] you your sins’” (Matt. XVIII [as cited]).

The angel: “Where did he take vengeance for himself?”

The devil: “It is not written, ‘if you take vengeance,’ but ‘if you do not forgive from your hearts.’”

The angel: “Let us be judged before the Lord.”

The devil: “It is written: ‘Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven’” (ibid.). “This man did not fulfil that.”

The angel: “Where was he proud?”

The devil: “It is not written, ‘Do not be proud,’ but: ‘Unless you are converted,’ and so forth.”

The angel: “Let us be judged before the Lord.”

Confounded, the devil withdrew. Then the angel said to him: “Look upon the world.” Looking, he saw four fires in the air, separated from one another by certain intervals: those of lying, covetousness, dissension, impiety, and fraud. Each kindled the other. When Furseus feared these fires, the angel said: [Col. 0777B] “What you did not kindle shall not burn in you.”

Then the angel divided the flame into two walls, and Furseus saw opposite him four demons, one of whom said: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII [as cited]).

The angel: “What did he fail to do of his Lord’s will?”

The demon: “He accepted gifts from wicked persons.”

The angel: “He believed that they had done penance.”

The demon: “He ought first to have tested their repentance and perseverance, and then to have received them.” And he added: “Every offence which is not cleansed on earth, God has said is to be avenged in heaven. This man has not cleansed himself of this, nor does he here receive punishment.”

The angel: “So long as repentance is hoped for, God’s grace accompanies a person.”

The demon: “This is not a place of repentance.”

The angel: “You do not know God’s hidden judgments: [Col. 0777C] perhaps there will be repentance.”

The demon: “It is written: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself’” (Rom. XIII [as cited]).

The angel: “This man did good works towards his neighbours.”

The demon: “It is not enough for a person unless he has loved them as himself.”

The angel: “The fruit of love is to do good works.”

The demon: “But he did not fulfil the command in loving.”

The angel: “Let us be judged before the Lord.”

The demon: “He promised to renounce the world, yet contrary to the Apostle’s command he loved the world.”

The angel: “He loved the things of the world not for himself alone, but for all who were in need.”

The demon: “However it may be loved, it is contrary to the Apostle’s command and contrary to the promise made in baptism.”

The angel: “Let us be judged before the Lord.”

The demon: “It is written: ‘Unless you announce to the wicked man his [Col. 0777D] wickedness, I shall require his blood from your hand’” (Ezek. III [as cited]). “This man did not do so.”

The angel: “Of this time it is written: ‘The prudent man shall keep silence in that time, because it is an evil time’” (Prov. XI [as cited]). For when hearers despise the word, the teacher’s tongue is impeded, when he sees that the preaching they have heard is despised.”

The demon: “Nevertheless, he ought to proclaim the truth until death.”

The angel: “Let us be judged before the Lord.”

When the demons had been overcome, the angels cried: “No labour ought to seem hard, no time long, by which the glory of eternity is acquired.”

After this Furseus saw two bishops, Beatius and Medanus, speaking with him, and he believed them to be dead. Delighting in hearing the heavenly songs, he said to the angel: “It is a great joy to listen to these things.”

The [Col. 0778A] angel replied: “We are often deprived of this hearing for the sake of the mystery of the ordering of humankind, lest the demons, by corrupting human hearts, undo what we labour to proclaim.”

Then he saw these two bishops, as though coming forth from the height of heaven, and commanding him to return to the world. But as he passed before the aforesaid fires, a man leapt from the fire, the demons throwing him upon Furseus’s shoulder; pressing his cheek against Furseus’s cheek, he burned him. This was the man who, at his death, had given Furseus his garment. The angel said to him: “What you burned burned in you, although you had accepted it in order to free his soul. Preach, therefore, that none of the property of a sinner who has died in his sins is to be accepted, nor is his body to be buried in a holy place.” Then he saw his body opened in his breast, [Col. 0778B] and so he revived.

For ten years he preached to the peoples of the Goths, preaching in Ireland with a few brethren. Crossing through Britain into Saxony, he was honourably received by King Sigebert, who built him a monastery; Furseus entrusted it to his brother Foillanus, and himself went to his brother Vultánus, a hermit. After spending one year with him, he went to Gaul. There he was received by King Clovis and by the patrician, and built a monastery at the place called Lagny.

## 649

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, and Odoenus, bishop of Rouen, were illustrious, as were Philibert, abbot of the island of Hério; Richarius, abbot in Ponthieu; Geremarus, abbot of Flavigny; Angadrisma near Beauvais; and Ansegisus, son of Saint Arnulf, whom Begga, [Col. 0778C] sister of Grimoald, had married.

Of these, Richarius was born in the village of Crintula in the province of Ponthieu. From a rustic he became a man widely renowned for his religious life. He was converted to a great religious life through the priest Caidoc, whom he received as a guest when he came from Ireland. He ate barley bread mixed with ashes, and water tempered with tears. He comforted lepers in baths, and then entered the same baths after them. He preached in Britain. The devil inflicted madness upon the horse that he rode; when it had been healed through his prayer and then set aside, he thereafter used an ass. He flourished in the time of King Dagobert and his sons. He died on 26 April.

The life of the blessed Eligius was written by Saint Audoenus. Eligius was born in the territory of the city of Limoges, in the village of Catelassus, [Col. 0778D] about six miles from the aforementioned city. His father was Eucherius; his mother was called Terrigia. While he was still in her womb, his mother saw in a vision a very beautiful eagle flying over her offspring; and three times it called out to her and, as it seemed, promised her something.

The boy was entrusted to an honourable man, Albanus, a goldsmith, who managed the public workshop of the fiscal mint in the city of Limoges. After some years he left his native land and went to Francia, becoming known to a certain treasurer of King Clothar, named Bolbo. The king gave him gold and gems for the making of one saddle; from them Eligius made two. He first presented one completed saddle to the king, then the other, saying: “What remained of the gold, lest it be wasted, I have applied to this work.” From [Col. 0779A] this time he became honoured in the king’s palace.

He was tall in stature, ruddy in face, handsome in his hair, with curling locks, angelic in countenance, and of a manner at once simple and prudent. He was especially resplendent in garments adorned with gold and gems: wearing belts ornamented with gold and jewels, bright linen garments worked with metal, boots [perhaps *hocas*] covered with Saracen gold, and clothing all costly, mostly of pure silk. Yet, to avoid display, he wore haircloth next to his body beneath them. All these things he afterwards expended upon the needs of the poor. Then he used cheap clothes, girded with a cord, and was often even stripped of clothing for the sake of the poor. The king would then give him his own garment and belt, because he loved Eligius as his own soul. He had even built him a dwelling adjoining his own.

[Col. 0779B] King Dagobert also, handsome and illustrious, who had no equal among all the preceding kings of the Franks, loved him so greatly that he often withdrew from the nobles in order to be alone with Eligius. Whatever Eligius asked of him he obtained without delay, and he expended everything upon the poor, captives, and the infirm. From the time of Queen Brunhild until the time of Dagobert, the Simoniacal plague prevailed in Gaul; Eligius and Audoenus then worked diligently to remove it.

Eligius was then elected to the church of Noyon after Acatius, bishop of that city; and together with him his companion Audoenus was elected to the church of Rouen. Eligius presided over the metropolitan see of Vermand, and also over Tournai, once a royal [Col. 0779C] city, as well as Noyon, Flanders, Ghent, and Kortrijk. He and Audoenus were consecrated on the same day by Deodatus, bishop of Metz, in the third year of Clovis the Younger, on a Sunday before the Litany.

Eligius had a place set apart, into which, on fixed days, he admitted poor and infirm persons and ministered devoutly to them. He washed their foul heads, shaved their unsightly hair with his own hand, gave each of them drink and food, and dismissed them clothed if they had been naked. When they went out, he admitted others if any were present and comforted them in the same way. If at times a very large crowd gathered, he did the same for all of them. Every day he refreshed twelve persons in this manner, himself eating with them at the appropriate hour; but first he poured water over the hands of each one and with his own hand gave wine and bread.

[Col. 0779D] He built at Noyon a monastery of handmaids of Christ. The Lord revealed through him the body of Saint Quentin. But before he became bishop, there was at the king’s palace a certain Mauritius, religious in dress and a praised singer; yet he was puffed up in mind on that account, insolent in heart, and disordered in conduct. He began to boast that he would find the body of this precious martyr. But as soon as he began to dig the ground with a hoe, the handle of the digging-tool stuck to his hand. Abandoning the work he had begun, he miserably expired the following day, with worms swarming out from his hands.

When Eligius found the body of this holy martyr, he was struck by an immense light and an indescribable fragrance and could scarcely remain standing. For a globe of splendour issued from the tomb at the blow of the striker and, dazzling the eyes of all bystanders, changed the greater part of that region into the brightness of day. Yet it was midnight, very dark and gloomy. From the jaw of this holy martyr Eligius took a tooth for the healing of the sick; and a quantity of blood flowed from the tooth’s root. He also removed, as relics for himself, nails of wondrous size driven into his skull and other limbs. Then, wrapping the martyr’s body in most precious pure silk, he transferred it with the greatest care near the altar. He also constructed above it a tomb of gold, silver, and gems, of marvellous workmanship. He magnificently adorned the church as well, which had seemed small.

[Col. 0780B] After this, with great labour and persistence, he found the holy martyr Piaton in the district of Médan, in a place called Salcisnum. Similarly, the people displayed as proof the long nails removed from his body. At Soissons he also found the holy brother-martyrs Crispin and Crispinian; bringing them out of a crypt, he laid them to rest splendidly. Likewise, in the district of Beauvais, he found the blessed martyr Lucian, formerly a companion of Saint Quentin, and similarly transferred and laid him to rest.

At Paris he gave sight to a blind man on the bridge. Again at Paris, the custodian of Saint Columba informed him that in the night thieves had stripped her church of all its ornaments. Eligius then went to the oratory of Saint Columba and said: “Hear what I say, holy Columba. [Col. 0780C] My Redeemer knows that, unless you quickly restore the stolen ornaments of this shrine, I shall have thorns brought and cause this door to be barred in such a way that from today onward no veneration shall ever be offered to you in this place.” Having spoken thus, he departed. The next day the custodian rose early and found all the hangings restored as they had been before, down to the smallest covering.

Moreover, he obtained from the king permission to take down and bury the bodies of all condemned persons wherever he could find them, whether in villages or cities, from gibbets, wheels, and nooses. He appointed from among his communities corpse-bearers to attend to this duty. Accordingly, while he was in the king’s retinue in Austrasia, near the city of Strasbourg, he found a man who had ended his life by a noose that very day. As his companions were preparing his burial, Eligius came nearer and began to feel and stroke the body, soothing it from head to foot. When he perceived that the soul was present, modestly disclaiming the power of the act, he said: “What a great crime we might have committed, unless the Lord had helped us: burying this body in the earth while its soul is still within it!” He ordered the revived man to be clothed and allowed to rest. When they heard this, his persecutors again sought to put him to death. Eligius scarcely rescued him from their hands; withdrawing himself from the man’s company to avoid glory, he obtained from the king a charter of protection for him.

[Col. 0781A] These are the tombs which he made of gold, silver, and gems: those of Germanus, Severinus, Piaton, Anticus, Lucian, Genevieve, Columba, Maximian, and Julian; and especially that of blessed Martin of Tours, King Dagobert providing the expenses. He also made the tomb of Saint Brictius, and another where the body of blessed Martin had formerly lain; the mausoleum of Saint Denis the martyr in the city of Paris; and a marvellous marble canopy over it, adorned with gold and gems. He covered in gold the crypt, the frontal ornaments, and the beams around the altar-throne; upon them he placed round golden apples set with jewels. He also carefully overlaid the lectern and doors with silver. He covered the roof of the altar-throne with silver beams as well. He made a screen at the place of the former tomb, and constructed outside, at the feet of the holy martyr, an altar which is almost without equal as an ornament in Gaul and remains, to the great admiration of all, to this day. In that same church of Saint Denis King Dagobert was buried under an arch on the right-hand side.

## 650

Itta, widow of Pippin, at the admonition of Saint Amand, devoted herself and her possessions to God. She founded the monastery of Nivelles and placed over it her daughter Gertrude, a virgin worthy of God. Authbert, bishop of Cambrai, was illustrious.

(651.) King Sigebert, despairing of having offspring, built twelve monasteries for God in various places. Among them Stavelot and Malmedy were outstanding. His mayor of the palace Grimoald and Remaclus, bishop of Maastricht, assisted him in these works. Not long afterwards Remaclus, weary of worldly tumults, assumed the monastic habit at Stavelot itself.

Saint Landelinus, also called Morasus, then flourished. Authbert, bishop of Cambrai, converted him from a robber to Christ, and Pope Saint Martin ordained him to preach. He was founder of the monasteries of Lobbes, Aulne, Wallers, and Crespin, where his body rests with his disciples Adelènus and Domitianus.

At that time also flourished Gislenus of Celle; Duke Madelganus, also called Vincentius of Hautmont and of Soignies; his wife Waldetrudis of Castrilocus; Waldetrudis’s sister Aldegundis of Maubeuge; and Trudo of Hesbaye, who was growing into a novice of Christ. Besides these, many from England and Scotland were travelling as pilgrims in Gaul, namely Erto, Bertuinus, and Eloquius.

[Col. 0781D] The monastery of Fleury was founded by Abbot Leodebold. Not long afterwards the body of Saint Benedict was brought there from the fortress of Monte Cassino by the monk Agilulf. The body of his sister, Saint Scholastica, was transferred to Le Mans. After Rodoald, Aripert ruled the Lombards for nine years.

(652.) Emperor Constantine, deceived by Paul, bishop of Constantinople, decreed that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ were to be confessed—as though Christ were to be believed to will or to act in no way. For this reason Paul himself, the bishop, overturned the altar of the Apostolic See which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia. Martin therefore gathered at Rome a synod of 105 bishops and anathematized the heretics: Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul of Constantinople.

[Col. 0782A] (653.) King Sigebert adopted Grimoald’s son Hildebert as his son and heir to the kingdom. Emperor Constantine, having sent the exarch Olympius into Italy, attacks the Church of God. Jodocus, son of the king of the Britons, despising the world and his kingdom, rests in Christ as a pilgrim and hermit in the district of Ponthieu.

## 654

Fire fell from heaven, and great fear came upon humankind. There was a most grievous pestilence for three summer months. At night a good and an evil angel visibly appeared to all, circling the city; and as often as, by the command of the good angel, the evil angel struck with the spear which he seemed to carry in his hand the door of any house, so many persons from that house died on the following day. At this time Saint Foillanus of Fosses was martyred.

## 655

[Col. 0782B]

The Saracens, having captured Rhodes, overthrew its famous colossus; nine hundred camels were laden with its bronze. This is one of the seven wonders of the world. For how could so great a mass of bronze either have been cast, or, once cast, raised?

## 656

Emperor Constantine, engaging the Saracens in a naval battle, was disgracefully defeated. King Sigebert of the Austrasians died, entrusting his son Dagobert, still very small, to the fidelity of Grimoald, so that by Grimoald’s aid he might be advanced to his father’s kingdom.

After King Oswald, his brother Wius, the first of the English to be famous for miracles, ruled among the Bernicians; and Oswinus, son of Ostiti, among the Deirans. Oswin was at last killed by Oswiu, after, avoiding battle, he had secretly withdrawn to an outlying estate. He was a generous man and devoted to God.

Afterwards this same Osvius, king of the Northumbrians, having made a vow to the God of heaven, fought King Penda of the Mercians with no large army, slew King Penda amid the immense slaughter of the Mercians, and brought the Mercian people to conversion to Christ. He also subjected the Picts to the kingdom of the English. From that time he ruled over nearly all the English, and increased Christianity through Bishops Angilbert and Wilfrid, and finally through Archbishop Theodore. He built many dwellings for the servants of God. The chief among them was then a monastery of women, now of monks, thirty miles north of York, called in its ancient name *Sceneshalh*, but now Whitby. Begun by Hilda, a woman of distinguished religious life, [Col. 0782D] it was greatly advanced by Ethelfreda, daughter of the same king.

## 657

Olympius, patrician and exarch, sent into Italy by Emperor Constantine to kill Pope Martin or bring him to Constantinople, ordered his *spatharius* (sword-bearer) to kill him at Mass while he offered Olympius communion. But the Lord blinded the *spatharius*: when Martin gave communion or the peace to Olympius, he did not see him. The *spatharius* himself later affirmed this upon oath. Thus Olympius was compelled by necessity to make peace with Martin.

Afterwards he went with an army against the Saracens in Sicily; and, through sin, a greater destruction came upon the Roman army, which afterwards perished entirely by disease. Grimoald, mayor of the palace, having had his lord Dagobert, son of Sigebert, tonsured and sent into Scotland through Dido, bishop of Poitiers, made his own son Hildebert king of the Austrasians.

[Col. 0783A] Hothmen, *ammira* of the Saracens, having been killed, Muhamas, made *ammiras* from an *ammireo*, ruled for twenty-five years.

(658.) The Franks, grieving over Grimoald’s treachery against Sigebert’s son, seized him and sent him to prison at Paris. When they presented him for the judgment of Clovis, Clovis caused him to waste away in chains in prison by a bitter death, and made his younger son Hildric king of the Austrasians. Itta, mother of Saint Gertrude, died.

After Bishop Theodard was martyred, Saint Lambert, son of Count Aper, brought glory of noble birth and grace of holiness to the bishopric of Maastricht. At Arras, when the body of Saint Vedastus was transferred by Authbert, bishop of Cambrai, in the presence of Lambert of Tongeren, Audomarus of Tarascon, and other holy bishops and abbots, Audomarus—blind through old age—was given sight by the prayers of the bishops present and the merits of Saint Vedastus. Grieving that he had been freed from the blindness which he rejoiced to think God had sent him for his salvation, he was blinded again according to his desire. In certain chronicles it is read that King Clovis died in this year.

(659.) After Olympius, Theodore the exarch, surnamed Calliopas, was sent with Theodore, the imperial chamberlain. They took Pope Martin from the church of the Saviour, called the Constantinian, and brought him to Constantinople. He was sent [Col. 0783C] into exile at Cherson, where he ended his life on 17 September. He made thirty-three bishops.

After him Eugenius, the seventy-seventh pope and first of that name, sat for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. He was a Roman by nation, from the first Aventine district, a cleric from the cradle; kind, gentle, meek, gracious to all, and especially distinguished for holiness. Emperor Constans subjected Slavonia to himself.

## 660

Muhamas, *ammiras* of the Saracens, made an agreement with Emperor Constantine that the Saracens should pay the Romans every day a tribute of one thousand coins, a slave, and a horse.

King Clovis, uncovering the body of Saint Denis of Paris with insufficient reverence, though greedily, broke off and stole the bone of his arm; he immediately fell into perpetual madness. Aripert, king of the Lombards, having died, his sons Godepert and Perctarit spent a year not so much arranging the kingdom as contending over it.

Pope Eugenius commanded that, on the day of his death, alms should be distributed in full to the poor, the clergy, and the household of the presbytery. He made twenty-one bishops. He died on 2 June, and the see was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days.

(661.) After him Vitalian, the seventy-eighth pope, a native of Segni in the province of Campania, sat for fourteen years and six months. As Bede says, soon after Vitalian had been ordained, Emperor Constantine sent to Saint Peter golden Gospels adorned all around with white gems of marvellous size. [Col. 0784A] He himself, some years later—that is, in the sixth indiction—came to Rome and offered upon the altar of Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold.

Saint Amandus of Elnone died.

For thus it is read in the account of his death:

“In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 661, in the fourth indiction, the fifteenth epact, with the fourth concurrent, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; Easter falling on the fifth day before the Kalends of April; on the twenty-first moon; on the eighth day before the Ides of February, a Sunday, on the first moon—Saint Amandus died, about ninety years old. He was born in the year of the Lord 571, on the Nones of May, in the province of the Agenais, in the district of that region called Herbatilicus, of his father Serenus and his mother Amantia, [Col. 0784B] in the seventh year in which Justinian’s successor, the younger Canus, held the height of imperial power in the commonwealth with his wife Sophia.

“At that time John, the sixty-third pontiff in the order of the bishops of the Roman Church, governed the chair of that city in the eighth year of his episcopate. At the ordination of Pope Saint Gregory, Saint Amandus was in the twenty-second year of his age; at that pope’s death, in his thirty-fifth. That was the year 605 from the Lord’s Nativity and the second year of Phocas’s reign, as Bede relates in his chronicles. The same Saint Amandus was very intimate with Pope Martin. He died in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Vitalian, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.”

There survives a decretal letter of Pope Martin to this Saint Amandus, in which it is stated that Amandus wished to lay down his pastoral office because of the disobedience of those priests and deacons who, after their ordinations, were defiled by falling into sin. The same most blessed pope dissuades him from that intention, urging patience and admonishing him to show them no indulgence in their offence, but to depose all who had fallen from office and assign them to continual penance.

“For if,” he says, “we seek for advancement to sacred orders such persons as no blemish and no contagion of life can hinder from sacred orders, how much more, if a man has fallen after his ordination and is found liable for the sin of transgression, must he be entirely forbidden [Col. 0784D] to handle, with filthy and polluted hands, the mystery of our salvation? Let such a one always be deposed in this life according to the statutes of the sacred canons, so that, when He who searches the inner mind and does not rejoice that any of the sheep should stray sees his sincere repentance, He may have him reconciled at the dreadful judgment.”

The saint himself built the monastery called Blandinium in the fortress of Ghent; another called Marchiennes; and another to which he himself gave the name Lochosa, or Rotnace, almost adjoining the aforementioned monastery. He also built the cell called Barisiacus, a place which King Childeric and Queen Brunhild seem to have granted to him with its adjoining appurtenances. Finally, after founding the monastery at Elnone, he there [Col. 0785A] happily served Christ with his followers until the day of his death.

Leaving his country and parents, he was received, after his youth had already passed, on the island of Ora, forty miles from the shore of the Ocean. There, by prayer, he drove away an enormous serpent. Afterwards he went to Tours, to Saint Martin; there cutting off the hair of his head, he entered upon the rank of the clergy. Afterwards, having received a blessing from the abbot of that place and the brethren, he went to Bourges to Austregisilus. He was received by him and by his archdeacon Sulpicius, and a cell was built for him beside the church upon the upper wall of the city. There, covered in haircloth and ashes, content with barley bread and a little water, he lived for nearly fifteen years.

[Col. 0785B] After this, the thought occurred to him that he should visit the thresholds of the Apostles; and he did so, taking with him only one companion. There by day he went about the holy places, and by night returned to the church of Saint Peter. One day, when everyone had gone out, he remained there out of devotion, wishing to keep vigil through the whole night; one of the guards found him and, treating him contemptuously and with insults, expelled him from the church. But as he sat in a trance of mind before the church doors, Saint Peter appeared to him, warning him to return to Gaul for preaching. On his return he was compelled by the king and bishops to become a bishop. He redeemed captives and boys from overseas by paying a price. Having also regenerated them in the spiritual washing, he ordered that they be thoroughly instructed in letters; [Col. 0785C] and, after granting them freedom, he placed them in various churches. We have heard that many of them became bishops, priests, or distinguished abbots.

Returning from Rome, he embarked a second time and reached the place called Centumcellae. There, while one night he was praying alone, as was his custom, an unclean spirit seized one of his servants by the hand and dragged him toward the sea, intending to drown him there. As he was being dragged, he cried out: “Christ, help me! Christ, help me!” The malignant spirit answered him mockingly: “What sort of Christ?” And while the boy who was being dragged was silent, Saint Amandus said: “Tell him, son: ‘Christ, the crucified Son of the living God.’” At once, at this utterance, the enemy vanished like smoke.

Not long afterward, while he was sailing through the open sea and speaking the word of the Lord to the sailors, [Col. 0785D] a fish of extraordinary size appeared. The sailors cast a net into the sea and caught that same fish. While they feasted and rejoiced, a violent storm arose. The sailors ran to the servant of God, who ordered them to have confidence. As he sat in the stern, Saint Peter appeared to him and said: “Do not fear: neither you nor those with you shall perish.” At these words the storm was immediately calmed.

He converted the people of Ghent, who were still idolaters at that time. When his companions had left him alone there because of the barrenness and sterility of the place, he earned his food by the labour of his hands, while diligently attending to the office of preaching. A certain companion of Frankish stock, named Dortho, was residing in the city of Tournai to settle lawsuits. And behold, a certain accused man was brought before him, whom the whole crowd had shouted [Col. 0786A] was worthy of death; he had been beaten with many blows and was already half-alive in body. Dortho decreed that he ought to be fastened to the gallows. But Amandus, arriving, requested that he might deign to spare his life. Dortho refused and ordered him hanged; once hanged, he breathed out his spirit. Saint Amandus went to the gallows and ordered the man, taken down from the wood, to be carried to his own cell. When the brethren had left the cell, he lay upon the dead man’s body and, praying with tears, restored him to life. Having washed his body and scars, he restored flesh to flesh in such a way that no trace appeared of the wounds he had formerly suffered. Thus, sending him back to his own home, he restored him unharmed to his parents. By this miracle he made converts to Christ.

After this, crossing the Danube, he went into Slavia [Col. 0786B] to preach, in hope of martyrdom; after converting a few people there, he returned to his own sheep. King Dagobert, excessively devoted to the love of women and inflamed by every filthiness of lust, seemed to have no offspring. For this he earnestly prayed to the Lord and was at last heard. When he had received a son, he caused Saint Amandus to be sought out—the man whom he had earlier ordered expelled from his kingdom because Amandus reproved him for capital crimes, something no bishop had dared to do. He came to the king at the royal estate called Clichy. The king threw himself at his feet and begged forgiveness; Amandus quickly raised him from the ground and graciously pardoned him. The king said to him: “I deeply repent that I acted foolishly against you; but I beg you, do not remember my injury. The Lord has given me [Col. 0786C] a son, not through my merits. I ask you to deign to wash him in the sacred font and receive him as your spiritual son.”

Amandus strongly refused, knowing it is written that one serving as a soldier for God ought not to become entangled in secular affairs, and that a man of quiet and retirement ought not to frequent royal palaces; he withdrew from the king’s presence. Immediately the king sent to him the illustrious man Dodo and, with him, the venerable man Eligius, who at that time lived in the king’s palace in secular dress. They persuaded him to yield to the king’s requests. He at once made the forty-day-old child a catechumen; when the prayer was finished, no one of those standing around responded “Amen.” The Lord opened the child’s mouth, and, with everyone hearing, [Col. 0786D] he answered in a clear voice, “Amen.” Amandus then immediately baptized him, giving him also the name Sigebert.

After this he was ordained bishop of the people of Maastricht. For three years, going round villages and fortified places, he preached the word of the Lord diligently. But many—an unspeakable thing!—priests and levites rejected his preaching. In accordance with the Gospel, he shook the dust from his feet upon them and hastened to other places. Finding a small island called Canelaus near the river Scheldt, he lived there with the brethren for some days. But for two years a great plague crushed the despisers of God’s word, so that houses were overthrown, fields turned into wilderness, and villages and fortified places destroyed; scarcely anyone remained in those regions who had despised Amandus [Col. 0787A] as he preached.

After this he preached in Vasconia. A certain mime-actor despised and slandered him; seized by a demon, he began to tear himself with his own hands. Forced publicly to confess that he suffered these things because of the insult he had inflicted upon the servant of God, he breathed out his spirit amid the torment itself.

After this he was received as a guest in a certain city by the bishop of that city. While the bishop himself, according to the custom of hospitality, poured water over his hands, he privately ordered a servant to preserve that same water in the church sanctuary. Later, at the bishop’s instruction, a certain blind man washed his eyes with it and regained sight.

In the district of Beauvais, in a place called Rossoton beside the river Oronne, he healed a blind woman who had always practised augury and [Col. 0787B] worshipped idols, and who adored a tree dedicated to a demon. He restored to health the provost of his monastery, who had been disobedient and had consequently become paralysed, by blessing a cup of wine and a piece of bread, sending them to him, and ordering him to take a portion thereof.

A certain Muntinolus, bishop of the city of Oise, distressed that Amandus had received from the king a place for building a monastery, was inflamed by the torches of envy. He sent swift men [lacuna] to drive him from the place with insults, or punish him in that same place. On coming to him, they deceitfully told him that they ought to show him a suitable place for building a monastery, and that he should therefore go with them. Their deceit did not escape him, God revealing it. At last they came to the brow of a mountain, where they had resolved to cut off his head. Suddenly a storm of rain and hail arose; clouds covered the entire place of that mountain so completely that those attendants, deprived of light, saw absolutely nothing. [Col. 0787C] Having now no hope of life, they fell at his feet and begged forgiveness, asking him to allow them to depart alive. Praying, he restored light to them and sent them home terrified.

This saint was buried in the monastery which he himself built, called Elnone from the name of the little river flowing there; King Dagobert had given him this place. In the same year in which Saint Amandus died, Emperor Constans killed his brother Theodosius; and Grimoald, duke of the people of Turin, treacherously killed Godebert, son of King Aripert, [Col. 0787D] seized his kingdom, married Godebert’s sister, and reigned nine years. Saint Nivard, archbishop of Rheims, and his successor Reolus, and Bercharius the martyr, first abbot of Hautvillers; likewise Saint Bertha, martyr and abbess, flourished in holiness in Gaul.

662.

Emperor Constantine attacks Italy, captures many cities of the Lombards, and besieges Benevento; there King Grimoald severely crushes his army. Clovis, king of the Franks, dies in a frenzy. By Queen Balthild he had three sons: Lothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. After him Lothar reigned four years. After Erchinoald, Ebroin was mayor of the palace to this Lothar. From this point onward, as the Frankish kings declined from their customary courage and knowledge, the power of the kingdom was administered by the mayors of the palace, while the kings reigned in name alone. Their custom was to rule by reason of lineage, but to do or arrange nothing except irrationally to eat and drink and remain at home; and on the Kalends of May to preside before the whole people, greet and be greeted, receive and return services and gifts, and thus remain until the following May.

At that time Queen Balthild, Lothar’s mother, built for God the monasteries of Corbie and Chelles. She had been seized in lands beyond the sea, brought into Francia, and sold at a cheap price; she was redeemed by the venerable man Erchinoald, who then governed the palace. She was of distinguished Saxon blood, beautiful in appearance, cheerful of countenance, dignified in bearing, chaste, sober, prudent and cautious, humble and gracious. [Col. 0788B] She so pleased the aforesaid prince that he appointed her cupbearer. Even in that position, she served all the elders in her lord’s household so humbly that she removed and cleaned their shoes, brought water for washing, and promptly prepared their clothes, without any complaint or flattery, but with a good and pious spirit.

After Erchinoald’s wife died, the same prince wished to marry her. When she learned this, she secretly and deliberately withdrew from his sight. For when she was summoned to the prince’s chamber, this shrewd young woman hid herself secretly in a corner of the roof-space and threw very cheap rags over herself, so that no one thought anyone could be concealed there. Therefore, when she was not found, the prince married another woman. She was later sought again and found, but was not touched by the prince. Subsequently, by God’s grace, she became the wife of Clovis, son of King Dagobert—and deservedly so, for she too was of royal blood.

She gave many alms to churches and the poor through the hand of Abbot Genesius, whom the king assigned to assist her and who was then constantly at the palace; he later became bishop of Lyons. By this queen Clovis begot Lothar, who reigned after him. At that time Crodebert, a venerable man, was bishop of Paris, and Saint Audoenus was at Rouen. From that time the Burgundians and Franks were united in peace, though they had previously been at discord.

This queen [Col. 0788D] extirpated the Simoniacal plague from Francia and caused the most impious public exactions to cease. They had oppressed the people so severely that many preferred their children to die rather than live. She built a monastery of holy women in the Paris district, called Kala (Chelles), on an island in the river Marne; and to this monastery she gave a royal charter, marked with her own seal and those of her royal sons. In that charter, by invocation of the Holy Trinity and under an imprecation extending to the day of the dreadful judgment, she decreed that no ruler of that place in succeeding times should remove anything from the estates which she had bestowed for the various uses of the inhabitants of the monastery, nor hold any of it as a benefice. Whoever did so was to be delivered to infernal punishments with the most wicked and avaricious Judas, [Col. 0789A] to be punished without end.

She appointed as the first mother of this monastery the very devout servant of Christ Bertila, whom she summoned from the monastery of Jothro. She also built the monastery of Corbie in the district of Amiens, which she magnificently endowed with estates and properties. She established there as its first father the venerable Theudofred, whom she summoned from the monastery of Luxeuil and who later became a bishop. To the most holy man Philibert, abbot of the monastery of Jumièges, she granted a great forest from the royal fisc for building a monastery. To Laigobert, abbot of the monastery of Turdion, she gave an estate with many talents of gold and silver, as well as the royal belt which she herself wore. She bestowed very great benefactions on the monasteries of Fontenelle and Logium. Upon Luxeuil and the other monasteries of Burgundy [Col. 0789B] she conferred numerous estates and countless sums of money. To the monastery of Jothro, from which she had summoned the consecrated virgins with Bertila to Kala, she gave Villeneuve in the district of Vermandois, along with many other benefactions. To the monastery of Saint Fara she gave an estate with many other gifts. She granted immunities to the chief churches: Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain, Saint-Médard, Saint-Pierre de Fossés, Saint-Pierre de Lagny, Saint-Amand, and Saint-Martin.

She prohibited the sale of human captives and ordered throughout the cities of the Franks that no one in the Frankish kingdom should transfer a captive person to another kingdom. She redeemed many captives, set many free, and placed many in monasteries. She established men and girls of her own people, whom she herself had reared, in the practice of the regular life. She honoured the basilicas of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul at Rome with many gifts, and sent many presents to Roman recluses and poor persons.

At length, when contention arose among the Frankish nobles because of the pride of Bishop Sigebrand—for which he himself was killed—she was enabled to fulfil her long-desired intention. Led by certain senior nobles of the kingdom to the monastery of Kala, she received the religious habit there. During her assigned week she served in the kitchen office, like the other sisters, and performed cleaning duties, even more than the other sisters, removing with her own hands the filth of excrement. At length she was afflicted with iliac disease, from which, however, with God’s aid and that of physicians, she recovered.

[Col. 0789D] As her death approached, a splendid vision was shown her. A ladder seemed to stand raised before the altar of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, its top reaching heaven; and by its steps she seemed, accompanied by holy angels, to penetrate the heavenly mysteries. She had a certain goddaughter, whom she had received from the sacred font, and for her she prayed to the Lord that the girl might die before herself. This came to pass, and Balthild immediately followed her in death. At the departure of her soul from the body, divine radiance shone most brilliantly upon her little body. Those present saw a choir of angels coming to meet her, along with her most faithful friend Bishop Genesius. The angels were seen carrying her soul up to heaven, raised by the rowing-motion [Col. 0790A] of their wings and by their hands.

The monastery of Kala had first been built by Queen Clotild, wife of the great Clovis, whom Saint Remigius baptized; she built it in honour of Saint George. But because the enclosure of that church was too narrow and insufficient for the great flock of holy women, Queen Balthild had it demolished and caused a larger one to be built. The aforesaid Clotild, niece of King Gundobad, brought not only her husband but also many Frankish nobles to faith in Christ, and built the church of the monastery of Saint-Pierre de Fossés. The wife of King Childebert, Ultrogotha, too, was a nurse of orphans, comforter of wards, supporter of the poor, and helper of faithful monks. Queen Radegund, wife of the elder King Clothar, as stated above, received the sacred veil while her husband was still alive.

663.

Emperor Constantine attempts to transfer the imperial government from Constantinople to the city of Rome, but the people of Constantinople resist him.

664.

Constantine came to Rome and removed everything made of bronze that served for the adornment of the city. He stripped the church of Saint Mary of the Martyrs, which had been roofed with bronze tiles, and sent all these things to Constantinople. On his return, through assessments or poll-taxes (*diagrapha seu capita*) and naval levies over many years, he imposed such afflictions upon the peoples of Calabria, Sicily, Africa, and Sardinia as had never existed from the beginning of the world, so that no hope of life remained to anyone. Moreover, taking away sacred vessels and treasures of the holy churches, [Col. 0790C] he left nothing.

In England a great dispute arose between the English and Scots concerning the observance of Easter, through the agency of the glorious King Oswiu, who also agreed with the English celebrating Easter according to the Roman custom. Saint Gertrude of Nivelles died. When Sisebut, king of the Visigoths, died, Chintila reigned sixteen years. (665.) Eorconbert, king of the English, died; after him his son Egbert reigned nine or eight years. This Egbert either killed, as is said, his paternal uncle’s sons, Æthelbert and Ealhbert, or calmly allowed them to be killed.

666.

Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, died. Lothar, the child king of the Franks, died; after him his brother Theuderic was raised to the kingship by Ebroin. His brother Childeric was reigning [Col. 0790D] in Austrasia. (667.) King Theuderic was rejected by the Franks because of Ebroin’s insolence, and his brother Childeric, king of Austrasia, was summoned by all to reign. Theuderic and Ebroin were tonsured: Theuderic was confined at Paris in the monastery of Saint Denis, and Ebroin at Luxeuil. Childeric’s mayor of the palace was Wulfoald. In the district of Verdun, above the Moselle, he founded the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel.

668.

Archbishop Theodore and Adrian flourished in England: learned men who had absorbed every branch of learning to the marrow; they had been sent to England by Pope Vitalian. (669.) Emperor Constantine, also called Constans, hated by all his own people, was killed by his followers at Syracuse in a bath, on 15 July, in the twelfth indiction. His son Constantine ruled after him for seventeen years. (670.) A certain Mizius, having planned a usurpation in Sicily, was quickly put to death. Pope Vitalian ordained ninety-seven bishops and died on the sixth day before the Kalends of February; the episcopal see was vacant for two months and thirteen days. After him, the seventy-ninth pope, Adeodatus, a Roman by nation and formerly a monk, sat for four years, two months, and five days. He was most kind and gentle, so that he willingly received everyone, from the greatest to the least, and everyone obtained what he requested.

Then Mezetius seized kingship in Sicily; his head was carried to Constantinople. When Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, died, his son Ecgfrith reigned fifteen years. [Col. 0791B] He was his younger legitimate son, more commended by the merits of his most holy wife Æthelthryth than by his own. Yet he is to be praised in this respect: he graciously permitted that queen, who wished to live in continence, to do so; and by weeping he obtained the blessed Eadbert as bishop. Nevertheless, he caused the blessed Wilfrid to go into exile. He devastated the Irish, a race of innocent people which by native simplicity never contrived any evil, with widespread slaughter. He lost the sovereignty of the Mercians, being routed in battle by their king Æthelred, son of Penda.

King Grimoald of the Lombards, on the ninth day after bloodletting, took up a bow and tried to strike a dove; the vein of his arm burst, and he died after physicians applied poisonous remedies. After him, Tharith, son of King Aripert, was by divine providence recalled from exile and restored to the Lombard kingdom; he reigned seventeen years.

At this time Saint Praejectus, bishop and citizen of Clermont, flourished. He was martyred by the nobles of that city in revenge for Hector, patrician of Marseilles, who had been killed by Childeric, king of the Franks, because of the injustices which Hector had inflicted upon the Church of Clermont. In the territory of Cambrai, the virgin of God Maxellendis, fleeing her lover Harduin in order to keep her vow of virginity, was martyred by him. He was immediately blinded, and after three years was given sight by her.

(671.) Emperor Constantine, suspecting his brothers of wishing to rule jointly with him, cut off their noses. At this time a certain man in Britain, rising from death, recounted many things that he had seen concerning places of punishments and purgatorial fire; Bede speaks of him. There was a householder in the region of Northumbria called Incimmemmaum. He died early in the night, revived at dawn, and put those watching him to flight. His wife, however, though very frightened, remained. He said to her: “Do not fear. I have risen from the death in which I was held, and I have been permitted to live again among human beings; but from now on I must live very differently from before.”

He immediately rose and went to the village oratory, where he prayed until day; then he divided his substance into three parts, giving one to his wife, another to his children, and immediately distributing the third to the poor. Not long afterward he came to the monastery of Melrose, which is encircled by the river Tweed. Receiving the tonsure, he obtained from the abbot a secluded dwelling, and remained there until death in a remarkable manner of life.

He recounted the following:

> “A man radiant in appearance and splendid in clothing led me. We proceeded silently toward the rising of the summer sun. We came to a valley, exceedingly broad, long, and deep, which lay on our left. One side was terribly hot with raging flames; the other was exceedingly dreadful with driving hail and the cold of snow. Both were full of souls violently tossed back and forth in turn. Since they could not endure one side, they leapt across to the other. I thought within myself that this was hell. But my guide answered my thought: [Col. 0792B] ‘No; this is not hell, as you suppose.’
>
> “As we went on, I saw places filled with darkness so dense that I saw nothing at all except the appearance and clothing of my guide. Then behold, frequent globes of flame rose from a pit and fell back into it. At once my guide disappeared and left me alone. The summits of the flames were full of human spirits, ascending and falling back like sparks with smoke; an intolerable stench boiled up with them. Meanwhile a crowd of demons, laughing and mocking, dragged five human souls into the darkness. One of them was tonsured like a cleric, one a layman, and one a woman; they descended with them into the middle of the burning abyss.
>
> “Some spirits rose from that abyss and, blowing foul fire into my eyes, nostrils, and mouth, threatened to seize me with the fiery tongs they carried; yet they could not touch me. Then, as though the flash of a glittering star amid darkness, my guide appeared behind me. He immediately drove them away. Turning to the right, he began to lead me toward the rising of the winter sun. I was soon brought out into clear light and saw an immense wall, whose length and height seemed to have no limit. No door, window, or means of ascent could be seen in it. Immediately, I do not know in what manner, we were on its summit. Beneath us was a field most broad and delightful, full of blooming little flowers, the sweetest fragrance, and light [Col. 0792D] brighter than the midday sun. In it were very many companies clothed in white and many seats of people rejoicing. As he led me among them, I thought this to be the kingdom of heaven, as you suppose.
>
> “Proceeding from there, I saw a far greater splendour of light, heard the sweetest voice of singing, and perceived a most magnificent fragrance. When I hoped that I was about to enter, my guide immediately turned his steps back along the way by which I had come. As we returned, he said: ‘The valley you saw is the place in which the souls of those who delay confessing and correcting their crimes until death are examined and punished. They nevertheless leave the body penitent and confessing, and all shall reach the kingdom of heaven on the day of judgment through God’s mercy. Many, however, are freed before the day of judgment by the almsgiving, fasting, and prayers of the living, and especially by the celebration of Masses.
>
> “‘The pit you saw is the mouth of Gehenna; whoever has fallen into it even once will never be freed. The flower-filled place is that in which are received the souls of those leaving the body with good works, though not of such perfection as immediately to deserve entry into the kingdom of heaven. All these shall enter it on the day of judgment. But whoever is perfect both in deed and thought reaches that kingdom immediately upon leaving the body. Near it lies the place where you received the sound of sweet song and the most sweet fragrance. I departed from you for a time in order to learn what was to be done with you.’”
>
> “Although I again abhorred living in a body, suddenly, I do not know in what manner, I found myself alive among you.”

[Col. 0793B] He recounted these things not indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those who either feared eternal punishments or desired eternal joys. Near that cell lived a certain monk and holy priest named Englis, who is still a solitary on the island of Ireland, sustaining his old age on bread for food and water; through him the things that this man had seen became known. King Aldfrith also, a man most learned in every respect, listened to him attentively. Aldfrith himself finally became a monk in the aforesaid monastery, whose abbot at that time was the holy man and priest Hedwald, now bishop of Lindisfarne.

The brother who had seen these things was called Drycthelm. He very often immersed himself in the nearby river to quench the heat of his body, so that even crusts of ice flowed down around him from his garment. For he never removed his wet and icy clothing from the river until it had been warmed and dried by his body. When he was asked why he endured such severe cold, he replied: “I have seen colder things.” And when he was asked why he maintained such rigorous austerity of self-restraint, he replied: “I have seen harsher things.”

672.

The Saracens invade Sicily and inflict great slaughter upon the people; they carry to Alexandria all the bronze that was at Syracuse, brought from Rome, and immense booty. Amatus, bishop of Sens, is long afflicted by King Theuderic with harsh and irreversible exile.

673.

[Col. 0793D]

Egbert, king of the English, campaigning against the Picts, was killed by them with almost all his forces. Cuthbert, foreknowing future events, attempted to hold him back from that expedition; and at the very hour when Egbert died, he prophesied that he had been slain. His brother Lothair, also called Lothar, succeeded him, entering upon the kingdom through an evil quarrel. For Egbert’s son Eadric harassed him for fifteen years, and Lothair, pierced in the body by a final missile, breathed out his soul while he was being treated. This Lothair mocked the innocent men whom his brother Egbert had killed after they had been proclaimed martyrs. Egbert, however, lamented this deed and granted the mother of his cousins a portion of the island of Thanet for building a monastery. Lothair reigned twelve years.

(674.) A rainbow appeared in the sky [Col. 0794A] in March, and all flesh trembled, so that everyone said the end had come. Theodore, having held a synod in England, established many things useful to the Church. He wrote a book of Penitentials, distinguishing with marvellous and cautious discernment the manner of penance for individual sins. A few extracts from that book must be given here.

Steps must not be made before the altar. Incense should be burned on the feast-day of saints, in reverence for the day, because they gave forth a fragrance of sweetness like lilies. A layman ought not to recite the reading in churches or say “Alleluia,” but only a psalm or responsories, without “Alleluia.” A bishop may confirm in the open country if necessary. A bishop ought not compel an abbot to go to a synod unless there is some reasonable cause. The sacrament must not [Col. 0794B] be received from the hand of a priest who cannot perform the offerings or readings according to the rite.

This ruling may be questioned as to whether it ought always to be observed. For what if a sick person in extremity finds no one else from whom to receive communion? How many uneducated priests are tolerated in the Church even today?

[If a fornicating priest baptizes after his offence has become known, those whom he baptized are to be baptized again.] I wonder how the Church did not condemn this ruling, since even those baptized by heretics in the form of the Church ought not to be rebaptized.

[If an ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, let him be baptized and ordained again; and likewise all whom he previously baptized.]

Here one may ask whether anyone can rightly be baptized by one who is himself unbaptized [Col. 0794C]; and it seems that, in a case of necessity, anyone may be baptized by anyone else, provided that the baptizer baptizes in the faith and according to the form of the Church. For one not yet baptized may possess faith, either unaware that he has not yet been baptized, or knowingly still postponing his own baptism.

[At the ordination of a monk, the abbot ought to celebrate Mass and complete three prayers over his head; and for seven days he shall cover his head with his cowl; and on the seventh day the abbot shall remove the veil, as a priest customarily removes the coverings of infants at baptism; because it is, according to the judgment of the Fathers, a second baptism, in which all sins are remitted, as in baptism. A priest may consecrate an abbess during the celebration of Mass.] Today this is reserved to bishops alone.

[At the ordination of an abbot [Col. 0794D], the bishop ought to celebrate Mass and bless him while he is bowed down, in the presence of two or three witnesses from among his brethren; and he shall give him a staff and foot-coverings.] Elsewhere it is read that he should be given a staff and a rule.

[According to the Greeks, a priest may consecrate a virgin with the sacred veil, reconcile a penitent, make exorcized oil, and, if necessary, chrism for the sick. According to the Romans, this is permitted to no one but a bishop. Likewise, the Greeks bless a virgin and a widow together, and consecrate both. The Romans do not veil a widow. Gregory Nazianzen says that tears are a second baptism. Those who have been baptized may not eat with catechumens or give them the kiss: how much less with pagans or Jews.]

[Col. 0795A] The prohibition against giving them the kiss seems sufficiently consonant with reason; but not so the prohibition against sharing a meal with them. For Peter was rebuked by Paul because, when the Jews were absent, he ate with the Gentiles (Gal. II); but when they were present, he withdrew himself from fellowship at table with the Gentiles. And blessed James gave the kiss to the unbaptized man who suffered with him. Therefore, even in such a case, the kiss ought not to be denied to catechumens.

[According to the Roman Church, it is customary to carry deceased monks and religious persons into the church, anoint them on the breast with chrism, celebrate Masses there for them, carry them to burial with chanting, and cover them with earth or stone. Mass shall be celebrated for them on the first, third, ninth, and thirtieth days, and thereafter after a year; because the Lord rose on the third day and gave up the spirit at the ninth hour; and the children of Israel mourned Moses for thirty days (Deut. XXXIV). No reason is given for the anniversary, but perhaps it signifies the Day of Judgment after the year of this age, on which we shall all rise again.

[The relatives of the dead ought to fast for seven days and offer an oblation at the altar, as is read in Jesus son of Sirach (Ecclus. XIV); and the children of Israel fasted for Saul (II Kings I). Dionysius the Areopagite says that one who offers Masses for an evil man commits blasphemy against God. Augustine says that this ought to be done for all Christians, because it either benefits them or those who offer and pray. If an abbot sins, not even a bishop may take away the possessions of the monastery, but he shall send him to another monastery, into [Col. 0795C] the authority of another abbot. A monk may not make a vow without the abbot’s consent; otherwise it must be broken. According to the Greeks, a woman may make an offering at the altar; not according to the Romans. On Sunday Greeks and Romans sail and ride: they do not make peace settlements, nor travel in a cart except only to church, nor bathe themselves. On Sunday the Greeks do not write publicly, but privately at home in cases of necessity. Greek monks have no slaves; Roman monks do. During a deadly pestilence, Greeks and Romans say that the sick themselves ought to be visited, as the Lord commanded. The Greeks do not give the flesh of animals that have died of themselves to pigs; nevertheless, it is permissible to take their hides and skins, shoes, wool, and horns [Col. 0795D], but not on any holy day. The head may be washed on Sunday, and feet may be washed in lye. But this washing of feet is not a Roman custom. If a man is tormented by a devil and knows nothing except to run about everywhere and kill himself, prayer may be made for him if he had previously been religious; for others it is not permitted. A man may put away his wife because of fornication and take another. But if she wishes to do penance, after two years she may take another man. A woman, however, may not put away her husband, even if he is a fornicator, unless perhaps in order to enter a monastery. Basil so ruled. If an adulterous woman’s husband does not wish to live with her, and she wishes to enter a monastery, she shall receive a fourth part of her inheritance. Men may not have women as nuns [Col. 0796A], nor women men as monks; nevertheless, let us not destroy what is customary in this land. If a woman has been taken captive, her husband shall wait five years; likewise the woman if such things happen to her husband. If the man has taken another wife and the first returns from captivity, he shall take back the first and dismiss the later one. In the third degree of blood relationship, according to the Greeks, as is written in the Law (Lev. XVIII), marriage is permitted; among the Romans, in the fifth. In the third degree they dissolve the union after it has been made. Therefore they should be joined in the fifth generation. If persons are found in the fourth degree, they shall not be separated; in the third, they shall be separated. A husband ought not to see his wife naked. A girl of fourteen has authority over her own body; a boy does not have it until his fifteenth year. If anyone purchases as free a pregnant woman [Col. 0796B], the child born of her is free. If a king possesses another king’s land, he may give it for the sake of his soul. A thing found on the road must be taken up; if its owner is found, it must be returned. He who fasts for a dead man helps himself. The sick may take food and drink at any hour, when they desire or are able. Romans reconcile a penitent within the apse; Greeks outside it. Reconciliation is absent from this province because public penance is absent. And the Nicene synod, Pope John, and the Gallican canons appear to maintain that clerics caught in adultery, whether confessing it themselves or convicted by others, cannot return to office. What kindness hostile to justice is this: to flatter criminals and preserve their wounds, closed over, until the Day of Judgment? What mercy is it to spare one person in every respect and, through a bad example, bring all into danger?

[Col. 0796C] Blessed Cyprian does not advise this, saying: “He who flatters a sinner with fawning words supplies fuel for sinning; he does not suppress offences but nourishes them.” Again: “An unskilled physician is one who touches the swollen cavities of wounds with a sparing hand; by preserving the poison hidden in the depths, he makes it worse.” Again Chrysostom: “An unskilled physician is one who draws a scar over a wound before its corruption has been discharged.” Saint Faustus, in a letter: “Whoever wishes to perform the office of a husband loses the grace of consecration.” He who is sent unwillingly to a monastery in order to perform penance—what else should he be called but unrepentant?]

Thus far from Theodore’s Penitential; now let us return to [Col. 0796D] history.

## 675

A Saracen fleet arrived against Constantinople; after attacking the Christians unsuccessfully for several years, they were, on their return voyage, for the most part drowned.

(676.) When Saracens and Arabs engaged with the Roman army, thirty thousand Saracens were killed. King Hilderic, by the savagery of his character, kindled against himself the hatred of the Franks; by him Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun, was shut away at Luxeuil. Pope Adeodatus made forty-six bishops; he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, and the see was vacant for four months and fifteen days. After his death, such rains and such thunder occurred in Italy as no age of humankind [Col. 0797A] remembers, so that people and cattle even perished by lightning. Unless the Lord had been appeased through the litanies held daily, people could not have threshed or stored grain in barns; indeed, from those very rains legumes sprouted anew and came to maturity, which was very remarkable.

(677.) After him Donus, the eightieth pope, a Roman by nationality, sat for one year, five months, and ten days. In Rome, in the Boetian monastery, he found Nestorian heretics—Syrian monks—whom he distributed among various monasteries as Roman monks. He paved the courtyard before the church of Saint Peter with great marble slabs.

In his time the Church of Ravenna subjected itself to the Apostolic See, from which it had separated itself over the matter of autocephaly. Reparatus, bishop of that church, died immediately afterward. When he was elected, a star appeared in the east from cockcrow until morning for three months; its rays penetrated the heavens, and all peoples marveled at its appearance. After it disappeared, having withdrawn into itself, a great mortality followed in the eastern regions.

## 678

Callinicus, an architect from Heliopolis in Syria, fled to the Romans and invented sea-fire. By its use the Romans burned the Saracens’ ships and utterly burned them together with their souls, and so gained the victory.

(679.) Pope Donus made six bishops and died on the thirtieth day before the Ides of April; the see was vacant for two months and [Col. 0797C] fifteen days. After him Agatho, the eighty-first pope, a Sicilian by nationality, sat for two years, six months, and three days. He was kind, gentle, cheerful, and pleasant.
