Contrary to custom, he became treasurer of the Roman Church, personally arranging the treasurer’s cases, issuing with his own hand funds received through the nomenculator, or offerings covered with a veil. Peace between the Romans and Saracens was confirmed for thirty years, so that the Saracens were annually to pay the Romans three thousand pounds of gold, fifty captive men, and fifty noble horses. Bodilo the Frank, whom King Hilderic had ordered to be beaten while bound to a stake, slew Hilderic when he encountered him on a hunt, together with his pregnant wife Blithild; and Theoderic was restored to the kingdom. [Col. 0797D] His mayor of the palace was made Leudesius, son of Erchinoald, through the counsel of Bishop Leodegar and the other princes, as Einhard says. The Merovingian people, or line, failed in Hilderic; yet it had long previously possessed no strength. For the kingdom’s resources and power lay with the palace prefects, who were called mayors of the palace. The king possessed an estate of permanent revenue and, wherever he needed to go, traveled in a cart drawn in rustic fashion by yoked oxen and an ox-driver.

## 680

Ebroin, having left Luxeuil, sent to Saint Audoen to seek counsel; Audoen sent him only this message: “Let Fredegund come to your memory.” Then Martin and Pippin, son of Ansegisel, dukes of Austrasia, came against [Col. 0798A] Ebroin; Ebroin put them to flight. Martin fled to Laon-sur-Clamart. Ebroin swore to him upon empty reliquary-cases that he would not kill him; Martin believed him and was killed. Thus Ebroin crushes his adversaries, attacks King Theoderic, plunders his treasures and those of the Church, and kills Leudesius, mayor of the palace. Pretending that a certain Clovis was the son of King Lothair, he makes him king; by threats and blandishments he compels as many as he can to swear allegiance to him.

Pope Agatho received an imperial command from the emperors, in accordance with his request. By this the amount of money customarily paid for the ordination of a pope was remitted; provided, however, that if an election should occur after his death, the person elected ought not to be ordained until, after a general decree, he has been brought into the imperial city according to ancient custom, so that the ordination may take place with their knowledge and command.

After the death of King Chintila, his son Tholga, still a boy, reigned over the Visigoths for four years. The people of the Bulgars, coming out of Scythia under their leader Bathara, ravaged Thrace. Constantine’s army met them, was disgracefully driven away by them, and severely crushed. Their incursions consequently became so powerful throughout the Roman commonwealth that Constantine, after making peace with them, was compelled to pay them annual tribute. From this point the kingdom of the Bulgars began.

Pope Agatho, having fallen ill, appointed a treasurer according to custom. The moon [Col. 0798C] suffered an eclipse in June, on the eighth day; and a most grievous mortality followed in the same month, and in August and September, in the city of Rome, such as is not remembered to have occurred in the times of other pontiffs. Parents with children, and brothers and sisters, were carried two by two from their beds to graves.

(681.) The Sixth Ecumenical Synod was assembled at Constantinople, with one hundred and fifty bishops. At it George of Constantinople was recalled from the error of the Monothelites. But Macarius of Antioch and all who denied two wills and operations in Christ were anathematized. At the synod itself, Basil, bishop of Treca, rose up and stripped him of his orarium by command of the synod and emperor; and, after anathematizing him, they threw him out of the synod. [Col. 0798D] Roman clerics carried his throne and Stephen his disciple out of the synod on their shoulders.

At that same hour, and before it, very black spider webs fell among the people, so that all marveled that the filth of heresies had been expelled and that, with God’s help, the Churches had been united and cleansed. In Macarius’s place Theophanius, abbot of the island of Boras in Sicily, was ordained. Macarius and his adherents—that is, Stephen and another Anastasius, former priests, and Leontius, a former deacon—were sent into exile at Coma and confined. Then the names of the patriarchs Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter were removed from the diptychs of the churches and from church paintings wherever they could be found. Then John, bishop of Porto, who was one of the envoys of the lord pope, publicly celebrated Mass in Latin, before the emperor and the patriarchs, on the Lord’s Day [Col. 0799A] in the octave of Easter, in the church of Saint Sophia.

(682.) Saint Leodegar was seized by Ebroin and harshly tortured together with his brother Gerinus. Not long afterward Gerinus was crushed beneath stones. In Italy, during three summer months, there was a most grievous mortality among humankind—the one, namely, described three years before this year, after the eclipse of the moon, in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. After Muhania, Greith his son reigned among the Saracens for three years.

(683.) In England Queen Etheldreda, daughter of Anna, king of the English, flourished. Though married to three husbands, she remained a virgin. After her death, according to Bede, her body was found incorrupt eleven years after its burial, together with the garment in which it had been wrapped. [Col. 0799B] Agatho made eighteen bishops and died on the fourth day of January; the see was vacant for one year, seven months, and five days.

(684.) After him Leo the Younger, the eighty-second pope, second of that name, a Sicilian by nationality, sat for ten months and seventeen days. He was most eloquent, adequately instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in Greek and Latin, outstanding in singing and psalmody, and scholarly in speech. He accepted the Sixth Synod lately celebrated, in which the Monothelites had been condemned; afterward Anastasius the priest and Leontius the deacon recanted that heresy. Leo decreed that one ordained archbishop should pay no customary fee for the use of the pallium or for the various offices of the Church.

In his time, on 16 April, in the second indiction, the moon bore a bloody appearance for almost the whole night, and after cockcrow began gradually to become clear. He was the first to ordain in June. He was ordained by three bishops: those of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri, because the Church of Albano had no bishop. He made twenty-three bishops. [Col. 0799C] By imperial decision, the Church of Ravenna was restored under the ordaining authority of the Apostolic See: namely, so that whoever was elected bishop there should come to the city of Rome to be ordained. King Egfrid grievously devastated the innocent people of Ireland. Tholga, rejected by the Visigoths because of the frivolity of his youth and tonsured as a cleric, was succeeded by Chindaswinth, who reigned for twenty years. Pope Leo the Younger died on the fifth day before the Nones [Col. 0799D] of July; the see was vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days.

## 685

After him Benedict the Younger, the eighty-second pope, second of that name, a Roman by nationality, sat for ten months and twelve days. From his earliest age he served in the Church, and he so conducted himself in the dignity of the priesthood as befitted a man worthy of his name. In the church of Saint Valentine he made a covering over the altar with nails in little baskets, and around it a most precious *palergium* of gold-threaded cloth; and in the church of Blessed Mary at the Martyrs, a purple covering with a cross and little gems, four gold nails, and around it a most beautiful wholly-silk *palergium*. Together with the clergy and the army, he received locks of hair from the lord Justinian [Col. 0800A] and Heraclius, sons of the emperor, and the decree in which he stated that he had sent those locks.

In his time, for several days, while the sky was clear, a star appeared by night near the Pleiades, between the Nativity of the Lord and Theophany, completely obscured like the moon beneath a cloud. Again, in February after the feast of Saint Valentine, a star rose from the west at midday and declined toward the eastern regions. Then in March Mount Vesuvius in Campania erupted for days, and all the surrounding places were devastated by the abundance of its ash. After his death he left thirty pounds of gold to all the clergy, monasteries, diaconiae, and church custodians. He made twelve bishops. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of May; the see was vacant for two months and fifteen days.

After the death of Gizith, Marhuan reigned over the Saracens for one year. King Theoderic received Ebroin into favor and, following his counsel, convened a synod of bishops. At Ebroin’s direction he deprived many of them of the episcopate and condemned others to irrevocable exile. During this persecution Saint Lambert was removed from the bishopric of Maastricht and sought the leisure of peace in the monastery of Stavelot, where he lived safely for seven years. Saint Leodegar, long tortured by Ebroin, after hunger and the squalor of prison, after the gouging out of his eyes, the cutting off of his feet, and the severing of his tongue and lips, at last completed his martyrdom by decapitation.

Ansegisus, father of Pippin, was killed by Gunduin, whom he himself had found and raised, received from the sacred font, and [Col. 0800C] advanced to the highest honors of military service. Lother, also called Lothair, king of the English, wounded by a spear, as was said above, died while being treated. After him reigned Egdric, also called Edric, son of Egbert, for not quite two years; he had as perpetual enemies Edunalla and his brother Mollo. Mollo, compelled to flee into a certain hut, breathed out his life amid flames when it was set on fire. Then for six years there was no king in Kent.

Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians and husband of Queen Etheldreda, was killed this year by the Picts, as stated above. After him his brother Alfrid reigned for nineteen years, in the greatest peace and joy of the province, except that he persecuted the great Wulfrid. Picts, Scots, and Britons greatly press the English [Col. 0800D]; they recover the liberty once lost through the English and invade a great part of England. Saint Amatus, bishop of Sens, was exiled by King Theoderic on Ebroin’s advice. Saint Kilian, a Scot and bishop of Würzburg, flourished.

## 686

Pope John, fifth of that name, a Syrian from the province of Antioch, sat as the eighty-fourth pope for one year and fourteen days. In accordance with the ancient custom, he was elected in the Church of Constantine and thence brought into the episcopal residence. Begga, widow of Ansegisus, devoted herself and her possessions to God and founded the monastery of Andenne. Upon the death of Emperor Constantine, his son Justinian ruled for ten years. After Marhuan, Habdalam reigned over the Saracens [Col. 0801A] for one year.

It is read in the deeds of the Roman pontiffs that, in the time of Pope John, Justinian established peace with the Saracens for ten years, by land and sea, and the province of Africa was subjected to the Roman Empire. Pope John left one thousand and ninety solidi to all the clergy, monasteries, diaconiae, and church custodians. He made thirteen bishops. He died, and the see was vacant for two months and fourteen days.

(687.) After him Conon, the eighty-fifth pope, descended from a Thracian father but brought up in Sicily, then came to Rome and served the same Church; he sat for eleven months. He was angelic in appearance, venerable in his white hair, truthful in speech, mature in age, simple in mind, peaceful in character, and religious in life. He had never committed himself to secular [Col. 0801B] causes or affairs. Without the clergy’s consent, through the intervention of evil men, he appointed Constantine, a wicked and evasive deacon of the Church of Syracuse, as administrator of the Sicilian patrimony; and he gave him also mantles [lacuna].

Saint Cuthbert, bishop of the English, died. Abd al-Malik ruled the Saracens for twenty-two years. Between him and Justinian peace was agreed, on terms that the Saracens should pay the Romans each day a thousand coins, a slave, and a horse. Upon the death of Wulfrid, mayor of the palace, Pippin son of Ansegisus held power in Austrasia with Duke Martin. Ebroin engaged them, as stated above, killed Martin, and won the victory. Among the Lombards, after Perctarit, his son Cunipert reigned for twelve years. [Col. 0801C] After the death of Egdric, king of the English, foreign kings of nations devastated and divided the kingdom of England for four years, or, according to others, six years. Pope Conon, afflicted by a long illness, died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October; the see was vacant for two months and twenty-three days.

## 688

After him Sergius, the eighty-sixth pope, a Syrian by nationality, born in the region of Antioch, of a father named Tiberius, at Palermo in Sicily. Coming to Rome under Pope Adeodatus, he was diligent and capable in the office of singing; by this favor he rose in due order to the episcopate. Theodore the archpriest and Paschal the archdeacon were elected with him. Theodore humbled himself and withdrew; Paschal, however, did not consent until compelled to accept him.

[Col. 0801D] Yet Paschal secretly continued to send to Ravenna and promise John the exarch, surnamed Platyn, one hundred pounds of gold. When the latter came to Rome, he could not assist Paschal, because Sergius had already been confirmed; nevertheless, he exacted the gold promised from the Church of Saint Peter. For this reason Sergius had the lamps and crowns which hung before the altar of Saint Peter taken down and given as security. But the exarch was not softened even by this until he had received one hundred pounds of gold. Not long afterward Paschal was removed from the archdiaconate, not only for this matter but also because of a certain incantation, and the lights which he worshipped, and the lots which he handled with other diviners. He was confined in a monastery and died unrepentant after five years.

Zacharias, a protospatharius sent by Justinian the heretic to bring Pope Sergius to Constantinople, hid under the pontiff’s bed for fear that the Romans would kill him. There, through fear, he lost his senses; nevertheless the pope comforted him. He was expelled from Rome amid injuries and insults.

Sergius found in the sacristy of Saint Peter an ancient silver casket in a very dark place, so old that its silver was not visible, and this by God’s revelation. A seal was impressed upon it, and over the seal lay a wholly-silk cloth called a *stauracium* (“little cross”). When this was removed, he found a cross adorned with diverse precious stones. Having drawn from it four petals, in which gems of marvelous size were enclosed, [Col. 0802B] he found deposited there an ineffable portion of the Lord’s wood. This wood is adored and kissed by all the people on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

He decreed that, at the hour of the breaking of the Lord’s body, the *Agnus Dei* (“Lamb of God”) should be sung by clergy and people; and that on the day of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of the Holy Mother of God, and Saint Simeon—called Hypapante (“Meeting”)—litanies should proceed from Saint Adrian’s and the people should gather at Saint Mary’s. By divine revelation he transferred the body of Pope Leo I. He ordained Berthoald, archbishop of Autun, and Clement, that is, Willibrord of the Frisians. He made one hundred and seven bishops. He sat for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days. The innocence and merit of Saint Leodegar [Col. 0802C] were manifested by many miracles.

## 689

Justinian broke the peace made with the Saracens, inflicted evils upon them, and suffered worse ones from them. Ermenfrid killed Ebroin, mayor of the palace of Neustria, who was oppressing the Franks, and fled to Pippin. Waratto was appointed mayor of the palace in Ebroin’s place. Justinian broke the peace made with the Bulgars and, engaging them, first defeated them; afterward, being caught by them, he barely escaped. A battle was fought between Pippin and Giselmar, son of Waratto, near the fortress of Namur. Not long afterward Giselmar was divinely punished, Waratto died, and Berthar, Waratto’s son-in-law, became mayor of the royal palace.

(690.) The Franks, alienated from Berthar, sought Pippin’s friendship through hostages and incited him against Berthar. Saint Audoen, [Col. 0802D] Theodore archbishop of the English, and Saint Amatus died. King Theoderic, together with Berthar, was defeated when he engaged Pippin. Berthar was killed by his own men; Theoderic was captured by Pippin.

(691.) Pippin subjected Neustria to himself and, ruling alone over the whole kingdom under Theoderic, improved the condition of affairs. He restored Saint Lambert to the episcopal see of Maastricht. Wicred, son of King Egbert, strengthened by religion and industry, freed the English people from the oppression of foreigners and reigned over them for six years. By his enterprise he had overcome envy among his own people, and by money had established peace with the enemy; he was drawn to the kingship by the great hope of the citizens. Peaceful at home, unconquered in war, and most Christian in religion, [Col. 0803A] he extended his power very widely. Saint Remaclus died. Duke Alahis, having worn down Cunipert, seized the kingdom of the Lombards; Cunipert killed him in battle. Willibrord, arriving from England with twelve companions, flourished in Gaul through holiness.

## 692

After Saint Audoen, blessed Ansbert became bishop of Rouen. He was from the district of Vexin and from an estate named Calorgium. The virgin Andragesina, daughter of Robert, an illustrious man and bearer of King Clothair’s ring, was betrothed to him. When she prayed that her beauty might be changed into ugliness, she at once appeared leprous. Physicians were called in; but the more they worked, the more unsightly she appeared. Her father asked whether she wished to remain in virginity; she answered that she had always desired this. [Col. 0803B] Her betrothed Ansbert rejoiced and drew up an irrevocable document, so that she should now be called not his bride but Christ’s bride. When this had been done, holy Angadersina was sent to Rouen to Saint Audoen; consecrated and veiled by him, she was restored to her former beauty.

Then she was made head of the convent of the Oratory, which was situated beside the walls of the city of Beauvais. After this, when blessed Ansbert heard musical instruments before King Clothar and the princes, he said to himself: “O good Creator, what must it be like for those who love you to hear in heaven the unending song of angels, if such are the songs of men on earth!” Afterwards he became a monk in the monastery of Fontenelle, situated in the district of Rouen upon the Seine; where at that time [Col. 0803C] blessed Wandregisel, also called Wando, was superior—nephew, through his brother Walchis, of Ansegisel, mayor of the palace. He founded the two distinguished monasteries of Fécamp and Fontenelle. Seeing Ansbert to be of keen intellect, he caused an abundance of various books to be supplied to him. In the assembly he presented himself for prayer before all the others. He also asked blessed Wandregisel that he might be permitted, with his father’s leave, to undertake daily work beyond the customary work of the brethren. He was ordained priest by blessed Audoenus. He foretold to the youth Theoderic that he would become king. In confirmation of this prophecy, the field in which he then was put forth green grass in winter, remaining ever greener than the other parts of the field.

After blessed Wandregisel, who had been abbot for almost twenty years, Lambert of Taverny was elected. [Col. 0803D] King Theoderic granted his estate beyond the Rhône, in the region of Provence, to supply the monastery of Fontenelle with oil and other necessities. This Lambert afterwards became bishop of Lyons, after blessed Genesius; and blessed Ansbert then became abbot of Fontenelle after that same Lambert. He was humble in dress and moderate in food. In his monastery he established a hospice for feeble and aged poor persons, in which twelve poor persons were to be received; and two other houses for the sick, in which eight were to be received.

Under the aforementioned Lambert, Erembert, bishop of Toulouse, and the holy priest Condred, an anchorite from the island of Britain, became monks in the monastery of Fontenelle. [Col. 0804A] After blessed Audoenus, Saint Ansbert became bishop. At that time the king resided at the estate of Clichy, in the district of Paris; Ansbert was his counsellor when matters of the kingdom were discussed. Once made bishop, he increased in graces and diminished in wealth. One day, after the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he ordered all the inhabitants of Rouen, noble as well as humble, to be brought in to prepared banquets. When all had been seated in due order, he himself sat down at the table of the poor. The revenue which was customarily paid from public estates, by canonical rule, to the bishop’s share, he granted to the priests for the restoration of churches. He gave the monks of Fontenelle a privilege that they should always elect an abbot from among themselves; but in that privilege he bound [Col. 0804B] them under the bond of anathema if they themselves or their successors should depart from the Rule of Saint Benedict. This privilege was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 682, the sixteenth year of Theoderic, the fifth year of blessed Ansbert’s episcopate, in the tenth indiction, at Rouen, in a general synod.

He translated the body of blessed Audoenus to a more prominent place in the church of Saint Peter in the suburb of Rouen, and constructed over his tomb a shrine of extraordinary size, adorned with gold, silver, and gems, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension. When the solemnities of Mass had been completed, he had an innumerable multitude invited to a banquet. At this banquet he himself served the poor and needy. At this feast, provided at his expense, all the citizens of Rouen and the inhabitants of the surrounding monasteries, clerics [Col. 0804C] and consecrated women, were fed.

Accused before Prince Pippin, he was, by Pippin’s command, carried off into exile at Hautmont, situated in the territory of Hainaut on the river Sambre, where Haldulf was then abbot. He endured this exile humbly, though no crime had been established against him, remembering that he had read somewhere: “Great men suffer much; and they are born as examples in order that they may instruct others.” Reconciled with the king, he humbly asked him that it might be permitted for the members of his body to be brought back to the monastery after his death. When he had died, as a shroud was placed upon his head, he was seen to open his eyes. A lamp lit by the faithful before his tomb not only burned unceasingly but also overflowed, so that a vessel was placed beneath it to receive its overflow.

[Col. 0804D] We ought to have placed earlier what we now set down. At that time Saint Hildevert flourished, born in the city of Meaux, over which he presided as bishop. At the age of five he was entrusted to Saint Faro for instruction in sacred letters. He bore the insults of his companions with the greatest patience. From the time when he was made priest by Saint Faro, he always wore haircloth next to his flesh. At Saint Faro’s urging he entered a monastery; after blessed Faro he became bishop.

Near the city of Meaux there stood a church of the Holy Cross, in which the body of Saint Faro had once been buried. In the courtyard of this church the people of Meaux buried their dead. It happened that certain wicked men approached blessed Hildevert, asking that it might be permitted to build another church for themselves in that courtyard [Note: [Col. 0805D] This means gloves.], [Col. 0805A] and this was done. But that same temple, built out of avarice, collapsed utterly on the night before it was to have been dedicated on the following day. Struck by fear and moved to repentance, blessed Hildevert went to Pope Boniface, that he might impose penance on him for this sin. After making satisfaction, he was sent by him to preach.

Entering each house, he said, “Peace to this house; peace to those entering and going out”; and thus, beginning the word, he carried it through to the end. He did this as far as Jerusalem, both going and returning. In the seventh year after his departure he reported to the pope what he had done. Returning to Gaul with the authority of the lord pope, at a place called Lagny he found a monk named Fursa, outstanding in holiness. [Col. 0805B] An angel of the Lord had stood beside Fursa in a vision and said: “Bishop Hildevert will come to you tomorrow; know that his sins have been forgiven by the Lord. Take care, therefore, to receive him with honour.” When Saint Hildevert came to him, he threw himself at Fursa’s feet. Seeing this, Fursa fell upon his face.

Then Hildevert came to a village seven miles from the city of Meaux, where he himself had founded a church in honour of the Blessed Mary. He afterwards dedicated it and celebrated Mass there. When there he drew out the *utrantos* (2) with his hands—an uncertain reading—and placed them in a ray of sunlight; they were supported by it for three hours. Then he raised to life a certain boy who had died unbaptized. Baptizing him, he called him Aldebert [Col. 0805C] after his own father, and ordered that he be buried beside himself, to die seven years later. Blessed Hildevert died on 26 May, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. Blessed Abbot Majolus, by angelic revelation, afterwards raised the bodies of these two from the earth, together with many bishops.

## 693

King Theoderic of the Franks died; after him his son Clovis reigned four years, or, according to others, two years. Theoderic had reigned nineteen years and had begotten this Clovis by Queen Clothild. Berthar, mentioned above, Waratto’s son-in-law, was small of stature, foolish, and useless. The Saracens crushed the Romans in a very severe war. Abbot Ewald and Ewald the Black, priests who had come from England, were martyred in Gaul and, by Pippin’s command, buried at Cologne.

## 694

Pippin defeated Radbod, duke of the Frisians, in war, and sent Willibrord to preach to that people. Aruval, disciple of Kilian, bishop of Würzburg; Abbot Adaman; and the bishops Aldhelm and Winfrith flourished in England.

## 695

The heretic Justinian attempted to undermine the holy Sixth Synod; he vainly endeavoured to drive from the Church Pope Sergius, who resisted him. An eclipse occurred at the third hour of the day, with the stars clearly visible in heaven.

**(696.)** The venerable priest and monk Bede [Col. 0806A] flourished in England, being in his thirtieth year.

**(697.)** Leo the patrician deprived Justinian of the kingdom, mutilated his nose and tongue, sent him into exile, and reigned three years. Bede says that Saint Cuthbert died at this time, speaking as follows in his book *On Times*:

> “Cuthbert, most reverend bishop of the church of Lindisfarne in Britain, formerly an anchorite, led from infancy to old age a life made illustrious by signs of miracles. Eleven years after his burial, his body was found incorrupt, as though he had died that very hour, together with the garment in which it was wrapped. We ourselves have recently set forth this matter in the book *On His Life and Virtues*, in prose, and some years ago in hexameter verses.”

King Clovis died while still a boy. After him his brother Hildebert—also called Childebert—reigned eighteen years, or, according to others, seventeen. [Col. 0806B] His mayor of the palace was Grimoald, Pippin’s son by his noble wife Plectrude; by her Pippin also begot Drogo, duke of Champagne. Willibrord, surnamed Clement by Pope Sergius and consecrated bishop of the Frisians, established his episcopal see at Utrecht—that is, the town of *Vulcarum*—from Pippin’s household; he was of the island of Britain, of the English people.

Saint Kilian, bishop, with his disciples Cholomannus and Tholmannus, was martyred at the fortress of Würzburg in eastern Franconia by Geilana, wife of Gozbert, prince of the Würzburg people. She feared that he would separate her from her husband, because Kilian rebuked him for having his late brother’s wife. For a long time the death of these men was unknown to all, [Col. 0806C] but Geilana and the murderers of the martyrs were seized by a demon, and through their confession it was made public.

## 698

Through the intervention of Prince Hildulf, Saint Ursmar undertook the governance of the monastery of Lobbes. A synod was held at Aquileia. Because of ignorance in matters of faith, as Bede says, it hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, celebrated at Constantinople under the great Justinian and Pope Vigilius, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of Pope Sergius, it consented.

Saint Lambert dared to rebuke Prince Pippin because he had brought in his concubine Alpaida in addition to his lawful wife Plectrude. He was martyred at Liège by Dodo, brother of that same Alpaida, and was buried at Maastricht; Saint Hubert was appointed bishop in his place. Bede says that Leo [Col. 0806D] ruled three years, but the chronicles count only two years as his reign. Tiberius, also called Apsimar, had this Leo’s nose cut off and confined him in custody; after him he ruled seven years.

## 699

Drogo, Pippin’s son and duke of Champagne, died. His brother Grimoald was appointed by Pippin mayor of the palace in the court of King Childebert, and Theudesinda, daughter of Radbod, duke of the Frisians, was given him in marriage. This Grimoald begot Theudoald by a concubine. When Cunipert, king of the Lombards, died, his young son Liutpert reigned, with Ansprand as guardian. Dodo, murderer of Saint Lambert, was afflicted with dreadful pain, consumed by worms, and, because of his unbearable stench, thrown into the river Meuse. All accomplices in this crime were divinely punished within the year. [Col. 0807A] The murderer of the holy martyr encountered his own brother, and each was slain by the other.

## 700

The Romans, ranging through Syria, killed two hundred thousand Saracens. Reginbert, duke of Turin, defeated Ansprand, guardian of King Liutpert, in war and ruled for one year.

## 701

Terbel ruled over the Bulgars. After Reginbert’s death, his son Aripert defeated Ansprand in battle, captured and killed King Liutpert, compelled Ansprand to flee to Bavaria, and allowed Ansprand’s younger son Liutprand to flee to his father. He reigned nine years. Chindaswinth, worn out with old age, relinquished the kingdom of the Visigoths. After him his son Flavius Recceswinth reigned. Saint Benedict, abbot of the English, died.

## 702

Pope Sergius died on 7 September, the seventh day before the Ides of September; the episcopal see was vacant for one month and twenty days. After him, John V, a Greek by nation, the eighty-seventh pope, sat for three years, two months, and twelve days; he ordained sixteen bishops. Justinian, fleeing from exile, went to the Khagan, king of the Avars.

## 703

Khagan, bribed by Emperor Leo, wished to betray Justinian to him; Justinian fled to Terbel, king of the Bulgars.

**BEDE.** Gilvifer, duke of the Lombard people at Benevento, devastated Campania with fire, sword, and captivity. Having sent many gifts with priests, Pope John, Sergius’s successor, redeemed all the captives and caused the enemies to return home, since there was no one to resist them. [Col. 0807C] This John died, and the episcopal see was vacant for five months and eighteen days.

**(704.)** After him another John, John VI, a Greek, son of Platon, the eighty-eighth pope, sat for two years, six months, and seventeen days, a man most learned and eloquent. In his time King Aripert of the Lombards restored to Saint Peter, in a document written in golden letters, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps, which had been held by that people. Among other distinguished works, this John made a most beautiful oratory of the holy Mother of God [Col. 0807D] within the church of Saint Peter.

After the death of Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, Osred reigned twelve years. He began to reign as a boy of eight and spent his whole life disgracefully in the seduction of consecrated women; at last he was killed by the plots of his kinsmen.

**(705.)** Justinian the exile regained the kingdom with the assistance of Terbel, king of the Bulgars. He captured Leo, who had occupied his place, and Tiberius, Leo’s successor, who had expelled him from the kingdom and had kept him in custody in the same city throughout his own reign. In the middle of the circus, before the people, he ordered them beheaded. He sent the patriarch Callinicus to Rome after putting out his eyes, and gave the bishopric to Cyrus, who had been abbot in Pontus and had supported Justinian in exile. Whenever Justinian wiped away a drop of mucus flowing from his cut-off nose, [Col. 0808A] he ordered someone among those who had conspired against him to be beheaded—almost as often as he did so. He ruled a second time with his son Tiberius for seven years, or six years according to Bede.

Pope John ordained nineteen bishops, died on 18 October, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven months. After him Sisinnius, a Syrian by nation, the eighty-ninth pope, sat for twenty days. He was so crippled by gout that he could not take food with his own hands; yet he was steadfast in spirit and concerned for the inhabitants of this city, and he had lime-kilns procured for repairing the walls. He ordained one bishop in the island of Corsica. He died suddenly and was buried on 6 November, the eighth day before the Ides of November; the episcopal see was vacant for one month and [Col. 0808B] eighteen days.

**(706.)** After him Constantine, a Syrian by nation, the ninetieth pope, sat for six years and fifteen days. Under him there was a severe famine at Rome for three years; afterwards there was such abundance that the former scarcity was forgotten. At the same time Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, was deprived of sight by Justinian and sent into exile in Pontus because he had instigated rebellion against him. The Slavs harassed Italy.

## 707

Kings Coenred and Offa of the English came to Rome; there they were tonsured as monks and served Christ. Offa, king of the Mercians, was at that time most powerful.

**(708.)** Justinian broke the peace concluded with the Bulgars and, having engaged them in battle, barely escaped. The Picts and Scots adopted the rite of Paschal observance.

[Col. 0808C] **(709.)** After Abd al-Malik, al-Walid ruled the Saracens for seven years. While Hildebert held the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom, the archangel Michael appeared to Autbert, bishop of Avranches, and warned him once and again to found, in the place in the sea called the Tomb because of its height, a church in his memory. Michael wished there to be paid to him in the sea the same veneration as was paid on Mount Gargano. Meanwhile, a bull secretly stolen by a thief was tethered in that place. The bishop was therefore warned a third time to lay the foundation where he found the bull tethered; and, as he saw it tread down the earth with its feet, to trace for himself the circuit of the church. He established a church in honour of Saint Michael in the place now [Col. 0808D] called “In Peril of the Sea.” It is more commonly called Mount Saint Michael.

It should be known that I have not been able to find the history of the veneration of Saint Michael on Mount Gargano, whose commemoration is recited once a year in the Martyrology on 29 September, the third day before the Kalends of October. Yet in many churches, at this feast, a commemoration of this second apparition is read, for what reason I do not know—unless perhaps because the history of that first veneration on Mount Gargano is not found. I nevertheless believe that some possess it, but it has not yet come into my hands.

## 710

Adrian, abbot of the English, who had been sent to England with Archbishop Theodore by Pope Vitalian, died. In the same year, according to William of Malmesbury, Aldhelm died, [Col. 0809A] having held the episcopate for four years; he wrote the book *On Virginity* for the virgins of Barking. Emperor Justinian, having embraced the orthodox faith, invited Pope Constantine to Constantinople, and honoured him on his coming and return with glory worthy of the apostolic office. Thus one reads in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*:

> “Pope Constantine went to Constantinople at Justinian’s command; he and his chief men entered the city with gilded saddles and bridles and with cloths, carrying the *comelantum*, as he was accustomed to proceed at Rome. Then he met the emperor at Nicomedia; and the emperor, prostrate upon the ground, kissed his feet.”

On his journey there and back he ordained forty-two bishops. Saint Hubert, admonished by heaven, brought the body of Saint Lambert [Col. 0809B] from Maastricht to Liège amid great glory of miracles, and transferred the episcopal see to that same city. Ansprand returned to Italy with the Bavarians and fought Aripert. Aripert fled and was drowned in the river; Ansprand recovered the Lombard kingdom. He died after three months. After him his son Liutprand reigned thirty-two years.

## 711

Saint Oda, wife of Hocco, duke of the Aquitanians, flourished in holiness in Gaul. By her generosity she enriched the churches of God, and, dying, rested in the diocese of Liège.

**(712.)** Philippicus, also called Bardanes, murdered Emperor Justinian and ruled for two years after him. Pope Constantine and the Roman people refused to accept his name, letters, or image, as those of a heretic.

## 713

[Col. 0809C]

Grimoald, mayor of the palace, was killed at Liège while praying before the altar of Saint Lambert by Taingarius, a retainer of Radbod, duke of the Frisians. Theobald, son of Drogo, was appointed mayor of the palace by his grandfather Pippin. So Sigebert says. It should nevertheless be known that this Theudoald was said above not to be Drogo’s son but the son of that same Grimoald, begotten by a concubine.

**(714.)** Saint Ursmar, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, died, and Saint Erminus succeeded him. In the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, three months after Justinian had received Pope Constantine so gloriously, Justinian himself was killed by Philippicus. On account of Philippicus’s erroneous doctrine, an image, which the Greeks call a *botarea*, containing the six holy [Col. 0809D] and ecumenical synods, was recited in the church of Saint Peter. At that time Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, moved by repentance, returned to his own see, although deprived of sight. At this time two kings of the Saxons, coming with many others to the thresholds of the apostles, died swiftly, as they wished.

Then Benedict, bishop of Milan, contended on behalf of the church of Pavia but was defeated, because it belonged to the consecration of the apostolic see. Pope Constantine ordained fourteen bishops and died on 8 January, the sixth day before the Ides of January; the episcopal see was vacant forty days. After him Gregory II, a Roman by nation, the ninety-first pope, sat for sixteen years, nine months, and eleven days, in the times of Anastasius II, Leo, and Constantine.

[Col. 0810A] **(715.)** Artemius, also called Anastasius, deprived Philippicus both of empire and of sight and ruled. This Gregory had charge of the library under Saint Sergius. At the beginning of his episcopate he ordered lime to be burned and began to restore the city walls, but was impeded in many ways. He established that Thursday also should be a fast day in Lent, which had not previously been done.

Petronax, a citizen of Brescia, by divine prompting and encouraged by Pope Gregory’s exhortation, nobly rebuilt the monastery of Saint Benedict at the fortress of Cassino. Under his rule he gathered many to serve God according to the Rule, after more than one hundred and ten years had elapsed since it had been devastated by the Lombards.

Bede says in his *Chronicles* that Philippicus ruled for one year [Col. 0810B] and six months; that he expelled Cyrus from the episcopate and sent him back to Pontus to govern his monastery in the capacity of abbot; and that he sent Pope Constantine letters of erroneous doctrine, which the latter rejected with the counsel of the apostolic see. On account of this, he caused paintings to be made in the portico of Saint Peter containing the acts of the six holy synods. For Philippicus had ordered such paintings removed when they were kept in the imperial city. The Roman people also decreed that neither the name, documents, nor coin-image of the heretical emperor should be received. Therefore his likeness was not brought into the church, nor was his name spoken in the solemnities of Mass.

Bede likewise says that Anastasius ruled three years and sent letters to Constantinople through the scholar Paternus [Col. 0810C] and the exarch of Italy, showing himself to be a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Council.

Prince Pippin died and left as heir to his principate his son by Alpaida, Charles Tudites, or Martel. Plectrude, Pippin’s widow, had Pippin’s Charles taken captive and committed to custody in the city of Cologne; with her grandson Theudoald, mayor of the palace, she usurped the governance of the kingdom. When Childebert, king of the Franks, who, as is recorded, was a holy man, died, his son Clovis, also called Dagobert, reigned four years. Childebert was buried in the monastery of Chelles, in the basilica of Saint Stephen. The Franks fought against Theudoald in ruinous war on both sides; when he had been defeated, [Col. 0810D] they appointed Ragenfrid mayor of the palace and Chilperic king. By divine direction Charles was delivered from the custody of his stepmother, and immediately tried to wrest his principate from the hand of Ragenfrid. First, attacking Radbod, duke of the Frisians, who was assisting Ragenfrid, he sustained heavy losses to his army.

## 716

Saint Giles, coming from Greece, flourished in holiness in Provence. Emperor Anastasius sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens; but they turned to another plan, returned to Constantinople, and compelled the orthodox Theodosius to become emperor. Anastasius fought them, but was defeated and compelled to become a cleric; he was ordained priest. Theodosius, being indolent and uneducated, and a collector of public revenues, was compelled by force [Col. 0811A] by the army to assume the empire. Emir al-Walid died; after him Sulayman ruled the Saracens for three years.

After the death of Osred, king of the Northumbrians, Coenred reigned three years, or, according to others, two. Ina, king of the West Saxons, is said in the *Chronicle* to have had no brothers, but he had sisters, Cuthburga and Quenburga. The first was married to Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, and shortly afterwards left him. First at Barking under Abbess Hildelith, and then as herself mistress of the rule at Wimborne, she lived a life pleasing to God. The place is now an obscure village; at that time it was distinguished and possessed many consecrated virgins.

Ina also had a wife, Æthelburh, a woman of royal lineage and spirit. While she repeatedly urged into her husband’s ears that they should take leave of worldly matters even in their final years, and he deferred from day to day, she at last overcame him by this stratagem. On one occasion at an estate they had displayed royal luxuries with great pomp. On the following day, when they had departed, the steward, by the queen’s order, made the palace as hideous as he could, defiling it both with dung of cattle and heaps of rubbish; and in the place where they had slept he put a sow that had just farrowed. When they had already gone a mile, the queen approached the king with wifely endearments, begging that they return to the place they had left and asserting that there would be great danger if they did not. He assented. Seeing the place which on the preceding day had been equal to Sardanapalus’s, now disfigured by foul desolation, he marvelled.

[Col. 0811C] Then she seized the opportunity and, smiling pleasantly, said: “Where, my lord, are yesterday’s noises and curtains drunk with Sidonian dyes? Where is the bustling insolence of parasites? Where are Daedalian vessels, adorning the very tables by the weight of their metal? Where are the delicacies sought by land and sea for the seduction of the appetite? All have passed away like smoke and wind. Woe to those who have clung to them, for they too will pass away. Consider, I beg you, how miserably the flesh that is nourished in luxury wastes away. We who gorge ourselves more abundantly shall rot more miserably: ‘The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and stronger punishment awaits the stronger’ [Wisdom 6].” Having said no more, she compelled her husband to agree, and together they went to Rome. So as not to make a display of their conversion, they did not cut off their hair before public eyes, but concealed themselves in common dress. They had now grown old and, as we have heard, were illustrious for many miracles.

[Col. 0811D] Ina reigned fifty-eight years; after him his kinsman Æthelheard reigned fourteen years; after him his relative Cuthred sixteen years; after him Sigebert, cruel and infamous, one year—he was stabbed by a swineherd in a cave. **(717.)** After him Cynewulf reigned fourteen years; after him Beorhtric sixteen years, who married the daughter of Offa, then most powerful king of the Mercians; after him Egbert.

Egbert, coming from Ireland, flourished in Gaul in holiness and learning. Egbert, a holy man of the English people, who adorned his priesthood with a monastic life and was also a pilgrim for the sake of the heavenly homeland, converted by devout preaching many regions of the Scottish people to the canonical observance of the Paschal season, [Col. 0812A] from which they had long strayed, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 717.

Saint Germanus was transferred from Cyzicus to the episcopate of Constantinople. Theodosius, elected emperor, as Bede says, defeated Emperor Anastasius in a severe battle near Nicaea and, after receiving an oath from him, caused him to become a cleric and be ordained priest. But Theodosius himself, as soon as he received the kingdom, being Catholic, restored to its former place the venerable image in which the six holy synods were depicted, which Philippicus had cast down.

**BEDE.** In these times many of the English people—noble and humble, men and women, leaders and private persons—were accustomed, prompted by divine love, to come from Britain to Rome. Among them was my most reverend abbot [Col. 0812B] Ceolfrith, who, after having been a priest for forty-six years and an abbot for thirty-five, died when he reached Langres and was buried there in the church of the holy twin martyrs. Among other gifts that he had intended to bring, he sent to the church of Saint Peter a pandect translated by blessed Jerome into Latin from Hebrew or Greek speech.

Pope Gregory consecrated Boniface, who had come from Britain, as bishop; through him he preached the word of God in Germany and converted that people to Christ. The same Gregory made into a monastery the hospital which had stood behind the apse of the holy Mother of God at the Manger. King Liutprand of the Lombards confirmed Aripert’s donation. The moon appeared blood-red until midnight. Theodo, duke of the Bavarians, [Col. 0812C] was the first of that people to come to pray at the thresholds of the apostles.

The river Tiber overflowed its bed and passed beyond the walls of the City, so that in the Via Lata the water rose to one and a half times a man’s height, extending from the gate of Saint Peter to the Milvian Bridge. Thus it overthrew houses, devastated fields, uprooted shrubs and crops; the greater part of the Romans could not sow. The water held Rome for seven days; but when litanies were held, it withdrew on the eighth day. Theodosius laid down the empire; after him Leo II ruled twenty-four years according to Sigebert, but nine years according to Bede, because he carried his *Chronicle* down to that year.

## 718
Zeulimen, the emir, with his fellow emirs and a fleet of nearly three thousand ships, besieged Constantinople for three years. [Col. 0812D] The Bulgars killed thirty-two thousand Saracens. Charles engaged Chilperic and Raginfrid at Vinchy in the district of Cambrai, on the Sunday before Easter, which fell on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. Raginfrid, defeated, was put to flight. Charles pursued them as far as Paris.

Radbod, duke of the Frisians, having been brought by the preaching of Bishop Wulfram to the point of being baptized, put one foot into the font; but, drawing back the other, he asked where the greater number of his ancestors were—in hell or in paradise. Hearing that more were in hell, he withdrew the foot which he had dipped in the water, saying: “It is better to follow the many than the few.” Thus mocked by a demon who promised that on the third day from then [Col. 0813A] he would give him incomparable goods, he perished on that very third day by a sudden and eternal death.

This Wulfram, bishop of Sens, came from the district of Vexin. His father, Wulbert, served in the court of King Dagobert and of his sons Louis. He succeeded Lambert of Sens in the bishopric of Sens, in the time of the younger kings Lothar and Theuderic. He was warned in a vision to preach the word of God to the Frisian people. In order to do this he then went to the monastery of Fontenelle, whose superior at that time was the blessed Ansbert, bishop of Rouen; from that monastery he took fellow-workers with him for preaching.

While they were sailing toward Frisia and were in the middle of the sea adjacent to the country of the Norwegians, when the hour came for Saint Wulfram to celebrate Mass, the ship remained [Col. 0813B] motionless with its anchors set. When they came to the point at which the minister ought to offer the paten to the bishop, the bishop held out his hand awaiting it. But when the minister wished to wash it, it fell into the sea; and he threw himself at the bishop’s feet and begged forgiveness. The bishop sent him to the place where it had fallen and, by prayer, caused the paten to be brought up from the bottom of the sea and to adhere to the minister’s hand.

After this, the son of Duke Radbod was baptized by blessed Wulfram and, clothed in the white baptismal garment, expired. Among the Frisians it was customary that whomever the lot selected should be offered to demons as a sacrifice. A certain boy named Ono was selected by lot for this. When Saint Wulfram asked for him, the duke replied: “If your Christ rescues him from the torment of death, let him be yours.” He was hung [Col. 0813C] upon a gallows. But as Saint Wulfram prayed, the bonds constricting his throat were broken, and he fell unharmed to the ground. Held by the saint, he rose up whole. Having been baptized and afterwards ordained priest by Regesland, bishop of Rouen, he copied many books for the monastery of Fontenelle.

After this Duke Radbod, when he was to be baptized, as stated above, drew his foot back from the font. Being greatly uncertain, he sent to blessed Willibrord, bishop of that people, to ask whether he ought to be baptized. Willibrord replied: “How will he believe me, when he does not believe our holy brother Wulfram? I,” he said, “saw him this night bound with a fiery chain. It is therefore clear that he has already [Col. 0813D] undergone eternal damnation.” And as he was going to the prince’s house, he was told that Radbod was already dead; he at once returned home.

The aforesaid Ono recounted how Radbod had been deceived by the devil. He said that the devil had appeared to him transformed into an angel, his head covered with a golden diadem set with gems, and clothed in a garment woven with gold. As Radbod gazed at him, the devil said: “Most valiant of men, who has so led you astray that you wish to depart from the worship of the gods? Do not do this, but remain in what you have learned; and you will come to the golden dwellings which I am soon to give you forever. Tomorrow therefore summon Wulfram, the teacher of the Christians, and ask him what is that dwelling-place of eternal brightness which he promises you. When [Col. 0814A] he cannot show it to you, let envoys from both sides be sent; I shall be their guide on the way and shall show them the golden and most beautiful dwelling which I promise you.”

Upon waking, Radbod told everything to Saint Wulfram. Wulfram said that the mocking devil wished to deceive him. The duke answered that he would become a Christian if that beautiful dwelling were not shown to him by Wulfram’s God. At once, therefore, a Frisian was sent on the duke’s behalf and a deacon on Saint Wulfram’s behalf. When they had gone a little way from the town, they met a certain companion on the road, who said to them: “Hurry quickly, for I shall show you the most beautiful dwelling prepared for Duke Radbod.”

Proceeding along a very broad road and through unknown places, they saw a road adorned with polished work in various kinds of marble. From afar they saw a house as though of gold; and they came to a square before the house, as though paved with gold and gems. Entering the house, they saw that it was of marvelous beauty and unbelievable splendor, and that in it stood a throne of extraordinary size. Then their guide said: “This is the dwelling prepared for Duke Radbod.” At this the deacon, astonished, said: “If these things are made by God, may they remain forever; if by the devil, may they quickly perish.” When he signed himself with the sign of the holy cross, that guide changed into a devil, and the golden house into mud. The deacon and the Frisian remained amid marshy places full of very long rough bushes. After travelling for three days over an immense distance, [Col. 0814C] they returned to the town and found the duke dead; and they recounted to Saint Wulfram what they had seen.

The Frisian was baptized; he was called Ingomar, or Cuningus, and followed Saint Wulfram to the monastery of Fontenelle. Duke Radbod died, as is read in the Life of Saint Wulfram, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 719, the sixth year of Prince Charles. Blessed Wulfram was among the Frisians for five years, and afterwards returned to the monastery of Fontenelle, where he assumed the monastic habit, having ordained the venerable Gericus bishop in the city of Sens.

At Fontenelle the saint himself went for many years without a bed, clothed in haircloth beneath his cowl. Nowhere, [Col. 0814D] out of regard or fear for the rich, did he keep silent if they had done wrong; rather, he rebuked them with harsh invective. But he chanted more gently, not raising his voice on high, but shedding tears from the depths of his breast. He died at Fontenelle on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 720. He was buried beside blessed Wandregisil in the church of Saint Paul, where he lay for nine years. Blessed Wandregisil lay there for forty years, and Saint Ansbert for eleven.

At this time, in Britain, a certain hermit was shown by an angel a marvelous vision concerning Saint Joseph the decurion, who took down the Lord’s body from the cross, and concerning that dish or platter in which the Lord supped with his disciples. The hermit wrote a history of it, [Col. 0815A] called the history of the Gradale. “Gradalis,” or in French “gradale,” means a broad and somewhat deep dish, in which costly foods with their sauce are customarily served to the rich in successive courses—one morsel after another in different ranks. It is called in the vernacular *graalz*, because it is pleasing and welcome to the person eating from it: both on account of its container, because it may perhaps be of silver or another precious material, and on account of its contents, that is, the manifold arrangement of costly foods.

I have not been able to find this history written in Latin; it is preserved only in French, written by certain nobles, and, as they say, it cannot easily be found complete. Nor have I yet been able to obtain it carefully for reading from anyone. As soon as I can, I shall briefly translate into Latin [Col. 0815B] the more probable and useful parts.

**719. BEDE.**

The Saracens abandon Constantinople; very many of them perish from hunger, cold, and plague. On their return they attack the people of the Bulgars, who dwell beyond the Danube; defeated by them, they flee and make for their ships. As they sought the open sea, a sudden storm arose; many ships were sunk or shattered, and many men were killed along the shores by the ships.

The emir Ceuleimen dies, after whom Haumar rules the Saracens for two years. Against him the people of Constantinople resist stoutly through persistence in prayer and battle, and steadfastness; under him Saracens perish without number. It is related that they perished miraculously in the following manner.

At Constantinople, in the monastery of the Holy Mother of God beside the palace, on the sea near Saint Sophia, there was [Col. 0815C] an image of blessed Mary holding the infant in her arm, painted on a panel by Saint Luke while Saint Mary was still living. This image is called the *Hodēgētria*, that is, “the Guide,” because Saint Mary appeared to two blind men, led them to her church, and gave them sight. A procession with this image is held every Tuesday throughout the city.

When therefore, as stated above, the city was under siege and the citizens were fasting, praying, and fighting at the same time, a certain citizen advised that the image be brought forth and that everyone pray to it thus: “Holy Mother of God, who have so often delivered us, deliver us now from the enemies of your Son; and, if you desire that we should not sink your image in the sea, sink them.” When they had said this, he secretly held the image [Col. 0815D] beneath the waves; immediately a storm arose and either sank or broke all the ships of the Saracens.

After the death of King Dagobert, Lothar reigns for two years. After Conred, Osric reigns over the Northumbrians for eleven years. These two—Conred and Osric—killed Osred, who had reigned before them. Constantine, son of Emperor Leo, while being baptized by Saint Germanus the patriarch, defecated in the holy font, giving a great omen that he would prove a scandal to the Church of God.

The Saracens depart in confusion from the siege of Constantinople, their ships having been partly sunk and partly destroyed by a storm of fiery hail. Of so great a multitude of ships scarcely five remained; the power of God became known to all. [Col. 0816A] Within the city, however, three hundred thousand people died of plague.

**720.**

Haumar persecutes Christians and makes many of them martyrs. Chilperic and Raginfrid enlist the aid of Eudo, duke of Aquitaine; defeated by Charles in battle, they scarcely escape by flight. On returning, Eudo takes Chilperic away with him. Saracens from Africa, led by Abdita, son of the emir Muhania, cross into Spain and claim it for themselves. Thus the kingdom of the Visigoths and Sueves was destroyed and reduced beneath the Saracens, about three hundred and forty-six years after the Visigoths had been driven out of Scythia by the Huns; and about two hundred and fifty-six years after, when the Vandals had withdrawn and the Sueves had been conquered, they began to rule in Spain.

The kingdom of the third part of Spain, called that of the Galicians, [Col. 0816B] neither the Visigoths then nor the Saracens later could subdue; it still flourishes unharmed and, protected by faith in God, remains unconquerable.

**721.**

After Haumar, Gizid rules the Saracens for three years. When King Lothar dies, Charles receives Chilperic back from Eudo through envoys and makes him his king. King Liutprand of the Lombards, hearing that the Saracens had ravaged Sardinia and defiled the place where the bones of Saint Augustine, the great teacher, had long ago been transferred and honorably buried because of barbarian devastation, sent for them; having paid a price, he received them and transferred them to Pavia. There he buried them with the honor due to so great a Father.

Up to this point [Col. 0816C] Bede wrote his Chronicle, reckoning from the beginning of the world to this Leo, according to the Hebrew Truth, four thousand six hundred and eighty years.

**(722.)**

Emperor Leo labored often and greatly to have Pope Gregory killed, but in vain, since the Italians and Lombards steadily resisted the emperor in Gregory’s defense. The *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* recount this as follows. Duke Basil, the *chartularius* Jordanes, and the subdeacon John surnamed Lurion planned how they might kill the pontiff, with the agreement of Morinus, an imperial *spatharius*, in accordance with the emperor’s command. Morinus became crippled and departed from Rome. When their plan had been exposed, the Romans killed Jordanes the *chartularius* and John Lurion. Basil became a monk [Col. 0816D] and died.

The exarch Paul wished to accomplish the crime through another *spatharius*, but the Lombards’ attack upon the Romans prevented this. The Lord’s pontiff had allowed them to impose a tax in the provinces, as the emperor did elsewhere. In Campania of Italy wheat, barley, and legumes were burned; these were sent from heaven in rain [reading uncertain].

Charles, pursuing Raginfrid, besieges Angers; after taking it and defeating Raginfrid, he grants it to him as a residence and assumes the leadership of the entire kingdom. King Liutprand besieges Ravenna and, having taken the city by means of the Ravennates’ fleet, destroys it; from there he carries off many ships and countless riches.

**723.**

Charles defeats the Saxons. Rigobert, bishop of Rheims, is deposed from his bishopric by Charles, his godson, because when Charles was setting out against Raginfrid, Rigobert had refused, out of fear of Raginfrid, to open the city of Rheims to him. Eucherius also, bishop of Orléans, was deprived of his bishopric for a similar reason and exiled to the Saxon village of Hasbania; in the monastery of Saint Trudo he attained perfection in holiness. [Col. 0817A]

**724.**

Charles subdues the Bavarians by arms. A certain wicked Jew, promising Gizid that he would reign for forty years, persuades him to decree throughout his kingdom that images of God and the saints should be removed. Deceived by hope of a long reign, he did indeed issue the edict, but soon died. After him Eluelid reigned for twenty years.

**725.**

[Col. 0817B]

Emperor Leo, deceived by a certain Beser, an apostate and renegade from the faith, declares war against the images of Christ and his saints and decrees that they everywhere be removed and burned. For this error Pope Gregory rebukes him much in writing, but in vain. The exarch Paul and his son are killed by the Romans. The Romans wished to elect another emperor for themselves, but the pontiff forbade it, hoping for Leo’s conversion.

A star called Antifer appeared in the western sky with rays; its rays faced toward the north and extended to the middle of the heavens. Tiberius, coming from parts of Tuscany, wished to make himself king; he was killed and his head was sent to Constantinople. The patrician Eutychius and King Liutprand devised a plan to kill the pontiff, so that the king might have the duchy of Spoleto and the patrician Rome. When the pontiff met them in the Field of Nero, he so bent the king’s mind that he prostrated himself in worship before him and laid down a gilded mantle, *armelansia* [an uncertain vestment], belt, and sword, together with a golden crown and a silver cross. [Col. 0817C]

**(726.)**

Charles fights against Lantfrid, duke of the Alemanni; having defeated him, he subdues Alemannia.

**727.**

After Childeric’s death Charles makes Theuderic his king, and he reigns for fifteen years. Meanwhile Charles defeats the Saxons. At Constantinople the images of all the saints, [Col. 0817D] of the Saviour, and of the Holy Mother of God are removed and burned with fire, and all painted churches are whitewashed. Those who did not agree with the emperor were either killed or mutilated. Saint Germanus is deposed from his bishopric. Anastasius, supporting the emperor, is made bishop. Charles defeats the Sueves and, for a second time, the Bavarians.

Wicred, king of the English, dies; after him his son Edilbert reigns. This Wicred, or Wifred, son of Egbert, as was said above in chapter sixteen of the forty-fifth book of this volume, reigned thirty-six years. For the six years immediately before him there had been no king in Kent. He left three children. Edbert maintained the kingdom for twenty-three years, Edbert for eleven, and Alric for thirty-four, retaining their father’s institutions and ending their reigns not dishonorably. [Col. 0818A] Coemes is the first to reign over the Bulgars.

**(728.)**

Charles crosses the Loire, defeats Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, in war, puts him to flight, and devastates Aquitaine grievously. Since Pope Gregory sees Emperor Leo to be incorrigible, he causes Rome, Italy, and all Hesperia to withdraw from Leo’s jurisdiction and forbids the payment of tribute.

**(729.)**

Eudo, duke inferior to Charles in every respect, invites the Saracens from Spain against him.

**730.**

Saint Egbert, priest of the English, dies. The Saracens cross the Garonne with all their households, as though intending to settle in Gaul; they devastate everything and burn the churches of God. Charles, relying on God’s aid, meets them in battle and kills three hundred and seventy-five thousand of them together with their king Abdirama, [Col. 0818B] while losing only twelve hundred of his own men. Eudo also, reconciled with Charles, bursts into the Saracens’ camp and crushes their remnants. So Sigebert says.

But the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* recount this battle thus. The Saracens, who had then held Spain for ten years, attempted to cross the Rhône and occupy the Frankish lands, where Eudo was in command. Joining battle against them, he killed 375,000 of them in one day. Only fifteen hundred Franks died. In the preceding year this Eudo had received three sponges as a blessing, sponges which are placed for use at the Roman pontiff’s table. At the hour when battle was to be joined, Eudo himself, prince of Aquitaine, distributed very small portions of them to his people for them to consume; and of those who partook, [Col. 0818C] not one was wounded or died.

After the death of Osric, king of the Northumbrians, Cednulf reigns. Pope Gregory gave to monasteries, diaconiae, mansionarii, and all the clergy 2,160 solidi, and for the lamps of Saint Peter one thousand solidi. He made one hundred and fifty bishops. He died and was buried on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, while Leo and Constantine were emperors; the bishopric was vacant for thirty-five days.

**731.**

After him sat the ninety-second pope, another Gregory—the third of that name—a Syrian by nation, for ten years, eight months, and twenty-five days; a mild and wise man, learned in Greek and Latin, retaining all the psalms by heart. [Col. 0818D] He sent the priest George to the emperors Leo and Constantine; afraid, George did not present the letters. On returning he was almost deposed from the priesthood; but at the request of the bishops of the whole council, Gregory spared him, imposed penance upon him, and sent him again to Constantinople. But the emperors caused the letters to be detained in Sicily and banished their bearer for a year.

Accordingly Pope Gregory turned the Roman people and the revenues of all Hesperia away from Leo. Raginfrid dies, and Bede, the venerable priest, according to Sigebert; but according to William, two years later—which seems truer, as we shall show below. Charles, having taken Lyons and other cities, subdues Burgundy. Constantine, [Col. 0819A] Leo’s son, marries Irene, daughter of Cajan, duke of the Avars. Baptized, she remained orthodox although her husband apostatized.

**(732.)**

Charles fights Eudo in Gascony and deprives him of both principality and life. Liutprand takes many towns and castles belonging by right to the Roman pontiff. Cedulf, king of the Northumbrians, is captured and tonsured as a cleric, and after this is restored to the kingdom. So Sigebert says.

William of Malmesbury, however, says: “After Osric, Cednulf, the seventh from Ida, reigned, a man learned in letters; to him Bede presented the history of the English to be polished by him.” He adds: “In Cednulf’s fourth year Bede died, in the year of the Incarnation 733, at the age of fifty-nine. Born at the farthest corner of the world, he illumined all lands with the shining splendor of learning. In the nineteenth year of his life he was made deacon, and in the thirtieth priest; from then until his fifty-ninth year he never ceased either teaching or writing. He produced thirty-six volumes, divided into seventy-eight books. It is said that he went to Rome in order personally to affirm that his books accorded with ecclesiastical teaching, or, should they meet opposition, to correct them at apostolic admonition. Yet I do not firmly assert that he was at Rome; but I declare without doubt that he himself was invited there by Pope Sergius.”

For there survives Sergius’s letter to Ceolfrith, abbot of Bede, in which, among other things, the following is written:

> We exhort the God-beloved goodness of your religious devotion that, because certain ecclesiastical matters have arisen which cannot become more widely known without examination, and we need persons trained in the art of letters for conference, you should not fail, as becomes a helper devoted to God’s universal mother Church, to give obedient devotion to this our exhortation. Rather, without any delay, do not hesitate to send to the thresholds of the princes of the apostles, my lords Peter and Paul, your lovers and protectors, and into the presence of our humble self, the religious servant of God Bede, priest of your venerable monastery. With the Lord’s favor and your holy prayers, do not doubt that, after the desired solemn examination of the aforesaid matters has been accomplished with God’s help, he will return safely to you. For, as we believe, whatever shall shine forth as bestowed through his excellence upon the universal Church will benefit all believers.

Thus so celebrated was his reputation that the Roman eminence needed him even for resolving questions. [Col. 0819D] His eloquence was unstudied but sweet. For seven continuous weeks before his death, nauseated by an illness of the stomach and drawing breath with laboured breathing, he nevertheless did not abandon his literary pursuits; throughout those days, besides the appointed duty of psalmody, he devoted himself to them, and during those days translated the Gospel of John into English.

He said to his disciples: “Learn, little sons, while I am with you.” On the Tuesday before Ascension a slight swelling appeared in his feet. He then summoned the community, was anointed and received communion, and, having given every one the kiss of peace, asked each separately to remember him in the future. To some, on account of more intimate friendship, he also gave little gifts which he kept in private. [Col. 0820A]

On Ascension Day, lying opposite the oratory where he used to pray, on a haircloth spread beneath him, with his mind unimpaired and a joyful face, he said: “O King of glory! Lord of hosts,” and so forth, to the end of the antiphon. When it ended, he breathed out his spirit. So sweet a fragrance followed that all who stood by said that they were in paradise. He was buried in the same monastery; but now he is said to lie at Durham with blessed Cuthbert. His epitaph is this:

> Here rests Bede the priest, buried in the flesh.  
> Christ, grant his soul eternal joy in heaven;  
> and grant that he may be made drunk from Wisdom’s spring,  
> for which he has longed in rejoicing, ever with intent love.

So William. Therefore Bede the Venerable, priest, died [Col. 0820B] in the fourth year of King Cednulf, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 733, as has been said.

In the same year Pope Gregory, the third of that name, assembled at Rome a synod of nine hundred and three bishops, confirmed the veneration of holy images, and by a general sentence anathematized those who violated them. In the same year Charles, having defeated Tudites, Wailfer, and Huvald, sons of Eudo, in battle, subdues Aquitaine.

**(734.)**

Charles attacks Frisia, kills Poppo, duke of the Frisians, with many others, and subjects Frisia to himself.

**(735.)**

Charles besieges Avignon, a city of Gaul captured by the Saracens through the treachery and agreement of Maurontus, duke of Provence. Having recovered it by force, he destroys the Saracens to utter extermination. Saint Hubert dies. [Col. 0820C] From this point the kingdom of the English is not recorded. So Sigebert.

William, however, says this: King Cednulf, in whose fourth year Bede died, became a monk in the church of Lindisfarne after eight years of rule, placing in the kingdom Egbert, son of his father, who reigned twenty years and had a namesake brother, archbishop of York. Paulinus, the first bishop of this city, driven from his see by hostile force, died at Rochester and left there the distinguished pallium which he had received from Pope Honorius. Many bishops after him, content with the simple title of bishop over so great a city, had aspired to nothing higher. But the distinguished pallium of an archbishop was regained by many appeals to the apostolic throne. This Bishop Egbert founded a most noble library at York, an armory—or rather a treasury—of all the liberal arts. This Archbishop Egbert was Alcuin’s teacher. [Col. 0820D]

**(736.)**

King Egbert, emulating his brother in religion, had his hair cut and gave place to Molon, who ruled vigorously for eleven years before being killed by the plots of Alred. Alred was driven out by the provincials in the tenth year of his reign. After him King Alfunold was treacherously killed by the same men in the eleventh year of his reign. Before him, however, Ethelbert, also called Adeldred, son of King Molon, was expelled by the same men in his fifth year. After him no one dared to ascend the throne.

While the Saracen king Athima was besieged by Charles in the Gallic city of Narbonne, Saracens came from [Col. 0821A] Spain to his aid with another king, Amor. They engaged Charles; both kings were killed, the city was recovered, and the Saracens were almost utterly annihilated. The survivors, fleeing from Charles as he pursued them, were drowned in the deep.

**737.**

Charles captures Nîmes, Agde, and other cities of the Gothic region which had been invaded by the Saracens, and destroys them to their foundations. Saint Erminus, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, dies.

**(378.)**

After the city of Arles had been captured by the Saracens and all the surrounding region destroyed, Charles summoned King Liutprand of the Lombards to assist him, met the Saracens, put them to flight by the terror of his name, and removed from them all hope of invading Gaul thereafter.

**739.**

Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, rebels against Liutprand [Col. 0821B] and flees to the Romans. Charles defeats Maurontus, duke of Provence, who had invited the Saracens, and subdues Provence. King Liutprand severely harasses Rome because it has given refuge to Trasamund.

**(740.)**

Charles makes the Saxons tributaries. Signs appear in the sun, moon, and stars. After Theuderic, king of the Franks, Hilderic reigns for nine years.

**(741.)**

Having pacified and enlarged the kingdom of the Franks, the warlike prince Charles dies, leaving as heirs to his principate his sons Carloman and Pippin. Pope Gregory is said twice to have sent him from Rome keys of the venerable tomb, with Saint Peter’s chains and many gifts. He gladly received the embassy and sent to Rome with many gifts Grimoald, abbot of Corbie, and Sigebert, recluse of the basilica of Saint Dionysius. Charles died at the estate of Quierzy (Cressy), on the river Oise, in the twenty-fifth year of his principate, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November; he was buried in the basilica of Saint Dionysius. After Leo, his son Constantine rules as emperor for thirty-five years.

Constantinople is severely shaken by earthquakes for a full year. Before Leo’s death, Peter the *defensor* was sent to Constantinople to Bishop Anastasius. He brought to Rome six twisted columns given him, and placed them in the church of Saint Peter before the confession, near the presbytery—three on the right and three on the left. Upon them he placed beams, [Col. 0821D] which he covered with the purest silver; on one side were represented the figures of the Saviour and the apostles, and on the other the Mother of God and holy virgins.

Pope Gregory, making a screen (*pergula*), bestowed gifts of various kinds: two golden bowls, five other *saxiscas* [vessels; term uncertain], an image of the Holy Mother of God, a gem-studded golden diadem, a gem-studded golden necklace, and the other things arranged for the ornament of his screen. He made an image of the Holy Mother of God embracing the Saviour, wholly of gold and set with various gems, weighing five pounds.

At that time King Liutprand came to Rome, pitched his tents in the Field of Nero, ravaged Campania, and in Lombard fashion tonsured and clothed many Roman nobles. Therefore [Col. 0822A] the pontiff, distressed with grief, took the sacred keys from the confession of Saint Peter and sent them to Charles, prince of the Franks, through Bishop Anastasius and the priest Sergius, asking him to free the Romans from the Lombards.

He made Vulgatius, from the regions of Francia, bishop of Vienne; established the feast of All Saints; and made eighty bishops. He was buried on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, and the bishopric was vacant eight days.

**(742.)**

After him sat the ninety-third pope, Zacharias, a Greek by nation, for ten years, three months, and fourteen days; a man praiseworthy in every respect, advancing even his persecutors to honours. King Liutprand restored to him four cities which he had taken from the Romans, as well as many other things which he had taken from Saint Peter. He made peace with the Roman duchy for twenty years and returned to the pope all captives whom he had carried away from the Roman provinces.

Zacharias constructed from the foundations a portico, tower, bronze doors, and railings before the Lateran archive. Upon the same tower he made a triclinium and bronze railings, where he depicted a map of the world and decorated it with various little verses. He had the books of the *Dialogues* translated into Greek. He found the head or body of Saint George the martyr, together with Greek letters identifying it as such; having gathered all the people, he caused it to be brought into the second district to the Golden Veil. He made eighty-five bishops.
