King Liutprand of the Lombards dies. Hildebrand, whom he had designated king, having been rejected by the Lombards, Ratchis reigns [Col. 0822C] for seven years. Prince Pippin meets Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, who has rebelled against him, while Carloman ravages Alemannia. Artabald seizes imperial power against Constantine. Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, founds the monastery of Fulda in the forest of Buchonia.

**743.**

Carloman advances into Saxony, captures the fortress of Ostoburg, and takes Theuderic the Saxon as a hostage for peace. Duke Egdilo of Bavaria, having abducted Pippin’s sister, rebels against him; Pippin defeats him in battle, though with losses.

**744.**

Constantine captures Artabald, puts out the eyes of him and his sons, and sends them into exile. The eyes of many of his friends also are put out. Emir Elvelid dies; after him Gizid reigns for [Col. 0822D] one year.

**(745.)**

Ash falls from heaven. Pippin defeats Theodoald, son of Duke Godefrid. Bishop Peter of Damascus and Peter of Mavimene are martyred by the Saracens in Syria. After the city of Aix had been taken and laid waste by the Saracens, the body of blessed Mary Magdalene is transferred by Gerard, count of Burgundy, to the monastery of Vézelay which he had built; although some write that she rests at Ephesus and has no covering over her.

**(746.)**

Carloman, Pippin’s brother, sets out for Rome, abandons the kingdom, and is tonsured as a monk by Pope Zacharias. At first he dwelt on Mount Soracte, in a monastery which he himself founded; later, because of the crowds of visitors coming to him and burdening that house, he moved to Monte Cassino, [Col. 0823A] where he shone in a praiseworthy life. It is read in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* that he received the yoke of clerical office from the holy pontiff. Afterwards he departed for Saint Benedict’s, situated in the country of Aquino, and there bound himself by oath to end his life.

The priest Athalongus, warned by blindness inflicted upon him to seek the bodies of Saint Kilian and his companions, recovered his sight when he found them. On this account Saint Boniface decreed that the fortress of Würzburg should be distinguished by the privilege of an episcopal see in honour of Kilian the martyr, who had there been ordained by Pope Conon to preach and had there received from God the place of his death and repose; he first ordained Saint Burchard bishop there.

After Gizid was killed, Histes reigns one year.

**(747.)**

After him Muruham reigned for six years.

**(748.)**

Pippin pursues his brother Grifo, who rebels against him, into Saxony. The Saracens clash with one another in civil war. Pippin captures in Saxony Grifo and his accomplices Tassilo, Lantfrid, and Suidiger, defeated in battle. He makes Tassilo duke of Bavaria and grants Grifo twelve counties in Neustria. This does not satisfy Grifo; he flees to Waifer in Aquitaine. In Calabria and Sicily there is plague and excessive human mortality. Little crosses, as if marked with oil, appear on people’s clothing and on church veils. [Col. 0823B]

**749.**

Ratchis, king of the Lombards, breaks the treaty, harasses Rome, and besieges the city of Perugia. Pope Zacharias goes to him, taking leading men from his clergy, gives him many gifts, and begs him to desist from the siege. He preaches God’s word to him so effectively that Ratchis becomes a cleric and, together with his wife and children, puts on the monastic habit at Rome. Aistulf succeeds him for seven years.

**(750.)**

Hilderic, king of the Franks, is tonsured as a monk. Prince Pippin, by apostolic authority and the election of the Franks, is anointed and consecrated king by Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, and reigns for eighteen years—about eighty-eight years after mayors of the palace had begun to exercise power over the kings of the Franks.

**751.**
Pippin the king fights against the Saxons; by his own efforts he improves the churches of Gaul with chants authorized by Rome; his brother Grifo is killed. Remigius, [Col. 0823D] another of his brothers, shines as bishop of Rouen. (752.) Pope Zacharias died on the Ides of March, and the episcopal see was vacant for twelve days. After him Stephen II, the ninety-fourth, sat for five years and twenty-nine days. Along with him another Stephen, a priest, was elected; on the third day, after rising from sleep and sitting down to arrange household affairs, he suddenly became deranged and speechless, and died the following day. After him this Stephen was unanimously elected by all the people. He immediately restored four hospices at Rome and founded five others. Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, came to the thresholds of the Apostles, where he promised to persevere; afterward breaking his vow and going out to the Lombards, whom he wickedly incited, he was stoned. Aistulf, [Col. 0824A] king of the Lombards, began to oppress the Romans. In the third month of his ordination Pope Stephen sent him many gifts for peace. He made a treaty with them for forty years, which he broke in the fourth month; he wished to impose a gold solidus upon each person and to subject Rome to himself. The pontiff sent to Constantinople for aid. Meanwhile Aistulf grievously oppressed them. The pope himself, walking barefoot, bore on his own shoulders in procession an image of our Lord Jesus Christ, of His Mother, and the holy cross, ashes having been placed upon everyone’s heads. He ordained that every Saturday, all other neglect set aside, a litany should be held. He made curtains before the altar of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin at the Manger, which he overlaid with silver. Maruha, after killing Muhammad, reigned five years. Pope Stephen sent to Pippin king of the Franks for help against Aistulf. Pippin sent Rodgang, first an abbot and afterward a bishop, and Duke Aucharius, to bring the pope into Francia. As he was travelling, a fiery globe appeared in the southern sky, moving away from the borders of Gaul toward the regions of the Lombards. The pontiff came to the monastery of Saint Maurice, where Pippin hastened to meet him with his wife and sons, having sent his son Charles ahead. At his own palace of Ponticone Pippin dismounted, and, prostrate upon the ground with his wife, sons, and nobles, received him; he himself also performed the service of a groom as far as a certain place near the pope’s saddle-horse [lacuna]. On the holy day of Epiphany [Col. 0824C] he received him and immediately directed his army toward Ravenna. Since it was winter, he brought the pontiff with him to Paris and caused him to winter at Saint-Denis. In that monastery Pippin stayed some days with the pope and was anointed king, together with his sons. There the pope became seriously ill; and when in the morning he was thought dead, he suddenly recovered on the next day. Then Aistulf sent Carloman from Monte Cassino into Francia to his brother Pippin; he achieved nothing, but became a monk there. Afterward Pippin moved his army against Aistulf. Defeated, Aistulf made a treaty, which he broke after Pippin’s departure; he besieged Rome for three months and cast out many bodies of saints from their cemeteries. Again the pope sent [Col. 0824D] to Pippin, who hurriedly besieged Pavia. Aistulf immediately restored to Saint Peter everything he had taken and confirmed it in writing; afterward he was struck down by a divine blow while hunting. He was the brother of King Rachis, who became a monk.

**SIGEBERT.** Thus Pippin was anointed king by Pope Stephen together with his sons Carloman and Charles; through them their line is blessed forever with the inheritance of royal succession, and every foreigner is forbidden, under apostolic anathema, from invading their kingdom. Pippin again enters Italy, defeats Aistulf, and compels him to act according to his will. Carloman the monk attempts to remove the bones of Saint Benedict the abbot from the church of Fleury and carry them to [Col. 0825A] the fortress of Cassino; but, by miracles shown by God and by Frankish resistance, he is prevented from his undertaking. (753.) A terrible earthquake occurred: some cities were overthrown in part, others altogether; still others, entire and unharmed, with their walls and inhabitants, moved from mountainous places to the plains below, more than six miles away. In Mesopotamia the earth split open for as much as two miles; and other earth, exceedingly white and sandy, rose from the depths, and from it came forth an unclean animal speaking with a human voice, announcing the incursion of a people from the desert against the Arabs. (754.) Carloman the monk dies at Vienne. Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, is martyred with his companions in Frisia and is honourably buried at the monastery of Fulda, which he himself had built and founded in Thuringia. This Boniface, an Englishman by nation, wrote a letter to Æthelbald, king of the English; William of Malmesbury records his genealogy in this manner:

“In the year of the Lord 626, a certain Penda, son of Pybba and tenth from Woden, assumed the royal title among the Mercians, after he had, already fifty years old, nourished his boldness by frequent raids against neighbouring peoples. Either not knowing, or pretending not to know, what a crime it was to conquer allies by war, he destroyed Edwin and Oswald, kings of the Northumbrians; Sigebert, Egric, and Anna, kings of the East Angles. He drove Cenwalh, king of the West Saxons, into exile—and deservedly, for although at first a Christian, he had afterward renounced the faith and repudiated Penda’s sister. At last he was slain by Oswine, brother of Saint Oswald, more through God’s power than by a military hand. By Queen Koneswita he had five sons: Weda, Welfenus, Æthelred, Menwald, and Mercelin; and two daughters, Kyneburga and Kynewita, both Christians and of holy continence. After him his son Weda reigned among the southern Mercians, son-in-law of Oswi, whose daughter he had received, while his pagan father was still living, on the condition that he should become a Christian. He was killed through the treachery of his wife. Oswi took his kingdom and held it for three years. But after Oswi’s leaders had been expelled by the provincials, Waifer, Penda’s son, reigned. Becoming a Christian at once, he was the first simoniacal [Col. 0825D] king of the English. For he sold the bishopric of London to a certain ambitious Wina. He married Ermenhilda, daughter of King Eorcenberht of Kent; by her he begot Reured and the most holy virgin Werburga, who lies at Chester. His brother Merewalh married Ermenburga, daughter of Eormenred, brother of that same Eorcenberht; by her he begot daughters, Milburga, who lies at Wenlock, and Mildrith, who lies in Kent at the monastery of Saint Augustine, and a son, Metesinus. Ælfrid, king of the Northumbrians, married Kyneburga, Penda’s daughter; later she took the habit of a nun in the monastery which her brothers Wulfhere and Æthelred had built. Wulfhere reigned nineteen years; after him Æthelred, more devout than warlike, who in the thirtieth year [Col. 0826A] of his reign was regularly tonsured at Bardney and changed first into a monk, then shortly afterward into an abbot. He was contemporary with Ine, king of the West Saxons. He married Ostgyth, sister of Ecgfrith, king of the Northumbrians, and by her received a son, Ceolred. After him reigned Cenred, son of his brother Wulfhere, a man of excellent character. In the fifth year of his reign he went to Rome and spent the rest of his time there in religious life, pierced with remorse and terrified by the pitiable end of his soldier who, as Bede relates, had proudly refused, while healthy, to confess his crimes; when brought to death’s door, he openly saw demons dragging him to punishments. After him Ceolred, son of his uncle Æthelred, reigned eight years; he lies at Lichfield. He left as heir Æthelbald, Penda’s great-grandson through his brother Alweo, [Col. 0826B] who reigned in peace forty-one years, until Brenred killed him; Brenred himself was soon killed by Offa.”

The aforesaid Boniface, bishop and martyr of Mainz, wrote a letter to this Æthelbald, from which I have excerpted the following:

“To the most beloved lord Æthelbald, to be preferred in the love of Christ above the other kings of the English: Boniface, archbishop, German legate of the Roman Church, a perpetual greeting of charity in Christ.

“We have heard that you devote yourself to almsgiving, forbid thefts and robberies, love peace, and are a defender of the poor and widows; and for this we give thanks to God. But that you despise lawful marriage, [Col. 0826C] if you did so for chastity’s sake, would be praiseworthy. Yet because you indulge in lust and adultery, even with nuns, it is blameworthy and condemnable. For it confounds the renown of our glory before God and men, and places us among idolaters, because you have violated the temple of God. Therefore, dearest son, repent, and remember how shameful it is that you, who by God’s gift rule over many peoples, should be a slave of lust, to His dishonour. We have further heard that nearly all the nobles of the Mercian people, following your example, abandon their lawful wives and violate adulteresses and nuns. How foreign this is to decency the customs of foreign peoples teach you. For in ancient Saxony, where there is no knowledge of Christ, [Col. 0826D] if a virgin in her father’s house or a married woman under her husband is adulterated, they burn her after strangling her with their own hands, and hang the seducer over the grave of the buried woman; or chaste matrons, with the woman’s clothing cut off to the waist, scourge and stab her with knives; and, sent from village to village, new women meet her to scourge her until they kill her. The Wends also, a most foul race of men, have this custom: when her husband dies, the woman throws herself onto the pyre in which he is being burned, to burn with him. If, therefore, peoples ignorant of God have zeal for chastity, what befits you, dearest son, who are a Christian and a king? Spare, then, your own soul; spare the multitude of people perishing through your example, for whose souls you must render an account. Consider also that, if the English people, as we are reproached by those in Francia and Italy and by the pagans themselves, reject lawful marriages and lapse into adultery, there will arise from such a mixture [Col. 0827A] an idle people, despising God, which by its corrupt morals will ruin its country—as happened to the Burgundians, Provençals, and Spaniards, whom the Saracens harassed for many years because of their former sins. Furthermore, it has been reported to us that by taking away many privileges of churches and monasteries you incite your dukes by your example to dare the same. But consider, I beg you, what terrible vengeance God inflicted upon former kings, conscious of the guilt for which we rebuke you. For Ceolred, your predecessor, violator of holy nuns and breaker of ecclesiastical privileges, while feasting splendidly with his companions, was seized by an evil spirit; without confession or viaticum, while speaking with the devil and detesting God’s law, he gave up his soul. Osred also, king of the Deirans and Bernicians, guilty of the same crimes, was driven to such unbridled conduct that he lost both his kingdom and his youthful life by a contemptible death. Charles [Note: [Col. 0827D] He means Charles Martel.] also, prince of the Franks, destroyer of many monasteries and converter of ecclesiastical revenues to his own use, was consumed by prolonged torment and a shameful death. Dearest son, nothing is more salutary for a good king than willingly to correct his offences when rebuked. We entreat and beseech you, by the living God the Father, by His Son [Col. 0827C] Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit, to remember how fleeting the present life is, how short and momentary is the pleasure of impure flesh, through which eternal torments are purchased, and how disgraceful it is for one whose life is brief to leave evil examples to posterity forever.”

Boniface sent Archbishop Cuthbert a letter of the same tenor, adding that he should rebuke clerics and nuns for the scantiness and splendour of their clothes; further, that he should not wonder why Boniface concerned himself with another’s business, although it did not affect him how and with what morals the English people lived. He should know that Pope Gregory III had bound him by oath not to withhold the morals of neighbouring peoples from apostolic knowledge. If gentle admonitions [Col. 0827D] did not succeed, he would act lest such vices remain hidden from the pope. From these things one may judge the prudence of this blessed man and his freedom of spirit in publicly rebuking the sins of kings and princes; through this, joined to the holiness of his earlier life, he happily attained the crown and glory of martyrdom. Lullus succeeded Boniface; the Life of Saint Goar speaks of him, and these verses say:

> Bishop Lullus—none is holier than he—  
> Strong in healing granted by God’s gift.  
> He comes to meet diseases, as the whole world proclaims.

Offa succeeded King Æthelbald, Penda’s descendant in the fifth generation, a man of great spirit, who proposed to carry out whatever he had conceived in his mind. Thus he defeated Wulf, king of the West Saxons, a most valiant warrior, in open battle; he caused King Æthelbert, summoned to him by great promises, to be unexpectedly beheaded within his palace, and deceitfully obtained the kingdom of the East Angles. He caused the relics of Blessed Alban, hitherto obscurely concealed, to be placed in a shrine of gems and gold, after a basilica of most beautiful workmanship had been built there and monks assembled. He gave his daughter Eadburh to Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons. Anselm, an illustrious man whose sister was the wife of King Aistulf, transferred the body of Saint Sylvester to the monastery of Nonantola, founded by himself.

## 755

Emperor Constantine convenes at Constantinople a synod of three hundred and thirty bishops, [Col. 0828B] in which, after an edict was promulgated ordering the removal of images of God and His saints, he gravely scandalizes the Church of God and tyrannizes against the orthodox. King Aistulf, having broken the peace treaty, besieges Rome. Pippin, returning to Italy, besieges him shut up in Pavia and compels him unwillingly to renew the peace treaty; he causes everything belonging by right to Saint Peter to be restored. Fulcadus, abbot of Saint Denis the martyr, translated the body of Saint Vitus the martyr from Rome to Paris. (756.) Duke Tassilo is reconciled to his uncle Pippin. King Aistulf dies, struck by God’s judgement. After him Desiderius, formerly duke in the regions of Tuscany, reigns eighteen years; but he would not have reigned unless Pope Stephen had summoned him [Col. 0828C] on condition that he restore to Saint Peter what he had taken away. This Stephen made fifteen bishops; while he was in Francia he made Rotgang an archbishop and bestowed the pallium upon him. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopal see was vacant one month and five days. Up to this point the book *On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* is found written continuously, but who wrote it after Damasus is unknown. From Saint Peter until this point there are together seven hundred and eight years, 344 months, and 1,070 days, during which ninety-four pontiffs sat, excluding the years, months, and days in which the Roman episcopal see was vacant. From Saint Peter to this Stephen it was vacant, at intervals, nine years, [lacuna] months, and 1,464 days. [Col. 0828D] The Roman pontiffs, from Saint Peter to this Stephen II, made 1,251 bishops in different places. Moreover, Innocent, who was the forty-second, Boniface, the fifty-seventh, and Conon, the eighty-fifth, are not recorded as having made bishops. Between Silverius and Vigilius, and between Martin and Eugenius, the episcopal see is not said to have been vacant. From this point different authors treat of the Roman pontiffs sporadically and in varying ways. (757.) After Stephen, Paul, the ninety-fifth pope, sat at Rome for ten years and one month; but neither his nationality nor his deeds are stated. Habdallas presides over the Saracens for nineteen years. Pippin vigorously storms the Saxon fortifications and, after much slaughter, reduces them to tribute.

## 758

Waifer, son of Eudo and duke of Aquitaine, incurs Pippin’s wrath by unjustly harassing Frankish affairs. When Pippin enters Aquitaine, a treaty of feigned peace is made. Walpert, abbot in Italy, and Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, nephew of King Pippin through his sister Landeata, flourish in Gaul; he founded the monastery of Gorze in the diocese of Metz. The body of Saint Petronilla, virgin and daughter of the Apostle Peter, is transferred at Rome by Pope Paul. In her marble sarcophagus there was read an inscription written by the hand of the Apostle Peter himself: “To Aurea Petronilla, most beloved daughter.” (759.) Abdallah persecutes the Church of God. Waifer, having turned away from the peace [Col. 0829B] treaty, King Pippin devastates the district of Arumnicum, captures many strongholds and the city of Arumnis itself, and carries away Blandinus, count of the city, with many others. Saint Gengulf flourishes in Burgundy.

## 760

Pippin captures the city of Bourges and fortifies it after capture. Thelexis reigns over the Bulgars. Chilping, count of Arumnis, and Aming, count of Poitiers, meeting Pippin’s soldiers, are killed with many others.

## 761

The head of John the Baptist is transferred to the city of Memissa. (762.) Many are martyred by Constantine the heretic. Thelexis, engaging Emperor Constantine, is defeated with great loss and disgrace to the Bulgars; for this he is rejected by the Bulgars and killed by them with the leaders of the people. After [Col. 0829C] him Sabinus reigns. Duke Tassilo entirely turns away from King Pippin. The Turks, breaking out from the Caspian Gates, ravage Armenia. In their country, when a plague had arisen in ancient times, at the advice of Christians they cut their hair in the form of a cross; and because by this sign their country recovered safety, they afterward maintained this rite of tonsure. Waifer, despairing of his own position, razes the walls of Aquitaine’s cities to the ground; Pippin restores them and entrusts them to loyal princes for the protection of his own people. (763.) Pippin devastates the district of Limoges with slaughter and fire. Sabinus the Bulgar makes a treaty with the Romans; rejected by his own people for this, he flees to Constantine. After him Pagan reigns. A great frost lasts from the Kalends of [Col. 0829D] October until February. Stars were suddenly seen to fall from heaven; all were so terrified that they thought the end of the world was at hand.

## 764

Bishop Chrodegang transferred from Rome to Gaul the bodies of the martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius, placing Gorgonius at Gorze, Nabor at Illirac, and Nazarius in the monastery of Lorsch, which the illustrious Count Cancor had founded and given to the church of Metz in the previous year. (765.) King Pippin devastates Agen, Périgueux, and Angoulême, cities of Aquitaine, and subjugates a great part of Aquitaine to himself. Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, dies. At this time, in Syria, in the city of Berytus, subject to Antioch, Jews found an image of the Saviour Jesus Christ in the house of a certain [Col. 0830A] Jew; it had been left there by a Christian who had lived there. They took it down insultingly and inflicted upon it all the insults which, according to the Gospel, were inflicted upon Christ: they mocked it, spat upon it, struck it with fists and open hands, reviled it with shameful insults, fastened its hands and feet with nails, and offered it vinegar and gall. From the wound blood and water came out; they caught it in a vessel placed beneath it. To test whether the miracles they had heard Jesus perform were true, they gathered all the sick into their synagogue, sprinkled them with this blood, and all were healed from whatever illness afflicted them. At length the Jews, stricken with remorse, all ran to Adeodatus, bishop of the city; relating the event, they returned the image with the blood to him. [Col. 0830B] After they had been baptized, the bishop distributed the blood in vessels far and wide, preached God’s mighty works, and exhorted all that every year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, the Passion of the Lord’s image should be celebrated.

## 766

Constantine and Habdallas rage with equal madness against the orthodox and kill many of them for Christ. Constantine, moreover, bitterly resenting the glory of saints made resplendent by miracles, orders even their relics everywhere to be dug up and thrown into the depths. In the presence of King Pippin, a synod is celebrated concerning the Holy Trinity and the veneration of holy images. King Pippin hangs on a gallows Temistanus, brother of Eudo and uncle of Waifer, who had defected from Waifer to Pippin and from Pippin to Waifer, after he had been captured by Pippin’s own men in battle. Arminintes, king of the Saracens, seeks the friendship of King Pippin from Spain through envoys sent and gifts given and received.

## 767

Pippin crushes Aquitaine with final devastation, captures Saintes, and carries away captive Waifer’s mother, sisters, and nieces. After Pope Paul’s death, a certain Constantine, suddenly ordained priest from a layman, seized the papacy in tyrannical ambition and became a great scandal to the Church of God. Against him, some Romans set up Philip as pope, but he was deposed not long afterward. Saint Gengulf bought a certain spring in Gaul and caused it to rise in Burgundy. When its seller mocked the purchaser, he suddenly saw his own spring dry up. One day, therefore, while Gengulf was sitting beside that spring, miraculously rising in his garden, with his adulterous wife, he began to accuse her of the disgrace of her adultery. When she vehemently denied the crime, he proposed a very easy test of her innocence: “If you want me to believe that you are falsely burdened with this disgrace, bare your arm and bring me a little stone from the bottom of this spring. If you draw back your arm unharmed, I shall believe that you are innocent.” Hearing this, she confidently immersed her arm in the spring and immediately drew it back burned as if by fire. Then the saint said to her: “Behold the truth of your offence. Keep, then, what is yours, and remain by yourself or with your adulterer, for you shall no longer be my companion.” Having given her half his property, he lived apart from her. Not long afterward, [Col. 0831A] while sleeping in his house, he was killed by a certain cleric who was accustomed to commit adultery with his wife. As his body was carried in a bier to burial, many sick persons were healed by touching it. When her maidservant reported this to his wife—namely, that her master, like a holy martyr, was performing miracles—she laughed and sneered: “Yes,” she said, “Gengulf works miracles just as my anus sings.” Immediately, whether she wished it or not, her anus began to emit shameful and rhythmic noises. Thereafter, throughout all her life, every Friday, whenever on that day—the day on which her husband became a martyr—she uttered any word with her mouth, she emitted from her anus an indecent sound for every word. When King Pippin heard this, he deemed it worthy of trial, for the greater glory of the martyr Gengulf. After Pope Paul’s death, Master Hugh says in his *Chronicles*, the episcopal see was vacant for one year and one month; and the aforesaid Constantine sat for that same period, that is, one year and one month, as the ninety-sixth pope. But this pseudo-pope was erased from the order and number of popes, and therefore the whole duration of his tenure is called a vacancy of the episcopal see.

## 768

The long struggle between Pippin and Waifer ends, because Waifer is killed by his own followers, weary of so many evils, in Pippin’s favour; not long afterward Pippin dies, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans. He died at Paris from dropsy. His son Charles succeeds him, surnamed “the Great” because of the greatness of his good fortune, like Alexander and Pompey. Sharing the kingdom with his brother Carloman, Charles reigned forty-three years. After the pseudo-pope Constantine had been driven from the Church by the zeal of the faithful and deprived of his eyes, Stephen III, the ninety-sixth, presides for three years, five months, and twenty-eight days, according to Master Hugh. He convenes at Rome a synod from both Gaul and Italy, in which he reordains all those ordained by Constantine, except with respect to baptism and chrism. The synod decrees that bishops ordained by him should return to the rank which they had held before, and, if judged worthy, be ordained again. Priests and deacons ordained by him likewise should return to their former rank [Col. 0831D] and, if worthy, be consecrated again; but they should never ascend to a higher rank or order. Laymen ordained by him as deacons or priests should be altogether degraded and remain in religious dress. That synod also confirms the veneration of holy images and anathematizes their profaners. It also ordains that *Glory to God in the highest* be sung at Mass on every Sunday. Pope Symmachus, the fifty-second, had nevertheless earlier ordained that the *Glory to God in the highest* should be sung every Sunday and on the feast-days of martyrs. Charles is made king at Noyon, and his brother Carloman at Soissons.

## 769

When Hunald planned rebellion in Aquitaine, Charles marched into Aquitaine and received all the Aquitanians [Col. 0832A] and Gascons into submission. Hunald, who had fled to Lupus, duke of the Gascons, was handed over to Charles by Lupus with his wife, and Charles carried him away; thus the Aquitanian war ended. Desiderius, king of the Lombards, entered Rome under the pretext of prayer and blinded certain captured Roman nobles. (770.) Constantine the heretic, wholly turned away from God, martyred by a bitter death the holy man Pope Stephen, who had been confined for eleven years and was revered even by the nations. He compelled all his subjects to swear upon the wood of the holy cross that they would venerate no image of God or of His saints. Those who invoked the Mother of God, kept vigils for God, lived devoutly in regular attendance at churches, abstained from oaths and impurities, or possessed relics of saints—these and such persons he condemned, deprived of their estates, and tortured in every manner. Those who were especially devout he burned, after smearing their beards with wax and pitch. He compelled monks to take wives and nuns to take husbands. Many who avoided this were martyred; under no pagan persecution did more people suffer martyrdom than under this one. Thelergius reigns over the Bulgars. (771.) King Carloman, brother of King Charles, dies at Salmontiacum; part of his kingdom joins Charles’s dominions. His wife, with her sons and Autharius the Frank, flees to Desiderius, king of Italy. Hunald, duke of Aquitaine, came to Rome as though intending to persevere there; fleeing to the Lombards, he apostatized. There, not long [Col. 0832C] afterward, he perished, overwhelmed with stones. Emperor Constantine, intending to fight the Bulgars by sea, loses almost his entire army when nearly two thousand of his ships are shattered by a north wind.

## 772

After Pope Stephen’s death, Adrian, the ninety-seventh pope, sat, according to Master Hugh, for twenty-three years, ten months, and eighteen days. He laboured greatly to restrain the rage of heretics who execrated images of God and His saints; publishing a book against them, strengthened by many citations from Scripture, he refuted their errors and established the right faith firmly. In the verses of the offertories, he doubled what is doubled. Charles directs his attention to the Saxon war. He captures the Saxon fortress of Eresburg. [Col. 0832D] He destroys the Irminsul; when his army there suffered from thirst, by divine direction a most abundant stream of water suddenly poured forth. Charles, having obtained what he had wished, receives hostages from the Saxons. This Saxon war, as Einhard says, lasted thirty-three years against Charles. (773.) Pope Adrian came to Charles at Rome to protect the possessions of the Church. Proceeding there, Charles besieged Pavia; leaving his army there, he arrived at Rome and celebrated Easter there. Returning, he captured Pavia; and returning again to Rome, he established a synod with Pope Adrian and one hundred and fifty-three other bishops and abbots. In it Pope Adrian, with the whole synod, gave him the right to elect the pontiff and appoint the Apostolic See, as well as the dignity of patriciate. Furthermore, he decreed that archbishops and bishops in every [Col. 0833A] province should receive investiture from him, and that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless approved and invested by the king. He anathematized all rebels against this decree, and ordered their goods to be confiscated unless they repented.

[Note: [Col. 0833C] What the author here says concerning the investiture of benefices allegedly granted to Charles by the pontiff is taken from Sigebert, whom Helinand commonly follows. Baronius and Spondanus demonstrate very well, however, that this assertion is false; Spondanus’s words are worth quoting:

“What Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle*—that after Pavia had been captured Charles returned to Rome and, in a synod of 153 bishops and abbots held by Pope Adrian, was given the right to elect the Roman pontiff, and that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investitures from him—was written by Sigebert no less than 338 years after the event, namely in the year of the Lord 1112. Since no author at all of an earlier age knew of it—not even those who recorded most diligently the life of Charles, his deeds year by year, and every assembly that he held—it is rightly believed that this fabrication was contrived at that time [Col. 0833D] in favour of the schismatic Emperor Henry, whose party Sigebert supported with all his strength. For all authors affirm that Charles did not come again to Rome after taking Pavia, but returned as swiftly as possible to Gaul in order to prepare an expedition against the rebellious Saxons. Indeed Einhard, or Eginhard, Charles’s secretary, who constantly attended him and wrote his *Life*, expressly states that he went to Rome only four times: first in this year, during the expedition against the Lombards; second, in fulfilment of a vow, in 780; third, against the duke of Benevento, in 786; fourth, to restore Pope Leo, in 800, when he was also made emperor. Where, then, is this fifth arrival of Charles in the city, invented by Sigebert and asserted nowhere else? Yet it happened that, without any more careful investigation of the fraud, what he had stated most falsely was believed true. Thus pious ecclesiastical writers did not turn to refute these claims [Col. 0834C] but laboured to show that what Adrian had granted Charles was later revoked. Among them was Gratian, who, excessively credulous, copied Sigebert’s fraud word for word and added another of the same kind, fabricated by schismatics under the name of Leo VIII in favour of Emperor Otto. Moreover, neither the very term *investiture* in this sense nor its use by the bestowal—as they add—of ring and staff is found in any writer of that period. As for the election of the pontiff, the practice and laws of other emperors after Charles, to be discussed below in their proper places, contradict these claims. Finally, Charles was so far from wishing to arrogate to himself episcopal elections that he instead established by his published decree that they should be free and determined according to the prescription of the sacred canons. But enough on this matter for the present. After the death of the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, Melchior Goldast, a Calvinist, published his *Rationale* [Col. 0834D]—as he calls it—of imperial constitutions. Professing to set forth the rights of the Roman Empire against the censures of Baronius’s *Annals*, and treating the matter in Calvinist fashion, to say nothing further, he savagely attacked a most modest and sincere historian. But a most powerful defender of truth soon appeared in reply: Jacob Gretser, theologian of the Society of Jesus. Undertaking an apology for the most illustrious cardinal, he demolished all Goldast’s arguments; and when Goldast nevertheless published an even more irrational reply, Gretser, in another defence, stopped his mouth again. Therefore, whatever this Calvinist heretic insolently babbled in this controversy on behalf of the schismatic Sigebert, you may, if you wish, see it excellently examined and refuted by that distinguished professor of the illustrious Society. So says Spondanus under the year 774. In the manuscript Chronicle of Sigebert preserved in the library of Saint-Geneviève, moreover, this fable of his is omitted, and not a word of it occurs.”]

Offa, king of the Mercians, seeks Charles’s friendship by frequent embassies. He attempted to transfer the archiepiscopal see formerly founded at Canterbury to Lichfield, and obtained from Pope Adrian that there should be an archbishopric of the Mercians at Lichfield; he deprived Lambert, archbishop of Canterbury, of all estates within his boundaries and of jurisdiction over bishoprics. Alcuin, sent by the kings of England to Charles on a mission of peace, was entertained by him and remained with him: a man most learned in every respect, [Col. 0833B] who instructed Charles in dialectic, rhetoric, and especially astronomy. After Blessed Aldhelm and Bede, he was the most learned of all Englishmen, and demonstrated his talent in many books.

Alcuin himself was appointed by Charles to the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours. In a letter to Cumbald, Egbert’s third successor, he says:

> “Send me the choicest little books of scholarly learning, such as I had in my native country through the good and most devoted industry of my master Ecbert; and, if it please you, some of our boys to copy from them whatever is needed. I shall send back those who will carry into Francia the flowers of Britain, so that there may not be only [Col. 0834A] a garden enclosed at York, but at Tours also the outpourings of paradise.”

The same Alcuin says:

> “It is read in the book of Gildas, the wisest of Britons, that the Britons themselves lost their country because of the avarice and plundering of their rulers, the injustice of their judges, the slothfulness of their bishops’ preaching, and the luxury and evil morals of the people. Let us beware lest these same vices take root in our own times.”

The same man, in a letter to Æthelard, bishop before Cuthbert and successor of Lambert, says among other things that, when going to Rome and visiting the great Emperor Charles, grandson of that Charles of whom Boniface spoke, he should not bring clerics or monks dressed in multicoloured and ostentatious clothes, since Frankish clerics were accustomed to dress only in religious [Col. 0834B] garments.

## 774

The Saxons harry the borders of the Franks with fire and slaughter; but they cannot burn the church at Fritzlar, which Saint Boniface blessed and foretold would never be burned. Therefore Charles, returning to Saxony, attacks the Saxons with his army divided into three parts, and victory attends him in every encounter.

Charles, offended by the discordance of ecclesiastical chant between Romans and Gauls, sent two clerics to Rome to learn the authentic chant from the Romans and teach it to the Gauls. Through them the Church of Metz first, and then through it all Gaul, was restored to the authority of Roman chant.

While the siege was under way and his army divided, Charles took many cities beyond the Po, among them [Col. 0835A] Verona. There Autharius the Frank, hiding with Carloman’s wife and son, surrendered himself and them to the king. Adelgis, however, son of King Desiderius, who had fled there, escaped and fled to Constantinople. As a deadly pestilence worsened the siege of Pavia, the city was opened to King Charles. Desiderius, with his wife, daughter, and all the leading men, was captured and sent into perpetual exile in Gaul by Gilcred, bishop of Liège. Whatever the Lombards had taken from the Romans over many years Charles restored to them. Having destroyed the kingdom of the Lombards, he brought all Italy under the law of the Frankish kingdom, 204 years after the Lombards had begun to reign in Italy.

Italy, as Einhard says, extends in length from Augusta Praetoria to Lower Calabria [Col. 0835B], where the territories of the Greeks and Beneventans meet, for more than a thousand Roman miles. Charles had married the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, but repudiated her after a year, for an uncertain reason.

## 775

Constantine marches against the Bulgars, but peace is agreed between them. Not long afterward, when the Bulgars broke the treaty, Constantine attacked them unexpectedly and triumphed over them nobly. Charles captured the Saxon fortress of Sigiburg; then he fought them and received hostages for peace from the defeated.

## 776

The Emperor Constantine, divinely struck by the scourge of a terrible fire, dies miserably, still alive and crying: “I am delivered to unquenchable fire.” After him, in the same year, the emir Abdallah [Col. 0835C] died; after him Madar reigned nine years.

When some in Italy planned rebellion against the Franks, Charles marched against them, captured the city of Forum Julii, and had its duke Rotgaud, instigator of the rebellion, beheaded. Having captured the city of Treviso, he struck terror into the rest through the majesty of his name.

While the Saxons were besieging the fortress of Eresburg, the glory of God appeared above the church to all: two shields blazed blood-red and made certain movements in the air as in battle. Charles crushed Saxony like a tempest, broke into its fortifications, and pressed the Saxons to surrender themselves and their country to him and, after giving hostages, pledge that they would become Christians.

(777.) After Constantine, his son Leo ruled five years [Col. 0835D]. Witichind, duke of the Saxons, fled to Normandy. The baptized Saxons make an agreement that they will forfeit their free status and all their possessions if they should ever abandon fidelity to Christ and the king.

Charles devastates Caesaraugusta in Spain, besieges Pamplona, destroys the walls after taking it, subdues the Basques and two petty Saracen rulers, and receives several cities in surrender. At Witichind’s urging, the Saxons ravage Francia; but defeated by Charles, they seek safety in flight. The Bulgar Thelicus fled to Emperor Leo; Leo baptized him and made him a patrician.

(778.) Emperor Leo invades Syria. Charles subjugates the Westphalians in Saxony.

(779.) Chardamus rules the Bulgars. Hildebrand, [Col. 0836A] duke of Spoleto, submits to Charles and purchases his favor with many gifts. Saint Sturmius, first abbot of Fulda, died.

(780.) Charles crossed the river Elbe; there the Bardowicks and Nordalbingians were baptized to win his favor. Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, rebelled against Charles at his wife’s urging. She was the daughter of King Desiderius and sought to avenge her father’s exile through her husband.

## 781

The Emperor Leo, mad with desire for precious stones, coveted the great crown of the Church; he took and wore it, carbuncles broke out on his head, and he died, carried off by fever. The emir Mady made many men and women martyrs for Christ.

Charles went to Rome for prayer, and there his sons were anointed as kings. Pippin, Charles’s son by a concubine, was baptized by Pope Adrian and anointed king of Italy. Louis was anointed king of Aquitaine; he was four years old, born to Hildegard, with his twin brother, in the year of the Lord 778, and his brother almost died before he was born. This boy, though still only four years old, was dressed in arms suited to him.

In the same year Charles’s daughter Gisela was baptized at Milan by Archbishop Thomas. Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, was reconciled to Charles through Pope Adrian.

(782.) After Leo, his wife Irene ruled with her son Constantine for ten years. At Constantinople a certain man found a golden tablet, and on it a man lying down with this inscription: “Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under Constantine and Irene, O sun, you shall see me again.”

The Saxons rebelled [Col. 0836C], and, defeated by Charles, handed over to him up to 4,200 rebels and gave him hostages.

(783.) The Saxons rebelled again and were almost annihilated by Charles. Queen Hildegard died on the day before the Kalends of May, on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension; and in the same year the blessed queen [died].

## 784

Likewise the Saxons and Frisians rebel and are defeated. The Westphalians are defeated by Charles, son of Charles.

(785.) Charles lays Saxony waste. The emir Mady dies; Moses reigns after him for two years. Witichind and Albion, leaders of the Saxons, are reconciled to Charles and baptized; the Saxon disturbances are suppressed.

(786.) Charles sends his seneschal Adulf against the Bretons; through him he takes many Breton [Col. 0836D] fortresses and their leaders. Offa, king of the Mercians, reigned thirty-nine years. Before dying he made his son Egfrith king; he reigned only four months. Cenwulf succeeded him. Louis, Charles’s eight-year-old son, rides well. The sign of the cross appears on people’s clothing.

(787.) After Moses, his brother Aaron ruled the Saracens for twenty-one years. Charles came to Rome and marched against Arichis, duke of Benevento. Arichis purchased Charles’s favor by giving gifts and hostages. War arose between the Avars and Franks. Blood flowed from heaven and earth.

(788.) Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, is judged guilty of treason against Charles. Charles therefore had him tonsured and confined him in a monastery with his son Theodo. In Italy [Col. 0837A] there is fighting between Greeks and Romans; likewise between Franks and Avars; thirdly between Avars and Bavarians; and fourthly between Avars and Franks. In all these wars Charles rejoices that victory has come to his side.

At the urging of Patriarch Tarasius and Pope Adrian, the second universal synod of 350 bishops was held at Nicaea. There the Catholic faith, in the presence of Irene and her son Constantine, was confirmed by the subscription of all; and the heresy of those who execrate the images of God and his saints was rejected forever.

A powerful conspiracy against Charles was formed by the Austrasians, with Harderic as instigator. This is Count Harderic, of whom the History of Amelius and Amicus speaks; that history is believed to belong to this period. When the conspiracy was discovered, many [Col. 0837B] were either mutilated or exiled.

(789.) Charles built and fortified two bridges over the Rhine at Cologne. Entering Slavonia, he subjugated it. Adelgis, son of Desiderius, encouraged by Greek counsel and support, came into Italy. Having begun war with the Franks, he was captured by them and put to death cruelly. In Saxony Charles built two bridges over the Elbe, with a wooden fortress at either end of one of them.

## 790

Charles carefully reformed the discipline of reading and chanting. Alcuin, born in Britain but of Saxon stock, was his beloved teacher and outstanding in literary learning; chiefly through his instruction the king himself learned all the liberal arts. In grammar, however, he had as teacher [Col. 0837C] Peter of Pisa, a deacon; in the other disciplines, Albinus, surnamed Alcuin. With him he devoted much time to learning dialectic and rhetoric, but especially astronomy.

He also tried to write, and for this purpose kept tablets and notebooks under his pillow; but the labor, begun late and contrary to proper order, had little success. He regularly attended church in the morning, evening, night hours, and at the time of the sacrifice, insofar as his health allowed. He admonished the church custodians not to leave anything unseemly or dirty there. He provided such an abundance of gold and silver vessels and sacred vestments that even doorkeepers, who were of the lowest rank, had no need to minister in private clothing [Col. 0837D].

He reformed most diligently the discipline of reading and chanting. He did not read or sing alone, but softly and together with others. During dinner he listened either to some musical performance or to a reader. He delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially *The City of God*. He supported the poor not only in his own kingdom but also beyond the seas—in Syria, Egypt, Africa, Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage. For that reason he sought the friendship of foreign kings, so that some relief might result for the poor Christians under their rule.

He had the laws of all nations subject to him, which had not been written down, committed to writing. He wrote down barbarian and very ancient songs in which the deeds and wars of old kings were sung. He also began a grammar of his native [Col. 0838A] language. He gave the months names in his own language, and designated the twelve winds by their proper names. He had his sons and daughters trained in liberal studies: his sons in riding and hunting; his daughters in wool-working, distaff, and spindle.

Whenever he was at home, he never ate without his children; he never travelled without them. His sons rode alongside him; his daughters followed behind. Although they were very beautiful, he would not give any of them in marriage, but kept them all in his household until his death, saying that he could not do without their company. Fortunate in other respects, he was unfortunate in his daughters; nevertheless, he concealed their disgrace as though nothing ill had been said about them.

He was broad and robust in body, of imposing stature, though not exceeding the proper height of seven of his own feet. [Col. 0838B] He had a round crown of the head, very large and lively eyes, a somewhat long nose, beautiful white hair, a cheerful and bright face, and a clear voice, though one less suited to the form of his body. He was very skilled at swimming. He wore a tunic bordered with silk; in winter he protected his chest with a cuirass made from otter and marten skins. He wore a blue cloak. He was always girded with a sword whose hilt and belt were of gold or silver, sometimes even set with gems, especially when embassies from foreign peoples were present.

On feast days he wore a garment woven with gold, gemmed footwear, and a gold clasp fastening his cloak; he also wore a diadem of gold and gems. On other days his clothing differed little from that of ordinary people. Moderate in food, he was more moderate still in drink. His daily dinner consisted of four dishes, apart from roast meat, which hunters brought in on spits. After dinner he rarely drank more than three times. In summer, for three hours after midday, he rested naked as at night. At night he interrupted his sleep four or five times. He admitted litigants even while putting on his shoes or clothes. He was eloquent; he understood Greek better than he spoke it.

Thus far Einhard describes Charles’s character and appearance. Archbishop Turpin, however, says of him:

> “King Charles had dark-brown hair, a ruddy face, and a handsome body, but a fierce expression. His height was seven feet—his own feet, I mean, which were very long. He was exceptionally broad across the loins, proportionate in the belly, thick in arms and legs, and extremely strong in every limb; most skilled in combat, a most vigorous soldier. His face was one palm and a half in length, his beard one palm, and his nose about half a palm. His forehead was one foot [Col. 0838D]; his lion-like eyes sparkled like carbuncles. His eyebrows were half a palm long. Whoever, when he was angry, he looked upon with open eyes was immediately terrified. The belt with which he girded himself measured eight palms, besides the part that hung down.

> “He ate little bread, but consumed a quarter of a ram, or two hens, or one goose, or a pork shoulder, or a peacock, or a crane, or a whole hare. He drank a little wine and water soberly. His strength was so great that with a single blow of his own sword he cut through an armed soldier seated on a horse, from the crown of the man’s head down to the horse’s hooves, man and horse together. He could easily straighten four horseshoes at once with his hands; with one hand he swiftly lifted an armed soldier from the ground above his own palm to the level of his head.

> “He was most generous in gifts, most just in judgments, and brilliant in speech. At the four chief feasts of the year, holding his court in Spain, he wore the royal crown and carried the sceptre: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and Saint James’s Day. A naked sword was borne before his tribunal. Around his bed, every night, 120 strong men kept constant watch. Forty kept the first night watch: ten at his head [Col. 0839B], ten at his feet, ten to his right, and ten to his left, holding a naked sword in the right hand and a burning candle in the left. The others kept the subsequent watches in the same way, sleeping in turns.

> “Galafer, the Admiral of Toledo, equipped him in military dress in the palace of Toledo when he was an exile in childhood. This same Charles later killed in battle Braimant, the great and proud king of the Saracens and enemy of Galafer. He placed many bodies of saints in [lacuna].”

Thus far Turpin.

Albinus, Charles’s teacher, wrote many works, among which the books *On the Holy Trinity*, written for Charles himself, are outstanding. At the king’s command, therefore, he corrected sacred history. For when Attila, persecutor of the Church, was reigning, he destroyed nearly all volumes of the Christian religion. Therefore, as John Beleth says [Col. 0839C], Alcuin composed an office for the Holy Trinity and for Blessed Stephen, and offered them to Pope Adrian. Adrian rejected the one concerning the Trinity, saying:

> “Just as there is no office of Unity, so neither is there one of Trinity. But since God is three and one—both Unity and Trinity—why should an office not be made for the Holy Trinity, which is God, just as one is made for God himself, who is both first and one?”

## 791

Charles attacks the kingdom of the Avars, that is, the Huns, by land and sea and puts them to flight. Constantine deprives his mother Irene of imperial power and rules alone for seven years.

## 792

Constantine marches out against Chardamus the Bulgar and is disgracefully defeated. Chardamus enriches himself by taking all the royal [Col. 0839D] equipment. The Felician heresy is condemned at Regensburg before Pope Adrian by Felix himself. He maintained that the Son of God is true in his divine nature but adopted in his human nature, dividing the one person of God and man into two persons: the true Son and the adopted son.

Pippin, Charles’s son by a concubine, handsome in face but hunchbacked, was enticed by a promise of the kingdom by certain Frankish nobles and conspired against his father in Bavaria. After the fraud was uncovered and the conspirators condemned, he lived religiously—both willingly and under compulsion—in the monastery of Prüm, and there served God until the end of his life. Some accomplices in the conspiracy were exiled; a few were put to death.

## 793

The Saxons waver in faith toward God and loyalty to the king. [Col. 0840A] A bridge of boats was made with anchors and ropes so that it could be joined together and taken apart.

## 794

For the third time the Felician heresy was condemned at Frankfurt. Queen Fastrada died there and was buried at Saint Alban’s. The Greek pseudo-synod, falsely called the seventh, held for the worship of images, was rejected by the bishops. Emperor Constantine deprived many subject nobles of their eyes. Charles, learned in many languages, wrote down barbarian and very ancient songs in which the wars and deeds of old kings were sung; he named the twelve winds by their proper names, whereas previously only the four cardinal winds had been named.

## 795

The Saxons, terrified by Charles’s power, surrender themselves [Col. 0840B] to the faith of Christ and loyalty to the king. Charles adorned churches with sacred vessels and vestments. He built at Aachen a basilica of exceptional beauty, for whose construction he had columns and marbles brought from Rome and Ravenna. He built it in honor of the Blessed Virgin. He also made there baths tempered with hot and cold water, and a palace next to the church. He had that church painted with histories from the Old and New Testaments, and the palace with Spanish wars and the seven liberal arts.

Pope Adrian died; when news of his death was brought to Charles, he wept as though he had lost a son. Once, when Charles was besieged in the city of Worms by three kings—the kings of the Vandals, Frisians, and Saxons—and their armies, in a certain tower, his nephew Roland was then besieging the city of Gratianopolis, which he had besieged for seven years. Suddenly a messenger came to him from Charles’s father, asking him to bring aid. Then Roland, greatly troubled about what he should do, neither ate nor drank for three days but remained in prayer with his armies. On the third day, while he prayed, the walls of Gratianopolis fell; having defeated the pagans, he set out to free his uncle, whom by God’s aid he did free.

It is related that Julius Caesar, in order to subdue the Spaniards who would not pay him tribute, sent three peoples: Nubians, Scots, and tailed Cornishmen, ordering them to kill all males and preserve the women. Entering the land by sea and smashing their own ships, from the city of Barcelona to Caesaraugusta, and from the city of Bayonne [Col. 0840D] to the mountain, they devastated everything alike with sword and fire. They could not advance farther, however, because the Castilians assembled and drove them out. Fleeing to the coastal mountains between Nájera, Pamplona, and Bayonne, toward the seacoast in the land of Biscay and Álava, they settled there and built many castles. They killed all the males and seized their wives by force; by them they begot sons, who are called Navarrese, as though *non veri*, “not true,” that is, illegitimate and not born of true descent.

The Navarrese were also formerly said to be named from the city of Nadaver, which Saint Matthew converted to the Lord. Charles gave this land of the Navarrese together with the land of the Basques to the Britons for settlement after he had acquired Spain; [Col. 0841A] the land of the Castilians to the Franks; the land of Nájera and Caesaraugusta to Greeks and Apulians; Aragon to the Poitevins; Andalusia along the coast to Germans; Portugal to Danes and Flemings. The Franks refused to inhabit Galicia because it seemed harsh to them. How Charles acquired this whole land of Spain we shall later recount in the appropriate place.

## 796

After Adrian, Pope Leo, the ninety-eighth pope, sat for twenty years, five months, and sixteen days. He immediately sent Charles the keys of Saint Peter’s confession-shrine together with the banner of the city of Rome. Withan, king of the Abrodites, was killed by the Saxons.

(797.) Henry, duke of Friuli, despoiled Yringo, prince of the Avars, in Pannonia and sent his incalculable treasure to King Charles. Thudin, prince of the Avars, surrendered himself and his country to Charles and received the grace of baptism.

## 798

Alfonso, king of Galicia and Asturias, sent Charles a pavilion of remarkable beauty. Irene was made empress after her son Constantine had been blinded by his own people. She sent ambassadors to Charles at Aachen concerning peace: Michael, patrician of Phrygia, and Theophilus, a priest.

This year the star called Mars could not be seen anywhere in the whole sky from July of the preceding year until July of this year. Alfonso, king of Galicia and Asturias, having plundered Lisbon, the furthest city of Spain, sent Charles through the envoys Froia and Basiliscus the trophies of his victory: coats of mail, [Col. 0841C] mules, and captive Moors. Irene ruled four years. Thatin, the Spanish governor of Barcelona, surrendered himself to Charles and restored Barcelona, which had revolted from him. Charles defeated the Saxons in a severe battle. The sun was darkened for seventeen days.

## 799

The Emperor Constantine died, blind. Barcelona, restored to the Saracens, was besieged by Charles’s soldiers. Henry, duke of Friuli, was killed by his own men. The Romans seized Pope Leo while he was celebrating the solemnity of the Greater Litany, tore out his tongue and eyes. These men were relatives of Pope Adrian. But after his voice and sight had been divinely restored to the pope, they again tore out his eyes and tongue from the roots. Rescued from their hands, he fled to Charles.

The Balearic Islands [Col. 0841D] surrendered to Charles because they had been plundered by the Saracens in the preceding year. The keys of the city of Huesca were brought to him. The whole island of Britain was subjugated to Charles. There was a rain of blood at York during Lent.

Egbert, king of the Kentish people, surnamed Præn, was bound and carried away by King Cenwulf of the West Saxons. Yet at Winchcombe, where he had built for God the church that still remains, on the very day of its dedication he released the captive king, in an assembly of thirteen bishops and ten dukes, none of whom went away disappointed of royal generosity. Besides the gifts which the great men received, he gave utensils, clothes, and horses of incalculable value and number to all who had no lands. King Cenwulf gave a pound of silver to the priests, a mark of gold, one solidus to the monks [Col. 0842A], and finally distributed much to all the people. He enlarged many monasteries with very ample revenues. He sent Pope Leo 120 *mancusae* for a blessing, and obtained from him the restoration to Bishop Æthelard, Lambert’s successor, of the former dignity which King Offa had taken from him.

King Egbert of the Kentish people came to Francia to Charles, in order to receive from the Franks instruction in ruling. For that people is easily foremost among all western peoples both in military exercise and in refinement of manners. After the death of Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, he returned to Britain and ruled in the year of the Lord 800, when Charles was reigning in Francia in the thirty-fourth year of his reign.

(800.) The people of the Avars falls away from the faith. Charles goes to Rome and remains there all winter; he restores Pope Leo to his seat [Col. 0842B], legally condemns the accused, and quiets all Roman disturbances. The Balearic Islands are defended against the Saracens with Frankish help. Through Guido, Charles’s duke, the Bretons are defeated and received into submission. Gerard, duke of Bavaria, fighting the Avars in Pannonia, is killed. It is read concerning him in the vision of Wetti that he was numbered among the martyrs. In July there was, contrary to nature, severe frost solidified twice; but it harmed no crops.

(801.) The Romans, who had long been alienated in spirit from the emperor at Constantinople, seized the occasion that a woman who had blinded her own son ruled them. With unanimous consent they acclaimed imperial praises to King Charles and crowned him through the hand of Pope Leo III, calling him Caesar and Augustus. [Col. 0842C] For on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, when the king rose from prayer at Mass before the confession-shrine of Saint Peter, Pope Leo placed a crown on his head; and all the Roman people cried: “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor of the Romans, life and victory!” After the acclamations of praise, he was adored by the apostolic pope in the manner of ancient rulers; and the name of patrician being removed, he was called emperor and Augustus.

Pippin, son of Charles, was installed as king of Italy. A few days later the emperor ordered those who had deposed the pope in the preceding year to be brought forward; after an inquiry had been held concerning them, they were condemned to death, according to Roman law, as guilty of treason. The pope, however [Col. 0842D], mercifully interceded for them, that they should lose neither life nor limb; they were therefore deported into exile. The leaders of this faction were Paschal the nomenclator, Campulus the sacellarius, and many other Roman nobles.

When the emperor wished to hear the crimes alleged against the pope and no accuser appeared to prove them, the pope himself, carrying the Gospel book before all the people in the basilica of Saint Peter, ascended the ambo. Having invoked the name of the Holy Trinity, he cleared himself of the accusations by oath.

## 802

Charles, the first of the Franks, ruled the Romans for thirteen years, after the Roman Empire had been divided from Constantinople, about 468 years having passed since Byzantium, a city of Thrace, had been enlarged by the first Constantine into a new and imperial [Col. 0843A] city. To it all the glory of Roman dignity was transferred; it was consecrated as the seat of the Roman Empire and called New Rome.

Throughout his empire Charles sent envoys to administer judgment and justice, and established twenty-three chapters of law. Amimuelim, who was also Aaron, king of the Persians, sent Charles the only elephant he possessed; the elephant’s name was Abulabat. He also sent other gifts.

While the emperor was at Spoleto, on the day before the Kalends of May, in the second hour of the night, a very great earthquake occurred which shook all Italy. In this quake the roof of the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle fell for the most part together with its beams; in some places cities and mountains collapsed. In the same year certain places near the Rhine in Germany [Col. 0843B] and Gaul trembled. A pestilence arose because of the mildness of the winter weather. Barcelona, already under siege for two years, was captured. Its governor Zatus and several other Saracens were taken. The Italian city of Rieti was captured and burned. Its governor Rozelinus was sent into exile with Zatus.

Saint Salvius, bishop, coming from Aquitaine to the royal estate of Valenciennes, was martyred by Winigard, son of Genard, steward of that place. Winigard had coveted the sacred garments which Salvius used in celebrating Mass, because they were costly. Charles was divinely warned three times to seek the martyr’s body. Having found it, he buried it honorably and punished its killers severely; nevertheless, divine vengeance did not for this reason cease against them.

Envoys of Charles returning from the emir Aaron [Col. 0843C] brought into Francia, among other gifts, also the bodies of Saint Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage; Speratus, first of the Scillitan martyrs; and the head of the martyr Pantaleon. But it is not stated where they were placed.

And it should be noted that all these events, and the first year of Charles’s empire, are recorded in some chronicles under the preceding year, namely the year of the Lord 801. Nicephorus deposed Irene from imperial power, sent her into exile, and ruled eight years.

The patriarch of Jerusalem sent Charles, as a blessing, the keys of the Lord’s Sepulchre and of the place of Calvary, together with the keys of the city and mountain and a banner. It is related that at the time when the Roman Empire was granted to Charles, the patriarch of Jerusalem, expelled from the city by pagans, came to Constantinople to Emperor Constantine and his son Leo, together with John, priest of Naples, and David, archpriest of Jerusalem. He sent them to Charles with a letter written in the hand of Patriarch John himself and a letter written in the hand of Constantine himself; together with the two aforesaid men were two other Hebrew envoys, Isaac and Samuel. In the final [Col. 0844A] part of this letter was written:

> “One night, having fallen into ecstasy, I saw a certain young man standing before my bed. Gently calling me, he touched the little stake and said: ‘Constantine, you have asked the Lord for help in this matter; behold, receive Charles the Great, king of Gaul, the defender of the Church in the Lord.’ And he showed me a certain armed soldier, wearing greaves and a cuirass, with a red shield and a sword at his side, whose hilt was purple; with a very tall spear, whose point often emitted flames; and in his hand he held a golden helmet. He himself was an old man with a long beard, handsome in face and tall in stature; his eyes shone like stars, and his white head gleamed.

> ‘Come now, Augustus: one who refuses obedience to visions from God can in no way escape blame. [Col. 0844B] Emmanuel … Jesus, rejoice in the Lord; mindful of him, perform his praise. May Christ bind upon you, with perpetual honor, the belt of justice upon your loins and the crown upon your head. There is no need for pretence where the Lord’s command is spoken. Therefore hold the Lord’s domain according to his commandments.’”

This same Constantine had driven the pagans six times from Jerusalem, but they nevertheless prevailed. These envoys found the king at Paris and delivered the letters. When they had been read, the king began to weep for the Lord’s Sepulchre. The king ordered Archbishop Turpin to expound these letters before all the people.

When they heard this, all begged the king to set out. On hearing it, the king at once issued an edict that all who were able to bear arms should go with him against the pagans; and whoever did not go, he and his son should be slaves for four years. Accordingly, he assembled a larger army than he had ever possessed before, and they set out.

[Note: What the author relates concerning Charlemagne’s pilgrimage to the holy places of Jerusalem, their rescue from Saracen domination, and the little bird that led him through forests and unknown routes, is fabulous, as historians rightly demonstrate from Einhard, the eyewitness and historian of Charlemagne’s deeds. From this arose the story, says Du Pleix, that Aaron, king of the Persians and lord of all the East, in order to win Charlemagne’s favour, sent him very many gifts and transferred to him dominion and possession of the holy places; whence it was later believed that those same places had been recovered by Charlemagne’s arms.]

When they had come near Jerusalem, into a certain wood which can scarcely be crossed in two days, where there were griffins, bears, lions, tigers, and other various wild beasts, Charles, thinking that he could cross it in a single day, entered it with his army. When night came and the army had lost its way, Charles ordered the camp to be laid out. After the stillness of the night had passed, the king, lying in his bed, began the psalms; and as he said this verse, “Lead me in the path of thy commandments, for I have desired it” (Ps. 118), behold, a bird’s voice crying near his bed was heard distinctly in his ears. Those present heard it and awoke. The king continued the psalms as far as the passage, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141), etc. As he said it, the bird cried again: “Frank, what are you saying? Frank, what are you saying?” The king followed this bird along a narrow path until they recognized the track which they had lost on the preceding day. Pilgrims say that from that time birds speaking in this manner began to be heard in that land.

Having driven out the pagans and recovered the land, the king asked leave to return home from the emperor of Constantinople and the patriarch of Jerusalem. The emperor kept him for one day at Constantinople and meanwhile caused animals of various kinds and colours, gold, and gems to be prepared before the city gates. But Charles, lest he should seem uncivil if he accepted nothing, sought counsel from his nobles as to what he should do. They answered that he ought to accept no gift from anyone in return for the labour which he had undertaken solely for the love of God. Approving their counsel, he ordered all his men not even to deign to look at the things set out. At length, adjured and compelled to accept some gift for God’s sake, he asked for relics of the Lord’s Passion.

Accordingly, after deliberation, a three-day fast was imposed upon all our people and upon twelve Greek persons chosen to divide this sanctuary. On the third day Charles confessed his sins to Ebroin, archbishop; then the clergy of both parties began psalms with a litany. When Daniel, bishop of Naples, opened the casket in which was the crown of thorns, so great a fragrance came forth that all thought themselves to be in paradise. Then Charles, prostrate on the pavement and full of faith, prayed the Lord that, for the glory of His name, He would renew the miracles of His Passion and Resurrection. When he had prayed, dew descending from heaven soaked and drenched the wood and caused it to put forth flowers; and so great a light, together with fragrance, was present that all thought their garments celestial.

When Daniel began to cut into the solid wood with hooked pincers, it began to bloom more and more. Then Charles, in a wooden glove which he had prepared for this purpose, received some of the flowers and filled his right glove; then, preparing another glove to receive the thorns, he handed that one with the flowers to Archbishop Ebroin. And since both men’s eyes were hindered by tears, one thinking that he had received it and the other that he had given it, each let go of the glove; it hung in the air for almost an hour. When the king had filled the other glove with thorns and wished to hand it to the bishop, he saw the first glove hanging in the air.

After this, when he wished to throw the flowers out of the glove, they were turned into manna; and this manna is now at Saint-Denis. Many think it to be that ancient manna which the Lord rained down in the wilderness. All present there were made well by the fragrance of the flowers. When these things had taken place, behold, an innumerable crowd violently entered the church and began to cry, “Truly, today is the day of resurrection.” For the fragrance issuing from the flowers had filled the whole city and healed three hundred and one sick persons. There was there a certain sick man who had been afflicted for twenty-three years and three months, blind, deaf, and mute. At the extraction of the thorny crown he received sight; at the cutting, hearing; and at the putting forth of the flowers, speech.

After this the aforesaid Daniel, with hands raised, gave the Lord’s nail to the king. When it was drawn out from the alabaster in which it had been enclosed, a certain boy was healed who had had his left hand and his whole left side withered from the womb. He ran to the church, saying that, while lying in bed at about the ninth hour, he seemed, as though placed in an ecstasy, to see a grey-haired smith draw with hooked pincers from his left hand, and likewise from his similarly withered left foot, a nail, and from his side a lance. There were further given to King Charles a fragment of the Lord’s cross, the Lord’s shroud, the chemise of the Blessed Mary, the band with which she girded the child Jesus in the cradle, and the arm of holy old Simeon. The king placed all these things in a sack made of buffalo hide and hung it from his neck like a wallet.

On arriving at a fortress named Ligné, he raised a dead boy to life by the touch of the relics, and fifty sick persons of both sexes were healed there. Charles remained there six months and one day. When he came to Aachen, countless blind persons were healed, countless sufferers from fever, twelve demoniacs, eight lepers, fifteen paralytics, fourteen lame persons, thirty maimed persons, fifty-two hunchbacks, sixty-five epileptics, several with throat diseases, and very many people from neighbouring places. Finally, he proclaimed throughout the whole world that on the Ides of June they should come to Aachen to see the relics which he had brought from Jerusalem and Constantinople, having first confessed their sins. It was established there that this exhibition of relics should always take place on the Wednesday of the Ember Days in June. Present at this council were Pope Leo, Archbishop Turpin, Achilleus bishop of Alexandria, Theophilus of Antioch, and many other bishops and abbots. A dead man was also raised there.

It is very remarkable that, concerning this entire Jerusalem journey of Charles, in which such a distinguished work was performed—the acquisition of the Jerusalemite land and so many miracles wrought through these relics—nothing at all is found recorded among Latin chroniclers. Yet the present narrative seems to clash with historical truth when it says that the patriarch of Jerusalem came to Constantinople to Emperor Constantine and his son Leo at the time when the Roman Empire was given to Charles, since both of these—that is, Constantine and his son Leo—were already dead at the time when the Roman Empire was given to Charles. It may, however, be understood that the Roman Empire was given to Charles in their time, that is, offered to him; for it is recorded that Charles for more than thirty years was content with the simple title of king, refraining from the imperial designation, although he was often invited to it by Pope Hadrian.

## 803

The Empress Irene died in exile. SIGEBERT. Charles transferred into Francia all the Saxons dwelling beyond the Elbe, and gave their districts to the Obodrites. EINHARD. Charles, having finished the Saxon war, transferred into Gaul ten thousand persons from among those who inhabited both banks of the River Elbe, with their wives and little children, and distributed them through different places. Likewise SIGEBERT. In Italy, the cities of Ostana and Luceria, which were hostile to Charles, were received into submission. Charles administered justice throughout his whole empire and established twenty-nine chapters of law.

Aaron the amir advanced against Nicephorus with three hundred thousand men. Unable to withstand this, Nicephorus entered into a disgraceful treaty, agreeing to give him annually thirty thousand coins and three thousand as tribute for his own head and three thousand for his son’s head. In other chronicles the following is read for this year: Irene, deposed by the Greeks, is succeeded in rule by Nicephorus. He sent ambassadors to Charles. In winter an earthquake occurred around the Palace, and a mortality followed. In the city of Mantua, the blood of Christ is said to have been discovered.

## 804

Pope Leo came to Charles in Francia. Nicephorus, having broken his treaty with the Saracens, brought many misfortunes upon his empire. Godfrey, king of the Danes, behaving with much insolence toward neighbouring peoples, sought peace from Charles. The Avars, who are also the Huns, conquered after a long war against the Franks, lost in this final war all their glory and nobility. In no battle were the Franks enriched so greatly. So much gold and silver, and so many precious spoils, were found in the royal treasury of the Khagan that one may rightly believe the Franks justly took from the Huns what the latter had unjustly taken from others.

## 805
