The Romans and Greeks always regarded Frankish power with suspicion. Hence there is this Greek proverb: “Francorum Philon Kexisgiton loy Kexis” [the Greek is corrupt or unrecovered as printed]. Therefore, since the emperors at Constantinople were angry against Charles and regarded his power with suspicion, Charles reconciled them to himself by frequent embassies and a most binding treaty.

The Avars, unable to endure the attacks of the Slavs, obtained from Charles a place to live between the Sava and Carantania; there they settled, without the title of a kingdom, under Frankish rule. Charles, son of Charles, defeated the rebellious Bohemians and killed their leader Lechon.

TURPIN, archbishop, in the History of the Acquisition of Spain. After Charles had acquired many kingdoms, he proposed to rest from battles. Immediately he saw in the sky a certain road of stars beginning at the Frisian Sea and stretching between Germany and Italy, between Gaul and Aquitaine, passing straight through Gascony, Basque country, Navarre, and Spain, as far as Galicia, where the body of blessed James then lay hidden and unknown. Charles looked upon this road every night and wondered what it signified. As he reflected, a man of form surpassingly excellent and beautiful beyond what may lawfully be expressed appeared to him at night in an ecstasy, saying: “What are you doing, my son?”

Charles replied, “Who are you, lord?”

“I,” he said, “am the apostle James, foster-child of Christ, son of Zebedee, brother of John the Evangelist, whom the Lord, above the Sea of Galilee, deigned by His ineffable grace to choose for preaching to the peoples; whom King Herod killed by the sword; whose body rests unknown in Galicia, which is still shamefully oppressed by the Saracens. Therefore I wonder why you have not yet liberated my land, you who have acquired so many and such great cities. Wherefore I inform you that, just as the Lord has made you more powerful than all earthly kings, so He has chosen you above all others to prepare my road and free the land from the hands of the Moabites, so that He may thereby prepare for you the crown of eternal recompense. The road of stars which you saw in the sky signifies that you, with a great army, will go from these regions as far as Galicia to overcome the faithless pagan nation, to free my road, and to visit my sarcophagus; and after you, all peoples will do so from the present time to the end of the age.”

The apostle appeared to Charles in this fashion three times. After this Charles went there with a great army; and when he had besieged Pamplona for three months and could not take it because of its impregnable walls, he prayed Saint James that, for the honour of his name, he would grant him to capture the city. Then its walls fell utterly. Those Saracens who wished to be baptized were preserved alive; those who did not wish it were killed.

When these marvels were heard, all the cities surrendered, and the whole land was made tributary. Finally, having visited the sarcophagus, he came to Petronium and planted his lance there in the sea, giving thanks to God and Saint James, who had led him so far. Afterwards he travelled throughout all Spain from sea to sea. In Galicia he then acquired fourteen cities, among which Compostela was then small. There are ninety-six cities in Spain, among them Huesca, from which blessed Vincent came, and in which there were formerly ninety towers. At Petronissa the finest silver is produced. In the city of Accinctina lies blessed Torquatus, who was a follower of blessed James; at his tomb an olive tree, flowering by divine power, is laden with ripe fruits every year on his feast, the first day before the Ides of May.

Then the whole land of the Spaniards was subject to Charles: namely, the land of al-Andalus, the land of the Pardians, the land of the Castilians, the land of the Moors, the land of the Navarrese, the land of the Portuguese, the land of the Saracens, the land of the Alavans, the land of the Biscayans, the land of the Basques, and the land of the Palargians. Charles took some of their cities without fighting, but some with great war and the greatest skill. The very strongly fortified city of Lucerna, which is in the Green Valley, he could not capture until the end. At last he besieged it for four months; and, prayer having been made to God and Saint James, its walls fell, and it remains deserted to this day. For a certain whirlpool of the River Atti rose in its midst, in which black fish are found.

These are the cities Charles cursed because he acquired them with grievous labour; therefore they remain without inhabitants to this day: Lucerna, Ventosa, Caparra, and Adonia. All the idols and images which he then found in Spain he utterly destroyed, except an idol in the land of Andalus called Salam Cadis—that is, “the god of Cadis”; for Cadis is properly the name of that place, while *salam* in Arabic means “god.” The Saracens relate that Muhammad, while still alive, made this idol in his own name and, while still living, sealed within it a certain legion of demons by magical art. This legion holds the idol so strongly that it has never been possible for anyone to break it. Whenever a Christian approaches it, he is immediately endangered; but whenever a Saracen approaches in order to worship or to beseech Muhammad, he goes away unharmed. If any bird happens to alight upon it, it immediately dies.

It is an ancient stone, most skilfully carved in Saracen workmanship, situated on the shore of the sea, broad and square below, narrow above, and as high as a raven ordinarily flies upward. Upon it stands that image, cast in the form of a man from the finest brass, erect upon its feet, with its face turned southward and holding in its right hand an enormous key. This key, as the Saracens say, will fall from its hand in the year when the king is born in Gaul who, in the last times, will subject all Spain to Christian laws. As soon as the Saracens see the fallen key, they will bury their treasures in the ground and all flee.

From the gold which kings and princes then gave Charles, he enlarged the church of Saint James while remaining in those parts for three years. He established there a bishop and canons according to the rule of blessed Isidore, and suitably adorned it with bells, hangings, and books. From the immense remainder of gold and silver which he brought from Spain, he made these churches: that of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Aachen; Saint James’s in the same town; likewise Saint James’s near the city of Bourges; likewise Saint James’s near Toulouse; likewise Saint James’s in Gascony, between the town of Ax and Saint-Jean-Sorde, on Saint James’s road; likewise Saint James’s at Paris, between the Seine and Montmartre; and besides these, innumerable abbeys throughout the world.

## 806

Charles, having returned to Francia, divided his kingdom among his sons and thereafter confirmed the resulting testament by his own authority and that of Pope Leo. The Bethemani, aided by the Slavs, ravaged everywhere, but were vigorously defeated by Charles, son of Charles. On the fourth day before the Nones of September there was an eclipse of the moon, the sun being in the sixteenth degree of Virgo and the moon in the sixteenth degree of Pisces.

## 807

Chumeid, an amir sent by Aaron to destroy Lycia, came to Myra and attempted to smash the coffin of Saint Nicholas; instead he broke another one. For his presumptuous audacity he lost his entire fleet, pursued by an unavoidable storm. On the day before the Kalends of February, with the moon in its seventeenth day, there was an eclipse of the sun at midday, both heavenly bodies being in the twenty-fifth degree of Aquarius. Likewise, on the fourth day before the Kalends there was an eclipse of the moon, and battle-lines of marvellous size appeared in the same night; the sun was in the eleventh degree of Virgo. Moreover, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, the planet Mercury was seen in the sun like a small black spot, though somewhat above the central middle of that luminary; it was visible to us for eight days. But cloud cover prevented observation of when it first entered or departed. Likewise, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, there was an eclipse of the moon in the third hour of the night, the sun being in the fifth degree of Virgo and the moon in the fifth degree of Pisces. Thus, from September of the preceding year to September of the present year, the moon was darkened three times and the sun once.

An ambassador of the Persian king, named Abdella, brought gifts to Emperor Charles: a pavilion and tents of various colours, of marvellous size and beauty. All were of fine linen, both tents and ropes, dyed in diverse colours; besides these there were many precious silken hangings, fragrant spices, ointments, and balsam. In addition, there was a clock of brass marvellously constructed by mechanical art. In it, the course of twelve hours was turned by a water-clock, with the same number of golden balls which fell at the completion of the hours, and by their fall caused a little cymbal placed beneath them to ring. There were added to it an equal number of horsemen, who came forth through twelve windows when the hours were completed; by the motion of their departure they closed the same number of windows which had previously been open. There were many other things in that clock. Among the gifts were also two candelabra of brass, of marvellous size and height.

TURPIN, in the History of Charles. After Charles had returned to Gaul, a certain pagan African king, having assembled armies, conquered Spain, driving out and killing the guards of towns and cities whom Charles had left behind. When these things were heard, Charles collected great armies and returned to Spain; Milo of Angers, father of Roland, was commander of the armies. When Charles’s army had lodged near Bayonne, a city of the Basques, a certain knight named Romaricus, sick and near death, having received penance and the Eucharist, instructed a kinsman to sell the horse which he had and give the price to clergy and the poor. After he died, the man sold the horse for a hundred solidi and quickly spent the money on food, drink, and clothing.

After thirty days had passed, the dead man appeared to him in an ecstasy and said: “Since I entrusted my possessions to you, to be given in alms for the redemption of my soul, know that God has forgiven me all my sins. But because you unjustly kept back my alms, know that I have been in the punishments of Tartarus for thirty days. Know that tomorrow you will be placed in that same infernal place from which I have come forth; but I shall be in paradise.” Having spoken thus, he disappeared. The other awoke trembling; and while on the same day he related his dream to his companions, suddenly a cry arose in the air, like that of lions, wolves, and bears. Behold, he was suddenly snatched away by demons to the place already appointed for him by divine judgment. Sought by his companions, he was found only with difficulty on the twelfth day, lying dead upon a very high mountain, his whole body shattered. The mountain was four days’ journey from the place where he had been snatched away. There the demons had thrown him three leagues high above the sea.

After this Aigoland sent Charles a challenge to battle on whatever terms he chose: twenty against twenty, forty against forty, one hundred against one hundred, one thousand against one thousand, two against two, or one against one. Therefore a hundred knights were sent by Charles against a hundred, and the Saracens were killed. Then another hundred were sent by Aigoland against a hundred; all were killed. Then Aigoland sent two hundred against two hundred, who were immediately slain. Then he sent two thousand against two thousand; some of them were killed, the rest put to flight. On the third day Aigoland cast his lots and learned of Charles’s loss; he sent word that on the following day he should fight a full battle, if he wished. This was undertaken by both sides.

Then certain Christians, who late on the day before the battle were making their martial preparations with utmost care, planted their upright spears in the ground before the camp, in meadows beside the river called Cera. Later, in that place, by Charles’s command and assistance, a vast and excellent basilica of the blessed martyrs Famundus and Primitivus was built, together with a great and most fertile settlement. Early in the morning, those who were about to gain the palm of martyrdom in the near battle for faith in God found these spears adorned with bark and foliage. Marvelling beyond expression and ascribing so great a miracle to divine grace, they cut them off close to the ground. The roots left in the earth afterward of themselves produced large trees like poles, which are still visible in that place. For many of their spears were of ash wood. A wondrous thing: great joy to souls, and immense harm to bodies.

What more need be said? On the following day forty thousand Christians were killed, along with Duke Milo, Roland’s father, and Charles’s horse. Then Charles, standing on foot with two thousand Christian infantrymen, drew his sword, named Joyous, and cut many Saracens in two. As evening came, Saracens and Christians returned to their camps. On the next day four marquises from regions of Italy came to Charles’s aid with four thousand fighting men. When Aigoland learned this, he turned to flight; then Charles returned with his armies to Gaul. The winter was very mild and pestilential.

## 808

In Britain, after Kenulf, who reigned twenty-four years and whose son Kenelm, a boy, was innocently killed by his sister and became a martyr, his brother Kednulf reigned for one year. In the second year, expelled by Bertulf, he came to Charles; through him, as Sigebert says, he was restored to kingdom and homeland. Pope Leo III sent ambassadors to Britain: Adulf, a deacon by nationality a Saxon; with him Emperor Charles sent two abbots, Linotfrid the notary, and Nantarius of Saint-Omer. Crumnis ruled among the Bulgars. Aaron the amir died; after him Muhammad ruled for five years.

## 809

Pippin, king of Italy, subdued Venice to himself and not long afterward died at Milan; Charles restored Venice to Nicephorus. Nicephorus, by new and unjust laws, exasperated all his subjects and increased God’s wrath against himself. After the death of Godfrey, king of the Danes, his son Hemming sought peace from Charles. Walchandus assumed the bishopric of Liège; in the Ardennes he built the monastery of Andage. In Tuscany, the maritime city of Populonium was plundered by Greeks called Crabiotae. In November the emperor held a council at Aachen concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, a question first broached at Jerusalem by a certain monk John. To settle it, Bernard, bishop of Worms, and Adalard, abbot of Corbie, were sent to Pope Leo at Rome.

[Note: We have omitted what followed concerning the war of Aigoland, the giant Ferracutus, the slaughter of the Franks at Roncevaux [yet that disaster did indeed occur, though not in the manner fabulously narrated by Archbishop Turpin], etc., from Turpin, whether genuine or fictitious, as fabulous and rejected by learned men. Although some matters already brought forward are likewise sprinkled with fables, we allowed them to remain as a specimen, lest the omission of the remaining fables be charged against us.]

## 810

Ruoltona, the emperor’s elder daughter, died on the eighth day before the Ides of June; and Pippin, his son and king of Italy, on the eighth day before the Ides of July. There was a great mortality of cattle throughout all provinces subject to the emperor. The sun was eclipsed on the seventh day before the Ides of June and on the second day before the Kalends of December; the moon, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July and on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January. Charles sent three armies into three parts of his kingdom: one beyond the Elbe, which defeated the Hillones; another into Pannonia, which subdued the remnants of the Huns and the Slavs; and a third against the Bretons, which crushed their treachery.

## 811

Charles, the emperor’s elder son, died on the second day before the Nones of December. Hemming, king of the Danes, died; after him, two contenders for the kingdom fought one another, and almost eleven thousand Danes were slain. At Mainz, a bridge five hundred paces long across the Rhine, which Charles had built of wood over ten years with immense labour and marvellous workmanship, so that it seemed capable of enduring forever, was accidentally burned within three hours, so completely that not even a single splinter remained upon the water.

Charles made Christ heir of his possessions by testament, dividing into three parts all that he possessed as property. He assigned one third to the poor and to those serving the palace; he subdivided the remaining two thirds into twenty-one portions and distributed them to the metropolitan bishops subject to him in the same number. Thus the metropolitan church was to have a third of its allotted share and divide the other two thirds among its suffragan bishops. Their names are these: Rome, Ravenna, Milan, Forum Julii—that is, Aquileia—Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Juvanum, also called Salzburg, Trier, Sens, Besançon, Lyons, Vienne, Rouen, Reims, Arles, Tarentaise, Embrun, Bordeaux, Tours, and Bourges. He placed each portion, sealed in its own casket, adding the name of the metropolitan city to which it was to be sent.

For the last four years of his life Charles was afflicted by frequent fevers; in the end he also limped in one foot. Then he acted more according to his own judgment than that of the physicians, whom he hated because they forbade him roast meat, to which he was accustomed. He delighted in naturally warm water vapours. Nicephorus entered Bulgaria; because he did not know how to moderate his victory, he was killed by the Bulgars, together with a great number of the senatorial order. After him his son Stauratius ruled for one year.

## 812
Charles places the imperial crown upon his son Louis [Col. 0853B], and makes Bernard, son of Pippin, king of Italy. At the monastery of Elnone, St. Amand was raised from his tomb by Lautharius the custodian, about the one hundred and fifty-second year after his deposition, on the twentieth day of September. Yet in his legend this raising of his body is placed in the year of the Lord 809, the one hundred and fiftieth year after his death. On that day the same saint was seen in his tomb: a venerable man with grey hair, pale from abstinence and fasts, fragrant as though with aromatics because of the incorruption of his sweet-smelling limbs, wholly untouched in body, and very like one asleep, adorned in pontifical vestments of honourable beauty. The nails of his hands had grown so far that, by their growth, they even pierced [Col. 0853C] the sleeves of his garments. Lautharius, or Lotharius, took these as relics; he likewise cut off the growth of his beard and, with a craftsman’s instrument, drew two teeth from his gums—he could not do otherwise. Drops of blood flowed after them, and are still kept in an ivory casket.

After Stauracius was deposed, Michael, son-in-law of Nicephorus, ruled for two years. His envoys, Michael the bishop, Arsasius, and Theonostus, protospatharii, came to Aachen and spoke acclamations to the emperor in Greek. On the Ides of May, after noon, there was an eclipse of the sun. The body of St. Salvius was discovered.

This saint had first come into the district of the royal estate of Nonensis, called Valenciennes. Departing from there, he celebrated Mass in the church of St. Martin [Col. 0853D] on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, where he also instructed the people. After Mass a certain Genardus, who administered the estate under his lord Abbo, invited him to dinner. St. Salvius possessed golden church vessels, garments adorned with gold and gems, and a golden belt woven with precious stones and pearls. He deliberately carried all these things with him everywhere, openly before all men, in order thus to attain the palm of martyrdom.

Winegardus, Genardus’s son, a frivolous and insolent man, coveted these things. He had them all taken from him; from the chalice and paten he ordered a chair made for himself; he sent the man of God to prison; and he sent a servant to kill him and his disciple in prison. And so it happened. Yet the servant did not dare [Col. 0854A] do this until the saint commanded him. These two saints were from the territory of the Arumni.

Winegardus ordered their bodies secretly carried to the enclosure of his herd and hidden there in a pit in the earth. In that same enclosure was a very large bull, which always prevented the other animals from approaching the place where the saints’ bodies lay, driving them away with his horns. The body of St. Salvius had first been placed in the pit, and the body of his disciple was thrown over it in the form of a cross. If by chance any filth fell there, the bull did not cease throughout the whole night until he had cleansed the place with his feet.

A certain woman, keeping watch by night and walking around her house in the village of Breniticum, saw an immense [Col. 0854B] brightness in the place where the herd was. She ran to the door and saw two lighted lamps illuminating the whole place as at midday; and she summoned her neighbours to see this miracle. This happened one night and the next, and the matter was reported to the priests.

At the same time it was revealed by an angel to King Charles that he should send to Valenciennes and seek with the greatest care where St. Salvius rested with his disciple. This was told him for three successive nights. They were found, Genardus betraying them; and Genardus, his son Winegardus, and Winegarius the servant who had killed them were brought forward. The king ordered Genardus and Winegardus to be castrated and their eyes torn out; Winegarius [Col. 0854C] the servant was to have only his eyes torn out.

The saints’ bodies were placed upon wagons to be taken to the church of St. Vedast, but they could not be moved even when a multitude of oxen had been brought. Leaving only two oxen yoked to the wagon, they allowed them to go wherever they wished. With the greatest speed these two oxen brought the bodies to the church of St. Martin, near Valenciennes, where St. Salvius had been accustomed to pray; and there they were placed. Charles gave St. Salvius a third part of that estate.

At that time two sisters of a certain duke of the Franks came before King Charles, complaining that their brother was taking away their inheritance. Summoned by the king concerning this, he replied that he was taking nothing from them. The king made him swear upon the body of St. Salvius [Col. 0854D] that he owed his sisters nothing of what they claimed. After he had sworn joyfully, he immediately burst open at the middle, and excrement broke forth through the secret passage of his belly. Blood issued from his eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils; and after two hours he ended his life.

Genardus also, having been blinded, gave St. Salvius everything that he possessed. His son Winegardus, when he came to the church in which the saint rested and prayed for forgiveness, caused the whole church to shake. Terrified, he turned to flight and came to the monastery of St. Amand; there he remained grieving and repentant all the days of his life. Genardus likewise, his father, having lost his bodily eyes, received spiritual sight, remaining in his own house and doing penance. Winegarius the servant came to [Col. 0855A] St. Salvius and, prostrate before his body with a great flood of tears, received sight in one eye; until the day of his death he fed flocks in the service of St. Salvius.

(813.) Throughout all Gaul, councils were held at Charles’s command by bishops for the condition of the churches. The first was at Mainz, the second at Reims, the third at Tours, the fourth at Chalon, and the fifth at Arles. The Moors ravaged Centumcellae, a city of Tuscany, and Nicea in the province of Narbonensis. The emperor Michael, fighting the Bulgars, was defeated; returning home, he laid aside the diadem and became a monk. Leo, son of the patrician Bardas, succeeded him. Grumas, king of the Bulgars, who two years earlier had killed Nicephorus and driven Michael from Moesia, puffed up with pride, besieged Constantinople. As he rode about beneath the city walls, Leo made a sortie and compelled him, badly wounded, to flee. [Col. 0855B] Muhammad the emir fought against his brother Abdallah; defeated by him, he unwillingly permitted him to reign jointly with him. By this war the kingdom of the Saracens was divided for several years. Leo ruled eight years after Michael.

## 814

Charles dies and is buried at Aachen, in the seventy-second year of his life and the thirteenth of his Roman emperorship. In certain chronicles it is read that he died on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, the forty-third after the conquest of Italy, and the fourteenth year of his Roman empire. His son Louis ruled after him for twenty-six years.

## 815

Peace is confirmed between Louis and Leo. [Col. 0855C] Hariold, king of the Danes, driven from his kingdom and homeland by the sons of Godefrid, came to Louis and begged for his help.

(816.) Chrunus the Bulgar, insolent because of success, attacked the people of Constantinople, roaming in repeated raids as far as the city gates. At Constantinople a great earthquake continued for several days, by which many buildings of the city and of other towns collapsed. In Aquitaine, at Saintes, an earthquake occurred in September. The River Rhine, swollen by Alpine snow, overflowed beyond its usual bounds.

(817.) Pope Leo died in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June. After him sat Stephen, the ninety-ninth pope, third of that name, for seven months. He immediately came to Reims to the emperor and crowned him. Louis sent an army against the Danes [Col. 0855D] and received hostages through it. Pope Stephen died in the third month after his return, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February. After him sat Paschal, the hundredth pope, first of that name, for seven years and seventeen days. The moon was eclipsed on the Nones of February at the second hour of the night. A comet appeared in the constellation of the Charioteer. The portico through which the emperor was walking collapsed upon him and more than twenty-nine persons. A conspiracy against the emperor was made by his nephew Bernard. Its leaders were Aegidius, foremost among the king’s friends; Reginardus, his chamberlain; Reginarius, son of Count Reginarius; Anselm, bishop of Milan; Volfoldus of Cremona; and Theodulf of Orléans. The Gascons rebelled against Louis.

## 818

[Col. 0856A]

Scloamir, king of the Abodrites, deserted Louis and fled to the Danes. Louis subdued the Bretons; their duke Murnianus, who had assumed the title of king, was killed by them.

(819.) Bernard, king of Italy, accused of conspiring against the emperor and found guilty of treason, was first deprived of his eyes and kingdom, then of his life. Bishops detected in the conspiracy were deposed by synodal decree and consigned to monasteries. Other more noble men were ordered to be blinded along with King Bernard. Queen Ermegardis died at Angers on the fifth day before the Nones of October. Ariold was restored by Louis to the kingdom of the Danes.

## 820

Scloamir, king of the Abodrites, and Lupus, duke of the Gascons, condemned to death, were exiled by Louis. [Col. 0856B] When a general council was held at Aachen by Louis’s direction, certain chapters concerning the use of regular monks were added by bishops and abbots; and, after a large compilation from the Holy Scriptures had been made, rules were established for clerics and for religious women who were clerics.

Louis himself, while still thirty-four years old, trained the Aquitanian clergy—who had previously lived under tyrants and devoted more effort to riding, military exercise, and the throwing of missiles than to divine worship—to read and chant, bringing in teachers from various places. At this council he caused a book containing the perfection of canonical life to be compiled; in it he also ordered included a summary of food, drink, and all necessities. [Col. 0856C] He had this book copied in every city and monastery of his kingdom.

Then bishops and clerics began to put aside golden belts, gems, ornamented knives, elaborate garments, and long robes burdening their ankles. For he considered it a monstrous thing for an ecclesiastical man to aspire to the adornment of secular glory. He especially loved monks, and would himself have become a monk had his father not forbidden it. Many monasteries were built or restored under him, especially these: the monasteries of St. Philibert, St. Florent, Carof, Conques, St. Maxentius, Menat, Maguelone, Nearciacum, St. Savin, Masciatum, Nontliacum, St. Theofild, St. Pascentius of Sora, Solemniacum, St. Mary’s nunnery, St. Radegund’s nunnery, Devera, Deutera in the district of Toulouse, [Col. 0856D] Vadala in Septimania, Amane, Galune, St. Lawrence, St. Mary called “in Rubine,” Cannes, and very many others.

## 821

From this point the account of the kingdoms of the Bulgars and Saracens fails. Pope Paschal found, at her own revelation, the body of the virgin St. Cecilia, clothed in golden garments and still stained with her own blood; he transferred her, and the bodies of the holy martyrs Valerian her husband, Tiburtius, Maximus, and Pope Urban, to the church which he had built for them.

Louis confirmed the partition of the kingdom made among his sons by the oath of his nobles. Emperor Leo was killed in his palace through a conspiracy of his nobles, especially of Michael, count of the household troops, who ruled after him [Col. 0857A] for nine years.

According to certain chronicles, in the preceding year there was a pestilence among cattle and human beings throughout all Francia. Because of continual rains and an atmosphere dissolved by excessive moisture, grain and legumes were spoiled: they either could not be gathered, or, once gathered, decayed. Wine failed because of a lack of warmth; what remained was sour and unpleasant. Autumn sowing was so impeded that absolutely no crops were sown before spring’s mild weather. The moon was eclipsed on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, at the sixth hour of the night.

Again, according to certain chronicles, in the present year Bernard was reconciled with Louis, restored to his kingdom, and Adalard, abbot of Corbie, recovered his abbey, from which he had been exiled into Aquitaine. Autumn sowing was impeded in certain places [Col. 0857B] by the persistence of rain. It was followed by a winter so long and severe that the most famous rivers—the Rhine, Danube, Elbe, Seine, and other rivers throughout Gaul and Germany—were frozen so solidly that for thirty days or more they bore wagons linked together as if upon bridges. Their thaw caused great damage to many persons settled near the Rhine.

## 822

In the region of the Thuringians, at a certain place beside a river, a long turf-bank, fifty feet long, fourteen wide, and six high, was cut and lifted from the ground without human hands and moved twenty-five feet. Likewise, in the eastern part of Saxony adjoining the borders of the Sorbs, in a deserted place beside a lake called Tusco, [Col. 0857C] the earth swelled up like an embankment; over the space of one night, without the effort of human work, it rose in the likeness of a track and stretched for a distance of one league.

At a council held at Attigny, the emperor publicly confessed that he had sinned against all the bishops whom he had made tonsure against their will.

(823.) Drogo, Louis’s brother, became bishop of Metz. Lothair, the emperor’s son, was sent by his father into Italy; consecrated by Pope Paschal, he received the crown of the kingdom and the title of emperor and Augustus. Theodore, primicerius of the Roman Church, and Leo the nomenclator, his son-in-law, were first blinded in the Lateran patriarchal palace and then beheaded. Some said this had been done because they seemed already to be less prompt than was right in loyalty to the young Lothair. Some [Col. 0857D] also said it was done by Pope Paschal’s order or counsel. But he adequately excused himself before the emperors; regarding this accusation, before the pope and Louis’s envoys in Rome, in the presence of a great number of bishops, he cleared himself by oath and defended the killers because they belonged to the household of St. Peter; he said that those killed had been guilty of treason.

Then Adalung, abbot of St. Vedast, and Hunfrid, count of Chur, were sent to Rome. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, by the emperor’s counsel and the authority of the Roman pontiff, went to the Danes to preach and baptized many of them. An earthquake occurred at the palace at Aachen. In Saxony, in the district called Frizai, twenty-three villages were burned by heavenly fire; people and animals [Col. 0858A] were struck dead by lightning; crops were devastated by hail; and stones of immense weight fell with the hail. A great mortality of human beings followed these prodigies, on account of which the emperor ordered fasts.

In this year his son Charles was born to him by Queen Judith. Lightning fell from a clear sky in daytime. In the territory of the Italian city of Cremona, in the village of Grabadona, in the church of St. John the Baptist, an image painted in the apse of that church of the holy Mother of God holding the boy Jesus in her lap, while the Magi brought gifts, had been darkened and nearly effaced by excessive age. For two days it shone with such brilliance that it seemed to surpass, by the beauty of its charm, all the splendour of a newly painted image. Yet that brightness did not illuminate the images of the Magi, except for the gifts [Col. 0858B] which they were offering.

In the territory of Toul, near the village of Commercy, a girl of twelve years, after receiving holy communion from a priest at Easter, first abstained from bread for ten months, then from all food and drink for three years, and afterwards returned to ordinary life.

## 824

A severe and prolonged winter occurred, which destroyed not only other animals but also some human beings through the cruelty of the cold. The moon was eclipsed on the second day before the Nones of March, at the second hour of the night. Pope Paschal died. After him sat Eugenius, the hundred and first pope, first of that name, for three years and two months, [Col. 0858C] formerly archpriest of the title of St. Sabina, the party of the nobles prevailing.

A few days before the summer solstice, in the territory of Autun, when a sudden change in the air turned into a storm, an immense mass is said to have fallen with hail, fifteen feet long, seven broad, and two high. The bodies of St. Severus, bishop of Ravenna, his wife Vincentia, and his daughter Innocentia were transferred to Mainz by Otgar, archbishop of Mainz. Among other gifts, the envoys of Emperor Michael brought Emperor Louis books of Dionysius the Areopagite, written by him, *On the Hierarchy*, translated from Greek into Latin at Louis’s own request. The books were received at Paris with joy on the sainted martyr’s feast day itself; the power of the holy martyr increased that joy when nineteen sick persons were healed there that night. [Col. 0858D] Valchandus, bishop of Liège, transferred the body of St. Lambert from Liège to the monastery of Andage. Rabanus became abbot of Fulda and wrote much on the Holy Scriptures.

## 825

Heriold, king of the Danes, with his wife, sons, and his party among the Danes, was baptized at Mainz. Emperor Louis honoured him with gifts and a portion of Frisia bestowed upon him as a benefice. He was baptized at St. Alban’s.

## 826

According to certain chronicles, the following occurred in the following year. Hilduin, abbot of St. Denis, sent to Rome and, with Pope Eugenius consenting to his prayers, received the bones of the most blessed Sebastian and placed them at Soissons in the basilica of St. Medard. While they still lay unburied in the chest in which they had been brought, [Col. 0859A] they performed innumerable and almost incredible miracles. The bodies of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter were transferred from Rome to Francia and became renowned for many signs. The body of St. Gregory, pope, is also said to have been transferred to the city of Soissons. Battle-lines were seen in the sky, and terrible nocturnal flashes of lightning darted through the air.

## 827

Pope Eugenius died. He was succeeded by the deacon Valentine, surviving scarcely one month, the hundred and second pope. After he had died, according to some forty days after his pontificate, Gregory, priest of the title of St. Mark, succeeded as the hundred and third pope, Constantine, the ninety-sixth pope, having been erased from the number of popes. This Gregory, fourth of that name, who was also called Leo IV, sat for [Col. 0859B] sixteen years and was greatly troubled by a continual flow of blood from his nostrils.

In this year, according to certain chronicles, Heutardus, the wisest man of his age, sent to Rome for the bodies of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, which he buried at his own expense in his territory; but it is not said in the territory of which city.

(828.) A conspiracy was made against the emperor by his sons. In Gascony beyond the River Garonne, grain resembling wheat is said to have rained from heaven, though it had grains somewhat shorter and rounder. Abbot Rabanus published commentaries on the Book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus for Archbishop Otgar. Amalarius wrote a book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and Angelomus wrote commentaries on the Books of Kings for the emperor. Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, [Col. 0859C] arranged in two booklets the edicts of Charlemagne and his son Louis relating to ecclesiastical law. The Italian army of Louis, carried by fleet to Africa, inflicted a great slaughter upon the Africans. The bodies of Saints Valentine and Genesius were transferred to the monastery of Resquingia.

(829.) At Aachen there was an earthquake and a wind so violent that it stripped not only humble houses but also, for the most part, the lead roof of the church itself. The sons’ disturbance and conflict against the emperor became evident. In this year, which is the 4,738th year from the beginning, the ninth great year of 524 years comes to an end. Thus far I have found the chronicle [Col. 0859D] of an anonymous author, from the year of the Lord 746 down to this year.

(830.) Pope Gregory, grieved that the suburbs of the Roman city around the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, were continually harassed and ravaged by Saracen raids, intended to build a new city there. Encouraged by the counsel and aid of the emperors, he began the new construction.

## 831

At Constantinople Theophilus ruled for fifteen years. The Saracens, invading Sicily, ravaged the island of Lipari, where rested the body of the Apostle Bartholomew. Formerly, because pagans could not bear that it was venerated by all men owing to the excessive brilliance of its miracles, the body had been placed in a leaden coffin and sunk in the sea; it had made its own way from India to this island. Its bones, now scattered here and there [Col. 0860A] by the Saracens, were afterwards gathered by a certain monk at the saint’s own revelation and transferred to Benevento. Emperor Louis deprived some opponents of office, exiled others, and stripped others of their property; thereby he further exasperated his sons and nobles against himself.

## 832

Pope Gregory, coming into Gaul, acted with the sons against the emperor. The emperor repudiated his wife Judith as though she were the cause of the evils.

## 833

Emperor Louis, deserted and betrayed by his own men and reduced to the power of his sons, laid aside his arms by the judgment of bishops and was confined to do penance. The sun and moon were eclipsed.

(834.) Emperor Louis was released, recovered his former empire and his wife, and compelled his son Lothair to return to Italy.

## 835

[Col. 0860B]

At Pope Gregory’s urging, and with all the bishops consenting, Emperor Louis decreed that the feast of All Saints should be celebrated in Gaul and Germany on the Kalends of November, as the Romans celebrated it by Pope Boniface’s institution. At this time the relics of the martyr Vitus were transferred from Paris to Corbie in Saxony. The Franks themselves testified that from that time the glory of the Franks passed to the Saxons. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, was deposed; many others who had conspired with him in Louis’s overthrow were also condemned and exiled.

## 836

Pope Gregory solemnly dedicated the completed construction of the New City and called it the Leonine City, or Roman City: either after Leo III, who had formerly laid the foundations of this [Col. 0860C] work, or after himself, who was called Leo IV.

## 837

The Northmen grievously ravaged Gaul, devastated Dorestad, burned the town of Antwerp and the market-town of Wilclant situated near the mouth of the Meuse, and received tribute from the Frisians. Pope Gregory restored many cities of Italy, ruined either by age or warfare, with new constructions or walls. When the Saracens came as far as the Roman harbour to plunder, the Romans, at Pope Gregory’s urging and aided by the Neapolitans, met them in battle. With divine aid in a violent storm of winds, they destroyed the defeated enemy almost to total annihilation. A comet appeared in the sign of Libra.

## 838

The Northmen ravaged the island of Walcheren and [Col. 0860D] exacted tribute.

(839.) Emperor Louis was reconciled with his son Lothair, who came to him under pledge of faith, and granted him the dignity of the empire and the royal crown.

## 840

A comet appeared in the sign of Aries; after several days, very many little fires, like stars, were seen running through the sky. Louis died. A comet-star appeared in the sign of Virgo, in that part of the sign which encompasses beneath it her mantle, and likewise the serpent’s tail and skin. Contrary to the course of the seven wandering stars, it proceeded eastward; marvellous to say, then passing through the signs of Leo, Cancer, and Gemini, it finally ended beneath the Charioteer’s feet, at the head of Taurus, the fiery globe and the great length of its radiance which it had extended in every direction. [Col. 0861A]

A short time afterwards, when the emperor was sick, for forty days his food was only the Lord’s body on Sunday. When he saw a demon standing by, he said, “Huis, huis,” meaning, “Out, out.” He had ruled Aquitaine for thirty-seven years. He died in the forty-fourth year of his life and the twenty-seventh of his empire, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. He received with the greatest joy the priest George, who promised to make an organ in the Greek manner. After him Autharius usurped the empire and ruled for fifteen years, according to others for nine years.

**WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY.** This Louis, son of Charlemagne, had four sons: Lothair, Pippin, Louis, and Charles the Bald. Lothair, while his father lived, assumed the imperial title and ruled for fifteen years over the part of Germany now called Lotharingia—as if “Lothair’s kingdom”—[Col. 0861B] and over all Italy with Rome. He was the cruelest of all men before him, and repeatedly bound his own father, taken captive, in prisons, because, after Ermegard, by whom he had had his earlier children, had died, his father kissed more frequently Charles, born of his wife Judith.

Pippin, son of Louis, ruled in Aquitaine and Gascony. Louis, the third son of Louis, besides Noricum which he possessed, held the kingdoms which his father gave him: namely Alemannia, Thuringia, Austrasia, and the kingdom of the Avars. Charles, however, held the western half of Francia, all Neustria, Lesser Brittany, the greater part of Burgundy, Gothia, and Gascony, after Pippin son of Pippin had been removed from there and tonsured in the monastery of St. Medard. Later Pippin escaped by flight, [Col. 0861C] returned to Aquitaine, and hid there for a long time while fleeing. Again, treacherously deceived and seized by Prefect Ranulf, he was brought to Charles and thrust into perpetual exile at Senlis.

Lothair, eighteen years before his father’s death, was anointed emperor. After his father’s death, he led an army against his brothers, King Louis of the Bavarians and Charles, having joined Pippin to himself with the people of Aquitaine.

## 841

Charles and Louis, grieving that their brother Lothair deprived them of their rightful share, prepared to rise against him.

## 842

A comet appeared in the sign of Aquarius. While the three brothers were therefore disputing over the partition of the kingdom, [Col. 0861D] battle was joined between them in the district of Auxerre, at the village of Fontenoy. So great a slaughter was made on both sides that no age remembered so great a destruction of men among the Frankish people. Their strength was so reduced there that afterwards they could not even defend their own borders from foreigners. Yet victory fell to Charles and Louis, and Lothair was put to flight. There the Franks, together with all the nations subject to them, struck one another down in mutual slaughter.

(843.) Since the brothers had not yet ceased from war, forty leading men were at last selected from each of their parties, by the counsel of the nobles, to meet together and divide the kingdom equally; and thus a truce was made until the following year. Meanwhile Louis proceeded into Saxony and vigorously suppressed a very strong conspiracy of freedmen who wished to oppress [Col. 0862A] their lords; the authors of the sedition were condemned to death.

**WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY.** Ethelwulf, son of Egorith, king—whom some call Atamachus—became king of the West Saxons in the year of the Lord 838. Content with the ancestral kingdom of the West Saxons, he assigned to his son Estatius the dependent kingdoms which his father had acquired. This Ethelwulf granted to Christ’s servants the tithe of all estates within his kingdom, free from every public obligation and released from every burden. Having set his kingdom in order, he went to Rome, where he offered before Pope Leo IV to St. Peter the tribute which England pays even today. Leo had also honourably received Eifred, Ethelwulf’s son, sent to him earlier, and had anointed him king.

Having remained there for a whole year, [Col. 0862B] Ethelwulf splendidly restored the English school, said first to have been established by King Offa and burned down in the preceding year. Returning home by way of Gaul, he married Judith, daughter of Charles. From this it is apparent that Charles the Bald had both a mother Judith and a daughter Judith. In certain chronicles Charles the Bald is placed immediately after Louis the Pious, Lothair his elder son being omitted; and there Charles the Bald is said to have ruled for forty-five years.

## 844

The Moors occupied Benevento. Pope Gregory died. After him sat Sergius, the hundred and fourth pope, second of that name, for three years. To confirm his election, Louis, son of Emperor Lothair, was sent by his father and was anointed king of the Lombards by that pope. After the kingdom had been divided into three parts, the brothers met at Verdun, a city of Gaul, [Col. 0862C] and made peace among themselves, giving and receiving oaths in turn.

Charles received the western kingdoms, from the British Ocean to the River Meuse; in that part the name Francia remained from then until now. The eastern kingdoms fell to Louis, namely all Germany as far as the waters of the Rhine, together with certain cities beyond the Rhine and their adjacent regions, on account of the abundance of wine. Lothair, the eldest, held all the kingdoms of Italy, including Rome itself, as well as Provence and the middle part of Francia between the Scheldt and the Rhine; this, after its name was changed, was called Lotharingia after him. Thus, after the division, Charles ruled in Francia for thirty-four years, and his brother Louis [Col. 0862D] in Germany for thirty-three years.

(845.) Louis, king of Germany, overcame in war the Abodrites, who were attempting to desert him, after their king had been killed; he organized through dukes their people and land, divinely subjected to him.

(846.) At Constantinople Michael and Theodora ruled for eleven years. The Northmen grievously harassed Charles’s kingdom and came by ship as far as Paris. They fought three battles with the Frisians: they were defeated in the first and victorious in the two others. Louis had fourteen Bohemian dukes baptized with their followers. Charles fought unsuccessfully with the Bretons.

(847.) Pope Sergius died, and the episcopal see was vacant for two months and fifteen days. After him sat Leo, the hundred and fifth pope, for eight years, three months, and six days. He decreed that, while the sacred solemnities of Mass are celebrated, [Col. 0863A] no layman should presume to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except only the sacred people appointed for the service of the sacred office; and that the Octave of the Assumption of St. Mary should be celebrated in the Church, which had not previously been done.

## 848

Rabanus was ordained archbishop of Mainz from being abbot of Fulda. At a synod held at Mainz by order of King Louis, he decreed many things useful to the Church. A certain false prophetess, claiming that the day of judgment was imminent, stirred up Mainz so greatly that she even drew some men in holy orders to herself. Seized by Rabanus, she confessed that she had done this at the instigation of a certain priest for the sake of gain.

(846.) Gottschalk, a heretic—though it is not said in what respect he was heretical—was refuted reasonably, as it seemed to many; [Col. 0863B] yet he persisted in his error. St. Helena, Constantine’s mother, whom her son Constantine had buried at Rome in the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, was transferred to Francia by the monk Theogisus and venerated with great devotion by the Franks in the diocese of Reims.

(850.) The Franks were defeated by the Bohemians in a severe battle. An evil spirit publicly declared through the mouth of a possessed man that it had presided over the war and, together with its companions—the spirits of pride and discord—had brought it about that the Franks turned their backs in flight.

(851.) The relics of the martyr St. Hermes were sent into Gaul by Emperor Lothair and honourably deposited in the monastery of Inda. A severe famine afflicted Germany, so that [Col. 0863C] a father wished to devour his own son. At that time Rabanus showed great generosity toward the poor.

(852.) Charles, king of the Franks, captured Pippin and Charles, the sons of his brother King Pippin, who were disturbing his kingdom; after tonsuring them as monks, he shut them in a monastery.

(853.) The Northmen entered the mouths of the Loire by the British Sea, attacked the city of Nantes, butchered the bishop while he was celebrating baptism on Holy Saturday of Easter, killed clergy and people, occupied Angers and Tours, burned the church of St. Martin, and, like a tempest, laid everything waste.

## 854

Hincmar, bishop of Reims, flourished; he wrote the *Life of St. Remigius*. Pope Leo died, and the episcopal see was vacant for two months and fifteen days. [Col. 0863D] In the fourth year of this pope, as is read in certain chronicles, Lothair ruled with his son Louis for five years—although he is certainly read to have ruled with that same son for eleven years, from the first year of Pope Sergius II. After this Leo sat Benedict II, the hundred and sixth pope. When he had been deposed through the conspiracy of certain wicked men, Anastasius seized the prelateship. But Anastasius was deposed by Lothair’s envoys and thrown into prison; Benedict was honourably restored and sat for two years, six months, and ten days.

The Northmen, who for twenty years had grievously worn down Francia, returned to their homeland and destroyed one another in civil war almost to total annihilation, so that none remained [Col. 0864A] of their royal line except a single boy.

(855.) Earthquakes, an unusual disturbance of the air, whirlwinds, storms, hailstorms, and lightning brought many hardships upon people in many ways. A certain man was consumed by heavenly fire, his clothing unharmed. Lothair divided the kingdom among his sons, renounced the world, assumed a monk’s habit at the monastery of Prüm, and not long afterwards rested in the Lord. After him his son Louis, formerly anointed king by Pope Sergius, ruled for twenty-one years. His brother Lothair held Lotharingia.

This Lothair died (from Malmesbury) in the year of the Lord 855, the thirty-third of his reign. By Ermengard, daughter of Hugh, he had three sons: Louis, to whom he gave the kingdom of the Romans and Italy; Lothair, to whom he left the imperial seat; and Charles, [Col. 0864B] to whom he left Provence to govern.

(856.) Maginrad the hermit was martyred. Rabanus died. At Constantinople Michael alone ruled for thirteen years. Pope Benedict died, and the episcopal see was vacant for fifteen days.

## 857
After him Nicholas I, the first pope of that name, the one hundred and seventh pope, sat for 9 years, 6 months, and 20 days; in certain chronicles he is placed in the fourth year of this Louis, son of Lothair. Emperor Louis confirmed the ordination of this Nicholas by his presence. When a storm arose at Cologne and the people fled to the basilica of St. Peter, a thunderbolt in the likeness of a fiery dragon suddenly split and penetrated the basilica, killing three men in different places with one stroke and leaving six others half-dead from the same blow. [Col. 0864C] Ethelwulf, king of the West Saxons, after a long pilgrimage during which he had stayed at Rome, returned to England, having married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald. From him, in a certain chronicle, the genealogical line of the kings of England is traced upward as far as Adam. [Note: [Col. 0863D] This fabulous genealogy is omitted here.] In the year of the Lord 857, the two sons of Ethelwulf divided their father's kingdom: Ethelbald ruled in Wessex and Ethelbert in Kent.

858.

The Franks complained to Louis, brother of their king Charles, about the latter's cruelty, and invited Louis to rule over them against Charles. He rashly undertook this and shamefully withdrew from another's territories. In the diocese of Mainz an evil spirit gave a manifest proof of its wickedness. For [Col. 0864D] first it troubled people by throwing stones and striking the walls of houses as if with hammers; then, speaking openly, it revealed thefts and sowed discord among neighbours. Finally, it stirred everyone's minds against one man, as though the others suffered such things because of his sins. It burned his crops after they had been gathered into one heap; wherever he entered, the house was immediately burned, so that he had nowhere to remain except in the fields. Therefore, while priests performed litanies and sprinkled blessed water, the enemy, throwing stones and wounding many, at last became quiet for a time. But when the priests had departed, the enemy howled mournfully; finally [Col. 0865A] naming a certain priest explicitly, it professed that, whenever blessed water was sprinkled, it had hidden beneath that priest's cloak as though beneath that of its familiar companion, accusing him of having slept with the steward's daughter. Thus it persisted for three years, until it consumed all the buildings there by fire.

859.

Louis, king of Germany, fought many battles valiantly against the Slavs, whose ruler was called Rastrix; because he had broken faith, Louis ordered his eyes to be put out. While King Charles's leading men were at variance among themselves, the Bretons, invading a land deprived of assistance, came as far as Poitiers, laying all waste. Charles pursued them as they returned and entered Brittany; battle was joined and the Franks were defeated, amid whose slaughter the Bretons ranged freely.

860.

[Col. 0865B]

Numenius, king of the Bretons, while he persisted in devastating the kingdom of the Franks, saw St. Maurilio, formerly bishop of Angers, standing beside him. Struck on the head with his staff by this saint, he experienced the wrath of God in death. At this time Lentulf, duke of the Saxons, father of Duke Otto and grandfather of King Henry, transferred the body of St. Innocent, pope, from Rome into Saxony.

861.

Herispous, son of Numenius and king of the Bretons, entered into alliance with King Charles; enriched with gifts by him, he submitted himself to his lordship.

862.

Lothair, brother of Louis and king of Lotharingia, taking Waldrada, his concubine, in addition to his wife Thieberga, with the consent of the archbishops Gunthar of [Col. 0865C] Cologne and Thietgaud of Trier, brought great disaster upon himself. Ethelbert, king of Kent, died and was buried at Sherborne; his brother Ethelbald obtained his entire kingdom. In his time a band of pirates landed at Southampton and plundered the populous city of Winchester.

863.

Hubert, abbot and duke, brother of Queen Thieberga, rose against Lothair because of the repudiation of his sister. The archbishops Gunthar and Thietgaud, examined at Rome by Pope Nicholas, having been convicted both by the synodal proceedings which they brought with them and by their own mouths, were deprived of their bishoprics and sacred ranks, anathematized, and allowed lay communion only.

864.

Waldrada the concubine having been excommunicated, King Lothair, seeing that excommunication was also threatened against himself, took back his wife Thieberga. But not long afterwards he repudiated her again and received back his concubine; nor could he thereafter be separated from her by any form of correction. (865.) The bodies of the holy martyrs Eusebius and Putianus, transferred to Gaul by the gift of Pope Nicholas, are honourably buried in monasteries of religious men granted to St. Peter. The king of the Bulgars, converted to Christianity with his people, received sacred ministers of ecclesiastical order sent to him by the Apostolic See, and also received assistance from King Louis. He was so firmly established in the faith that, not long afterward, after appointing his elder son king, he himself renounced the world and became a monk. But when his son, behaving youthfully, wished to return to [Col. 0866A] the worship of the pagans, the father resumed the military belt and royal dress, pursued and captured his son, put out his eyes, and cast him into prison. Having placed his younger son on the throne, he resumed the sacred habit and persevered in it until the end of his life. Louis, king of the Noricans—that is, the Bavarians—son of Louis the Pious, after the feast of Easter divided his kingdom among his sons. To Charles he gave Noricum, that is, Bavaria, and the marches against the Slavs and Lombards; to Louis, Thuringia, the East Frankish lands, and Saxony; to the other Charles, Alemannia and Curvalam, that is, the county of Cornwall. (866.) Herispous having been killed by his own men, Solomon his son ruled over the Bretons and made an alliance with Charles, who was advancing against him. The Northmen, returning to Gaul, [Col. 0866B] devastated the territories of Nantes, Angers, Poitiers, and Tours. When Ranulf, duke of Aquitaine, and Robert the Strong, Malchio, rushed against them, they themselves were rashly killed in battle, while the rest were struck down by the Northmen in heaps, like sheep by wolves.

867.

When the Saracens invaded the region of Benevento, Emperor Louis met them courageously. Lothair his brother hastened to assist him and indeed fought many battles stoutly with him; but his army, severely afflicted by unseasonable weather, illnesses, and the bites of spiders, returned with great loss of men. In this year Ethelred, son of Ethenulf, began to reign; he fought many wars [Col. 0866C] with the Danes. In one year he fought nine times with hostile battle-lines drawn up. On the Danish side nine earls, one king, and countless people were killed. Pope Nicholas died; after him Adrian II, the one hundred and eighth pope, sat for 5 years. But according to a certain chronicle he is placed two years later.

868.

A comet appeared plainly. Michael, emperor of the Greeks, impaired in mind, ordered his intimates to be killed, though when he returned to himself he demanded that they be presented to him. Basil, whom Emperor Michael had taken into his household as a poor man from the family of an abbot and, after making him a chamberlain, had raised to such honours that he was called “the second after the emperor,” was repeatedly ordered by the emperor in his madness to be killed. Fearing that he might be killed on such a pretext, Basil chose rather to kill the emperor himself than to be killed by him, and ruled for 17 years.

869.

The body of St. Maurus, disciple of St. Benedict, was transferred from Glanfeuil in Burgundy, for fear of the Northmen, to the monastery of Fossatus, founded by St. Balbert, disciple of St. Columbanus.

870.

King Lothair went to Pope Adrian, who was excommunicating him. For the proof of his innocence, both he and his magnates had been invited to the testing of the body and blood of the Lord; and he himself, together with all who with him presumed rashly to receive the Lord's body, perished within that same year, Lothair himself dying immediately on his return at Piacenza.

871.

[Col. 0867A]

At Cologne, during a synod held for the dedication of a church by the three metropolitans Liutbert of Mainz, Bertulf of Trier, and Willibert of Cologne, when the greater church of St. Peter was to be dedicated by them, voices of evil spirits were heard on the preceding night, lamenting and complaining to one another that they must be expelled from seats they had long possessed. King Charles of the Franks, after the death of his brother Lothair, sought to seize Lotharingia for himself alone; but through the moderation and skill of his brother Louis, king of Germany, he was brought to divide the kingdom equally between the two brothers. Louis's army waged various wars against the Slavs with varying success.

872.

A domestic calamity among his [Col. 0867B] sons afflicted King Charles of the Franks. For his father seized and blinded Carloman, who had advanced in the clerical state as far as the office of deacon, because he had turned to apostasy and, disturbing the kingdom by every kind of mischief, had become another Julian. His other son Charles, having rashly wished to test the courage of a certain soldier named Albuin, was killed by that same Albuin, who did not know who he was. Basil, emperor of the Greeks, among other gifts sent to Louis, king of Germany, a crystal of extraordinary size adorned with gems and gold, together with a substantial piece of the Holy Cross. Ethelred, son of Ethenulf, king, died. After him reigned Ofred, son of the younger Etheuf, who had formerly received royal anointing [Col. 0867C] and a crown from Pope Leo V. He ruled for 28 years and 6 months. For nine continuous years he fought against enemies. Once, when he was shut up on an island and was alone in his dwelling, while his companions had scattered along the riverbank to fish, he gave his body, sick with cares, to sleep. And behold, St. Cuthbert, formerly bishop of Lindisfarne, addressed him as he slept:

> “I am Cuthbert, if you have heard of me. The Lord has sent me to announce good things to you. England has long paid the penalty for her sins. But now at last, regarded by the Lord through the merits of her native saints, she is restored. You, pitiably driven from your kingdom, will after a short time be gloriously restored to the throne. And this shall be your sign: today your fishermen will come bringing out in baskets a great multitude of fish—an astonishing thing, since, with the river water frozen, nothing of the sort is expected, and the cold season defeats every art of fishermen. When you have attained better fortune, remember your deliverer and his messenger.”

The same vision appeared in a dream to his mother. When both awoke, they told one another their dreams; and behold, the fishermen arrived with a great abundance of fish. Not long afterward he dared to escape from the prison in which the Danes held him, and attempted the danger with great cunning. For he entered the Danish king's tents in the guise of a messenger, confiding his secret to one man only, his most faithful companion. There, posing as a practitioner of the art of seeing, he perceived with eyes and ears every secret, even in the innermost rooms of the dining-hall. After remaining there several days, he returned to Ebungia, disclosed everything to his companions, and suddenly rushed upon [Col. 0868A] the unguarded barbarians. After very many of them had been killed, the remainder, with their king, gave hostages that they would become Christians and depart from England—and they did so. Their king Gedrum, whom our people call Gurmindus, was baptized with thirty nobles and almost all the people, and was received as a son by King Elfred. The remaining Danes who did not wish to become Christians crossed the sea with Hasting. According to certain chronicles, the eighth synod was held under Pope Adrian. After him the one hundred and ninth pope, John VIII, sat for 10 years and 2 days.

873.

For this John, John, deacon of the Roman Church, wrote the Life of the first Pope Gregory, commendably composed in four little books. Adalgisus, [Col. 0868B] duke of the Beneventans, seduced by the Greeks, rebelled against Emperor Louis and caused many cities of Italy to revolt from him. The emperor courageously resisted him and took Benevento and Capua; but, persuaded by Adalgisus's deceit to dismiss his army, he was so entrapped by him that he could not escape unless, forced to make a shameful compact, he swore to Adalgisus never during his life to enter the territory of Benevento. On this account Adalgisus was declared guilty of treason and a public enemy by the Roman senate; war having been decreed against him, he fled to Corsica. Charles the Younger, son of Louis, king of Germany, was grievously tormented by a demon in the presence of his father and his magnates; during the torment he confessed that this had happened to him because he was plotting [Col. 0868C] to form a conspiracy against his father.

874.

At Brescia in Italy, blood is said to have rained from heaven for three days and nights. The Northmen, demanding tribute from the kingdom of Germany, were heavily defeated by Louis's army. Countless locusts devastated Gaul, larger than other locusts, having six wings, six feet, and two teeth harder than stone. Flying in squadrons like battle-lines, they sent commanders with a few men a day's journey ahead to mark out places for the coming multitude; arriving at the appointed place around the ninth hour, and waiting there for sunrise, they covered the air for the space of one day's journey, darkening the brightness of the sun itself. With broad mouths and extended entrails they devoured every green thing among grasses [Col. 0868D] and trees, extending four or five miles over the length of a day's march. Reaching the British Sea in a miserable spectacle, they were at last submerged in the depths of the sea by the winds; but cast back upon the shore by the tide of Ocean, they corrupted the air with their decay and caused many to perish. A severe famine followed and consumed many by starvation, so that almost one third of the people of Gaul perished.

875.

The winter was harsher and longer than usual: snow and frost lasted from the Kalends of November to the vernal equinox. Louis, king of Germany, saw in a dream his father Louis the Pious, who admonished him in the name of the Holy Trinity to rescue him from the torments in which he was detained, so that he might at last deserve to have eternal [Col. 0869A] rest. Therefore the son earnestly assisted his father by assigning alms to various monasteries. From this it may be understood that, although that emperor had done many things pleasing to God and men, he nevertheless allowed more things contrary to God to be done in his kingdom. Among these the graver appeared to be that he did not resist the heresy of the Nicolaitans, and did not endeavour to observe the admonitions of the archangel Gabriel, set forth in twelve chapters, which Emarchus offered him to read and keep. The Northmen occupied the city of Angers with all their people, as though they intended to live there. King Charles, having summoned Solomon king of the Bretons, besieged it for many days in order to attack it. But when the Northmen had been reduced to desperation, the king, having accepted money from them, allowed them to depart with their large army, and by this agreement gave them opportunity to do worse things.

876.

A comet appeared more brilliant than usual. In June there was a sudden and enormous overflowing of waters, so that in Saxony a certain village, far removed from torrents and rivers, was in an instant wholly swallowed up with its people and beasts, its trees and buildings, its church and altar, leaving no trace of habitation. Emperor Louis died in Italy. His uncle Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, went to Rome, where, having won over Pope John and the Romans by gifts, he was made emperor and ruled for 2 years. After their king Solomon had died, the Bretons clashed among themselves in civil war [Col. 0869C] over the contest for the kingship, and thus unwillingly ceased from the devastation of Gaul.

877.

After obtaining the empire, Charles the Bald became exalted beyond himself. Disregarding Frankish customs, he affected Greek splendours and unusual dress; wearing a long dalmatic, girded over it with a belt hanging down to his feet, his head wrapped in a silk covering and crowned with a diadem, he strutted about. Being more timid than a hare and readier to flee enemies [Col. 0870A] than to put them to flight, he provoked his brother Louis, king of Germany, threatening that he would hire forces so great that, after the river had been drained by horses, he himself would enter the German kingdom through the dry riverbed. The monk Henry offered to Emperor Charles a Life of St. Germanus of Auxerre, splendidly written in heroic metre in six little books. Louis, king of Germany, died, leaving his three sons as heirs, among whom he divided his kingdom, as we have said above. He ruled over his sons in all piety for ten years and died in the fifty-fourth year of his reign. His sons were Louis the Younger; Charles, who not long afterward became emperor; and Carloman, father of Emperor Arnulf. Emperor Charles the Bald, rejoicing at his brother's death and prepared to carry out against his brother's [Col. 0870B] sons the injustice he had conceived against his brother, invaded their kingdom with fifty thousand men and more, reaching as far as Cologne while Louis's sons were occupied elsewhere. Louis the Younger sent an embassy to his uncle and asked for terms of peace. When he could not obtain them, he met him bravely in war, defeated him, compelled him to flee with enormous loss to his army, and covered him with great disgrace. When a plague among cattle broke out in Germany, dogs gathered from all sides to feed upon the carcasses, but vanished so completely that neither living nor dead ones could be found.

878.

Charles the Bald, travelling to Rome for the second time, gave Boso, his wife's brother, a niece—the daughter of Emperor Louis—as wife; and, granting him Provence, crowned him king, as though he would even rule over kings. Hearing that his nephews Carloman and Charles were bringing an army against him, he was overcome by fear and prepared to return. On the return journey he was badly poisoned by a certain Jewish Zedekiah and died at Mantua, in the beginning of the third year of his empire and the thirty-eighth of his reign, on the third day before the Nones of October; he had been crowned emperor at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

## BOOK XLVI

[Col. 0869]

[Col. 0869D] This Charles the Bald founded and completed the monastery of St. Cornelius near Compiègne. He himself had planned to make a castle in the likeness of Constantinople; the castle which Charlemagne had established at his own estate of Aachen, he established at the estate of St. Denis. Since he had seized many things belonging to the church of St. Denis which others had given, he offered it the Lord's crown of thorns, one of the nails, wood of the Cross, and certain other things. But he left the shroud at Compiègne. He established these things in the time of Pope Nicholas. Before these relics were shown to the people, there used to be such famine in Gaul that people ate asses and horses; afterward, through the Lord's mercy, this ceased. Sigebert says that this Charles died at Mantua on his return from Rome. [Col. 0870D] Elsewhere I have read that, while going to Rome, he died on the journey and was buried near Lyons in the monastery of Mantonay. After a long time he appeared in a vision of the night to a monk of St. Denis named Erthongarius, and on the same night to a cleric of St. Quentin of Vermand named Alpho, telling each that he was Charles the Bald and had appeared to them by God's command so that he might tell them that God and St. Denis were displeased because his body had not been buried in the church of St. Denis, to which he had bestowed such great gifts for God's honour. They were therefore to go and tell his son Louis and the magnates of the kingdom to bring him back. Thus he was brought back in the time of Walter, abbot of St. Denis, and buried in the church of St. Denis before the altar of the Holy Trinity. At this time [Col. 0871A] John Scotus flourished, a man of penetrating intellect and honeyed eloquence. Long before, when the clashes of war resounded on every side throughout Gaul, he had crossed over to Charles the Bald; at Charles's request he translated, word for word, the *Hierarchy* of Dionysius the Areopagite from Greek into Latin. He also composed the book entitled *On the Division of Nature*, very useful for resolving questions, provided that he is forgiven certain points in which he departed from the Latin path while fixing his gaze intently upon the Greeks. In subsequent years, attracted by the generosity of Elfred, he came to England; at the monastery of Malmesbury he was, it is said, pierced with writing-styluses by the boys whom he taught, and was even regarded as a martyr. This was his epitaph:

[Col. 0871B]

> Holy sophist John lies enclosed in this tomb,  
> Who while living had already been enriched with wondrous doctrine;  
> At last, by martyrdom, he merited to ascend to Christ's kingdom,  
> Where all the saints reign through the ages.

These verses are rough and lack the polish of modern times. At the same time Milo, monk of St. Amand, flourished. He composed the Life of St. Amand in verse and wrote a book *On Sobriety* for Charles the Bald. Under this Milo his nephew Hubald was growing up; famous for his mastery of the seven liberal arts, he was especially distinguished in music above all else, and composed chants concerning many saints in sweet and regular melody.

879.

After Charles the Bald, his son Louis, surnamed the Stammerer, ruled in Francia for 2 years. [Col. 0871C] But Charles the Younger, son of Louis, king of the Germans, obtained the empire through the support of certain Roman nobles, although Pope John made every effort to transfer the empire to Louis the Stammerer. Because of this John was insulted by the Romans, since he did not support Charles; he came into Francia and remained with King Louis the Stammerer for nearly a year. More than five thousand Northmen were slain by the Franks in Gaul. Hasting, driven from England by King Elfred, as was said above, crossed the sea with his men and, emptying Paris, Tours, and many other cities situated along the Seine and Loire of their inhabitants, ranged as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea.

880.

ODO, abbot of Cluny. This Hasting, after devastating [Col. 0871D] the upper parts of Gaul, besieged Tours. When its wall was repeatedly battered by the ram, people ran to the body of St. Martin and carried it to the weaker place, making the dead man a defender of the living. Immediately the Danes fled, and the people of Tours pursued them as far as the sixth milestone. There the church of St. Martin was built, at the place where the holy body had halted.

There were there ruins of ancient walls, where it was said that the hall of Valentinian had stood, in which, while seated, he had not deigned to rise for Martin until, terrified by a fire that burst forth, he rose. After three lustra of Hasting's flight, Rollo came from the same regions. Having defeated the Bretons and Flemings and burned their cities and [Col. 0872A] towns, he came to Le Mans and besieged it; he sent commanders of his army to Tours. But then, by God's providence, the Cher and Loire had overflowed so greatly that they could not approach Tours. Moreover, sixteen monks were struck down by the sword; the abbot and another twenty-four, hiding in caves, escaped. They were preserved for this purpose: to accompany the body of their patron. Yet Abbot Herbern, dragged out of his hiding place, could not be compelled by any torments either to reveal the Church's treasures or the monks in hiding. No survivor remained whom Martin did not appoint to the governance of the Church. Then, after the Danes had departed, the abbot and those twenty-four were received reverently by the canons of St. Martin, brought to the city, and sustained there. Six months later Rollo captured Le Mans. Then [Col. 0872B] the body of St. Martin was transferred to Orléans. Its guardians were Abbot Herbern with twenty-four monks, twelve canons, and twelve burghers of Nevers, who supplied them with all necessities. Afterwards they reached Saint-Benoît. Then, hearing that Rollo had now arrived at Orléans, they proceeded to Chablis, and afterwards to Auxerre, where innumerable miracles were performed in the church of Blessed Germanus.

GUILLELMUS. As very many people coming for the sake of remedies made offerings, a dispute arose between the people of Tours and Auxerre over the division of the money. To settle this dispute, a leper was placed between the bodies of the two saints. All human guard was excluded for the whole night. At dawn it appeared that the part [Col. 0872C] of the leper nearest Martin had been entirely cured, while the other remained leprous. The body was turned around, and the diseased side was turned toward Martin. On the following morning he was found wholly cured, Germanus yielding to the honour of his guest. At that time the Danes harassed Gaul for thirteen years, until at last, defeated by Emperor Arnulf in many battles, they fled back to England. During that period Elfred brought under his authority the whole island, except what the Danes possessed. He gave Cinidonia, the capital of the kingdom of Mercia, to a certain nobleman together with his daughter Egelfreda.
