By her this nobleman, named Ethelred, had children, Ethelenda and Edward, who afterwards ruled. This Elfred, already twelve years old, was wholly without learning. [Col. 0872D] Yet his mother graciously invited him, as a game, to receive as a gift the book she held in her hands if he learned it quickly. Thus, beginning letters in play, he drank them in with thirsty eagerness. He translated these books into English: Orosius; the *Pastoral Care* of St. Gregory; the *Deeds of the English*; and Boethius's book *On Consolation*. He divided the day in this manner: he spent eight hours writing, praying, and reading; eight caring for his body; and eight dispatching the affairs of the kingdom. For this reason there was in his chapel a candle divided into twenty-four portions, and a sacristan who, by the burning of the candle, reminded the king of each duty. He assigned half of all his revenues, provided they were justly acquired, to monasteries. He divided all his other revenues into two parts, and then the first into [Col. 0873A] three: one of these he gave to his court servants; the second to workers, whom he continually employed in constructing new buildings by a remarkable manner unknown to the English; the third to strangers. The second part of the revenues was divided so that the first share was given to the poor of his realm, the second to monasteries, the third, [lacuna], the fourth to churches beyond the sea.

He always carried in his breast a little book containing the daily course of the Psalms, so that whenever he had leisure he might take it up and pray. He gave his daughter Ethelfelda in marriage to Baldwin, count of Flanders; by her Baldwin had Arnulf, from whom the counts of Flanders descend, and Adulph, who received the county of Boulogne from his father. He was buried at Winchester in his own monastery. This Rollo, of whom mention was made above, descended indeed from a noble but, through antiquity, decayed stock of the Norican kings. Driven from his country by the king's command, he drew after him, with great hopes, many men whom either debt or consciousness of crimes troubled; he undertook piracy and did not abandon it. The citizens, trusting neither in arms nor walls, worship the *semperatum* of Blessed Mary—that is, her shift—which Charles the Bald had caused to be brought from Constantinople with other relics. They displayed this shift like a banner over the defenders' battlements. When the enemy saw it, they laughed and directed arrows at it. Their eyes were immediately darkened, and they could neither advance nor retreat. Seeing this, the townsmen satiated themselves with a marvellous slaughter of them. Rollo nevertheless escaped, whom God preserved for His own faith. Not long afterward he acquired Rouen and the lands adjoining [Col. 0873C] that city, in the year of the Lord 836, namely one year before the death of Charles the Bald. Louis, Charles's son, defeated the Northumbrians indeed, but did not drive them out. This is William's account, who always places Charles's death one year earlier than Sigebert does. Sigebert never gives this Charles a surname, since he never calls him “the Bald,” but simply Charles. Others, with the historical account, call him the Bald. At the ninth hour of the day the sun was so darkened that stars appeared in it. Louis the Stammerer died in the palace at Compiègne on the sixth day before the Ides of April, leaving his wife pregnant: according to William, in the year of the Lord 870; according to Sigebert, two years less—that is, later. While opinions differed concerning the Frankish empire, [Col. 0873D] some judging that it was owed to the son of Louis the Stammerer by a concubine, others supporting Boso, petty king of Provence, in his unjust seizure of it—he had as his wife a niece of Charles the Bald—and others wishing it to be reunited to the kingdom of Germany, Louis the Stammerer's posthumous son was born meanwhile. He was named Charles after his grandfather. Yet the sons of Louis the Stammerer by a concubine, Louis and Carloman, meanwhile divided the Frankish kingdom between themselves and ruled for 5 years; they constantly pursued Boso. (881.) More than nine thousand Romans were killed in the Charcoal Forest of Francia. GUILLELMUS. Louis, brother of Carloman, fighting the Normans, won a victory in the district of Merminiac and died not long afterward, on the day before the Nones of August in the year of the Lord [Col. 0874A] 882. He ruled for 2 years, 3 months, and 24 days. His brother Carloman succeeded him and ruled for 3 years and 6 days.

882.

Charles, king of the Germans, after the death of his brother Carloman and, not long afterward, the premature death of his other brother Louis, obtained the whole kingdom of Germany together with the Roman empire, after renowned victories over his enemies. Charles was blessed at Rome by Pope John. The Normans, joined by the Danes, ranging through Francia and Lotharingia, devastated Amiens, Arras, Corbie, Cambrai, Thérouanne, the lands of the Noricans, Menapians, and Bredatensians, all the territory around the river Scheldt, and the monasteries of Saints Waltricus and Richarius with fire and sword. Entering Walcheren, they burned all Butina and also the palace at Nijmegen. [Col. 0874B] In the same year Godefrid and Ligefrid, kings of the Normans, encamped beside the Meuse at a place called Hastan with an immeasurable multitude. They burned Liège, Maastricht, Tongeren, Cologne, Bonn, and the neighbouring forts. At Aachen, stabling their horses in the palace, they burned the town itself and the palace. They burned the monasteries of Stavelot, Malmedy, Inda, and Prüm. Ministers of the sacred order of both sexes hid themselves wherever they could most suitably do so, and concealed the bodies and relics of saints in safer places. To these evils were added Hugh, son of Lothair by the concubine Waldrada, tyrannizing in Lotharingia, and the aforesaid Boso in Burgundy. (883.) The Normans burned Trier and came as far as Metz; there, battle being joined, [Col. 0874C] they defeated the Christians. In that battle Walo, bishop of Metz, was killed. Emperor Charles, summoned by Gauls and Germans to give aid, besieged the Normans. King Godefrid then made a treaty: Frisia was to be given to him as a province and Gisela, daughter of King Lothair, as his wife. He was baptized and received from the sacred font by the emperor. King Sigefrid, too, being greatly weakened, was made to withdraw from his kingdom. The Normans soon returned to Francia and, after many incursions, demanded from Carloman, king of the Franks, twelve thousand marks of tested silver as tribute; promising peace for twelve years, they returned to the sea. At this time a certain Rodulf transferred from Rome to Francia the body of St. Callixtus, pope and martyr, who instituted the fasts of the four seasons. [Col. 0874D] (884.) GUILLELMUS. In this year Carloman, king of the Franks, died on the eighth day before the Ides of December, struck by a solitary weapon in the forest of Ennelin, on Mount Aerius. Then Charles, king of the Suevians, son of Louis, king of the Bavarians, assumed the sole rule of the whole Roman and Frankish empire in the year of the Lord 885.

885.

Accordingly, after the deaths of the two brothers who were kings of the Franks, the Normans returned to Francia, saying that they had made a peace treaty with the king of the Franks alone, not with the Franks. Therefore the Franks were compelled to invite Emperor Charles to their aid and to submit Francia to him, according to Sigebert. Against the Normans encamped at Louvain, [Col. 0875A] he sent an army once and twice, but accomplished nothing worthy of note. Nevertheless, from this year he ruled in Francia for 5 years. Hincmar became bishop of Reims.

886.

Sigebert places Pope Marinus in this year, though in other chronicles he is placed three years earlier, that is, in 883. He was the one hundred and tenth pope and sat for 1 year and 5 months. Hugh, son of King Lothair by the concubine Waldrada, hoping through rebellion to obtain his father's kingdom of Lotharingia, persuaded Godefrid, king of the Normans, to ask the emperor to add imperial estates freely to his own domains. He promised him half the kingdom he sought; Godefrid had married his sister Gisela. Hugh thought by this means to entrap the emperor in either case: if he agreed, Danes and Normans, enemies of the kingdom, would be admitted into the kingdom's very heart; if he refused, Hugh would seem to have [Col. 0875B] a just cause for rebellion. When, at the emperor's command, Duke Henry and Godefrid met in Batavia to negotiate this matter, Godefrid and his men were killed in the course of the proceedings. Not long afterward Hugh too was blinded by Henry and finally tonsured as a monk at Prüm. At Constantinople, Emperor Basil died, and his son Leo ruled for 18 years.

887.

The Normans, leaving Louvain, besieged Paris. Duke Henry led an army against them; while riding carelessly, he fell into a pit which the Normans had made and covered with rubbish, and was killed. Duke and Abbot Hugh, a man of remarkable piety and prudence, died. Agapitus became pope after Marinus. [Col. 0875C] Yet he is not recorded in certain books. He was the one hundred and eleventh pope, for scarcely one year.

888.

Since Emperor Charles could not drive out the Normans, he finally made a treaty with them and granted them the lands beyond the Seine, whose inhabitants were rebelling against him. That part of Francia was called Normandy from the Normans.

GUILLELMUS. The following vision of this Charles is related.

“In the name of God Most High, King of kings, I, Charles, emperor—by the free gift of God king of the Germans, patrician of the Romans, and emperor of the Franks—on the holy night before Sunday, after the divine office of the nocturnal hours had been celebrated, when I went to rest and wished to sleep, a terrifying voice came to me, saying: ‘Charles, your spirit will shortly depart from you for no small time.’ [Col. 0875D]

“Immediately I was caught up in the spirit; and he who lifted me up was exceedingly bright, holding in his hand a ball of thread emitting a most brilliant radiance of light, as comets commonly do when they appear. He began to unwind it and said to me: ‘Take hold of the end of the shining ball, and bind and knot it firmly around the thumb of your right hand; for by it you will be led through the labyrinthine punishments of hell.’ Having said this, he went swiftly before me, uncoiling the thread of light from his ball, and led me into the deepest fiery valleys, which were full of pits burning with pitch, sulphur, lead, wax, and fat. There I found the bishops of my father and of my uncles. When I asked them in fear why they suffered such grievous torments, [Col. 0876A] they answered:

“‘We were bishops of your father and your uncles; and when we ought to have exhorted them and their people to peace and concord, we sowed discord and were instigators of evil. Therefore we now burn in these Tartarean punishments, both we and other lovers of murder and robbery. Your bishops and retainers, who likewise now love to act in this way, will also come here.’

“And while I listened trembling, behold, blackest demons flew toward me with fiery hooks, wishing to seize the thread of the ball which I held in my hand and pull it toward themselves. But, repelled by the rays of that ball, they could not touch it. Then, running behind me, they wished to hook me and cast me down into the sulphurous pits. But my guide, [Col. 0876B] who carried the ball, threw the thread of the ball over my shoulders and doubled it, and drew me strongly after him. Thus we ascended exceedingly high fiery mountains, from which arose boiling marshes and rivers, and every kind of bubbling metal. There I found innumerable souls of men, of my father’s nobles and of my brothers’, cast down—some up to their hair, others to their chin, others to their navel—and they cried out to me lamenting:

“‘While we lived, we loved, together with you, your father, your brothers, and your uncles, to wage battles, hold carousals, and commit robberies for earthly greed. Therefore we are tortured in these boiling rivers and in the various kinds of metals.’

[Col. 0876C] “As I approached these things in fear, I heard souls crying behind me: ‘The mighty shall suffer mighty torments’ (Wisdom 6). I looked and saw, on the banks of a boiling river, furnaces of pitch and sulphur, full of huge dragons, scorpions, and serpents of various kinds. There also I saw certain nobles of my father, my brothers, and my uncles, saying to me: ‘Woe to us, Charles! You see how grievous are the torments we endure because of our wickedness, pride, and evil counsels, which from greed we gave to our kings and to you.’

“As I trembled in sorrow, dragons rushed upon me, their open jaws full of fire, sulphur, and pitch, wishing to swallow me. But [Col. 0876D] my guide tripled the thread over me; the fiery mouths were overcome by its rays of brightness, and he drew me onward more forcefully. We descended into a valley which on its lower side was dark and burning like a fiery furnace, but on the other side was so delightful and splendid that I cannot describe it in any way.

“I turned toward the dark, flame-spewing side and saw there certain kings of my lineage amid great punishments. Greatly distressed by this, I thought that I would immediately be plunged into those punishments by the blackest giants, who set that valley ablaze with kinds of fire. Trembling greatly, while the thread of the ball illuminated my eyes, I saw a light somewhat whiten on the side of the valley, and there two springs flowed. One was exceedingly hot, the other bright and lukewarm; and there were two vats. As I went there, the thread of the ball guiding my steps, I looked intently upon one in which water was flowing and saw my father Louis standing there up to his thighs. Overwhelmed by deep grief and anguish, [Col. 0877A] I heard him say to me:

“‘My lord Charles, do not fear. I know that your spirit will return again to your body; and God has allowed you to come here so that you might see for what sins I, and all whom you have seen, endure such punishments. For one day I am in this bath of a boiling vat; on the next I am transferred into that other most pleasant vat of water. This is through the prayers of Saint Peter and Saint Remigius, by whose patronage our line has hitherto ruled while governing. But if you, my bishops, abbots, and the whole ecclesiastical order quickly assist me [Col. 0877B] with Masses, offerings, prayers, psalm-singing, vigils, and alms, I shall quickly be freed from this vat of boiling water. For my brother Lothair and his son Louis have already been released from these punishments through the prayers of Saint Peter and Saint Remigius, and have been led into the joy of paradise.’

“And he said to me: ‘Look to your left.’ I looked and saw two exceedingly high boiling vats. ‘These,’ he said, ‘are prepared for you, unless you reform yourself and repent of your abominable sins.’ Then I began to shudder violently. But my guide, seeing me in such terror, said to me: ‘Follow me to the right side of the most radiant valley of paradise.’

“I beheld, in immense brightness, my uncle Lothair seated with glorious kings upon a topaz stone of wondrous size, crowned with a precious diadem, and beside him his son Louis, likewise crowned. Seeing me, he graciously summoned me, saying in a gentle voice: [Col. 0877C] ‘Charles, my successor, now third in the Roman Empire, come to me. I know that you have come through the place of punishment where your father, my brother, has been placed in the baths appointed for him. But through God’s mercy he will very soon be freed from those punishments, just as we were freed through the merits of Saint Peter and the prayers of Saint Remigius. God gave him great apostolic authority over kings and over the Frankish race; unless he supports the remnant of our line, our genealogy will now cease to reign and rule. Therefore [Col. 0877D] I know that power will soon be taken from your hand, and afterward you will live only a very short time.’

“Then Louis his son, turning toward me, said: ‘The empire which you have hitherto held ought by hereditary right to be assumed by Louis, the son of my daughter.’ And when he had said this, it seemed to me that the infant Louis was brought into their presence. Lothair looked upon him and said to me: ‘The child appears such as was that child whom the Lord set in the midst of the disciples and said: “I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18). But you must restore to him the power of the empire by means of the thread of the ball which you hold in your hand.’

“Therefore, untying the thread from the thumb of my right hand, I gave him [Col. 0878A] the entire monarchy of the empire through that thread. Immediately that shining ball, united like the radiance of the sun, was gathered wholly into his hand. Thus, after this remarkable event, my spirit returned to my body, greatly weary and terrified.”

After this vision, this Charles survived scarcely two years.

889.

Adrian III sat as pope, the one hundred and twelfth, or the one hundred and eleventh, because Agapitus is not counted in certain books. He sat one year and four months. The emperor Charles was jealous of his wife because she behaved more freely than was right with Liuthard, bishop of Vercelli. At a public assembly he declared that he had never carnally lain with her; she, boasting that she was a virgin, accepted repudiation and sought a monastery. [Col. 0878B]

890.

The emperor Charles, failing in body and mind, was rejected by the magnates of the realm; Arnulf, son of King Carloman, his cousin, was raised to the kingdom and reigned twelve years. This Arnulf assigned estates in Germany to his uncle Charles, now ex-emperor and even lacking necessities; Charles died the following year.

GUILLELMUS: Charles the Boy succeeded him in the kingdom of the Franks, son of that Louis who died at Compiègne; while Arnulf, of the imperial line, succeeded him in the empire, guardian of that boy Louis concerning whom the preceding vision had spoken. Arnulf reigned eleven years. This Charles married the daughter of Edward, king of the English.

891.

SIGEBERTUS. The Roman Empire and the kingdom of Francia were miserably torn apart. In Italy Berengar and Guy contended for the kingdom. The Franks, however, disregarding the boy Charles, scarcely ten years old, son of Louis the Stammerer, set over themselves as king Odo, son of Duke Robert, whom we said above had been killed by the Northmen. Rudolf, moreover, having placed the crown upon himself, was established as king of the Burgundians; his kingdom endured for a long time.

SIGEBERTUS. From this time Liutprand, deacon of the Church of Pavia, begins his history. Basil became the one hundred and twelfth pope. He is not found in certain books. The Northmen captured Paris, attacked Burgundy, and besieged the city of Sens, but did not capture it. In Italy the Saracens, occupying a certain fortress, Fraxinetum, seized it to Italy’s great destruction. [Col. 0878D]

GUILLELMUS. Alfred, mentioned above, was highly learned, and always in poor health, continually troubled either by piles or by some internal ailment. They say that he obtained this from the Lord through prayer, so that he might embrace worldly pleasures less readily. He established hundreds and tithings and bestowed such peace upon his country that he ordered golden bracelets to be hung even on the public causeways where paths divide at crossroads, mocking travellers’ poverty because there was no one to steal them. He sent many gifts to Rome and to Saint Thomas in India. The envoy sent for this purpose was Sighelm, bishop of Sherborne, who penetrated India and brought back many gems and very many spices; Pope Marinus sent the king a portion of the Lord’s wood. [Col. 0879A]

He built one monastery at Athelney, where he had once been captive, and there appointed as abbot John, a native of Old Saxony; another at Winchester, called the New Monastery, where he installed Grimbald as abbot. Grimbald had become known to him because, when the king, as they say, had once travelled through the place as a boy, Grimbald had kindly entertained him, having been sent at the archbishop’s request. The reason for his summons was that by his own industry he might revive the study of letters, then almost buried in England. He likewise founded the monastery of Shaftesbury, which he filled with nuns, appointing his daughter Æthelgifu as abbess there.

He had with him a certain Asser, nobly educated, from St David’s, whom [Col. 0879B] he made bishop of Sherborne. This man explained in plainer words the sense of Boethius’s books *On Consolation*, which the king himself translated into English. He summoned from Mercia Werferth, bishop of Worcester, who at the king’s command translated the books of the *Dialogues* into the English tongue.

After him reigned Edward, whose mother, Æthelflæd, widow of Æthelred, king of the Mercians, having experienced the difficulty of her first childbirth, abstained from her husband forever, declaring that it did not befit a king’s daughter to expose herself to such danger. Edward reigned twenty-three years and gave his daughter Edith to Charles, king of the Franks, son of Louis the Stammerer. He arranged for his daughters first to be educated in letters and then to be trained in distaff, spindle, and needle; he likewise had his sons first instructed in letters and afterward taught the governance of the kingdom.

892.

[Col. 0879C]

SIGEBERTUS. The Northmen return from Sens to Paris, are driven thence by the river Marne, burn the city of Troyes, and ravage everything as far as the cities of Verdun and Toul. Guy drives Berengar, twice defeated in battle, into flight. Odo, king of the Franks, defeats the Danes in battle on the river Aisne.

893.

King Arnulf, adding the duchy of the Moravians to Duke Svatopluk’s duchy of the Bohemians, thereby made the Bohemians hostile to himself and gave Svatopluk, by increasing his power, an occasion to rebel against him. Since he was unable to subdue him, he admitted into the realm the Hungarian people, enemies of God; with their aid he defeated Svatopluk and made him tributary.

894.

[Col. 0879D]

Saint Waldrich, or Ulrich, is born in Bavaria. The Northmen, again driven back from Paris, attack the territory of the Bretons and are at first victorious, but afterward are defeated by the Bretons, twelve thousand of their men being killed in two battles. While King Odo, by the counsel of the Franks, remained in Aquitaine, the Franks themselves recalled the boy Charles, son of Louis the Stammerer, to his paternal kingdom and had him anointed king at Reims by Archbishop Fulk; and a long conflict arose between him and Odo. Sunderold, archbishop of Mainz, was martyred by the Northmen at Worms. Stephen became the one hundred and twelfth pope.

895.

If this Stephen, the fourth of that name, first sat in this year, then either Basil sat four [Col. 0880A] years; or, if no one sat between Adrian and Stephen, as certain books say, then the bishopric was vacant for so many years; or this Stephen sat earlier than is written here, and sat for several years, according to Hugh the Great, immediately after Adrian in the year of the Lord 886. He sat six years and thirteen days.

The Northmen, returning to Lotharingia, fight the Christians near Liège and are victorious. Emperor Arnulf, on hearing of the slaughter of his men, hastens with a strong army from Bavaria against the Northmen. Attacking them in an infantry battle on the river called the Dyle, he inflicted such slaughter that scarcely anyone survived from their countless multitude to carry news of the disaster back to the fleet. The remaining Northmen crossed the Meuse, roamed through Ripuaria and the Ardennes laying waste, [Col. 0880B] and withdrew across the sea.

At this time Remigius of Auxerre flourished, devoted to expounding divine and human writings. At this same time Berno flourished in Burgundy: from a count, he became abbot of the monastery of Gigny, which he had founded; and, from a gift of Countess Aura, he also built the monastery of Cluny as a cell of Gigny.

896.

The emperor made his son Svatopluk, born of a concubine, king of the Lotharingians. King Charles begged Emperor Arnulf for help against Odo. Arnulf sent an army to aid him, but it accomplished little. King Charles received Hundeus, king of the Northmen, from the sacred font.

GUILLELMUS. Charles, son-in-law of Edward king of England, summoned Rollo, made him a Christian, [Col. 0880C] and gave him Normandy together with his daughter Gisela, who was to be a vessel of peace, on the condition that Rollo should hold Normandy as a gift from the Franks, as from his lord. When those present urged him to kiss the giver’s foot, he disdained to cast himself at the king’s knees; instead, standing, he seized the king’s foot and drew it to his mouth. The king was thrown backward, and laughter followed among the Northmen. When the Franks reproached him, Rollo excused the action by alleging that such was the custom of his country. The same Charles also gave Rollo the county of Maine and Brittany, which are dependencies of Normandy.

ODO, abbot of Cluny. After Rollo’s conversion to the faith, the body of Saint Martin was brought back from Auxerre [Col. 0880D] to Tours. On its return, whoever were detained by any kind of infirmity—even if they were not brought there, did not ask for it, or did not wish it—were healed. For two paralytics, making their living from their illness, heard what was happening; after taking counsel together and fitting staffs under their armpits, they tried rather to crawl than to flee, but as they went on their way were healed. They themselves afterward confessed this, not daring to conceal it.

When Martin entered the bounds of his own diocese in wintertime, every shrub was clothed with leaves and flowers. Both candles and lamps were lit by fire sent from God, especially in the two basilicas consecrated in his name, at Marmoutier and in the church of Castrum Novum, where this is preserved even now. On right and left, in all [Col. 0881A] the churches, the bells were rung by divine power, though no one touched them. This happened in the year after his translation, on 19 December; and by synodal authority it was decreed that this feast should be celebrated by Adelard, archbishop of Tours, and his provincials: Ranno of Orléans, Adelard’s brother; Mainard of Le Mans; Lupus of Angers; and the suffragan bishops of the whole province.

According to Sigebert, it appears that this Charles caused two leaders of the Northmen to be baptized: Hundeus, king of the Northmen, whom he names, and this Rollo, whom he names nowhere and who was never called king.

897.

Emperor Arnulf, appealed to by Berengar for assistance against Guy, sent his son Svatopluk [Col. 0881B] with an army into Italy. But Guy, relying on his strength and corrupting the leading men of the army with gifts, caused them to return without effect.

898.

Emperor Arnulf entered Lombardy in force and captured the city of Bergamo by arms. He hanged its count, Ambrose, before the city gate with a noose; striking terror into the other cities, he brought them all into obedience to himself. Odo the musician, formerly a cleric of Tours, professed himself a monk under Abbot Berno.

(899.) Odo, king of the Franks, died, urging the leading men to receive Charles as king. Charles, having recovered the whole kingdom of the Franks, reigned twenty-seven years. A synod was held at Tribur against laymen who attempted to diminish episcopal authority; many decrees concerning the condition of the holy Church [Col. 0881C] were issued.

900.

Formosus, bishop of Porto, became the one hundred and fourteenth Roman pope, against the wishes of certain Romans who had wanted to make Sergius, deacon of the Roman Church, pope, but had not prevailed. When Formosus had at one time come under the hostile suspicion of Pope John, he fled in fear of him, abandoning the bishopric of Porto. Because, when recalled by the pope, he refused to return, he was anathematized. At last, coming into Gaul to make satisfaction to the pope, he was reduced even to lay dress, swearing that he would never again enter Rome or seek the bishopric of his city, and affirming in a document written in his own hand that he would remain in lay communion.

[Col. 0881D] Later, restored to his bishopric by Martin, John’s successor, contrary to the oath he had given, he not only entered Rome but also assumed the papacy of the Roman Church. Because of this, a question and controversy was debated in the Church for many years with great scandal. Some prejudged that his ordination and those of persons ordained by him ought to be invalid; others, on the contrary, judged more soundly that, whatever Formosus had been, all his consecrations ought to be valid on account of the dignity of the priestly office and the faith of those who had been ordained by him—especially because Formosus himself had been released by Pope Martin from his oath and perjury.

Arnulf the emperor came to Rome under this Formosus; but, not admitted, he besieged the Leonine City. When a hare happened to flee toward Rome and the army followed with a great shout, the Romans, in fear, threw themselves from the wall and by the heaps thus formed gave the enemy a place to climb the wall. [Col. 0882A] Rome having thus been taken, Arnulf had those who had wronged the pope beheaded, and was duly anointed emperor of the Romans by the pope.

GUILLELMUS. In the time of Edward, king of the English, Formosus was pope at Rome. He sent letters into England excommunicating Edward and all his subjects because for seven full years the whole region of the Gewisse—that is, Wessex—had been without bishops. A council was therefore assembled; one bishop was appointed for each province, and what two bishops had formerly held was divided among five.

[Col. 0882B] SIGEBERTUS. Fulk, archbishop of Reims, was killed by Winemar, retainer of Baldwin, count of Flanders, because he had received from Charles, as a benefice, the abbey of Saint-Vaast at Arras, which Baldwin had already seized for several years without anyone granting it to him.

901.

King Guy, unable to endure Emperor Arnulf pursuing him everywhere—for neither naturally fortified cities nor castles could resist him—while trying to save himself by flight, besieged the emperor’s wife. She, now despairing of her position, bribed one of the emperor’s attendants with much money and gave Arnulf a deadly drink. Having swallowed it, for three days he could not be roused; with his eyes open, he could neither speak nor perceive anything. This compelled him to withdraw. [Col. 0882C] Guy pursued him as he withdrew, but, struck by God, died.

(902.)

GUILLELMUS. In this year Edward, son of Alfred’s daughter, mentioned above, began to reign. Boniface became the one hundred and fifteenth pope. Emperor Arnulf, worn out by a long illness—or, as some relate, afflicted by tiny worms called “pedunculi,” which swarmed so abundantly in his body that no physician could diminish them—died. After him his son Louis reigned ten years.

GUILLELMUS. This is that boy Louis of whom Charles’s preceding vision tells. According to Guillelmus, this Louis was the son of that Charles who gave Normandy and his daughter Gilla to Rollo; according to Sigebert, he was Arnulf’s son. Perhaps he speaks not of a natural son [Col. 0882D] but of an adopted one.

Stephen became the one hundred and sixteenth pope, for four months. First ordained bishop of Anagni by Pope Formosus, he persecuted Formosus himself, decreed that all his ordinations ought to be invalid, and committed against him other deeds horrible to recount. For it is read that he—not Sergius—had Formosus’s body drawn from its tomb in a council, stripped of papal vesture, clothed in lay dress, deprived of two fingers of the right hand, and cast into the Tiber.

Romanus became the one hundred and seventeenth pope. In Italy, Guy’s son Lambert reigned against Berengar for a very short time; after Lambert’s death Berengar obtained the kingdom of Italy. Theodore became [Col. 0883A] the one hundred and eighteenth pope. Disagreeing with Pope Stephen, he reconciled those ordained by Formosus, whom Stephen had forcibly unordained within Rome, though not outside it; Stephen had nevertheless not presumed to consecrate them anew. After reconciling them, Pope Theodore restored the written renunciations and ordered them to be burned.

John became the one hundred and nineteenth pope. To confirm Formosus’s ordination, which Stephen had deposed, he convened a synod at Ravenna of seventy-four bishops, in the presence of the Frankish archbishops and king; before them the synod which Stephen had held for Formosus’s condemnation was burned.

The barbarian Hungarian people, which had remained shut in by certain barriers and had previously had no opportunity to emerge either southward or westward, was released when Arnulf broke down the barriers. While Arnulf lived, it had somewhat restrained its fury; now that he was dead, it spread like a storm through all Gaul, Germany, and Italy. [Col. 0883B] King Svatopluk was killed by the Lotharingians in battle. In that conspiracy and battle, whoever was wounded either did not escape death or could never afterward be healed.

After Francon, bishop of Liège, died, Stephen was substituted as bishop, a man distinguished for holiness and learning. He produced in a more polished style the life and passion of Saint Lambert the martyr for Bishop Herimund; he also composed, in sweet and regular melody, a nocturnal chant concerning the same martyr, the Holy Trinity, and the Finding of Stephen the Protomartyr.

Conrad, father of that Conrad who reigned after Louis, was killed in battle by Count Albert. (905.) King Louis, having engaged the Hungarians in battle, was miserably defeated. Benedict became the one hundred and twentieth pope. At Constantinople, when Emperor Leo died, his son Constantine and Alexander, brother of “Vincfko” [reading uncertain], reigned one year.

906.

Leo became the one hundred and twenty-first pope. Thirty days after his ordination, his priest Christopher seized him and thrust him into prison, becoming by usurpation the one hundred and twenty-second pope. The Hungarians, elated by the previous year’s victory, reduced Louis’s kingdom to tribute.

Among the Greeks, Romanus, low-born but considered a man of proven courage because he had killed a fierce lion, was for this reason appointed by Emperor Leo commander of the naval force. Wishing to become guardian of the emperor Constantine, who was very young, he seized outside the city Constantine’s guardian appointed by his father and all the leading men of the palace whom he had summoned to himself; he expelled them from the palace and honoured his own servants with court offices. [Col. 0883D] Phocas, however, who had led the land army against Simeon, king of the Bulgarians, terrified by this news fled from the battle and made everyone flee; thus he gave the Bulgarians spirit and strength to fight the Greeks more fiercely. Romanus captured Phocas and deprived him of his eyes.

907.

The Hungarians made the defeated Bulgarians tributary. Sergius became the one hundred and twenty-third pope. This is Sergius, rejected from the papacy because of Formosus. Formosus had made him bishop from being a deacon; he nevertheless withdrew to the Franks, and with their help captured the usurper Christopher and thrust him into prison. Entering Rome secretly, he seized the papacy and compelled the Romans by threats and terrors to hold all Formosus’s ordinations invalid. In revenge for his own rejection, in an act wicked even to tell, [Col. 0884A] he ordered Formosus, dragged from the tomb, clothed in priestly vestments upon the pontifical throne, to be beheaded; then, after three fingers of his right hand had been cut off, he had him thrown into the Tiber. He unjustly unordained all those ordained by Formosus and still more unjustly ordained them again.

Certain images of saints were publicly seen to adore and reverently salute Formosus, after fishermen had found him and carried him in a coffin to the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. [Col. 0884B]

Among the Greeks Romanus became the father-in-law of Basil, and, to act more securely, married the mother of Emperor Constantine while betrothing his own daughter to Constantine himself.

908.

Having obtained from the leading men permission also to receive imperial dress and the diadem of empire, Romanus appeared no longer to be the emperor’s guardian but emperor over the emperor. He even associated his son Christopher with the empire and gave him precedence over Emperor Constantine when they went in procession. (909.) But Christopher died not long afterward. While the Hungarians devastated Italy, King Berengar attacked them in battle and was miserably defeated. Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, made a treaty and checked the Bulgarians, who were vigorously fighting the Greeks. [Col. 0884C]

910.

Saracens sent from Africa by their king into Italy to bring Apulia and Calabria, which had rebelled against Emperor Romanus, under his dominion by warfare, defeated the Apulians and Calabrians forcefully. Turning toward Rome, they occupied Mount Garigliano, fortified themselves there, and conquered many cities of Italy.

Regino, abbot of Prüm, brought his chronicle, begun from the Nativity of the Lord, down to this year. A certain Adelbert, one of the leading Austrasians, who had rebelled against King Louis for seven years, was brought before the king through the treachery of Hatto, bishop of Mainz, and beheaded.

911.

The Hungarians ravaged Germany. Berengar met in battle Louis, son of Boso by a daughter of Emperor Louis, who had been invited from Burgundy by the Italians to become king; he compelled Louis to swear that, if permitted to return, he would never again come into Italy. [Col. 0884D]

(912.) Louis, king of Germany, died. Because of the insolence of tyrants in Italy and the great onset of evils, he did not obtain the empire and the blessing. After him reigned Conrad—son of the aforementioned Conrad who had been killed by Count Albert—for seven years; Conrad too lacked the imperial blessing.

As Abbot Berno was dying, he appointed Odo, formerly Conrad’s musician, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, on the condition that the Church of Cluny should pay the Church of Gigny an annual rent of twelve denarii.

(913.) Louis, [Col. 0885A] son of Boso, again invited by the Italians to rule, so quickly forgot his oath that he went into Italy against Berengar; having expelled him, Louis usurped the kingdom of Italy.

(914.) The more powerful princes of the realm planned rebellion against King Conrad: namely Arnulf of Bavaria, Burchard of Swabia, Eberhard of Francia, Gilbert of Lotharingia, and—more eminent than them all—Duke Henry of Saxony and Thuringia. By the king’s wisdom and strength they were restored to his favour. Arnulf alone fled with his wife and sons to the Hungarians and remained there until the king’s death.

915.

Louis, however, was retaken by Berengar, who entered the city after bribing its guards with gold, and was deprived of his eyes. The Hungarians, allied with Berengar, ravaged Alemannia and were severely slaughtered by the Bavarians and Alemanni. Charles, king of the Franks, recovered the kingdom of Lotharingia. [Col. 0885B]

916.

This is Charles, son-in-law of Edward king of England, who gave Normandy and another daughter, Gisela, to Rollo. The Saracens, coming out from Fraxinetum and Mount Garigliano, occupied Calabria, Apulia, Benevento, and likewise Roman cities to such a degree that the Romans held one half and the Saracens the other half; they oppressed Italy very severely. Anastasius, the one hundred and twenty-fourth pope, sat. After him came Lando, the one hundred and twenty-fifth.

The Hungarians, devastating all Alemannia, reached as far as Fulda.

918.

[Col. 0885C]

Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, made his sons Stephen and Constantine rule as emperors over their lord, Emperor Constantine—while Emperor Constantine earned his livelihood by the work of his hands, that is, by skilfully practising painting. King Conrad also incited Hatto, bishop of Mainz, through whose treachery Adelbert had formerly perished, against Duke Henry of the Saxons because Henry’s power made him suspect. When the bishop had already made a golden collar to be placed about the duke’s neck while he dined with him, the plot was disclosed and frustrated. After three days he died from sickness and anguish, or, as others say, from a stroke of lightning. The accomplices in the plot were likewise expelled from the country by the duke.

When the king sent an army against Henry, the Saxons raged against them with such [Col. 0885D] slaughter that minstrels declaimed: “Where is that hell which can contain so great a multitude of slain?” The Hungarians passed through Alemannia into Alsace and as far as Lotharingia.

919.

As King Conrad was dying, before the princes of the realm he designated as king Henry, son of Otto, duke of the Saxons, who reigned eighteen years. John, bishop of Ravenna, became the one hundred and twenty-sixth pope.

(920.) King Henry marched with an army into Bavaria against Arnulf, returned from the Hungarians, and by his courage and wisdom brought him into his favour, granting him the appointment of the bishops of Bavaria. He likewise brought Burchard, duke of Alemannia, intimidated by war, into submission.

Duke Robert, brother of King Odo, seeking the kingdom of the Franks against Charles, disturbed Francia; at his instigation almost all the leading men of Francia opposed Charles. [Col. 0886A]

(921.) After Stephen, bishop of Liège, died, Richer, a Catholic man, was ordained bishop at Rome by Charles through papal authority, Hilduin being rejected; Hilduin, after giving money to Duke Gilbert, was seeking the bishopric. At this time Saint Wibert was prominent among the nobles of Lotharingia. He founded the monastery of Gembloux; illustrious in wealth, nobility, and power, he laid aside the belt of worldly knighthood and became a monk.

Duke Ziptandus of Bohemia was converted to the faith of Christ and ruled Bohemia justly and devoutly. After him his son Watislaus, eminent in justice and holiness, ruled; his brother Boleslaus was fiercely hostile to him. [Col. 0886B]

(922.) While the Hungarians ravaged Francia, Alsace, Alemannia, and Saxony, King Henry met them near the city of Merseburg. Vowing to God, if he obtained victory, that he would eradicate the Simoniacal heresy from his realm, he destroyed them almost to extermination. The same King Henry, whenever he saw thieves, robbers, or assassins strong of hand and fitted for war, granted them pardon, gave them lands and weapons, formed them into a legion, and deployed them to fight the barbarians, strictly adding that they should spare citizens only.

Charles, king of the Franks, fighting with Lotharingian aid near the city of Soissons against Robert, brother of King Odo, who was seizing the kingdom of the Franks against him, killed many men and submitted himself and Francia to King Henry. As a pledge of perpetual alliance and love, he sent him the hand of the precious martyr Dionysius of Paris, enclosed in gold and gems. [Col. 0886C]

923.

Kings Henry and Charles made an alliance at Bonn. Charles restored the kingdom of Lotharingia to King Henry; bishops and counts on both sides confirmed the settlement by oath. The Africans who, from the fortification of Mount Garigliano, were ravaging all Italy, were so crushed in battle with the aid of Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, that not even one survived who was not either slain [Col. 0886D] or captured. Many testified that the apostles Peter and Paul had been seen there helping the Christians.

924.

Henry, king, makes peace with the Hungarians for nine years. Charles, king of the Franks, is captured by Count Herbert and thrust into custody at Péronne because of the killing of Duke Robert, whom he had slain. Rudolph, king of the Burgundians, invited by the Italians to rule against Berengar, joined battle with Berengar and, having defeated and expelled him, held the kingdom of Italy for three years. William: in this year, after Edward, who reigned for 23 years, his son Ethelfinnus reigned for 16 years.

[Note: Col. 0885D: Below, Ethelstimus, Etelstanus, Etheltanus.]

He is said to have been born of a concubine. [Col. 0887A] There was scarcely any ancient monastery in all England which he did not adorn with buildings, ornaments, books, or estates; he established new monasteries, as it were, deliberately, while he distinguished ancient ones by a generosity of craftsmanship as though incidentally. He gave one of his sisters in marriage to Sitrico, king of the Northumbrians; when he died after a year, he subdued that province to himself. He expelled Widnalius, king of the Welsh, and [lacuna] from their kingdoms; later, however, moved by pity, he permitted them to reign again under his authority in their former realms.

His final conflict was with Adelanus, son of Sitrico. Fearing the king, who was approaching him with an army, Adelanus pretended to be a minstrel; taking a harp in his hand, he came to King Ethelstan’s tent, singing before its doors, and was therefore readily admitted. [Col. 0887B] While singing among the psalmody, he scrutinized everything with his eyes. After the banquet he was ordered to leave and received payment for his song; scorning to carry it away, he buried it in the ground beneath himself. This was noticed by a certain man who had formerly served him and was immediately reported to Ethelstan. When the king reproached the man because he had not exposed an enemy placed before his eyes, he received this reply:

> “I once swore to Adalanus the same oath that I recently swore to you, O king. But move your tent from here until the troops left behind arrive in the morning, so that you may break by prudent delay an enemy exulting in reckless confidence.”

Adalanus therefore came by night and killed, with his entire household, a certain bishop who had arrived at the army in the evening. Proceeding further, he found the king unprepared, [Col. 0887C] for the king had thought that the enemy would dare nothing of the kind. The king, then, roused from his bedding, was exhorting his men to battle when his sword accidentally fell from its scabbard. Calling upon God and Saint Aldhelm, who was his blood-relative from an ancient lineage, he put his hand back to the scabbard and found the sword. It is preserved even today as a miracle in the royal treasury; it is sharp on one side and can never receive gold or silver. Trusting in this gift of God, he pursued Adalanus and his army tirelessly throughout the whole day until evening.

There fell there Constantine, king of the Scots, a man of treacherous boldness and vigorous old age, along with five other kings, twelve counts, and almost the whole multitude of the barbarians. The few who remained were spared in order that they might embrace the faith of Christ. [Col. 0887D] The petty kings of the Norwalenses—that is, of the northern Britons—paid him annually, under the name of tribute, twenty pounds of gold, three hundred of silver, twenty-five oxen, and as many hunting dogs and hunting birds as he wished. He took the city of Exeter from the Orthonuwalenses and fortified it with towers and a wall of squared stone. A certain Aroldus, king of the Naurici, sent him a ship with golden beaks, a purple sail, and an interior closely covered with a shell-like roofing of gilded shields.

After his father’s death, Ethelstan’s rivals wished to cut him down in the city of Winchester. Their leader was one Helfredus, who, when caught, was sent to Rome to clear himself by oath before Pope John. Having sworn before the altar of Saint Peter, he fell down and was carried by servants to the English school; he died on the third night. [Col. 0888A] Rabaudus, provost of Archbishop Samson, sent the same Ethelstan the bones of Saint Senator, Saint Paternus, and Saint Stabilio, who had been Saint Paternus’s teacher and departed to Christ with Paternus on one day and at the same hour. Those saints had then been transferred from Lesser Brittany and Normandy to safer places. Many other relics were likewise transferred at that time, while the Normans ravaged Gaul, and were readily available for sale.

This Ethelstan is said to have been born of a concubine in the following manner. In a certain village there was a shepherd’s very beautiful daughter. In a night vision she saw the moon shining from her womb and illuminating all England with its light. [Col. 0888B] When she reported this to her companions, and they in turn told it to the steward’s wife who was nursing the king’s sons, that woman took her in and treated her as a daughter. Later Edward, son of King Alfred, fell in love with her in that woman’s house, and by her begot Ethelstan. Henry, son of Conrad, king of the Germans and emperor of the Romans, sent to Ethelstan, requesting his sister for his son Otto. Louis, prince of the Aquitanians and surviving descendant of Charlemagne, had another of Ethelstan’s sisters.

(925.)

King Henry captures Brennaburg, a city of the Slavs, and imposes tribute upon the defeated Slavs. After this, reviewing the rural soldiers, he ordered that eight of them should remain in the fields and the ninth in the city, so that the eight might labour in the fields both for themselves and for the ninth, while the ninth should store [Col. 0888C] in buildings constructed by himself for that purpose a third part of all their produce, so that in time of war none of them should lack anything and the cities should be full of supplies and men. Berengar, king, is wickedly murdered by the Italians. The Hungarians, under their leader Salardus, range through Italy, besiege Pavia, and burn it.

(926.)

Charles, king of the Franks, dies in exile and captivity under Herbert, a martyr; after him Rudolph, king of the Burgundians, rules in Francia for two years. Simeon the Bulgarian, from philosopher becoming monk and from monk soldier, rules the Bulgarians and grievously crushes the Greeks; but Romanus, emperor of the Greeks, moderates his madness by making a treaty.

(927.)

[Col. 0888D]

After the death of King Charles, when the Lotharingians refused to submit to Henry, a certain Lotharingian named Christian, feigning illness, deceitfully summoned Duke Gislebert to himself, captured him, and sent him to the king, so that through him he might bring Lotharingia under his control. But the king, observing Gislebert’s skill and power, betrothed his daughter Terberga to him and again appointed him governor of Lotharingia. Louis, son of King Charles, fleeing men who were plotting against him, crossed the sea to England; for his mother had been a daughter of the king of the English. King Rudolph is rejected by the Italians, and Count Hugh of Arles is put in his place in the kingdom of Italy.

(928.)

Hugh, king of Italy, brought under his control certain Italians whom he suspected, after they had been surrounded by the counsel and valour of Count Samson. Ratherius, monk of Lobbes, [Col. 0889A] a man of excessive simplicity but renowned for his learning in the liberal arts, set out with Hilduin—who had formerly sought the bishopric of Liège—for Italy to King Hugh. Hugh made Ratherius bishop of Verona and ordained Hilduin at Milan. King Henry captures Ranna, a city of Dalmatia, and imposes tribute upon Dalmatia. Louis, returning to Francia, though with hardship, is nevertheless restored to his kingdom and reigns for 27 years.

(929.)

King Henry obtains from King Rudolph of Burgundy and Italy, through prayers, threats, and gifts—also adding part of the province of the Swabians—the lance of marvellous workmanship, sanctified by a nail of Jesus Christ and said to have belonged to Constantine the Great. Count Samson had given it to King Rudolph. Henry left it to posterity as an emblem and safeguard of the Empire.

930.

[Col. 0889B]

Pope John, captured by the soldiers of Marquis Guido and thrust into custody, was most cruelly strangled by having a pillow placed over his face. After him another John becomes the 127th pope, brother of Alberic the Roman, after Hugh the ruler had been expelled. Elsewhere Leo is read in this place. This Leo, the sixth of that name, sat as the 127th pope for seven months. Wenceslaus, prince of Bohemia, besieged by King Henry in the city of Prague, surrendered himself and the city to the king and paid the tribute fine imposed on Bohemia.

931.

King Henry makes the kings of the Normans and the Abrandari Christians. [Col. 0889C] The Redocrii, up to two hundred thousand persons conspiring against King Henry, rebel and grievously trouble his kingdom; they also incite neighbouring peoples to rebellion. But, defeated in a severe battle by the king’s commanders Bernard and Thietmar, nearly all either die or, fleeing into the neighbouring sea, drown. By this event the neighbouring peoples are deterred from rebellion.

932.

Arnold, duke of the Bavarians, coming into Italy against King Hugh, is received by the Veronese and, engaging Hugh, is defeated. Bishop Ratherius, driven from his bishopric by Hugh because he had supported the Bavarians, is exiled at Pavia, where he eloquently composed a book concerning his afflictions. He also wrote many other works useful to readers.

933.

[Col. 0889D] The Beneventans, waging war against the Greeks, emasculated as eunuchs every Greek whom they captured. Stephen VII becomes the 128th pope, for two years and one month.

934.

The Hungarians, demanding tribute from the Saxons, are either killed or captured by King Henry’s army, to extermination. The tribute demanded is distributed in churches and among the poor as an offering of thanksgiving to God. Otto, son of King Henry, marries the daughter of King Edmund of the English. This is the sister of King Ethelstan of whom William spoke above: she was not King Edmund’s daughter, but King Edward’s; but Sigebert sometimes gives other names for the kings of England than William does. John XI becomes the 129th pope, for four years and ten months; in his first year Berengar III is said to have reigned for eight years.

935.

[Col. 0890A] King Henry defeats the Danes, who made piratical incursions against the Frisians, makes them tributary, and causes their king Chuppa to be baptized. In the city of Genoa a fountain of blood flowed abundantly, perhaps portending the city’s impending destruction. That same year the Africans came there with a fleet, captured it, seized or killed all the citizens except little children and women, and stripped it even of its treasures.

936.

Rudolph, king of Burgundy, dies. Leo VII becomes the 130th pope, for three years, six months, and ten days. From this it is apparent that Sigebert did not correctly record the years of the papacies: for that John who sat immediately before this Leo sat for four years and ten months according to Master Hugh, but according to Sigebert for no more than one year. Yet Sigebert, in his chronicles, never gives their precise years; he merely says that they sat at that time, rather than for so many years or so many months. I, however, give their numbers everywhere from the chronicles of Master Hugh.

[Col. 0890B] Inger, king of the Rus’, knowing that the Greek armies had been led against the Saracens and dispersed for the protection of islands, came with a thousand ships and more to storm Constantinople. He was so certain already of victory that he ordered Greeks to be killed, not taken prisoner. But the Roman emperor met him bravely with a small force, cast Greek fire all around, and burned nearly all of them together with their ships. Of the few who escaped, he ordered all captives to be beheaded.

937.

The sun was darkened under a clear sky, while through the windows of houses it sent forth bloody rays. [Col. 0890C] A certain man’s left hand, cut off with iron, was restored to him while sleeping, after nearly a full year; as a token of the miracle, a line like blood remained at the point of joining. King Henry dies. Although he had been glorious in defeating enemies, since he was peaceable he made no effort to receive the imperial blessing after driving from Italy the tyrants who, like hired mercenaries succeeding one another, were tearing the Empire apart. William, however, as stated above, says that he was emperor of the Romans, but is mistaken. After him his son Otto, by Matilda, daughter of Theodoric, duke of the Saxons, ruled for 36 years. The hill where King Henry was buried later emitted flames in many places. [Col. 0890D] Odo, first abbot of Cluny, died; Adhemar succeeded him.

938.

[Col. 0891A] The first to rebel against Otto was Everard, count palatine, and with him Gislebert, duke of Lotharingia, who had as wife Gerberga, the emperor’s own sister. The Hungarians ravage Gaul as far as the Ocean, after passing the Rhine at Worms and devastating Austrasia and Alemannia, with many cities consumed by fire and sword; they return through Italy. Wenceslaus, holy prince of Bohemia, is killed by his brother Boleslaus, who had been seduced by ambition to obtain the principality. In vengeance for this, King Otto both declared war, and a long struggle between them was drawn out for fourteen years.

939.

Everard and Gislebert capture Henry, Otto’s brother, while he is under siege; by their deception they detach him from loyalty to the emperor and join him to their faction, alleging that the kingdom belonged more properly to one born in his father’s kingdom than to Otto, who had been born before his father became king. Stephen VIII becomes the 131st pope and sits for three years, four months, and fifteen days. The Hungarians are severely slaughtered by the Saxons. Otto, returning meanwhile from the Bavarians who were resisting him, exiles Everard; attacking the Bavarians again, he subdues them all except one son of Arnold. The same Otto builds the city of Magdeburg, also called Parthenopolis, that is, “city of virgins.” The heresy of the Anthropomorphites troubles Italy; against it Ratherius, bishop of Verona, protests both in speech and writing.

940.

[Col. 0891B]

Otto comes into Lotharingia as far as Capremont. Berengar the Younger, grandson through a daughter of Berengar the Elder, fearing that King Hugh would persecute him because he aspired to the kingdom of Italy against him, flees to Hermann, duke of the Swabians, and through him to King Otto. King Otto overcomes Boleslaus in war; but Boleslaus, catching off guard those made confident by victory, massacres the commander of the king’s army with many others, while the king devastates Bohemia.

William: this year Edmund, Ethelstan’s brother, began to reign at the age of eighteen; he reigned six and a half years. He enriched Glastonbury Church with great estates and honours, and confirmed his donation by a privilege written in golden letters in an elegantly prepared book of the Gospels, which he gave to that church. [Col. 0891C] This Edmund had banished a robber named Leo. After six years he returned and, on the feast-day of Saint Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, unexpectedly sat among the king’s guests at Pucklechurch; for the English then customarily held festive banquets in memory of Saint Augustine’s preaching. That robber happened to be reclining beside the duke. The king had scorned to give him portions from the meal. When he alone recognized him, while the others were foaming with wine, the king, inflamed by anger, seized the robber by the hair and dashed him to the ground. The robber secretly drew a dagger from its sheath, plunged it into the king’s breast, and the king immediately died. As the king’s retainers rushed in, the robber was torn limb from limb, after first wounding several men.

[Col. 0891D] Blessed Dunstan, then abbot of Glastonbury, had foreseen this end of the king, being instructed by the gestures and buffoonish clapping of a demon dancing before him. Immediately mounting his horse and hurrying to court, he received news of the event midway on the journey. Edmund was buried in Glastonbury Church; the estate in which he died was granted as a funeral offering.

941.

Louis, king of the Franks, invading Lotharingia, came as far as Alsace under the leadership of Everard and Gislebert. King Hugh, having been sent Greek fire by the Greek emperor, attacks Fraxinetum; after burning the ships of the Saracens, he captures it and drives them from it. Tagmarus, brother of King Otto, goes over from him to his enemies and, among other evils, takes the fortress of Herhesburg. There, shut in by the king, he confessed his guilt within a church and died.

[Col. 0892A] Marinus becomes the 132nd pope and sits for three years, six months, and fourteen days; Master Hugh, however, places him in the following year, not this one. When Saint Waldericus came to Rome, he learned from Marinus that he would become bishop of Augsburg; this occurred fifteen years later. From this it is inferred that Pope Marinus possessed the spirit of prophecy.

Sigebert: Gislebert and Everard, together with Henry, brother of the emperor, prepare for war against Otto near the Rhine, but encounter Otto’s soldiers. After many engaged with few, while Otto lay prostrate in prayer on the other bank of the Rhine before the nails fixed into the Lord’s lance, the defeated men turned their backs; Henry was incurably wounded in the arm.

[Col. 0892B] When a dispute arose among the princes concerning a difference of law—whether, while grandfathers survived, grandsons should inherit after their deceased fathers, or whether, with cousins disinherited, the inheritance should return to the paternal uncles—the investigation of truth, by the decision of King Otto and all the princes, was entrusted to judicial combat. Victory went to those who judged that brothers’ sons ought to inherit together with their fathers.

King Otto besieges the Alsatian town of Brisach, which King Louis held through the soldiers of Gislebert and Everard. During this siege, at the urging of Frederick, bishop of Mainz, who had already defected from Otto in his heart, many defect from Otto; and by this event, while others were terrified, the king alone remained undaunted. Meanwhile the king’s faithful men—namely Udo and Conrad, brother of Hermann, duke of the Swabians—unexpectedly attack Everard and Gislebert, who were confidently occupied in plundering the kingdom near the Rhine, and defeat them fiercely. Everard is killed by the sword and Gislebert drowned in the waters of the Rhine. Scarcely any of the rest was not either slain or captured. At this report the king’s faithless followers are broken in spirit; Louis departs from Alsace; and the king and his faithful men rejoice with him.

[Col. 0892C] King Louis marries Gerberga, formerly wife of Gislebert and sister of King Otto. Otto gives Gislebert’s daughter, his niece, to Bertold, duke of Bavaria, and Bavaria’s duchy is given to Otto. Adhemar, abbot of Cluny, appoints Abbot Majolus as his successor.

[Col. 0892D] William: this year William, son of Rollo and duke of Normandy, is treacherously killed in Francia by Alson, surnamed Curto. At his belt was found the key to a familiar chest, in which were found monastic garments. He had always intended to wear these in the conflicts at Jumièges, a place abandoned since the time of Hasting, which he himself had cleared of thorny brushwood and raised to the condition it has now. His son was Richard.

944.

Sigebert: Otto, duke of the Lotharingians, dies; Conrad, son-in-law of King Otto, succeeds him. [Col. 0893A] The emperors Stephen and Constantine, sons of the emperor Romanus, bitterly resent being restrained from youthful frivolity by their father’s just severity. They set an ambush in the palace and, without the knowledge of the other Constantine, son of Emperor Leo, depose their father from the palace throne. Having shaved his head, as custom requires, they send him to a neighbouring island where cenobites practised their religious warfare.

The sun suffered a terrible eclipse on Friday, at the third hour of the day. On that day in Spain Abdaram, king of the Saracens, was defeated in battle by Radamir, the most Christian king of Galicia. In Italy a comet of extraordinary size appeared, portending the famine that followed.

945.

King Otto transfers the body of the martyr Innocentius to the city of Magdeburg; he subjugates all Lotharingia to himself, with only Adalbero, bishop of Metz, resisting him. Stephen and Constantine, seeing that after their father’s overthrow Constantine, son of Emperor Leo, was preferred to them by everyone and that they themselves were now scarcely regarded as second in rank, planned to do to Constantine what they had done to their father. [Col. 0893B] Their plan was made public by the Devil, promoter of that plan. When they had sat down at a banquet by agreement and were disputing with deliberation over precedence in sitting, a signal was given by Constantine’s men; both brothers are thrown down from the throne and, their heads shaved, are themselves sent to the same monastery to which they had sent their father. Thus, the palace having been emptied of usurping emperors, Constantine himself and Romanus, his son by a daughter of Emperor Romanus, rule for nineteen years.

[Col. 0893C] King Otto subjugates Burgundy. Count Gero bravely and repeatedly defeats the barbarians, who on every side break in upon the occasion of civil war. Count Hugh of Paris is exceedingly hostile to Louis, king of the Franks; Hugh was son of Robert the tyrant, slain in the battle of Soissons by King Charles.

946.

Agapetus II becomes the 133rd pope and sits for ten years, six months, and ten days. Henry, brother of the emperor, is besieged by his brother in the city of Metelburg. Casting down his arms, he falls at his feet and begs mercy, and is confined in custody. Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, is expelled by the citizens. King Otto captures many who were plotting rebellion against him and kills many. When Duke Bertold dies, King Otto gives the duchy of Bavaria to his brother Henry and thus restrains him from rebellion.

[Col. 0893D] William: this year Edred, the third of Edward’s sons, reigned for nine and a half years. Dunstan, hearing news that he was ill, hastened thither on horseback and heard a voice sounding from above: “King Edred has now fallen asleep in the Lord.” He was buried at Winchester in the bishopric.

947.

Seeing Berengar return from Swabia into Italy and himself abandoned by the Italians, King Hugh commends his son Lothair to the loyalty of the Italians, so that at least he might reign jointly with Berengar. Hugh himself returns to Arles, whence he had come. He dies after a year; after his death Lothair, his son, reigns in Italy in name alone for two years.

948.

[Col. 0894A] Berengar, king in fact and power, acceptable to all, tyrannizes throughout Italy. Henry, duke of Bavaria, captures Aquileia in Italy, twice defeats the Rundati, crosses the Ticino, and returns with much booty. Louis, king of the Franks, is trapped by his own dukes, captured by the Normans, and, at Hugh’s counsel, sent to Laon and delivered into public custody. His elder son Carloman, carried off by the Normans, dies at Rouen.

949.

[Col. 0894B] Taxis, king of the Hungarians, comes into Italy and receives from Berengar ten bushels of coins in order to return. King Otto undertakes an expedition into Francia with thirty-two legions to free Louis. Louis is released from custody out of fear of him. King Otto captures Laon, confines Hugh within Paris, captures Rheims, expels Hugh’s nephew, who had usurped the bishopric of Rheims, and restores the lawful bishop. He advances powerfully as far as Rouen; restoring to Louis the castles and cities that he had captured, he returns to Saxony. King Otto sets out for Bohemia against Boleslaus.

950.

Boleslaus is reconciled to the king and finally submits to him faithfully; after a peace treaty had been made according to the king’s will, he gives him his hand. As King Otto prepares a second expedition into Francia, Hugh, unable to bear his power, meets him near the river Carus; after a treaty of peace had been made according to the king’s will, he gives him his hand.

951.

[Col. 0894C] Mainz is besieged by King Otto. Archbishop Frederick is captured and thrust into custody, then not long afterward released through the king’s clemency. King Otto designates by testament his son Liudolf, born of the daughter of the king of the English, to succeed him as king.

952.

Liudolf, son of King Otto, at the instigation of Duke Conrad, rebels with him against his father; he captures Regensburg and many other cities, and turns princes from his father to himself. The king besieges him while shut up within Mainz.

953.

There is a war on the Meuse between Conrad and Count Rainer of Hainaut. When Wichfrid, archbishop of Cologne, dies, Bruno, brother of King Otto, succeeds him; Roger wrote his life. Through this Bruno’s efforts the bodies of Saints Eligius, Patroclus, Privatus, and Gregory, together with Saint Peter’s staff, are transferred from Rome to Cologne.

954.

[Col. 0894D] King Otto takes a second wife, the widow of Louis, king of the Italians, and through her receives Pavia. Ratherius, twice driven from the bishopric of Verona, is ordained bishop of Liège after Fatabert, through the action of Archbishop Bruno.

955.

Liudolf having been restored to his father’s favour, Duke Conrad, deserter from God and king, goes over to the Hungarians and leads them into Lotharingia as far as the Carbonarian Forest. God’s power is displayed against them at Lobbes; forbidden to advance farther, they return empty-handed. Berengar, king of Italy, comes to King Otto in Germany and, giving himself and his son into Otto’s hands, commits himself to him. When Louis, king of the Franks, dies, his son Lothair, by Gerberga, Otto’s sister, reigns for thirty-one years.

[Col. 0895A] William: this year Edwy, son of the aforesaid King Edmund, begins to reign—a wanton and lustful young man who married his kinswoman. On the very day on which he had been consecrated king, amid a very crowded assembly of magnates conducting serious affairs, he suddenly rushed out from their midst, as if in play, into the dining hall and threw himself into the embrace of a prostitute. Dunstan violently dragged the dissolute youth from the chamber and, by compelling him to repudiate his mistress, made him his permanent enemy.

Soon, supported by most wretched retainers, Edwy subjected all the monks throughout England—first stripped of their resources and then driven into exile—to shameful sufferings. He expelled Dunstan himself into Flanders. [Col. 0895B] He turned Malmesbury monastery, inhabited by monks for more than 270 years, into a stable for clerics. Then the body of blessed Aldhelm, hidden in the ground for so many years, was lifted up by the clerics and placed in a shrine; the king gave it a very extensive estate. But toward the other monasteries he was excessively inhuman, both because of the instability of his age and because of his mistress’s counsel. He reigned four years.

Sigebert: The Bavarians fight successfully against the Slavs. John XII becomes the 134th pope and sits for seven years.

956.

In Italy a stone of marvellous size, hurled from heaven amid thunder and a turbulent storm, presented a great miracle to those who saw it. In many places churches were shaken by a violent tempest; priests of both orders died by lightning strike, and many prodigies terrible to tell were shown. [Col. 0895C] On the death of Frederick, bishop of Mainz, William, son of King Otto, succeeds him. Ratherius is expelled from the bishopric of Liège and Baldric succeeds him, through the efforts of his uncle Rainer, count of Mons. Liudolf, son of King Otto, dies in Italy.

957.

Meanwhile, while the Hungarians were ravaging Otto’s kingdom under the leadership of Duke Conrad, Otto met them in battle. Conrad fled back to Otto from the Hungarians in repentance, praying God that, as punishment for his treachery, he might be killed by the Hungarians. In that battle the Hungarians were so utterly defeated and diminished that thereafter they dared not even murmur; none, or scarcely any, escaped. Conrad nevertheless fell there in accordance with his prayer. Three petty kings of the Hungarians, captured in battle, perished by hanging. [Col. 0895D] Bruno, archbishop, having obtained the duchy of the Lotharingians after Conrad, built the monastery of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne. Henry, duke of Bavaria and brother of King Otto, dies; his son Henry succeeds him.

958.

Archbishop Bruno causes many Normans, together with their princes, to be baptized. Viemannus, fleeing from King Otto beyond the Elbe, brings Slavs into his kingdom. The king defeats them bravely, kills their petty king with many others, and has seven hundred captives beheaded.

959.

[Col. 0896A]

Saint Gerard, founder of Bronien monastery, dies. Bruno, archbishop and archduke of Lotharingia, exercising the second place in his brother’s kingdom with power and skill, summons Count Rainer of Mons, surnamed Long-neck, to Valenciennes, captures him, and condemns him to irrevocable exile. This was because he disturbed the kingdom by wars, or, as is said to be truer, because, after the death of Duke Gislebert, his kinsman, he had presumed violently to take from Gerberga, the emperor’s sister and Gislebert’s wife, those things which Gislebert had granted her as dower. Rainer’s goods being confiscated, his sons Rainer and Lambert flee to Lothair, king of the Franks.

A prodigious event terrifies many and restrains them from vices: marks of the cross appear on the clothing of very many, while the clothes of certain others are stained as though by leprosy.

William: this year Edgar, son of Edmund and brother of Edwy, begins to reign, a youth of sixteen. [Col. 0896B] At his birth Dunstan is said to have heard an English voice saying: “Peace of England, so long as that boy shall reign and our Dunstan shall live.” He reigned sixteen years. There was scarcely a year of his reign in which he did not found a new monastery. He bound by a perpetual oath of loyalty King Kynadius of the Scots, Malcolm king of the Cumbrians, Maccus the arch-pirate, and all five kings of the Welsh, when they had been summoned to his court. Meeting him at the city of Chester, they were conveyed in a single boat along the river as a spectacle of triumph: he sat in its prow, while they rowed.

Stirred by his fame, Saxons, Flemings, and Danes came to see him. From them the English then learned unpolished fierceness of spirit from the Saxons, enervating softness of body from the Flemings, and drinking from the Danes. [Col. 0896C] Dunstan flourished at that time in England: first abbot of Glastonbury, then bishop of Winchester, soon archbishop of Canterbury; a man of great power in the world and great favour with God; after King Alfred a wonderful reviver of the liberal arts and a magnificent restorer of royal foundations. To curb his countrymen’s drinking, he ordered golden or silver nails to be fixed to drinking vessels, so that, as each man knew his limit, modesty would prevent him either from seeking more himself or compelling another to seek it.

His pupil was Athelwold: first monk of Glastonbury, then abbot of Abingdon, and afterward bishop of Winchester. In the chief city of a single see, he did works so many and so great as the king of all England himself would scarcely have seemed able to perform. He expelled the clerics from Winchester and introduced monks in their place. [Col. 0896D] Oswald also flourished then, nephew of Archbishop Odo; before Dunstan he had been a monk of Fleury and bishop of Worcester, and afterward archbishop of York. He built Ramsey monastery in a marshy place, expelled clerics from Worcester, and put regular monks in their place.

960.

Sigebert: At this time, through the efforts of King Otto, the condition of the Empire and Church having been improved, many monasteries and religious houses are restored, enlarged, or built to the praise of God.

961.

[Col. 0897A] Gaul and Germany now being well pacified, King Otto turns his attention also to pacifying Italy, especially since Pope John and the other bishops anxiously summoned him to free them from the hands of the tyrants Berengar and his son Adalbert. On the holy day of Pentecost at Aachen, he has his son Otto, a boy of seven, anointed king. Having entrusted him to the archbishops—his brother Bruno and his son William—he sets out for Italy. At Constantinople, after the death of Emperor Romanus, Nicephorus rules for ten years.

962.

Saint Wibert, founder of the monastery of Gembloux, dies in Christ at Gorze, where he served God because of his love for the fervent religious observance there. His body is brought back to the monastery of Gembloux.

963.

Otto, having traversed Italy and terrified the tyrants by fear of himself, so that they hid in places fortified by nature or sought the aid of the Saracens, is blessed as emperor at Rome by Pope John; the tyrants are renounced both by Pope John and by the Romans. When he was returning home, Adelbert was recalled to Rome from Fraxinetum by Pope John; but when the emperor returned, they fled. A council of bishops from all Italy having been assembled, Pope John was charged with infamous crimes. Summoned three times, he delayed to come and defend himself; at length, after he had been condemned beforehand by all, Leo—still a layman—was installed as pope by the election of all and with the emperor’s consent. Thus Leo, presiding over the Apostolic See, performed ordinations and the acts proper to the Apostolic office. But before long the Romans, having broken faith with the emperor, received Pope John back. He, having assembled a synod, deposed Leo and annulled his acts. It was decreed by the public judgment of all that the synod held by Leo was not even to be called a synod, but a brothel favouring adulterers. Therefore all whom he had ordained, having been condemned, were ordered to present their own condemnation in a document containing these words: “My father gave me nothing.” Thus they remained deposed to the ranks which they had previously held. But if any were judged worthy, they were ordained again, without recognition of their former consecration; the same decree being imposed on them as on those condemned by Constantine the Neophyte.

The Romans, therefore, bribed by Pope John, suddenly attacked the emperor while he was staying at Rome with few men. They were so crushed by the emperor’s army that, unless the emperor’s soldiers had been recalled from slaughter by the emperor and Pope Leo, the Romans would have been exterminated to the last man. Having been reconciled to the emperor through Leo, they later, after the emperor’s departure, prepared plots against Pope Leo; perceiving this, he fled to the emperor. John, meanwhile, having ceased to be pope and indulging himself with a certain man’s wife, was struck by the devil in the act and died without the viaticum.

The Romans, contrary to the oath they had made to the emperor—that they would never elect a pope without the consent of him and of his son Otto—appointed Benedict as their pope.
