But the emperor, having besieged Rome, afflicted the Romans so severely by slaughter and famine that they promised to receive Pope Leo. Thus Benedict was rejected from the papacy and priesthood, and William was deprived of orders by Leo. In this year of the Lord 963, Benedict V, the one hundred and thirty-fifth pope, sat for two months; after him Leo VIII, the one hundred and thirty-sixth pope, for one year and four months.

### 964

On the death of Adalbero, bishop of Metz, who had been brother of Duke Frederick, he was succeeded by Theodoric, the emperor’s cousin. It is said that, when Theodoric examined letters bearing the names of all the bishops of Metz—letters which an angel of the Lord is said to have given to Saint Clement, the first bishop of Metz, marked in gold, silver, or baser metal according to the quality of their merits—and saw that the first letter of his own name was marked in silver, he declared that he would accomplish such great good in the episcopate that the very letter of his name ought to be marked in gold.

The beginning of this good intention was shown in the monastery of Saint Vincent, martyr and deacon, founded on an island of that city. Arnulf the Elder, count of Flanders, died. Lothair, king of the Franks, grievously harassed and devastated [the land].

### 965

John XIII became the one hundred and thirty-seventh pope—or the one hundred and thirty-sixth, if the preceding Benedict is not counted—and sat for seven years and eleven months. Emperor Otto celebrated Pentecost at Aachen. There gathered there from Francia his sisters: Gerberga, queen of the Franks, mother of King Lothair and Duke Charles; and Hawide, wife of Hugh, count of Paris, whose son was Hugh, who later reigned in Francia. There all that royal line was filled with great joy of mutual rejoicing.

Archbishop and Duke Bruno, setting out for Francia to reconcile his nephews, King Lothair and the sons of Hugh, was seized by fever near Compiègne and returned to Reims. There, having assigned by testament to churches of saints whatever movable property he possessed, he died. His body was conveyed to Cologne by Theodoric, bishop of Metz. Otto returned to Italy. William says that Pope John assembled a general synod this year.

### 966

William, archbishop of Mainz and son of the emperor, died. At this time the Danes, who worshipped Christ and idols together, disputed at a feast with the cleric Poppo concerning the worship of God and gods. The Danes maintained that Jesus Christ was indeed God, but that the gods were greater and more ancient than he. Poppo, on the contrary, affirmed that Jesus Christ alone was the true God, one God in substance and three in persons. King Alradus of the Danes required the cleric to prove the faith he had set forth by a testimony of truth. Poppo assented, and a mass of iron of immense weight, heated intensely, was laid upon his hands to carry. When the cleric had carried it for as long as all pleased, without any injury, the king wholly rejected idolatry and converted himself and his people to worship the one true God; the cleric was made bishop.

Wichmann, long a rebel against the emperor, was killed by Misaca, a Slavic petty king, friend and soldier of the emperor.

**WILLIAM.** Edgar, king of England, while hunting one day, lay wearied and overcome by sleep beneath a wild apple tree. Behold, a pregnant hunting-bitch lay down beside his feet and startled him as he slept. For although she herself was silent, the puppies enclosed in her womb uttered varied and resonant barks. Astonished, the king raised his eyes to the top of the tree and saw one apple and then another fall into the river. As they struck one another, with equal bubbles rippling together, an articulated voice sounded thus: “Vel his te,” that is, “It goes well with you.”

Not long after, as the masses of water rolled on, a little pitcher appeared upon the water, and behind the little pitcher a large water-filled jar. The former was empty; and although the larger, by frequent thrusts of the current, pressed the smaller, as though to pour its waters into it, it could never accomplish this, because the empty little pitcher withdrew and again, as though in proud triumph, assailed the larger jar.

[Col. 0899B] The king returned home anxious after this vision and disclosed everything to his mother, to whom, as to a holy woman, God was accustomed to reveal many things. She was called Elfiga. She was so devout and gentle that she secretly ransomed even criminals whom public judgment had condemned; whenever she saw a poor person, she at once gave away whatever precious garment she wore. She was most beautiful in body, most skilful in handiwork, and devoted to every good work.

The next morning she said to her son: “The barking of the puppies, which they uttered while their mother rested, signifies that, after your death, when those who are now strong and alive are at rest, villains not yet born will bark against God’s Church. The fact that one apple followed another, so that from the collision of the second with the first there seemed to sound the voice, ‘Vel his te’—that is, ‘It goes well with you’—indicates this: from you, who like a great tree overshadow all England, two sons will proceed. The supporters of the second will destroy the first. Then the instigators of the opposing party will say to both boys, ‘Woe to you’; because the dead one will reign in heaven, the living one in the world.

“The fact that the greater jar could not fill the smaller signifies that northern peoples, more numerous than the English, will attack England after your death. Although by the frequent arrival of their countrymen they fill their bellies, they will nevertheless never be able to fill this corner of the world; rather, our English, when they appear most thoroughly defeated, will drive them out.”

King Edgar was so severe in his holiness that in his time there was no private robber and no common plunderer, unless one preferred, at the cost of his own life, to prey upon another’s property. Indeed, he planned to exterminate from the kingdom every kind of beast hungry for blood. He commanded Widialo, king of the Welsh, to pay him annually a tribute of three hundred wolves. When Widialo had done so for three years, in the fourth he stopped, declaring that he could find no more.

Edgar was very slight of body and of immense strength, so that he voluntarily challenged to combat any bold man, fearing above all that he might be feared in such a contest. Every summer after Easter he ordered ships to assemble from all coasts at the western part of the island with the eastern fleet; then with the western fleet he would sail again to the north, and thence, accustomed to row with the northern fleet to the east, in order to investigate whether pirates were causing disturbances. In winter and spring he rode through all the provinces, inquiring into the judgments of the more powerful, lest they violate justice.

Once, when he was a young man, he came to the monastery situated at Wilton. There a certain girl of noble English birth was being reared among nuns in the common habit. Seeing her and desiring her, he sent for her. Fearing for her chastity, she snatched a veil from a nun and put it upon her head, and so went to the king. Seeing her, he said, “How suddenly you have become a nun!” He removed the veil and forced himself upon her despite her resistance.

When Dunstan learned this, he came to the king greatly distressed. As the king came to meet him and wished, as usual, to lead him by the hand, Dunstan angrily drew back his hand and would not allow the king to touch it. Rebuking him for adultery, he said: “First wash your hands by repentance, so that you may hold the hand of a bishop.” Terrified by this, the king fell at Dunstan’s feet and begged forgiveness. Dunstan imposed upon him a penance of seven years, which he devoutly completed. From that virgin, called Wulfrith, King Edgar begot Saint Edith.

He loved another, the very beautiful daughter of a certain duke, and ordered her brought to him by night. But her mother, indignant at even the king’s concubinage with her daughter, substituted her maidservant for her daughter; she too was beautiful.

At one time the king had gone hunting and asked Dunstan, who happened then to be with him, to delay Mass until he returned. As the third hour approached, the man of God put on the sacred vestments and awaited the king, standing with his elbows resting upon the altar and giving himself to tears. Then, suddenly overcome by a light sleep, he was caught up into heaven. Mingled with the angels, he heard them sing to the Holy Trinity in modulated voices: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.” Retaining their chant, he returned to himself and asked whether the king had come. He was answered, “No.”

Therefore he prayed again, and again was caught up into heaven. There he heard said in a resounding voice: “Go, it is the dismissal.” When the response, “Thanks be to God,” had been made, the king’s clerics ran in, saying that the king was present. Dunstan answered that he had already heard Mass, and that he would neither hear nor celebrate another that day. Asked why, he disclosed the vision; and taking occasion from it, he forbade the king thereafter to go hunting on the Lord’s Day. He taught his clerics the *Kyrie eleison* which he had heard in heaven, and it is sung in many places in England to this day.

When Edgar was born, his father Edmund sent word to Dunstan that he wished to speak with him. As Dunstan went to him, he met the devil in the likeness of a mime, playing and leaping. Recognizing by the Spirit what it intended to signify, he ordered it to appear visibly before all as it appeared to him; and this came to pass. Asked what the demon’s joy meant, Dunstan said that the king would soon die and that the kingdom would suffer many tribulations. Accordingly, before seven days had passed, the king was murdered at a feast by a robber, as we have said above; his brother Edred succeeded him.

Edred loved Dunstan and wished to make him bishop of Winchester, since Bishop Elfege, surnamed the Bald, Dunstan’s kinsman, had already died; but Dunstan refused. The king therefore asked the queen to entreat him to accept the bishopric. He replied that he would not become bishop while the king lived. A certain Elfin was then appointed.

On the seventh day Dunstan saw in a dream that he had arrived at Rome, worshipped blessed Peter in his church and blessed Paul in his, and immediately, leaving the city, had returned to his homeland. When he reached the Mount of Joy, Peter, Paul, and Andrew appeared to him, each holding a sword inscribed in gold, and conferred these upon him as a gift of apostolic blessing. On Peter’s sword was written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). On Paul’s sword was written the name Paul; on Andrew’s, the name Andrew. Andrew, looking gently upon him, sang in a modulated voice: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11 [printed: II]). Peter then told him to stretch out his hand and struck his palm with a rod in a gentle blow, saying: “Do not henceforth cast off the Lord’s yoke.”

When he awoke, he related the vision to King Edred, who interpreted it by saying that Dunstan would become bishop of Canterbury, because there was a church there built in honour of the Son of God, who is the Word in the beginning. After this, the same king fell ill and sent for Dunstan. On his way, when he had completed half the journey, Dunstan heard a voice from heaven saying: “King Edred rests in peace.” At that voice the man of God’s horse fell to the ground without any injury and died. Dunstan came to the king and found him dead and abandoned by all, everyone having withdrawn from the dead man’s funeral; Dunstan himself buried him.

After him reigned Edwy, son of Edmund, whom Dunstan left because he saw him to be incorrigible. There was then a noble and beautiful woman who had a beautiful daughter. Both mother and daughter were the king’s shameless concubines, and each strove to become queen. Through that woman Dunstan was expelled from his monastery. Certain brothers of that same monastery, moved by envy and desiring to be rid of him, also assisted her. When the property of the Church was being plundered, a demon in the temple court let out a burst of laughter. Recognizing this, Dunstan said: “You rejoice over that which causes me grief; but know certainly that the joy which you now have at my departure is nothing compared with the grief you will have at my return.” Hearing this, the demon fled.

Dunstan then fled to Flanders. The aforesaid woman sent men after him to tear out his eyes, but they could not overtake him. He stayed at Ghent, where Saint Andrew the Apostle often visited and strengthened him. He carried one of that apostle’s teeth in a staff. For one day, when the devil attacked him in the form of a bear, Dunstan beat him with the staff he held, so that the staff itself broke into three pieces. As he struck him, he said: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee before his face” (Psalm 67 [Vulgate numbering]); and added: “If Dunstan lives, know, enemy, that he will make such a staff, which will not break from slenderness as this one has.”

He therefore made another staff, strong and thick, decorating its upper end with silver formed into a hollow sphere. In it he placed Saint Andrew the Apostle’s tooth, and he was often comforted by that apostle’s familiar conversation. One day while praying at Ghent, he fell asleep and saw himself at Glastonbury with the brethren chanting the evening office. After the *Magnificat* the antiphon was sung: “Why have you disparaged words of truth?” When they had sung as far as the words, “Nevertheless, fulfil what you have devised” (Job 6), all suddenly fell silent. While they kept silence, Dunstan urged them by expression, voice, and gestures to sing it through; but they persisted mute and confused. Then a voice was heard from above, coming crosswise: “Never, never shall it happen that they fulfil in deed what they have devised. For they shall never tear themselves away from your authority, O Dunstan; they shall never remove you from the leadership of that monastery.”

After this Edwy was driven beyond the Thames, and his wicked harlot was killed.

Then his brother Edgar was made king from the river Humber to the river Thames, and the kingdom was divided into two. He recalled Dunstan from Flanders. Dunstan was then chosen bishop of the Wiccii. When Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated him, omitting the title of the Church of the Wiccii, he designated him for the archbishopric of Canterbury. Meanwhile King Edwy died. His soul was presented to Dunstan while he prayed, by certain exceedingly hideous men. Dunstan wept and laboured so much for him, forgetful of Edwy’s injuries, until he knew that he had been heard. Consequently, after no long interval, those Moors returned to Dunstan, empty of their prey, saying that they would take vengeance on him. Dunstan, making nothing of their threats, gave thanks to God.

After this he was made bishop of London and—though under compulsion—governed the two churches of Worcester and London simultaneously. Thus his earlier vision was fulfilled, for the church of Worcester was consecrated in the name of the Apostle Peter, and that of London in the name of Paul. Later, when Archbishop Odo died, Dunstan was transferred to the see of Canterbury.

Elfin, bishop of Winchester, had previously obtained that see from the king through the princes of the realm, whom he had won over with gifts and promises. Going to Rome for the pallium, he died in the Alps from excessive cold. After him Birtelm, bishop of Dorset, modest and humble, was appointed; but because he was not firm in correcting vices, he was ordered to return to his own church.

At that time a certain count had married his own kinswoman. Rebuked by Dunstan, he would not obey the command to leave her and was excommunicated. He went to the king, complaining against Dunstan. The king ordered the archbishop to absolve him; Dunstan refused and excommunicated him more severely. The count sent many gifts to Rome. The Apostolic Lord ordered Dunstan to absolve him. Dunstan said: “Far be it from me that, for the cause of any mortal man, I should despise the law of my God!” Seeing this, the count repented and repudiated his wife. Barefoot and clothed in woollen garments, bearing a rod in his hand, he fell at Dunstan’s feet while Dunstan was holding a general council, and then for the first time he was absolved.

Three makers of counterfeit coin were once captured and immediately condemned to suffer the punishment promulgated in England for such a crime, namely the cutting off of their hands. This did not escape Dunstan. Therefore, on the day of Pentecost, when he was about to celebrate Mass, he asked whether the law had been carried out. The answer was that, out of reverence for the feast day, the punishment had been deferred to the following day. “Never,” he said. “I shall not approach the altar today until they have endured their due punishment, for the matter concerns me”: the men were under his authority. In saying this, he wept much for those who were to lose their hands, showing with what feeling he had spoken. When they had been punished, he went up to the altar with a joyful face, saying: “Now I trust that the Almighty will receive the sacrifice from my hand.”

While at that Mass he said, “May you deign to grant peace to, guard, unite, and govern your Church”:

> [Note: Col. 0903D. In the canon of the Mass.]

a snow-white dove, seen by many, descended above him and remained silently with wings spread over his head until the sacrifice was completed. When it was completed, the dove moved above the tomb of the aforesaid Archbishop Odo, embracing it with its wings and kissing it with its beak. For this reason, whenever Dunstan later passed before Odo’s sepulchre, he always bent his knees; and thereafter he called him Odo *sododem*, that is, “Odo the good.”

As Dunstan withdrew from the altar, the ministers, dispersing in different directions because of the sign which had occurred, left no one to take up his chasuble. It hung in the air and did not touch the ground, lest it disturb the servant of God in his concentration.

He was once dedicating the church of a certain nobleman. When water failed for the service and the nobleman was troubled, the man of the Lord, after a prayer, struck the ground with his staff and a spring burst forth. He was dedicating another church and, observing that it was not oriented toward the east, pressed it slightly with his shoulder; it is said that it immediately turned toward the east.

One night, while asleep, he was caught up in a vision into the heavenly places. He seemed to see his mother joined in marriage to a most mighty king, amid the immense joy of assembled magnates. Everywhere hymns and praises resounded to the glory of that king, with diverse instruments sounding together. As he himself gazed upon these things in great delight, a young man covered in a most shining garment approached him and said: “Why, when all the others rejoice and sing, are you alone silent at your mother’s wedding?” He answered that he did not know what to sing in praise of the king. The young man said: “Do you wish to be taught what you should sing?” He answered, “I desire it.” The other said:

> “O King of the nations, ruler of all,  
> Because of the throne of your majesty, grant us forgiveness,  
> O Christ the King, of our sins, alleluia.”
>
> [Note: Col. 0904D. Antiphon.]

As he repeatedly sang and repeated it, he was delighted in a wonderful manner. On waking, he immediately ordered that antiphon to be written down.

Dunstan was born of noble English stock. His father was called Herstanus, his mother Kynederta. While pregnant with him, she went with her husband on the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary to the church of Glastonbury, carrying candles in their hands to offer. When Mass had begun, under a clear sky, all the lights suddenly went out. Then, while all were amazed, astonished, and looking at one another, fire suddenly fell from heaven and lit Kynederta’s candle. From it all the other candles borrowed their light. The child was baptized and called Dunstan, which is interpreted “mountain-stone.”

One day his parents brought him to the aforesaid church. While they were spending the night there on his behalf, a figure of angelic appearance appeared to them, took the boy by the hand, and led him to and fro through the court with measured movement, saying: “Thus shall this place be built for the way of life of those who are to be formed in God’s service, whether from childhood or through conversion from depravity of conduct into the newness of grace by this boy.”

Accordingly, he was entrusted to a teacher in that church. One day he became very ill and seemed to be breathing his last. Suddenly, at midnight, he leapt from his bed and ran to the church to give thanks for health restored to him. But the devil, envying his devotion, feigned a great pack of barking dogs. Knowing these to be demonic illusions, Dunstan signed himself, invoked Christ’s name, brandished against them a staff which he found lying on the road, and compelled them to flee.

When he reached the church, he found it shut and a ladder fastened to the wall. Climbing it and finding no entrance, he began to descend from the other side of the roof. God, pleased by his devotion and innocence, directed his steps; and suddenly he was lifted by an angel and set down before the altar, although the church was locked on every side and he did not know what was being done around him. In the morning he was found there asleep. Asked how he had come there, he simply replied that he did not know.

At that time Athelmus, archbishop of Canterbury and Dunstan’s paternal uncle, commended him to King Athelstan. Dunstan was skilled in writing, painting, carving, and working in wax, wood, bone, gold, silver, and bronze, as well as in musical instruments. Once he came to the home of a certain matron to gild a service-book for her for use in the Church. The work already in his hands, a harp which he had hung on the wall began of itself, though no one touched it, to sing in modulated tones the whole antiphon, “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.”

Courtiers envied him and accused him before the king of magic. Seeing this, he went to his kinsman Elfege, bishop of Winchester. On the way he was overtaken by envious plotters, thrown from his horse, and severely beaten. Yet, lest he be killed, by God’s grace a multitude of dogs unexpectedly rushed upon the attackers and defended him. On arriving at the bishop’s house, he was made a monk by him, although he had intended to take a wife.

Later, having become a priest, he came to Glastonbury and made for himself a cell at the place where his mother’s candle had been divinely lit. It was only four feet long and two and a half feet wide; its height accommodated a man’s stature. There was a window in the middle of the doorway. There he prayed and, wonderful to relate, worked with his hands.

One day while he was engaged in smith’s work, the devil came to him in human form, asking him to make something, I know not what, for him. As Dunstan prepared in charity to do what was requested, the devil began to change form and speech, appearing now as an old man, now as a boy, now as a wanton girl. Seeing this, Dunstan understood the deception and, concealing his knowledge, began patiently to endure the demon’s antics. Taking red-hot tongs, he seized the demon fiercely by the nose and held him tightly as he squeezed. When the demon tried to escape, Dunstan dragged him inside and, after tormenting him for a long time, finally cast him out disgracefully.

Running through the street, the demon cried out in lament: “Why did that bald devil do this? I asked him for an act of mercy, and he cruelly afflicted me and burned me with prolonged fire.” After this the enemy did not dare attack him further in that place. A certain rustic heard this while sitting by his hearth. Jealous of blessed Dunstan and pleased to hear the devil’s slander, he received the demon into his house under the pretext of pity. Shortly afterwards the demon seized his son, threw him into the fire, and departed.

This same saint was accustomed, after vigils, to visit holy places, accompanied by only one companion. While doing so, he heard in the church of Blessed Mary, near the church in which Saint Augustine rests, a loud singing of the whole antiphon, “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven.” Approaching the door and looking through the cracks, he saw the whole church filled with immense light and a company clothed in white singing that antiphon in joyful voices.

At another time he sought the aforesaid church of the Virgin for the same reason. Behold, Blessed Virgin Mary, accompanied by a numerous choir of virgins, came to meet him. Having received him with the highest honour, she began to lead him to her church, while two girls from the choir sang in front:

> Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing his honour;  
> Let the sweet love of Christ resound from the devout mouth.

The choir of virgins repeated these verses in response. Afterwards the aforesaid girls sang the following pair of verses:

> First, the proud one fell from great light into the depths.  
> Thus man too, when he grows proud, first falls into the depths.  
> (SEDULIUS.)

And so, until the man of God was brought into the oratory, the choir of virgins sang the first verses and the two virgins sang the paired verses, as they occur in the aforesaid poem of Sedulius.

At that time Dunstan obtained from Pope John that clerics unwilling to live chastely should be expelled from their churches and monks introduced in their place. Hearing this, Athewold, bishop of Winchester, often urged his clerics to leave their women. They promised to do so, but never did it. Seeing this, he prepared many monks’ cowls. On the day when, after Communion, “Serve the Lord in fear,” etc., is sung, he had the garments he had prepared carried into the choir. Throwing them into the middle, he said: “Have you noticed what you have just sung?” They replied, “We have.” “Then,” he said, “serve the Lord in fear and take hold of discipline—that is, the monastic habit—lest, as you have sung, you perish from the right way.”

They asked for a delay, but he would grant no more time. He expelled all who refused to become monks. Some of them immediately became monks, and monks from Abingdon were summoned by the same bishop to instruct them. The rest went to the king, demanding justice for themselves.

A council was convened at Winchester. Dunstan argued that things given to churches were given so that clerics living holy and upright lives, sustained by the offerings of the faithful, might be heard on behalf of the donors. The king begged him to spare the clerics on this one occasion and, if they did not reform, to expel them then. Dunstan was silent, his head bowed to the ground as he considered the business; all were silent, awaiting his answer. Then the image of the Crucified, fixed high above, said for all to hear: “It shall not be so: you would change things well done into things not well done.” All trembled. Dunstan said: “What more do you want, my brothers? The divine judgment has decided the matter.” They said: “Truly, we have heard.” Thus the monks remained at Winchester in peace as long as those clerics lived.

After those clerics had died, their sons, wishing to recover what they had lost in their fathers, hired a certain man then in Scotland, said to possess extraordinarily great eloquence, named Bernelm, to oppose Dunstan. They therefore assembled at Calne. When they had put forward their old complaint, Dunstan replied: “The calumny has already been decided by the Lord’s own mouth. I am now old and unable to bear labour; I commit the cause of his Church to the Lord God.” When he had said this, the floor collapsed with all who were present, except only that part where Dunstan and his companions sat. Thus that calumny was silenced.

Accordingly, forty-eight monasteries of monks or nuns were established in England through Dunstan, with the cooperation of Oswald, bishop of Worcester and later bishop of York, and Athewold, bishop of Winchester. After this Dunstan crowned King Edgar. Edgar had lived without royal insignia from his sixteenth year until his thirtieth; in his thirtieth year he was magnificently crowned at Bath on Pentecost, and lived only three years longer.

One day, as Dunstan departed from Canterbury accompanied by the aforesaid Athewold and the bishop of Rochester, the two bishops went their separate ways and asked him for his blessing. They moved him to tears. Asking why he wept, they heard him say: “Because you will soon die, and you will see me no more, nor I you.” And so it happened. The bishop of Rochester fell ill as soon as he entered his city and died not long afterwards. The bishop of Winchester fell ill before reaching his city and died not long afterwards. After him Elfege, abbot of Bath, was appointed bishop, the Lord commanding this to his servant Dunstan through Saint Andrew the Apostle.

### 967

At that time the sons of Symeon, Peter and Bajanus, ruled the Bulgarians. Bajanus was so powerful in magical art that whenever he wished, he appeared to become a wolf or any other beast.

### 968

Otto the Younger, summoned to Rome by his father, was blessed as emperor by Pope John. Otto the elder, by his power, brought the dukes of Benevento into submission to himself. He was also the first, by his enterprise, to open veins of gold and silver in Saxon territory.

### 969

[Col. 0907C]

A certain count, intimate with Emperor Otto, was seized by the devil at Rome before the eyes of all, so that he tore himself with his teeth. By the emperor’s command he was brought to Pope John, so that the chain of Saint Peter might be placed around his neck. Deceitful clerics first and second put another chain upon the raging man, but no remedy resulted where there was no power. At last the true chain of Saint Peter was brought and placed around the madman’s neck; the devil departed crying out and foaming greatly.

Theodoric, bishop of Metz, seized this chain and declared that he would not release it unless his hand were cut off. At length the emperor settled the dispute and obtained from Pope John that the bishop might receive a ring cut from this chain. When Emperor Otto had sent part of his army to the Greeks to obtain a wife for his son Otto, the Greeks attacked them, plundered their camp, killed many, captured many others, and sent them to Constantinople.

To avenge this disgrace, Otto sent his more eminent men into Calabria. Attacking the Greeks, they killed many, dishonoured many by cutting off their noses, and exacted tribute from the Greeks throughout Apulia and Calabria. Hearing this, the people of Constantinople rose against their emperor Nicephorus.

### 970
Deoderic, bishop of Metz, while serving for three years in the Italian expedition under Emperor Otto, collected by every means he could the bodies of saints from various places in Italy: from Marsia, Saint Elpidius the confessor [Col. 0908A], whose companion, Bishop Eutychius, the emperor himself had already carried off; from Amiternum, the martyr Eutyches, with the relics of Maro and Victorinus, his companions; from Foligno, Felician, bishop and martyr; from Perugia, Asclepiodorus the martyr; from Spoleto, Scenas the martyr together with Gregory, martyr of Spoleto; from Corduno, the relics of Vincent, levite and martyr—long before brought from Spain to Capua by two monks, and from Capua transported there; from Mevania, another Vincent, bishop and martyr; from Vinoritium, Leontius, bishop and martyr; from Florence, Minias the martyr; from the city of Todi, Fortunatus, bishop and confessor; from Corsinium, Lucy, the Syracusan virgin and martyr, formerly translated there [Col. 0908B] from Syracuse by Faroald, duke of the Spoletans; and from the Sabines, portions of the bodies of Protus and Hyacinthus.

All these things, together with a portion of the chain of Saint Peter the Apostle, with hair of the same saint, the blood of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and part of the gridiron of Saint Lawrence the martyr, given to him by Pope John, together with many other relics of saints, Bishop Deoderic brought into Gaul in this year; and he placed them in the church of Saint Vincent the martyr, which he had built on an island in the city.

971.

At Constantinople, Emperor Nicephorus, fearing that his sons would drive him from the empire because he was old, wished to make them eunuchs. Their mother, the empress, since she could in no other way free them, persuaded John to kill Nicephorus and assume the empire. John therefore secretly entered the palace with ropes [Col. 0908C], killed Nicephorus, and ruled for six years.

972.

Emperor Otto united his son Otto, also emperor, in lawful marriage with Theophania, niece of John, emperor at Constantinople, who had been crowned by Pope John. Notger became bishop of Liège. He enclosed the city with a wall, adorned it with fine buildings, rebuilt from its foundations the greater church, distinguished by the body of Saint Lambert, and founded the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist on the island.

973.

Benedict VI became the one hundred and thirty-seventh pope; he sat for one year and six months. Otto the elder, emperor, died; Widukind the monk wrote his life, and also composed a history of the Saxons down to this year. After him [Col. 0908D] his son Otto ruled as emperor for ten years. Reginar and Lambert, sons of Reginar Long-Neck, gradually recovering their strength, returned from France; and, with Garno and Rannald, who had occupied their father’s county, they fought at Parrona, killed them with many others, and, fortified in the castle of Buxidae on the river Haine, ravaged Lotharingia. Wenceslaus, prince of Bohemia, murdered by his brother Boleslaus in order to seize the principality, made the city of Prague, where he rests, illustrious by many miracles.

974.

Donus became the one hundred and thirty-eighth pope; he sat for one year and seven months. Ratherius died at Lobbes; of him there is this one-line verse:

A bishop at Verona, but Ratherius an exile three times. [Col. 0909A]

His cousin Henry, duke of Bavaria, rebelled against Otto. Emperor Otto besieged the castle of Buxidae, destroyed it after capturing it, and banished those taken there; nevertheless Reginar did not desist from rebellion.

975.

Boniface VII sat as the one hundred and thirty-ninth pope, for one year and one month. Otto subdued Duke Henry. Majolus, abbot of Cluny, was illustrious for holiness and religious devotion. There was a great frost from the Kalends of November to the vernal equinox. King Edgar died and was buried at Glastonbury. After him his son Edward reigned for eight and a half years. Then a comet was seen.

At the royal village called Calne, clerics once expelled from their churches raised fresh hostilities. One of them, Olferius, destroyed nearly all the monasteries which the most reverend Athelwold [Col. 0909B] had built. A meeting was first held at Winchester, where, as we have said above, an image of the Lord spoke openly against the clerics, yet they were not pacified. A meeting was held again at Calne, where, as said above, the floor collapsed. The king was absent because of his youth; but the councillors of all England were seated in an upper chamber when suddenly the entire floor, with its boards and beams, fell. All were dashed to the ground; Dunstan alone escaped upon a single beam which remained standing. The rest either died or suffered permanent illness. Then and thereafter all the English adopted Dunstan’s judgment, abandoning the clerics.

The same Dunstan had made Edward king against the will of the nobles [Col. 0909C] and of the stepmother, who wanted to make king a little boy not yet seven years old, so that she herself might rule in his stead. Hence, enraged at Edward when he returned from hunting, his companions scattered here and there, and when he was very thirsty, she offered him a cup; as he drank, an attendant pierced him with a dagger. Lights were shown from heaven there, and a lame man recovered his step and a mute man his speech. When Queen Elfrida came there, her horse, standing on the spot, could not be moved by any spurs. The horse was changed, and the second too could not be moved.

Then that cleric Elferius, who had destroyed the monasteries, paid royal funeral rites at Shaftesbury after the sacred body had been raised from an obscure place; but a year later he was consumed by worms which we call lice. Elfrida, however, performed harsh penance, wearing haircloth next to her flesh and sleeping on the ground without [Col. 0909D] a pillow. She was a beautiful and chaste woman, but overbearing; by her arrogance she brought long servitude upon her country through Edward. At Shaftesbury there is a monastery of women devoted to God.

976.

SIGEBERT. Emperor Otto marches against the Slavs. The sons of Reginar Long-Neck, supported by the aid of the Franks, and especially of Charles, later duke, wage war against Counts Godfrey and Arnulf, who after Warner had seized the county of Mons. They besiege the fortress of Mont-Cassel; after many on both sides had fallen in the conflict, the siege was raised, and the victory was uncertain; yet the palm was awarded to the counts. Saint Waldric, bishop of Ansburg, died; what his life had been like was soon revealed by the glory of miracles. [Col. 0910A] Benedict VII sat as the one hundred and fortieth pope, for nine years and six months.

977.

The people of the Liutici return to idolatry. Saint Vojtěch, bishop of Prague, surnamed Adalbert, is distinguished among the Wends by holiness and learning. The sons of Reginar, encouraged by Frankish counsel to act bravely for themselves—for Reginar had married Hawide, daughter of Hugh, later king, and Lambert had married Gerberga, daughter of Duke Charles—were restored to the land of their fathers. The duchy of Lotharingia is given to Charles, brother of Lothair, king of the Franks, with many benefits added, so that he too might desist from insolence and oppose the disturbances of his brother Lothair.

From this point Sigebert is silent concerning the empire at Constantinople. Master Hugh says in his Chronicles that John Simbolius, who killed Nicephorus, ruled in his place together with the boys Basil and Constantine. When John died, the aforesaid Basil and Constantine reigned.

978.

With the kingdom everywhere at peace, while Emperor Otto was staying at Aachen, Lothair, king of the Franks, suddenly hastened to invade Lotharingia. Since the emperor withdrew because he was unprepared for battle, the king returned home after much devastation. Otto pursued him with an incalculable army and, on the appointed day, namely the Kalends of October, entered France. Ranging through it until the Kalends of December, he ravaged the territories of Reims, Laon, Soissons, and Paris with varied destruction, granting complete immunity only to the churches of God. On the return journey, however [Col. 0910C], he lost part of his baggage near the river Aisne. A certain recluse foretold of these events that all the instigators of this evil would die within seven years.

979.

Fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky throughout the whole night, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. This year completes one thousand years from the Nativity of Christ according to the truth of the Gospel; according to the cycle of Dionysius, that thousand years end in the twenty-first year from now. Thus, in the calculation of the year of the Lord’s Passion, the Dionysian cycle conflicts with Gospel truth.

GUILLELMUS. This year Æthelred, son of Edgar and Elfrida, began to reign; he reigned for thirty-six years. When this little boy was baptized, with bishops standing around, he defecated in the sacred font and defiled the sacraments. [Col. 0910D] Therefore Dunstan, disturbed, said: “By God and His mother, that man will be worthless.” When he was ten years old and heard his murdered brother being mourned aloud, his weeping so moved his raging mother that, because she had no whip at hand, she seized candles and beat the innocent boy with them, not ceasing until she had nearly deprived him of life and drenched him with her own tears. For this reason he so abhorred candles throughout his life that he never allowed their light to be brought before him.

When Saint Dunstan placed the crown upon his head for his coronation, he said before all: “Because through your brother’s death you have aspired to the kingdom, therefore hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God: The sin of your shameful mother, and the sin of the men who took part in her wicked counsel [Col. 0911A], shall not be blotted out except by much blood of wretched provincials; and evils shall come upon the people of the English such as they have not suffered up to that time.”

980.

Emperor Otto goes to Italy. Otto and King Lothair meet over the river Chiers and are reconciled, having exchanged oaths; and King Lothair renounces Lotharingia. The bodies of Saints Landuald, Adrian, and Amantius are translated from Wintershoven, a village of Hesbaye, to Ghent, with great glory of miracles.

981.

Emperor Otto attempts to transfer Apulia and Calabria, provinces of Italy dependent upon the kingdom of the Greeks, to the Roman Empire, especially because of the kinship which he had with the Greek emperor through his wife Theophania.

982.

[Col. 0911B]

The Greeks, hostile because Emperor Otto was invading Greek provinces, having hired the aid of the Saracens, engage the emperor in battle in Calabria. In that battle almost all the Roman forces were destroyed to the point of annihilation. The emperor, striving to escape by swimming, was captured by sailors who did not know him. Recognized but not betrayed by one of them, a Slav merchant, he was with difficulty freed through the Slav and Bishop Deoderic, after the matter had been reported to the empress and to the bishop, who were awaiting the outcome at the city of Rossano. While the sailors greedily waited for money brought to ransom him, the emperor barely escaped by mounting a horse. But when all were dismayed in spirit by the disaster to the commonwealth, the empress alone, with feminine [Col. 0911C] and Greek frivolity, mocked them because the Romans had been defeated by an army of her own nation; and for this reason she began to be hated by the leading men.

983.

Emperor Otto, overcome by weariness and anguish of mind, dies at Rome; and the leading men disagree over appointing an emperor. Some contend that the empire is due to his son Otto; others, hating the empress, wish to transfer the empire from her son to Duke Henry, son of Henry, who had been brother of the first Otto. This Henry kept the boy Otto himself, treacherously abducted, in custody; but the princes wrested the boy from his hand and raised him to the kingdom. He reigned for nineteen years.

984.

Lothair, king of the Franks, again striving to invade [Col. 0911D] Lotharingia, captured the city of Verdun and Godfrey, count of that city. John XIV sat as the one hundred and forty-first pope for nine months. Deoderic, bishop of Metz, died; and according to the prophecy of a man of God, scarcely any of the princes who escaped the Calabrian battle survived long. Adelbero, a holy and noble man, son of Duke Frederick, assumed the bishopric of Metz.

985.

John XV sat as the one hundred and forty-second pope for ten years and seven months. King Lothair, seeing King Otto advance by the strength of his soldiers, restored Verdun and Godfrey.

986.

When Lothair, king of the Franks, died, his son Louis reigned for one year. Guillelmus counts this Louis [Col. 0912A] and Louis, Lothair’s father, almost as one person. For he says:

“The son of that Charles who gave his daughter Gisela to Rollo was Louis. Provoked by a certain Isambard, who had turned to paganism and made a mockery of the faith, he summoned his nobles to single combat for assistance. When they made no reply, a certain young warrior named Hugh, of no great renown, son of Robert, count of Montdidier, voluntarily sought the duel for his lord and killed the challenger. Louis followed with his whole army to Pontoise; having either killed or put to flight all the barbarians whom the other had brought, he obtained a splendid lance. But not long afterward, weakened by a grave illness because of the exertion of that campaign, he appointed that Hugh heir of the kingdom, either because his wife had been barren or because, owing to the shortness of his life, he was without offspring.” Thus the line of Charlemagne failed.

987.

When Louis, king of the Franks, died, and the Franks wished to transfer the kingdom to Duke Charles, brother of Lothair, while Charles referred the matter for deliberation, Hugh, son of Hugh, count of Paris, by Hawide, sister of Otto I the emperor, usurped the kingdom of the Franks.

See what great discrepancy there is. Guillelmus says that this Hugh was the son of Robert of Montdidier; but Sigebert says that he was son of Hugh of Paris. Likewise, Guillelmus says that this Hugh married the daughter of Edward, king of the English, sister of King Æthelstan, who had reigned long before this time—namely in the time of Henry, king of the Germans, father of Otto I. Otto I had married one sister of that Æthelstan; Louis, prince of the Aquitanians, another; and this Hugh married the third, who was most beautiful. He sent her father exceedingly splendid gifts for her: spices, precious gems, and especially emeralds; many chariot-horses with trappings; and a vessel of onyx, so carved that corn seemed to wave in it, vines to put forth buds, and human figures to move; and it was so bright and polished that it reflected the images of those looking into it like a mirror. He also sent the sword of Constantine the Great, upon which the name of its ancient owner was read in golden letters. On its hilt, too, a single iron nail was fixed upon thick plates of gold, one of the four nails which had been fastened to the Lord’s body [Col. 0912D]; likewise the lance of Charlemagne, which, whenever that most unconquered emperor, leading an army against the Saracens, hurled it at the enemy, he returned victorious. It was said to be the very lance which, driven by the hand of a soldier into the Lord’s side, opened paradise to mortals; likewise the banner of the most blessed martyr Maurice, commander of the Theban Legion, by which King Charles customarily broke and routed however dense the enemy’s formations in the Spanish war; likewise a diadem of much gold and precious gems, whose brilliance dazzled the eyes of beholders; likewise a fragment of the Holy Cross enclosed in crystal, so that through the crystal itself the color and size of the wood could be discerned; and likewise a small portion of the crown of thorns enclosed in the same manner.

The leader of this embassy [Col. 0913A] was Adulphus, son of Baldwin, count of Flanders, by Helvida, daughter of King Edward and sister, through their father, of Æthelstan himself. These are the words of Guillelmus, who says that this same Æthelstan, son of Edward, began to reign in the year of the Lord 924 and reigned only sixteen years. Yet this Hugh first reigned in the present year, that is, in the year of the Lord 987, almost sixty years later than that Æthelstan, for whose sister he says Hugh sent so many gifts to her father Edward; nor do I see how the times of both kings can be reconciled. This Hugh reigned for nine years. Herluin, first abbot of Gembloux, died.

988.

Duke Charles claims against Hugh, his nephew, the kingdom of the Franks, due to him through paternal and ancestral succession. Pressing him by war, he captures the city of Laon. Hugh besieges Charles at Laon; but in the second month of the siege, the besieged sally out, burn the besiegers’ camp, and the king, after very many had been killed, barely escapes by flight.

GUILLELMUS. This year Saint Dunstan died. His Life was written by Osbern, cantor of Canterbury, second to none of our age in literary style and first of all in music. Osbern writes thus concerning the death of that saint:

“The day of the Lord’s Ascension was at hand; and after the vigils had been performed, Dunstan remained alone praying in the church. And behold, he saw an innumerable multitude of white-clad beings, wearing upon their heads golden crowns glittering with inestimable brightness, rush through the church door and stand gathered before him. With one voice they greeted him thus: [Col. 0913C] ‘Hail, our Dunstan, hail! The Son of God, whom you desire so greatly, commands you that, if you are ready, you should come and celebrate with us this day, for whose joy you long.’

“Remaining undaunted, he asked who they were. ‘We are cherubim and seraphim,’ they said, ‘and tell us what you wish.’

“Then he said: ‘Today is a most solemn day, and it lies upon me to refresh the people with the bread of the word of God and show them how they may attain this joy. Many have gathered for this purpose, and I ought not deceive them; therefore I cannot come today.’

“They said: ‘Come then, be ready to come hence with us to Rome on the Sabbath, and before the supreme pontiff sing “Holy, holy, holy” for ever.’ He assented, and they departed.

[Col. 0913D]

“Therefore, when the Gospel had been read at Mass that day, he spoke to the people as he had never spoken before; then he returned to the altar and celebrated the mysteries. But when the time came for the blessing over the people, he came back from the altar to preach again, so that you would have thought not a man but an angel was speaking. Again he returned to the altar; and, after giving the blessing, he returned again to the people, while all were astonished. As soon as he opened his mouth to speak, his face shone with such brightness that no one could look at him. He foretold that his death was near, promising that he would never fail them. Then he went back to the Lord’s table.

“That same day, when he had risen from the table [Col. 0914A] after taking food, he went to the oratory and indicated the place in which he wished to be buried. Immediately illness seized him. On Friday he took to his bed, urging all who came to follow in Christ’s footsteps. On Saturday he received communion again; and while awaiting his hour, he was suddenly raised from the bed on which he lay up to the roof-beams, and, the beams blocking his way, was gently lowered to the ground. After he had been lowered, as those who had fled returned to him as though he were resting, he was again lifted with his bed up to the beams, as before, and gently lowered again. This occurred a third time.

“Then he said to those around him: ‘You see whither I am called. If you wish to come with me, go by the way by which I have gone. May God who calls me himself direct your hearts and bodies to his will in peace.’ And when all answered ‘Amen,’ he passed away.

“A certain priest, noble among his own people, had become paralysed. Brought to the saint’s body, he felt someone pass a hand over his entire body and make his limbs firm again. He was healed and accordingly held a great feast. While the guests rejoiced and praised Dunstan, he became puffed up and said: ‘Do you count me among the poor? Even if Dunstan had not existed, I would have been healed.’ Upon saying this he was immediately struck by his former illness; and, crying out piteously, he gave up his spirit.

“A certain German had been excommunicated by the holy bishop for the sins of lust and arrogance; handed over to Satan for seven years, he trembled in his whole body, having completely lost his senses. At last he was dragged to Dunstan’s tomb [Col. 0914C] on the night of the Purification of Blessed Mary. When the responsory *Behold the miracle* began, he vomited up his demon with much blood.

“A certain virgin blind from birth was beside the saint’s tomb at the vigils of the feast of Saint Andicenus, on the second day before the Kalends of September. While the responsory was sung, ‘Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning’ [Luke 12], she received sight.

“A certain boy lame from the womb was brought there by his mother. While his mother prayed, he held an apple; suddenly the apple began to roll as far as the saint’s tomb. Not wishing to lose it, he at once ran after it, healed.

“It was customary in that monastery for all boys to be beaten before the fifth day of the Nativity of the Lord, not for their faults but solely by custom. The masters were asked to remit that day; they refused, and all prepared themselves with rods. That night Dunstan appeared in a vision to one of the boys and said: ‘Why are you so frightened, boys?’ ‘Because, lord,’ he said, ‘the masters’ anger cannot be calmed.’ ‘Do not be afraid,’ he said, ‘I shall calm it. I am Dunstan, father of this monastery. This shall be your sign that I shall set you free: go and tell the guardians of the church to remove from beside me and from the church the body of the son of Alred, whom the hateful flattery of certain persons buried beside me with rash presumption, though he was a pagan. Unless they do this quickly, this whole church will suffer grave loss.’

“Dawn was already breaking—the dreadful hour for the boys—and the masters stood [Col. 0915A] armed with knotted straps, waiting for the boys to pass before them. And behold, suddenly all the masters fell asleep; and as the boys passed through their midst, there was no one to touch them. But the youth delivered the commands to the guardians, who despised them.

“Afterward Dunstan was seen by certain monks departing from the place. When they held him back and asked why he was leaving, he replied that he could not endure the stench of pagan flesh and the wickedness of certain people living there. ‘If this matter is not corrected,’ he said, ‘this entire city and church will pay the penalty.’ Not long afterward the city was burned, and the whole church with its offices, except the refectory and dormitory with the cloisters attached to them.

“A certain archdeacon of London, most learned in letters, was converted in the same monastery and began to live religiously. A year after becoming a monk, he performed the office of secretary; and, as he enjoyed greater freedom than the others, he gradually began to grow cold in religion. At length he was preparing to flee with a certain young man who knew of his plan, though his mind still wavered about what he intended to do. He resolved, however, not to leave the monastery without Saint Dunstan’s permission. He therefore came to his tomb, complained about the others, and sought his blessing to continue their journey, saying that he would be Dunstan’s wherever he went.

“Coming behind the choir, he found there a certain most reverend monk, holding a staff, standing supported by it, and looking at him with bright eyes. Seeing him [Col. 0915C], he was terrified and wished to turn aside from him. The other, holding the staff across his path, said: ‘Where are you going?’ He indicated that he ought not speak. But the other said: ‘If I speak to you, tell me where you are going.’ ‘Where it concerns me,’ he said. The saint replied: ‘That is nothing; return to the tomb where you were just now, and with your will changed pray more earnestly.’

“He returned and prayed as he had prayed before. On returning, he met in the same place the one whom he had met earlier, who asked where he was heading. He said to him: ‘What is that to you?’ ‘Very much,’ he replied, ‘for you too, unless you amend yourself, will experience this soon. Now therefore go back again, change your mind, change your prayer.’ Since he tried to pass on rather than return, the other brandished his staff against him and compelled him to go back.

“He returned in great fear and prayed a third time the same prayer; on returning, he did not find there the one whom he had found before. Thinking that he had prayed well, he hurried to the cloister gate, where he encountered the one he had encountered before, standing against him with a troubled face and asking where he was going. He answered: ‘Who are you, who restrain me with such authority?’ He said: ‘Do you ask who I am? Hear: I am Dunstan, overseer and archbishop of this place, lover and helper of those who are truly sons of this church. And how do you seek my help, when you wish to abandon me and this place? By my leave you shall never depart from here; whether willing or unwilling, you shall remain here, you shall die here. And because you have despised listening to me, behold, in your punishment you shall prove that you have not done well.’

“And raising his staff [Col. 0916A], he struck him hard three times, threw him to the ground, and disappeared. He was found lying there and carried to the infirmary. His illness increased daily, and no one could determine what kind it was; but he did not wish to reveal it. At last he was laid upon haircloth, and the litany began to be said for him. When it was said, ‘Saint Dunstan, pray for him,’ he asked to be laid upon his bed, saying that now he would not die. He summoned Prior Henry and confessed everything to him, including that he could not die until he had confessed this. Having received penance and the prior’s blessing, he gave up his spirit.

“The chasuble of Saint Dunstan, in which he customarily sang, was at London, without any gold ornament. A certain London matron, gravely ill, believed that she would never recover. To her, as she seemed about to die, Saint Dunstan appeared and asked whether she wished to recover. When she answered that she wished it very much, he said: ‘Take the gold embroidery which is in your chest and put it on the chasuble which is at Westminster; and you shall recover.’ And so it happened. What was marvelous was that the embroidery was found neither smaller nor larger than the adornment of the chasuble required.”

GUILLELMUS. Not long after the death of Blessed Dunstan, the Danes ravaged England, as he had prophesied. They burned the city of Canterbury and carried off in chains the most reverend Archbishop Ælfheah. When they forced him to strip his own peasants in order to ransom himself, and he refused, they stoned him, struck him with an axe, and made him a martyr. As his blood dripped, dry ground immediately became green. Because of so great a miracle, the Danes permitted his body to be carried to London, where it was buried. After ten years it was found incorrupt; down to the present time fresh blood remains, as does the body’s uninjured wholeness. In England there are thirty-two districts, sixteen of which the Danes then invaded.

(989) SIGEBERT. There was a frequent and long-lasting inundation of waters beyond the usual measure; afterward an exceedingly hot summer, harmful to many, and consequently the crops ripened late. Duke Charles stormed Montaigu and advanced as far as Soissons, ravaging as he went. From there he attacked Reims and returned to Laon with much plunder. There was great spring drought, so that the first sowing was hindered and a severe famine followed. Excessive snow fell, followed by continual rain [Col. 0916D], which entirely prevented the autumn sowing.

(990.) Duke Charles occupies Reims; he captures the archbishop appointed by King Hugh and certain leading men, and relegates them to Laon.

991.

Duke Charles dies, and his son Otto succeeds him. At Reims, a synod of all France having assembled, Arnulf, nephew of Duke Charles, whom Charles himself had appointed bishop at Reims, is condemned and deposed by the judgment of all. Adelgarius the priest, who betrayed the city and opened its gates to Charles, is excommunicated without possibility of release; Gerbert is substituted in his place. But when some argued that Arnulf could not have been deposed without the knowledge and authority of the Roman pope, Gerbert, deposed, went to Emperor Otto [Col. 0917A]. The emperor made him archbishop of Ravenna and afterward Roman pope. Hence arose the following one-line verse:

Gerbert passes from R[heims] to R[avenna], and becomes a pope flourishing at R[ome].

GUILLELMUS. This Gerbert, born in Gaul, grew up from childhood as a monk at Fleury. Then, as a young man, he left the cloister and went to Spain, which had formerly been held by the Romans but, in the time of Emperor Honorius, had passed under Gothic rule. The Goths had been Arians until the time of Pope Gregory; but then, through Leander, bishop of Seville, they became Catholics, and through King Reccared, brother of Hermenegild, whom his father killed on the night of Easter for his confession of the faith. Leander was succeeded by Isidore, a holy and learned man, whose body Alfonso, king of Galicia, in our own age translated to Toledo, purchased for its weight in gold.

The Saracens who had subdued the Goths were themselves defeated by Charlemagne and lost Galicia and Lusitania, the greatest provinces of Spain; but they possess the upper regions to this day. And, just as Christians have Toledo, so they have Seville, which they commonly call Sibilia, as the capital of their kingdom, devoted, according to the custom of their people, to divinations and incantations. Coming among them, Gerbert surpassed Ptolemy in the astrolabe, Alcander in the intervals of the stars, and Firmicus in fate. There he learned the songs of birds, the mystery of their flight, and how to summon slight figures from hell. He also so thoroughly absorbed the quadrivium that he recalled to Gaul those disciplines long obsolete there. He was the first to take the abacus from the Saracens, and gave rules which can scarcely be understood even by sweating abacists.

He lodged with a certain philosopher, whom he first won over by many expenses and then by many promises. This philosopher possessed a single book containing the knowledge of the whole art, which Gerbert could by no means wrest from his master. At last, assisted by the philosopher’s daughter, with whom frequent association had made him intimate, he stole it at night from beneath his pillow and fled with the theft. Awakened from sleep, the philosopher pursued the fugitive by the indications of the stars. But the fugitive, learning by the same art of the danger, hid beneath the nearest wooden bridge [Col. 0917D], suspended between bridge and water and clutching the bridge [Col. 0918A], so that he touched neither earth nor water; and in this way he eluded his pursuer.

> **[Note: [Col. 0917D]** Learned men rightly judge these matters, which the author copied from William of Malmesbury, to be fabulous; and still more so the following accounts, which we have cut out, concerning Gerbert’s dedicating himself to a demon and his dreadful murder at Rome, inflicted by a demon in the church of the Holy Cross. Sigebert, the aforesaid William of Malmesbury, and others drew these accounts from Benno the schismatic, who wrote almost one hundred years after the death of Sylvester II, or Gerbert. Yet in that uncultivated age there was some occasion for inventing this tale, because Gerbert was exceptionally learned in mathematics and especially in astrology. Certainly no one before Benno is found to have written such things concerning Sylvester; Benno also, with the same malice, accused other predecessors of Gregory VII of magic.
>
> On the contrary, those who lived in Sylvester’s time wrote honorably of him: for example, the weighty writer Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg in Saxony, Book VI; and Helgaud, monk of Fleury, in the *Life of Robert, King of the Franks*, of whom Gerbert was master. What utterly destroys the tale is the epitaph placed upon Sylvester’s tomb in Rome, in the Lateran basilica, by his successor Sergius—an epitaph worthy of any Roman pontiff of great name. A man with so disgraceful an end as Benno invents, openly destroyed by a demon, could in no way have been commended by such high praise.
>
> The story also sufficiently indicts itself when it discusses—or rather babbles about—a treasure discovered by magical art in the Campus Martius and a palace filled with immeasurable riches. Dreams of this sort belong to deranged old women rather than to a historian. See Baronius, under the year 909, and Bellarmine, Book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 12. Moreover, the author afterward disapproves magical observances in the following words:]

How laborious it is to consider such things! Certainly there is no benefit in them. For the answers of demons, in their desire to deceive human beings, are always delivered through ambiguities, for two reasons: first, because they are uncertain about all future events that depend upon free will; secondly, because, even if they were certain, they would nevertheless take greater pleasure in deceiving those who consult them by their ambiguity than in instructing them by a certainty which they do not possess. Not only is there no benefit in knowing these curiosities; there is also great danger.

Hence St Augustine, in Book X, chapter 9, of *The City of God*:

> “Miracles were wrought in the Old Testament by the simple faith and devout confidence of piety, not by incantations [Col. 0918B] and chants composed by the art of impious curiosity, which they call either magic, or, by the more detestable name, *goetia*, or, by the more honorable name, *theurgy*. They make a kind of attempt to distinguish these things, condemning as blameworthy some persons devoted to illicit arts, whom the common people also call sorcerers—for they say that these belong to *goetia*—while wishing others, to whom they assign theurgy, to appear praiseworthy; although both are bound by the deceitful rites of demons under the names of angels.
>
> “For Porphyry promises a certain supposed purification of the soul through theurgy, though with hesitant and, as it were, shamefaced argument; but he denies that this art can provide anyone’s return to God, so that you may see him wavering, amid alternating opinions, between the vice of sacrilegious curiosity and the profession of philosophy. [Col. 0918C] At one moment he warns that this art, as deceptive, dangerous in its very practice, and forbidden by law, must be avoided; at another, as though yielding to its admirers, he says that it is useful for cleansing a part of the soul—not indeed the intellectual part, by which the truth of intelligible things, which have no bodily likenesses, is perceived, but the spiritual part, by which images of bodily things are apprehended.
>
> “He says that this part is made fit and suitable, through certain theurgic consecrations, which they call *teletae*, for receiving spirits and angels and for seeing gods. Yet he admits that from these theurgic *teletae* no cleansing accrues to the intellectual soul that makes it fit to see its God and to discern [Col. 0918D] what is true. From this it can be understood what kind of [Col. 0919A] gods, or what kind of vision, he says is produced by theurgic consecrations: a vision in which the things that are true are not seen.
>
> “Finally, he says that the rational soul—or, as he prefers to call it, the intellectual soul—can escape to the things above, even if that which is spiritual in it has been cleansed by no art of theurgy. But he says that the spiritual part is cleansed by the theurgist only so far as not, by that means, to attain immortality and eternity. Although, therefore, he distinguishes angels from demons, assigning airy regions to demons and ethereal or empyrean regions to angels, and advises making use of the friendship of some demon so that, with the demon carrying him, one may be raised, even a little, from earth after death, while declaring that another way leads to the heavenly fellowship of angels: nevertheless, he testifies, in a manner of explicit [Col. 0919B] confession, that association with demons must be avoided, when he says that the soul, after death and while paying penalties, shudders at the worship of the demons by whom it was deceived.
>
> “Nor could he deny that theurgy itself, which he commends as though it reconciled angels and gods, operates among powers of such a kind—powers which either themselves begrudge the purification of the soul or serve the arts of the envious. He brings forward the complaint of some Chaldean concerning this matter: ‘A good man in Chaldaea,’ he says, ‘complains that, despite great efforts to purify his soul, his success was frustrated, because another man, powerful in the same practices and moved by envy, had bound the powers summoned by sacred prayers so that they would not grant what was requested. Therefore,’ he says, ‘the one bound, and the other did not loose.’ By this evidence he said that theurgy appeared to be a discipline for accomplishing both good [Col. 0919C] and evil among gods and human beings, and that even gods are subject to and drawn into those disturbances and passions which Apuleius commonly attributes to demons and humans.”

Thus Augustine.

993.

In Burgundy, Odilo, a native of Auvergne, having professed as a monk from being a cleric of Brioude, became abbot of the monastery of Cluny after Majolus. For fifty-six years he was conspicuous for remarkable religious fervor. Distinguished above all by piety, he was illustrious not only through examples of life but also through miracles during his lifetime. When he was reproached because he seemed more merciful than was right toward sinners, he said: “If I am to be condemned, I would rather be condemned for mercy than for hardness.” Otto is consecrated emperor.

994.

[Col. 0919D]

At this time the following flourished in literary learning: in Lotharingia, Heriger, abbot of Lobbes; Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht; in France, Fulbert, bishop of Chartres; and Abbo, abbot of Fleury, who wrote a commentary on the calculation of Victorius. When Hugh, king of France, died, his son Robert reigned for thirty-four years. (995.) This King Robert was by no means unlearned in ecclesiastical chants. Indeed, he composed the very beautiful sequence, “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with us,” and this responsory, “O Judah and Jerusalem”; he is also said to have composed this Alleluia: “Deliver me from my enemies.” When he was once at Rome on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul, he offered a certain little sheet upon the altar. Those present thought that he had offered something great, but they found [Col. 0920A] that he had placed nothing else on the altar except a little sheet upon which was written the responsory with its verse, “Cornelius the centurion,” which the king himself had composed together with its melody.

John, surnamed Belet, says that Notker, abbot of St Gall in the German lands, was the first to compose sequences, and that Pope Nicholas instituted their singing. After him Hermannus Contractus, inventor of the astrolabe, composed “Almighty King” and “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with us.” Let the reader therefore decide to whom he prefers to defer, William or John.

996.

Gregory becomes the one hundred and forty-third pope, for two years.

997.

Herbert is ordained bishop of Cologne, and was eminent in many forms of holiness. Also illustrious at this time among the Gauls was Ansfrid, who, having been count of the Brabanters, famous no less for justice than for secular power, laid aside the belt of military service and was tonsured as a cleric; he advanced so far as to become bishop of Utrecht.

998.

John XVI becomes the one hundred and forty-fourth pope, for ten months. After him, as Sigebert says, Gerbert—also called Sylvester—becomes the one hundred and forty-fifth pope, and he too was outstandingly eminent among those distinguished for literary learning. Some, however, passing over this Sylvester, place Agapetus here, because Sylvester is said not to have entered by the door; he is also accused by some of necromancy and is said to have died after being struck by the devil.

WILLIAM. The collapse of the dukes arose from the pride of King Æthelred. For, without any grounds existing, he drained the English of their wealth upon fabricated charges; and, on slight suspicions, he ordered all the Danes throughout England to be massacred in one day. He was so shameless toward his wife that he scarcely considered her worthy of his bed, while he wallowed with concubines. She too, conscious of her high birth, behaved arrogantly toward her husband. For she was the daughter of Richard, count of Normandy, son of William, who governed that duchy for fifty-two years after his father and ended his life in the eighteenth year of this King Æthelred. He lies at the monastery of Fécamp, which he enlarged with certain revenues and endowed with monastic discipline through William, abbot of Dijon: an outstanding man, who also often reproved King Æthelred for his wrongs. [Col. 0920D]

When this was heard at Rome, the Apostolic See did not permit two Christian princes to fight one another, but sent Leo, bishop of Trier, into England to arrange peace. This was done in the year of the Lord 991.

SIGEBERT. At this time a certain religious man, returning from Jerusalem to Sicily, was refreshed for some time by the kindness of a certain recluse. Among other things, he learned from him that in that region there were places vomiting forth flames, called by the inhabitants “Vulcan’s cauldrons,” in which the souls of the dead suffered different punishments according to the quality of their merits, demons being appointed there to execute them. He said that he had often heard their voices, rage, and terrors, and sometimes their howlings, as they lamented that the souls of the faithful were snatched from their hands [Col. 0921A] through the alms and prayers of the living faithful—and, at that time especially, through the prayers of the Cluniacs, who prayed tirelessly for the repose of the dead.

When Abbot Odilo learned this through that religious man, he established throughout all monasteries subject to him that, just as the solemnity of All Saints is celebrated on the first day of November, so on the following day all those resting in Christ should be commemorated. This rite passed to many churches and caused the memorial of the faithful departed to be solemnly observed. (999.) In Italy, Crescentius, having seized the patriciate of the Romans, rebels against Emperor Otto.

1000.

In the year of Jesus Christ 1000, according to the reckoning of Dionysius, many prodigies were seen, and a very great earthquake occurred. A comet appeared on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, about the ninth hour. Under a clear sky, something like a burning torch fell toward the earth with a long trail and such brightness that not only those in the fields but even those indoors were struck by the sudden light. As the cleft in the sky gradually vanished, there meanwhile appeared a figure like a serpent, whose head was growing, with blue feet.

1001.

Emperor Otto attacks the patrician Crescentius at Rome. Crescentius is defeated, seized after being dragged back from flight, placed backwards upon a vile beast of burden, and paraded around. Then, after his limbs were gradually cut off, he was finally hanged before the city.

1002.

While Emperor Otto was residing at Rome and dealing rather leniently with the Romans, considering how he might restore the rights of the kingdom and of the Church to their former state, the Romans were thereby led to despise him. They suddenly [Col. 0921C] conspired against him, killed several of his soldiers, and besieged him in the palace. By the ingenuity of Henry, duke of Bavaria, and Hugh, margrave of Italy, he was scarcely brought out under a pretended agreement and withdrew from Rome with Pope Sylvester. Because Crescentius’s wife had enticed the emperor into love for her by hope of sovereignty, she grieved at his departure and administered poison to him. Wasted by it, he died in Italy while returning.

The transalpine soldiers, bearing the emperor’s body together with the imperial insignia toward Gaul, were harassed by repeated attacks of the Italians and made a way for themselves by force of arms. But when the matter was already thought secure, Henry, duke of Bavaria, having wronged Heribert, bishop of Cologne, upon whose word all depended, violently wrested the insignia from him as though they belonged to himself by hereditary right. [Col. 0921D] For he was the son of Duke Henry, who had been begotten by Henry, brother of Emperor Otto I. Accordingly Duke Henry, having won over the minds of certain princes of the realm, was anointed king by Willigis, bishop of Mainz, and ruled for twenty-one years.

1003.

John XVII sat as the one hundred and forty-sixth pope for eleven months; after him John XVIII sat as the one hundred and forty-seventh pope for five years. Abbo, abbot of Fleury, is martyred in Gascony. King Henry swiftly overcomes the more powerful men of the realm who wished to stir up wars against him, and makes tributary to himself the kings of the pagan peoples dwelling in inner Germany, who are called the Wends.

1004.

[Col. 0922A]

Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, and Adelbold of Utrecht are held in high esteem in the Church and at court. King Henry raises the Church of Bamberg to the honor of an episcopal see; and, because it lacked books, makes it heir to all his possessions. Therefore Theoderic, bishop of Metz, grieved that the emperor was assigning the dowry and patrimony of his sister, Empress Cunigunde, to the Church of Bamberg, rebels.

1005.

A dreadful comet was seen in the south. After the death of Duke Otto, the duchy of Lotharingia is given to Count Godfrey, son of Godfrey of Ardennes. Helperic wrote *On the Method of Computation* in this year.

1006.

Famine and pestilence prevailed almost throughout the whole world, so that living people, still drawing breath, were buried with the dead because those burying them were weary. Emperor Henry besieges the castle of Valenciennes, situated on the frontier of France and Lotharingia, which Baldwin, count of Flanders, had seized; Robert, king of the Franks, and Richard, count of the Normans, coming together to assist him.

1007.

Because Emperor Henry had returned unsuccessfully from the siege of Valenciennes, he marched against Baldwin and attacked the castle of Ghent. Having devastated the land, he captured several leading men of Flanders; therefore Baldwin, terrified, made satisfaction to him. He returned Valenciennes and, after providing hostages and swearing fealty, gave him his hand. Later the emperor, compelled by a rebellion among his own men, granted Valenciennes as a benefice to Count Baldwin so that Baldwin might aid him against his subjects’ uprising; [Col. 0922C] moreover, he also added Walcheren to him.

1008.

Baldric is ordained bishop of Liège, and Burchard bishop of Worms. Burchard, a diligent student of the Scriptures, compiled that great volume of canons, with the collaboration of Abbot Ausbert, a man most learned in every respect.

1009.

An eclipse of the sun occurred at the second hour of the day. Sergius IV sat as the one hundred and forty-eighth pope for two years and nine months.
