The Normans, ravaging Frisia, burn the town of Tiel. Emperor Henry besieges the city of Metz because Theoderic, his wife’s brother, had rebelled against him and usurped that city’s bishopric. For Duke Theoderic of the Moselle country, after his brother Albero, had given the bishopric of Metz to his own son, still a boy, appointed that same Theoderic as the boy’s guardian. Theoderic expelled the boy from the city, usurped the bishopric, and even captured Duke Theoderic himself in war. Thus, after the city had been almost laid waste by siege, peace was finally agreed.

1010.

Bishop Bruno is martyred. The Normans return to Frisia; after many had been killed, the town of Utrecht was burned. The Hungarian people, hitherto devoted to idolatry, are converted to faith in Christ at this time through Gisela, the emperor’s sister. Married to the king of the Hungarians, she brought him, through her persistence, to request baptism for himself and for the entire Hungarian people. In baptism he was called Stephen; throughout Hungary his merits are commended by the glory of many miracles.

1011.

[Col. 0923A]

In Lotharingia, near Mount Castrilocum, a little spring whose water was highly health-giving to many was changed into blood. A woman proved this when she showed many people that her face, washed with water from that spring, was bloodstained. (1012.) Albert is ordained abbot of Gembloux. Benedict VIII becomes the one hundred and forty-ninth pope and sits for twelve years.

WILLIAM. This year the following occurred in a certain village of Saxony where there was a church of Magnus the martyr. On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, a priest named Robert had begun the first Mass of the night. But in the cemetery a certain Otbert, leading dances with eighteen companions—fifteen men and three women—and noisily singing secular songs, so disturbed the priest that their very words involuntarily resounded amid the sacred solemnities of the Mass. [Col. 0923B] He ordered them to be silent; when they disregarded this, he pronounced a curse, saying: “May it please God and Saint Magnus that you remain singing thus until a year has passed.”

The words took effect. John, the priest’s son, seized his sister, who was singing, by the arm; immediately it was torn from her body, yet not a drop of blood came from it. She nevertheless remained throughout the entire year with the others, leading dances and singing. Rain did not fall upon them; neither cold nor heat, hunger nor thirst, nor weariness affected them. Their clothing and footwear were not worn away, but they sang as though out of their senses. First they sank into the earth as far as the knees, then as far as the thighs. By God’s will, a roofed structure was at times raised over them to keep off rain.

When the year had elapsed, Heribert, bishop of Cologne, released them from the bond by which their hands were bound and reconciled them before the altar of Saint Magnus. [Col. 0923C] The priest’s daughter, together with two others, immediately died. The rest slept continuously for the next three days and nights; some later died and, it is said, shone with miracles because they repented deeply. The others showed their punishment by trembling of their limbs. Otbert himself, one of those people, left this account in writing; and at the end of his writing it is written: “Letters were given to us by Lord Peregrinus, successor of blessed Heribert, in the year of the Lord 1013.”

1013.

Emperor Henry, marching into Italy to assist his men, whom the Greeks were oppressing through ravaging about Benevento, [Col. 0923D] Salerno, and Capua, captures the city of Troia. When Bishop Baldric was fortifying a castle in the village called Duguardis, Count Lambert of Louvain attacked him. Lambert prevailed, and the bishop, with many of his men captured and killed, suffered a grave misfortune. A very great earthquake occurred about midday on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.

1014.

King Henry is consecrated emperor. He sent Duke Godfrey with an army into the district of Brabant to besiege the castle of Louvain, but he returned unsuccessfully. Bishop Baldric founded the monastery of Saint James the Apostle on the island at Liège. Duke Godfrey defeated in war Count Gerard, who was disturbing the kingdom in many ways. After Gerard’s son was killed there with many others, he intimidated Gerard’s accomplices. At this time Saint Guiteth, also called Adalbert, bishop of Prague, is martyred. The county of Beauvais is given to Bishop Roger.

1015.

Duke Godfrey ravages the county of Hainaut. Rainer, pursuing him with his uncle Lambert of Louvain, joined battle at Florennes, where more than five hundred men were killed and Lambert himself fell. There a remarkable thing occurred. For when Lambert already had hope of victory—for he wore hanging from his neck to his breast a reliquary filled with relics of saints, through whose protection he believed himself safe in dangers—at the approach of the end of his life, the reliquary came off his neck and leapt upon a mound in the field. [Col. 0924B] Immediately the count, previously unconquered, was killed. One of the soldiers took the reliquary and hid it in his boot; but when his thigh and leg swelled, the matter was revealed, and he gave the reliquary to his lord Ethelo, namely the duke’s brother.

1016.

Simeon, a native of Syracuse in Sicily and later a monk on Mount Sinai, flourished at this time. Coming to Jerusalem, he undertook a long pilgrimage for Christ; coming to Gaul with Poppo, archbishop of Trier, he was enclosed at Trier in a high tower. There, after many persecutions from human beings and temptations from demons, he rested in a blessed death. The frequent glory of miracles showed his merit.

1017.

A comet, more remarkable than usual, in the form of a very great beam, appeared for four months. Cobold becomes bishop of Liège after Baldric.

1018.

In Frisia, when Count Theoderic, son of Arnulf of Ghent, was fighting the Frisians in vengeance for his father, whom they had killed, Duke Godfrey was sent by the emperor to fight against him. When battle had been joined, suddenly a voice was uttered, no one knew from where: “Flee, flee!” As all fled, many were killed by a few Frisians, while the duke was captured.

1019.

After Duke Godfrey had obtained from the emperor for the Frisians impunity for all their wrongdoing, he was released from captivity and died not long afterward. His brother Gothelo succeeded him in the duchy.

1020.

King Rudolph of Burgundy, angered by the insolence of the Burgundians, considers giving the kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Henry; but a pretended act of satisfaction by the Burgundians turns him away from this intention. Pope Benedict comes into Gaul to Emperor Henry.

1021.

Emperor Henry, celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne, appeases Archbishop Heribert, whom he had formerly treated unjustly, by humble satisfaction. Reconciled to him, the archbishop foretold that he would die shortly. Not long afterward he died and began to shine through great miracles; Bishop Pilgrim succeeded him. This Pilgrim was called Peregrinus above by that Otbert who was one of those leading the dances; but it is remarkable how that same Otbert says at the end of his writing that [Col. 0925A] letters were given to him by Lord Peregrinus, successor of blessed Heribert, in the year of the Lord 1013, whereas Sigebert here says that blessed Heribert died in the year of the Lord 1021.

WILLIAM. Cologne was first called Agrippina after Agrippa, Augustus’s son-in-law; afterward it was called Cologne after Trajan, who, having been raised to the imperial office there, brought colonies of Roman citizens to that place. There was in this city a bishop, renowned for piety but ugly in body, who became bishop as follows. On Quinquagesima Sunday, the emperor went hunting and, his companions having scattered here and there, came alone to a clearing in a forest. There was there a church belonging to a rustic priest, very deformed and almost a marvel of nature. The emperor, pretending to be a soldier, humbly requested Mass. The priest immediately prepared himself.

Meanwhile the emperor was considering why God, from whom all beautiful things proceed, allowed such a deformed man to perform his sacraments. They came to the verse of the tract: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Psalm 99 [Vulgate Psalm 99; English Psalm 100]). As the priest’s boy sang discordantly at these words, the priest answered in a louder voice, as though replying to the emperor’s thought: “He made us, and not we ourselves.” [Col. 0925B] Struck by this utterance and thinking him a prophetic man, the emperor made him bishop against his will.

This was the cause of his action. In a convent of nuns in the same city there was a certain virgin who, by her beauty and sweet speech toward everyone, inflamed her lovers. One of them, rich and noble, carried her away and kept her in the place of a lawful wife. The bishop orders that the woman be restored to the monastery, and this is done. Again, while the bishop is absent, she is taken away. Her abductor is excommunicated, so that none of the citizens dared dine or speak with him. The excommunicated man then went away to his country estates.

But when the bishop was approaching death, his fellow citizens assembled and pleaded for the excommunicated man. He answered them: “If that wretch abandons that accursed woman, let him be absolved; but if he persists, let him be ready, on the next year, on this same day and at the same hour at which I depart, to render account before the Lord. You shall see me breathe out my spirit when the signal for the sixth hour sounds.” Thus all was fulfilled: both died in this manner. For in the following year, on the very day and hour he had foretold, that excommunicated man [Col. 0925D] was struck down and died together with his mistress.

Likewise WILLIAM.

At that time Æthelred, fleeing the Danes, came to Normandy to Richard, brother of his wife Emma, son of Duke Richard, who completed the monastery of Fécamp which his father had begun. At night, evading the watch of his servants, he went to the monks’ Matins, bending his knees in prayer until dawn. One night, on his way to the church, he found the door bolted. Having forcibly thrust aside the bolt, he disturbed the sacristan’s sleep. Rising from sleep and seeing him dressed in common clothing, the sacristan flew at his hair and gave him many blows. The next day he lodged a complaint in chapter and [lacuna]. On the appointed day, the monk, by the judges, [lacuna]. [Col. 0926A] …which produces excellent wine, he assigned to the office of sacristan, declaring that he was a good monk who faithfully guarded the duty entrusted to him and who, even when angry, did not break silence.

This king died in the twenty-eighth year of his duchy and ordered himself buried before the church door, so that everyone might tread upon him and rain might fall upon him. Later Abbot William removed him from there and placed him before the altar. His brother Robert was archbishop of Rouen. Abusing his rank, he committed many shameful deeds; but as he declined into old age, he expiated some of them by many alms. This Richard had a son of his own name, who was duke for one year; he is said to have been poisoned by his brother Robert. Robert himself therefore went to Jerusalem seven years later; on his return home, he was killed by poison at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. This Robert was succeeded by the boy William.

Edmund was the son of King Æthelred, not by his wife Emma but by another woman, whom obscure report has consigned to obscurity. He was of great strength, both in courage and body; therefore the English called him “Iron-side.” He divided England with Cnut, keeping Wessex for himself and yielding Mercia to Cnut. Not long afterward he died and was buried at Glastonbury. It is said that Eadric brought about his death through agents—namely, on his advice, an iron hook was driven into his private parts while he was seated to relieve nature. His maternal half-brother Edwin, at Cnut’s command and through the traitor Eadric, left England. After long wandering, he finally died while living in concealment after a secret return; he was buried at Canistochium. [Col. 0926C]

His sons Edwy and Edward were sent to the king of the Swedes to be killed, but were preserved through his mercy and went to the king of the Huns. There the elder died; the younger married Agatha, the sister of the queen. Their half-brothers by Emma, Alfred and Edward, lay safely concealed in Normandy as long as Cnut lived. Their uncle Richard gave his sister in marriage to Cnut. Cnut consequently began to reign in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1017 and reigned for twenty years.

1022.

Durandus becomes bishop of Liège, of the humblest, poorest, and servile condition, so that he was now lord of his temporal lords. When a royal and synodal assembly had been held at Aachen for several days, such drought and violent disturbance of the air arose that many fainted from the excessive heat; many animals also suddenly died. The pavement and marble columns were so wet with sweat that those who did not know thought they had been sprinkled with water. (1023.) Emperor Henry and Robert, king of the Franks, meet on the river Cher near Évaux to deliberate on the state of the Church, kingdom, and empire. They agreed that, in order to confirm these matters, both together should meet the Roman pope at Pavia at a suitable time. The emperor bestowed such generosity upon the king and his people, and upon many also who had come merely to behold the imperial majesty, that the king’s munificence might be compared with the riches of Persian or Arab kings.

1024.

[Col. 0927A]

At Easter an eclipse of the sun occurred. John, bishop of Porto, brother of the recently deceased Stephen, becomes the one hundred and forty-ninth pope, according to Sigebert. But it is remarkable whose brother this John was—what recently deceased Pope Stephen—since between the preceding Benedict and this succeeding pope no Stephen, indeed no other pope, is placed. Master Hugh says thus in his chronicles: “In the year of the Lord 1024, John XIX, the one hundred and fiftieth pope, sat for nine years and nine months.”

SIGEBERT. Roger, the illustrious bishop of Beauvais, died. Among other benefactions, he gave to the church of St Peter, over which he presided, Abacum in Normandy and Montciacum in the territory of Vermandois. He also obtained the county of the same city from Odo, count of Champagne, giving him in exchange the castle of Sincratium, situated in the territory of Bourges, which belonged to him by right of marriage. [Col. 0927B]

Emperor Henry dies, designating as the future king after him Conrad, a man of royal lineage and outstanding independence and generosity, who had never submitted himself to anyone’s servitude. When the exceedingly powerful Duke Cono sought the empire, he was rejected through the influence of Abbo, bishop of Mainz, and certain leading men of the realm; and Conrad, elevated to the empire, ruled for fifteen years.

1025.

Stephen, the brother of Pope John, appeared to him and said that he was being tortured by infernal punishments, but hoped that through the intervention of Odilo, abbot of Cluny, he might obtain pardon. Odilo labored so long in prayer for him [Col. 0927C] that it was revealed to him that he had been heard on Stephen’s behalf. Reginard becomes bishop of Liège; at Liège, on the public hill, he established the monastery of Saint Lawrence and appointed Stephen abbot over it.

1026.

Robert, king of the Franks, sets his mind upon invading Lotharingia, but quickly abandons this undertaking. When Duke Gantelo, who through private hatred was burdening Conrad’s kingdom, and other princes had been brought to unity of peace, prosperity increased for the king and advantage for the realm.

1027.

At Aachen King Conrad elevates his son Henry, still a boy, to the kingship. He himself, consecrated emperor at Easter, suppresses the uprising of certain Italians raging against him. At this time the following abbots flourished: Odilo of Cluny, distinguished for piety; William of Dijon, revered for severity; Richard of Verdun, notable for devout seriousness and serious piety; Poppo of Stavelot; Elias of Cologne; Albert and Stephen of Liège; and Berno of Reichenau.

1028.

At this time Guido of Arezzo also flourished, a great name among musicians, and deserving preference even above philosophers in this respect: by his rule, even boys learn unfamiliar chants more easily than from a teacher’s voice or the use of an instrument. For, with six letters or syllables assigned melodically to the six notes that alone music regularly admits, and with these notes distinguished by the bends of the fingers of the left hand, the tension and relaxation—the raising and lowering—of these same six notes throughout the full octave are presented before their eyes and ears. [Col. 0928A]

1029.

Emperor Conrad marches against the rebellious Slavs to defeat them, and in the same year likewise against the rebellious Hungarians.

1030.

WILLIAM. King Cnut of England went to Rome and returned to England by ship; soon afterward he subdued the rebellious Malcolm, king of the Scots. At that time in England there was a most wise man, Æthelnoth, archbishop of Canterbury, second after Living, and, after Ælfheah the martyr, raised from dean to the episcopate. He brought Saint Ælfheah back from London to Canterbury. Returning from Rome, he sent to Coventry an arm of Saint Augustine, the great teacher, purchased at Pavia for one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. [Col. 0928B]

At his counsel King Cnut also sent money to churches overseas, and especially to the church of Chartres, where Fulbert, bishop most renowned for holiness and philosophy, then flourished. He laid the foundations of the Church of the Holy Mother of God and completed it with a remarkable stone roof. He is also said to have been visited in his sickness by that same Mother of God and restored by her most holy milk. For he burned with great and most blessed love in honor of the blessed Virgin, Mother of God, as is shown by the chants concerning her that he composed, sounding forth heavenly vows. Among his other works there survives a volume of letters; in one of them he gives thanks to Cnut because he had poured out the abundance of his generosity upon the expenses of the church of Chartres.

In the fifteenth year of this Cnut, Robert, king of the Franks and son of Hugh, died—a man devoted to almsgiving, to such an extent that, on feast days, when he put off or put on his royal garments, if he had nothing else at hand, he distributed the very garments to the poor, unless the wardrobe officials deliberately kept needy persons who pressed him importunately at a distance. He had two sons, Odo and Henry. Odo, the elder, was dull; the younger was shrewd and forceful. The father favored the elder, the mother the younger. By great sums of money and promises, as women are obstinate in what they have undertaken, she won over all the dukes of France to her wishes. He was crowned, with Robert of Normandy especially striving for it, before [Col. 0928D] his father had wholly breathed his last.

In return for these benefits, the same Henry very vigorously assisted William, Robert’s young son, against deserters when his father went to Jerusalem. Henry reigned for thirty years. King Cnut of Sceptonia died and was buried at Winchester.

SIGEBERT. At this time, by order of Emperor Conrad, a royal and synodal council was held at Tribur. Among other matters, the bishops wished to decree this chapter: that if the fast of the first month should occur in the week in which the beginning of the fast falls on the fourth feria, the observance of both fasts should be completed by the performance of the office. But Gerard of Cambrai and a few with him opposed this decree of the many, and obtained that the fast of the first month should be celebrated, according to ancient custom, in the other week [Col. 0929A] in which the office occurs.

1031.

Saint Bardo becomes bishop of Mainz. Robert and Richard, departing from Normandy and France at this time to lessen the number of people in their household, make for Apulia. Since the Italians were divided among themselves, and the two sides provided aid against one another, Robert and Richard, seizing this opportunity, cleverly and bravely defeat the Italians; by pressing their successes, they extend their name and prepare for themselves a path to future prosperity. An eclipse of the sun occurred about midday on the third day before the Kalends of July.

1032.

Such a decree was issued by the bishops of France, to be observed by the peoples subject to them. One of them said that letters had been brought down to him from heaven, urging that peace [Col. 0929B] be renewed upon earth; he communicated this matter to the others and gave them these directions to be handed on to the people. No one was to bear arms or reclaim plunder; being in no way the avenger either of his own blood or that of any neighbour, he was to be compelled to forgive those who struck him. They were to observe every Friday a fast of peace and water, and on Saturday abstain from meat and broth; content with this fast alone, they were to know that no other penance was to be added for them for the remission of all sins; and they were to confirm by oath that they would observe it. Whoever refused was to be deprived of Christianity; and no one was to visit him as he departed this world, nor commit him to burial. They also issued very many other unbearable commands, which it is burdensome to repeat.

When many people, eager for innovations, embraced this novelty of commands more readily than was right [Col. 0929C], Girard, bishop of Cambrai—who alone of the Lotharingians was attached to a French diocese—could by no exhortation be induced to accept them. Rather, he refuted each article, saying that humankind had from the beginning been divided into three classes: those who pray, those who fight, and those who cultivate the land, so that one class needs the assistance of the other two, and the two that of the one. Therefore arms ought to be borne and plunder restored; by the authority of law and grace, the avenger of one struck or killed should not be provoked by compulsion, but should be reconciled through the holy Gospel. A fast on the sixth or seventh day should not be imposed alike upon all, because not all have equal capacity; nor should all be content with this one fast, because not all have an equal need of repentance. To confirm these things by an oath, or to compound breach of the oath by perjury [Col. 0929D], is not useful. To excommunicate those who oppose these measures, to deny visitation to the sick or burial to the dead, is plainly contrary to the Gospel and altogether detestable. The authoritative decrees of the Fathers suffice, together with a suitably imposed measure of penance for neglect of them.

Benedict IX, the one hundred and fifty-first pope, sat for fourteen years. When Frederick, duke of the Mosellans, died, since he had no male children to whom the duchy might belong, Duke Gothelo, having obtained from the emperor the duchy of the Mosellans as well, ruled more powerfully in Lotharingia.

Since the Burgundians did not desist from their customary insolence against their king [Col. 0930A], King Rudolf transferred the kingdom of Burgundy to Emperor Conrad. From the time of Emperor Arnulf, they had had kings of their own race for more than 130 years; and thus Burgundy was again reduced to a province.

**WILLIAM.** After Cnut, his son—according to report, by the daughter of Earl Ælfhelm—reigned for four years and four months. Once established in the kingdom, he banished his stepmother. She crossed into Flanders to Count Baldwin. After Harold, however, Harthacnut reigned for two years less ten days. He died while drinking at Lambeth, near the Blindava. He was buried at Winchester beside his father. He had Harold’s exhumed body beheaded and thrown into the Thames. Caught in a net by a fisherman, it was buried in London [Col. 0930B]. He imposed upon England a harsh and intolerable tribute.

Ælfred, the eldest son of Æthelred, is said to have entered upon the kingdom in the interval between Harold’s death and the expected arrival of this Harthacnut; through the treachery of his countrymen, especially Godwine, he was blinded at Guildford. Thence he was sent to the monastery of Ely, where for a short time he sustained a wretched life on ordinary bread, after all his companions except ten had been beheaded. For this reason Harthacnut was hostile to Huno, bishop of Ernutun, by whose counsel this was said to have been done; he expelled him from his bishopric, but restored him after a year, having been corrupted by a bribe. Godwine too was compelled to take an oath of purgation. After the oath he also presented the king with a ship, its prow covered in gold, carrying eighty soldiers, who had on each arm two bracelets, each of sixteen ounces of gold; golden helmets on their heads; a Danish axe on the left shoulder; and an iron-shafted spear in the right hand [Col. 0930C].

## 1034

Odo of Champagne, claiming from Emperor Conrad the kingdom of his maternal uncle King Rudolf, demanded that he might govern Burgundy under him. Henry, son of King Conrad, married the daughter of the king of the English.

## 1035

**WILLIAM.** King Harthacnut sent his sister Gunhild, daughter of Emma, from Tynemouth to Henry, son of Conrad. She was conducted to the ship by all the nobles of England, who contributed lavishly to the expenses. Having reached her bridegroom, she remained with him for a long time. At last, accused of adultery, she set against her accuser—a man of gigantic stature—in single combat a certain young foster-child of hers, whom she had brought with her from England, while her other retainers withdrew in fear. When the duel was joined, the accuser was miraculously disabled by God, his knee cut through [Col. 0930D]. After her victory Gunhild gave her husband a repudiation; she consented neither by threats nor by entreaties to remain with him any longer, but took the habit of a religious woman and remained in God’s service.

**SIGEBERT.** Rebelling against the emperor, Odo invaded Lotharingia and attacked castles; he besieged the city of the Leuci, called Toul, and nowhere restrained his fury.

## 1036

[Col. 0931A]

Odo besieged and captured the castle of Bar. Duke Gothelo, however, deeply offended by the insolence of the French, met Odo with the Lotharingians. In the battle joined at Bar, Odo was killed, and the French army, worn down by heavy slaughter, was compelled to flee from Lotharingia.

## 1037

The Normans, having gradually assembled their forces in Apulia, were encouraged to invade Apulia by their own courage and the weakness of the Italians. Having seized castles and cities either by force or by stratagem, they acted powerfully in Apulia and inspired neighbouring peoples with terror at their name. Henry, count of Louvain, was killed in his own home by a captive, Herman. He was succeeded by his son Otto; when Otto was cut off by untimely death, his paternal uncle Baldric, also called Lambert, succeeded him.

## 1038

[Col. 0931B]

On the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the same month, a fiery beam of extraordinary size was seen in the sky between the south and east. Passing above the sun as it was already declining toward sunset, it seemed to fall to earth; its traces remained visible for a long time.

## 1039

Emperor Conrad went to Italy to crush those plotting rebellion. Since all the Lombards had conspired not to endure any lord who might wish or do anything other than they themselves wished, he put certain bishops in chains. Because the bishop of Milan escaped by flight, the emperor burned the suburbs of Milan. On the day of Pentecost, while the emperor was being crowned at Mass in a small church beside the city [Col. 0931C], the thunder and lightning were so severe that some lost their reason and others even expired. Bishop Bruno, who was singing the Mass, and the emperor’s secretary, together with three others, said that amid the solemnities of Mass they had seen Saint Ambrose threatening the emperor. Then the emperor withdrew from Italy. On the day before the Ides of May there was an eclipse of the sun, and on the day before the Nones of June the emperor died. After him his son Henry ruled for seventeen years, or eighteen according to William.

## 1040

This Henry subdued the Vindelici, peoples bordering on the Swabians. These Vindelici, William says, worship Fortune even to this day. Setting her image in a very celebrated place, they place beside her right hand a horn full of the drink made of water and honey which they call *hydromel*, mead. Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah, affirms that the Egyptians and almost all Eastern peoples did the same. Therefore, on the last day of November, sitting together, they taste it beforehand; and if they find the horn full, they applaud with great noise, since abundance in a full horn is thereby, they suppose, promised them in all things in the coming year; but if the reverse is the case, they groan [Col. 0931D].

Henry made these peoples tributary, so that at all solemnities at which he was crowned, four of their kings carried to the kitchen on their shoulders, by two poles passed through four rings, the cauldron in which meat was prepared. This same Henry was cheerful and merry. He had a sister who was a religious woman. During one winter [Col. 0932A], harsh with snow and frost, she was detained for a long time in one place; a certain court cleric, more intimate with the girl than was proper, kept frequent vigils in her chamber. Since it is difficult for a face not to betray a crime, someone noticed this; and though the matter was already commonly discussed, the emperor alone did not believe it.

One night, when they slept together later than usual, until morning, snow covered the whole ground. The cleric, fearing that he would be discovered by footprints in the snow, persuaded his mistress to let him escape the narrow passage mounted on her back. Raising her cloak behind her, she carried him out beyond the court. By chance the emperor had risen to urinate and saw them through a window. Later an opportunity arose for him to give a vacant bishopric to the cleric, and he whispered to him: “Take this bishopric [Col. 0932B], and see that henceforth you do not ride women.” Likewise, when granting an abbey to his sister, he said: “Be an abbess, and henceforth I shall not allow you to bear a cleric as a rider.” Ashamed, they abandoned their disgraceful conduct.

The same emperor had a cleric quite learned and with a fine voice, but passionately in love with a worthless prostitute. After he had lain with her on a certain festal night, he stood at the emperor’s Mass in the morning. Concealing his knowledge, the emperor ordered him to prepare to read the Gospel, because he wished, that is, to enjoy his singing; for he was a deacon. Conscious of guilt, the man refused. The emperor pressed him, to test his steadfastness. Finally, when he persistently refused obedience, the emperor ordered him to go into exile from his country. Accepting the sentence, he departed at once. A messenger was sent after him, when he had already packed everything and put it into a small bundle [Col. 0932C], and had hastened on his journey. Smiling happily, the emperor said: “You have done well, and I rejoice in your uprightness: you value the fear of God more than your country, and God’s anger more than mine. Therefore receive the first bishopric in the empire that becomes vacant, provided only that you renounce this shameful love.”

The same Henry celebrated Pentecost at Mainz. Shortly before Mass, while seats were being prepared, a quarrel arose in church between the chamberlains of the archbishop and those of the abbot of the monastery of Fulda, over which lord should sit beside the emperor. For the monastery of Fulda, famous in Saxony for the body of Saint Gall and richly endowed with very great estates, provides the emperor with sixty thousand armed men for military service; and by ancient privilege its abbot sits at the emperor’s right hand on great feast days. Thus they came to blows, and as fury raged through the church the pavement was flooded with blood. But when the bishops rushed together, peace was immediately established among the remaining disputants; the church was purified and Mass was celebrated with festal acclamations [Col. 0932D].

Then the sequence was sung; and, when its final verse had been uttered—“You have made this day glorious”—a voice fell from the air: “I have made this day warlike.” As all were frozen with fear, the emperor, concentrating intently and rejoicing at the enemy’s discomfiture, said: “You, inventor and instigator of every evil, have made the day warlike and sorrowful for the arrogant; but we, by the grace of God, who made it glorious [Col. 0933A], shall make it gracious for the poor.” Immediately the sequence was begun again, and with solemn weeping he invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, understanding that He had come among those who wept, those who sang, and all who together beat their breasts.

When Mass had ended, the poor were summoned by heralds; he expended for their use all the food that had been provided for himself and his court, serving the dishes himself, standing at a distance in accordance with the servants’ discipline, and himself clearing away the leftovers. In the time of his father Conrad, this same Henry had taken from a cleric a silver tube, with which boys at play squirt water, promising him a bishopric when he became emperor. When he came of age, he promptly gave the promised office to the man who claimed it. Not long afterward he fell ill with a severe sickness; as it worsened, he lay for three days senseless and mute [Col. 0933B]. The bishops present proclaimed a three-day fast and besought the Lord for his life.

On recovering, he summoned the bishop whom he had made for the tube and deposed him by judgment of a council. He declared that throughout those three days he had seen hostile demons shooting flames at him through the tube—flames, he said, so fierce that our fire would seem a jest by comparison. Meanwhile there had come a half-burned young man, carrying an enormous golden cup full of water; by the sight of him and the sprinkling of its liquid he had escaped the flames, which were extinguished. This was the blessed and glorious martyr Lawrence, whose church roof, ruined by long decay, Henry had caused to be repaired, and whom he had honoured with that church, among other gifts, by a golden cup. On one occasion a doe carried this same Henry, while fleeing enemies, across an impassable river [Col. 0933C].

**SIGEBERT.** Emperor Henry went to make war upon Odalric, duke of the Bohemians; but since the Bohemians resisted bravely, he returned without success.

## 1041

Emperor Henry, having secured God’s help through the prayers of holy men, avenged the misfortune of the preceding year and defeated Odalric, duke of Bohemia.

## 1042

When civil war arose among the Hungarians, King Peter was driven from the kingdom and sought help from Emperor Henry, who devastated Hungary on his account. Wazo, formerly a cleric of Saint Lambert’s, a man distinguished by a spirit of wisdom and knowledge and by religious fervour, became bishop of Liège.

[Col. 0933D]

**WILLIAM.** In this year Edward, son of Æthelred, began to reign; he reigned for nearly twenty-four years. He was so gentle that he did not know how to hurt even lowly persons with a word; yet he was held in great reverence by those of his household and in great fear by outsiders. For God so protected his simplicity that one who did not know how to be angry could nevertheless be feared. On holy Easter Day he was crowned in London with great ceremony by Archbishop Eadsige. He took as wife Edith, daughter of Godwine, into whom almost all liberal arts had flowed. During her husband’s life and after his death she was not free from suspicion of shame; but when dying, in William’s time, she voluntarily gave satisfaction under oath concerning her chastity. The king treated her so that he neither put her away from his bed nor knew her in the manner of a husband [Col. 0934A].

This Godwine once sat at table beside the king, when conversation arose about Ælfred, the king’s brother. “You look at me, O king,” he said, “with a furrowed face, as I see, whenever your brother comes to mind. But may God not permit me to swallow this morsel if I was privy to anything concerning his danger or your injury.” Having said this, he was choked by the morsel he had put into his mouth, rolled his eyes, and died. His son Harold, who stood beside the king, then dragged him away from beneath the table.

Godwine had previously had as wife the sister of Cnut, by whom he begot a boy. While this child rode boastfully upon a young horse, he was carried by it into the river Thames and drowned. His mother too was struck dead by lightning. She was said to be accustomed to buy companies of slaves in England and send them to Denmark, especially beautiful girls. This King Edward was renowned for miracles and for the spirit of prophecy. He was kind and generous to the poor and to guests, especially those from overseas.

On holy Easter Day, sitting crowned at table at Westminster and surrounded by a throng of magnates, while the others ate greedily, Edward’s mind was withdrawn from earthly things as he contemplated something divine, and he burst into laughter [Col. 0934B]. When the tables had been removed, his magnates who were present asked why he had laughed. After much and long hesitation, he answered: “The Seven Sleepers rest upon Mount Coelius; for two hundred years they have lain quietly upon their right sides, but at this very hour of my laughter they turned their sides to the left. For seventy-four years they will lie thus: a most dreadful omen for wretched mortals. For during those seventy-four years everything will come to pass which the Lord foretold would happen near the end of the world: nation will rise against nation, kingdom against kingdom, and there will be earthquakes, pestilence, famine, terrors from heaven, wars of pagans against Christians, and Christian victories over them.”

As those who heard marvelled at such assertions, he described to them the passion of the Seven Sleepers and the appearance of each one—things taught by no written record—as though he had lived with them every day. Among the magnates questioning him were Earl Harold, one abbot, and one bishop. Hearing this, Earl Harold sent one soldier to investigate the truth, the abbot a monk, and the bishop [Col. 0934C] a cleric, to the emperor at Constantinople, with letters and gifts from their king. The emperor received them kindly, sent them to the bishopric of Ephesus, and provided a letter called sacred, so that the bodies of the Seven Sleepers might be shown to the envoys of the king of England.

And it happened according to King Edward’s prophecy. For all the Greeks then swore that they had received from their fathers the tradition that the seven rested on their right sides; but after the Englishmen entered the cave, they found them on their left. Without delay all the things he had foretold followed. For the Hagarenes, Arabs, and Turks ravaged Syria, Lycia, and Asia Minor, and many greater cities, including Ephesus and Jerusalem. In the next seven years three popes died—Victor, Stephen, and Nicholas [Col. 0935A]. At Constantinople Constantine the monk reigned.

**1043.** Master Hugh, in his *Chronicles*, after Basil and Constantine, brothers whom he had previously named, places Constantine alone, brother of Basil; after him Romanus, his son-in-law, with his wife Zoe; then Michael the Etheriarch with Zoe; then Michael Archontopantui with Zoe; then this Constantine the monk with Zoe, but he gives no years for them.

Emperor Henry entered Hungary again with a small force, routed King Aba in battle, and recovered the king’s famous spear. He restored Peter, whom Aba had expelled, to the kingdom of the Hungarians and made Hungary tributary to himself.

## 1044

[Col. 0935B]

A severe famine afflicted Gaul and Germany. Duke Gothelo died. When his son Godfrey was denied the duchy of the Mosellans, he rejected the other duchy and rebelled against the emperor.

## 1045

Godfrey, induced by the persuasion of certain faithful men to regain the emperor’s favour, was seized by the emperor and committed to custody. But after giving his son as a hostage, he was released; when that son died in hostage-status, he rebelled again.

Benedict, who had seized the Roman papacy by simony, being unlearned in letters, caused another man to be consecrated pope, Sylvester, to perform the duties of ecclesiastical office in his place. Since this did not please many, a third man, Gregory, was brought in, to perform alone the functions of both.

**Master Hugh.** Sylvester III, the one hundred and fifty-second pope, sat for fifty-six days; after him Gregory VI, the one hundred and fifty-third pope, sat for two years. This Benedict IX, as Peter Damian says, was nephew of the earlier Benedict VIII, and was called Benedict the Younger in comparison with that elder Benedict. Concerning the elder Benedict, Peter Damian reports as follows:

“A certain bishop of Capua saw Pope Benedict the Elder riding upon a black horse, as though bodily. ‘Alas!’ he said, ‘are you not Pope Benedict, whom we know to have died?’ ‘I am,’ he replied, ‘that unhappy man himself.’ ‘How is it with you, Father?’ ‘I am grievously tormented,’ he said, ‘but I do not despair of God’s mercy, if help is given me. Go, however, to my brother John, who now occupies the Apostolic See [Col. 0935D], and tell him on my behalf that he should especially distribute for me among the poor that large sum which is stored in such-and-such a chest, and that I must thus be redeemed. Yet whenever divine mercy has decreed this, let him know it. For all the other things distributed on my behalf to the needy have done me no good whatever, because they were acquired by robbery and injustice.’”

Having heard this, the bishop went promptly to Rome and reported his brother’s words to Pope John. He then immediately resigned his bishopric and became a monk.

The nephew of this same Benedict, Benedict who was third after him and succeeded Pope John II in the papacy, as Archbishop Humbert told me, appeared to a certain Vasso, riding near a mill [Col. 0936A]. He appeared in the form of a monstrous animal, whose ears and tail were those of an ass and whose remaining parts were those of a bear. As Vasso, terrified, began to flee, the monster cried out: “Do not be afraid, man. Know that I was a human being, as you are. But because I lived like a beast, after this present death I have assumed a beast’s appearance.” Vasso said to him: “Who were you?” “I,” he replied, “was Benedict in name alone, who recently held the Apostolic See though unworthy.” Vasso asked: “What recompense do you have?” “Now,” he replied, “until the day of judgment, I am seized and dragged through thorny, desolate, sulphurous, foul, and boiling places. But after the final judgment, my body together with my soul will be swallowed by the irremediable torment and irrevocable cauldron of the hellish abyss [Col. 0936B], so that no hope of recovery will remain for me thereafter.” After these words he disappeared.

From the beginning of his pontificate until the end of his life he had wallowed in the mire of lust; therefore he ended in an ass’s ears and tail. He had lived all his life carnally; therefore the rest of him was a bear. Oh, how much better it would have been for him had he abandoned the bishopric! After this Benedict, Sylvester sat, as stated above, for thirty-six days—fifty-five days. After him came Gregory VI, previously called Gratian, a man of great religion and holiness, of whom William reports as follows:

“He found the condition of the Roman Apostolate, diminished through the indolence of his predecessors, such that, besides a few towns near the city and the offerings of the faithful, he had nothing by which to support himself [Col. 0936C]. Cities and distant possessions belonging by right to the Church had been taken away by robbers. Public routes and highway roads throughout Italy were crowded with bandits, so that no pilgrim could pass safely except with a large company. Travel to Rome had ceased from every province. In the City itself assassins roamed in the middle of the forum. Anyone wishing to see the church of the Apostle who fell among these assassins could by no means return home without loss either of property or of life.

“Over the very bodies of the holy apostles and martyrs, over the sacred altars, swords were drawn. Offerings of worshippers, scarcely laid down, were snatched from their hands; once snatched, they were spent in feasting and the abuse of prostitutes. At first Gregory began to confront such great evils gently and as befitted a pontiff, acting more by love than fear, more by words than blows [Col. 0936D]. He ordered the citizens to cease harassing pilgrims and plundering sacred things. For it is against nature that one who breathes the common air should not enjoy the common peace; and a Christian ought to travel freely among Christians, since all belong to one household and are joined by the bond of one blood, redeemed at one price. It is also against the commandments of God, who commanded that those who serve at the altar should live from the altar (1 Cor. 9). The house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of robbers (Matt. 21), not an assembly of gladiators.

“Let them permit the offerings of the faithful to be used for priests’ needs or the expenses of the poor. He would somehow provide for those whom poverty drove to robbery; but those stirred by greed should impose restraint upon themselves, for fear of God and for worldly honour. By commands and letters he invited those who had seized ecclesiastical property either to restore what they held unlawfully or to prove before the Roman senate that they possessed it by right. If they would do neither, they should recognize that they were not members of the Church [Col. 0937A]. Though he preached such things frequently, he made little or no progress.

“Then he excommunicated all who either committed such deeds or joined those committing them in table-fellowship or conversation. But the excommunicated raged in response, terrorized ears with threats, and surrounded the city wall with the clash of arms, so that they almost killed the pope. Then the pope judged that the sword of excision must be used. He procured arms and horses from every quarter and equipped soldiers and cavalry. First, securing the church of Blessed Peter, he either destroyed or drove out the plunderers of offerings. Having killed those who resisted him, he restored to their former legal possession estates and towns that had long been lost.

“Meanwhile, the Roman citizens, accustomed to live by plunder, called him bloodthirsty and unworthy to offer sacrifice to God, since he was implicated in so many killings. The cardinals themselves said this. Thus, when he lay ill with the sickness from which he died, they first conferred among themselves and then dared to admonish him not to order his burial in the church of Saint Peter with the other apostles, since he had defiled his office with the deaths of so many persons [Col. 0937B].

“Then he recovered his spirit; glaring fiercely and threateningly, he delivered this speech:

“‘If there were in you even a spark of human reason or knowledge of divine authority, you would not approach your pontiff with so reckless an exhortation. So long as I lived, I spent my estate for your benefit and disregarded worldly renown for your liberation. If others had attached to these acts which you denounce the interpretations you now place upon them, it was proper for you to resist, softening fools’ opinions by better interpretations. For whom, I ask, did I amass treasure? Perhaps for myself? Yet I possessed the treasures of my predecessors, sufficient for any greed. To whom did I restore health? To whom liberty? You would indeed say, “To me.” Yet I was worshipped by the people and freely did whatever I wished [Col. 0937C]; all prayers applauded me, and every day praises were shouted for me.

“‘The sight of your poverty took these praises and applauses from me. I turned my attention toward you and judged that more stern measures must be taken. An impious robber babbled over the little purses of your fortunes. You maintained a poor life on daily bread, while he bought precious silks for himself out of your offerings. You excited concealed ridicule by your common and tattered garments. Therefore, because I could not endure this, I declared war on others, that at the cost of citizens’ losses I might purchase glory for the clergy. But, as I now discover, I have lost benefits bestowed upon the ungrateful. What others mutter in corners, you vomit out in public. I approve liberty, indeed, but require dutiful feeling. Sons assail their dying father concerning his burial [Col. 0938A].

“‘Will you deny me the common house of mortals? A prostitute is not barred from entering the church; neither is a usurer nor a robber; and will you forbid the pope to enter? What difference is there whether one views the sanctuary dead or alive, except that the living person is still tempted by many enticements, so that even in the Church he is not free from stain—often finding material for sinning there, where he came to wash away guilt. The dead do not know how to sin; indeed, they cannot, being without the final provision. What savage barbarity, then, is it to exclude from God’s house one who lacks both the will and the capacity to sin? Therefore, my sons, repent of such headlong audacity. You have spoken foolishly and bitterly. But lest you think that I rely upon authority alone, receive an argument too.

“‘Every human action must be judged according to the intention of the heart, so that judgment concerning the deed may tend toward that from which the plan of doing it proceeded. For, as Truth says: “If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6) [Col. 0938B]. A wretched needy man repeatedly begged me to relieve his poverty. Ignorant of what would follow, I did not refuse, but sent him away laden with various coins. As he departed, he encountered a robber; seeing that he carried money, the robber struck and killed him with the club he bore. Am I then to be judged guilty because I gave a pilgrim that through which he incurred the cause of death?

“‘In ecclesiastical and civil laws the same act is punished and praised according to differing considerations. The robber who kills a man in secret is punished; the soldier who has struck down an enemy in war is commended. Thus homicide is praiseworthy in the one, blameworthy in the other. Our predecessor Adrian I, of most laudable memory, was once praised for granting Charlemagne the investitures of churches, so that no one elected should be consecrated by a bishop until he had first been invested by the king with staff and ring. For Charles’s mind was unconquered by greed; no one could then easily find an entrance unless he entered through the door. Moreover, over such distances the Apostolic See could not be consulted, to give its assent to every elected person, when the king was nearby and arranged nothing out of greed [Col. 0938C].

“‘Now luxury and ambition occupy all royal palaces. Therefore Christ’s bride rightly asserts her freedom, lest a tyrant prostitute her to an ambitious usurper; and the pontiffs of our age are praised for having taken these grants away from princes. Certainly it is not a bishop’s office to command that a battle be joined. Yet it belongs to a bishop’s duty, if he sees the shipwreck of innocence, to intervene by hand and tongue. Ezekiel accuses the priests because they did not stand in opposition, did not oppose themselves as a wall or shield for the house of Israel. There are two offices in the Church appointed for cutting off vices: one which whets speech, the other which supplies the sword. As you yourselves bear witness, I did not neglect my part. So long as I hoped to make progress, I armed my tongue; I notified by messenger the man whose business it was to act with the sword. He wrote back that he was occupied in the war against the Vindelici [Col. 0939A], requesting that I should not be burdened to drive out the assemblies of robbers at my own labour and at his expense.

“‘If I had refused, what excuse could I have offered God, when the emperor had transferred his own duty to me? Should I see the slaughter of citizens and the injury of pilgrims, and sleep? Whoever spares a robber kills an innocent person. But it is objected that a priest ought not to defile himself with anyone’s bloodshed. True; yet one who restrains the guilty and frees the innocent does not defile himself. Indeed, “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Ps. 105). The priests Phinehas and Mattathias were famous for the highest praise; both avenged wrongdoers with their own hands. One pierced lovers in an embrace with a dagger; the other mingled with sacrificial blood the blood of one sacrificing to idols. Zachariah the priest expelled a king who was burning incense; and beyond doubt he would not have hesitated to kill him, had God not hastened to slay him. Divine punishment forestalled that very hand, so that leprosy consumed the body of one whose mind had usurped unlawful things [Col. 0939B].

“‘The king’s devotion is driven out—and shall the robber’s greed not be driven out? It is too little that I am excused; what I did must even be praised. For I bestowed a benefit upon those to whom I appear to have brought destruction. I lessened their punishment by hastening their death. The wicked person, after all, will sin more the longer he lives, unless perhaps God has regarded someone by a singular exception. Death is universally good for all: through it the righteous are placed among heavenly things; the unjust put a holiday to their crimes. By it the evil person puts an end to wickedness; the good person presses on toward the prize [Col. 0939C]. The saint approaches the palm; the sinner looks toward pardon, because death sets a limit to his sins. In their stead thanks ought to be given to me, since by my action they were freed from such great miseries.

“‘These are the things I had to say in my own defence, to nullify your assertions. But since both my threats and yours may prove false, let us commit ourselves to divine judgment. Lay out my body, prepared according to the custom of my predecessors, before the doors of the church; let the doors be secured with bolts and bars. If God wills that I enter, applaud the miracle; if not, do with my corpse whatever pleases you.’ Thus it was done.”

For as soon as his body had been placed before the church doors, which had been shut with bolts, a great whirlwind sent by God burst the bars and obstacles apart, flung open the doors with violent force, and dashed them against the wall with a great crash [Col. 0939D].

At the same time, at Berthelery, a village in England, there lived a woman who was a diviner and sorceress. One day, while she was threatening a little crow which she kept as a pet, the bird uttered some threat more loudly than usual—I know not what. On hearing it, the woman’s knife fell from her hand; at once her face grew pale, and, groaning for a long while, she said: “Today my plough has come to its last furrow; today I shall hear and receive a great misfortune.” While she was still speaking, a messenger came to her and said: “Your son is dead, and your whole household has perished in a sudden collapse.” On hearing this she was immediately struck down by grief; and she summoned her surviving children, a monk and a nun, and said to them through sobs:

“I have, by a certain wretched fate of my own, always served demonic arts. I have been a cesspool of every vice and a mistress of enticements; yet I hoped in your religious life, while I despaired of myself. Now therefore, because I know that in punishment I shall have demons as exactors whom I had as advisers in sin, I beg you by a mother’s womb to try to lessen my torments. For you will not revoke the sentence of condemnation upon my soul. Therefore sew my body into a deerskin, enclose it in a stone sarcophagus, bind the lid with iron and lead, and encircle the stone itself with three great chains. If I lie thus safely for three nights, bury me in the earth on the fourth day—although I fear that the earth may refuse to receive me because of [Col. 0940B] my sorceries. Let fifty psalm-singers be present at night, and let Masses be sung for me for as many days.”

It was done as she had commanded, and it availed nothing. For on the first two nights, while choirs of clerics sang psalms around the body, individual demons easily smashed the church door, though it was shut by a huge bar, and broke the two outer chains; the middle one, made with greater workmanship, remained unharmed. On the third night, around cockcrow, the whole monastery seemed to be shaken from its foundations by the noise of hostile arrivals. But one demon, more terrible of countenance and taller in stature than the rest, shattered the doors, violently shaken, into fragments; and with an arrogant bearing approached the sarcophagus. Calling her by name, he commanded her to rise. When she answered, “I cannot because of the bonds,” he said, “You shall be released—and to your ruin.” Immediately, without effort, he tore asunder like tow the chain that had resisted the savagery of the others; he kicked off the lid of the tomb, seized her by the hand, and drew her openly from the church to its doors. There a black horse stood ready, neighing proudly, with iron hooks projecting over its entire body. The wretched woman was placed upon it, and immediately vanished from the sight of the beholders with the whole company; yet for almost four miles there could be heard pitiable cries begging for help.

## 1046

Thus far WILLIAM. From this point, SIGEBERT.

At Godfrey’s instigation, Baldwin, count of Flanders, rebelled against the emperor. At Rome, while one contender argued against two, and two against one, concerning the papacy, [Col. 0940D] the emperor went to Rome. Having deposed them by canonical and imperial judgment, he made Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, who was also called Clement, the one hundred and fifty-fourth pope; and King Henry was blessed by him as emperor. He reigned ten months and seven days. The Romans swore never to elect a pope without the consent of Emperor Henry.

When Theodoric, bishop of Metz, died, his kinsman Adalbero, a man of great prudence and holiness, succeeded him. The church of Saint Gertrude at Nivelles, which some years earlier had been burned through negligence and through the outrage of the shedding of the Lord’s blood, was rebuilt anew and consecrated in the emperor’s presence.

## 1047

Such snow fell in the West that it broke the forests. Damasus II became the one hundred and fifty-fifth pope; he reigned twenty-four days. Godfrey burned the palace at Nijmegen and destroyed it beyond repair. He likewise burned the city of the Clavarians, called Verdun, together with its principal church of Saint Mary.

Franco, schoolmaster of Liège, was distinguished both by learning and by upright character. He wrote for Bishop Herman a book on the squaring of the circle [Note: [Col. 0941D] See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII, col. 1373.], concerning which Aristotle says: “The squaring of the circle is knowable; it is not yet knowledge, but it is knowable.”

## 1048

Berno, bishop of Toul, became the one hundred and fifty-sixth pope, and was called Leo IX. He reigned five years, two months, and six days. As he was travelling to Rome to assume the apostolic see, [Col. 0941B] he heard angels singing: “Thus says the Lord: I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction.” He composed chants for many saints, and did and wrote many things useful to the Church. While pope, he encountered a poor leper before the doors; after carefully tending him, he laid him in his own bed. When, upon opening the door, he did not find him there, he was astonished that he had received Christ in the poor man.

It should nevertheless be known that Master Hugh places this Leo two years later, that is, in the year of the Lord 1050; and this is truer, as we shall prove later.

Odilo, abbot of Cluny, died, and Hugh, a native of the territory of Autun, succeeded him. His father was a Dalmatian consul, lord of the castle of Semur. While his mother was pregnant with him and suffering from the discomfort of childbirth, she consulted a certain religious man. As he stood at Mass in contemplation, he is said to have seen the form of an infant marvellously radiant beyond human measure.

As a youth he was sent with companions on a raiding expedition, and unwillingly plundered the small property of a certain peasant; afterward, each year he repaid what he had taken once. When Odilo—called the archangel of monks—died, Hugh, then prior, was elected abbot. Adalmann first named him; this man, old and a cook, had for forty years been the provider of the cloister. He had assigned many of his brethren this duty: to go about outside purchasing bread, meat, and various foods, together with manifold kinds of cloth. Around Hugh’s bed were found various supplies bought for the use of the poor: bundles of shoes, leggings, and tunics in one place; masses of bread and heaps of meat in another. He himself mended the tunics of the poor together with monks or household servants.

His father was killed by the duke of Burgundy, who had married Hugh’s sister, and so lost the opportunity for penance; for him the most devout Hugh strove to mortify himself, so that, in addition to fasts, alms, and Masses, he even wore a coat of mail. He received at Cluny a certain knight who had killed his brother, the Dalmatian. At times he saw his guardian angel. King Alfonso of Spain honoured him above all others because, by Hugh’s prayers, he had escaped captivity under his brother. This brother, named Sancho, had been admonished by a certain bishop on behalf of Saint Peter, who had appeared to him, to release his brother Alfonso and advance him even to the throne. Afterwards the blessed apostle Peter himself threatened the same Sancho with death unless he did this. At once Sancho arose in alarm and freed his brother, granting him a doubled paternal revenue. Once freed, Alfonso decreed that he would pay his Cluniac intercessors two hundred ounces of gold annually and left them the day of his liberation as an annual feast.

One day, while sleeping, Hugh saw in a dream a multitude of serpents lying beneath his head. He suddenly shook his pillow and found a book of Virgil placed beneath it; throwing away the secular volume, he rested in peace.

At times, according to the custom of peace, he strengthened the brethren of the monastery of Blessed Mary of La Charité with a kiss. As each came in turn to kiss him, a monk came in his proper order; the saint rejected him. Asked afterward by his abbot, the monk replied that he was a craftsman and infected by the deceptions of necromancy. Saint Hugh immediately had him expelled from the monastery.

While sleeping one day at Saint John the Baptist’s at Angély, he saw in the spirit a lightning-bolt descend from on high and split the assembly hall at Cluny. He immediately thought that one of the brethren had committed an offence which would be imputed to the whole community unless they ran there without delay. At once, interrupting what they had begun, he pressed his companions to return; and, to everyone’s amazement, arrived unexpectedly at Cluny. Entering the chapter house and looking about at all, he severely rebuked the man who had caused the scandal. “Peter,” he said, “reveal your fault to the prior; uncover the wound, that you may experience the remedy.” Thus Peter of Tournus confessed what he had done.

A certain brother, Durannus of Brendon by name, at first appearing unlearned, afterwards became abbot of Moissac and finally bishop of Toulouse. Though prudent in other matters, he often carelessly uttered words that provoked laughter. The saint rebuked him many times for this and did not sufficiently succeed. Thereafter he warned him prophetically:

“Certainly, brother, unless while living you wholly abandon these joking words forbidden to a monk, after death, when more strictly corrected, you will appear monstrously, returning to the heights with foaming lips.”

The following day he appeared thus to Siguin, chaplain of that same father, and tearfully begged that Saint Hugh intercede for him. When Siguin reported this to Saint Hugh, he ordered seven brethren to observe continuous silence for the deceased for one week. One of them broke the silence. Again the same bishop revealed himself to the same man and complained bitterly of the brother who, by not keeping silence, had interrupted that man’s healing. Hearing this, the saint ordered that this breach of silence be repaired by seven more days of silence. When this was done, the same bishop appeared in apostolic dress and gave thanks for his purification [Col. 0943A].

At Silviniac, a brother deceived by the devil laid hands upon himself and killed himself in the woods, as though to anticipate the crown of martyrdom. He was, however, grievously prone to anger, and perhaps for that reason the adversary prevailed against him. When his soul was dragged to judgment, he had as an accuser one displaying the deadly knife. The wretch, prodigal of his own soul, obtained through apostolic intercession—stripped of his monastic cowl—that he should remain before the entrance of the cloister at Cluny, holding the cowl in his hands, until by the prayers of Saint Hugh and the brethren he should deserve to put it on and receive his order again. The pious father immediately ordered prayer, almsgiving, and sacrificial offerings to continue until the spirit of the deceased appeared in another vision wearing his habit; his body too was judged not unworthy of burial in the cemetery.

A brother who saw this vision did not report it immediately, as he ought. Therefore, during Rogationtide, while the others went out for the procession, he remained alone in choir because he was lame. Saint Odilo then appeared visibly to him with two men. And behold, after prayer before the altar, having summoned him, Odilo entered the chapter house and rebuked that brother’s sloth with great severity, ordering his attendants to inflict the sharpest discipline upon him. After the litanies he reported to the abbot both the vision and his own punishment and suffering.

Hugh had with him a chasuble of the blessed apostle Peter, worn at Antioch. Touching with it at Paris a distinguished paralytic named Robert, he said: “The apostle Peter said to the paralytic: ‘May the Lord Jesus Christ heal you; rise and make your bed’” [Note: [Col. 0943D] Antiphon of the Church.]; and immediately he was made well.

Urigo, an honourable man with a festive voice, had become hoarse at Christmas. Grieving because he could not sing, while sitting at the abbot’s footstool he put his hand behind the abbot’s back, took his cap, and wrapped the hair-cord around his own neck; immediately his voice was restored.

Hugh restored the church of Cluny so that it was fit to contain a thousand brethren. He was prompted to this by an admonition of the blessed apostle Peter, who had appeared to a certain old man and instructed him to tell the abbot on Peter’s behalf to restore the church and begin a new one. Then the apostle himself was seen holding and stretching cords and setting out the boundaries for the intended size.

In that church, on Christmas Day, after exhorting the brethren in chapter, Hugh recounted this vision:

“Someone saw in the chapel the Mother of Mercy, the most blessed Mother of God, holding the divine child in her bright lap. Clapping with pure hands, he joyfully said: ‘Come now: this night, wholly dedicated to me, recalls my Nativity; it proclaims that glory has come to heaven, peace to humankind, and release to the prophets. This night serves my glory; this night shall shine with the light of great splendour. Where now is the wickedness of the most evil enemy, in which he used to rejoice before I arose, the Sun of Justice? I have arisen from you, illustrious mother, most worthy by my divine and royal birth.’”

“While he said these things,” he continued, “he who had the word in his power was seen to see the devil standing nearby, and rebuked him thus: ‘Blush, tempter, and flee. My praises, which resound through the house of my beloved, disgracefully exclude you.’ Rebuked by these words, the confounded one withdrew farther away. But the child, surrounded by the compassionate Mother and the host of angels, celebrates with you, beloved brethren, this splendid feast: meet the Saviour with rejoicing voice and heart.”

It once happened that Saint Hugh gave the most holy Eucharist to a leper who had been bodily excluded from human fellowship, but was then receiving communion. With swollen lips and an ulcerated mouth, the man chewed the Lord’s body irreverently and cast out a small portion by an unseemly severing, followed by nausea and dreadful foam. A certain Goberannus, a foster-child of Blessed Remigius who had transferred from his own house to Cluny, was present. Placing both hands beneath the expelled portion, he cast it all into his own mouth, faithfully swallowing the sick man’s vomit. Hugh, astonished, declared without hesitation that Lawrence’s gridiron had been more tolerable.

The same Hugh customarily chanted the entire Psalter every day throughout Lent.

## 1049

Pope Leo came into Gaul in order to calm the disturbances of the Empire stirred up by Baldwin. He reconciled Godfrey to the emperor; but as Baldwin acted more obstinately, the emperor led an army against him. At last Baldwin yielded and, on the appointed day at Aachen, made satisfaction to the emperor.

Pope Leo, having held synods in Gaul and Germany, improved the condition of the Church. At that time the body of blessed Remigius was translated at Reims. At this council blessed Hugh, questioned concerning his own advancement, answered: “The flesh desired it; the spirit resisted.” Therefore, at this council Simoniacs, both laypeople and clerics, and married priests were, through Saint Hugh’s persuasion, excluded from the communion of Catholics and from the churches. At this same council Hugh acted praiseworthily by command of the lord pope and at the persuasion of a very renowned man, Saint Constantius, canon of Reims.

## 1050

While Pope Leo strove to drive the Normans from Roman territories, he suffered great disaster, for he too was captured with many others. Yet he refused to be released unless his own men were released as well.

At this time Saint Theobald, not least among the nobles of the Franks, was famous. Renouncing the world and himself and following Christ, he lived as a recluse at Vincenza, a city of Venice, and in the twelfth year of his religious life rested in a blessed death. The greatness of his miracles after death showed how acceptably he had served God. His bones were translated into Gaul and won great reverence in many places.

Bardo, bishop of Mainz, died; his holiness was evident through an abundant grace of miracles. Baldwin, count of Laon, having seized the county of Hainaut, rebelled against the emperor.

## 1051

WILLIAM. At that time there were two old women on the road to Rome, living in one hut and skilled in the same sorcery. Whenever a guest arrived alone, they transformed him into a horse, donkey, or pig, sold him to merchants, and drank the price. One day they received a young man who earned his living through theatrical performances and transformed him into a donkey. They made considerable profit from him, since the donkey detained passers-by by the marvel of his gestures. For the donkey moved in whatever way the old woman commanded. He had not lost his understanding, only his speech. The old women amassed much gain from this.

Hearing of it, a wealthy neighbour bought the donkey for a high price; [Col. 0945B] and the old women told him to keep it from entering water. The donkey was kept from water for a long time; finally, finding less careful guardianship, he threw himself into a nearby lake, rolled about there for a while, recovered his human form, and lost the form of a donkey. His keeper asked a passer-by whether he had seen the donkey. The man said that he himself was it. The servant reported to his master, and the master to the apostolic Leo, a man most holy in our age. The old women, convicted, confessed it.

Peter Damian confirmed the pope when he hesitated, producing the example of Simon Magus, who made Faustinus appear in Simon’s form. From this it is evident that what is done through necromancy cannot deceive a person looking upon it in water; just as with that powder mentioned above which changed into gold whatever it touched—not because it was truly so, but because it appeared so until it was washed away by water.

At Rome in the same period there was a wealthy and noble young man who had recently taken a wife and prepared a large feast for his companions. After eating they went into a field to play. The master of the feast, leader of the game, called for a ball. Meanwhile he placed his betrothal ring upon the outstretched finger of a nearby bronze statue of Venus. When almost all had set upon the ground, he first withdrew from the game, suspicious as his heated entrails warned him. Returning for the ring, he found that the statue’s finger had bent down to its palm. He struggled there a long time, unable either to remove the ring or to break the finger; he silently departed and concealed the affair from his companions.

Late at night he returned with a servant and found the finger outstretched and the ring stolen. Concealing his loss, he returned to his bride. When he lay beside her in bed, he felt something misty and dense rolling between himself and her: it could be felt but not seen. Prevented from embracing her by this obstacle, he also heard a voice: “Sleep with me, for today you betrothed me. I am Venus, upon whose finger you placed the ring. I have it and will not return it.”

Terrified by this great marvel, he neither dared nor could report it. He spent that night sleepless, deliberating much within himself. For a long time, whenever he wished to sleep with his bride, he felt and heard the same thing. In other respects he was well and capable, both at home and in military service. At length, prompted by his wife’s complaints, he told the matter to his parents. Having taken counsel, they revealed it to a suburban priest named Palumbus. He was a necromancer and powerful in sorcery. Enticed by many promises, he gave the young man a prepared letter and said:

“Go at that hour of the night to the crossroads where four roads meet; stand silently and watch. Figures of people of both sexes, every age, rank, and condition, mounted and on foot, will pass there—some joyful, some sad. Whatever you hear, do not speak. A certain one, taller and more corpulent in form, will follow that crowd; he is himself a god. Go to him and silently hand him the letter to read. What you ask will immediately be done.”

So it happened. Among the other passers-by he saw a woman dressed as a prostitute, riding a mule, her hair loose and thrown over her shoulders, bound above with a golden band. She held a golden rod in her hands, with which she guided the mule; because of the thinness of her clothing she appeared almost naked, making indecent gestures.

The lord of the company came last. From a proud chariot adorned with emeralds and pearls, he fixed terrible eyes upon the young man and asked the reason for his journey. The young man said nothing in reply, but stretched out his hand and offered him the letter. The demon did not dare disregard the familiar seal and read what was written. Immediately, lifting his arms to heaven, he said: “Almighty God, how long will you endure the wickedness of the priest Palumbus?” Without delay he sent attendants from his side to tear the ring from Venus. She delayed greatly, but at last with difficulty returned it. Thus the young man obtained his desire and long-sighed-for love without hindrance.

But when Palumbus heard the demon’s cry to God, he understood that the end of his days was foreshadowed for him. Therefore, with all his limbs internally mutilated, he died in miserable torment, confessing before the Roman people unheard-of crimes.

(1052.) The Gallican Church was disturbed by Berengar of Tours, who maintained that the Eucharist which we receive at the altar is not truly the body and blood of Christ, but a figure of body and blood. Much was disputed against him, both orally and in writing, by many people. Among them Lord Guido, abbot of the Cross of Saint Leufroy, published against him an elegant book on the body and blood of the Lord.

WILLIAM. Pope Leo held a council at Vercelli against him. But after Leo’s death, Hildebrand—when he was archdeacon at Tours and soon pope—assembled councils at Rome and compelled him to anathematize his own doctrine. Lanfranc, archbishop, answered him, but especially and vigorously Guimundus, formerly a monk of Saint Leufroy in Normandy and afterwards bishop of Aversa in Apulia, the most eloquent man of our time.

Yet Berengar in the end repented so fully that some consider him a saint without qualification: full of almsgiving and humility, he distributed the revenues of great possessions rather than hoarding and worshipping them, and allowed no woman to be admitted into his sight. Nevertheless Berengar, though he had corrected himself, could not convert those whom he had led astray. So very evil is it to weaken others away from the good by example or word; for perhaps another’s sin will weigh upon you when your own has been erased. They say that Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, foretold this.

When Fulbert lay at the point of death, many visited him and the house could barely contain those gathering. Looking far about between the opposing crowds, he judged that Berengar should be expelled as forcefully as possible, declaring that a monstrous demon stood near him, seducing many toward following him with a flattering hand and corrupting them with enticing breath.

Berengar himself, dying on the Feast of the Epiphany, remembered how many wretches, when he was once a young man in the first heat of his error, he had infected with his sect. With a groan he said: “Today, on the day of his manifestation, my Lord Jesus Christ will appear to me: because of my repentance, I hope, unto glory; because of others, I fear, unto punishment.”

In this year Abbot Adilprad found the body of King Edgar, buried at Glastonbury, incorrupt. Because the coffin he had prepared was too narrow for the body’s size, he rashly dared to cut the royal remains with iron; immediately blood flowed forth in waves.
