The royal body was then placed upon the altar in the shrine which Edgar himself had given to the church, together with the head of Saint Apollinaris the martyr and relics of Saint Vincent the martyr, which he had bought at great price. The abbot who had profaned the sacred body immediately lost consciousness, and not long afterward death found him after he had left the church. There a madman and a blind man were healed.

Nowhere among the nations, I think, will you find so many bodies of saints uncorrupted after death as in England; they display an image of future incorruption. I believe this was divinely done so that a nation situated almost outside the world might be encouraged in hope of resurrection by contemplating so many bodies that remain uncorrupted. These are Theocam, Beldrica, and Wulburga, virgins; King Edmund; Archbishop Ælfheah; and the ancient Father Cuthbert: all with skin and flesh unharmed and joints flexible; the last also possessing a certain vital warmth, indicating the appearance of those asleep.

Cenwulf, king of the Mercians, entrusted his seven-year-old son Kenelm to the loyal care of his sister Quendryda. She, falsely foreseeing the kingdom for herself, ordered a retainer who was the boy’s fosterer to remove the child. Taking the boy hunting, the man killed him among the thickets. Though concealed in England, this was immediately made known by God at Rome. For a parchment, dropped from above upon the altar of Saint Peter and borne by a dove, was written in English characters and disclosed in order both the murder and the grave. It was interpreted by a certain Englishman, and the pope’s letter immediately informed the kings of England about their compatriot martyr. Accordingly, the innocent boy’s body was solemnly raised up with frequent veneration.

As it was being carried to Winchcombe, Quendryda, that parricidal woman, was roused by the singing of clerics and applause of laypeople. From the window of the upper room where she stood, she put out her head. Holding, by chance, a psalter in her hands, in the continuation of her reading she had reached the psalm, “O God, do not keep silence at my praise” (Psalm 108). Reciting it backwards from the end by some sorcery, she tried to weaken the joy of those singing. But then, by divine power, the eyes of the sorceress were torn from their hollow sockets and stained with blood that verse: “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord” (ibid.). To this day the marks of blood remain, breathing forth the woman’s monstrous crime and God’s vengeance.

At the monastery of Selsey a plague broke out and killed many. A three-day fast was decreed. On the second day of the fast, the apostles Peter and Paul appeared to a boy lying ill with the same disease, saying that he ought not fear death, which is both the end of sickness and the entrance into everlasting life. Moreover, no one else of that monastery would die from this pestilence, because God had granted this through the merits of the illustrious King Oswald, who was praying that same day for his countrymen. For this was the day on which that king, killed by the faithless, entered the court of heaven. His day of death was sought out and found thus. From then on he was counted among the martyrs.

The Danish leaders Ivar and Ubba were devastating the province of the East Angles. The former beheaded King Edmund, who did not resist but, having cast away his weapons, lay prostrate on the ground in prayer, after inflicting certain tortures upon him. The executioner threw his head among the thickets. When the citizens searched for it, they heard the head’s voice calling all to itself; a wolf guarded it, clasping it in its forepaws. The wolf followed the bearers from behind as far as the tomb, harming no one and harmed by no one.

A wooden chapel was first built above Edmund’s body. When thieves wished to plunder it, invisible bonds entangled them in the very attempt. His head, joined to the rest of the body, displayed the mark of martyrdom in a scarlet scar. The hair and nails of this saint gradually grow; a certain holy woman, Oswen, used to cut and trim them every year, so that they might benefit posterity by their sacred veneration. When this saint ordered that his body be shown threateningly to him, a young man named Leostan, wishing—as he said—to test by the trustworthiness of his eyes a report of uncertain fame, became mad as soon as he saw it; shortly afterward, swarming with worms, he died.

As Bede is the authority, Æthelthryth remained a virgin despite being married to two men. Her father was Anna, king of the East Angles. She also had two other sisters, Æthelburh and Seaxburh. The first was first a nun and afterwards abbess in the Gallic monastery called Brie; she remained always incorrupt, before and after death, as did her sister. The other was given in marriage to Eorcenberht, king of Kent; by him she bore two daughters, Eorcengota, of whom Bede wrote much, and Eormenilda, who was given as wife to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians. By him she had a daughter, the virgin Werburh. The mother was abbess at Ely after her mother Seaxburh. The daughter rests at the city of Chester and is said especially to hear the prayers of women and children.

Wulfhere’s brother Merewald and Ermenburh, daughter of Eormenred, Eorcenberht’s brother, had two daughters, Mildrith and Milburga. The first rests in the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury; the other at Wenlock. When her mausoleum was broken open on one occasion, it gave forth a great fragrance like balsam.

Edward the Elder by his wife Eadgifu had many daughters. One of them, Eadburh, was tested by her father when she was scarcely yet three years old. He had placed in the dining room ornaments of different callings: on one side a chalice and the Gospels, on the other bracelets and necklaces. The little girl was carried there by her nurse and sat at her father’s knees. Ordered to choose whichever she wished, she despised the secular things at first glance and, crawling eagerly with her hands, adored the Gospel book and the chalice in childish innocence. The company sitting there exclaimed at this omen of her future holiness; the father himself kissed her with especially close kisses and said: “Go where divinity calls you.” Thus, clothed in a nun’s habit in the city of Winchester, she shone in great holiness, so that by night she secretly took the shoes of each of her companions, carefully washed and anointed them, and set them back beside their beds.

Egitha, the holy virgin daughter of King Edgar, lies in the monastery at Wilton. While blessed Dunstan was consecrating the basilica of Saint Dionysius which Edgar had built out of love for the martyr, he saw this young woman frequently extend her right thumb and make the sign of the cross upon her forehead. Delighted by this sign, [Col. 0949C] the bishop said to her: “May this finger never decay.” Immediately, amid the solemnities of Mass, he began to weep. Asked the reason, he said: “Soon this flowering rose will wither; soon this bird beloved of God will fly away.” So it happened. She died on the day foretold, namely six weeks after that day, when she was twenty-three years old.

Not long afterward Dunstan himself saw in a dream Saint Dionysius holding the same virgin by the hand and firmly commanding through a divine oracle that she should be honoured by servants on earth, as she was venerated by her bridegroom and lord in heaven. Even as a professed nun, she wore garments embroidered with gold. For this Saint Æthelwold, bishop, openly rebuked her. She answered: “The true and irrefragable judgment of God awaits the conscience alone of mortals. For pride may also exist in mournful rags. Therefore I think that a mind may be as incorrupt beneath these garments as beneath your torn skins.”

When her virginal body was raised up, it was found wholly dissolved into ashes except for the right thumb, the abdomen, and what lay beneath the abdomen. While some debated this, the virgin herself appeared in sleep to one of those who had seen it and said: “It is no wonder that those parts of my body decayed. For dead bodies naturally dissolve in this way; and I, being a girl, sinned with those members. But justly the belly did not decay, because lust did not touch it. I was free from gluttony and sexual intercourse.”

King Sigebert of Hungary disagreed with Emperor Henry. [Col. 0950A] Pope Leo came to the emperor to reconcile them; but friends of discord interfered, and it was in vain. Pope Leo, after holding a synod, decreed by apostolic authority that Gerard, bishop of Toul, the fifth bishop before him and remarkable for holiness of life, should be solemnly held in the Church among the holy confessors.

## 1053

Baldwin the count, raiding the borders of Lotharingia, burned the town of Huy. Godfrey rebelled again, because, having married the wife of Margrave Boniface, he was expelled from Lombardy by the emperor’s order.

The Greeks lapsed into manifold heresy through the influence of Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo, bishop of Ochrid among the Bulgarians. Pope Leo rebuked their errors in a book written against them and supported by firm testimonies of Scripture. But Nicetas, a monk of Constantinople surnamed Pectoratus, wrote against the Romans a book full of error and folly, entitled *On Unleavened Bread, the Sabbath, and the Marriages of Priests*.

WILLIAM. At that time the body of Pallas, son of Evander, was found at Rome intact, with this epitaph:

> Pallas, Evander’s son, whom the spear of Turnus,  
> A soldier, slew, lies here in his accustomed manner.

I would not believe that these verses were composed at that time, although Carmentis is said to have invented Latin letters; rather, they were by Ennius or some other ancient poet. Such is the nature of preserved bodies: as the flesh decays, the outer skin holds the sinews, and the sinews hold the bones. The opening of the wound which Turnus had made in the middle of his breast measured four and a half inches [Col. 0950C]. A burning lamp was found at his head. Since they could extinguish it neither by sprinkling any liquid nor by a violent blast, a man of subtler ingenuity made a hole beneath the flame, and as soon as air entered, the fire vanished. The body, placed against a wall, surpassed the height of the walls by its enormous size. But as days went on, moistened by falling dew, it underwent the common corruption of mortals: the skin dissolved and the limbs flowed away.

## 1054
SIGEBERT. Pope Leo, having won over Emperor Constantine’s mind by a letter written to him, sent his envoys to Constantinople: namely Humbert, cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida; Peter, archbishop of Amalfi; and Frederick, the seventh deacon and chancellor [Col. 0950D], to refute the heresies of the Greeks. For, like Simoniacs, they sold God’s gift; like Valesians, they promoted even castrated guests to episcopal office; like Arians, they rebaptized Latins baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity; like Donatists, they boasted that the Catholic Church existed in Greece alone; like Pneumatomachians, they cut the procession of the Holy Spirit out of the Creed; like Nazarenes, they observed Judaism. They forbade infants dying before the eighth day after birth to be baptized; women endangered in childbirth or menstruation to receive communion, or, if they were pagans, to be baptized. They called the Latins “Azymites,” and, persecuting them excessively, closed their churches [Col. 0951A]; they offered sacrifice with leavened bread; in the persons of their children they anathematized the Roman Church and preferred the Church of Constantinople to it.

Therefore the envoys of the lord pope, having been kindly received by the emperor, defeated before him the monk Nicetas, so thoroughly that he anathematized and burned the book he had written against the Romans. But since Patriarch Michael refused to confer with them, they placed upon the altar of Saint Sophia, before clergy and people, a document excommunicating him, and departed. Michael seized and destroyed this document, read it to the people, and, after the emperor had recalled the envoys, summoned a synod in the emperor’s absence so that they might be stoned by the populace. When the emperor prohibited this, Michael stirred the people against him; but, having been convicted of falsifying the document of excommunication [Col. 0951B], Michael and all his party were removed from the emperor’s favour and from the palace.

Humbert of Silva Candida wrote these things; and he refuted the writings of the monk Nicetas and of Leo of Anidani. Translated from Latin into Greek by command of Emperor Constantine, these writings were received by the Greeks.

Emperor Henry, having elevated his five-year-old son Henry as king at Aachen, marched against Baldwin. Baldwin fled, and Henry crossed the river Scheldt, devastating everything. Moreover, when the gates of the barrier [perhaps “of the Meuse,” f. *Mosae*] were opened to him, he inflicted a great slaughter upon his enemies; advancing farther, he killed Count Lambert, Baldwin’s retainer, with many others. He also shut up within the city of Tournai many Flemish nobles who were pursuing his army, and captured them while besieged. Pope Leo dies [Col. 0951C]; many miracles were shown at his tomb in Rome.

William says that this Leo was formerly called Bruno, that he was made pope from being bishop of Speyer, and that he possessed great sanctity. Sigebert says that he was called to the papacy from being bishop of the Leuci—that is, from the city of Toul. Let the reader decide which is more credible. Yet each bears witness to his holiness.

Peter Damian, however, a man of great holiness and learning who flourished at that time, writing to Pope Hildebrand, says among other things:

> “You are accustomed to relate of Pope Leo that, contrary to his merit, he had received from the Lord the grace of miracles, even to the driving away of demons. [Col. 0951D] Similar is what the bishop of Novara related: while he was travelling in Germany as companion to a certain bishop, and the hour of refreshment was approaching, that bishop had nothing to set before him. Strengthened by faith, as cranes flew overhead, he said: ‘Lord, command one of these cranes to be cast down to us.’ It happened immediately. Yet that bishop who prayed and obtained this was a man of carnal life.”

See: this Peter Damian plainly alleges that Pope Hildebrand himself had said that this Leo had received from the Lord the grace of miracles contrary to his merit. Whether this is true, Hildebrand must consider.

Here Sigebert again says: “There was a battle by the Dead Sea,” but he does not say what battle it was, or what that Dead Sea was.

1055.

[Col. 0952A]

Anno is ordained bishop of Cologne. Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, becomes the one hundred and fifty-seventh pope and is called Victor II. He sat for two years, three months, and thirteen days.

PETER DAMIAN. I learned from the report of Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, that when he himself had been sent by Pope Victor as envoy to Gaul, he assembled a synod in which he deposed six bishops for various crimes. Among them was a bishop made by simony, who could not express “the Holy Spirit” in words, although he pronounced “the Father” and “the Son” freely and readily. Convicted by this difficulty, he resigned his episcopal office.

This Archdeacon Hildebrand declared in the chapter-house at Cluny that he had seen Christ, Judge of the world, standing beside Saint Hugh [Col. 0952B]; seated at Hugh’s right hand, He supported regular discipline with His favour. Later, when made pope, he used to call Hugh “a gentle tyrant”—a lion to the fierce, a lamb to the meek.

SIGEBERT. While the emperor was established in Italy, his soldiers engaged the Slavs and the Lutici in war; many were captured or killed. Baldwin of Flanders, together with Godfrey, besieged his uncle Duke Frederick within Ardroverperum; but when the Lotharingians came running up, he abandoned the assault.

1056.

Pope Victor, coming into Gaul, was received gloriously by the emperor; and, not long afterward, with Victor present, Emperor Henry died. William says that he died when the eighteenth year of his reign had been completed. He was buried at Speyer, which he himself had so named from the very ancient and ruined Nemetes [Col. 0952C].

SIGEBERT. After him his son Henry reigned for fifty years.

1057.

A general assembly having been held at Cologne, Baldwin and Godfrey, through the mediation of Pope Victor, were restrained and restored to the king’s favour and to peace, and all disturbances of war were settled.

1058.

In Frisia, after Emperor Henry had captured several castles, the Frisians were checked in their rebellion. Frederick, son of Duke Gozelo, formerly a cleric of the holy Roman Church and its seventh deacon, was hated by Emperor Henry because Henry hated his brother, Duke Godfrey. After his embassy to Constantinople, he became a monk among the monks of Cassino, then abbot; changing his name to Stephen, he became the one hundred and fifty-eighth pope [Col. 0952D]. This Stephen IX sat for nine months.

Paderborn, a city of Germany, was burned together with its greater church. In the monastery a certain Scottish monk named Paternus had long lived enclosed. Though he had often foretold this fire, he refused to leave because of his commitment to enclosure, and allowed himself to be burned.

Peter Damian relates it thus:

> In a certain German city there was a servant of God in a cell beside a monastery. It was revealed to him that unless the people quickly appeased God through penitence, the entire city would perish by fire within thirty days. The vision was proclaimed. They refused to repent. But he ordered every precious object of the monastery to be removed, so that it might be safe. At last fire suddenly arose from seven quarters of the city [Col. 0953A] and reached the cell of the man of God. Though urged to leave, he refused; committing all things to God’s judgment, he was burned with his cell.

1059.

In the district of Brabant near Tournai, multitudes of serpents gathered from either side and rushed into a prodigious battle against one another. Many having been killed on both sides, the defeated party fled and concealed itself in the hollow of a tree. The other party pursued in the manner of victors, hissing around it, until people threw fire around them and all were burned.

Stephen fell ill in the city of Florence. When Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, came, he said that the enemy was departing; when Hugh left, he said that he was approaching.

1060.

MASTER HUGH. After Stephen, Benedict X becomes the one hundred and fifty-ninth pope [Col. 0953B], and sat for nine months. Sigebert and William alike pass over this Benedict, placing Nicholas immediately after Stephen.

Henry, king of the French, dies—a valiant and good soldier—after drinking a draught. Not long afterward a comet appeared, trailing long flaming hair through the sky. Of it a monk of Malmesbury named Eilmer said:

> “You have come—you have come, lamented by many mothers. It is long since I saw you; but now I behold you much more terrible, threatening the ruin of this land.”

He was well educated and advanced in age, and in his first youth had attempted an act of astonishing daring. For he fastened wings to his hands and feet by some contrivance, so as to fly in the manner of Daedalus. Embracing the fable as truth, and catching the breeze from the summit of a tower [Col. 0953C], he flew for the distance of a stadium and more. But, trembling through the violence of wind and whirlwind, and also through awareness of his rash deed, he fell; ever afterward he was disabled, his legs broken. He himself maintained that the cause of his fall was that he had forgotten to fit a tail to the rear part.

1061.

SIGEBERT. After Henry, his son Philip reigned in France for forty-nine years. Gerard, bishop of Florence, who was also Nicholas IX, becomes the one hundred and sixtieth pope and sat for two years and six months.

Marianus the chronicler flourished. Coming from Scotland into Gaul, he was first a monk at Fulda in Cologne, then an enclosed recluse at Mainz.

WILLIAM. In the leisure of his long life, he examined chroniclers and discovered that Dionysius’s chronological cycles disagreed with English truth [Col. 0953D]. Therefore, counting every year from the beginning of the age, he added twenty-two years missing from those stated cycles. Yet he had few or no followers of his opinion. Thus the learned man of our time often meets with this misfortune: scarcely anyone receives the full praise due to learning. So nearly no one grants serene assent according to their merits to discoveries that are new, even if probable; with all his efforts he is drawn toward the opinion of the ancients. Everything recent is despised; and because favour alone nourishes talents, when favour ceases, everything has grown dull.

(1062.) WILLIAM. At that time a marvel was seen on the border of Normandy and Brittany in one—or rather two—women. There were two heads and four arms; everything else was double down to the navel [Col. 0954A], but below that everything was single. One laughed, ate, and spoke; the other wept, hungered, and was silent. They ate with two mouths but digested through one passage. When one died, the other survived, carrying the dead woman for nearly three years, until she too failed through the weight of the burden and the stench of the corpse.

Some believed, and recorded in writing, that these women signified England and Normandy: although divided, they are united under one lord. Whatever money they swallow with greedy throats flows into one pit, namely either the avarice of princes or the ferocity of surrounding peoples. England, flourishing in wealth, sustains Normandy, dead and almost exhausted, until England too perhaps succumbs to the violence of tax-gatherers.

[Col. 0954B] SIGEBERT. Anno, bishop of Cologne, acting on the counsel of the leading men of the realm, who resented that the kingdom of Emperor Henry was not being governed manfully through his mother Agnes, violently and unjustly seized the boy and took him into his guardianship, removing the government of the empire from his mother. Having given an account of the matter before all, he received his lord the emperor’s favour, and through the son returned to the mother’s favour. But, turning the emperor’s necessity into his own choice, so as to stop the mouths of those who spoke wickedly of him, he rejected not merely royal honour but also the burden of worldly life, and went to Rome, to the thresholds of the apostles. There, until the end of his life, he was an example and a miracle to all.

1063.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, becomes Pope Alexander II and sat for eleven years, six months, and twenty-five days. He was the one hundred and sixty-first pope [Col. 0954C]. Against him, Cadalus, bishop of Parma, sought the papacy, to the great scandal of the Church; for a long conflict between them broke out even into killings.

A large army departed from Gaul for Spain against the Saracens; but because the entire region had been devastated by Saracens, it returned ineffectually under pressure of famine.

King Edward, dying, gave the succession to England to William, count of Normandy. The line of the West Saxons, which had reigned in Britain for five hundred and seventy-one years from Cerdic and for two hundred and sixty-one years from Ecgberht, failed in him. On Christmas Day he wore the crown at London; and there, struck by the illness through which he knew he would die [Col. 0954D], he ordered the church of Westminster to be dedicated on the feast of the Holy Innocents, and was buried there on the feast of the Epiphany. He was the first in England to build that church in this style of construction.

1064.

This is William’s account; but Sigebert has it thus: Harold, king of the English, dies; Harold succeeds him. In this year was completed the third great cycle of five hundred and thirty-two years from the Lord’s Nativity, twice elapsed, containing twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles; it is completely useful for every calculation of Easter and turns back into itself from age to age without error. But it seems blameworthy in this respect: the years of the Lord’s Incarnation having been rashly prefixed to it, it disagrees with the truth of the Gospel by asserting that in the year of the Lord’s Passion the fourteenth moon of April fell that year on the first weekday. This is entirely false, because according to the testimony of the Gospel, in that year the fourteenth moon fell on the fifth weekday, and the Lord suffered on the sixth weekday, the fifteenth moon, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0955A].

King Frederick having died, Godfrey received the duchy. The third great cycle begins this year; in other accounts its beginning is falsely assigned to the preceding year. For twice five hundred and thirty-two makes one thousand and sixty-four, not one thousand and sixty-three. I say this because nearly all chronicles must be condemned for this error.

A comet appeared throughout Easter week. Harwic, king of the Norwegians, came with nearly a thousand ships to rule England; and in the city of York he killed more than a thousand laymen and one hundred priests. Harold, king of the English, came upon him with seven legions, killed him with many others, and then William, count of the Normans, entered England with the French. Battle was joined with the English; he killed Harold with many others and reigned there for twenty-six years [Col. 0956A]. How this happened must be narrated more fully at the beginning of another book. For of this William, as William of Malmesbury says, things may be told that will encourage the sluggish, serve as an example to the ready and energetic, be useful to those present, and give pleasure to those who come after.

# BOOK XLVII

[Col. 0955]

[Col. 0955B] WILLIAM. Robert, another son of Richard II, caught sight of a woman dancing and did not refrain from joining her to himself by night. Thereafter he loved her alone and for some time kept her in the place of a lawful wife. A son was born from her: William, called “Albani” [uncertain]. His mother foresaw in a dream his future greatness: she saw her own entrails stretched and spread across all England and Normandy. Moreover, when the child first touched the ground at birth, he filled both hands with the rushes used to sweep dust from the floor. The midwife, struggling to take away what he had grasped tightly, cried out under a favourable omen that he would be king.

When he was seven years old, as his father set out on the journey to Jerusalem, Count Gilbert was appointed guardian of the boy. At a council convened at Fécamp [Col. 0955C], the guardianship of the boy was entrusted to King Henry of France. At his father’s command, all swore allegiance and faithfulness in the boy’s name. As soon as he reached maturity, he received the insignia of knighthood from the king of France and married Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, count of Flanders. He was count of Normandy for thirty years.

He built and richly endowed the monastery of Saint Stephen at Caen, appointing Lanfranc as abbot there. Lanfranc later became archbishop of Canterbury, a man comparable to the ancients in learning and religion. Another monastery of Saint Martin was at Hastings.

While he was still almost a boy, he removed his uncle Malger from the archbishopric of Rouen. Malger was sufficiently learned; but, mindful of his birth, he had forgotten his profession, giving himself too frequently to hunting and contests of birds, and spending ecclesiastical treasures on overly lavish banquets [Col. 0955D]. As the report of this spread, he lacked throughout his life the use of the pallium, because the Apostolic See denied this privilege to one who neglected the sacred office. Therefore, repeatedly summoned and reproved by his nephew, and nevertheless behaving still more irreverently, he was deposed under final compulsion.

Some report that the secret cause of the deposition was that Malger had excommunicated his nephew together with his wife Matilda because they were joined in consanguinity. For that reason William devised pretexts for removing the persecutor of his crimes. In expiation for this sin, William later built the monastery of Saint Stephen at Caen, and Matilda that of the Holy Trinity.

Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp, succeeded Malger. He was full of many virtues, especially abstinence. As he approached his end, deprived of the breath of life, he lay apparently dead for almost half a day. At last, when preparations were being made to carry him into the church, his soul returned, and he said to those standing around:

> “Receive the last words of your shepherd. I died naturally, but I have been restored so that I might tell you what I saw; I shall not remain long, because it delights me to sleep in the Lord. My guides were adorned in garments [Col. 0956C], and their faces possessed every elegance. Nothing was more delightful than their bright speech. Rejoicing, I went with them, as it seemed to me, toward the east; I was promised a place in paradise, which I would enter not much later. In a moment, crossing Europe, we entered Asia and came to Jerusalem. There, after the saints had been venerated, we made our way to the Jordan. The inhabitants of the nearer bank, joined to the fellowship of my guides, made a more joyful company. I hastened to cross, eager to see what lay farther on. Then my companions said that the Lord had commanded that I first be terrified by the sight of demons, so that venial sins which I had not washed away by confession might be cleansed by the terror of those dreadful forms. While they were still speaking, there stood opposite us such a host of demons brandishing sharp spears and breathing fire that the field seemed iron and the air aflame. [Col. 0956D] I was so shaken with horror that I judged there to be no safe refuge either in heaven or on earth. Thus, fearful and uncertain how I might escape, I recovered my breath so that, while saying these things, I might not neglect to provide for your salvation—though I shall immediately breathe it out again.”

He spoke, and almost with the word gave up his spirit. His body was buried in the church of Saint Mary and, by divine miracle as they say, was elevated above the ground for three days.

Pope Alexander, having heard William’s case, sent him a banner for the whole kingdom of England [Col. 0957A]. They assembled at Saint-Valery and waited many days for a breeze to cross the sea. When the delay became excessive and William’s people murmured, he ordered Saint Valery’s body to be brought out to request wind. At once a favourable wind filled the sails, and they reached Hastings.

As he was leaving the ship, his foot slipped, and he heard a nearby soldier cry out to him: “You hold England, count who is to be king.” Harold, returning from the battle in which he had defeated the king of the Norwegians, sent scouts. Captured within the camp, they were ordered by William to be led around the tents, then generously fed and sent unharmed back to their lord. On their return they reported the duke’s magnificent confidence and added that nearly everyone in that army appeared to be priests, since they had their entire faces shaved, including both lips. The English, however, allowed the upper lip to be covered with hair continually flowing over it.

William sent a monk as envoy, bearing three proposals: that Harold should either withdraw from the kingdom according to the agreement, or rule under William, or settle the matter by the sword while both armies looked on. Harold did not deem the envoy worthy even of an answer, but drove him away angrily.

That night, as we have heard, the English spent wakefully in songs and drink; but the Normans gave themselves to confession and then little to sleep, and in the morning received communion in the Lord’s body. The count asked for his arms and by chance put on his hauberk inside out, while his attendants made an uproar. Correcting the omen with a laugh, he said: “My county will be turned into a kingdom.”

Then the song of Roland was begun [Col. 0957C], and battle was joined. Both sides fought fiercely. The fleeing English entered a certain steep ditch by a shortcut familiar to them; there they trampled so many Normans that the mound of corpses levelled the plain of the field. Harold died, struck in the brain from afar by an arrow. One of the soldiers cut open the thigh of his fallen body with a sword; William marked him with disgrace and expelled him from military service.

On that day William, charging about, fighting, and exhorting, lost beneath him three very strong horses, all pierced through. His bodyguards whispered that he should withdraw from danger, but he remained until nightfall. No blood was drawn from his body, although he was attacked with many missiles. He returned Harold’s body without payment to his mother, though she had offered much through envoys.

On Christmas Day he was crowned by Aldred, archbishop of York, unwilling to receive this office from Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, because Stigand had not lawfully become archbishop. He sent Harold’s royal banner to the pope at Rome; it bore the image of a fighting man, skillfully woven at great expense in gold and jewels.

He subdued the rebel city of Exeter with little trouble when part of its wall fell of its own accord and gave him entrance. He had attacked it more boldly after declaring that, with God’s help, the irreverent men must be cast down, because one of them, standing on the wall with his groin exposed, had offended the ears of the Normans by the sound of his lower part in contempt of them. Harold’s brother Harugar secretly served in the army of the emperor at Constantinople [Col. 0958A]. At the emperor’s command, for violating a noblewoman, he was thrown to a lion; he strangled the beast by the bare force of his sides.

1067.

Saint Theobald died enclosed at Vicenza, a Venetian city. Many people, as many as seven thousand, travelling to Jerusalem in fulfilment of a vow to pray, were besieged by Arabs in a certain fortress on Good Friday. So many were killed or wounded that, out of seven thousand and more, scarcely two thousand returned.

Cono, also called Conrad, chief chanter of Cologne, had been sent by Emperor Henry to assume the archbishopric of Trier. He was captured by Count Theoderic of Trier, led into the forest by Theoderic’s retainers, hurled from a cliff three times, and, still uninjured, pierced through with a sword. His body was covered with forest leaves [Col. 0958B]. A peasant found it, carried it to a village, and buried it. From there Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, transferred it to the monastery of Tholey, where God immediately glorified it through many miracles.

At this time the city of Beauvais was deprived of its bishop. Guy, dean and guardian of the Church of Saint Quentin at Vermand and archdeacon of Laon, was made bishop of Beauvais and consecrated by Gervase, metropolitan of Reims. Grieving deeply that he lacked the presence of the martyr Quentin, he built a church in Quentin’s honour and memory not far from the walls of Beauvais.

As two men contended for the papacy at Rome, a synod assembled at Mantua. Through the intervention of Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Alexander was cleared of simony and confirmed in the Apostolic See [Col. 0958C], while Cadalus was rejected as a Simoniac.

1068.

JOHN, in the *Policraticus*. King William, having assumed the crown and established peace, sent envoys to foreign nations, so that they might bring back whatever seemed magnificent or wonderful from every illustrious household. Not so Gaius Caesar, who, following the principle of the sumptuary law, decreed that a civic rather than imperial household should be content at the first table with three customary dishes or courses; provided, however, that sweet dishes, as supplementary additions, could be mixed among the courses of the first table according to necessity, the rank of persons, the exercise of generosity, or the solemnity of the occasion.

The customary dishes are those served to everyone, which the Greeks call *katholika*, “general.” Supplementary dishes are those which, owing to necessity or courtesy, are added for some reason to the prescribed portion; they are so called because they are customarily inserted among the regular dishes. Sweet dishes designate every kind of second-table fare, because the more attractive and delicate foods are customarily put there.

Thus VARRO: “Those sweet dishes are especially honeyed which are not honeyed.” This may perhaps refer to the fact that what necessity desires is more pleasing to its user than what the irritation of the palate invents.

SIGEBERT. Theoderic, count of Trier, guilty before God and men for the martyrdom of Cono, was exiled by the emperor. Having undertaken a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, what befell him and all who travelled in his company is still unknown. As Frenchmen on one side and Scots on the other invaded England [Col. 0959A], the English were consumed by famine; many of them ate human flesh.

1069.

Guy, bishop of Beauvais, dedicated the church, completed over two years, in honour of his patron, the martyr Quentin, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].

With the rivers bound by icy cold, Emperor Henry entered the land of the Lutici, struck them down in excessive slaughter, and greatly devastated their land.

1070.

Gerard, duke of the Mosellans, dies, and Duke Godfrey. Gerard is succeeded by his son Oderic; Godfrey by his son Godfrey. Godfrey, though physically hunchbacked and small, was outstanding in spirit. The Hungarians plan rebellion against their king Solomon, but are restrained by fear of Emperor Henry, whose sister had married Solomon.

1071.

[Col. 0959B]

Duke Godfrey attacked the further Frisians in war and nearly annihilated them. At Trier, in the subterranean crypt of the church of Saint Paulinus, the body of Saint Paulinus himself is found. It had long before been brought back from Phrygia, where he had lived in exile, and hung there by Bishop Felix in iron chains. Beside him lay many bodies of saints: at his right, Palmacius, consul and patrician of Trier; at his left, Tyrus, one of the leaders of the Theban Legion, martyred in that same city by Rictiovarus with many Thebans. At his head were seven senators of the same city: Maxentius, Constantius, Crescentius, Justinus, and three brothers, Leander, Alexander, and Sother. At his feet lay Hormisda, Papirius [Col. 0959C], Constans, and Jovianus. Though many others lay there, golden letters written on the wall indicated only the names, the time, and the day of the martyrdom of these persons; and it was said that they had all suffered under Rictiovarus.

1072.

When Baldwin the Younger, count of Flanders, died, his brother Robert, with Flemish consent, seized Flanders from his nephew Arnulf. Arnulf, together with Philip, king of the French, met his uncle Robert. Battle was joined; Arnulf was killed and King Philip escaped by flight. After many had been slain, Arnulf’s mother Richildis was captured on one side and Robert on the other. When each was released in exchange for the other, the war between them was prolonged with varying fortune.

1073.

In this year, two great cycles after the fifteenth year of Tiberius had elapsed, all things according to the course of sun and moon agree with the year in which the Lord was baptized: namely, the eighth day before the Ides of January [6 January], a Sunday, the Epiphany; the beginning of His fast on Monday; His temptation on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February], on Friday.

When two brothers, kings of the Rus’, contended for their kingdom, one of them, driven from sharing the throne, appealed to Emperor Henry, submitting himself and the kingdom of the Rus’ to him if through his help he should be restored. But this was in vain, because a most grievous dissension arising in the Roman Empire advised Henry to defend his own possessions rather than acquire others. For the Saxons, suffering many great wrongs and injustices from the emperor, rebelled against him; and the emperor hurried urgently to subdue them.

Pope Alexander rose respectfully to meet Archbishop Lanfranc when he came to Rome [Col. 0960A], declaring that he had rendered that mark of reverence not to the honour of the archbishop but to the love due to his teacher. This Lanfranc had become archbishop of Canterbury from being abbot at Caen.

At Lanfranc’s Mass, a young monk read the Gospel. When he offered the paten to the bishop after the *Pater noster*, he saw before him certain utterly hideous faces of evil spirits. Terrified by the sight, he tightly embraced with both arms the bishop as he held the sacred things in his hands, crying horribly and saying: “Christ conquers; Christ reigns.” All present were terrified, and soldiers carried him to the bishop’s chamber.

After Mass they assembled in chapter. The man, strongly bound and possessed by a demon, was brought in. Lanfranc spoke concerning him and ordered common prayer to be made for him. At once he appeared to be healed and was brought to the tomb of Saint Dunstan to give thanks. But while Compline was being sung, he was suddenly snatched from his stall and ran to Prior Henry. Henry immediately seized him, led him into the dormitory, and remained awake before him through the night. At midnight, crying out, the man disturbed everyone. He was taken, resisting violently, to Saint Dunstan’s tomb. When he arrived, he began to rage and spewed forth endless blasphemies against Christ until daybreak.

In the morning he was taken back to the infirmary, where he was tormented for many days. Whoever came to him, if that person had committed some sin not yet confessed, he publicly exposed them as destined to be joined with him in everlasting punishments [Col. 0960C]. Hence some, ashamed, confessed fully. When they appeared before him again, he asked who they were, where they had come from, how they had so suddenly been washed clean, and how they had lost his company.

After this, when he was placed amid holy relics, he leapt up together with the bed upon which he lay, wanting to flee the saints. When he was kept there, the demon ran through his belly like a little cat, now toward his mouth, now toward his lower parts, seeking an exit. As the brothers were taking their meal, the brother left to guard him, greatly devoted to Saint Dunstan and trusting in God’s help, took the cross which Saint Dunstan had customarily had carried before him in the manner of an archbishop. He laid it on the possessed man [Col. 0960D], crying tearfully: “Saint Dunstan, help!” Immediately the demon left.

Then the sick man raised his eyes to heaven and, bathed in tears, said: “I give you thanks, holy Father Dunstan, and to you, dearest brother; because by your merits, most holy lord, and by your loving prayer, dearest brother, I have been delivered from the enemy.”

After this the bishop of Bayeux, who was earl of Kent, raised certain claims against Lanfranc concerning the lands and customs of the Church of Canterbury. When the day of the hearing came, Lanfranc earnestly invoked Saint Dunstan. That night the saint appeared to him in a vision and said: “Lanfranc, do not be sad. I shall be with you; and if you do not defeat them, know that I am not the one speaking with you [Col. 0961A].” Thus it happened: the next day Lanfranc, to the astonishment of all, nullified everything alleged against him.

1074.

SIGEBERT. Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Romans, became the one hundred and sixty-first pope, Gregory VII, and sat for twelve years, one month, and three days. GUILLELMUS. This Hildebrand, as I heard from someone who had heard Abbot Hugh of Cluny relate it, announced other people’s thoughts by the prophetic insight of his mind; for this reason Pope Alexander had placed him at the head of the apostolic chancery. By virtue of this office Hildebrand, as chancellor, travelled through the provinces in order to correct wrongdoings. One day, as he was riding with a great throng of attendants, Abbot Hugh was following at the rear of the procession with his [Col. 0961B] monks. Seeing from afar the great honour paid to the man, he began to think to himself how such honour could belong to a little man of slight stature and lowly parentage; undoubtedly, he thought, it came to him from pride, since he had so many persons walking about him. He had scarcely turned this over in his mind when the archdeacon wheeled his horse about, spurred it on, and, shouting from a distance and calling to the abbot, said: “Tutu, you have thought wrongly. For I neither attribute this glory to myself, if it can be called glory, since it quickly passes away, nor wish it to be attributed to me; rather, it belongs to the blessed apostles, by whose privilege it is shown to me.”

Blushing, the abbot answered only this: “I beg you, lord, how did you know my thought?” “It came,” he said, “from your mouth to my ears, as though through pipes.”

Again, once when the abbot and archdeacon entered a church together [Col. 0961C] to pray, they prostrated themselves more devoutly, their sides held close and joined. Then the archdeacon looked at the abbot, gnashing with an angry grimace. When the abbot had gone outside, he asked the cause of his agitation. Hildebrand said to him: “If you wish to love me, beware of afflicting me any further with this injury. For my Lord Jesus, that one ‘fairer than the sons of men’ [Ps. 44], stood visibly at my petitions, attending to my words and favouring me with serene eyes. But, constrained by the force of your prayer, he left me and turned to you. I consider it a kind of injury to rob a friend of the author of his salvation. Moreover, know that mortality among men and destruction threaten this place. For I saw [Col. 0961D] an angel of God standing over the altar with a drawn [Col. 0962A] sword, and already this province is being encircled by thick, misty air. Let us therefore flee as quickly as possible.”

Having said this, they entered their lodging and sat down to care for their bodies. Immediately, when food had been set before them, mourning arose in the house, several members of the household having suddenly died. As the plague spread through neighbouring houses, they quickly mounted mules and fled.

The same archdeacon had presided in Gaul at a council in the pope’s stead. There several bishops were accused of simony. One of them, charged with this crime, could neither be convicted by witnesses nor refuted by arguments, so skilled was he in eloquence. Then the archdeacon said: “Let human speech cease; let the divine oracle be produced. It is certain that episcopal grace is a gift of the Holy Spirit; and anyone who deserves the episcopate believes that the gift of the Holy Spirit can be bought [Col. 0962B] with money. Therefore, before us who have assembled by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, let this man say: ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’ If he says it plainly and without stumbling, it will be established in my judgment that he is not a simoniac.”

The man gladly accepted this condition, considering nothing less difficult than saying this. Indeed, he pronounced “Glory be to the Father and to the Son” in full; but he stuck at “the Holy Spirit.” When all raised an outcry, he was unable, by any effort either then or for the rest of his life, to name the Holy Spirit. The aforementioned abbot often took this man, deposed from the episcopate, about with him as evidence of the miracle. This Gregory excommunicated all elect persons who received the investiture of churches from a layman’s hand.

[Col. 0962C] SIGEBERT.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] If anything seems offensive in our author toward certain pontiffs, especially Hildebrand, or Gregory VII, it must be ascribed to Sigebert; indeed, these are Sigebert’s own words. He was hostile to this pontiff and supported the emperor’s party, since the emperor and Pope Gregory were bitter enemies. Concerning this Sigebert, Cardinal Bellarmine says in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Sigebert,” he says, “in his *Chronology* was rather unfair to Gregory VII because of his attachment to the emperor; for this reason he told not a few lies, especially when he recounts Gregory’s death.”

Sigebert himself, under the year 1074, says that Gregory VII prohibited married priests from celebrating divine offices, “by a new and inconsiderate precedent.” Helinand also reports these words and does not condemn them. But what sort of accusation is this? Who today would tolerate such priests standing at the altar and celebrating divine offices? Thus, also in defence of Pope Gregory, against Sigebert’s slanders, as Bellarmine says in the cited passage [Col. 0962D], Saint Anselm wrote in his eighth letter to Abbot William, where he says:

“Concerning priests who openly show themselves reprobate before God by a reprobate life of lust, it must altogether be maintained what apostolic foresight has established with ecclesiastical and just severity. For it is in no way fitting that they should stand there irreverently, where, stubbornly stinking with open and shameless lust and despising God’s and the saints’ prohibition, they minister at the sacred altars; indeed, they do not minister, but, so far as concerns themselves, defile them. This is not because anyone should think the things they handle contemptible, but because those handling them should be detested: so that, repelled by men’s abhorrence when they do not reverence the presence of God and angels, they may cease to contaminate sacred things.”

See what we have noted on this passage of Sigebert in *Patrologia*, vol. CLX, cols. 217, 218, 221. EDITOR.]

Pope Gregory, having held a synod, anathematized simoniacs, removed married priests from divine office, and forbade lay people to hear their Mass, by a new precedent and, as many thought, an inconsiderate judgment, contrary to the opinion of the holy Fathers. They wrote that the sacraments performed in the Church—baptism, chrism, the body and blood of Christ—are dispensed within God’s Church by good men and bad alike, the Holy Spirit secretly at work, so that the effect of the sacraments is neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by the sins of bad ones. For this reason it is said: “This is he [Col. 0962D] who baptizes” [John 1]. Likewise, this is he who consecrates.

[Col. 0963A] From this matter such a grave scandal arose that at no time of any heresy had the holy Church been divided by a more serious schism. Some acted for justice, others against justice; some did not shrink from simony, while others covered the stigma of avarice with an honourable name. While they boasted of giving freely, they sold under the name of charity. And, as Eusebius says of the Montanists, under the name of offerings they more cunningly accept gifts. Further, while few maintained continence, some feigned it merely for gain and display, and many added perjury or repeated adultery to incontinence. Moreover, as on this occasion laymen rose against holy orders and shook off every submission to the Church, laymen profaned the sacred mysteries and, disputing about them, baptized infants, sometimes using filthy moisture in place of sacred oil and chrism.

[Col. 0963B] At life’s end they thought little of receiving the Lord’s viaticum and the Church’s customary funeral rites from married priests. They burned in fire the tithes assigned to priests; and, to judge all the rest by one example, laymen often trampled underfoot the Lord’s body consecrated by married priests and poured out the Lord’s blood upon the altar. Many such things contrary to law and right were done in the Church; and on this occasion many false teachers arose in the Church, turning the people away from ecclesiastical discipline by profane innovations.

## 1075

Emperor Henry defeated the Saxons in a most severe [Col. 0963C] battle; pressing them with a renewed campaign, he forced all their princes, bishops, dukes, counts, and other powerful men to surrender. The Hungarians rebelled against the emperor and tortured their king Solomon, driven from his kingdom, under prolonged confinement. (1076.) Pope Gregory fiercely attacked Emperor Henry and, by writings and words, turned from him whomever he could; he even alienated from him the heart of Agnes, the emperor’s mother. An assassin killed Duke Godfrey in Frisia. Baldwin, a boy and brother of the slain Arnulf, fought at Davingium against the army of his uncle Robert, whom he defeated in battle. There was great frost and very severe ice from the Kalends of November to the middle of April.

In this year, which is the thirteenth year of the new nineteen-year cycle in the repeated great year of Dionysius, two great years having elapsed since the Lord’s Passion, everything pertaining to the course of sun and moon agrees with the year of the Lord’s Passion. It is therefore evident that Dionysius did not rightly attach the years of the Lord to his cycle, since he began his cycle from the year of the Lord 532. Clearly, he meant that Christ himself had been born in the second year of the preceding great cycle; and accordingly this year agrees with the year of the Lord’s Passion. Thus the year of the great cycle ought to be not the thirteenth but the thirty-second, because that was the year [Col. 0964A] of the Lord’s Passion. Consequently, in setting the Nativity of Christ twenty-one years later than he should have done, Dionysius made the solar and lunar courses agree with evangelical truth.

## 1077

Emperor Henry, having summoned at Worms a council of thirty-four bishops and many leading men of the realm, ordered it decreed that all Hildebrand the pope’s decrees and acts should be invalid. There, all except a few renounced Hildebrand and judged that he must be removed from the papacy. Hildebrand, conversely, excommunicated the emperor, so that the leading men of the realm might oppose the king as though he had been excommunicated for a just cause. On Palm Sunday, about the sixth hour, a star appeared in a clear sky.

When the Saxon princes who had surrendered were released by those to whom they had been entrusted, the Saxons rebelled at the instigation of Pope Hildebrand. The pope himself met the emperor in Lombardy and absolved him under a false hope. For all those who had earlier renounced Hildebrand, adding perjury to perjury, renounced the emperor and set Rudolf, king of Burgundy, over themselves as king. The pope sent him a crown inscribed:

> The Rock gave to Peter; Peter gives the diadem to Rudolf.

Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, blessed him as king; and when the people of Mainz raised a revolt against them, Rudolf fled by night with the archbishop. Pope Hildebrand absolved all who opposed the emperor from disloyalty and from perjury. The emperor, with the Alpine passes fortified against him, frustrated their ambushes everywhere [Col. 0964C], came by way of Aquileia to Regensburg, attacked Rudolf, and compelled him to flee; then, in a renewed campaign, he ravaged Swabia. (1078.) Emperor Henry, having ravaged Swabia, destroyed castles; by laying all waste he filled his enemies with fear and gave his friends courage, and drew back to himself many who had abandoned him in despair of their fortunes. Bishop Herman bound himself in allegiance to Pope Hildebrand and was therefore expelled from the city of Metz as a rebel against the emperor.

From this time the canonical order of Blessed Quintin of Beauvais began to flourish anew in the Church: first instituted regularly by the apostles, then by Blessed Augustine the bishop, under Master Ivo, the venerable provost of that same church, afterwards bishop [Col. 0964D] of Chartres. At this time Peter Damian wrote to Pope Hildebrand, giving the reason why he had resigned his bishopric.

For he was a man most renowned for religion and wisdom. He relates there certain matters which I have decided should be considered here: “Because,” he says, “I refused ecclesiastical government, a penance of one hundred years was imposed on me, according to the remedies of the monastic rule.”

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Observe Bellarmine, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he treats of Peter Damian and assigns his death to the year 1072, making the following consequent observation: “From this,” he says, “the tale of Helinand and Vincent of Beauvais is refuted, concerning the penance of one hundred years imposed upon him [Col. 0964D] by Pope Gregory VII; for Peter Damian died before Gregory VII was elected pontiff.”

But it is not a tale; it is certain history reported by our Helinand. For Helinand copied the very words of Peter Damian, which are also found in the published works of Peter Damian: “Because,” he says, “I refused ecclesiastical government”—that is, because I resigned my bishopric—“a penance of one hundred years was imposed upon me, according to the remedies of the monastic rule.” These are not Helinand’s words but Peter Damian’s, addressed to Hildebrand. Yet neither Peter nor Helinand says that this penance was imposed by Hildebrand himself; indeed, he suggests the opposite by writing it as though it were less well known to Hildebrand. Moreover, that penance could have been imposed by Hildebrand as the pope’s legate, an office he held before becoming pope.

You will say: Peter recounts this penance to Hildebrand as pope; yet he died before Hildebrand became pope. I answer: he recounts it to Hildebrand who afterwards became pope, not to one who was pope at that time. [Col. 0966D] If Helinand thought Hildebrand had then been pope, he erred only in a circumstance of the action which he reports; the penance of one hundred years imposed on Peter is not therefore a fiction. How this penance was fulfilled even by delicate and noble women, see in Peter’s very letter to Hildebrand. But observe that our author makes no mention of the female pope or papist Joan, because that tale had not yet been invented; nor does he mention the Parisian doctor who raised his head from the bier while prayers were being said for him in church before he was buried. If so memorable an event was known to him and to Sigebert, it is very strange that they passed it over; but that it was unknown to them is stranger still.]

Perhaps he speaks here of remedies such as those he describes when he says: “Dominic,” he says, “was clad in an iron cuirass next to his flesh, girt on his body with two iron bands and with two about the upper arms. Armed in this way, with each hand holding scourges, stripped of his clothes, he recited twelve psalters, remaining awake throughout the whole night; on the next day he completed them, and from the thirteenth [psalter] as far as ‘Blessed are they whose…’” [Ps. 118:1].

By this man’s example, the custom took root in our regions that not only men, but also noble women, eagerly undertook this kind of purgatory. For the widow of Tethald, a woman of great lineage and high rank, told me that by the prescribed rule of this discipline she had completed a penance of one hundred years, reckoning three thousand scourges as one year. Such, therefore, was the penance of one hundred years imposed upon him because he had resigned his bishopric from love [Col. 0965B] of religion, though he was very fit to govern the Church.

But in giving his reason, he says that many saints before him had done the same. “Valerius,” he says, “of Hippo appointed Augustine as his successor. Lucidius of Evodius, when death was imminent, fled to a monastery; and, as Gregory says in the *Register*, Blessed Andrew appeared to him and announced the hour of his death. Adalbert, bishop of Vienne, became a monk and deserved to find the palm of martyrdom. Likewise, a certain holy penitent, having resigned his bishopric, was at last visited by an angel and commanded to return to the episcopate; but he refused, until Blessed Remigius, promptly arriving at the warning of the same angel, commanded him to do so, and then for the first time he obeyed.”

And below: “It is better to cast off the burden than to perish with a broken neck to the loss [Col. 0965C] of the Lord, whose servant I am.” Therefore it is written: “Why did you not put my money on the table, so that when I came I might have demanded with interest what is mine?” [Luke 19]. That is, says Jerome, you should have deposited at the altar what you could not carry. For while you, an idle trader, retain the coin, you occupy the place of another who could have doubled the money.

“Do not some bishops have royal banquets every day, display every day, a wedding feast every day? And from resources with which they ought to refresh the needy, they entertain soldiers; men belonging elsewhere belch at their table amid abundant delicacies, while those whose entire substance it is, excluded outside, waste away through want of food. And, what seems to equal diabolical [Col. 0965D] wickedness, after estates have been squandered on military service and all landed possession, tithes [Col. 0966A] and congregations besides are granted as secular benefices. This most evil liberality both deprives the poor of the means of living and frightens diocesan people from paying tithes—killing the former in body and the latter in soul.”

The bishop of the city of Florence presided over a game of chess. While I was still a bishop, rebuking him, I imposed upon him the duty of reciting three psalters, washing the feet of twelve poor men, feeding them, and giving each one a denarius, so that he might wash away with his hands what he had polluted with his hands.

I have thought it worthy to insert here certain remarkable occurrences of this period which Peter Damian himself recounts here and there in his books. The doge of Venice, at Constantinople, had a wife who lived so tenderly and delicately, and pampered herself with such elaborate pleasure, that she disdained to wash herself in ordinary water; instead, her servants collected dew from heaven on every side and laboriously prepared her bath. She did not touch her food; rather, eunuchs cut each item of nourishment into very small pieces, which she then greedily brought to her mouth with certain golden two-pronged forks. Her chamber was fragrant with so many spices and incenses that it is foul even to tell of it and incredible to hear. But while she was still alive, the sword of judgment was brandished over her: her whole body rotted away, so that it filled the entire chamber with an intolerable stench. No one could bear her—not her attendant, not a little servant. Scarcely one maid remained in her service, and not without the aid of fragrant substances; even she approached hurriedly [Col. 0966C] and withdrew quickly. Long consumed by this disease and miserably tortured, she ended her final day while even her friends rejoiced.

To her may be applied: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her torment and mourning” [Rev. 18]. And again: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and a stronger punishment presses upon the strong” [Wis. 6].

Sophia was sister of two marquises, sons of Ugo, and daughter of Rainer. While healthy and sound, she asked the abbot of Saint Christopher to prepare a burial-place for her in that monastery. Although he resisted and told her that she was speaking idly, she nevertheless obtained it, though with difficulty. Her tomb was therefore made in the monks’ cloister. As soon as she entered [Col. 0966D] and saw it, by some judgment of God unknown to me, she fell ill; soon afterwards she miscarried and died, and was buried there [Col. 0967A]. Although her tomb was of gypsum and had been most carefully strengthened by masons’ skill, for about a whole year it nevertheless gave off such a foul discharge that it did not allow the brothers to remain in that entire half of the cloister. For the more tenderly and softly all flesh is reared, the worse it turns to corruption.

A certain monk, while carrying some fried food in a small vessel to the refectory, had an itching appetite and secretly threw one piece into his mouth and ate it. Immediately such a heat of lust seized him that, though he had never done this before, he could not restrain himself by any means until he emitted semen with his own hands. Thus, after the morsel, Satan entered into him.

At the monastery of Blessed Vincent, situated not far from the monastery called Pierced Rock, we had established [Col. 0967B] a regular ordinance that during Lent, for three days, all should take only a little bread and water; should utter no words, nor reading, nor prayer within hearing; should go barefoot; and, after the Psalter had been completed, should cleanse themselves each day by mutually scourging one another with whips. A certain brother violated this rule by eating. He was skilled in writing, musical notation, turning, and construction. He knew divination, monastic practices, medicine, magic—everything. In the middle of Lent this fat, sleek, corpulent man suddenly fell sick. I had heard that he had been excluded from the celebration of Masses because of his sins. I admonished him about this matter, but he denied it. On the next day, sitting anxiously in bed, he demanded the Lord’s body from me.

When the abbot, who was standing with us, rebuked him on this account—because no signs of death appeared in him—he nevertheless persisted. When the priest was already standing there with the sacrament, he drew one of the brothers close to himself and whispered some grave sin into his ear. The brother, astonished and not knowing what penance to impose, finally imposed fifteen years of penance on him. As soon as the man received the Lord’s body, he vomited out his soul together with bile. This bile did not cease to flow until his burial.

In the aforesaid monastery it had been established, and had already been observed for three years, that the offices of Blessed Mary ever Virgin should always be said at the canonical hours. A certain monk named Gozo—a man of reprobate life, but eloquent, witty, and precise—began to complain about this [Col. 0967D], and by his arguments secured the discontinuance of the hours of the Blessed Virgin. Immediately innumerable adversities arose against the same monastery: plundering, robbery, conflagrations, and the slaughter of servants and dependents of that place. They went to the German emperor, but in vain. They came to me. I told them that these things had happened because they had cast away from themselves the mother of peace. The messengers at once fell prostrate upon the ground and said that thereafter they would never omit the praises of the Blessed Virgin. Thus shortly afterward they recovered peace.

A certain monk joined us to live with us, and for eight years remained with us chastely and commendably, according to the brothers’ testimony; he wrote many volumes for us, for he was skilled in writing. Afterwards [Col. 0968A], though he was fat in body and seemed stronger than usual, he began obstinately to demand leave to return to his own monastery, at the devil’s prompting, as later became clear. For as soon as he reached the monastery, he committed incest with another monk, an old man of evil days, equally skilled in letters and book-copying. A sickness immediately fell upon him; he took to his bed, and not long afterwards, confessing and ashamed, died.

A certain monk of the city of Faenza made water burn in a lamp in place of oil; afterwards he fell into lechery and was publicly beaten with rods and disgracefully shaven bald.

An angel of the Lord used customarily to come to a priest of the same city and take the sacrament of the Lord’s body from the hands of the celebrant, while the prince watched. At length the same priest fell into lechery [Col. 0968B]; and behold, while he was offering, the angel of the Lord came as usual and, with the prince looking on, squeezed a sponge filled with water over his head, pouring again over all his limbs all the filth and defilement which he had previously contracted from that man’s body. Astonished, the prince privately admonished the priest. He at first denied it, but afterwards confessed that on the preceding night he had fallen with one of the prince’s chambermaids.

Two men among the foremost citizens of the same city appeared together in a vision to a certain deacon. They seemed clothed down to the ankles in iron chasubles in the manner of priests. When he questioned them and asked, “Do you who are in that life continually bless the Lord?” they replied: “We who are tortured in hell by eternal fire never bless the Lord.”

[Col. 0968C] A certain prince of Salerno, once seeing flames burst forth from Mount Vesuvius, immediately said: “Without doubt some wicked rich man nearby is about to die and descend into hell.” For in those regions there is such a custom that, when the death of a reprobate rich man is imminent, that mountain vomits forth pitchy, sulphurous flames. Having said this, on the following night, while the same prince lay securely with a prostitute, he died. As she later related, not knowing what had happened, she bore down upon him more harshly and only at last with difficulty cast away from herself not a man but a corpse.

A certain Neapolitan priest, wishing more certainly to learn what it was not lawful to learn, presumed to draw near to the place where the infernal abyss belched forth more fiercely. After the solemnities of Mass, he proceeded mitred, as if armed. But when this rash investigator went farther than men ordinarily did, unable to return, he was seen no more afterwards.

Another priest left his sick mother at Benevento. While he was escorting his lord through the territory of Naples, looking at the surging flames, he heard a cry which he recognized as his mother’s. He noted the hour and then learned that his mother had died at that moment.

A certain cleric, living in lechery with his concubine for five years, was found burned with her in one house when the city was set alight by an accidental fire. A certain priest, promising conversion and postponing it, fell from his horse into a small stream and was drowned.

[Col. 0969A] John, bishop of Comacchio, took a widow’s pig. She wept but was not heard. While he was eating it, he was struck in the throat; physicians could not heal the wound as long as he lived. He then turned to religion, which he had promised long before but had refused to fulfil. Yet he lived a long time afterwards in conversion, suffering such severe distress in his throat that he received food with great difficulty; and when he reclined at the common meal of the brothers who succeeded him, he could scarcely take in enough over so long a period to restore his stomach.

A rich man named Harduin had promised me in firm devotion that, if he could not do so earlier, at least when ten years had elapsed he would enter religion at the monastery of Blessed Vincent, which is situated at Arpinga. [Col. 0969B] When the term was completed, he began to evade the matter; and the abbot of the same monastery favoured his wishes and dissuaded him from conversion, since he was of course supported by Harduin’s necessary assistance. Meanwhile, seized by illness, he made confession and gave much to poor persons and churches. As though safe because all things had been properly arranged, he bound the kinsmen and relatives attending him under this solemn charge: “I beseech you,” he said, “by the charity which is God, that no one should seek to restore me to this mortal life, lest—God forbid—sudden death find me unprepared.”

He died, and some time after his death appeared in a vision by night to that abbot. “I seemed,” said the abbot, “to see on a broad plain of a field an emperor, or some other exalted power, assembling with a plentiful army of his entire realm. As I looked in astonishment this way and that, behold, Harduin was being hurried along by certain guards. ‘Hey!’ said I, ‘stop your step a little. Will you not speak to me, Harduin? Come, brother, how are you? Are you joyful, or do you suffer? Are you in punishment or in glory?’”

Then he, sad and weeping, said: “Why do you ask me about glory, when I am afflicted with unceasing punishments?” The abbot replied: “What then has Blessed Vincent done to you?” But he said: “Saint Vincent long made me hope for his conversation; but because, weary long ago, I was unable to obtain this, I have now utterly lost this hope in disappointment.” Thus he was plainly disappointed in promises by the one whom he had likewise disappointed through promises.

[Col. 0969D] In the monastery founded by Blessed Gregory within the walls of the city of Rome, a certain boy was offered by his parents. When he grew up, he returned to the world and took a wife. Having become a young man, he was struck in the throat by divine judgment and began to be ill unto death. At last he asked to be carried back to the monastery. There he received repentance for his wicked deeds and the monastic habit.

While his wife and several others stood beside his bed, he began groaning and howling and babbling in a disorderly voice. When he was rebuked and asked why he would not be quiet, he said: “Do you not see Blessed Andrew the apostle and Saint Gregory scourging me with their most severe blows?” Then he rested and caught his breath briefly, saying: “They have just beaten me [Col. 0970A] because I left the monastery and took a wife.” Again, after weeping and roaring, he rested and said: “They have just beaten me because I gave nothing at all to poor beggars, especially the Scots; indeed, what is worse, I often mocked them.” Again: “I have just been punished because I borrowed six coins from a certain poor little widow and refused to repay them. For as many steps as she took in labour while coming to demand them from me, so many blows I have now suffered from the hands of both saints as they beat me together. And, so that you may know that I am not lying,” he said, “the day after tomorrow at the sixth hour I shall depart from this world.”

It was then Friday. But on the night when the Lord’s day dawned, on Palm Sunday, he leaped from bed after all had departed; he suddenly snatched up the scapular and hair-shirt [Col. 0970B] which lay beside him and immediately entered, amazed and hurried, the Church of Saint Andrew. There, laid out upon a bed, he said to the brothers present: “Behold, scourged by the saints’ blows, I depart from the body as purified as I emerged clean from the font of baptism.”

Accordingly, during the sacred solemnities of Mass, when the account of the Lord’s Passion had scarcely been read through, he died at the hour which he had predicted. When his body was stripped to wash it, bruises and marks of wounds were found upon it. In the same monastery there is a crypt, and in it a spring from which Blessed Gregory drank, and a stone bed in which he rested during summer. Once a pregnant little dog entered this crypt to give birth there. As soon as she approached the aforesaid bed [Col. 0970C], she fell down dead.

Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, told me: “A servant of God in the region of Naples dwelt as a solitary on a steep cliff beside the public road. While chanting psalms at night and opening the window of his cell to observe the hours, he saw many Ethiopians travelling along the road and driving pack-animals heavily laden over a long stretch with hay. He asked who they were and why they carried this fodder for beasts. ‘We are evil spirits,’ they said. ‘We are preparing these not as food for beasts to be fed, but rather as fuel for fires in which men are to be burned. For we are awaiting nearby the prince of Capua, who is already lying sick, and John, commander of the soldiers of the city of Naples [Col. 0970D], who is still living in health.’”

The man of God immediately hurried to John and told him what he had seen and heard. At that time Otto II was going into Calabria against the Saracens. On hearing this, John said: “I now need to meet the emperor and discuss carefully the state of this land. After his departure, I promise that I shall leave the world and become a monk.” To test whether what the man related was true, he sent a messenger to Capua, who found Pandulf already dead. John himself, commander of the soldiers, died fifteen days before the emperor reached those regions.

Martin, who lives in the Camaldolese hermitage, a man of many virtues and especially of the grace of tears, related the following. [Col. 0971A] There was a monk in a monastery in the maritime region, called Adpinum, entangled in many bonds of sins. When a great and lengthy penance had been imposed on him, he asked help from a certain dependent of his in carrying the burden of the penance. This man devoutly accepting the burden, commanded the monk to remain responsible for so great a part to be discharged. The man thus bound died not long afterwards. His life among the brothers had been blameless and his reputation honourable.

Not many days later he appeared in a dream to the penitent monk. When asked how he was, he said: “Badly and harshly, but because of you. For free from my own obligations, I bound myself in your bonds and did not discharge another’s surety; I testify under harsh scourges. But I beg you, keep vigil on my behalf and free me. Go, therefore, and entreat the community [Col. 0971B] to fulfil what I promised and rescue me.” When this had been done, he again appeared to the aforesaid monk with a joyful and serene face, saying that he had been delivered from punishments through the brothers’ prayers and joined to the saints.

In the regions of Gaul, a great dispute arose between an abbot and a certain powerful layman concerning a possession, so that, after lengthy quarrels, supporters of each side agreed to take up arms. The lay potentate, attended by troops of armed men, entered the field intending to fight. But the abbot forbade all his following who had come to fight for him; he placed only his monks on horses, ordered their heads to be covered with hoods, and thus armed came to the place of combat [Col. 0971C]. Immediately the opponents were struck with such terror that they promptly dismounted from their horses, cast down their arms, humbly threw themselves upon the ground, and begged pardon.

If it is objected that Pope Leo waged wars, I answer: Peter was not made prince of the apostles because he denied Christ, nor was David made a prophet because he committed adultery. Evils and goods must be judged not from men’s merits but from their own qualities. Gregory suffered many robberies and acts of violence from the Lombards, Ambrose from the Arians; each fought by patience alone.

Dusinus, a bishop, on Ash Wednesday had a lavish banquet prepared for himself and his knights; suddenly paralysis seized his countenance, [Col. 0971D] his face, and his mouth, and he lived for a long time afterward with this infirmity. A certain man had stolen another’s pig. Now this man was very hospitable. Meanwhile Jesus appeared in the form of a poor man, and, being as it were long-haired, needed a barber. The man at once rose reverently, took up scissors, and began to cut his hair. While doing so, he found two hidden eyes on the back of His head. Alarmed, he asked what this meant. The other replied: “I am called Jesus, who despise all things everywhere; and these are the eyes with which I saw the pig that you have just shut up in a pen.” And immediately He disappeared.
