A certain bishop, being very thirsty, ordered wine brought to him. When the cupbearer had poured all that was in the vessel into a cup and brought it to the bishop, behold, an importunate poor man asked that it be given to him, saying [Col. 0972A] that unless he drank at once, he would immediately expire. The bishop ordered it given to the poor man; and though he was thirstier than before, he ordered the wine-vessel inspected again, in case anything might perhaps remain; and it was found full. A certain abbot ordered a lamprey bought; one was bought for twenty Pavia coins, cooked and served. And behold, a poor man at the door urgently requested that the very thing set before the abbot be given to him. The abbot sent him the fish, still whole. Immediately the poor man, with the dish full of fish, rose up into the air and, before all who watched, passed into heaven. Behold the proof that what we hide in the bosom of a poor man, we store up in heaven.

A certain bishop ordered a lamprey prepared; and while he was singing Mass, he was tempted by a pleasurable desire for the taste of that fish. He was ashamed; and, when Mass had ended, [Col. 0972B] ordered the feverish fish to be given to a poor man. A certain householder had only one coin in his chest, with which to buy something to eat with bread. Meanwhile a poor man came and asked for mercy. He gave him that coin. He returned home, and his usual bread was set before him. And behold, an unknown man, whom he had never seen before, hurriedly and anxiously placed in his hand twenty shillings in coins tied up in a linen cloth, saying that they had been sent by his lord; and, as though expected, immediately departed.

A certain man noble by birth but degenerate in character married his kinswoman in the kingdom of Clavomac. He was excommunicated by a pious bishop, but treated this with contempt. As a sign of divine indignation, it happened that loaves [Col. 0972C] from the wedding tables, cast out into the streets before everyone, were not touched by dogs. Not long afterward, while he slept in his chamber, he was struck by lightning.

When I was studying at Parma, on the vigil of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, a certain man rose early and led his oxen to more distant pastures. A neighbor of his entered the house and, pretending to have a fever, got into the man’s wife’s bed. Gnashing his teeth and trembling, he caused her, pitying him as if he were her fevered husband, to embrace him and cover him with a blanket. After violating her, he immediately departed. Not long afterward the husband returned and found the bed; reproaching him, his wife said: “You will indeed be well able today to enter the church [Col. 0972D] of the holy martyrs, which stands next to you, together with the other Christians.” When he, astonished, asked what she meant and learned the entire matter in order, both recognized that they had been deceived and were greatly distressed. At last, recovering their courage and laying aside all shame, they joined the others for the night office, laid their complaint before everyone, and begged the Lord to exact vengeance for so great a crime by making the hidden adulterer known.

Immediately the adulterer, filled with a demon and tearing himself, entered the church: now flying aloft, now hurling himself with the greatest force into the depths; now dashing his head against a wall, now in frenzy throwing himself down upon the pavement. At last he breathed out his unhappy soul before the people.

[Col. 0973A] It is reported that in the region of Puteoli in Apulia, amid black and foul-smelling waters, there is a rocky and craggy promontory. From these waters, according to their accustomed pattern, most hideous little birds are seen to rise; from the Saturday evening hour until dawn on Monday they appear to human eyes and roam freely as though released from chains, stretching their wings and shedding their feathers. They are never seen to eat, nor can they be caught by any device of a bird-catcher. On Monday morning a huge raven, like a vulture, pursues them and croaks after them; they at once plunge beneath the water and appear no more until the evening of the next Saturday. Some maintain that these are souls of human beings assigned to Gehenna, but that on Sunday, together with the adjoining nights, they receive refreshment for the glory of the Lord’s Resurrection.

Prudentius agrees with this assertion in a hymn, saying:

> Even for spirits often harmful,  
> there are holidays from punishments . . . .

[Note: [Col. 0973D] *Cathemerinon*, hymn V, verses 125–26.]

That night was made a holiday when God returned victorious from the depths of Acheron. But Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, entirely denies that the matter is so. Nevertheless Archbishop Stambertus, in Desiderius’s presence, related that he had heard this from the inhabitants of Apulia.

The same Humbert related that, in the monastery of Saint Silvester in the territory of Urbino, a certain monk died and lay as an inanimate corpse, with the brethren lying around him, from the beginning of the nocturnal cockcrow until the second hour of the day. While at Mass [Col. 0973C] the *Agnus Dei* was being said for him, he rose. When the astonished brethren approached more closely to hear words from his mouth, he began to spew curses and insults against God, to spit upon the cross offered to him for kissing, and to assail the undefiled Mother of God with shameful reproaches. He said: “Why do you chant psalms for me or offer sacrifices? I was in the very flame of Tartarus, and there my teacher and lord Lucifer put upon my head his brazen crown, ever glowing with unquenchable fire; and he clothed me in a cloak of the same metal, which he himself wore.” The cloak was so long that it flowed down to his ankles, and was so fiercely ablaze that it seemed to emit drops.

When the brethren urged him to do penance, he pronounced anathemas and with sacrilegious mouth condemned all the mysteries of our Redeemer. Then the monks prayed for him with all their hearts. Stripping off their clothes, scourging themselves, and beating their breasts with their fists, they labored in every kind of prayer within their power. And behold, that desperate man returned to himself, praised the omnipotence of the Savior, renounced Satan’s deceptions, worshipped the cross, and begged for penance. He confessed that, after renouncing the world, he had fallen into fornication, which he had hitherto concealed. Praising and blessing God, he lived until the following day and departed in holy confession.

Hildebrand related to me that in Germany there was [Col. 0974A] a certain count, of good reputation and, in human estimation, of innocent life, who had died ten years before. After his death, a certain religious man, descending in spirit to the lower regions, saw that same count on the highest step of a ladder. The ladder appeared to be set up amid hissing and crackling flames, to receive all those descended from the same noble lineage. This ladder rose out of an immeasurable abyss. Those succeeding one another were arranged in this order: each newcomer occupied the top step of the ladder, while the one found upon it descended to the next lower step. When the man who saw this asked why that count of his own time, who had lived so justly, was being tortured there, [Col. 0974B] he heard the reason: it was because of a certain possession of the Church of Metz, which his great-grandfather had taken from Saint Stephen; and he himself was now the tenth successor in the inheritance.

In the regions of Babylon the Apostolic See possessed an estate from which it annually received so much balsam income as sufficed to keep the lamp hanging before the altar of Saint Peter supplied and perpetually burning. The pope sold this estate for money and lost the payment in spices which he had been accustomed to receive. Some time later, while the same pope stood praying before the holy altar, seemingly devoutly, behold, a dreadful and very aged old man—whose face even seemed to have a beard—struck him violently with an uplifted arm and said: “You have extinguished [Col. 0974C] my lamp before me; and I extinguish your lamp before God.” He immediately disappeared. The pope at once fell down and died shortly afterward.

A certain boy of five, son of the most noble man Hubald, who lives with me in the wilderness, had become a monk in my monastery. Having rested in his bed in the evening, he was found in the morning in the bakehouse, though both doors were shut. He said that certain men had led him there to a great banquet, where every delight of feasting was visible, and had made him eat there. He also said that, carrying him as far as the castle which overlooks the mountain, they placed him upon the very bell that hangs nearby on high.

In the district of Bologna two friends and equals were dining, [Col. 0974D] and a cock was brought to them. One of them, taking a knife, as was customary, cut this dish into pieces and poured crushed pepper with sauce over it. When he had done so, the other said: “Certainly you have so thoroughly disposed of this cock that even Peter himself, if he came, could not cure it.” The other immediately added: “Indeed, not only if blessed Peter commanded it, but even if Christ Himself commanded it, this cock will never rise again.” At these words the cock suddenly leapt up alive and covered with feathers, beat its wings, crowed, shook out its feathers, and sprinkled all the sauce over those who were dining. Immediately the sacrilegious blasphemers were struck with leprosy amid the scattering of pepper; [Col. 0975A] and this plague of leprosy remained hereditary among their descendants until death. Therefore they were reduced to servitude to the church of Bologna, which bears the name of Saint Peter.

Certain Venetian merchants, having made landfall, saw a lion entangled in the coils of a dragon not far from the shore and violently dragged by the dragon into a cave. The innkeepers, who had suddenly gathered for this spectacle, boldly attacked the dragon, killed it, and freed the lion. The lion, not ungrateful, for several days during which the innkeepers remained there, brought them every day the hide of one animal it had caught.

A certain man was going with his companion to cut wood; and behold, a serpent of beam-like size, raising two necks with two heads, attacked them [Col. 0975B]. One of them, who held an axe, cut off one of its heads; but his axe immediately fell to the ground. Enraged, the serpent at once seized it in its teeth with the other head and, winding the man in its coils, carried him into its cave. As he was dragged away, he cried to his companion to defend him or give him the axe which he held in his hands. But the companion, afraid, would not do so, and fled; for this reason he was compelled by the priests to undergo exile as one guilty of death.

Thus far Peter Damian. Now let us return to the sequence of the history.

SIGEBERT. In this year the monastery of Saint Savior was begun on the island called Aquicinctus by the distinguished men Sicher and Walter. At this time in the East the Turks prevailed over the Arabs and Saracens, and, invading Armenia and [Col. 0975C] Syria, captured many cities and Antioch itself. At Pentecost, after holding an assembly at Mainz, Emperor Henry decreed that Hildebrand should be deposed from the papacy; and, proceeding to Lombardy, he appointed Guibert, bishop of Ravenna, pope in Hildebrand’s place.

Pope Hildebrand, as though by divine revelation, foretold that in this year the false king would die. This was true indeed, but his conjecture concerning the false king deceived him, being interpreted according to his own wish as referring to King Henry. For King Henry engaged the Saxons in a great battle; and in the encounter the false king Rudolf was slain, together with many princes of Saxony.

## 1081

[Col. 0975D] A great earthquake, with a grave roaring of the earth, occurred on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the first hour of the night, portending an imminent evil which resounded throughout the whole world and by which the earth suffers and has suffered. For Emperor Henry entered Italy to wage war against Pope Hildebrand. Against him the pope, having fortified cities and castles, prepared for rebellion and would not receive him when he came hostilely to Rome. Henry, however, having captured the cities and castles which stood against him for Hildebrand, besieged the Leonine City of Rome.

WILLIAM. When he heard this, Guiscard, son of Bohemond, marched to Rome. Terrified by his reputation, Henry fled with the false pope. Hildebrand returned, but not long afterward was again driven away by Henry.

## 1082

[Col. 0976A] In Gaul, the knight Hermann, placing a crown upon himself, exercised tyranny in Saxony after Rudolf. Marianus Scotus brought his chronicle, which he began from the birth of Christ, down to this year, which was the fifty-sixth year of his age. He labored greatly to correct the error concerning the years of the Lord found in the Dionysian cycle; this is easy to see, since he set down the years of the Lord according to the Dionysian cycle on one side, and according to the truth of the Gospel on the other.

## 1083

Emperor Henry, having breached the Leonine City, besieged Rome. A day having been appointed between emperor and pope to settle their dispute, peace was not reached between them because the pope evaded the matter; therefore the Romans and many peoples of Italy withdrew from the pope. Fleeing, he withdrew to the Normans in Apulia. [Col. 0976B] (1084.) The Romans received the emperor into the city, and Hildebrand was deprived of the papacy by their judgment. Guibert was made pope and was called Clement.

Those who supported the emperor maintained that Hildebrand had been justly deposed as guilty of treason, because he had set up another king against the emperor and undertaken the audacity of rebellion. Those holding the contrary view protested that the universal pope could not be removed from the pontificate by the judgment of a few men, by lay shorn heads, or by imperial power, rather than by a universal judgment; and, what was more serious, that to appoint another in the place of a bishop who was still living was contrary to canonical authority, and other things of that kind.

King Henry was made [Col. 0976C] patrician of the Romans and was blessed as emperor by his Clement. Baldwin, count of Mons, married Ida.

At Mainz, after holding a royal and synodal assembly, Emperor Henry demanded of all that they depose Hildebrand and approve Guibert’s ordination by subscription. Some favored him in hand and mouth, but in heart still clung to Hildebrand. Hermann of Metz, though deprived of the bishopric in his absence, was again driven from the city by the emperor; in the bishopric of Metz [lacuna] he installed a hireling, but Christ’s sheep did not hear the voice of strangers. The emperor attacked the Saxons. They sought and obtained peace, on the agreement that all those proscribed for this rebellion should have their possessions restored. Because this was not done, they rebelled again, [Col. 0976D] with Count Ecbert, the emperor’s kinsman, above all others as instigator.

Walter, one of the clergy of Saint Lambert in England, a bishop of the English, was attacked without cause by their hatred and, while celebrating Mass, was martyred by them like another Stephen, the pope. He does not say in what city this occurred; and it is remarkable that William, who writes the history of the English of this period, reports nothing of it.

Pope Hildebrand, also Gregory VII, died in exile at Salerno.

WILLIAM. A man of happy favor with God, and perhaps of excessive austerity toward men. Indeed, it is reported that, at the beginning of the first disturbances between himself and the emperor, he would not admit the latter even at the doors when he came barefoot, carrying scissors and a broom; for he abhorred [Col. 0977A] the man as sacrilegious and guilty of incest with his sister-in-law. This repulse caused the deaths of many.

SIGEBERT. I found this written concerning him: “We wish you, who are concerned for the care of the Church, to know that the apostolic lord, Pope Hildebrand, also Gregory VII, now at the point of death, summoned to himself one of the twelve cardinals, whom he loved above the rest; and he confessed to God, to Saint Peter, and to the whole Church that he had sinned greatly in the pastoral charge committed to him for governance, and that, at the devil’s persuasion, he had stirred up hatred and anger against humankind. He then said that the famine which had spread over the world had begun for the increase of charity. Finally he sent his aforesaid confessor to the emperor and to the whole Church [Col. 0977B] to seek pardon for him, because he saw the end of his life and was soon to put on the angelic garment. He remitted and dissolved all the rights [lacuna] of his bans against the emperor and all Christian people, living and dead, clergy and laity; and ordered his followers to leave the house of Theoderic and the emperor’s friends to enter.”

(1086.) The Saxons were besieging the city of Lüneburg, in order to restore to his see its bishop Albero, who had been expelled by the citizens. Emperor Henry attacked them, but the army, divinely terrified, gave way; more than four thousand of them fell, while only fourteen were killed on the Saxon side. An excessive flooding of waters caused damage and danger in many places. In Italy the inundation was so great that melting cliffs destroyed several villages [Col. 0977C] in their collapse.

Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, became the one hundred and sixty-third pope and reigned for two months. He was also Victor III and, according to Sigebert, was wasted by dysentery and died not long afterward.

WILLIAM. At his first Mass he was afflicted by some disaster, I know not what; the chalice, if it is worthy of belief, had been poisoned.

SIGEBERT. Anselm, bishop of Lucca, Hildebrand’s indefatigable collaborator, died in exile at Mantua. He produced commentaries on Jeremiah and the Psalms and confirmed Hildebrand’s teaching in an eloquent book. His holiness was manifested by miracles. Domestic birds—peacocks, hens, and geese—left their homes and all became wild.

Augustine, in Book III of *The City of God*, recounts that a similar portent occurred, saying: [Col. 0977D] “Before the Latin confederacy rose in arms against Rome, all animals subject to human use—dogs, horses, asses, oxen, and whatever other livestock were under human dominion—suddenly became wild; forgetting their domestic gentleness, they left their shelters and wandered freely, shunning the approach not only of strangers but even of their masters. Nor could anyone venture near to restrain them without death or danger. What great evil it signified, if it was a sign; and how great an evil it was, even if it was not a sign!”

## 1087

[Col. 0978A] The emperor and the Saxons frequently fought, with varying outcome. While the Venetians were planning to remove the body of Saint Nicholas from Myra in Lycia, devastated by the Turks, the citizens of Bari forestalled them: forty-seven men came from Antioch to Myra and compelled the four monks whom they found there to show them the saint’s tomb. Breaking it open, they removed the bones of Nicholas in their full number, floating in a liquid of oil, and carried them gloriously to Bari. This translation took place in the 745th year after the deposition of Saint Nicholas. John, archdeacon of the church of Bari, wrote the account of his translation at the command of Urso, archbishop of the church of Bari and Canosa.

At that time a certain great man of the Palatine court, sent by his emperor, to whom the land of the Myrans was subject, came and prayed to Saint Nicholas to deign to show him some small portion of himself which he might kiss. The church minister therefore drew something from the liquid of the urn with a brush, [Col. 0978B] and one tooth came out. The magnate concealed it in a golden pyx and placed it upon the altar there. A little later, looking at it, he saw oil flowing from the pyx. He wrapped it in a cloak, thinking that the oil could thus be contained; but it flowed all the more. He therefore despaired of keeping secret what the Lord had revealed to him. Saint Nicholas appeared to him in a vision, saying: “Behold, I have satisfied your request; but you cannot carry it away, because I do not permit so tiny a portion to be separated from the other members.” The next day he did not find the tooth where he had put it.

The men of Bari therefore set out with three ships for Antioch on business; they visited the island of Cacava, then came to the islands of Magestra, then to the places of Macri [lacuna] [Col. 0978C] The port of Saint George is five miles distant from Bari. The body of Saint Nicholas was placed by those who transferred it in the church of Saint Benedict. On the first day more than thirty sick persons were healed there. A man from the region of Ancona, his body bent and deprived of the use of hands and feet, was healed by kissing the shrine. A priest from the territory of Camerino, suffering from gout in the spine, came to Bari to the saint; from the place at which he could first see Bari, he began gradually to straighten up and arrived wholly healed. Parents brought from Amalfi a handsome demoniac, who was healed at the aforesaid place from which Bari is first seen, where a cross had been erected by those who had been healed.

There were healed from a certain castle [Col. 0978D] a little girl weak throughout her body, and a little boy who could keep no food in his stomach. A poor man from Dyrrhachium brought back his wife, disabled in every limb except her tongue, cured. A leprous woman from Dalmatia was healed. A maidservant of a certain man of Siponto, bent over at the back, was healed. A woman who had recently given birth and lacked milk was healed; likewise a little son of a man from Macerata, who had never been able to move in a natural gait; likewise a poor man living at Taranto, unable to walk on his feet and scarcely able to sit. A certain image said to him in a dream: “Why do you not go to Bari?” “How can I?” he said. “Go,” it replied, “for you can.” And he rose up healed.

A certain knight had lost some possessions; suspecting one of his retainers [Col. 0979A] of having done it, he struck his shin with a dagger’s two-edged blow. Worms bred in the wound, making the shin ulcerous. Coming to the saint, he was healed. From Cisalpine Gaul two women were healed, one blind and the other demoniac. The woman who had been blind offered the saint silver eyes set with precious stones.

## 1088

SIGEBERT. In the same year fish died in the waters. In Spain King Aufal of Galicia fought the Saracens bravely and at last captured Toledo, their greatest city, after besieging it for several years; he extended Christian worship there. Urban II, the one hundred and sixty-fourth pope, reigned eleven years and four months.

WILLIAM. This man was first Odo, archdeacon of Reims, then prior of Cluny, [Col. 0979B] afterward bishop of Ostia.

SIGEBERT. Odo, formerly a monk of Cluny and bishop of Ostia, was made pope against the emperor and Guibert, under the name Urban. From this arose scandals in the Church and growing divisions in the kingdom: one dissented from another; kingdom and priesthood disagreed; one excommunicated the other; the other despised the excommunication, whether from prejudice against the case or against the person; and each more abused the authority of excommunication against the other according to personal inclination than with regard to justice. Thus the authority of Him who gave the power of binding and loosing was despised [Col. 0979C].

Indeed, to speak with the peace of all good men, this novelty alone—lest I call it heresy—had not yet appeared in the world: that the priests of Him who calls the king “apostate” (Job 34), and who “makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people,” should teach the people that they owe no submission to evil kings; that, although they have sworn an oath of fidelity, they nevertheless owe no fidelity; that those who oppose the king should not be called perjurers; indeed, that he who obeys the king should be held excommunicated, while he who acts against him should be absolved from the guilt of wrong and perjury.

## 1089

The duchy was at last given to Godfrey, nephew through a sister of Godfrey the Hunchback. It was a pestilential year, especially in the western part of Lotharingia. There many, with the holy fire consuming their entrails, rotted away, their limbs eaten off and blackened like coals, and either died miserably or were preserved for a more miserable life, their hands and feet putrefied and cut off [Col. 0979D]. Many others, twisted by the contraction of their limbs, went mad.

(1090.) Emperor Henry entered Italy to subdue those opposing him. Hermann the tyrant, returning from Saxony to Lotharingia, labored to stir up disturbances in the kingdom. When he carelessly approached the wall of a certain castle, he was struck on the head by a stone hurled from a tower and died. At Metz the body of Saint Clement, first bishop, appointed there by the apostles, was found and raised up. In Saxony Count Ecbert, while pursuing the emperor’s faithful men in war, was himself slain. The barrenness of the earth’s crops increased, and famine gradually crept in. Emperor Henry captured the castles and fortifications of those opposing him in Italy; he also besieged and took Mantua.

(1091.) Robert, son of Guibert, [Col. 0980A] king of England, resented that Normandy was denied to him while his father still lived. In anger he went to Italy to marry the daughter of Marquis Boniface, by whose help he might oppose his father. Frustrated in this hope, he stirred up King Philip of France against his homeland. Therefore he lost his father’s blessing and England, and after his father’s death scarcely retained Normandy.

Richard, the other son of William, while hunting deer in the New Forest, is said [Col. 0980B] to have contracted a fatal illness from a mist of pestilential air. This was a place which his father William had turned, after destroying villages and demolishing churches, for thirty miles and more into woodland and lairs for wild beasts. For this sin William his son, who reigned after him, and Richard his grandson, son of Robert count of Normandy, perished there: the first struck in the breast by an arrow; the second pierced in the neck by a branch of a tree—or, as some say, caught by the throat as his horse passed beneath.

William’s daughters were Cecilia, abbess of Caen; Constance, countess of Brittany, who by the severity of her justice provoked the people of the province to administer a deadly drink to her; Adela, countess of Blois, who took the religious habit at Marcigny. A fourth, promised to Harold, died before the wedding. A fifth, pledged to Alfonso king of Galicia, obtained from God a virgin’s death. On the knees of this deceased woman a callus was found from frequent prayer.

Thus King William, living in Normandy at the end of his life, incurred hostility with Philip, king of France. Philip said of him: “The king [Col. 0980C] of England lies at Rouen, warming his bed like women after childbirth, making sport of the belly which he has relieved by drink.” Stung by this insult, William replied: “When I go to Mass after my confinement, I shall offer him a hundred thousand candles.”

Not long afterward, in the month of August, he invaded France and burned the town of Mantes by setting fires in it. While himself kindling the flames at close range, he contracted illness from the heat of the fire and the unseasonableness of autumn. Some say that his charger, leaping a steep ditch, ruptured his internal organs, because his belly protruded in front.

(1092.) Almost all instigators of the Saxon war having been killed, the Saxons, weary of evils, made peace among themselves and ceased all military disturbances. Lord Ivo, provost of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais [Col. 0980D], consecrated by Pope Urban, became bishop of Chartres. William II, king of the English, of singular strictness and severity, died; his son William succeeded him.

AUTHOR. William says: William died at Rouen on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-second year of his reign, the fifty-ninth of his life, and the year of the Lord 1087. His body was carried down the Seine to Caen and buried there; yet he could not obtain that resting place without a challenge. For a certain knight, to whose inheritance that place had belonged, publicly denounced the seizure and forbade the burial, saying that the place had been violently taken from him by William. Therefore Henry, the only one of the king’s sons who was present, paid the knight one hundred pounds of silver. Robert, the eldest son, was then waging war against his father in [Col. 0981A] France; William had sailed for England before his father breathed his last.

At that time, in the province of Wales, the tomb of Gawain was discovered. He was Arthur’s nephew and ruled in that part of Britain which is still called Gawain’s land. Although a knight of great renown, he was expelled from his kingdom by Hengist’s brother and nephew. His tomb was found on the seashore, fourteen feet long. Arthur’s tomb, however, is nowhere seen.

Lanfranc, archbishop, brought up William, son of King William, made him a knight, and consecrated him king on the day of Cosmas and Damian. He was so generous as to be prodigal, so high-minded as to be proud, so severe as to be cruel. He had little reverence for God and none for men, although God is to be feared at all times and man according to the occasion. [Col. 0981B] He wanted the price of his clothes raised beyond measure, taking offense if anyone lowered it.

One morning, when about to put on new stockings, he asked his chamberlain how much they had cost. When the man replied, “Three shillings,” the king, indignant and raging, said: “Son of a whore, since when does a king have stockings of so paltry a price? Go and bring me some bought for a mark of silver.” The man went and brought much cheaper stockings, and lied that they had been bought for the price commanded. “Yet,” said the king, “these suit royal majesty.” From then on the chamberlain set the price of the king’s clothing as he pleased, trafficking thereby extensively for his own advantage.

At last, exhausted by expenses, the king turned his mind to plunder, assisted in this crime by Ranulf the clerk, raised from the lowest rank of men to the highest by his eloquence and cunning. At his instigation, the sacred offices of churches were sold whenever their pastors died. For as soon as the death of any bishop or abbot was heard, the king’s clerk was immediately sent there to record in writing everything found and to bring all subsequent revenues into the royal treasury. Any person was appointed in place of the deceased, not according to proof of character but according to proof of money.

Troops of effeminate men and herds of gluttons followed the court, so that a certain wise man rightly said: “The court of the king of England is not a lodging-place of majesty, but a brothel of catamites.” It belongs to the disgrace of that time that Archbishop Anselm tried to correct these things, but, abandoned by the support of his suffragans, voluntarily departed, yielding to the wickedness of the age. When he was on the point of sailing and waited for the winds in harbor, by the king’s order [Col. 0981D] he was stripped like a public robber: all his bags and packs were brought out and searched.

The Jews whom his father had transferred from Rouen to London, when they approached him on a certain feast day with gifts, he dared to encourage to fight against Christians, declaring that, if they won, he would join their sect. The matter was therefore handled with great fear by bishops and clergy, who in pious concern feared for the Christian faith. The Jews gained nothing from this contest except disgrace, although they repeatedly boasted that they had been defeated not by argument but by faction.

When his brother Robert wished to undertake the journey to Jerusalem, Normandy was mortgaged to him [Col. 0982A] for ten thousand marks of money. Therefore an edict imposing an unbearable levy ran throughout all England. When bishops and abbots frequently came to the king to complain of this, he replied: “Do you not have chests fashioned of gold and silver, full of the bones of the dead?” Thus they were compelled to strip the shrines of saints, despoil crucifixes, and melt down chalices—not for the use of the poor, but for the royal treasury.

The hunting rights which he had at first permitted he prohibited so strictly that it was a capital offense to catch a stag. On account of these and similar acts, the nobles often conspired against him. William of Eu, accused of treason before the king and challenging his accuser to judicial combat, was blinded and castrated. This accusation implicated several innocent persons, one of whom was William of Alderie, a handsome man and the king’s spiritual kinsman. Ordered to be affixed to the gallows, he confessed to Bishop Osmund of Salisbury; he was scourged through all the churches of the town, his garments distributed among the poor, and went naked to the hanging, bleeding his delicate flesh by frequent kneelings upon stones. With bishop and people following to the place of punishment, he said: [Col. 0982B] “So may God help my soul and deliver it from evils, as I am innocent of the matter of which I am accused.”

Having heard of the dispute between Pope Urban and Guibert of Ravenna, he withheld the payment owed to the Roman See, though he was more inclined to Guibert’s favor. This was the first cause of the dissension between him and Anselm.

In the second year of his reign, on the third Ides of August, a great earthquake terrified all England, with the dreadful [Col. 0982C] marvel that all buildings sprang apart at a distance and immediately settled again into their former condition. A shortage of every kind of produce followed, and grain ripened so late that the harvest was scarcely stored by the feast of St Andrew. In his fourth year there was a disturbance of lightning and violent whirlwinds. On the Ides of October at Winchcombe, a blow sent from heaven struck the side of a tower with such force that the weakened material made an enormous opening, about the size of a human body, at the junction of the roof. Entering through it, it shattered a very large beam throughout the church and cast down the head and right leg of the crucifix, and the image of St Mary. An intolerable stench followed. At last the monks, boldly rushing in, drove away the enemy’s illusions by sprinkling holy water. There was also a conflict of mutually opposing winds, coming from the south-east, on the sixteenth Kalends of November; in London it destroyed more than six hundred houses. Churches collapsed along with houses, boundary-walls with walls. The same fury of winds likewise lifted the roof of the church of St Mary, called “at the Arches,” and two men there were crushed. Timbers and beams were borne through the air, to the amazement of those standing far off and the terror of those standing near. Four beams, twenty-six feet long, were driven together into the ground with such force that scarcely four feet remained above it—a marvellous sight, how they had broken through the hardness of the public roadway—set there in the same order in which the builder had placed them in the roof. Because they obstructed passers-by, they were cut down level with the ground, since they could not otherwise [Col. 0983A] be pulled out. In his fifth year, the same violence of lightning at Salisbury completely shattered the roof of the church tower and damaged much material, on the fifth day after Osmund, bishop of illustrious memory, had dedicated it.

(1093.) Conrad, son of Emperor Henry, went over into Italy to his father’s opponents. This greatly obscured his father’s previous victories and weakened his strength. On the Kalends of August, at the first hour of night, a fiery staff was seen borne through the sky from south to north.

**WILLIAM.** In the sixth year of King William, there was such a flood in England, from the abundance of rains, as no one remembered. Soon, when winter came, the rivers froze so hard that horses, carts, and wagons could cross them. (1094.) When the frost thawed, bridges were broken by the force of the [Col. 0983B] masses of ice. Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, died; Walcher succeeded him, but after Walcher himself was driven from the bishopric, Manasses was ordained bishop. In France and Germany there was a grave mortality among humankind. In Italy, those who had gone over to the emperor from his enemies, after he returned to France, almost all crossed back again to his enemies and fortified against him the strongholds which he had captured.

**WILLIAM.** In the seventh year of King William, agriculture failed because of the taxes which the king, being in Normandy, had imposed. When agriculture failed, famine followed; as it increased, a mortality among men followed, so frequent that the dying lacked care and the dead burial. At that time also the Welsh, made savage against the Normans, ravaged the district of Chester and part of that of Salisbury, and seized England by arms.

## 1095

**SIGEBERT.** The famine long in preparation grew most severe, and the year became calamitous: many suffered hunger, while poor people grievously harassed the wealthier through thefts and arson. Amid a strong hurricane of winds, an earthquake also occurred at midnight on the fourth Ides of September. The king of the English was troubled by his brothers in Normandy and England. In many parts of the world, on the second Nones of April at about dawn, very many stars were seen to fall from heaven to earth.

Among these, when a certain man in France marvelled that one very large star had fallen to earth, he marked the place where it seemed to fall; when he poured water there, he marvelled still more to see smoke issuing from it with the sound of boiling. Henry, count of Louvain, was killed. The king of Hungary died. In the county of Namur we saw ash-baked bread as though stained with blood. Pope Urban, holding councils through Burgundy and France, renewed and confirmed Hildebrand’s decrees. He excommunicated King Philip of France, who, while his own wife was alive, had taken to himself the living wife of another.

**WILLIAM.** Fulk was an early count of Anjou. As an old man he went to Jerusalem. There, after binding two servants by oath to do whatever he commanded, he was dragged naked in public to the Lord’s Sepulchre, while Turks watched. One put a wooden rope around his neck; the other drove his stripped back with whips. Amid this he cried: “Receive, Lord, wretched Fulk, your perjurer, your fugitive.” Yet he returned home peacefully, though against his desire. Some years later he had a son, Geoffrey, surnamed Martel, “the Hammer.” He had assumed this surname because he seemed, by a certain good fortune, to crush all who opposed him. For he captured his lord, the count of Poitou, in open war, bound him in iron chains, and forced him to accept the terms of an ignoble peace: to cede the city of Bordeaux and its territory, and to pay an annual tribute from his remaining lands. The captive died after three days because of the injury from the iron and the lack of food. Martel married his stepmother, taking his brothers into his guardianship. Soon, entering the territories of Count Theobald [Col. 0984B] of Blois, he besieged Tours and Theobald himself within it. Captured and confined in prison, Theobald renounced the city for himself and all his heirs forever.

At his death this Geoffrey gave the county to Geoffrey, his sister’s son, who was simple and unwarlike. His brother Fulk seized the duchy; he was surnamed Rechin, because, often grinding his teeth at his brother’s simplicity, he finally deprived him of his rank and held him in perpetual custody. This Fulk had a wife who left him and married Philip, king of France. Philip was so captivated by love of her that she commanded him in everything, though he wished to command everyone else. In the end he endured for several years being pointed out by every finger and excommunicated by the whole Christian world on account of her lust. The sons of this Fulk were Geoffrey, Martel, and Fulk. The first was killed by the plots of his own people.

At that time, in the city of Nantes, there were two clerics, not yet permitted by their age to be priests, abundantly trained in letters and greatly attached to one another. They made a pact: whichever of them died first would appear to the other, awake or asleep, within thirty days; they gave and received a solemn bodily pledge. Not long afterward one died. On the thirtieth day he stood before the other, who was awake and engaged, I know not in what work, dead in appearance, bloodless and pale. Addressing the living man first, he said: “Do you recognize me?” “I recognize you,” the other replied, “and I wonder why you delayed so long.” The dead man first excused his delay: “At last,” he said, “at last [Col. 0984D] I come; and, if you wish, my coming will benefit you, but it is wholly without profit to me. For I have been assigned to everlasting punishments.” “I,” said the other, “will help you by prayers, fasts, and many alms.” But he replied: “God’s judgments admit no repentance. In hell, while the pole turns the stars and the sea beats the shores, I shall be punished for my crimes. Though the whole world sought remedies for me, I should nevertheless suffer eternal and innumerable kinds of punishments. And so that you may recognize one of my innumerable punishments—here is one.” He stretched out a hand dripping with a festering sore. “Does it seem light to you?” he asked. When the other said that it seemed light to him, the dead man bent his fingers into his palm and cast three drops of flowing corruption upon him. Two struck his temples and one his forehead; they pierced the skin as though with a fiery dart, making a hole large enough to admit a nut. The living man testified by a cry of pain that this was a great punishment. “This,” said the dead man, “will remain with you as long as you live: a grievous proof of my punishments and, unless you neglect it, a singular reminder of your salvation. Go, then, while you can; change both your clothing and your mind; become a monk at Redon, under St Melanius.” When the living man would not answer this proposal, the dead man fixed him with the force of his gaze: “If, wretch, you hesitate to convert, read these letters.” Saying this, he stretched out a hand inscribed with grim characters. In them Satan and all the host of hell gave thanks from Tartarus to the whole ecclesiastical body, because, although that body in no respect lacked its pleasures, it permitted so great a number of souls subject to it to descend to hell through neglect of preaching as no former age had seen. After these words, the appearance of the speaker vanished. The hearer sold everything, gave it to the poor, went to St Melanius, became a monk there, and lived an excellent religious life.

**WILLIAM, likewise.** In this year, that is, in the year of the Lord 1095, Pope Urban came to France and held a council at Clermont. Among other decrees it was determined:

- That bishops, abbots, or any member of the clergy should not receive any ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of princes or any lay persons.
- That clerics should not hold prebends in two cities or churches.
- That no one should at once be abbot and bishop.
- That no ecclesiastical dignity should be sold or bought by anyone.
- That no person in any sacred order should engage in sexual commerce; that ecclesiastical dignities should be removed from those who knowingly had bought them either themselves or through their parents.
- That those who did not know such purchase to have been forbidden by the canons should be pardoned.
- That no layman from the beginning of Lent, and no cleric from Quinquagesima until Easter, should eat meat.
- That on Easter Saturday the office should be celebrated only after the ninth hour.
- That from Advent until the octave of Epiphany; from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter; from the first day of the Rogations until the octave of Pentecost; and at every season from Wednesday at sunset until Monday at sunrise, . . . should be observed.
- That whoever seized a bishop should be held altogether outlawed.
- That whoever seized men in sacred orders or their servants should be anathema.
- That whoever seized the goods of dying bishops or clerics should be anathema.
- That no one should be elected bishop unless he were a priest, deacon, or subdeacon and possessed the distinction of legitimate birth—except in extreme necessity and with the pope’s permission.
- That sons of priests or concubines should not be advanced to the priesthood unless they had first entered religious life.
- That one who fled for refuge to a church or to a cross should, with immunity from bodily mutilation, be handed over to justice or, if innocent, set free.
- That each church should retain its own tithes, and that they should not pass to another.
- That a layman should neither sell nor retain tithes.
- That no payment should be demanded for the burial of the dead.

At the same council the pope excommunicated the king of France and all who called him king or lord and obeyed him. He likewise excommunicated that accursed wife of his and those who called her queen or lady, until they made amends, so that each should separate from the other. Likewise he excommunicated Guibert of Ravenna, who called himself pope; Emperor Henry, who supported him; and all who agreed with them. After this he addressed the people, exhorting them to take up the cross, and among other things said: “As Solomon says: ‘Nothing is more timid than wickedness, nothing more toilsome’ [Wisdom 17]. Now labour and fear alike are required of you for a better reward. Do you not know that life is calamity for men, but death happiness? For death hastens the good to their homeland and cuts off wickedness from the wicked.”

**SIGEBERT.** There was an eclipse of the moon on the third Ides of February, and again on the third Ides of August. Western peoples, grieving that the holy places at Jerusalem were being profaned by the pagans and that the Turks had already overrun a large part of Christendom, were moved by one inspiration. Encouraged by one another through many signs shown to them, leaders, counts, powerful men, nobles and commoners, rich and poor, free and enslaved, bishops and clerics, old men and young, boys and girls—all with one mind and under no compulsion—came together from every direction: from Spain, Provence, Aquitaine, Brittany, Scotland, England, Normandy, France, Lotharingia, Burgundy, Germany, Lombardy, Apulia, [Col. 0986C] and other kingdoms. Marked and armed by the power and sign of the holy cross, they prepared to avenge upon the enemies of the Christian name the injury done to God. And the more inclined each had formerly been to practice worldly soldiery, the more readily he now became willing to practice God’s soldiery voluntarily. Meanwhile a most firm peace having been established everywhere, they first attacked the Jews in the cities where they lived and compelled them to believe in Christ. Those unwilling to believe they stripped of goods, slaughtered, and expelled from the cities. Some Jews, led by zeal to maintain the law of their ancestors, slaughtered one another; others pretended belief for a time and later returned to Judaism. Prominent in this warfare against God’s enemies were Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia; his brothers Eustace and Baldwin; Anselm of Ribemont; Baldwin, count of Metz; Robert, count of Flanders; Stephen, count of Blois; Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of France; Robert, count of the Normans; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; and Bohemond, duke of Apulia.

**WILLIAM.** Never had so many peoples agreed upon one purpose. Their number surpassed human expectation, although it was reckoned at six million, all of whom were proceeding to Jerusalem. Raymond was the son of William, a very ancient count of Toulouse, whose wife Almodis, married many times, first married the count of Arles and then this William. After bearing him two sons, she chose the count of Barcelona in preference to him. At his death this William gave the county of Toulouse to his son William and that of Cahors to Raymond. Raymond afterward added by his prowess Arles, Narbonne, Provence, and Limoges; he later also bought Toulouse from his brother. By one of his concubines he had a son, Bertrand, whom he appointed his heir. In his old age he married the daughter of the king of Tarragona. On this Jerusalem expedition he was the first of all laymen to receive the cross, encouraged by the bishop of Le Puy, who had undertaken Urban’s responsibility in preaching after Urban himself had died on the journey to the Council of Clermont. There was also among the others the count of Maurienne, a man notorious for every bodily obscenity, and for that reason no less inexorable toward the offenses of others. For his father’s slight offense, he took a little boy as a hostage and blinded him, tearing out the poor child’s eyes with his accursed nails.

**SIGEBERT.** A comet appeared in the west throughout the first week of October. Excessive flooding prevented autumn sowing, and barrenness of the earth’s crops followed. The army of God attacked the borders of the pagans and acted bravely. Its first battle was at the bridge over the river Farfar, on the ninth Kalends of March, where many Turks were killed. Its second battle was at Nicaea on the third Nones of March; there the pagans too were defeated, and Nicaea and Laodicea were captured. Although there were more than three hundred thousand armed men in the Christian army, such abundance of every necessity was available to them that a ram sold for one coin and an ox for scarcely twelve coins.

**WILLIAM.** For forty years the Turks had possessed Bithynia, a part of Asia Minor called Romania by the Romans. Its lord was then Soliman. But after abandoning their bows, the Turks fled for three continuous days. The Soldan among the Persians is what Augustus is among the Romans: ruler of the whole East and of all Saracens. Their empire—that is, the empire of the Persians—lasts so long, I think, because that people, little warlike and lacking vigorous blood, does not know how to unlearn the servitude once accepted, being ignorant, as Lucan says, that swords were given so that no one might be a slave. In this year, which was the tenth year of King William II of England, a comet appeared on the Kalends of October for fifteen days, casting a larger tail toward the east and a smaller one [Col. 0987D] toward the east-south-east. Other stars also appeared, as though shooting darts at one another. In the same year Anselm, primate of England, fled the darkness of error and went to Rome.

Baldric, formerly abbot of Bourgueil and archbishop of Dol, who wrote a history of Jerusalem, says that the Turks at Jerusalem allowed the Lord’s Sepulchre to be maintained with somewhat greater honour—not because they cared greatly about the Christian religion, but because by this means they satisfied their own interests and greed through the offerings of visitors. They had already extended their dominion as far as Antioch. He also says that the bishop of Le Puy, named Aimar, was the first of all at the Council of Clermont itself to receive Pope Urban’s permission to go to Jerusalem. He further says that, in the year of the Lord 1095, on the day before the Nones of April, Wednesday, the twenty-fifth day of the moon, innumerable observers in Gaul saw such a flight of stars that, had they not shone, they would have been thought hail because of their density; some thought they had fallen. Some interpreted their motion as the movement of Christendom. For in the following year both the synod at Auvergne was held and the expedition begun.

Before this synod, however, Pope Urban had held a general council at Piacenza. The remedy exceeded its measure, because the desire to go to Jerusalem came upon some more strongly than it should have done. Many hermits, recluses, and monks, unwisely leaving their dwellings, set out on the expedition. Some departed with their abbots’ permission, granted for the sake of prayer; but more withdrew by flight. Many of the common people boasted and displayed crosses miraculously imprinted upon themselves; certain little women presumed the same thing. This was discovered to be wholly false. Others applied hot iron to themselves in the form of a cross, either from the contagion of boasting or for the display of good will. Tancred, Bohemond’s nephew, and Richard of the Principate followed Bohemond, son of Robert Guiscard and brother of Duke Roger.

In the first two battles, the Turks prevailed over a people without king or commander. The first was at the castle of Exerogorga, which the Christians entered empty of all inhabitants but full of every provision. Whether the inhabitants had left it from fear or strategy was uncertain. The spring and well supplying the castle lay outside it. When these were taken away from the Christians, a certain Rainald, whom they had made their leader, conspired with the Turks to betray his brethren to them, if he could, and to defect to them. Many there became apostates; others were either shot at as targets, sold, or carried away captive. The Christians suffered this first persecution on the third Kalends of October. When the Turks heard that Peter the Hermit and Walter, surnamed “Pennyless,” were in a city named Civetot near Nicaea, they marched against them. Running up, they encountered Walter and killed him with many others. Peter had already returned to Constantinople, because the quarrelsome people would not obey [Col. 0988D] him. The Turks besieged and captured the castle of Civetot, and killed or captured the Christians found there. The Christians suffered this likewise in October.

While this was occurring, Godfrey with his brothers Baldwin and Eustace, and Baldwin of Le Bourg with their troops, were approaching Constantinople by way of Hungary; the bishop of Le Puy and Count Raymond were travelling through Slavonia. Hugh the Great, Count Robert of Flanders, and the other Robert, count of Normandy, went ahead to Rome with their men and came into Apulia. When Bohemond heard the news of their arrival, after examining each man’s prowess and insignia, he ordered a fine cloak brought to him. Cutting it into pieces, he distributed a cross to each of his men and retained one for himself. Emperor Alexius of Constantinople was plotting evil against the army of God.

They came to Castoria, where they celebrated Christmas. From there they came to Palagonia, a most strongly fortified castle of heretics, full of every good thing. Having utterly destroyed it, they reached the river Vardar. There Tancred with his men put the emperor’s soldiers to flight, killed some, and brought others bound to Bohemond. This battle occurred on Ash Wednesday. From there they came to the city of Serra, where they had a sufficient market. There Bohemond made friendships with two Corpalatii. From there they came to the city of Cusa on Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper. They arrived at Nicaea on the day before the Nones of May. The city was besieged for seven weeks and three days, and at last captured and restored by the Christians to Emperor Alexius, who had received peacefully the Turks who had fled from it to him.

From there the army of God reached a certain bridge. On the third day the Turks displayed innumerable forces: Saracens, Angulans, Persians—three hundred and sixty thousand—and innumerable Arabs. Many thousands of barbarians were slain there. William the marquis, Tancred’s brother, fell there, as did Geoffrey of Mont-Scabieux and many others. The Turks boast that they are descended from the stock of the Franks and that their ancestors departed from Christianity; and that by nature none but themselves and the Franks ought to wage war. This battle occurred on the Kalends of July. In their tents were found very much gold and silver, horses, oxen, [Col. 0989C] camels, mules, rams, donkeys, and abundant furnishings.

Soliman, son of the elder Soliman, fleeing Nicaea, found ten thousand Arabs and persuaded them to flee. Coming to cities and castles inhabited by Syrian Christians, he deceitfully told them, “We have defeated the Franks,” and thus his men were admitted within their gates. Entering their houses and churches, they plundered them, took away all that they desired, and carried off their sons and daughters. Hearing this, the Christians pursued them and came to Iconium, then to the city of Heraclea, which, after expelling the Turks, surrendered itself to them. Then Tancred and Baldwin, brother of Duke Godfrey, came to Tarsus and captured it. There, through a dispute, Baldwin held Tarsus alone. Not long afterward two cities, Adana and Mamistra, and many castles were restored to Tancred. The city of Alfia was restored to other nobles. A certain knight native to that land, named Simeon, requested it and received it. Then they came to Caesarea in Cappadocia, which had been destroyed down to the ground, though its ruins still showed what it had been. Then they came to the beautiful and wealthy city of Plastentia, which the Turks had besieged for three weeks but could not capture. It immediately opened itself to the Christians. Peter of Alfia requested it and received it. Then they came to Copon, a noble and wealthy city, which surrendered to them. Then they entered the valley of Antioch. Peter of Roa, separating from the others, entered the valley of [Col. 0990A] Rugia; he overcame and put to flight very many Turks found there, and the Armenians surrendered to him the city of Ruzah and certain castles. The main army, however, came with great difficulty into the valley of Antioch, metropolis of Syria.

**WILLIAM.** After Rome, Constantinople, and Alexandria, this city was ranked fourth among all cities in the world. There is a river there, now called the Fannus, formerly the Orontes, which flows into the sea twelve miles from the city. With its swift currents, made colder by their very force, it refreshes the city with a healthful moderation of air and brings provisions to its inhabitants by ship. It mocks the perseverance of besiegers for however long a time. Moreover, the city itself is defended by walls and made inaccessible by mountains. The church of St Peter and the church of Blessed Mary remained unharmed as long as the Turks were there.

**BALDRIC.** Bohemond first besieged it from three gates on the third Kalends of November, Wednesday. There were many Armenians and Syrians in the city, Christians indeed but subject to the Turks. Pretending to flee, they boldly went out to the camps as beggars, explored the plans of the camp, and brought them back into the city. This greatly harmed the Christians. In the camp such a famine arose that a donkey-load sold for eight *purati*, worth 120 shillings in denarii. William the Carpenter and Peter the Hermit secretly fled. Tancred found and seized them; after reviling them disgracefully, he forced them to return. The fifth battle took place before Antioch, in which many Turks were killed and their horses captured. In that battle there were no Turkish infantrymen, but all were cavalry. One hundred heads of the slain were sent to the envoys of the Emir of Babylon. This battle took place on the Ides of February, Tuesday before Ash Wednesday. Moreover, in another battle the Turks killed more than a thousand Christians. In the sixth battle the Turks were again defeated; twelve Turkish princes, whom they call *adnatalii*, and fifteen hundred very brave soldiers, defenders of the city, died. The Christians sent four packhorses laden with the heads of the slain to the port where the envoys from Babylon were. Tancred seized the Armenians and Syrians who were carrying abundant necessities into the city and took everything from them. Thus famine arose in the city.

[Col. 0990D] **SIGEBERT.** Twenty-one monks from the monastery of Molesme, together with Robert, father of that monastery, came to Cîteaux. Relying upon the counsel and strengthened by the authority of the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and then legate of the Apostolic See; the religious man Walter, bishop of Chalon; and Duke Odo of Burgundy, they began to establish in the wilderness they had found an abbey. The aforesaid Robert was appointed abbot by the bishop of Chalon, and the others, under him, established stability in that place. But not long afterward Robert himself was recalled by the monks of Molesme and was returned to Molesme by Pope Urban’s command and with the permission of Walter, bishop of Chalon; Alberic was substituted in his place.

**WILLIAM.** In the time of William II, king of England, the Cistercian religious order began. It belongs to England’s glory that she produced such a man, who was the founder and mediator of this order. His name was Harding; from boyhood he was a monk at Sherborne. Later, weary of those garments, he went to Scotland and then to France, where he studied for several years. He then set out for Rome with a clerical companion; as they went and returned, they sang the entire Psalter every day. Returning afterward to Burgundy, he received the tonsure at Molesme, a new and large monastery. There, when certain practices were proposed to him which were not drawn from the Rule, he began to examine their rationale. He disputed for so long with one person and another concerning some superfluities that he brought the abbot himself and twenty-two others around to his view. Thus they came to Cîteaux, a place formerly salt-marsh; and there they remained with the support of the archbishop of Vienne, who is now pope. At last the abbot who had come with them was summoned by his own monks and returned to them, seemingly compelled but willingly. All who had come with him from Molesme returned with him, except eight, who appointed as their abbot a certain Alberic from among themselves and as prior Harding, who was also Stephen.

**BALDRIC.** In besieged Antioch there was a certain Turkish emir named Pyrrhus, who had made a treaty of friendship with Bohemond through trustworthy intermediaries. Attracted by Bohemond’s reputation, Pyrrhus sent him his son as a hostage and surrendered the three towers which he held; thus the city was captured. Cassian, commander of the Turks, hid among the fugitives; Armenians cut off his head and brought it to Bohemond. Corbaran, leader of those who had assembled to aid Antioch, having obtained from the caliph—the apostolic head of his people—permission to rage against the Christians, had gathered innumerable peoples to himself, including the emir of Jerusalem and the king of Damascus. As these approached Antioch, Solisadol, son of Cassian, gave Corbaran a most strongly fortified stronghold commanding the city. Having done this, Corbaran besieged the city. His hundred-year-old mother came to him, a diviner and sorceress, predicting that, if he fought the Christians, they would overcome him.

Out of fear of the Saracens, William [Col. 0991D] of Gentamenil and his brother Alberic, Guy Trissel, and Lambert, perpetually poor of his own resources, fled from the Christian army by lowering themselves over the wall; thereafter they were called “Rope-Walkers.” Famine prevailed in the city. But the Lord appeared to a certain priest with his most blessed Mother and the apostle Peter; a cross shone above the Lord’s head. He reproached the Christians for the benefits he had bestowed upon them and for their ingratitude in fornicating with women. When he threatened to take vengeance on them and repay them according to their evils, the Mother of Mercy and blessed Peter fell at his feet, begging him not to be angry with all for the offenses of a few. Yielding to their prayers, he said to the priest:

[Col. 0992A] “Go and tell my people: Remove from among yourselves the brothel and prostitution and every abuse; and within five days, if you return to me, I will turn to you and provide suitable help for you. Meanwhile, let them daily chant:

> [Note: [Col. 0991D] Responsory of the Church.]  
> Our enemies have gathered together and glory in their strength. Break their power, O Lord, and scatter them, that they may know that there is no other who fights for us except you, our God. Destroy them in your power and cast them down, O Lord, our protector.

Saint Andrew the apostle also appeared to a certain pilgrim named Peter, showing him the place in the church of St Peter where the Saviour’s lance was to be found. Not long afterward, fire from heaven was seen to fall by night into the Turks’ camp. A very poor and very small loaf of Byzantine bread was sold for a Byzantine coin. Horseflesh and donkey-flesh were valued at imperial coins. A hen was priced at fifteen shillings, an egg at two shillings, and a walnut at one denarius. They endured this continuous suffering for thirty-six days. Meanwhile Stephen, count of Blois, had withdrawn because of illness to Alexandretta, not far from Antioch, in order to recover. Everyone awaited his return because he was a man of counsel. But when he heard that the Turks had surrounded the city, he secretly climbed into the mountains and hurriedly departed in concealment, thinking that his men had perished or would shortly perish. Coming to the emperor, who was advancing with a large force of Greeks and Franks to aid [Col. 0992C] our people, he persuaded him to turn back. Later, touched by contrition of heart and shame, that same Stephen atoned for this offense and disgrace by returning from his homeland to Jerusalem; and thus he made satisfaction to all. Thirteen industrious and vigorous men dug from morning until evening and found the Lord’s lance buried very deep.

It now appears that the opinion advanced above by William of Malmesbury concerning Charlemagne’s lance is false—the claim that it was the very spear which, driven by a centurion’s hand into the Lord’s side, opened paradise to mortals. For this spear, newly found, had not been seen since the time of the apostles, as Sigebert says. How, by whom, or when it was buried there, I do not remember having read. [Col. 0992D] Yet I greatly wonder why William says that Charlemagne’s lance, whatever it was, was driven by a centurion’s hand into the Lord’s side, since John’s Gospel plainly says that one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance (John 19). “One of the soldiers,” it says, not “one of the centurions”—unless perhaps he was both soldier and centurion. But in the martyrology, under the Ides of March, we read of this saint: “At Caesarea, of blessed Longinus the soldier, who opened the Lord’s side with a lance.” And in his Acts we read:

> Longinus, the soldier who pierced the Lord’s side with a lance, served under the centurion who, standing by the cross, believed. When he had struck the side and saw the wonders that were [Col. 0993A] taking place, he beat his breast and cried out in a loud voice: “Truly this man is the Son of God.” Leaving military service, he believed, having heard from the apostles the faith which is in the Lord.

Therefore the lance was driven into that Lord’s side not by a centurion’s hand, but by the hand of Longinus the soldier; nor, after that, before this time was it in the use of any other person, prince or private man.

When the Christians left the city to fight Corbaran, a certain sweet little shower, like a dewy drop, fell upon them, gladdening horses and riders so greatly that the horses neighed and the riders’ spirits were exhilarated. The rain was so fine and slight that it could be felt rather than seen, like certain drops of dew. Not long afterwards an innumerable army was seen issuing from the mountains themselves, [Col. 0993B] mounted on white horses and carrying white banners in their hands. The leaders of this host were Saint George, Saint Demetrius, and Saint Mercurius, he who killed Julian the Apostate. The Turks, therefore, defeated, fled. There were taken many horses, sheep and oxen, and countless treasures, and these were brought back into the city.

This battle took place on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, on the eve of the apostles Peter and Paul. Hugh the Great was sent to Emperor Alexius, that he might take possession of Antioch and preserve the agreements inviolate. Not long afterwards the bishop of Le Puy died at Antioch. After this, the count of Saint-Gilles subjected to himself Albara, a considerable city of the Saracens.

[Col. 0993C] Below the city of Antioch are four rather high mountains; on one of them, namely the highest, is a castle which commands the whole city. Below lies the city, suitably built and surrounded by a double wall. The inner wall is broad and high, constructed of squared stones; on it are four hundred and fifty towers, adorned with handsome battlements and defended by projecting works. The outer wall is not of such height, but is nevertheless of admirable beauty. It contains three hundred and forty churches; it has a patriarch, to whose patriarchate one hundred and fifty-three bishops are subject. On the east it is enclosed by four mountains; on the west the river Farfar flows past the city walls. Eighty-five kings raised it to greatness in founding it, [Col. 0993D] the greatest and first of whom was Antiochus, from whom it took its name.

The Christians had besieged and taken it for eight months and one day. Afterwards, though the city had already been taken, the pagans held them under siege within it for three weeks. In that siege so great an army of pagans assembled that no one remembers having seen or heard of a more numerous one. The Christians rested there for five months and nine days.

After this they came to the wealthy city of Ma‘arrat, which was taken at evening on Saturday, the third day before the Ides of December. The Franks remained there for a full month and three days. There the bishop of Orange died. There the Christians suffered such severe hunger that they ate the flesh of Turks. [Col. 0994A] The count of Saint-Gilles, abandoning the dispute which he had with Bohemond concerning the city of Antioch, left Ma‘arrat with barefoot pilgrims on the Ides of January. The king of Caesarea made peace with them.

After this they plundered a certain castle of five thousand animals and much food; and the men of the castle gave the army horses, a great quantity of gold, and much money. From there they came to the exceedingly beautiful city of Cephalia, full of every good thing, which its inhabitants abandoned and fled. Having taken possession of it, the Franks came to a fertile valley, where they rested for twelve days. Then they found a castle empty of people but full of every good thing: wheat, wine, oil, flour, and barley. There they celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary. There the king [Col. 0994B] of the city of Carmel and the king of Tripoli sent their envoys to them; they rejected the latter’s gifts.

From there they came to the town of Arqa. There fourteen Christian knights defeated sixty Turks. Afterwards they made peace with the emir of Jebail. Then the king of Tripoli gave them three hundred pilgrims and granted them a market. After this they came to the city of Beirut, then to Sidon, then to Tyre, then to Acre, then to the Castle of Caiphas, and then near Caesarea, where they rested on Pentecost, the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

From there they went to Ramla, near which a venerable church is shown, in which the most precious body of blessed George had rested, where, held by pagans, he is said to have completed his martyrdom. There they restored a bishop anew, to whom they offered tithes of their possessions, [Col. 0994C] because he had nothing on which to live. Ramla is twenty-four miles from Jerusalem. But when they came to the place from which Jerusalem could be seen, they wept exceedingly for joy; and, falling on their knees in worship, they kissed the ground and besieged it on the seventh day before the Ides of June, a Tuesday.

## 1099

**SIGEBERT.** While the Christians were vigorously fighting the Turks and by warfare claiming their cities and castles for themselves, it happened near a very strongly fortified castle called Arqa, situated eight day-stages from Jerusalem, that many of them perished; and Anselm of Ribemont, struck on the head by a stone, died, repeating only three times after receiving the wound: “God, help [Col. 0994D] me.”

But the army of God, proceeding by divine instruction into the interior of Spain [Palestine], was refreshed by God’s generous hand, because the citizens and castle-holders of that region sent envoys beforehand to them with many gifts, and were even ready to surrender towns or cities to them. Having received assurances from these people, and having imposed tribute upon the cities, while many also of those who had withdrawn were meanwhile returning to them at Tyre, the Christians at last came to Jerusalem. While they laboured in besieging it, especially from lack of water, all, by common resolution, went barefoot every day around Jerusalem in prayer.

Therefore, on the eighth day of such humiliation, but the thirty-ninth of the siege, on the Ides of July, a Friday, Jerusalem was taken. In Solomon’s Temple and its portico, the Christians, joining battle with the pagans, [Col. 0995A] raged in slaughter against them so greatly that they rode in the blood of the slain up to their horses’ knees.

When it had been decided who should retain Jerusalem, and the princes were already discussing their return home, behold, the king of the Saracens came to Ascalon to fight them, with one hundred thousand horsemen and four hundred thousand infantry. When the army of the Lord, containing no more than five thousand horsemen and fifteen thousand infantry, met them—God fighting for his servants as they cried to him, and a cloud shielding them from the sun’s heat—the Saracens, terrified merely by the Christians’ charge, all fled after throwing away their arms. In this battle, fought on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, one hundred thousand pagans were killed. [Col. 0995B] At the gate of Ascalon about two thousand were suffocated. The number of those who perished in the sea and who were destroyed among the thorn-brakes of the forests is uncertain.

Jerusalem was taken about four hundred and sixty years after it had for the second time been captured and possessed by the Saracens under Emperor Heraclius.

**WILLIAM.** Mount Sion, enclosed within the city of Jerusalem, rises like a citadel. There the Lord’s Temple and the temple called Solomon’s Temple—built, it is uncertain on whose authority—were frequented with great devotion by the Turks. In the Lord’s Temple there stood an image of Mohammed. There was also the spacious church of the Holy Sepulchre, built in rounded workmanship by Constantine the Great; it had never suffered any injury from enemies of the faith, [Col. 0995C] I suppose through fear of the heavenly fire which, every year on the vigil of Easter, suddenly shines bright in the lamps. When this miracle began, or whether it existed before the time of the pagans, is known from the report of no history.

In the book of Bernard the monk, we read that 251 years ago, namely in the year of the Lord 970, he himself went to Jerusalem and saw that fire. He lodged in the hospice which Charlemagne ordered built there, and where he also assembled a library at immense expense. Bernard recalls such peace as Christians enjoyed under Saracen rule in Egypt and throughout those places that, if a traveller’s beast of burden, carrying necessities, happened to die or fail at the crossroads, the traveller could go unencumbered [Col. 0995D] to the nearest town to seek help, leaving his loads behind, and would find everything he had left untouched.

The first fifteen bishops of Jerusalem were circumcised; those who followed were uncircumcised. Gaius, the twenty-first bishop, was the first there to celebrate Easter according to Roman custom. In the time of Macarius, the twenty-ninth bishop, the Holy Cross was found there by Helena. Cyril, the forty-second bishop, established the churches of the Holy Sepulchre, Mount Calvary, Bethlehem, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Up to this Cyril, all were called bishops. After them patriarchs arose, the eighth of whom was Zacharias, in whose time Chosroes, king of the Persians, destroyed the churches of Judaea and Jerusalem. His army killed thirty-six thousand Christians. After him Modestus was appointed by Emperor Heraclius. After him came Sophronius, [Col. 0996A] in whose time the Saracens came and drove all Christians from Jerusalem, except the patriarch, whom they left there out of reverence for his holiness.

That was the time when the Saracens overran all Egypt and Africa, Judaea and Spain, and the Balearic Islands. Charlemagne took part of Spain from them; they have possessed the remainder and all the lands named up to the present day, now for about five hundred years. In the eighth place after Sophronius was Theodosius, whom the aforesaid monk Bernard says was carried off from his monastery, fifteen miles from Jerusalem, and made patriarch. He also says that Michael was then patriarch of Babylon over Egypt, the patriarchate having been transferred from Alexandria to [Col. 0996B] Babylon.

Again, eighth after him was Horestes, in whose time Achim, Sultan of Babylon and nephew of Patriarch Horestes, came. He sent his army into Jerusalem, destroyed all the churches, caused his uncle the patriarch to be taken to Babylon, and had him killed there.

After him came Theophilus, and after him Nicephorus. The latter built the present structure of the Holy Sepulchre, with the favour of Sultan Achim. After him came Sophronius, in whose time the Turks came to Jerusalem, killed all the Saracens, and gained possession of the city; the Christians, however, remained under Turkish rule. After him came Euthymius, [Col. 0996C] and after him Simeon, in whose time the Franks came, captured Jerusalem, and delivered it from the hands of the Turks and the king of Babylon.

Jerusalem was taken on the fifteenth day of July. A certain Syrian gave back a portion of the Lord’s wood which had been kept at home by hereditary succession. There Duke Godfrey, son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, was elected king; through his mother’s line he belonged to the lineage of Charlemagne. His mother Ida, daughter of the elder Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, had a brother Godfrey, surnamed Beocard. The wife of this Godfrey was Matilda the marchioness. Godfrey, Ida’s son, served Emperor Henry against Pope Hildebrand; and while Rome was being assaulted, he was the [Col. 0996D] first to break through the section of wall assigned to him.

Later, exhausted by excessive labour and suffering great thirst, he drank too much wine and contracted a quartan fever. But on hearing of the expedition to Jerusalem, he vowed that he would go there if God restored him to health. Once this vow had been made, his strength immediately flourished again completely. During the siege of Antioch, he cleft in two from the sides with a Lotharingian sword a Turk who had demanded single combat.
