One severed half, still twitching in armour, remained; the horse on which he sat carried away the other—so firmly had that Turk been seated on his horse. The same Godfrey met another Turk in like fashion and, striking his head with a swung sword, split him from crown to groin; with the same blow he completely cut through the saddle and the horse’s spine.

In the same siege, one of his soldiers, who had gone out to forage, was attacked by a lion and eventually killed while defending himself with his shield. Godfrey grieved so deeply [Col. 0997A] that he pierced the beast with a hunting-spear. Wounded, and raging more fiercely from pain, it rushed at him and, with the iron protruding from its wound, wounded his leg. He immediately disembowelled the beast with his sword.

In this year, which was the twelfth year of King William II of England, a sea-wave rose up the River Thames and drowned many villages with their inhabitants.

## 1100

**SIGEBERT.** Guibert and Urban, contending for the Roman papacy, each brought his contest to an end by dying. Rainerius, who became Pope Paschal, succeeded.

**MASTER HUGH.** In the year of the Lord 1108, in the seventy-sixth eighth indiction [the reading is uncertain]—that is, the sixteenth of Henry III—Paschal II, the one hundred and sixty-fifth pope, sat for eighteen years, five months, and seven days. [Col. 0997B]

**AUTHOR.** It should be known that this Henry was the third among the Henries, but the second among emperors. For the first Henry, as was said above, was not emperor but only king; therefore he says, “in his sixteenth year,” because this Henry III had in this year been emperor for sixteen years, although he had already reigned for forty-four.

**SIGEBERT.** King Godfrey dies.

**WILLIAM.** William was made king. He is said, through becoming unaccustomed to rest, to have revived an old fever. He reigned one year. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was buried beneath the rock of Godgothana. Asked concerning a successor, he named no one, but only said: “the man who was worthy.”

After him his brother Baldwin was elected king. Fulcher of Chartres, his chaplain, wrote in part the deeds of this Baldwin. But Robert, count of [Col. 0997C] Normandy, stained his lineage with an indelible blot. Although he was the son of a king and the kingdom of Jerusalem was offered him by the unanimous consent of all the nobles, he would not accept it, fearing hardship. On his return he married in Apulia a daughter of William of Conversano, of very beautiful appearance. By her he had a son, William, who died after a few years from an illness, they say, contracted through the contrivance of a concubine, by tightly binding her breasts to prevent an abundance of milk. At last Robert himself, having squandered everything through foolish liberality, was reduced to such poverty that he procured a precarious livelihood from townsmen, and was finally put in chains by his brother Henry.

In this year, which was the last year of the life of King William of England, [Col. 0997D] the devil visibly appeared to people in woods and remote places, addressing passers-by. Moreover, in the district of Berkshire, in the village of Hanstead, a spring flowed blood so copiously for fifteen consecutive days that it stained the neighbouring ford. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, with whom all religion alike had gone into exile, came in this year to Cluny. As he conversed there with Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the abbot replied that, on the preceding night, King William had been brought before God and condemned to damnation.

The same king, on the day before he perished, saw in sleep that he was letting blood from a phlebotomy wound and that a stream of blood stretched as far as heaven, so that it obscured the light. That same night a certain monk from overseas saw in a dream that the same king entered a certain church [Col. 0998A] proudly and insolently, as was his custom, looking disdainfully upon those standing about him. Then, gripping the crucifix fiercely with his teeth, he gnawed away its arms and almost severed its legs. The crucifix endured this for a long time, but finally kicked the king so that he fell backward. From the mouth of the king as he lay there issued such a flame that whirling masses of smoke licked even the stars.

When someone reported this dream to him, he replied: “He is a monk, and for money he dreams like a monk. Give him one hundred shillings.” That same day he was struck in the breast in a forest by an arrow shot by Walter Tirel, a certain knight from France, who had been trying to hit a stag and was standing near the king. He died in the year of the Lord 1100, the thirteenth of his reign, the forty-first of his life, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. In his time [Col. 0998B] he allowed no ecclesiastical council to be held. He kept saying that sacred offices belonged by right to his own authority. On the day he died, he held in his own hand three vacant bishoprics and twelve abbacies.

## 1101

**SIGEBERT.** William was succeeded in the kingdom by his brother Henry. Robert, count of Flanders, returning home from Jerusalem, brought with him the arm of Saint George the martyr, which he sent to the church of Anchin. Conrad, son of Emperor Henry, still in rebellion against his father, died in Italy. Emperor Henry defeated Henry of Limburg, who opposed him; after taking his castles he compelled him to surrender, but, when he had redeemed the emperor’s favour for a great sum, the emperor also granted him the duchy of Lorraine.

**WILLIAM.** King Baldwin was crowned at Bethlehem by Patriarch Daimbert on Christmas Day in the year 1101. [Col. 0998C] At that time there were scarcely four hundred knights in the entire Christian force, together with as many foot-soldiers, to guard Jerusalem, Ramla, Haifa, and Jaffa. That year the sacred fire on Easter Eve was delayed until the morning of the Lord’s Resurrection. But when one lamp at the Sepulchre had been divinely lit, all the other lamps throughout the church were immediately divinely kindled.

Afterwards Baldwin took Caesarea of Palestine. There the emir of the city and their bishop were captured; a Turk, called there Archudius, having been struck in the neck by a Christian’s fist, vomited up bezants. For men had concealed bezants inside their gums, women inside their private parts. [Col. 0998D] The same king afterwards subdued Tiberias, Sidon, Accaron, and all the coastal cities. The countess of Sicily came to Jerusalem to seek marriage with him, bringing with her infinite treasures. He indeed married her then, but later dismissed her because, as they say, a cancerous disease was consuming her genitals.

While Robert, count of Flanders, was troubling the city of Cambrai, Emperor Henry marched against him; and, having captured some of his castles, was compelled to return because of the severity of the approaching winter.

**BALDRIC.** While Bohemond of Antioch enjoyed every prosperity and brought all his neighbours under his control either by force or by affectionate allegiance, it happened in July that a certain Gabriel the Armenian [perhaps “Armenian”] offered to surrender himself and his city of Melitene to him. [Col. 0999A] While Bohemond was going with a few men to receive it, he was surrounded by the ambushes of a Turkish emir named Danishmend, and was captured and held not far from the aforesaid city.

## 1103

**SIGEBERT.** At Liège, after a general assembly had been held, Robert, count of Flanders, was received into the emperor’s favour.

**BALDRIC.** By God’s grace Bohemond was released from chains.

**WILLIAM.** This Bohemond, even as a boy, kept nothing for himself, but distributed even childish gifts. He went with his father to make war on Dyrrhachium. Since the townspeople boasted, trusting in their walls, that the city was called Dyrrhachium because it endured all sieges unafraid, Guiscard, Bohemond’s father, said: “I am called Durandus; therefore I shall endure [Col. 0999B] in the siege until I take the name away from the city, so that it shall henceforth be called not Dyrrhachium but Mollitum.” Terrified by the firmness of this reply, they immediately opened their gates to him.

Bohemond, after being captured and released, brought with him to Antioch the silver fetters in which he had been bound. Not long afterwards he came to Gaul, offering the chains to Saint Leonard. He married a daughter of the king of the Franks. Because of suspicion of a harmful drink, he kept a knife ready; when it was set before the face of one eating, sweat appearing on its handle revealed whether any definite poison had been added. After him his nephew Tancred ruled Antioch; Roger, son of Richard, succeeded Tancred.

**BALDRIC.** William, count of Poitou; Stephen, count of Blois, who had returned home from the siege of Antioch; Hugh the Great, who had returned home after Antioch was taken; Raymond, count of Provence, who after Jerusalem was taken had gone to Constantinople to the emperor [Col. 0999C]; Stephen, count of Burgundy; and many other noble and powerful men entered the borders of Romania with an innumerable army. Marching overland, subduing cities and castles, they were making for Jerusalem. Soliman the emir opposed them—the man from whom Nicaea had been taken by the first leaders of the expedition. He laid ambushes for them with an innumerable band of Turks.

Many women there perished by the sword; more were led away captive; many men were slaughtered or consigned to iron fetters. There the count of Poitou lost almost all his men, horses, mules, pack animals, [Col. 0999D] and almost everything that he had; at last he reached Antioch in mourning. Count Raymond, fleeing through byways with part of his army, barely escaped. Stephen of Blois, Stephen count of Burgundy, Hugh the Great, and Hugh of Lusignan, brother of Count Raymond, reached Tarsus by a remote route in another part of the army. There Hugh the Great died.

Other nobles, proceeding toward Jerusalem, took Tortosa, killed all the Saracens found there, and recovered somewhat from their spoils. Count Raymond remained at Tortosa and kept it for himself; this displeased the others because he knew the routes by which they were to pass. The others came to Jaffa with King Baldwin, who had gone out to meet them. [Col. 1000A] He led them to Jerusalem, where, after the Easter festival had been celebrated, they returned to Jaffa.

Then the count of Poitou, because he was poor, needy, and lacking everything, went home, embarking on a ship. The others also, wishing likewise to return home, entrusted themselves to winds and sea; but adverse wind compelled them to return to Jaffa. They were therefore at Jaffa with the king when the king was informed of the enemy’s attack upon the people of Ramla. Thinking that certain scouts had been sent out for plunder and could easily be intercepted, the king immediately mounted his horse and set out with a few men.

But Stephen, count of Blois, warned him not to go out heedlessly and without foresight and counsel. Angrily the king answered him that, even if Stephen and his companions were then in [Col. 1000B] France, he would not refrain from attacking them. He went out with a few men. The aforementioned counts immediately armed themselves and followed him with their troops. They had scarcely two hundred knights; the enemy had more than twenty thousand. Thus they were cut down by enemies on every side.

The king fled into Ramla. At night, attended only by an armour-bearer, he mounted a very swift horse called Gazelle because of its speed and made his way through the midst of the enemy to the mountains. Stephen of Blois and Stephen of Burgundy lost their heads. Hugh of Lusignan, Geoffrey of Vendôme, and many others were slaughtered there. Others were carried captive to Babylon. Of all the knights whom the king had brought out of Jaffa, scarcely three escaped: the king’s armour-bearer, Luithard, and the viscount of Jaffa. [Col. 1000C]

Not long afterwards King Baldwin, with Hugh of Tiberias, an excellent knight who had come to his aid, killed many Saracens near Jaffa; and in the same year they took the city of Accaron with the help of the Genoese and Pisans.

## 1104

A certain clerk of Vendôme, while studying in the schools at Lyons, saw in a vision by night a certain valley beneath a mountain, on top of which stood a most beautiful city. Its appearance delighted those who looked upon it exceedingly, so that whoever saw it could not be satisfied with the sight of it and strove in every way to discover how he might be able to reach it.

Meanwhile he saw a river running below, indeed around, the foot of the mountain. [Col. 1000D] As he walked around it, seeking a way to cross it, he saw on the riverbank twelve poor men, or fourteen, washing their tunics in the river. Among them was one clothed in a most white garment, very unlike the others, who helped them wash their tunics; after helping one, he went to help another.

Then the clerk who saw these things approached the one helping the others and said to him: “What people are you?” He replied: “These are poor people doing [Col. 1001A] penance and washing themselves from their sins; and I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Without my help neither these nor others can do good. This beautiful city which you see is paradise, where I dwell; and when each person has washed his tunic—that is, has performed penance—he shall enter it. You yourself have long sought the way by which one goes there; but no way other than this leads to it.”

Having said this, the clerk awoke from sleep and began to wonder at the vision. But not long afterwards, when he returned from school to his own country, he recounted this vision to the bishop of Chalon, with whom he was familiar. When he heard it, the bishop urged him to leave the world and enter religious life, commending to him above all the Cistercian order. He came to Cîteaux and found the place uncultivated and deserted, with brothers living among wild beasts.

At the gate of the monastery, made of wicker, there hung an iron hammer; by its sound those wishing to enter called the porter to the gate. Called by this sound, the porter [Col. 1001B] came outside to him and bowed in greeting. Looking at him, the clerk immediately recognized him as the very man whom he had seen among those washing their tunics in the river. He asked him to bring the abbot to him. Then the abbot and the whole community came to him; and the clerk recognized that he had seen all of them washing their tunics in the river. At once he fell at the abbot’s feet, begging with tears to be received. He was received and, not long afterwards, became prior.

## 1105

Henry, son of Emperor Henry, turned away from his father, turned away from him all whom he could, and rose against him under the pretext of improving the realm, contrary to right and justice. How shamefully he treated his father is shown by the letter which his father wrote to King Philip of France. [Note: [Col. 1001D] Sigebert reports this letter under the year 1106.]

At this time Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, flourished: a pupil of Berengar of Tours, an outstanding poet and prose stylist. He wrote a magnificent epitaph for Berengar himself in fifty-two verses; he composed this couplet about Rome:

> Happy city, if only that city lacked lords,  
> or, having lords, it were shameful to lack faith.

**WILLIAM.** At that time a deadly pestilence raged in the monastery of Fulda. It first seized the abbot and soon carried off many of the monks. At first the survivors feared for themselves and made more generous prayers and almsgiving. But as time went on, as is the nature of everyone, their fear gradually diminished and they omitted these things—especially the cellarer, who constantly cried out that the store of provisions could not meet so many expenses. He had always hoped for some relief through so many funeral processions; no hope remained, he said, if the dead consumed what the living could not manage. [Col. 1001D]

Thus, on a certain night, after he had long delayed sleep on account of necessary tasks, he finally slipped the bonds of delay and was going to the dormitory. Behold, he saw in the chapter house the abbot and all those who had died that year, seated in the order in which they had died. Trembling and eager to escape, he was forced back, rebuked, and scourged according to monastic custom. He heard the abbot speak to this effect:

> “It is foolish to desire profit from another’s death, since the lot of each person hangs under the same fate. It is also impious that, when a monk has spent his whole life [Col. 1002A] in the service of the Church, he should lack even the stipend of one year after death.
>
> “Know, therefore, that you will die very soon; but whatever is done for you shall be assigned to the benefit of the others from whom you withheld it. Go now, and correct others by your example, whom you corrupted by your words.”

He went away; and that he had seen no vain thing was shown both by his still-fresh wounds and by his approaching death.

At that time Walstan, bishop of Worcester, having been challenged on his slight learning, went outside the council in order to prepare his reply by more careful deliberation. With his mind freed from the uproar, he said to his companions: “Believe me, we have not yet sung the sixth hour.” But when his companions urged that they first do what they had come to do, since there would be more than sufficient time for chanting, he said: “The king and nobles, if they hear of this, will think they are being made a laughingstock. Believe me: we shall first perform God’s service, and afterwards conduct the litigation of men.” [Col. 1002B]

When the hour had been sung, without contriving any evasion or inventing any deceptive show of truth, he went immediately to the court. Although his supporters tried to restrain him, they could not persuade him. Indeed, as they feared for his case, he said: “Know for certain that I visibly see here the blessed archbishops Dunstan of Canterbury and Oswald of York, who today, protecting me by their prayers, will blunt the sharpness of the false speakers.” Accordingly, a blessing being given to a monk of very slight eloquence but knowledgeable in the Norman language, he pleaded the case and won it.

It should be known that Dorobernia is Canterbury itself; Durham Church is Lindisfarne. Chester was formerly called the city of the Legion, and its bishop was called the bishop of Lichfield, from a certain town. Furthermore, the bishop of Cirencester and of Selsey are the same; the bishop of Elmham and of Norwich are the same; the bishop of Sherborne and of Salisbury are the same. The bishop of Dorchester and of Lincoln are the same; the bishop of Wells and of Bath are the same.

The bishoprics of Ripon, Lichfield, Sidnacester, Dunwich—by some means unknown to me—and Hexham have long since perished through hostile violence. In the time of Edward the Simple, the bishoprics of Cornwall and Crediton were united, and the bishopric was transferred to Oxford. [Col. 1002C]

The archbishop of Canterbury, presiding in council, has the archbishop of York on his right and, beside him, the bishop of [Col. 1002D] Winchester; on his left is the bishop of London. If the archbishop of Canterbury cannot be present at a council, the archbishop of York shall preside, with the bishop of London on his right and the bishop of Winchester on his left. The rest recognize their seats according to the dates of their ordinations.

The archbishop of Canterbury has under him the bishops of Ireland and Wales. The archbishop of York has under his authority all bishops beyond the River Humber: the bishops of Ripon and Hexham, now extinct; Lindisfarne; Candida Casa, now called Whithorn; and all the bishops of Scotland and of Orkney.

## 1106

[Col. 1003A]

**BALDRIC AND SIGEBERT.** King Baldwin and the Jerusalemites crush an innumerable multitude of pagans in a glorious victory between Jaffa and Ramla.

SIGEBERT. On the fourth day before the Nones of February, a star was seen in the sky by day, from the third hour until the ninth, seeming to stand a cubit’s distance from the sun. While Emperor Henry was staying at Liège, his son came to Aachen; and, wishing to proceed to Liège against his father, on the Thursday of Holy Week he sent his knights ahead to seize the bridge at Visé, lest anyone oppose his approach. But when his father’s soldiers rushed to recover the bridge, the son’s soldiers were driven from it: some were captured, some drowned in the Meuse, and some killed. Among them Count Bruno was also killed. [Col. 1003B] Thus the son, advancing against his father, returned without glory. Although the people of Cologne kept faith with the emperor, their archbishop encouraged the emperor’s son against his father; Cologne was besieged and attacked, but not taken. Meanwhile Emperor Henry died at Liège.

WILLIAM. This Henry, Hildebrand’s enemy, was eloquent in speech, keen in intellect, and lavish in almsgiving. Sixty-two times he fought in pitched battle; many of his enemies ended their lives in a miserable death. One of his opponents, a powerful and factional man, while reclining at a banquet with his neck thrown back, was suddenly surrounded by mice, so that he could never escape. The number of these little beasts was so great that no one would have thought so many existed in any large province. Though they were long beaten back with clubs and benches, they could not be driven away. [Col. 1003C] They tried to harm no one but him alone, whom they pursued with their teeth and with a certain terrible clamour.

His servants carried him more than an arrow-shot out to sea, but in vain. For immediately such a flood of mice poured in that one might have sworn the marble was covered with straw. When they had begun to gnaw through the ship’s planking, and the water entering through the cracks threatened certain shipwreck, the servants turned the stern toward shore. The wretched man was put ashore and at once, torn wholly to pieces, satisfied the horrible hunger of the mice.

Yet I judge this less wonderful because it is certain that in Asian regions, if a leopard has bitten someone, a multitude of mice immediately comes to urinate upon the wounded person; and an unclean deluge of urine accompanies the man’s death. But if, through the diligence of those keeping them away, the danger has been avoided for nine days, the skill of physicians may be called in, and recovery will certainly follow. My informant saw a man wounded in this manner who, despairing of safety on land, put out to sea after weighing anchor. Without delay more than a thousand mice swam after him, enclosed—marvellous to relate—in pomegranate rinds whose pulp they had eaten; but, when the sailors made an uproar, they were drowned. For that Parent of all things created leaves nothing without an innate faculty, nothing harmful without a remedy. [Col. 1003D]

SIGEBERT. When Emperor Henry died, his son Henry succeeded him. Duke Henry, who, shifting in allegiance from the emperor to his son, had encouraged the latter by his counsel against his father, and then, returning from the son to the father, had fought against the son’s party, surrendered himself to the king’s son after the emperor’s death as guilty of treason against majesty. He was captured and committed to custody; yet he escaped from that confinement by his own ingenuity. His duchy was given to Count Godfrey of Louvain. [Col. 1004A]

(1107.) Henry the ex-duke, seeking to recover his duchy, occupied the town of Aachen against Duke Godfrey. Godfrey, unable to endure this, forcibly broke into the town, frightened its inhabitants away from Henry’s support, and captured certain powerful men, counts, and many nobles. Henry himself barely escaped with his sons by flight. The duke considered it unworthy to capture Henry’s wife. He brought the counts and more eminent persons whom he had captured into allegiance to himself, having won them over on the condition that they should serve under him. [Col. 1004B]

A battle took place at Tinchebray between Robert, Count of Normandy, and Henry, King of England.

Alberic, abbot of Cîteaux, died. After him Stephen, an Englishman by birth, a most ardent lover and most faithful imitator of religious life, poverty, and regular discipline, was made abbot. In his days all honoured the holiness of the Cistercian Order, but recoiled from its austerity; they drew back from imitating those whom they approached in devotion. Then thirty persons together—clerics and laymen alike, each noble and powerful in the world—entered the novices’ cell. Within twelve years he founded twenty abbeys.

Then the Charter of Charity was made by Stephen himself, abbot of Cîteaux, and twenty abbots, and was confirmed by the authority of the apostolic seal. [Col. 1004C] From that time they rejected from the Order frocks and pelisses, woollen garments and hoods, breeches, combs, coverlets, bed-straw, varied dishes in the refectory, fat, and everything contrary to the purity of the Rule. They also renounced churches, altars, offerings, tithes, the burial of other people, ovens, mills, villages, and peasants; because neither in the life of Saint Benedict nor in his Rule did they read that the saint possessed such things, that women entered his monastery, or that the dead were buried there, except his sister Saint Scholastica. [Col. 1004D] They said that blessed Benedict had commanded that a monk make himself a stranger to secular occupations.

They also said that the holy Fathers had divided tithes into four portions: one for the bishop; another for the priest or clergy; a third for guests coming to that church, or for widows and the sick; and a fourth for poor people having no other means of support, for the repair of the church. Since in this reckoning they could not find the place of the monk who holds his own land so as to live by working it himself and through his own cattle, they refused unjustly to usurp such things for themselves as though they were another’s right.

I remember hearing Master Peter the Chanter of Paris, a most just and learned man, relate the following concerning this Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux. One day his cellarer informed him that there was nothing in the monastery by which even that small number of brethren could be supported for one day. He replied: “Saddle two asses for us.” When they had been saddled, he took his lay-brother up with him and ordered him to beg bread door to door in one village for the use of the brethren, while he himself would do likewise in another; and, after they had done this, they were to meet at a place appointed by him. [Col. 1005A]

So it was done; and as they were returning to meet one another in the specified place, the abbot saw that the lay-brother’s sack was much fuller than his own. Smiling, he said: “Where did you beg? I see that you collected in a richer street than I did. Where, I ask you, did you collect? Who gave you more?” The lay-brother replied: “That priest whom you know very well almost filled my entire sack by himself.” Hearing this, the abbot groaned and said: “Woe to us! Why did you accept anything there? Did you not know that that priest was ordained there simoniacally, and that whatever he receives is leprosy and robbery? As the Lord lives, we shall taste absolutely nothing of all that he gave you. Far be it from us to eat his sin and incorporate it into ourselves!” He summoned the shepherds of the sheep, who were not far away, and emptied the lay-brother’s entire sack into the folds of their garments. [Col. 1005B]

1108.

SIGEBERT. Emperor Henry marched against Robert, Count of Flanders; but, since the pact of peace was more pretended than settled on both sides, he returned without effect. Bohemond, Duke of Apulia, having assembled an army from every quarter, prepared to invade the Byzantine Empire. In the diocese of Liège a sow gave birth to a piglet with a human face. A four-footed chick was also born. Emperor Henry marched against the Hungarians, but returned after making a treaty. Philip, King of the French, died; after him his son Louis reigned for twenty-nine years.

(1109.) Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, died, as did Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in the sixtieth year of his ordination, according to Gilo, who wrote his Life. A few days before Hugh died, a vision of saints appeared to a peasant labouring in a field. They were led by a certain royal lady, whose back he saw as she passed, but not her face. A certain old man followed that holy company. [Col. 1005C] He stopped and said: “Farmer, to whom belongs this field that you cultivate?” The man replied: “To blessed Peter and the lord abbot of Cluny.” The old man then said: “The field, the abbot, and the servant are mine. Hurry and tell my abbot to make provision for his lady whom he has nourished, for she will soon reach the end of this life. Tell him that Peter the Apostle has announced this to you. And proclaim that those who go before me are the Mother of God and the saints who minister to her.”

Hugh himself, at the point of death, remembered the anniversary commemorations of Archbishop Geoffrey and Abbot Guy, and reminded those who had forgotten them. His memory was so exact and his charity so great that he did not forget a brother’s welfare where scarcely anyone remembers his own. On the very night in which he died, he assigned the blessings of the readings to the readers. His last word to those around him was: “Bless [me].”

His body, in the chapter house, was clothed in white by the brethren, then washed first with water and afterward with wine. Finally, the whole great body was abundantly anointed three times with the little balsam that remained in a small vessel. It would scarcely have sufficed for his handsome head alone, had it not been multiplied by heavenly blessing and overflowed in the hands of those ministering. [Col. 1006A]

Blessed Denis appeared to a brother at Nogent, telling him to hurry to Cluny so that he could bid farewell to Saint Hugh, who was about to die. The brother said:

“I came, unhappy man that I am, but did not find the holy man as he departed. Yet what was denied to the body was granted to the spirit. For I saw heavenly beings mingled with mortals; and amid the company of monks I saw the Mother of God, the Star of the Sea, shining more brightly. Her presence so terrified and routed certain appearing archers, as a strong wind is accustomed to cast down autumn leaves. Among them Martin, the jewel of priests, and Benedict, the sun of abbots, escorted Saint Hugh’s spirit and placed it within a vineyard, beautiful and most fruitful, that he might rejoice there and remain there for a little while. [Col. 1006B]

“There Saint Hugh himself invited me as I watched: ‘Dearest, eat of the white clusters, which abound for us, and keep solemn fellowship with me. For I shall rest here only a little while, until a certain swelling subsides which I contracted in my dusty feet during my long circuit of the earth. But when my steps are immediately healed and worldly dust has been shaken off, I shall pass free to higher things. Tell my successor Pons to guard the treasures of humility and innocence; to regard the needs of all as his own; to devote himself to mercy; and wisely to order the zeal of the monastic Order according to my example. For by acting manfully in this manner, he will obtain help from God, who does not abandon those who hope in him.’” [Col. 1006C]

On the same night in which the blessed Father fell asleep in the Lord, an abbot saw in a vision two beds handsomely adorned, lifted to the stars by the hands of angels. He heard voices on high saying: “By merit of their lives we shall place two heroes, reformers of themselves and of the world, upon gold-radiant couches: namely, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Abbot of Cluny, who are fathers of many sons in glory.” These two indeed died at almost the same time. [Col. 1006D]

AUTHOR. Concerning the abbots of Cluny from the first down to this Hugh, these verses were composed:

> Berne came first in rank; Odo stands more blessed in honour.  
> From these arose holy Majolus, the model of men,  
> scarcely restraining his burning spirit with fire.  
> Then sacred Odilo was sent from the coasts of Auvergne,  
> gentler in disposition than fierce in authority.  
> Next comes Hugh, using the reins with discernment,  
> later in order, first in usefulness.

SIGEBERT. In this year many were afflicted with sacred fire, their limbs becoming black like coals.

AUTHOR. Three scourges are customarily assigned to three regions: famine to the English, fire to the French, leprosy to the Normans. Yet in the territory of Beauvais the punishment of fire is very rarely known to occur; this, they assert, was granted by God to blessed Gummarus as a special gift. [Col. 1007A]

1110.

SIGEBERT. In June a comet appeared, directing its rays toward the south. Many inferred that this sign portended King Henry’s future expedition toward Italy.

(1111.) King Henry went to Rome to settle the discord that existed between kingship and priesthood. It had begun under Pope Gregory VII [Note: [Col. 1007D] See what we noted above, under the year 1074, concerning Sigebert’s invectives against Gregory VII.] and, stirred up by his successors Victor and Urban, and more than all by Paschal, had become a scandal to the whole world. For the king, wishing to employ the authority, custom, and authentic privileges of the emperors who, from Charlemagne onward, had ruled for more than three hundred years under sixty-three popes and had lawfully bestowed bishoprics and abbeys by staff and ring, asserted this as his right. [Col. 1007B]

Against this authority of their predecessors the popes decreed by synodal judgment that a bishopric, any ecclesiastical dignity, or investiture could neither be nor ought to be conferred by staff or ring from a lay hand; and those who received a bishopric or another investiture belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction in this manner were excommunicated. Principally for this reason the king advanced toward Rome; and he forcefully crushed any Lombards who in any way wished to resist him.

MASTER HUGH. In the year of the Lord 1111, the twelfth of Pope Paschal, Henry IV ruled among the Germans. In the first year of his reign he captured Pope Paschal. Yet the same Henry is found already to have reigned four years; for this was the fifth year of his reign. But Master Hugh, I suppose, counts this as the first year of his imperial rule because in this year, through the reconciliation made between him and the pope, he became Emperor of the Romans. Hence Sigebert writes as follows in his Chronicles. [Col. 1007C]

“In the reconciliation made between the emperor and the pope, after he had taken the pope together with the bishops and cardinals on Easter Day, and Henry had been crowned emperor, the pope, after the Gospel had been read, handed him before the altar of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, in the sight of all the princes, a privilege concerning the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys [Note: [Col. 1008D] The emperor extorted from the pontiff the investitures of benefices by force.], both by ring and by staff: namely, that he might confer the investiture of staff and ring upon bishops or abbots of his realm freely elected without violence or simony. After investiture, however, he was to receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom it belonged.

“The confirmation of peace between the apostolic lord and the emperor, while he handed him the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ in the celebration of Mass, was this: ‘Lord Emperor, we give you this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and suffering for us on the cross, as the holy and apostolic Church holds, in confirmation of true peace between me and you. Given on the Ides of April, in the fourth indiction.’” [Col. 1007D]

[Col. 1008A]

WILLIAM, Abbot of Saint-Thierry. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1111, the fifteenth year from the foundation of the house of Cîteaux, blessed Bernard, twenty-two years old, entered the novices’ cell under Abbot Stephen with more than thirty companions. Among them was Hugh of Mâcon, who built the monastery of Pontigny and was afterward made bishop of Auxerre.

Saint Bernard’s father was called Tescelin, lord of the town of Fontaine; his mother was called Aleth, from the castle of Montbard. She had seven children: six sons who were to become monks, and one daughter who was to become a nun. She refused to entrust them to the breast-feeding of others, instilling in them the nature of a good mother with her mother’s milk. Nor did she allow them to become accustomed to more delicate foods. [Col. 1008B]

When she had Bernard, the third in order, in her womb, she dreamed that she carried a little dog wholly white, reddish on its back, and barking. The answer was that this child would utter great barks against the enemies of God, would lead a pure life, and would furnish a great example of patience. When grown, the boy was entrusted to a master at Châtillon. The church of that castle was later, through Bernard’s efforts, advanced from secular observance to the order of regular canons. On the night of the Nativity of the Lord, the gracious child Jesus appeared to him as a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber.

The aforementioned Aleth, Bernard’s mother, when she was labouring at the point of death, was chanting with the clerics and reciting the litany. When the words were said, “By thy passion and cross, deliver her, O Lord,” she raised her hand to make the sign of the cross and gave up her spirit; thereafter she could not lower the hand which she had raised to sign herself. [Col. 1008C]

One night, by the devil’s prompting, a naked girl was put into the bed where Bernard slept. Feeling her, he turned himself to the other side and slept. Though she touched and provoked him, he remained unmoved; overcome and ashamed, she fled. At another time he was tempted by a female host, who threw herself into his bed and enticed him to sexual intercourse. But he, not lacking a plan, shouted, “Thieves! Thieves!” On hearing this she fled; and this happened three times. When he was becoming more tightly entangled by love of secular learning, he thought he saw his mother complaining and saying that she had not nourished him for such frivolity. [Col. 1008D]

After every meal, he was accustomed to weigh how much he had eaten. He had spent a year in the novices’ cell while still thinking there was only one glass window at the east end of the church, though there were three. Thus those asleep seemed to him to be dead among men, just as the dead are sleeping before God.

SIGEBERT. God, offended by human sins, caused the church of Saint Michael of the Peril of the Sea to be struck by lightning and burned, together with all its buildings. Baldwin, Bishop of Laon, while attempting to withdraw the citizens of that city from the fellowship bound by an unlawfully sworn oath, was, horrible to say, stabbed to death by a sword when the seditious rushed to arms, on Thursday of Easter week, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the Greater Litany. [Col. 1009A] In the violent tumult of the confused crowd the bishop’s house was also set on fire. Consequently the mother church itself of Blessed Mary, and the church of Saint John the Baptist in the nuns’ abbey, together with all other adjoining churches, were consumed by fire.

Louis, King of the French, punished the authors of the sedition so severely that the example could deter both those present and those to come from a like crime. This affliction of the people of Laon was preceded by a disturbance which was the seed and root of the coming calamity, and in a sense its forewarning. A certain noble prince and castellan of Laon, Gerard of Chérisy by name, was praying devoutly on his knees in that same church of the holy Mother of God. His enemies, who did not dare attack him elsewhere, treacherously surrounded him. As he rose from prayer, they killed him there with various sword wounds. [Col. 1009B]

When the pavement of the church, sprinkled with his blood, could not be completely washed clean though water was poured over it many times, and many who came to see it wondered greatly at this, Master Anselm, then dean of the church of Laon—a man widely renowned for learning and eloquence—is reported to have foretold secretly to certain persons that the shedding of that blood could be washed away only by the burning of the same church, since so great a crime was to be expiated not with water but rather with fire. And so it happened. [Col. 1009C]

SIGEBERT. In June, rye and trees, scorched by sacred fire, disappointed the hope of their fruit; and some grapes besides were dried up. [Col. 1010A] A severe and prolonged sickness of men followed, with diarrhoea and death.

AUTHOR. Here Sigebert means by “sacred fire,” unless I am mistaken, a heavenly flash of lightning. Properly speaking, however, “sacred fire” is the name commonly given to a kind of inflammation in human beings which physicians call erysipelas. Here he therefore uses it in the former sense.

Likewise SIGEBERT. At Ravenna and Parma, cities of Italy, blood rained in June.

AUTHOR. Here ends Sigebert’s chronological history, which he himself wrote from the first year of Gratian—that is, from the year of the Lord 380—down to this seventh year of Emperor Henry, fourth year of Louis, son of Philip, King of the French, and thirteenth year of Henry, King of the English. From this point onward (1113) I have found no chronographer and no historian writing continuously concerning the following times. [Col. 1010B]

In certain Chronicles of Sigebert, however, after the end of his history I have found chronological years noted, and very brief entries—no more than a single line—placed under certain years. They are not continuous as Sigebert’s work was, for he left no year in which he recorded nothing, but are interrupted, some years being left empty without a historical entry, as Jerome and Prosper do in their Chronicles. Such brief and interrupted notices, as I have said, I have found from this place down to the twenty-sixth year of Philip, the King of the French now reigning, son of King Louis and father of Louis not yet king. What I shall therefore set down from this point I have collected most diligently from certain authors everywhere. Let the forty-seventh book therefore end here. [Col. 1010C]

# BOOK XLVIII

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009C] In the aforesaid year, that is, in the year of the Lord 1113, Bartholomew was elected bishop of Laon, most renowned throughout the provinces of Laon and Rheims alike for the nobility of his lineage, the integrity of his character, and the abundance of his resources. He was consecrated by Ralph, Archbishop of Rheims. [Col. 1009D] He found the greater church of Saint Mary of Laon and twelve other churches burned, together with the bishop’s house and many other houses of clerics and laypeople.

Seven canons of the church of Laon and six attendants were therefore chosen to carry the shrine of Saint Mary and other reliquary chests through various churches, seeking alms from the faithful for rebuilding the churches. These relics were made illustrious by many miracles, which the canons of the church of Laon wrote down. From them we have briefly extracted a few for edification.

At Issoudun two crippled men were healed, their heels being joined to their buttocks. Geoffrey, lord of that castle, had for God’s sake long fed them in his own house. At the castle of Buzançais, the fifteen-year-old son of the lord of the castle, who was an exceedingly wicked robber, was healed. He had been deaf and mute from birth. [Col. 1010C] When this had happened, the boy’s father ran barefoot to the church and offered forty solidi to Saint Mary’s shrine. For he did not have much money. He also set the shrine of Saint Mary upon his shoulders with the other knights, and carried it barefoot for two miles to the next castle. [Col. 1010D]

Hearing of this, the enemies of that robber, and of the miracle worked upon his son, likewise hurried barefoot to meet it. Having peacefully received the shrine from them, they carried it into their own castle. From there they came to Tours. There a certain woman who for eight years had been unable to rise from bed or go anywhere unless carried was healed in this manner. The Mother of Mercy appeared to her in sleep and commanded that she have herself carried to her shrine in the church of Saint Maurice. She was carried in a waggon and placed beneath the shrine; at once she fell asleep and rose healed. [Col. 1011A]

There also, at Saint Martin’s, a young man deaf and mute from birth was healed. As sweat poured from his entire body and the veins around his ears swelled, blood flowed copiously from his ears. Afterwards he went with the shrine to Laon.

After this, the shrine came to Saint-Laurent-de-Cala on the feast of that martyr. A monk living there could not endure that the shrine of the Blessed Virgin should be placed upon the altar of Saint Lawrence; rather, fearing the loss of the customary offerings on that feast, he had it placed upon a smaller altar in one part of the church. When the people from Tours who had followed the shrine related the miracles they had seen and invited all pilgrims arriving to come to the shrine, the monk, struck with envy, had the shrine and all the relics thrown out of the church. [Col. 1011B]

But the provost of the castle gave the bearers of the shrine a spacious tent which he had prepared for himself. Matrons brought many curtains and adorned the tent most fittingly, making it brilliant throughout the night with abundant lights.

That monk was seized severely with epilepsy toward evening; before all the people he fell to the ground and filled the onlookers with great terror. The great bell also fell from the tower and broke, and the tower itself cracked and split in its upper part. The monk, therefore, repenting late, prostrated himself barefoot on the ground before the shrine and humbly made satisfaction to the heavenly Queen, begging that the shrine be returned to the high altar; but the people of Laon refused. [Col. 1011C]

At Angers, a woman suffering in childbirth unto death drank water in which the relics had been washed; having immediately given birth, she was delivered, and in thanksgiving offered a silver spoon. At Le Mans, a wealthy and barren matron gave birth to a son in the same year and came to Laon in thanksgiving.

On the Nativity of Saint Mary, the same shrine came to Chartres. The venerable Bishop Ivo met it with the entire procession of canons as far as the vineyards, and the shrine was placed in the greater church upon the altar of Saint Mary. There was a crippled woman who for five years had been in the house where the bishop’s bread was baked. In the first hour of the night the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to her in a dream and ordered her to rise as quickly as possible, go to the greater church, and seek the shrine from Laon. [Col. 1011D]

She woke at once, ran healed to the church, and cried out joyfully through the streets, shouting and repeatedly exclaiming: “Lady Saint Mary!” Immediately the bishop commanded all the bells to be rung for a long time, and himself began: “We praise thee, O God.” While it was being sung, another crippled woman entered, healed; and she set upon the altar the two little stools with which she had been accustomed to drag herself about. Again the bells were rung and the *Te Deum* was sung, begun by the bishop. Before it was finished, a young knight who was being held captive in chains in a certain castle unexpectedly entered the church, released. His mother, advancing with citizens who met him toward the altar, knelt before the shrine and, saying that he had been delivered through blessed Mary, offered forty solidi. [Col. 1012A]

At the bishop’s command, bells were again rung through all the churches, and he began the *Te Deum laudamus* for the third time. Much weeping for joy took place there. Thus, from the offerings of the faithful collected throughout France during the whole autumn and winter, the church of Saint Mary of Laon was constructed in large part.

In the following Lent, while the greater part of the work still remained and money was gradually failing, seven of the canons of Laon were chosen. The shrine of Saint Mary and many other saints’ relics were entrusted to them. Among these, one reliquary stood out in form and dignity; it bore this inscription:

[Col. 1012B]

> A sponge, the Lord’s cross, together with the shroud and the face-cloth;  
> and thy hair, O Mother and Virgin, consecrates me.

With these relics they set out for England, which at that time flourished in great abundance of riches because of the peace and justice maintained there by King Henry. On Monday after the Sunday *Isti sunt dies*, they departed from Laon, and in the same year, about the Nativity of Blessed Mary, returned to Laon, recounting the miracles which had meanwhile occurred.

At Nigella in the district of Vermandois, one John, deaf and mute from birth, was healed by drinking water in which the relics had been washed. During the entire time after he slept beneath the shrine, he sweated, while blood flowed copiously from his nostrils, ears, and swollen veins around his neck. He followed the shrine as far as the sea. [Col. 1012C]

Around Good Friday they came to Arras. There was an old goldsmith there who had been deprived of sight for twelve years. Hearing that the shrine of Saint Mary of Laon had been brought there, he asked about its form and appearance. When he learned it, immediately drawing deep sighs from the bottom of his breast and weeping profusely, he said: “I, a sinner, made this shrine with my own hands in my youth, by command of Lord Elinand, Bishop of Laon.” That bishop had placed in it most precious relics, among them the head of Saint Valery the abbot and the head of Saint Montan, monk and recluse, who foretold the birth of blessed Remigius and received sight from the milk of Remigius’s mother Cilinia, as he had foretold. [Col. 1012D]

“O most merciful Mother, if only you would show me this mercy: that, receiving sight like Saint Montan, I might again deserve to see your shrine which I made!” Saying this and weeping, he begged that his eyes might be touched with the water used to wash the relics. This was done; he drank of the same water and remained awake throughout the night in prayer before the shrine. At daybreak he received sight.

At Saint-Omer a girl whose hand had been withered from birth was healed. On the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist they came to Wissant; summoned by sailors, they boarded a ship. With them were many merchants travelling to England to buy wool, who hoped to make the crossing more safely with the shrine. They carried more than three hundred marks in their purses. The master of the ship was called Coldistan. [Col. 1013A]

In mid-sea they saw pirates sailing, with gleaming spears, swords, and shields aboard their vessel. Then, from fear, each confessed sins to the other; even a priest confessed to a layman. The aforementioned merchants, now despairing of life, offered their purses with all their money to the shrine. Weeping and praying to blessed Mary, they asked her to deliver them from the pirates’ hands and from the danger of death, and to retain all their money for restoring her church.

As the pirates drew near, the shipmaster urged the priest Boso to take the relics of the Mother of God and forbid the pirates power to harm them. At once he took the reliquary containing the hair of blessed Mary, ascended with fear and devotion to the higher part of the stern, supported by the shipmaster with both hands, and raised his hand against the enemies. By the authority of Christ and his Mother he sternly adjured them not to come farther or have power to harm them. [Col. 1013B]

As soon as he made the sign of the cross against the enemy with that reliquary, more swiftly than speech, a violent contrary wind drove the pirates’ ship backward; its mast broke, and part of the mast fell upon one of them, dashed out his brains, and hurled him dead into the sea. Shortly afterward the ship carrying the shrine reached harbour safe and joyful. The delivered merchants took back the purses that they had offered.

After travelling all around England and spending their money on purchasing great heaps of wool, they filled a large house above the seashore, called Dover, with that wool. On the very night before they were to cross back, the house was burned with all the wool. [Col. 1013C]

After this the shrine came to Canterbury. There the people of Laon were honourably received by Archbishop William, who formerly, seeking Laon in order to see and hear Master Anselm, had stayed many days in the bishop’s house and had taught there the sons of Ralph, chancellor of the King of England.

There was there a very wealthy matron who had been tortured for eight days by the pains of labour. She sent her husband to the people of Laon to ask whether any of them perhaps knew some remedy. The priest Boso advised him to counsel his wife to make a truthful confession of sins to her priest and confidently to drink water in which the relics had been washed. [Col. 1013D]

She had already completely lost both speech and memory through pain. Yet, strengthened at once somewhat by the very heat of faith, she faithfully confessed her sins to the priest who came to her. She added that on the same night a most beautiful lady seemed to have appeared to her in a vision, coming from France, commanding her to confess her sins truthfully and promising that she would thus be healed. Therefore, immediately after drinking the water of the relics, she gave birth and was healed. She offered many gifts and ornaments to blessed Mary.

No one there could be healed unless he belonged to that very diocese and had confessed his sins, provided that he was of a suitable age. [Col. 1014A]

At Winchester a certain knight, the king’s cupbearer, was healed after having been blind for eight years; and another, a very wealthy man named Walter, who had lain bedridden for six years and, besides this, suffered from diarrhoea. He offered three gold rings to the three clerics who had brought the relics to him; then, running before the bier, he offered three silver cups, much money, and other ornaments. When some people, seeing these things carried through the street, said that he had offered little in proportion to his great wealth—for he was reported to have more than three thousand pounds of English currency in his treasures—he replied that for the present he did not wish to give more, until he had repaid all the interest which he had received from his debtors, as he had promised God. Accordingly he immediately had heralds proclaim throughout the whole city that whoever had paid him interest should come and receive back what was his. Besides him, another twelve persons were healed: blind, lame, deaf, and mute.

After this the bier came to the village called Christ-Keccam, that is, “Christ’s Church,” on the octave of Pentecost, when there was a very large gathering of merchants. There was there a dean with twelve canons, who refused to receive the bier lest they lose the merchants’ offerings, because their church was not yet finished. Since there was a heavy rain, the dean at last, and only with difficulty, permitted the bier to be placed on a lesser altar in a remote part of the church. But when he saw that nearly all the merchants who had heard of the miracles performed at Winchester were going to the bier and making offerings, he angrily ordered the bier to be expelled from the church. Thus the horses and garments of the men of Laon were soaked by the rain, and because of the multitude of merchants they found no lodging in the whole village.

Then a certain matron, taking pity on them, asked her husband to lend to the Queen of Heaven, who had been driven out of the church, the new house which they had built and had already let to merchants for two marks; and to permit her and her clerics to lodge there the following night, while they sought other lodging for themselves. He agreed, received into that house the clerics, who were by then almost overcome by the rain, had their mud-soiled garments washed and dried, and placed the bier of the Blessed Virgin in a suitable place, decently adorned with curtains. Thereafter he showed them every hospitality. One of the merchants struck three bells which he had for sale and which were hanging from the ceiling of the house, summoned his companions by their sound, and, mounting to a higher place, related how the dean had expelled the bier from the church. He urged that no one should go to the church, but that they should instead assemble at the lodging of the bier of Saint Mary to hear the divine office. Finally, all unanimously issued a decree that anyone who went to the church should pay five shillings to his companions.

It was then the Saturday before the octave of Pentecost. This host had near the town a house [Col. 1015A] in which oxen and livestock were kept; there lived there a poor peasant assigned to guard the animals. His little daughter had had a twisted foot from birth, so that the heel was at the front and the toes at the back. Drinking water from the relics and sprinkling her foot with it, she kept vigil before the bier and was healed in the morning.

The next day a certain fire-breathing dragon came out of the sea and flew into that village. First it set fire to the church, then to certain houses, with flame which it emitted from its nostrils. The bier of Saint Mary had barely departed by half a stadium. Afterward riders came on horseback and begged the men of Laon to assist the burning village. Thirsting from human curiosity to see so great a wonder, they appointed suitable guards for the bier and quickly rode back to the settlement. They saw a dragon of incredible length, having five heads and emitting sulphurous flames through its nostrils, flying from place to place and setting the houses alight one by one. The church was so utterly burned that not only its timbers, but also its walls, enormous stones, and even the altars themselves, were reduced to ashes; there was no indication whatever that a church had stood there.

The dean, seeing both his church and his house on fire, hastily gathered and bound up his garments and household goods and had them carried to a ship moored on the nearby seashore. But the dragon, as though it had come for this purpose alone, flew toward the ship and set fire to everything in it, and even to the ship itself—an incredible thing to tell. Yet the house of the host who had received the bier remained sound and unharmed, together with everything within it; so also did the more distant house in which his livestock were kept. The merchants likewise, who had shown much goodwill to the men of Laon, were so preserved by God’s grace that they lost either nothing or little of all their possessions.

But the dean who had expelled the bier from the church, moved by late repentance, followed it barefoot and, prostrating himself before it, solemnly acknowledged God’s judgments and begged forgiveness. At Exeter Robert the archdeacon received the men of Laon and the bier honourably; he had long remained at Laon to hear the lectures of Master Anselm. Sixteen sick persons were healed there. There was, however, a certain cripple from the diocese of Salisbury who could not be healed until the bier came into his own diocese.

From Salisbury they came to the abbey of nuns called Wilton, where they were shown the tomb of the Venerable Priest Bede, beside whom was buried that celebrated woman poet. A man who had long suffered from fever lay there at the tomb of the Venerable Priest Bede, because many were accustomed to be healed there. On the very night before the bier from Laon arrived, that woman poet appeared to the sick man and said: “You cannot now be healed here through Bede, because the Blessed Mother of God has come down among us.” When the sick man reported this to the men of Laon the next day and drank water from the washed relics, he was immediately healed.

From there they came into the district of Devonshire, where the natives showed them the chair and oven of that famous king Arthur, according to British tales. There the cleric Algard, later bishop of Coutances in Normandy, honoured them greatly; he had been at Laon a pupil of Master Anselm. There, near the village called Bunnia, a girl of ten, blind from birth, received sight; and a young man deaf from birth received hearing. But a man with a withered hand began to quarrel with one of the servants of the men of Laon about Arthur, and therefore could not be healed.

Near the castle of Bannistuplum there lived a lord named Joel of Totnes, whose wife was Germana, daughter of Wermund of Pinquengni. He received the men of Laon and the bier honourably for three days, and offered them a silver cup, a precious chalice, curtains, and other ornaments, together with a horse to carry them and many other things, to the value of fifteen pounds in Laon currency. In his house was a girl of twelve, bent over in her whole body, who was not healed as long as the bier remained there. But when, as they departed, she cried with great weeping, “Alas, most merciful lady, holy Virgin Mary! Will you then depart thus and leave me unhealed?” immediately, before all who saw, she was made well; throwing away her little crutches, she sprang up, stood, and ran to the bier, giving thanks. A monk from La Charité, afflicted with sciatica, was similarly healed there.

[Col. 1016C] At Totnes an old man, lame from birth and brother of the provost of that castle, was healed. When he had been healed, his brother offered forty sterling shillings before the bier; after him an innumerable crowd added many gifts.

There were there three young men of the same district, close blood-relatives. Seeing so much money carried to the bier, they began to disparage the men of Laon, saying that they worked miracles by magical art for the sake of profit. One of them urged the others to go with him to the bier, pretending to kiss it, and then to fill their mouths by licking up the coins laid upon the altar. When they refused to do this, that faithless man did what he had said. Licking with his mouth, he snatched as much as he could from the heap of coins; returning to his companions, he showed them the coins he had stolen and invited them to go with him to the tavern. When they would not follow him, the wretched man entered the tavern and came out satiated. The other two returned to the gathering of the people.

But he mounted his horse and entered the nearest wood, scarcely half a stadium away. Having fastened a wooden rope around his neck, he hanged himself from the branch of a tree. The horse on which he had ridden returned empty to the gathering of the people. Seeing it, the two aforementioned young men examined and swiftly followed its tracks, quickly reached the wood, and found him hanging and dead. Unfastening the purse which hung from his belt, they found the coins he had stolen still stained with fresh saliva. They immediately carried them, with loud lamentation, to the bier and restored them upon the altar. Throwing themselves upon the ground, they implored the mercy of the Mother of God for the soul of their kinsman and reported before all the crime which the deceased had committed. All marvelled at God’s so swift vengeance and, beating their breasts, shed copious tears.

At the city of Bagea a boy of twelve, bathing in hot baths, was drowned. His parents carried him to the bier. He was placed between two fires, and his body was suspended head downward and feet upward; his mouth was opened, with a small stick inserted between his upper and lower teeth. When he had vomited a great quantity of water and his body had been sufficiently warmed, he was taken down and carried back to the bier. He was washed with water used for washing the relics, and a little of the same water was dripped into his mouth. He at once revived whole and sound and returned home.

Thus far the miracles of the bier of Laon, performed in France and England in the year of the Lord 1114 and 1115. But that which occurred under Elinand, bishop of Laon, at Conciacum—concerning the woman who caused her son-in-law to be killed because she was accused of committing adultery with him, and was therefore condemned to be burned, but was preserved unharmed amid the flames by Blessed Mary because she cleared herself of guilt by a true confession—although she survived only three days, lest malice change her understanding, belongs to another time. For this reason we did not place it in its proper time, because I am not sufficiently certain at what time that bishop, who bore the same name as I, lived. Yet, as we have from the miracles previously mentioned, he was before Bishop Baldric. In this work I have resolved to record nothing unless I know at what time it occurred.

Accordingly, at this time that Master Anselm and his brother Ralph flourished in France at Laon. In this same year, namely A.D. 1115, the monastery of Clairvaux was founded under Saint Bernard, its first abbot; likewise the monastery of Pontigny, by Hugh of Mâcon, who later became bishop of Auxerre. These two men became abbots in the third year after their conversion. For they had entered the house of Cîteaux together in the year of the Lord 1113, as William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, writes, and in the fifteenth year from the foundation of the house of Cîteaux—although Sigebert, in his chronicles, says that they entered the house of Cîteaux with thirty companions in the tenth year from the foundation of that house, namely the first year of Abbot Stephen.

Blessed Bernard was twenty-two years old when he was converted, and twenty-seven when he became abbot of Clairvaux. When he went to Châlons to receive his blessing, since the bishopric of Langres was then vacant, he was received with great reverence by William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons. Seeing the young man so thin and wasted in body, William threw himself prostrate upon the ground and asked the chapter of Cîteaux to place Bernard for one year under his care; and he obtained this. During that period, through the error of a most negligent and ignorant servant, he often ate raw lard offered to him instead of butter and drank oil offered to him instead of water. For because of excessive abstinence he had then lost the faculty of taste as regards distinguishing flavours, so that he testified that cold water alone had taste for him. Blessed is he to whom alone is reckoned as a fault what others are accustomed to take as glory.

Near the river Aube, Clairvaux had formerly been a den of robbers, called the Valley of Wormwood, either because of the abundance of wormwood or because of the bitterness that befell those who encountered robbers. At that time the brothers of Clairvaux often made pottage from beech leaves. Their bread was like that prophetic bread made from barley, millet, and vetches. [Col. 1018B] (Isaiah 28.)

At that time Saint Bernard saw a boy standing beside him in divine radiance and commanding him with great authority to speak confidently whatever should be suggested to him when he opened his mouth; for it would not be he himself who spoke, but the Spirit of his Father speaking in him. A certain brother, whom Bernard had ordered to abstain from communion for a secret offence during an especially great solemnity, was ashamed to remain alone without communicating and went to receive communion with the others. When the saint saw him, he did not wish to deny him communion, but prayed silently that God might ordain something better from so great a presumption. The brother, therefore, could not by any means swallow the Body of the Lord which he had received. After Sext he drew the saint aside and confessed his presumption. The saint rebuked him and, by praying, enabled him to swallow the Body of the Lord without difficulty.

He ordered beer which he had blessed to be given to certain knights going to a tournament to drink, and they were immediately converted. When Valcher of Montmirail had been brought as an infant by his mother to be blessed by Bernard, who was lodging in her house, the saint, while speaking, stretched out his hands several times; the infant repeatedly kissed his hand, drawing it to his mouth. A cleric named Nicholas obtained through him from the Lord the grace of tears.

## 1116

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, who had excommunicated Philip, king of France, because he had taken a mistress in addition to his wife, died: a man of many virtues and of learning alike. He abridged the decrees and wrote many other useful works. In the suburb of Antioch, the earth opened by night and swallowed houses with their inhabitants. This annotator does not say whether the chasm occurred with an earthquake or without one. But it is more credible that this happened with some earthquake; for the earth can scarcely gape in so wide a fissure as to swallow whole houses without also shaking. We have set forth above the reasons concerning the natural causes of earthquakes, in Book 29 of this work, comprised in eighteen chapters. Let them be sought there.

## 1117

In this year I have found nothing recorded, as also in the fourth year preceding this one, namely A.D. 1114. But just as under that year I set down the miracles of the bier of Blessed Mary of Laon performed throughout France, which I had on the authority of a booklet of the church of Laon describing those same miracles, so under this year the death of Baldwin, king of Jerusalem and brother of Godfrey, should be recorded. This Baldwin, after his brother Godfrey, who had reigned for one year, was crowned king, as Baldric and William write, in the year of the Lord 1101; and, as the aforesaid William writes, he reigned for seventeen years. It is therefore evident that he died in this year. For, as William writes, he died in the seventh year of his reign, in the fourth month. Another Baldwin, his kinsman and count of Edessa, succeeded him. This Edessa is twenty miles from the Euphrates and one hundred from Antioch. The Greeks call it Edessa; the Syrians, Rothasia. It is not read how many years this Baldwin reigned. Thus far William of Malmesbury wrote his history, addressed to Robert, count of Normandy.

## 1118

An earthquake is said to have occurred this year, so violent that it threw down parts of certain cities; but it is not said which cities, nor in what part of the world this earthquake occurred. Thus the event is recorded far too negligently, since it is recorded in this manner.

## 1119

Gelasius II became the one hundred and sixty-sixth pope, for one year.

## 1120

Master Hugh says in his chronicles that this was the eighth year of Henry IV, which must be understood of the empire, not the kingdom. Pope Calixtus II, the one hundred and seventh pope, sat for five years, ten months, and thirteen days. This Calixtus, as Lord Geoffrey of Auxerre says, became Pope Calixtus from being Guy, archbishop of Vienne. He was the first to plant the Cistercian order in the territory of Vienne, at the monastery of Bonnevaux; its first abbot was John of Lyons, later bishop of Valence. A most joyful and beautiful vision, which this same John saw before his conversion, was a foretoken of that future dignity, as follows.

Geoffrey on the Apocalypse. When the first foundations of our Cistercian order were being laid, there was in the church of Lyons an upright and honourable cleric, John. Moved by reports of our order, he silently resolved within himself to join their community. But a few days afterward, another thought entering his mind, he changed his purpose; and, by way of some compensation for abandoning that purpose, he undertook a pilgrimage to Saint James. Having devoutly completed it, he returned, was joyfully received by his household, and, exhausted from the journey, withdrew to his chamber. As he rested, God and our Lord Jesus Christ immediately appeared to him in a vision, with the two blessed apostles Peter and James.

Peter held in his hand a book which the Lord ordered to be opened. It was written in golden letters and contained the names of the predestined. The apostle, being commanded, began to read; and when he read there the name of that John, the Lord said: “Take him away; erase him, erase him, for he promised that he would be mine and recoiled from his promise.” But blessed James drew nearer and, pleading, said: “Lord, he is my pilgrim; I beseech you, do not erase his name.” The Lord answered: “He ought to have been my citizen, not my pilgrim. Is it not greater to be my citizen than your pilgrim?” But the Apostle James persisted in his prayer: “Do not erase him, most merciful Lord; do not erase him, I beseech you. I stand surety to you for him: he will do what he had resolved.” And the Lord said to him: “When will he do it?” The apostle replied: “Within fifteen days.”

Awakened by these words, John threw himself upon the ground and gave thanks to his surety with a most abundant outpouring of tears, saying: “I will indeed do it, holy apostle; I will do what you have so mercifully promised on my behalf.” Not long after his great weeping he fell asleep again. Again the Lord appeared with the aforementioned apostles and ordered the book to be opened again. In it John heard blessed Peter reading: “We will make for you little chains of gold, adorned with silver.” (Song of Songs 1.) John immediately rose, anticipated the appointed day, and fulfilled his vow.

He became the first abbot of the monastery of Bonnevaux and afterward bishop of the church of Valence; his life and death shone with many merits and miracles. With full justice the Israelites are reproached for returning in heart to Egypt (Acts 7), when this John, who recoiled from Cîteaux, was ordered to be erased from the book of life.

At the same time we should consider with what devotion the intercessory aid of the saints must be sought by us: they stand surety for us so lovingly and intercede so effectively. This example most plainly refutes the heretics of our time, called Paterines—that is, Manichaeans or Publicans—who say that pilgrimages are vain and their invocations vain, and that our prayers cannot come to the knowledge of those who now have nothing in common with our life. Yet the saints themselves are in heaven, of whom it is written: “The prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the heavens” (Ecclesiasticus 25). And in the Apocalypse it is written that an angel stood before the golden altar, holding a golden censer in his hand; much incense was given to him so that he might offer it from the prayers of the saints upon the golden altar before the throne. “And,” it says, “the smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints rose from the hand of the angel before God” (Revelation 8).

By the same reasoning, our prayers would not reach the knowledge of angels either, with whom our life has nothing in common; nor likewise God’s knowledge, and especially not Christ’s, who now has nothing in common with our life, although formerly he had, as he himself says: “I am the first and the last, and living; and I was dead” (Revelation 1). Moreover, the apostle Peter says in the Second Epistle: “I judge it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by reminder, knowing that the putting off of my tabernacle is near. But I will take pains that you may frequently keep these things in memory after my death” (2 Peter 1). Behold: the apostle confidently promises that even after death he will not fail in timely help to those who had believed through him.

That rich man of the Gospel, buried in hell, retained memory and concern for his brothers still living in the flesh, and begged Abraham that they might not come to the place of torments where he was (Luke 16). Shall the souls of saints who recline in heaven with the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8) have no memory of those dear to them, and shall they let the prayers of those invoking them pass by with a deaf ear? The devil sends his promptings into human hearts through evil angels (Psalm 77); likewise God sends his through good angels. Hence: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matthew 18). For why are they called their angels, if they do them no good, if they do nothing for them? The angel says to Daniel: “There is no helper for me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Daniel 10). The angel Raphael says to Tobias that he had offered Tobias’s prayers, tears, and alms to God (Tobit 12); and the angel who appeared to Cornelius, who was not yet reborn, says the same thing (Acts 10). All, as the Apostle says, are ministering spirits, sent for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Hebrews 1).

The souls of saints, stripped of their bodies and joined to the hosts of angels, possess the same power and charity as the angels, as is plainly read in the lives of the saints. Thus, after the apostle Paul had been beheaded, he returned to the matron Plantilla her veil stained with his most holy blood; and as he had foretold Nero, “When my head has been cut off, I shall appear to you alive.” At about the ninth hour, although the doors were shut, he visibly stood before Nero and said: “Caesar, behold, I am Paul, a soldier of Christ, the eternal and unconquered King. Believe even now: for I am not dead, but live to my God.” The lives of the saints are full of miracles of this sort, demonstrating how saints, now stripped of flesh, powerfully help those in the flesh who invoke them.

This error, now general and common to all Paterines and Bulgars, whom we call Publicans by the popular name, was formerly peculiar to Vigilantius the priest. He said that it was sacrilege to pray at the relics of saints. As Jerome says, he received his name by antiphrasis; for he ought more rightly to have been called Dormitantius (“Sleepy”) than Vigilantius (“Wakeful”).

Certainly, he was true to his lineage, as one born from the stock of robbers and Convenae. Pompey the consul, after subduing Spain and hurrying back for a triumph, brought these people down from the Pyrenean heights and gathered them into one town; hence the town also received the name of the Convenae. Pompey did the same in the regions of the East: after defeating the Cilician and Isaurian pirates and brigands, he founded between Cilicia and Isauria a city bearing his own name. To this Vigilantius—or rather Dormitantius—Jerome replied among other things as follows:

“Was the Emperor Constantine sacrilegious because he transferred the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople, where demons roar before them? Is the present Emperor Arcadius also to be called sacrilegious because, long afterward, he transferred the bones of blessed Samuel into Thrace?” And shortly afterward: “You put before me an apocryphal book, read under the name of Ezra by you and persons like you, where it is written that after death no one may dare to pray for others. I have never read that book.
