For what need is there to take into one’s hands what the Church does not receive?” And shortly afterward: “Unless perhaps, in the manner of the pagans and the impious Porphyry and Eunomius, you pretend that these are deceptions of demons, and that the demons do not really cry out but feign their torments.” And shortly afterward: “You will freely proclaim yourself either Mercury, because of your greed for money; or Nocturninus, after Plautus’s *Amphitryon*, while Jupiter, during his sleep, joined two nights together in adultery with Alcmena so that Hercules, a man of great strength, might be born; or certainly Father Liber, because of drunkenness, the drinking-cup hanging from your shoulders, your ever-red face, foaming lips, and unbridled insults.” And shortly afterward: “Whenever,” he says, “I have become angry, thought some evil in my heart, or been deluded by a nocturnal phantom, I do not dare enter the basilicas of the martyrs; thus I am wholly terrified in both mind and body.” Thus Jerome.

How much better it is to hear and read that book of 2 Maccabees, where it is written: “It is therefore a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, that they may be released from sins” (2 Maccabees 12), than that apocryphal book worthy of burning, which forbids prayer for the dead! But these things have been said briefly against this detestable heresy. Now let us return to the history.

This year Henry, king of the English, is said to have fought Louis, king of the French, between Andely and Nonge; but it is not said to whom victory fell, nor what the cause of the war was. These ought to have been recorded together, so that it might be known whose cause was more just.

This year I have found nothing recorded; but from the statements of Lord Geoffrey of Auxerre, who wrote the Life of Blessed Peter of Tarentaise, it may be inferred that this same Peter left the world in this year and was converted in the monastery of Bonnevaux. He was twenty years old when he was converted and seventy-three when he died. But he died in the year of the Lord 1174; therefore he was born in 1102, from which this present year is the twentieth. He was born in the territory of Vienne, to parents humble in worldly condition but great and noble before God in faith and conduct. For already, when this Peter as a little boy was handed over to letters, they had begun to devote themselves to abstinence and, by mutual consent, to abstain from marital intercourse. They allotted the better bedding to the poor and themselves remained on straw.

Peter, a boy who loved letters and avoided games, undertook the study of letters, with anointing rather than learning as his teacher; so that in his first year he could sing all David’s psalms by heart. His father wore haircloth next to the flesh; both parents refused to allow any ecclesiastical benefices to be given to their sons, though clerics. From the beginning of his conversion Peter drew his brother Lambert with him; Lambert later became abbot in the monastery of Chézery. Peter himself, not long afterward, became abbot in the monastery of Tamié, so called because it stands, as it were, midway between two provinces and two counties. From that time the brethren of Tamié began to acquire a great reputation for generosity and humanity.

Already at that time Peter carried pieces of bread and cheese about and hid them in the bosoms of poor people whom he met. He practised this still more when he was bishop, sharing pious burdens even with his companions. If, while travelling, he needed to dine, he sought side-turnings and sat down beside the public road, so that his table might then also be shared with poor people and pilgrims. The Lord had provided a suitable elm for this vine: Amadeus, marquis of Italy and count of Savoy and Maurienne.

## 1122

An earthquake is said to have occurred this year during the Advent of the Lord, on the fourth Ides of December; but it is not said where, nor should it be believed to have been universal.

## 1123

Henry IV, emperor, dies; Lothair succeeds him and reigns for twenty-two years. When a sedition arose at Tours between clergy and laity, the church of Saint Martin burned.

(1124.) Christians fight Saracens between Jerusalem and Ascalon, and victory fell to the Christians. Pope Calixtus dies. He wrote a book *On the Miracles of Saint James*, compiling into one volume matters that he had read in scattered sources. He was never able to lose this little book: although he was at one time stripped of all his other possessions by robbers; though the house in which he was lodging burned with all his household goods; and though he himself suffered shipwreck at sea, his little book always escaped every danger from fire, water, and robbers. From this book I have excerpted a few things for edification.

In the letter of Pope Leo it is written that Blessed James suffered in the eleventh year after the Lord’s Ascension, during the time of Unleavened Bread, with his disciple Josiah. This Josiah, Calixtus says, is said to have been Herod’s steward. But since the day of the apostle’s passion had long been unknown, a faithful man known to me had a vision on the night of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary: as Blessed James was being led into Herod’s court to be tried, a great dispute arose between the Gentiles and the Jews over the apostle. At last he was judged by Herod, led outside the city, and beheaded. Immediately a certain distinguished man, who was as if a prelate, spoke of him tearfully to the people as follows. He was judged in the royal court about the third hour and suffered about the ninth, like Christ: that is, at the same hour and day at which master and disciple suffered.

Jerome, however, in the Martyrology which he wrote for the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, wrote that his passion should be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August; Pope Alexander II also ordered this to be done, because of the days of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection. This Alexander placed in storage the chains of Saint Peter brought from Jerusalem to Rome, after they had been washed with water and oil. For on the eighth day before the Kalends of August Blessed James is said to have been carried from Syria as far as Compostela, and on the third day before the Kalends of January to have been committed to burial. King Alfonso of Galicia observed this solemnity with great splendour, because Galicia had received the apostle’s body on the third day before the Kalends of January. On that day, in honour of the twelve apostles, he annually offered upon the altar of Saint James twelve marks of silver and twelve talents of gold; he made new knights and held a general banquet to which all were summoned by herald and trumpet.

Bede relates that a certain Italian man had committed a very great sin, which he finally confessed with difficulty to his priest and bishop. The bishop sent him to Saint James, to act according to the counsel of Theodemir, bishop of Compostela, carrying a slip of paper on which that sin was written. He ordered him to lay it upon the altar and humbly pray the apostle James to intercede for him. This was done. When Archbishop Theoderic, about to celebrate Mass, found the folded paper and asked who had placed it there, the man confessed in tears before all who heard what he had done. When the bishop looked again at the paper, it was found not written upon but wholly without letters. Archbishop Theodemir did not dare impose any other penance upon him, except that thereafter he should fast every Friday.

Master Hubert, canon of the church of Saint Mary Magdalene at Besançon, wrote that in the year of the Lord 1080 thirty men of Lorraine resolved to visit Saint James and entered into a pact among themselves to preserve mutual fidelity. Yet one of their number refused to bind himself by this oath of fidelity. At length, setting out all together, they came as far as a Gascon city called Porta Clausa, “the Closed Gate.” There one of them fell ill and could go no farther. Because of their pact of loyalty, his companions supported him with great labour for fifteen days as far as the pass of Cisa, although persons in good condition ordinarily cross that entire distance in five days. At last, wearied by the burden, they abandoned him there.

The man who had not ratified the pact remained with him and kept watch beside him during the following night in the village of Saint Michael. At dawn the sick man told his companion to try to climb the mountain if he would help him. The companion replied: “I will help you as long as I live.” After they had climbed the mountain, day came to an end and the sick man died. His distressed companion called upon Saint James for aid. James appeared to him in the form of a knight seated upon a horse and said: “Give me this dead man, and sit behind me upon the horse until we come to the place of burial.” Thus, in that night, he carried them a journey of twelve days to the Mount of Joy of Saint James, where he set them down; and he ordered the living man to go to the canons of Saint James and ask them to help him bury his dead pilgrim of Saint James.

Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, wrote that three knights of the diocese of Lyons, from the town of Dumezei, while travelling to Saint James, found a poor woman going there and carrying her little belongings in a certain bag. She asked them to relieve her [Col. 1025A] of her small burden. One of them therefore undertook to carry her satchel. Every day at evening the woman caught up with the knights and took from her little bag what she needed; and at the first crowing of the cocks, when pilgrims travelling on foot are accustomed to set out, she returned her satchel to the knight. Thus he went on his way the more cheerfully because he was less encumbered; and in this the knight served the woman for love of Saint James.

When he was still twelve days’ journey from the city of Saint James, he found a poor man who begged him to lend him his horse to ride, so that he might be able to reach Saint James. For he was falling ill and would otherwise die, since he could go no farther. The knight agreed, set him upon his horse, took the man’s staff in his own hand, and began to go on foot, carrying the poor woman’s little burden around his neck [Col. 1025B].

As he proceeded in this manner, he fell ill from fatigue and the heat of the sun. When he realized this, he remembered that he had offended God in many ways. He would not spare himself, but endured his illness by travelling in this way all the way to Saint James. When he arrived, he worshipped God and His apostle, was received into lodging, and lay down in bed. His companions visited him and urged him to confess, receive communion, and be anointed with holy oil. But he turned his face away. Alarmed, his companions prayed to Saint James for him.

He remained for three days without food or drink. At last he sighed and said: “Thanks be to God and Saint James, because I have been delivered. As soon as I felt myself become ill,” he said, “I wished to confess, receive communion, [Col. 1025C] and be anointed. But while I was silently considering this, a crowd of demons came upon me and oppressed me so greatly that from that hour I could not even make a sign to indicate anything conducive to my salvation. Yet I understood what you were saying, but I could not reply. For one demon bound my tongue, while others turned my head and body, against my will, wherever they wished. At last blessed James came, carrying in his left hand the poor woman’s bag which I had borne, as though it were a shield for himself, and in his right the staff of the poor man to whom I had lent my horse, as though it were a lance; and he drove the demons away. Send quickly, therefore, for a priest.”

They sent for one; and while the priest delayed in coming, the man publicly warned one of his companions, saying: “Friend, henceforth do not serve your lord Girinus [Col. 1025D] the Bald as a knight. For he is truly damned, and will shortly die an evil death.” And so it happened. For not long afterward, while he was killing a knight by attacking him with weapons, he was pierced through by that knight’s lance. The pilgrim himself said of his own case that he would not remain much longer in this world. Not long afterward, having confessed and received communion, he rested in a good end.

Pope Calixtus. In the year of the Lord 1090, a certain German was travelling to Saint James with his son. Arriving near Toulouse, he lodged with a certain man who, coveting his money, devised a plan to hide his own silver cup in their bag, so that he might accuse them [Col. 1026A] of theft. On the following day he overtook them with an armed band, accusing them of theft. They said to him: “Whomever you find with your property, condemn him justly.” When the cup was found in their bag, he seized their goods and dragged them before a public tribunal.

Moved by pity, the judge ordered one to be released and the other hanged. The father and son then began to dispute over which should be hanged. At last the son, though his father refused, compelled the matter so that he himself was hanged in his father’s place. The father, utterly grief-stricken, went on to Saint James. Returning after thirty-six days, he turned aside to the body of his son, who was still hanging. As he wailed, saying, “My son, why do I live while I see you hanging?” the son comforted his father and replied: “Father, do not mourn over my punishment, for there is none; rather rejoice, because it is sweeter for me now than it ever was in all [Col. 1026B] my life. For blessed James, sustaining me with his own hands, refreshes me with every kind of sweetness.”

Hearing this, the father ran into the town and had his son taken down. When the townspeople understood that their host had accused them out of greed, they hanged him there. In the year of the Lord 1105, in Italy near the castle of Coizanum, a certain Bernard was captured, chained, and thrown by his enemies into the depths of a tower. As he called upon blessed James day and night, the apostle appeared to him and said: “Come, follow me to Galicia.” He broke Bernard’s chains and disappeared. Immediately this pilgrim, though fetters were hanging from his neck, climbed to the summit of the tower without any help except that of the apostle alone. From the summit [Col. 1026C] of the tower he made a single leap to the ground; its height was sixty cubits.

In the year 1106, a certain knight had a swollen throat and could be cured by no physician. He was healed by touching a little cross which a pilgrim was carrying. In the following year, a certain merchant was captured by a baron and imprisoned because of his possessions. He called upon Saint James, who appeared to him at night and, commanding him to rise, led him to the top of a tower. The tower bent down so far that its summit seemed to be laid upon the ground; he departed from it without leaping and went away free. The guards awoke and pursued him, coming close to him; but, divinely blinded, they did not find him. He went to Saint James with the chains by which he had been bound.

[Col. 1026D] Count Pontius of Saint-Gilles went to Saint James with his brother. When they arrived, they asked the warden to allow them to keep vigil before the apostle’s body. For it was the custom that, after sunset, the doors of that oratory should be closed until morning. He refused. Saddened, they withdrew to their lodgings; gathering all the pilgrims of their company, they provided themselves with lights to hold in their hands. Strengthened in faith, nearly two hundred pilgrims came to the closed doors and prayed, saying aloud: “Saint James, if our pilgrimage pleases you, open your oratory to us.” They had not yet finished speaking when, behold, the doors opened with such a crash that they thought them broken into fragments [Col. 1027A]. The bars, bolts, and chains by which they had been fastened were broken.

A certain bishop from Greece, named Stephen, left his bishopric and came to Saint James in poor clothing. There a cell of reeds was made for him, in which he devoted himself day and night to fasting, vigils, and prayer. While he was praying one day, a crowd of country people near his cell began thus to entreat the apostle: “Blessed James, good knight, deliver us from our pressing evils.” Hearing this, he rebuked them, saying: “O foolish rustics, call blessed James not a knight but a fisherman.”

That same night blessed James appeared to him in the whitest garment, holding two keys in his hand and bearing armour more brilliant than the rays of the sun. Calling him a third time, he said: “Stephen, servant of God, because you ordered that I be called not a knight but [Col. 1027B] a fisherman, I appear to you thus, so that you may know that I serve God as a knight. I have obtained from the Lord that I should be the helper of all who hope in me. And, that you may believe this more firmly: with these keys which I hold in my hand, I shall open the gates of the city of Coimbra, which has been oppressed by siege for seven years by Fernando, king of the Christians. Tomorrow, at the third hour, when the Christians have entered, I shall deliver it into their power.” And so it happened.

There once arose a most fierce war between the count of Mont-Calcaria and his knight named William. William was captured by the count and brought before him. When the count ordered him beheaded, the knight cried: “James, apostle of God, whom Herod slew by the sword at Jerusalem, help me and deliver me from the executioner’s sword!” With his bare neck exposed and his hands raised to heaven, he endured three tremendous blows [Col. 1027C] and was not injured at all. Then the executioner drove his sword-point into his belly; but blessed James so blunted it that he did not even feel the stroke.

Then the count ordered him confined in his castle. When he invoked blessed James, the apostle appeared to him in the morning, standing by him and saying: “Behold, I am here, whom you invoked.” The house was then filled with such sweetness of fragrance that all who were there believed themselves to be in paradise because of the scent and because of the immense light that appeared there. Then, amid that radiance, blessed James led him out before all, holding his hand, and brought him to the farthest gate of the castle, the guards being as though blinded. When the doors were opened, both went together for one mile [Col. 1027D] beyond the walls. Then the knight, inflamed with love for the apostle, went to Galicia to visit the apostle’s body.

A certain citizen of Barcelona went to Saint James and asked nothing else of him except that he might be freed from captivity by his enemies if he should happen to fall into it. Later it happened that he was captured and sold thirteen times through markets and fairs. Yet whoever bought him could not keep him, because blessed James broke his chains and every bond. The thirteenth time, while he was bound with double chains by a Saracen, the apostle appeared to him and said: “Because, while you were in my basilica, you asked of me only the liberation of your body and not the salvation of your soul, you have fallen into these dangers. But because the Lord has had mercy on you, [Col. 1028A] He has sent me to draw you out of these prisons.” Having broken his chains, he disappeared.

The man went out free, taking with him as testimony a piece of the chain. He showed it to all the pagans whom he met and who wished to capture him, and immediately every opponent fled from him. Thus he came safely through the land of the Saracens to the land of the Christians. Many bands of lions, bears, leopards, and dragons also wished to devour him as he crossed the wilderness; but when they saw the chain which the apostle had touched, they immediately fled from him. I, Calixtus, found this man, when he was again travelling to Saint James in the year 1100, between Stella and Grugnum, barefoot and with his feet skinned; and he told me all these things.

Among the Spaniards, at Vindelionum [Col. 1028B], on the feast day of Saint James, a certain peasant threshed wheat on the threshing floor. Afterwards, when he went to the bathhouse and sat there, the skin of his back, from his shoulders to his legs, adhered to the walls of the bathhouse, and there, before all who saw, he breathed his last. Among the Basques, at Albinetum, the people refused to observe the apostle’s feast. That same night the whole village was burned, by a fire said to have been sent from heaven. In the village of Saint-Damian, in the territory of Montpellier, a certain peasant woman was ordered to make bread baked under the ashes. When it was brought to the table and broken, blood flowed from it. These last three miracles are not from the book of Calixtus.

1125.

After Calixtus, Honorius II sat as the one hundred and sixty-eighth pope, for five years and two months. Blessed Bernard [Col. 1028C] wrote several letters to this Honorius. Tyre is said to have been captured, but it is not stated by whom—whether Christians or Saracens. Therefore the man who noted this, striving to be brief, became obscure.

1126.

A most severe winter occurred, and a great famine. In Haspengouw a monster was born, human in front and dog behind. Charles, count of Flanders, was murdered by the treachery of certain of his magnates while praying in church at Bruges.

1127.

Louis, king of the French and son of Philip, exacted a most severe punishment upon the perpetrators of the crime, so that some were even condemned to the wheel. Their whole offspring was exiled, and many innocent people who had not plundered paid the penalty. Among them were [Col. 1028D] my father Herman and his brother Ellebaud. Though noble and very handsome boys, after losing great inheritances they fled from Flanders into France.

1128.

Geoffrey, bishop of Rouen, died. After him Hugh, formerly a monk of Cluny, became archbishop, a religious and learned man. He wrote an elegant book on various questions for Matthew of Albano, who had likewise been promoted from Cluny. Blessed Bernard wrote to this Hugh, writing among other things as follows:

“If the evil of the day grows stronger, let it not prevail. If it disturbs, let it not throw you into confusion. The billows of the sea are wondrous, but more wondrous is the Lord on high. Graciously—if you do not ignore it—has the mercy from above dealt with you until now, illustrious Father [Col. 1029A]. For by provident dispensation you were not set over evil men before you had been joined to good men, so that by their fellowship and example you might become good, and might afterwards be able to live as a good man even among bad men.

“To be good among good people indeed brings salvation; but to be good among bad people brings praise. The former belongs to as much intimacy as security; the latter to as much virtue as difficulty. For it is a great thing to touch pitch and not be defiled by it; to dwell in fire unharmed, and to remain amid darkness without gloom. David says: ‘I have dwelt with the dwellers of Kedar’ (Psalm 119 [120]). He does not say ‘in Kedar,’ but ‘with the dwellers of Kedar,’ as one who always lived in the light, although he had bodily cohabitation with dwellers in darkness—that is, in Kedar.

“Thus, when long ago the Egyptians were feeling their way through darkness, wherever the children of Israel were—though they were certainly among them—there was light [Col. 1029B]. Hence the same prophet rebukes certain false Israelites: ‘Mingled among the nations, they learned their works, and it became a stumbling-block to them’ (Psalm 105 [106]). Formerly, among your Cluniacs, it was enough for you to preserve innocence; but among the people of Rouen, patience is needed, as the Apostle says: ‘A servant of God ought not to quarrel, but rather to be patient with all’ (2 Timothy 2).

“Not merely patient—not wishing to be conquered by evil—but also peaceable, overcoming evil by good, so that you may bear the bad and heal those whom you endure, possessing your soul in patience. But be peaceable also, so that you may possess those entrusted to you. Be patient because you are among evil men; be peaceable because you preside over evil men. Let your charity have zeal, but let severity apply moderation according to the occasion. Discipline, indeed, when never relaxed, often makes more progress when it is nevertheless temporarily suspended. Let the vigour of justice always be fervent, but never rash. As not everything that pleases is lawful, so not everything lawful is immediately expedient. You yourself know these things better than I do; therefore I refrain. I ask that you pray for me without ceasing, because I sin without ceasing.”

1129.

HUGH FARSITUS. In the year of the Lord 1129, in the district of Soissons, power was granted to the Adversary to strike many persons of different ages and sexes with an invisible plague, so that, once their bodies were ignited, they burned with intolerable agony. This disease is wasting: beneath stretched, livid skin, it separates and consumes the flesh from the bones; and, as time passes, it gains increases of pain and burning, compelling the wretched to die moment by moment. Yet death does not come to those who desire it, until, after their limbs have been consumed, that swift and deadly fire attacks the vital members. And what is very remarkable: this fire, though powerful in consuming without heat, drenches the miserable with a cold like ice so intense that they cannot be warmed by any remedies.

Likewise, no less remarkable is this: once it has been extinguished by divine grace, and the deadly cold driven away, so great a heat pervades the diseased parts that the disease of cancer very often joins itself to that burning unless remedies are applied. For six days in the month of September they were in the church of the Blessed Virgin [Col. 1030A]. At the prayers of the people, who were flocking to that church from other churches and from the principal church, the blessed Mother of God came, drawing with her strong hosts of holy spirits. At her presence hell would fear and the gates of death tremble.

So great a trembling, heralding her coming, filled the church that everyone fled, thinking that an earthquake had occurred or that the church had been shaken from its foundations. But when they returned and perceived that there was no danger, they found that the burning of the sick had been reduced and every pain lulled by a most swift bestowed sweetness. Some sick people say that, on the day before this heavenly benefit, abundant brightnesses had poured through the glass windows of the church, as though they were heralds [Col. 1030B] of the gift which was to follow. Within fifteen days, one hundred and three persons are recorded by name as having been extinguished from this fire. Many also affirm that stars of marvellous size drove away the dark gloom of night beyond the church.

A certain woman named Gendrada, wife of a man named Theoderic, living in Riparia beyond the River Aisne, which flows past the city of Soissons, came to the church from a village called Andiguncurtis along with the others. The fire had consumed her face, nose, upper lip, and flesh down to her breasts, gums, and molar teeth; and the fire was extinguished from her face. But she had become burdensome and hateful to every person she encountered, unpleasant for all—even her own people—to behold. Therefore she was compelled to cover her whole face except her eyes with a damp cloth [Col. 1030C].

She returned to the church of the Blessed Virgin, made a candle to offer, and went to sleep. Waking earlier in the same night, she felt the soaked cloth slip loose. As she tried to secure it and draw it upward again, but made little progress, she was compelled to call for the help of those around her. While they delayed, sluggish from sleep or cold, she asked that a lamp be lit and help brought to her. Meanwhile she felt the flesh pressed beneath her fingers and the cloth grow soft, and did not know that it was the flesh of a restored lip and nose. As she repeatedly unfolded the cloth and correspondingly felt the newly formed creation again and again, she cried out three times in a very loud voice: “God and holy Mary, help!”

Those present, awakened and alarmed by that cry [Col. 1030D], quickly brought in a light and saw a newly formed nose and lip. A boy eleven years old, a keeper of livestock, whose feet were burning, was brought by his mother. Having received relief from pain within a few days, he was carried back home. He was from Vallibus. But when, by divine prompting, the same boy, not unmindful of so great a benefit, burned with desire to see the house of the Blessed Virgin, and daily pressed his mother insistently about it while she wholly refused to agree, he said: “Let the illness return to me, so that I must be carried there.” And so it happened.

He was therefore brought back there by his mother. At the entry of the procession of the mother church, roused from rest, he broke the air with cries of thanksgiving. He told [Col. 1031A] everyone that he had been taken up before God and had seen our Lady, the Mother of God, pleading for the people: that God might deign to turn away and overthrow this disease from the people, and remove this spark which had befallen them. From her Son she graciously received this answer: “Mother, you are the star of the sea; let all your will be done.” When the same Virgin again asked about her own house, which was inferior and despised in comparison with the others, he heard from her Son that money should be brought from beyond the sea and beyond the Rhine, from which her house should be built, and that He would adorn it with great brightness and glory before the eyes of all beholders.

He also foretold that evils would come upon the people of Soissons from God, because they would not restore the church of His Mother. Indeed, the fire attacked many from that same city; what remains, and of what sort, we do not know [Col. 1031B]. The same boy testified that he would die shortly afterward, and so it occurred, for he did not survive a month. A very remarkable thing about this boy was that, recounting all history from the beginning of the world, he set forth his whole account rapidly in rhythm. He rehearsed the text of the Gospel and the deeds of the Lord in such order as if he were reading all things in a book and pronouncing words dictated by others.

Among other things, he said of Joseph, husband of the Blessed Virgin: “He who holds the sceptre of the flowering rod was guardian of the glorious woman.” He told these things with his eyes closed, as though he hated transitory light. He scarcely deigned to speak to laymen and the unlettered, as though wearied beyond endurance by their ignorance. When he died, so great a grace suffused his body that the whiteness and brightness of his face indicated something angelic and divine, I know not what [Col. 1031C].

In a village called Kala, in the territory of Soissons—an estate of the mother church of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius—a woman suffering from a difficult childbirth was in peril for three continuous weeks. Persuaded by neighbouring women, she vowed that she would go barefoot to blessed Mary of Soissons; she was newly delivered, but in a wondrous manner. For first she expelled from her womb three stones: the first the size of a goose’s egg, the second nearly the size of a hen’s egg, and the third no smaller than a certain nut. As soon as these stones had been discharged, the child’s birth followed; it received the grace of baptism and survived for a few days.

A certain married woman of Blericurt [Col. 1031D], a village near Cociacum, was struck blind. She was brought to Soissons, where she was recognized by the mayor of Austrechia, her kinsman, while she embraced the altar. Asking why she had come, he said, in the presence of Abbess Matilda: “Rightly, my kinswoman, have you been struck with blindness, because, although you are a servant of our lady Saint Mary, you denied the Lord to her. Confess the truth, therefore, if you wish to be healed by the Mother of Truth.” This was done, and she was healed.

The monastery of Ourscamp is founded. After Honorius, Innocent III sat at Rome as the one hundred and sixty-ninth pope. Peter Leonis was ordained against him through faction. To quell the plague of this schism, Saint Bernard was summoned from Clairvaux and laboured greatly [Col. 1032A], accomplishing much. Once, when Bernard was in the town of Noyon, in the house of Bishop Simon, Hervaeus of Baugency was brought to him: a most charming boy, of royal blood and Bernard’s own nephew. On the following night Christ revealed to His servant what would happen after a long time.

For Bernard seemed, during the celebration of Mass, to give the kiss of peace to a certain angel, to carry to the boy. Certain of the revelation, Bernard foretold that Hervaeus would renounce the world and one day become a devoted servant of Christ. Later the venerable Valeran, first abbot of Ourscamp, made him a monk; fulfilling an angelic office, he imparted to Hervaeus the peace which he himself had received from the mouth of the holy father. Hervaeus succeeded the aforesaid [Col. 1032B] Valeran in the government of Ourscamp. Finally, while still healthy and sound, he foresaw and foretold his approaching death, Valeran himself announcing it to him by revelation.

Innocent’s life, reputation, and learning were considered worthy of the supreme priesthood. But Peter Leonis, aspiring to this height of honour, was called Anacletus by supporters corrupted with money. He had amassed countless riches both from the exactions of the curia and from the business of legations, which he had reserved for the anticipated market-day. Moreover, great stores of paternal revenues, hitherto sealed up but now distributed among the people, armed for every lawful and unlawful purpose a populace purchasable with money.

After these resources had been distributed, he tore the royal gifts—the ornaments of the church—from the altars themselves [Col. 1032C]. When even irreverent Christians blushed or feared to break up chalices and divide golden crucifixes limb by limb, Jews were sought out to shatter boldly the sacred vessels and images consecrated to God. Meanwhile, at a council convened at Étampes, Saint Bernard persuaded the assembly to receive Innocent. Innocent was honourably received at Orléans by Louis, king of the French. From there he was brought to Chartres by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, a man of great virtues; Henry, king of the English, also met him there.

1130.

A monastery at Beaumont was founded under its first abbot, Alexander, by the venerable Robert of Candoe.

1131.

[Col. 1032D]

A great synod was held at Reims by Pope Innocent. After making many arrangements for the honour of God, he crowned Louis king in place of his brother Philip, who had been thrown from a horse and killed by a pig, while their father was still alive. The same Innocent dedicated the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons, which stands across the river. Among those present was a woman from the district of Laon. She proceeded with others to enter the monastery of the Blessed Virgin, but was repelled from the entrance by an invisible power. Then she began to be afflicted with extreme terror and to tremble throughout her body. Having confessed and received absolution, she was granted entry.

1132.

A great synod was held at Pisa by Pope Innocent and the bishops of the whole West. When the council had been dissolved, the lord pope sent from his side Saint Bernard, Guido of Pisa, and Matthew, bishop of Albano [Col. 1033A], to reconcile the Milanese and cleanse away the schism created in that city by Anselm. At the abbot’s request, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, was joined to them. Many possessed persons were healed there.

1133.

An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third day before the Nones of August [3 August]. Emperor Lothair died. Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy flourished in holiness, learning, and much glory of miracles. So too did Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, whom blessed Bernard visited. On seeing Bernard, the bishop prostrated himself and adored him to the ground; seeing this, Saint Bernard likewise fell before him. Thereafter those two sons of brightness became one heart and one soul.

1134.

[Col. 1033B]

Conrad, nephew of the elder Henry, ruled after Lothair. He ruled among the Romans and Germans for twenty-two years. At that time Mascelin, an upright and honourable cleric of Mainz, was converted and followed blessed Bernard at Clairvaux. Abbot Alexander, with his whole community and with the assent of Henry, king of the English, came into the forest of Luins and built his monastery in the hermitage called the Dead Sea.

(1135.) Henry, king of the English, died in the thirty-fifth year of his reign. He was succeeded, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], by his nephew Stephen, who reigned for nineteen years.

(1136.) At that time Geoffrey of Péronne was converted; he later became prior of Clairvaux. His father also, a noble and powerful man, became a monk and prefect at Clairvaux [Col. 1033C], and was buried by Saint Bernard. At that time the whole province of Bordeaux suffered under the oppression of schismatics. In Aquitaine there was no one able to resist the prince whose heart God had hardened. At the persuasion of Girard, bishop of Angoulême, who instilled seeds of dissension into his heart, he had become defender and author of the schism.

Girard sent to Peter Leonis, asking that he grant him a legation; he himself would swear fidelity and obedience, and would moreover bring the prince of the land and all whom he could under Peter’s authority. The man of perdition rejoiced that he had found a place in which to spread his wickedness; he quickly and gladly consented. He sent to Girard Giles, cardinal-bishop of Tusculum, who alone among the Romans, with Peter of Porto, had adhered to him. Thus Girard, resuming the horns [of authority], began publicly to appear wearing a mitre, which he had not done before.

By these two, William, bishop of Poitiers, an upright and Catholic man, was violently expelled from his see [Col. 1033D], and another man was intruded in his place—noble in lineage but degenerate in faith. Likewise they intruded a certain Ranulf of Dorat into the church of Limoges. Not long afterward, falling backward from his horse on a level road, he died when a single avenging stone, left there for this purpose, struck his head and shattered his brain.

When Geoffrey, venerable bishop of Chartres, to whom Pope Innocent had entrusted the legation of Aquitaine, heard these and similar reports, he took Saint Bernard with him. They came to Nantes. There a woman was healed by the holy man, having for six years been oppressed by an incubus demon [Col. 1034A].

The dean of the church of Poitiers dared to break apart the altar at which Saint Bernard had sung Mass. Shortly afterward he was struck by God; as he was already breathing out his life, he saw his house full of demons. Crying that a demon was cutting his throat, he asked those standing around for a knife to thrust into his own throat to draw out the demon. Amid these words he died. The archpriest who announced the synod of Peter, invader of the church of Poitiers, was seized by the devil in the presence of those whom he was inviting to the assembly of perfidy. God’s hand also visibly inflicted vengeance upon many others who had been more fervent in that schism [Col. 1034B].

At last the prince was reconciled and the bishops who had been expelled were restored to their sees. Girard alone persisted in evil; he was suddenly found dead in his bed without confession or viaticum, monstrously swollen. His nephews buried him in a certain basilica, but Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, had him removed from there and cast elsewhere. His nephews too were driven from the same church, and the whole offspring and planting, uprooted from the root, went into exile through foreign kingdoms, bearing the complaints of so great a judgment.

Roger, king of Sicily, alone among the princes disobeyed Innocent. Trusting in Peter of Pisa’s eloquence, he sent to Peter Leonis that he might delegate Peter of Pisa to him from his side. But the holy abbot reconciled Peter of Pisa himself to Pope Innocent. Three days later Peter Leonis died unrepentant. His corpse was buried in concealment, and to this day that grave is unknown to Catholics.

(1137.) Abbot Alexander joined the house of the Dead Sea to the Cistercian Order; Valeran, abbot of Ourscamp, received it as a daughter-house and transferred his monks there.

(1138.) Abbot Alexander resigned the care of the abbacy. Adam, formerly prior of Ourscamp, succeeded him. King Louis died in the twenty-ninth year of his reign.

(1139.) Louis, son of Louis—father of the present Philip—ruled among the Franks for forty years. This Louis had already been crowned king seven years earlier.

(1140.) [Col. 1034D] The abbey of Froidmont was founded under its first abbot, Manasses. At that time Henry, brother of King Louis, became a monk at Clairvaux; not long afterward he was raised to the bishopric of Beauvais.

(1141.) England was laid waste by famine and the sword, while the princes of that land were at discord among themselves.

(1142.) At that time Pope Innocent founded, at Tre Fontane, the monastery of Saint Anastasius the Martyr, constructing monastic dwellings there; and he requested a community and abbot from Clairvaux. Bernard, formerly vice-lord of the church of Pisa, was sent there with a community.

At that time there was Peter Abelard, a distinguished master, most celebrated for his reputation for learning, but teaching treacherously concerning the faith. Pope Innocent condemned his writings to fire and [Col. 1035A] their author to silence. Blessed Bernard identified objectionable propositions in his books in the letter which he wrote about him to Pope Innocent. Yet his books are still eagerly kept by many, to whom stolen waters are sweeter and hidden bread more pleasant. I myself have found much in them that is objectionable.

Geoffrey of Auxerre, who for a long time was blessed Bernard’s secretary, had once been Peter’s disciple. Among other things, he says of Peter:

“I remember that I once had a master who, either himself devouring or serving to his disciples nothing further of the Paschal lamb than its feet and entrails, defrauded both himself and his followers of no small part of it. For, emptying the price of redemption of its force, he commended to us nothing else in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 1035B] except an example of virtue and an incentive to love. What the Scriptures declare, namely that the human race was redeemed from the devil’s power by that precious blood, he said consisted solely in this: that an example had been shown us of striving even unto death for truth and justice, and that, as it were, an incentive to love had been applied, since the love bestowed gave occasion for loving in return.

“As though these two things had not already been shown to us in the deaths of prophets slain for truth and justice; and these indeed are great and true things, but not the only things. Blessed be God, who afterward gave both me and you a better master, through whom he rebuked the former man’s ignorance and refuted his presumption. For he, as a true Hebrew [Col. 1035C], eagerly devoured and carefully commended to us for eating the head of the lamb with its feet and entrails: preaching that the suffering Lord should be imitated and the loving Lord loved in return, while professing and worshipping human redemption in Him as the principal cause of this sacrifice, like the lamb’s head.

“For Christ set before us three special things in His Passion: an example of virtue, an incentive to love, and the sacrament of redemption. To the heretic who empties this third of force, the rest could be of no benefit. For He strove to death for virtue’s sake in vain, providing us an example of patience; and in vain displayed and commended the affection of this immeasurable love, if captivity, long since consigned over, does not receive the effect of abundant redemption.”

Thus Geoffrey wrote strongly and in a Catholic manner against Peter, formerly his master [Col. 1035D]. My own master, who taught me from childhood, was also a disciple of this Peter Abelard: Ralph, an Englishman surnamed the Grammarian, a man of the church of Beauvais learned both in sacred and secular letters.

1143.

Celestine II becomes the one hundred and seventieth pope.

1144.

Lucius II becomes the one hundred and seventy-first pope. The city of Rouen was surrendered to Geoffrey, count of Anjou. A most violent wind overthrew trees, towers, and many houses.

1145.

Great famine grows severe in France. Saint Bernard performs many miracles in Germany. [Col. 1036A] There, near the city of Speyer, such was the crowd that King Conrad, lest the people crush him, took him up in his own arms after laying aside his cloak and carried him out of the basilica. Bernard, abbot of Saint Anastasius, is elected Roman pope and becomes the one hundred and seventy-second pope, being called Eugenius III. When a sedition arose among the people, he shook the dust from his feet upon the disputants and, leaving them, came into France. In his company Saint Bernard performed many signs. To this pope the same holy man wrote a book of great subtlety and usefulness, entitled *On Consideration*.

1146.

William, a boy in England, is crucified by the Jews on Good Friday in the city of Norwich. Concerning him the following vision is read. A boy named William, [Col. 1036B] fifteen years old, while asleep saw a radiant man saying to him: “Follow me.” At once he began to see a dark shadow on his left; but he was encouraged by the gentle appearance of his guide.

Thereafter he saw a dark valley, having fire on one side and exceedingly cold water on the other, where souls continually passed from one to the other. After this the old man led the boy to other torments, where he saw innumerable fiery seats, and an innumerable multitude being driven onto these seats. Demons brought flaming coins from purses and threw them into the mouth of each person; they expelled it through throat and gullet, but the demons again thrust it back into their mouths.

Afterward he saw flesh that seemed to have the shape of a fully formed human being cast by demons into cauldrons; and within a moment [Col. 1036C] it appeared as a newborn infant. Cast out of the cauldrons with fiery forks, these beings seemed to be transformed into their former age; and thus they were repeatedly boiled anew in the cauldrons.

Led thence to another fire, he saw countless people cast into it and dissolved at each separate joint; and the joints, cast again from the flame, returned to their places. Afterward he saw many fastened upon revolving wheels: men by their genital organs, women by their sexual members; and all cried, “Woe, woe!”

After this he saw many hanging head-downward above fiery seats, like thieves in a field. Others, dying of cold, saw garments laid beneath them but could not touch them. Others, tormented by hunger, could not touch the desirable foods placed beneath them. Those who had not aided others placed in any necessity [Col. 1036D] received no help in that same distress.

Afterward he saw Tartarus open, which seemed deeper in its descent than the length of the road from Canterbury to London. There the ancient enemy sat in the midst of the flame, stretched out into six parts. As the boy stood trembling beside the rim of the pit, the foul spirit which had continually clung to his left side since he left the house began to accuse him, saying: “I have always suggested every evil thing to this boy.” But it said absolutely nothing of those things which the boy had confessed before Easter—for this happened after Easter. Yet it brought so many and such grave charges against him that they seemed sufficient for eternal condemnation.

Then, at his guide’s prompting, when the boy protected himself with the sign of the cross, the pit disappeared. When that guide departed, [Col. 1037A] the boy stood trembling in darkness for a long time. But when the guide returned, he led the boy to a bright radiance; and immediately there appeared a wall of immeasurable length and breadth, in which no entrance was visible. When they came there, in an instant they found themselves carried beyond it.

In that desirable country there appeared a round house with twelve gates, as it is written: “Three gates on the east,” and so forth (Ezek. 48). Having entered it, they saw it to be so vast that all those in the world could not fill a tenth part of it. There he saw many in great glory, but others still more glorious. Then he saw ten companies of the blessed.

Coming to the eastern gate, he saw, about the middle of the doorway, a certain altar, around which radiant men were seated; all of them served one person as [Col. 1037B] pre-eminent above them. He wore on his head a golden crown adorned with twelve golden crosses. His guide addressed the boy, who rejoiced in this vision: “This will be your place if you live well. Know that this is the boy William, whom the Jews crucified at Norwich. Although he is already in great glory because of his brief suffering, he will nevertheless have far greater glory still. Yet he has not deserved to behold the Redeemer’s face, nor have his companions whom you see in such great glory.”

Again the guide departed from him, but immediately returned and said: “Follow me, for by God’s command I shall bring you back to the place where I took you. But if you strive well, you will come to this glory.” At once he returned to his body, although unwillingly. He began to sleep on Monday, shortly before None. On Tuesday, about the third hour, [Col. 1037C] he raised himself upon his face and made the sign of the cross—namely, when he saw Tartarus open. On Thursday, about midday, he revived.

1147.

An eclipse of the sun occurred on Sunday, the fifth day before the Nones of November, at the third hour. King Louis, with the French, undertakes the journey to Jerusalem in the ninth year of his reign.

1148.

A council is held at Rheims by Pope Eugenius. At this council blessed Bernard publicly refuted Master Gilbert, surnamed Porretan, disputing alone with him as the unrivalled champion of his age. This Gilbert was bishop of Poitiers, greatly trained in sacred letters; but, investigating matters too lofty for himself, he became foolish. For, holding no simple view of the unity of the Holy Trinity and the simplicity of the Godhead, [Col. 1037D] and writing without fidelity, he set hidden loaves before his disciples and served them stolen waters. Nor did he readily acknowledge before authoritative persons what he thought—or rather, how foolishly he thought. For he feared what they say Peter Abelard told him at Sens:

> Your own affair is at stake when the neighboring wall burns.

At last, however, when the scandal among the faithful over this matter was already growing strong and the murmuring increasing, he was summoned before the assembly and ordered to surrender the book in which he had vomited forth grave blasphemies, although enclosed in a certain wrapping of words. Saint Bernard therefore first drew out, by subtle questions, all that the other was trying to conceal by verbal quibbles; then, in a two-day disputation, [Col. 1038A] refuted it both by his own arguments and by the testimonies of the saints.

But observing that some of those presiding now recognized the blasphemy in the teaching, yet still diverted the reproach from the person, he was fired with zeal and convened separately his own Gallican Church. Finally, by the common counsel of the Fathers of ten provinces and of many other bishops and abbots, a new creed, dictated by the man of God, was set against the new doctrines. The names of every one of them were also subscribed, so that the irreproachable zeal of them all might become known to others. Thus at length, by apostolic judgment and the authority of the universal Church, that error was condemned.

Bishop Gilbert was asked whether he consented to the same condemnation. Consenting, and publicly retracting what he had earlier written [Col. 1038B] and affirmed, he himself obtained pardon—especially because from the outset he had prudently entered the disputation on the condition that he promised, without any obstinacy, freely to correct his opinion in accordance with the judgment of Holy Church.

Certain disciples of these two masters, namely Peter Abelard and Gilbert of Poitiers, excessively zealous for them, afterward began to disparage blessed Bernard and the whole Cistercian Order. One of them, Master Stephen, surnamed of Alinerra, told me that he himself had been present at that Council of Rheims, and that our Bernard had accomplished nothing against his Gilbert; but that, on the contrary, Gilbert himself had entirely confirmed his opinion by arguments and authorities; that certain bishops and abbots of France, out of private regard for our Bernard, had preferred his dream to that teaching, and had induced Pope Eugenius to condemn it.

He further added that our Bernard had suffered great humiliation at Auxerre at that time, where he had foretold that he would raise a certain dead man in the presence of all the people, but, after many prayers poured forth in vain, was unable to raise him. This Stephen was one of the clerics of Henry, Count of Champagne; a canon of Beauvais and of Saint Quiriacus at Provins; and exceptionally practiced in every sort of wit in both languages, Latin and French. Yet he was most avaricious, as one who had always pursued idleness and other people’s food. In the same year [Col. 1038D] in which he told me these things, he died—I believe in vengeance for Saint Bernard, whom he had disparaged.

1149.

In this year Saint Malachy died, as is read in a vision which a certain Mark wrote for Abbess G.; from this I have decided to excerpt certain matters here. For he says:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1149, which was the second year of the Jerusalem expedition of Conrad, King of the Romans, and the fourth year of Pope Eugenius; in which year that pope himself returned from the regions of France to Rome, and in which Saint Malachy also died at Clairvaux—this vision was seen.

“There are two metropolitan sees in Ireland: Armagh, of the northern Irish, and Cashel, of the southern. From the latter came a certain man named Tundal, noble by birth, cruel in conduct, distinguished in bodily appearance, strong in courage, and wholly unconcerned for the salvation of his soul. He took it badly if anyone so much as briefly spoke to him about the salvation of his soul. He neglected church; he did not wish even to see Christ’s poor; whatever he had, he gave to mimes and jongleurs for vain glory.

“Though he had many friends and companions, among them he had one to whom, by the obligation of comradeship, he owed three horses. When this man was awaiting the appointed term, after the time had passed he approached him. Having been well received by him, he stayed three nights; then he began to discuss certain matters. When the other answered that he did not presently have at hand what he sought, he departed angrily.

“But the debtor, wishing to appease him, asked him to take food with him before leaving. He sat down [Col. 1039B] and, laying aside the axe he held in his hand, began to eat with him. Immediately, struck invisibly, he could not draw back to his mouth the hand which he had stretched out, and he began to cry out terribly. He entrusted his axe, which he had set down, to his companion’s wife, saying: ‘Keep my axe, for I am dying.’ Immediately his body fell lifeless, as though it had never had life.

“All the signs of death are present. The household runs together; the food is removed; the squires cry out; the host weeps; the body is laid out; the bells are rung; the clergy assemble; the people marvel; the whole city is disturbed by the death of a good knight. From the tenth hour on Wednesday until the same hour on Saturday he lay thus dead. Yet a slight warmth in the left part of his breast was felt by those carefully touching him; therefore they were unwilling to bury him.

“After this he recovered his spirit and began to breathe with a weak breath, as it were, for the space of one hour. To the astonishment of all, he began to look about with a feeble gaze. Asked whether he wished to receive communion, he indicated that the body of the Lord should be brought to him. Having received it and drunk wine, he began, in thanksgiving, to praise God and say: ‘O God, your mercy is greater than my iniquity, though it is exceedingly great. How many great and grievous tribulations you have shown me! Yet you turned and restored me to life, and brought me back from the depths of the earth.’

“Having said this, he immediately disposed by testament of all that he possessed and gave it to the poor. He ordered himself to be signed with the sign of the cross and vowed utterly to abandon his former life. [Col. 1039D] He recounted all that he had seen and suffered, saying:

‘When my soul put off its body and knew that it was dead, the consciousness of its guilt began to terrify it, and it did not know what to do. It was afraid, indeed, but did not know what it feared. It wished to return to the body, but could not enter; it wished to go outside, but was terrified everywhere.

‘Therefore, weeping and groaning, not knowing what to do and trusting in nothing except God’s mercy, it at last saw coming toward it so great a multitude of unclean spirits that they filled not only the house and its courtyard, but even the lanes and streets of the city. Surrounding the miserable soul, they said: “Let us sing for this wretched soul the song owed to death; for she is the daughter of death, food for unquenchable fire, friend of darkness, and enemy of light.”

‘Turning toward her, they gnashed their teeth at her; in their extreme frenzy they tore their hideous cheeks with their own claws, saying: “Behold, wretch, the people you chose, with whom you shall enter hell to burn. Nurse of scandal, lover of discord—which we too love—why are you not proud now? Why do you not commit adultery? Why do you not fornicate? Where are your vanity and vain joy? Where is your unrestrained laughter, where your strength with which you insulted so many? Why do you not now make signs with your eyes, scrape with your foot, speak with your finger, or devise evil with a crooked heart, as you used to do in your frivolities and buffooneries?”

‘While they said these and similar things, it saw coming from afar [Col. 1040B] something like a most brilliant star. At once it fixed on this an unwearied gaze, hoping to receive some consolation through it. It was its angel. When he drew near, he greeted it by its own name, saying: “Hail, Tundal; how are you?”

‘Seeing the exceedingly beautiful young man and hearing itself greeted by its own name, it answered thus in both fear and joy: “Alas, Lord Father! The pains of hell surround me; the snares of death have overtaken me.”

‘The angel said: “Now you call me lord and father, though I was always with you and you never judged me worthy of such a name.”

‘But it said: “Lord, where did I ever see you, or where did I ever hear your most sweet voice?”

‘The angel replied: “I always followed you from your birth, wherever you went; and you never wished to yield to my counsels.” Stretching out his hand toward one of the unclean spirits, who above the rest was reviling it insultingly, he said: “Behold the one whose will and counsel you always obeyed. But the mercy of God, which you have not deserved, will assist you. Therefore be confident and glad, because you will suffer few of the many things that you deserved. Follow me, and retain in memory whatever I show you, for you will return again to the body.”

‘Then it, exceedingly terrified, left its body over which it had stood and came nearer. Hearing this and seeing that they could not inflict the evils with which they threatened, the demons blasphemed God, calling him unjust because he did not render, as he had promised, to each according to [Col. 1040D] his works. After this they rose against one another and struck each other with whatever blows they could; then, leaving behind a dreadful stench, they withdrew in sadness and indignation.

‘The angel, going before, said to the soul: “Follow me.”

‘It answered: “Alas, my lord! If you go before, those behind will seize me and deliver me to eternal fires.”

‘The angel replied: “Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them. If God is for us, who is against us? (Rom. 8.) A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you. With your eyes you shall behold and see the recompense of sinners (Ps. 90).”

“Having said this, they set out. As they traveled together farther on [Col. 1041A] and had no light except the angel’s radiance, they finally came to a valley terrible, very dark, and covered with the gloom of death. It was deep and full of burning coals, and had an iron cover six cubits thick. This cover, through its extreme heat, surpassed the burning coals themselves; its stench surpassed all the tribulations that the soul had suffered thus far.

“Over that plate descended a multitude of wretched souls; there they were burned until they melted like grease in a frying-pan. What was worse, they were strained through the aforesaid plate, as wax is usually strained through cloth, and were again renewed for torment in the burning coals of fire. This was the punishment of parricides, fratricides, and murderers, whether by deed or consent.

“‘But after this punishment,’ said the angel, ‘they are led to greater ones. You, however, although you are a murderer, will not suffer this now.’

“After this they came to a mountain of astonishing size, great horror, and vast desolation, which afforded passers-by a very narrow path. On one side of this mountain was foul, sulphurous, dark fire; on the other, icy snow and a dreadful wind. The mountain was full of torturers, who had fiery iron forks and very sharp tridents. With these they pierced the throats of souls trying to pass and drew them to their punishments; alternately they hurled them from snow and hail into the fire, and back again.

“‘This,’ said the angel, ‘is the punishment of plotters and traitors.’

“After this, the soul, following the angel step by step in fear, [Col. 1041C] came to a deep valley, exceedingly foul and dark. The soul itself could not see its depth, but it heard the sound of a sulphurous river and the howling of those suffering in it. From it rose foul smoke from sulphur and corpses, surpassing all the punishments it had seen before.

“There was there a very long plank extending from one mountain to another, stretched like a bridge above the valley. It was one thousand paces long and one foot wide. No one but one of the elect could cross this bridge. It saw many fall from the bridge, and only one priest pass over unharmed. He was a pilgrim, carrying a palm branch and clothed in a pilgrim’s cloak; before all others, he crossed first and fearlessly.

“But the angel, comforting the frightened soul, said: ‘Do not fear. You will be freed from this punishment, but you will suffer another.’ Going before, he took it and led it unharmed beyond the bridge, saying: ‘This is the dreadful valley and the punishment of the proud.’

“As the angel went before, they traveled along a dark, winding, difficult road. While it toiled greatly in proceeding through the darkness, the soul saw at a distance a beast of incredible size and unbearable terror, greater than all the mountains it had seen previously. Its eyes were like burning hills; its mouth was so wide and open that it seemed able to hold nine thousand armed men. [Col. 1042A] In its mouth it had two giant parasites, very grotesquely placed with their heads reversed. One had its head upward toward the upper teeth of the aforesaid beast and its feet downward toward the lower teeth; the other the reverse. They stood like columns in its mouth, dividing it into the likeness of three gates.

“Unquenchable flame came from that mouth, divided into three parts through the three gates; and souls to be condemned were forced to enter against that flame. An incomparable stench likewise issued from the mouth itself, and through the same mouth was heard the lamenting of the multitude within its belly. For inside were many thousands of men and women paying the penalty of dreadful torments. Before its mouth also stood a multitude of unclean spirits forcing souls to enter, afflicting them with many blows and beatings before they entered.

“When Tundal’s soul had long looked upon so horrible a monster, it said to the angel in extreme terror: ‘Lord, why are you approaching there?’

“The angel replied: ‘We cannot otherwise complete our journey. None but the elect can escape this punishment. This beast is called Acheron, and it devours all the avaricious. Of it it is written: “It will swallow up the river and not marvel; and it is confident that the Jordan will flow into its mouth” [Job 40]. Those who appear in its mouth and set opposite one another among its teeth are giants and, in their own times, were faithful to the devil in their wickedness.’

“Having said this, the angel drew nearer, went before the soul, and stood before the beast. The soul followed, though unwillingly. When they stood together before the beast, [Col. 1042C] the angel disappeared and the wretched soul remained alone. The demons surrounded it like rabid dogs, flogged it, and dragged it with them into the beast’s belly.

“How much it suffered there was later shown by its countenance and its changed conduct. It suffered bites and tearing by dogs, bears, lions, serpents, and innumerable other unknown and monstrous savage animals; blows of demons; the heat of fire; the harshness of cold; the stench of sulphur; darkness before its eyes; a flow of burning tears; gnashing of teeth; an abundance of afflictions. There the miserable soul accused itself for its former deeds; in overwhelming sadness and despair it tore its own cheeks. And when it thought itself eternally damned there, it felt itself, by some means unknown to me, outside the beast. Lying weak at some distance from it, it opened its eyes and saw near it the angel of light who had gone before. [Col. 1042D] Then, joyful though afflicted, it greatly praised the Lord for his mercy; and the angel touched and strengthened it.

“Going thence, they saw farther on a very broad and stormy lake, whose towering waves did not allow them to see the sky. There was a very great multitude of terrible beasts, roaring in order to devour souls. Across the width of the lake was a very narrow bridge, two miles long. Its width was one palm; it was longer and narrower than the bridge above.

“That plank was full of extremely sharp iron nails set into it, which pierced the feet of all who crossed. All the beasts gathered at that bridge in order to take food from it—namely, souls unable to cross. The beasts were so large that they resembled great towers; fire came from their mouths so fierce that onlookers thought the lake itself was boiling.

“It saw there a certain soul weeping intensely on the bridge and accusing itself of many crimes. It was burdened with the heavy weight of sheaves of grain and was compelled to cross this bridge. Though it suffered acutely from the nails piercing the soles of its feet, it feared even more to fall into the lake and into the open mouths of the beasts.

“When Tundal asked what this meant, the angel said: ‘This punishment is especially appropriate for you [Col. 1043B] and for those like you who commit theft, whether great or small. Yet those who offend in small matters and those who offend in great do not suffer in the same way—unless that small thing is sacrilege. A person is guilty of sacrilege who steals either a consecrated thing or anything from a consecrated place. Most especially guilty are those who sin under the habit of religion.

‘You must cross this bridge, lead an untamed cow with you, and return it unharmed to me beyond the bridge, because you once stole your godfather’s cow.’

“Tundal replied: ‘Lord, did I not return it?’

“‘You did,’ he said, ‘but when you could not hide it. Therefore you will not suffer the full punishment, because it is a lesser evil to will than to accomplish, though both are evil before God.’

“Having said this, the angel showed him the untamed cow. Therefore Tundal, willing or unwilling, took hold of the cow and tried with whatever threats he could to drive it onto the bridge. The roaring beasts came and waited for their food from the bridge. Tundal began the journey, but the cow would not follow him. When Tundal stood, the cow fell; and when it stood, Tundal fell. Thus, taking turns falling and standing, they came to the middle of the bridge.

“When they had come there, they saw the man carrying sheaves of wheat approaching them. He begged Tundal’s soul, which was leading the cow, not to block the bridge for him; and Tundal likewise [Col. 1043D] begged him to allow him to complete his journey, because he had already crossed half of it. Neither could return, I do not say, but could not even look back. So they stood and wept, making the bridge bloody with the blood of their feet. When they had remained thus for a long time, not knowing how, each saw that the other had passed him.

“Tundal then saw before him his angel, whom he had left behind. The angel said: ‘Welcome. Be anxious no longer about the cow, because you owe nothing further on its account.’

“When Tundal showed his feet and said that he could go no farther, the angel replied: ‘You must remember how swift your feet were to shed blood; therefore ruin and misery are in your ways.’ Touching him, he healed him and so went on before.

[Col. 1044A] “When Tundal said, ‘Lord, where are we going now?’ the angel answered: ‘A most foul torturer awaits our arrival, whose lodging we cannot pass by. This lodging is always full of guests, but its host still desires to find other guests for punishment.’

“As he went through dark and dry places, there appeared to them a vast open house, like a steep mountain because of its enormous size, round like an oven. A flame came from it which, for a thousand paces, burned whatever souls it could find. Seeing this, Tundal said to the angel: ‘Behold, we are approaching the gates of death. Who will free me, wretched as I am?’

“The angel said to him: ‘You will indeed be freed from this outer flame, but you will enter the very house from which it proceeds.’

“As they came nearer, they saw executioners standing amid the flames with axes and knives, double-edged adzes, augers, sickles, exceedingly sharp pincers, spades, digging-tools, and other implements by which they could flay, behead, split apart, or mutilate souls. Under their hands was a multitude of souls enduring all these things.

“Seeing this, Tundal said to the angel: ‘I beg you, lord, if it pleases you, free me from this punishment alone, and allow me to be handed over to all the others that follow.’

“The angel said: ‘This is a greater punishment than all you have seen until now; but you will yet see one greater still. Enter this punishment, for rabid dogs await you.’

“Tundal, trembling [Col. 1044C] and failing from distress, begged not to enter, but gained nothing. When the demons saw that he had been yielded to them, they surrounded him; heaping great insults upon him, they tore him to pieces with the aforementioned instruments. The lord of this house was called Phistrinus.

“In this house were groaning and sorrow, weeping and gnashing of teeth; a slow fire outside and a vast conflagration inside. There was an insatiable craving for food there, and the excess of gluttony could not be satisfied. Sexual parts were tortured with most grievous pains. The very genitalia, corrupted by decay, seemed to teem with worms; and into these private parts of men and women—not only laypersons but religious persons as well—certain dreadful beasts entered.

[Col. 1044D] “There Tundal’s soul acknowledged that it justly suffered such things. But when it pleased God, it found itself outside the torments, though it did not know by what means. It sat in darkness and the shadow of death. Seeing its angel, it said: ‘Alas, my lord, where is what we have heard: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord”?’ (Ps. 32.)

“The angel answered: ‘This saying has deceived many. For although God is merciful, he is also just. He exacts many penalties, but forgives more. You have justly suffered whatever you have suffered. But then you will give thanks when you see what torments you have escaped through God’s mercy.

‘If God forgave everything, why would anyone be just? And if one did not fear punishments, why would one fear sinning or turn away from one’s pleasures? What need would there be [Col. 1045A] for those who have confessed to repent, if they did not fear God?

‘God mercifully spares sinners who do not perform penance while in the body. Yet they are destroyed according to their deserts. Likewise, temporal prosperity is justly taken away in this bodily life from the righteous for their offenses; but good things without end are mercifully reserved for them with the angels. God forgives many evil deeds, yet he leaves no good work unrewarded. No one is free from sin, not even an infant one hour old’ (Job 14, according to the Septuagint).

‘Many, however, are delivered from punishment, so that the shadow of death does not touch them. The righteous, therefore, who do not suffer punishments after death are nevertheless led to see them, so that, having seen the torments from which they are delivered by God’s grace, they may burn more ardently in love of God [Col. 1045B] and in praise of their Creator. Conversely, souls worthy of eternal punishments are first led to the glory of the saints [Note: [Col. 1045D] Read with caution.] so that, seeing the rewards which they freely abandoned, they may afterward suffer more greatly. For no punishment is so grave as to be separated from fellowship with God and the saints.

‘For this reason the priest whom you saw cross the first bridge safely was led to punishment, that, seeing the penalties, he might praise more ardently him who called him to his glory. For he was found a faithful and prudent servant, and therefore will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him. But since we have not yet seen all the evils, let us hasten.’

“Therefore, with the angel going before, Tundal saw a beast very unlike the others he had previously seen, [Col. 1045C] having two wings, a very long neck, an iron beak, and iron claws. From its mouth it belched unquenchable flame. This beast sat upon a lake frozen solid with ice and devoured souls; in its belly they were reduced to nothing through torments, and it bore them again into the lake frozen with ice, where they were renewed once more for punishment.

“All souls descending into the lake, both men’s and women’s, became pregnant and, thus pregnant, waited for the time of giving birth. Within, they were bitten in their entrails, after the manner of vipers, by the offspring conceived; and the wretched beings were thus kept alive in the cold water, frozen solid by the ice of the Dead Sea. When the time came [Col. 1045D] for them to give birth, they filled hell with howling cries and so gave birth to serpents.

“Not women alone but men also gave birth; and they did so not only through the members which nature has established as fitting for such an office, but also through arms and breasts alike. Beasts erupted through every part of their bodies, having burning iron heads and most sharp beaks; with these they tore apart the very bodies from which they emerged. Since those beasts wished to come out but could not draw their tails along with them, they did not cease to turn their burning iron beaks back into the bodies from which they emerged, until they consumed them down to the sinews and dry bones.

“Thus, together [Col. 1046A] the crashing of swelling ice, the howls of souls enduring this punishment while burning, and the bellows of the beasts issuing from them rose to heaven. On all their various limbs and fingers were heads of different beasts, which bit those limbs down to sinews and bones. They had living tongues like asps, which consumed the entire palate and windpipes down to the lungs. Their genitalia too, both men’s and women’s, were like serpents, which tore the lower parts of the belly and strove to pull out the entrails from there.

“Then the angel said: ‘This is the punishment of monks, canons, nuns, and other churchmen, who are known to lie to God by their tonsure and habit; who have sharpened their tongues like serpents and have not restrained their members from unclean deeds. Those who defile themselves by immoderate lust will undergo this punishment; and therefore you must undergo it.’

“Having said this, the demons seized it violently and gave it to the beast to be devoured.”

After the aforesaid torments, while she was in the brood of vipers, an angel of light came to her; touching her, he healed her and commanded her to follow him. Apart from the angel’s radiance they had no light, and they went through terrible places, more dreadful than many of those preceding, by a very narrow path which seemed to lead from the summit of a very high mountain into a precipice. The farther that soul descended, the less [Col. 1046C] she hoped to return to life. She said to the angel, “Lord, where are we going?” The angel replied, “This way leads to death.” And the soul said, “What then is meant by what is written: ‘Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many are they who enter by it’ (Matt. VII), when we see no one here except ourselves?” The angel replied, “This was not said of this path, but of the shameless, unlawful, and worldly life which leads to it.”

Going farther, and suffering beyond measure, they came to the valley of smiths. There they saw workshops in which exceedingly great lamentation was heard. Then the angel said: “This torturer is called Vulcan; through whose craft many have fallen, [Col. 1046D] and by whom they are tormented.” “Lord,” said the soul, “must I suffer his punishment?” “You must,” he said, who went before her as guide. Weeping, she followed him. And behold, the torturers, with red-hot tongs, the holy angel saying nothing, seized her and cast her into a furnace of burning fire; and, blowing bellows, as iron is commonly tested in the forge, so they tested her, until the souls suffering there were reduced to nothing.

And when they melted so that they appeared to be nothing but water, they were pierced with iron tridents; and, laid upon an anvil, they were struck with hammers until twenty or a hundred were reduced to one mass. Yet, what was more grievous, they did not perish even thus; for they desired death and could not find it. The torturers spoke among themselves, saying, “Is it enough?” And others in another workshop replied, “Throw them to us, so that we may see whether it is enough.” And they threw them; and the others caught them in iron tongs before they touched the ground, and, like the first, likewise gave them over to the fires.
