Thus miserably they were thrown now here, now there, and were burned everywhere until skin and flesh, sinews and bones alike were reduced to ashes and flame. After many sufferings Tundal’s advocate came, and, taking him from the midst of the ashes, said: “How are you? Were the pleasures of the flesh so sweet to you that for them you must endure so many and such great evils [Col. 1047A]?” He was wholly unable to answer, because after such punishment he had no strength to speak.

Then the angel said: “Take courage, for the Lord brings down to hell and brings back. Although the things you have suffered thus far are great, yet greater are those from which, through God’s mercy, you shall be delivered.” And he added: “All whom you saw above await God’s judgment. But those who are still in the lower regions have already been judged. For you have not yet reached the lowest hell.” As usual, touching and strengthening her, he went on before.

As they went together and conversed while walking, behold: sudden terror, unbearable cold, intolerable stench, and darkness incomparable with the former darkness. [Col. 1047C] Distress and anguish seized Tundal’s soul, so that it seemed to her that all the foundations of the earth were trembling; compelled, she said to the angel who went before her: “Alas, my lord, what is this, that I cannot stand as before?” Having said this, she could not move for fear; and behold, the angel quickly disappeared, and she could no longer see him. At once she began to despair. “For there is neither knowledge, nor work, nor reason in hell, whither she hastened” (Eccl. IX).

She heard the cries and howlings of a wondrous multitude, and thunder so horrible that neither our weakness could comprehend it nor her tongue describe it. Looking about, therefore, to see if she might somehow discern whence she had come, she saw a square, four-sided pit like a cistern. This well sent forth a foul column of flame [Col. 1047D] and smoke, extending to heaven; and within it was a vast multitude of souls and demons rising with the flame like sparks, and, reduced to nothing, falling again with the demons into the furnace, down into the abyss.

When she saw this, Tundal’s soul wished to draw herself back, but could not lift her feet from the ground. And when she tried this repeatedly and could not do it, filled with extreme frenzy she burned with rage against herself; tearing her cheeks with her nails, she cried: “Woe is me! Why do I not die? Why do I not die? What madness has deceived me?” Hearing this, the demons rising with the flame surrounded her with the instruments by which they dragged souls to torments, saying: “O [Col. 1048A] wretched soul, worthy of punishments and tortures, whence have you come here? You have experienced nothing yet. You shall still see a torment worthy of your deeds, from which you will neither be able to escape nor perish within it; but, living ever in torment, you shall burn without refreshment, without light, without consolation, without any aid. Henceforth you can hope for no mercy. You have drawn near to the gates of death, and without delay you shall be brought before the lowest hells. He who brought you here has himself deceived you; let him free you from our hands, if he can. You shall see him no more.”

And they said among themselves: “Why do we delay any longer? Let us drag her away and give her to Lucifer to devour.” Thus brandishing their weapons, they threatened her with eternal death. Those unclean spirits were black as coals; [Col. 1048B] their eyes were like burning lamps of fire; their teeth whiter than snow; they had tails like scorpions, very sharp iron claws, and wings like those of a vulture.

Meanwhile the angel of the Lord came. Having put the spirits of darkness to flight, he comforted his accused charge, saying: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of light, because you shall obtain mercy and not judgment. You shall indeed see great punishments, but you shall not suffer them. Come, then, and I shall show you the worst enemy of the human race.” Going before her to the gates of hell, he said: “Come and see. Know, however, that no light shines upon those assigned here; but you will be able to see them, and they will not see you.”

Approaching, [Col. 1048C] the soul saw the prince of darkness and the abyss of hell. What unheard-of torments, and of what kind, she saw there, she could in no way recount, even if she had a hundred heads and a hundred tongues in each head. There was seen the prince-devil, surpassing in size all the beasts she had seen before; the soul knew nothing among the things she had seen with which to compare the magnitude of his body. That beast was black as a raven, having the form of a human body from feet to head, except that it had very many hands and a tail. It had not fewer than a thousand hands, each about a hundred cubits in length and ten in thickness. Each hand had twenty fingers, and its fingers were a hundred palms in length and ten in thickness; its claws [Col. 1048D] were thicker and longer than soldiers’ lances, and were of iron; and there were as many on its feet. Its beak was exceedingly long and thick; its tail harsh and long, fitted with very sharp stings for injuring souls.

That horrible monster lay on an iron grating, with burning coals beneath it, while an innumerable multitude of demons blew bellows. Around it was such a multitude of souls and demons as no one would believe the world could have produced from the beginning over so many years. That ancient enemy was bound, limb by limb and joint by joint, with iron and bronze chains, fiery and very thick. As he tossed upon the coals and burned on every side, inflamed with excessive rage, he turned himself from [Col. 1049A] one side to the other and stretched all his hands out into the multitude of souls. Filling his hands with souls, he squeezed them as a thirsty peasant presses clusters of grapes in order to draw wine from them—so that no soul there was not deprived by that squeezing of head, feet, or hands. Then, sighing, he blew them forth and scattered the souls through the various parts of Gehenna.

Immediately that pit, of which we spoke above, belched foul flame; and when that dreadful beast drew in his breath, he drew back to himself all the souls he had scattered before, and devoured them as they fell into his mouth with smoke and sulphur. Whatever souls escaped his hands so as not to be squeezed, he struck with his tail. Thus that miserable beast, while continually striking others, is itself continually struck; and, while inflicting torments upon souls, is tortured in every torment more than all others.

Then the angel said to the soul: “This is Lucifer, the beginning of the ways of God, who moved amid the delights of paradise. If he were loosed, he would throw heaven and earth alike, down to hell, into confusion. All those who are with him are partly angels of darkness and partly sons of Adam; they have already been judged and await many others, who either denied Christ or performed the deeds of those who deny him. They first suffered the lesser torments which you saw, and afterwards were led to these; from these torments no one who has once entered them will ever be able to depart. These are evil prelates and rulers, of whom it is written: ‘The mighty shall suffer mighty torments’ (Wis. VI), [Col. 1049B] because they did not make good use of the power given them by God.”

Then the soul said to the angel: “Why is power not given to good people, so that they may govern well?” The angel replied: “Either the sins of subjects demand this, so that they may not have good rulers; or the good themselves are spared in this way, so that they may provide better for the salvation of their souls. But this unhappy one is called prince of darkness, not because of the power he has, but because of the primacy which he holds in darkness. All other punishments, however great, are counted as nothing in comparison with this.”

The soul said: “That is certainly true. For merely seeing this place troubles me more, and enduring its stench burdens me more, than suffering all that I suffered before. [Col. 1049D] Therefore I beg you, if it can be done, quickly take me away from here and do not permit me to be tortured here any longer. For I see here many relatives, companions, and acquaintances of mine, whose company I rejoiced to have with me in the world; and I greatly abhor their fellowship here. I know for certain that, unless divine mercy comes to my aid, my merits requiring it, I shall suffer no less than they do.”

The angel replied: “Come, happy soul, return to your rest, for God deals kindly with you. You shall not suffer these things, nor shall you see them again unless you deserve it. Until now you have seen the prison of God’s enemies; henceforth you shall see the glory of his friends.” The soul turned and followed the angel going before her. When they had not gone far, the stench vanished; the darkness was destroyed [Col. 1050A] and light appeared; fear fled and security returned; sorrow was laid aside, and that soul was filled with joy and gladness. She marvelled that she had changed so quickly and said: “O Lord, how have I been changed so quickly?” The angel replied: “Blessed are you. Do not wonder: this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. We must return to our region by another way. Therefore bless God and follow me.”

As they went, they saw a very high wall. Beneath it, on the side from which they had come, was a very great multitude of men and women enduring rain and wind. They were very sad, suffering hunger and thirst; nevertheless, they had light and did not smell the stench.

Then the angel said: “These people were evil indeed, but [Col. 1050B] not very evil. They lived honourably, but did not bestow their temporal goods upon the poor. Therefore, for some years they suffer rain and wind, hunger and thirst; but afterward they shall be led to good rest.” Going a little farther, they came to a gate which opened of its own accord to them. Entering it, they saw a beautiful, fragrant field, full of flowers, bright and very pleasant, in which were many souls of both sexes rejoicing. Night was never there, nor did the sun set for them, and there was a fountain of living water.

Then he said: “Here dwell the good, but not very good: delivered from torments, they do not yet deserve to be joined to the fellowship of the saints. This fountain is called Living. Whoever tastes of this water shall live eternally and thirst no more.” Proceeding a little, they saw [Col. 1050C] laypersons known to them, among whom were the kings Cantaber and Donatus. On seeing them, the soul said to the angel: “Lord, what is this? These two men were exceedingly cruel during their lives, and greatly hostile to one another. By what merit, then, have they come here?” The angel replied: “Before their death they repented of this hostility. Cantaber was ill for a long time and made a vow that, if he lived, he would become a monk. Donatus, bound in chains for many years, gave to the poor all that he possessed; therefore his righteousness remains for ever and ever. And you shall tell all these things to the living.”

When they had gone a little way, they saw a house wonderfully adorned, whose walls and whole structure were of gold and silver [Col. 1050D] and every kind of precious stone. Yet it had neither windows nor door, and nevertheless all who wished to enter entered. Inside it was as brilliant as if—not merely one sun, but many suns, as it were—shone there. It was exceedingly large and round, supported by no columns; even its whole vestibule was paved with gold and precious stones.

Looking around, Tundal saw a golden seat adorned with gems and silk and every ornament, and King Chormarc seated upon the throne, clothed in wondrous and most precious garments, beyond any earthly price. As he stood in amazement, very many came into that house with gifts for the king, and each joyfully offered his own gifts. [Col. 1051A] While Tundal stood for a long time before his lord King Chormarc—for he had been his lord in the world—many priests and Levites came, dressed as for singing Mass, in silk chasubles and other very precious ornaments; and that royal house was adorned on every side with marvellous splendour. They placed golden and silver cups and chalices, and ivory pyxes, upon pegs and tables; and the house was adorned so that, if there were not a greater glory in God’s kingdom, this might seem sufficient.

All those who ministered, coming before the king and bending the knee, said: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII). Then Tundal said to the angel: “Lord, I marvel at so many attendants, among whom I recognize not [Col. 1051B] one from his household.” The angel replied: “They are not of his household, but the poor of Christ and pilgrims, to whom the king bestowed his goods; and therefore eternal reward is rendered through their hands.”

Then Tundal said: “Lord, has my master suffered any torments?” “He has suffered,” he replied, “and still suffers daily, and will yet suffer. Wait a little, and you shall see.” When he had waited a little, the house grew dark, and all its inhabitants were immediately dismayed; the king went out sorrowfully and weeping. As Tundal followed him, he saw that multitude which he had previously seen within, with hands stretched out to heaven, most devoutly beseeching God and saying: “Lord God [Col. 1051C] almighty, as thou wilt and as thou knowest, have mercy upon thy servant.” Looking, he saw the king in fire up to the navel, and from the navel upward clothed in haircloth.

“This punishment,” said the angel, “he suffers daily for three hours, and rests for twenty-one hours. This is because he defiled the sacrament of lawful marriage; therefore he suffers up to the navel. He wears haircloth because he ordered a count to be killed near St Patrick’s and broke his oath. Except for these two offenses, all his sins have been forgiven. But now let us ascend.”

When they had gone a little farther, they saw a wall exceedingly splendid. It was entirely of silver, very bright and beautiful. Though no gate appeared there, Tundal nevertheless entered, without knowing how, [Col. 1051D] and, looking around, saw choirs of saints rejoicing and saying: “Glory to thee, God the Father; glory to thee, God, Son of God; glory to thee, Holy Spirit, God.” Men and women were clothed in white and most precious garments, without spot or wrinkle, glad and cheerful and rejoicing, and praising the holy Trinity. The whiteness of their garments was like fresh snow struck by the sun’s ray. Their harmonious voices produced sounds like a musical melody. Brightness, delight, pleasantness, cheerfulness, beauty, dignity, health, eternity, concord, and charity were equal in all. The fragrance of the field in which they were surpassed every [Col. 1052A] spice and perfume.

Then Tundal said to the angel: “I beseech you, my lord, let us remain in this rest.” The angel replied: “May it go well with you; you shall see greater things still. These are the joys of married people who kept faith in marriage, governed their households well and justly in the fear of God, and shared their goods with the poor, pilgrims, and Christ’s churches; who shall hear at the judgment: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matt. XXV).”

Tundal earnestly begged to remain there, but did not obtain it. After this they went on. He felt no weariness in walking; and wherever they passed, people came to meet her with bowed heads and joyful faces, with immense gladness, greeted her by her own name [Col. 1052B], and glorified God who had delivered her, saying: “Praise to thee, Lord, king of eternal glory, who dost not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXI); “who, according to thy mercy, hast deigned to rescue this soul from the torments of hell and join it to the fellowship of thy saints.”

After they had passed through very many crowds in this manner, another wall appeared, as high as the first, but made of most pure and brilliant gold, so that any soul seeing it would delight more in the mere brightness of its metal than in all the glory she had seen before. Having entered it as they had the first, they saw very many seats made of gold, gems, and every kind [Col. 1052C] of precious stone, covered with most precious ornaments. Upon them sat aged men and women, clothed in silks and white and variegated robes, and in every adornment such as Tundal had neither seen before nor been able to conceive. Each one’s face shone like the sun shining at noon; they had hair like gold and golden crowns adorned with the same gems.

Golden lecterns stood before them, on which lay books written in golden letters. They sang to the Lord *Alleluia* in a new song, with a melody so sweet that the soul who once heard their voices forgot all past things.

Then the angel said to Tundal: “These are the saints who gave up their bodies for God’s covenant and [Col. 1052D] washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb [Note: [Col. 1051D] Antiphon of the Church.]; also the continent, who turned from worldly life to God’s service; and those who, crucifying themselves together with their vices and desires, lived soberly, justly, and devoutly.”

When curious Tundal looked around, he saw what seemed like many camps and tents, made in marvellous variety from purple, fine linen, gold, silver, and silk. Within them he heard chords, organs, and lyres, with organists and cymbals sounding; he also heard all other kinds of musical instruments making music with sweetest sounds. He asked what these were. The angel replied: “This is the rest of religious persons—monks, converts, canons [Col. 1053A] and nuns—who cheerfully and devoutly render the obedience promised to those set over them; who rejoice more in being subject than in presiding; who abandon their own will and obey another’s; who, while in the body, savour heavenly things; who restrain their tongues not only from evil but even from good, out of love for silence.”

Then Tundal said: “Lord, if it please you, I wish to come nearer and see those who are inside.” “It pleases me,” he said, “that you should see and hear them; but you shall not enter among them. For they enjoy the presence of the Holy Trinity; and whoever has once entered among them, forgetful of all former things, is thereafter never separated from the fellowship of the saints—unless perhaps he is a virgin and deserves to be joined to the choirs of angels.”

Coming [Col. 1053B] nearer, they saw inside souls of both sexes, likened to angels, whose brilliance, delightful fragrance, and most sweet sound surpassed all the glory they had seen before. Yet the voices of those spirits surpassed every such sweetness. They experienced no effort in raising their voices; their lips did not seem to move, nor did they trouble to lift their hands to musical instruments, and yet each produced melody at will.

The firmament above their heads shone greatly. From it hung chains of the purest gold intermingled with silver rods, woven in a most beautiful variety. From these hung golden cups and bowls, little bells and cymbals, lilies and small spheres. Among them moved a vast multitude of flying angels [Col. 1053C] with golden wings, who, flying gently amid the chains, produced for their hearers a most sweet and delightful sound.

When Tundal, exceedingly delighted, wished to remain there, the angel said to him: “Look.” Looking, he saw a single tree, very great and broad, with greenest foliage, most beautiful flowers, and extraordinary abundance of every kind of fruit and crop. In its leaves dwelt many birds of diverse colours and kinds of voice, singing and making music. Under its branches grew lilies and roses, and every kind of fragrant herb and plant. Beneath the same tree were many men and women in golden and ivory cells, always blessing [Col. 1053D] and praising God for all his benefits and gifts. Each had upon his or her head a wonderfully adorned golden crown, a golden sceptre in hand, and clothing like that in which the monks mentioned above had appeared.

Then the angel said to Tundal: “This tree is a figure of the holy Church. Those beneath it are builders and defenders of churches; and because of the benefits which they bestowed upon the holy Church, they attained the fellowship of its members, since, through those persons’ admonition, they abandoned secular dress and lived religiously.”

When they had proceeded, they saw a wall unlike the others in height, beauty, and splendour. It was built from every kind of precious stone, with metals of diverse colours set between them [Col. 1054A], so that it seemed to have gold for mortar. Its stones were crystal, chrysolite, beryl and jasper, hyacinth and emerald, sapphire and onyx, topaz and sard, chrysoprase and amethyst, turquoise and garnet. With these and similar stones the wall shone exceedingly and strongly drew to itself the minds of those beholding it.

Ascending the wall, they saw without doubt what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. II; Isa. LXIV). There they saw the nine orders of angels, with blessed spirits mingled among them; there they heard ineffable words which a human being cannot, and is not permitted, to utter.

And the angel said to Tundal’s soul: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people [Col. 1054B] and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. XLIV). Behold how great is the pleasantness, delight, dignity, and exaltation of being present among the choirs of angels and all the saints; and, surpassing every joy, of perceiving as merciful and gracious him who is the bread of angels and the life of all.

From the place where they then stood, they saw not only all the glory they had previously seen but also the punishments described above. More wonderfully still, they saw the world itself, as though beneath a single ray of sunlight, as it is written: “They shall see the land from afar” (Isa. XXXIII). The sight of a creature cannot be dulled once it has been granted to see the Creator of all. In a marvellous way, while they stood in the same place where they had stood before, without turning in any direction, they nevertheless saw from that same place all things placed before and behind them. Not only sight, but an extraordinary knowledge of all things, was given them, so that there was no further need to ask anyone; there Tundal openly and completely knew everything he wished to know.

While Tundal was there, Saint Ruadan the confessor came to him. Greeting and embracing him with great joy, in the depths of tender charity he said: “May the Lord preserve your going out and your coming in, from this time forth and for ever” (Ps. CXX). “I am Ruadan, your uncle, to whom you are rightly indebted for burial.” Having said this, he stood there and said nothing more.

[Col. 1054D] Looking around, Tundal saw Saint Patrick, apostle of the Irish, with a great crowd of bishops. Among them he saw four whom he knew: namely Coelestinus, who had been archbishop of Armagh, and Malachy, who succeeded Coelestinus. Malachy came to Rome in the time of Pope Innocent and was made legate and archbishop by him; he distributed all that he could possess among the saints and the poor. He was the founder of forty-four monasteries of monks, canons, and nuns, supplying them with all necessities and retaining absolutely nothing for himself. There also Tundal saw Christian, bishop of Lismore, Malachy’s brother by the same mother, a man of remarkable continence and a lover of voluntary poverty; and Nehemiah, bishop of the city of Cluain [Col. 1055A], a simple and modest man, likewise distinguished above the rest for wisdom and chastity. He recognized these four bishops.

Beside them was a wonderfully adorned seat, upon which no one sat. Tundal said: “Whose is this seat, and why does it stand empty?” Saint Malachy replied: “It belongs to one of our brethren who has not yet departed from the body; when he departs, he will sit here.”

While Tundal’s soul delighted greatly in all these things, the angel of the Lord who had preceded her came and gently addressed her: “Have you seen all these things?” She replied: “I see them, lord. I beg you, let me remain here.” The angel said: “You must return to your body and remember everything you have seen, for the benefit of your neighbours.”

[Col. 1055B] On hearing this, the soul, sorrowful and weeping, answered: “Lord, what evil have I done so great that, leaving such glory behind, I must return to the body?” He replied: “None deserve to enter here except virgins, who keep their bodies from unclean touch and their hearts from every unclean desire, and who would rather be burned for so great a glory than be defiled by any shameful desire. You were unwilling to do this and to believe my words; therefore you cannot remain here. Return, then, to your body, and abstain from the things you did before. My counsel and help will not fail you, but will remain with you truly and faithfully in presence.”

When the angel had said this, the soul, turning, immediately felt herself weighed down by the mass of her body. No interval, nor any [Col. 1055C] moment of time, intervened; but at one and the same point of time she was speaking with the angel in heaven and felt herself on earth clothe herself in her body. Then, weak, she opened her bodily eyes; sighing and saying nothing, she looked at the clerics standing around and received the body of the Lord with thanksgiving. She distributed everything she possessed and gave it to the poor, and ordered the sign of the holy cross to be affixed upon the garments she wore. All that she had seen and could remember she afterwards related to us. She urged us to lead a good life, and preached God’s word—which she had previously not known—with great devotion, humility, and learning.

But we, who cannot imitate her life, have at least endeavoured to write these things for the benefit of readers.

**AUTHOR.** Thus far concerning Tundal’s vision, which occurred in the year in which Saint Malachy died. Saint Bernard set forth the life of this Malachy, glorious in miracles and full of virtues, in a truthful and elegant style. Now let us return to the sequence of the history.

## 1150

At that time Peter of Tarentaise, bishop, flourished in great grace of miracles. When the fame of his virtues reached the city of Lausanne, three men imprisoned there—while their guards played before the barred prison door—began, weeping and mourning, humbly and faithfully to invoke his name. The invoked bishop immediately appeared, loosed the shackled men, extended his hand, opened the door, and ordered them, once outside, to follow him. Thus visibly appearing to them, and seen by many others, [Col. 1056A] he drew them out and led them away. Since there was no opportunity to turn aside, following their guide who went before them, they passed over the boards on which the guards were playing, through the midst of those guards. Nor is this surprising: they could not be seen as present by their enemies, since in this way they seemed to themselves to be absent. The bishop did not disappear from them until they had escaped the danger and knew themselves to have reached a safe place.

They therefore bound themselves by a vow and tasted no food until they came into the presence of their deliverer, proclaiming God’s new and wondrous mighty works. He frequently extinguished implacable enmities and inveterate hatreds, and restrained exceedingly grave wars. He brought about desperate reconciliations even between the greatest princes, [Col. 1056B] the Lord working with him and confirming his word by the signs that followed (Mark XVI). Between his own prince, Count Imbert, and Count Raymond of Toulouse, then ruling in the region of Grenoble, he with much labour brought to an end a war long waged, not without many burnings and killings.

On account of this affair, being urgently desired, he went to King Henry of England. On this journey divine power worked through him a remarkable miracle at Saint Symphorien, a castle of the Church of Lyons, a few leagues from the city. There lived a faithful man, Peter of Fraxinet, known and honoured among his neighbours, a diligent and attentive host to religious men, [Col. 1056C] of both excellent conduct and reputation. He at one time drew the holy man to his lodging almost by force. This man had a young daughter suffering from a pitiable affliction.

For a certain female sorceress, induced through the malice of an envious mother-in-law, had caused her to waste away in a hopeless illness, so that she could in no way endure either her husband’s presence or his sight. Persuaded by maternal feeling, her mother summoned a notorious sorcerer so that Satan might cast out Satan. He came, investigated, recognized the condition, and declared that the young woman was filled with iron (*inferrata*). He ground tree bark and gave her drinks infused with words and herbs. He also bit the poor woman’s arm with his own teeth in two places around the bend of the elbow, so that the upper and lower bites were each about a palm’s breadth from the elbow joint. [Col. 1056D]

A strange and marvellous thing: she recovered from that illness; but from time to time, feeling as though a needle were moving out from her heart, she was cruelly tormented until an unseen force drew the needle out through the upper bite in her arm. No scar had formed over this bite, nor over the lower one. More than thirty needles had already emerged in this manner at intervals over time: some, as people say, with heads; others bearing holes suitable for receiving thread.

The daughter was therefore presented by her father to the holy man, who explained her mournful story. And behold, the young woman immediately felt a needle and, groaning, lamented. One of the lay brothers attending the man of God came near and drew it out, bloodstained; it was preserved for many years as evidence. The saint prayed and, touching the place of the wound, promised in the power of faith that neither iron nor steel would come forth thereafter. And so it happened. Yet, though the material changed, the malice was not entirely extinguished: through the lower bite of the arm, which the holy man had not touched—because nothing had yet come out from it—small wooden stakes, commonly called *brochae*, made of oak or ash, began to emerge in place of iron needles. They were thicker than thorns and a little longer, though not all of one length or thickness, any more than the needles had been. [Col. 1057A] Within a year and a few months sixteen pieces of wood had already emerged from the woman.

Then the reverend bishop Peter came, for whom the fullness of so great a miracle was divinely reserved. The woman was presented to him while he celebrated the solemnities of Mass, [Col. 1057B] as he had ordered on the preceding evening. At that very hour a seventeenth piece of wood emerged from the woman’s flesh, and the chaplain drew it out before everyone’s eyes. The bishop then absolved the confessing woman and, giving her the sacrament of the Eucharist, commanded her henceforth to be free from fear of any further emergence of material whatsoever. Thus released from all deceits, she remained united to her husband and bore children; for many years afterwards she proclaimed the power of the holy man which she had deserved to experience in herself.

Those who practise such sorcery are called *vultivoli* [image-workers]: to imitate people’s affections, they fashion, in a softer material such as wax or clay, likenesses of those whom they seek to corrupt. Virgil mentions this delusion in the *Pharmaceutria* [Col. 1057C], saying (*Eclogue* VIII):

> As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts  
> By one and the same fire, so may Daphnis melt with love for me.

Naso also, in the book of the *Heroides* (*Epistle* VI):

> She curses those who are absent and makes waxen images,  
> And drives slender needles into the wretched liver.

Even when their malice does the greatest harm, it is, as some say, undone by an easy device: if those under suspicion are confronted by someone, they deny the accusation; or, if they confess, they are asked to revoke the sorcery. But if this is true, why did that notorious sorcerer, who first recognized the enchantment, not apply so easy a remedy?

1151.

The continual and prolonged flooding caused by rains delayed and hindered the harvest [Col. 1057D]. Saint Bernard instituted in our Order a third procession for the Ascension of the Lord. For previously only two had been observed: that of the Purification, namely, and that of Palm Sunday. But that holy man judged it fitting that we should accompany Christ returning from earth to heaven, just as they had accompanied that angel when he came down from heaven to us; and in the book of the Roman Order, the station on that day is entitled “at Holy Jerusalem.”

1152.

Henry, Count of Anjou and Duke of Normandy, afterwards King of England, married the wife whom Louis, King of the French, had repudiated. Hence war arose between them. Louis had repudiated her because of that woman’s incontinence [Col. 1058A]: she conducted herself not as a queen, but almost as a prostitute.

1153.

After Eugenius III, who sat for eight years, Anastasius, the one hundred and seventy-third pope, sat for one year. In the same year Saint Bernard died.

1154.

Stephen of Blois, King of the English, died in the nineteenth year of his reign and the sixteenth of King Louis of France. Adrian, an Englishman by birth, became the one hundred and seventy-fourth pope. Adam II, abbot of Mortuum Mare, died; Stephen, prior of Ourscamp, succeeded him.

John of Salisbury, himself English by birth, was an intimate of this Pope Adrian and reports the following words of him:

> I heard Pope Adrian say that no one is more wretched than the Roman pontiff, and that no condition is more miserable than his. For he acknowledged [Col. 1058B] that he had found such miseries in that see that, by comparison with his present circumstances, all preceding bitterness had been joy and happiness. He said that the chair of the Roman pontiff was thorny, his mantle everywhere sewn with exceedingly sharp prickles, and so heavy that it bruised and crushed the shoulders even of the strongest; that the crown and tiara rightly seemed splendid, because they were fiery. He said that he would never have wished to leave his native soil of England, or to have remained forever hidden in the cloister of Saint Rufus near Valence, rather than enter into such straits—were it not that he dared not resist the divine dispensation.
>
> He added this also to me very often: although he had ascended step by step, from a cloistered clerk through every office to the supreme pontificate [Col. 1058C], nothing whatever of happiness or tranquil rest had been added to his former life by that ascent. And, to use his own words: “The Lord has always enlarged me upon the anvil and under the hammer; but now, if it please Him, may He put His right hand beneath the burden He has imposed upon my weakness, for it is unbearable to me.”
>
> Is not a man worthy of pity who struggles for so great a misery? Let him who is chosen be ever so rich: on the following day he will be poor and held bound to almost innumerable creditors. Therefore to seek the supreme pontificate, and to ascend to it not without a brother’s blood, is to succeed Romulus in acts of parricide, not Peter in feeding the sheep. Thus the supreme pontiff is rightly called—not merely by title but in substance—the servant of servants. For he must serve the Roman servants of avarice, to such a degree that [Col. 1058D], unless he serves them, he becomes either an ex-pontiff or an ex-Roman.

(1155.)

Henry, grandson through his daughter of Henry the Elder—for he was the son of the Empress Matilda, whose father was Henry, son of William the Bastard, who acquired England, and brother of William Rufus, who was struck by an arrow from a knight while hunting—reigned in England for thirty-five years. From this point I have found nothing concerning the times of the emperors of Germany; accordingly, in their place the years of the kings of France must be recorded.

At this time Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, taken from the monastery of Bec, flourished: a man wholly praiseworthy in life, magnificent, and most experienced in both secular and ecclesiastical affairs.

(1156.)

The sign of the cross appeared in the moon. Alberic, a knight of Beauvais [Col. 1059A], suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ. It is not said where or how he suffered; this has therefore been recorded most negligently.

1157.

Three moons were seen, with the sign of the cross in the middle one. Thomas, Archdeacon of Canterbury, was made chancellor of King Henry through the influence of Archbishop Theobald.

1158.

The daughter of Louis, King of the French, was given to the son of Henry, King of the English, so that peace between them might be secured. (1159.) On the Nones of September [5 September], three suns were seen in the western quarter; but when two gradually disappeared, the sun of the day, which had been in the middle, remained until sunset.

1660.

The miracles of Blessed Mary of Rocamadour belong to this period. At that time a certain Briton [Col. 1059B] died one night at the beginning of the night and came back to life in the morning. He related this:

> A beautiful angel in a most shining garment led me into a very deep valley which, on one side, was full of a great fire, and on the other of snow, hail, and ice. There many souls passed alternately from the waters of snow to the utmost heat, and back again. When I thought that hell was there, the angel answered my thought: “This is not hell, as you suppose; you will yet see something else.”
>
> He led me farther on, and darkness began to thicken before us so that I could see nothing except the brightness of the angelic garment. Then, behold, great balls of flame began to appear to me, rising from a certain pit as far as the clouds and falling back again into [Col. 1059C] that pit. Then the angel who was leading me left me in that thickness of darkness. There I saw a great multitude of souls, like sparks, rising and falling into the pit with the dark ball of flame; and from the mouth of that pit there issued an immeasurable and intolerable stench. And behold, I heard the loud howlings of weeping souls and the loud laughter of demons dragging them to torments.
>
> There were five souls: one tonsured like a cleric, one a woman, and three laymen. Then very black spirits came out of hell, casting sulphurous flame from their nostrils and holding tongs with which they wished to drag me to themselves, but could not. As they surrounded me, I looked about to see whether help might perhaps come to me from somewhere. And [Col. 1059D], behold, the brightness of a certain star appeared to me. When it drew near, those foul spirits departed.
>
> The angel seized me and led me back toward the east, and we came to a certain high and long wall in which no entrance appeared; yet suddenly we were above it. Within it was a most beautiful field, full of fragrant flowers; through their fragrance I was freed from the stench of hell which I had endured. There was a great brightness there, seemingly greater than sunlight. There were great companies of those clad in white, seated upon most beautiful seats. And when I thought that the kingdom of God was there, the angel answered my thought: “This is not the kingdom of God.”
>
> Afterwards we went farther [Col. 1060A], and I saw a brightness a hundred times greater than before. There I heard angels and souls singing in an ineffable melody. When I thought that I was about to enter there, my guide stopped and led me back along the way by which he had brought me, as far as the place of the former brightness. He said: “Do you know what those things are that you have seen?”
>
> The soul said: “I do not know, lord.”
>
> He said: “That valley full of burning heat, snow, and hail is the place of souls being purged, who deferred confession and penance for their sins until death. But because they repented at least then, they will be delivered through God’s mercy on the day of judgment. Meanwhile, however, they can be relieved of punishments by the prayers and alms of the faithful, and especially by the celebration of Masses. That pit is the mouth of the infernal [Col. 1060B] abyss. This flowering field is the place of holy souls who departed from the body in good works and await God’s kingdom with great joy and exultation. You too, if you are solicitous for the salvation of your soul, will receive it with those blessed spirits—you who are to return to your body.”

When I begged him to allow me to remain there, because I did not wish to return to the body, suddenly I found myself among people living here.

After this vision, this man became a convert in the house of the Cistercian Order called Melrose. Near it was a running stream in which, to subdue his flesh, he often stood in the winter cold up to his chin. When that water was frozen solid, he broke the crust of ice and stood there in his clothing [Col. 1060C] as long as he could endure it. On coming out, he did not change his garment but allowed it to dry upon his body. Those who saw him, pitying him, said: “How, brother, can you endure such bitter cold?” He answered: “I have seen harsher things.”

1161.

At that time there was in England a man of great bodily strength and, because of that strength, of great renown. After many sins, rebuked by his conscience, he resolved to go to Jerusalem, that there he might expend his strength in God’s service, according to the saying, “I will keep my strength for thee” (*Psalm* LVIII [LIX]). Concerning this vow he consulted a certain abbot of the Cistercian Order, who persuaded him to take up the cross of religious life and hasten to the heavenly Jerusalem.

He did so, and began to be exceedingly fervent in religion. Afterwards, tempted by Satan, he changed his intention and resolved to go bodily to Jerusalem, as he had first vowed. But because the abbot was not then present, he postponed his departure against his will until the next day. That same night, returning from the latrine to his bed, he saw a demon seated upon a beam of the dormitory in the form of an ape. He began to think that it was the devil, because such beasts are not kept in that Order. The devil, perceiving that he had been recognized, leapt from the beam upon him and beat him so severely that blood came from his nostrils and mouth. Having done this, he vanished.

As the man cried out, the brothers were alarmed [Col. 1061A]. Seeing the novice so gravely injured, they carried him into the infirmary. He lay senseless in his bed for three days and seemed more dead than alive; with his eyes open, he saw nothing. As he lay thus, Saint Benedict appeared to him and said, “Bless.”

He answered, “The Lord [bless].”

And he asked: “Who are you, lord?”

“I,” he said, “am Brother Benedict. Follow me.”

He followed him in spirit. They began to climb lofty steps, and on every step were two demons who bewitched those ascending and struck that novice on every step. Wearied by the demons’ blows, the novice could scarcely now follow his guide. But Saint Benedict, looking back, laid his hand upon the novice’s head [Col. 1061B] and strengthened him.

Having ascended those steps, the novice saw a place of great brightness and verdure in the region of the pure ether. There he saw a chapel hanging in the air, so easily accessible that he wondered why such a small chapel had been made.

Saint Benedict said to him: “Do not wonder at the chapel’s outward narrowness, for you do not know how broad and spacious, how lofty and precious, it is within. Mortal man ought not to wonder at the works of God, who alone knows the reason for His works.”

Saint Benedict entered and ordered the novice to stand behind the door. There was a company of those clothed in white seated around the inner circumference of the chapel, and among them sat the Mother of Mercy, shining like the sun among the stars. Approaching her, Saint Benedict said: “Bless.”

She answered: “The Lord [bless].”

“Lady,” he said, “behold the novice whom you ordered to be brought.”

She said: “Bring him before me.”

When he had approached, the Lady said to him: “Do you wish to remain with me in my house, serving me as you promised?”

He said: “Yes, Lady.”

“Then,” she said, “swear to me upon that altar and vow that you will always serve me and will perform and keep the works of the Lord.”

When he had sworn, our Lady said to Saint Benedict: “Take him back whence you brought him.”

Then Saint Benedict placed him behind the door and said: “Look carefully and hold fast what you are about to see, for it will be useful to you to have seen these things.”

Saint Benedict then took a basin, girded himself with a towel, and gave the basin to our Lady [Col. 1061D]. She began to wash in order the feet of all those seated there, and Saint Benedict, kneeling, wiped them dry after her.

When this command had been carried out, Saint Benedict led the novice back through flowering, delightful, sweetly fragrant places. And behold, a multitude of monks and novices met them. Some had beautiful crowns upon their heads; others did not yet have them but awaited them confidently.

Among them was a monk who by a sign requested Saint Benedict’s permission to speak with the novice, and received it. Having obtained permission, he said to the novice:

> Brother Gunthelm, I was a monk of your house. I beg you to tell your abbot, who was also mine, on my behalf, that Brother Matthew, once his monk [Col. 1062A], bids him correct himself and take more diligent care than he has hitherto done to observe his Order. Let him believe this on the following tokens: when I departed from the body, I saw a certain crown descending from heaven which I thought would be mine; but it was given to a monk who had died before me. I was saddened by this and envied my brother’s good. I confessed this matter to that same abbot and repented. I admonish you yourself to remain in your purpose, humble and obedient; flee honours; never delight in doing your own will; and always fear God.

After these words Saint Benedict ordered Saint Raphael to lead the novice where he was to be led. Saint Raphael led him into paradise. As they drew near [Col. 1062B], the novice saw a certain city of gold, whose gate was of immense beauty. While he marvelled at it, the angel sent him through the gate. Within paradise he saw most beautiful grasses and trees, and birds singing. Beneath one tree was a most clear spring whose streams flowed through the middle of the city.

When the novice wished to rest by the spring, the angel led him to another tree of remarkable height and beauty. Upon it was a most beautiful man, of enormous stature, almost a giant, clothed in a garment of many colours from his feet to his breast.

“This,” said the angel, “is the first father of the human race, Adam the first-formed, redeemed through the blood of Jesus Christ, Son of God [Col. 1062C]. His garment is that robe of glory of which the enemy of humankind despoiled him through transgression of the divine command. Beginning with his son Abel, the first righteous man, he himself began to recover his garment through the good works of his sons and daughters. When he is wholly clothed, the number of the saints will be complete and the age will come to an end.”

After this the angel and novice came to the region of the shadow of death and the land of darkness. The novice saw what seemed to be dreadful towers and thought that hell was there. But the angel said: “It is not. Those towers are the furnaces of hell, through which the smoke and flame of eternal fire come forth.”

Afterwards they saw a man seated upon a burning chair. Before him stood figures like beautiful women, holding lighted candles [Col. 1062D]. They thrust them into his face and mouth, then drew them back, still burning, through his entrails; and they continually endured this punishment.

“This man,” said the angel, “was a friend to his flesh and an enemy to his soul, gluttonous and lustful. The chair signifies that he was powerful in wickedness. He loved women; therefore malignant spirits torment him in such a form.”

Afterwards they saw a man whom very black spirits flayed alive, rubbed with salt, and roasted upon a gridiron.

“This man,” said the angel, “was powerful and cruel toward his subjects.”

Afterwards they saw a man on a burning horse, carrying a fiery shield, holding a goat upon the horse’s neck, and dragging a monk’s habit behind his horse’s tail.

“This man,” said the angel, “was poor [Col. 1063A], but lived by robbery. He stole a goat from a poor woman. Near the end of his life he wished to become a monk, not through true repentance, but in order to conceal his disgrace for a little while. For, if he had lived, he intended to return to his former life. Therefore he drags the religious habit, since he esteemed it so little. The goat and the fiery shield are the torments of his damnation.”

Afterwards they saw various religious persons—monks, nuns, and bishops. Some laughed and guffawed, others uttered insults, others strove to satisfy gluttony, others to gratify lust. This was not because such pleasures exist after death, but because, for greater shame and torment, likenesses of past sins are represented in their very punishments, demons forcing them to this. Afterwards the demons beat them with clubs through the middle of their heads, until their brains were dashed out and their eyes expelled [Col. 1063B], and they did this without ceasing.

After this the angel Raphael led the novice to the depths of hell. There he saw a dreadful fiery wheel, with a man stretched out upon it. As the wheel turned, a voice said to the terrified novice: “You see a dreadful thing, but you will see something yet more dreadful.”

And behold, the wheel descended with such rapid motion to the depths of hell and made so great a crash in falling that the whole world seemed to have fallen—heaven, earth, and sea. While the wheel fell, all the captive souls that were there, and all the demons, struck that man, cursed him, and excommunicated him [Col. 1063C]. This was Judas the betrayer.

As the angel Raphael and the novice returned from there, the angel who governed the sun for the service of humankind appeared to them. Afterwards Saint Raphael said to the novice: “You must return to your body. Tell this vision to no one except your abbot, and tell it in confession.”

Then the novice, who had lain dead for three days, came back to life. He began to yawn and to utter groans and lamentations. Forgetting the angel’s command, he immediately began to tell what he had seen, saying to those who stood around him and asked what he had seen: “I saw hell; I saw paradise.”

As he said this, Saint Benedict came before him with a staff and struck the disobedient sick man’s mouth. The sick man [Col. 1063D], raising his hand against the blow, was struck severely on the finger. Asking why he had been struck, he heard from Saint Benedict: “Because you were disobedient; and if you have been injured in the flesh, know that you have been injured more in your soul. Because you sinned by speaking, you will lose speech for nine days.” Having imposed penance upon him, he disappeared.

For those nine days he was gravely ill and his hand swelled. After nine days he was made well and told his abbot alone what he had seen. The abbot, who had received no command of silence, disclosed the vision for the edification of hearers and readers.

1192.

At that time a certain man of Le Mans, named Christian, a young man, became a convert in a certain hermitage in the archbishopric of Tours [Col. 1064A], called Gastine. There, while he was severely tempted by his flesh, he afflicted himself. In Lent he fasted, abstaining from every drink except on one day of the week. In winter he stood, clothed, in cold water up to his neck. He scourged himself until the rods broke.

One day, as he did this and struck himself until he bled, he heard a voice from the west saying: “What you are doing profits you nothing. This God whom you call upon will not give you what you ask. Turn instead to me, and I shall help you.”

On hearing this, he understood that it was the enemy’s voice. After praying to God to aid him against the temptations, he resolved to undertake a pilgrimage to various saints and thus end his life in pilgrimage. Having pondered this for a long time [Col. 1064B], he took up a staff and went out barefoot. When he came before a certain church, he knelt and asked God to give him good counsel.

He had scarcely risen from prayer when, behold, he perceived a great stench. By it he knew that the devil stood near, suggesting that he abandon his religious habit and his place. Giving thanks to the Lord for such a sign, he returned to his brothers.

Once, at Matins on the feast of Saint Stephen, he was asleep when the lesson was read in which it says, “And they stoned Stephen” (*Acts* VII). Awakened by these words, he rebuked himself for drowsiness, saying: “Woe to me, who fall asleep in God’s service like this. That saint was not asleep when he was being stoned; and I, wretch that I am, ought to have asked this holy martyr [Col. 1064C] to pray for me.”

After this he began to keep watch with the utmost devotion and to ask Saint Stephen to pray for him. On the next day, as he was in the refectory before tasting anything, a voice came to him saying: “You are intent on receiving earthly food and do not think of the glorious protomartyr, who prays for you.”

Then his eyes were opened, and raising them to heaven, he saw the martyr praying for him, as the voice had said. At once he rose, sought a private place in which to pray, and said: “Saint Stephen, what thanks can I give you for this great kindness? I possess nothing of my own to give you; yet I give you this: for love of you I shall not clothe myself in linen, but only in wool.” This he did.

Later, while exhorting others to persevere in their good resolve [Col. 1064D], he told the following story:

> Once I was lying at Gastinet in a bed full of straw, in a certain upper room. When I wished to rest, I felt something moving beneath my loins. I told this to my master, but the motion did not cease. One day, the Lord inspiring me, I began to turn over the straw of my bed. When the straw had been overturned and I found nothing, I lifted one of the boards of the upper room. Beneath it I found an old foot-covering [*pedule*], and in it a great mass of coins.
>
> When I had found them, I left them there, ran to our master, and confessed what I had discovered. He ordered me to bring them to him. When I had done so, he ordered all the brothers [Col. 1065A] to gather. They all excommunicated the man who had done this. When a certain carpenter heard this, he said that he had done it and humbly asked pardon, promising amendment. The master forgave him and imposed penance; but he would not keep the ill-gotten coins and instead divided them among the poor.

After this, hearing reports of the Cistercian Order, Brother Christian began to urge his companions to transfer to it. They would not do so; but they determined among themselves that any of them wishing to transfer to the Cistercian Order might transfer. They sent Christian himself to the abbey of La Charité, accompanied by his prior and one companion.

After his year of probation had been completed, malignant spirits often appeared to Christian in visions by night, threatening to expel him from that house. They said that he laboured in vain, because he would not endure in that Order. But he had recourse to prayer.

While he waged this battle with demons, one day a voice came to him from the head of his bed, saying: “Remember this verse from the Psalter: ‘Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy power’” (*Psalm* LIII [LIV]). When he heard this he recited it, and afterwards always armed himself against all temptations of the devil with this verse as with a shield.

When the demons saw that he had confidence in this verse, they said: “Fool, it was we who taught you this; we want you to say it.” He was therefore uncertain whether [Col. 1065C] he ought to say it or not. Since he was simple and unlettered, he asked clerics what the voice meant. When he learned from them that it was the beginning of a psalm, by God’s grace he learned the entire psalm. He remained long in this battle against demons.

One night in winter, after Vigils, the brothers were sitting and reading by lamplight in the chapter house, while he remained praying in the cloister. As he prayed, a voice from heaven said to him: “Those good men whom you see in the chapter house are God’s martyrs.”

In the same year Christian saw the whole community surrounded by demons so numerous that they seemed to cover everything between heaven and earth. Seeing this, he said: “Lord God, what can this be? Who will be able to escape these dangers [Col. 1065D]?”

He heard a voice saying to him: “Whoever can possess humility will be delivered from all these snares.”

Not long afterwards a brightness came from the east. When the malignant spirits perceived it, they vanished. The glorious spirits who were in that light drew near and filled the place in which those holy men were with a solar brightness. In that brightness the Queen of Angels appeared.

As he gazed upon her and said inwardly, “Good God, where is our Lady, our advocate, the saviour of the world, going?” that same Lady answered him: “I come to assist this place, which needs my help. I come to aid this poor abbey and the places of other poor people who trust in me.”

1163.

Stephen, Abbot of Mortuum Mare, was recalled [Col. 1066A] to the care of the abbey of Ourscamp; Geoffrey IV succeeded him in the abbacy of Mortuum Mare.

1164.

Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, died, and Rothold, Bishop of Évreux, succeeded him in the archbishopric. (1165.) Philip, son of Louis, now reigning, was born in the twenty-seventh year of his father’s reign.

The Archbishop of Tarentaise came to Montcaux, on the frontier of France and Normandy, to restore peace between Kings Louis and Henry. There the Lord performed many miracles through him in the presence of the two kings, Henry the younger King of England, and Philip, Count of Flanders. On Ash Wednesday he imposed blessed ashes upon the head of the King of England at Mortuum Mare.

In the same year Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, fled in exile from England [Col. 1066B] to France and came to Sens to Pope Alexander III, bringing with him the written customs of the King of England for whose sake he was exiled. Holding them, he unfolded and spread the document before the pope’s feet, saying:

> Behold, father, the sacred—or rather sacrilegious—customs of the King of England, contrary to canons and decrees and even to the laws of earthly princes themselves. We are compelled to endure exile because of them, and have come to show them to your Holiness. Therefore let your Holiness, if it please you, order them to be read and heard. For whoever hears these things, it would be remarkable if both ears did not ring: hearing Christians act against the law of Christianity, and the venerable ordinances of the holy Fathers condemned, while new and unheard-of abuses, presumptuously adopted from the old tyrants, are introduced into the Church [Col. 1066C].

Having spoken these words on bended knees, he rose at the pope’s command and stood in the midst of the crowd of his clerics surrounding him. When, at the lord pope’s command, those customs were read and the reader had pronounced the first chapter, the venerable bishop began to argue remarkably against the proposed chapter and to make plain and expose more fully the king’s purpose. By decrees and laws he showed and proved in what respects, and in how many, the provision that had been pronounced opposed the canons of the holy Fathers; and how great a danger threatened the Church if the king obtained what he intended.

He did likewise with every chapter [Col. 1066D], while the lord pope willingly listened and carefully noted his arguments point by point. The cardinals, however, who, having accepted money from the king, supported his side, caused the blessed man much vexation in his case—especially William of Pavia, who was more friendly and intimate with the king than the others.

Seeking by every means to hinder the blessed man, William rose against every point and opposed himself to him, advancing many propositions and questions. The venerable man, like threads of a spider’s web, either unravelled or refuted them without difficulty or hesitation. William supposed that the archbishop used another’s speech rather than his own, and that, if he could turn him aside from the course of his discourse, he would immediately expose him to mockery and confusion.

But the saint himself, recognizing that William directly opposed him [Col. 1067A], sometimes so entangled and ensnared him by a reciprocal turn of argument with his own objections that it became manifest to all that he not only employed his own powers and eloquence, but moreover possessed an unconquerable intellect and eloquence.

Since a great part of the day had been consumed both in the exposition of his cause and in argument with his opponents—for there were sixteen chapters of those customs to which he had replied while standing—the lord pope, at last admiring his wisdom, greatness, and distinction, summoned him to himself. Ordering him to sit beside him, he said: “Welcome, dearest brother.” Rejoicing with him and repeating several times that he had come welcome, the pope began to give him thanks [Col. 1067B] for having undertaken so great a burden and difficult business, and for having presumed to defend the Church of God in such perilous times against the attacks of tyrants.

The venerable bishop likewise returned many thanks to the lord pope with due honour and reverence, because he had been deemed worthy of so great an honour. Then the lord pope condemned those customs forever and subjected their observers and enforcers to perpetual anathema.

The man of God remained at the curia for some time and then, with the lord pope’s permission and counsel, withdrew to Pontigny, where he remained for nearly two years. There, among other pursuits of holy zeal, he also desired and received the monastic habit. Sending a secret messenger to the lord pope, then residing at Sens [Col. 1067C], he requested and obtained from him the making, blessing, and dispatch of a religious habit for himself. Among other things, the lord pope wrote back:

> We have sent you, beloved brother, a habit—not such as we wished, but such as we had.

When the King of England learned in how great honour the venerable bishop had been received by the lord pope, and that he had chosen Pontigny as his dwelling-place, he could no longer rage against him personally. Instead, with an unheard-of kind of cruelty, he vented his fury upon his people. He ordered that wherever any man or woman of the archbishop’s kindred might be found, that person should be disinherited, despoiled of private goods, and expelled from the kingdom—after first exacting an oath that he or she would go to Pontigny in order to grieve the archbishop and present himself or herself to him. [Col. 1067D]

Then old men and young belonging to his kindred were driven out, as were women with nursing children, and some pregnant women.

In this year, 1,830 from the coming of the English into Great Britain, 634 from their baptism, and 100 from the entry of the Normans, a certain storm in the district of Rouergue chastised God’s people with a grievous scourge. For savage wolves snatched little children from their mothers’ breasts and devoured them with cruel bites. A certain woman, named . . . phane de Venere, whose brother had already fallen victim to this destructive calamity—his mother retaining only an arm torn from the child’s body—entered a garden on the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary to gather ears of grain. For the weather was misty [Col. 1068A]. And behold, two wolves came running with such a din that horsemen were thought to have arrived. One wounded her in the throat; the other, lifting her garments as far as her navel, inflicted various mortal wounds. They dragged her to the wood, not by the direct road to the village, along which they were often driven away by dogs, but leaping over two walls, and often three, as though they were nothing. The wood was half a mile from the town.

Still breathing, but about to give up her last breath, the woman, through the power of the Holy Spirit and the kindness of the Virgin Mary, commanded the savage beasts not to tear her body further, and forbade them to attack her any longer. At once they ceased from mangling her, carefully guarding her bloodless body from the attack of other beasts that might come. [Col. 1068B] Meanwhile she was being sought with dogs; and on the following day, after she had lain exposed through the cold of the night, she was found and brought back to the village. She was so torn that scarcely any human shape could be recognized in her. Worms and pus boiled forth from her mangled body; she was terrible to behold, even for her own blood-relations, who had also pitilessly rejected her. Her tongue could not move to form a word. Food poured into her mouth came out through openings in her throat and breast, with only a slight or moderate amount being absorbed. Because of the contraction of her sinews and injuries to her limbs, her knees adhered to her breast; and the wounds from which no small amount of flesh had been stripped could not be covered with skin.

Her relatives therefore placed her upon a vehicle and carried her by night to a distant village [Col. 1068C]. Left before the doors, she was thought by those entering to be a monster; and, lest she remain with them longer, they had her tied to an ass and taken far away like a log. As the ass was descending a steep place on a mountain to drink from a torrent rushing down into the valley, it lowered its head, and the woman, who had been loosely bound, fell into the water. But Blessed Mary did not allow her to drown; rather, lifting her above the river’s wave, she placed her on the bank.

Drawn from the river, she lay alone in the barn of a certain nobleman, whose heart the Lord had touched, secluded from human company; for the stench of her body and the enormity of her wounds oppressed both the sight and smell of those attending her. The knight, taking charge of her [Col. 1068D], ordered wine and oil poured into her wounds. Meanwhile the woman was restored, though only slightly, by the care of healers and the aid of food. She continually pondered the Mother of God in her mind, hoping to be healed through her; and by signs, gestures, and such little words as she could manage, she begged to be carried to Rocamadour. At last she was brought to that church through the compassion of many. There, though bent over and unable to look upward, she persisted in prayer and contrition of heart, and was granted both an answer and healing.

## 1167

At that time Henry, bishop of Beauvais, was transferred to the archbishopric of Reims.

## 1168

He was succeeded in the bishopric of Beauvais by Bartholomew (1169). Henry, king of England, caused his elder son Henry, son-in-law of Louis king of France, to be consecrated king by Roger, bishop of York, out of hatred for St Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1069A]; although this belonged to the archbishop of Canterbury alone.

## 1170

At that time in the eastern regions and in the Promised Land, because of human sins, an earthquake overthrew many cities, churches, towns, and villages. The gaping earth swallowed innumerable thousands of people alive and covered the dead beneath the collapse of buildings. Among those falling in so sudden a destruction was a certain Hermann, a Viennese by birth, raised in Antioch. He was in Caesarea Castle, which belonged by right to the patriarchate of Antioch, in the church of St Peter, when he saw flashes, lightning [Col. 1069B], and thunder. After a fissure in the earth had swallowed alive more than 140 of those who were in the church alone, he too had already sunk as far as his neck; but he invoked the most merciful Mother of the Lord, who gives protection at Rocamadour, and immediately found his prayers heard. For while those around him roared as they died and fell into the depths of the earth, he, though compressed by the ground and almost suffocated, was drawn out of the earth by the aid of the Queen of Virgins and escaped alive. This dreadful event occurred on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

(1171.) Henry, king of England, as he had promised the lord pope and Louis, king of France, being about to make peace with the archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1070A], caused a Mass for the faithful departed to be sung, knowing that peace would not be granted to him, because he was unwilling to receive peace from the archbishop. Hence that same holy archbishop suffered martyrdom in that year in the church and for the Church.

## 1172

Robert, provost of Arras, governed two bishoprics, Arras and Tournai. He was the son of a smith, a peasant from Chartres; and, as they say, he employed a familiar demon, through whom he had attained such high honours. (1173.) The city of Rouen was besieged by Louis, king of France, Henry the new king, and Philip, count of Flanders.

## 1174

[Col. 1070B]

St Peter, bishop of Tarentaise, died; Geoffrey IV, abbot of Mortemer, also died, and was succeeded by Richard I, abbot of La Valasse. (1175.) The provost of Arras was killed by ruffians, with James of Avesnes, an illustrious knight, said to have arranged his death. (1176.) Not long afterwards—indeed, in that same year—Henry, archbishop of Reims, died. There had been great rivalry between them over power, because the one ruled Flanders and the other France; and both were extinguished in a short time. (1177.) An eclipse of the sun occurred at the sixth hour on the Ides of September.

# Book XLIX

[Col. 1069]

## 1178

[Col. 1069C]

Philip, son of King Louis, was crowned king in the fortieth year of his father’s reign, while his father was still living; the latter died in that same year.

## 1179

Therefore, in the seventh year of Henry, king of England, Philip son of Louis reigns. He had been crowned king at Reims in the preceding year, on the Kalends of November, by William, archbishop of Reims. This William had been transferred from the archbishopric of Sens to become archbishop of Reims. After Richard, William the Englishman became the sixth abbot of Mortemer and the second abbot of La Valasse.

## 1180

Philip, son of Robert of Brena, nephew of Louis, king of France, and kinsman of this present Philip, was elected bishop of Beauvais through the influence of his uncle Henry, archbishop of Reims. Returning from the journey to Jerusalem, he was consecrated in the fourth year of his election [Col. 1069D].

## 1181

Pope Alexander III, the one hundred and seventy-fifth pope, died. When someone once called him a good pope, he replied: “I would be a good pope if I knew how to preach, judge, and impose penance.”

## 1182

Lucius became the one hundred and seventy-sixth pope.

## 1183

Henry the Younger, king of England, died, as did Rothold, archbishop of Rouen; he was succeeded by Walter of Coutances.

## 1184

[Col. 1070C]

At this time Peter One-Eye, abbot of Clairvaux, flourished. He always concealed the eminence of his birth as far as he could, by dissimulation. He became a novice at Igny. In food he never took anything beyond the common allowance, and from that common allowance he often and greatly withheld from himself. He possessed only a cowl and a tunic. In winter, beyond the usual provision, he had one cowl or one tunic. He never used boots, nor stockings except simple ones. He attended vigils continuously and perseveringly. He wished to seem insignificant, not to be proclaimed humble. He neither possessed nor sought worldly graces: polished speech, beauty of person, practical skill in secular affairs, or a winning generosity. He possessed inward goods; in outward things he rejoiced to be obscure [Col. 1070D].

Yet he was not so obscure and lowly as he supposed, but was greatly revered and loved by those who judged rightly. One night, before he came to Igny, he saw in a vision of the night that he entered a most beautiful hall. A seat had been placed there, and upon it sat a lady of most venerable appearance. As he entered the hall, black and terrible dogs ran to meet him and, rushing upon him, wished to tear him apart. But that great and venerable lady splendidly drove the dogs away by her authority; then, calling Peter to herself, she caressed him with gentle hands and sweet speech, and commanded him to be secure.

He was always in the same state. When a certain abbot who was his close friend asked him how he could always remain the same, he replied: “When I was a novice, a certain spirit was visibly perceived to enter into me. From then until now, that spirit, power, or disposition in some way rules me, governs me, and leads me like Joseph’s sheep. It frequently gathers inward what has been scattered among lower things; it compels me, though I may wish to attend to other matters, to prayer. It sometimes makes me not perceive things which enter through my eyes or sound in my ears.” As Gregory says: “Whomever the love of eternal life has perfectly absorbed, it renders as if insensible to earthly desires outside.”

While still a novice in the order, he sometimes attended the vigils. While the others sang psalms, he stood in choir asleep; and he felt as though someone touched him, gently striking him to wake him. He thought it was the prior; but when he woke and opened his eyes, he saw no one. When this often happened to him, and he repeatedly did not see the one who woke him, he understood that it was a divine power. He was troubled because it presented itself to him but did not show itself to him. One night, therefore, when he felt the customary awakener, he woke and swiftly opened his eyes. Looking intently, he saw standing beside him a radiant and beautiful youth, as though with golden hair. Immediately departing from him, the youth walked through the middle of the choir, proceeding slowly and plainly. After appearing thus for a long time, he vanished.

At midnight on Sunday the brethren were singing psalms, and he with them. Then a pain in his head seized him so violently that he thought of leaving the choir. As he moved to do so [Col. 1071C], he heard a voice saying to him: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Psalm 17). Strengthened by this voice, he remained. Soon afterwards the pain again grew stronger; again he intended to leave, and again the aforesaid voice sounded. Throughout that night and the following Sunday, until the end of the conventual Mass, that conflict of pain and the strengthening voice did not cease. When, in his order, he came to the corner of the altar to receive communion, at the very moment of bowing it seemed to him that a stone of great weight fell from his head. Immediately rising and receiving Holy Communion, he was healed of all that pain.

A religious man, his close friend, once troubled about the grounds of our faith, asked him in confession whether he himself had ever felt such a temptation. He said: “I do not deny that I have often been assailed by such a thought; but manifold experience of faith has strengthened every such weakness in me.” The other asked what this experience was. “I have experienced many things concerning God,” he said, “and on one occasion something such that, when I ceased to experience it, I bore it more heavily than if I had been thrown into a blazing furnace.”

He was made prior of Igny, then abbot of Val-Roi. Such a vision preceded that election: the abbot then presiding over Igny saw a burning and shining lampstand placed before the high altar suddenly go out through the great window; shortly afterwards Peter was elected.

A certain hired man of Val-Roi could not obtain his wages from the cellarer, who maintained that by right they were not owed to him [Col. 1072A]. When the hired man wished to report this to the abbot, who was then ill, he could not, because the cellarer would not permit him to enter. Enraged, he went to a neighbouring grange, carrying glowing coals in a cooking-pot in order to burn it down. While he was contemplating this, behold, the abbot came and asked what he meant to do. Terrified by the sight of the abbot, he was overwhelmed with astonishment and confessed his entire intention and the reason for it. The abbot said to him: “Do not do this. Come to me tomorrow in the infirmary, and I shall order your wages restored to you.” The man did as he had been commanded.

After the man had been sent away with certain hope of receiving his wages, the abbot said to Brother Nicholas, who attended him: “Truly, brother, if we thought of the Lord [Col. 1072B], the Lord would think of us.” This brother, guessing that he had seen something remarkable, pursued the departing man. Wisely and ingeniously promising both to keep the matter secret and to hasten its settlement, he elicited the account of what had happened.

The illness called a fistula afflicted him. He concealed the disease, though he could not conceal that he was ill. A monk of Clairvaux, famous in the art of medicine, passed through that place. The brothers informed him of the abbot’s illness, and he urged and persuaded the abbot to let him inspect it. He saw it and told the brethren that it was a fistula, situated where it could not be cut and therefore could not be healed. He added: “If this man sees Easter, he will never die again.” Yet he recovered and lived many years thereafter.

He was summoned to the election of the abbot of Igny, taking with him for companionship and consolation a certain Robert, monk of Igny, a devout and learned man. He prayed earnestly that the Lord might inspire him concerning whose election he ought to support. While he pondered and prayed, he heard a voice say: “When you come to that place, you will know what you seek.” He was already approaching the place and had not yet obtained his desire. As he prayed more intently, the voice again said: “Ask that monk who is travelling with you; he will tell you who is going to be abbot.” Immediately summoning Robert, the abbot said: “We are going to Igny, and I believe that the election will depend very greatly upon me. You, who know the brothers’ characters, tell me whom you judge more worthy of this office.” Without hesitation Robert said: “I judge no one more worthy than you; therefore I predict that you will be abbot.” The abbot replied: “I know that you would wish my promotion; but this is not placed in your power. I wish you to name someone else whom you consider worthy of election.” But he said: “I shall name no one else. All desire you; you will be abbot.” They came to Igny, and by the unanimous agreement of all, without any contradiction, he was elected abbot [Col. 1072D].
