Moreover, before he was elected, a devout brother named Nicholas, who had long performed the office of cantor, continually prayed that the Lord would provide them with a suitable abbot. Once, while he was praying, a voice plainly said: “Nicholas, you shall have an abbot, and he will show you what you ought to do.” For Peter was to show everyone an example of true religious life and holy fervour. After Peter had become abbot, Nicholas wished to undertake something beyond the common rule; but because he was delicate and weak, he did not dare. While thus wavering, he once heard a voice saying: “Nicholas, never be afraid to do penance.”

Once, when a religious friend was eating with him and saw fish set before him which he did not taste, he reproached him for excessive abstinence. Peter replied: “Indeed, I would eat more sparingly, if I did not spare my body.” Gilbert, abbot of Foigny, used to say of him: “I have never seen anyone for whom singularity has turned out less badly.” To very many who did not know him intimately, he seemed simple and dull, because he was slow of speech and, when he spoke, spoke like a layman [Col. 1073B]. For he concealed all his good qualities.

Baldwin, a knight illustrious by birth and very rich, left no evil undone except what he was unable to do. Yet he greatly loved Peter, abbot of Igny, and protected his possessions from every injury, while inflicting many evils upon other houses. When he fell ill, he summoned the abbot. After hearing his confession, the abbot urged him to renounce the world. He agreed, but could not obtain permission from his wife. The abbot returned to the monastery. Not long afterwards, when Baldwin despaired of life, his relatives brought him to the monastery. He was assigned to a cell, clothed in the sacred habit, and guardians were appointed for him. That night, when the board was struck for him, the awakened brethren came running. The abbot performed the office and the seven psalms were also said, but he had not yet departed. The brethren returned to their places.

Meanwhile two of the brethren saw two visions concerning the sick man. One saw the entire convent standing before him; and, as he humbly bowed, it gave him the kiss of peace. The other saw the sick man lying in bed and wishing to rise but unable to do so. When he came near to help him, the sick man said: “Do not help me; I do not need your aid. For blessed Benedict is helping me, and he also commands the abbot himself to make me a crown.” Without delay, the board was struck a second time. The brethren were present [Col. 1073D]; the sick man departed and was carried into the choir. Vigil was kept around him. The abbot, who was then himself somewhat ill, went to rest.

Lying awake in bed, he began to think and say to himself: “Lord God, what will become of this man, whom the bonds of so many sins bind? What does it profit him that he confessed his evils, repented at the end, and received the habit of religion? Where is he now? Is he well, or ill?” As he thought this, he heard a voice saying: “He greatly needs help.” Hearing this, the abbot immediately went in spirit to the church and, as though bending his knees before each of the altars of saints that were there, implored their patronage with all the devotion he could, that they might obtain mercy for Baldwin from the Lord.

After this was done [Col. 1074A], the abbot’s eyes closed and he suddenly slipped into sleep. As soon as he began to sleep, he felt himself weighed down as though by a great mass. He understood that it was an evil spirit oppressing him, which said: “What are you attempting to do?” The abbot replied: “What is it that I intend to do?” And the devil said: “Do you think that you can take Baldwin from me, when he remained in his sins until the end of his life?” The abbot answered: “Did he not confess his sins? Did he not repent at the end and flee to God’s mercy? Even if I say nothing of all else, do you not know that Christ’s blood was shed for sinners for the remission of sins? By that precious blood which flowed from the side of the one sleeping upon the cross, I adjure you, accursed one: depart from here at once, and have no power over him.”

Defeated and confounded, the devil fled. Rejoicing in the victory, the abbot began to sing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—and sang while asleep as far as the words, “Thou art the King of glory, O Christ.” Waking, he completed the entire hymn in praise of God. While he still had upon his lips the verse, “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be confounded,” the bell sounded. The abbot rose for vigils, mindful of the voice which had told him that Baldwin needed help. He prayed all night for him. In the morning, when the brethren had assembled in chapter, he imposed upon each a thirty-day observance for Baldwin, which he himself also resolved to perform. During those thirty days Baldwin often appeared in the guise of a suppliant, as though asking for help, especially when the abbot’s devotion was lukewarm and languid [Col. 1074C].

One day the abbot was going to a grange and could not sing Mass that day. Baldwin appeared to him on the road, much sadder than usual. On the thirtieth day, Good Friday before Easter, while the second reading was being read, the abbot saw two exceedingly beautiful men clothed in purple coming to the middle of the choir. They led Brother Baldwin, clothed in dark brown (*isembrunus*), into the midst. Having brought him before the abbot at the place where he sat, they presented him to him, saying: “This is Baldwin.” As the abbot considered what they would do with him, they led him to the altar and offered him there. When this had been done, the vision disappeared. Afterwards Baldwin did not appear to the abbot. [Col. 1074D]

The abbot understood from that offering that Baldwin had been reconciled, but from the black garment that he was still subject to punishment. A little before this Baldwin died, a certain knight at the point of death had sent for the abbot to visit him. The abbot came, heard his confession, and advised him to renounce the world and receive the religious habit at Val-Roi, which was nearer to his house. This he did. Returning to Igny, the abbot began to reflect: “What good will this habit of religion, assumed in such circumstances, do this knight?” And he heard a voice saying: “It will profit him greatly. Know that in this man, and in every person who dies in the Cistercian Order, the devil will have no power until judgment has been passed concerning him.”

[Col. 1075A] Henry, count of Champagne, once asked the servant of God to pray to the Lord for him. Peter celebrated Mass in order to intercede for him. When the mystery had been completed and he had turned to his ministers to say the final collect, the absent count appeared to him, bearing upon his garment the sign of the cross, as those do who intend to go to Jerusalem. Yet, as the count later confessed, he had not then attached the cross to himself; but that very day, after much wavering, he had resolved without doubt that he would do so.

The blessed man was once sitting in chapter on the anniversary of a certain brother’s death. The cantor, whose office this was, reminded him to absolve that brother according to custom. But the abbot replied: “He needs absolution.” Having said this, he absolved him.

An elder named John, sitting not far from him, noted these words and, when an opportunity arose, asked him the reason for them. He replied: “Recently he visibly appeared to me while I was awake. When I asked whether he yet saw the Lord, he answered, ‘The time has not yet come.’ Having said this, he vanished.” John further testified that the man had lived long and devoutly in the order and had been afflicted for two years before his death by a most grievous illness, which he himself believed to be purgatory. But surely the way leading to the vision of God is not only narrow but long (Matthew 7); and “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). Yet who shall boast that he has a clean heart? [Col. 1075C] Through many tribulations—that is, purifications—we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14). For this, prolonged labour with the file is required.

The saint was once praying in a certain church, and St Bernard and St Malachy stood beside him as he prayed. Turning towards them, he directed his prayer and intention to them. One of them said to him: “You will be abbot of Clairvaux.” Having said this, they vanished, and he remained terrified, because he would never have wished this to happen.

Not long afterwards Gerard, abbot of Clairvaux, came to Igny. Hugh of Basoches was then there, having grievously offended against the order; the aforesaid Gerard had punished his offence with regular severity. Hugh was among the brethren who were physically ill, while he lay sick in mind. Intending to kill the abbot, Hugh lay in wait. A devout brother named Haymo, a native of Reims, was seated in the vestibule [Col. 1075D] of the infirmary. Haymo then saw two figures of horrible appearance enter the infirmary.

That night Abbot Gerard attended vigils. As he went to the dormitory for a necessity, Hugh, lying in ambush with a weapon prepared for the crime, mortally wounded him. Gerard survived until the following day. Toward evening, when the brethren had been placed before him, he said: “Lead me, Lord, in thy truth, and teach me; for thou art God, my saviour, and on thee have I waited all the day” (Psalm 24). Saying this, he fell asleep in the Lord. Peter escorted his body as far as Clairvaux, greatly fearing that he himself might be made abbot. But at that time a certain Henry was made abbot, a man powerful in deed and word [Col. 1076A], who shortly afterwards was made a cardinal bishop.

Gilbert, then prior of Clairvaux and afterwards abbot of Foigny, was considering transferring Peter from Igny to Clairvaux. As he thought this, a certain brother said to him: “It seemed to me that we were being told that Christ the Lord was coming to this house. We went out to meet him at the gates of the monastery. We saw him with neither form nor beauty: short in stature, poor in dress, contemptible in appearance. Yet no one doubted that he was the Lord Jesus Christ himself.” Hearing this, Gilbert understood that Christ had appeared in Peter’s form.

Peter, summoned to the election, fled, but was elected in his absence. On that same journey, as the monks of Clairvaux were carrying the body of Abbot Gerard to Clairvaux and had arrived with it at Châlons, Peter sorrowfully accompanied the body. Gerard himself appeared to Peter, abbot of Igny, saying: “Do not be grieved at my death, for I am with our Lord Jesus Christ. When you come to Clairvaux, you shall perform my funeral service and bury me.”

Accordingly, when Peter, at the request of the other abbots, sang Mass for the dead man and was in the canon of the Mass, St Bernard and St Malachy appeared to him, one at one side of the altar and the other at the other, saying: “Do not doubt that Abbot Gerard is a companion of the angels and in eternal glory.” Therefore, while Peter was concealing himself so that he might not be made abbot of Clairvaux, he was sought out and found at a certain grange, living among the lay brothers and turning hay in the meadows that day [Col. 1076C]. Brought from there to Igny, he could not be overcome by entreaties; but compelled by the authority of the order, he assumed the government.

On the following day, as they were about to depart, Gilbert was seized with fever. The abbot said to him: “Why are you leaving me in need?” He replied: “Because I have a fever.” The abbot said: “Rise; let us go from here. The fever will harm you no longer.” He rose and was healed shortly afterwards.

After some time Peter was visiting the abbeys of Clairvaux, with Gilbert accompanying him. Gilbert sat upon a horse which carried him gently but often stumbled. Seeing this, the abbot rebuked him for using so dangerous a horse. Gilbert replied: “Because it is not spiteful and carries gently. But if you fear for me, pray to the Lord [Col. 1076D] that it may suffer from this fault no more.” The abbot said to him: “Does God care for beasts of burden? Yet I pray to God that it may not fall in such a way as to harm you.” Gilbert used it for many years afterwards. But as soon as he became abbot of Foigny, he abandoned the horse and Boheries. A brother of Boheries mounted that horse, beneath which—or rather, upon which—the horse fell so heavily that the brother broke his leg.

The Roman pope, having heard of Peter’s reputation, summoned him, confessed his sins to him, and received the Holy Eucharist from his hand. He would even have received the habit of the Cistercian Order if the man of God had permitted it; but he gave him the necessary funds to establish an abbey of that order.

In a certain French church a dispute arose among the clerics about the election of a bishop. A Roman cardinal was present. The clerics entrusted the decision to him: of the two men whom they had named, they would elect whichever one he named. The cardinal consulted the holy man about which of the two seemed better to him. He replied: “Among two counterfeit coins no better one can be found.”

While he was still abbot at Val-Roi, through the violence of a disease of the head one of his two eyes was wholly dissolved and flowed out, and he became one-eyed. He later used to say jokingly that he had escaped one of his enemies, and that he feared the one remaining more than the one lost. He said this to comfort those who bore bodily losses with difficulty, identifying with them through compassion and likening himself to them through humility. [Col. 1077B] For the man, already most fully perfected, did not fear for his bodily senses.

While he was still abbot of Igny, the brethren at one time had no prior. Since he delayed appointing one, an elder asked him the reason for the delay. He replied: “I do not cease to ask the Lord about this, but I receive no answer from him.” The elder named someone whom he considered suitable. But Peter said: “The Lord does not wish this man.” From this it is sufficiently clear how intimate he was with God.

When riding, he carried the scapulars of the boys travelling on foot, wearing a loose and worn cloak. A devout friend once said to him as he rode beside him: “Let us pass those who are ahead of us, so that we may escape this cloud of dust.” He replied: “If we pass them, they will be in the lot in which we now are, and the punishment will return upon its own head.”

During harvest-time he went out with the brethren to work. While the monks rested silently, the abbot saw three most beautiful women coming among the brethren, one of whom marvellously excelled the others. The abbot went to meet them and said: “Certainly you are very bold to come thus among us. Do you not know well that a woman ought not to come among us, that is, among brothers of our order?” Then she who was more splendid than the rest said: “I have every right to come among my own. For I am Mary, Mother of the Lord Jesus Christ, and I come to visit my harvesters; this is Mary Magdalene, and this is Mary of Egypt.” [Col. 1077D] Hearing this, the abbot fell at her feet. When he wished to embrace them, she vanished.

After his death, a certain brother thought to extract one of his teeth as a relic. He thought he could easily do so, because the dead man’s mouth was open. But when he prepared to do it, he found the mouth so closed and obstructed that he could not fulfil his intention.

A monk, prior of a certain small cell, used frequently to visit the holy man. Troubled by a grievous temptation and entangled in the bonds of sin, he sought Peter’s counsel and help. Peter had instructed him to hold good hope of divine consolation. On hearing that Peter had died, he began to grieve greatly. After his death the saint appeared to him in a dream, consoling him and declaring that he had been healed from all his temptation [Col. 1078A]. Upon waking, the man believed the dream and awaited the fulfilment of the promise. A few days later, a certain person to whom he was bound by unlawful love, and while that person lived he had not hoped that he could be healed, died. Hearing this, he rejoiced and said: “The snare is broken, and we have been delivered.”

## 1185
At the same time Hugh, the venerable abbot of Bonneval, flourished in abundant grace of holiness. While still a young man, he had left the world and entered a house of the Cistercian Order called La Macière; there he began to live with great religious devotion. Afterwards he was sorely tempted and considered returning to the world. While entertaining this thought, he entered the church to pray. He prayed with tears; kneeling, he stretched his hands toward heaven and raised to heaven eyes full of tears. [Col. 1078B] He saw above the altar the Mother of Mercy, clothed in light as with a garment. It seemed to him that he saw Jesus, her Son, beside her, and how He had been announced by the angel, born of the Virgin, and proclaimed to the shepherds; how He was circumcised, seized by the Jews, scourged, mocked, and crucified; how He rose on the third day and ascended into heaven on the fortieth. As he saw all this, Our Lady said to him: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened in the Lord; and be assured that henceforth you shall not be assailed by such temptations.”

After this he began to afflict himself with excessive abstinences, so that he seemed almost to lose his senses and memory. Meanwhile Saint Bernard, who was still alive at that time, came to him by God’s providence. He ordered him [Col. 1078C] to be sent to the infirmary; that the vigils should be sung for him every night before those of the other sick, so that he might afterwards sleep sufficiently; and that he should have general permission to speak wherever he wished. Thus, through God’s mercy, he soon recovered. Then great religious fervour began to burn in him. Not long afterwards he was made abbot of Bonneval.

Under this holy man, a certain young man became a novice, very fervent at the beginning of his conversion. Afterwards he too was grievously tempted and contemplated returning to the world; and he confessed this thought to the abbot. The abbot began to urge him to remain, but achieved nothing, for the young man insisted in every way that he would leave. Then the abbot said: “Son, have mercy on your soul by pleasing God, and do not lose the glory prepared for you. [Col. 1078D] For I promise you—and I constitute myself guarantor of this promise—that, if you remain, you shall be the eternal companion of the holy angels.” Strengthened in the Lord by these words, he persevered, and afterwards lived most excellently.

Two years before he died, he suffered from a most severe illness, so that the brethren greatly pitied him when they saw the extremity of his pain. Saint Job was sent to comfort him, in such great brightness that the entire eastern side of the infirmary was filled with it. When the sick man marvelled at the brightness, Saint Job said to him: “Do you know who I am?” He answered, “I do not know, lord.” “I,” he said, “am Job, whom the Father of mercies and God of all consolation has sent to comfort you. As I was patient in such infirmity, [Col. 1079A] so are you; and therefore you shall flourish with me in my glory, and tomorrow you shall be with me, and shall reap what you have sown.” And this came to pass.

Not long afterwards he appeared to his abbot in great glory, thanking him because through his admonition he had persevered in the Order. Under the same holy man, a cleric and a treacherous and deceitful knight became novices. In the same year this knight had surrendered and destroyed two castles. As he slept, it seemed to him in a night-vision that he fell into a well so deep that he spent three days falling before reaching its bottom. When he related this to the holy abbot, the latter interpreted the well as the abyss of hell, into which he would fall if he left the Order; therefore he urged him to remain. [Col. 1079B] But he would not, and departed; on the third day he was killed by his enemies.

The cleric was tempted but not overcome, and confessed his temptation to the abbot. Consoling him, the abbot promised that, if he remained, the Queen of the world would come for his soul and lead it into her rest. This too came to pass. For on the day before his death Our Lady appeared to him, saying that she came for him and that on the following day he would be in eternal rest; and so it happened.

On the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary, while the same abbot was rousing the brethren in choir for vigils, he saw the devil standing in the middle of the choir in a horrible form, so that the abbot himself fell down in terror. Raised by the brethren, he signed himself and returned to his seat. [Col. 1079C] On the following day the abbot related in chapter what he had seen, and said that one of the brethren was guilty of a grave crime, on account of whom the devil had come. At this all were afraid; but the guilty man concealed his conscience. On the second following day the abbot again said that the devil was still among them. Then all the brethren confessed and each received discipline, praying the Lord to reveal the guilty conscience to the abbot; and this happened. The abbot then drew the culprit aside and told him his sin. On hearing it, he fell at the abbot’s feet, begging that he might be forgiven and that a penance according to the abbot’s will might be imposed upon him. Once this was done, the devil appeared no more.

In a certain daughter-house of Bonneval, an abbot noble by birth [Col. 1079D] but degenerate in character was, for deserving reasons, deposed by this holy man, and another, more worthy man, put in his place. After this had been done, as Saint Hugh was departing, a garrulous dependant of the deposed abbot began to slander him publicly, saying that he had deposed him from envy rather than justice. On hearing this, Saint Hugh stretched out his hands to heaven and prayed God to make known that he had acted with a pure and upright intention. Immediately the garrulous man went mad and began to run about the entire court of the abbey, eating the dung of the cattle there. When the holy man saw this, he took pity on him, prayed for him, and he was healed.

In the house of Bonneval there was a fervent monk who, although weak in body, nevertheless always attended [Col. 1080A] the conventual observance. At last he suffered paralysis and lay ill in the infirmary for a long time. There was there a master of novices, named John, sick unto death. John said to him: “Brother Benedict, do you hear what I hear?” He answered: “I hear nothing. What do you hear?” “I hear,” he said, “the voices of angels chanting, like the sound of many harpists, who are coming for the soul of our paralytic; and tomorrow I too shall follow. Hurry to strike the board, for his soul is greatly hastening to depart.” Then Brother Benedict ran to strike the board; and before all the brethren had assembled, the paralytic departed; John did so on the next day.

A servant of the cellarer of Bonneval fell ill unto death and confessed his sins to the monk-confessor of the poor. He disclosed a certain sin which the monk feared to receive in confession, and he enjoined the sick man to confess it to the abbot; the man agreed, if he lived. In the meantime the servant died. When the abbot returned from a journey after Compline and sat upon his bed, intending to remove his shoes, he saw the dead man ascending the stairs of the dormitory. Coming before him, he fell at his feet, asking pardon and humbly begging him to hear his confession, saying that he had been sent to him for this purpose. He confessed with such an abundance of tears that the abbot too was moved to tears; they wept so much that the sleeve of the abbot’s cowl became very wet. After absolution, [Col. 1080C] the dead man humbly begged the abbot to pray for him, because he was in great torments. And as the abbot wished to test by touch whether he was in the body or in the spirit, the dead man vanished.

On the following day the abbot asked the confessor of the poor whether the deceased had confessed such a crime to him. He replied: “Yes. But how do you know it?” “I heard it,” he said, “from his own mouth.”

A young monk had recently died in the same house. Afterwards, when his mother saw the abbot, she began to weep anxiously for her son. Consoling her, he said: “Do not weep; be assured that your son is in great glory. I know how he lived, and how holy his life was.” Hearing this, his mother received consolation. Not long afterward, as the same abbot prayed, [Col. 1080D] that monk appeared to him with a most radiant countenance and greeted him. Recognizing him, the abbot said: “How is it with you, son?” “Well, lord,” he replied, “as you see. Did you not say to my mother the day before yesterday that I was in great glory? Certainly you spoke truly.” Having said this, he vanished.

A lay brother from another house had been sent to Bonneval for his offence, where he fell sick unto death. When the abbot visited him, he urged him to confess openly the sin of which he was accused—a sin which he had never wished to confess, not even to his own abbot. But he denied everything and asked to be given the body of the Lord. Abbot Hugh urged him not to presume to receive the body of the Lord unless he had confessed well. But he maintained that he had confessed well, [Col. 1081A] and ordered that the body of the Lord be brought to him. When the priest brought it and placed it in his mouth, the man immediately began to cry: “What shall I do, wretch that I am? What shall I do?” Then the priest removed from him the body of the Lord, which he held upon his tongue, and at once he expired.

The same abbot once fell ill and entered the infirmary. He saw a dove whiter than snow upon the shoulder of the infirmarian monk. When that monk wished to seize it, it flew to the abbot and entered his bosom; afterwards it came out through the opening of his tunic, thrust its beak into the abbot’s ear, and spoke to him in human words: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: prepare yourself, prepare yourself, prepare yourself. Saint Bernard commands you to go and make peace [Col. 1081B] between the pope and the emperor.” This peace he afterwards made.

1186.

Urban III becomes the one hundred and seventy-seventh pope. (1187.) Geoffrey, count of Brittany, third son of the king of England, dies near Paris. (1188.) Saladin subjects the whole East to himself. In this year the form of visitation was established and written down which is read to this day in visitations of each house of our Order. King Philip captures Tours. (1189.) Henry, king of England, dies at Le Mans, in the thirty-fifth year of his reign; his son succeeds him. (1190.) Philip, king of the Franks, and Richard, king of England, go to Jerusalem, each with a great retinue; and at Messina, a city of [Col. 1081C] Apulia or Sicily, they incur enmity toward one another. (1191.) The king of the Franks subdues Acre, otherwise called Ptolemais, a maritime city. King Richard, envying the glory of King Philip of France, withdrew from every opportune assistance and accepted gifts from Saladin. Philip, count of Flanders, dies on the Jerusalem expedition. King Philip of France, fearing the treachery of Richard, king of England, and, as they say, led still more by desire for the land of Flanders, returns from the land of Jerusalem against the will of almost all the nobles of France. He first confirms to Richard by oath that within forty days after he returns to France he will not harm [Col. 1082A] his lands.

(1192.) King Philip begins to subdue Normandy. Returning from the Jerusalem expedition, King Richard is captured and imprisoned by the duke of Austria, handed over to Emperor Henry, and placed in custody at Speyer. In that captivity, after Richard had confessed his sins to a certain bishop and resolved thereafter to be continent, not long afterward a certain bishop of England, visiting him and seeking his favour, persuaded him, as though for the preservation of his bodily health, . . . and thus strengthened the wretched man in his wickedness. A certain bishop of Spain, a close acquaintance of mine and a most religious man, told me this. He had heard it from another bishop to whom Richard, at the point of death, confessed that he had been thus deceived by another bishop.

(1193.) When Saladin knew that death was imminent, he summoned his standard-bearer and said: “You who are accustomed to carry my banners in war, carry the banner of my death—a worthless little rag—upon a spear throughout all Damascus, crying: ‘Behold, the dying king of the East will take with him nothing but this worthless cloth.’” And so he died.

(1194.) King Richard redeems himself from captivity after despoiling the churches of England and Normandy of golden and silver chalices and their other ornaments: more than two hundred thousand marks being given in part to the emperor and other barons, and in part promised under hostages. (1195.) King Richard begins to recover the land of Normandy. By gifts and promises alike, the same king binds almost all the nobles of Gaul to himself, and deprives Philip, king [Col. 1082C] of France, of all the strength of his military forces.

(1198.) Innocent III, the one hundred and eighty-first pope. King Richard dies, struck by an arrow. His brother John succeeds him. William, abbot of Mortemer, dies. (1199.) A most severe winter lasts for more than three months; as a result there follows a very great mortality among animals, especially sheep and wild wethers, from the severity of the cold, followed by famine. (1200.) The city of Rouen, with all Normandy, is subdued by Philip, king of France. John, king of England, flees to England, fearing that the barons would hand him over to King Philip. The city of Constantinople is captured by the Franks (1204).

[Col. 1081]

## Extracts from Helinand’s Poem, Written in the French Language, Entitled *On Death*

(*Literary History of France*, vol. XVIII, Paris: Firmin Didot, 1835, quarto, p. 100 ff.)

The author indicates that he has taken leave of the world.

[Col. 1081D]

> Death, who have made me moult in a mew,  
> Into such a sweating-room where the body sweats  
> For what it did in the world of excess.  
>
> [Col. 1082D] [lacuna]  
>
> Therefore I have changed my heart,  
> And have abandoned play and rage:  
> He is badly drenched who does not dry himself.  
>
> [lacuna]

### IV. The author addresses Death and begs her to grant a reprieve to his friends.

[Col. 1083A]

> Death, I send you to my friends,  
> Not as to enemies,  
> Nor as to people whom I hate in the least;  
> Rather, I pray God, who has placed in my heart  
> That what I have promised them may be theirs:  
> May He give them long life and the grace  
> To live well throughout all their days.  
>
> But you, who play at the hunt  
> For those in whom God has placed no fear,  
> Do much good by your menace;  
> For your fear purges and sifts  
> [Col. 1083B] The soul, as through a sieve.  
>
> [lacuna]

### XVI. On the Bishop of Beauvais

[Note: [Col. 1083B] He means Philip of Dreux, who governed the Church of Beauvais from 1175 until 1217.]

> Death, run straight to Beauvais,  
> To the bishop who loves me so much  
> [Col. 1084A] And has always held me dear.  
> Tell him that without contradiction  
> He will one day belong to you, though I do not know when.  
> Let him therefore strive to cleanse  
> His life, to empty out his ship,  
> And to illumine it with good morals, etc.  
>
> [lacuna]

### XVII. On the Bishops of Noyon [Note: [Col. 1083B] Stephen of Nemours, 1188–1221.] and Orléans [Note: [Col. 1084B] Henry of Dreux, brother of the bishop of Beauvais, who died in 1199. But if one reads “of Amiens,” understand Theobald of Heilly, who held the see of Amiens from 1169 to 1204.]

> Death, who holdest the great in prison  
> Just like some poor dog  
> Whom the world holds in contempt,  
> Greet my two bishops,  
> The one of Noyon and the one of Orléans [variant: Amiens].  
>
> [Col. 1084B] Tell them that they have many delays  
> Which are not written on their faces:  
> You make a long term short.  
> Let them now guard themselves against your snares.  
> You take the sleeper in his bed;  
> You take delight from the rich;  
> You make beauty become dung.
